en: The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Necklace (Ratnavyūha). Chapter One: The Necklace.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, within the Great Stūpa—the original dwelling place of the Buddhas of the past—which is praised by the great Bodhisattvas; its ground is pure and subtle, the most excellent Dharma-seat of all Buddhas;
where devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others constantly offer hymns of praise, and which can further increase immeasurable roots of goodness.
There is always the subtle, wondrous radiance of all Buddhas, which accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit and fulfills the spheres of practice traversed by all Buddhas.
Once the Tathāgata has attained the path of Bodhi, he turns the sublime wheel of Dharma, taming immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, and attains mastery over all phenomena.

The World-Honored One has attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena; he is able to skillfully discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, and has forever severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Without relying on external adornments, he fully understands all dharmas. Together with a great assembly of sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus—all of whom are tamed, have severed the habitual tendencies of affliction, are sons of the Buddha who well understand profound meanings, and are fields of merit capable of severing all states of existence—they have attained the fruit of pure precepts: non-arising and non-ceasing.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas, endowed with unimpeded wisdom, profound wisdom, and the wisdom that is beyond conceptualization; they showered down the rain of Dharma with great loving-kindness and great compassion, able to bestow the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma upon all. Toward all sentient beings, their minds were as impartial as the earth, increasing and bringing to fulfillment the factors conducive to enlightenment.

The light of wisdom can shatter the darkness and illuminate all paths of good and evil; it can open the lotus flowers of the virtuous minds of sentient beings and cause their roots of goodness to ripen. It increases the sprouts of virtue and dries up the ocean of afflictions; possessing the wings of wisdom, one soars through space without obstruction—thus it is likened to the sun.
It skillfully increases or diminishes the good and evil of sentient beings—thus it is likened to the moon. As the foundation of all virtues, it is like Mount Sumeru;

with a sincere and tranquil mind, one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), unmoved by worldly discourses, dwelling securely in the unsurpassed way of renunciation, and able to behold all the worlds of the Buddhas.
The treasury of accumulated wholesome dharmas is like the great ocean;
he has fully accomplished all *dhāraṇīs*, possesses tranquil noble conduct and great compassion, and his two eyes of concentration and wisdom are pure and adorned.
Having long since been far removed from fear regarding the profound Dharma, he shall never cease until the Bodhi cultivated throughout immeasurable eons is finally perfected.
At rest, they accomplish all the merits of a bodhisattva, namely: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Unobstructed Eye of Wisdom Light;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Adorned Necklace Who Sees All Fields;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Whose Supramundane Intention Never Ceases the Tathāgata-nature; and [the one] who manifests for the sake of all sentient beings...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Subtle Conduct Divine Power; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Banner of Renown for Immeasurable Eloquence and Unhindered Divine Power;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sovereign King Born of Pure Multitudinous Radiance;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Skillful in Discourse and Analysis of Word-Meanings with Extensive Exposition of Discursive Principles and Divine Power.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas adorned with immeasurable merit and wisdom, and other such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
always dwell together and reside in the same place as the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata constantly expounds for them in detail the dharmas of the gateways of practice for Bodhisattvas.

At that time, it had been sixteen years since the Tathāgata attained the Way of Buddhahood; he knew extensively that many within the assembly who had extensively cultivated the pure life (brahmacarya) had all gathered together in this great assembly, being capable of receiving and upholding the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Tathāgata had this thought:
"I shall now, amidst this immeasurable assembly of elephant kings, proclaim the Dharma practiced by bodhisattvas."
"First, I shall manifest the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, so that the bodhisattvas may come to know the profound realm of the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered a samādhi called "The Supernormal Power of the Buddha’s Realm: Truly Seeing Sentient Beings."

By the power of the Buddha’s merit and majestic spiritual authority, a great courtyard was manifested between the two realms of the desire and form heavens, equal in scale to a trichiliocosm. It was accomplished through the twin powers of meditative concentration and wisdom; it was a place fit for the Buddha’s dwelling and travel. Furthermore, a great light was emitted—luminous, pure, and clear—which shone throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to attain a mind of contentment. Most excellent among all celestial palaces, it was able to exhort the heedless bodhisattvas of the ten directions.

Surrounding that courtyard on all four sides were trees of white lapis lazuli, with walls made of pure gold. There were chambers of merit-gems with eaves draped in agate, and railings of various jewels. A net of white pearls covered them from above, adorned with all kinds of banners and canopies. The ground was smeared with various fragrances, and diverse incenses were burned and scattered. All the most exquisite and sublime adornments belonging to sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions appeared therein.

He established immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lion Dharma-thrones; each throne was provided with immeasurable multicolored, soft, and supple coverings, capable of causing sentient beings to feel joy, delight, and affection.

In each of the four continents, four stairways were constructed from the seven treasures; the diamond steps were ten yojanas wide, and as one walked upon them, they emitted subtle and wondrous sounds.
As it was with the four continents, so it was with the trichiliocosm.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi, and the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways, while he also emitted a supreme and most magnificent radiance.
Then, surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas before and behind him, he set out for that monastery.

All the devas honored and praised him, making offerings of incense, flowers, music, ointments, powders, burning incense, māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers. These offerings caused immeasurable and boundless worlds to tremble; their radiance shone everywhere, leaving no place unilluminated, manifesting the supernatural powers and merit of all the Buddhas.
At that time, the entire great assembly on Vulture Peak suddenly vanished, and the steps of the staircase ascended into the void.

Then, immeasurable billions of devas, nāgas, and others—including the *anupālaka* spirits, the *mālakāra* spirits, the asuras, the garuḍa-dance spirits, the crawling spirits, the flesh-eating spirits, the benevolent hungry ghosts, the jar-ear ghosts, the latrine-dwelling rākṣasas, the man-haunting ghosts, the madness-inducing ghosts, the shadow ghosts, the postpartum rākṣasas, the hair-bearing ghosts, and the ever-intoxicated ghosts—all these hosts attended upon the Buddha, making offerings with celestial incense, flowers, and exquisite celestial music.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings joined their palms, knelt for a long time, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The radiance of the Tathāgata surpasses all; It can destroy the darkness of the three evil realms.
Now we take refuge and joyfully rely upon him, The unsurpassed Honored One, Sarvārthasiddha.”
When the Four Heavenly Kings and the various devas had finished praising the Buddha in verse, they immediately attended upon his rear.

At that time, Śakra and the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven beheld the Buddha from the steps of their realm; they made offerings to him with celestial incense, flowers, and exquisite music, and praised the Buddha in verse:
"The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers; The great compassion he has attained is unsurpassed."
"Adorning the ten directions with the Buddha’s merits, I now pay homage to the One who is without equal.
At that time, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, having praised the Buddha in verse, immediately attended upon the Buddha's rear.

At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven and the sons of the Yāma devas beheld the Buddha upon the successive tiers of his realm. They made offerings with celestial fragrant flowers and exquisite music, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
"Your unimpeded wisdom is boundless; You skillfully understand the three times of all sentient beings.
With a single mind, you can know infinite minds; Therefore, we bow our heads in homage to the Unsurpassed One."
At that time, having praised the Buddha with verses, the King of the Yāma Heaven and the sons of the Yāma devas followed closely behind the Buddha.

Then, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven and the sons of the Tuṣita devas saw the Buddha from the steps of their own realm; they made offerings to him with celestial flowers, incense, and exquisite music, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The Buddha knows all phenomena to be like illusions and mirages, Without reception, without action, and beyond verbal expression.”
"Out of compassion for the multitudes, he speaks that which is unspeakable; he proclaims non-self and knows the nature of phenomena.
Then, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, together with the sons of the Tuṣita gods, having praised the Buddha in verse, immediately attended upon him.

At that time, the Deva King of Nirmāṇarati and the Devaputra Sunirmāṇarati, upon the steps of their realm, beheld the Buddha. They made offerings with celestial flowers, incense, and exquisite music, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the ten powers; He knows all dharma-realms to be like space.
Though formless, out of compassion he manifests forms; His mind is impartial as he regards all sentient beings.”
The Tathāgata constantly practices the conduct of a World-Honored One, yet for the sake of sentient beings he performs worldly deeds;
opening the non-discriminative realm of all phenomena, I now pay homage to him who is neither god nor man.
Then, after the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the various devaputras had praised the Buddha with verses, they followed behind the Buddha as his attendants.

At that time, the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and the devaputras of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven beheld the Buddha upon the steps of their celestial realm; they made offerings to him with divine fragrant flowers and exquisite music, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Abiding in the state of tranquility according to the precepts, You have cultivated and perfected the unsurpassed samādhi.”
His wisdom is unimpeded and boundless; I pay homage to the one who has attained ultimate liberation.
With great kindness and great compassion, his speech is subtle and wondrous; he truly knows what is the path and what is not the path.
Possessing courageous and vigorous power that is unsurpassed, I now reverently bow to the one who cannot be shaken.
Constantly able to cultivate and gather the three liberations, no one can fully praise their virtues;
though a crow differs from a golden bird in flight, it too can soar and wheel according to its own strength.
Now, like a crow, I offer praise according to my strength; may you, out of compassion, graciously accept this humble hymn.
Without sowing, there is no harvest of fruit; without praising the Tathāgata, there is no liberation.
Compassion is the stalk, wisdom is the leaf, samādhi is the filament, and liberation is the blossom.
The Bodhisattva, king of bees, partakes of nectar; I now pay homage to the Dharma-lotus of the Buddha.
With the light of great compassion and wisdom fully perfected, He can shatter the darkness of ignorance in sentient beings.
His precepts are pure and all delight in beholding him; I now reverently pay homage to the Dharma-moon of the Buddha.
His mind is as impartial as space; whether anointed with fragrance or pierced by a blade, his heart remains undivided.
Able to purify the defilements of immeasurable sentient beings, I now pay homage to the Buddha, the River of Dharma.
At that time, having praised the Buddha with verses, the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and the various devaputras followed behind the Buddha.
Each of the devas, having likewise offered praise to the Buddha, [did so].

At that time, the Tathāgata manifested immeasurable supernormal powers and spiritual faculties, gradually proceeding to that monastery of the seven treasures; as those in the four continents saw the Buddha ascend, so too did those throughout the trichiliocosm see him do the same.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the Jewel Monastery and ascended the lion throne; the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas each sat in order upon their respective jewel seats.

Then, the World-Honored One entered a buddha-samādhi called "Unobstructed Liberation. From every single pore, he emitted great rays of light, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, illuminating immeasurable worlds in the eastern direction; it was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.

Those in the hells who were touched by this light found relief from their manifold sufferings, while the remaining sentient beings were cleared of greed, anger, and delusion, regarding one another with a heart of loving-kindness as if they were father and son.
At that time, through the power of the Buddha’s merit, such verses were spoken within that radiance to exhort the heedless bodhisattvas:
“The Tathāgata’s diligence is boundless; The power of his diligence transcends immeasurable kalpas.
Who could praise the Buddha’s merit of radiance? Only the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions.”
To exhort the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who delight in negligence and do not cultivate dhyāna,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata emits this light, summoning all bodhisattvas to gather in this realm.
Having fully accomplished the ten powers of a Buddha, he is able to shatter all the Māras of the world;
unstained by worldly dharmas like a lotus flower, his radiance is immeasurable.
The Tathāgata turns this unsurpassed wheel, which neither gods nor worldlings can turn;
for the sake of all sentient beings he turns the wheel of Dharma, just as it was turned by the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past.
The Tathāgata now assembles this great assembly; he is difficult to behold, like the udumbara flower.
Those who possess faith and have achieved accomplishment all come to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma.

The verses spoken within this radiance resounded throughout the ten directions, exhorting and encouraging all bodhisattvas; they caused the great earth of all worlds to tremble, universally bestowing peace and happiness upon all sentient beings, purifying the afflictions of all beings, and destroying the darkness of ignorance and delusion in sentient beings.
This light eclipsed the palaces of all celestial Māras, its brilliance pervading the ten directions before returning to enter through the crown of [the Buddha’s] head.

At that time, in the eastern direction, there was a buddha-world named Infinite Merit Jewel Accumulation Supernatural Power. There dwelt a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled King of Uninterrupted Light of Pure Great Pure Radiance and Seven Factors of Enlightenment Jewels.

In that world, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakusumaputra Sarvadharmeśvara. Having encountered this light, he set out together with as many great bodhisattvas as there are sands in ten Ganges Rivers, arriving at the Great Jewel Monastery in the Sahā world. There he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right ten thousand times, and made offerings of exquisite fragrant flowers. Then, before the Buddha, he praised him in verse:

"Having reached the further shore of all merits, Constantly extolled by the Buddhas of the ten directions, Your unimpeded name pervades the ten directions— Great Compassion and Great Kindness, the Lion of the Śākyas."
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm is without differentiation, yet for those of dull faculties he speaks of differentiation;
he proclaims a single dharma as being immeasurable, like a great illusionist manifesting various phenomena to the multitude.

Then those bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the east of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the southern direction, there was a Buddha-world named Buddharaśmi. Therein dwelt a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Anantaguṇaratna.

A bodhisattva named Ratnadaṇḍa, having encountered this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. They arrived together at the Great Jewel Monastery in the Sahā world, where they beheld Śākyamuni Buddha. They prostrated themselves before him in reverence, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha.
Then, before the Buddha, they praised him in verse: "The Great Compassionate Cloud of Dharma sends down the rain of Dharma; He constantly speaks of impermanence, emptiness, and the absence of self."
With the water of the Eightfold Path, he extinguishes the fire of the fetters; He can cause the various roots of goodness in sentient beings to grow.
The Buddha’s light can shatter the darkness of ignorance; He can instruct all heedless bodhisattvas.
He can scorch the seeds of craving within the three realms of existence; He can reveal the true path and that which is not the path.

Then the bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated themselves before his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the south of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the western direction, there was a buddha-world named Radiance (*Prabhāsa*), where the Buddha was named Universal Light (*Samantaprabhāsa*).

Therein was a bodhisattva named King of the Power of Renown (*Yaśasbalarāja*). Having encountered this light, he immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, arriving at the Great Jewel Monastery (*Mahāratnavihāra*) in the Sahā world. There he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated himself before him in reverence, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha.
Then, before the Buddha, he praised him in verse: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas you have made virtuous vows; Therefore, you have attained a body pure and free from outflows."
The Tathāgata’s deeds are like space; His unimpeded voice pervades the ten directions.
The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice is like the sound of thunder; This voice does not arise from karma or non-causes.
There is no hearing, no receiving, and no sentient beings; For what reason does Great Compassion speak through this voice?

Then the bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to magically create seats to the west of the Buddha and sat down in order.
At that time, in the northern direction, there was a buddha-world named Ratnavyūha, where the Buddha was named Anantaguṇavyūha.

Therein dwelt a bodhisattva named Mahāsāgarajñāna, who, upon encountering this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. Arriving at the Great Jewel Monastery in the Sahā world, he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated himself before him in homage, and circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right. He made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha and, further, praised him before the Buddha with these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Golden Light Is able to destroy all darkness in the world.”
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, those who encounter it are all able to destroy their afflictions.

Even if one’s body were to rise above the great trichiliocosm, and one’s spiritual powers and divine strength were boundless, such a person could not see the mark on the crown of his head; what karma did Great Compassion create throughout vast ages?

Then those bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to magically create seats to the north of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the southeast direction there was a buddha-world named *Aśoka* (Sorrowless), where the Buddha was named *Sarvāndhakāravidhvamsana* (Destroyer of All Darkness).

There was a bodhisattva there named *Ajeyaprabha* (Invincible Light) who, upon encountering this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. They arrived together at the Great Jewel Enclosure in the Sahā world, where they beheld Śākyamuni Buddha. They prostrated themselves before him in reverence, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha. Then, before the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
“Immeasurable realms enter into a single pore, Yet no harm is inflicted upon any sentient being.”
The realm of the Tathāgata is beyond the reach of knowledge; therefore, his supernormal powers are inconceivable.
He can manifest a single body as infinite, yet his true body neither increases nor decreases.
Although he displays miraculous transformations for the sake of sentient beings, his inner mind remains free from pride.

Then those bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the southeast of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the southwest direction, there was a buddha-world named Sudarśana, where the Buddha was named Samacitta.

There was a bodhisattva there named Mahākaruṇācitta who, upon encountering this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. They arrived together at the Great Jewel Monastery in the Sahā world, where they beheld Śākyamuni Buddha. They prostrated themselves before him with their heads to the ground in reverent salutation, circumambulated him to the right ten thousand times, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha. Then, before the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable ages you have guarded the prohibitions and precepts, Just as a yak loves its own tail."
Seeing those who violate the precepts, he gives rise to a heart of compassion; He is neither arrogant nor does he praise his own person.
The Tathāgata’s mind is like Mount Sumeru, Which cannot be shaken by wrong views from the ten directions.
His wisdom is profoundly deep and bottomless, Just like the great ocean, difficult to conceive.
The Buddha himself is liberated from all existence, and he also causes those bound by suffering to attain liberation;
the liberation thus attained is truly without distinction, yet there are differences according to the path one follows.

Then the bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the southwest of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the northwest direction, there was a buddha-world named Destroying Darkness, where the Buddha was named King of Great Supernatural Powers.

There was a bodhisattva there named Jewel Net who, upon encountering this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. Arriving together at the Great Jewel Monastery in the Sahā world, he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated himself before him in reverence, and circumambulated him to the right ten thousand times. He made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha and further praised him in verse before the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like an illusion, Yet for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of illusory matters.”
Because there is no real substance, it is called an illusion; though there are no sentient beings, one speaks of "sentient beings.

Just as a person sees various forms in a dream, yet upon waking finds that truly no such forms exist, so too the Tathāgata manifests worldly conduct to deliver sentient beings, while in reality the Tathāgata has no worldly conduct.

Then those bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the northwest of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the northeast there was a buddha-world named Pure Abode (*Vimalavihāra*), where the Buddha was named Mind Equal to Space (*Gaganasamacitta*).

There was a bodhisattva there named Boundless Pure Intention (*Anantavimalamati*) who, having encountered this light, immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. Arriving at the Sahā world, he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Buddha. Then, before the Buddha, he praised him in verse:
“The Buddha knows the profound realms of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); He always delights in tranquility and cultivates the state of non-conceptualization.”
They know the various thoughts and intentions of sentient beings, and they also teach that all phenomena are like empty space.
Abiding in a single moment of mind, they know the three periods of time and are likewise able to know the various karmas [of beings].
Without giving rise to the thought of "mind" or the thought of "sentient beings," they have cultivated the perception of signlessness throughout immeasurable eons.

Then those bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats to the northeast of the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the direction below, there was a buddha-world named Sukhāloka, where the Buddha was named Ratnāmbujapuṣpa.

There was a bodhisattva there named Vyūharatiprabhāsa who, having encountered this light, immediately set out together with as many great bodhisattvas as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers to arrive at the Sahā world. Upon seeing Śākyamuni Buddha, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite fragrant flowers to the Buddha. Then, before the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
"The true sons of the Buddha, the One of Immeasurable Wisdom, Are as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions."
Though one were to question the Buddha for immeasurable eons, one could never exhaust the meaning of even a single syllable of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is boundless; his merit, dhāraṇī, and likewise his renown, power, and majesty are without limit, like the great ocean throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Then the bodhisattvas praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated themselves before him; by their own supernatural power, they manifested seats beneath the Tathāgata and sat down in succession.
At that time, in the zenith there was a buddha-world named Adorned with Necklaces, where the Buddha was named Great Renown.

There was a bodhisattva there named King of Supernatural Powers of All Dharmas; having encountered this light, he immediately set out together with a multitude of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, arriving at the Sahā world. Upon seeing Śākyamuni Buddha, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him ten thousand times to the right, and made offerings of exquisite incense and flowers. Then, before the Buddha, he praised him in verse:
“The body and bodily karma of the Buddha are boundless, And so too are his mind, speech, and their karmic activities.
Only a Buddha can know the three karmas of a Buddha; others cannot know them, for they are like the limits of space.
The Tathāgata has no teacher and requires no instruction; therefore, sentient beings call him the Great Teacher.
The Dharma-realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable: the wheel of Bodhi and the entry into Nirvāṇa.

Then the bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha with verses and prostrated with their heads at his feet, used their own supernatural powers to manifest seats in the space above the Buddha and sat down in succession.
At that time, within a single thought-moment, immeasurable great Bodhisattvas from the ten directions gathered simultaneously in the Great Jewel Monastery.

Then, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi; the sound of his clearing his throat reached throughout the ten directions, and all sentient beings heard it. Having heard it, they immediately conceived faith and reverence for the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

All the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as humans and non-humans, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, attained tranquility of body and mind upon hearing the Buddha’s voice.

By the power of the Buddha’s merit and majestic spiritual authority, they all beheld the jeweled staircases and steps; in a single thought-moment, they all ascended the jeweled stairs and reached the midst of the jeweled pavilion, where each sat down in their respective order according to their rank.

The various Brahma devas and celestial beings also heard that sound; the Brahmakāyika, Mahābrahmā, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha devas likewise arrived at the Jewel Monastery in a single moment of thought. Having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat down in succession upon seats that had been miraculously transformed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the great assembly had all gathered, emitted a ray of light from between his eyebrows. This light was named "Manifesting the Power of Bodhisattvas"; after circling the bodhisattvas seven times, it entered into the topknots of their heads.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Guṇakusumaputra Sarvadharmeśvara who immediately entered a samādhi.
This samādhi was named "Adorned with Garlands. By the power of this samādhi, a lion throne emerged from within the jeweled pavilion.

The height of the seat was eighty trillion *tāla* trees; adorned with the seven treasures and strewn with various flowers, it was a sight for all sentient beings to delight in, capable of purifying the minds of all sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmavaśitaguṇakusumamati, having manifested such lion thrones, arose calmly from his samādhi. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and, before the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“The light of the sun and moon dispels the appearance of darkness, But the Buddha’s light can destroy the gloom of the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of supernatural faculties, Surpassing the radiance of all the devas.”
The Buddha realizes that the dharma-realm is devoid of cognition; Like illusions, water, or the moon, it has no coming or going.
Without arising, without sensation, and without an agent— Having known this truth, he speaks for the sake of the multitudes.
Knowing that within form and mind there is neither form nor mind, yet employing skillful means to speak of form and mind for the sake of the multitudes;
the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers are like an illusion, and he knows that all dharma-realms are likewise so.
The minds of all sentient beings are eternally pure, yet at times they are defiled by adventitious afflictions;
the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have attained liberation and manifest supernatural powers that are like illusions.
Space has no ground and no place of abiding; the Tathāgata’s mind is likewise.
For the sake of the multitudes, he ascends the lion throne and, like all Buddhas of the past, proclaims the nectar of the Dharma.
The entire great assembly has neither coming nor going; There is nothing heard or spoken, and no one who receives.
All phenomena are entirely like empty space; I only pray that you will reveal and expound the realm of reality.
World-Honored One, accept this lion throne for me; I pray you roar the lion’s roar for the sake of all sentient beings.
Out of compassion for the masses, manifest the Brahma-sound, And kindle the lamp of wisdom to shatter the darkness of delusion.
The multitudes from the ten directions who have come to hear the Dharma have all assembled here in this precious monastery;
may the Buddha now bestow the great gift of the Dharma, shattering the bounds of poverty throughout immeasurable ages.

At that time, out of great compassion and pity for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guṇakusumaprabha Dharmeśvara, the World-Honored One ascended the lion throne of precious jewels offered to him. Desiring to expound the unimpeded Dharma-gate of all bodhisattva practices—which is fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas:

the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the Dharma-gate of the *dhāraṇī* of mastery over all dharmas, the Dharma-gate of entering the four types of unhindered knowledge, the Dharma-gate of entering the great supernormal powers, and the wheel of non-retrogression—[he sat upon it].
The stage of non-retrogression, which encompasses all vehicles and is endowed with the non-discriminative dharma-realm of the entire dharma-realm;
it thoroughly knows the mental faculties and roots of all sentient beings; its true reality within the dharma-realm is firm and indestructible;
it can destroy all four Māras and enemies, subdue all evil views and afflictions, and attain—
Through uncommon and skillful means of wisdom, one attains the great mind of equanimity because it is non-dual;
this is the sphere where all Buddhas enter equally, the sphere free from obstruction, wherein it is taught that all dharmas are entirely real,
wherein the teaching of all dharmas is neither awakening nor non-awakening, and wherein the equal characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination are contemplated.
Because they are fully endowed with the great adornment of wisdom; because they adorn the body and voice of a Buddha;
because they possess inexhaustible mindfulness, intention, conduct, and wisdom; because they proclaim the true Four Noble Truths; because they are able to purify the bodies and minds of śrāvakas;
because they cause pratyekabuddhas to sit upon the throne of succession; and because Mahāyāna bodhisattvas attain...
Because of mastery over the Dharma; because of extensively proclaiming all the merits of the Buddhas; because of explaining and revealing all phenomena;
because of expounding the great merits of all Bodhisattvas; because of tearing asunder the net of doubt in the minds of all sentient beings;
because of destroying all evil and heterodox doctrines; and because of increasing the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
To manifest the Buddha’s spiritual power over sentient beings, and for such causes and conditions as these, the Tathāgata ascended the lion throne of jewels.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jewel Staff, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength, entered the Buddha-Garland-Adornment Samādhi; by the power of this samādhi, he enabled the entire great assembly to obtain various kinds of garland adornments.

At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Renowned Power, further empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Lotus Samādhi; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire assembly to obtain exquisite flowers, with which they made offerings to the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsāgaraprajñājñāna, also empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Samādhi of Sublime Fragrance; by the power of this samādhi, he enabled the entire great assembly to obtain sublime fragrances, with which they made offerings to the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jewel Net (Ratnajāla) also, sustained by the Buddha’s power, entered the Samādhi of Radiance; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the bodies of the entire great assembly to obtain radiance.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Compassionate Mind (Karuṇācitta) also, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the Samādhi of the Unblinking Eye; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire great assembly to gaze up at the Tathāgata with eyes that never blinked.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantaviśuddhamati, also empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Samādhi of Joy; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire great assembly to listen to the Dharma with joy and delight.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Adhiṣṭhāna-pratibhāna-vyūha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the samādhi of the Tranquil Mind; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire assembly to be completely free from the five hindrances.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvadharmarddhi-rāja also, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered the samādhi of non-forgetfulness; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire great assembly to single-mindedly contemplate the bodhicitta so as not to forget or lose it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Courageous and Strong (Vīrakrama), empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Samādhi of Invincibility (*anabhibhūta*). By the power of this samādhi, he caused the entire assembly to subdue all Māras.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māras (Mārabhañja), empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Samādhi of Demolishing Māra. By the power of this samādhi, he summoned one hundred million Māra kings from this trichiliocosm to assemble at the Jewel Monastery before the Buddha. They prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and all spoke these words:
“We pray only that the Tathāgata—”

He extensively opens the gate of ambrosia for all sentient beings; because of the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra, we shall all be able to remain far removed from all demonic activities, and our minds shall encounter no obstacles among the great assembly.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
You have now already become free from the activities of Māra; by this cause and condition, you shall further become free from all activities of Māra in future ages.
O sons of good family!
For example, a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a room that has been dark for a hundred years;
you all are likewise able today to dispel the black darkness of ignorance from throughout immeasurable eons.
Just as the sun, the moon, and precious jewels emit light, so too do those who abide in faith, morality, generosity, wisdom, and meditative concentration.
Son of good family!

Since you have now requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma, by this cause and condition, you shall be able to shatter the darkness of ignorance and become a bright light of wisdom for all sentient beings.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmeśvararāja who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.”

Why is this? When the Tathāgata resolves to teach the Dharma, he is able to cause the entire great assembly to gather like clouds. For the sake of Bodhi, he performs the great adornment of the Great Dharma and its supernormal powers; he attains great renown throughout immeasurable worlds; his body and mind are tranquil as he achieves liberation; and he is praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions within the inconceivable Dharma-realm. He is fully endowed with all ten *pāramitās* and has accomplished mastery in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). He can tear asunder the net of doubts of all Māras, extinguish the evil and heterodox arguments of sentient beings, and skillfully discern the entire Dharma-realm. Having attained complete and unimpeded wisdom, he possesses mindfulness, mental conduct, wisdom, and heroic vigor, and is fully endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

He skillfully knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings; he knows the realms of sentient beings and preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations; he is constantly able to proclaim the pure dharma-realm; he is well-versed in all regional dialects; he is able to attain all pure Brahma-sounds; he is fully endowed with and has accomplished a heart of compassion; he cannot be moved by any heterodox or erroneous views, and is indestructible like a mountain of adamant.

“Having fully cultivated the three characteristics and established the banner of the Dharma, he has already crossed the profound river of the twelve links of dependent origination; having severed both views of annihilation and permanence, he is able to discipline the great assembly, and throughout immeasurable eons, he has attained an inconceivable accumulation of dharmas.”

He is able to heal all ailments like a great king of physicians; having heard the profound Dharma, he gives rise to no fear; his body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; and he fully accomplishes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eight liberations.

Their actions of body, speech, and mind are purely good and untainted, enabling all sentient beings to come and listen to the Dharma; they cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas, constantly experience peace and bliss, perpetually cultivate the Dharma-realm, and unwearyingly bestow the jewel of the Dharma as a gift.

Their minds are unstained by any conditioned phenomena, just as a lotus flower is unsullied by dust or water; their brilliance surpasses all lights, and their wisdom is as deep as the ocean. They succeed to the nature of the Triple Gem, harmonize the realms of sentient beings, open the treasury of the Buddhas, and protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.

Endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom, having cultivated and accumulated immeasurable adornments of merit throughout immeasurable eons, and constantly desiring to attain a mind of single practice, a single color, and a single location—all such Bodhisattvas possessing these merits have gathered here in this assembly.

“I only pray, Tathāgata, that you will expound the Dharma-gate of the unimpeded conduct of Bodhisattvas, for the benefit of all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, so that those who have newly resolved their minds may attain non-retrogression; those who have long since resolved their minds may attain further growth; those practicing the path to Bodhi may purify their intentions; those Bodhisattvas who do not yet retreat may study the Buddha-dharma; those Bodhisattvas in their final birth may be adorned with its ornaments; those Bodhisattvas in their last body may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; those of fixed nature may increase their causal conditions; those of unfixed nature may be provided with causal conditions; those who have not yet entered the Buddha-dharma may be led to enter it; those who have already entered the Buddha-dharma may revere the Buddha-dharma; those who delight in the Three Vehicles may be taught the One Vehicle; and so as to bestow the happiness of gods and humans upon the world.”
“World-Honored One!
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are such inconceivable matters as these.
World-Honored One!”
Now, every single bodhisattva in this great assembly is able to manifest all manner of great supernatural powers.
For this reason, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that sentient beings are so heavily burdened by ignorance and craving?
Although they witness such supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva, they nevertheless give rise to an inferior attitude toward the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they have already surpassed all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
World-Honored One!”

For example, it is as if there were someone who would discard beryl to take up crystal; all sentient beings are likewise, for they abandon the Mahāyāna and instead delight in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If there are sentient beings who have already resolved, or wish to resolve, their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such persons shall all obtain these merits.

At that time, within the assembly, there were thirty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings—both devas and humans—who gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Two: The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Two, Part One: The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that all the bodhisattvas had assembled in great numbers, reflected thus:

"Today, these good men and women all desire to know the true meaning of all dharmas; they are able to uphold the profound Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, and they wish to hear and receive the unimpeded dharma-gate of the bodhisattva practices."

Thereupon, he emitted from between his eyebrows a white tuft of light named Fearlessness, which circled the great assembly seven times and entered the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharanīśvararāja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, manifested a jeweled canopy as vast as a trichiliocosm, adorned with the seven treasures, which he spread over the Tathāgata’s precious throne.
He prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"The Tathāgata has attained mastery over all dharmas; His radiance can shatter the darkness of the world.
The World-Honored One’s Buddha-eye is without obstruction, Able to perceive the true meaning of all phenomena."
Endowed with immeasurable virtues, you have awakened alone to all realms of phenomena without a teacher;
O Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings you emit light—by what cause and condition do you now enter my body?
What I previously knew and remembered was not clear; the same was true for the roots of dhāraṇī.
Now this light has entered my body, and I clearly perceive all realms of phenomena.
Body and mind have attained great purity; I experience unsurpassed and boundless bliss.
Now I have known the realm of the Buddha, And have also attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech.
The Buddhas of the ten directions are difficult to approach; the foolish are unable to serve them as teachers.
Now, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, I wish to pose a few questions for the benefit of sentient beings.
By what causes and conditions is the bodhicitta generated?
Furthermore, for what purpose does a Buddha appear in the world?
For what reason is light emitted throughout the ten directions, and by what cause are supernatural powers displayed?
For what reason does the Buddha bestow predictions upon the assembly?
We pray that you will explain this in detail for the sake of the great multitude.
This present assembly is supreme and unsurpassed; they are all fully capable of receiving and upholding the Buddha’s realm of Dharma.
This assembly is free from Māra and the works of Māra; it exists solely to reveal the treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
My own wisdom is shallow, limited, and finite; how could I possibly inquire of the Unsurpassed Honored One?
I now inquire of the Tathāgata’s boundless wisdom: how may one come to know all skillful means?

I pray that you will now instruct all disciples; once I have studied and attained mastery over the Dharma, and having attained it, am able to bestow the great rain of the Dharma, I shall repay the kindness of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are inconceivable, and the conduct of Bodhisattvas is boundless. Therefore, I now wish to question the Tathāgata—the Unsurpassed Dharma King and the Mass of Great Compassion—regarding the profound meaning for the benefit of sentient beings:
What is called the practice of a Bodhisattva?”
By what kind of necklace is a bodhisattva adorned so that the conduct of the bodhisattva may become pure?
How can one destroy the various darknesses of ignorance?
How can one sever the mind that is ensnared by the net of doubt?
How does a bodhisattva cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva protect sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva truly cultivate the deeds of a bodhisattva—wholesome deeds and deeds that do not lead to harm?
I only pray that the Tathāgata will, out of compassion, proclaim this teaching.

Furthermore, this great assembly possesses sharp faculties and wisdom; they are able to understand the Buddha’s words, know the dharma-realm, and penetrate the unimpeded dharma-gates of the bodhisattva’s practice. They are able to destroy all Māras and the works of Māra, shatter great doubt, and comprehend the profound realm of all Buddhas. They know the realms of sentient beings and the nature of their minds, can behold immeasurable Buddha-worlds, protect the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata, and attain great mastery over all dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family!”

One who is able to inquire about the profound meaning of the Tathāgata and is able to skillfully practice the immeasurable conduct of the Buddha is capable of posing such a profound question as you have.
Since you now possess a sincere mind, I shall explain it for you: if a bodhisattva can achieve and fulfill such merits as these, they shall attain great mastery over all phenomena.
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time; please deign to proclaim it.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! A bodhisattva has four kinds of necklace adornments:
first, the adornment of the necklace of ethical discipline;”
Second, the adornment of the necklace of samādhi;
third, the adornment of the necklace of wisdom;
fourth, the adornment of the necklace of dhāraṇī.
There is one kind of adornment of the necklace of precepts, namely, the absence of any harmful intent toward sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva is free from a malicious or harmful mind, all sentient beings will always delight in seeing them.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, closing off the evil paths;
second, being able to open the gates of goodness."
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, purity of body; second, purity of speech;
[and third, purity of mind]."
Third, purity of mind.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, obtaining all that is sought;
Second, the fulfillment of one's vows;
third, the accomplishment of one's vows;
fourth, the ability to perform what one desires.
"Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, faith; second, precepts;..."
Third is concentration;
fourth is mindfulness; fifth is wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are six kinds:
first, non-broken precepts;
second, non-leaking precepts;..."
Third, the precept of non-confusion;
fourth, the precept of non-regret;
fifth, the precept of mastery;
Sixth, the precept of non-attachment.
"Furthermore, there are seven kinds, namely the seven purities:
first, the purity of giving;..."
Second, purity of patience;
third, purity of diligence;
fourth, purity of meditative concentration.
Fifth, purity of wisdom;
sixth, purity of skillful means;
seventh, purity of excellent skillful means.
"Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely the eight perfections:
first, the perfection of non-action;
second, the perfection of the stages;"
Third, the perfection of an unforgetting mind;
fourth, the perfection of non-laxity;
fifth, the perfection of the sense faculties.
Sixth, the perfection of the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
seventh, the perfection of freedom from adversity;
eighth, the perfection of spiritual friends.
"Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
first, immovability; second, fearlessness;"
Third, concentration and wisdom;
fourth, tranquility;
fifth, sincerity of heart.
Sixth, purity; seventh, loosening the bonds;
eighth, harmonizing the mind.
Ninth, abiding on the stage of subduing.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, purifying the body for the sake of the thirty-two marks;
Second is purity of speech, because one's words are non-dual;
third is purity of mind, because of liberation;
fourth is purity of the field, because it causes the merit and virtue of sentient beings to increase.
Fifth is the purity of mind, for the sake of harmonizing sentient beings;
sixth is the purity of existence, for the sake of practicing the transformation of sentient beings;
seventh is the purity of the bodhisattva’s name, for the sake of attaining all the merits of the Tathāgata.
Eighth is pure wisdom, because of its great supernormal powers;
ninth is pure skillful means, because it destroys all hosts of Māras;
tenth is pure precept, because it constitutes the unshared dharmas.
“Good son! Such matters as these are called the adornment of the precept-garland.
There is one kind of adornment of the samādhi-garland, which is the cultivation and accumulation of a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of all sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, straightforwardness;
second, gentleness."
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, not being deceptive;
second, not being harsh."
Third, freedom from crookedness and flattery.
There are further four kinds:
first, conduct free from attachment;
Second, the practice of non-anger;
third, the practice of fearlessness;
fourth, the practice of non-delusion.
"Furthermore, there are five kinds, namely the samādhi of being far removed from the five hindrances.
Furthermore, there are six kinds, namely the samādhi of cultivating and accumulating the six recollections."
“Furthermore, there are seven kinds, namely, the cultivation and accumulation of the seven factors of enlightenment samādhi.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely, the cultivation and accumulation of the eightfold noble path samādhi.”

"Furthermore, there are nine kinds: first, the Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates the bodhicitta and the mind of great compassion; he cultivates and accumulates mindfulness toward all immeasurable sentient beings; he remains far removed from evil desires and unwholesome dharmas; with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), he attains the joy and bliss of tranquility, thereby realizing the first dhyāna.

Second, being far removed from directed and sustained thought, he inwardly attains a joyful mind; through mental concentration, he reflects without directed or sustained thought, attaining the joy and bliss born of samādhi, thereby realizing the second dhyāna.
Third, leaving behind joy, he cultivates equanimity and is endowed with a mindful mind; free from negligence, his body experiences bliss, thereby realizing the third dhyāna."

Fourth, being far removed from suffering and pleasure, and with the extinction of sorrow and joy, one dwells in equanimity and mindfulness, having attained the fourth dhyāna which is neither painful nor pleasant;
fifth, being far removed from the signs of form, one cultivates the sign of immeasurable space;
sixth, being far removed from the sign of space, one cultivates the sign of immeasurable consciousness.
Seventh, they distance themselves from the marks of consciousness and cultivate the mark of nothingness;
eighth, they distance themselves from the mark of nothingness and cultivate the mark of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
ninth, although they have not yet perfected the wisdom of skillful means, they transform sentient beings through the power of samādhi.
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, observing phenomena without error;
second, fully accomplishing śamatha."
Third, to practice diligence without rest;
fourth, to be skillfully able to discern the proper timing;
fifth, to wholeheartedly receive and uphold wholesome dharmas.
Sixth, to pacify the mind;
seventh, to contemplate the body;
eighth, to constantly contemplate the dharma-realm.
Ninth, attaining mastery over the mind;
tenth, obtaining the noble nature.
These are called the adornments of the samādhi necklace.
“Good son! There is one kind of adornment for the necklace of wisdom, namely, having no net of doubt in the mind.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:”
First, to distance oneself from doubt;
second, to distance oneself from anger.
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
First, to be far removed from ignorance;
second, to break the shell of ignorance;
third, to produce great radiance.
“Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, knowing suffering;
second, abandoning the origin [of suffering];”
Third, the realization of cessation;
fourth, the cultivation of the path.
"Furthermore, there are five kinds:
First, purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline;
second, purity of the aggregate of meditative concentration;
third, purity of the aggregate of wisdom.
Fourth, the purity of the aggregate of liberation;
fifth, the purity of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Furthermore, there are six kinds:
First is the purification of the *dānapāramitā*, which has three aspects:
first, internal purity, viewing all phenomena as like an illusion;
second, the purity of sentient beings, viewing them as like a dream.
Third, regarding the purity of bodhi, one does not seek karmic retribution.
Second, there are three aspects to the purity of the śīla-pāramitā:
first, viewing the body as being like a shadow;
Second, contemplating the mouth as an echo;
third, contemplating the mind as an illusion.
Third, there are three kinds of purifying the *kṣānti-pāramitā*:
First, not becoming angry when hearing disparagement;
second, not feeling joy when hearing praise;
third, being able to contemplate the dharma-realm when one's body is mangled or one's life is taken.
Fourth is the purification of the *vīrya-pāramitā*, which further has three aspects:
first, non-conceptualization; second, firmness.
Third, not perceiving the characteristics of dharmas.
Fifth, the purification of the dhyāna-pāramitā has three aspects:
first, non-attachment to all dharmas; [the other two follow].
Second, the non-retrogression of the mind;
third, the purity of the object of focus.
Sixth, the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) has three aspects:
First, gathering in sentient beings for the sake of their liberation;
second, purifying dhāraṇīs for the sake of upholding the Dharma;
third, purifying one's vows for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, practicing the four foundations of mindfulness without grasping or attachment;
second, practicing the four right efforts without emergence or cessation."
Third, cultivating the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) so that body and mind are pure;
fourth, cultivating the five faculties (indriya) so as to know which faculties are present and which are absent;
fifth, cultivating the five powers (bala) so as to be able to destroy afflictions (kleśa).
Sixth, by cultivating the factors of enlightenment, one knows the true reality of the dharma-realm;
seventh, by cultivating and gathering the noble path, there is no coming or going.
"Furthermore, there are eight kinds:
First, the cultivation of meditative concentration for the sake of ultimate purity;
second, the cultivation of wisdom for the sake of destroying darkness;
third, the cultivation of knowledge of the aggregates for the sake of knowing the collection of phenomena.
Fourth, one cultivates the knowledge of knowing the elements (*dhātu*) in order to realize that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is equal to empty space;
fifth, one cultivates the knowledge of knowing the sense-bases (*āyatana*) in order to know the equality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
sixth, one cultivates the knowledge of knowing the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by contemplating the absence of self and what belongs to self.
Seventh, one cultivates the wisdom that discerns the truths in order to destroy the four inversions;
eighth, one cultivates the wisdom that discriminately knows the dharma-realm in order to know reality as it is.
"Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
first, contemplating the perception of impermanence;
second, contemplating the perception of impermanence as suffering;"
Third, the perception of suffering as being without self;
fourth, the perception of food as impure;
fifth, the perception that the world is not to be relished.
Sixth, the perception of the many faults and afflictions inherent in all births and deaths;
seventh, the perception of liberation;
eighth, the perception of detachment from craving.
Ninth, contemplating the perception of exhaustion.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, contemplating all phenomena as being like illusory manifestations;
2. like the perception of a dream;
3. like the perception of a mirage;
4. like the perception of an echo;
5. The perception of being like a plantain tree;
6. The perception of being like the moon reflected in water;
7. The perception of being like a shadow;
Eighth, one contemplates the dharma-realm as being without the notion of increase or decrease;
ninth, one contemplates all dharma-realms as having neither going nor staying;
tenth, one contemplates the unconditioned as being without arising or ceasing.
This is called the adornment of the wisdom-garland. "Good son!
There is one kind of adornment for the dharani-garland, namely, the mind of mindfulness."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, initial reception;
second, ultimate ability to maintain."
"Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, knowing the meaning;
second, knowing the words."
Third, knowing how to speak.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, right speech;
Second, speech that is clear;
third, speech that is unimpeded;
fourth, speech that is unerring.
"Furthermore, there are five kinds, namely the five reliances:
first, rely on the meaning and not on the letter;
second, rely on gnosis and not on consciousness."
Third, rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning;
fourth, rely on the Dharma and not on persons;
fifth, rely on that which transcends the world and not on that which belongs to the world.
"Furthermore, there are six kinds:
first, upholding [the teachings] exactly as they were spoken;
second, being truthful in one's speech."
Third, speech that people delight to hear;
fourth, speech of compassion;
fifth, speech that produces the sprouts of goodness.
Sixth is timely speech.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, beneficial speech; [and so forth].
Second, adorned speech;
third, unimpeded speech; fourth, unhindered speech.
Fifth, no double-tongued speech;
sixth, speaking with prior knowledge;
seventh, clear speech.
"Furthermore, there are eight kinds:
first, knowing the dialects of various regions;
second, knowing the language of ghosts and spirits;"
Third, knowing the languages of all devas;
fourth, knowing the languages of all nāgas;
fifth, knowing the languages of gandharvas.
Sixth, knowing the language of asuras;
seventh, knowing the language of garuḍas;
eighth, knowing the language of animals.
"Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
first, fearless speech; second, uncontracted speech;..."
Third, speech that is free from difficulty;
fourth, speech that knows liberation;
fifth, speech that knows how to answer in accordance with the Dharma.
Sixth, knowing the discourse of extensive explanation;
seventh, knowing the discourse of sequential order;
eighth, speaking the discourse on impermanence;
Ninth, inexhaustible speech.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of speech:
first, speech that destroys the net of doubt; [and so forth].
Second, the discourse that reveals the realms;
third, the discourse that reveals the Dharma-gates;
fourth, the discourse that reveals wisdom;
Fifth, speech that dispels darkness;
sixth, speech that explains each and every syllable;
seventh, speech that praises the Buddha;
Eighth, words that rebuke afflictions;
ninth, words that distinguish between sharp and dull faculties;
tenth, wondrous words that reveal the Buddha’s merits.
“Good son! This is called the adornment of the *dhāraṇī*-necklace.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The four ornaments and garlands can make the Mahāyāna majestic and dignified;
namely, precepts, concentration, wisdom, and the unsurpassed dhāraṇī.
These can purify the three karmas and cause one to be beloved by all people."
Forever severing the three evil realms—this is called the garland of precepts.
Fulfilling all wishes as desired and attaining the bodies of humans and devas;
Being able to cultivate diligent and energetic effort—this is called the garland of precepts.
Able to cultivate the unsurpassed concentration, Attaining the two kinds of liberation, And beholding unsurpassed nirvāṇa— This is called the necklace of precepts.
One's precepts are neither broken nor leaking; The unsurpassed precepts are untainted.
One who attains great mastery is called "Adorned with the Necklace.
Pure precepts can purify giving; pure precepts can purify patience.
Pure precepts purify the five perfections; this is called the adornment of the precept-necklace.
Purity of precepts can purify existence; it purifies great heedfulness.
With a fearless mind free from regret, this is called the "garland of precepts.
Through purity of precepts, one attains the noble nature and can likewise purify body and mind.
Attaining the boundless concentrations—this is called the necklace of ethical discipline.
Fearless and unshakable, one attains the purity of meditative absorption and is able to sever the bonds of affliction; this is called the necklace of ethical discipline.
One who can discipline the difficult-to-tame faculties, Who can attain great renown,
And who adorns the mind with mastery— This is called the "garland of precepts.
One who can act according to what they have spoken, And can purify the four types of verbal conduct,
To remain far removed from all afflictions is called the adornment of a necklace.
To be able to purify one’s own buddha-field, to be able to discipline all sentient beings,
and to be able to cultivate great compassion is called the adornment of a necklace.
Not committing any evil deeds, Cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva,
Possessing great power and fearlessness— This is called the adornment of the necklace.
It can adorn Great Nirvana, And it can attain the great cause and fruit.
Filling all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness is called the adornment of the necklace.
Being able to leave behind stinginess and deceit, practicing the four means of attraction with gentleness,
and severing attachment, anger, fear, and delusion is called the adornment of the necklace.
Able to shatter the five evil hindrances, Cultivating and gathering the tenfold mind of mindfulness,
Assisting the path through non-negligence— This is called the adornment of the necklace.
Fully endowed with the two wings, One contemplates the meaning according to the Dharma.
Delighting in abiding naturally in tranquility is called the adornment of a necklace.
Having no doubt regarding the Dharma and being free from a deluded or distracted mind,
truly understanding the Four Noble Truths is called the adornment of a necklace.
Maintaining the precepts with a mind free from attachment, and likewise not giving rise to pride;
one who does not grasp at the precepts or the precept-holder is called "adorned with a jeweled necklace.
Possessing unsurpassed wisdom and pure concentration, they also know the two kinds of pure wisdom.
To be able to fully understand the three realms is called the adornment of the necklace.
When the mind is pure and conceit does not arise, and one sees impurity without disparagement;
to know that dharmas are inexpressible is called the adornment of the necklace.
Wisdom adorns knowledge, and knowledge likewise adorns wisdom;
purifying the bodhi of oneself and others is called the "ornament of the necklace.
Knowing that phenomena are like dreams and illusions, one does not say that all phenomena are non-existent.
To be able to speak in accordance with the world is called the adornment of a necklace;
wisdom can adorn precepts, and precepts can adorn wisdom.
When body and speech are pure in bodhi, it is called the adornment of a necklace.
Seeing phenomena as like the moon in water, And also like a mirage in the heat;
Explaining the Dharma as having the character of an echo, Like a city of the gandharvas—
Not treating what is not the Dharma as the Dharma— Is called the adornment of the wisdom-garland.
Wisdom can adorn patience, and patience can adorn wisdom;
when body and speech are purified by bodhi, this is called the adornment of a jeweled necklace.
Following the Dharma without increase or decrease, one understands and then disciplines sentient beings.
To contemplate the Dharma-body with a sincere mind is called the adornment of the necklace.
Wisdom can adorn progress, and progress can adorn wisdom;
when the moving mind is purified without regret, it is called the adornment of the necklace.
Wisdom can adorn meditative concentration, and meditative concentration can adorn wisdom;
one who can expound the profound realm of phenomena attains unsurpassed supernormal powers,
understands all skillful means, and achieves the supreme dhāraṇī.
The purity of the Dharma-realm and its sentient beings is called the adornment of the necklace.
Knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of the multitude, destroying afflictions and all demons,
and attaining mastery over body and mind— this is called the adornment of the necklace.
The Way has neither going nor coming, Nor is there anyone who goes or comes;
It is not of the past, nor of the future, Neither present nor something to be cultivated.
Without discriminating within the dharma-realm, One can purify ultimate concentration.
To know the aggregates, sense bases, and elements is called the adornment of the torch of wisdom.

That the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are like space—devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self—and that their arising and ceasing have the twelve links as their cause: this is called the purity of wisdom.
Truly knowing the ultimate truth, and likewise knowing the aggregates, bases, and elements,
they do not give rise to disputes regarding phenomena and understand the three periods of time without obstruction.
Discerning the three groups of beings, they are able to preach the three vehicles for them.
Able to employ the teachings of the Triple Gem, one cultivates the three concentrations on signlessness.
Through signlessness, one knows the single mark; through non-illusion, one knows that which is like an illusion.
Where there is no speech, one is able to speak; one speaks of emptiness within the non-empty.
All phenomena are impermanent and subject to change, yet they do not destroy the dharma-realm.
Because they arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they circulate throughout the dharma-realm;
this is called true wisdom, which does not conceptualize the dharma-realm.
Knowing the two as moving and unmoving, Knowing the two as shallow and deep,
Knowing the two as permanent and impermanent— This is called the wisdom of great purity.
Constantly not losing the mind of mindfulness, One thoroughly understands the dharma-realm.
Knowing the letters and knowing their meanings, one is not obscured regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Having heard the Dharma once, one is able to retain it; one understands the languages of sentient beings, is able to destroy all false paths, and cultivates unsurpassed wisdom.
Relying on the four supreme reliances, this great dhāraṇī-garland;
I speak this garland of merit to adorn the bodhicitta,
to teach fearlessly among the masses, and to skillfully understand the language of the devas.
They can destroy the web of doubts, open up all realms of phenomena,
and praise the Triple Gem; they exhort others to make offerings,
draw near to the Buddhas and their assemblies, and cultivate and accumulate supreme wisdom.
"I speak of the four kinds of necklaces, Which can adorn Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
If one possesses sincere faith, One shall immediately attain this adornment.

Postscript to the Collation of the First Scroll of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra: According to this sūtra, both the Guo edition and the Song edition consist of sixty scrolls in total, comprising seventeen chapters.
In the Tibetan (Dan) canon, it consists of thirty fascicles and eleven chapters.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the sutra, the names of the "Garuḍa-Necklace Chapter" (Yingluo pin) appear in both the Liang and Song editions, which are absent from the Tibetan canon.
Regarding the "Gaganagañja" chapter, in both editions it follows the "Avaktavya" chapter, whereas in the Danzang (Dunhuang canon) it precedes the "Anabhilāpya" chapter.

Furthermore, following the "Ratnacūḍa" chapter, both editions contain the four-fascicle "Akṣayamati" chapter, which is absent from the Danzang; instead, the Danzang contains the three-fascicle "Sūryaguhya-parivarta."
Why are they thus different?
Now, summarizing and synthesizing the preceding and following texts of the *Kaiyuan lu*, it is clear that there are six versions of this scripture in total.
The Record states:
"According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra-śāstra* by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou, there are twelve sections of discourse that together constitute a single sutra:

first, the 'Garuḍa-ornament Chapter' (*Āmuktamālya-parivarta*); second, the 'Dhāraṇī-vaśavartin-rāja Chapter'; third, the 'Ratnāvalī Chapter'; fourth, the 'Animiṣa Chapter'; fifth, the 'Sāgaramati Chapter'; sixth, the 'Anabhilāpya Chapter'; seventh, the 'Avaktavya Chapter'; eighth, the 'Gaganagañja Chapter'; ninth, the 'Ratnaketu Chapter'; tenth, the 'Gaganacakṣus Chapter'; eleventh, the 'Ratnaśikhin Chapter'; and twelfth, the 'Akṣayamati Chapter'."
The commentary states: "This is the first version.
Verifying it now by means of the sequence of chapters, it constitutes the first thirty fascicles out of the sixty fascicles of these two versions."
It further states: "Now, upon examining the manuscript of the sutra, it differs from Sengyou’s record:

first, the *Dhāraṇī-īśvara-rāja-bodhisattva-parivarta*; second, the *Ratnāvalī-parivarta*; third, the *Animiṣa-parivarta*; fourth, the *Sāgaramati-parivarta*; fifth, the *Gaganagañja-parivarta*; sixth, the *Avacanīya-parivarta*; seventh, the *Anabhilāpya-parivarta*; eighth, the *Ratnaketu-vibhāga*; ninth, the *Gagananetra-vibhāga*; tenth, the *Ratnaśikhara-parivarta*; and eleventh, the *Sūryaguhya-vibhāga*."
The commentary states:
"This is the second version.
Verifying it now by means of the sequence of chapters, it is precisely this thirty-fascicle *Danzang* (Dan-zang) edition of the sutra."
Furthermore, it says:

"During the Sui dynasty, the monk Jiu compiled the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, taking the title of the *Prajñāpāramitā-pañcāśat-prakaraṇa-sūtra* as the 'Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions,' placing it after the 'Candragarbha' chapter; together with the 'Akṣayamati' chapter, this formed fifty-eight fascicles."
The commentary states:
"This is the fourth version.
It further states:

Regarding the compilation of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, there is also a version consisting of sixty fascicles; this is achieved because the thirty-first and thirty-second fascicles both contain the "Ratnacūḍa-parivarta," thereby completing the total of sixty fascicles. This "Ratnacūḍa-parivarta" precedes the "Sūryagarbha[-parivarta]," and it is found in fascicles twenty-six and twenty-seven.
This has been compiled again, yet its underlying intention remains unclear.
Furthermore, since the Sanskrit originals for the *Sūryaguhya* and *Sūryagarbha* are no different, to compile and record them repeatedly is a grave error.
The commentary states: "This is the fifth version.
Verifying it now by means of the sequence of chapters, it corresponds to the sixty-fascicle version of the sutra currently found in both the Northern and Southern Tripitakas."
However, it does not include the "Ratnacūḍa-parivarta," which is the only minor difference.

Specifically, from within the fifty-eight fascicles of the aforementioned fourth edition, the ten fascicles of the "Sūryagarbha-vibhāga" were divided into twelve fascicles to complete the total of sixty.
As for the third and sixth versions, since they are not found in any of the extant canons, I shall not trouble myself to describe them.
It is because the manuscript copies of the sutra differ in this way that such discrepancies have arisen within the canon.

I have carefully examined the textual sequence of the *Kaiyuan lu* (Kaiyuan Catalogue); as for these two editions of the canon consisting of sixty fascicles, they cannot be relied upon for practice because they contain six errors.
The Catalogue states:
"There is also a version of the scripture that divides it into the *Yingluo-pin* (Garuḍa Chapter); this is not correct, for this is a single section and should not be divided into two.
According to the Commentary:
To divide this sutra [in this manner] is the first error.
Furthermore, it is said:

"The *Sengyou Ji* does not contain the 'Dayim Fen' (Division of Dayim), but includes the 'Wujinyi Pin' (Chapter on Akṣayamati); this is not so. Although the *Akṣayamati Sūtra* is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, it was not translated by Kumārajīva, nor does its sequence correspond; thus, it should not be included therein."
The commentary states:
