There are those who can be transformed and those who cannot; knowing whether the faculties of sentient beings are mature or immature, he preaches the Dharma according to their mental dispositions, skillfully knowing when to reprove them and when to soothe them with gentle words.
Knowing there are those who do not accept his instructions, he cultivates a mind of equanimity toward them.
The Tathāgata, well-versed in all skillful means, adorns his wisdom to destroy afflictions;
for the sake of destroying the afflictions of sentient beings, he expounds the fifth activity of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata truly knows the path that leads to the destination.
How does he know it?

He knows the group of those fixed in the right [path], the group of those fixed in the wrong [path], and the group of those who are not fixed; he knows the power of causes and the power of karmic retribution; he knows the causes and conditions of merit from past lives; he knows the causes and conditions for adornment in the present life, whether they are difficult to discipline or easy to discipline; and he knows how to provide a brief explanation for what is extensive, and an extensive explanation for what is brief.

They know which sentient beings are able to attain liberation and which are unable to attain liberation; they know that those who are indeterminate will dwell in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) if they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), but will lack liberation if they do not obtain a virtuous friend.
Having known this, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to their inclinations; having heard the Dharma, they apply their mindfulness and reflection to obtain wholesome fruits.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is solely for the sake of those who are indeterminate; he never teaches the Dharma to those who are fixed in error.
Why is this? Because they are not suitable vessels and cannot attain true liberation; this is called the Tathāgata’s cultivation of a mind of equanimity toward such persons.

Having known this truly, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently practices adornment in order to shatter such beings of false certainty; for this reason, the bodhisattva resolves upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that there are three kinds of greed:
first, that which arises from the perception of purity;
second, that which arises from the condition of sensation.”
Third, it is because of fundamental causes and conditions. There are three kinds of anger: first, anger due to its causes and conditions;
[the second is anger due to its objects; the third is anger due to its habitual tendencies].
Second, because of the condition of sensation;
third, because of the primary condition.
Ignorance is also of three kinds:
First, the causal condition of ignorance;
second, the causal condition of the view of self;
third, the causal condition of the net of doubt.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows that among sentient beings, some attain supernormal powers with difficulty and slowly, while others attain them with difficulty and quickly; he knows that those who attain them with difficulty and slowly can attain happiness quickly, and those who attain them quickly with ease can attain suffering slowly, while those who attain them with ease and slowly can attain happiness quickly."

One knows there is the power of cultivation and the power of wisdom; furthermore, one knows that there are those who possess the power of cultivation but lack the power of wisdom, those who possess the power of wisdom but lack the power of cultivation, those who possess both the power of cultivation and the power of wisdom, and those who possess neither the power of cultivation nor the power of wisdom.

Furthermore, one knows that there are paths capable of purifying the mind but not adorning it; those capable of adorning it but not purifying the mind; those capable of purifying the mind and also possessing adornment; and those that neither possess purification of the mind nor possess adornment.

Furthermore, he knows that there is a path which purifies the body but not the speech or mind; there is one which purifies the speech and mind but not the body; there is one which purifies the body, speech, and mind; and there is one which does not purify the body, speech, or mind. This is called the sixth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata well knows the destination to which one goes, And he also knows the various causes and conditions of sentient beings;
He can fully understand those who are fixed and those who are not, And he penetrates with clear insight those who are disciplined and those who are undisciplined.”
He does not preach the Dharma for those of false resolve, nor does he seek to discipline those of inferior faculties;
he knows the teachings on the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, and he also understands the light and heavy characteristics of all fetters.
He knows when the four paths turn back and when they do not; therefore, the Buddha has realized the ultimate limit of the path.
He truly knows the power of cultivation and the power of wisdom; likewise, he knows the lower, middle, and superior powers.
He knows whether body, speech, and mind are pure or impure, and the same applies to the mind and its adornments.
The Tathāgata, having known the realms of the faculties and afflictions of sentient beings, has destroyed them;
for the sake of those sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, he proclaims the sixth activity of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata knows dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, affliction, and liberation from affliction.
How does he know this?
One knows that all sentient beings, due to causes and conditions, crave and delight in birth-and-death; and due to causes and conditions, they crave and delight in nirvana.
What is called "cause"? What is called "condition"?
If sentient beings contemplate what is unwholesome, this is called the causal condition for birth and death.
Because of unwholesome contemplation, ignorance arises and grows; therefore, unwholesomeness is the cause and ignorance is the condition.
Because of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise; therefore, ignorance is the cause and the various formations are the condition.
Because of the various formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; therefore, the formations are the cause and consciousness is the condition.
Because of consciousness, name-and-form arise; therefore, consciousness is the cause and name-and-form is the condition.
Because of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; therefore, name-and-form is the cause and the six sense bases are the condition.
Because of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa) arises; therefore, the six sense bases are the cause and contact is the condition.
Because of contact, feeling (vedanā) arises; therefore, contact is the cause and feeling is the condition.
Feeling gives rise to craving; therefore, feeling is the cause and craving is the condition.
Craving gives rise to grasping; therefore, craving is the cause and grasping is the condition.
Because grasping gives rise to becoming, grasping is the cause and becoming is the condition.
Because becoming gives rise to birth, becoming is the cause and birth is the condition.
Because birth gives rise to the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth, birth is thus the cause and old age and death are the conditions.

Afflictions are the cause and various karmas are the conditions; various views are the cause and the fetter of craving are the conditions; afflictions are the cause and the five hindrances are the conditions. These are called causes and these are called conditions, yet all sentient beings, by means of these causes and conditions, greedily delight in birth and death.
"For what causes and conditions do they delight in Nirvana?
There are two causes and two conditions that cause all sentient beings to delight in Nirvana:
first, they delight in hearing the Dharma with joy."
Second, delighting in right reflection.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, śamatha; [second, vipaśyanā].
Second is vipaśyanā. It further has two kinds:
first, the wisdom of non-departure; [second, the wisdom of non-arrival].
Second is the knowledge of non-coming.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, contemplating birth and death; [second, contemplating nirvana].
Second, the contemplation of nirvana.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, maintaining it in accordance with the Dharma; [and second, realizing its true nature].
Second, the attainment of realization.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, the cultivation of the gates of liberation; [second, the actualization of those gates].
Second, attaining the fruit of liberation.
This, in turn, has two aspects: first, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna); [and second, the knowledge of non-arising].
Second is the knowledge of non-arising.
This, in turn, has two types:
first, the knowledge of the truths; [second, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows].
Second, he contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). He discerns what is called "cause" and what is called "condition.

Furthermore, he knows that all sentient beings take delight in *nirvāṇa* through these causes and conditions. Having fully understood such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), samādhis, and liberations (*vimokṣa*), the Tathāgata abandons desires, evils, and unwholesome states; with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the joy and bliss born of seclusion, he enters the first dhyāna. Entering the first dhyāna, he emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*); entering the cessation of perception and feeling, he emerges from the first dhyāna. This continues in the same manner up to the eight liberations.

"All sentient beings are unable to know the places where the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, enters and emerges; the Tathāgata fully knows his dwelling in meditative equipoise, as well as its higher and lower states."
Sentient beings say that the Buddha enters one samādhi, yet the Buddha actually enters all samādhis;
sentient beings see the Buddha arise from all concentrations, yet the Buddha actually remains in one specific samādhi.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi has no fixed sequence, yet it is not indeterminate; it is something that none of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas can fully know.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows that through certain causes and conditions for teaching the Dharma one attains the samādhi of a śrāvaka, through certain causes and conditions for teaching the Dharma one attains the samādhi of a pratyekabuddha, and through certain causes and conditions for teaching the Dharma one attains the samādhi of a bodhisattva. Having known this, he expounds the teachings according to their inclinations; this is called the seventh activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata fully understands the causes of birth and death, And likewise thoroughly penetrates the causes of liberation.
Having understood them, he preaches the Dharma for others, Destroying the unwholesome causes of birth and death."
Improper reflection is the cause of ignorance; with ignorance as a causal condition, birth and death are prolonged.
With afflictions as a causal condition, one receives the fruits of karma; with various views as a causal condition, the fetters of craving increase.
If one succeeds in drawing near to a virtuous friend, And with a sincere heart listens to and receives the unsurpassed Dharma,
Observing the samādhi of inner and outer emptiness, One will then be able to cross over the ocean of birth and death.
Cultivating and gathering supreme concentration and wisdom, one contemplates that all phenomena are equal, without coming or going.
If one can perceive that there is neither arising nor ceasing, one will immediately attain the clear and lucid eye of tranquility.
Cultivating and gathering the three unsurpassed gates of liberation, Fully endowed with the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
Having already attained for oneself unimpeded wisdom, They are further able to expound it for the sake of all sentient beings.

Entering the first dhyāna and emerging from the cessation samādhi, Entering the cessation samādhi and emerging at will— The Tathāgata’s samādhi has no fixed sequence; Therefore, he is said to be "always in samādhi."
The various samādhis entered by the Tathāgata are no different from the dharma-realm;
the followers of the two vehicles do not know the Buddha’s dwelling place, nor do bodhisattvas know his profound samādhi.
Sentient beings constantly wander in the darkness of ignorance, unaware of the places where the Tathāgata enters and emerges.
The Unsurpassed World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings, has thus proclaimed this seventh karma.

Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata thoroughly knows all the karmas of his own past lives—whether one birth, two births, or up to immeasurable births; whether one calamity, two calamities, or up to immeasurable calamities; whether one kalpa, two kalpas, or up to immeasurable kalpas. He recollects their names, clans, food and drink, physical appearance and form, as well as their suffering, pleasure, and lifespan. He knows that these sentient beings created such karmic causes and thereby obtained these present bodies.
He contemplates that death in one existence leads to birth in another.

Just as with his own self, so it is with others; he also knows the karmic causes possessed by sentient beings, understanding that these various beings create such karmic causes and thereby obtain bodies in other existences.

To know the minds and causal conditions of sentient beings, and how after such a mind has ceased, another mind arises in succession—such matters are beyond the comprehension of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The Buddha’s knowledge of past lives fully knows that throughout the three periods of time there is neither beginning nor end; such wisdom is beyond measure. He exhorts all sentient beings: "You should now reflect upon the good and evil you have experienced in past lives. By the power of the Buddha, you shall be able to recollect them all—the immeasurable roots of goodness planted in the past, whether planted in the presence of a Buddha, or planted in the presence of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"Once he has recollected this, the Tathāgata immediately teaches the Dharma according to their inclinations so that they do not fall back; this is called the eighth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata recollects immeasurable eons, Whether the wholesome or unwholesome karma of himself or others."
He clearly perceives events throughout immeasurable eons, as if gazing at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.
He fully knows their lineage, birth, and names; likewise, he knows their physical form, eons, and the processes of arising and ceasing.
He also knows their lifespans and dwelling places, and similarly, the causes of their wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Knowing the immeasurable sequential minds of the multitude, as well as the causes of their arising and ceasing,
he fully knows their births throughout immeasurable eons, yet his unimpeded wisdom remains inexhaustible.
The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and beyond compare; the followers of the two vehicles do not know its realm.
To cause sentient beings to remember the past, he has proclaimed the eighth karma according to their inclinations.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Tathāgata’s divine eye is pure and subtle; he sees all sentient beings being born, passing away, and falling [into other realms], whether they receive beautiful forms or ugly forms, whether they are born into happy states or miserable states, and he is also able to clearly know the causes of their various karmas."

Knowing that these sentient beings have committed evil through body, speech, and mind, slandering the noble ones and increasing their false views, they will, due to this evil karma, fall directly into hell after casting off this body.

Knowing that these sentient beings have performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, do not slander the noble ones, and have increased their right view, they will, by virtue of these karmic conditions, be reborn in a favorable existence immediately after casting off this body.
The Tathāgata’s divine eye can see the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, which are without boundaries like empty space and without limits like the dharma-realm.

They see all sentient beings as they are born and as they perish; they see all worlds as they form and as they dissolve; they also know when sentient beings give rise to the thought of enlightenment and when that thought ceases; and they see all Buddhas from the moment they first attain perfect enlightenment, through their turning of the wheel of the true Dharma, until their entry into nirvana.
He saw the śrāvakas realizing liberation, and having attained liberation, entering parinirvāṇa;
he saw the pratyekabuddhas, through their supernormal powers, repaying the kindness of sentient beings' offerings of faith.
Such matters as these cannot be seen by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

The Tathāgata’s divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is accomplished with such immeasurable merit that, by means of this divine eye, he observes all sentient beings: who should be converted and delivered by the Buddha, and who, moreover, should be converted and delivered by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

If there are those who are to be delivered by the Buddha, the Tathāgata immediately manifests his body for them, while all other sentient beings see nothing at all; this is called the ninth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Having cultivated wholesome karma throughout immeasurable kalpas, One obtains such a pure divine eye;
It can see all sentient beings in the ten directions, Fully manifesting their forms of both good and evil.”
He beholds all sentient beings—superior, middling, and inferior—and likewise sees them receiving the existence of good and evil;
he is able to know the wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, as well as the various retributions obtained through the causes of such karma.
They also know the spheres of wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
they see the Buddhas of the ten directions destroying the armies of Māra, turning the wheel of the true Dharma, and entering nirvāṇa.
Seeing all the śrāvakas attain liberation, and teaching and transforming sentient beings to bring them to nirvāṇa;
seeing the pratyekabuddhas manifest supernatural powers, thereby repaying the kindness and virtue of their donors.
The true Dharma taught by the Tathāgata—having heard it, one can cross the ocean of birth and death;
yet Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas cannot know the sphere of the Buddha’s vision.
The Tathāgata perceives even the most subtle atoms, And likewise beholds immeasurable and boundless realms;
The Tathāgata teaches and delivers those who are to be saved— Therefore, he proclaims this ninth activity.
"Furthermore, noble son!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, knows that all outflows are exhausted and he is ultimately liberated; 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. "

The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is pure and subtle; "pure" means being free from all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The knowledge of the śrāvakas, however, has limits and measure. Why is this?
Because there are residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the wisdom of the *pratyekabuddha* also has limits. Why is this?
Because there is no great compassion.
The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is immeasurable and boundless. Why is this?

Because they know all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because they have fully accomplished all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and because they have forever severed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they embrace great loving-kindness and great compassion, adorn themselves with the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and do not habitually grasp at signs in any phenomena. They cannot be surpassed by anything in the world, and whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they are free from all faults.

Just as space is pure, clear, and unadulterated by smoke or clouds, so too is the Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna), which is likewise unmixed with any habitual tendencies of affliction (kleśavāsanā).

The Tathāgata has accomplished the pure and complete knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), which he is able to proclaim and expound for the sake of sentient beings, causing those who hear it to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva generates the great armor (*mahā-saṃnāha*) in order to sever afflictions; this is called the tenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is boundless; It is pure and untainted by the habits of affliction.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the residual breath of habitual fetters; Therefore, their knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is not pure.”
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with great compassion; therefore, his wisdom is boundless.
Having fully accomplished all practices, he knows the spheres of the outflows of sentient beings.
That which is expounded as impermanent and non-self, Causes sentient beings to know emptiness and the absence of pleasure;
By practicing wholesome reflection, they attain the pure eye, Knowing there is no sentient being and no person.

Out of great compassion, he takes pity on all sentient beings; endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, his wisdom is unimpeded in severing afflictions; for this reason, he proclaims the tenth activity.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses and accomplishes the deeds of a Tathāgata;
as for the deeds of a Tathāgata, he has thoroughly awakened to and known all dharmas."
Whether it be a deva, a human, a Māra, a Brahmā, a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa, to say truthfully that the Tathāgata does not awaken to or know the Dharma—such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is called the Perfectly Awakened One because he has awakened to the equality of all dharmas.

Whether they be the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of noble ones, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, the dharmas of Buddhas, the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of those beyond training, worldly dharmas, supramundane dharmas, wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, outflowing dharmas, non-outflowing dharmas, conditioned dharmas, or unconditioned dharmas—he has perfectly and equally awakened to such dharmas as these; therefore, he is called the Perfectly Awakened One.
As for "equality," it means the equality of seeing emptiness, because phenomena are truly real;
the equality of signlessness, because all signs are destroyed;
and the equality of wishlessness, because one does not cling to the three realms.
The equality of non-arising, because of the nature of non-arising;
the equality of non-activity, because of the nature of non-activity;
the equality of non-emergence, because of the nature of non-emergence.
The equality of the non-attainment of any destination, because of the nature of having no destination;
the equality of reality, because of the absence of the nature of the three periods of time;
the equality of wisdom and liberation, because of the absence of the nature of ignorance.
Nirvāṇa is equanimous, for it lacks the nature of birth and death;
seeing all such phenomena as entirely equal, the Tathāgata is therefore called the Perfectly Awakened One.

Having observed this, out of great compassion, he proclaims and expounds it for the sake of all sentient beings: those who are not the World-Honored One yet conceive the notion that they are the World-Honored One, those who are not the Perfectly Awakened One yet conceive the notion that they are the Perfectly Awakened One, and those who have not exhausted their outflows yet conceive the notion that they have exhausted their outflows.
“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses and is able to destroy such evil conceptions as these; this is called the eleventh activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Buddha knows that all dharmas are equal, Therefore he is named the All-Knowing One.”
The karmic activities of ordinary beings, sages, bodhisattvas, and buddhas— whether mundane or supramundane, wholesome or unwholesome—
are all seen in their true reality as empty, signless, wishless, and without arising or ceasing.
Because the Tathāgata perceives all things with equanimity, he expounds these eleven types of karma for the sake of the multitudes.
"Furthermore, good son!

The Tathāgata has truly and eternally exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, he declares: 'I have exhausted all outflows. I do not see among humans, devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas anyone who could truthfully say that the Buddha’s outflows are not yet exhausted."
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)?

The Buddha has attained liberation of the mind from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); he has attained liberation of the mind from all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and all outflows of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). For this reason, the Tathāgata is said to have exhausted the outflows.

In the ultimate sense, the noble ones possess true knowledge; there is no awakening, no abandonment, no realization, and no cultivation. It is for the sake of dissemination that it is said, "the outflows are exhausted. Why is this?

That which is exhausted is precisely without arising and without cessation; that which is inexhaustible cannot be proclaimed. Because it cannot be proclaimed, it is named the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); now, that which is unconditioned has no emergence, cessation, or abiding.

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the dharma-nature remains eternally constant. The Tathāgata does not perceive a self nor the cessation of a self; rather, the Tathāgata abides in great loving-kindness and great compassion, and for the sake of sentient beings, proclaims the cessation of the self. This is called the twelfth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has forever severed all outflows and fetters, As well as all boundless habitual tendencies;
Therefore, worldly dharmas cannot defile him, Just as a lotus in the mud remains unstained by water.”
The Great Compassionate Lion-King among Men, for the sake of sentient beings, proclaims and disseminates [the teaching];
he knows with truth that there is neither arising nor cessation, and likewise that there is no self or what belongs to a self.
All phenomena are without increase or decrease; He speaks according to their true nature and characteristics.
The Tathāgata, having attained the power of great mastery, Speaks of the twelve karmas for the sake of the multitudes.
"Furthermore, noble son!

The Tathāgata speaks truthfully regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path; among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, I do not see anyone who can say that these dharmas cannot act as obstructions."
What is meant by "obstructing"?
What is meant by "not obstructing"?
There is one dharma that can obstruct the Path, namely, heedlessness.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
namely, lack of shame and lack of remorse.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
That is to say, the evils of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
namely, desire, hatred, fear, and delusion.
Furthermore, there are five things:
namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.
Furthermore, there are six things:
These are: lack of reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, samādhi, and heedfulness.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas: first, pride;
Second, great pride; third, pride of pride; fourth, false pride;
Fifth, wrong speech; sixth, wrong livelihood;
seventh, wrong mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas:
first, wrong view; second, wrong thought;
Third, wrong speech; fourth, wrong action;
fifth, wrong livelihood;
Sixth, wrong effort; seventh, wrong mindfulness;
eighth, wrong concentration.

Furthermore, there are nine things: namely, when someone intends to commit various evils, whether they are currently committing them or have already done so, and inflict them upon their own kin; or when someone bestows goodness upon their own enemies; or when someone inflicts evil upon themselves—it is the same in each case. These are called the nine.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas, namely the ten unwholesome actions: first, killing;
second, stealing; [and so forth].
Third, sexual misconduct;
fourth, false speech; fifth, divisive speech;
Sixth, harsh speech; seventh, frivolous speech;
eighth, covetousness and envy;
Ninth is ill will; tenth is wrong view.

"If a bhikṣu gives rise to evil thoughts, by reason of these causes and conditions, he does not understand that conditioned phenomena abound in faults. Because he does not understand this, he gives rise to a perverted mind; through the conditions of this perversion, the five hindrances increase."

Because the five hindrances increase, they cause various afflictions to obstruct wholesome dharmas; through the causes and conditions of these afflictions, the actions of body, speech, and mind produce all manner of evils. The Tathāgata knows such dharmas as they truly are to be able to obstruct the Path. Having realized this for himself, he expounds it for the sake of the assembly in order to destroy such obstructive dharmas that hinder the Path. This is called the thirteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one cultivates and accumulates heedlessness, One will truly be unable to attain liberation.
The various evil karmas of body, speech, and mind, And the afflictions of shamelessness and lack of remorse."

Associating with unwholesome dharmas can obstruct the Path; The Great Compassion and Great Benevolence perform thirteen activities, Expounding the antidotes and non-antidotes of right awakening In order to destroy the afflictions.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata truly teaches that the noble path is ultimate.

If there are sentient beings who draw near to right mindfulness, they will certainly attain liberation. Among humans, devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, I do not see anyone who can truthfully declare that one who cultivates the path shall not attain ultimate, unsurpassed liberation."
What is called the true and holy path?
There is one kind, namely the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Furthermore, there are two kinds.
That is to say, śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, there are three kinds: namely, the emptiness samādhi, the signless, and the wishless.
Furthermore, there are four kinds: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are five kinds, namely the five faculties such as faith.
Furthermore, there are six kinds, namely the six foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds, namely the seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely the Eightfold Noble Path.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds, namely the first dhyāna up to the attainment of cessation.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds, namely the ten wholesome actions.
This is called the ultimately true noble path.

Furthermore, as for the ultimate path, it is that which cannot be increased or decreased, nor can anything be grasped or discarded; it is without attachment and without relinquishment; it is neither correct nor deviant, neither one nor two. This is called the truly ultimate path.
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all, has taught such a path for the sake of all sentient beings; this is called the fourteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata fully understands the dharma of tranquility; Those who draw near to him attain liberation."
The Tathāgata, having no teacher and no instructor, spontaneously attained the flavor of the nectar of immortality.
By practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the fetters of affliction are extinguished and liberation is attained.
Contemplating and skillfully knowing the true Dharma, one does not cling to the nature of phenomena; this is true liberation.
The Tathāgata perceives phenomena as being like space, Like illusions, transformations, or mirages in the heat;
Possessing the ten powers and an infinite body, He speaks of the fourteen karmas for the sake of the multitudes.
"Furthermore, noble son!
The bodily karma of the Tathāgata is free from fault; whether they be foolish or wise, none are able to declare that the Buddha has any fault."

Why is this? Whether the Tathāgata walks, sits, or stands; whether he puts on his robes, holds his alms bowl, or receives food and drink; whether he sees, hears, or speaks; or when he enters or leaves cities, villages, or dwellings—his feet do not tread upon the ground, for he always walks upon thousand-petaled lotuses.

If there are sentient beings who encounter the touch of the Buddha’s shadow, they will enjoy peace and happiness for seven days without any desire for food or drink; after casting off this body, they will be reborn in a favorable state of existence.
The Tathāgata’s robes remain four inches away from his body, such that even the most violent and fierce winds cannot move them.
Although the Tathāgata possesses such matters as these, his inner mind has never been anything other than concentrated; therefore, the body of the Tathāgata is free from fault. Good son!
The Tathāgata’s verbal karma is likewise free from fault. Why is this?

Because he speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks reality, speaks correctly, speaks with purpose, speaks meaningfully, does not speak excessively, speaks in accordance with what he maintains, speaks purely, understands all speech, speaks subtly, speaks without contradiction, and speaks with a single voice; therefore, the Tathāgata has no faults in his speech.
The mental karma of the Tathāgata is likewise free from fault.

Why is this? The Tathāgata constantly performs all buddha-activities, yet within his inner mind he is never subject to arrogance; without exerting intellectual deliberation, he knows the Dharma exhaustively. This is called the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom; therefore, the Tathāgata’s mind is free from fault.
"To destroy such faults of sentient beings, he proclaims the Dharma; this is called the fifteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata are tranquil; Therefore, none are able to say he has any fault."
In truth, it cannot be said that this is for the sake of dissemination; this which is neither karma nor non-karma is spoken of as karma.
"Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata does not engage in dispute with devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas."
Why is this? Because they are free from attachment and aversion.

When all the world offers them honor and respect, their minds do not become elated nor do they feel joy; when all the world reviles and treats them with contempt, they do not give rise to sorrow or distress.

Whatever wholesome deeds he performs are never unsuccessful, and he never engages in unwholesome karma. The Tathāgata truly has no worldly disputes; he constantly cultivates and accumulates the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-dispute). The Tathāgata is without self and without what belongs to a self (*anātman* and *anātmīya*). To destroy the disputes and contentions of sentient beings, he teaches such karma; this is called the sixteenth karma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has cultivated and accumulated the concentration of non-contention; Therefore, his mind is free from both anger and joy.
The Tathāgata acts to sever all afflictions; Therefore, he proclaims these sixteen karmas.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The mind of the Tathāgata is free from forgetfulness or error; he does not lose his mindful awareness regarding the eight liberations. He constantly observes the mental activities of all sentient beings, and having observed them, he is able to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Regarding the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge as well, he never loses his mindfulness."

To recollect and never forget throughout the three periods of time, such that one’s own mind of recollection is never lost and one further preaches this dharma of mindfulness for the sake of sentient beings—this is called the seventeenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has cultivated and accumulated the eight liberations; Therefore, regarding all phenomena, he does not lose mindfulness.
Knowing the minds of sentient beings, he speaks according to their inclinations, In order to cause them to attain mindfulness—this is the result of such karma.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata is truly without an unconcentrated mind.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent, he always knows the profound and subtle meaning of all dharmas."
Whether all those in the world have entered meditative concentration or have not entered it, none are able to know the mind of the Tathāgata, except for the Buddhas who borrow his power of the Way.
“Because he wishes to cause all immeasurable sentient beings to always abide in meditative concentration, he speaks of such karma; this is called the eighteenth karma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is always in meditative concentration; In all his deeds, there is no distraction.”
"Constantly entering samādhi, he is without cognition; for this reason, he proclaims the eighteen karmas.
Furthermore, son of good family, the Tathāgata is truly without various perceptions.

That is to say, he has no conceptual discrimination between fields of merit and non-fields of merit, nor does he have conceptual discrimination regarding sentient beings, nor regarding phenomena, nor regarding the thought of perfect enlightenment, nor regarding the dharma-realm."

He does not differentiate between thoughts of upholding the precepts and thoughts of violating them; nor does he differentiate between thoughts of enmity and thoughts of intimacy, or thoughts of receiving and not receiving; nor does he differentiate between thoughts of right view and wrong view. Therefore, the Tathāgata has no manifold perceptions.
"To destroy such conceptions among sentient beings, he proclaims this activity; this is called the nineteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata has forever severed all conceptions; Therefore, he thoroughly understands all dharma-realms."
To shatter the manifold conceptions of sentient beings, He proclaims the nineteen activities of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, noble son, from his wisdom,
the Tathāgata’s mind of relinquishment knows nothing that is not relinquished."

Why is this? Because of the cultivation of the body, the cultivation of morality, the cultivation of the mind, and the cultivation of wisdom; because of the severing of delusion, the Tathāgata’s relinquishment of the mind emerges from the world. This is the noble relinquishment, the ultimate relinquishment, the relinquishment that turns the Brahma-wheel, the relinquishment shared with great compassion, the relinquishment for the benefit of sentient beings, and the relinquishment that knows the remedies.

Such relinquishments as these are without increase or decrease, neither high nor low; they are unmixed with afflictions, neither one nor two; they do not observe temporal conditions, being unimpeded and without counterpart; they do not abide or move, neither hidden nor manifest, and are true and not false.
“The Tathāgata accomplishes such great equanimity (*upekṣā*) and is thus able to preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; this is called the twentieth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata cultivates the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; From wisdom, he cultivates a mind of equanimity.”
Toward all sentient beings, he is free from love and hatred; Unwavering and non-abiding, his equanimity is true.
The Unsurpassed Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, Is fully endowed with such great equanimity.
With unimpeded wisdom, he tames sentient beings And proclaims the twenty pure karmic paths.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The desire-activity of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
What is called 'desire'? "

Desiring to dwell in wholesome dharmas—namely, to preach the Dharma with great kindness and great compassion to deliver beings and establish them in tranquility, and to exhort all bodhisattvas to study the path to enlightenment so that the lineage of the three vehicles may continue without interruption.
Such desires do not arise following after desire, but rather arise following after wisdom.
Because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he expounds the true Dharma; this is called the twenty-first activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s desires neither increase nor decrease; Out of great kindness and great compassion, he preaches the Dharma.
Without ceasing the Three Vehicles, his boundless body Expounds such karma for the sake of the multitudes.”
"Furthermore, good son!
The Tathāgata’s diligence is without rest.
How is it without rest?

Regarding what is called taming sentient beings through preaching the Dharma and transforming them for their deliverance: even if there were a single person who listened to the Dharma from the Buddha for immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata would continue to preach for them without ceasing.
If there is a single Buddha who expounds the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata likewise listens with a mind free from weariness or neglect.

Even if there is a single sentient being to be transformed beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, the Tathāgata will surely follow them without abandoning, without ceasing to eat, without resting, and without giving rise to a mind of fatigue, regret, or retreat; he constantly exhorts sentient beings to be diligent and energetic. This is called the twenty-second activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Lion-King of Men, endowed with diligence, Praised diligence amidst the great assembly;
He preached the Dharma with diligence without ceasing— Therefore, the practice of diligence is the twenty-second."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata’s mind of mindfulness neither increases nor decreases. Why is this?

When the Tathāgata first attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he universally observed the minds of all sentient beings of the past, future, and present; subsequently, when teaching the Dharma, he did not lose his prior mindfulness. He maintained awareness of the original three clusters and the three types of faculties, and in everything he proclaimed, there was nothing done without mindfulness. This is called the twenty-third karma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When the Tathāgata first attained Bodhi, He universally observed the true minds of all sentient beings.
In whatever Dharma he taught, he never lost mindfulness; These twenty-three karmas were spoken by the Buddha."
"Furthermore, noble son!

The Tathāgata’s samādhi is equal toward all phenomena and never diminishes; therefore, all Buddhas are entirely equal. Toward one hundred million kinds of greed, anger, and delusion, as well as one hundred million kinds of non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion, their minds are equal and without distinction. It is likewise with respect to the conditioned and the unconditioned, and birth-and-death and nirvāṇa."

Possessing such samādhis of equality as these, one is not confused by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; the four great elements and the three realms are neither this nor that, and are neither all things, nor increasing, nor decreasing.
"To cause sentient beings to attain this samādhi, he proclaims the True Dharma; this is called the twenty-fourth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata contemplates all dharmas with equanimity; Therefore, his mind is always in samādhi, free from distraction."
Not encompassed by the three realms, so too are the sense faculties and the four great elements.
All phenomena are without distinction; one observes the wholesome and the unwholesome with equanimity.
Such is the karma taught by the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings attaining this samādhi.
"Furthermore, good son! The wisdom of the Tathāgata is eternally without decrease.
By means of this power of wisdom, he knows all dharmas and is able to preach the Dharma in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings."

Attaining unimpeded wisdom, one knows all meanings, knows all syllables, and knows all phrases; throughout immeasurable eons, one may expound upon a single phrase of the Dharma, producing immeasurable meanings to sever all doubts, preaching the teachings of the Three Vehicles as well as the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, and also expounding the eighty-four thousand clusters of dharmas—this is called immeasurable and boundless wisdom.
"In order to cause sentient beings to attain this wisdom, he proclaims the True Dharma; this is called the twenty-fifth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is unimpeded and boundless, Able to proclaim unimpeded and boundless teachings."
Expounding a single syllable as immeasurable phrases, and expounding a single phrase as immeasurable meanings;
proclaiming the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, as well as that many collections of dharmas,
in order to cause sentient beings to attain unimpeded wisdom— for this reason, such activities are proclaimed.
"Furthermore, good son! The liberation of the Tathāgata is without deficiency.
The śrāvaka attains liberation by hearing from others; [the Tathāgata does not]."
Pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through causes and conditions;

the Tathāgata, however, is self-awakened without a teacher, having forever severed both afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). He does not continue with the past, does not cling to the future, and does not dwell in the present. Furthermore, he does not crave or adhere to the two dharmas of the eye and forms, and it is the same for everything up to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*).
Knowing that the nature of the mind is pure, the Tathāgata proclaims that he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single thought-moment.
In order to cause sentient beings to likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single thought-moment, he expounds the True Dharma; this is called the twenty-sixth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

“For the sake of the śrāvakas who hear and attain liberation, And for the sake of the pratyekabuddhas who awaken through causes and conditions, The Tathāgata’s liberation does not dwell in attachment;
It does not dwell in the three periods of time, for the nature of the mind is pure.”
Whatever he expounds is for the sake of liberation, exhorting all sentient beings toward the unsurpassed path;
because the twenty-six karmas are neither karma nor non-karma, he dwells in great kindness and great compassion to preach among the multitudes.
"Furthermore, good son! The physical actions (*kāyakarman*) of the Tathāgata proceed in accordance with wisdom and are encompassed by wisdom.

By virtue of these actions, sentient beings—whether hearing or seeing him preaching the Dharma or remaining silent, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating or drinking, or entering and leaving cities, towns, and villages—are all brought to subdual through his thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
Therefore, all the bodily actions of the Tathāgata proceed in accordance with wisdom; this is called the twenty-seventh activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The bodily actions of the Tathāgata are for the sake of sentient beings; Thus he manifests various kinds of wondrous marks and signs.”
"Whatever actions he performs to harmonize and guide sentient beings, he teaches these deeds out of great compassion.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
the Tathāgata’s verbal karma proceeds in accordance with wisdom."
Why is this? Because the teaching of the Dharma is pure; because it is free from error or omission;
because it is speech that is authentic, easy to understand, easy to comprehend, neither lofty nor base, neither crooked nor coarse, and not evil.
Speech that is not obscure, gentle speech, not frivolous speech, not hurried speech, not fearful speech,
not speech whose meaning is unintelligible, not speech with harsh sounds, not slow speech, ambrosial speech, lovely speech,
sequential speech, adorned speech, respectful speech, and speech that is pleasant to hear.
...speech free from greed, speech free from defilement, pure speech, ultimate speech, non-deceptive speech,
non-deluded speech, unimpeded speech, expansive speech, truthful speech, non-artificial speech, inexhaustible speech,
speech of peace and happiness, speech of tranquility of body, speech of tranquility of mind, and speech of tranquility of craving...
Speech that is tranquil; speech that pacifies anger; speech that pacifies delusion; speech that destroys Māra; speech that refutes heterodox arguments; the voice of Brahmā;
the voice of the kalaviṅka bird; the voice of Śakra; the voice of the great ocean tide; the voice of the kroñca crane;
the voice of the peacock in autumn; the voice of the kokila; the voice of the jīvajīvaka bird.
The voice of the king of geese, the voice of the king of deer, the sound of the lute, the sound of the drum, the sound of the conch, the sound of musical instruments,
the voice pleasant for humans to hear, and the sound pleasing to the faculty of hearing; speech that increases wholesome dharmas, inexhaustible speech regarding the meaning of phrases,
speech that accords with the meaning of syllables and phrases, timely speech, concise speech, speech on contentment, and the disciplining of the sense faculties.
Speech that is adorned by generosity; speech of pure ethical discipline; speech accompanied by the practice of patience;
speech endowed with diligence and supernormal powers; speech that is detached from the desire realm; speech possessed of wisdom; speech of loving-kindness and compassion;

speech of sympathetic joy and equanimity; speech that expounds the three vehicles; speech that ensures the non-interruption of the Three Jewels; and speech that understands the three categories of beings.

...understanding the discourse on the three periods of time, understanding the discourse on the three liberations, discerning the discourse on the four truths, the discourse on cultivation and accumulation,
the discourse of praise, the discourse of the Buddha, the discourse of the noble ones, the discourse of the boundless, and the discourse of non-action.

"Good son! The Tathāgata accomplishes such speech as this; therefore, all the verbal karma of the Tathāgata proceeds in accordance with wisdom. This is called the twenty-eighth karma of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"What the Tathāgata speaks is like a pure jewel, Accomplishing immeasurable merits;
His voice pervades the realms of the ten directions, And with a single sound, he enables various understandings."
In all that he expounds, he forms no thought, nor does he further observe the mental realms of others;
the Tathāgata’s voice is like an echo, and so too are non-speaking and non-hearing.
With great kindness and great compassion, his speech is pure; for the sake of sentient beings, he explains various dharmas.
Therefore, he proclaims the deeds of the Tathāgata—twenty-eight deeds, just as those of the Buddhas of the past.
"Furthermore, noble son, the mental karma of the Tathāgata proceeds in accordance with wisdom. Why is this?

The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the mind, intellect, and consciousness of all sentient beings, yet he does not follow their whims, conditions, greed, anger, or delusion. He is far removed from deception, the notions of "I" and "mine," and the dark obscuration of ignorance; he is equal, pure, and boundless, like space. Therefore, the mental karma cultivated by the Tathāgata proceeds in accordance with wisdom; this is called the twenty-ninth karma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The mind of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, Like lifting Mount Sumeru with a single hair;
Constantly observing the objects of sentient beings' minds, He remains far removed from the realms of Māras and afflictions."

The Elephant-King among Men has explained wholesome karma; To destroy the various evils of sentient beings, And to purify the body, speech, and mind of sentient beings, These twenty-nine types of karma have now been explained.
"Furthermore, good son!
The Tathāgata’s wisdom knows the past; that wisdom is unimpeded and without obstruction.
What is meant by this wisdom?

He knows the past Buddhas, immeasurable and innumerable, as well as the number of all grasses, trees, and sentient beings in their worlds; he also knows the various sounds that were the objects of their minds, and how much Dharma those Buddhas taught. He knows how many sentient beings attained the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. Furthermore, he knows the lifespans—long or short—of those Buddhas and their worlds, the number and variety of their names, their breathing and eating, and the realms of their faculties, the realm of their minds, the realm of phenomena, the realm of their consciousness, and the realm of their activities. He understands, in accordance with reality, the successive arising and ceasing, the appearing and disappearing, of their minds.
"Knowing their number is not known through inferential knowledge; this is called the thirtieth activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is unimpeded and unobstructed; Therefore, he is able to know all immeasurable lands."
He fully understands all the deeds of the Buddhas, as well as the faculties of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.
This Lion among Men knows the past as clearly as if he were looking at an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of his hand.
The One of Boundless Body speaks of the thirty karmas in order to cause sentient beings to know the world of the past.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata’s wisdom knows the future world; that wisdom is unimpeded and without obstruction.
What is this wisdom? It is as follows:"
He knows the future, whether things arise or perish, and the number of kalpas in which all worlds will be destroyed by water, fire, or wind, as well as the cycles of their formation and destruction.
He knows how many Buddha-worlds there are, how many Buddhas appear in the world, and how many atoms exist within those worlds.

He also knows how many śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas there are; he further knows how many times those Buddhas eat, breathe, walk, stand, sit, and lie down. He knows how many people attain the liberation of a śrāvaka, how many attain the liberation of a pratyekabuddha, and how many attain the liberation of a perfectly enlightened one (samyaksaṃbuddha). He also clearly understands how many sentient beings successively give rise to thoughts and successively extinguish thoughts as they cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
To clearly and fully know such matters as these, which is not through inferential knowledge, is called the thirty-first activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the future world, And the arising and ceasing of all phenomena.
Knowing the Buddha-worlds and the Buddhas, as well as the successive arising and ceasing of the minds of all beings,
and having gained such knowledge, being free from pride— this is called the thirty-first Tathāgata-activity.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata’s wisdom knows the present age; that wisdom is unimpeded and without obstruction.
What is this wisdom?

The Tathāgata fully knows the number of Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas currently in the worlds of the ten directions; he knows the suns, moons, and stars; the grasses, trees, and atoms of dust; the drops in the four great oceans of earth, water, fire, and wind; and the various forms, colors, and characteristics of sentient beings, as well as the successive arising and ceasing, appearing and disappearing of their minds and thoughts. He also knows the present karmic retributions of those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts—including for how long they will remain in the world and when they will attain liberation;
he likewise knows the causes and conditions of karma and its fruits for humans and devas—including for how long they will remain in the world and when they will attain liberation.
Furthermore, he knows the realm of afflictions, the realms of the various faculties, the mind-realm, and the dharma-realm.
Although the Tathāgata possesses various kinds of knowledge, he does not give rise to pride, nor does his mouth utter two-fold speech; this is called the thirty-second activity of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Tathāgata is inconceivable; No one knows the objective realm of the Buddha’s perception.
That which the Tathāgata knows is like space— Immeasurable, ineffable, and boundless."
The subtle and supreme ultimate truth that has been taught— so that sentient beings may attain this karma—
the one who possesses mastery over dhāraṇī asks the Buddha, and the Unsurpassed World-Honored One answers according to his wish.
“Good son! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, being fully endowed with these thirty-two karmas, is able to subdue immeasurable sentient beings. Good son!”
"Although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks of these various karmas for the sake of sentient beings, the karma of the Tathāgata is truly immeasurable and beyond calculation. Good son!"
Regarding the deeds of the Tathāgata, all sentient beings in the entire world are unable to conceive of them, unable to comprehend them, and unable to proclaim them.
Such deeds enable him to know all lands as being equal to empty space.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the ten directions are entirely equal. Good son!

As taught by all Buddhas, when observing sentient beings and Buddha-worlds, liberation and nirvana are without distinction; having perceived that the Dharma-realm is of a single flavor, the Buddha turns the irreversible wheel of the True Dharma.

“Good son! It is like a skilled artisan who knows genuine jewels, who obtains a single gem from among the mountains of treasure. Having treated it with water and removed it from the water, he places it in fermented rice gruel; having removed it from the rice gruel, he places it in bean broth, yet his mind is still not satisfied. He then places it in bitter vinegar; having removed it from the vinegar, he places it in various medicinal herbs. Having removed it from the herbs, he polishes it with felt wool. This is called a genuine blue lapis lazuli gem.”
Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise;
because he knows that the realm of sentient beings is not luminously pure, he teaches impermanence, suffering, and impurity in order to destroy the mind that craves the pleasures of birth and death.

The Tathāgata’s diligence never ceases, and he further expounds upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) so that they may understand the True Dharma of the Buddha.

The Tathāgata’s diligence still does not rest, and he further preaches the Dharma so that they do not retreat from the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), knowing that the dharmas of the three periods of time constitute the path to enlightenment; this is called the great jewel, the auspicious field of merit.
Therefore, you should know that the various karmas of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, immeasurable, and ineffable. The Tathāgata is endowed with thirty-two karmas;

although he knows his own body to be like empty space, he manifests his body within the world and likewise proclaims the ineffable Dharma. He has forever severed all causes and conditions of the mind, fully knows the mental realms of all sentient beings, and also knows the spheres of all bodhisattvas.
“Good son! The true activity of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is that he never severs the bodhisattva’s prediction of enlightenment; this is called the true activity of the Tathāgata.”

At that time, as the World-Honored One was speaking of this karma, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, a great light shone everywhere, and immeasurable, boundless fragrant flowers rained down.

All the great assemblies of devas and humans, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans present in this monastery, having heard of the Tathāgata’s deeds, rejoiced greatly in their hearts; they further made offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of incense, flowers, music, precious banners, flags, canopies, and other articles of worship.

Among them, some offered to the Tathāgata crests of *cūḍāmaṇi* jewels, jeweled hair, bracelets, various gems, necklaces, sun-jewels, moon-jewels, signet rings, pearl belts, jeweled pendants, and hair ornaments; others offered earrings.
That is to say: blue lapis lazuli, lotus-gem, garuḍa-gem, jambū-river gem, Śakra-gem, fire-gem, light-gem, immeasurable-light gem, immeasurable-color gem, soft-pure gem, diamond-gem, and white pearl.
Furthermore, there were various fragrances, namely powdered incense, sandalwood incense mixed with golden sand, tagara incense, aloeswood, and mikaradamarapa incense.
Furthermore, they scattered various flowers, namely: *māndārava* flowers,
*mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, *kovidāra* flowers, *pārijātaka* flowers,
*nandana* flowers, *sāla* flowers, *mahāsāla* flowers, and hundred-petaled flowers.
The *chattrā* flower, the *prapattrā* flower, the *mahāprabha* flower, the *gandhapattrā* flower, the *sugandhā* flower,
the *priyadarśanā* flower, the *anantavarṇā* flower, the *aniyatavarṇā* flower, the water-born flowers— namely the *utpala*,
the *padma*, the *kumuda*, and the *puṇḍarīka*— and the land-born flowers.
Flowers, *pāriyātraka* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *sumanā* flowers,
*kunduru* flowers, *tānḍulīya* flowers, *atimuktaka* flowers, *campaka* flowers, and *aśoka* flowers.

With various kinds of music, banners, and canopies, the bodhisattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions each ascended into the sky above the precious pavilion and cast their bodies down as an offering to the Buddha. Once they had cast themselves down and scattered [the offerings], their bodies disappeared; instead, nets of the seven treasures appeared, covering everything above. Then, their bodies reappeared within those pearl nets.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions each sent a pārijāta tree to offer as an act of worship to Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
By the power of the Buddha, each of these trees arrived at the jeweled monastery and adorned that place.

At that time, immeasurable sentient beings within the assembly resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Three;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty at Guzang.
Chapter Two, Part Four: The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned his entire body to look upon the great assembly, like an elephant king turning its head, and spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!

Who can protect these offering implements and this jeweled monastery so that they are not destroyed, lost, or diminished, but remain until Maitreya has attained perfect enlightenment, and sixteen years later, may they be used to make offerings to that Buddha and the five hundred Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa?

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sovereign King of the Supernatural Powers of All Dharmas. He rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

I am able to protect these offerings and this jeweled monastery, ensuring they are not destroyed, lost, or diminished, so that after Maitreya has attained perfect enlightenment, I may offer them to that Buddha and to the five hundred Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa sixteen years later.
At that time, there was a Māra in the assembly named Abhijñā (Supernatural Power), whose realm was called the Four Continents. He spoke to the Bodhisattva Dharmābhijñā-vaiśāradyarāja, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Now that you have prepared these offerings as well as the jeweled pavilion, in what kind of vessel will you place them to guard and protect them so that they do not perish? "O Noble Son!"
Generally speaking, that which is called a "vessel" is by nature impermanent, whereas this body of mine is eternally abiding and unchanging. Good son!
You should now carefully contemplate my body.

At that time, having heard these words, the Māra-king contemplated as instructed and saw within his navel a world named Water-King Radiance; therein was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Jewel-Utpala, and in that world there was a great mountain of jewels.
The Tathāgata sat cross-legged in the center, proclaiming the True Dharma to the various bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Māra King, having witnessed this event, was filled with great wonder and immediately prostrated before the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas and Spiritual Powers, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Great Being!
Only now do I realize that you possess a sublime vessel, capable of protecting and upholding such offerings and this jeweled monastery so that they shall not perish.
At that time, the Māra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When I had not yet seen such bodhisattvas nor heard such subtle and wondrous Dharma, I desired to train as a śrāvaka and enter nirvāṇa.”

Having now witnessed the power of the spiritual penetrations and the majestic authority of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Dharmas, I have immediately resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"World-Honored One!

Even if my body were to undergo the sufferings of the hells for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, and only thereafter were I to attain the Unsurpassed Way, I would never abandon the Bodhicitta."
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
“You have been able to skillfully resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; you, too, shall attain such immeasurable power of supernatural faculties.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly named Siṃhadhvaja, who addressed the bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, saying: “Good son!

By obtaining what kind of dhāraṇī-gates do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enable themselves to receive and uphold all the words of the Buddhas, such that whatever syllables, phrases, and meanings they expound are inexhaustible?
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja said: "Good son! There are eight dhāraṇīs;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains them, he will be able to receive and uphold all the words of the Buddhas, and whatever syllables, phrases, and meanings he expounds will be inexhaustible."
What are the eight?
First, the dhāraṇī of the radiance of pure sound;
second, the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible vessel;
Third, the Dharani of the Immeasurable Limit;
fourth, the Dharani of the Great Ocean;
fifth, the Dharani of the Lotus;
Sixth, the dhāraṇī of entering the gate of non-obstruction;
seventh, the dhāraṇī of the four types of unimpeded knowledge;
eighth, the dhāraṇī of the Buddha’s ornaments and necklaces—these are called the eight.

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in these eight dhāraṇīs, they will be able to receive and uphold all the words of the Buddhas; whatever syllables, phrases, and meanings they expound shall be inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhadhvaja said: "Excellent, Great Being!"
"I only pray that you will explain this extensively; having heard it, the bodhisattvas shall be able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja said:
"O son of good family!"
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you.

Regarding the *Dhāraṇī of the Radiance of Pure Sound*, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains it, they will be able to fully accomplish immeasurable merit in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas and attain purity of the four great elements; by these causes and conditions, their voice becomes subtle and exquisite.

When he proclaims the Dharma, his voice pervades one Buddha-world, two Buddha-worlds, five Buddha-worlds, ten Buddha-worlds, twenty Buddha-worlds, thirty Buddha-worlds, forty Buddha-worlds, fifty Buddha-worlds, a hundred Buddha-worlds, a thousand Buddha-worlds, ten thousand Buddha-worlds, and even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds—beyond all measure and calculation—and wherever the Dharma is preached, it is heard everywhere.

"When he preaches the Dharma, whether he sits upon a lion throne as his Dharma seat for one yojana, or like Mount Sumeru, or in a place like the Brahma realm—sitting in such a location—if there are immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Way, he hears them all universally, receives and upholds them without forgetting, and skillfully understands their words, phrases, and their underlying meanings."
"When preaching the Dharma oneself and when listening to the Buddha preach, there is no obstruction in either of these two matters.
Within a single syllable, one preaches all dharmas; that which is called a single syllable is 'A'."
"A" is the beginning of all letters. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva utters the letter "A," they are able to expound upon all dharmas.

"A" signifies non-existence. That which is non-existent means that all dharmas have no root; all dharmas have no birth; all dharmas have no beginning; all dharmas have no end; all dharmas are inexhaustible; all dharmas have no agency; all dharmas have no coming; all dharmas have no going; all dharmas have no abiding; all dharmas have no intrinsic nature; all dharmas have no emergence; all dharmas have no activity; all dharmas have no increase; all dharmas have no height; all dharmas have no decrease; all dharmas have no master; all dharmas have no utility;
all dharmas have no aspiration. All dharmas are free from conceptual proliferation and lack both vitarka and vicāra; they are without speaking, without listening, without location, and without entry.
All phenomena are without self and without sentient beings; they are without purity, without life-force, without name, without master, without a person (*puruṣa*);
they are without interior, without exterior, impermanent, signless, incalculable, immeasurable, unconditioned, traceless, phraseless, letterless, and unimpeded.
Common, not following others, not following oneself, without grasping, without releasing, without taking up, without discarding,
without number, without body, without purity, without defilement, without transition, without change, without sensation, without sound,
without characteristic, without fetter, without stain, without madness, and without outflow.
...non-existent, unrestrained, unobscured, non-turbid, non-obstructive, formless, without sensation, without perception,
without mental formations, without consciousness, without cause, without fruit, without aggregates, bases, or elements, without causal conditions,
without objective spheres, without feeling, without desire, without form, and without the formless;
It is without guidance, without black, without white, without dregs, without thought, without time, without refuge,
without purity, without mixture, without burning, without practice, without house, without support,
without movement, without abiding, without solidity, without fragility, without visibility, and without tangibility.
...neither light nor darkness, neither crookedness nor fault, neither reality nor unreality,
neither delusion nor contemplation, neither seeing nor cultivation, neither seeing nor hearing, neither cognition nor wisdom,
neither contact nor consciousness.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this Pure Sound Radiance Dhāraṇī, they explain all dharmas within this single syllable.”
Within this single syllable, the Bodhisattva expounds immeasurable meanings without error, neither violating the Dharma-realm nor losing the meaning of the words.

Once the Bodhisattva has attained this dhāraṇī, their body, speech, and mind are purified; their every movement and gesture is such that sentient beings delight in beholding them—this is called purity of body.
Whatever he expounds, sentient beings delight in hearing; this is called purity of speech.
Cultivating and gathering the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—this is called purity of mind.
Once a bodhisattva has attained this dhāraṇī, he is able to purify the two kinds of giving: material giving and the giving of the Dharma.
They are able to purify their precepts, giving rise to no ill will upon seeing those who violate them;
they are able to purify their patience, giving rise to no anger or vexation upon seeing sentient beings being harmed;
they are able to purify their diligence, practicing wholesome dharmas without rest.
It can purify meditative concentration by destroying arrogance;
it can purify wisdom by eliminating ignorance;
it can purify karma by destroying evil causes.
It can purify the eye, because one attains the three eyes;
it can purify the ear, because one obtains the divine ear to hear the voice of the Buddha;
it can purify the nose, because one smells the fragrance of the pure precepts of all Buddhas.
It can purify the mouth, because one does not crave or cling to the taste of ambrosia;
it can purify the body, because one attains the transformation body;
it can purify the mind, because of skillful reflection.
It can purify form, by means of the thirty-two marks;
it can purify sound, by means of preaching the sublime Dharma;
it can purify fragrance, by means of attaining purity through precepts, learning, and giving.
They are able to purify tastes, because they attain the unsurpassed taste;
they are able to purify tangibles, because they cultivate and accumulate the unsurpassed samādhis;
they are able to purify phenomena, because they contemplate the dharma-realm as being without discrimination.
He is able to purify mindfulness, because he does not forget or lose the Dharma as it was heard;
he is able to purify the mind, because he is never bound to the factions of Māra;
he is able to purify conduct, because he contemplates the profoundly deep realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
“Good son! Once a bodhisattva abides in this dhāraṇī, wherever the sound of their speech reaches, the radiance of their body likewise illuminates that place.”
"Good son! This dhāraṇī accomplishes such immeasurable merit.

As for the 'Inexhaustible Vessel Dhāraṇī,' once a bodhisattva abides in this dhāraṇī, they can speak of the impermanence of form without end; they can speak of the suffering of form without end; they can speak of the selflessness of form, and speak of form as being like foam, like an illusion, like the moon in water, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, or like a flame, all without end."

To speak of the absence of intrinsic nature in form is inexhaustible; to speak of form as being without marks, ineffable, beyond aspiration, unconditioned, neither arising nor ceasing, belonging neither to the past, future, nor present; neither internal nor external; neither pure nor defiled; neither self nor what belongs to a self; neither going nor coming; neither opposed nor obstructed; and neither one nor two.

It is not a sentient being, nor is it a life-span, nor is it a person; it is not greed, hatred, or delusion; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither with outflows nor without outflows; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is not blind, not deaf, not lame, not crippled, not insane, and not deranged; it is not grass, wood, or stone; it is not a tree, not earth, not water, fire, or wind; it is not a house, not a dwelling, not a city, not a walled town, not a great village, not a mountain; it is not round, not square; it is not composed of the four great elements; it is not an agent, not a recipient, not sound, not hearing, and it is not something that can be described.

The twelve links of dependent origination are inexhaustible; they are neither eternal nor annihilated, without karma and without fruit, not the aggregates, bases, or elements; they do not abide in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they are neither identical nor different; furthermore, they are neither affliction, nor purity, nor defilement, nor level, nor crooked. Thus does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speak of the inexhaustibility of form.
"Good son! This *Akṣayakaraṇḍa* dhāraṇī has immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable divisions.
If one were to divide even a single portion of it into a thousand parts, I could not exhaustively explain even one of those thousand parts."

"Regarding the 'Dhāraṇī of the Immeasurable Limit' (*apramāṇakoṭi*): the 'limit' (*koṭi*) refers to the view of eternalism and the view of nihilism; the 'immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*) refers to the twelve links of dependent origination.
