The 'limit' refers to the accumulation of all suffering from ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, up to old age and death; furthermore, the 'immeasurable' refers to birth and death."

Furthermore, "limit" (koṭi) refers to that which has neither beginning nor end; furthermore, "limit" refers to that which is without grasping or abandoning; furthermore, "limit" refers to that which is without arising or ceasing; furthermore, "limit" refers to that which is neither defiled nor pure, because its nature is pure; furthermore, "limit" is what is called the visible; furthermore, "limit" is what is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa); furthermore, "limit" refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.

Furthermore, as for the "limit" (koṭi), it refers to the karmic fruits of the internal and external actions of the three periods of time; the absence of karma and the absence of fruit; the wholesome and the unwholesome; outflowing and non-outflowing karma and afflictions; self and non-self; birth-and-death and nirvana.
“Good son! That which is immeasurable refers to motes of dust; that which is the limit refers to earth, water, fire, and wind. This is called the ‘Dhāraṇī of the Immeasurable Limit.’”

Once a bodhisattva abides in this dhāraṇī, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas; yet the words, phrases, meanings, and flavors of what they teach can never be exhausted. This dhāraṇī accomplishes such immeasurable merit and virtue.
“Regarding the Great Ocean Dhāraṇī, son of good family:

it is just like the great ocean, wherein all forms existing within the four continents—sentient beings, herbs, trees, medicinal plants, and seeds of grain; the sun, moon, stars, clouds, mists, thunder, and lightning; and kingdoms, towns, villages, cities, palaces, gardens, ponds, mountains, and rivers—all such various kinds of forms appear therein.”

When a bodhisattva dwells in this dhāraṇī, it is likewise so: the physical, verbal, and mental actions of all sentient beings each appear as individual seals within the body of this bodhisattva; and all the verbal actions of all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions are entirely manifested as seals within the mouth of this bodhisattva. Therefore, whatever the bodhisattva speaks is entirely true.

The seal is called "non-existence," meaning that all phenomena are without applied or sustained thought, without speech, without limit, without action, and without craving; this is called the foremost meaning of ultimate reality.
"Furthermore, there is the seal of 'Ccha' (遮). 'Ccha' signifies 'eye'; the eye is impermanent, yet it can be purified and seen.
Furthermore, there is the seal of 'Na' (那). 'Na' signifies 'name'; all dharmas are so called because they are disseminated, yet in reality, they are nameless."
Furthermore, there is the seal of *lo*; "lo" signifies "world," for all worlds are subject to craving and ignorance.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *da*; "da" signifies "ten," for the Buddha possesses the ten powers and is able to transform sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the *pa* seal; "pa" signifies five. The Tathāgata distanced himself from and extinguished the five desires, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there is the Seal of Killing; "killing" refers to the six. Because the Tathāgata truly and fully understands the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), he is able to subdue all sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is the Seal of Killing; "killing" refers to the six. Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the six foundations of mindfulness (*ṣaṭsmṛtyupasthāna*), he attains great sovereignty.

Furthermore, there is the seal of "killing" (sa); "killing" signifies "six. Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), he is able to teach and transform sentient beings through these powers.
Furthermore, there is the seal of "va"; "va" signifies "left. Because the World-Honored Tathāgata has departed from the left-hand path (vāmamārga), he has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, there is the "Mu-in" (Many Seal); "many" signifies reality. Because the Tathāgata perfectly awakens to the nature of reality, he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
Furthermore, there is the "Ya-in" (Other Seal); "other" signifies "that. The Tathāgata knows that this and that are equal.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *bha*; "bha" means "bondage. Because the Tathāgata has distanced himself from all afflictions (*kleśa*), he is named *Ariha*.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *ja*; "ja" refers to birth and old age. Because the Tathāgata has already transcended the realm of birth and old age, he is named the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
Furthermore, there is the seal of *dharma*; *dharma* means "phenomenon" (or "teaching"), signifying that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is pure and stainless.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *śamatha*; *śamatha* means "calm abiding," signifying that the Tathāgata has perfected the cultivation of *śamatha*.
Furthermore, there is the Kha-mudrā; "Kha" means space (*ākāśa*). The Tathāgata knows and perceives that all phenomena are identical to space.
Furthermore, there is the Ka-mudrā; "Ka" signifies asceticism (*kaṣṭa-caryā*). The Tathāgata has distanced himself from all ascetic practices.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *bha*; "bha" signifies reality (*satya*). That which the Tathāgata has taught as the Four Noble Truths is precisely this reality.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *ma*; "ma" signifies the path (*mārga*). The Tathāgata is able to teach the Eightfold Noble Path.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *gā*; "gā" signifies "profound," for the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught is exceedingly profound.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *kṣānti*; "kṣānti" signifies "patience," for the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, there is the *hu* seal; *hu* means to praise, for the Tathāgata constantly praises all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, there is the *ruo* seal; *ruo* means universal knowledge (*sarvajña*), and for this reason the Tathāgata is named "All-Knowing One."
Furthermore, there is the seal of *bha*; *bha* signifies existence (*bhava*), for the Tathāgata has already understood all forms of existence.
Furthermore, there is the seal of *tha*; *tha* signifies desire (*chanda*), for the Tathāgata desires all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the *pa* seal; *pa* means "before," for the Tathāgata constantly teaches the Dharma in the presence of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the *pha* seal; *pha* means "fruit," for the Tathāgata constantly speaks of the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
“Good son! By means of such letters, all dharmas are expounded; all these letters are manifested as seals within the vocal karma of the bodhisattva. This is called the Great Ocean Dhāraṇī.”

"As for the Lotus Dhāraṇī, once a bodhisattva abides in this dhāraṇī, wherever they preach the Dharma, pure and wondrous lotus flowers made of the seven treasures constantly emerge to serve as their Dharma seat; seated upon them, the bodhisattva proclaims the Dharma to transform sentient beings."

Furthermore, immeasurable lotus flowers rained down in abundance; these lotus flowers also produced various sounds of the pure Dharma—sounds that were profound and vast, containing many metaphors, the sounds of the twelve divisions of scripture, the sound of purity, and the sound of severing afflictions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva remained silent; yet all these lotus flowers were able to expound the Dharma and emit various immeasurable rays of light. All sentient beings saw the Bodhisattva seated upon the flower pedestals performing the work of a Buddha; this is called the Lotus Dhāraṇī.

"Regarding the 'Dhāraṇī of Entering the Unobstructed Gate,' when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaks of one dharma, there is no obstruction; likewise, when speaking of two dharmas, three dharmas, four dharmas, or even up to hundreds of thousands, immeasurable, boundless, and Ganges-sand-like dharmas—dharmas as numerous as the atoms within the four continents, or the atoms within a trichiliocosm, or even the atoms within Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—there is likewise no obstruction regarding their syllables, phrases, or meanings. This is called the Dhāraṇī of Entering the Unobstructed Gate."

"The dhāraṇī of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge consists of: the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), the unimpeded knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid)."
In the immeasurable worlds of the east, for those sentient beings who inquire about the Dharma, the Bodhisattva responds accordingly with unimpeded knowledge of the Dharma;
in the immeasurable worlds of the south, for those sentient beings who inquire about the meaning, the Bodhisattva responds accordingly with unimpeded knowledge of the meaning;
in the immeasurable worlds of the west, for those sentient beings who inquire about the phrasing, the Bodhisattva responds accordingly with unimpeded knowledge of expression.
When sentient beings in immeasurable worlds to the north ask questions of one who delights in eloquent exposition, the bodhisattva responds accordingly with the wisdom of eloquence;
this is called the dhāraṇī of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.

"Regarding the 'Buddha-Necklace Adornment Dhāraṇī,' if there is a bodhisattva who attains these seven dhāraṇīs, an image of the Buddha will appear upon the crown of his head; it will be the color of pure gold, emitting great radiance, and endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics."
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body, speech, and mind all perform the deeds of a Buddha, and his thoughts are identical to those of a Buddha.
Having perfected such Buddha-deeds, the Bodhisattva is able to know the various minds of the great assembly; having known them, he preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations.

Whether for one day, two days, or even for immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of years, one could not exhaustively fathom the words, phrases, and meanings of the Dharma-gates known by him.
"Furthermore, they are fully endowed with four kinds of wisdom. What are these four?
First, knowing the minds of sentient beings;..."
Second, knowing all syllables and phrases;
third, knowing that what is taught is inexhaustible;
fourth, knowing the ultimate reality.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four kinds of wisdom, they are able to discipline sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! This is called the Buddha’s Garland Ornament Dharani.

“Good son! These eight dhāraṇīs have immeasurable divisions; within these divisions, one division is further divided into a thousand parts, yet even if one were to speak of only one of those parts, one could not exhaustively describe them. Such are the immeasurable merits accomplished by these dhāraṇīs.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja spoke these verses:

“The Tathāgata has taught eight dhāraṇīs; if a bodhisattva fully attains them, they will be able to understand the various meanings of all sūtras, and their words, phrases, and meanings will be inexhaustible.”
Endowed with virtuous karma, one attains a sublime voice, Which enables immeasurable worlds to hear;
Having heard it, sentient beings cultivate wholesome dharmas, And having cultivated them, they attain liberation.
Throughout immeasurable eons he speaks of the non-existent dharma; Based on the root of a single dharma, he speaks inexhaustibly;
He also understands manifold meanings through a single syllable— This is called the Tathāgata’s retention of the ultimate limit.
The Bull-King among Men has severed the two extremes; he teaches the meaning of the Middle Way, which is boundless.
Possessing perfect wisdom, he observes with equanimity; though he maintains this, there is no one who attains it.
The colors and forms of the four directions appear as a great ocean; All seals of syllables seal the Bodhisattva.
When preaching the Dharma, there is no obstruction; One accomplishes the dharani of the great ocean.
Seated upon a precious lotus flower, he expounds the Dharma; He also rains down lotus flowers, scattering them among the great assembly.
The lotus flowers also proclaim immeasurable teachings; This is called the "Holding of the Tranquil Lotus."
He speaks a single syllable without obstruction, and likewise does so among immeasurable syllables;
he explains immeasurable meanings without impediment, fully possessing such unimpeded retention.
The profound meaning of the Dharma they preach is inexhaustible; their eloquence and skillful exposition are boundless.
They are able to shatter the net of doubt within the minds of sentient beings and attain the dhāraṇī of supreme wisdom.
From his topknot, images of the Tathāgata constantly emerge; in body, speech, and mental action, he is no different from the Buddha.
One who possesses these eight dhāraṇīs cannot be fully praised even throughout kalpas;
endowed with these eight dhāraṇīs, they remain unstained in the world, like a lotus flower.
Supreme in the world like Mount Sumeru, Incalculable and likewise beyond measure,
The worldly evils cannot move him, and so it is. This person,
fully endowed with such upholding, Can destroy all false views of the worldly path, Just as a lion roars among the beasts.
If one attains the unsurpassed dhāraṇī, one can master the pure conduct of the world,
increase immeasurable wholesome dharmas, and also teach and transform many sentient beings.
Possessing such a dhāraṇī, one can destroy the darkness of ignorance in sentient beings;
acting as a great radiance like the morning sun, one is also able to dispel all obscurity.
He preaches the Dharma without obstruction, like space; for the sake of sentient beings, he acts like a fierce wind.
Bestowing the medicine of the Dharma to destroy afflictions, he is like a skilled physician of the world who rescues the sick.
If one attains the complete and unsurpassed dhāraṇī, its praised merits can never be exhausted;
it can bring about refreshing clarity like the autumn moon, and the growth of wholesome dharmas is likewise so.
When Bodhisattvas achieve such upholding, they are able to transform immeasurable sentient beings;
if they possess such dhāraṇīs, they obtain mastery like a great king.
Able to transform sentient beings for the Great Vehicle, Able to bestow the wealth of Dharma to destroy poverty,
Able to let fall the rain of Dharma like a dragon king, And able to crush and destroy afflictions like fierce hail.
If one attains such a dhāraṇī, one can transform sentient beings toward bodhi;
one cannot exhaustively speak of its merits, as Indra cannot, for its words and meanings are as inexhaustible as space.
If one attains the accomplishment of dhāraṇī, all the great assemblies will joyfully see and hear them;
their minds undistracted, they always abide in meditative concentration, cultivating and accumulating immeasurable compassion,
practicing pure brahmacarya, and roaming through supernormal powers— all these four are like the Great Brahmā Heaven.
If one attains the accomplishment of dharani, one is then able to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
clearly perceiving the realms of the ten directions, one transforms sentient beings within those worlds.
If one possesses such a dhāraṇī, one will immediately attain the full perfection of the Buddha’s virtues;
one will be constantly held in the thoughts of the Buddhas of the ten directions, just as parents cherish their only son.
If there is a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī, they can extol the immeasurable garland of merits;
fully accomplishing morality, mindfulness, and wisdom, they are able to understand the mental activities of sentient beings.
If one attains the accomplishment of dhāraṇī, One will be free from arrogance, stinginess, and greed;
Skillfully knowing expedient means to harmonize sentient beings, One cultivates and gathers compassion and mercy to destroy afflictions.
If one attains the accomplishment of dhāraṇī, Defilements will not stain them, like the void;
They skillfully understand the intentional speech of sentient beings, And are likewise able to expound the Dharma according to their inclinations.
If one possesses such a dhāraṇī, one can fully understand the faculties of all sentient beings;
one can comprehend the various inclinations of sentient beings and preach the Dharma according to those inclinations,
preaching the Dharma through the gates of remedial measures, and using the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to discipline sentient beings.
If one attains such a dhāraṇī, one cultivates boundless śamatha;
If one attains such a dhāraṇī, one becomes fully endowed with the six perfections like all Buddhas.
Thoroughly understanding the realm of all afflictions, one penetrates their tranquility and destroys them.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are all utterly tranquil, And likewise so are walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
If one achieves such mastery of this retention, There will be no further afflictions or habitual tendencies.
One attains the pure Dharma-body, boundless and infinite; Not born by birth, one is always born through transformation.
The actions of body, speech, and mind proceed in accordance with wisdom; all meditative concentrations and mindfulness are likewise so.
If one attains such mastery of this dhāraṇī, those who offer praise could never exhaust it.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"You have long since attained this dhāraṇī; therefore, you are able to skillfully analyze and explain the meaning of all its immeasurable merits.
Not only today, but in the past as well, at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas, you have likewise performed such analysis and explanation."
“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Pure Radiance; the world was named Pure, and the kalpa was also named Pure.”

The world-system was composed of pure lapis lazuli, like a clear mirror; the ground was as level as the palm of a hand; all the groves and trees were formed of the seven treasures; and there were exquisite jewel lotuses as large as chariot wheels, pure and pristine, a sight that all people delighted to behold.
The people of that land all dwell in palaces, halls, and towers made of the seven treasures, no different from those in the heavens; their greed, anger, and delusion have gradually become slight.
That land has neither sun nor moon, but only the light of the Buddha; when blue lotuses bloom, they know it is night, and when red lotuses unfold, they know it is day.

"At that time, that Buddha had a sangha of sixty trillion great bodhisattvas; the number of those who had left the household life was beyond reckoning. They were all devoted to and delighted in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, and in that world, even the names of the two vehicles did not exist; they were all bodhisattvas who were non-retrogressive."

That Buddha’s lifespan was a full half-kalpa; there was no distinction between humans and devas, for those who dwelt on earth were humans and those who resided in space were devas, with the exception of the Dharma-King.

The people of that land do not worship various devas or heterodox deities, nor do they take refuge in them; furthermore, there is neither the female form nor even the mention of violating the precepts.
They are fully endowed with the threefold training.
What are the three?
First, the precept derived from the precepts;
second, the precept derived from the mind.
Third, regarding the precepts derived from wisdom:
generating the bodhicitta and feeling weary of and repentant toward birth and death is called the precept derived from morality;
cultivating samādhi and wisdom is called the precept derived from the mind.
"By cultivating and gathering wisdom, one attains great wisdom; this is called the 'precept derived from wisdom.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Prabhāśikhin. Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, circumambulated him to the right in reverence, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
Regarding what is called *dhāraṇī*, why is it named *dhāraṇī*?
Abiding in which *dhāraṇī* can a bodhisattva maintain the names of all Buddhas and provide detailed explanations for the sake of all sentient beings?
The Buddha said:

"Good son! There is a dhāraṇī called 'Jewel Torch. When a bodhisattva dwells within this dhāraṇī, they are able to uphold the names of all Buddhas, analyze and explain them for the sake of all sentient beings, according to the various languages of those beings."
The Bodhisattva Prabhāśikhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this in detail; having heard it, we shall practice and uphold it.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, listen attentively and with a sincere mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Far removed from all afflictions, Pure, stainless, and truly real;
Its mind can produce great radiance— This is named the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī."
The actions of body, speech, and mind are all utterly tranquil, Like the bright purity of the autumn moon;
Cultivating and gathering great compassion with an impartial mind— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
That mind is free from all discursive thought and examination, having completely distanced itself from the two views;
it is neither with perception nor without perception—this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Fully endowed with mindfulness, intention, and wisdom, One is able to enter the unsurpassed great Dharma-gate;
Pure and stainless like space— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Far removed from the three stains of worldly affliction, Having perfected the three kinds of pure wisdom,
And having attained liberation within the three realms of existence— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
It can utterly destroy greed, anger, and delusion, And one also attains freedom from the turbidity of afflictions;
It eliminates the various false darknesses of ignorance— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
The high, middle, and low voices of sentient beings— One can thoroughly and clearly know them all;
Being able to preach the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings, This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
It is fully endowed with profound and immeasurable meanings, And likewise fully endowed with all syllables and phrases;
Being far removed from "I" and "mine," This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Fully accomplishing the four reliances, And likewise possessing the four unhindered knowledges,
With a mind always abiding in the four dhyānas— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Able to extensively analyze the ultimate truth, Fully possessing and attaining the four Brahma-vihāras,
Cultivating and perfecting the five supernormal powers— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Upholding and mindfully recollecting the four foundations of mindfulness, Attaining the four right efforts through diligence,
And accomplishing the adornment of the four bases of power— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Having accomplished the five faculties and the five powers, one cannot be moved by any adverse winds;
having cultivated and gathered the unsurpassed seven factors of enlightenment—this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.

Having perfected the two wings of concentration and wisdom, one soars upon the level path of the Eightfold Noble Way, proceeding toward supreme knowledge and liberation; this is called the Ratnajvālā Dhāraṇī.
Able to tread the stages of the bodhisattva path, And to abide in supreme, true liberation,
Forever severing all afflictions and habitual tendencies— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
It can produce immeasurable great radiance, like the sun and moon in the world;
it can purify the three kinds of pure eyes—this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
It can purify all afflictions and enable one to remain far removed from all demonic activities;
by observing the faults inherent in the flavors of the five aggregates, this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Skillfully knowing how to discipline all sentient beings, Forever departing from the causes and conditions of the six sense faculties,
Expounding the Dharma for the sake of the multitude so they may attain mindfulness— This is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
Abiding in such a dhāraṇī, one can reach the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions;
seeing the Buddhas, one listens to and receives the Dharma with a sincere heart, and is likewise able to extensively expound such teachings.
Having heard the Dharma, one upholds it with a sincere heart and is able to explain the meaning of the words for the sake of sentient beings.
By virtue of the causal conditions of great mindfulness, one is able to understand the subtle and wondrous speech of all Buddhas;
one can expound upon impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and that all phenomena obtain their fruits through conditions.
To clearly and thoroughly observe the realms of all phenomena—this is called the Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī.
One achieves the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence; the three types of clear knowledge and the three kinds of wisdom are likewise so.
If there is one who dwells in this dhāraṇī, they shall be able to attain the meaning of the eight liberations.
The Buddha has taught immeasurable dhāraṇīs, all of which are gathered within this retention;
if one attains such a dhāraṇī, it is called the accomplishment of the immeasurable retention.
If one enters immeasurable meditative concentrations And attains immeasurable supernormal powers, It is all due to the power of such dhāraṇīs; Therefore, it is called the King among Holders.

Just as the four great oceans are without obstruction, and all rivers and springs flow into them, so too are the various streams of all dharmas; they all ultimately converge in this ocean of upholding.
Having attained a boundless body and inexhaustible mind, Able to extensively analyze and expound the dharma-realm,
Those who have accomplished immeasurable merit Are able to obtain this dhāraṇī.
If one attains such a subtle and wondrous dhāraṇī, One immediately obtains the thirty-two marks and signs;
One’s complexion becomes supreme and of noble lineage, Abounding in wealth and treasures, one attains mastery.
Amidst all states of existence, one realizes non-arising, And is able to extensively analyze the meanings of all dharmas.
Abiding securely in the stage of immovability and non-retrogression, all is due to having attained this dhāraṇī.
If a bodhisattva wishes to cultivate awakening, they should practice such a dhāraṇī;
once this retention is obtained, the cultivation of the path becomes easy, enabling them to expound the Dharma and harmonize sentient beings.
While preaching the Dharma throughout immeasurable eons, the two aspects of words and meanings can never be exhausted;
it is by attaining such a dhāraṇī that one is able to purify the afflictions of all sentient beings.
They are able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of the true Dharma, Able to cause sentient beings to be liberated from all sufferings,
And able to advance sentient beings toward the unsurpassed path, Because they have attained such a dhāraṇī.
Even if there were sentient beings numbering in the millions, and each possessed a million tongues,
they could not fully describe the immeasurable merit obtained by one who upholds this [sūtra].
“Good son! At that time, when the Buddha Pure Radiance was preaching this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Light-Crest and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas all attained this dhāraṇī.”
"Good son! Do you know that at that time, that Bodhisattva Light-Crown was anyone else?
He was none other than yourself."
"Therefore, you are now able to extensively distinguish this dhāraṇī; among this great assembly, you who have attained this retention are the foremost.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Prajñākūṭa, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the Ratnaprabhā-dhāraṇī, and having obtained it, not lose it, and by means of this dharma, subdue sentient beings? "Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells securely in the faculty of wisdom and performs the deeds of wisdom, such a bodhisattva is able to attain this dhāraṇī; having attained it, they do not lose it, and is able to tame sentient beings by means of this dharma.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa spoke again, saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain:
what is the faculty of wisdom?
What is the activity of wisdom?
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Good son! If a good man or a good woman has not previously heard of wisdom and now hears it, this is called the "root. Having heard it, to explain it extensively is called the "activity."
Initially, contemplating all phenomena is termed the "root"; having contemplated them, explaining them extensively is termed the "activity.
Initially, contemplating the roots of goodness is termed the "root"; subsequently, transforming others through this contemplation is termed the "activity."
Contemplating heedfulness is called the root; transforming others through that [contemplation] is called the activity.
Taming one's own mind is called the root; taming the minds of others is called the activity.
Abiding in tranquility is called the root; purifying body, speech, and mind is called the activity.
Knowing the One Vehicle is called the root; teaching it for the sake of sentient beings is called the activity.
"Cultivating śamatha is called the root; possessing the three kinds of wisdom is called the function.
Cultivating the three gates of liberation is called the root; realizing the three kinds of wisdom is called the function."
Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness is called the root; not dwelling on mindfulness is called the function.
Cultivating the four right efforts is called the root; being free from the nature of afflictions is called the function.
Cultivating the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is called the root; knowing that there is no psychic power is called the function.
Cultivating and gathering faith is called the root; relinquishing all things is called the function.
Cultivating fearlessness is called the root; being able to explain it extensively is called the function.
Cultivating and gathering samādhi is called the root; knowing the sequence of meditative concentrations is called the function.
The cultivation and accumulation of wisdom is called the root; knowing all phenomena is called the function.
Adorning bodhi is called the root; attaining bodhi at its time is called the function.
Realizing suffering, its origin, and the path is termed "roots"; realizing cessation is termed "action.
That which does not rely on the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is termed "roots"; that which relies on the definitive sūtras (*nītārtha*) is termed "action."
Initially receiving and hearing the Dharma is called the root; relying upon its meaning is called the function.
Not relying on the person is called the root; relying upon the Dharma is called the function.
To perceive that phenomena are impermanent is called the root; that phenomena are without arising or ceasing is called the function.
To know that all phenomena are suffering is called the root; to know that phenomena are without agency is called the function.
Knowing that phenomena are without self is called the root; knowing that the nature of phenomena is pure is called the function.
Knowing that nirvāṇa is pure is called the root; knowing that phenomena are fundamentally pure is called the function.
To hear the righteous without fear is called the root; to rely upon the righteous is called the function.
To hear the truth without dread is called the root; to rely upon the true Dharma is called the function.
Knowing the syllables without fear is called the root; knowing them and delighting in their exposition is called the function.
Hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s power of unimpeded wisdom and not giving rise to fear is called the root; relying upon the Tathāgata’s power of unimpeded wisdom is called the function.
The two conditions for the arising of phenomena are called the "roots," while compassion that is without such conditions is called the "activity.
Taking pity on sentient beings is called the "root," while being able to destroy suffering is called the "activity."
To contemplate the wholesome and attain joy is called the root; for the mind not to cling to phenomena is called the activity.
To be without craving, hatred, or equanimity is called the root; to be neither one nor two is called the activity.
Mindfulness of the Buddha is called the root; mindfulness of the Dharma-body is called its function.
Mindfulness of the Dharma is called the root; knowing the purity of the Dharma-nature is called its function.
Mindfulness of the Sangha is called the root; knowing the unconditioned nature of the Sangha is called its function.
Mindfulness of the precepts is called the root; knowing that there is no one who upholds them is called its function.
Mindfulness of giving is called the root; being able to relinquish afflictions is called its function.
Mindfulness of the heavens is called the root; attaining birth in the pure heavens is called its function.
To hear and then contemplate is called the root; to be unattached to the world is called the function.
To know that which was originally non-existent yet is now produced is called the root; to be without production and without reception is called the function.
Knowing nirvana is called the root; attaining great liberation is called the function.
Self-benefit is called the root; benefiting both self and others is called the function.
"Upholding the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma is called the root; penetrating their meaning is called the function.
Being able to expound the Dharma is called the root; understanding ignorance and so forth is called the function."
Exhorting all sentient beings toward the path of Bodhi is called the "root"; exhorting them to cultivate wisdom and skillful means without regression is called the "activity.
Not fearing any existence is called the "root"; aspiring to be born in various existences is called the "activity."
Attaining patience through hearing is called the "root"; attaining it through reflection is called the "activity.
Attaining patience according to one's will is called the "root"; attaining it because of non-arising is called the "activity."
That which remains for one more lifetime is called the root; the final body is called the karma.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree is called the root; fully comprehending all phenomena is called the karma.
When these words concerning the faculty of wisdom and the karma of wisdom were spoken, all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as well as this Jewel Monastery, shook in six ways.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wisdom-Cluster addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and condition do the worlds of the ten directions and this courtyard of the Seven-Jeweled Monastery within the void tremble in this way?
"Good son! This is the faculty of wisdom and the karma of wisdom, which has also been taught by all the Buddhas of the past; for this reason, this earth undergoes such a great trembling."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Endowed with the Four Unhindered Knowledges addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition is the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Heap named 'Heap'?"
The Buddha said:

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Guṇagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The land was named Śubhavati, and the eon was named Vimalā; all the sentient beings in that land were purely virtuous.
At that time, the Buddha had an assembly of thirty-two thousand great bodhisattvas and an assembly of eighty-four thousand śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to test the bodhisattvas, questioned them with ten billion matters, saying:
"O sons of good family!
Among this assembly, who is able to explain such meanings as these?"
Among them, some said:
"I shall contemplate it; only after one month will I be able to understand it.
Others, again, said:
"I shall pass after half a month," another said,
"I shall pass after seven days."
Or some said: "I shall be able to understand it after one day and one night have passed.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Smṛtimatī, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I can now understand this meaning without rising from my seat.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva had uttered this lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, the earth immediately shook in six ways and emitted a great radiance, exhorting the earth deities up to the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, so that they all came to the place where the Tathāgata was.

At that time, the place where the great assembly sat was a full million *yojanas* in length and breadth. When the Bodhisattva Cintāmati saw that the entire great assembly had gathered, by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), the power of wisdom and mindfulness (*prajñā-smṛti-bala*), the power of dhāraṇī, the power of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid-bala*), the power of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya-bala*), and the Buddha’s spiritual power, he understood a billion meanings within each of those billion individual matters, without prior deliberation and without any impediment.

Having spoken these meanings, sixty thousand sentient beings within the great assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and forty thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From the earth spirits and various devas up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, everyone heard the sound of the Dharma being preached.
“Good son! Do you know who the Bodhisattva Smṛtimat was at that time?
It was none other than Prajñākūṭa.”
"For these reasons, it is called the 'Accumulation of Wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Because of hearing the Dharma, it is called the 'Root'; Because of expounding the Dharma, it is called the 'Action'."
Contemplating all that is wholesome is called the root; explaining the profound meaning is called the activity.
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma is called the root; preaching the Dharma according to the inclinations of others is called the activity.
Cultivating śamatha is called the root; possessing the three types of wisdom is called the activity.
The four foundations of mindfulness are called the roots; the four right efforts are called the activity.
The five faculties, such as faith, are called the roots; the five powers, such as faith, are called the activity.
The seven factors of enlightenment are called the roots; the eightfold noble path is called the activity.
Not relying on words is called the root; relying on the meaning is called the function.
Not relying on persons is called the root; relying on the Dharma is called the function.
Not relying on the provisional meaning is called the root; relying on the definitive meaning is called the function.
Not relying on consciousness is called the root; relying on wisdom is called the activity.
Thoroughly understanding non-action is called the root; penetrating non-arising is called the activity.
The two types of compassion regarding arising phenomena are called the root; objectless compassion is called the activity.
Fearlessness is called the root; being able to proclaim the True Dharma is called the function.
The six bases of mindfulness are called the root; the meaning of the six recollections is called the function.
Being able to benefit oneself is called the root; benefiting both oneself and others is called the function.
Upholding the True Dharma is called the root; being able to explain it for others is called the activity.
Having one remaining birth is called the root; the final body is called the activity.
If a bodhisattva’s mind does not regress, they then understand and realize the root and activity of wisdom.
"One can attain the supreme patience of non-arising, and can open the gate to unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is inconceivable, and unsurpassed bodhi is likewise inconceivable.

Why is this? Because it is not expressed by words, nor is it encompassed by words; because that which is spoken by the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless; because it enters into immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates; because the twelve links of dependent origination are profound and difficult to understand; because those attached to dualistic dharmas cannot know it; because those of sharp wisdom come to know it gradually; because it is not something known or seen by the six sense-faculties; and because it is also not the realm of the wisdom of the two vehicles.
“World-Honored One!
Such bodhi is the seal of all dharmas; it is unconditioned like space, for it is not a dwelling place, being free from any dwelling place.”

He knows all conditioned phenomena and the causes and effects of all sentient beings; his wisdom is vast and boundless, adorning all immeasurable wholesome dharmas; he serves as a worthy vessel for wholesome dharmas and can manifest supernatural powers to others.

For those abiding in the two paths, it demonstrates non-duality; it demonstrates that all Buddhas are equal and without distinction, being without words and without meaning, ineffable and inaudible. It can demonstrate to sentient beings the true assembly of the Triple Gem, as well as the three gates of liberation for deliverance from the triple world, and it demonstrates the causes for the three kinds of wisdom and the vajra-samādhi.
Abiding in the true Dharma of all Buddhas, they hear the wisdom of all Buddhas in its entirety; they benefit all sentient beings and are likewise able to proclaim the teachings of all Buddhas.

If there are good sons or good daughters who can thus praise all the merits of bodhi, and who hear such Vaipulya sutras, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain them, they are said to be able to repay the kindness of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is,
son of good family!
As you have said, you shall obtain immeasurable merit.

"If there are those who can receive and uphold this sutra, transcribe it, read and recite it, and explain its meaning, the merit they obtain will be no different [from that of others].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas: "Good sons!..."
"Who among this assembly is able, after my parinirvāṇa, to protect and uphold such unsurpassed bodhi, and to extensively expound this meaning so that the Dharma may long endure?"
At that time, there were sixty trillion bodhisattvas and devas within the assembly who spoke with one voice:

“After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we are able to protect and uphold such unsurpassed bodhi, and widely expound this sutra so that the Dharma may long endure; we only pray that the Tathāgata will bestow upon us the power of his vows.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If I am truly equal to the Buddhas of the ten directions, And have forever crossed the great ocean of suffering of birth and death,
Then this supreme Dharma of such merit Should abide for a long time without destruction."
If I have cultivated loving-kindness for immeasurable eons, Truly acting for the sake of all sentient beings,
Observing all with equality and without duality, Therefore, the True Dharma shall abide for a long time.
If I were to fulfill these two adornments, I would benefit sentient beings throughout immeasurable ages;
by transforming sentient beings through these two dharmas, the True Dharma shall endure for a long time.
If one can destroy the fetters of affliction, And eliminate all false views,
Being fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas, One is thus able to skillfully give rise to this power of aspiration.
“Good son! It is not only you, but all humans and devas, as well as all Māras and Brahmās, who will be able to protect and uphold such true Dharma after my parinirvāṇa.”
“Good son! Space may be made into form, and form may become identical with space, but the power of my vows and supernormal faculties cannot be made otherwise.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings spoke these words:
"If there be anyone who, after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain the meaning of this sutra, we shall constantly follow and protect them."
The Brahmā devas said:
"We shall relinquish the sublime bliss of meditative concentration to protect this person.
The Tuṣita devas said:
"We, too, shall protect such disciples who uphold this sutra.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“If there is anyone who can receive and uphold this sutra, I shall never perform demonic deeds or demonic activities against that person.
The Devaputra Guṇagarbha said:
“World-Honored One!
The bodhi attained by all Buddhas is entirely contained within this sutra.
If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and expound it, you should know that such persons shall immediately attain bodhi.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
I shall extensively proclaim such an unsurpassed sūtra as this in that Tuṣita Heaven.”
The Venerable Kāśyapa spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Although the wisdom of us śrāvakas is slight, we ought to receive, uphold, recite, and proclaim its meaning according to our capacity."
Ānanda spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
I shall truly receive and uphold this sutra, not losing so much as a single word or a single phrase; it shall be no different from what has issued from the Buddha’s own mouth.”
"If there are sentient beings who resolve to attain bodhicitta, I am also able to explain it extensively for them.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good sons! You are all capable, after my parinirvāṇa, of protecting and upholding the True Dharma so that it shall not perish. Good sons!"

If there are sentient beings who seek the Mahāyāna and, though they have not yet attained the stage of dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti), receive, uphold, and maintain this sutra, you should know that such persons will receive their prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) before seven Buddhas have passed.
If there are śrāvakas who uphold it, they shall be present in the first assembly when Maitreya attains Buddhahood.
If there are pratyekabuddhas who uphold it, they shall attain the realization of the Way after my parinirvāṇa.

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; immeasurable sentient beings achieved patience; immeasurable sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind; and immeasurable worlds shook in six ways.
The bodhisattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions made offerings to the Buddha with fine incense, flowers, music, banners, and canopies, all saying:
"We have come here to this monastery of the seven treasures and attained great and wholesome benefit."

If I possess even the slightest power of merit, by this power I pray that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni may long remain in the world, and that such a sublime scripture may spread throughout the worlds of the ten directions without ever being destroyed.
"If there are upāsakas, upāsikās, and others who uphold this sutra, may they be freed from all sorrow and fear, and be without the suffering of illness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja said:
"World-Honored One!..."

The Dharma now being taught is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; it cannot be shaken by any heterodox teachings. It is the root of all wholesome dharmas and the foundation for the three vehicles, as well as the primary gateway to all phenomena.
If there are sentient beings who come and ask me, saying:
"What is the name of this Dharma?
How should it be received and upheld?"
"How should one answer?
I only pray that you will explain this. The Buddha said:

“Good son! This is called ‘The Great Compassionate One Preaching the Dharma of Great Compassion,’ and it is called ‘The Tathāgata’s Deed of Bestowing Prophecy upon Bodhisattvas. You should uphold it thus.”
When this sutra had been spoken, the great assembly of humans and devas rejoiced, received it upon their heads with reverence, and, having faith and acceptance, practiced it accordingly.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty at Guzang.
Chapter Three: The Jewel Woman (Ratnāvalī). Part One.

At that time, the World-Honored One was still dwelling between the realms of desire and form, upon a lion throne within the Great Jewel Enclosure, surrounded by the great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, there was a young girl in the assembly named Ratnā who rose from her seat, took a string of white pearls in her right hand, and spoke these words:

"If it be true that I am able, throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, to uphold this sublime scripture of the *Mahāsannipāta*, to read and recite it, to copy it, to expound its meaning, and to cause it to be widely disseminated, may this pearl necklace be fixed upon the uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha and upon those of all the bodhisattvas."
Having spoken these words, he immediately cast the string of pearls.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power and through his sincere words, the pearl string was instantly upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head and also spread across the heads of all the bodhisattvas;

and within the pearl strings upon each of their own heads, those bodhisattvas beheld the world-systems and the trees of enlightenment that would exist at the time they themselves attained buddhahood in future lives.
They clearly perceived and understood the taming of sentient beings and the power of past vows; having seen this, each conceived a sense of wonder and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
As for this Jewel Woman, how is it that she possesses such immeasurable and great merit?
All the vows I have made throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas are now clearly perceived and fully understood in a single thought-moment.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

It is truly as you have said. This Jewel Woman has, in the past, planted various roots of goodness and made great, virtuous vows before ninety-six billion nayutas of Buddhas; in every place where she was born, she always attained the truth. Therefore, whatever this woman contemplates or speaks never fails to be realized.
If he wishes to cause this great trichiliocosm to be filled with precious flowers, they appear as soon as he speaks;
if he says he wishes to fill this great trichiliocosm with various sublime fragrances, they exist immediately upon his speaking;

if he wishes to manifest various forms and colors—the form and color of a wheel-turning monarch, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, or Brahmā; or the form and color of a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa; or the form and color of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā—they are obtained exactly as he speaks.

If a wind calamity arises, it turns into a fire calamity; when a fire calamity arises, it turns into a water calamity; and when a water calamity arises, it turns into a wind calamity—just as one says, so it immediately changes.

If there should be a Mara King who leads his hosts, wielding swords, staves, bows, crossbows, arrows, spears, lances, halberds, and shields, and desires to transform them into precious flowers, they shall become so immediately as he speaks.

If one encounters a desolate place lacking water and suffering from great scarcity, one should make a great vow for the sake of all sentient beings; thereupon, cities, towns, and villages will appear, and the people, both great and small, will have no lack of drink or water.
If one wishes that all forms within the trichiliocosm be like the form of a Tathāgata, they immediately become the wondrous form of a Buddha exactly as spoken.
If one says that the entire great assembly shall abide in space, as soon as the words are spoken, they abide there.
“Good son! If this Precious Woman wishes to hear everywhere throughout the void of this place the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, she hears them exactly as they are spoken.”
“Good son! The maiden Ratnadattā has accomplished such immeasurable and boundless great merits.
At that time, the maiden Ratnadattā spoke these verses in praise before the Buddha:
“I have now accomplished this great treasury of jewels, And am thus able to praise the Unsurpassed Honored One,
Who is far removed from all afflictions And is fully endowed with the great jewels that assist enlightenment.”
The Tathāgata is endowed with the unsurpassed jewels; His great radiance can illuminate the boundless worlds.
To the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Unsurpassed Jewel Banner, I now present these treasures as an offering:
Coral, agate, and blue lapis lazuli, Vajra, pearl, and the jewel of sun and moon.
With such jewels he makes offerings to the Buddha, so that all sentient beings may attain bodhi.
The World-Honored One’s bodily radiance surpasses all jewels; sentient beings delight in beholding it without weariness.
Standing in one direction, he sees the ten directions, causing each being to see the Buddha before them.
Some see the Tathāgata’s body walking or standing, Some see him sitting, reclining, or preaching the Dharma;
Some see him in silence, proclaiming nothing at all, Or see him entering meditative absorption to cultivate wisdom.
The light from each and every pore of the Tathāgata Is able to illuminate all worlds throughout the ten directions.
"The radiance is pure and most unsurpassed, Like the autumn moon and the pure lotus.
At that time, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the Jewel Woman further spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now wish to inquire briefly regarding the meaning within this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra; if the Tathāgata permits it, I shall venture to pose my questions.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"O Jewel Woman!
Ask whatever you wish.
If there is any web of doubt, I shall eliminate it for you."
At that time, the Jewel Woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is truthful speech?”
What is reality? What is the Dharma-discourse?
And what is the Dharma?
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Jewel Woman!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have three kinds of reality.
What are these three?
First, not deceiving the Buddhas;
second, not deceiving oneself.
Third, not deceiving sentient beings.
What is meant by not deceiving the Buddhas, oneself, and sentient beings?
O Jewel Maiden!

If there is a bodhisattva who, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becomes greedily attached to the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called deceiving all the Buddhas, oneself, and sentient beings.
What is non-deception? Jewel Woman!

If there is a bodhisattva who, having already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, should experience great suffering and affliction while in hell; or encounter demonic activities and dwell together with those of false views; or be born in an evil land where evil afflictions arise; or have their bodies met with swords and spears, being hacked, pierced, burned, and roasted—at such times as these, they never abandon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). They do not cease, do not rest, do not fear, and do not regret, but cause the mind of enlightenment to increase and expand further, undergoing great suffering and affliction for the sake of all sentient beings.

Seeing those who suffer, his mind becomes even more expansive; he diligently cultivates vigor with the desire to attain bodhi, and is not deceived or deluded by false speech. He cannot be shaken by any perverse winds; this is called a bodhisattva not deceiving the Buddhas, himself, or sentient beings.
“O Jewel Woman!
If there is a bodhisattva who does not deceive the Buddhas, himself, or sentient beings, this is called the true reality of a bodhisattva.
O Jewel Woman!”
There are four further matters by which one does not deceive the Buddhas:
first, the firmness of one's mind;
second, abiding in the ultimate destination.
Third, being endowed with power;
fourth, diligently cultivating vigor.
"Not deceiving oneself also has four matters:
First, a pure mind; second, a sincere mind;
third, non-deception.
Fourth is being without crookedness.
There are also four matters regarding not deceiving sentient beings:
first, adornment; [and so forth].
Second, the cultivation of loving-kindness;
third, the cultivation of compassion;
fourth, the practice of gathering [beings].
“Precious Daughter!
This is called the foremost truth of a bodhisattva.
As for the truth of a bodhisattva, it is that at the time of first generating the aspiration, they do not abandon sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
A Bodhisattva who is truthful does not speak much; he guards his speech, does not use harsh words, and speaks with truth.

Whether in private, in a great assembly, or in the presence of a king, his speech is sincere. He does not deliberately tell lies for the sake of wealth, nor does he deliberately tell lies for the sake of power."
If there were a trichiliocosm filled with the seven treasures, one would still not utter a falsehood for their sake, much less for the sake of a minor matter!
“Precious Daughter!
Such a reality has thirty-two purities.
What are these thirty-two?
First, speech of shame;
second, speech of merit;
third, speech of remorse.
Fourth, gentle speech; fifth, truthful speech;
sixth, speech free from derision or reproach.
Seventh, speech that is free from greedy attachment;
eighth, speech that is fearless;
ninth, speech that closes off all evil paths.
Tenth, speech that opens up all wholesome paths;
eleventh, speech on noble conduct;
twelfth, speech on wise conduct.
Thirteenth, speech that is pure within;
fourteenth, speech that is pure without;
fifteenth, speech that is pleasant to receive.
Sixteenth, delighting in listening to speech;
seventeenth, speech that is not harsh;
eighteenth, subtle and exquisite speech.
Nineteenth, speech that is analytical;
twentieth, speech with sublime tones;
twenty-first, speech that is purely wholesome;
Twenty-second, refraining from deceptive speech;
twenty-third, refraining from harsh speech;
twenty-fourth, speaking with joy.
Twenty-fifth, words of self-exhortation;
twenty-sixth, words of exhorting others;
twenty-seventh, words that are not lost.
Twenty-eighth, speech that brings peace and security;
twenty-ninth, speech regarding the field of merit;
thirtieth, speech that accords with the Buddha’s words.
Thirty-first is speech that is surrounded by truth;
thirty-second is pure speech of the mouth.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!
Regarding the reality of a bodhisattva, whatever they speak is consistent with their speech and intention.
What is meant by "consistency between speech and intention"?
Because they cultivate and accumulate generosity, they attain bodhi; it cannot be attained through stinginess or greed. This is called speaking in accordance with one's intention and speech.
To be able to bestow all things is called "truth.
One attains bodhi by cultivating and accumulating pure precepts; it cannot be attained through the violation of precepts. This is called speech that accords with one's mind and mouth.
To abide according to the precepts is called reality.
One attains bodhi by cultivating and accumulating patience; it cannot be attained through anger. This is what is meant by speech that accords with one’s mind and mouth.
To fully cultivate patience is called truth.
Diligently practicing vigor leads to the attainment of Bodhi; it cannot be attained through indolence. This is called speech that accords with one's mind and words.
Because one cultivates diligence, it is called "reality.
One attains bodhi by cultivating and accumulating meditative concentration; it cannot be attained through a distracted mind. This is what is meant by speech that accords with the intention.
Cultivating and gathering a concentrated mind is called reality.
Cultivating wisdom leads to the attainment of Bodhi; it cannot be attained through ignorance. This is what is meant by speech that accords with the intention.
Because one cultivates wisdom, it is called "reality.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment and the four immeasurable minds are likewise so.
Furthermore, O Jewel Woman!
That which is called reality is what is known as noble practice (*ārya-caryā*). Noble practice consists of the contemplation of suffering and impermanence.

Furthermore, noble practice refers to the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path. To know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) possess no characteristic of arising is called the knowledge of suffering.

Regarding the cause of the five aggregates: it is the ultimate distancing from the fetter of craving—being without greed or attachment, neither praising nor seeking, neither departing nor arriving. This is called being detached from the accumulation and extinguishing all marks; yet, at the time of its extinction, not a single dharma is extinguished.
To transform unequal phenomena into equal phenomena is called the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha*).

When *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are equal in their characteristics—being without applied thought (*vitarka*), without sustained thought (*vicāra*), without equality, without attachment, without grasping, without activity, and without transformation—this is called the cultivation of the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*).

Truly understanding such truths as these, and further being able to analyze and explain their meaning in detail, this is called the reality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; when he speaks this true Dharma, ten thousand bodhisattvas attain the patience of reality (*bhūtakoṭi-kṣānti*).

“Jewel Woman! One who speaks according to the Dharma speaks in accordance with the Dharma in all that they proclaim; they contemplate the Dharma, keep the Dharma in mind, and practice the Dharma. They travel by means of the Dharma, seek the Dharma, desire the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, and cultivate the Dharma. They are the banner of the Dharma, the staff of the Dharma, and the ornamented vessel of the Dharma;

they are the lamp of the Dharma, the light of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Dharma, the intention of the Dharma, and the certainty regarding the Dharma—adorned with these as their jeweled necklaces.”
The Dharma-seat, the Dharma-ritual, the Dharma-protection, the Dharma-wealth, and the inexhaustibility of the Dharma are vast and boundless.
The Dharma-action, the Dharma-body, the Dharma-speech, and the Dharma-mind—when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fully accomplishes such dharmas as these, it is called "Dharma-discourse."

“The Dharma consists of truthful speech and the preservation of the words of the Dharma; it teaches people to honor their parents, preceptors, elders, and those of virtue, and it extols bodhi and the path to bodhi.”

It causes one not to abandon the bodhicitta; with a sincere mind, one remains mindful and does not forget awakening; one does not depart from the adornments for cultivating the dharmas of awakening; one draws near to the noble ones and virtuous spiritual friends; one cultivates and accumulates faith, listens to the Dharma with single-minded focus, yearns for the true Dharma, and exerts oneself in diligence.

They do not greedily cling to dharmas; they recognize and repay kindness; they delight in tranquility and do not sever the noble lineage; they instruct others in the dhūta practices and exhort them to practice the ten wholesome paths of action; they praise generous giving; and they dedicate all wholesome dharmas toward awakening.

With a sincere mind, one upholds the pure precepts, cultivates and accumulates patience, eliminates laziness, practices pure meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; one cultivates the Four Noble Truths and proceeds toward those truths.

Having attained the four unhindered wisdoms and great supernormal powers, they accord with the gift of Dharma by practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the cultivation and accumulation of the eightfold noble path. Through the two dharmas of concentration and wisdom, they attain knowledge-liberation, according to the liberation of the various vehicles: Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.

"In praising and expounding upon all merits, one should contemplate the twelve profound links of dependent origination, discerning the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, remaining free from fear."

He taught that the five aggregates are like illusions and transformations; he taught that the eighteen elements have the characteristic of space; he taught that the nature of the sense bases is identical to the nature of emptiness; he constantly spoke of the seven riches, the six recollections, and the six respects; and he explained the complete fulfillment of the six pāramitās.

He speaks of the six constant practices and cultivates the six supernormal powers; he is fully endowed with the five eyes and speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). He disseminates throughout the world the language of accomplished action, and his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings as he praises the Buddha’s words.
“Precious Daughter!

If there is a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with such discourse on the Dharma, their mouth shall never utter the language of a self, nor the language of a sentient being, nor the language of a life-span, nor the language of a person; they do not speak of annihilation, nor of permanence, nor of the view of existence, nor of the view of non-existence, nor of dualistic severance, nor do they cling to the language of the middle; they do not speak of accumulation, nor of cessation, nor of contention, nor of partiality, nor of that which is not cognized, nor of inversion, nor of speech that increases doubt, nor of speech that opposes the Dharma; rather, they speak of observing the dharma-realm and of destroying pride.”

“The Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma abides in accordance with the Dharma and speaks in accordance with the Dharma, uttering words of truth and words of the Dharma—words that are uninterrupted and unrefuted. This Bodhisattva who preaches the Dharma cannot be debated by anyone in all the worlds; those who see him are struck with awe.”

The Bodhisattva of Dharma-speech can expound upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); he does not cling to the three realms or to any forms of existence, nor does he beg from others. He is without mind, thought, or consciousness; he is free from dust and defilement, ignorance, and darkness. He is not bound to others, nor is he bound to himself. There is no high or low in him; he is unmixed with the causes and conditions of all objective spheres. Pure and tranquil, he has no leader. He is difficult to know and difficult to awaken to; he cannot be conceptualized, yet he acts without conceptualization. Only those of pure wisdom can truly know him.

Without sensation and without a sensor, one eternally severs all sensations, transcending the three periods of time. It is neither extinction nor characterized by extinction; neither arising nor characterized by arising. There is neither abundance nor scarcity; no birth, no cessation, no increase, no decrease, no future existence, and no past existence. It is not cultivation, not seeing, not the vision of Māra, and not the vision of reality. It is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic, and yet it is not a single characteristic, while also being a single characteristic.

It is not a dwelling, nor is it apart from a dwelling; it is neither near nor far, neither separate nor distinct, neither bound nor liberated, neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows (*anāsrava*), and it is not even similar [to these].

It is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither complete nor incomplete, neither name nor form, neither attachment nor liberation, neither broken nor whole; though it is not diamond, it possesses an indestructible nature.

Reality is thus: it is neither near nor far; it is without form and without cause; it is neither dull nor deaf; it is neither this nor that; it is neither internal nor external; it is neither self nor other; it is neither seen nor heard; it is neither remembered nor forgotten; it is neither consciousness nor cognition; it is not the sphere of consciousness, nor is it the sphere of cognition.
"O Jewel Woman!
This is called the Dharma.
If one can extensively expound such teachings as these, it is called 'expounding the Dharma.'"
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! A Dharma-speaking Bodhisattva does not contend with any in the world;

they do not disparage or treat with contempt others who have not yet studied; their minds do not mock nor give rise to arrogance; they do not praise themselves nor slander others; they do not preach the Dharma to others for the sake of food and drink; and they do not obstruct the goodness of others or cause them to fall into doubt."
When seeing others commit offenses, one never speaks of them; one does not give rise to contempt for the teachings of others, nor does one obstruct the practices they cultivate.

Whatever Dharma one teaches is never divorced from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). One never discriminates within the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), remaining unmoved by the realm of phenomena and unmoved by true nature (*tathatā*). One does not rely on letters, consciousness, persons, or the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); though not relying upon these, one does not disparage them either.

"One does not give rise to discrimination between oneself and others, nor does one revile the twelve links of dependent origination. One does not purify the world by remaining within the world; one does not purify dharmas by means of dharmas. One is without greed or stinginess, without breaking the precepts or abandoning those who have broken them, without anger or envy, and without indolence. One does not lose the mind of the Way and does not forget bodhi. Desiring to adorn supreme wisdom, one exerts oneself without ceasing or resting, never giving rise to regret."

One should have no envy or jealousy toward the teachings of others; one should not, out of attachment to what is not the Sūtra, slander the Sūtra, and the same applies to the Vinaya and the Māyā (monastic discipline).
Regarding the True Dharma, one ultimately never perceives it as wrong; one does not increase pride because of pride, nor does one slander causes and conditions or the retribution of karma.

Within the True Dharma, the mind never regresses; one recognizes kindness, remembers kindness, and repays it without forgetfulness. One never harbors a heart of resentment, does not cling to the view of self, and does not envy the benefits of others.

"Regarding enemies and kin, one holds no dualistic thoughts; even when subjected to the insults of others, one never retaliates. One does not engage in double-tongued speech to incite strife between this party and that. One harbors no flattery or deceit to appear extraordinary and delude the masses. One does not, out of a desire for the pleasure of others, receive the bodhisattva precepts, bhikṣu precepts, bhikṣuṇī precepts, śikṣamāṇā precepts, śrāmaṇera precepts, śrāmaṇerī precepts, upāsaka precepts, or upāsikā precepts. Instead, dwelling in secluded places, one contemplates in silent stillness and with diligent mind receives and recites the twelve divisions of the sūtras."

One does not uphold and guard such precepts for the sake of defeating others; one does not practice contentment merely for the sake of receiving offerings; one does not cultivate contentment for oneself merely to demonstrate the discontent of others; and one does not believe that the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas is something produced by another.

Not committing evil deeds or wrong livelihoods; not abandoning the seven riches and not being greedy for food; not severing the noble lineage; not slandering others nor praising oneself; not making quantitative calculations regarding the Buddha-dharma; and praising the Mahāyāna with a mind that knows no satiety—this is called "Dharma-speech."

At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Jewel Maiden: "Regarding the meaning of 'Bodhisattva,' what is meant by this term? It refers to one who, when practicing the adornment of faith, is free from falsehood;

who, desiring to adorn all roots of goodness, single-mindedly and with focused intent cultivates wholesome dharmas; who destroys the doubts of sentient beings without seeking karmic retribution; who bestows peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; who guards the prohibitive precepts without losing the mind of patience; who diligently practices vigor to increase wholesome dharmas; who cultivates tranquil concentration to gather in all distractions; who possesses unsurpassed wisdom to destroy the darkness of ignorance; who cultivates a heart of loving-kindness to treat all sentient beings as equals; who cultivates a heart of compassion to personally attend to and manage whatever sentient beings do; who cultivates a heart of sympathetic joy to bestow the joy of the Dharma upon the multitude; and who cultivates a heart of equanimity to neither dwell on suffering nor pleasure."

Having relinquished material wealth, his mind is free from regret or stinginess; his speech is gentle, destroying the evil intentions of the multitude; he benefits others with profound completeness; and through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose), he exhorts them toward the Mahāyāna. By means of these four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he tames sentient beings.
One perceives that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, thereby purifying all afflictions (*kleśa*).

One relies on the meaning (*artha*) and not on the letter; one relies on wisdom (*jñāna*) and not on consciousness (*vijñāna*); one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and sets aside those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); and one relies on the Dharma and not on the person (*pudgala*).
He possesses unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning, which is inexhaustible, yet remains free from conceptual discrimination within the dharma-realm;
he possesses unimpeded eloquence regarding expression, attaining liberation through speech;
and he possesses unimpeded eloquence regarding inspiration, speaking in accordance with the Dharma.

Adorning generosity with insatiable practice; adorning ethical discipline through the fulfillment of virtuous vows; adorning extensive learning by acting in accordance with the Dharma; adorning merit by being endowed with the primary and secondary marks; adorning wisdom by knowing the distinctions between the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; adorning meditative concentration for the sake of mental purity; and adorning knowledge by attaining the three types of insight.

One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness so that the mind is not distracted; one cultivates the four right efforts to attain roots of goodness; one cultivates the four bases of psychic power to travel to all directions; one cultivates the five faculties to discern and analyze phrases; one cultivates the five powers to destroy afflictions; one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment to know all dharmas; one cultivates the eightfold noble path so as not to be moved by evil; and one cultivates the superknowledges so as not to fall back or lose them.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands such meanings as these, it is called "the meaning";
if there is a Bodhisattva who can explain these meanings, it is called "explaining the meaning.
Furthermore, O Ratnā, Daughter!

Furthermore, as for the meaning: by cultivating and accumulating the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one destroys all phenomena of existence; by cultivating and accumulating the signless (*animitta*), one destroys the signs of all phenomena; and by cultivating and accumulating the wishless (*apraṇihita*), one does not seek the three realms.
If one can expound these three kinds of emptiness, this is called "explaining the meaning";
that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not to be practiced is what is called "the meaning.
When a Bodhisattva speaks of this non-practice, it is called "explaining the meaning."
The severance of all arising is what is called "meaning.
If a bodhisattva speaks of the non-arising of all phenomena, this is called "speaking of the meaning";
that all existents have no emergence is what is called "meaning."
To speak in this manner is called "explaining the meaning";
the Four Noble Truths are what is termed "the meaning.
To speak in this manner is called "explaining the meaning."
The absence of self and what belongs to self is called "meaning.
To speak in this manner is called "speaking of meaning.
That which cannot be expressed by words is called "meaning."
To speak in this manner is called "explaining the meaning";
the true meaning is what is termed "meaning.
To speak in this manner is called "explaining the meaning."
All dharmas of enlightenment are beyond measure and calculation; this is called "meaning.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks in this manner, it is called "speaking the meaning.
When a person of great learning acts in accordance with the Dharma, this is called "meaning."
To speak in this manner is called "explaining the meaning";
that among all vehicles the Mahāyāna is supreme is what is called "the meaning.
To be able to speak in such a way is called "explaining the meaning."
Furthermore, Jewel Woman! That which is without discrimination is called "meaning" (*artha*).

Therein, there are no sentient beings, nor is there any recipient of life. It is of a single flavor, unmoving, inexhaustible, and not a single thing. It is neither born nor produced; it does not come nor go, it is not extinguished, and it is non-dual.
