It cannot be perceived, it is without fabrication, it is unconditioned and without action, and the mind is not crooked or deceitful.

The three periods of time are equal, and the three parts are without distinction; there is neither loss nor gain, neither heat nor cold, neither purity nor impurity. It does not act yet is as it is; it neither grasps nor abandons; it is not the path yet reveals the path; it is neither eternal nor annihilated, nor is it even the Middle Way.
Without anger or turbidity, one does not contemplate dharmas or non-dharmas; it is not comprised of any syllables, sounds, or speech.

Being without mind, intellect, or consciousness, one does not give rise to discrimination regarding greed, anger, or delusion. Regarding all dharmas—whether they are characterized by activity or marks—the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are themselves empty. Truly entering into the equality of all dharmas, whether equal or unequal, one attains liberation through wisdom.
"O Jewel Woman!
If a bodhisattva can thus possess the meaning, this is called 'meaning';
to speak of such meaning is called 'speaking of the meaning.'"
“O Jewel Woman!
How does a bodhisattva explain the Vinaya?
The Buddha has taught that there are generally two kinds of Vinaya.”
What are these two?
First, the vinaya of transgression;
second, the vinaya of afflictions.
What constitutes an offense?
What is the Vinaya?

An offense is that which arises when, having committed an act, one subsequently recognizes it as unwholesome reflection; when, due to ignorance, inversion, falsehood, deception, and afflictions, one clings to a self, sentient beings, and doubt; when one fails to attain liberation due to restlessness and regret, pride, negligence, and lack of learning—it is because of such factors that it is called an offense.

If one shatters the doubting mind and attains liberation, because of this attainment of liberation, one perceives the locus of transgression as being neither a locus nor a non-locus; it is not of body, speech, or mind; it is neither grasped nor abandoned, and cannot be seen; it is not produced by the body, nor produced by the mind or speech; if it were produced by these three, it would be a phenomenon subject to extinction.
If it is a phenomenon that ceases, who acts and who transgresses?
As with transgression, so it is with all phenomena: all phenomena are without root, without action, and without location.
If one can destroy such doubts as these, this is called purity; this is called being without feverish distress.
To act in accordance with the teacher’s instructions is called having faith, it is called having concentration, and it is called vinaya.
"What are the afflictions?
What is the discipline (vinaya)?
The twelve links of existence—namely, from ignorance up to old age and death—are called the afflictions."
That which skillfully subdues all afflictions is called *vinaya*. Why is this?
For emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) can subdue all phenomena.
If dharmas are empty, devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, and beyond aspiration, how can there be greed, anger, delusion, and so forth?
Since non-action is able to harmonize all dharmas, if all dharmas are non-active, how can there be afflictions and various fetters?
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; if they arise from conditions, how can they be perceived?
By perceiving these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), one also comes to know afflictions (*kleśa*) and the characteristics of afflictions.
If this empty wisdom can contemplate bodhi, then by means of this very emptiness, one is emptied of afflictions.
If one can observe such equality, this is called vinaya.
If one can expound the meaning in this manner, they are called a bodhisattva capable of teaching the *vinaya*.
If this *vinaya* can know me, it is precisely the thorough knowledge of the *vinaya* of afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is called "knowing the Vinaya of the self"? It means:

contemplating non-self and contemplating the nature of the self; knowing the purity of the self and the reality of the self; knowing the differentiation of the self, the emptiness of the self, and the cultivation of the self; and knowing that the self is immovable, unspoken, unattached, and neither arising nor ceasing.
If one can understand the "self" in this way, it is precisely the thorough knowledge of the vinaya of afflictions (*kleśa-vinaya*).
It is likewise when one conceives the notion of a self where there is truly no self, or conceives the notion of afflictions where there are no afflictions;
if the self is fundamentally non-existent, afflictions are also thus.
"If one is fully endowed with vipaśyanā, one can thus observe and understand; this is called knowing the vinaya of my afflictions.
Afflictions do not exist in the past, future, or present; if one does not act toward them, does not dwell on them, and does not seek them, this is called knowing the vinaya of afflictions."

The Vinaya is likewise neither past, future, nor present; just as the mind is not form, being neither internal, nor external, nor in between, so too are the afflictions—not form, nor internal, nor external, nor in between.
Why is this? Because there is no cognition, no contention, no purification, and no conditioning.
If one can know in this way that all afflictions neither arise nor cease, this is called thoroughly understanding the vinaya of afflictions.
“Precious Daughter!
If a bodhisattva attains such knowledge of the vinaya of afflictions and also preaches this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva’s exposition of the vinaya.”
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Jewel Maiden was filled with great joy and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
The true meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, as well as the Vinaya, are inconceivable.
If there is a bodhisattva who can speak in this way, that person is able to truly know and truly see.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the Jewel Maiden:
"Now that you have already perfected such dharmas as these, are you able to expound them?
The Jewel Maiden replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra! True name is non-attachment; non-attachment is the meaning. Such a meaning is inexpressible, and that which is inexpressible is the Vinaya.”
"Venerable One! If it is thus, how can it be explained? Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Reality is cessation; cessation is the Dharma; the Dharma is purity; purity is meaning; meaning is the Vinaya.
Such dharmas as these have no words or letters. If there are no words or letters, how can they be spoken?
"Venerable One! Reality is suchness;
suchness is the Dharma; the Dharma is non-dual; non-duality is the ultimate meaning. Now, that which is non-dual cannot be regulated. If it cannot be regulated, how can it be called 'regulated'?"
“Such dharmas as these are all non-existent; if they are non-existent, how can they be spoken of? Śāriputra said:
“By virtue of what jewel have you now achieved this?”
"Is she who is given such a name truly called 'Jewel Woman'? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
There are thirty-two kinds of bodhisattva jewel-minds; within these minds, there is entirely no mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
What are the thirty-two?
First, the generation of the mind for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
Second, they resolve their minds so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed;
third, they resolve their minds to uphold the Buddha-dharma so that it does not perish;
fourth, they resolve their minds to protect and guard the Saṃgha.
Fifth, they resolve their minds to bestow upon sentient beings the joy of the sublime Dharma;
sixth, they resolve their minds to cultivate and accumulate great loving-kindness for all sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from the various sufferings of affliction;
seventh, they resolve their minds to cultivate and accumulate great compassion by relinquishing both internal and external things.
Eighth, they resolve to guard and uphold the precepts in order to subdue those who violate them;
ninth, they resolve to cultivate patience in order to destroy impatience, arrogance, malevolent minds, deranged minds, intoxicated minds, crazed minds, and the mind of heedless self-indulgence;
tenth, they resolve to exert diligence in order to shatter laziness, fear of retreat, and regretful minds, thereby subduing all sentient beings who are indolent.

Eleventh, they resolve to cultivate meditative concentration in order to destroy distracted minds, deranged minds, and false thoughts; to cause sentient beings to attain the four dhyānas and the eight liberations, and to subdue all sentient beings within the desire realm.
Twelfth, they resolve to cultivate wisdom to shatter all darkness, attaining true knowledge and vision as they enter the Dharma-realm.
Thirteenth, they resolve to know that sentient beings are equal and non-dual, for all are of one single flavor.

Fourteenth, they resolve their minds to attain freedom from greed and hatred; to remain undivided in mind amidst gain and loss, defamation and praise; to abide securely in wholesome dharmas, unmoved by suffering or pleasure; and for the sake of protecting sentient beings through such means as these.
Fifteenth, they resolve their minds to attain fearlessness and intrepidity, desiring to understand the profound twelvefold dependent origination and to depart from all views.
Sixteenth, they resolve their minds out of a desire to adorn their wisdom and merit with never-ceasing satisfaction.
Seventeenth, they resolve their minds desiring never to be separated from seeing the Buddhas and constantly hearing the Dharma;
eighteenth, they resolve their minds desiring to preach according to what they have heard;
nineteenth, they resolve their minds desiring to attain the vast collection of the Dharma without greed or stinginess.
Twentieth, they resolve their minds to praise pure precepts, abiding according to what they have heard, in order to teach, transform, and console those who violate the prohibitions;
twenty-first, they resolve their minds to shatter the seven kinds of pride of all sentient beings;
twenty-second, they resolve their minds to know the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
Twenty-third, generating the mind of enlightenment to destroy the evil karma of all Māras;
twenty-fourth, generating the mind of enlightenment to bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings;
twenty-fifth, generating the mind of enlightenment with the desire to shatter and eliminate all the sufferings of sentient beings, without the mind giving rise to regret.
Twenty-sixth, they resolve their minds for the sake of fully accomplishing and attaining the Buddha-dharmas;

twenty-seventh, they resolve their minds for the sake of knowing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and having known this, their minds do not abandon it nor do they feel weary or regretful;
twenty-eighth, they resolve their minds for the sake of joyfully cultivating and accumulating all factors conducive to enlightenment.
Twenty-ninth, they resolve their minds to perceive emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet do not realize [nirvana] for the sake of sentient beings;
thirtieth, they resolve their minds to protect all realms of existence even while fearing them;
thirty-first, they resolve their minds to see the faults of birth and death without becoming weary or regretful.

Thirty-second: They resolve their minds to experience supreme bliss upon approaching enlightenment, yet they renounce this sublime joy for the sake of sentient beings and instead undergo the suffering of poverty.
Śāriputra! These thirty-two jewels of the arousal of the mind are entirely devoid of the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; for this reason, the bodhisattva is called a "Gathering of Jewels."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Jewel Woman, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

You have spoken truly regarding the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. That bodhicitta accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit; it cannot be fully described by means of thirty-two matters alone."

Why is this? It is not by means of the jewel of the śrāvaka that one can obtain the jewel of the Buddha; it is not by means of the jewel of the pratyekabuddha that one can obtain the jewel of the Buddha; it is only by means of the jewel of the bodhisattva that one can obtain the jewel of the Buddha.
"Having obtained the Jewel of the Buddha, one then obtains the Jewels of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas; for this reason, the Bodhisattva is called a 'Gathering of Jewels'.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"What the Jewel Maiden has spoken is inconceivable; as I observe her discourse, it appears that this maiden has attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is only now that you say this maiden has not yet attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge!"
"This woman has long since accomplished and perfected [these qualities].
The words of this Jewel Woman’s teaching on the Dharma are inexhaustible; its phrases, meanings, and flavors are likewise inexhaustible.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the Jewel Woman:

“Virtuous One, you should now extensively analyze and explain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), so that they may accomplish their purpose regarding all phenomena. “Venerable Sir,
the bodhicitta is called the ‘unimpeded word.’”
Why is this? Because the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) encompasses all meanings, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid);
because the entire dharma-realm enters into the mind of awakening, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
To speak of words when, in reality, there are no words is called the unimpeded knowledge of dharma (dharmapratisaṃvid);
to speak of the ineffable Dharma without interruption is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
The meaning being ineffable is called non-obstruction regarding meaning;
all phenomena being like illusory appearances is called non-obstruction regarding phenomena;
the absence of verbal activity is called non-obstruction regarding expression.
To be without obstruction regarding the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) is called the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
To thoroughly comprehend the meaning is called the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);
to delight in tranquility is called the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
The fact that characters do not deviate from the dharmas and the dharmas do not deviate from their meanings is called the unimpededness of dharma and meaning (*dharmārtha-pratisaṃvid*).
That which is spoken is sound; this is called the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is the very meaning of bodhi; this is called the unimpededness of dharma and meaning.
The meaning of *bodhi* is that which can give rise to phenomena; this is called the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Phenomena can be formulated into phrases; this is called the unimpededness of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
Having spoken, one attains the meaning; this is called the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
The meaning of the Dharma is called unimpededness regarding names;
liberation is called unimpededness regarding phenomena;
and the exposition of the characteristics of dharmas as being without intrinsic nature is called unimpededness regarding language.
To discern the dharma-realm and that which is not the dharma-realm is called the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
That the Saṅgha is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);
that all members of the Saṅgha share a single flavor is called the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
Because of the harmony of the Saṃgha, it is called the unimpededness of diction;
because of expounding the merits of the Saṃgha, it is called the unimpededness of eloquence.
O Virtuous One!
"These four kinds of unimpeded knowledge pervade all dharmas.
At that time, Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!"
“How long has it been since this woman first resolved her mind [on enlightenment]?
Under which Buddha did she plant these various roots of goodness?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vibhaktadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land was named Mahāviśuddha, which was like the Tuṣita heaven. He was accompanied by a community of seventy-six thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were pure in their brahma-conduct and had attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of non-retrogression."
"At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Pure Virtue Retribution (Śubhavarṇavipāka), who ruled over a thousand worlds with sovereign power.
He had eighty-four thousand ladies of the inner palace and a full complement of a thousand sons, all of whom possessed strength equal to that of the Lotus-Wielding Malla."

At that time, for thirty-six thousand billion years, the holy king made various kinds of offerings to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, namely: dwellings, bedding, clothing, food and drink, and medical provisions for the sick and infirm.
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One,
I wonder how long the lifespan of that Buddha will be?”
“Śāriputra! That Buddha’s lifespan will last for ten full intermediate kalpas.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, together with his harem, retinue, court ladies, and ninety-two trillion nayutas of subjects from outside the palace, will bring various kinds of immeasurable and boundless offerings and proceed to the place where the Buddha dwells.”
He scattered eight thousand billion exquisite and precious jewels over the Buddha, prostrated with his head at his feet, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Regarding the articles of offering I have now prepared, is there perhaps any other more excellent offering that surpasses mine?
At that time, the Buddha replied: "Great King!"

There is another form of offering that surpasses all other offerings; compared to this offering, all other offerings do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a ten-thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of offering is this?"
"I wish to hear it with joy; I only pray that you will speak of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with exquisite jewels, and one were to take them and offer them as a gift,..."
Though one possesses such immeasurable merit, it is not equal to the generation of bodhicitta out of compassion.
Even if one were to offer pure and exquisite flowers and incense to as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges across immeasurable billions of eons,
such merit would still not equal the seven steps taken after generating the mind of enlightenment.
Such a resolve to awaken is itself giving; It is also morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom.
If one generates this great mind out of compassion, Its merit is immeasurable and inexhaustible.
One who possesses supreme physical power and wealth, supreme lineage, and is able to give rise to bodhicitta—such a person rules over a thousand worlds up to the Brahma heaven;
only one who has attained great sovereignty is able to give rise to it.
If one joyfully resolves to attain bodhicitta, one will thus be able to sever the existence of evil;
one can open the path of rectitude for humans and devas, and close off the treacherous, perilous paths of the eight difficulties.
Possessing all faculties complete, neither blind nor deaf, This is entirely due to generating bodhicitta with a sincere mind;
One can behold the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions And hear the flavor of the nectar of the heavens.
If one can wholeheartedly resolve upon Bodhicitta, this person can shatter doubt and arrogance;
attaining mastery over immeasurable wisdom, they are able to expound the Dharma-realm for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings regard him as their parents, And likewise cherish him with the thought of a skilled physician or a friend;
He can heal the afflictions and diseases of sentient beings, Instructing and exhorting them to advance upon the path to Bodhi.

At that time, when the Holy King heard the Buddha speak of the merit obtained from generating the bodhicitta, his heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation. Together with his retinue and the people both within and without his realm, he all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I have therefore generated this bodhicitta.
If one wishes to attain great sovereignty, One must not regress in this life.”
In the measureless cycle of birth and death, one undergoes suffering and affliction, yet it brings no benefit to oneself or others;
it would be better to give rise to this resolve and endure great hardship than to remain without such resolve and experience worldly ease.
If there are sentient beings who resolve upon Bodhicitta, they shall immediately obtain the bliss of gods, humans, and noble kings;
they shall also obtain the bliss of tranquil, untainted liberation, as well as the bliss of unsurpassed Bodhi.
The samādhi of supreme wisdom-patience, Possessing the four immeasurables and the six perfections,
The three kinds of pure wisdom and the six supernormal powers, The four unhindered knowledges and great mastery,
The unsurpassed ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, As well as the three foundations of mindfulness and great compassion.
Accomplishing and perfecting the eighteen dharmas— All such things arise from the arousal of bodhicitta.
One can shake all worlds throughout the ten directions, And also know the minds of sentient beings in the ten directions;
One can deliver immeasurable sentient beings— All this arises from the arousal of the bodhicitta.
"Śāriputra! When these verses were spoken, forty thousand ladies and immeasurable sentient beings all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the holy king again made offerings to that Buddha for ten billion years; having finished making these offerings, he grew weary of the world and left the household life.
Once he had gone forth, he contemplated four propositions:
first, the proposition of reality; [and so forth].
Second, the phrases of the Dharma;
third, the phrases of meaning;
fourth, the phrases of discipline—having constantly contemplated the meaning of these four phrases for one hundred million years.
“Śāriputra, you should know: was the Wheel-Turning Sage King of that time anyone other than this very Jewel Woman?”
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!
By what karmic conditions has she received this female body?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
No bodhisattva ever takes birth through the karma of a woman; rather, it is solely by the power of their supernormal knowledges and wisdom that they manifest in a female body!”
It is for the sake of taming all sentient beings.
Śāriputra, do you truly think that the Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī is a woman? Do not form such a view.
Why is this? To receive a female body is itself the power of wisdom and the power of supernormal faculties. Śāriputra!

This woman has long since been free from the bodies of male and female throughout immeasurable kalpas; such a body belongs neither to the past, nor to the future, nor to the present. This body is a body of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyakāya*). By means of this body of skillful means, she has inspired ninety-two thousand women in this world to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, she manifests this body of skillful means.
At that time, the Jewel Woman said to Śāriputra:
"Virtuous One!
Are you now able to preach the True Dharma with this female body?"
Śāriputra said: “I have already conceived weariness and regret even for this male body, how much more so for a female body!
[The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!...”
"Do you feel revulsion and regret regarding this male body? Śāriputra replied, "It is so, it is so."
“Venerable Sir! For this reason, the bodhisattva surpasses all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like. Why is that?
That which you, the śrāvakas, loathe and regret, the bodhisattva experiences with joy and without regret.
While the śrāvaka seeks not to be born in any realm of existence, the bodhisattva willingly accepts and delights in them.
Śrāvakas give rise to the notion of contentment regarding all merits, whereas Bodhisattvas have no sense of satiety.
Śrāvakas feel weary of and seek to leave afflictions, whereas Bodhisattvas dwell within them without fear.
Śāriputra said: “Precious Woman!
What kind of power does a bodhisattva possess, by virtue of which their mind never experiences weariness or aversion?”
The Jewel Maiden replied:
"Virtuous One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses eight kinds of power, through which they never grow weary.
What are the eight?
First is the power of loving-kindness, because the mind is without obstruction;
second is the power of compassion, for the sake of subduing [sentient beings].
Third is the power of reality, because it does not deceive the Buddhas, oneself, or sentient beings;
fourth is the power of wisdom, because it is free from afflictions;
fifth is the power of skillful means, because the mind has no regrets.
Sixth is the power of merit, because it is free from fear;
seventh is the power of wisdom, because it destroys ignorance;
eighth is the power of diligence, because it overcomes negligence.
"These are called the eight powers.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these eight powers, his mind feels no regret. Śāriputra said:
“Precious Daughter!
Have you now fully perfected the eight powers? She replied:

“Venerable One! That which is called ‘endowment’ is itself inversion; inversion is itself the two marks; the two marks are themselves the conditioned; the conditioned is itself non-existence; and non-existence is itself equality.”
Venerable sir!
If they are equal, how can one have power and the other lack power?
How can one speak of the numbers one or two? "Venerable One!

All dharmas are like space. And this space cannot be said to be internal, nor can it be said to be external; it cannot be said to be light, nor can it be said to be darkness. All dharmas are likewise so."
If all phenomena are identical to empty space, how can one speak of strength, weakness, or the numbers one and two?
"Virtuous One!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses both strength and weakness."

What is power? What is lack of power? There is no power of afflictions, but there is the power of wisdom; no power of stinginess, but there is the power of generosity; no power of breaking precepts, but there is the power of upholding precepts; no power of anger, but there is the power of patience; no power of laziness, but there is the power of diligence; no power of distracted mind, but there is the power of meditative concentration; no power of ignorance, but there is the power of wisdom. For this reason, the bodhisattva distances himself from unwholesome dharmas and cultivates and accumulates wholesome dharmas.
"Therefore, the Bodhisattva possesses no power of unwholesome dharmas, but possesses the power of wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Jewel Woman, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"If there are good sons or good daughters who can speak in this way, they are speaking the truth.
When the Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī spoke this Dharma, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the mind of patience (kṣānti).
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Five.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty at Guzang.
Chapter Three, Part Two: The Chapter on the Jewel Maiden.
At that time, the Jewel Maiden again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As it is said in the sutras, regarding the Tathāgata who is endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*): is the World-Honored One identical to these ten powers, or does the World-Honored One exist apart from the ten powers?
If the World-Honored One were identical to the ten powers, this would constitute two distinct dharmas; if there were two, they would be impermanent.
If the World-Honored One existed apart from the ten powers, how could the Tathāgata say that all dharmas are equal?
World-Honored One!
If a single power contains the ten powers, why does the Tathāgata not speak of a hundred powers?
If he does not speak of a hundred, one should know that a single power is neither ten nor a hundred.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Jewel Woman, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is neither one nor two.
If he is neither one nor two, why speak of ten?
Why speak of a hundred?
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by remaining detached from both the one and the two.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is neither identical to the ten powers nor separate from the ten powers; yet he is able to expound upon the ten matters, and for this reason, the Tathāgata is said to be fully endowed with the ten powers.
"Although the Tathāgata speaks of these ten powers, within each single power there are contained immeasurable powers; it is for the sake of dissemination that he speaks of them as 'the ten powers.
The Jewel Maiden spoke again: "Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will extensively explain these ten powers.
The Buddha said to the Jewel Maiden:
"Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall analyze and explain this for you.
Jewel Woman!
When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, it is impossible that they would seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas or commit evil deeds."
By means of this firm resolve, at the time of attaining bodhi, he accomplishes the first power.
Because the Tathāgata has accomplished such power, he utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and is able to turn the wheel of Dharma;
such a wheel of Dharma cannot be turned by devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!
When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they understand that all karmas are in fact a single karma.

By this power, they understand all past, future, and present karmas, as well as their causes, conditions, bases, and what constitutes a non-base; when they attain enlightenment, they achieve the second power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, he discerns the faculties of sentient beings; having known them, he teaches the Dharma.
By the power of this, when he attains enlightenment, he accomplishes the third power."
“Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, he contemplates the realm of sentient beings; having contemplated it, he teaches the Dharma in accordance with that realm. Because he contemplates the realm, when he attains enlightenment, he achieves the fourth power.”
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, he observes the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; having observed them, he teaches the Dharma according to their understanding. Because he knows their understanding, when he attains enlightenment, he achieves the fifth power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they contemplate the path that leads to the destination—whether it be the conditioned path, the unconditioned path, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva. By virtue of this contemplation of the path, when they attain enlightenment, they perfect the sixth power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, he reveres and honors the cultivation of various meditative concentrations (dhyāna). For the sake of disciplining sentient beings, he expounds the essential points of the Dharma; because of this cultivation and accumulation, at the time he attains enlightenment, he achieves the seventh power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they do not disparage past roots of goodness; they achieve mindfulness and do not become negligent. Because they are not negligent, when they attain enlightenment, they perfect the eighth power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they do not give rise to a mind of contempt toward those who have not yet studied; having already studied themselves, they do not give rise to arrogance. They are able to bestow upon sentient beings the light of wisdom, and because they bestow this light, when they attain enlightenment, they achieve the ninth power."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they teach all sentient beings to distance themselves from the phenomena of outflows (*āsrava*) so that they do not increase; they praise liberation and the cultivation of the path free from outflows, and they also preach the path free from outflows for the sake of sentient beings. Because they cultivate the path free from outflows, when they attain enlightenment, they achieve the tenth power."
“Precious Daughter!
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates these ten powers, they are able to fully possess the ten kinds of power of a Tathāgata.
Precious Daughter spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
By practicing what dharmas do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique dharmas?
The Buddha told the Jewel Woman:
"When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they do not give rise to greed or stinginess regarding the sublime Dharma they have attained, nor do they think:
'If I teach this to another, they will surpass me.'"

"His mind is impartial toward all sentient beings; he is able to relinquish both internal and external things as gifts to all, and he observes the dharma-realm as being devoid of diverse characteristics.
By these causes and conditions, when he attains bodhi, he achieves the first fearlessness."
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they clearly understand all factors that obstruct the path. Because they understand them clearly, they do not engage in or follow such obstructing factors; nor do they praise them or teach others to do so. Having recognized the obstructing factors, they remain far removed from them."
By these causes and conditions, when they attain bodhi, they achieve the two forms of fearlessness.

Furthermore, Jewel Woman, when a bodhisattva practices the path to bodhi, they constantly cultivate the pure path and constantly preach the pure Dharma; because they cultivate and adorn themselves to attain the pure Dharma, they thus adorn themselves through both personal cultivation and by teaching sentient beings.
By these causes and conditions, when one attains Bodhi, one achieves the three fearlessnesses.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to Bodhi, they never give rise to a mind of arrogance; they never claim for themselves 'I know' or 'I see,' nor do they conceal their virtues or expose their faults."
By these causes and conditions, when they attain Bodhi, they achieve the four fearlessnesses.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to Bodhi, they show the correct path to sentient beings who have lost it; they remove tiles, stones, and thorns from the road; they construct bridges over dangerous and impassable fords; they provide lamps and illumination in places of darkness; and upon seeing those who have committed offenses, they are able to subdue them."

They are able to remove all doubts and regrets of sentient beings; they do not insist that those who have not committed an offense have done so, thereby eliminating the minds of sentient beings that harbor doubts regarding the Dharma. They bestow the light of the Dharma, exhorting others to preach it, and upon seeing those who preach the Dharma, they praise them, saying "Excellent! With reverence and respect, they do not give rise to thoughts of contempt.
They desire to understand the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, and they do not look down upon those who speak incorrectly.
By these causes and conditions, when one attains Bodhi, one achieves the first perfection of being without fault.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to Bodhi, they speak words that are truthful, words that accord with the Dharma, words that accord with the meaning, words spoken at the proper time, words that are disciplined, words that are unerring, words free from all evil speech, and the speech of the noble ones."

Having heard the Dharma, they in turn explain it to others for the sake of their own benefit and the benefit of others; when speaking, they do not disparage [the teaching] nor give rise to contention. They place faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and cause sentient beings likewise to have faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, while contemplating that all dharma-realms are ineffable.

By these causes and conditions, when they attain Bodhi, they will know all speech and obtain the skillful means of immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī; therefore, from every one of the marks and signs upon their bodies, and from every single pore, there shall issue the subtle and wondrous voices of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they constantly cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and also transform sentient beings, causing them to cultivate the six recollections.

By these causes and conditions, when they attain enlightenment, they do not lose their mindful mind; they also attain the skillful means of the dhāraṇī of dharma-realization. Thus, even if immeasurable sentient beings, over immeasurable eons, contemplate profound meanings and come to question [the Buddha] all at once, the Tathāgata does not rely on the power of deliberation, yet is able to answer each one simultaneously according to their respective questions."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they constantly protect the minds of all sentient beings, refraining from creating causes for their distracted minds or causes for their various sufferings and afflictions;
when they see sentient beings practicing wholesome dharmas, they do not obstruct or disturb them."
They skillfully know that all phenomena are entirely like illusory forms; their minds are impartial toward all sentient beings, and they know that all dharma-realms are of one single flavor.

By these causes and conditions, when they attain Bodhi, their minds are always in samādhi. They attain the skillful means of boundless hearing and dhāraṇī; having attained this retention, their minds remain constantly in samādhi as they perform the Buddha-work.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, their perceptions are non-perverted and their mind is non-perverted. Because they are non-perverted, within the state of non-self, they do not form notions of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a person, a human, a male, a female, pride, afflictions, permanence or annihilation, existence or non-existence, good or evil, defilement or purity, the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing, the mundane and the supramundane, birth-and-death and nirvana;
it is because all sentient beings possess perversion that they have such notions.
If there is no inversion, then there is no such perception, and one proceeds by way of the Middle Way.
For this reason, when attaining Bodhi, one achieves a single perception and is free from dualistic perceptions.
By practicing this samādhi, one attains the skillful means of the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible vessel.

By the power of this retention, the mind constantly cultivates and accumulates the samādhi of non-conceptualization; out of compassion for sentient beings, one cultivates and accumulates great compassion, preaching the Dharma without ceasing.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they cultivate and accumulate the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), relinquishing suffering, pleasure, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, lack of joy, lack of grief, lack of attachment, and lack of aversion."

By these causes and conditions, their minds remain undivided by gain or loss, praise or blame; they constantly contemplate impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and likewise transform sentient beings to cultivate such equanimity.
By these causes and conditions, when one attains Bodhi, it is called "Great Renunciation" (*mahopekṣā*).
Having attained this renunciation, one obtains the skillful means of the *dhāraṇī* known as the "Ocean Seal.

By the power of this retention, although one receives the respectful offerings and veneration of humans, devas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, and Brahmā, one does not feel any joy therein.
When people with wrong views treat them with contempt or insult them, they do not feel resentment.
Their minds are impartial, like earth, water, fire, and wind—neither rising nor falling, neither moving nor turbid—as they cultivate great loving-kindness and compassion.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they seek with a sincere mind the various roots of goodness within the profound dharma of enlightenment, and do not seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas."
One cultivates and gathers such states of mind as great compassion, without ever regressing.

By these causes and conditions, at the time of attaining bodhi, one fulfills the aspirations of a Tathāgata, which neither increase nor decrease; one attains the *dhāraṇī* of the Vajradhvaja and achieves great sovereignty.
They know how to speak, they know what is spoken, they know when to speak, they know where to speak, and they know for which sentient beings they speak.
Furthermore, O Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they are always diligent and energetic, never knowing satiety regarding all wholesome dharmas; they reverently serve and make offerings to their preceptors and virtuous friends, and they also constantly associate with them, delighting in hearing the true Dharma and retaining it exactly as they have heard it.

Such diligence is for the sake of taming sentient beings, for the desire to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, and to cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain the Unsurpassed Way, as well as to enable them to obtain such diligence and enter the Dharma-gate.

By these causes and conditions, they attain the skillful means of the dhāraṇī of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, when a bodhisattva attains bodhi, they achieve such irreducible diligence, and through this diligence, they become fully endowed with supernatural powers (abhijñā).
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they fulfill the faculty of mindfulness and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, contemplating the body—both internal and external—as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; and they do the same for sensation, mind, and phenomena."

He cultivates the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness for the sake of the Tathāgata-body; while contemplating the application of mindfulness to the body, he does not realize liberation.

By these causes and conditions, when he attains Bodhi, he achieves the undiminished mindfulness of the Tathāgata and gains the supernormal power of knowing the mind. He knows the faculties, elements, inclinations, karma, afflictions, habitual tendencies, and mental states of all sentient beings; the roots of goodness and unwholesome roots, the arising and ceasing of karmic retribution, the successive stages of existence, the various Buddha-worlds, the assemblies of the various vehicles, and the bodhisattva practices leading to the bestowal of predictions. He knows his parents, kinsmen, teachers, and preceptors—knowing such things as these, his mindfulness never fails.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they constantly cultivate wisdom that is sharp, swift, boundless, profound, liberating, pure, immovable, unimpeded, and unsurpassed; they fully comprehend the wisdom of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as supreme wisdom and insatiable wisdom, being endowed with such wisdoms as these."

Seeking wisdom and seeking the Dharma, upholding the Dharma and expounding the Dharma, they take sweet delight in the Dharma; because of this delight in the Dharma, they do not give rise to greedy attachment toward internal or external things.

Toward their teachers and preceptors, they are able to endure all manner of suffering, offering them whatever items they require as gifts. For the sake of the meaning of even a single word or a single phrase, they are able to offer the precious treasures of the worlds of the ten directions to the masters of the Dharma, and for the cause of a single verse, they would sacrifice their own lives.
Though one might practice generosity for immeasurable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is not equal to the joy arising in the mind upon hearing even once of the matter of Bodhi.

One who delights in hearing and speaking of the True Dharma will always be held in the thoughts of all Buddhas and devas; by the power of that mindfulness, they will be able to thoroughly penetrate all the sutras and treatises existing in the world.
By these causes and conditions, when one attains Bodhi, the Buddha-wisdom realized is neither increased nor diminished; such wisdom as this is called "unimpeded.

It knows the minds of sentient beings—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; with outflows or without outflows; mundane or supramundane; defiled or pure phenomena; birth-and-death or Nirvana; all dharma-gates, all matters of Bodhi, all paths to Bodhi, all worlds, all kalpas, and all atoms, throughout the past, future, and present.
Being unimpeded in penetrating such matters and inexhaustible in their exposition, for these reasons, the Tathāgata is able to expound immeasurable teachings within a single dharma.

"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they do not delight in remaining at home to seek the five desires; rather, they delight in dwelling in seclusion to cultivate the dharma of renunciation. They delight in cultivating profound meanings and the three gates of liberation. By the power of such cultivation, they attain the dharma-gate of non-obstruction and unhindered wisdom. They transcend the realm of Māra and become fully adorned with its ornaments; they remain far removed from afflictions and all evil views. They expound the most profound meanings to shatter the doubting minds of the multitude, eliminate all evil thoughts and reflections, and destroy the realms of desire, form, and formlessness."

For sentient beings who are greedy, he expounds the True Dharma to cause them to leave greed behind; for those who delight in anger, he expounds the mind of loving-kindness to cause them to leave hatred behind; for those who are deluded, he explains the twelve links of dependent origination to cause them to leave ignorance behind; for those who are stingy and greedy, he explains the *dāna-pāramitā*; for those who break the precepts, he explains the *śīla-pāramitā*; for those who are wrathful, he explains the *kṣānti-pāramitā*; for those who are indolent, he explains the *vīrya-pāramitā*; for those with distracted minds, he explains the *dhyāna-pāramitā*; and for those lacking wisdom, he explains the *prajñā-pāramitā*.

"For ordinary persons, he teaches the Four Noble Truths; for those who hold perverted views, he teaches impermanence, impurity, suffering, and non-self; and for those bound by fetters, he teaches the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."

When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with such dharmas as these, by virtue of these causes and conditions, at the time of attaining bodhi, they achieve liberation that is neither increasing nor decreasing. Such liberation cannot be shaken; it is ultimately pure and ultimately liberated.

They are able to know and see all the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they also attain the skillful means of pure dhāraṇī; by the power of this retention, they are able to expound liberation and attain great mastery over all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they revere wisdom and thereby attain the power of wisdom and the radiance of wisdom.
They know the wisdom regarding retinues; they know the mind free from greed; they know the mind free from hatred; they know the mind free from..."
With a mind of delusion, he knows the mind free from attachment, knows the mind free from defilement, knows the mind free from contention,
knows the mind free from nutriment, knows the mind free from greed, knows the unsurpassed mind, knows the unobstructed mind,
knows the indeterminate mind, knows the wholesome mind, knows the unwholesome mind, knows the evil mind, and knows the pure mind.
He knows the impure mind; he knows the great mind and the small mind, the narrow mind and the broad mind, the pervasive mind and the non-pervasive mind;

he knows the greedy mind and the renunciant mind, the mind that upholds the precepts and the mind that violates the precepts, the patient mind and the impatient mind, the lazy mind and the diligent mind, the concentrated mind and the distracted mind, the deluded mind and the wise mind, and the ordinary mind.
The noble mind: the mind of the group of those fixed in rightness, the mind of the group of those fixed in error, and the mind of the group of those not fixed;

the mind of the śrāvaka, the mind of the pratyekabuddha, and the mind of the bodhisattva; and the mind of the truth of suffering, the mind of the truth of the origin, the mind of the truth of cessation, and the mind of the truth of the path.

"Although he knows this, he does not realize it for himself; rather, in order to discipline sentient beings, he constantly preaches the True Dharma—namely, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
He remains far removed from the view of nihilism and the view of a self, teaching that causes and effects arise from conditions, and do not depend upon a self, a person, a life-force, or a soul."

One understands that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations; volitional formations are the condition for consciousness; consciousness is the condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the condition for contact; contact is the condition for feeling; feeling is the condition for craving; craving is the condition for clinging; clinging is the condition for existence; existence is the condition for birth; and birth is the condition for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and the mass of affliction. Through the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; through the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; through the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; through the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and the mass of affliction cease—the great mass of suffering ceases.
Having made this contemplation, he further reflects:
"Such phenomena as these are truly not created by a self, nor by sentient beings, a life-force, or a person; they are neither eternal nor annihilated."
If it is not produced by sentient beings, persons, or the like, this is called emptiness.
That which is empty is devoid of self, sentient beings, life-span, and persons; it is neither eternal nor annihilated.
Being neither eternal nor annihilated, it is without arising and without ceasing.
That which is without arising or ceasing is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
that which is not subsumed within the three periods of time is termed "non-existence";
as such non-existence, it cannot be calculated or numbered.
Because it is beyond calculation, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
that which is the ultimate truth is the speech of the Tathāgata;
that which is the speech of the Tathāgata is free from contention.
"The absence of strife is called the dharma of a śramaṇa;
the dharma of a śramaṇa is itself space.
To be able to understand such dharmas as these is called true knowledge.
"If one contemplates and reflects thus: 'From various unwholesome conditions, ignorance arises, leading up to this entire mass of great suffering;
with the cessation of unwholesome reflection, ignorance ceases, and so on, until this entire mass of great suffering ceases.'"

Having performed this contemplation, one does not cling to the view of eternalism nor cling to the view of nihilism; one knows that all phenomena arise from conditions and cease from conditions, and one knows that all phenomena are devoid of self, sentient beings, life-span, or personhood, seeing neither "this" nor "that," nor anything in between.
Why is this? If there were neither "this" nor "that," how could there be "middle"?
For this reason, the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma in this way.
By these causes and conditions, at the time of attaining Bodhi, one achieves the wisdom of liberation, which neither increases nor decreases, and also attains boundless *dhāraṇī* skillful means.

Because of this mastery, one contemplates the realm of space based upon the *dharmadhātu*, expounding what is possible and what is impossible, up to the power of the exhaustion of outflows, the four fearlessnesses, and great kindness and great compassion. One proclaims the profound treasury of secrets and simultaneously transforms sentient beings through these teachings; this is called that which is not shared with the two vehicles, wherein the body, speech, and mind are fully endowed with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, all bodily actions follow wisdom; they do not deceive sentient beings or create obstacles for them. They are without greed or stinginess and harbor no harmful intent. Their pure conduct is pristine as they diligently cultivate vigor, gathering the factors conducive to enlightenment without sparing their own body or life, giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings."
By these causes and conditions, when one attains bodhi, one is called a Tathāgata; all bodily actions follow the movement of wisdom, and one attains the skillful means of the *dhāraṇī* of all lights.

By the power of this upholding, one is able to manifest various bodies through skillful means—namely, the bodies of devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Brahmās, Śakras, the Four Heavenly Kings, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Having manifested such various bodies, one preaches the Dharma to the great assemblies according to their inclinations.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he immediately vanished and became invisible, so that the entire assembly did not know where he was;

or, after his body had vanished, he would continue to preach the Dharma, such that all sentient beings could gaze upon him with their six sense-faculties without ever feeling satiated, and when they could no longer see him, their minds remained constantly focused on him in recollection.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, all vocal actions follow wisdom; they do not deceive sentient beings. They avoid false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. They always speak words that are peaceful and secure, words of Dharma, words of Vinaya, words that are not feverish, words of the Buddha, words of meaning, words pleasant to hear, and words delightful to behold."
By these causes and conditions, when one attains bodhi, one is called a Tathāgata whose all vocal actions follow wisdom, and one obtains the skillful means of the threefold dhāraṇī.
By the power of this retention, one skillfully understands the languages of all sentient beings and explains all the karmic actions of those beings.

The words spoken by the Buddha are words of truth, words of the twelve links of dependent origination, words of liberation according to circumstances, words of non-attachment, words of tranquility, and words of causal conditions.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, all mental actions follow wisdom; they do not deceive sentient beings, nor are they envious or harmful. They do not harbor false views but cultivate right view, giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity. They never forget the mind of enlightenment and, being endowed with wisdom, they cast aside arrogance."
By these causes and conditions, when one attains bodhi, one is called the Tathāgata whose every mental action accords with wisdom, having obtained the skillful means of the stainless dhāraṇī.
By the power of this retention, while abiding in a single state of mind, one is able to know the various minds of all sentient beings.
One observes that the minds of all sentient beings are entirely equal, like illusory transformations, pure by nature;
one observes that the physical actions of all sentient beings are equal, all being like the moon reflected in water.

They see all sentient beings within their own bodies, and their own bodies likewise within the bodies of sentient beings, appearing like reflections; they are able to cause all sentient beings to become Buddha-bodies and their own bodies to become the bodies of sentient beings, such that nothing whatsoever can move or alter this.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they have faith in the wisdom of the Buddhas of the past and possess no net of doubt regarding their excellence of physical, verbal, and mental karma."
If one hears that the Buddha’s deeds are inconceivable, one is neither startled nor terrified.
One has faith that the sentient beings of the worlds of past Buddhas have already been tamed;

one has faith that the Tathāgata’s body travels through the worlds of the ten directions with unimpeded coming and going, is able to understand the languages of all sentient beings, and preaches the Dharma to them according to their various needs.

Possessing unimpeded wisdom regarding all three periods of time, they thoroughly understand all dharma-realms and all vehicles of the past; they possess the supernormal power of knowing the karmic fruits of all sentient beings and the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding such matters as these, he possesses faith in his heart without doubt, and he also transforms sentient beings so that they likewise share his faith.

By these causes and conditions, when he attains Bodhi, he is called the Tathāgata whose wisdom regarding the past is unimpeded; because he previously cultivated and accumulated the *vīryavanta-samādhi* (the samādhi of courageous vigor), he obtained the *vikrāntagāmin-dhāraṇī* (the dhāraṇī of heroic stride) and its skillful means.

By the power of this retention, one is able to know the lifespans and lineages of all past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; one also knows the karmic fruits, supernatural powers, and activities of all past bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings.

One also knows all past kalpas—those in which a Buddha appeared and those in which none appeared—as well as their names, whether pure or impure, extensive or narrow, coarse or subtle, like a mote of dust, and whether inverted or sequential. Regarding all such matters, one attains complete understanding as clearly as if observing an *āmra* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they have faith in the wisdom of the Buddhas of future ages and possess no net of doubt regarding their virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind."
If one hears that the Buddha’s activities are inconceivable, one does not give rise to fear or alarm.
One believes that all sentient beings in future worlds shall be tamed;

one believes that the Tathāgata travels through the worlds of the ten directions with unimpeded coming and going, is able to understand the languages of all sentient beings, and preaches the Dharma for them according to their various capacities.

His wisdom regarding all three periods of time is unimpeded; he thoroughly understands all realms of phenomena and all vehicles in the future; he knows the karmic fruits and supernormal powers of all sentient beings; and he possesses the knowledge of others' minds. He has faith and is free from doubt regarding such matters as these, and he also transforms sentient beings, causing them to share his same faith.

By these causes and conditions, when one attains Bodhi, one is called the Tathāgata whose wisdom regarding the future is unimpeded; through the cultivation of the samādhi of compassion, one attains the skillful means of the Lion’s Roar Dhāraṇī.

By the power of this retention, one is able to know the lifespans and lineages of all future Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; furthermore, one knows the karmic fruits, supernormal powers, and [the states of] all sentient beings, including future bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

He also knows all future kalpas—those in which a Buddha appears and those in which no Buddha appears—as well as their names, whether pure or impure, broad or narrow, coarse or subtle, like a mote of dust, and whether inverted or upright; he thoroughly understands all such things as if looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When a bodhisattva practices the path to enlightenment, they have faith in the wisdom of the Buddhas of the present age and possess no net of doubt regarding their excellent deeds of body, speech, and mind."
If one hears that the Buddha’s deeds are inconceivable, one is neither startled nor terrified.
One believes that all sentient beings in the worlds of the present Buddhas have been fully tamed;

one believes that the Tathāgata’s body travels through the worlds of the ten directions with unimpeded coming and going, able to understand the languages of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma to them according to their various needs.

His wisdom regarding all three periods of time is unimpeded; he thoroughly understands all dharma-realms and all vehicles of the present, knows the karmic fruits and spiritual powers of all sentient beings, and possesses the knowledge of others' minds. Regarding such matters, his mind has faith and no doubt, and he also transforms sentient beings so that they share the same faith as himself.

By these causes and conditions, when one attains bodhi, one is called the Tathāgata whose wisdom regarding the present world is unimpeded; through the cultivation of pure concentration, one obtains the skillful means of the Vajra-dhāraṇī.

By the power of this retention, one is able to know the lifespans and lineages of all present Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; one also knows the karmic fruits, supernatural powers, and the states of all present bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings. One also knows all present kalpas—those in which a Buddha appears and those in which none appears—including their names, whether pure or impure, broad or narrow, coarse or subtle, like a mote of dust, and whether inverted or sequential. Regarding all such things, one is able to understand them completely, as if looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of one’s hand.
"O Jewel Woman!
These are called the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses another unique quality, namely, the invisible crown of the head."
Why is this? Because his body is boundless and there is no one who can surpass him, it is called an "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because all things are fully present therein, those who see them are relieved of their afflictions; this is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this so?
Because his body is like a medicinal tree, he dwells among the multitude without fear; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because all things are pure, one is without timidity when among the assembly; this is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this?
Because of the four fearlessnesses,
knowing the minds of sentient beings is called an unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because he teaches the Dharma according to his will, his assembly remains tranquil; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because he follows the instructions of his teacher, his speech is pure; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because he does not speak meaningless words, whatever he proclaims causes those who hear it to rejoice; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because he is free from the notions of enemy and friend, the sound of his preaching the Dharma is heard equally by all; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?

Because there is no other benefit [to be gained], each person perceives the Buddha standing directly before them; while gazing upon him, their eyes never blink—this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this so?
Because the body is inconceivable.
To hear what the Buddha has taught and thereby give rise to the sprouts of goodness is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because they have accomplished immeasurable virtues, those who behold them never tire of doing so; this is called an "unshared quality" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because he has awakened to all phenomena, he turns his entire body to look back as an elephant king gazes; this is called an unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because his deportment is pure, he utters the great lion’s roar; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because he is endowed with great power, his deportment is purely virtuous; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because all bodily actions follow wisdom, his verbal actions are purely wholesome; this is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this?
Because all verbal karma proceeds in accordance with wisdom,
all eyes are called the "unshared dharmas" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because all mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, sentient beings delight in hearing them; this is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this so?
Because his speech is subtle and exquisite, he receives supreme offerings; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because it is the unsurpassed field of merit,
its inexhaustible qualities are called the "unshared dharmas" (āveṇika-dharmas). Why is this?
Because they do not seek karmic retribution, nothing can destroy them; this is called the "unshared dharma" (āveṇika-dharma). Why is this?
Because each and every joint possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa, his records are not false;
this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this so?
Because he knows all the faculties, he is the teacher of all; this is called an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because it penetrates all things, its life-span is inexhaustible; this is called an uncommon dharma (āveṇikadharma). Why is this?
Because they have attained the Dharma-body, those who draw near to them obtain great benefit; this is called the uncommon dharma (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because they have accomplished all wholesome dharmas, the wisdom they attain cannot be defiled; this is called an unshared dharma (*āveṇika-dharma*). Why is this?
Because the nature of the wisdom that knows the three periods of time is pure, those who shed the Buddha’s blood incur the five heinous crimes; this is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this?
Because they have accomplished all roots of goodness, their habitual tendencies of affliction are exhausted; this is called the "unshared dharma. Why is this?
Because he thoroughly understands the causes of all afflictions,
his knowledge of all conditioned phenomena is called an uncommon dharma. Why is this?
Because they awaken to all dharmas,
Jewel Woman!
This is called the unique quality of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Jewel Woman again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for the thirty-two marks attained by the Tathāgata, by what karmic causes and conditions are they accomplished?”
The Buddha told the Jewel Woman:
"The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable merit; therefore, he has attained the thirty-two marks.
Of these immeasurable matters, I shall now speak briefly."
Because the Tathāgata wholeheartedly upholds the pure precepts, he attains the mark of level soles;
because he practices various deeds of giving, he attains the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel;
because he does not deceive any sentient beings, he attains the mark of high heels.
Because he protected the True Dharma, he obtained the mark of long, slender fingers;
because he did not disrupt the assemblies of others, he obtained the mark of webbed hands and feet;
because he offered exquisite garments as gifts, he obtained the mark of soft hands and feet.
Because of giving pure food and drink as alms, one obtains the mark of the seven parts being full;
because of delighting in hearing the Buddha-dharma, one obtains the mark of the antelope-like calves;
because of concealing the faults of others, one obtains the mark of the concealed organ.
Because he cultivated wholesome dharmas, he attained the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion;
because he constantly transformed sentient beings through wholesome dharmas, he attained the mark of the collarbones being level and full;
because he rescued and protected those in fear, he attained the mark of the arms and elbows being rounded and fleshy.
Because he delighted in assisting others in their undertakings, he obtained the mark of hands that reach the knees;
because he constantly practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, he obtained the mark of a pure body;
because he constantly gave medicine to the sick, he obtained the mark by which all food appears as it reaches the throat.
Because he constantly generates adornments by cultivating wholesome dharmas, he attains the mark of lion-like jaws;
because his mind is impartial toward all sentient beings, he attains the mark of forty teeth;
and because he reconciles disputes, he attains the mark of closely set teeth.
By the gift of rare treasures, one obtains the mark of even teeth;
by the purity of body, speech, and mind, one obtains the mark of two white canine teeth;
and by guarding against the four faults of speech, one obtains the mark of a broad and long tongue.
Because he has accomplished immeasurable merit, he attains the mark of having the supreme flavor among all flavors;
because he always speaks with gentle words toward sentient beings, he attains the mark of the Brahma-voice;
because he has cultivated and accumulated a mind of loving-kindness, he attains the mark of deep blue eyes.
Because he sought unsurpassed bodhi with a sincere mind, he obtained the mark of the dewlap of a bull-king;
because he praised all the merits of others, he obtained the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows;
because he reverenced his parents, teachers, elders, and preceptors, he obtained the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
Because he delights in expounding the profound Dharma, he attains the mark of a supple body;
because he gives bedding and seats, he attains the mark of golden light;
because he stays far away from congregating to discuss worldly affairs, he attains the mark of a single hair growing from each pore.
Because he delighted in the instructions and admonitions of virtuous friends and teachers, he obtained the mark of body hairs that curl upward;
because he did not inflict evil upon sentient beings, he obtained the mark of hair as golden and lustrous as refined gold;
and because he constantly exhorted sentient beings to cultivate samādhi, he obtained the mark of a body as perfectly symmetrical as a nyagrodha tree.
Because he creates images of the Buddha wherever he is born, he attains the mark of Nārāyaṇa’s strength.
Jewel Woman!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such immeasurable merits, he obtains these thirty-two marks.
The Jewel Maiden spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable.”
"How wonderful!
The Tathāgata has excellently expounded the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Jewel Maiden, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Just as you have said, all sentient beings who hear this meaning shall immediately attain the fulfillment of immeasurable merit.”
"Those who hear this and believe it shall likewise achieve immeasurable merit.

When this Dharma was spoken, the ten directions of immeasurable and boundless worlds shook in six ways; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The devas in the void rained down various kinds of flowers and played manifold musical instruments as an offering to the Buddha.

If there are sentient beings who have planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, they shall then hear of these ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the unique dharmas, and the thirty-two marks.
Having heard this, such a person is able to give rise to deep faith; having gained faith, they are able to roar the lion’s roar within the great assembly and preach such a Dharma. Why is this?
Inferior persons are unable to hear such true Dharma; even if they should hear it, they will not necessarily gain faith.

Superior persons, who are fully endowed with the observance of precepts and wisdom, are able to hear it; having heard it, they revere and believe it, and having believed it, before long they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Jewel Woman spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha is inconceivable; the Dharma and the Saṅgha are likewise inconceivable; and hearing and believing this sutra is also inconceivable.”
"If there are those with faith, such persons will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva practice the practice of the Dharma?"

“O Jewel Woman! A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abandon his kin and old friends; he recognizes kindness and repays it, feeling compassion for all beings. He never forsakes those who come to him for refuge, and with a sincere heart, he contemplates the path to Bodhi. He cultivates patience, practices what is difficult to give, and gathers in sentient beings. With a compassionate mind, he guards the precepts, reflects upon the meaning of the good, upholds the True Dharma, delights in the Dharma, is mindful of the Dharma, maintains the Dharma, and rejoices in tranquility.”

Dwelling alone in seclusion, his mind was free from regret or retreat; he skillfully protected the purity of the body, speech, and mind of sentient beings; for the sake of the four immeasurables, he donned the great armor of adornment; and he constantly exhorted sentient beings toward the path of Bodhi.

In all their discourses, they first praise the Mahāyāna; they do not first grant someone permission and later feel regret; they purify their conduct, being contented and possessing few desires; they are neither stingy nor envious, never severing the lineage of the sages; their minds are free from contention, and they thoroughly understand cause and effect.

One should possess faith, learning, ethical discipline, generosity, shame, and wisdom; draw near to virtuous friends and follow the instructions of teachers and elders; be free from arrogance in mind; pay respectful homage to those who are senior and endowed with virtue; remain detached from greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as from the notions of "I" and "mine"; and constantly keep in mind the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, generosity, ethical discipline, and the devas.

When receiving offerings, his mind does not become elated; he constantly and diligently practices the six pāramitās and the skillful means of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He does not perceive the marks of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, or a person. He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma-path.

"Furthermore, one who practices the Dharma has no eye, no forms, and no mental formations regarding the perception of forms; no ear, no sounds, and no mental formations regarding the perception of sounds; no nose, no odors, and no mental formations regarding the perception of odors; no tongue, no tastes, and no mental formations regarding the perception of tastes; no body, no tangibles, and no mental formations regarding the perception of tangibles; no mind, no phenomena, and no mental formations regarding the perception of phenomena."

The practice of non-form, the practice of neither form nor non-form, the practice of suffering regarding non-form, the practice of neither suffering nor non-suffering regarding non-form, the practice of self regarding non-form, the practice of neither self nor non-self regarding non-form, the practice of emptiness regarding non-form, the practice of neither emptiness nor non-emptiness regarding non-form, the practice of signlessness regarding non-form, the practice of wishlessness regarding non-form, the practice of non-practice regarding non-form, the practice of nature regarding non-form, the practice of reality regarding non-form, the practice of tranquility regarding non-form, the practice of arising regarding non-form, the practice of departure regarding non-form, the practice of causes and conditions regarding non-form, and the practice of aggregation regarding non-form—these are called the practice of dharmas. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
“Precious Daughter!
