“Venerable One!
It is not because of the activity of the eye that it is called the holy life (brahmacarya); it is not because of the activity of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind that it is called the holy life.
It is not because of the activity of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena that it is called the holy life.”
Furthermore, because it does not proceed by way of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, it is called the Brahma-faring.
It is neither sign nor condition; it is neither seen nor heard; it is neither known nor cognized.
"Venerable One!
Such dharmas as these have no going, coming, or abiding; they are without pulling or dragging, without measure or number, and without high or low. This is called the holy life (brahmacarya)."
Subhūti said: “Good son! That which is called ‘brahma-faring’ (brahmacarya) is the Eightfold Noble Path.”
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said: "Virtuous One!
Why is the Eightfold Noble Path called the Brahma-faring?"

If one takes right view as the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then not seeing any phenomena is called right view; seeing all phenomena with equanimity is called right view; the very seeing of non-seeing is what is named right view.
If one does not see, how can it be called right view?
If there is no right view, how can it be called the holy life (brahmacarya)?
That which is without mental application is called right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa).
Indeed, conceptualization is called inversion; if it is an inversion, how can it be called right conceptualization?
All sounds are entirely equal—whether good or evil, one or two, past, future, or present, whether they be all syllables or all noises—these are called echoes.
If it were an echo, how could it be called correct speech?
As for the equality of sounds: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and nirvāṇa is tranquility.
If one can equally contemplate all dharmas as having the characteristic of nirvana, and can expound this, it is called right speech.
There is no body and no bodily action; no mouth and no verbal action; no mind and no mental action.
Why is this? Because there is no locus for karma.
If there were a locus for karma, then there would be "I" and "mine"; if there were no "I" and "mine," then there would be no fruit of karma.
If one contemplates in this manner, it is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

If one would otherwise engage in wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*) for the sake of sustaining life, by distancing oneself from such wrong livelihood, it is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). If one contemplates these things as being without self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), and as being devoid of a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-force (*jīva*), or a person (*pudgala*).
If they do not exist, for what reason are they called "right livelihood"?

When one does not give rise to defiled attachment toward forms through eye-consciousness, the nature of eye-consciousness is empty; because the nature of consciousness is empty, the eye and forms are also empty. If the eye, forms, and consciousness are empty, this applies likewise up to the mind-consciousness and mental phenomena.
If one contemplates in this manner, it is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
Being free from inversion and severing all forms of striving is called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
There is no dharma of striving, no striver, no one who fully accomplishes striving, and no one for whom striving brings benefit.
If one can contemplate such dharmas as these, it is called right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).

If one can maintain equanimous mindfulness toward all dharmas as being equal to space, and if one understands that all dharmas are likewise so, and that the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are also like this—just as all dharmas are.
If one can contemplate such dharmas as these, it is called right mindfulness.
To contemplate all dharmas as entirely equal, being without self or what belongs to a self—if one can thus contemplate with equanimity, it is called right concentration.

"Venerable One! If one can thus contemplate the equality of the nature of all dharmas, this is called the Eightfold Noble Path; this is called the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya). It is not by way of number that it is called the Eightfold Noble Path;

it is not because the Eightfold Noble Path is itself called the Brahma-faring; it is not because it is a worldly path that it is called the Brahma-faring; it is not because of a mind of attachment that it is called the Brahma-faring; it is not because of dualistic marks that it is called the Brahma-faring; it is not because of the mark of conditioned activity that it is called the Brahma-faring. If one sees that all dharmas have no place of abiding, only then is it called the Brahma-faring."
At that time, while the Bodhisattva Animiṣa was preaching such dharmas of pure conduct to the great assembly, five hundred bhikṣus were freed from all afflictions and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Subhūti said: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
"Please explain this Dharma; it shall be no different from what is proclaimed by an Arhat who is free from afflictions. "Venerable One!

I am now likewise free from afflictions and am also an Arhat. I have likewise distanced myself from the afflictions and dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; because I abide in accordance with the Dharma, I am called an Arhat."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva Asaṃkṣepa possesses delightful, unimpeded, and inconceivable eloquence; with sharp wisdom, he answers whatever questions are posed to him."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa has attained the samādhi of mastery over all dharmas; for this reason, he is able to answer according to whatever question is asked.”
"If there is a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi, no one among the people, devas, māras, or brahmās of all the worlds will be able to obstruct their unhindered eloquence.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
If there are people who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, have fully perfected their merits, they will be able to see the Bodhisattva Animiṣa and hear what he teaches.
World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain to others, or even merely hear this sutra, and all of them resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that all such persons shall, like the Bodhisattva Animiṣa, let out the lion’s roar.
“World-Honored One!
I shall protect such persons as these.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!
You now protect and uphold the True Dharma with a sincere heart.”
At that time, the Brahma King again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I shall joyfully cultivate the samādhi of the meditative concentration on equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*). Renouncing the bliss of dhyāna-concentration, I shall come to protect the Buddha-dharma and its preachers, ensuring they are free from the suffering of illness. To whatever land there may be a place where the Dharma is being preached, I shall go there and listen with a sincere heart.”

If there be any land that believes in and accepts this sutra and makes offerings to the Triple Gem, I shall likewise eliminate all evil omens for them, causing that realm to be pure, peaceful, and governed by the True Dharma.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent,
Brahmā King!
"You are truly a protector of the Dharma.
If there is anyone who can protect the Dharma in this way, you should know that such a person will never be separated from the Treasures of the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, am able to protect those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain such a Dharma as this.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
One who knows the Dharma is indeed able to protect this Dharma. Having heard the Dharma from me, you have immediately attained the Dharma-eye and severed all evil paths.”
"If one further protects and upholds the True Dharma with a sincere mind, one shall before long sever all forms of existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold such a sutra as this, and extensively explain its meaning for the fourfold assembly."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to receive and uphold such a sutra exactly as the Buddha has spoken it, without any difference, and shall extensively proclaim, explain, and analyze it for the fourfold assembly.”
At that time, the great assembly of humans, devas, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard the sutra, rejoiced and praised it, saying: "Excellent!"
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Seven;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty at Guzang.

Chapter Five: The Chapter on Bodhisattva Sāgaramati (Part One) At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Great Jewel Enclosure between the realms of desire and form, surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, the great trichiliocosm was filled with water as if it were a vast ocean, like when the calamity of water at the end of an eon arises.

Yet, all the worlds—the countries, towns, villages, cities, dwellings, mountains, forests, and trees—up to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), remained entirely unharmed and just as they were before; nevertheless, the entire great assembly saw this water.

At that time, immeasurable *puṇḍarīka* flowers emerged from the water, with stems of blue lapis lazuli and petals of pure gold; they had pedestals of merit-gems and stamens of Śakra’s jewels, surrounded by many countless flowers.
Measuring ten *li* in length and breadth, they stood within the jeweled monastery, reaching a height of one *tāla* tree.
At that time, the great assembly each saw themselves upon these flowers; those flowers then emitted a great radiance, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the great assembly felt joy in their hearts, thinking:
"We shall surely now hear the supreme and wondrous Dharma.

Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt for a long time upon a lotus flower with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions is this great trichiliocosm filled with vast waters like a great ocean?

Furthermore, as when the calamity of water at the end of a kalpa arises, immeasurable *puṇḍarīka* flowers emerge, and their great radiance thus shines universally throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions?”
The Buddha said, “Maitreya! Below this world,
past as many worlds as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems, there is a world named Ratnavyūha.”

In that land there is a Buddha, titled Sāgarajñānarddhinirvṛtta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

There is a bodhisattva there named Sāgaramati who wishes to come here to this great jeweled pavilion together with countless bodhisattvas; having already severed all notions of numerical reckoning, he desires to come and hear this Mahāsannipāta Sūtra.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That buddha-world is extremely far from here; since Sāgaramati is there, would he be able to hear what this Buddha has spoken?"
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, just as you have now heard before me, so it was with them as well."
"Just as you and this great assembly behold me today, so too does the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati behold me.
"World-Honored One!

The supernormal powers possessed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inconceivable; though they dwell in infinitely distant worlds, they possess such unimpeded divine eye and unobstructed faculty of hearing."
World-Honored One!
Who, upon hearing of such inconceivable matters, would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Only those who are base, inferior, and unworthy would do so!

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, endowed with immeasurable power of supernatural faculties, vanished from that land in a single thought-moment and suddenly appeared within this Great Jewel Monastery.

He immediately entered into samādhi, causing this great assembly to see from afar all the inhabitants, cities, towns, villages, houses, palaces, mountains, forests, trees, birds, and beasts of that Buddha-world, as well as seeing that Buddha preaching the Dharma surrounded by his great assembly.

Having manifested these things, he arose serenely from samādhi, approached to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Then, with all the fragrant flowers and various musical instruments from his own world, he made offerings to the Buddha and spoke these words:
“The Tathāgata Jñānarddhivikrīḍita from the ocean of worlds below sends his greetings in measureless abundance.”
"Is the Tathāgata’s body and life, as well as the great assembly, all in peace and security?
Having spoken thus, he sat to one side upon a precious lotus flower.
At that time, there was a Brahmā King named Śubhakṛtsna (or Viśvabhū), who reflected thus:
"For what cause and condition does this great water exist, filling this trichiliocosm, yet it is not a calamity of water?
I shall now go and ask the World-Honored One."

He immediately went together with sixty-eight thousand Brahmās to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what cause and condition is this trichiliocosm filled everywhere with lotus flowers made of the seven precious jewels, with immeasurable bodhisattvas each sitting in succession upon these jeweled flowers, and the great waters filling the entire trichiliocosm?
The Buddha said to Brahmā:
“Good son! This is the power of the supernatural faculties of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati.”
The Brahmā said: “World-Honored One!
Has the Tathāgata’s teaching of this sublime scripture of the Great Assembly not yet been concluded?”
The Buddha said,
“Brahmā! The Tathāgata’s unhindered eloquence is inexhaustible.”

"Brahmā! The Buddha, together with a great assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas, contemplates the dharma-realm and discourses upon the dharma-realm; the subtle and wondrous joy of the dharma is likewise inexhaustible."
The Brahmā said: “World-Honored One!
Who is this Bodhisattva Sāgaramati of whom the Tathāgata speaks?”
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!
Do you not now see me seated upon a precious lotus flower, ten yojanas in length and breadth, which is revered and praised by all the bodhisattvas?”
"The radiance of his physical form and appearance is so brilliantly resplendent that none but the Tathāgata can equal him.
At that time, Brahmā, having seen this, immediately conceived a heart of reverence; he prostrated himself with his head at [the Bodhisattva's] feet and spoke these words:
"If anyone should behold such a True Being (samyaksatpuruṣa), they would obtain great benefit; my meeting with him now is likewise so."
“World-Honored One!
How long will this True Dharma remain?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Just as this True Dharma is like the lifespan of the Tathāgata, so too shall these bodhisattvas protect this Dharma after my parinirvāṇa. Why is that?
“This sutra is the seal of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and manifested the power of his own wisdom. In order to inspire faith in the great assembly and to adorn this sutra, he spoke these verses:
“In lands below as numerous as atoms, There is a Buddha, Honored One of Ocean-like Wisdom and Supernatural Powers.”
Constantly expounding the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, I have heard it, been able to receive it, and shall explain it to others.
I have now come into this great assembly to make offerings and pay respect to the Honored One of Ten Powers,
as well as the bodhisattvas who are his retinue, in order to shatter the subtle doubts within the Dharma.
I now pay homage to the Most Unsurpassed One, making the highest offerings according to the Dharma;
desiring to adorn supreme Bodhi, I shall transform sentient beings through the Unsurpassed Way.
If one contemplates all forms as being without marks, and is likewise able to sever and abandon the three types of sensation;
if there is neither appearance nor seed-nature, such a person can pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one is not greedily attached to "self" or "what belongs to self," And further cultivates and accumulates the Middle Way,
Contemplating all phenomena as being like space— Such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one does not greedily cling to various sense objects, And is likewise able to bring the internal sense bases to stillness,
Not giving rise to attachment toward any realm of phenomena— Such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one perceives the Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body, One can raise the unsurpassed great banner of Dharma;
Seeing all phenomena as having the nature of an illusion, Such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one perceives neither giver nor receiver, and likewise neither agent nor recipient;
if one is free from both right view and wrong view—such a person can pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Neither fixed within enlightenment, nor determined to remain in birth-and-death,
having distanced themselves from all afflictions— such a person is able to pay homage to the Tathāgata.
If one cultivates wholesome dharmas with a sincere mind, purifying the three karmas of body, speech, and mind,
and is likewise able to subdue the various sense faculties, such a person can pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one endures that all phenomena are without self, yet does not abandon sentient beings for the sake of attaining bodhi,
but maintains pure precepts for the sake of bodhi— such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one contemplates all phenomena as being like a mirage, and views sentient beings as equal to space,
with a pure mind free from conceptualizing thoughts— such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Undergoing great suffering for the sake of all sentient beings, practicing patience for the sake of Bodhi,
and contemplating all phenomena as like the moon in water— such a person is able to pay homage to the Perfectly Awakened One.
Observing that there is no self, life-force, or person, yet cultivating bodhi for the sake of sentient beings;
observing that all phenomena possess the characteristic of perishing moment by moment—such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Though undergoing the sufferings of hell, their resolve does not waver; they apply themselves with diligent vigor to cultivate and gather the Path.
Hearing that all phenomena are empty, their minds are not afraid; such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Unimpeded in all spheres of experience, like one moving their hand through space,
and perceiving the equality of the characteristics of the three times— such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If Māra cannot know their mind, this person can attain great supernormal powers;
if they preach the Dharma with inexhaustible words and meanings, this person can pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
If one can hear the voices of all Buddhas everywhere, and having heard them, receive and uphold them and proclaim them widely,
seeing no marks of distinction among the Three Jewels— such a person is able to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The Tathāgata is endowed with the six pāramitās; Like space, he has no coming or going.
He clearly understands the realms of all sentient beings; Therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The Tathāgata has accomplished great merit, And never gives rise to even a semblance of pride;
I now pay homage to the Buddha’s physical form, Which the world and its inhabitants cannot create.
The Buddha’s light surpasses all other lights, And his mind is sublime and most supreme.
All sentient beings cannot see [the Buddha’s] crown; therefore, I pay homage to all the Victorious Ones.
The Tathāgata knows the understandings of all sentient beings and expounds the Dharma according to those understandings;
he is able to know the remedies for afflictions—therefore, I pay homage to the World-Honored One.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati had praised the Buddha with verses, he descended from the air and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a few questions; I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me leave to do so."
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
"World-Honored One!"
I have previously heard that there is a samādhi called the Seal of Purity; if a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will expound this samādhi, so that all bodhisattvas may hear it universally; having heard it, they shall all adorn their practice for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Listen with a sincere mind and attend closely; I shall now speak."
"Good son! It is like a pure jewel that has been polished and refined by a craftsman; its value is immeasurable and it is held in high esteem by all people. Good son!"

Once a bodhisattva has first resolved upon awakening, they cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas through extensive hearing and reflection. They observe the dharma-realm and purify their initial resolve; once that initial resolve is purified, they are revered and remembered by all buddhas and bodhisattvas, and they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
“Good son! A pure jewel is free from nine kinds of impurities. What are these nine?
First, the nature of gold;
second, the nature of silver;
third, the nature of lapis lazuli.
Fourth, the nature of crystal;
fifth, the nature of agate;
sixth, the nature of lotus.
Seventh, the nature of musāragalva;
eighth, the nature of ratna-guṇa;
ninth, the nature of coral—these are called the nine.

Free from these nine natures, it is called a pure jewel, its value being immeasurable; it is utilized by the wheel-turning sage kings, and the radiance of this jewel cannot be matched by any other light.

“Good son! It is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), attains the Samādhi of the Pure Seal by departing from nine kinds of natures.
What are these nine?
First, the nature of ordinary persons;
second, the nature of those who practice through faith;
third, the nature of those who practice through the Dharma.
Fourth, the nature of the eight patiences;
fifth, the nature of the srotāpanna;
sixth, the nature of the sakṛdāgāmin;
Seventh is the nature of an anāgāmin;
eighth is the nature of an arhat;
ninth is the nature of a pratyekabuddha.

Free from these nine natures, one enters the lineage of the Buddhas and attains the Samādhi of the Pure Seal; because of its purity, it surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, bestowing light upon all sentient beings.
"Good son! A pure jewel can withstand being ground, pierced, and pressed; therefore, this jewel is called 'without flaw. Good son!"
The Samādhi of the Pure Seal is also like this.
"Good son, what is the Samādhi of the Pure Seal?

They cultivate and assemble the three types of precepts and are endowed with the ten wholesome dharmas; they practice loving-kindness and compassion, feeling pity for sentient beings. When seeing the affairs of others, they go personally to manage them. They cherish all beings, cultivating a mind of equanimity and purity, and constantly keep sentient beings in mind. They gather in all beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), maintain focused mindfulness of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) to subdue the sense faculties, and possess few desires and contentment so as not to sever the noble lineage. They cease all strife and litigation, destroy arrogance, and respectfully honor their teachers, preceptors, elders, and senior monastics. They do not disparage others, seeking the Dharma and protecting the Dharma while remaining far removed from unwholesome dharmas. Their faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha remains unshakable.

The mind constantly takes all wholesome dharmas as its object of contemplation; it does not praise itself but always extols the virtues of others. It recognizes kindness and repays it, purifies all modes of deportment, and possesses patience. It seeks *śamatha*, cultivates *dhāraṇī*, and maintains a mind equal to wind, earth, water, fire, and space. It always delights in leaving the household life to cultivate and accumulate tranquility, upholds the precepts with diligence, draws near to virtuous friends, and purifies the sense faculties.

The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unimpeded; they contemplate impurity to destroy the fetters of greed, cultivate a heart of loving-kindness to break down enmity and attachment, and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination to destroy ignorance. They remain far removed from all obstructive dharmas, bestow the Dharma without stinginess, and fully accomplish the six pāramitās.

They do not seek other vehicles; they contemplate the faults of birth and death with inner and outer purity; their resolve for the path to bodhi never regrets or regresses; and they teach and transform sentient beings within the Mahāyāna.

"Good son! When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with such dharmas as these, purifies both the pure and impure intentions, and resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called a 'precious jewel'."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"If one cultivates and accumulates the mind of great compassion, And fully perfects the ten wholesome dharmas, Such a person will certainly behold Maitreya Buddha; Therefore, the bodhicitta is inconceivable."
Cultivating and gathering great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, And constantly teaching and transforming others in the Mahāyāna,
Practicing the mind of equanimity to eliminate afflictions— Therefore, the bodhicitta is inconceivable.
Fully cultivating and gathering mindfulness and wisdom, And being able to subdue one's own mind, One can practice contentment and few desires; Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Distant from all unwholesome dharmas, With a mind gentle toward sentient beings,
Increasing all wholesome dharmas— Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Reverently making offerings to one's teacher and preceptor, Successively inheriting and increasing the noble lineage,
And remaining far removed from all forms of pride— Therefore, the bodhicitta is most supreme.
Their minds are upright and free from deception; they always delight in tranquility while transforming sentient beings.
Having eliminated arrogance, they do not slight others; therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.

One who upholds the True Dharma can hear and expound it; transforming all sentient beings to leave afflictions behind, they single-mindedly and with a sincere heart focus on the Unsurpassed Vehicle. Therefore, the Bodhicitta is supreme.
Making offerings to the Triple Gem and believing in the Four Truths, Staying far removed from all evils and cultivating wholesome dharmas,
Being free from anger and malice toward sentient beings— For these reasons, the bodhicitta is supreme.

When adventitious afflictions arise, one feels shame and remorse; One immediately confesses before the Buddhas of the ten directions, Cultivates and accumulates wholesome dharmas, and disciplines the faculties; Therefore, the bodhicitta is most supreme.
Purifying body, speech, and mind, one understands the fruits of karma; Knowing gratitude and mindfulness of kindness, one knows how to repay it;
With faith in the twelve links of dependent origination, one purifies one’s deportment; Therefore, the bodhicitta is most supreme.
Possessing śamatha and cultivating wisdom, Fully maintaining the precepts and delighting in bodhi, The mind remains unmoved even amidst great suffering; Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Their mind is as impartial as the four great elements, They regard all sentient beings as like space;
Always delighting in leaving home to cultivate bodhi, Therefore, the bodhicitta is most supreme.
Delighting in tranquility, one purifies body and mind; practicing the conduct of the Dharma, one contemplates the Four Noble Truths.
With speech that is truthful, in accordance with the Dharma, and expressive of ultimate meaning—for these reasons, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Abiding securely while teaching the Dharma, Diligently cultivating vigor to destroy the works of Māra,
And never being indolent regarding the qualities one cultivates— Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.

By drawing near to virtuous friends, one attains the Buddha’s bodhi; One can cross the ocean of birth and death for all sentient beings, And purify all six sense objects; Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.

Far removed from obstacles, having eliminated the five hindrances, With the faculties purified and free from pride, It is the antidote to greed, hatred, and delusion; Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Observing with right reflection and a mind endowed with mindfulness, Cultivating the aids to enlightenment and attaining supernormal powers,
Fearless toward birth and death, delighting in nirvāṇa— Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Whatever Dharma one preaches is not for the sake of food; one’s mind is free from stinginess regarding all dharmas;
one practices wholesome dharmas without seeking reward; therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
One does not gather sentient beings through other vehicles; rather, one causes them to accept and uphold the various joys that are taught.
Because their minds are immeasurable and boundless, the bodhicitta is therefore supreme.
Pure within and without, free from fault, One does not fear birth and death while cultivating bodhicitta;
When cultivating bodhicitta, the mind feels no regret— Therefore, the bodhicitta is most supreme.
Knowing the realms of sentient beings and purifying their lands, one adorns enlightenment not for oneself, but to show the right path to deluded beings; therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
Thoroughly knowing the true nature of the dharma-realm, Inconceivable non-conceptual wisdom can shatter the fearful thoughts of sentient beings; Therefore, the bodhicitta is supreme.
If one can be fully endowed with such qualities, this is the pure generation of the bodhicitta;
it cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas, nor likewise by the afflictions or the works of Māra.
If there is one who can generate the bodhicitta, they shall thus surpass all vehicles.
It can purify the minds of all sentient beings, and it can also expound the unsurpassed path.
"Good son! What is meant by the bodhicitta being pressed down yet not destroyed?"

The one who presses [the seal] is named Great Compassion; he takes all sentient beings as his object, ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is inherited and never severed. For the sake of the Buddha-dharma, he adorns his roots of goodness, purifies the world with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and protects the True Dharma without begrudging his own body or life.

“Good son! If you are struck, touched, troubled, disturbed, or harmed by evil sentient beings, you should endure it all. Furthermore, you should not abandon any sentient being; your mind should be free from regret, free from sorrow, and free from vexation, as you apply yourself with diligent vigor to discipline sentient beings.”
If one encounters insults, anger, or physical assault, one should accept them in silence and never retaliate, reflecting thus:
"The Great Vehicle does not contend with the world."
Why is this? All sentient beings follow the current of birth and death, whereas the Dharma of the Mahāyāna flows against the current of birth and death;
all sentient beings engage in mutual strife and litigation, whereas the Dharma of the Mahāyāna destroys contention and strife.
All sentient beings are ablaze with anger and hatred, whereas the Dharma of the Mahāyāna extinguishes the mind of anger;
all sentient beings are each deceitful and false, whereas the Dharma of the Mahāyāna is upright and free from falsehood.
If there are sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who, with various weapons and staves, pursue a bodhisattva and say:
"Whoever has resolved upon this bodhicitta, I shall cut their body into pieces like sesame seeds!"

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva never retreats from the mind of enlightenment, nor does he ever relinquish loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; nor does he abandon generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects:

"Throughout immeasurable and boundless lifetimes, I have taken on the bodies of those in the great hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; I have practiced unwholesome dharmas, and thus have been unable to benefit myself or others."
If, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I were pursued by wicked people with swords and staves and had my body dismembered limb by limb, I would never abandon the bodhicitta nor all sentient beings.
Why is this? If I am unable to endure such sufferings within this world, how could I possibly endure the various sufferings of hell?
When practicing wholesome dharmas, many unwholesome dharmas arise as obstacles; if I do not endure them, how can I perform these various wholesome dharmas?
When all sentient beings inflict evil upon me, I shall surely bestow the wholesome Dharma upon them;
when sentient beings inflict weapons, staves, abuse, or insults upon me, I shall bestow upon them the unsurpassed Great Patience.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can contemplate and reflect in this manner, it should be known that before long they will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having contemplated thus, they are able to endure the three oppressions, namely those of body, speech, and mind.
"What is 'pressing the body'?
If a bodhisattva’s body is being dismembered, at that time they comply with the evil person according to the Dharma, fully accomplishing the six pāramitās."
How does a bodhisattva, when their body is being dismembered, fulfill the six pāramitās?
If a bodhisattva, when their body is being dismembered, does not begrudge their own life or limb, at that time they fulfill the dāna-pāramitā;
if they cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness toward those evil persons, at that time they fulfill the śīla-pāramitā.
When one does not become angry, does not revile others, and does not retaliate with evil deeds, at that time one fulfills the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
When one practices diligence (*vīrya*) for the sake of all sentient beings and never abandons the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), at that time one fulfills the perfection of diligence.
If others should strike or revile them, their mind remains unmoved; they do not lose right mindfulness, and their intention remains pure.
At that time, one fulfills the dhyāna-pāramitā;
contemplating the body as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, like grass, trees, tiles, stones, and the like, at that time one fulfills the prajñā-pāramitā.
Having fully perfected these six *pāramitās*, one remains unbroken even under pressure; this is called "pressing the body.
What is "pressing the mouth"?

It is to endure all evil speech, insults, and revilements—whether true or false—and to blame only one's own afflictions and fetters rather than harboring resentment toward others, while cultivating and accumulating compassion for all sentient beings.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates such patience while enduring abuse and insults, he immediately attains the fulfillment of the six pāramitās.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva encounters verbal abuse and humiliation, he reflects thus:

"This person, due to the causes and conditions of stinginess and greed in past lives, and by associating with evil friends, has acquired this wicked mind. I, however, have destroyed stinginess and greed, cultivated and accumulated the practice of giving, and associated with virtuous friends; therefore, I am able to relinquish this anger."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, fully endowed with the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), when encountering insults and abuse, reflects thus:

"This person has broken the precepts and does not believe in the retribution of karma; for this reason, he reviles me. I, however, uphold the precepts and believe in the ripening of karmic results; therefore, I cultivate patience, remain mindful of bodhi, protect and maintain the True Dharma, and act in accordance with sentient beings."
At that time, being fully endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva encounters abuse and insult, they reflect:

"This person is indolent and does not cultivate wholesome dharmas; for this reason, they revile me. I shall apply myself with diligent vigor to cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas, abandon all thoughts of anger, and never feel satiety regarding these wholesome dharmas. I must now employ great skillful means: first, I shall cause this person to sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and only thereafter shall I attain the fruit of enlightenment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, fully endowed with the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), when encountering abuse and insult, further reflects:
"This person has lost mindfulness, is deranged, negligent, and defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*); I shall now destroy all afflictions and give rise to the bodhicitta for the sake of such evil beings."
If all sentient beings were already completely pure, for what further reason would I have generated the bodhicitta?
Therefore, I shall single-mindedly focus my thoughts on the bodhicitta without any distraction.
At that time, being fully endowed with the perfection of dhyāna, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters insults and abuse, he further reflects:

"This person clings to 'I,' 'mine,' sentient beings, life-span, and the person (pudgala). I rely upon the dharma-realm; within the dharma-realm, who is there to insult and who is there to receive it? Furthermore, I do not perceive even a single dharma that constitutes the insult or the insulter."
At that time, one is fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one can wholeheartedly receive, uphold, and practice the five *pāramitās*, then at that time one is fully endowed with the *kṣāntipāramitā*; this is called "restraining the mouth."
"What is meant by 'pressing down the mind'?

It is not fearing the hosts of Māras as to retreating from the bodhicitta; it is not fearing any of the various heterodox and erroneous views as to retreating from the bodhicitta; it is not fearing the manifold sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals as to retreating from the bodhicitta."
If one sees a Buddha image approaching and it speaks these words:

"You are likewise unable to resolve upon bodhicitta; the path to enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain. It would be better for you to early cultivate the vehicle of the śrāvakas and quickly realize nirvāṇa to enjoy great peace and bliss."
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he immediately reflected upon whether the path to bodhi was difficult or easy:
"I shall never retreat; I will certainly reach the foot of the Bodhi tree and sit upon the diamond throne."
In the past, I already made a request to all sentient beings, promising that I would bestow the Dharma as a gift upon them.
Since I have not yet given it to them now, how could I deceive them?
I shall act in accordance with the mind of all Buddhas.
"To endure such matters that press upon the mind, and not to deceive the Buddhas, the great assemblies of devas and humans, nor one's own self—this is called 'pressing upon the mind'.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The mind toward the path to Bodhi is indestructible, And so too are Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion."
Furthermore, they do not sever the lineage of the Three Jewels, but cultivate immeasurable adornments for the sake of Bodhi.
For the sake of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
they have relinquished wealth and practiced giving throughout immeasurable ages, and likewise endured all manner of great suffering and affliction.
To attain the various merits of the Triple Gem, they uphold and extensively expound the True Dharma;
to deliver sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death, they are thus able to endure all manner of suffering.
Though the wicked beings of the worlds in the ten directions Should seize me with swords and staves and threaten my person,
My mind shall never waver nor lose its Bodhi; Out of compassion for all sentient beings,
I shall endure suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable kalpas, Neither seeking self-benefit nor the benefit of others.
Now this patience of mine brings great benefit, and it shall also enable me to attain the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues.
Even if my body were crushed for the sake of the Buddha’s merits like sesame seeds, my mind would feel no regret;
my heart would never retreat from the Unsurpassed Way, and I would undergo manifold sufferings for the sake of Bodhi.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one should remain mindful of bodhicitta;
with a mind that is tranquil and free from afflictions, if the desire to give rise to anger toward sentient beings arises, one should first hold oneself and one's own afflictions in contempt.
Enduring all manner of sufferings within the three evil realms, for the sake of all sentient beings attaining the Buddha-way,
they do not seek the pleasures of humans or devas, but joyfully accept all sufferings for the sake of the multitude.
Whatever suffering one undergoes among human beings does not equal even a hundred-thousandth part of that in hell;
though one may endure immeasurable suffering in the three evil realms, one shall never retreat or lose the bodhicitta.
Contemplating that the body is impermanent and without self, Its nature of the four elements being like four venomous snakes,
One who wholeheartedly relinquishes such a body Will be able to attain the unsurpassed path of wisdom.
Wandering through the various realms of existence, they undergo all manner of suffering because they are unable to contemplate the true nature of the body;
the Bodhisattva, however, is able to contemplate the true nature of the body, and therefore remains forever free from all afflictions and distress.
When practicing evil there is no hindrance, yet in cultivating wholesome dharmas there are many obstacles;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bear witness to this, and for this reason I undergo various sufferings.
I am now able to endure such things—immeasurable sufferings of body, speech, and mind;
by these causes and conditions, my bodhicitta is firm and ultimately unshakable.
Sacrificing the body to fulfill the six pāramitās, one is without greed for the body and thus fulfills dāna;
Giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward those evil persons, one thereby fulfills śīla;
Being able to endure the cutting of the body without giving way to anger, by these causes and conditions one fulfills kṣānti.
When experiencing suffering, the mind does not waver; therefore, one is fully endowed with *vīrya*.
Without losing mindfulness, one delights in tranquility; therefore, one is fully endowed with *dhyāna*.
Contemplating that the body is without self and without what belongs to a self; at that time, one is fully endowed with *prajñā*.
If I can achieve such adornment, I shall surely attain the Unsurpassed Way before long;
if I cannot endure the karma of harsh speech, how could I destroy the manifold afflictions?
If I discipline my body, speech, and mind, Then I shall be able to endure all the oppressions of suffering;
I shall be able to destroy all the hosts of Māras, And though there be many heterodoxies, I shall remain unmoved.
If you wish to fulfill the perfections, the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata,
and obtain the unsurpassed, priceless jewel, you should train in the discipline of body, speech, and mind.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘piercing the bodhicitta’?

Once a bodhisattva has already generated the bodhicitta, they never give rise to a semblance of pride (*māna*). They do not cling to the bodhicitta, do not crave the bodhicitta, do not love the bodhicitta, and do not dwell upon the bodhicitta. In this way, they are able to bring the mind to stillness and contemplate the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and all the Buddha-dharmas.”

The profound realm of reality (dharmadhātu) refers to the twelve links of dependent origination being free from the two extremes; it means that the nature of all phenomena is inherently selfless, and when observing the nature of the self, one sees that the nature of all phenomena is empty and without a master, abiding in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

He knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are devoid of volitional construction; he contemplates form as being like foam, sensation like a bubble, perception like a mirage, formations like a plantain tree, and consciousness like an illusion. He contemplates the elements (*dhātu*) as inactive and unwavering, the sense bases (*āyatana*) as being like the deaf and blind, and the mind as having no momentary abiding. Thus, the fetter of pride finds no place to arise.
All dharmas are non-dual and without discrimination; they are of one flavor, one vehicle, one path, and one source.
One contemplates all sounds as being devoid of the characteristic of sound; all vocalizations are sequential and do not coalesce, and all dharmas are inexpressible.

One thoroughly understands the characteristic of suffering; one knows that there is no "mine" in the origin [of suffering]; one finds no increase in cessation; and one knows the ultimate nature of the path, because it is free from obstruction.
One contemplates the mindfulness of the body, knows feelings of the past and future, maintains mindfulness of the arising and ceasing of the mind, and knows the dharma-realm.
Observing that the elements (dhātu) are not elements, one thus cultivates right effort;
desiring to attain mastery, one thus cultivates the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
Being free from all afflictions is called the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya).
Delighting in tranquility is called the faculty of diligence;
because it is not [merely] mindfulness, it is called the faculty of mindfulness;
because it is not [mere] reflection, it is called the faculty of concentration.
To be far removed from all things is called the faculty of wisdom;
to not follow others is called the power of faith;
to be without obstruction is called the power of diligence.
Because it is non-retrogressive, it is called the power of mindfulness;
because the mind attains mastery, it is called the power of concentration;
because it does not discriminate between good and evil, it is called the power of wisdom.
Because of non-laxity, it is called the awakening factor of mindfulness;
because of entering into all phenomena, it is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena;
because of acting in accordance with the Dharma, it is called the awakening factor of energy.
Because it is far removed from evil, it is called the factor of enlightenment of joy;
because body and mind are tranquil, it is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility;
because it knows the true samādhi, it is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
Not observing duality is called the awakening factor of equanimity;
being far removed from all views is called right view;
and being free from all applied and sustained thought is called right intention.
To know the nature of all sounds is called right speech;
to give rise to no attachment regarding body, speech, or mind is called right action;
to be free from a jealous heart is called right livelihood.
Neither increasing nor decreasing is called right effort;
not giving rise to craving or attachment toward the wholesome or unwholesome is called right mindfulness;
and observing the realms of the mind is called right concentration.
“The nature of true reality is quiescent; its ultimate meaning is termed impermanence, suffering, and non-self, yet it is conventionally designated as pure and supremely pure.”
To be able to discipline the mind is called giving;
for body and mind to be pure is called precept-keeping;
that all phenomena are impermanent is called patience.
Diligently cultivating this wisdom is called diligence;
internal and external purity is called samādhi;
and contemplating reality is called wisdom.
To know that the nature of the minds of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
to contemplate all things as equal to space is called compassion (*karuṇā*);
and to sever all forms of attachment to joy is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

To distance oneself from all conditioned phenomena is called the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*); all dharmas are pure in the future, and the various [phenomena] of the past and the present are without self. "Good son!..."
If one can truly observe and understand such dharmas as these, it is called "piercing the jewel of the bodhicitta.
Having observed these dharmas in this manner, the bodhisattva successively attains the *dhāraṇī* of mastery over all dharmas.

“Good son! It is like the sun and moon, which do not form the intention to travel back and forth or to illuminate; yet, by the power of the merit of all sentient beings, they naturally move to and fro and destroy all darkness.”
"Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can contemplate and comprehend such dharmas as these in this same way, they do not form the thought:
'I shall benefit immeasurable sentient beings and cause those sentient beings to obtain great benefit.'"
"Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can perform this contemplation, it is called the dhyāna-pāramitā and the prajñā-pāramitā. Why is this?

Only by entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can one perform such contemplation; a distracted mind cannot do so. Concentration is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and contemplation is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). In this way, one is able to contemplate reality and clearly perceive the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
What is meant by "seeing the characteristics of all phenomena"?
The characteristics of all phenomena are called the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
That which is called signlessness is non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*); this very non-activity is designated as the characteristic.
If one can forever sever such signlessness, that is the mark of signlessness.

Furthermore, "signlessness" is called the mark of non-arising; the "mark of signlessness" is called the mark of non-ceasing; and "non-arising and non-ceasing" is called the mark of the signlessness of signlessness.

If one perceives that there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither activity nor non-activity, neither oneness nor duality, neither anger nor contention nor existence—and thus knows the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it is, unmoving and unchanging—this is called true nature, this is called the nature of phenomena, and this is called real nature.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly knows such dharmas as these, it is called ‘abiding in non-abiding.
When this teaching was spoken, twelve nayutas of sentient beings resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and sixteen thousand devas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who can shatter all marks of phenomena, With the pure and unsurpassed bodhicitta—
If one can observe in this manner, One will immediately attain non-attachment to all dharmas."
Clearly seeing the profound realms of all phenomena, they do not fear nirvana;
because of this cause for fearlessness, they are able to increase the Buddha-dharma.
Clearly understanding causes and their karmic retributions, The twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so;
Far removed from the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism, He expounds the True Dharma in various ways according to the needs of beings.
The mind does not cling to permanence or impermanence, and one is further able to expound the Middle Way;
knowing that all phenomena are empty in nature, there is no sentient being and no life-span.
All phenomena are empty and signless, and likewise there is no sequential arising;
their nature is originally and eternally quiescent, incapable of being produced, like space.
Not observing the characteristics of any phenomena, one clearly awakens to the knowledge that nothing arises;
one observes form as foam, sensation as a bubble, perception as a mirage, formations as a plantain tree, and observes the mind as an illusion and the four great elements as empty;
one observes the sense bases as being like those who are deaf and blind.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the mind and its objects have neither interior nor exterior; the mind has no place of abiding, and the realms are non-dual.
Without clinging to any phenomena or their various forms and characteristics, although such knowledge exists, there is no pride.
One contemplates that all dharmas are equal—of a single flavor, a single vehicle, and the source of the single path.
One who can know such true meaning clearly perceives the dharma-realm.
There is no sound that can perceive sound;
there is no mind that can perceive the mind.
To contemplate syllables while there are no syllables—this is to truly know the dharma-realm.
The meaning of all phenomena is ineffable; sound and syllables are likewise so.
Truly knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, Fully binding the mind to the four foundations of mindfulness,
Without discrimination regarding the dharma-realm, One’s mind attains great mastery.
Far removed from all afflictions, One practices the four right efforts with diligence;
To attain unimpeded great sovereignty, One zealously cultivates and accumulates the four bases of power.
Not being greedily attached to any phenomena, one cultivates the faculty of faith;
Always delighting in dwelling in great tranquility, one thus cultivates and accumulates the faculty of diligence;
With a mind free from discursive thought, knowing reality as it is, one thus cultivates and accumulates the faculty of mindfulness.
They are able to fully subdue all mental conceptions; therefore, they cultivate and accumulate the faculty of concentration.
They are able to thoroughly investigate the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); therefore, they cultivate and accumulate the faculty of wisdom.
Desiring to thoroughly understand all dharma-realms, one thus cultivates and accumulates the seven factors of enlightenment;
not observing the numerical distinctions of "one" or "two" among all dharmas, one thus cultivates and accumulates the eightfold noble path.
If one can give away wealth and possessions as desired, And likewise observe the precepts as desired,
Furthermore purifying both the internal and external, This is what is called "great supernormal power."
All phenomena are pure by their very nature; therefore, one cultivates and gathers loving-kindness and compassion.
Having severed all afflictions of delight, one therefore cultivates and gathers sympathetic joy.
All phenomena are pure by their very nature; this is likewise true for the past, the future, and the present.
"If one contemplates that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, this person shall immediately attain true knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:

"Once a bodhisattva has attained this pure and great purity, their mind is truly without deception; they are equal and non-dual toward all sentient beings, attaining the samādhi of the seal of ultimate great purity and true wisdom, and abiding in the foundation of the seal of purity samādhi."
“What is called the root of samādhi? It is to cultivate great compassion for all sentient beings;

though one receives offerings, the mind does not become elated, and even when met with anger or insult, the mind does not sink. Because the mind is not elated, one can give rise to the dharma-nature of non-arrogance and the name of non-arrogance, and likewise does not give rise to a semblance of pride. The actions of body, speech, and mind arise from wisdom; therefore, all deeds performed do not fail to follow wisdom.”
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s physical actions following wisdom?

The physical form they obtain is exceptionally sublime and subtle; sentient beings who see it are immediately tamed, and even their four modes of conduct can tame others. They are free from all physical faults, physical crookedness, and physical impurities."

His body is pure and adorned with the primary and secondary marks; his faculties are complete without deficiency. He does not give rise to arrogance by relying on this body, nor does he look down upon those of inferior appearance.

They do not give rise to attachment toward their own bodies; observing the body as the dharma-realm and through bodily action, they know this to be form and remain mindful of the dharma-body. They do not seek a body of food, taking meditative concentration as their sustenance, yet they manifest the acceptance of offerings for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, constantly cultivating noble conduct.
That is to say, they uphold the pure precepts and protect the True Dharma not out of desire, hatred, or delusion.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, being endowed with such bodily actions that accord with wisdom, attains great supernormal powers and the power of fearlessness; by virtue of these powers, he manifests his body throughout all Buddha-lands.

Just as this physical body is manifested in this world, so it is in all other worlds; it emits great radiance that shines universally throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions. This light is supple and gentle, such that sentient beings who encounter it are freed from the heat of afflictions. Having been freed from afflictions, they experience great bliss. This is called the bodhisattva’s bodily action that accords with wisdom.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s verbal karma following wisdom?
It refers to remaining far removed from sixty-four types of verbal karma of harsh speech:
coarse speech, turbid speech, untimely speech, false speech, leaking speech, loud speech, haughty speech, ...”
Speech that is harsh, frivolous speech, divisive speech, unintelligible speech, distracted speech, low-voiced speech,
upraised speech, erroneous speech, evil speech, fearful speech, stammering speech, contentious speech,
drowsy speech, playful speech, deceitful speech, vexatious speech, timid speech, perverse speech, sinful speech, and mute speech.
Entering into speech, burning speech, hellish speech, false speech, arrogant speech, contemptuous speech,
unlovely speech, speech that proclaims faults, lost speech, speech of separation, harmful and malicious speech, double-tongued speech,
meaningless speech, unprotected speech, joyous speech, mad speech, and murderous speech.
Harmful speech, binding speech, obstructing speech, fettering speech, striking speech, singing speech,
unrighteous speech, self-praising speech, speaking of others' faults, and slandering the Triple Gem— these are called the sixty-four [types of speech] (the Dan edition says: ...).
Eleven types were missing, and I could not find their original source. "Good son!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva remains far removed from such things as harsh speech. Whatever he speaks, he speaks what is real, speaks what is true, speaks of liberation, speaks according to reality, speaks in accordance with the truths, speaks for the benefit of sentient beings, speaks of the reality and unreality of sentient beings' minds, speaks what all delight to hear, speaks all sounds, speaks all languages, speaks to purify the faculties of sentient beings, speaks to cause sentient beings to leave behind afflictions, speaks the words of the Buddha, speaks the nectar [of the Dharma] whose sound is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions, speaks to cause sentient beings to forever leave behind suffering and distress, speaks of profound meanings, speaks to harmonize sentient beings, and speaks of not committing evil. This is called the Bodhisattva’s vocal karma following wisdom."

"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mental karma following wisdom? Abiding in a single state of mind, they are able to know the minds of all sentient beings; constantly dwelling in meditative concentration, they manifest various dignified demeanors such that all Māras, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot know the objects of their mental focus. They never give rise to the thought of wishing to harm themselves or using means to harm others. Having fully understood all dharmas, they attain unimpeded penetration; having attained such a mind, they do not accept what can be accepted, nor do they realize cessation. This is called a bodhisattva’s mental karma following wisdom; this is called the root of the Samādhi of the Pure Seal."
"Furthermore, these roots are of ten kinds:
first, purifying the initial resolve for enlightenment;
second, purifying the path to bodhi."
Third, purifying the six pāramitās;
fourth, cultivating samādhi for the sake of purifying the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā);
fifth, purifying signs (nimitta).
Sixth, purity; seventh, pure dhāraṇī; eighth, purity of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
Ninth, purifying that which is without fault;
tenth, purifying the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
These are called the ten.
“Good son! The Samādhi of the Pure Seal possesses thirty qualities:
the first is internal purity;”
Second, purity of the external;
third, purity of the mind;
fourth, purity of pride.
Fifth, purity of body;
sixth, purity of eyes;
seventh, purity of all sentient beings through the absence of sentient beings.
Eighth, the purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
ninth, the purity of the single flavor of all phenomena;
tenth, the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Eleventh, the purity of the gateway to liberation;
twelfth, the purity of all phenomena entering the Dharma-realm;
thirteenth, the purity of all phenomena entering into a single nature.
Fourteenth, the purity of unshakable faith;
fifteenth, the purity of non-obstruction;
sixteenth, the purity of all liberations.
Seventeenth, the purity of the unconditioned;
eighteenth, the purity of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination;
nineteenth, the purity of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Twentieth, the purity of being unsurpassed;
twenty-first, the purity of the knowledge of all dharmas;
twenty-second, the purity of past karma.
Twenty-third, purity through compassion;
twenty-fourth, purity through not abandoning sentient beings;
twenty-fifth, purity through destroying all demonic activities.
Twenty-sixth, purity through being free from internal craving;
twenty-seventh, purity through being free from all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
twenty-eighth, purity through knowing all phenomena in a single thought-moment.
Twenty-ninth is the purity of not losing mindfulness;
thirtieth is the purity of being fully adorned with adornments.
When a bodhisattva is complete in such dharmas as these, it is called the Samādhi of the Seal of Purity.
“Having attained this samādhi, one attains the eight unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas). What are these eight?
The world one attains has the ground made of vajra;”
Upon a single tree there were various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
all sentient beings gave rise to no afflictions;
and those of the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals all saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, and having seen him, they immediately attained subtle and wondrous bliss.
Golden light shone everywhere throughout immeasurable worlds;
the entire great earth shook in six ways;
and not a single sentient being was harmed or afflicted.
"The wisdom of a single thought-moment knows all phenomena;
this is called the eighth.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one knows that all phenomena are like space, Pure by their very nature, neither arising nor ceasing,
Then one can purify the seal of the Tathāgata And likewise abide in the root of meditative concentration."
Though receiving offerings, the mind feels no joy; though rebuked or insulted, the mind feels no anger.
Cultivating and accumulating compassion with an equanimous mind—this is called the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
Far removed from all forms of pride, Having abandoned them, his mind does not exalt itself;
Able to censure the afflictions and their various fetters— This is called the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
Their bodies are forever free from all evil karma, adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence;
their faculties are pure and complete, and they never give rise to the fetter of pride.
Even upon seeing those of inferior appearance or who are ugly, or those who are poor and lowly, their minds do not treat them with contempt.
To purify the teaching of the Dharma for the sake of Bodhi—this is called the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
By observing the true nature of the body, one destroys the sentient beings' conceptualization of a body;
thus, one attains the supreme Dharmakāya, far removed from all bodies of mixed food.
Always dwelling in meditative concentration, nourished by the joy of the Dharma, one partakes of solid food for the sake of sentient beings;
as the supreme flavor of ambrosia increases the life-force of the Dharma, this is called the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
Delighting in noble conduct and upholding the Buddha’s precepts, they remain far removed from greed, hatred, delusion, and the like;
first the Bodhisattva disciplines their own body, and only thereafter do they preach for the sake of sentient beings.
With supernormal powers, they travel throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma to discipline sentient beings;
manifesting their bodies in forms like those of others, they preach the Dharma according to their inclinations.
From his body issues forth immeasurable golden light, Which universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions;
It can destroy the fever of afflictions in sentient beings, And increase the merit of the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings suffering from the three evil realms, upon encountering [him], they all obtain unsurpassed bliss;
they all become able to distance themselves from the sufferings of the evil paths and, with perfected faith, cultivate wholesome deeds.
The pure bodily karma taught by the Tathāgata is for the sake of purifying the Buddha-bodies of sentient beings;
if there are those who can cultivate such karma, they shall obtain a pure body like that of the Buddhas of the past.
If one distances oneself from the karma of harsh speech, One immediately attains a subtle voice born of wisdom;
Whatever is proclaimed will be joyfully heard by all, And those who hear it shall all give rise to the sprouts of goodness.
Far removed from the sixty-four kinds of harsh speech, such a person is able to speak the nectar of immortality;
they can expound the unconditioned Mahāyāna and also attain skillful understanding of the languages of sentient beings.
Capable of uttering speech free from greed, hatred, and delusion, He expounds the profound and true meaning;
His voice resounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, Proclaiming for the sake of the multitude the liberation of reality.
Though reviled, struck, or harmed, they do not give way to anger or contention; their minds are always compassionate and they speak with gentle words.
For the sake of the multitude, they expound that which is inexpressible, yet having spoken, no pride arises in their hearts.
If one can purify such karma, this person will remain far removed from all evils of speech;
as for the pure karma of speech taught by the Tathāgata, it is intended to grant sentient beings a broad and long tongue.
If there is one who cultivates and accumulates wholesome mental karma, that person knows all minds in a single thought-moment;
always abiding in meditative concentration and manifesting dignified demeanor, they destroy all demonic activities without their mind becoming arrogant.
Not receiving yet able to receive for the sake of sentient beings, Thoroughly knowing reality yet not realizing extinction;
All Māras do not know this mind, And the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise so.
Without giving rise to a harmful mind toward oneself or others, and being able to contemplate the profound realms of all phenomena—
if one wishes to attain this Samādhi of the Pure Seal, one should always cultivate and assemble these ten dharmas.
They purify and adorn the realm of the Buddhas, Purifying wholesome dharmas and the six perfections;
Endowed with merit and the marks of the physical body, They attain the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded exposition.
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma, they purify their minds; Without losing mindfulness, they preach non-self;
Free from all hindrances, their wisdom is unimpeded; Their intent is never faltering, and they are endowed with merit.
Cultivating the aids to enlightenment with heedfulness, they preach enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings;
their bodies are unimpeded throughout immeasurable worlds as they expound the True Dharma to transform living beings.
Endowed with the eight kinds of uncommon qualities, They obtain the unsurpassed, great benefit;
With the ground of vajra and various trees, They all see the Bodhisattva seated at the Bodhi tree.
If you wish to be fully endowed with such virtues, You should cultivate the samādhi of the Pure Seal (Vimalamudrā).
Because the Tathāgata cultivated and accumulated this concentration, He attained inconceivable merit.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Eight.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang at Guzang.
Chapter Five, Part Two: The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Pure Seal, he should cultivate and accumulate purity regarding awakening and remain far removed from all turbid states of mind."
“Good son! If one cannot perceive the intrinsic purity of all phenomena, then one is defiled by the afflictions of craving.

All phenomena are inconceivable; they are neither produced nor performed, being pure and quiescent. They are free from dust and stain, and devoid of fault; they are ultimately pure like the nature of liberation. The dharma-realm is indestructible and without discrimination; the true nature and the dharma-nature are without distinction.”
All phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless; just as the nature of liberation is unimpeded and equal, so too are all phenomena.
One who can thus correctly contemplate them is said to be "unturbid."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva can preach such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, this is called being ‘without dregs. Good son!”
"If there is a bodhisattva whose mind is free from turbidity and impurity, this person shall attain the Samādhi of the Pure Seal.
Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
"World-Honored One!"
The meaning of this samādhi is profoundly deep because it is ineffable;
it cannot be seen because it severs all numerical dharmas;
it is difficult to comprehend because it is invisible.
This is great wisdom, for it encompasses all dharmas.

All bodhisattvas are entirely equal—stainless and free from dregs, without any obstructions, and without a place of abiding; they are subtle and wondrous, difficult to clarify, and beyond metaphorical description.
Its nature is as firm and solid as a vajra;
it is neither born nor extinguished, neither broken nor destroyed, neither bound nor fettered, for it is a great radiance that is far removed from darkness;
it is inconceivable, stainless, and pure, for it is far removed from greed.
There is no contention, because one cultivates and accumulates loving-kindness;
there is neither perception nor observation, because one is detached from coming and going;
all things are equal, because they are like space.
“World-Honored One!
By contemplating what causes and conditions does one attain this samādhi?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! For example, it is like a person who wishes to travel through space; so too is a Bodhisattva who has greatly adorned himself. One who wishes to attain this samādhi should likewise practice great adornment, adorning all dharmas with equanimity.”
Why is this? Because worldly dharmas obtain their fruit from seeds. "Good son!
All conditioned phenomena have consciousness as their seed, yet this samādhi has no seed. Why is this?

Because this samādhi is not cognized by eye-consciousness, nor even by mind-consciousness; it is neither action nor form, neither sensation, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness. It contemplates all dharmas as universally equal; this is called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Good son! It is not because of different characteristics that it is called birth-and-death, nor is it because of different characteristics that it is called nirvana. Good son!”
The characteristics of birth and death are themselves the characteristics of nirvāṇa. Why is this?

Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is pure; that which is called "intrinsic nature" is termed "the absence of nature," and that which is the absence of nature is termed the "characteristic of the absence of nature."
If the nature of signlessness is non-action, then such non-action is the dharma-nature which is devoid of words; if there are no words, it is called Suchness.

As it was with the past, so it is with the middle and the future; these are called the three periods of time. Now, that which constitutes the three periods of time is itself emptiness, and emptiness is non-action. If there is thus no action, how can there be an agent?
Therefore, non-action is termed emptiness. If there is no action and no agent, one should know that there is no dharma;

if there is no dharma, there is no seeking and no wishing. If there is no wishing or seeking, then there are no actions of body, speech, or mind. The absence of actions of body, speech, and mind is termed unimpededness. That which is unimpeded is termed non-emergence. Non-emergence, non-extinction, and non-abiding—non-extinction and non-abiding are the marks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). That which has the marks of the unconditioned is termed non-abiding.

"Non-abiding" means that there is no activity whatsoever; the mind does not abide in form, nor does it abide in anything up to mental formations. If the mind does not abide in these four bases, this is called non-abiding.

If there is no abiding, then the semblance of ego-grasping does not arise; if there is no such semblance of ego-grasping, there is no increase; if there is no increase, there is no cause; if there is no cause, there is no applied or sustained thought; and the absence of applied and sustained thought is called silence.

“Good son! The meaning of such dharmas as these is profoundly deep; if one can have faith in them, one will immediately attain liberation, forever departing from the obstacles of inverted afflictions. One will then be able to receive and uphold the Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Such a person is a great captain, a guide, a merchant leader, a master of mantras, and a physician; they are able to make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and are thus called a child of the Buddha.”

Surpassing the works of Māra, you shall destroy the hosts of Māras; before long, you will attain the Samādhi of the Pure Seal (Vimalamudrā), whereby you will be able to grandly adorn a sturdy vessel to ferry sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death.
“World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva destroy all the factions of Māra?
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva is able to not seek after any dharmas, at that time they will be able to shatter the hosts of Māra and will not seek the causes and conditions of any objective realms.
Good son!..."
There are four kinds of māras:
first, the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra);
second, the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
Third is the Māra of Death;
fourth is the Māra of the Heavens. Good son!
If one can contemplate phenomena as having the characteristic of an illusion, such a person is able to destroy the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra).
If one sees that all phenomena are entirely characterized by emptiness, such a person is able to destroy the Māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
If one perceives that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, such a person is able to destroy the Māra of Death.
If one eliminates arrogance, one then destroys the Māra of the Heavens. "Furthermore, good son!

If one knows suffering, one can destroy the Māra of the aggregates; if one distances oneself from its origin, one destroys the Māra of afflictions; if one realizes cessation, one destroys the Māra of death; and if one cultivates the path, one destroys the Māra of devas.
"Furthermore, noble son!

If one perceives all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as suffering, one destroys the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); if one perceives the true reality of all phenomena as impermanent, one destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); if one perceives the true reality of all phenomena as selfless, one can destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and if one perceives the tranquility of all phenomena as *nirvāṇa*, one can destroy the Māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*)."
"Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva is able to be without attachment to the body and, when giving away the body as a gift, dedicates it toward Bodhi, they can destroy the Māra of the Aggregates (skandhamāra).
When giving, by remaining far removed from a mind of stinginess and greed, they destroy the Māra of Afflictions (kleśamāra)."
If one contemplates that all wealth and possessions are impermanent, one can destroy the Mara of Death;
