if one practices compassionate giving for the sake of sentient beings, one can destroy the Mara of Heaven. "Furthermore, good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who upholds the pure precepts not for the sake of the view of self, they can destroy the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); if they uphold the pure precepts not for the sake of craving for existence, they destroy the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); if they uphold the pure precepts for the sake of distancing themselves from the faults of birth and death, they can destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and if they can give rise to the thought that causes those who violate the prohibitions to all uphold the pure precepts, then by upholding the pure precepts, they destroy the Māra of devas (*devaputramāra*).
"Furthermore, good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who does not perceive a self yet practices patience, he destroys the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). If he does not perceive the existence of sentient beings who practice patience, he destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*). If he does not perceive birth and death, he destroys the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). If he does not perceive awakening (*bodhi*), he destroys the Māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*)."
"Furthermore, noble son!

If there is a bodhisattva who diligently cultivates vigor and whose body is tranquil, he destroys the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). If he diligently practices vigor and his mind is tranquil, he destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*). If he diligently practices vigor and contemplates the non-arising of phenomena, he can destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). If he diligently practices vigor for the sake of disciplining sentient beings and causing them to transcend birth and death, he destroys the Māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*)."
"Furthermore, noble son!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) without being attached to the five aggregates (skandha), they can destroy the Māra of the aggregates; if they cultivate meditative concentration without attachment to the elements (dhātu) or sense bases (āyatana), they can destroy the Māra of afflictions (kleśa-māra); if they cultivate meditative concentration without attachment to the sense bases, they can destroy the Māra of death (mṛtyu-māra); and by dedicating all roots of goodness toward Bodhi, they can destroy the Māra of the devas (deva-māra)."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva who knows the skillful means regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), he can destroy the Māra of the aggregates; knowing the skillful means regarding the elements (*dhātu*), he destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa*); knowing the skillful means regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*), he can destroy the Māra of death; and by dedicating these various kinds of skillful means toward enlightenment, he can destroy the Māra of the devas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates all dharmas as having the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they can destroy the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); if they contemplate all dharmas as being entirely without characteristics (*animitta*), they can destroy the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); if they contemplate all dharmas as being entirely without aspiration (*apraṇihita*), they can destroy the māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and by possessing these three dharmas and dedicating them toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), they can destroy the māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*)."
"Furthermore, good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the body and the locus of the body without sensation or attachment, they can destroy the Māra of the aggregates (skandha-māra). Contemplating sensation and the locus of sensation without sensation or attachment, they destroy the Māra of afflictions (kleśa-māra). Contemplating the mind and the locus of the mind without sensation or attachment, they can destroy the Māra of death (mṛtyu-māra). Contemplating phenomena and the locus of phenomena without sensation or attachment, they can destroy the Māra of the devas (devaputra-māra);
by performing such contemplations, they never lose the Bodhicitta, and this person is thus able to shatter the four Māras."
“Good son! If one clings to a self, then the works of Māra increase. A bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows both that there is a self and that there is no self.
If there were a dharma that was neither with a self nor without a self, then not a single dharma would undergo increase or decrease; yet all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance.”
Therefore, the bodhisattva, desiring to adorn the unsurpassed Great Vehicle, does not initiate this adornment for the sake of a self; having initiated the adornment, he reflects thus:
"Who is it that adorns the Dharma so that it remains firm and indestructible?"
I shall adorn [them].

Furthermore, I do not practice adornment for the sake of destroying the notions of a self, sentient beings, life-force, or a person; rather, I practice adornment in order to shatter the attachment of sentient beings to the false delusions of views regarding a self, sentient beings, life-force, a person, and so forth.

Sentient beings possess inverted views, perceiving these five aggregates as permanent, blissful, self, and pure; I shall therefore preach to them such [truths] as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, so that sentient beings may attain true wisdom.
If there are sentient beings whose minds harbor desires and aspirations, you should know that such persons are called "attached.

If they do not desire or aspire, then they have no attachment. One who is unattached is not deluded; one who is not deluded attains true wisdom, knowing the past, future, and present, yet remaining unattached to the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide.

If one does not form attachments to these three periods of time, it is called non-perversion and is termed the practice of a bodhisattva. One thoroughly understands the various activities of all sentient beings; having understood them, one clearly explains karma and its results, and likewise knows the conduct of greed, the conduct of hatred, and the conduct of delusion.

He knows that there are sentient beings who practice desire yet adorn it with hatred; who practice hatred yet adorn it with desire; who practice delusion yet adorn it with desire; who practice desire yet adorn it with delusion; who practice hatred yet adorn it with delusion; and who practice delusion yet adorn it with hatred.

“Good son! There are sentient beings who give rise to desire for forms and anger toward sounds; again, there are sentient beings who give rise to desire for sounds and anger toward forms; again, there are sentient beings who give rise to desire for fragrances and anger toward tastes; again, there are sentient beings who give rise to desire for tastes and anger toward fragrances; again, there are sentient beings who give rise to desire for tangibles and anger toward mental objects (*dharma*); again, there are sentient beings who give rise to desire for mental objects and anger toward tangibles. Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose desire is weak while their anger is fierce; again, there are sentient beings whose desire is fierce while their anger is weak. Again, there are those whose desire is weak while their ignorance is strong; those whose ignorance is weak while their desire is strong; those whose anger is weak while their ignorance is strong; and those whose ignorance is weak while their anger is strong.”
There are sentient beings who are to be disciplined by form, but not by sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
some are to be disciplined by sound, but not by form, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
some are to be disciplined by odor, but not by form, sound, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
It is the taming of conditioned flavor, not for the sake of form, sound, odor, or tangibles;
it is the taming of conditioned tangibles, not for the sake of form, sound, odor, taste, or mental objects;
it is the taming of conditioned phenomena, not for the sake of form, sound, odor, taste, or tangibles.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain taming through the tranquility of their minds, rather than through the tranquility of their bodies;
or there are sentient beings who attain taming through the tranquility of their bodies, rather than through the tranquility of their minds.
There are some sentient beings who attain taming upon hearing the teaching of impermanence, but do not attain taming because of suffering, impurity, or non-self.
There are some sentient beings who attain taming upon hearing the teaching of suffering, but do not attain taming because of impermanence, impurity, or non-self.
There are some sentient beings who are tamed by hearing the teaching on impurity, rather than being tamed by means of impermanence, suffering, or non-self.
There are some sentient beings who are tamed by hearing the teaching on non-self, rather than being tamed by means of impermanence, suffering, or impurity.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are tamed by seeing the supernatural powers of the body, but not by the knowledge of others' minds.
Or there are sentient beings who are tamed because of the knowledge of others' minds, but not because of supernatural powers.

“Good son! There are sentient beings who, though they practice with diligent vigor, attain liberation slowly; there are those who, with little vigor, attain liberation quickly; there are those who, with diligent vigor, attain liberation quickly; and there are those who, with little vigor, attain liberation slowly.”

There is liberation through causes but not through conditions; there is liberation through conditions but not through causes; there is liberation through both causes and conditions, and there is liberation that is neither through causes nor through conditions.
There are sentient beings who attain liberation by contemplating internal phenomena but not external ones;
and there are those who attain liberation by contemplating external phenomena but not internal ones.
There are those who attain liberation by contemplating both the internal and the external, and there are those who attain liberation without contemplating either the internal or the external.
Among sentient beings, there are those who attain liberation through the practice of pleasure and not through the practice of suffering;
and there are those who attain liberation through the practice of suffering and not through the practice of pleasure.
Some attain liberation through suffering or pleasure;
others attain liberation without depending on either ascetic practices or pleasurable practices.
There are sentient beings who are tamed by praise rather than by reproach.
Some are tamed through censure rather than praise;
some are tamed through both praise and reproach;
and some are tamed without such causes.
There are sentient beings who are tamed by teaching through contradiction rather than by teaching through conformity;
some are tamed by conformity rather than by contradiction;
and some are tamed by both contradiction and conformity.
There are those who are tamed by teachings given through causes that are either contrary or conformable;
there are sentient beings who are tamed by hearing a brief exposition rather than an extensive one,
while others are tamed by an extensive exposition rather than a brief one.
There are those who attain discipline through extensive or concise teachings;
there are also those who attain discipline without depending on the extensive or concise exposition of the Dharma.

There are sentient beings who attain discipline through the Four Noble Truths; some attain discipline through the Foundations of Mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), some through the Right Efforts (samyakprahāṇa), some through the Bases of Psychic Power (ṛddhipāda), some through the Five Faculties (indriya), some through the Five Powers (bala), some through the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and some through the Eightfold Path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).

“Good son! The conduct of sentient beings is inconceivable; the minds of sentient beings are also inconceivable; the taming of sentient beings is inconceivable; the Dharma-gates they enter are inconceivable; and the realms of sentient beings are inconceivable.”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained such inconceivable wisdom, they then come to know that the conduct practiced by all sentient beings is inconceivable.
“Good son! It is like a net that has many knots; if there is a person within it who, by the power of incantations and arts, breaks through the net and emerges to go wherever they please.”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering among sentient beings, by the power of the mantra of wisdom, he destroys the net of afflictions with sovereign ease according to his will; although he has not yet realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he is able to penetrate the conduct of sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, to hear that sentient beings possess such conduct as this and yet remain neither startled nor terrified is truly difficult; it is inconceivable."
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, what do you think?"
“Suppose there were a lion cub; although it has only just been born, would it feel fear upon hearing the lion’s roar?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, their hearing of the conduct of sentient beings is likewise so.
Śāriputra, what do you think?”
“Even though the fire is small, would it fear dry fuel? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, the attainment of the fire of wisdom is likewise so. Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata now employs a non-example as an example.”
Śāriputra! It is as if a fierce fire were to make a pact with various dry logs that they would engage in a great battle for seven days.
At that time, all the dry trees, grasses, and shrubs, along with their various branches and leaves, would gather together in a mass like Mount Sumeru.
At that time, a close friend of the fierce fire spoke to him, saying:
"For what reason do you not now adorn yourself and seek much assistance?
The fuel is vast and numerous, while you are but alone; how could you possibly withstand it?"
Then the fire replied:
"Though those enemies be many, my power is sufficient to oppose them; I have no need for allies. Śāriputra!
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
although all afflictions may combine together with such fierce intensity, the power of the bodhisattva’s wisdom is able to extinguish and subdue them.
Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of power: first, the power of afflictions;
[second, the power of wisdom].
2. The Power of Wisdom.

If a bodhisattva lacked the power of afflictions (*kleśa*), they would be unable to act together with all sentient beings, nor would they be able to know the spheres of activity of sentient beings; furthermore, they would inevitably realize the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Therefore, by means of the power of afflictions, the bodhisattva wanders through all realms of existence without giving rise to fear; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means (*upāya*).
“Śāriputra, just as a small venomous snake does not require a companion, so it is with one who has first resolved their mind [on awakening]. Śāriputra!”
For example, although there may be immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of fireflies, they cannot obscure the radiance of the sun;
likewise, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva may have immeasurable and innumerable afflictions, they cannot obscure the light of the bodhisattva’s wisdom.
“Śāriputra! Just as a single pill of agada medicine can neutralize a great poison, so too is the wisdom of a bodhisattva:
a small medicinal dose of wisdom can destroy the immeasurable poison of afflictions.”
“Śāriputra! For example, when heaven sends down water of a single flavor, it acquires various flavors according to the differences in the ground;
the single wisdom of liberation of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise, manifesting various distinctions according to the faculties of sentient beings.”
“Śāriputra! Just as beneath the Jambū tree there is golden mud, and within that golden mud there are various kinds of jewels;
so too, within the golden-mud-like mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening (bodhicitta), there are likewise the jewels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“Śāriputra! Just as all other minor kings are entirely subject to a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), so too it is with all humans and devas;
they all come to take refuge in and submit to a bodhisattva at the first stage of resolve.”
“Śāriputra! Just as a person of meager merit does not encounter a rain of jewels;
so too, if one cannot plant various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, one will be unable to give rise to the bodhicitta.”
“Śāriputra! Without sugarcane seeds, there would be no various flavors of rock honey;
likewise, without the bodhicitta, there would be no various flavors of the Three Jewels.”
“Śāriputra! It is as the physician-king Jīvaka often says:
‘There is nothing in the world that is not medicine.’”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; he teaches that there is no dharma whatsoever that is not bodhi. "Śāriputra!
Just as the Asura King, even by exhausting all his power, cannot obstruct the path of the sun and moon;"
All the hosts of Māras are likewise; even exerting their full power, they cannot obstruct a bodhisattva who diligently practices the path to awakening. “Śāriputra!
Just as the celestial palaces and dwellings of the gods in the realm of form abide supported by space,
so too does the bodhi attained by a bodhisattva who practices with diligence abide supported by space.
“Śāriputra! For example, just as empty space can fully contain all myriad things, yet this empty space never increases or decreases;
so too it is with the immeasurable Buddha-dharma: although there may be bodhisattvas who resolve their minds to seek it, these Buddha-dharmas neither increase nor decrease.”
“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a person who travels through space according to his strength, yet the nature of space neither increases nor decreases;
so it is with the bodhisattva, who dwells in the power of faith and practices the Buddha-wisdom, yet this Buddha-wisdom likewise neither increases nor decreases.”
“Śāriputra! For example, when a potter has not yet completed a vessel, it does not receive the name ‘vessel’;
the wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva are likewise: as long as they have not yet generated the resolve [for awakening], they do not receive that name.”
“Śāriputra! Just as when a person has already seen a Wheel-Turning Sage King, they no longer seek to see other minor kings;
so it is with a bodhisattva: once they have generated the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), they no longer generate the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
“Śāriputra! Just as various jewels do not emerge from other places, but must necessarily emerge from the great ocean,
so it is, Śāriputra!”
Among the jewels of the śrāvakas, the Three Jewels do not emerge; the Three Jewels must emerge from the jewel of the bodhisattva. “Śāriputra!
For example, a crown prince is not yet called a king, yet he is not not called a king;”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is not called a Buddha, yet he is not not called a Buddha.
"Śāriputra! For example, even a small jewel must not be treated with contempt."
Why is this? Just as these small jewels can perform great deeds and bring about manifold benefits, so too it is with a bodhisattva;
when they first resolve their mind on enlightenment, they must not be looked down upon.
“Śāriputra! I now speak such parables for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; if there are bodhisattvas who hear these parables, they shall immediately attain peace and happiness.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to realize the Buddha-way, One should eliminate the mind of doubt and delusion.
Those who diligently cultivate supreme faith Shall be able to attain Bodhi."
If one cultivates the Samādhi of the Pure Seal, Proclaiming that all phenomena are like dreams,
And purifies the mind throughout immeasurable lifetimes, One shall be able to realize the path of Perfect Enlightenment.
The path attained by the Buddha is not a physical action, nor is it the two actions of speech and mind;
its unconditioned, true nature is likewise such that it cannot be described through metaphors.
The Buddha-way is without counterpart and cannot be seen; it is not the realm of eye-consciousness, being like empty space.
It is not any of the sensory faculties, nor is it the domain of those faculties.
It is neither marks, nor aggregates, nor sense-bases or elements. It is not mind, intention, feeling, perception, or consciousness.
Neither knowledge nor the realm of non-knowledge—therefore, the Buddha-realm is unknowable.
The great compassion of all Buddhas is inconceivable; it is immeasurable, boundless, and unobstructed.
Without letters, without sound, and ineffable—therefore, none can know the Buddha-realm.
If there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, have drawn near to virtuous friends and heard the true Dharma, having heard it they immediately attain great merit and virtue;
they constantly experience wondrous bliss like that of the former Buddhas, such that no demons can find any flaw in them;
their faculties are tamed and they dwell in the realm of joy.
Able to destroy the four māras through skillful means, One dwells according to the Dharma within the realm of the Buddhas.
If one practices such a path to enlightenment, One will immediately attain bodhi and preach it for others;
One can ferry sentient beings across the sea of birth and death, And shatter all great false views.
One immediately attains the unsurpassed marks and signs, And achieves the ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
Able to know the afflictions and conduct of sentient beings, One is able to destroy all paths of existence.
If there is a bodhisattva who exerts diligent effort, they will be able to destroy all afflictions;
just as fire can burn dry grass and wood, the bodhicitta can incinerate the afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying: "Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices with diligent vigor, it is easy to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Whoever practices with diligent perseverance should know that such a person possesses bodhi.

Whoever possesses such diligence is one who is fully endowed with the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā; they are able to benefit themselves and also benefit others.

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vīryavīra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land was named Sudarśana, and his kalpa was named Kusumasaṃcaya.”

At that time, the world was filled with vast waters, from which eighty-four thousand exquisite lotus flowers emerged; each was ten yojanas in length and breadth, and they possessed immeasurable billions of golden rays of light.
The fragrance was subtle and wondrous; when the devas of Akaniṣṭha saw it, they experienced great peace and happiness, and spoke thus:
"There are many lotus flowers in this world; one should know that many Buddhas will likewise appear."
"For this reason, this kalpa is named 'Cluster of Flowers' (*Puṣpasaṃcaya*).

At that time, that land was tranquil and free from sound; because of its tranquility, the bodhisattvas of immeasurable worlds constantly delighted in observing it, and through such observation, each attained the *pramuditācaryā-samādhi*. Therefore, that world is named 'Good Vision' (*Sudarśana*)."

"In that land, there are many groves of trees made of the seven treasures, as well as towers, pavilions, and palaces; sentient beings enjoy peace and happiness like those in Tuṣita Heaven. Food and drink are abundant, spiritual powers are easily attained, and there are no female bodies—all are born by transformation. Furthermore, there are no two vehicles; all cultivate the Mahāyāna."

“At that time, that Buddha had thirty-six thousand renunciant bodhisattvas who had all attained the mind of non-retrogression; immeasurable humans and devas had first resolved upon bodhicitta with firm, non-retrogressive resolve. That World-Honored Buddha constantly delighted in proclaiming the practice of diligent vigor.”

At that time, there was a bodhisattva within the great assembly named Dṛḍhavyūha. He rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing diligence with vigor? The Buddha said, "Good son!
There are four dharmas for the diligent practice of vigor. What are these four?
First, the arousal of the mind;
Second, forming the mind;
third, observing the mind;
fourth, abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
These four dharmas are precisely the causes and conditions for fulfilling the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?
O son of good family!

To initiate is the cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas; to act is called the cause for the increase of wholesome dharmas; to contemplate is called the cause for benefiting sentient beings; and to abide in accordance with the Dharma is called the causal condition for entering all Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, "one who initiates" seeks to hear the true Dharma; "one who acts" is able to explain it after having heard it; "one who contemplates" skillfully reflects upon its meaning; and "one who abides according to the Dharma" abides as taught.

Furthermore, "generating" refers to subduing the mind of stinginess; "acting" refers to being able to practice universal giving; "contemplating" refers to dedicating the gift to awakening for the sake of sentient beings; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to not seeking the fruits of giving.

Furthermore, "one who initiates" seeks out a recipient; "one who acts" gives rise to a mind of compassion upon seeing a petitioner; "one who contemplates" observes that wealth is impermanent; and "one who abides in accordance with the Dharma" does not seek karmic retribution.

Furthermore, "one who initiates" seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma; "one who acts" seeks a pure livelihood; "one who contemplates" cultivates the enduring Dharma within non-enduring things; and "one who abides according to the Dharma" gives rise to no arrogance when relinquishing all things.

Furthermore, "to resolve" means to distance oneself from all unwholesome precepts; "to act" means to wholeheartedly receive and uphold all pure prohibitions; "to observe" means to sincerely discipline those who violate the prohibitions; and "to abide according to the Dharma" means to purely maintain the prohibitions without giving rise to arrogance.

Furthermore, "to resolve" means to purify verbal karma; "to act" means to purify bodily karma; "to contemplate" means to purify mental karma; and "to abide according to the Dharma" means to cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas.

"Furthermore, 'to resolve' means to distance oneself from a mind of anger; 'to act' means to cultivate and accumulate patience; 'to observe' means to protect oneself and others; and 'to abide according to the Dharma' means that having cultivated patience, one does not give rise to arrogance."

Furthermore, "one who sets out" always delights in transforming sentient beings with wrong views; "one who acts" is able to destroy the hearts of anger in sentient beings; "one who contemplates" perceives neither the internal nor the external; and "one who abides according to the Dharma" remains far removed from all afflictions and fetters.

Furthermore, "to resolve" means to distance oneself from indolence; "to act" means to diligently cultivate vigor; "to observe" means to subdue all indolent sentient beings; and "to abide according to the Dharma" means to exhort all sentient beings to cultivate vigor.

Furthermore, "setting forth" is called "excellent compassion"; "acting" means having completed what was to be done; "observing" means not seeking other vehicles; and "abiding according to the Dharma" means not losing the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, "arousing" adorns the factors of dhyāna; "practicing" adorns samādhi; "contemplating" ensures that one never gives rise to a semblance of pride; and "abiding according to the Dharma" destroys the minds of sentient beings that engage in evil conduct.

Furthermore, "to set forth" is to adorn the mind of mindfulness; "to act" is to adorn all states of existence; "to contemplate" is for one's intention to be firm; and "to abide according to the Dharma" is to be courageous and free from fear.

Furthermore, "arousing" is called the cause in accordance with the Dharma; "acting" is called skillful means; "contemplating" is called the gateway; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" is called liberation.

Furthermore, "arousing" refers to seeking names; "acting" refers to grasping at syllables; "contemplating" means that syllables are inexpressible; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" means being far removed from syllables.

"Furthermore, 'to resolve' means to distance oneself from evil associates; 'to act' means to draw near to virtuous friends; 'to contemplate' means to listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind in the presence of virtuous friends; and 'to abide according to the Dharma' means not to misinterpret the meaning."

Furthermore, "one who resolves" delights in renouncing the household life; "one who acts" distances themselves from both enemies and kin; "one who contemplates" seeks the wholesome Dharma; and "one who abides according to the Dharma" does not follow the will of others.

Furthermore, "arousing" refers to having few desires; "acting" refers to being content; "observing" refers to being easy to support and easy to satisfy; and "abiding according to the Dharma" refers to knowing what is appropriate for the occasion.

Furthermore, "one who resolves" trains in the precepts; "one who acts" is without transgression regarding the precepts; "one who contemplates" trains in the precepts according to their intention; and "one who abides in accordance with the Dharma" trains in the precepts according to wisdom.

Furthermore, "arousing" refers to the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) and the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā); "acting" refers to the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā); "contemplating" refers to the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā); and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the perfection of knowledge (jñāna-pāramitā) and the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).

Furthermore, "one who initiates" gathers others through the practice of giving; "one who acts" gathers them through gentle speech; "one who contemplates" gathers them through benefiting others; and "one who abides in accordance with the Dharma" gathers them through sharing common interests.

Furthermore, "arousing" refers to great loving-kindness; "acting" refers to great compassion; "contemplating" refers to great sympathetic joy; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to great equanimity.

Furthermore, "to resolve" means to uphold and protect the True Dharma; "to act" means to purify the field of merit; "to contemplate" means to adorn oneself with the primary and secondary marks; and "to abide according to the Dharma" means to tame and transform sentient beings.

"Furthermore, 'setting out' means truly knowing the māra of the aggregates; 'acting' means being free from the māra of afflictions; 'contemplating' means destroying the māra of death; and 'abiding according to the Dharma' means subduing the māra of the devas."

Furthermore, "setting forth" refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body; "acting" refers to the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; "contemplating" refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.

Furthermore, "one who sets out" clearly understands suffering; "one who acts" distances themselves from the origin; "one who contemplates" realizes true cessation; and "one who abides according to the Dharma" refers to cultivating the path.

Furthermore, "setting forth" refers to the faculty of faith; "acting" refers to the faculty of diligence; "contemplating" refers to the faculty of mindfulness; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the faculty of wisdom.

Furthermore, "setting forth" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment; "acting" refers to the eightfold noble path; "contemplating" refers to śamatha; and "abiding in accordance with the Dharma" refers to vipaśyanā.

“Good son! Just as all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) are called ‘arousing,’ the cultivation of all virtues is called ‘acting,’ all pure minds are called ‘contemplation’ (*vipaśyanā*), and knowing all karma is called ‘abiding in accordance with the Dharma.’”
“Good son! That Buddha again addressed Sthiravyūha: ‘Good son!’”
One who exerts diligent effort calms the mind; when the mind is calm, that is itself diligence.
To destroy attachment to the body is diligence;
to understand the body and the mind is diligence.
To sever the notions of "I" and "mine" is itself diligence;
to sever all fetters is itself diligence;
to exhaust the hindrances of afflictions is itself diligence.
If one can remain far removed from all obstacles, this is diligence;
if one can eliminate the ten types of arrogance, this is diligence;
and if one can destroy greed and anger, this is diligence.
If one can distance oneself from ignorance and craving for existence, this is diligence.
If one who is heedful cultivates wholesome dharmas, this is diligence.
If one can truly contemplate the internal and external sense bases, this is diligence.
To know truly the aggregates, elements, and sense bases is diligence;
for the mind to be tranquil is diligence;
to destroy doubt is diligence.
If one does not discriminate regarding the three periods of time, that is diligence;
if one contemplates the dharma-realm without wavering or shifting, that is diligence;
if one is without leakage, that is diligence.
If there is no harming, that is diligence;
if there is no giving rise to regret, that is diligence;
if there is no seeking, that is diligence.
If there is no cessation, that is diligence;
if there is no acting, that is diligence.
If there is neither increase nor decrease, that is diligence.
To be without superior and without inferior is itself diligence;
to neither abandon nor cling is itself diligence;
to be neither bound nor liberated is itself diligence.
Neither going nor coming is itself diligence;
neither arising nor ceasing is itself diligence;
neither being negligent nor being non-negligent is itself diligence.
The absence of action and actor is itself diligence;
the absence of darkness and light is itself diligence;
that which is neither seeing nor not seeing is itself diligence.
“Good son! When that Buddha preached this Dharma of diligence, immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Good son!”
Now, within this assembly, five thousand bodhisattvas have likewise attained this dharma of non-arising patience (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
Seven thousand devas and humans have resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Firm Adornment (Dṛḍhavyūha) practiced with diligent vigor in order to attain such immeasurable Dharmas and thereby achieved the stage of ‘lower patience’ (mṛdu-kṣānti). For the sake of seeking the Dharma, he neither sat nor lay down until the end of his life.”

Having relinquished his body, he was reborn in the Brahma world and attained the body of a Brahmā deity. For immeasurable eons, he made offerings to the Buddhas and listened to the True Dharma. During that kalpa, he universally made offerings to eighty-four thousand Tathāgatas, listening to the True Dharma and practicing with diligent vigor.
“Good son! Do you know that the one named Dṛḍhavyūha at that time was anyone other than myself? It was indeed I.”
"Good son! Because I have long been fully endowed with this diligence, I have surpassed Maitreya and all other great bodhisattvas to attain perfect enlightenment first. Therefore, I say:"
Whoever possesses diligence, you should know that such a person possesses bodhi. "Good son!
Even though I practiced with diligent effort, it was still difficult for me to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how much more so for one who is indolent!"
"If there are bodhisattvas who are able to be diligent, these people will be able to benefit themselves and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I recall in immeasurable past ages, during the Flower-Cluster Kalpa, the Buddha Diligent (Vīrya)."
The world of Sudarśana is filled with water, from which eighty-four thousand flowers emerge.
That land is like the Tuṣita heaven; it abounds in food and drink, and there are no women.
Beings are not born of parents but are all miraculously born (*upapāduka*); furthermore, there are no two vehicles, but only the Single Vehicle.
The bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions behold the land of Sudarśana enjoying peace and bliss;
thirty-two thousand monastics and immeasurable humans and devas have resolved to attain bodhi.
At that time, that Buddha praised diligence, speaking only for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sthira:
"If one can resolve to cultivate goodness with vigor, binding the mind in thought and abiding in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, for my sake, the World-Honored One analyzed and extensively expounded these four lines:
"Awaken the mind of bodhi and practice according to the Dharma; contemplate and attain patience, abiding according to the Dharma."
If one seeks the True Dharma, this is called the first aspiration; to speak in accordance with the Dharma is called "action";
to receive its meaning without error is "skillful reflection"; and to cultivate patience is "abiding according to the Dharma."
If one diligently practices giving, this is the initial aspiration; seeking out a recipient is called "action.
Clearly seeing impermanence and reflecting well, one does not perceive dualistic marks but abides in accordance with the Dharma.
Seeking wealth in accordance with the Dharma is the initial resolve; a pure livelihood is what is called "action.
Destroying the mind of stinginess through right reflection, one does not seek arrogance but dwells in accordance with the Dharma.
To distance oneself from unwholesome precepts is the initial undertaking; to guard the precepts without leakage is what is called "action.
To subdue the violation of precepts through skillful reflection, one dwells in accordance with the Dharma, pure in discipline and free from pride.
Abstaining from harsh speech is the initial undertaking; the tranquility of the mind is what constitutes its practice.
With a tranquil mind and right reflection, all phenomena abide in tranquility according to the Dharma.
To distance oneself from a harmful mind is the initial undertaking; to cultivate and accumulate patience is called the practice.
To protect oneself and others through wise reflection, and to abide in accordance with the Dharma without giving rise to pride, is the perfection of patience.
To admonish those who harbor anger is the initial undertaking; to distance oneself from evil people is what is called "action.
With inner and outer tranquility and virtuous reflection, one dwells in accordance with the Dharma, free from attachment to a self.
To distance oneself from indolence is the initial resolve; Diligently cultivating vigor is what is called "action.
Knowing reality is right reflection; Cultivating and gathering the Path is dwelling according to the Dharma.
The initial seeking of the sublime Dharma is the first resolve; having sought it, its ultimate realization is called "action.
To maintain it with mindfulness and right reflection is to not lose the Dharma, abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
Seeking the factors of dhyāna is the initial setting forth; cultivating and accumulating samādhi is called "action.
Being free from pride regarding resemblance and possessing correct reflection, one dwells according to the Dharma without fault.
The mind of mindfulness and wisdom is the initial aspiration; attaining the Dharma-gates is called "action.
Protecting the True Dharma through skillful reflection, one dwells according to the Dharma with courageous and vigorous diligence.
Right mindfulness regarding causes and conditions is the initial setting forth; practicing skillful means for the cultivation of goodness is called "action.
Contemplating internal phenomena with correct reflection, one attains liberation and abides in accordance with the Dharma.
First seeking out words and letters is the initial aspiration; Thoroughly penetrating and understanding them is called "action.
Knowing that they are inexpressible is skillful reflection; Realizing there are no words or letters is abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
To distance oneself from evil friends is the initial undertaking; to associate with virtuous spiritual friends is called the practice.
Having heard the teaching, one reflects well upon it as it was heard; not departing from the Dharma, one abides in accordance with the Dharma.
Leaving home for the Buddha-dharma is the initial aspiration; abandoning enmity and kinship is called "action";
cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas through right reflection, one abides according to the Dharma without following the whims of others.

Having few desires and being content is called "arousing [the mind]"; delighting in tranquility and practicing right reflection, once established in tranquility, one speaks of non-contention and likewise cultivates for oneself abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
Training in the precepts is the initial undertaking; not practicing defiled precepts is called "action.
The precept of no-precept is well-considered reflection; through the precept of wisdom, one abides according to the Dharma.
Not speaking of worldly affairs is the first undertaking; constantly delighting in tranquility is what is called "action.
Being easy to support and easy to satisfy, one reflects well and dwells according to the Dharma by contemplating impermanence.
Delighting in the cultivation of giving and precepts is the initial aspiration; patience and diligence are called "action.
Cultivating dhyāna and wisdom through right reflection, one dwells according to the Dharma by practicing wisdom and skillful means.
Gathering others through the practice of giving is the initial undertaking; gathering them through gentle speech is called the performance [of the act].
Benefiting sentient beings through virtuous reflection constitutes abiding in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Cultivating and gathering compassion is called "arousing"; not distinguishing between the three periods of time, one reflects with wholesome thought.
To purify the body and mind for the sake of all sentient beings, one cultivates and gathers joy and equanimity, abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
Attaining the True Dharma is the initial aspiration; Purifying the field of merit is called "action";
Adorning one's own person through skillful reflection, Taming sentient beings while abiding according to the Dharma.
Destroying the Māra of the Aggregates is the initial resolve; Leaving behind the Māra of Afflictions is called "action";
Being able to destroy the Māra of Death is "skillful reflection"; Subduing the enemy Māras is to abide according to the Dharma.
Cultivating the mindfulness of the body is the initial undertaking; cultivating the mindfulness of sensation is called "action";
cultivating the mindfulness of the mind is right reflection; cultivating the mindfulness of phenomena is dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
To know suffering clearly is the initial aspiration; to distance oneself from its origin is called "action";
to realize cessation through true and virtuous reflection, one cultivates the right path and abides according to the Dharma.
Cultivating the faculty of faith is the initial aspiration; cultivating and gathering the various powers is called "action";
cultivating mindfulness, samādhi, and wise reflection, one dwells in accordance with the Dharma through the cultivation of wisdom.
The tranquility of body and mind is the initial setting forth; being free from wrong views is called "action.
Contemplating name-and-form with right reflection, one dwells according to the Dharma with diligence and without regret.
The absence of self and what belongs to self is called "arising"; the absence of bondage and liberation is called "action.
To contemplate well that there is no going and no coming is for the nature of phenomena to abide immovably according to the Dharma.
To distance oneself from arrogance is the first undertaking; to eliminate greed and hatred is called "action.
To contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination is right reflection; to be free from delusion and craving is to abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If one can remain far removed from all signs, Destroy all obstacles,
and be endowed with the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, One will be able to speak of merits and exert diligent effort.
When the Tathāgata preached this Dharma of diligence, ten thousand sentient beings realized non-arising,
five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma, and immeasurable humans and devas resolved to attain Bodhi.
It is I who am thus adorned with firmness; my diligence surpasses that of all bodhisattvas.
If you wish to attain the supreme true path, you should cultivate diligence as did the Buddhas of the past.
At that time, the Brahma-deva Bhāvanā said to the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati:
"Regarding what is called 'Buddha-dharma,' what is meant by the term 'Buddha-dharma'?"
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“Brahmā, the Buddha-dharma is called all dharmas; all dharmas are called the Buddha-dharma.”
As the nature of the Buddha-dharma is the nature of all phenomena, so the nature of all phenomena is the nature of the Buddha-dharma.

There is no distinction between the nature of the Buddha-dharma and the nature of all phenomena; all phenomena are quiescent, and the Buddha-dharma is also quiescent; all phenomena are empty, and the Buddha-dharma is also empty.
"Brahmā! All dharmas are the twelve links of dependent origination, and bodhi is likewise the twelve links of dependent origination. Brahmā said:
“Good son! Is the Buddha-dharma not, after all, nothing more than the dharmas of the triple world? “Brahmā!”
"The nature of the three realms and the Buddha-dharma is without distinction; the three realms are equal and the Buddha-dharma is equal, for there are no two separate characteristics. "Good son!"
"Just as space has neither increase nor decrease, so too is the Buddha-dharma: it neither increases nor decreases; because its nature is empty, it is without superior or inferior.
"Brahmā! [he said].
If a son of good family wishes to see the Buddha-dharma, he should contemplate it in this way:

"Furthermore, Brahmā, the Buddha-dharma is neither a locus nor a non-locus; it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is not blue, yellow, red, white, variegated, lapis lazuli, or the color of the realm of space; it is neither multicolored nor formless."

It has no material form, neither square nor round, neither long nor short; it is signless and the sign of signlessness, without bondage and without liberation. That which is without such signs is called the Buddha-dharma.

It is signless, without phrases, and without letters; it is pure and tranquil—the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of signlessness, the meaning of non-accumulation, the meaning of ultimate non-emergence, and the meaning of awakening and knowledge.
That which cannot be proclaimed, cannot be beheld, and cannot be seen is called the meaning of tranquility (*śānta*).

The meaning of tranquility is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the meaning of emptiness is the meaning of non-accumulation; the meaning of non-accumulation is the meaning of reality (*tattva*); the meaning of reality is the meaning of ultimate non-emergence; and the meaning of ultimate non-emergence is the meaning of non-extinction.
The meaning of non-extinction is the meaning of having no location; the meaning of having no location is precisely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The nature of phenomena is the Buddha-dharma; it is called the Dharma of training, the Dharma of the Arhat, the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha, and the Dharma of the Buddha.

"In this way, the Buddha-dharma and all other dharmas likewise have no place of abiding; they neither arise nor cease. They possess no color, form, substance, squareness, roundness, length, or shortness. They have no characteristics of wisdom, no ignorance, and no darkness. All dharmas are equal and without distinction."
Those who seek the Buddha-dharma refer to the Buddhas, the Buddha-dharma, and all dharmas.
It is only when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree that they are able to know and see them with perfect clarity and reality.

Why is this? Because the true Dharma of all Buddhas has no place of abiding; likewise, all phenomena have no place of abiding. The Buddha-dharma cannot be apprehended, and all phenomena cannot be apprehended either.
The Buddha-dharma is equal, and all dharmas are likewise equal.

If there are no causes and conditions, there is no lineage; if there is no lineage, there is no arising or ceasing; if there is no arising or ceasing, it is called the reality. One who knows reality is the true nature; the dharmas of the past, future, and present are themselves the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? Because they have attained unimpeded penetration through the three periods of time.

That which is unimpeded is precisely the Buddha-wisdom; Buddha-wisdom is precisely the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). These unique qualities encompass all phenomena (*dharma*); therefore, all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma. All phenomena and the Buddha-dharma are non-dual and without distinction.
The Brahmā said:
"Good son! Do you now clearly see the Buddha-dharma?"
“Brahmā! The Buddha-dharma is not form and cannot be seen; how can you say that you see it clearly?
All dharmas are entirely invisible. That which is truly clear is itself the Buddha-dharma, for it possesses no dual characteristics.”
The Brahmā said: "Good son, for what reason does the Tathāgata say that the Buddha knows and sees all dharmas?"
“Brahmā! If the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata possessed a fixed characteristic, one could say that it is known and seen with complete clarity. “Good son!”
"Is the Buddha-dharma non-existent?
"Brahmā! If dharmas have no fixed nature, they cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist."
"If it cannot be said that there is the characteristic of existence or non-existence, how can one say that there is clear knowledge and vision? "Good son!
How does the Tathāgata speak of the Buddha-dharma?"
“Brahmā! As it is said regarding space, the nature of space truly has no fixed characteristic; the Buddha-dharma is likewise. “Noble son!”

The Buddha-dharma is thus inconceivable; when a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, that they hear such a teaching without being startled or terrified is inconceivable, and the nature of perfect awakening is likewise inconceivable.
“Brahmā! That which is taught by the Buddha is precisely what enables one to give rise to this bodhicitta; therefore, hearing it does not produce fear. Brahmā!”
If there is attachment, fear arises;
if there is no attachment, fear does not arise.
Those who cherish their bodies and lives give rise to fear; those who do not cherish their bodies and lives have nothing to fear.
Those who possess obstructions give rise to fear; those without obstructions have nothing to fear.
Those who are attached to a self and what belongs to a self give rise to fear; those who have severed the notion of a self and what belongs to a self have nothing to fear.
“Good son! By what power does a bodhisattva mahāsattva hear the profound Buddha-dharma and not give rise to fear?
“Brahmā! [the Bodhisattva replied.]
There are eight kinds of powers by which one hears the profound Buddha-dharma and does not give rise to fear.
What are these eight?
First, the power of faith;
Second, the power of virtuous friends;
third, the power of extensive learning;
fourth, the power of roots of goodness.
Fifth, the power of skillful reflection;
sixth, the power of destroying arrogance;
seventh, the power of great compassion;
Eighth is the power of abiding in accordance with the Dharma. Brahmā!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these eight powers, they will not give rise to fear upon hearing the teaching of the profound Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"You have skillfully proclaimed the various powers of the bodhisattvas.
It is truly as you say; endowed with such powers, a bodhisattva does not give rise to fear upon hearing the profound Buddha-dharma."

"Good son! All verbal expressions are called 'sound. The nature of bodhi is neither expressible nor visible; that which cannot be expressed or seen is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The Tathāgata clearly knows and sees this which cannot be proclaimed, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, he proclaims it."
“Awakening is neither mind nor mental factors, much less sound or syllables!

‘Good son, it is because the Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings that he awakens to the extremely profound Dharma. Having awakened to this extremely profound Dharma, there is no knowing and no awakening, no mind and no mental factors, no sound and no syllables, and it cannot be proclaimed. Yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of the sequence of written characters, sounds, and voices.”
“Good son! For example, space is not a material phenomenon; it cannot be seen, it is neither resistant nor created. Good son!”
Suppose there is a person skilled in painting who draws images upon the empty sky—whether of men or women, elephants or horses—is such a person conceivable?
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
This may still be considered credible;
however, that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, knows that which is ineffable yet is able to expound it—this matter is exceedingly difficult.
Although he thus speaks this ineffable Dharma, the true nature of reality remains ineffable.

"Good son! If, upon hearing this Dharma, one is neither startled nor terrified, you should know that this person has long planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Tathāgatas."

"Good son! Such a sutra as this is inconceivable. If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain it, that person will be able to uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and will encompass the liberation of all sentient beings."

“Good son! If there were a bodhisattva who could clearly perceive all the Buddhas in immeasurable worlds, and having seen them, were to take the most excellent and wondrous seven treasures to fill these worlds and offer them to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—would the merit of this person not be great?”
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
Such merit is difficult to describe through analogy.”
“Good son! It is not as if someone were to protect the True Dharma out of compassion, receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining this sutra. Why is that? Because—”
The gift of the Dharma surpasses the gift of food.
Indeed, the gift of food is a worldly gift, whereas the gift of the Dharma is a supramundane gift. "Good son!
If a person can protect the Buddha’s True Dharma, they are encompassed by the four [modes of] gathering. What are these four?
First, they are gathered by the Buddha.
Second, being embraced by the devas;
third, being embraced by merit;
fourth, being embraced by wisdom.
"The Buddha’s gathering of sentient beings further involves four matters:
first, they always attain close proximity to all Buddhas;
second, no māras can find an opportunity against them."
Third, they obtain the inexhaustible dhāraṇī;
fourth, they dwell in the stage of non-retrogression.
"The celestial beings who gather sentient beings also have four matters: [the same four as above]."
First, the deities purify the place where the Dharma is preached;
second, at the time of preaching the Dharma, the assembly joyfully listens;
third, one is never harmed by external causes or conditions.
Fourth, to inspire faith in those who lack it.
There are also four matters by which merit gathers in sentient beings:
first, the adornment of the body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
Second, adorning the mouth, such that whatever one proclaims is joyfully heard by sentient beings;
third, adorning the Buddha-lands;
fourth, adorning one's lineage, namely as Śakra, Brahmā, or a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
“Wisdom that gathers sentient beings also has four aspects:
first, knowing the faculties of sentient beings and preaching the Dharma according to their needs;
second, knowing the illnesses and sufferings of sentient beings and administering medicine according to their ailments.”
Third, they attain great supernormal powers and travel through all Buddha-lands;
fourth, they clearly and thoroughly penetrate the Dharma-realm. "Good son!
"If you wish to obtain such merit as this, you should diligently protect and uphold the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one can protect the Dharma with compassion, Uphold this sutra and explain it extensively,"
I say that one part out of a thousand is like taking a single drop from the great ocean.
One who knows gratitude, remembers kindness, and keeps the Tathāgata in mind—such a person may be entrusted with the Dharma-treasury;
they shall make offerings to the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions and thus be able to protect the Buddha-dharma.
Though one may bestow immeasurable treasures of the nations as gifts, it is not equal to reciting a single verse with a sincere heart;
the gift of Dharma is most wondrous and surpasses the gift of food. Therefore, the wise should protect the Dharma.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, along with devas, nāgas, and spirits, are embraced by their merit and wisdom;
they adorn themselves with the various marks and signs through their practice—all these beings do so because they protect the True Dharma.
They constantly encounter all Buddhas and spiritual friends, And constantly hear the unsurpassed, true path;
They swiftly attain immeasurable dhāraṇīs— All these people do so by virtue of protecting the True Dharma.
Their precepts of body, speech, and mind become pure; Possessing great supernormal powers, they travel through all lands;
Never regressing from Bodhi and endowed with the six perfections— All such people do so by virtue of protecting the True Dharma.
The atoms of the world may be fully described, But the merit of protecting the Dharma is immeasurable.
If one wishes to attain that which cannot be proclaimed, One should protect the True Dharma with a firm mind.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Guṇaratnaprabhāsa. He rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet in reverent salutation, knelt on both knees with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In this great sūtra, the Tathāgata has stated that the Buddha-dharma cannot be expounded.
If it cannot be expounded, how can it be protected?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, it is so, it is so.”

The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is truly ineffable; the Tathāgata awakens to the Dharma that cannot be spoken. Although such True Dharma is ineffable, it possesses syllables and phrases, and by means of these syllables and phrases, it can be proclaimed and revealed.
To thus receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, explain, and elucidate these words and phrases is called "protecting the Dharma.

"Good son! Furthermore, there is another way to protect the Dharma: seeing those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, explain, and elucidate [the teachings], one should respect, make offerings to, attend upon, prostrate to, honor, and praise them; one should conceive of them as teachers and provide protection, supplying them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, dwellings, and lamps and candles. Upon hearing what they say, one should exclaim 'Excellent! One should protect their lineage and their residences, and likewise protect their servants and attendants. When hearing evil of them, one should conceal it; when hearing of their goodness, one should proclaim it."
"Good son! If one can protect those who uphold this Dharma, such a person is able to protect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Furthermore, good son!"
If there are those who can cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, such persons are indeed upholders of the True Dharma. Furthermore, good son,

if one does not dwell together with those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, but instead restrains their transgressions through speech and discourse, such a person is indeed an upholder of the True Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son!

If there is anyone who can cultivate and accumulate a heart of compassion, free from thoughts of food and drink, and out of pity for sentient beings proclaims the True Dharma, this is called 'protecting the Dharma.'"
"Furthermore, good son!
To receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain such sutras as these without begrudging one's own body or life is called 'protecting the Dharma.'"
"Furthermore, good son!

If there is one who listens to even a single word or a single phrase of the Dharma, traveling for a distance of one yojana or even walking seven steps in the time it takes to breathe out once, this is called 'protecting the Dharma.'"

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahājñānasvarabala Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The land is named Pure Light, and the eon is named Lofty Manifestation.
That realm consists entirely of blue lapis lazuli jewels.

The assembly of bodhisattvas has all achieved immeasurable power; they are fully endowed with supernormal powers and unimpeded wisdom. All these bodhisattvas have attained celestial bodies and listen to the Dharma with sincere hearts, without any distinction between those who have left the household life and those who remain at home.
At that time, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, the World-Honored One proclaimed the Right Dharma to the great assembly.
At that moment, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmamati who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What is this Dharma that you speak of as being protected? The Buddha said, "Good son!
Now, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) delight in seeking after objects; if one can restrain them, this is called "protecting the Dharma.
Good son! When visual consciousness engages with forms, this is called "unrighteousness" (adharma); if one can distance oneself from it, this is called "protecting the Dharma."
It is the same for the mental consciousness regarding phenomena. Good son,
if one sees that the eye is empty, and having seen this, does not contemplate forms nor cling to consciousness, this is called the Dharma.
If one can truly know such dharmas as these, this is called "protecting the Dharma.
Furthermore, if one perceives the emptiness of the mind, and having perceived it, does not contemplate dharmas nor cling to consciousness, this is called "the Dharma."
If one can truly know such dharmas as these, this is called "protecting the Dharma.
"Good son! If a dharma can give rise to another dharma, yet within that dharma one does not seek it, does not grasp it, and the mind has no greedy attachment, this is called 'protecting the Dharma.'"

If there are views that can give rise to wrong views, and one does not seek them, does not grasp at them, and the mind does not become attached to them within those views, this is called protecting the Dharma.

If there is ignorance that cannot purify the mind, and one does not seek it, does not grasp at it, and the mind does not become attached to it within those defilements, this is called protecting the Dharma.
“Good son! If there is a single dharma which, once acquired, cannot be bestowed upon others, this dharma is neither the True Dharma nor the Vinaya.
If one can bestow it, that is the True Dharma and that is the Vinaya.”
If there is no grasping, no seeking, and no giving, that is the True Dharma and that is the Vinaya.
Indeed, grasping and seeking are the non-path.
If one does not give, that is the non-Dharma and the non-Vinaya.
If one is able to practice giving, this is itself the True Dharma and itself the Vinaya.
Not grasping, not seeking, and not giving is itself non-emergence, non-arising, and non-extinction.
If there were no arising and ceasing, how could anything be bestowed?
That which cannot be bestowed is called the Dharma; it is called the Vinaya. Why is this so?
Because it serves as the causal condition for the arising of afflictions that act as obstacles, it is therefore inexhaustible.
That which is inexhaustible has no emergence; that which has no emergence is called the Dharma and is called the Vinaya.
To neither seek nor grasp at such a Dharma is called "protecting the Dharma."
“Good son! At that time, when that Buddha was preaching this Dharma, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, both dharma and non-dharma are called ‘dharma.
Why is this? Because...”

If there is one who discriminates between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, that person is not said to be upholding the True Dharma; if one forms conceptual marks of phenomena, this is called non-Dharma, World-Honored One!
If one can thoroughly understand and see that all phenomena are non-phenomena, this is called the primary meaning of reality.
World-Honored One!
If there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon, that is the "innumerable"; if it is innumerable, it is the true nature; and the true nature is named "space."

The nature of space is boundless and without joints; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise. There is no distinction between the nature of phenomena and their true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Why?
Because they are boundless and without joints.
If there is a bodhisattva who sees such things as these, that is true seeing.
World-Honored One!
I do not see a single dharma; because I do not see it, I do not see increase, nor do I see decrease.
World-Honored One!
Having seen it in this way, would I not be slandering the Tathāgata?
Is this a true vision?
“‘Good son! One who views it in this way does not slander the Tathāgata; this is the true view.
When this Dharma was spoken, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati and ten thousand devas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
“Good son! Do you know that the Bodhisattva Dharmamati at that time was anyone other than myself? It was I who was he.”
"Therefore, the True Dharma that I have sought throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I now entrust to you.
At that time, sixty trillion bodhisattvas and others within the assembly raised their voices in unison and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We shall together protect, uphold, and widely proclaim the True Dharma.
The Buddha said,
"Virtuous sons!..."
"How do you now abide in accordance with the Dharma to protect and uphold the True Dharma?
Bodhisattva Śailendra then spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
“Those who cherish their own bodies and lives cannot protect the Dharma; I do not cherish my life, but abide according to the Dharma, and therefore I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Guṇaparvatarāja said, “World-Honored One!
"Those who possess greed for gain cannot protect the Dharma; because I am free from greed for gain, I am able to protect the Dharma.
Bodhisattva Ratnaketu said, "World-Honored One!..."
"If one perceives the two marks of 'dharma' and 'non-dharma,' one cannot protect the Dharma; because I am free from these two marks, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyagarbha said, "World-Honored One!"
"One who possesses afflictions cannot protect the Dharma; because I possess the power of wisdom and have already distanced myself from them, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Holder of the Torch said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"One who does not destroy darkness cannot protect the Dharma; because I have now destroyed darkness, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha said, "World-Honored One!"
"If one follows the minds of others, one cannot protect the Dharma; because I follow my own intention, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vyūharāja said, "World-Honored One!"
"One who does not regulate the sense faculties cannot protect the Dharma; because I have now brought them under control, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Pure Light said, "World-Honored One!"

"If one were to construct various conceptual marks of phenomena, one would be unable to protect the Dharma; because I am now free from various conceptual marks regarding phenomena, I am able to protect the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vardhamāna said:
"World-Honored One!..."

fourth, they revile and disparage the gift of Dharma.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, impure bodily action; second, failure to guard verbal action;
[third, failure to guard mental action; fourth, wrong view]."
Third, not relinquishing mental action;
fourth, feeling weary of and regretting the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, to engage in divisive speech for the purpose of breaking up harmonious communities;
second, to utter words of anger toward one's teacher or preceptor;
third, to engage in meaningless speech for the purpose of destroying what is beneficial.
Fourth, deceiving humans and devas by giving rise to false speech.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, not guarding the causes of the precepts;
Second, the cause for disturbing meditative concentration;
third, lack of faith in future lives;
fourth, delighting in and attachment to worldly affairs.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, coarseness; second, arrogance; [third, ...]; fourth, ..."
Third, delighting in worldly talk;
fourth, constantly delighting in sleep.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:"
First, they falsely assume the name of a bodhisattva while receiving offerings;
second, they are unable to care for those suffering from illness;
third, they do not plant the seeds of goodness.
Fourth, not turning toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, self-deprecation;
Second, disparaging the Dharma;
third, disparaging merit;
fourth, frequently thinking of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, there are four things:
first, craving for the body;
second, craving for the mind."
Third, craving for life;
fourth, craving for precepts.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:"
First, craving for dwellings;
second, craving for patrons;
third, craving for wrong views.
Fourth, greed for breaking the precepts.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, doing much;..."
Second, speaking much; third, receiving much;
fourth, looking about much.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, the view of a self;
second, false views;..."
Third, the view of annihilationism;
fourth, the view of eternalism.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, not doing it; second, turning away after having done it;
third, feeling regret in one's heart.
Fourth, lack of joy. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, not tending toward the stage of the Path;
Second, not cultivating meditative concentration;
third, falling away from wisdom;
fourth, taking no delight in skillful means.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, obstructing the Dharma;
second, obstructing wholesome karma;"
Third, the obstacle of afflictions;
fourth, the obstacle of Māra’s activities. "Good son!..."
"Such dharmas as these are called obstructions to the Mahāyāna.

When this teaching was spoken, forty-four thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and twenty-eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The great earth of the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and immeasurable devas and humans in the void spoke with one voice in these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
World-Honored One!
Today the Tathāgata has let out the great lion’s roar, out of compassion for sentient beings, opening the gate of the Mahāyāna.
World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who obtain even a small portion of this Dharma, they shall immediately sever the sufferings of the three evil realms and gradually attain the immeasurable treasures of the Dharma.
It is like a person who, seeing a great heap of jewels outside a village or town, feels compassion upon seeing it and immediately returns to the village to tell the people:
"Whoever wishes to sever poverty, let them come with me."
When this person speaks these words, some may believe and others may not.

Among them, those who believe follow him together to the place of treasure; they gather as much as they wish and immediately overcome their poverty and suffering, yet that mass of treasure neither increases nor decreases.
Furthermore, it does not think: "I permit this person to take, but not that person; I relieve this person's poverty, but not that person's; I permit this one to carry it away, but not that one."

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise so: throughout immeasurable ages he diligently sought this unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma; having sought it and attained its vision, he gives rise to great compassion and addresses all sentient beings with a Brahma-like voice:
"If there are those who wish to destroy the poverty of birth and death, you should listen with a sincere heart."
There are sentient beings of meager merit who lack faith; they are thus unable to destroy the poverty of birth and death.

Among them, those who do have faith may, according to their respective intellectual capacities, take up the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, or the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva. This great mass of jewels neither increases nor decreases.
If there are those who come to this treasury of jewels and are unable to take even a single jewel, such persons shall dwell forever within the three evil realms.

If there are those who can take up even a single word or a single phrase, or who can receive and uphold it for even a single thought-moment, such persons will be able to destroy the poverty of birth and death.
"How much more so, then, for one who takes up even a single chapter or two of this Mahāyāna sūtra, and fully listens to, receives, recites, and explains it to others?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the devas and humans:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O sons of the gods!

If there are those who receive and uphold such a sutra as this, these persons will be endowed with all wholesome dharmas; they will carry upon their heads the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom of the Tathāgata; they will be a great mass of wisdom, capable of bringing great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Among all vehicles, the Great Vehicle is supreme; Like space, it is without limit or boundary.
Far removed from all existence within birth and death, It proceeds toward the Bodhi tree without obstruction."
If one can purify the mind, bestow all gifts upon all beings,
and wholeheartedly uphold the pure precepts, one will proceed toward the Bodhi tree without obstruction.
Maintaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, Constantly observing the afflictions and various transgressions,
One can surpass all inferior vehicles And discipline sentient beings within the Mahāyāna.
If there are those who with a sincere heart receive and recite the sutras, Possessing the precepts of tranquility and patience, and endowed with wisdom to destroy the hosts of Māra;

Out of compassion for sentient beings, they proceed to the Tree of Enlightenment, Adorned with kindness and mercy, riding upon the four dhyānas; With the sharp blade of wisdom, they crush the hosts of Māra.
Beneath the Tree of Enlightenment, he contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination; having arisen, out of compassion for the multitudes, he preached the Mahāyāna.
Beings of the ten directions ride upon the Mahāyāna; this vehicle neither increases nor decreases, being like empty space.
The supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna are inconceivable; therefore, the Tathāgata has cultivated and gathered them.

Abiding securely in the foundations of mindfulness and adorning himself with right exertion, taking the bases of psychic power as his feet and the faculties as his strength, he traverses the Eightfold Path to gather the jewels of awakening; for this reason, the Tathāgata proceeded to the Bodhi tree.
His mind is tranquil and free from afflictions; having destroyed all darkness, he has attained the light of wisdom.
Therefore, Brahmā and Śakra pay homage to the Tathāgata who rides the Great Vehicle.
Fully endowed with the six perfections and the six supernormal powers, Possessing skillful means and cultivating the three liberations,
Able to destroy all māras and false views— Therefore, the Tathāgata rides upon the Mahāyāna.

If there are those who possess all roots of goodness, And those who have accomplished roots of unwholesomeness, Whoever has faith shall break through the afflictions; Therefore, the Mahāyāna is inconceivable.
All worldly dharmas whatsoever, as well as the unsurpassed supramundane dharmas,
whether they be the dharmas of those in training or the dharmas of those beyond training— all are subsumed within the Mahāyāna.
