If there are sentient beings who walk upon evil paths, Who associate with wrong views and evil friends,
Out of compassion for such as these, he cultivates skillful means And, for the sake of their subduing, preaches the Mahāyāna.
Inferior beings take no delight in the Mahāyāna; their minds are narrow and they cannot sever the fetters of others.
Constantly seeking their own pleasure while abandoning others, they give rise to terror upon hearing the Mahāyāna explained.
If there is a wise person endowed with power and influence, who out of compassion for sentient beings brings them benefit,
hearing the teaching of the Mahāyāna their heart rejoices, and they destroy all suffering and affliction without regret.

If one wishes to fully understand the conduct of sentient beings— The various elements and faculties of all living beings—the Bodhisattva can penetrate them in a single thought-moment; Therefore, the Mahāyāna is inconceivable.

One attains the physical tranquility adorned with marks, One attains verbal tranquility that all delight to hear, And one attains mental tranquility endowed with supernormal powers; All such things arise from entering the Mahāyāna.
If there are those who can practice the Mahāyāna, they shall not sever the lineage of the Triple Gem;
they can bring benefit to sentient beings and destroy all the sufferings of poverty.
Able to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions, Directly beholding immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones—
Those who thus advance toward the Mahāyāna Shall immediately obtain immeasurable merit.
Unconquerable by anyone in all the worlds, those who proceed toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna possess great power that destroys the hosts of Māra; therefore, the Mahāyāna is inconceivable.
Attaining mastery over form and power, The bodies of Brahmā, Śakra, and the Universal Monarch—
If there are those who ride this Great Vehicle, Such persons shall enjoy the bliss of the triple world.
Having given, one never gives rise to a mind of regret; One does not begrudge or cling to that which is most cherished.
Sacrificing one’s own body in giving, one cultivates loving-kindness and compassion; Therefore, the Mahāyāna is inconceivable.
Upholding the precepts with diligence and delighting in the holy life, they can use their supernormal powers to obstruct the sun and moon;
without craving for the body or its virtuous rewards, they cultivate such a vehicle to harmonize sentient beings.
When preaching the Dharma, whether it is accepted or rejected, one gives rise to neither anger nor attachment;
with body and mind, one diligently practices great vigor in order to attain the Mahāyāna that is so difficult to find.
One can attain the state of the unsurpassed Great Dharma King, and likewise achieve the forbearance that is difficult to endure;
though one may undergo suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable eons, it is for the sake of attaining the Mahāyāna that transcends all.
Diligently performing what benefits many sentient beings, with the actions of body, speech, and mind all being supple;
cultivating and accumulating compassion and supernormal powers, for the sake of abiding in the Great Vehicle’s great benefit.
Fully understanding the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the dharma-realm, Being selfless, without contention, and having harmonized the faculties—
If one can abide securely in the Mahāyāna, One shall receive peace and happiness just as the Buddhas of the past did.
Endowed with mindfulness and diligence, and possessing the great supernormal powers of the four bases of psychic mastery,
they rely upon the true Dharma and its ultimate meaning— all because they delight in abiding in the Mahāyāna.
Fully endowed with the unsurpassed fearlessnesses, the Unsurpassed Honored One can roar the lion’s roar;
adorned with the subtle and wondrous marks and signs, all this arises from delighting in abiding in the Mahāyāna.
Fully possessing the three kinds of supernormal powers, they tame and transform sentient beings;
their minds are tranquil and free from pride, and as they practice the Mahāyāna, they are endowed with patience.
Possessing the full Brahma-voice, subtle and exquisite, which all sentient beings greatly delight to hear;
if one delights in cultivating and accumulating the Mahāyāna, such a person skillfully understands the languages of all sentient beings.
All karmic deeds performed shall become a pure land; before long, one shall attain a boundless body.
If there are those who listen to this Dharma with a sincere heart, they shall receive boundless and unsurpassed bliss.

One may traverse the void to its furthest limits and know the number of drops in the waters of the great ocean, yet one cannot fully expound the virtues of the Mahāyāna; therefore, this vehicle is inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Sāgaramati Bodhisattva:
“Good son, if you wish to uphold such sūtras as these, and if you wish to bring profound stillness to your own deep mind, you should uphold the gate-words, the dharma-words, and the vajra-words.”
Regarding the gate-phrase of wholehearted observation: it serves as the gateway within all phenomena.
That is to say, the letter *A* is the gateway to all phenomena; *A* signifies "non-existence," for all dharmas are entirely impermanent.
*Pa* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *pa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
*Na* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *na* is the non-obstruction of all dharmas.
*Dha* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *dha* is the nature that can subdue the nature of all dharmas.
"Sa" is also a gateway to all dharmas; "sa" means to remain far removed from all dharmas.
"Ta" is also a gateway to all dharmas; "ta" means that all dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*).
Ka is also a gateway to all dharmas; Ka means that all dharmas are without action and without reception.
Sa is also a gateway to all dharmas; Sa means that all dharmas are without discrimination.
Ga is also a gateway to all dharmas; "ga" signifies that the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is profoundly deep and bottomless.
Ja is also a gateway to all dharmas; "ja" signifies being far removed from the marks of arising.
*Dham* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *dham* means that within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one does not give rise to discrimination.
*Sama* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *sama* means being endowed with *śamatha* and attaining the Eightfold Noble Path.
*Kha* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *kha* means that all phenomena are like empty space.
*Cha* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *cha* means that all phenomena are exhausted.
If it is also all dharma-gates, "if" means that all dharmas are unimpeded.
Ta-ho is also all dharma-gates; "ta-ho" means that all dharmas are either possible or impossible.
*Gu* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *gu* refers to obtaining great benefit after contemplating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
*Da* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *da* refers to the fact that all dharmas have no ultimate end.
*Ka* is also a gateway to all dharmas; because *ka* signifies the tranquility of the body, one attains great benefit.
*Tī* is also a gateway to all dharmas; because *tī* signifies the tranquility of the mind, one is freed from all evils.
"U" is also all dharma-gates; "U" refers to upholding, protecting, and purifying the precepts.
"Śe" is also all dharma-gates; "Śe" refers to skillful reflection.
"Substitution" (*ti*) is also a gateway to all dharmas; "substitution" means abiding in all dharmas.
"Cultivation" (*xiu*) is also a gateway to all dharmas; "cultivation" means that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is liberation.
*Vī* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *vī* means that all dharmas are entirely *vinaya*, and *vinaya* means the taming of one's own self.
*Kāla* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *kāla* means that the nature of all dharmas is unstained.
"A" is also a gateway to all dharmas; "A" means that the nature of all dharmas is luminosity.
"Sa" is also a gateway to all dharmas; "Sa" means practicing the Eightfold Noble Path.
*Bha* is also a gateway to all dharmas; *bha* means that all dharmas are neither internal nor external.
Son of good family!
This is called a "gate-word" (*mukhapada*); it can purify the mindful mind, it can purify the mind, and it enables one to know the faculties of sentient beings.
“The Dharma Verses are the seal of liberation for all dharmas; the seal of non-duality for all dharmas;
the seal of impermanence and non-annihilation for all dharmas; the seal of neither increase nor decrease for all dharmas;
the seal that all dharmas are equal to space; the seal of the path of the five eyes for all dharmas; [all] dharmas...”
Like the seal of space, all dharmas are without discrimination; like the seal of space, all dharmas enter the seal of the Dharma-realm;
all dharmas are like a seal; all dharmas are without past, future, or present, like a seal;
all dharmas are the seal of the purity of their own nature; all dharmas are the seal of emptiness.
The seal of all phenomena being signless; the seal of all phenomena being wishless; the seal of all phenomena being neither having a location nor lacking a location;
the seal of all phenomena being suffering; the seal of all phenomena being selfless; the seal of all phenomena being tranquil;
the seal of the nature of all phenomena being without fault; and the ultimate truth of all phenomena.
The seal of grasping; the seal that all phenomena abide according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
the seal of the ultimate liberation of all phenomena; the seal that all phenomena are timeless; the seal that all phenomena transcend the three periods of time;
the seal of the single flavor of all phenomena; the seal of the unimpeded nature of all phenomena; the One.
The seal that the nature of all phenomena is unborn; the seal that the nature of all phenomena is without contention;
the seal that the nature of all phenomena is without applied and sustained thought; the seal that all phenomena are non-material and invisible;
the seal that all phenomena have no abode; the seal that all phenomena have no antidote; all phenomena...
The seal of the absence of karmic fruit; the seal that all phenomena are without agent and without recipient;
the seal that all phenomena are without arising or cessation. Good son!
This is called the Dharma-phrase.
Such Dharma-phrases are the bodhi of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Such phrases of the Dharma-seal encompass the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma.
"Good son! If one can contemplate the aggregates of phenomena in this manner, one will immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Good son!"
If there are those who have not yet planted roots of goodness, upon hearing this Dharma they will immediately plant them and destroy the works of Māra. Good son!

If one contemplates in this way, one can obtain the *Akṣayakara-dhāraṇī* (Inexhaustible Vessel Dhāraṇī), and through such dharmas as these, one is able to encompass the eighty-four thousand samādhis and the eighty-four thousand types of conduct and dispositions of sentient beings; this is called the "Dharma-phrase."
“Regarding the ‘vajra-phrase’: its body is indestructible, just like a vajra. Why is this?
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indestructible, and the nature of wisdom is capable of destroying ignorance; therefore, wisdom is called the vajra-phrase.”
The five heinous crimes destroy all roots of goodness; therefore, the five heinous crimes are called adamantine phrases (*vajrapada*).
The meditation on impurity can destroy lustful desire; therefore, the meditation on impurity is called an adamantine phrase.
The contemplation of loving-kindness can destroy hatred; therefore, loving-kindness is called a vajra phrase.
The contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination can destroy delusion; therefore, the contemplation of conditions is called a vajra phrase.
The mind of a single sentient being encompassing the minds of all sentient beings is called a vajra phrase.
The mind of a single sentient being and the minds of all sentient beings being entirely equal is called a vajra phrase.
All Buddhas and each individual Buddha are entirely equal; this is called a vajra phrase.
A single field of merit and all fields of merit are inexhaustibly equal; this is called a vajra phrase.
All phenomena are equal to space; this is called a vajra phrase.
All phenomena are of one single flavor; this is called a vajra phrase.
All phenomena and the Buddha-dharma are equal and non-dual; this is called a vajra phrase.
The Vajra Samādhi can destroy all the evil karma of Māras; it is called a Vajra Phrase.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous voice destroys all evil sounds; it is called a Vajra Phrase.
To contemplate that which is without arising or ceasing as transcending birth, old age, and death is called a vajra phrase. "Good son!
Such dharmas as these are called vajra phrases, called firm phrases, called indestructible phrases, and called..."
The indestructible phrase is called the phrase of equality, the phrase of reality, the phrase of non-duality,
the phrase of non-retrogression, the phrase of great tranquility, the phrase of being incapable of committing transgressions, the phrase of neither increasing nor decreasing,
the phrase of the non-existence of existence, the phrase of the non-existence of dharmas, the phrase of truth, the phrase of existence, and the phrase that does not slander the Buddha.
The phrase of the Dharma, the phrase of relying on the Dharma, the phrase of being with the Saṃgha, the phrase of suchness,
the phrase of discerning the three periods of time, the phrase of valor, the phrase of the Brahma, the phrase of loving-kindness, the phrase of the mind,

the phrase of space, the phrase of bodhi, the phrase of non-depression, the phrase of the characteristics of dharmas, the phrase of signlessness, and the phrase of the non-abiding of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
The phrase of Pāpīyān; the phrase of destroying Māra; the phrase of the unsurpassed; the phrase of the invincible; the phrase of the extensive;
the phrase of acting within one’s own domain; the phrase of entering the Buddha’s domain; the phrase of being without vitarka and vicāra;
the phrase of non-discrimination regarding the dharma-realm; the phrase of no-phrase.
“Good son! If there are bodhisattvas who can understand the meaning of such phrases as these, they shall surely sit beneath the Bodhi tree upon the Vajra-Lion Dharma-seat.”
When this Dharma was being taught, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for entering the Dharma-gate and also acquired the samādhi of equality toward all sentient beings.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of music, and spoke these verses in praise:
“I now pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, Who is able to know the voices of all sentient beings.”
You teach that the characterized and the uncharacterized are in truth a single characteristic, yet you attain the thirty-two wondrous marks.
If there are sentient beings with every single thought, you impartially encompass the minds of all sentient beings;
you teach that practice and non-practice are in truth a single practice. Therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The Tathāgata truly knows cause and effect, And thus he proclaims karmic retribution for the sake of sentient beings;
Since the Dharmadhātu of True Suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, I therefore praise the Unsurpassed Honored One.
All sentient beings lack discursive thought and investigation; their minds are fundamentally pure and free from greed.
Yet, through the power of causes and conditions, craving arises. Therefore, I pay homage to the cause of true wisdom.
I see the Buddha’s body in various colors, yet the Tathāgata’s body is truly colorless;
out of compassion for sentient beings, he displays color where there is no color—I pay homage to the Lion-King among Men.
All fields of merit enter into a single field, yet this one field neither increases nor decreases;
it does not move within the dharma-realm nor does it shift—therefore, I pay homage to the Human Elephant King.
Observing that the minds of all sentient beings are like illusions, and that all phenomena and awakening are likewise so;
knowing that all phenomena are entirely equal, I therefore pay homage to the one who is beyond equality.
Observing that all dharma-realms are entirely equal, He thus teaches that all dharmas are neither one nor two;
Neither existent nor non-existent is liberation— Therefore, I pay homage to him who has severed the two views.
One might say that the sun and moon fall to the earth; one might say that a fierce wind can be bound with a rope;
one might say that Mount Sumeru can be moved by blowing upon it with the mouth; but one cannot say that the Buddha has two words.
You speak words of truth, words of reality, and pure words; your body and mind are as pure as space.
Unstained by worldly dharmas like a lotus flower, I therefore pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Whoever is able to praise such virtues as these, shall immediately obtain such merit as these;
for the sake of such merits, I pay homage to this mass of merit.
At that time, having offered their praise, the bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that which is called the Great Jewel is the Buddha.

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of bliss; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of faith; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of mindfulness; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of wisdom. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of the knowledge of the meaning of the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination. The appearance of a Buddha in the world is the emergence of all wholesome dharmas: the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Prajñākūṭa who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The emergence of birth, old age, sickness, and death in the world is the emergence of the Buddha; the emergence of ignorance and craving is the emergence of the Buddha; the emergence of greed, anger, and delusion is the emergence of the Buddha; and the emergence of all nets of doubt and afflictions is the emergence of the Buddha.”
"Why is this? If such dharmas as these did not appear in the world, for what reason would the Buddha appear in the world?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family,
it is truly as you have said.”
At that time, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One,
if there are those who do not see such dharmas as these, does the Tathāgata appear in the world or not appear in the world?”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they truly do not know such dharmas as these; therefore, I have proclaimed them for their sake.”
“Good son! There are four kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who have initially resolved to attain bodhicitta;”
Second, practicing the path to enlightenment;
third, being firm and non-retrogressive regarding enlightenment;
fourth, being destined to succeed to the Buddha's position in a single lifetime.
A Bodhisattva who has resolved to attain enlightenment sees the physical marks of the Buddha; having seen them, they immediately resolve upon bodhicitta.
A Bodhisattva who is practicing the path sees the Buddha endowed with all wholesome dharmas; having seen them, they immediately resolve upon bodhicitta.
A non-regressive bodhisattva perceives the body of the Tathāgata and all phenomena as entirely equal;
a bodhisattva in their final birth does not perceive the specific merits of the Tathāgata nor all phenomena as distinct.
Why is this? Because the wisdom-eye they have attained is perfectly clear and pure; because they have severed the two views; and because their wisdom is purified.
If one perceives neither purity nor impurity, nor that which is neither pure nor impure, such a person is then able to clearly see the Tathāgata.

“Good son! In the past, I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in this way; having seen him, I immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and was also able to clearly know that there is neither attainment nor non-attainment.”

Having attained it, he immediately ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees. Abiding in the void, he clearly and thoroughly understood the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Having clearly understood it, his mind abided nowhere; having no place of abiding, he attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara immediately bestowed upon me this prediction: "Māṇava!

In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
"At that time, I did not hear this sound of the prophecy at all, nor did I have the perception of a Buddha or the perception of a prophecy.
At that time, through my threefold pure wisdom,
I did not perceive the perception of a self, nor the perception of a Buddha, nor the perception of a prophecy."
Furthermore, there are three purities:
not seeing a self, not seeing sentient beings, and not seeing the true Dharma.
Again, there are three purities:
One does not perceive names, one does not perceive forms, and one does not perceive causes.
Furthermore, there are three purities:

seeing that all aggregates (skandhas) entirely enter the aggregate of phenomena (dharmaskandha); seeing that all elements (dhātus) entirely enter the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu); and seeing that all bases (āyatanas) entirely enter the base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, there are three purities:
the past is already exhausted, the future does not arise, and the present does not abide.
Furthermore, there are three purities:
Contemplate the body as being like the moon in water; contemplate sound as being ineffable; contemplate the mind as being invisible.
Furthermore, there are three purities:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
If one views it in this way, that is the true vision regarding the bestowal of the prediction [of enlightenment]. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva forms such a view, it is called the vision of reality."
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Ten.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Five, Part Four: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such views as these, what kind of vows should they make?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

Such a person acts according to their original vow; whether the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind is in meditative concentration or not in concentration, for the sake of sentient beings, they act in accordance with their original vow.

“Good son! It is like a person who has a field of sugarcane or rice, one *qing* in size, with level and even ground. When he wishes to irrigate it, he opens the watergate and lets the water flow out; no further effort is required, and it naturally spreads everywhere.”

Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: whether he is in meditative concentration and focuses his mind in contemplation, or when he is not in concentration and is not contemplating, for the sake of sentient beings he makes vows as originally intended; whatever roots of goodness he performs, he vows to share them all with sentient beings, and having shared them, he dedicates them toward the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is pure, and his morality, patience, concentration, and wisdom are likewise pure; he contemplates the Buddha-dharma and all sentient beings as equal and non-dual.

Although he possesses such vows, from the outset there is no [grasping] mind; therefore, although the Bodhisattva is without such a mind, the power of his vow never fails to reach all sentient beings. He shares all his roots of goodness with them, and having shared them, he dedicates them toward unexcelled bodhi.
“Good son! It is like a śāla tree that someone cuts down; once its roots are severed, it falls in the direction it was cut. Good son!”
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: practicing and cultivating samādhi, they constantly turn toward bodhi.
Suppose someone were to cry out:
"Do not cut down this tree; let it fall where it stands!"
"Even this tree still falls in the direction it was cut;
likewise, it is impossible for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that the wholesome dharmas they have cultivated should not be directed toward unexcelled bodhi."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The wholesome dharmas cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva are solely for the purpose of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed; for purifying the buddha-fields; for adorning the body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; for adorning the mouth so that sentient beings delight in hearing the Dharma when it is preached; for adorning the mind so as to contemplate all sentient beings as equal and non-dual; and for attaining the various samādhis of the Buddhas and the Buddha-dharmas.
Although a bodhisattva does not crave such dharmas, they are able to attain them with mastery.
Why is this? It is due to the power of their vow.
“Good son! It is like a potter:
when the clay is on the wheel, it does not yet receive the name of an object; once it has been fashioned into a vessel, its name is established according to that object.

The wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva are also like this: as long as they have not yet made a vow, they cannot receive the name of ‘pāramitā. Therefore, a bodhisattva must certainly make vows regarding all wholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! It is like a goldsmith:
before the gold has been fashioned into a vessel, it does not yet receive a name; once it has been completed, it receives the name ‘necklace.
The wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva are also like this: as long as one has not yet made the vow, they cannot be called ‘pāramitās.’”
“Good son! It is like a bhikṣu who, wishing to enter the meditative absorption of cessation, first makes a vow:
‘I shall now enter this concentration.’”
"When the gong sounds, one should then arise and depart.
Yet within this samādhi there is no sound of a gong; it is by the power of his vow that he emerges from samādhi precisely when the gong is struck.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who out of compassion for sentient beings makes this vow:
"I shall deliver those who have not yet been delivered; I shall liberate those who have not yet been liberated."

"When cultivating bodhi, one enters deep samādhi; by the power of compassion, one keeps all sentient beings in mind and does not realize the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, although the bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he does not attain their fruit."
“Good son! The conduct of a bodhisattva is inconceivable; although they enter deep meditative absorption, they do not realize the fruits of the śramaṇa path. Good son!”

It is like two people who wish to cross a raging fire: one person, clad in a diamond armor, is able to pass through it; the other person, whose body is covered in dry grass, is consumed by the flames.
Why is this? Because grass is easily burned, whereas gold is firm. It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

out of compassion for sentient beings, they focus their thoughts on Bodhi and adorn themselves with profound and immeasurable samādhis. By the power of these samādhis, they are able to pass beyond the fixed positions of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas without taking the realization of their fruits; having arisen from meditative concentration, they attain the path of perfect enlightenment, the samādhi of the Tathāgata.

Those covered with dry grass are likened to the śrāvakas; because these śrāvakas loathe and repent of saṃsāra and lack compassion for all sentient beings, they are unable to transcend the fixed positions of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Why is this? Because those of the Two Vehicles conceive a sense of contentment regarding merit, whereas Bodhisattvas have no sense of satiety in their hearts regarding merit.

The diamond armor is a metaphor for emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the great fierce fire is a metaphor for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, they are nevertheless able to refrain from realizing the fruits of the śramaṇa path.
“World-Honored One!

It is inconceivable that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are fully endowed with these qualities: they cultivate this samādhi yet do not realize its fruit; they enter the fires of birth and death yet are not burned by them. Because they have accomplished skillful means, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter all meditative concentrations and yet are not deluded or deceived by those concentrations, for they possess skillful means.”

"Though he practices all various conducts, his mind is free from defiled attachment; though he speaks of the fruits of śrāmaṇya for those with wrong views, he himself does not personally realize the fruits of the śrāmaṇya path.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"
"It is exactly as you have said, son of good family!
It is like three dyes—namely lac, saffron, and indigo—placed in a single vessel to dye three kinds of materials: namely wool, cotton cloth, and silk garments."

If wool is soaked in dyeing solution, it becomes blue; if fine cotton cloth is washed clean, it becomes yellow; and if silk (kauseya) is first soaked in lye, it becomes red. Thus, although these three substances are placed in the same vessel, the colors they receive are each different.
Good son! It is the same for those of the three vehicles.
The vessel is a metaphor for emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The three kinds of colors are a metaphor for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
the way the cloth takes on color according to its nature is a metaphor for the three kinds of bodhi.
Even emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness do not give rise to the thought: "I shall grant such a fruit" or "I shall not grant such a fruit."
"Good son! Woolen cloth is a metaphor for the śrāvaka; fine cotton cloth is a metaphor for the pratyekabuddha; and silk cloth is a metaphor for the bodhisattva vehicle.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as being like one who is deaf or blind, seeing that no sentient beings exist, at such a time his mind is free from defiled attachment and there is no regret or regression."
At that time, one truly understands within the mind:
"I neither bring benefit nor lack of benefit to sentient beings, yet I cultivate and accumulate great compassion for the sake of sentient beings."
“Good son! It is like a subtle and pure lapis lazuli gem; even if it remains in the mud for a hundred years, its nature is eternally pure, and once extracted, it returns to its original state.”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he thoroughly understands that the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure, though it is obscured and defiled by adventitious afflictions; yet these adventitious afflictions truly cannot defile the pure mind, just as a pearl in the mud is not defiled by the mud.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects thus:
"If my own mind-nature were defiled by afflictions, how could I possibly transform sentient beings?

For this reason, the bodhisattva always delights in cultivating and accumulating the adornment of merit, delights in making offerings to the Triple Gem while dwelling within the realms of existence, and delights in running errands and serving sentient beings.

He does not give rise to a mind of greed toward objects that provoke desire; he protects and upholds the True Dharma, delights in practicing generosity, is fully endowed with pure precepts, adorns himself with patience, diligently exerts vigor, adorns himself with the factors of dhyāna, cultivates and accumulates wisdom, never tires of extensive learning, maintains pure brahmacarya, and practices the great supernormal powers and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

"Good son! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice such dharmas, they are not defiled by afflictions and do not cling to the three realms. Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess the power of the merit of skillful means, although they move within the three realms, their bodies and minds remain undefiled."
“Good son! It is like a householder who has an only son whom he loves and cherishes deeply. While playing, the son accidentally falls into a latrine.

When the mother sees this, she is repulsed by the foul impurity. Later, when the father sees it, he rebukes the mother; he then enters the latrine, pulls the child out, and washes him clean. Because of the bond of affection, he forgets the stench and filth.”

Good son! The parents of the elder represent the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the latrine represents the triple world; the son represents sentient beings; the mother’s inability to pull him out represents the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the father’s ability to rescue and deliver him represents all bodhisattvas; and the causal condition of love represents great compassion.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, endowed with skillful means, enters the triple world yet is not defiled by the triple world.
Therefore, there are two kinds of paths: the first is that of the Śrāvaka; [the second is that of the Bodhisattva].
Second, the Bodhisattva.
Those on the path of the Śrāvaka are weary of the triple world, whereas those on the path of the Bodhisattva are not weary of the triple world. Good son!

The Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; though they traverse all realms of existence, they do not fall into existence. Since they do not fall into existence and yet do not realize [nirvana], their traversing of the three realms is called skillful means, and their non-realization is called wisdom.

“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as being without dual characteristics—contemplating that dharmas are equal and sentient beings are also equal, and that those who are thus equal are also equal in nirvāṇa—this is called wisdom.”
If one can thus contemplate sentient beings in such a way as not to realize nirvāṇa, this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Pure and unattached giving is called wisdom (*prajñā*); making vows and dedicating [merit] is called skillful means.
“World-Honored One!
What are called pure wisdom and pure skillful means? “Good son!
If a bodhisattva perceives no self, no sentient being, no life-span, and no person, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
If they cultivate and accumulate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, dedicating all roots of goodness and sentient beings toward awakening (*bodhi*), this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
To know the inferior, middling, and superior faculties of all sentient beings is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Having known them, to preach the Dharma according to their inclinations is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Because their wisdom is pure, though they engage in all realms of existence, their minds are free from defiled attachment; because their skillful means are pure, though they cultivate the two vehicles, they do not realize their fruits. "Good son!
If one is not defiled by any afflictions, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To be able to discipline sentient beings and cause them all to incline toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is called skillful means (*upāya*).

The Bodhisattva makes a vow that all sentient beings shall obtain inexhaustible wealth and inexhaustible merit, and that their roots of goodness shall increase; furthermore, that all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—whether in training or beyond training—as well as all Bodhisattvas, shall obtain the Dharma according to their wishes, which is called "pure skillful means."

If one is able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, explaining them extensively and analytically, speaking without end, speaking without obstruction, speaking not in vain, and speaking according to the inclinations [of others], this is called pure wisdom.
That a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not lose the mind of unsurpassed bodhi in every place of rebirth is called pure wisdom.
That in every place of rebirth one dedicates the wholesome dharmas performed toward sentient beings is called pure skillful means.

"Through the causal conditions of pure wisdom, one knows that the bodhicitta is without abode and without root; through pure skillful means, one transforms all sentient beings so that they proceed toward bodhi.
"World-Honored One!"
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is endowed with these two purities, all the karma they perform is none other than bodhi. Why is this?
Within all dharmas there is darkness and obstruction; because destroying this darkness and obstruction is itself bodhi, the Bodhisattva is therefore never separated from bodhi.
If a bodhisattva should form such a thought as,
"I am separated from enlightenment," it should be known that this person shall not attain enlightenment.
If one thinks, "I now possess bodhi," then for that person, bodhi would be subject to purity and impurity.
If one can contemplate all phenomena in this way, one immediately attains bodhi; this is precisely the skillful means of pure wisdom.

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Anantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān;
his land was named Acakṣu, and the kalpa was named Prabhārasa.”

At that time, when the World-Honored One had first sat beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment but had not yet attained Buddhahood, the non-regressive bodhisattvas who were in their last birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) from the worlds of the ten directions all came to behold him. Having arrived at his location, they made offerings with various kinds of flowers, which remained suspended in mid-air at a height of seven tāla trees.

Having attained Buddhahood, he emitted a great radiance that shone throughout the ten directions. In the worlds of the ten directions, there were many devas who, upon seeing the Buddha’s light, each spoke these words:
"The Buddha of Boundless Light has truly appeared in the world."

The adornments and splendors of that Buddha-world were as magnificent as the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas. Ten thousand years after the beginning of that eon, a Buddha appeared in the world named Prabhārasa; for this reason, that eon was called Prabhārasa.

“Good son! During the Prabhārasa kalpa, fourteen hundred million Buddhas, Tathāgatas, appeared in the world. That Buddha-world contained ninety-six thousand small kingdoms; each kingdom was eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Each kingdom had eighty-four thousand cities, each city being one full yojana in length and breadth, and in each city there dwelt eighty-four thousand people.”
That land is fully endowed with such things as these.

Its ground is purely adorned with the four jewels—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and it abounds in food and drink, lacking nothing. The people of that land are free from the notions of "I" and "mine," just like those in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
That Buddha’s lifespan will last for ten full intermediate kalpas; his assembly of śrāvakas will number ninety-six thousand koṭis, and his assembly of bodhisattvas will number twelve thousand koṭis.
In that land there are two cities:
one is named Joy (Rati), and—
The second is named Pure (*Śuddha*).
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, was born in the City of Purity and dwells in the City of Joy.
In that land there is a king named Pure Sound (*Śuddhasvara*), who possesses the seven treasures and rules over a trichiliocosm.

The ladies of the inner palace numbered thirty-six thousand; their countenances were so upright and majestic that they were indistinguishable from those of the heavens. He had one hundred thousand sons, all of them heroic, fierce, and courageous, each possessing half the strength of Nārāyaṇa. Each was endowed with twenty-eight marks of excellence, and all had resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

There were eighty thousand women, pure and stainless, whose forms and features were as exquisite and extraordinary as those of celestial beings, without any difference; they all likewise gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

During that time, for the span of two kalpas, the king made offerings to the Tathāgata and the great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas. For the sake of the Tathāgata, he constructed a jeweled monastery five yojanas in extent; within this jeweled monastery, there were furthermore hundreds of thousands of jeweled pavilions, which he provided as offerings to the Saṃgha.
"At that time, the noble king and his retinue all practiced the pure brahma-faring.
Then, the Buddha transformed immeasurable sentient beings in the Mahāyāna Dharma, and further transformed countless others in the Śrāvaka-yāna."

At that time, having made offerings to the Buddha, the king, together with his retinue, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right in reverence, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva practice the Mahāyāna without following the words of others?
How does a bodhisattva attain ultimate realization from birth?
How does a bodhisattva attain non-abiding?
How does a bodhisattva attain unshakable wisdom?
How does a bodhisattva attain pure wisdom?
How is it that a bodhisattva’s power enables them to see afar?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s faculties being sharp and keen?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with a buddha-field?
What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing heedfulness?
"How does a bodhisattva hear the profound Dharma and have no fear in their heart?
How does a bodhisattva receive the name 'bodhisattva'? The Buddha said:
“Great King! There are four dharmas by which one who practices the Mahāyāna does not follow the words of others.
What are these four?
First, they are fully endowed with noble faith and have transcended the world;
second, they are fully endowed with wisdom and contemplate the nature of all phenomena;
third, they are fully endowed with the various supernormal powers.
Fourth, one cultivates pure diligence for the sake of transforming sentient beings. Great King!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they practice the Mahāyāna and do not follow the words of others.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that lead to the attainment of the ultimate. What are these four?
First, knowing that wholesome dharmas serve to tame the mind;
Second, not being greedy for one's own pleasure;
third, cultivating and accumulating compassion for all sentient beings;
fourth, always delighting in the Mahāyāna.
These are called the four.
Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains non-abiding.
What are the four?
First, purifying the mind;
second, purifying adornment.
Third, abstaining from falsehood;
fourth, cultivating firm wisdom to be endowed with merit and virtue.
These are called the four dharmas.
"Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains pure wisdom. What are these four?"
First, pure eyes; second, gathering in sentient beings through the four means of attraction;
third, purifying the body with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Fourth, contemplating the purification of the Buddha-fields and the pure Dharma-realm; these are the four,
Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that enable one to see far and achieve sharpness of the faculties. What are these four?
First, to mindfully contemplate the Bodhi tree without abandoning the bodhicitta.
Second, mindfulness of the Buddha’s wisdom while remaining unattached even to that wisdom;
third, mindfulness of the Dharma-body, cultivating and accumulating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
fourth, mindfulness of the Buddha’s nirvana, yet having no weariness or regret within the cycle of birth and death.
These are called the four.
Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas for fully accomplishing the practice of a Buddha-field through heedfulness. What are these four?
First, he assumes the body of Śakra, in order to transform the various devas and cause them to be free from negligence;
second, he assumes the body of Brahmā, in order to transform the various devas and cause them to be free from negligence;
third, he assumes the body of a Cakravartin king, in order to transform sentient beings and cause them to be free from negligence.
Fourth, they receive the bodies of great ministers and elders, endowed with precious treasures, in order to transform sentient beings and cause them to be free from negligence;
these are called the four.
"Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one hears the profound Dharma without fear in the heart.
What are these four?"
First, associating with virtuous friends;
second, being taught the profound Buddha-dharma by those virtuous friends;
third, being well able to contemplate it.
Fourth, to abide in accordance with the Dharma;
these are called the four,
Great King!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one obtains the name of a bodhisattva.
What are these four? First, seeking the pāramitās;
Second, to cultivate and accumulate compassion for all sentient beings;
third, to joyfully seek the Buddha-dharma;
fourth, to have no weariness or regret in one's mind when transforming sentient beings.
"These are called the four.

"Good son! At that time, King Pure Sound, having heard this Dharma from that Tathāgata, together with all his retinue, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). They abandoned their kingdom and left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the king, saying: "Great King!

Your present renunciation of the household life is itself a repayment to the Buddha. If you can thus give rise to faith and renounce [worldly attachments], this is called a great repayment; it is called merit; it brings great benefit."
"Great King!
There are twenty-four benefits to a bodhisattva’s renunciation of the household life.
What are these twenty-four?"
First, by relinquishing worldly affairs, one attains great mastery;
second, by relinquishing afflictions, one obtains liberation;
third, by donning dyed robes upon the body, one attains the path free from defilement.
Fourth, by being fully endowed with the four requisites, one attains the four types of spiritual lineage;
fifth, by delighting in the dhūta practices, one remains far removed from all great desires and evil cravings;
sixth, by not abandoning the aggregate of precepts, one enjoys the bliss of humans and devas.
Seventh, not abandoning bodhicitta so as to attain the Buddha-dharma;
eighth, always delighting in tranquility and remaining aloof from worldly discourse;
ninth, attaining a mind of great purity by not being attached to dharmas.
Tenth, they are endowed with the factors of dhyāna, because they attain meditative concentration;
eleventh, they seek extensive learning, because they attain wisdom;
twelfth, they destroy arrogance, because they attain wisdom.
Thirteenth, they eliminate false views because they have attained right view.
Fourteenth, they do not give rise to applied and sustained thought because they truly know all dharma-realms.
Fifteenth, they regard all sentient beings with equanimity because they have attained great loving-kindness.
Sixteenth, transforming all sentient beings with a mind free from weariness, because they have attained great compassion;
seventeenth, not sparing their own bodies or lives in order to protect the Dharma;
eighteenth, quieting the mind in order to attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Nineteenth, mindfulness of the Tathāgata for the sake of seeing the Buddha;
twentieth, practicing wholesome reflection for the sake of attaining the profound wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination;
twenty-first, attaining the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti);
Twenty-second, attaining the patience of non-arising;
twenty-third, believing in all meritorious qualities;
twenty-fourth, attaining the wisdom of the Buddha.
"These are called the twenty-four.

"Good son! At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Holy King further used it to transform and teach all his male and female attendants, ministers, and subjects; at that moment, ninety-nine thousand billion sentient beings in that kingdom all went forth as monastics together."
“Good son! After the bhikṣu Viśuddhasvara had left the household life, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One!’”
"How can I now be said to have left the household life? The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
"You are named Pure Sound; you should purify your own realm. Once your own realm is purified, you are called a bhikṣu, you are called one who has gone forth.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the bhikṣu delighted in tranquility and reflected thus:

"The 'realm' is the eye; he who contemplates the emptiness of the eye is one whose realm is pure. That which is a pure realm is a buddha-field. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. The 'realm' is the mind; if one contemplates the emptiness of the mind, that is a pure realm. That which is a pure realm is a buddha-field. It is the single realm, the realm of emptiness, the realm of sentient beings, the signless realm, the wishless realm, the effortless realm, and the unconditioned realm."

“Good son! After the bhikṣu Pure Sound had observed in this way, he immediately attained lightness of body and lightness of mind. Having attained lightness of body and mind, he attained immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having attained supernormal powers, he attained the dhāraṇī gate of unhindered eloquence (*pratibhāna-asaṅga*)."
"Good son! Do you know who that bhikṣu Pure Sound was at that time?
It was none other than yourself."
"The male and female attendants are precisely this assembly of bodhisattvas whom you have brought here to hear the Dharma.

When he had spoken these *ityuktaka* verses, eighteen thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eight thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
“Good son! If there are those who wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should speak according to the Dharma and abide as they have spoken.
What is meant by ‘speaking according to the Dharma’ and ‘abiding as one has spoken’?
"Good son! If someone should say:
'I shall become a Buddha and invite all sentient beings, promising them the flavor of the Dharma.'"

Having made this request, they are unable to receive, uphold, recite, or analyze and explain the subtle and wondrous sūtras; they cannot maintain pure prohibitions and precepts, nor do they cultivate diligence with vigor; they do not practice contentment, being easily satisfied with only a small measure of wholesome dharmas. This is called deception; it is to speak contrary to the Dharma and to abide contrary to what has been taught.

If someone says: "I shall become a Buddha and invite all sentient beings to partake of the flavor of the Dharma," and having so invited them, upholds, recites, and explains [the teachings], guards the prohibitive precepts, and practices with diligent vigor;

if they have few desires and are content, gaining much wholesome dharma without conceiving thoughts of sufficiency—this is called being non-deceptive, speaking in accordance with the Dharma, and abiding according to what one has spoken.
“Good son! It is like a king who invites many guests; having invited them, he fails to prepare the provisions for his guests, only saying they are not yet ready once the guests have already arrived.”
Thereupon, the guests each spoke these words:
"Yesterday we accepted the King's invitation, yet our households prepared no food; today we have come upon the King's summons, yet again we have received nothing.
Thus they rebuked themselves, grieving, enraged, lamenting with resentment, and weeping.

Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva invites sentient beings and promises them the food of the Dharma, yet does not seek extensive learning, nor maintain the precepts, nor practice diligence, nor cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, sentient beings will reproach him, and gods and humans will weep.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can act as he should act and speak as he should speak, he must not deceive any sentient beings.
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who request of a bodhisattva,
"Please preach the Dharma for me," and the bodhisattva grants their request, saying:
"I shall speak for you. Having given this promise, he became heedless.
When sentient beings saw that the Bodhisattva had become heedless, they exhorted him; only after they had exhorted him did he then preach the Dharma for them.

While teaching, if someone asks about a profound meaning, they may be unable to answer due to negligence; because they cannot answer, shame arises in their heart, and thus, out of concern for their own body and mind, they deceive sentient beings and abandon them.
"Good son! If a bodhisattva wishes to abide according to what has been taught, they should not begrudge their own body or mind in order to protect sentient beings. Good son!"
In a past age, there was a lion king who lived in a cave in the deep mountains and constantly thought to himself:
"I am the king among all beasts; my strength is capable of overseeing and protecting all other animals."
At that time, there were two monkeys living on that mountain who had fathered two sons together.
Then the monkeys spoke thus to the lion king:
"If Your Majesty can protect all beasts, we now entrust our two sons to you; we wish to go elsewhere to seek food and drink."
Then the lion king immediately granted his permission; thereupon, the monkey left his two sons behind, entrusted them to the beast-king, and departed.
At that time, there was a vulture king in the mountains named Li-jian (Sharp Sight); while the lion king was sleeping, he seized the monkey’s two sons and stayed upon a precipice.
When the king had awakened, he addressed the King of Vultures with these verses:
"I now entreat you, Great King of Vultures; I pray that you will sincerely accept my words.
For my sake, I beg you to release him, so that he does not lose his integrity and fall into shame."
The Vulture King spoke this verse in reply to the Lion King:
“I am able to fly and roam through the void; having already passed beyond your domain, my mind is free from fear.
If you must protect these two children, you should sacrifice this body for my sake.”
The Lion King said: "Now, for the sake of protecting these two children, I would cast away my body without regret, as if it were withered grass.
If I were to protect my own life and speak falsely, how could I be called one who 'acts according to what he says'?"
Having spoken this verse, he immediately went to a high place, intending to cast off his body.
At that time, the King of Vultures spoke again in verse:
"If one sacrifices body and life for the sake of others, That person shall receive unsurpassed bliss."
"I now give you this monkey as a gift; I pray that the Great Dharma King will not harm himself.
"Good son! At that time, the lion king was none other than my own self."
The male monkey was Kāśyapa; the female monkey was the bhikṣuṇī Sughārā;
and the two monkey cubs were none other than Ānanda and Rāhula of the present day.
The King of Vultures at that time was none other than Śāriputra.
Noble son! For the sake of protecting those who rely upon him, a bodhisattva does not spare even his own body or life.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘acting according to what one says’?
If a bodhisattva says:”
"I shall practice generosity," and he immediately practices great giving— this is called a bodhisattva acting according to his word.
If a bodhisattva says:
"I am able to uphold the precepts," and thereby transforms all others to likewise protect the precepts as he does— this is called a bodhisattva acting according to his words.
If a bodhisattva says:
"I cultivate patience," and thereby transforms sentient beings so that they likewise cultivate patience— this is called a bodhisattva acting according to what he says.
If a bodhisattva says:
"I shall apply diligent effort for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, they transform sentient beings to practice diligence together for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; this is called a bodhisattva acting according to their words.
If a bodhisattva says,

"I cultivate meditative concentration," and accordingly transforms sentient beings by removing their distracted minds and cultivating meditative concentration, this is called a bodhisattva acting in accordance with what they say.
If a bodhisattva says,
"I cultivate wisdom," and discriminates in accordance with the Dharma, this is called a bodhisattva acting according to what they say.
"Good son! If a bodhisattva says:
'I shall destroy and break all evil dharmas.'"
He then cultivates and accumulates all wholesome dharmas; this is called a bodhisattva acting according to what he says.
"Good son, that which can adorn is called 'acting according to what is said,' and that which can bring things to ultimate completion is called 'acting accordingly.'"
One who is able to resolve their mind is called "one who acts as they speak"; one who attains the realization of the fruit is called "one who acts as they do.
One who is able to purify the mind is called "one who acts as they speak"; one who is able to apply their whole heart is called "one who acts as they do.
One who is able to resolve their mind is called "one who acts as they speak"; one whose mind does not regress is called "one who acts as they do."
Listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind is called "acting according to what is taught"; having heard it and abiding accordingly is called "acting according to what is done.
Purifying the mouth is called "acting according to what is taught"; purifying the body is called "acting according to what is done.
Receiving the precepts for the first time is called "acting according to what is taught"; guarding and upholding them with a sincere mind is called "acting according to what is done."
To resolve upon the bodhicitta is called "acting according to what is said"; to practice the bodhisattva path is called "acting according to what is done.
To attain the stage of patience is called "acting according to what is said"; to dwell in the stage of non-retrogression is called "acting according to what is done.
To obtain the body of one more birth is called "acting according to what is said"; to obtain the final body is called "acting according to what is done."
Approaching the Bodhi tree is called "acting according to what one says," and attaining the fruit of enlightenment is called "acting according to what one has said.
"Good son! This is what is meant by a bodhisattva speaking in accordance with the Dharma and acting in accordance with what they have spoken."
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas dwelt in the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Padma who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“As the Buddha has taught, so he speaks and so he acts; this is inconceivable. That in which the Buddha dwells is precisely what he speaks and precisely what he acts. “Good son!
“Are you able to understand this matter?
“I have understood it,
World-Honored One!”
“If one knows that the True Dharma is reality, this is called abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
Mount King Bodhisattva said,
“World-Honored One!
The dharma of non-abiding is called abiding in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this?
Because one perceives that all dharmas are without awakening; since there is no awakening, not perceiving even a single dharma is what is termed "awakening."
"If there is not a single dharma, how could there be abiding?
To see in this way is called 'abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
Bodhisattva Puṇyarāja said:
“World-Honored One!
If one follows the mind, one does not abide in accordance with the Dharma;
if a bodhisattva contemplates the mental faculty as being like an illusion, this is called non-abiding.”
"If there is no abiding, it is called 'abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara said,
"World-Honored One!"
The absence of a covetous mind is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
What is a covetous mind?
It refers to [the perception that] within the Dharma there is either loss or gain; if one is without a covetous mind, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Dayi said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who has any attachment, this is called ‘movement.’”
"If one has no attachment in the mind toward phenomena, this is called 'immovability.
If there is no movement, it is called 'abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Courageous and Valiant said:
“World-Honored One!
All worlds follow the movements of the mind.
If one knows the movements of the mind, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one undergoes suffering because of sensation."
If one can refrain from experiencing, all feelings will be severed;
if one can refrain from grasping, all attachments will be severed.
Although one neither grasps nor takes up, yet does not abandon sentient beings, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Gandhahastirāja said:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings carry a heavy burden, namely the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).”

If one can know the true reality of the five aggregates, destroy the view of the aggregates, cast off the heavy burden, and yet harbor no notion of a burden even toward all phenomena, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara said:
“World-Honored One!

If one acts in the world not in accordance with the Dharma, that is not abiding according to the Dharma; if one is correctly adorned, this is called abiding according to the Dharma. To be correctly adorned means to see all dharmas as equal to empty space.”
The Bodhisattva Resolute Mind said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva does not give rise to arising, does not cease with ceasing, and furthermore does not perceive the nature of arising and ceasing, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue, Radiant Universal Illumination, said:

"If one can know and see true nirvana, seeing that all phenomena are extinguished and without arising or ceasing, and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, cultivating adornments for the sake of attaining bodhi—this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Light said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a place of activity, that is the work of Māra; it is not dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
"If there is no place of practice, then one destroys the works of Māra.
If one destroys the works of Māra, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
Bodhisattva Viśuddhaprayoga said:
“World-Honored One!
If one forms the thought,
‘I shall attain the Dharma,’ and for the sake of attaining this Dharma exerts oneself with diligent vigor;”
Such diligence is empty diligence.
If one can observe that all phenomena are not fixed, and through this lack of fixity diligently cultivates diligence, it is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Transcending the Three Evil Realms said:
“World-Honored One!

All dharmas are without action and without transformation; they are without applied thought and without sustained thought. That which is without applied and sustained thought is called the nature of the mind.”
"If one perceives that the nature of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally pure,
this is called 'abiding in accordance with the Dharma. The Bodhisattva Acintyamatibhāṣin said,
"World-Honored One!..."
To know the minds of all sentient beings while not forming mental conceptions regarding their nature is called "contemplating that which is inconceivable.
If one can contemplate within this state of non-contemplation, it is called "abiding in accordance with the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Delight-in-Quietude said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who purifies the realm of the mind, they will then be able to leave behind all outflows.”
"If one can remain far removed from all outflows (āsrava), this is called right practice.
One who practices rightly is said to abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Caravan Leader.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva possesses pure wholesome dharmas—the adornment of merit and the adornment of wisdom—and contemplates these two adornments as equal and non-dual; if they contemplate the equality of wisdom through the equality of merit, and contemplate the equality of merit through the equality of wisdom, seeing them without distinction, this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
“World-Honored One!
Not perceiving duality is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma; if one does not disrupt or differentiate the Dharma-realm, it is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva Arthapratiśaraṇa said:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who relies on the true meaning and not on the letter, and for the sake of the true meaning upholds, recites, and studies it—extensively expounding the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma without error or wavering—this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva Pure Intention said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to the bodhicitta and with a sincere heart protects this bodhicitta, then when practicing for bodhi, they will know the nature of all dharmas.”
“Now, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither a state of possibility nor impossibility; it is called ‘abiding according to the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Ultimate Purity of Mind said, “World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who distances himself from defilements as one washes away dirt, such that afflictions cannot pollute his mind, this is called ultimate purity.
Once his mind is pure, he follows the practice of enlightenment; this is called dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who associate with evil friends, they do not abide in accordance with the Dharma; they do not cultivate the noble Dharma and do not abide in accordance with the Dharma. If they draw near to evil companions, they perform the deeds of Māra and fall into the realm of Māra.”
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who wish to leave behind all demonic activities, all demonic haunts, and all unwholesome dharmas, they should draw near to virtuous friends.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Do you now truly know the activities of Māra? “I know them.”
“World-Honored One!
” “Good son! You should now speak for the sake of the great assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas.”
“World-Honored One!
That which is the work of Māra is precisely the eye and forms.
If a person sees a form and gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment, that is the work of Māra; this applies likewise to the mind and mental phenomena.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they bestow as gifts those things they do not love, yet they remain greedy and stingy regarding their cherished wealth and refuse to relinquish it."
To give to those one loves and not to give to those one hates, thereby discriminating between recipients and material goods—
if one makes such a distinction between these two, it is called the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva practices the *śīlapāramitā*, if they guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts while associating with those who uphold them, yet praise themselves and disparage those who have broken the precepts, this is called the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they may give rise to forbearance toward those of great power, yet fail to give rise to forbearance toward those of little power; seeing those of great power, they speak gently and act with humility, but seeing those of little power, they use harsh speech and treat them with contempt. This is called the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor, they teach the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle."
When cultivating bodhi, one treats the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas with contempt and does not proclaim them;

one delights in worldly activities and takes no pleasure in making offerings or showing reverence to the Triple Gem—namely, with flowers, incense, banners, canopies, music, and songs of praise—and does not seek extensive learning, nor can one draw near to those who possess it; this is called the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, they may attain meditative concentration yet fail to subdue all sentient beings; consequently, they give rise to regret and weariness, becoming attached to the bliss of dhyāna."

To revile those who preach the Dharma; to take no pleasure in discussion; to praise tranquility while being greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna; to revile and disparage the two realms while craving the formless body; to have an extremely long lifespan yet fail to see the Buddhas, hear the True Dharma, or be far removed from virtuous friends; and to be ignorant of skillful means regarding the acceptance and relinquishment of cultivation—these are called the works of Māra.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they understand cause and effect yet do not gather and discipline sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and if they do not know the superior, middling, or inferior faculties of sentient beings, this is called the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva delights in empty and quiet seclusion, and having delighted in seclusion, experiences the bliss of seclusion, yet does not delight in hearing the Dharma, preaching the Dharma, or inquiring about doubts; because of this seclusion, afflictions do not arise; because they do not arise, he does not know that which should be known, does not abandon that which should be abandoned, does not realize that which should be realized, and does not cultivate that which should be cultivated, thereby failing to attain the true meaning—this is called the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates much learning, speaking words that are pleasant, delightful, subtle, gentle, and joyous."

If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of clothing, food, bedding, or gain; if one does not preach to those who have faith and understanding and are able to listen with a sincere heart; if one preaches to those who are negligent yet provide offerings; if one fails to preach to those for whom it is appropriate to preach; or if one conversely preaches to those to whom it is inappropriate—this is called the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if there is a bodhisattva who, when preaching the Dharma, conceals its profound meanings, there may be devas and humans who, possessing the knowledge of others' minds, understand this and become displeased, thinking:
'I have come for the sake of the Tathāgata’s true and authentic Dharma, not for the sake of worldly, shallow, and superficial speech.'"
Such a person who wishes to destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata will not be able to increase it.
If there is anyone who destroys the Buddha’s True Dharma, I take no pleasure in seeing or hearing what they say.
He then departs; this is called the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if there is a bodhisattva who conceives the notion of a 'good friend' toward a bad friend—wherein that bad friend does not gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), does not cultivate extensive learning, does not transform sentient beings, does not speak the Dharma but speaks worldly talk, and lacks knowledge of the Dharma, the proper time, and the meaning—this is called the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a bad friend is one who cannot reveal, distinguish, or explain the teachings of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharma; who does not transform sentient beings to cultivate compassion, distance themselves from the eight difficulties, and practice giving and precepts; who lacks the power to use gentle speech to approach others with equanimity and teach them patience; and who says that the Buddha-way is extremely difficult to attain, obtainable only after enduring diligent suffering through immeasurable lifetimes. This is called a bad friend, and it is termed the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

if a bodhisattva possesses a mind of arrogance, because of that arrogance they will be unable to make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, teachers, preceptors, parents, elders, fellow students, and those of the same master."
If one sees those superior to oneself but is unable to draw near them to listen to the Dharma or inquire about doubts, then although one has heard it, one loses it immediately upon hearing.

If one sees those inferior to oneself and draws near to them with affection and fondness, then unwholesome dharmas gradually increase; because unwholesome dharmas increase, one becomes distant from wholesome dharmas.
“World-Honored One!
Just as the great ocean gradually deepens so that all rivers flow together into it, so too is it with the bodhisattva who destroys pride: all wholesome dharmas gradually increase within them.”
If a bodhisattva does not destroy their pride, this is called the work of Māra.
"World-Honored One!

It is like a person who plants a *campaka* tree on high ground and dry land, yet constructs a dam where water constantly flows; since the ground is both high and parched and cannot obtain water, the tree gradually withers and turns yellow, unable to grow."
World-Honored One!
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: because pride increases, they do not associate with virtuous friends; they do not hear the true Dharma, and even if they hear it, they lose it again.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may possess a physical form that is complete, upright, and majestic, and may have many attendants and be adorned with merit; yet, if they have not yet fully attained the adornment of wisdom, they will give rise to arrogance because of these conditions."

Due to arrogance, if there is a bodhisattva who is adorned with wisdom and contemplates the true Dharma yet has a frail and emaciated body, [the former] sees them and treats them with contempt, failing to make offerings. Because of these causes and conditions, their arrogance increases further; through ignorance and negligence, they fail to subdue the activities of Māra.
"In this way, when a bodhisattva gives rise to pride because of form, this is called the work of Māra.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! You have skillfully distinguished and proclaimed the deeds of Māra. Noble son!"
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall now expound upon the destruction of the paths of Māra’s activities. "Good son!
The nature of all dharmas is empty and quiescent."
If one knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty, one also knows that all sentient beings are empty.
Having realized emptiness, one cultivates a mind of loving-kindness to subdue oneself; this is called a bodhisattva destroying the activities of Māra.

If one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is signless (*animitta*), yet cultivates and accumulates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) for the sake of sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva destroying the activities of Māra.

If one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is wishless (*apraṇihita*), yet seeks existence with a sincere heart for the sake of all sentient beings, and having so sought it, subsequently tames them accordingly, this is called a bodhisattva being able to destroy the activities of Māra.

To contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is free from greed, and that the nature of sentient beings is likewise free from greed, yet to embrace them in order to subdue their greed—this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.

If one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is without anger, and that the nature of sentient beings is likewise without anger, yet one gathers them in order to subdue their anger, this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.

If one contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is non-delusion, and that the nature of sentient beings is likewise non-delusion, yet one gathers them in order to subdue their delusion—this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.

To contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is without arising or ceasing, and to proclaim the True Dharma in order to destroy arising and ceasing—this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.
To contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is equal, and while teaching the three vehicles, not to abandon the Great Vehicle—this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.
