If one does not become greedily attached to mind, intellect, or consciousness, and is likewise able to remain far removed from all causes and conditions, cultivating the adornments of the Dharma for the sake of bringing liberation to all sentient beings, then even though one transcends all conditioned activities, one never abandons the conduct of a bodhisattva; this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to destroy the works of Māra.

When this Dharma was being taught, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān arrayed his fourfold army and approached the Jewel Monastery, just as he had previously approached the Bodhi tree. Having seen him, the Tathāgata addressed Sāgaramati, saying:

"You have described the works of Māra; I shall describe the destruction of Māra. For this reason, the Māra-king Pāpīyān has arrayed his fourfold army and come here. What stratagem do you intend to employ to repel him?"
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to take Māra Pāpīyān and his retinue and place them in the Land of Adornment, while I myself shall dwell in the place where Māra resides.”
At that time, Śāriputra said:
“Good son, how far is the world-system ‘Adorned’ from here?”
"What is the name of that Buddha?

"Śāriputra! To the east of here, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a land where a Buddha named Pure Light Dispelling Doubt (Poyi Jinguang) currently dwells in the world, preaching the pure bodhisattva conduct to all bodhisattvas."
In that land, within a trichiliocosm, there were one hundred million Māras; each Māra king had a retinue of ten thousand billion soldiers.
When that Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, all these Māras collectively arrayed themselves and went to where the Bodhisattva was.

At that time, the Bodhisattva first expounded the sublime scriptures for all the Māras, causing them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression; only thereafter did he attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of the true Dharma.
The great disciples and attendants of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, were also all māras; such māras as these were all able to teach, transform, and subdue sentient beings.
Therefore, I now take Māra Pāpīyān and place him in that land, desiring to destroy the demonic deeds he practices and to adorn the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata.

When Māra Pāpīyas heard these words, fear arose in his heart; he looked around in all four directions, seeking a place to retreat, but found himself obstructed on all sides and unable to follow his will. He further desired to extinguish his own body but could not do so; as his stratagems failed, his anxiety redoubled, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I only pray that, out of great compassion,
you will grant us some protection. The Buddha said, "Pāpīyan!"
"I have no mastery over this matter; you should turn toward the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati and seek his compassionate forgiveness.
Then Māra Pāpīyān immediately joined his palms toward Sāgaramati and said:
"O son of good family!
“From this day forward, I dare not again commit such demonic deeds; I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will accept my repentance.
Sāgaramati Bodhisattva said, “I harbor no anger toward you at all; it is the constant law of Bodhisattvas to practice patience toward all sentient beings.”
"Pāpīyān! You should go there to pay homage and visit that Buddha; your person shall thereby obtain immeasurable benefit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately stroked his head with his right hand and spoke these words:
"If there are bodhisattvas who are free from greed and stinginess regarding all dharmas, I shall, by means of my supernatural powers, cause you to reach that Buddha-world.
Having spoken these words, Pāpīyas immediately arrived in that land.
Having arrived in that land, they beheld the Buddha, paid him homage, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Those bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"In what kind of land do such impure people as these come to this place?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

To the west, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni; he is currently preaching the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra for an incalculable number of bodhisattvas and others.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva named Sāgaramati; when he was expounding upon the deeds of Māra, the fourfold army of that Māra’s adornments arrived at the assembly, and the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, by means of his supernormal powers, transported them here.
The bodhisattvas in that world said to Pāpīyas:
"O son of good family!
You should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and abandon your demonic activities; we shall become your fellow students."
When Māra Pāpīyān heard these words, he immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas invited Pāpīyān to ascend the lion throne and asked him:
"We have heard that the Tathāgata has preached the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* for the great assembly; what is the significance of this?"
"O Benevolent One, please explain it.
Then, by the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Māra Pāpīyān proclaimed what he had heard, without losing even a single phrase or a single word.
Those bodhisattvas then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish and desire to see that Buddha Śākyamuni and his assembly of bodhisattvas.
That Buddha then spoke to those bodhisattvas, saying:
“Wait but a moment, and you shall naturally behold this jeweled monastery.
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"We wish to see the Māra Pāpīyān; what is he doing in that world?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed the minds of the sentient beings in both this world and that world, addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying:
"O son of good family!
"You should now manifest this Buddha-world to those bodhisattvas.

At that time, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva emitted great radiance from his ten fingers; the light passed through as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers and illuminated that land entirely. The entire assembly here beheld the Buddha and the bodhisattvas in that land, and saw the Māra Pāpīyas seated upon a lion throne preaching the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra.

Then the bodhisattvas rose from their seats, bowed their heads in respectful salutation toward that Tathāgata, and scattered various kinds of flowers as an offering; the flowers thus scattered transformed into flower pedestals above that Buddha.
When those bodhisattvas saw these flower pedestals, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
from where have these flower pedestals come?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! This is the offering scattered by the assembly of bodhisattvas in the Sahā world.”
The bodhisattvas said:
“World-Honored One!
How may we come to see that land, the Sahā world?”
The Buddha said, “Good sons!
You should now pay homage to this light and maintain it with a sincere mind; you shall naturally come to see that buddha-world.”
Then that bodhisattva, as the Buddha had instructed, paid homage to the light and held it in mind with a sincere heart; immediately, he was able to see this Sahā world.
Having seen it, he rose and prostrated to Śākyamuni Buddha, making offerings from afar with various incenses and flowers.
Furthermore, he saw the trichiliocosm filled with pure, clear water like a great ocean.
The flowers scattered there reached this world’s Great Jewel Monastery and, above the Tathāgata, transformed into precious canopies.
Then Māra Pāpīyān addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How should I return to that world?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! If you wish to return, you should mindfully recollect Sāgaramati with a sincere heart.”
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān directed his wholehearted thoughts toward the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati; having done so, he was immediately able to return to this world.
When Śāriputra saw Māra Pāpīyān, he spoke these words: "Pāpīyān!
“Do you see that buddha-field? Pāpīyān replied, “Śāriputra!...”
"I have already seen it, as well as that pure land where the bodhisattvas dwell.
Śāriputra asked, "Do you not perform the work of Māra in that land?"
“Virtuous One! When I reach that land, I shall seek unsurpassed bodhi with a sincere and diligent heart; for what reason would I then create demonic karma?
If one who seeks bodhi with a sincere heart perceives demonic karma, that person will then be able to cultivate diligence and vigor.”

When the great assembly in this realm saw Māra Pāpīyān return here, sixty thousand sentient beings and ten thousand hosts of Māras together resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, saying:
"May the physical forms we receive be no different from the physical form of that Bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One,
there are many enemies and adversaries for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, you have established these supernormal powers.
"By virtue of my supernormal powers, this sutra shall remain in the world for a long time.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"The supernatural power of the virtuous vows I have now established is for the purpose of planting roots of goodness in all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:

"You should know that if my disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—uphold, recite, copy, and extensively expound such sūtras as these, you, the four kings, should provide deep protection and assistance, and do not become negligent through attachment to sensual pleasures."
"I have now appeared in the world to destroy negligence and protect the True Dharma.
And he spoke this mantra,
which is as follows:

"Samai, ramai-samamai, matunī, brahmavati-dhāni, dhanavati, dhonidhanavati, apasanti, amale, vimale, jayavirate, karate, karana, ali, aravati-alepasanti, nigadani, avati, mati, mahumati, marite, visute, visutavati, nisale, mokhani. "O son of good family!"
This is called the Mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings.

If there is a Dharma Master who receives and upholds this sutra, he should recite this mantra. Having recited it, he should cultivate loving-kindness and direct his mindfulness toward the ten directions, calling to mind the Four Heavenly Kings and their retinues with a sincere heart. At that time, the Four Kings shall appear to him in a dream or come in person to protect him.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Having heard this incantation, we four kings, together with our retinues, shall go to where the Dharma-preacher resides to protect and guard him."

"If there are any necessities of life required by this Dharma master, I shall employ skillful means to ensure he obtains them, so that he may remain free from the suffering of illness and his body may experience peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati: "Good son!..."
Now listen with a sincere mind to the mantra of Śakra, which is as follows:
“Jayā jayamati avadhi vadhi makule sthavadvī śunī śāntikele dandī dharmani takale kṣaya kṣaya mukha avatena nigațena svāhā svāhā santī. Come, Kauśika!
When the asuras are defeated, the devas will prevail; because the devas prevail, the Buddha-dharma increases.
Kausika! If you wish to experience peace and happiness, you should protect the True Dharma.
"Good son! This is called the 'Explanatory Mantra. Good son!"

If there is a Dharma Master who wishes to preach the Dharma, he should first bathe to make his body pure and clean, hold exquisite incense and flowers while facing due east in prostration, single-mindedly recollecting the Buddhas of the ten directions, and extend a heart of loving-kindness universally to all sentient beings. Only then should he ascend the lion Dharma-seat, recite this mantra, and speak these words:
"Kauśika, come! The Four Heavenly Kings, come! For the sake of the great assembly, remove all obstacles and extinguish all afflictions."

At that time, Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings, out of consideration for the Dharma Master, came together; therefore, the great assembly delighted in hearing the preaching of the Dharma. "Good son!..."
Listen now further to the mantras of the Māras of the ten directions and their retinues, which are as follows:

“Śame, śamabhaṭi, śamamiti, abulaimarakhuti, maṅgule, bharate, kayole, ṭikibhaṭi, akukani, piśācini, nimati, abhaṭi, kūkule, karasani, umuke, śamiti, paramumuke, bandhana-nirghaṭi, śamaghe. A mantra such as this has the power to bind all teachers of treatises and all hosts of Māras. It is called the Seal of the Buddha; it cannot be destroyed by the enemies who are the retinues of Māra.

"Good son! If there is a Dharma master who receives, maintains, reads, and recites such mantras as these while ascending the lion throne, he should single-mindedly contemplate the compassion of all Buddhas toward sentient beings."

If one conceives of oneself as a physician, the Dharma being taught as a potent medicine, those who listen to the Dharma as those suffering from illness, the Tathāgata as a virtuous friend, and the True Dharma as something eternal and constant—when one can speak the True Dharma in such a manner, Māra will be unable to approach within a distance of one yojana on all four sides of that place.
Then Māra Pāpīyān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are disciples of the Buddha who are able to recite such divine mantras, their bodies shall be pure; I shall protect them and refrain from performing demonic deeds.”
By the power of my ocean-like wisdom and supernormal faculties, I shall abandon all demonic activities.
In whatever lands, cities, towns, or villages this Dharma is taught, I shall manifest a transformation body and go there in person to listen and receive it.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Pāpīyan!"
If you can attain such a mind, you will destroy the works of Māra and shall likewise obtain dharmas such as these.
"Good son! You should furthermore listen with a sincere heart to the Brahmā-mantra."
That is to say:

*Mitakāle, kāruṇakāle, amṛtakāle, aupikākāle, buddhakāle, dharmakāle, saṃghakāle, sukṛtaviśaye, mahāvitanī, viśvatemire, nibhāledhaye, ujjavati, ujjayami, nandanī, dharmapratibhānī, satyadhyupavati viśvadhi, svajjhatopasami, ulukāya brahma, vilukāya brahma.* "If one wishes to fully receive and uphold such Brahmā-mantras, one should practice the pure conduct of Brahmā-carya, maintain the precepts, and recite these mantras while invoking Brahmā:"

"Brahmā, come and protect this great assembly, causing them to listen to the true Dharma with a sincere heart, to keep the Triple Gem in mind, to turn the wheel of the true Dharma, and to guard and uphold the city of the Dharma."

"If there is a Dharma Master who can discipline the sense faculties, who with a sincere mind purely guards body, speech, and mind, who diligently cultivates precepts, patience, vigor, and much learning, who gives rise to the bodhicitta and practices the four immeasurables, and who ascends the Dharma seat to recite this mantra."
"Having recited this mantra, the Brahmā King and his retinue have all come to assemble at this place where the Dharma is being preached.
At that time, the Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If there is a Dharma master who recites this mantra, once I have heard this mantra while in the first dhyāna, I shall abandon the bliss of meditative concentration and go to his place, where I shall bestow eight dharmas upon him.
What are the eight?
First is the gift of mindfulness, because it retains what has been heard;
second is the gift of wisdom, because it contemplates profound dharmas.
Third is the gift of analytical knowledge, because it discerns profound meanings;
fourth is the gift of unimpeded eloquence, because it destroys doubt;
fifth is the gift of unimpeded expression, because it understands the languages of all sentient beings.
Sixth, he bestows fearlessness, because he is unsurpassed among the multitudes;
seventh, he bestows the light of the Dharma, because his teachings are not erroneous;
eighth, he bestows unerring predictions of enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!
We, too, are able to extensively proclaim this Dharma. “Good sons!”
"After my parinirvāṇa, such devas as these shall protect the true Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said,
"World-Honored One!"
"After the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has entered parinirvāṇa, those who have faith should entrust this Dharma to such persons so that it may endure for a long time.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. Emanations of the Tathāgata filled its entirety, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, as numerous as the grasses, trees, stalks, joints, branches, and leaves of the trichiliocosm.
These emanated Buddhas spoke with one voice:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions and Śākyamuni Tathāgata share the same vow that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.
For what reason?..."
Although there may be all the hosts of evil Māras, they cannot destroy such dharmas as these.

The great earth may be destroyed, the vast oceans may be parched, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, may be crushed into dust; the minds of all sentient beings may be merged into one, the void may be painted, and the four great elements may be transformed—but the vows of the Buddhas cannot be altered.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound such sūtras as these.
Sāgaramati Bodhisattva then said:
“World-Honored One!
In this assembly there are now many immeasurable great bodhisattvas; for what reason does the Tathāgata look upon Ānanda and command him to receive and uphold this?”
At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with doubt, wondering:
"Between Sāgaramati and Ānanda, whose power of recollection is greater?
Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the doubts of the assembled multitude, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
“Are the sentient beings in a trichiliocosm numerous? “Very numerous,
World-Honored One!”

“Kāśyapa! Suppose that such immeasurable sentient beings were all to obtain human bodies and constantly question the Tathāgata; what the Tathāgata speaks would be inexhaustible and free from any obstruction.”
"Good son! Just as when the heavens send down rain without obstruction, all streams and currents converge and gather in the great ocean, yet this great ocean neither increases nor decreases."
"Whatever the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati upholds, the same is true for the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions. Kāśyapa,

even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were endowed with dhāraṇīs like those of Ānanda and others, they would not equal one-hundredth, one-thousandth, or even one-hundred-thousand-millionth part of the Dharma upheld by Sāgaramati."

When these words were spoken, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they offered exquisite flowers and incense as a tribute to the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Padma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who can believe in, comply with, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and explain the meaning of this sutra, and who offer worship and respect to such a scripture, how much merit will they obtain?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

“If one were to fill the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions, it would not equal the merit of one who, with faith and compliance, accepts, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra; the latter’s merit is far greater than the former.”
The various merits accomplished through these four dharmas, which the Buddha has described as being immeasurable and boundless in number,
arise from generating the bodhicitta, constantly practicing the gift of Dharma, abiding according to the Dharma, and cultivating compassion.
The Buddha taught that four phenomena are boundless; the wise, having heard this, feel no fear:
the nature of space, the realm of sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom, and the bodhicitta.

When this collection of Dharma jewels was thus proclaimed, the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of music; honoring and praising him, they spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, explain, and expound such sutras as these, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable; even the Buddhas of the ten directions could not exhaustively describe it.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If sentient beings hear such sutras as these, there are none who do not resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, this sutra is named "The Great Heap of Jewels."

At that time, the entire great assembly—humans and devas, all śrāvakas and Ānanda and his peers, the garuḍas, gandharvas, and other beings of the world—heard the sutra and were filled with joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Eleven;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Twelve.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Six: The Bodhisattva of Silence.
At that time, the World-Honored One was still in the Great Jewel Monastery between the realms of desire and form, surrounded by a great assembly, preaching the Dharma.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, General Siṃha gave birth to a son.
At the moment of his birth, many devas in the sky spoke these words: "O boy!..."

One should mindfully recollect the Dharma and contemplate the Dharma; regarding all speech, do not speak of worldly affairs, but always proclaim the supramundane Dharma. One should constantly guard the mouth, being cautious with words and speaking sparingly; do not give rise to discursive thoughts or mental investigations concerning worldly affairs, but rely upon the meaning rather than the literal words.

At that time, having heard these words, the boy no longer wept and was free from the appearance of an infant; for seven days his countenance remained harmonious and joyful, and whenever he saw someone, he was filled with delight, his eyes never blinking.
At that time, someone said to his parents:
"This child is inauspicious; he should not be raised. Why is this?..."
"Because he is mute and has no voice.

His parents replied, "Although this child is mute and does not utter a sound, his physical faculties are complete and without defect; you should know that this child must surely possess merit and virtue, and is not an inauspicious person of meager fortune."
Because he was established with a name, his name was "The Wordless.

As the youth Wordless gradually grew up like an eight-year-old child, wherever he traveled, people delighted in seeing him. Whenever there was a place where the Dharma was being taught and the Wheel of Dharma turned, he would gladly go to listen and receive it, yet no words would issue from his mouth.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the youth Aniruddha went with his parents, retinue, and kinsmen to the Jewel Monastery.

Having arrived, he saw the Buddha and his heart was filled with joy; he paid homage, made offerings, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Standing with palms joined, he also beheld the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions and gave rise to a mind of great joy.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The son born to General Siṃha possesses all his physical faculties yet is unable to speak; by what causes and conditions of evil karma has this come about?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You should not now speak such words to disparage this youth. Why is that?"
Such a person is indeed a great bodhisattva; having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, they are non-retrogressive on the path to enlightenment.
When this child was born, many devas came to admonish him,
saying: "Excellent, young man!

One should keep the True Dharma in mind and contemplate the True Dharma; one must not speak of worldly matters, but should always proclaim the meaning of the supramundane. One should always guard the mouth, being cautious in speech and sparing with words; do not give rise to discursive thoughts regarding worldly affairs, but rely upon the meaning rather than the literal text.
"Śāriputra! Thus, having received the instruction from the deva, the youth remained silent and in contemplation, thereby attaining the four dhyānas. Śāriputra!"
The Bodhisattva Wordless manifests such a body so as to be able to subdue immeasurable sentient beings; therefore, he remains silent and proclaims nothing. Śāriputra!
"I shall now proclaim this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra; the Bodhisattva Aghoṣa shall be able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings herein.

At that time, by the power of his own vows and the power of his supernatural faculties, the Bodhisattva Aghoṣa caused all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to each see within their own right hands a great lotus flower like a chariot wheel, perfect in color and fragrance, most subtle and supreme, a sight for which people long. Upon each lotus pedestal sat a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), his body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Wordless had manifested such great supernormal powers, he bowed his head, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
“Homage to the Buddha!”
“Homage to the Buddha!
All the bodhisattvas within the lotus pedestals likewise spoke these words in unison:
“Homage to the Buddha!”
"Homage to the Buddha!

Having uttered these words, the great earth in worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers shook in six ways, and the devas in the void made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite incense, flowers, and various kinds of music.

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and his own power of aspiration, the Bodhisattva Wordless (*Avāca*) leaped with the other bodhisattvas into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees. Facing the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata is formless yet manifests forms; He likewise remains unstained by form.
If sentient beings enter the Buddha-dharma, How should they know true form?”
The Tathāgata does not exist within the aggregate of form, nor does he exist apart from form;
having already transcended all aggregates of form, the Tathāgata manifests form out of compassion for sentient beings.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Tathāgata adorns his physical form with the various marks and signs;
though in reality he possesses no marks of form, he speaks of them for the sake of the multitude. Therefore, the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is without words; Once words are transcended, there is no sound.
Being without words, it cannot be spoken; It is profoundly deep, quiescent, and beyond cognition.
Just as when the Buddha was first at the Bodhi tree, the dharmas he awakened to were likewise thus:
these dharmas have no letters and no sounds; they are without fabrication and cannot be spoken.
Thus all these phenomena are without marks, And are likewise free from all characteristics;
If all phenomena are without marks, How does the Tathāgata expound them?

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with great compassion; therefore, out of pity and for the sake of benefiting others, he expounds that which cannot be spoken, while also knowing that reality itself is ineffable.
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that which is ineffable, And likewise knows that the nature of sound is empty and quiescent;
Truly knowing the meaning of all things, He is therefore called the Buddha, the Truly Awakened One.
The Dharma that is taught is called worldly truth; the Tathāgata has truly awakened to this.
Worldly truth does not emerge and possesses no intrinsic nature; it cannot be contrived and has no fixed limit.
In reality, there is no form or appearance; yet for the sake of the multitude, you manifest various forms.
Knowing that all phenomena are non-existent, O Unsurpassed Honored One, you preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
When I was first born, I received the words of the devas; therefore, I remained silent and said nothing.
With a sincere heart, I contemplated the Dharma and reflected upon the Dharma; therefore, I perceived neither form nor sound.
If one attains entry into the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), at that time there will be no forms, sounds, or the like;
if one can distance oneself from mental karma, one will immediately attain distance from verbal karma.
The absence of verbal expression is itself speech; though there is verbal expression, it is likewise without speech.
Speech is neither created nor uttered, for the intrinsic nature of language is quiescent.
Now with a sincere heart I contemplate Bodhi, and likewise with a sincere heart I cultivate its path;
now I speak these unsurpassed words, and I shall surely attain the true Way.
My mind does not attain the path to bodhi; Speech and the actions of speech likewise do not attain it.
Unsurpassed bodhi is itself emptiness; Its nature is fundamentally and eternally quiescent.
As is the nature of awakening, so too is sound; because the nature of phenomena is neither seen nor grasped, my voice is likewise invisible, and the awakening sought is also thus.
For the sake of bodhi there is practice; yet this practice has no destination.
Since such practice has no destination, the locus of bodhi is neither a place nor a non-place.
The six pāramitās are like bodhi; all wholesome dharmas are likewise so.
All speech is without speech; within this absence of speech, one is able to speak.
If there is the gift of wondrous sounds, the donor who bestows them, and the material objects themselves—all such acts of giving are themselves bodhi; all of these are ultimately ineffable.
If giving could be expressed in words, then the essence of bodhi could also be so expressed;
yet the nature of bodhi is like space, and all sounds are likewise so.
If there is a mind capable of knowing reality as it is, And having known it, is also able to proclaim the sound,
Yet that sound ceases in accordance with its cognition— This is the true mark of bodhi.
If one can distance oneself from the karmas of body, speech, and mind, all afflictions will likewise do so;
this is the perfection of all pāramitās, the true nature of phenomena as taught by the Tathāgata.
Generous giving does not exist within awakening, nor does awakening exist within generous giving;
these two dharmas are merely sounds, having neither a place of abiding nor a destination.
Whoever is able to understand such things as these is a true and great Bodhisattva;
if one does not give rise to pride at the time of giving, one is a supreme and unsurpassed great donor.
Upholding the prohibitive precepts is itself a sound; it has no form or color and reaches nowhere.
That all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished is the mark of supreme upholding of the precepts.
If such a precept cannot be produced, and likewise possesses no karma of body, speech, or mind;
if it neither arises nor ceases, and is not something created—how can it be called a "precept"?
To cause it to circulate, he utters sounds; for sentient beings, these are designated by the name "prohibitory precepts.
Just as with all prohibitory precepts, so too are these sounds; thus, both of these dharmas are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because that which is spoken by the mouth serves as a precept, various kinds of adornments are established;
yet in sound there are truly no adornments, for one knows in truth that they do not exist.
The actions of body, speech, and mind— One can turn these precepts toward enlightenment;
Yet both the sound of the prohibitions and enlightenment Are like space; these two phenomena are thus.

If there is one who can know in this way, that person will immediately practice the path of ethical conduct and will be able to reach the further shore of morality; that place is profoundly deep and difficult to perceive.
The sound of the teaching on patience is itself emptiness; Emptiness has no location and no activity.
Patience and emptiness are two dharmas, Yet they are without distinction, like space.
The sound of patience is not produced by form; it cannot be seen and has no location.
If one cultivates and gathers an impartial mind, that is the true characteristic of patience.
Although forbearance perishes moment by moment, it always accompanies the physical body;
all its verbal expressions are untainted, yet for the sake of sentient beings, the name "forbearance" is established.
If one is able to discipline body, speech, and mind, that is itself the unsurpassed patience;
if one is able to endure those who practice patience, that too is the unsurpassed patience.
If there are sentient beings who crush their bodies, breaking them joint by joint until they are as fine as sesame seeds,
and they contemplate the body as being like dry grass and wood— this is what is called patience regarding the body.
When hearing harsh words and insults, if one's mind remains unmoved and abides in accordance with the Dharma,
observing sounds as being like space— this is the unsurpassed patience of speech.
If one can thoroughly penetrate the causes of affliction And remain far removed from all defilements,
This is what is called "patience of mind," Being undefiled by any afflictions whatsoever.
As patience is itself the nature of bodhi, so too are the actions of body, speech, and mind;
if one can turn these toward bodhi, this is what is called attaining bodhi.
If there are sentient beings who apply themselves with diligent vigor— whether superior, middling, or inferior, coarse or subtle—
and cultivate and accumulate [merit] throughout immeasurable eons, they shall obtain nothing and find no ultimate end.
If one does not attain diligence, for that reason enlightenment is called "non-attainment";
if one can thus not attain any phenomena, that is itself the unsurpassed, diligent exertion.
If there is one who possesses such diligence, Unincreasing and undiminishing like space,
Such a person is indeed a Great Bodhisattva, Vigorously practicing diligence without fear.
All meditative absorptions have no accumulation; they are without fabrication and no place of arrival.
If one contemplates all phenomena in this way, that is the true perfection of dhyāna.
Far removed from all unwholesome forms, And likewise from evil body and speech,
Able to incinerate all afflictions— This is the true dhyāna-pāramitā.
If one can contemplate the true nature of the mind, One will not perceive anything within all phenomena;
If one can be mindless and remain detached from the mind, This is the true perfection of dhyāna.
If one can contemplate the mind and bodhi, this is the unsurpassed, true vision;
if one possesses such a true vision, it will not be difficult to attain bodhi.
If one can know and see that there are no words, And that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing—
One who practices such contemplation and vision Is what is called "Great Wisdom."
Although one may verbally speak of wisdom, wisdom does not abide in the sounds of speech;
if one knows that these vocal sounds are in reality soundless, this is the true nature of wisdom.
If phenomena have no such abiding as "this" or "that," Nor any place of abiding in between, The nature of all phenomena has no place of abiding; This is the unsurpassed, great wisdom.
Without letters and without activity, without characteristics and without nature,
without the dual marks of grasping and abandoning— this is called the one of supreme great wisdom.
If one contemplates all pāramitās, their nature is equal like space;
this is precisely what is called "equality of non-equality," which is able to contemplate the equality of all phenomena.
If one can regard all phenomena with equanimity, And likewise perceive all sentient beings as equal,
Being able to view all Buddhas with universal equanimity, The wisdom thus attained is beyond compare.
If there are wise bodhisattvas who can contemplate such peerless dharmas,
they will immediately attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi, just as the former buddhas have attained it.

When the Bodhisattva Wordless (Avāca) spoke these verses, twelve thousand nayutas of sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

At that time, the bodhisattvas within the flower pedestal all rose from their seats, prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and reverently made offerings of exquisite lotus flowers to the Bodhisattva Silent Speech, declaring these words:
“We are those who recognize kindness; we now repay that kindness.”
At that time, Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions does such a bodhisattva utter these words?"
"I am one who recognizes kindness; I now repay that kindness. The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!
Thus, all these bodhisattvas have generated the mind of enlightenment because of the Bodhisattva Wordless; for this reason, it is said:
"I am one who recognizes kindness, and I now repay that kindness."
"Now, furthermore, because the Bodhisattva Wordless has heard and received such a Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra as this, he has come to behold me and make offerings to me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wordless addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have a doubt that I now wish to request you to resolve; I only pray that the Tathāgata will, out of compassion, grant me leave to speak.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you.
Then Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Silent Speech: "O Noble One!"
"If there is no speech, how can one ask questions? "Venerable sir!
All dharmas are entirely without speech, without letters, and without explanation."
Why is this? Because the nature of all sentient beings is ineffable; it is through vitarka and vicāra that sound is produced.
If there were no vitarka and vicāra, how could there be sound?
How can it be spoken? How can there be words?
"O Virtuous One!"

In the midst of vitarka and vicāra there are neither words nor sounds; apart from vitarka and vicāra, there are likewise no sounds or words. The essence of vitarka and vicāra is not itself vitarka and vicāra.

When I produce written characters, I am also not in a state of vitarka and vicāra, yet it is because of vitarka and vicāra that I possess great merit. If one can contemplate such profound dharmas as these, this is what is called the twelve links of dependent origination.

If that which arises from conditions is itself empty and quiescent, then it has no fixed characteristic; if one possesses such true knowledge, this is precisely the true knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
“Venerable One!

All dharmas arise entirely from the conjunction of causes and conditions; yet within this conjunction, there is truly no agent, no producer, and no one who brings them forth. Therefore, all dharmas have no master, no sound, no voice, and no mind; they are without vitarka and vicāra, yet are not without vitarka and vicāra.”
Why is this? Because arising and ceasing exist due to inverted causes and conditions.
Therefore, whether there be one who asks, one who listens, or one who explains, these are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are of a single mark, which is the markless.
“Venerable Sir!
To pose a difficult question is itself great compassion; it is because I possess this great compassion that I question the Buddha.
Such questioning is a question of compassion, not a mere verbal inquiry.”

"Verily, 'questioning with the mouth' is the questioning of the śrāvakas; because śrāvakas are attached to sounds, they are called 'śrāvakas. Because Bodhisattvas possess universal compassion, they have no questioning with the mouth. Śāriputra said:
"O son of good family!"
If the nature of all phenomena is not fixed, then the nature of all sentient beings is also not fixed; if it is not fixed, for whom would a bodhisattva cultivate a mind of compassion?

“Venerable sir! If sentient beings possessed a fixed nature, then no bodhisattva would ever cultivate compassion. In reality, all sentient beings are not truly sentient beings; it is only due to perversion that they are conceived as sentient beings. Therefore, bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate a compassionate mind, and for the sake of destroying perversion, they proclaim non-self.”
"Venerable One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not preach the true Dharma for the sake of destroying existence; nor do they cultivate loving-kindness and compassion or proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of destroying the self, the life-principle, or the person. Rather, they proclaim the Dharma for the sake of knowing the profound and true realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
"The true dharma-realm is precisely the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent!"

"Good son! I too know this truly and authentically; therefore, I have questioned you merely to test your wisdom. I ask for the sake of causing the Buddha-dharma to increase, and I ask out of a desire to benefit sentient beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silence addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As it is said in the sutras, there are two causes and conditions that can give rise to right view: namely, hearing the sound [of the Dharma] and wise reflection.”
“I only pray that you will take pity on us and extensively proclaim this for the sake of all bodhisattvas: how is it that by hearing the sound and through correct reflection, right view is produced?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

"Good son! To listen to the Dharma for the sake of the bodhicitta is what is meant by 'hearing the sound. To mindfully recollect the bodhicitta with a sincere heart is 'skillful reflection. To contemplate the bodhicitta is called 'right view.'"
"Furthermore, noble son! To listen to the Dharma for the sake of the path to enlightenment is called 'hearing the sound.
Not to distance oneself from the path is 'skillful reflection,' and to abide in accordance with the Dharma is called 'right view.'"
To listen to the Dharma for the purpose of taming the mind is called "hearing the sound.
To distance oneself from an evil mind is "skillful reflection," and to attain a virtuous mind is called "right view."

Listening to the Dharma for the sake of adorning wholesome dharmas is called hearing the sound; cultivating and accumulating adornments is wise reflection; and aspiring toward bodhi is called right view.
To listen to the sublime Dharma is called hearing the sound; to increase the sublime Dharma is called skillful reflection; to aspire toward Bodhi is called right view.
To listen to the teaching on generosity is called hearing the sound; to be able to relinquish everything is skillful reflection; to seek no karmic reward is called right view.
To listen to the collection of precepts is called hearing the sound; to guard the precepts with a sincere heart is called skillful reflection; to aspire toward Bodhi is called right view.
To listen to the patience of the Dharma is called hearing the sound; to not retaliate when struck or reviled is skillful reflection; to aspire toward Bodhi is called right view.
To listen for the sake of diligence is called hearing the sound; to destroy indolence is skillful reflection; and to aspire toward Bodhi is called right view.
To listen for the sake of samādhi is called hearing the sound; to be able to purify body and mind is skillful reflection; and to aspire toward Bodhi is called right view.
To listen to the accumulation of wisdom is called hearing the sound; having heard it, to contemplate it correctly is skillful reflection; and to aspire toward bodhi is called right view.

To listen to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) is called hearing the sound; to gather in sentient beings is skillful reflection; and to know that these means of integration are without grasping, without action, empty, and non-existent is called right view.

Listening to the Dharma of the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) is called hearing the sound; attaining lightness of body and mind is called skillful reflection; aspiring toward Bodhi is called right view.

Listening to the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) is called hearing the sound; cultivating and accumulating these analytical knowledges is skillful reflection; aspiring toward Bodhi is called right view.
Hearing the four reliances is called "hearing the sound"; diligently practicing the four reliances is called "skillful reflection"; and aspiring toward Bodhi is called "right view.
Hearing the exposition of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is called "hearing the sound":

if one hears the teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness, that is the "foundations of mindfulness"; the teaching on relinquishment is the "four right efforts"; the teaching on the collection of concentration is the "four bases of psychic power"; the teaching on fearlessness is the "five faculties"; the teaching on being indestructible is the "five powers"; the teaching on the departure from afflictions is the "seven factors of enlightenment"; and the teaching on the true knowledge of phenomena is the "eightfold noble path"—this is skillful reflection.
Not clinging to the extremes of annihilation or permanence, but aspiring toward Bodhi by means of such a path—this is called right view.

Hearing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is called hearing the sound; knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path is called wholesome reflection; seeing that such dharmas are neither born nor extinguished is called right view.
To hear the three gates of liberation is called "hearing the sound";
to have faith in the samādhi of emptiness, not to fear signlessness, and not to doubt wishlessness is "skillful reflection";
to aspire toward bodhi by means of such dharmas is called "right view."

Cultivating the samādhi of emptiness to clarify the mind’s vision, cultivating the accumulation of signlessness to eliminate applied and sustained thought, and cultivating the accumulation of wishlessness to seek beyond all states of existence—this is called right view.
Listening to the Dharma for generating the bodhicitta is called "hearing the sound"; cultivating the path to enlightenment is "skillful reflection";

and the non-retrogression of that mind is called "right view. Gaining a virtuous friend is called "hearing the sound"; making offerings to and attending upon them is called "skillful reflection"; and receiving their instructions is called "right view."
To listen to the dharma-realm is called hearing the sound; to contemplate the dharma-realm is skillful reflection; to abide in accordance with the dharma is called right view.
To see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is called hearing the sound; to mindfully recollect all bodhisattvas is skillful reflection; to attain the ultimate path is called right view.

Hearing the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma at the outset is called the sound of hearing; contemplating such spheres of activity for all sentient beings is called reflection; and subduing the eighty-four thousand faculties is called right view.
“Good son! Whatever causes and conditions can give rise to wholesome dharmas is called ‘hearing the sound.
Having heard them, not being separated from those various wholesome causes and conditions is called ‘skillful reflection.’”
To direct one's aspiration toward bodhi by means of such dharmas is called right view. "Good son!
These two dharmas are without distinction; namely, skillful reflection and right view."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are equal and non-dual; this skillful reflection that is able to contemplate equality is right view.
That which is without increase or decrease is itself right view.
That which is without grasping or rejecting is right view.
That which is without action or agent is right view.
That which is without applied and sustained thought is right view.
The absence of thought and the locus of thought is right view.
The absence of action and the absence of volition is right view.
The absence of one and the absence of two is right view.
"One gate, one flavor, one vehicle, and one practice—their nature is one.

There are no afflictions, nor fetters such as pride; there is neither hearing nor speaking, neither defilement nor purity. The nature of the dharma-realm is beyond discrimination; it is suchness, immovable, and equal throughout the three periods of time."

There is no self or what belongs to a self; there are no sentient beings, no life-span, and no person. There are no letters and no sounds, and it cannot be proclaimed. It is neither known nor seen. Within all dharmas, one attains a mind of contentment, remains far removed from all marks, severs all joy, conceptualization, and discursive thought, as well as the dwelling-place [of the mind], and even when praising the Buddha, one does not give rise to the mark of a Buddha.
When entering meditative concentration, contemplating such a profound realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is called "skillful reflection.
Having arisen from concentration, proclaiming this profound realm of phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings is called "right view."
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained this right view.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Silent Speech, saying: "Good son!..."
"From whom did you hear the Dharma to attain right view?
The Bodhisattva Silence replied,
"Virtuous One!"
If there are those who have not attained the bodhicitta of the past, future, or present, I hear from them and thereby attain right view.

Contemplating the equality of the three periods of time and the equality of all phenomena, I give rise to neither discursive thought nor investigation regarding any phenomenon; my mind does not abide in the conditioned or the unconditioned.
He remains far removed from all signs of sentient beings, yet for the sake of sentient beings he practices various ascetic austerities; furthermore, he is also far removed from two kinds of signs:
first, the sign of a sentient being;
second, the sign of a mind.

They remain far removed from the two extremes and know the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This true nature of phenomena is neither existence nor non-existence. They penetrate all the profound teachings of the Buddhas and do not give rise to arrogance by claiming, "I know."
"Venerable Sir!
I have heard and received the True Dharma from this person; yet this person has not uttered a single word, and yet he causes all to delight in hearing it."
Knowing that the true nature of dharmas is ineffable, one proclaims them for the sake of sentient beings;

having emerged from the world, one is not defiled by the world, ultimately cultivating and accumulating that which can neither be known as cultivated nor uncultivated—it is from such a person that I have heard and received the True Dharma.

Abiding in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one does not give rise to discrimination regarding the nature of sentient beings; observing that the nature of sentient beings, the nature of phenomena, and emptiness are all entirely equal, it is from such persons as these that I hear the Dharma.
This person attains bodhi without sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, without rising, without walking, without sleeping, without reclining, without slumbering, and without waking.

Having attained awakening, he ultimately does not manifest the sign of having attained awakening; furthermore, all sentient beings do not know that he has obtained awakening, for it is by way of non-attainment that he attains, and thus there is no sign of attainment.
"Venerable Sir!
As for the True Dharma, it possesses no radiance; that which has no radiance has no location;
that which has no location is bodiless; that which is bodiless is fearless; and that which is fearless is—"
Non-emergence—non-emergence is precisely non-arising; non-arising is precisely non-extinction;
non-extinction is precisely non-attachment; non-attachment is precisely non-movement; non-movement is precisely non-change;
non-change is precisely neither haste nor darkness; neither haste nor darkness is precisely the absence of vitarka and vicāra.
That which is without applied and sustained thought is the absence of worlds; that which is without worlds is the absence of receptacle-worlds;
that which is without receptacle-worlds is the absence of greed; that which is without greed is the purity of nature; that which is the purity of nature does not conjoin with afflictions;
that which does not conjoin with afflictions is non-inverted; that which is non-inverted is equanimity.
That which is equanimity is reality; that which is reality is neither born nor extinguished.
That which is neither born nor extinguished is said to arise from causes and conditions. That which arises from causes and conditions neither comes nor goes.
That which neither comes nor goes has no objective realm. That which has no objective realm is the absence of verbal expression. That which is the absence of verbal expression is... [not defiled].
Madness; that which is not madness is the absence of hearing; that which is the absence of hearing is the absence of action;
that which is the absence of action is the absence of dwelling; that which is the absence of dwelling is the absence of words; that which is the absence of words is the absence of marks;
that which is the absence of marks transcends the categories of mind, intellect, and consciousness; and that which transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness is—
Quiescence; that which is quiescent is without fever; that which is without fever is without hatred;
that which is without hatred is ultimate; that which is ultimate is non-existence;
that which is non-existent is nirvāṇa—this is called the Dharma.
"Venerable sir!
This is the True Dharma; this is the teaching of the Dharma; this is the hearing of the Dharma; this is Right View.
Venerable sir!"

Now, right view does not perceive the body, nor does it perceive bodily conduct or afflicted conduct; it does not perceive views, nor does it give rise to craving or attachment; it is without conceptualization and without observation—this is called the noble view and right view of the Buddha-dharma.
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!
To contemplate that ignorance and craving are equal to liberation without any distinction is called right view.
Having seen thus, neither clinging nor grasping is called the noble vision."
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!

To contemplate greed, hatred, and delusion as equal and non-dual—empty, signless, and wishless—and not to perceive their signs, but to perceive the sign of signlessness: this is called the noble vision."
Not observing one or two, but regarding all phenomena as equal, is called noble right view. "Furthermore, Venerable Sir!

If one can contemplate that the self and sentient beings are equal—because sentient beings are equal, the Tathāgata is equal; because the Tathāgata is equal, the Buddha-dharma is equal; because the Buddha-dharma is equal, the Noble Saṅgha is equal; because the Noble Saṅgha is equal, great compassion is equal; and because great compassion is equal, space is equal—and by abiding in such equality through non-abiding, this is called noble right view."
“Venerable Sir! As it is with all phenomena, so it is with sound;
as it is with sound, so it is the noble vision, the right view.”
"Venerable sir!
Even noble right view has no arising; if there is no arising, from whom could one hear the Dharma? Śāriputra said:
"As I understand the meaning of what you have said, venerable sir, all dharmas are beyond verbal expression. "It is so, it is so, Venerable One!"
"All dharmas are in reality beyond speech.
"Good son, if one says that the Tathāgata has accomplished meritorious qualities, what kind of fault is incurred in such speech?"
“Venerable One! If one speaks in such a manner, you should know that this person commits a great transgression. Why is this?
Because the merits of the Tathāgata are not determinate.
Why is this? Because he is neither possessed of merit nor possessed of demerit, he is named the Tathāgata.
If one perceives the Tathāgata as possessing merit, this is called desire.
Now, one who has desire possesses a great desire; to have desire and a great desire is itself a fault.
“Good son! How is it that one obtains the name ‘free from fault’? “Venerable sir!”

Like a fifth great element, like a seventh sense-faculty, like a nineteenth realm—without exiting or entering, without arising or ceasing, without volitional activity, and without mind, thought, or consciousness—this is called being faultless.
If there is knowledge and vision that involves distancing oneself from realization and cultivation, this is called a fault.
If there are various elements (*dhātu*), this is called a fault; if there are no various elements, this is called being without fault.
At that time, the Buddha praised Bodhisattva Wordless, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"What you have said is indeed well said.
When this Dharma was spoken, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva Avacanā further addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, there are four kinds of powers for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
namely, the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, and the power of wisdom.”
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain in detail and distinguish: what are called the four powers of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Listen attentively with a sincere mind, and I shall also speak.
If there is a bodhisattva who possesses deep faith and compliant understanding toward the Buddha’s true Dharma, and does not harbor any doubt, this is called the power of faith.
If one diligently exerts vigor in seeking the Buddha-dharma, without ceasing, without resting, and without giving rise to doubt or regret, this is called the power of vigor (*vīrya-bala*).

If there is a bodhisattva who seeks wholesome dharmas, and having attained them, does not lose mindfulness of the bodhicitta, dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment, this is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).
If a bodhisattva reflects within themselves and does not follow the words of others, but thoroughly understands the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is called the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If one possesses faith and draws near to the noble ones, this is called the power of faith.
If one is able to make offerings to such noble ones, this is called the power of vigor.
To listen to and receive the words of the noble ones with a sincere heart, this is called the power of mindfulness.
Having heard the sublime Dharma, to abide in accordance with the Dharma is called the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family,
to have faith in karma and its results is called the power of faith.
Having already given rise to faith, one refrains from all evil; this is called the power of vigor (*vīrya-bala*).
Past wholesome karma continues to increase in the present life; this is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).
If one knows that all phenomena have causes and effects, this is called the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
"Furthermore, noble son! If one has faith that the nature of phenomena is ineffable, this is called the power of faith.
If, by means of this faith, one is able to subdue the mind, this is called the power of diligence."
If one can be wholehearted, this is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).
To contemplate all phenomena as being like an illusion is called the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). "Furthermore, good son!
If one perceives that phenomena are empty, this is called the power of faith.
If one abandons wrong views, this is called the power of vigor.
If one perceives that both the internal and external are entirely empty and quiescent, and thus gives rise to no fear, this is called the power of mindfulness.
If one can contemplate and perceive the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), this is called the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
Furthermore, son of good family,
if one can contemplate and perceive signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), this is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
To expound for others the signless and the wishless is called the power of diligence.
To observe the signless and the wishless with a sincere mind is called the power of mindfulness.
To thoroughly understand that these dharmas cannot be fully expressed in speech is called the power of wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son! To be able to give all things without seeking a karmic reward is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
To feel no regret after giving, and to practice continuously without ceasing, is called the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*)."
When giving, to mindfully contemplate bodhi and make vows for the dedication of merit is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).
To not observe the wealth, the recipient, the giver, or the karmic fruit is called the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
"Furthermore, good son! If there is one who upholds the pure prohibitions and precepts without seeking their karmic retribution, this is called the power of faith.
If one does not give rise to afflictions that destroy the prohibitions and precepts, this is called the power of diligence."
Thus, to protect and uphold pure precepts with a sincere mind, aspiring toward Bodhi, is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).
To contemplate the body, speech, and mind as being like the moon reflected in water, an echo, a magical illusion, or a mirage is called the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
"Furthermore, good son! If there is one who practices the dharma of patience without seeking its fruit, this is called the power of faith.
If there is one who can endure being struck or reviled, this is called the power of diligence."
To cultivate and accumulate loving-kindness, compassion, and heedfulness for the sake of patience, while aspiring toward enlightenment, is called the power of mindfulness.
To contemplate that body, speech, and mind have nothing at all to endure is called the power of wisdom.

"Furthermore, good son! If one understands that through diligent application of effort one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and that it is not attained through indolence, this is called the power of faith."

If one can subdue all sentient beings, protect, uphold, listen to, and make offerings to the True Dharma, serve as a messenger and attendant for sentient beings, and purify Buddha-fields, this is called the power of diligence.
To enable sentient beings to distance themselves from indolence, diligently cultivate vigor, and aspire toward Bodhi is called the power of mindfulness.
To cultivate vigor such that it neither increases nor decreases is called the power of wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son! If one delights in tranquility and refrains from speaking of worldly affairs, this is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
If one dwells in empty stillness and attains the four dhyānas and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), this is called the power of vigor (*vīrya-bala*)."
If one does not experience any decline or loss regarding the various dhyānas, this is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).
If one contemplates the various dhyānas as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, this is called the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
"Furthermore, good son!..."
If, upon hearing all the perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one believes them without giving rise to doubt, this is called the power of faith.
Having heard them, to then expound them for the sake of sentient beings is called the power of diligence.
Skillfully reflecting with the mind is called the power of mindfulness.
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma is called the power of wisdom. "Furthermore, good son!
To cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of all sentient beings is called the power of faith.
To feel compassion for sentient beings and cause them to leave suffering behind is called the power of diligence.
Having observed the Dharma and attained great joy in the mind is called the power of mindfulness.
To maintain an even mind toward both enemies and kin, cultivating and accumulating great equanimity (upekṣā), is called the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family,
to observe that this body is produced by immeasurable evils and deceives ordinary people like a magical illusion is called the power of faith (śraddhā).

When undergoing the suffering of death, to single-mindedly fix one's mindfulness upon the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha while disregarding body and life is called the power of diligence (*vīryabala*).

Furthermore, not giving rise to any evil thoughts—such as the mind of a *śrāvaka*, the mind of a *pratyekabuddha*, greed, anger, delusion, envy, stinginess, or the mind that violates the precepts—is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).
If one contemplates the dharma-realm and observes the dharma-realm with unimpeded wisdom, knowing the past, future, and present as well, this is called the power of wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son!
Joy is called faith;
non-retrogression is called diligence;
and the absence of derangement is called the power of mindfulness.
To know with complete clarity is called the power of wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son, by means of the power of faith,
one is able to accomplish what must be done;..."
By the power of diligence, one brings matters to completion;
by the power of mindfulness, one commits nothing to forget;
by the power of wisdom, one is able to teach in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Because one contemplates the net of doubt, it is called the power of faith.
Because one distances oneself from doubt, it is called the power of diligence."
To no longer give rise to doubt is called the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).
To say that one can destroy doubt is called the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). "Furthermore, good son!..."
To have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma is called the power of faith.
To practice for the sake of awakening is called the power of diligence.
To attain compliant patience is called the power of mindfulness.
Attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) is called the power of wisdom. "Good son!

There is no difference between the faculty of faith and the power of faith; it is likewise for the faculty of vigor and the power of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness and the power of mindfulness, and the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom."
When this Dharma was being taught,

one hundred thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and forty-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Padma who addressed the Bodhisattva Anabhilāpya, saying:
“Good son, when you previously questioned the Buddha, the Buddha immediately analyzed and explained it for you; was your mind filled with joy?”
The Bodhisattva Wordless said:
“Good son! I neither inquire about nor listen to a single dharma; how could joy arise?”
The Bodhisattva Padma said:
"Noble son, have you not heard the Dharma from the Buddha?"
The Bodhisattva Wordless said:
"All Buddhas and Tathāgatas have nothing at all to say.
How then could I listen?"
"Why is this? Because I am not a vessel for the Dharma.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Padma.
"If you are not now a vessel for the Dharma, what kind of vessel are you?
Bodhisattva Silence replied, "Good son!..."
"My own body is currently not even a fit vessel for the Dharma, let alone any other vessel!
The Bodhisattva Lotus Flower said,
"If you are not a true vessel for the Dharma, how will you ever attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Bodhisattva Wordless said: “Good son!
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is likewise not a vessel.”
"Good son! If there were bodhi apart from the Buddha-dharma, one should know that there would be a vessel for it.
All Buddha-dharmas are themselves bodhi, and bodhi is itself the Buddha-dharma."
"Good son! Therefore, even if I were free from afflictions, I would not see the Buddha-dharma, nor would I see bodhi; for there is no distinction between afflictions, bodhi, and the Buddha-dharma."
"If one perceives bodhi within afflictions, this is seeing according to reality;
if one perceives bodhi apart from afflictions, this is called a perverted view.
Padma Bodhisattva said:
“Good son! What is called ‘perverted view’?
To see a self, a life-span, a person (*puruṣa*), or a youth (*māṇava*), and to hold that apart from these there exist separately desire, hatred, and delusion—this is called perverted view.”

The nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the nature of awakening (*bodhitva*) are without distinction; they are without agent and without recipient. The self-nature of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a person (*pudgala*), or a youth (*māṇava*)—these are precisely desire, hatred, and delusion. Such phenomena as these are themselves awakening. This is called "seeing as it truly is. One seeks awakening within the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is derived from them, and not elsewhere.

What is meant by "seeking"? When seeking, one does not perceive any phenomena; that which is not perceived is "no place"; "no place" is "non-abiding"; "non-abiding" is the nature of all phenomena. If all phenomena have no nature, this is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark is neither eternal nor annihilated, and is called the ultimate limit (*atyanta-koṭi*).

If there are those who can perceive such sections as these, one should know that such persons do not flow and do not disperse; being neither flowing nor dispersing, they are without arising or ceasing, which is itself nirvana, and constitutes the true knowledge of all dharmas.
If those such as these were to attain nirvāṇa, it would mean that the noble words enter into nirvāṇa.

Therefore, the Tathāgata has said in the sūtras: "It is impossible for one who is not self-subdued to subdue others, for one who is not self-liberated to liberate others, for one who is not self-peaceful to pacify others, or for one who has not attained nirvāṇa oneself to cause others to attain nirvāṇa."

If one tames oneself and causes others to be tamed; if one liberates oneself and causes others to be liberated; if one pacifies oneself and causes others to be pacified; if one attains nirvana for oneself and causes others to attain nirvana—this is indeed possible.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the path to enlightenment, he understands the conduct of all sentient beings.
He does not give rise to discrimination regarding the characteristics of phenomena or the dharma-realm; and when practicing all wholesome dharmas, he likewise perceives no hosts of māras.”

Although they seek the Buddha-dharma, they do not perceive a seeker; although they discipline sentient beings, they do not perceive a self or a person; although they practice all dharmas, they are not defiled by afflictions; although they conform to worldly dharmas, they are not stained by them. Carrying the burden of the five aggregates, they have no place of abiding; remaining far removed from the various realms, they do not move from the dharma-realm. Cultivating the gates of liberation, they do not regress from wholesome dharmas; clearly seeing the three realms, they are not mixed with afflictions. Practicing the *dāna-pāramitā*, they do not give rise to arrogance; this is likewise true for everything up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Following all practices, yet truly not practicing any practices at all—if one can cultivate such practices as these, it should be known that this is precisely practicing the path to bodhi.

One does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the path to enlightenment or the practices of enlightenment; if one practices such a path of enlightenment, one perceives no self within all phenomena, and is without greed, without hatred, without favoritism, without enmity, and without any obstruction.
"If there is no obstruction, that is unconditioned practice; if there is unconditioned practice, one is a true and great Bodhisattva.
The Lotus Bodhisattva said:
"O son of good family!"
For what reason is one called a Bodhisattva?

"Good son! One is called a Bodhisattva because they can awaken sentient beings to that which they have not awakened to; one is called a Bodhisattva because they can rouse sentient beings from the sleep of ignorance; one is called a Bodhisattva because they expound the dharmas that accord with bodhi; and one is called a Bodhisattva because they cause sentient beings to deeply delight in tranquility."

They increase the Buddha’s word, erect the banner of the True Dharma, and protect and mindfully sustain the assembly of noble ones. They remain unshakable in their bodhicitta, do not dwell in the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and never abandon their heart of utmost sincerity. They make vows to ultimately deliver those not yet delivered and liberate those not yet liberated; they act as a refuge for those without refuge, extinguish what has not been extinguished, and tame the afflictions. Without being detached from the afflictions, they contemplate the faults of birth and death while still seeking within the realms of existence.

He cultivates the samādhi of emptiness without abandoning sentient beings; he cultivates and accumulates the state of non-conceptualization without abandoning the thought of enlightenment; he cultivates and accumulates the wishless while deeply delighting in the various realms of existence.

Although he delights in the Buddha-dharma, he is neither attached to nor detached from desire; though he knows that conditioned phenomena abound in faults and transgressions, his inner mind does not abandon the conditioned.

Although they have departed from all darkness, they do not yet attain the Great Illumination; rather, they take great wisdom as their armor and equipment, deeply delighting in giving and adorning themselves with the necklace of generosity.
They purify Buddha-fields, fulfill pure precepts, fulfill vows, and fulfill patience, being able to discipline all sentient beings who lack forbearance.

Diligently cultivating vigor to seek the indestructible body, he is able to destroy the inferior body that experiences the pleasant sensations of the desire realm; though he undergoes various forms of existence, his mind feels no regret, for he skillfully understands expedient means, constantly self-subduing as he seeks bodhi.

One cultivates a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of all sentient beings; one cultivates and accumulates a mind of compassion for the sake of destroying all sufferings; one cultivates a mind of sympathetic joy for the sake of taming those who are untamed; and one cultivates and accumulates a mind of equanimity that is not ultimate renunciation.

"Having thoroughly penetrated and understood the profound meaning—which is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—they rely on the meaning, the Dharma, definitive sūtras, and wisdom, rather than relying on worldly dharmas; furthermore, they serve as a refuge for sentient beings."
They adorn the body and speech for the sake of all sentient beings; they adorn the mind by acting according to their words; and they adorn spiritual powers for the sake of all sentient beings.

They benefit sentient beings like the great earth; they can purify all things like vast waters; they burn away all afflictions like a blazing fire; they are unimpeded regarding all phenomena like a fierce wind; and they are equal toward all phenomena like empty space.

They have attained dhāraṇīs that sustain all gateways; they possess unhindered eloquence in joyful exposition, causing the multitude to hear with delight; they mindfully recollect the Buddha with a sincere heart for the sake of purifying the mind; and they are able to bestow the great gift of Dharma because they give the gift of material food.

He sustains himself through right livelihood with pure deportment; he cultivates the samādhi of non-contention and deeply delights in tranquility; he rejoices in harmonizing sentient beings and avoids worldly talk, rebuking and instructing those who delight in the world; he possesses the seven kinds of wealth and has a supple mind; he delights in practicing generosity with firm resolve and never regresses; his retinue is not divided, he draws near to virtuous friends, and he recognizes and repays kindness while contemplating past karma.

According to the inclinations of sentient beings, he is able to destroy their doubts; observing that birth and death abound with many faults, his actions are performed with utmost sincerity as he understands all languages; he cultivates and accumulates the Mahāyāna without doubting the Three Vehicles; sentient beings delight in seeing him and receive answers according to their questions; having attained unimpeded wisdom, he is held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas.

"His speech is timely and not excessive; he is luminous and cool like the autumn moon; he is fully endowed with wholesome dharmas like the full moon; he is a joy for sentient beings to behold like the bright moon; he increases wholesome dharmas like the waxing crescent moon; he is of a single sweet flavor like the single flavor of the moon; and he contemplates all phenomena as being like the moon reflected in water."

Pure and stainless like the moon free from obscuration, easy to converse with and endowed with all faculties, he serves as a bridge for all dharmas, able to ferry sentient beings across the four swift currents. He performs the work of a Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings, yet his mind never wavers from the realm of the Bodhisattva; for these reasons, he is called a "Bodhisattva."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Padma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Bodhisattva Aśabdha has spoken thus, one should know that before long he will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma-treasure.”
"If there are those who can believe in, accept, and uphold these teachings spoken by the Bodhisattva Wordless, they too shall likewise attain such merit.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! It is as you have said:
