because the Bodhisattva Wordless has attained the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom, even if one were to expound the meaning of a single phrase for immeasurable kalpas, it could never be exhausted."
The Bodhisattva Padma said:
“World-Honored One!

We only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to show compassion and pity, so as to increase the various wholesome dharmas of sentient beings, and to adorn this unsurpassed Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, by briefly revealing for the great assembly such a Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom.”
If there are wise bodhisattvas who, having heard this, shall likewise attain such a samādhi, and having attained it, shall swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Listen with a sincere mind and attend closely; I shall provide you with a brief analytical explanation."

What is called the lamp of wisdom is the lamp of knowledge; the lamp of knowledge is that which destroys darkness; that which is without darkness is that which destroys doubt; that which destroys doubt is the lamp of wisdom; and the lamp of wisdom is the non-dual characteristic of all phenomena.
“Good son! It is the wisdom of clear realization, the wisdom free from doubt, the wisdom of non-loss, the wisdom that does not pull back, the wisdom that does not follow after,
the wisdom without darkness, the noble wisdom, the fierce and sharp wisdom, the swift wisdom, the analytical wisdom, and the vast wisdom.”
Great wisdom, singular wisdom, manifold wisdom, knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, knowledge of the present,
knowledge of the equality of the three periods of time, knowledge of the three realms, knowledge of the three gates of liberation,
knowledge of the three types of insight, knowledge of the Three Jewels, knowledge of the three vehicles, knowledge of the three eyes, and knowledge of the three defilements.

The wisdom of the *tathatā* (suchness), the wisdom of the three aggregates (*trikaṇḍaka*), the wisdom of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), the wisdom of the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandhāyatana-dhātu*),

the wisdom of the harmony of causes and conditions, the wisdom that sees the ultimate limit, the wisdom of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the wisdom of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*), the wisdom of all sounds and speech, the wisdom of all syllables, and unimpeded wisdom.
The wisdom of non-destruction; the wisdom of being able to expound the Dharma; the wisdom of knowing inferior, middling, and superior faculties;
the wisdom of non-action and non-reception; the wisdom of all mantras; the wisdom of all medical arts;
the wisdom of all worldly affairs; the wisdom of the adornment of dhāraṇīs; the wisdom of the sun and moon samādhis; the wisdom of entering samādhi; and noble wisdom.
The wisdom of the noble samādhi; the wisdom of the vajra samādhi; the wisdom of the samādhi of non-contention; the wisdom of the samādhi of the equality of mind;
the wisdom of the samādhi that destroys Māra; the wisdom of the sun-light samādhi; the wisdom of the samādhi of signlessness;
the wisdom of the jewel-banner samādhi; the wisdom of the samādhi of all dharma-gates; and the wisdom of all dharma-vessels.
The wisdom of non-obscuration, the wisdom of the samādhi of boundless light, the wisdom of the samādhi of merit, the wisdom of the samādhi of non-abiding,
the wisdom of the samādhi of joyous vision, the wisdom of the samādhi of excellent vision, the wisdom of the inexhaustible vessel,
the wisdom of ultimate exhaustion, all-knowledge, immovable wisdom, and the wisdom of the Nārāyaṇa samādhi.
Regarding all wisdoms of vision and knowledge, such as these sixty thousand gates of samādhi-wisdom,
I attained them all upon seeing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past. Furthermore,
all such gates of samādhi are entirely sustained by the Wisdom-Lamp Samādhi (Prajñā-pradīpa-samādhi).
“Good son! For example, when the sun rises, it can perform four things:
first, it provides great radiance;”
Second, it eliminates darkness;
third, it reveals various forms and colors;
fourth, it enables all sentient beings to carry out their activities.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they likewise can perform four things:
first, to destroy all the darkness of afflictions;
second, to emit the great light of wisdom.
Third, he demonstrates to all sentient beings their various modes of conduct;
fourth, he reveals to sentient beings what is the path and what is not the path, and so forth. "Good son!

For example, it is like a pure precious jewel placed atop a high banner; its radiance shines everywhere throughout a distance of four yojanas, providing all sentient beings with whatever things they require, yet the essential nature and appearance of the jewel neither increase nor decrease.

The Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom is likewise so. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they forever sever all afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). They purify their precepts, concentration, and wisdom; they purify their body and mind; they purify their skillful means and their dhāraṇīs. Cultivating and accumulating great compassion, they radiate a great light that universally illumines immeasurable Buddha-worlds, performing deeds in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Although the Bodhisattva performs such deeds as these, their characteristics and nature neither increase nor decrease. "Good son!

For example, just as space accommodates Buddha-lands without obstruction, and likewise does not obstruct any raindrops, or the calamities of wind, fire, and water, so too are all sentient beings infinite and boundless."

"Good son! The Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom is likewise. Bodhisattvas who abide in this samādhi preach all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings without obstruction. They skillfully transform and teach all sentient beings: for those with the power of causes, they expound skillful means to bring them to liberation, subduing and maturing them; for those fixed in error, they skillfully expound the teaching to destroy their false fixation; for those without the seeds of goodness, they cause them to plant the seeds of goodness; for those who are not vessels for the Dharma, they cause them to become vessels; and for those who are vessels for the Dharma, they analytically expound *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he employs skillful means to teach the Dharma so that they may attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
For those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, he provides skillful instruction so that they may attain the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, he employs skillful means to teach the Dharma gradually, causing them all to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.

To penetrate the eighty-four thousand clusters of teachings and to destroy the web of doubts in the minds of sentient beings, he reveals, distinguishes, and explains them in various ways; yet even if one were to explain a single matter for immeasurable eons, it could never be exhausted. Although he performs such immeasurable deeds, this samādhi neither increases nor decreases.

“Good son! For example, just as the power of a single lamp can manifest various forms and colors, so too is the Wisdom-Lamp Samādhi: within a single moment of mind, it can manifest various forms throughout immeasurable Buddha-worlds, yet this samādhi remains unshakable.”

Therefore, among the four foundations of mindfulness, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is the summit; among the four right efforts, the effort to produce unarisen wholesome states is called the summit; among the four bases of power, tranquility of body and mind is called the summit; among the five faculties and five powers, the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom are called the summit; among the seven factors of enlightenment, the investigation of phenomena is the summit; among the eightfold noble path, right view is the summit; among all the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of all non-Buddhists, these are called the summit; among the four noble truths, the truth of cessation is the summit; among the four reliances, reliance on the meaning is the summit; among the four unhindered knowledges, the unhindered knowledge of meaning is called the summit; and among the six supernormal powers, the exhaustion of outflows is the summit.

Among the four immeasurable minds, compassion is the summit; among the cultivation of pure conduct, wisdom is the summit; among all the *pāramitās*, *prajñā* is the summit; among all skillful means, knowing the minds of sentient beings is called the summit; among all the powers, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*) is called the summit; among the fearlessnesses, the first is called the summit; among the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), non-obstruction is the summit; among the thirty-two marks, the mark of the invisible crown of the head is called the summit; among the eighty minor marks, the unfailing preaching of the Dharma is called the summit; among the adornments of speech, understanding all languages is called the summit; among the adornments of mind, the destruction of pride is the summit; among all dharmas, wisdom is the summit—this is called the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom.

While this sutra was being spoken, the Bodhisattva Padma and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained this samādhi; the great earth of the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the entire assembly made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite flowers, incense, and various kinds of music, honoring and praising him with reverence.
At that time, the bodhisattvas in the assembly each spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
Since the past, we have never even heard the name of this samādhi, much less heard its detailed exposition and analysis!"
I have now attained all such samādhis; therefore, to repay their kindness, I have prepared this offering.
If anyone hears the names of these samādhis, they will immediately obtain great benefit and shall not lose the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"

As you have said, if there are sentient beings who, having already planted various roots of goodness and drawn near to spiritual friends under the guidance of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, only then shall they be able to hear this samādhi.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, from within his navel there emerged the body of a bodhisattva, the color of pure gold, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, emitting a great radiance such that none other could surpass it except for the Buddha’s own light.
At that time, the Bodhisattva prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata Prajñā-mada sends his boundless greetings, inquiring whether the World-Honored One is light and at ease in your daily life, free from illness, and whether the great assembly is at peace.”

"In this realm of mine, there are now sixty trillion bodhisattvas who wish to go and listen to and receive this sublime scripture of the Great Assembly; they also wish to behold Bodhisattva Silence and the bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions, and furthermore, they wish to hear of the Wisdom Lamp Samādhi."
Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni!
We pray that you will graciously reveal this teaching, so that all those who have gone forth may attain the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom and return once more to this land.
Then Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One,
in which direction does the Tathāgata Prajñāmadhi reside?"
How far is it from here?
What is the name of that world?
And what is the name of this bodhisattva?
"In what place do these sixty trillion bodhisattvas reside?
"Śāriputra, that buddha-world lies to the east of here, past as many worlds as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, and its name is Vajradṛḍhamūla. The Buddha there is named Prajñābhibhū."
“Śāriputra! For what reason and by what causal conditions is that world named Vajradṛḍhamūla? Śāriputra!...”
The ground of that Buddha-world is entirely composed of vajra; it has become thus through the power of that Buddha’s vows.
The bodies of both sentient beings and bodhisattvas therein are also entirely vajra; for this reason, the world receives such a name.

This bodhisattva is named Vajranābha. In a single thought-moment, this person can shatter all vajra mountains and proceed directly to the worlds of immeasurable buddhas, manifesting from within the navels of those buddhas. By means of the buddhas' spiritual power and his own power of vows, he is therefore named Vajranābha.
“Śāriputra! Regarding what you have just asked—where such bodhisattvas abide—you should now question Vajranābhi; he will answer you himself.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"Good son! As for those sixty trillion bodhisattvas you mentioned, where do they dwell?"
Vajragarbha said, “The Tathāgata has declared that you are foremost in wisdom; you should observe with noble wisdom the place where this bodhisattva dwells.
Thereupon, Śāriputra observed it with noble wisdom but did not see it, and he said to Vajragarbha:
“Good son, I do not see it through the perfection of noble wisdom.
“Venerable sir,” [he replied].
“Your fellow student Aniruddha is foremost in the divine eye; you should have him observe where he resides.
At that time, Aniruddha surveyed the trichiliocosm with his divine eye but was unable to see him, and said to Śāriputra, “With my divine eye, I cannot see him at all.”
The Bodhisattva Vajranābhi said: "Virtuous One!
If your fellow students cannot see with it, it should not be called the 'divine eye,' but rather the 'fleshly eye.'"
Śāriputra said: "Good son, what is the meaning of your divine eye?"
“Venerable sir! As for my divine eye, I am able to see forms that you and the other śrāvakas cannot see. Śāriputra said:
“Good son! What kind of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) cannot I see, yet you are able to see?
“Venerable sir! [he replied.]
"Do you now see the Tathāgata Prajñāmadhura and his bodhisattvas in the world-system Vajradṛḍhamūla?
"No, noble son."
"I have only heard its name but am unable to see it. "Virtuous One!
Such buddha-fields, as well as the Tathāgatas, bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings therein, I can see entirely with my divine eye; this is called the pure divine eye of a bodhisattva."
"Such a divine eye is not possessed by any of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others.
When this Dharma was being taught, sixty thousand beings who were seeking the state of a śrāvaka abandoned their original aspirations and resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, each saying:
"May we obtain the unimpeded Buddha-eye; let us not have the obstructed eyes of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi entered into samādhi; by means of the Buddha’s supernatural power and his own strength, he caused the entire assembly to see sixty trillion bodhisattvas sitting upon lotus pedestals within the Buddha’s body, listening with single-minded devotion to what the Buddha was saying. Yet they did not obstruct the Tathāgata’s body, and the Tathāgata’s body neither increased nor decreased, remaining entirely unimpeded.
At that time, when the great assembly had witnessed this event, they made offerings and paid homage, joyfully praising the inconceivable deeds of the Tathāgata, and further spoke these words:
"The body, wisdom, and samādhi of the Tathāgata are all entirely inconceivable."
"Why is this? It is because these sixty trillion bodhisattvas all abide within the body without obstruction.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi to the great assembly:
"O great assembly!
You do not know that the body of the Tathāgata is like empty space; it is the boundless body, the unobstructed body, the vast body of the Dharma-body, the formless body, and the infinite body!"
“O sons of good family!

If the Tathāgata wishes to place all things within himself—namely, kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, hamlets, mountains, rivers, trees, and forests—there is no obstruction whatsoever. For this reason, the Tathāgata is inconceivable.”

“Good son! From the immeasurable pure lands of the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable bodhisattvas come to the Tathāgata to hear the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, thereby accomplishing a wondrous physical form endowed with the twenty-eight marks of a great man; the Tathāgata likewise places them within his own body.”
For what reason?
Because the sentient beings of this land, including the Brahmās, Śakras, and various kings, would feel shame and humiliation upon seeing them; therefore, not a single person is permitted to see them.

At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One’s merit and the power of the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi, the entire great assembly was enabled to see these sixty trillion bodhisattvas, all emerging from a single pore of the Tathāgata.
Having emerged, he prostrated before the Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what reason, World-Honored One, is the Bodhisattva Nameless called 'Nameless'?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
"You should consult Vimalakīrti (the Bodhisattva of Silence) yourself; he will surely answer you.
Thereupon, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva asked Vimalakīrti:
"O son of good family!..."
"For what reason is the name 'Wordless' so?
Bodhisattva Wordless remained silent.
When asked a second and a third time, it was likewise.
Vajranābhi said: "Good son, why do you not answer?"
The Bodhisattva Wordless said:
"I seek for words and phrases, yet they are entirely unobtainable; therefore, I remain silent and have nothing to proclaim. "Good son!..."
"If words cannot be found when sought, how can there be such a thing as 'words that cannot be found'?
"Good son! I answer with all the words of the Buddhas and the words of the world."
“What is meant by ‘answering the Buddha’s words’? ‘Good son!

By the power of mindfulness, I receive and uphold all that is spoken by the Buddhas, neither forgetting nor losing it. Yet, I do not perceive any sounds, syllables, or phrases; I proclaim them for the sake of their dissemination, and I also preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may transcend these sounds, syllables, and phrases.’”
What is meant by "answering according to worldly speech"?
It means understanding the various languages and sounds of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma to them in accordance with their own words. "Good son!..."
"Has it been long since you were able to preach the Dharma in such accordance with reality?
"Good son! It has been so ever since I eliminated applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) and was able to speak thus."
“Good son! For what reason and by what causal conditions do you speak thus? Good son!”
"If there were no applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), how could sound emerge?
For these reasons, it is said thus:
'O son of good family!'"
"Now, as for sound that is produced, does it emerge from the body or from the mind?
"Good son! Sound does not reside in either the body or the mind."
Why is this? The body is like grass and wood; the mind is like an illusion or a magical transformation. Because of various causes and conditions, sound emerges.
If it emerges from conditions, it is impermanent; if it is impermanent, it is not fixed; and that which is impermanent and not fixed is empty and non-existent.
Sounds and voices are like space: they cannot be seen and cannot be described.
As with space, so it is with all phenomena.

If sound were non-existent, then the phenomena discerned by sound would likewise be non-existent. Because sound is empty, all phenomena are empty; because sound is quiescent, all phenomena are quiescent. Sound is invisible, and thus all phenomena are also invisible; sound does not arise, and thus all phenomena also do not arise.

If there is no arising, then there is no coming or going; if there is no coming or going, this is the profound twelvefold chain of dependent origination. This profound dependent origination is without action and without ownership; if there is no action or ownership, then there is no arising or production. That which is without arising and without production is the "no-phrase."

If there are no phrases, this is precisely the non-arising of the eye, forms, and consciousness, up to the mind and mental objects; there is no suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, and death; there is no perception of the sun and moon, light, or of friends and enemies; all conditioned activities are severed; it is difficult to behold, being neither near nor far.
Vajragarbha said: "Noble son, what kind of teaching is this teaching of such things?"
“Good son! In this way, it is ultimately non-emergence. “Good son!”
"What is meant by 'ultimately not emerging'?
"Good son! That which is neither near nor far is ultimately not emerging."
“Good son! What is meant by ‘neither near nor far’?
“Good son! [he replied.]
"This is precisely empty space. If one perceives all phenomena as being like empty space, this is called equality. "Good son!
For what reason are all phenomena said to be like empty space?"

“Good son! The dharmas of the past have no end; those of the future and the present likewise have no end. That the three periods of time are without end is precisely the true mark (dharmatā), which is non-duality.

Duality refers to that which is called the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects—these are termed duality.”

If there were duality, it would be expressible; if there is no duality, it is inexpressible. That which is inexpressible is without consciousness, without mind, and without mentation; for this reason, it cannot be proclaimed.
That which can be spoken of is duality; that which cannot be spoken of is non-duality. "Good son!
Who creates this duality?"
“Good son! That which is non-dual cannot be made dual, nor can that which is dual be made non-dual.
If something is solid, it cannot be made brittle, nor can that which is brittle be made solid.”

The dharma of birth and death does not constitute non-duality, and the dharma of nirvana cannot be made dualistic; the nature of right view does not constitute wrong view, and the nature of wrong view does not constitute right view.
The Bodhisattva Vajranābhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the liberation attained by the Bodhisattva Avacanīya, it appears that he has acquired such a Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
"Do you think that without speech one cannot attain the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom?
At that time, the bodhisattvas and others from the world-system Vajradṛḍhamūla addressed the Bodhisattva Avāca, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"In what stage do you abide that you are able to give such an answer?
Bodhisattva Silence replied,
"O son of good family!"
"As the Buddha has taught, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the stage of ethical discipline (śīla-bhūmi), they are able to answer in this way.
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
“I only pray that you will explain such a ground of precepts. “Good son!

If there is no dwelling in body, no dwelling in mind, no dwelling in intellect, no dwelling internally, no dwelling externally, and no dwelling both internally and externally, this is precisely dwelling in the precepts.”
"Good son! If there is no sign, no life-force, no volition, and no conditioned activity, this is abiding in the precepts.
If there is a bodhisattva who abides in such precepts, this is non-abiding."
If there were no abiding, one would ultimately not give rise to the thought, "I am able to produce sounds and deliver an exposition.
Son of good family!
As to your question regarding what stage one dwells in: [it is this very state].
One who can answer in this way does so by abiding in the dharma-nature, the true mark, and the dharma-realm.
If one knows the reality of dharmas in this manner, then there is no applied thought or sustained thought.
"If there is no applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), how can there be speech? The Bodhisattvas replied: "Good son!..."
"When these words were spoken, what was being taught? "Good son,
when these words were spoken, two dharmas were taught."
First, cessation; second, non-emergence. First, the past;
second, the future. Because it does not abide in the present, it cannot be described.
"Good son! The dharmas of the past cannot be characterized by signs; the same is true for those of the future and the present.

If anyone were to construct signs regarding the dharmas of the three periods of time, that would be a perversion. Therefore, the meaning of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed; the meaning of all dharmas cannot be expressed by body, speech, or mind."

Why is this? Because there is no karma and no action; there is no physical form, no vocal karma, and no applied or sustained thought; it is like the nature of an echo, for it is like a transformation of the Buddha.
Good son! Whatever the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak always contradicts worldly discourse; therefore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
All the wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inconceivable, inexhaustible, and unmoving within the Dharma-realm.
At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas praised the Bodhisattva Wordless with one voice:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully distinguished such a Dharma-gate, whereby we have obtained great benefit and have been granted the opportunity to behold such immeasurable great bodhisattvas.”
Vajranābhi said to the Bodhisattva Aśabdaka:
"Good son! I wish to return with you to the world Vajradṛḍhamūla to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Prajñāgarva."
The Bodhisattva Wordless said:
"Good son! The world-system Diamond Firm Root is precisely this Sahā world-system here."
"The Buddha Prajñā-mada is none other than the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Why should I go to that buddha-world? Vajranābhi said:
“Good son! The ground of this buddha-world is not made of vajra; why, then, do you say it is that very world?
The Bodhisattva Silence replied:

“Good son! Your supernormal powers can pass unimpeded through immeasurable mountains of vajra, yet you have not yet attempted to destroy the atoms of this land. Only when you succeed in destroying them shall you truly be known as ‘Vajra.’”

At that time, Wuyan immediately entered the Vajra-samādhi, whereby all the mountains, forests, grasses, trees, and even the finest motes of dust throughout this land were entirely transformed into vajra.
At that time, Vajragarbha exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he was unable to break even a single atom.
Then Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My divine power is able to destroy the vajras, mountains, and walls of all worlds; by what cause and condition am I now unable to destroy even this single atom in this land?
"Is this the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural penetrations,
or is it the power of the Way and its Virtue that is beyond words?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This Bodhisattva Wordless has entered the Vajra Samādhi; by the power of this samādhi, he causes everything that exists within this trichiliocosm to become entirely vajra.”
“If you wish to further cause immeasurable worlds to become vajra, your power is likewise capable of doing so.
Vajranābhi Bodhisattva said,
“World-Honored One!”
“By being endowed with how many dharmas can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain such a vajra-samādhi?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with four dharmas, they are able to attain such samādhi. What are these four?
First, to mindfully contemplate bodhi with a sincere heart.
Second, the completion of all wholesome dharmas one has performed;
third, adorning wholesome dharmas with a sincere mind and directing them toward Bodhi;
fourth, being able to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, the accomplishment of supernormal powers;
Second, they cultivate the three gates of liberation;

third, they maintain the precepts with diligence, constantly contemplating the dharma-realm to know that all phenomena have no fundamental basis, and that they are beyond discursive thought and cannot be described;
fourth, they understand meaning and understand timing, and they know reality—that all phenomena are entirely equal.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, seeking great wisdom from a heart of great compassion;
Second, seeking the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through skillful means;
third, observing all sentient beings as entirely equal through a mind of great compassion;
fourth, observing the Four Noble Truths through a mind of equanimity.
“Furthermore, there are four things:
namely, the actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the bodhicitta; these are indestructible, all like adamant. ‘Good son!
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully accomplish such dharmas as these, they are able to attain the Vajra-samādhi.
When this Dharma was spoken, sixty trillion bodhisattvas all attained the Vajra-samādhi.
At that time, Wu Yan addressed his father, General Siṃha:
"Venerable One!
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is itself the fulfillment of immeasurable merit; the great mass of merit is the Tathāgata."
When a Buddha appears in the world, immeasurable sentient beings obtain great benefit; this "great benefit" is precisely nirvana, and nirvana is eternal and unchanging.
"Venerable sir, for what reason have you not resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
His father replied,
"At the very moment of my birth, I already resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, there were also immeasurable devas who came to exhort him, no different from yourself.
Such a matter can only be witnessed and known by a Buddha.
General Siṃha and his retinue of five hundred people all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Silent One praised his retinue:
"Excellent, excellent! You have skillfully adorned the mind of enlightenment."
The retinue asked, "What is meant by 'adorned bodhicitta'?
Bodhisattva Silence replied:
“There are forty matters that adorn the bodhicitta.
What are these forty? They are:
having faith in the Buddha without doubt;”
Not wavering from the dharma-realm;
making offerings to the noble assembly;
and drawing near to virtuous friends.
Regarding all bodhisattvas, one should conceive of them as sovereign physicians;
regarding all sentient beings, one should maintain a mind of equanimity;
and one should offer worship and respect to all teachers and preceptors.
Having virtue, they respectfully receive the words of their parents;
they protect the Dharma and seek the Dharma;
and they listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Having received and upheld [the teachings], one extensively explains them for others;
one makes offerings to and reveres those who protect the Dharma;
and one preaches the Dharma to others.
Not conceiving thoughts of food;
destroying pride; knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
Constantly reflecting with skillful wisdom;
dwelling in accordance with the Dharma;
and being able to give what is difficult to give.
To guard the precepts with a sincere heart;
to diligently and vigorously cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
and to fully accomplish the adornment of merit.
With a mind free from envy, one protects all sentient beings;
one restrains the afflictions;
and one tames the mind as well as the spirit of generosity.
They discipline all sentient beings and are able to sever their afflictions;
they are content and tranquil;
and they cultivate the pure brahmacarya.
They do not sever the noble lineages;
they are untainted by worldly dharmas;
and they honor and respect those who preach the Dharma.
Conforming to the ways of the world;
remaining far removed from indolence;
being free from negligence.
They do not seek the inferior vehicles;
their bodhicitta remains unshakable from the very beginning;
and while dwelling within birth and death, their minds feel no weariness or regret.
To remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas;
and to be fully endowed with all purely wholesome and sublime dharmas as an adornment for the holy life.
This is called the fortieth.
At that time, General Siṃha said:
"May you manifest your body from time to time, so as to cause us not to regress from our resolve for unsurpassed bodhicitta."
The Bodhisattva Silence said:
"Venerable One!
By being endowed with ten dharmas, one always attains proximity to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
What are these ten? They are:
namely, renouncing one's own pleasure to bestow it upon sentient beings;
cultivating and accumulating patience to protect those who are weak and powerless;
Constantly exhorting sentient beings to cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas, transforming and guiding all to incline toward Bodhi;

wishing that all sentient beings may first attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, whereupon I shall make offerings to them, listen to their teachings, receive and uphold them, and protect them, and only then shall I realize the Unsurpassed Way;
knowing the true nature of phenomena, not begrudging body or life.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, upon hearing the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), one does not give rise to fear;
one contemplates that there is no bodhi and no one who attains it;

one contemplates oneself as equal, and all sentient beings as likewise equal; by contemplating the equality of sentient beings, one contemplates the equality of all phenomena (*dharma*); and by contemplating the equality of phenomena, one contemplates the equality of empty space.
One contemplates the suffering of birth and death yet does not abandon it;
seeing the faults of birth and death, the mind feels no regret.
One who is fully endowed with such wholesome dharmas will always be able to draw near to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
When this Dharma was being taught, General Siṃha and his retinue attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!"
You should receive, uphold, recite, and transcribe such a sutra as this.

Why is this? Because within this sutra, the characteristics of all phenomena are analyzed and expounded, and it also causes immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Ānanda! If there are those who have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas, these people will be able to believe and accept this sutra, and they will uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively analyze its meaning.
There are three matters for those who receive this sutra:
first, they will certainly resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi;
second, they will attain a non-retrogressive mind.
"Third, one is able to protect the True Dharma.
At that time, having heard these words, seven nayutas of bodhisattvas rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We are able, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, to receive, uphold, read, recite,
and copy this sutra. Bodhisattva Silence said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of Dharma has the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, attained such that these people are made to receive, uphold, and protect it?
"Good son! If one can protect those who uphold this Dharma, that is itself the protection of the Dharma."
That which is called writing, reciting, and explaining consists of words; while words can express the Dharma, the Dharma itself cannot be expressed.
Son of good family!
There are two kinds of people who can protect the Dharma:
"First, to abide in accordance with the Dharma;
second, to recite these words, for if there were no words, the Dharma could not be taught.

At that time, the entire great assembly, including the retinue led by General Siṃha, as well as the devas and the people of the world, having heard this Dharma, their hearts were filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Twelve;
Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: On the Bodhisattvas Who Are Ineffable.
At that time, the World-Honored One was still in the Great Jewel Enclosure between the realms of desire and form, surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Inexpressible (*Anabhilāpya*). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, approached to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these verses:
"Unimpeded wisdom and unimpeded conduct, Like the nature of space, they are inexpressible;
Equal throughout the three times, beyond thought and reflection— I now pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One."
Contemplating the signless, joyful, and tranquil, Subduing the sense faculties and remaining detached from signs,
Thoroughly understanding that the nature of all phenomena is non-dual— I pay homage to the Lion King among Men.
Observing the nature of sentient beings and the nature of phenomena, these two natures are without distinction;
with an impartial mind, one observes all sentient beings. Now I have forever severed all natures;
the bodhi attained is non-attainment. Just as the nature of bodhi is such, so too is form.
Adorned with the adornment of signlessness, I now pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The entire dharma-realm is free from applied and sustained thought, yet ordinary beings perceive it through signs and activities;
the nature of the dharma-realm is indestructible—because of the Buddha’s true wisdom, I pay him homage.
The bodily karma of the Tathāgata is ineffable; his verbal and mental karmas are likewise so.
The nature of all phenomena and of sentient beings, the Unsurpassed Honored One knows them clearly.
Abiding in the ground of reality, that which the Tathāgata expounds is without sound or syllables.
Sentient beings delight in hearing [the Dharma] and thereby attain great benefit; for this reason, the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
The various dharmas he teaches are without marks; he tames sentient beings and cuts off all modes of existence (*bhava*).
He skillfully explains that the dharma-nature of sentient beings is empty; for this reason, I pay homage to the Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Inexpressible (Avaktavya), having praised the Buddha with verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bodhisattvas in this assembly have each already finished their inquiries. I now wish to ask a few further questions within this Great Collection Sūtra; I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to grant me his compassionate permission.”
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"Ask whatever you doubt; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ineffable, having received this permission, immediately entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Having entered this state, he caused the entire great assembly to dwell upon a great precious platform. Above in the void of space, he rained down flowers, incense, and various kinds of music as offerings, and further uttered these words:
"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ineffable now wishes to inquire about a great matter herein."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ineffable addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bodhi of all Buddhas is pure and tranquil; it is the great stillness, stainless, and free from darkness—a great radiance. It is truly such as it is, its nature being equal, subtle and profound, devoid of applied and sustained thought, far removed from all defilements, and ineffable.”

It is without words, without phrases, and without sound; it is vast and immeasurable, without limit or boundary; it is free from all extremes, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither advancing nor retreating, and has no place of abiding.

It is neither steep nor level; it is neither existence nor non-existence. It is firm and indestructible, without self or what belongs to a self. There is no grasping and no relinquishing; it is neither broad nor narrow. There are no phenomena and no sentient beings; it is inexhaustible and ultimately exhausted.

The nature of the emptiness of non-emptiness is neither a locus nor a non-locus; it is neither mind, nor action, nor arising, nor ceasing. Like earth, water, fire, and wind, it is without limit and immeasurable; it is equally and universally present, without obstruction, like space. It is not the eye-consciousness element, nor even the mind-consciousness element. Having severed all existence, it is beyond analogy and free from all metaphors, for it is the true knowledge of all Buddhas and is thus not other than suchness.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings have fully attained it;
it is not different from suchness.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are entirely equal;
their nature exists.
Why is this? Because it is the true nature. That nature is real.
Why is this? Because there are no divisions of past, future, or present. There is no action and no recipient; it is formless and mindless;

it is without perception and severs all sensation; it is without ideation and severs ideation; it is without volitional formations and severs volitional formations; it is without consciousness and severs consciousness; it is without the aggregates, bases, and elements and severs the aggregates, bases, and elements; it is without beginning, middle, or end and is free from all demonic activities; it is without dissemination, untainted, and not included within any category.

It is neither practice nor litigation, without dispute and without fault; it abides eternally in its own nature, free from discrimination. It is neither birth nor that which gives birth, neither cessation nor that which causes cessation. It has no root; it is neither supreme nor inferior. It has no dwelling place, no direction, and no interval. It is neither wisdom nor discernment, nor is it the activity of discernment. It is not subsumed under the Truths, nor is it subsumed within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). It has no antidote and possesses no conditioned merits, being utterly remote from all signs (*nimitta*).
“World-Honored One!
If this meaning is called bodhi, it is a phrase of no change, a phrase of no awakening, a phrase of no craving,
a phrase of no contention, a phrase of firmness, and a phrase of indestructibility.”

The phrase "immovable" is the phrase "non-acting," the phrase "bodiless," the phrase "unborn," the phrase "without wisdom," the phrase "equality," the phrase "non-dual," the phrase "reality," the phrase "existence," the phrase "truth," the phrase "the ultimate meaning," the phrase "non-conceptualization," the phrase "single flavor," and the phrase "oneness."

The phrase of phenomena, the phrase of the One Vehicle, the phrase of inexhaustibility, the phrase of the equality of the three periods of time, the phrase of the differentiation of the three periods of time,
the phrase of emptiness, the phrase of signlessness, the phrase of wishlessness, the phrase of non-activity, the phrase of tranquility,
the phrase of nature, the phrase of suchness, the phrase of non-arising, the phrase of non-emergence, the phrase of exhaustion, and the phrase of non-existence...
The phrase of dwellings, the phrase of dharmas, the phrase of true nature, the phrase of self-nature,
the phrase of bodilessness, the phrase of non-action, the phrase of non-conception, the phrase of non-contention, the phrase of non-annihilation, the phrase of impermanence,

the phrase of the twelve links of dependent origination, the phrase of what is to be contemplated, the phrase of concentration, the phrase of the superior, the phrase of the supreme, the phrase of the non-existent.
The phrase of faultlessness, the unsurpassed phrase, the ultimate phrase, the pure phrase, the phrase without summit,
the phrase without superior, the phrase without equal, the phrase without dependence, the phrase of mindfulness, the phrase without resemblance,
the phrase that surpasses all worlds, the phrase of no-phrase, and the phrase upon which all phrases depend.
“Such enlightenment is neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white; it is neither form nor non-form; it is neither long, nor short, nor round, nor square, and it possesses no fixed dimensions.”
It is not comprised within the three realms; it is neither the path, nor the ultimate, nor practice, nor arrival. It has no location, and is neither grasping nor abandoning.
It is free from all afflictions and devoid of sorrow or fear; it cuts off all joy, being neither real nor transformative, and is detached from all spheres of perception.
There is no self or what belongs to a self; there are no sentient beings, no life-span, and no person. It is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
It is without divisions, like space, and its nature is ultimately inexpressible. To accomplish such immeasurable dharmas is what is called bodhi.
When this Dharma was being taught, the great earth of the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all the devas made grand offerings of incense, flowers, and music, each exclaiming:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Excellent, noble son! It is well said.

At that time, there were eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly who had attained the *akṣayabhājana-dhāraṇī* and the dharma-gate of the samādhi of mastery over all dharmas and unimpeded liberation.
"If there are those who can believe in this way, such people shall also obtain these benefits of the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Inexpressible again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The precepts of a bodhisattva cannot be fully described. Why is this?
Because the fundamental nature of the body is inexpressible, the precepts of the body likewise cannot be fully described.
The intrinsic nature of speech is also ineffable; therefore, the precept of speech cannot be proclaimed.
The intrinsic nature of the mind is also ineffable; therefore, the precept of mind cannot be proclaimed.
“World-Honored One!
If there are bodhisattvas who, while practicing the path to unexcelled bodhi, protect the ten wholesome dharmas, that [number] is also unspeakable.
If they exhort all sentient beings with these ten wholesome dharmas, the number of sentient beings exhorted is likewise unspeakable.”
The cultivation and accumulation of the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are also ineffable. Why is this?

Because in cultivating the mind of loving-kindness, one contemplates the non-existence of sentient beings; in cultivating the mind of compassion, there is no agent and no recipient; in cultivating the mind of sympathetic joy, one is free from arrogance and intoxication; and in cultivating the mind of equanimity, one remains far removed from dualistic characteristics.
"World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who thus cultivates and accumulates the four immeasurable minds, this is to cultivate pure brahmacarya and abide in the path of Brahmā; this is the skillful means of Brahmā that surpasses all others, and such a one is constantly honored by all the Brahmās."

Why is this? Because it transcends all forms of holy life (*brahmacarya*); because it does not cultivate the compassion based on sentient beings as its causal condition; because it does not cultivate the pity (*karuṇā*) based on dharmas as its causal condition; because it does not cultivate the sympathetic joy (*muditā*) based on the two marks as its causal condition; and because it does not cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*) based on internal and external conditions.
Because they have distanced themselves from all worldly conduct and abandoned all worldly forms of brahmacarya, they are therefore constantly honored by all those who practice brahmacarya.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, the precepts of a bodhisattva cannot be fully described.
As for the bodhisattva precepts, one ultimately does not deceive oneself, nor does one deceive the Buddha.”

Why is this? Because that which is self-natureless is non-existent; that which is non-existent has no arising; that which does not arise has no causes and conditions; that which lacks causes and conditions is without syllables; and that which is without syllables is ineffable.
If there is a bodhisattva who can train in this way, they do not deceive themselves.
What is meant by "not deceiving the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas"?
It is to realize that all dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. That which is neither dharma nor non-dharma is equality; such equality is inexpressible.
If there is a bodhisattva who trains in this way, they are said not to deceive the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, "self" is itself without self and without what belongs to a self; one knows that there is likewise no self and nothing belonging to a self.

If one who trains by practicing and accumulating [virtue] in this way is likewise without self and without what belongs to a self (*anātman* and *anātmīya*), and if one who contemplates and observes in this way does not deceive themselves, then such a person is a Tathāgata. To follow the Suchness (*tathatā*) is to follow sentient beings; to follow sentient beings is to accord with all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); to accord with all phenomena is to neither emerge, nor perish, nor abide. If a phenomenon neither emerges, nor perishes, nor abides, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is said that the unconditioned dharma has three characteristics, namely: no arising, no cessation, and no abiding.
For this reason, it is called "unconditioned."
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the noble (*ārya*), and the noble is named "without enmity.
Because the Tathāgata has distanced himself from all enmity, he is called noble.
Enmity refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); since the Tathāgata has forever abandoned all ignorance, he cannot be harmed by any enemy or adversary.
Because ordinary persons possess ignorance, they are constantly harmed by enemies.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is able to contemplate the realm of enmity and the realm of wisdom; he knows the realm of afflictions and the realm of tranquility; he knows the realm of birth and death and the realm of nirvāṇa; he knows the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); and he thoroughly understands the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha.

Contemplating the realm of form and the eye-realm, as well as the ear-realm, sound-realm, nose-realm, fragrance-realm, tongue-realm, taste-realm, body-realm, touch-realm, mind-realm, and mental-object-realm, one knows that the realm of ignorance and the realm of wisdom are entirely equal; this is the equal Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The two realms of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equal; this is precisely the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
Knowing that the realms of name and form are all entirely equal is precisely the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
To know that the realm of the six sense bases and the realm of the six supernormal powers are entirely equal is itself the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
That the realm of contact and the realm of cessation are entirely equal is itself the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of sensation and the realm of cessation are both entirely equal; they are the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of craving and the realm of cessation are both entirely equal; they are the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of grasping and the realm of cessation are both entirely equal; this is the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of existence and the realm of cessation are both entirely equal; this is the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of birth and the realm of cessation are entirely equal; this is the Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
The realm of old age, sickness, and death, as well as the realm of their cessation, are entirely equal; this is the equal Buddha-realm, the ineffable realm.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva can perform such contemplations as these, they will immediately be able to enter into all realms.

If a bodhisattva enters such realms as these, seeing those who possess greed, they do not give rise to anger; seeing those who have severed greed, they likewise do not give rise to attachment; and seeing those who possess anger, they do not give rise to a mind of resentment.”

One who sees one whose anger has been severed does not give rise to a mind of attachment; one who sees one possessed of delusion does not give rise to a mind of resentment; and one who sees one whose delusion has been severed does not give rise to a mind of attachment. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands these three kinds of realms with complete clarity, such a bodhisattva thoroughly knows the three groups.
"World-Honored One!..."
If a bodhisattva wishes to train in this way, they do not deceive the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because they know the dharmas realized by all Tathāgatas and train in accordance with them; therefore, the bodhisattva does not deceive the Tathāgata.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Abhayānanda who asked the bodhisattva Avaktavya:
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train so as to be said to deceive the Tathāgata?"
The Bodhisattva Inexpressible said:
"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who speaks these words himself:..."
"I am one who upholds the precepts, while he is one who breaks them"—
a bodhisattva who speaks thus is said to deceive the Tathāgata.
"I am a donor, while he is stingy and greedy."
"I am one who practices patience, while they are full of anger;
I am diligent, while they are indolent;
I am one established in concentration, while they are distracted."

"I am wise; he is foolish. I am one who knows contentment and has few desires, delighting in tranquility, easy to support and easy to satisfy, begging for alms and wearing rag-robes, possessing only the three robes and not dwelling among the crowds."

Being learned, they avoid contentious speech and speak with gentleness; sentient beings delight in receiving their words, which are endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. They purify all modes of deportment as well as verbal karma, possess the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and speak words that are true, real, and consistent with what they have said.

Having recognized the realm of Māra, they remain far removed from it; they are constantly able to practice and study the six pāramitās; they are able to skillfully expound the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, giving rise to great vows; and they are able to transform sentient beings so as not to allow them to become negligent.
"If one thus praises oneself and disparages others, this is called a bodhisattva deceiving the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva should say,
"I am able to observe such dharmas as being distant from cultivation and extinction," this is also called deceiving the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally constant. Because it is eternally constant, the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) cannot be known or seen, cannot be abandoned, and cannot be cultivated for cessation.
If a bodhisattva speaks of "self" and "what belongs to self," this is also called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why? Because there is no duality of characteristics.
If anyone should say, "I have already attained realization" or "I am able to remain far removed [from defilements]," this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because the nature is pure.
If one says, "I possess the four foundations of mindfulness," this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has awakened to the fact that all dharmas are devoid of mindfulness.
If one says, "I possess the four right efforts," this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has awakened to the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is detached [from conceptual constructs].
If one says, "I possess the four bases of psychic power," this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has awakened to the fact that all dharmas are without discrimination.
If one says, "I am endowed with the faculties, powers, and the path of awakening," this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the nature of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If anyone should say that the self is different and the path is different, this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because the body itself is the path.
If one says that ignorance is distinct from craving for existence, this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata. Why?
Because ignorance and craving are themselves wisdom and liberation.
If one were to say that the three poisons are distinct from the three gates of liberation, this too would be called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are themselves greed, hatred, and delusion.
If one says that the four inversions are distinct from the four fruits of the path, this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why? Because the four inversions are themselves the four fruits of the path.
If one says that the eight wrong paths are different from the eight right paths, this is also called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why? Because it is for the sake of destroying the eight wrong paths and cultivating the eight right paths.
If one says that the nine abodes of sentient beings are distinct from the nine successive stages, this is also called deceiving the Tathāgata.
Why? Because there is no duality of nature.
If anyone should say that the ten wholesome paths of action differ from those of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), this too is called deceiving the Tathāgata. Why?
Because all dharmas are without cultivation or study.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva studies such dharmas as these, this is called deceiving all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Good son!”
All sentient beings and a single sentient being are neither two nor distinct. Why is this?
Because their nature is without self.

It is said that a single sentient being and all phenomena are non-dual and undifferentiated; if one says that a single phenomenon and the entire dharma-realm are non-dual and undifferentiated, then a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the entire dharma-realm are non-dual and undifferentiated.

It is said that the realm of one Buddha and the realms of all Buddhas are non-dual and without distinction; it is said that one field of merit and all fields of merit are non-dual and without distinction; and that all fields of merit and empty space are non-dual and without distinction.
All noble ones are far removed from afflictions, and all ordinary beings are non-dual and undifferentiated, for their fundamental nature is pure.
The mind of one sentient being and the minds of all sentient beings are non-dual and undifferentiated, for their fundamental nature is pure.
"A single realm is all realms; a single sense-base is all sense-bases; the conduct of a single sentient being is the conduct of all sentient beings—there is no duality and no distinction.

If one says that all phenomena do not remain for even a single thought-moment, one does not commit various evils, does not cling to wholesome dharmas, and does not give rise to arrogance. Within non-attainment, one does not form the notion of attainment; within non-realization, one does not form the notion of realization."

One knows that within both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa there is neither action nor recipient; one knows that all afflictions have no root, being neither born nor growing. Accordingly, through the precepts of morality, mind, and wisdom, one remains far removed from afflictions while never abandoning sentient beings.
The purity of the dāna-pāramitā is the absence of precepts within precepts.
The purity of the śīla-pāramitā is the absence of persons within persons and the absence of self.
The purity of the kṣānti-pāramitā is the absence of action within action.
The purity of the *vīrya-pāramitā* is the absence of purification within purification.
The purity of the *dhyāna-pāramitā* is the absence of practice within practice.
The purity of the *prajñā-pāramitā* is the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*) through neither exhaustion nor arising.
They attain a mind of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta-citta*) and receive their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), yet they do not enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) nor do they regress.

They are born once more in the Tuṣita Heaven, yet they do not descend from there to dwell in a mother’s womb; their minds abide nowhere among all phenomena, nor do they say of themselves, "I have transcended birth, old age, sickness, and death."
He did not walk seven steps, nor did he declare himself to be the Unsurpassed Honored One of the World.

He did not dwell amidst the pleasures of the palace ladies, nor did he practice the worldly arts and crafts. He manifested as an old man to destroy attachment to the body; he manifested the suffering of illness to destroy attachment to life; he manifested the signs of death to destroy attachment to desire, as well as the notions of "I" and "mine"; and he manifested as a śramaṇa to cause sentient beings to seek neither the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, humans, nor devas.

Diligently seeking the unsurpassed Dharma that transcends the world, he departed from the palace city to manifest liberation from the bonds of the triple realm and to demonstrate the fruit of compassion; looking back and forth, he showed himself free from both hatred and attachment.

Adorned with the thirty-two marks upon his body, he manifested himself as a field of merit and a source of blessings for all sentient beings; shaving off his topknot and casting aside his jeweled necklaces, he sent back the horse Kanthaka and Chandaka, thereby demonstrating his complete departure from all afflictions.

"By currently shaving his beard and hair, he demonstrates non-attachment to all phenomena; by receiving and wearing the kāṣāya robe, he demonstrates the taming of sentient beings; and by inquiring about and receiving the Dharma from Udraka and Ārāḍa, he demonstrates the destruction of a self-exalting mind."

He practiced austerities for six years to refute the non-Buddhists; he manifested the acceptance of food and drink to demonstrate conformity with worldly customs; he manifested the acceptance of straw mats to demonstrate contentment; and he sat upon a bed of grass to demonstrate the destruction of arrogance.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits praised and looked up to him with reverence; he manifested the fruit of retribution adorned by his meritorious virtues.

He subdued the hosts of Māra to demonstrate his heroic power, pointed to the earth with his right hand to demonstrate the power of his past blessings, and caused the great earth to tremble to demonstrate his gratitude.
Having attained the path to unsurpassed bodhi and manifested the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of all phenomena, one who contemplates the equality of all dharmas is called a Buddha.
Because the wisdom of a Buddha is invincible, for this reason he is named Tathāgata.
To clearly know and see wholesome and unwholesome dharmas is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); because he speaks words of truth, he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Not emerging from all dharmas is called turning the wheel of Dharma; because there is no turning and no speaking, it is called "turning and speaking."
The entry that is without entering is called the Dharma-entry; the gate that is without a gate is called the Dharma-gate.
The activity that is without activity is called the Dharma-activity; the meditation that is without meditation is called Right Meditation.
Liberation that is without liberation is called "right liberation"; the nature of all phenomena is neither bound nor fettered.
If it were a phenomenon subject to cessation, it would belong to the past and would be non-arising; this is what is meant by "the appearance of a Buddha.
The appearance that is without appearance is precisely what is called "the appearance of a Buddha."
"If there is a bodhisattva who can train in this way, they are called one who does not deceive the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ineffable, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! You are well able to discern the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
If there is anyone who can believe in such an appearance of a Buddha, that person does not perceive even the subtlest characteristic of a single dharma."
If one does not perceive [this], then one can truly understand the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world.

Why is this? The appearance that is no-appearance is the appearance of the Buddha. It is without action and without an agent; without recipient and without a recipient; without outflows and without one who possesses outflows; without contention and without views; without entering and without turning; without arising and without ceasing. There is no enlightenment (*bodhi*); there is no flattery and no deception; there is no mind, thought, or consciousness; there is no eye and no duality. There is no activity of the eye, nor even of the mind; there is no speaking and no teaching. This is called the appearance of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and its ineffability—when it is said that a Buddha appears, who would believe it?"
At that time, the Jewel Maiden said to Abhayā:
"Brother in the Dharma!
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is inconceivable; it is difficult to adorn and difficult to realize."
If a person is indolent, lacks a sincere mind, is hypocritical, crooked, arrogant, prone to anger and envy, stingy and greedy;
if they do not recognize kindness or repay favors received; if their three precepts are impure, they are defiled by the three stains of attachment to the triple world;
if they do not revere the Three Jewels or cultivate the three liberations; and if they are coarse and foul-mouthed, delighting in speaking what is non-existent—[such a person...]
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, they outwardly manifest refined conduct for the sake of gain and offerings;
deceiving themselves and others, they crave sustenance while their faculties remain untamed. They take pleasure in seeking the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

their minds are insincere, they are of little learning and deluded, lacking mindfulness and prone to forgetfulness, ignorant of skillful means, and failing to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
With a mind of renunciation, they constantly roam the realm of Māra; they are greedily attached to persons, sentient beings, life, and soul;
they preach that there is no cause and effect and no karma or conditions; their minds are dissolute and they delight in committing evil deeds;

they abandon the dhūta ascetic practices and take pleasure in worldly dharmas; they praise themselves and disparage others; and they are covetous of the body, life, form, and the other five [sense objects].
Such a person delights in sleep, takes pleasure in hearing worldly matters, is ignorant of the proper seasons, associates with evil friends,
and is unable to practice the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
"O Dharma-elder!
Such people as these do not know of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, nor do they believe in his appearance.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Abhaya.
“Precious Daughter!
Have you now already distanced yourself from such evil dharmas?
Precious Daughter replied:
“Dharma-brother!
I have already distanced myself from such evil dharmas.
How did I distance myself from them?”
As with the limit of non-greed, what is non-greed?
It is just like the limit of greed.
What is the limit of greed?
Is it like the limit of true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
How is the limit of true reality like the limit of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)?
How is the view of self like the past limit? What is the past?
It is like the limit of ignorance.
What is ignorance? It is like the limit of craving.
What is the limit of ignorance, craving, and so forth?
It is like the limit of wisdom and liberation.
What is the limit of wisdom and liberation?
It is like the limit of an illusion.
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati said: “O Jewel Woman!
Illusion is neither mind nor intellect; wisdom and liberation are themselves the mind and intellect.”
“Dharma-brother!
The minds, intentions, wisdoms, and liberations of all sentient beings are entirely like illusions.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Fearless.
“Precious Daughter!
Can you believe what the Ineffable Bodhisattva has spoken?”
The Jewel Maiden said:
"Brother in Dharma!
That which is ineffable can never be spoken; if it were spoken, it would not be ineffable."
If there is nothing that can be said yet there is something that is said, how can it be called "unspeakable"?
It would simply be "speaking.
Because in reality there is nothing that can be said when it is unspeakable, it is therefore called "unspeakable."
"If it is unspeakable and there is truly nothing spoken, what have I heard now?
If there is nothing heard, what is there to believe?
Bodhisattva Abhaya said:
“O Jewel Woman!
That which is ineffable is truly that which is spoken; there is now witness to this, namely, this great assembly.
This entire assembly has heard what was proclaimed by that which is ineffable.”
The Jewel Maiden said:
"O Dharma-brother!
If anyone within this great assembly were to say:
To say, "I have heard that which is unspeakable," is itself false.
Why? Because that which is unspeakable truly has nothing that can be spoken.
"How is it that the great assembly says they have heard [the Dharma]? The Bodhisattva Abhayā said:
"O Jewel Woman!..."
"Do you now believe the Buddha's words? "Dharma-brother!
If there were anyone in the world without faith, that person would be the Buddha."
Why is this? Faith is itself craving and hatred; the Tathāgata has no craving or hatred, and therefore he has no faith.
If there is no faith, there is no realization.
Dharma brother!
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are truly without realization; therefore, the Tathāgata also has no realization.
Dharma brother!
"The true nature of the dharma-realm is unconditioned and uncreated; dharmas such as empty space are truly without realization. Therefore, the Tathāgata likewise has no realization.
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati said:
"O Jewel Maiden!"
"What serves as proof?
The Jewel Maiden replied,
"O Dharma-brother!"
"If there are those who do not see the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, such persons may serve as witnesses.
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati said,
"O Jewel Woman!..."
"Are these Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others witnesses to this faith?
The Jewel Maiden replied,
"Dharma-brother!"
So it is, so it is! This is what is realized and what is believed. Why is this?

The precepts of the śrāvakas have limits, whereas the precepts of the Tathāgata are without limit; it is likewise with his concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the Jewel Maiden: "Jewel Maiden!
The śrāvakas also possess the three gates of liberation, and the Tathāgata likewise possesses the three gates of liberation."
"Why do you now take a śrāvaka as your witness for faith, rather than the Tathāgata?
The Jewel Maiden replied,
"Virtuous One!..."
Just as the waters of eight flavors from Lake Anavatapta rain down upon Jambudvīpa, causing all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests to grow and flourish—
does that rainwater have any differentiation?
Śāriputra said: “No, Jewel Woman!”

“Venerable Sir! It is like the water of Lake Anavatapta, which is originally of a single flavor; yet when used by a person of virtue, it possesses various subtle and sweet tastes, whereas when used by a person of meager merit, its taste becomes uniformly coarse, foul, and unpleasant.”
"Virtuous One!
The three liberations of the Tathāgata and the śrāvaka are likewise so.
Therefore, while there is a distinction between the Tathāgata and the śrāvaka, in the nature of the dharmadhātu there is truly no distinction."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Jewel Woman, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Jewel Woman, you have skillfully analyzed and proclaimed this meaning."
When the Jewel Maiden had spoken this Dharma, thirty-two thousand gods and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Jewel Maiden then addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Virtuous One!"
For example, the waters of the great ocean are of a single flavor, yet it contains many jewels as well as water-crystals and pearls of inferior value.
The Dharma-realm is likewise; although it is equal throughout, when the Buddhas study it, they obtain priceless jewels, whereas when the śrāvakas study it, they obtain jewels of inferior value.
“Venerable Sir!
Just as on Mount Sumeru there are various devas who experience much happiness, and others who experience little happiness, yet Mount Sumeru itself has no distinction between them.”

The Dharma-realm is likewise; although it is without distinction, when a Tathāgata dwells within it, he experiences immeasurable bliss, whereas when a Śrāvaka dwells within it, he experiences limited bliss.
"O Mahābhāga!..."
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, though he may have a thousand sons, none of them can be called the successor to the sovereign position;
so it is with the śrāvakas: although they possess wisdom, they are not called Buddhas.

"Venerable One! It is like lighting a lamp-vessel: if it is of gold, the light is yellow; if it is of copper, the light is red. Although their colors differ, there is no distinction in the lamp itself.

The Dharma-realm is likewise: when the Buddhas kindle it, the light of wisdom is boundless; when the Śrāvakas kindle it, the light of wisdom is limited. Yet, the nature of the Dharma-realm is truly without distinction."
“Venerable Sir!
When a Wheel-Turning King enters a city, everyone knows it; yet when a person of little merit enters a city, even those who are close and dear do not even perceive it.”

When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, enters the Dharma-realm, it is likewise so: all devas and humans are fully aware of it; he eclipses all non-Buddhist heterodox teachers and surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
When a śrāvaka enters the Dharma-realm, even that śrāvaka does not perceive or know it, let alone others!
“Venerable Sir!

For example, when there is a lion’s roar in the mountains, or the calls of the *gokhila* bird, the *kalaviṅka*, the peacock, and so forth, as well as the voices of humans, cows, donkeys, and horses, an echo arises following each sound. Yet, this echo itself has no actual distinction; it is simply because it arises following various sounds that the echoes differ.”

The three gates of liberation of the Tathāgata and the śrāvakas are likewise in this regard: the Tathāgata can destroy all hosts of Māras, can overcome all heterodox views of external paths, can know the mental thoughts of all sentient beings, can know the various conducts of sentient beings, can discipline śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, and can produce the sounds of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
although the śrāvaka shares the same dharma-realm, he cannot perform such deeds as these.
“Venerable Sir!
It is like sugarcane, which, though its flavor is one and the same, produces white rock honey for those of great merit and black rock honey for those of meager merit.”

The Dharma-realm is likewise; the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the flavor of the ambrosia of great wisdom, unmixed with the flavors of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whereas the śrāvaka possesses only the flavor of limited wisdom.
“Venerable Sir!
For example, within the trichiliocosm there are many great oceans that benefit immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, yet there are also small rivers that benefit fewer sentient beings;
the Dharma-realm is likewise.”
“Venerable One!

Just as the sun, moon, and stars all travel through space, yet the brilliance of the stars does not equal that of the sun and moon, while the nature of space itself remains truly without distinction.”
The dharma-realm is likewise: although both the Tathāgata and the śrāvaka dwell within it, their light of wisdom is truly not equal, yet the nature of the dharma-realm remains without distinction.
“Venerable Sir!
It is like two people who study the same craft; one is skillful and gains much benefit, while the other is clumsy and gains little profit.”
The *dharmadhātu* of the Tathāgata and the *śrāvaka* is also like this. "Venerable One!
Just as there is no difference between a single layer of flowers, yet through skillful means one obtains a garment of high value, while through unskillful means one obtains a garment of low value."

The single nature of the Dharma-realm is likewise thus: it is by virtue of the causes and conditions of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, skillful means, great kindness, and great compassion that he attains the priceless wisdom of great quiescence;
whereas the śrāvakas attain an inferior wisdom that is not pure.
“Venerable Sir!
Just as in the great ocean there is the Asura King Rāhula, and there are also other classes of sentient beings, yet only the Asura King can reach its bottom while the others cannot.”
The dharma-realm is also like this: the Tathāgata attains ultimate wisdom, whereas the śrāvakas do not.
"Venerable One!..."
For example, when the great earth produces the thousand-petaled flower and the seven-leafed flower, gods and worldly people alike feel great joy upon seeing the thousand-petaled flower.

It is the same with the Tathāgata and the *dharmadhātu* of the *śrāvakas*: gods and worldly people feel joy and give rise to affection and delight upon seeing the Buddha, but not so for the *śrāvakas*.
“Venerable One!

For this reason, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless, whereas the wisdom of the śrāvakas is measurable and limited; yet, the nature of the dharma-dhātu is truly without distinction.”
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati said to the Girl Ratnā:
"This ineffable Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must certainly be your teacher; he is able to discipline you with the sublime Dharma."
The Jewel Maiden replied,
“Good son, it cannot be said that a bodhisattva has nothing to discipline.”
