Why is this? Such a bodhisattva perceives neither self nor other, nor this nor that; being thus, what is there to be disciplined? Noble son!
If there is one who does not perceive any realm of Māra or their own objective sphere, such a person is able to subdue them.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If one can know and see all phenomena, perceiving neither a self nor what belongs to a self, such a person is able to subdue them.
Furthermore, good son!

If there is one who can diligently practice asceticism for themselves, yet does not encourage others to do so, and whose mind does not become arrogant after practicing asceticism—such a person is able to subdue [the mind].
Furthermore, good son!

Just as the various bodhisattvas, for the sake of sentient beings, attain liberation while remaining within the great cycle of birth and death and do not enter nirvana, such persons are able to subdue; this is called the first, ultimate meaning of subduing.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Abhaya, saying: "Good son!
This Jewel Woman has truly been brought to discipline by that Ineffable Bodhisattva; because she has been disciplined, she shall in the future attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the Jewel Woman again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva truly has no discipline.”
If one is tamed, that is itself great compassion; it is compassion that is able to tame, not the person.
As for those who are śrāvakas, they must be tamed. Why is this?
Because they lack great compassion, World-Honored One!
It is like the mango fruit that ripens upon the tree; its flavor is sweet and delicious, and thus it is craved and relished by people.
If it grows in damp soil, its flavor is bitter and is held in low esteem by people.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: born from great compassion, it is therefore self-regulated and does not depend on others.
The Bodhisattva Abhayā said to the Girl Ratnā:
"Are you also able to repay the kindness of this Ineffable Bodhisattva?
The Girl Ratnā replied:
“Good son! If I were aware of your kindness, how could I fail to repay it?
Only those sentient beings who are unable to practice the path to enlightenment cannot repay such a debt.”
“Precious Woman! What is called ‘cultivating the path to enlightenment’?
The Precious Woman replied:
“Good son! Thirty-two types of action are called the practices of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
What are these thirty-two?
They never fall away from the mind of bodhi; they do not crave the mind of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
they practice with a sincere heart, free from flattery or crookedness; in all their practices, they encounter no obstacles;

they act for the sake of sentient beings without weariness or regret; though they traverse the cycle of birth and death, they remain free from greed and anger, and toward all sentient beings, their minds—
With impartiality, they are able to teach and subdue all beings, gathering them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

For the sake of the assembly’s attainment of happiness, they cultivate a mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*); for the sake of suffering sentient beings, they practice great compassion (*karuṇā*).
Acting according to their words, their diligence is firm and steadfast; they never deceive any sentient being. Thus they cultivate their adornment...

He practices austerity as an aid to awakening; he does not seek any worldly pleasures, his mind is free from attachment to worldly gain and honor, he does not commit various evils for the sake of his body, he does not crave life nor look for the faults of others;
with a disciplined mind, he purifies the three types of precepts and adorns himself by cultivating the karma that brings about the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.
Constantly mindful of leaving the household life as a repayment for past wholesome karma, always delighting in tranquility and insatiable in extensive learning;
possessing wisdom that can benefit both oneself and others, never harboring thoughts of food when preaching the Dharma;
able to relinquish all things without seeking karmic retribution, purifying the aggregate of precepts without giving rise to arrogance, and never praising one's own possessions.
For the sake of others, he diligently cultivates patience; for the sake of purifying the Buddha-land, he diligently practices vigor;
for the sake of knowing skillful means, he seeks all-knowledge; he forever severs all afflictions and habitual tendencies;
for the sake of attaining supernormal powers to protect and uphold the True Dharma, he draws near to virtuous friends, reflects with a wholesome mind, and remains far removed from Māra.
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma through one's karma, one attains the subtle and wondrous wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing. Good son!
If there are those who cannot practice such a Dharma, you should know that these people are unable to repay their debt of gratitude, nor can they understand the kindness of the Tathāgata.
“Good son, there are two kinds of people who will certainly die without being cured, and who ultimately cannot recognize or repay kindness:
first, śrāvakas; second, pratyekabuddhas.”
"Good son! It is like a person who has fallen into a deep pit; such a person can neither benefit themselves nor others.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also like this: they have fallen into the pit of liberation and are unable to benefit themselves or others."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhayā removed the upper garment he was wearing from his own body to repay the Jewel Woman for her kindness in preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the Jewel Woman was unwilling to accept it.
The Bodhisattva Abhaya said, "For the sake of the Dharma, I only pray that you accept it.
"Good son! [the Buddha continued.]
The Dharma is free from craving; therefore, one should not preach the Dharma [for gain].
Those who receive the Dharma have no grasping; therefore, one should not accept offerings.
The Dharma is without craving; therefore, one should not crave offerings.
The Dharma is without self and without what belongs to a self; therefore, one should not perform offerings with things that belong to a self.
The Dharma is pure; therefore, one should not perform offerings with impure things.
The Dharma is without body or mind; those who practice with body and mind do not offer true worship.
The Dharma is not mind, thought, or consciousness; those who employ mind, thought, and consciousness do not offer true worship.
The Dharma is without pulling or dragging; those who engage in pulling and dragging do not offer true worship.
The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, to have [the notion of] dharmas is not an offering.
The Dharma is not among all states of existence; therefore, to have perceptions is not an offering.
The Dharma is not discursive thought or investigation; those who possess discursive thought and investigation do not offer.
The Dharma neither increases nor decreases; those who perceive increase or decrease do not perform true worship.
The Dharma has no high or low; those who perceive high or low do not perform true worship.

The Dharma cannot be spoken and cannot be heard, and it possesses no name. It transcends all sounds and is remote from the [conventional] path of the sages; therefore, one cannot worship it with robes.

The Dharma has no objective sphere; it is not within the sphere of the eye, nor does it extend to the sphere of the mind. It has no dwelling place; therefore, one should not offer robes as an act of worship.
The Dharma is precisely the twelve links of dependent origination, which is neither eternal nor annihilated; therefore, one should not offer robes as an act of worship.

The Dharma is without obstruction and not inverted; it is immeasurable, devoid of self, sentient beings, persons, or life-span; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither emerges nor is it unconditioned. Therefore, one should not offer robes as a供养 (offering).
The Bodhisattva Abhaya said: "O Jewel Woman!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, likewise accepts such an offering of the Dharma."
“Good son! Although the Tathāgata accepts the offering of the Dharma, he does not engage in discrimination, for it is like the nature of the dharma-realm.
“Precious Daughter!”
"What is meant by 'discriminating the dharma-realm' (dharmadhātu)? "Good son!

If one says that the Dharma is distinct, that the offering of the Dharma is distinct, that the recipient of the gift is distinct, and that the giver is also distinct—this is what is called discriminating the dharma-realm."
"If one does not discriminate between the Dharma and its offerings, nor between the recipient and the donor, this is what is meant by 'not discriminating within the Dharma-realm.
Fearless Bodhisattva said,
"Precious Woman!..."
"If the dharma-realm is non-conceptual, why do you say that one conceptualizes the dharma-realm and yet does not conceptualize it?
The Jewel Maiden said,
"O son of good family!
Although the nature of the dharma-realm is without discrimination, sentient beings give rise to discrimination because their minds are inverted. Good son!
Just as things are called "intact" or "broken" because of their physical form, if there is activity or something to be grasped, it is then called "broken" and called "discrimination."
“Good son! Just as the space within a vessel cannot be destroyed even though the vessel itself is broken, the nature of the dharma-realm is likewise.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Jewel Woman, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can accomplish this Dharma, such a person is worthy of receiving the offerings of the humans and devas of the trichiliocosm.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the people in the great assembly each removed their *uttarāsaṅga* robes and offered them to the Jewel Woman.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Inexpressible addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Whatever can be expressed is the mundane; that which cannot be expressed is the supramundane.
That which can be proclaimed is the mind of craving; that which cannot be expressed is the state free from craving.
That which can be proclaimed is worldly conduct; that which cannot be proclaimed is supramundane conduct. World-Honored One!

The meaning of the supramundane is free from fabrication; that which is free from fabrication is without contention; that which is without contention is the Dharma of the śramaṇa; the Dharma of the śramaṇa is the supramundane Dharma; the supramundane Dharma is without fault or transgression; that which is without fault or transgression is non-appropriation, non-arising, and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing is the supramundane; and the supramundane Dharma cannot be proclaimed and cannot be demonstrated.
"For this reason, all dharmas cannot be proclaimed.
At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Vijñānamati, who spoke to the Bodhisattva Avaktavya, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!
"If all dharmas are ineffable, how can sentient beings speak of 'the ineffable'? "Good son!
"Do you know whether an echo has speech? Vimati said,
"O son of good family!"
All echoes exist by virtue of causes and conditions.
"Good son! Is the cause of this echo definitively located within?"
"Is it fixed outside?
The Devaputra said,
"O Son of Good Family!"
"Such causes are not fixed within, nor are they fixed without.
"O Son of Heaven! All sentient beings forcibly construct dualistic conceptions and thus speak; yet the nature of all phenomena is truly ineffable."
The devaputra said: "Good son!
If it is ineffable, why does the Tathāgata proclaim eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, causing all śrāvakas to receive, uphold, read, and recite them?"
“O Son of Heaven!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has in truth nothing that he speaks; that which has nothing to speak is itself the Tathāgata.
O Son of Heaven!”
What do you understand to be the Tathāgata?
Do you not think that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the Tathāgata?

Do you not say that the Buddha is comprised within the past, future, and present; the conditioned and the unconditioned; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; and the three realms—that he is cause, effect, and a composite?
"Is it perception, non-perception, both perception and non-perception, or neither perception nor non-perception?
"No, noble son."
“Devaputra! If such things as these are not the Tathāgata, how can they be spoken of?
If they cannot be spoken of, why do you say that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has expounded eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma?”
Therefore, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma are truly ineffable, and those who receive them as śrāvakas are likewise ineffable.
That which is ineffable is the true meaning; if there is no discourse regarding this meaning, that is the ultimate reality.
If it can be expressed, it is indeterminate; if it cannot be expressed, it is provable. That which can be expressed cannot be proven. Why is this so?
"It is because of perversion.
At that time, the Devaputra Vijñānagati addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"This which the Bodhisattva Ineffable speaks—whom would anyone believe?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ineffable, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested as a bhikṣu and spoke these words:
"I now have deep faith in what the Bodhisattva Ineffable has said."

Why is this? As I am, so too is the Tathāgata, and as is the Tathāgata, so too is the dharmadhātu. The aggregates (skandhas) of the Tathāgata cannot be described; likewise, my aggregates also cannot be described.
The realm and entrance of the Tathāgata cannot be described, and my own realm and entrance likewise cannot be described.
It is the same with the awakening of the Tathāgata and my own awakening; they are equal and without distinction.
Just as the Tathāgata thoroughly knows the realms of all sentient beings, so too do I thoroughly know the realms of all sentient beings.
Just as the Tathāgata turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, so too do I turn the wheel of Dharma.
"When the Tathāgata enters unsurpassed nirvāṇa, I too shall likewise enter nirvāṇa.
The devaputra said: "Bhikṣu!"
"Are you not now a creation of Māra,
speaking such words as if you were the Tathāgata? The bhikṣu said:
“Devaputra! If there is one who says that the self is distinct from the Buddha, you should know that such a person is a disciple of Māra.

If there is one who says, ‘By means of the equality of the self, I contemplate the equality of dharmas; because dharmas are equal, sentient beings are equal; because sentient beings are equal, the Tathāgata is equal’—such a person truly knows and is able to transcend the realm of Māra.”

When the transformed bhikṣu spoke these words, five hundred bhikṣus were liberated through the exhaustion of outflows, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of patience; they then made offerings of incense and flowers to the bhikṣu.
Śāriputra said: "Good sons, for what reason do you make offerings to this transformed bhikṣu?"
The bodhisattvas said:
"Venerable sir,
who created this transformation?"
“Sons of good family!
Do you not now know that this is a transformation created by the Ineffable One?
The bodhisattvas replied:
“Virtuous One!
For example, if a Tathāgata were to further transform another Tathāgata, and someone were to make an offering, to whom would they be making the offering?
“O sons of good family!”
"This person is indeed making an offering to the Tathāgata. "Venerable One!
If one makes an offering to this manifested bhikṣu, it is equivalent to making an offering to the Ineffable Bodhisattva."
Śāriputra said: "Good son! As for this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ineffable, what kind of offerings should one provide, whatever offerings may be made?"

"Venerable One! If there is a wise person who possesses no vocal activity, no letters, no forms, no names, no actions, nothing to be proclaimed, no self and no other, no dharma and no non-dharma, and neither purity nor defilement—if one makes offerings in such a manner, then that is truly worthy of offering."
Then the transformed bhikṣu said to Śāriputra,
"Venerable One! Do you not think that I am now different from you?"
Śāriputra said: “No, bhikṣu!”
Why is this? The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena are entirely like illusions; as the Tathāgata has spoken, so do I believe.
"Venerable One!"
"If there is anyone who can make offerings to the Tathāgata, it is no different from making offerings to a transformation-body.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Inexplicable: "Good son!
"Who has entered this transformation to now make such a statement? "Venerable sir!
It is like a reflection in a mirror; who is there within it for the reflection to appear?"
“Good son! There is no entity within it;
rather, an image appears solely due to the causes and conditions of the pure four great elements. “Virtuous One!”
Transformation is also like this; because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is pure, it is able to make such a statement. "Good son!
If that is so, why is it that all sentient beings cannot proclaim it in this way?"
“Virtuous One! Since both [the mirror and the object] are not separate from the mirror behind it, why does the image not appear? “Good son!
“Because the four great elements on the back of the mirror are impure. “Venerable Sir!
Sentient beings are likewise; because they cannot purify the nature of the dharma-realm, they are unable to proclaim it.”
“Good son! Your earlier and later words are inconsistent in meaning. Why is this?
“You have often said that the nature of all dharmadhātus is inherently pure; why do you now say that the dharmadhātu is impure?
“Venerable sir! If it were not so, how could you have attained the purity of the Dharma-eye through the bhikṣu Aśva?”
“Good son! I merely name it ‘the purification of the Dharma-eye’ because it opens the way, guides, and eliminates adventitious afflictions; in reality, nothing is attained. Good son!”
If someone were to say, "I have attained space," this meaning would not be correct. Why is that?
Because the nature of space is eternally and inherently pure.
If it is eternally pure, how can it be "attained"?
Because it is covered by adventitious clouds, sentient beings do not see it; when these adventitious clouds are removed, it is called "seeing.
The nature of the dharma-realm is likewise so; therefore, I truly have not attained the dharma-eye.
“Good son! Why do you now speak such inconsistent words, saying that the nature of the dharmadhātu is either pure or impure?
The Bodhisattva Inexpressible replied:
“Venerable sir!
That which you have spoken and that which I have spoken are both the realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; they are not within the scope of our knowledge or vision.”

Śāriputra said: "Good son, if you say that this teaching is the realm of the Buddha and is not within my knowledge, why do you further say that the nature of the dharma-realm is without differentiation?"
"If there were conceptual differentiation, one should know that the dharma-realm would be immeasurable and could not be described as such.
"Virtuous One! The nature of the dharma-realm is a single reality; it is not immeasurable."
Śāriputra said: "Good son, if the nature of the dharma-realm is one, why do you say that this is the realm of the Buddha and not something known by me?"
"If the dharma-realm is one, by what causes and conditions are all sentient beings not called Tathāgatas?
"Virtuous One! Do you wish to differentiate between sentient beings and the Tathāgata as having distinct characteristics?"
“Good son! As you have previously stated, I do not wish for there to be any notion of difference between sentient beings and the Tathāgata.
“Venerable sir!”
"Do you firmly believe that there is such a thing as non-arising?
"Virtuous man! There is that which is called the Dharma-realm."
“Venerable sir! Do you further maintain that there is such a thing as the heterodox and the orthodox? “No.”
“Good son! The assembly of the heterodox and the orthodox is precisely inversion. “Virtuous One!”
"Do you claim that there is a dharma that arises without arising? "No, Good Son."
"If it is non-arising, it is ultimately non-arising. "Venerable sir,
do you think that this dharma of non-arising possesses conceptual differentiation?"
"No, noble son! " "Venerable sir!"
If this were not so, why would you say that all sentient beings are not the Tathāgata?
If it were thus, who would be the sentient being and who would be the Tathāgata?
“Good son! Having already understood this meaning myself, I have asked this question in order to manifest wisdom. Good son!”
If there are sentient beings who do not understand what you have said, they shall fall into hell.
Why is this? Because they will give rise to slander.
The Bodhisattva Inexplicable said:
"Virtuous One! Regarding such a Dharma as this, no one can revile it, and no one can accept it."
For what reason?
If there are those who slander this teaching, you should know that such persons shall likewise obtain dharmas such as these,
O Virtuous One!
Just as a person of weak and inferior strength cannot conceive doubt regarding a mighty wrestler, so it is with my Dharma:
those who have not planted roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas will ultimately be unable to doubt it or uphold it.

“Good son! As I understand the meaning of what you have said, a person who has faith and complies with such Dharma-teachings surpasses one who practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the worldly perfection of wisdom for immeasurable eons.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.
If there are those who believe and understand these words, you should know that such persons have already practiced these six pāramitās for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
If there are those who cannot believe these words, they will be unable to receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If they can believe them, they will receive the prediction and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra! I recall that throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, while practicing the six pāramitās, because I could not believe such words, I did not receive the prediction [of my future enlightenment] and did not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thereafter, having gained faith, he immediately received a prediction of his future enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, you should know that if anyone can believe and understand these words, they shall likewise receive a prediction and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Ineffable addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what portion does one receive the prediction of enlightenment?”
If it were the case that one receives a prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on past factors, this meaning would not be tenable. Why?
Because those factors have already ceased.
If it were the case that one receives prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on a future portion [of existence], this too would not be so. Why?
Because it has not yet arisen.
If it were the case that one receives the prediction in the present, this too would not be so.
Why? Because it cannot be so described.
"If these three parts are without the prediction of enlightenment, why do you say that a bodhisattva receives the prediction?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who believes in the ineffable, knows the ineffable, and speaks of the ineffable, they will not give rise to fear regarding the ineffable; they know that the two dharmas of the ineffable and form are without distinction.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye up to the mind; the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels; birth and death, and liberation; and the dharma-realm—all these are likewise ineffable. This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the portion of patience, the portion of non-arising, the portion of non-issuance, the portion of non-grasping, the portion of non-defilement, the portion of non-existence, and the portion of non-action.
Fully accomplishing such equal parts, one does not give rise to dual characteristics regarding all phenomena, nor dual thoughts, dual intentions, dual divisions, or dual conditions.

If there is a bodhisattva who can contemplate in this way, they are said to neither go nor come, and to abide nowhere. Because they do not abide, they perform no action; because they perform no action, they have no aspirations or seeking; and because they have no aspirations or seeking, they are neither annihilated nor eternal.

If there is neither annihilation nor permanence, this is the Middle Way; the Middle Way is precisely the twelve links of dependent origination, and the twelve links of dependent origination are without action and without seeking.
For this reason, it is called "profound."
There is no agent and no recipient; for this reason, it is further called profound.
It is unarisen yet arises, and unemerged yet emerges; for this reason, it is further called profound.
For example, a blazing fire arises from causes and conditions; it has no agent and no recipient.
Once this fire is extinguished, it has no place of departure and no place of arrival.
All dharmas are likewise thus: there is no agent and no recipient.
Son of good family!
If there is a bodhisattva who can know this, you should know that such a person shall receive the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, they rose into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees, joined their palms in reverence, and spoke these verses:
“If one can contemplate this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) As being ineffable and of non-dual character,”
This person immediately attains impartial wisdom, Just as was attained by the Buddhas of the past.
If one contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, They likewise find no duality therein.
Being able to discern with clarity that which is ineffable, One immediately receives the prediction of enlightenment, just like the Buddhas of the past.
If one wishes to observe the sense bases, elements, and so forth, as well as the non-dual nature of all phenomena—
which are without sound, without letters, and without divisions— therefore, all phenomena are ineffable.
The unspeakable portion and the portions of the three times are, in truth, a single undifferentiated portion;
since their actual nature and true characteristics are entirely equal, one who contemplates in this way is called a Bodhisattva.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are entirely equal in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is likewise non-dual.
The meaning of all phenomena is ineffable; they are without arising or ceasing, like space.
They are without agent or recipient, like the nature of fire; they arise from conditions but are not extinguished by conditions.
Once extinguished, one knows not where it has gone; all phenomena are likewise so.
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; when causes and conditions are severed, they are called "extinguished."
If phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, And likewise neither eternal nor discontinuous,
This is the profound twelvefold dependent origination, Which does not arise further from conditions.
Originally there was no arising, yet now there is arising; originally there was no emerging, yet now there is emerging.
There is no agent of action and no recipient; there are no causes nor any retributive fruits.
Furthermore, it is neither existent nor non-existent, and it possesses neither of the two characteristics of "self" and "other."
Nor does it exist within, nor is it outside; this is the profound twelvefold dependent origination.
This dharma was originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, the dharma subsequently returns to non-existence.
If an existing dharma were encompassed by the three periods of time, one should know that its nature and characteristics are as previously explained.
If internal dharmas do not exist within the external, and the nature of external dharmas does not exist within the internal, all dharmas are likewise so;
this is called the meaning of the primary true emptiness.
The fundamental nature of the minds of all sentient beings Is pure and stainless like space;
Because ordinary people do not know the nature of the mind, They speak of it as being defiled by adventitious afflictions.
If various afflictions can defile the mind, it can never be purified, just like filth;
because it is obscured and covered by adventitious afflictions, it is said that the minds of ordinary beings are impure.
If the nature of the mind were inherently pure, all sentient beings would be liberated;
however, because they are shrouded by adventitious afflictions, they do not attain liberation.
The mind cannot produce the subsequent mind; the mind cannot see the subsequent mind.
All minds arise from conditions; therefore, the succession of minds is never interrupted.
If one can know and see this mind as being like space and like illusory forms,
that person will attain mastery over the mind and will also be able to understand the successive states of the mind.
Just as a magician creates illusions, so too are the karmic masters of immeasurable lifetimes;
as the mind is, so are sentient beings. If one knows this, one attains mastery over the mind.
If one can attain such patience, seeing that all phenomena are like illusions and devoid of causes and conditions;
if one knows this and does not give rise to craving, one will attain liberation without depending on causes and conditions.
The mental natures of all sentient beings are subsumed by the Tathāgata within the three periods of time;
just as illusory objects have no true nature, so too is the mind of sentient beings.
The mind can fully know all sentient beings, and sentient beings can also fully know the mind;
the mind is not form and cannot be seen, and as it is with the mind, so it is with sentient beings.
Just as the nature of sentient beings is the nature of all phenomena, The unconditioned nature is ineffable;
The Tathāgata has awakened to this true dharma-nature, And for this reason, it is called unimpeded wisdom.
All ordinary beings do not know or see; they wander through immeasurable births and deaths, shrouded by ignorance and deluded regarding reality, unaware of suchness and the dharma-realm.
The nature of the dharma-realm is like empty space; All worlds are unable to describe it.
The Tathāgata, having cultivated and accumulated great compassion, Expounds it within the wordless Dharma.
Just as the six flavors in the world cannot each perceive themselves, so too,
although sentient beings speak of the aggregates, bases, and elements, they are unable to comprehend their essential natures and characteristics.
The wisdom of sentient beings is neither born nor extinguished, Like space and like an illusion;
Because it is far removed from all perversions, It is called pure wisdom.
The Tathāgata has awakened to all phenomena, Which are without sensation or action, like grass and wood;
If one can contemplate phenomena in this way, That person will immediately attain the patience of non-arising.
If there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who have attained such patience as this,
those people shall become immeasurable Buddhas, and they will receive the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
If one can relinquish all internal and external things, even not sparing one's own body or life,
and is able to harmonize all sentient beings, that person shall receive the prophecy of Buddhahood.
If one can purify all sentient beings, and having purified them, does not give rise to pride,
proclaiming that all sentient beings are entirely pure— for this cause and condition, one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
If one knows that all phenomena perish moment by moment, yet for the sake of sentient beings practices patience and is further able to expound the patience of sentient beings,
it is because of this patience that one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
Distant from unwholesome dharmas, one exerts diligent effort; For the sake of cultivating wholesome dharmas, one does not rest.
If one can eloquently explain diligent effort, Then by virtue of that diligence, one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
All phenomena are pure by their very nature, Equal and without distinction, like space.
If one can expound this equality, One shall receive the prediction of enlightenment through samādhi.
If one can know that dharmas are ineffable, And feel no fear when teaching them,
Being able to transform sentient beings through skillful means— By virtue of this wisdom, one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, Māra, leading a fourfold army—
consisting of chariots, cavalry, elephants, and infantry— came to where the Buddha was.
Māra himself transformed his body into the likeness of a bhikṣu and spoke to the Bodhisattva Avaktavya, saying:
“Good son! King Māra Pāpīyān is now approaching the Buddha’s dwelling with his fourfold army; what expedient means do you intend to employ? Akṣayamati replied:
"If he should come, I shall cause him to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The bhikṣu said, "Good man!"
"That Māra Pāpīyān possesses no virtuous mind at all; how then can he be made to resolve upon *bodhicitta*? He replied:
"I shall subdue him so that he may attain a virtuous mind; once he has attained a virtuous mind, by this causal condition, he will resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"How shall I subdue him?
I shall go to that realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods and become their king; he shall then belong to me.
Once he belongs to me, I shall subdue him according to my will."
At that time, having heard these words, Pāpīyān felt anxiety and fear in his heart; he wished to retreat, yet was unable to do so.
He further thought to himself:
"Now I am neither bound nor released, and furthermore, I cannot exercise my supernatural powers."
Then Māra immediately heard a voice in the air saying,
"This is the power of ineffable supernormal penetrations.
King Māra Pāpīyān immediately stepped forward, prostrated himself before the Ineffable One, repented, and spoke these words:
"I now abandon all demonic activities.
One must not say: "Pāpīyān! [Stop!]"
"Who has bound you? Pāpīyān replied, "Noble son!"
"I am neither bound nor released, yet I am unable to proceed. One must not say:
"O son of good family!..."
Just as you now are neither bound nor released and yet cannot walk, so it is with all sentient beings: they are neither bound nor released, yet they cannot walk.
Why is this? Because they are bound by the perversions of ignorance, craving, and so forth, they do not attain liberation, Pāpīyan!
"If you now wish to destroy your bonds, you should swiftly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Pāpīyān replied, "Good son!..."
“By accomplishing how many dharmas can all sentient beings give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment? “Pāpīyān!
When sentient beings accomplish sixteen kinds of dharmas, they can give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

What are these sixteen? They are as follows: constantly cultivating the superior mind to polish and refine the sense faculties; diligently practicing all forms of goodness to adorn one's merit; upholding the precepts with a sincere heart without giving rise to regret or weariness; cultivating great compassion to have pity for sentient beings; believing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great kindness and compassion, undergoing and practicing various sufferings for the sake of all beings, and being able to destroy all the afflictions of sentient beings; subduing the sense faculties and being fully endowed with right mindfulness; having no fear in the mind and seeking no further existence within the realms of birth; joyfully seeking the wisdom of the Buddha and not delighting in the two vehicles; experiencing pleasure without arrogance and enduring suffering without regret; revering wisdom and destroying conceit; knowing gratitude and repaying kindness; possessing physical strength; protecting and upholding the True Dharma; and ensuring that the Three Jewels are never severed. These are called the sixteen.
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who possess such qualities as these, you should know that such persons are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Pāpīyān said: "Good son!

If sentient beings possess such dharmas as these and are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I now truly lack such dharmas; how then could I give rise to the mind of the unsurpassed path?"
One should not say: "Pāpīyān!
It is like planting a tree for its flowers, fruits, and seeds; although they do not yet exist at first, one should know that they will certainly be obtained later without doubt."
"If sentient beings practice toward the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), it is likewise: although these sixteen dharmas are not yet manifest, they shall gradually attain them.
Pāpīyān said, "Excellent, excellent!"
“Good son! It is as you have said.
When this Dharma was spoken, thirty-two thousand among the assembly of devas and humans gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Pāpīyān said: "Good son! What is meant by 'practicing toward the bodhicitta'?"
“Good son! There are thirty-two dharmas that cause the bodhicitta to increase.
What are these thirty-two?
First, the mind of utmost sincerity;
second, the concentrated mind;
third, the pure mind.
Fourth, the mind of desire;
fifth, the mind of non-negligence;
sixth, the cultivation and accumulation of wholesome dharmas.
Seventh, adorning the journey toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
eighth, being able to gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction;
ninth, delighting in the practice of skillful means.
Tenth, to discipline sentient beings;
eleventh, to bring sentient beings to maturity;
twelfth, to be able to know causes and conditions.
Thirteenth, diligent application of effort;
fourteenth, associating with virtuous friends;
fifteenth, being endowed with faith.
Sixteenth, because they are endowed with faith, they give rise to joy;
seventeenth, they make offerings to and revere their teachers, elders, superiors, and those of virtuous character;
eighteenth, they are able to attend to those suffering from illness.
Nineteenth, they are able to reflect skillfully;
twentieth, they abide in accordance with the Dharma;
twenty-first, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
Twenty-second, they achieve dhāraṇī;
twenty-third, they are endowed with mindfulness;
twenty-fourth, they are able to expound the profound Dharma.
Twenty-fifth, they are fully endowed with wisdom;
twenty-sixth, they are fully endowed with the powers;
twenty-seventh, they aspire toward bodhi.
Twenty-eighth, not abandoning sentient beings;
twenty-ninth, cultivating and accumulating the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
thirtieth, wandering through birth and death without giving rise to regret in one's mind.
Thirty-first, they adorn their merit by taking on a physical body, and they adorn their wisdom by giving rise to pure vows;
thirty-second, they know that all phenomena are inexpressible.
These are called the thirty-two.
If a bodhisattva can increase these dharmas, they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Good son!

Just as the new moon in the autumn night waxes, becoming both bright and pure, so too it is with sentient beings who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta but are fully endowed with these thirty-two qualities.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva can fulfill these thirty-two dharmas, they will attain wondrous physical marks and be constantly honored by devas and humans; they will be able to relinquish all things without seeking karmic retribution, and give rise to great vows to purify the three periods of time.”

Maintaining the precepts in their entirety, pure, without leakage or breach, one cultivates patience and attains excellence through hearing the Dharma. Adorned with the dharma of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, one’s body and mind are tranquil, remaining free from craving for roots of goodness.

They never cultivate or accumulate meditative absorptions that savor attachment, nor do they cultivate compassion directed toward sentient beings; rather, they cultivate only dharma-based and objectless compassion. They cultivate great compassion to act for the sake of others, recognizing kindness and repaying it, and never abandoning sentient beings.

They delight in hearing the true Dharma and speak it exactly as they have heard it; when expounding the Dharma, they harbor no thought of food; they are able to discipline themselves and others, remaining free from the minds of greed and anger; they gather in sentient beings through the four means of integration, and cultivate the two kinds of adornments: merit and wisdom.

Possessing both vipaśyanā and śamatha, they maintain a mind of mindfulness that purifies all modes of conduct; they achieve and attain the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and their physical, verbal, and mental actions proceed from wisdom. Their minds are firm and resolute, never regressing, and they are constantly able to benefit all sentient beings.

“Pāpīyān! For the sake of leading all sentient beings into the Buddha-dharma, one manifests written characters and vocal sounds to deliver teachings; yet in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there are no such written characters or vocal explanations at all. This is what is called the nature of all dharmas (sarvadharma-svabhāva), and the nature of all dharmas is ultimately ineffable.”
Pāpīyān said: "O son of good family!
If all dharmas are inexpressible, how can a bodhisattva give rise to the great vow directed toward bodhi?"
One should not say: "Pāpīyān!
For example, the nature of space is boundless; could one possibly construct a well or a pond within it?"
"No, noble son! O Pāpīyan!"
"If the nature of all phenomena is such that it cannot be described, then it can never be realized nor ever proclaimed.
Pāpīyān asked: "What is meant by 'generating the bodhicitta'?"
One cannot say: "To fully understand the nature of greed is called generating the mind [of enlightenment].

Furthermore, to fully understand anger, delusion, stinginess, and envy; the aggregates, bases, and elements; and ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, up to birth, old age, sickness, death, and the great suffering—this is called generating the mind."
Māra said: "What is the nature of all dharmas? [The Buddha replied: "Māra!..."
"All dharmas have no emergence from this nature.
Pāpīyān asked, "In what way is there no emergence?"
"Furthermore, that which is without emergence is precisely the absence of the traces of Māra.
The traces of Māra are 'self' and 'what belongs to self'; to be free from self and what belongs to self is called being without emergence.

Discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), the causal conditions for formations, the aggregates of perception and grasping, and the explanations of ideation and non-ideation, arising and ceasing, good and evil, outflowing and non-outflowing, conditioned and unconditioned, as well as the mundane and the supramundane—these are the traces of Māra."
"If there is no such [arising], then there is no emergence.
When this Dharma was being taught, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
From within the void, this sound emerged:
“Excellent, excellent, Pāpīyan! When this Dharma was spoken,
eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Pāpīyān said: "Good son!
By being endowed with what dharmas does a bodhisattva attain the patience of non-arising?"
A voice from the sky said:
"By cultivating and perfecting the six pāramitās, one attains the patience of non-arising.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Inexpressible addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, explain the ‘unspeakable.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who, when practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), contemplates the body as like an illusion, contemplates sensation as like a dream, and contemplates awakening as being like space, and at the time of practicing giving does not perceive a single dharma—this is called the perfection of giving that cannot be described.”

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates both the precepts and the stage of the precepts, as well as the violation of precepts and its stage; who contemplates that all sentient beings lack a self-nature and contemplates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is called upholding the precepts without violating them.
Having fulfilled the full precepts, one does not give rise to three eyes:
first, the eye of observing the precepts;
second, the eye of breaking the precepts; [and third, the eye of neither].
Third, the Bodhisattva’s eye:

although one maintains the precepts, one does not seek even a single dharma, nor does one perceive the coming, going, or present existence of bodhi; this is called the inexpressible perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who practices patience by contemplating that sentient beings neither arise nor emerge; who contemplates that awakening, sentient beings, and all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent; who, within the emptiness of sentient beings, possesses neither anger nor joy; and who practices patience without perceiving even a single phenomenon as having the mark of enmity, nor perceiving the removal of even a single phenomenon—this is called the ineffable perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).”

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who practices with diligent vigor, perceiving that not even a single dharma among body, speech, or mind arises, nor does a single dharma perish; yet he cultivates vigor without destroying the *dharmadhātu*, cultivating adornments for the sake of delivering sentient beings, giving rise to no confusion regarding emptiness and non-self, and practicing adornment desiring to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.

Hearing it said that the Buddha-dharma is itself no-dharma, one does not give rise to fear regarding this matter; one purifies and adorns the Tathāgata’s world, yet though adorned, one regards it as empty, and even without such adornment, one turns the wheel of Dharma.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inexpressible.
This is called the ineffability of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the dhyāna-pāramitā, having cultivated it, he does not perceive the nature of the past mind; having purified the fundamental nature, he does not perceive a place of abiding. Furthermore, he does not perceive minds of greed, anger, or delusion, nor minds that are superior, middling, or inferior, nor even the absence of greed, anger, or delusion; he likewise does not discriminate between minds of folly and wisdom.”

Why is this? Just as the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is, so too is the absence of greed, anger, and delusion. Having contemplated in this way, one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Yet, one cannot create equality where there is no equality, nor can one create equality through the method of inequality. Furthermore, one is able to fully comprehend the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*); the wholesome and unwholesome, the pure and impure, the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*), the mundane (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*), and the dharmas of birth-and-death, nirvāṇa, and their respective antidotes. This is called the ineffable perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
“Good son! What is called the ‘unspeakable Prajñāpāramitā’?

If there is no practice of wisdom, and no self, no what belongs to a self, no sentient beings, no life-span, no person, and no views such as permanence, annihilation, existence, or non-existence—nor the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—this is called ‘non-practice.’”
To be without dispute, without coming, and without going—this is called following the practice of wisdom.
To be free from the darkness of ignorance and evil, false views, and to contemplate such dharmas as these is true contemplation.
“Good son! When a fire arises, everything is consumed by it; there is no cause or condition for its persistence except for empty space.

Likewise, when a bodhisattva practices this ineffable Prajñāpāramitā, there is likewise no cause or condition. Seeing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is utterly extinguished, they nevertheless proclaim nirvāṇa to all sentient beings through skillful means.”

They also know that sentient beings have no names, yet for the sake of skillful means they proclaim names; and by the power of wisdom, they know the past and future, and speak of emergence and cessation.
Although they thoroughly understand that body and mind do not exist, they speak of body and mind by means of skillful expedients.
Although they know that all phenomena cannot be expressed in words, they speak of them through expedient means for the sake of sentient beings.
Although he knows that there is neither giving nor a recipient, he speaks of giving and recipients by means of skillful means.
Although he knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, he speaks of the existence of prohibitions and precepts by means of skillful means.
Although one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of the nature of anger, one cultivates and accumulates patience through skillful means.
Although one knows there is neither cultivation nor abandonment, one diligently practices vigor through skillful means.
Although they know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, they practice meditative concentration through skillful means.
Although they know there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana, they cultivate and accumulate wisdom through skillful means.
Although one knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is inherently extinguished, for the sake of skillful means, it is said that nirvāṇa is itself prajñā.

Now, Prajñā is without sound or name and cannot be proclaimed; it cannot be seen or heard, being without mind and without consciousness. It is neither grasping nor abandoning, neither "I" nor "mine. It has no location, form, or dimensions; it is neither high nor low, neither matter nor visible. It is neither oppositional, nor active, nor cognitive, nor conceptual. It has no place of abiding and is not of the past, future, or present. It is not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental objects, or the mind-faculty. It is neither light nor darkness, nor is it empty space. It is neither internal nor external, neither created nor existent. It is neither fat nor thin, neither increasing nor decreasing. Its original nature is pure, free from greed, hatred, and delusion. Furthermore, it is neither deranged nor chaotic; it is boundless, immeasurable, and is called the "Ineffable Prajñāpāramitā."
When this Dharma was being taught, the Māra Pāpīyān was released from his bonds; his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately spoke these words:
"Just as I have now heard this 'unpreachable' Dharma, I have attained liberation."
If there are good men or good women who hear this Dharma, they too shall attain liberation from within perversion just as I have, and no māras whatsoever shall find an opportunity against them.
At that time, twelve thousand beings within the assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the name of this True Dharma?
How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta'; it is also titled 'The Ineffable Dharma,' and it is also titled 'Entering All Buddha-Dharmas and Severing All Names of the Buddhas.'"
"If there are those who can receive and uphold such teachings as these upon their heads, they shall immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, many musical instruments, incense, and flowers were arrayed in the air as offerings to the ineffable number of bodhisattvas.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle 13;
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle 14.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Storehouse of Space. Section One of Chapter Eight: The Storehouse of Space. Chapter One: The Questions.

At that time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Hall of Wondrous Jewel Adornments, the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata. He was adorned with the majestic power of the Tathāgata and the marks of great merit; he had attained the retribution of the Buddha-ground through his original practices. His bodhisattva palace was praised as immeasurable; it was established by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. Entering the sphere of unimpeded wisdom, he gave rise to supreme joy. He contemplated the advancement of knowledge and skillfully explained its distinctions, endowed with all virtues and praised in future ages.

World-Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One has skillfully turned the wheel of Dharma and is well able to discipline and harmonize immeasurable sentient beings, attaining mastery over all phenomena.

He knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings and is skilled at discerning all their faculties. Having reached the other shore, he has skillfully severed the fetters and habitual tendencies until they are forever exhausted without remainder; the Buddha-works he performs are spontaneously accomplished.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of six million bhikṣus, whose minds were harmonious and supple, whose habitual tendencies had been severed, and who were all sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King. They practiced the profound Dharma and were well able to understand the dharma of non-existence; they were exceptionally sublime and upright, fully endowed with dignified deportment, and were great fields of merit, dwelling correctly within the teachings taught by the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a great assembly of bodhisattvas who had transcended all conditioned activities yet did not abandon the conduct of a bodhisattva; who had attained the patience of non-self; who did not forsake great compassion for all sentient beings;

who surpassed all worldly realms yet conformed to worldly laws to diligently transform sentient beings; and who were also able to skillfully enter the stages of the Tathāgata’s practice without ever departing from the stages of bodhisattva practice. Their names were as follows:

They were accompanied by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Samantaprabha, Asaṅgaprabha, Sarvadharmavaśavartirāja, Asaṅgagocarā, Vibhaktipratibhānabuddhi, Vimalānantajālinīpradīparāja, Anupaliptagocarā, and Māramaṇḍalavidhvaṃsanaraśmipramuñcana; together with such incalculable, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, limitless, and ineffable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke on the essential practice for all bodhisattvas, titled "The Adornment of the Bodhisattva Path through the Dharma-Gate of Non-Obstruction.
It brings about the accomplishment of the various powers and fearlessnesses of the Buddha-dharma, the attainment of mastery over all dharmas, the entry into the gateway of the *dhāraṇī*-seals,
the entry into the gateway of the discernment of various eloquences, and the entry into the gateway of great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Entering the gate of the equality of all vehicles through the teaching of the non-retrogressive wheel; entering the gate of non-discrimination within the single-mark dharma-realm;
entering the gate of teaching according to the differences in the capacities and understandings of sentient beings;
entering the gate of firm dharma-discrimination that destroys all demonic realms through skillful and compliant contemplation; and entering the unimpeded wisdom that severs all fetters and views.
They enter the gateway of skillful wisdom through peerless vows; they enter the gateway of the equal wisdom of all Buddhas;
they enter the gateway of discerning all phenomena as they truly are without obstruction; they enter the gateway of the unchanging and impartial Dharma;
they enter the gateway of the profound twelve links of dependent origination; and they enter the gateway of the firmness of the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind, adorned with merit and wisdom.
He firmly contemplates the thought of advancement and enters the gate of inexhaustible concentration; he enters the gate of the Four Noble Truths.
For the sake of taming the śrāvakas, he enters the gate of detachment from physical and mental activities.
To subdue pratyekabuddhas, they enter the gate of bestowing the prediction of omniscience;
to subdue bodhisattvas, they enter the gate of mastery over all dharmas.

In order to manifest the virtues of the Buddha—namely, to reveal, explain, manifest, and cause understanding; to teach, recite, establish, arrange in sequence, expand, analyze, and facilitate compliance with the correct teaching.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was thus skillfully distinguishing the skillful means of the Great Dharma,
all forms and images within this trichiliocosm appeared— whether the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Sumeru the King of Mountains,
and the various Black Mountains; the four continents and Jambudvīpa, and the villages and towns.
cities, towns, houses, the great ocean, rivers, springs, ponds, medicinal herbs, trees, and various groves;
as well as the palaces of the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth; and the earth.
The divine palaces, the various celestial palaces in the void, the palaces of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
as well as the palaces of the Brahmā heavens, up to the palaces of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven— all these great [palaces].
The earth and the sentient beings with physical bodies in the desire realm are all completely concealed and invisible to the eye,
just as when the fire disaster at the end of a kalpa has arisen and consumed the great earth, before the great waters have yet emerged.
At that time, not a single form confronted the eye.

At that moment, even the trichiliocosm was likewise thus, such that there was not even the slightest form subsumed within the realm of desire or the realm of form, with the sole exception of the forms and images seen within the Hall of Sublime Jewel Adornments.

At that time, in the midst of the sky within the Hall of Exquisite Jewel Adornments, there spontaneously appeared hundreds of thousands of nayutas of jewel terraces, unattached and without support, exquisitely adorned and a joy for all to behold; they were like the jewel terraces where the bodhisattvas dwell in the single-jewel-adorned buddha-field of the Great Exquisite Adornment World, and these various jewel terraces were likewise so.

He saw the great assembly seated within the precious pavilions; from within the Hall of Exquisite Jewel Adornments, there spontaneously emerged pure and wondrous lion thrones made of true gold, ten thousand yojanas in height.
From this lion throne, a wondrous and pure radiance issued forth, universally illuminating this trichiliocosm and eclipsing the light of all the bodhisattvas so that it was no longer visible.

At that time, the great assembly was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; their hearts were delighted as they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata must now proclaim the Great Dharma, for he has manifested this auspicious sign."

At that time, Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from the jeweled platform, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What auspicious sign is this, that such supreme joy has arisen and these great miraculous transformations have been manifested?
World-Honored One!
This entire great assembly has fallen into doubt; we pray that the Tathāgata will explain what cause and what condition have led to the manifestation of this unprecedented event.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“To the east of here, passing through as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in eight buddha-worlds, there is a world named Great Adornment.”

In that land there is a Buddha named Ekaratnavyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who is currently dwelling and preaching the Dharma.
For what reason is that world named Great Adornment?
If one were to describe in detail the matters of that world’s adornment, they would not be exhausted even in a single kalpa; therefore, that land is named Great Adornment.
For what reason is that Buddha named Single Jewel Adornment? Śāriputra!
That Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of a single jewel—namely, the jewel of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna—and for this reason, that Buddha is named Single Jewel Adornment.

That Buddha, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, each ascended a lion throne and leaped into the air to a height of eighty billion *tāla* trees, where he preached the Dharma-gate of the Space-Seal (*ākāśamudrā*) for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
"What is the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Space?
It is that all dharmas take space as their gate because they have no place of abiding;
all dharmas are the gate of non-abiding because they have no form or characteristics."
The gate of all phenomena being formless, because they transcend the sphere of conditioned activities;
the gate of all phenomena having no sphere of activity, because they are pure internally and externally;
the gate of all phenomena being pure, because their nature is unstained.
All phenomena are the gate of non-defilement, because their intrinsic nature is quiescent;
all phenomena are the gate of quiescence, because mind, thought, and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent;
all phenomena are the gate of fundamental non-existence, because they are free from both substance and non-substance.
All phenomena are the gate of non-substantiality, because they lack the characteristics of instruction;
all phenomena are the gate of non-instruction, because they lack formal segments;
all phenomena are the gate of non-formal-segments, because they are free from the sphere of causes and conditions.
The gateway of all phenomena being without causal conditions, because they possess the characteristic of quiescence;
the gateway of all phenomena being quiescent, because they are free from dualistic characteristics;
the gateway of all phenomena being non-dual, because they have abandoned differentiation.
All phenomena are the gate of non-differentiation, for they enter into the single characteristic;
all phenomena are the gate of the single characteristic, for their own-characteristics are pure;
all phenomena are the gate of the purity of own-characteristics, for they transcend the three periods of time.
All phenomena are the gateway of transcending the three periods of time, because they do not depart from equality;
all phenomena are the gateway of not departing from equality, because their illusory and transformative characteristics are non-characteristics;
all phenomena are the gateway of illusory and transformative characteristics, because their essence is not real.
The gate of all phenomena being without substance, because they lack the mark of activity;
the gate of all phenomena being without activity, because body and mind are detached;
the gate of all phenomena being detachment, because they are free from marks and signless.
The gate of all phenomena being signless, because signs are immovable;
the gate of all phenomena having immovable signs, because they have no place of dependence;
the gate of all phenomena having no place of dependence, because they abide in the boundless.
All phenomena are the gate of being without limits, because they have no abode;
all phenomena are the gate of having no abode, because they are without self and without what belongs to a self;
all phenomena are the gate of being without self and without what belongs to a self, because they have no master.
The gateway that all phenomena are without a master, because their nature is selfless;
the gateway that all phenomena are without a self, because they are inwardly pure. Śāriputra!
That Tathāgata Ekaratnavyūha extensively expounded this Dharma-gate of the Space-Seal (*ākāśamudrā*) for the sake of the bodhisattvas.

When that Tathāgata was teaching this Dharma, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas realized that the nature of all phenomena is equal to space, and they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) regarding all phenomena.
“Śāriputra! In that Great Adornment Buddha-land, at the place of the Buddha One Jewel Adornment, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gaganagañja, who adorns himself with great adornments.”

Among all inconceivable vows, they are the most preeminent; they have attained the unimpeded knowledge and vision that constitutes the sovereign majesty within all merits; they adorn themselves with the inconceivable merits of a bodhisattva; they adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks; and they adorn their speech by skillfully teaching the Dharma according to the needs of those to be liberated.

They adorn their mind with non-retrogression from meditative concentration; they adorn their mindfulness with various dhāraṇīs; they adorn their intellect by entering into subtle phenomena; and they adorn their diligence by contemplating the nature of phenomena in accordance with reality.

He adorns his pure devotion with firm vows; he adorns his activities with the certainty of accomplishment; he adorns his ultimate goal by proceeding from one stage to the next; and he adorns his generosity by relinquishing all that he possesses.

One adorns ethical discipline with a pure mind and virtuous speech; one adorns patience with a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings; one adorns diligence with the full completion of all tasks; one adorns meditative concentration with the playful mastery of supernatural powers upon entering samādhi; and one adorns wisdom with skillful knowledge of the habitual tendencies of afflictions.

“He adorns loving-kindness by rescuing and protecting sentient beings; he adorns compassion by dwelling in the non-abandonment of sentient beings; he adorns sympathetic joy by having a mind free from hesitation; he adorns equanimity by being detached from both hatred and love; he adorns supernormal powers by sporting in various meditative concentrations; and he adorns merit by attaining the hand of inexhaustible jewels.”

They adorn wisdom by discerning the mental activities of all sentient beings; they adorn awakening by teaching the wholesome Dharma to sentient beings; they adorn the clarity of wisdom by attaining pure and luminous insight; they adorn the various eloquences by attaining mastery in meaning, phenomena, phrasing, and response; they adorn the fearlessnesses by destroying Māras and non-Buddhists; and they adorn themselves by attaining the immeasurable merits of a Buddha.

"Constantly preaching the Dharma through all the pores of the skin is the adornment of the Dharma; seeing the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas is the adornment of one's own illumination; being able to illuminate the lands of all Buddhas is the adornment of light; and teaching without error is the adornment of one's prophetic records."

The adornment of teaching according to the inclinations of beings through supernormal powers; the adornment of transformations by reaching the further shore of the four bases of psychic power through supernormal powers; and the adornment of being sustained by all Tathāgatas by entering the secret realm of the Buddhas through supernormal powers.
Having realized for himself right wisdom, he possesses mastery over the adornment of the Dharma; acting according to his words, no one can thwart him, and he firmly adorns all wholesome dharmas.

"That Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such immeasurable merits as these. Together with twelve billion Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, he has resolved to come to this Sahā world to see me, to pay homage, make offerings, show respect, and surround me, also for the sake of distinguishing a small portion of the Dharma-gate within this Great Samantavyūha Sūtra."

Furthermore, it is because he wishes to generate the great light of Dharma for the bodhisattvas who have gathered from the ten directions; because he wishes to increase and open up the Mahāyāna Dharma; because he wishes to receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s Dharma; because he wishes to bring forth the roots of goodness in immeasurable sentient beings; because he wishes to subdue all māras and non-Buddhists through wholesome dharmas; and because he wishes to manifest the bodhisattva’s lion-like playful supernatural powers—this is the auspicious omen that the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha intends to come here.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, surrounded respectfully by twelve billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, went to the presence of the Buddha Ekaratnavyūha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage to him, and to make offerings.
That Buddha replied, "Go as you please; you should know that now is the time."

Having prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Single-Jewel Adornment and circumambulated him seven times to the right, he vanished from that Great Adornment Land by means of the Buddha’s effortless, playful supernormal power. In the space of a single thought-moment, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, he arrived here in this Sahā world, upon the exquisite jewel terrace in the Hall of Jewel Adornment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja rained down exquisite flowers and incense as an offering to the World-Honored One and to this Great Universal Assembly Sūtra.

These were the māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, pāriyātraka flowers, mahāpāriyātraka flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, rocanā flowers, and mahārocanā flowers. Flowers from both land and water, as large as chariot wheels—with a hundred petals, a thousand petals, or a hundred-thousand petals—all emitted light and fragrance that perfumed everywhere. These exquisite scents were pleasing to the mind, blooming with fresh purity; their variegated colors and radiant brilliance were a joy for the eyes to behold. He rained down such various and immeasurable exquisite flowers until they filled the Hall of Exquisite Jewels to a height of one tala tree.

They produced the music of the devas, the sounds of which all issued forth as the voices of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates: sounds corresponding to the *dāna-pāramitā*; sounds corresponding to the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*; sounds corresponding to the four immeasurables; sounds corresponding to the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*); sounds corresponding to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); sounds corresponding to the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); sounds corresponding to the four noble truths (*āryasatya*); and sounds corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha made offerings to the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ekaratnavyūha sends his greetings and inquires after you: Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light, easy, and peaceful?
That Tathāgata Ekaratnavyūha further said:

"There are twelve billion bodhisattvas who, together with the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, shall go to that Sahā world. We pray that the World-Honored One will preach such and such a Dharma so that these bodhisattvas may attain spontaneous wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna), and having likewise accomplished the great light of the Dharma, they may return here."
"Why is this? Because in the past, the World-Honored One has already transformed these sons of good family, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifested a great precious canopy above the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, ten thousand *yojanas* in width. It had a frame of blue lapis lazuli and a center made of genuine coral. Its hanging pendants were made of lapis lazuli and Jāmbūnada gold, while various exquisite pearls, jeweled nets, and necklaces formed a canopy of tinkling bells that resonated in harmony. The radiance of this canopy shone universally throughout the ten directions, intermingled with various wonderful flowers in a variegated splendor.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, having conceived profound reverence for the inconceivable merits of the Tathāgata, joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him with these verses:

"O Most Victorious Honored One, whose wisdom and meaning of the Dharma are supreme, Naturally pure, stainless, and free from attachment, Like space, you are untainted; I pay homage at the feet of the Immovable Sage."
His practice is peerless and boundless; manifesting in this life, his adorned body is most supreme.
The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like space, universally giving rise to great compassion to deliver and save all beings.
The Lion among Men can manifest the body of the World-Honored One, adorned with a hundred merits;
it is severed from all speech and devoid of sound, free from all verbal expression and without conceptual proliferation.
Though knowing this to be so, he speaks it forth to bring joy to sentient beings who lack such nature;
by means of a mind that is no-mind, he attains this mind, able to know the illusory mind that is no-mind.
He thoroughly knows the mental activities and natures of sentient beings, yet he does not dwell in the notions of self or other;
manifesting dignified conduct to save sentient beings, the body of the Sugata is neither active nor inactive.
The Buddha knows the inclinations of sentient beings and can manifest such forms accordingly;
the World-Honored One does not conceive of a self regarding the Dharma, nor does he give rise to thoughts of attachment toward the Dharma.
He knows by what means the Dharma should be received, and speaks according to his realization at the appropriate time;
the great assembly gazes up with thirsty longing for the World-Honored One, who is rare in the world and most peerless.
The World-Honored One has no intention to manifest; there is nothing that can cause the great assembly to rejoice.
These various phenomena arise from conditions; they are void, quiescent, and not real.
The World-Honored One well understands such dharmas, Having attained the path of cool Nirvana;
He has departed from the two extremes and does not cling to the middle, Knowing that the empty is not real and lacks intrinsic nature.
These phenomena have no creator; you have well explained that karmic retribution is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Phenomena lack a multitude, a life-force, or a person; they are quiescent and cannot be named, like space.
Discerning reality as it is, there are no sentient beings, yet you establish many multitudes in the nectar of immortality;
having practiced for inconceivable kalpas in the past, you sought the superior power of advancing toward Bodhi.
The sublime practices you undertook are now perfected; having reached the ultimate goal, you have awakened to all things without exception.
Regarding all phenomena—superior, middling, and inferior—you know them all to be equal and eternally without distinction.
The wise know what is known without attachment; therefore, the World-Honored One is never disturbed.
The aggregates, bases, and elements are like illusions; the three realms are all like the moon reflected in water.
The deceptive nature of sentient beings is like a dream; with wisdom one discerns and explains this Dharma.
Worldly people falsely claim to have attained the Way, yet in reality there is neither the mark of attainment nor non-attainment.

As the Way has no attainment and the wheel does not turn, and as the wheel does not turn and there is no one who crosses over, he is thus able to deliver the multitudes from the four currents; having delivered himself, he delivers others from the bonds of perversion.
Skillfully able to comfort those in suffering and distress, One extinguishes oneself and extinguishes others, reaching the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Sentient beings are neither born nor enter nirvāṇa; Sentient beings are fundamentally pure and ungraspable.
The Path and sentient beings are like illusions; having personally realized this limit, one awakens many multitudes.
Just as no form is seen within empty space, so too are the forms of all living beings.
All phenomena are devoid of form and the characteristics of form; one who can know this form attains liberation.
To praise the Buddha by means of various subtle metaphors is to praise him while clinging to views; that is actually to disparage him.
The Buddha’s virtues are like space, without distinction; To praise the Buddha is to find him immeasurable.
Therefore, I pay homage to the Pure Honored One who purifies others, Who enters the subtle mind without conditions or thought.
As the World-Honored One knows the Buddha’s merits, So do I now pay homage to the merit of Suchness.

One who can know that sentient beings are without self, Who knows the limit of all phenomena and is free from desire, And who sees the Dharma-body, sees the Buddha; This is itself making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

When the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha had spoken these verses, the Hall Adorned with Exquisite Jewels and all the jeweled terraces in the void shook in six ways. The entire assembly’s minds became pure and joyful; leaping for joy and filled with delight, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and all said:
