“The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is truly skilled in speaking these sublime verses.”

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to practice this Dharma, they will not perceive the existence of any phenomenon even within their dreams; gradually, they shall all attain the lion’s roar, just like the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, having praised the Tathāgata with such sublime verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a few questions; I only pray that you will grant me your permission."
"If you grant me leave to ask, then I shall venture to inquire. Why is this?
The World-Honored One possesses immeasurable knowledge and vision, capable of discerning whether the faculties of sentient beings are matured or immature."
The World-Honored One is luminously penetrating, for he has removed all darkness;
the World-Honored One has realized the definitive meaning, for he skillfully explains and distinguishes the meanings of all phrases;
the World-Honored One knows the proper time, for he does not transgress its limits.
The World-Honored One’s predictions are unerring, for his teachings are never mistaken;
the World-Honored One knows the proper time, for he preaches the Dharma in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings;
the World-Honored One is skilled in playful mastery, for he has attained full penetration of all supernormal powers.
The World-Honored One is skillfully observant, for he embodies the mental activities of sentient beings;
the World-Honored One is most undefiled, for he has attained mastery over all phenomena;
the World-Honored One is self-awakened, for he has realized and understood all phenomena.
The World-Honored One rightly guides sentient beings toward wrong paths, teaching them to enter the right path;
the World-Honored One is a great king of physicians, able to bring about the eternal severance of all ailments from beginningless worlds;
the World-Honored One possesses great power, having accomplished the ten powers of a Buddha.
The World-Honored One is fearless, for he has accomplished the four fearlessnesses;
the World-Honored One is unsurpassed, for he has accomplished the eighteen unique qualities;
the World-Honored One practices great compassion, for his mind is unimpeded as he rescues all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One practices great compassion, for he knows and perceives non-self in order to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings;
the World-Honored One practices great joy, for he enters into meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, reaching the other shore;
the World-Honored One practices great equanimity, for he has severed all hatred and attachment, and his mind is like empty space.
The World-Honored One has attained equanimity, because he has awakened to all Buddha-dharmas without obstruction;
the World-Honored One is free from hatred and affection, because his mind is ultimately pure and remains unmoved by blame or praise;
the World-Honored One is free from longing, because his wisdom is fulfilled and he has no desire for gain or praise.
The World-Honored One possesses all-knowing vision, for he has reached the further shore of all the spheres of action of the Buddhas.
I know and see that the World-Honored One is endowed with such immeasurable and boundless merits; therefore, I wish to ask a few questions regarding this Dharma-gate.
After the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha had spoken these words,
the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying:
"O son of good family!
"I shall listen to your questions; you may ask whatever you desire and inquire as you wish, and I shall satisfy your mind according to your questions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Merit and Radiance addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!..."
"For whose sake do you wish to question the Tathāgata?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha replied to the Bodhisattva Puṇyaprabhāsarāja with these verses:
"All sentient beings who possess an equal mind, Who are able to reach the further shore through equanimity,"
Within the stainless heart of compassion, you sport freely; for their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
You have reached stainless right view, free from all defilement; with hesitation gone, you have severed that doubt.
Having attained personal realization, you benefit sentient beings; for their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
Knowing that I am without self and peerless, I have resolved my mind for the sake of the multitude without clinging to them;
able to liberate sentient beings from their views of a self, I ask the World-Honored One on their behalf.
Able to guard their dignified demeanor and be cautious in their conduct,
with minds as pure as space and as firm and unshakable as Mount Sumeru— for these individuals, I inquire of the World-Honored One.
With boundless resolve and peerless wisdom, Brave and steadfast, you can destroy the enemy of afflictions;
Having bound and severed those fetters, you have cut them all asunder— For their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
Delighting in giving, with majestic deportment and a subdued mind, Ever abiding in the powers of learning, diligence, morality, and patience,
With meditative concentration, the various supernormal powers, and the clarity of supreme wisdom— For their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.

Delighting in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet manifesting in physical forms within the cycle of birth and death, they have reached the nectar of immortality, being neither born nor ending; for their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
Your knowledge and vision are profoundly deep and boundless, beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
yet you know the conduct of all sentient beings—for their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
Those who are well able to comprehend and delight in right practice, whose fetters regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma have been severed,
and who always abide in right concentration with undisturbed minds— for their sake, I ask the World-Honored One.
O worthy sirs who do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, who are able to protect the True Dharma and the Saṅgha,
and who are praised by the Buddhas of the three periods for their great learning— it is for the sake of such as these that I question the World-Honored One.
At that time, having answered the Bodhisattva Puṇyaprabhāsarāja with these sublime verses, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) so that it is equal to space?

How does he practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so that they are equal to space?
How does one practice so that merit is equal to space?
How does one practice so that wisdom is equal to space?
How does a bodhisattva not depart from suchness?

Regarding what the Tathāgata has permitted—namely, mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṃgha, mindfulness of giving, mindfulness of precepts, and mindfulness of the devas—how does a bodhisattva practice the equality of all dharmas as being like nirvāṇa?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully discern the characteristics of practice?

How does a bodhisattva uphold the treasury of the Dharma-jewels of all Buddhas, and having realized the characteristics and nature of phenomena exactly as they are according to the Dharma-characteristics and nature awakened by the Tathāgata, neither grasp nor reject them?
How does a bodhisattva distinguish that sentient beings have been pure from the very beginning, yet still teach and transform them?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully accord with the practice of the path to accomplish the Buddha-dharma?
How does a bodhisattva not regress from the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and attain complete mastery over all Buddha-dharmas?
How does a bodhisattva enter the gateways of the profound Dharma that cannot be entered by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
How does a bodhisattva, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, attain superior wisdom through skillful means and become free from the various views of the two extremes?
How does a bodhisattva receive the seal of the Tathāgata, [possessing] the skillful means of non-conceptualizing wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā*)?
How does a bodhisattva enter the gateway to the nature of the dharma-realm and perceive the equality of all phenomena?
How does a bodhisattva become as pure, steadfast, and firm as a diamond, so that their mind remains unmoving within this Great Vehicle?
How does a bodhisattva purify their own realm so that it is like the realm of all Buddhas?
How does a bodhisattva attain dhāraṇī and never lose mindfulness?
How does a bodhisattva attain the unhindered eloquence sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas?
How does a bodhisattva attain mastery in manifesting the experience of birth and death?
How does a bodhisattva destroy all enemies and remain far removed from the four māras?
How does a bodhisattva benefit sentient beings and adorn their meritorious virtues?
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to perform the work of a Buddha when no Buddha exists in the world?
How is it that a bodhisattva attains the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) and is well able to know the mental activities of sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva become able to know all realms of sensory objects without obstruction?

How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection in majestic deportment and conduct, leaving behind all darkness to attain supreme radiance, gaining spontaneous wisdom regarding all phenomena, and swiftly accomplishing the practice of omniscience?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
saying: "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"

"You have skillfully distinguished and questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a wondrous meaning as this. You have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past and planted various roots of goodness; your mental conduct is impartial, like space; you pay homage to all Buddhas and have reached the place of luminous wisdom; you have aroused diligent vigor, desiring to deliver all beings."

The Buddhas, in accordance with the Dharma, do not abandon any sentient beings; they have crossed to the further shore of great compassion and transcended the activities of all Māras, yet they do not depart from worldly dharmas. With a mind equal in measure to space, they bring to fulfillment this supreme Mahāyāna wondrous Dharma, the Space Treasury (Gaganagañja).

Your merit is boundless and difficult to measure; you have already in the past inquired about such matters before as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and you are yourself capable of explaining them.
Therefore, Ākāśagarbha!
Listen now attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain for you the matters concerning the bodhisattvas that you have asked;
furthermore, they will be able to attain the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom, and the knowledge of all modes.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha said:
“Indeed, how wonderful! I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha addressed Ākāśagarbha:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, their practice of the dānapāramitā is equal to space. What are these four?

"Good son! If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in all places without obstruction or discrimination, because the self is pure, giving is also pure; because giving is pure, the vow is also pure; because the vow is pure, awakening (bodhi) is also pure; and because awakening is pure, all phenomena (dharmas) are also pure."
“Good son! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), making it equal to space. Good son!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they can purify the dāna-pāramitā. What are these eight? They are: giving while free from the notion of "I";

giving while free from the notion of "for me"; giving while free from the fetter of craving; giving while free from views rooted in ignorance; giving while free from the marks of self and other regarding awakening; giving while free from various conceptualizations; giving while free from the expectation of reward; and giving while free from stinginess and envy, with a mind as equanimous as space. These are the eight dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes to purify the dāna-pāramitā.
"To be free from these eight dharmas is called pure giving; just as space reaches everywhere, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving with a compassionate mind."
Just as space is not form and cannot be seen, so too it is with the various acts of giving performed by Bodhisattvas, which do not rely upon form.
Just as space does not experience suffering or pleasure, so too it is with the various acts of giving performed by Bodhisattvas, which are free from all sensation.
Just as space is characterized by the absence of marks, so too is the wisdom of the bodhisattva’s various acts of giving, which are free from all conceptual fetters.
Just as space is characterized by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), so too are the various acts of giving performed by the bodhisattva unconditioned and effortless.
Just as space is illusory and signless, so too is the practice of giving by Bodhisattvas, which does not rely on consciousness or conceptualization.
Just as space benefits all sentient beings, so too does the practice of giving by Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings.
Just as space cannot be exhausted, so too it is with the various acts of giving practiced by Bodhisattvas; they are likewise inexhaustible within the cycle of birth and death.

“Good son! It is like a conjured person giving gifts to another conjured person; there is no discrimination, no conceptual proliferation, and no seeking of karmic retribution. The Bodhisattva is also like this.”

Like the characteristics of a conjured person, they practice various acts of giving while remaining detached from the two extremes; they do not engage in conceptual proliferation or discrimination, nor do they hope for karmic rewards.
Son of good family!

When a bodhisattva abandons all fetters through wisdom, yet does not abandon any sentient beings through the wisdom of skillful means, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) that is equal to space.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dīpāṇi who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What kind of bodhisattva is able to practice such dānapāramitā?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

If a bodhisattva transcends all worldly realms and attains supramundane dharmas—dharmas that are non-material, without substance, and without activity; whose knowledge and vision are pure; which are neither darkness nor light and are free from all marks; and who reaches the limit of signless wisdom and accomplishes inexhaustible patience.

Having approached the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, they have succeeded to the stage of the bodhisattva’s definitive realm; they have received the prediction of non-retrogression and are sealed with its seal; they have attained the consecration of the true station and have attained the practice of skillful means, knowing the characteristics of the conduct of sentient beings; though they reach all places, they do not go anywhere—such a bodhisattva is able to practice this dāna-pāramitā.

When this Dharma was being taught, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas, perceiving the nature of all phenomena to be like space, attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying: "Good son!..."
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) equal to space. What are these four?
O son of good family!

When a bodhisattva knows that the body is like a reflection in a mirror, knows that sound is like an echo, knows that the mind is like an illusion, and knows that the nature of all phenomena is like empty space—this is for a bodhisattva to accomplish four dharmas such that their practice of the *śīlapāramitā* is equal to empty space.
“Good son! A bodhisattva who accomplishes eight dharmas is able to protect pure precepts.
What are these eight?

"Good son! Bodhisattvas protect the precepts by not forgetting the bodhicitta; they protect the precepts by not seeking the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they protect the precepts by maintaining the precepts without being limited by them; they protect the precepts by not relying on those very precepts; they protect the precepts by not abandoning their original vows; they protect the precepts by not depending on any place of birth; they protect the precepts by accomplishing great vows; and they protect the precepts by skillfully restraining the sense faculties in order to extinguish afflictions. These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes and protects pure morality."
“Good son! Just as space is free from all longing, so too is the Bodhisattva’s protection of the precepts through a mind of non-seeking.
Just as space is pure, so too is the Bodhisattva’s purity in upholding the precepts.”
Just as space is free from defilement, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from defilement.
Just as space is free from feverish affliction, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts free from affliction.
Just as space has no high or low, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts neither high nor low.
Just as space has no nests or caves, so too is the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts without any dependence.
Just as space is without arising or cessation and is ultimately unchanging, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts without arising or cessation and ultimately unchanging.

Just as space is able to contain all sentient beings, so too is the bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts able to transport them all; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they are able to protect the true precepts.
“Good son! Just as the moon in the water has neither observance nor violation of the precepts, so too is the Bodhisattva.

To understand that all dharmas are like the reflection of the moon, having neither observance nor violation of the precepts—this is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Śīla-pāramitā, which is equal to space.”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, his practice of the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience) is equal to space. What are these four?
Good son! If a bodhisattva does not retaliate when reviled by others, it is because they have cultivated the perception of the non-existence of self;
if they do not retaliate when struck by others, it is because they have no perception of "the other."
He does not retaliate against anger because he is free from the perception of existence;
he does not retaliate against enmity because he has departed from the two views.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of four dharmas, whereby his practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is equal to space.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they can purify the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience).
What are these eight?
"Good son! A bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) by being thoroughly pure within and single-mindedly devoted;
he practices the perfection of patience by being thoroughly pure without and free from expectations."
One practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) by being ultimately without obstruction regarding the superior, middling, or inferior;
one practices the perfection of patience by following the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without any defiled attachment;
one practices the perfection of patience by remaining detached from all views and corresponding to emptiness (śūnyatā).
One should practice the perfection of patience by severing all discursive thoughts so as to be signless;
one should practice the perfection of patience by relinquishing all vows so as to be wishless;
one should practice the perfection of patience by eliminating all conditioned formations so as to be without action.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishing eight dharmas to purify the pāramitā of kṣānti. "Good son!
Just as space has neither aversion nor affection, so too is it when a bodhisattva cultivates the pāramitā of kṣānti: there is neither aversion nor affection."

Just as space is without change or alteration, so too is the ultimate mind of a bodhisattva without change or alteration when practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). It is likewise in this way.

Good son! Just as space is without deficiency or loss, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who ultimately cultivates the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); his mind is likewise without deficiency or loss.
Just as space is without birth or arising, so too is the mind of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) without birth or arising.
Just as space is without conceptual proliferation (prapañca), so too is the mind of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of patience without conceptual proliferation.

Just as space does not hope for a reward of gratitude, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who cultivates the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); they do not hope for any karmic fruit from any sentient being.

Just as space is without outflows and unconditioned by attachments, so too is it when a bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): they are free from all outflows and unconditioned by the three realms.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he does not form this thought:
‘That person comes to revile me, and I am able to endure it.’”
Furthermore, one does not perceive the one who reviles, the one who receives the revilement, nor the phenomena that are reviled;
one does not form such observations, nor engage in such conceptual proliferation by saying, "That is empty and I am also empty";
nor does one entertain such reflections as, "Sound is like an echo—by what cause does it arise?"
Furthermore, one does not form the view that "I am right and they are wrong";
nor does one hold the opinion that "they are impermanent and I am also impermanent";
nor does one entertain the thought that "they are ignorant and I am wise."
Nor do they form this thought: "We should practice patience. "Good son!

It is like a person who, seeking sālā branches, takes a sharp axe and enters a sālā grove; having reached a large tree, he cuts off one branch, yet the remaining branches do not think: [‘He is cutting us’]."
"He has already been struck; he does not strike us.
Likewise, the one who has been struck does not think:
"I have already been struck; the others have not been struck."
"Both are devoid of conceptualization, giving rise to neither hatred nor attachment. Good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), he contemplates and knows that the nature of all phenomena is like grass, trees, walls, tiles, and stones; yet, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, he manifests the cutting and dismemberment of his own body, remaining without hatred or attachment and free from recollection, thought, or discrimination."
"Good son! This is how a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) so that it is equal to space. Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) so that it is equal to space?
Son of good family!
A bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas such that their practice of the perfection of vigor is equal to space.
What are these four?
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva diligently seeks all wholesome dharmas, yet knows that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is not established;
With all the most excellent offerings, they serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;

yet they do not perceive the Tathāgata nor the dharmas that are served and offered. They are well able to receive and uphold the wondrous Dharma spoken by all Buddhas, yet they do not perceive any characters or words that can be received and upheld. Furthermore, they are able to bring immeasurable sentient beings to fulfillment, seeing the nature of sentient beings as being identical to nirvāṇa.
Ultimately, there is neither birth nor arising.
Son of good family!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), making it equal to space.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they can purify the vīryapāramitā. What are these eight?
"Good son! For the sake of purifying the body, the bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, knowing that the body is like a shadow and thus does not cling to it;
for the sake of purifying the mouth, he exerts diligent effort, knowing that speech is like an echo and thus does not cling to it."
To purify the mind, they exert diligent effort, knowing that the mind is like an illusion and devoid of discrimination, and thus do not cling to it;
to fulfill the various pāramitās, they exert diligent effort, knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are comprised of causes and conditions, and are beyond frivolous conceptualization;
to attain the factors conducive to enlightenment, they exert diligent effort, awakening to the true nature of all phenomena so as to be free from all obstructions and attachments.
To purify all Buddha-fields, they exert diligent effort, yet because they know that all lands are like space, they do not rely on what they have purified;
to attain all dhāraṇīs, they exert diligent effort, yet because they know that all phenomena are without thought and without non-thought, they do not form dualistic marks;

to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, they exert diligent effort, yet because they know that all phenomena enter into the equality of a single mark, they do not destroy the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
“Good son! These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the *vīryapāramitā*. Good son!”
Just as space never experiences weariness or fatigue,
so too is it with the Bodhisattva, who exerts diligent vigor throughout immeasurable eons without ever becoming weary or disheartened.
Just as space can fully contain all forms yet remains itself without any obstruction, so too is it with the Bodhisattva.
In the same way, the bodhisattva’s diligent application of energy, which is impartial and unobstructed for the sake of accommodating all sentient beings, is also like this.
Just as empty space can give rise to all medicinal herbs and forests, yet this empty space has no place of abiding;

so too, the bodhisattva’s diligent application of energy for the sake of increasing the roots of goodness in all sentient beings is likewise without dependence or attachment and has no place of abiding.
Just as space reaches all places yet has no going, so too it is with the bodhisattva who exerts diligent effort to reach all phenomena: there is neither reaching nor non-reaching.
It is like space, which is not itself form, yet within it various forms are seen;
likewise, the Bodhisattva exerts diligent effort for the sake of the One Vehicle, yet manifests the distinctions among the various vehicles in order to bring about their ultimate fulfillment.
Just as the nature of space is inherently pure and cannot be defiled by adventitious dust, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who exerts diligent vigor:
though their nature is inherently pure, they manifestly undergo birth and death for the sake of sentient beings, yet remain unstained by the accumulation of worldly dust.
Just as the nature of space is an eternal dharma and lacks anything impermanent,
so too is it with the bodhisattva who exerts diligent effort for the ultimate sake of ensuring that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
Just as space has no beginning and no end, and is neither grasped nor abandoned;
so too is it with the diligent vigor exerted by a bodhisattva, which has no beginning and no end, and is neither grasped nor abandoned.
“Good son! There are two kinds of diligence:
the diligence of initial exertion and the diligence of final accomplishment.”

A bodhisattva, by initiating diligence at the outset, practices and perfects all wholesome dharmas; by completing diligence at the end, they discern that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature. They perceive that the roots of goodness thus accumulated are equal, yet this perceived equality is itself not equality.

Good son! It is like a craftsman who carves a wooden figure complete with all its physical features; though it can accomplish every task for which it is made, the craftsman does not give rise to dualistic thoughts regarding what it does or does not do.

In order to fulfill the adornment of their original vows, Bodhisattvas exert diligent effort and cultivate all deeds; they do not give rise to dualistic thoughts regarding what is done or not done, and their departure from the two extremes is likewise so.
“Good son! This is how a bodhisattva’s practice of the *vīryapāramitā* is equal to space. Good son!”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the dhyānapāramitā so that it is equal to space?
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he practices the dhyānapāramitā so that it is equal to space.
What are the four?
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva concentrates his inner mind, he does not perceive an inner mind that obstructs external states of mind;
Nor does one perceive an external sphere of mental activity; because one’s own mind is equanimous, one knows that the minds of all sentient beings are equanimous.
Furthermore, one does not rely on dualistic dharmas such as the mind and its equanimous contemplation;
for the fixed nature of dharmas is neither grasped nor distracted, and one knows that the nature of all dharmas is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of the dhyānapāramitā, making it equal to space.
"Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they can purify the dhyānapāramitā."

What are these eight? Noble son, if a bodhisattva practices dhyāna without relying on the aggregates (skandhas), practices dhyāna without relying on the elements (dhātus), practices dhyāna without relying on the sense bases (āyatanas), practices dhyāna without relying on the three realms (tridhātu), practices dhyāna without relying on the present life, practices dhyāna without relying on future lives, practices dhyāna without relying on the path (mārga), and practices dhyāna without relying on the fruit (phala)— these are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the purification of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"Just as space has nothing upon which it relies or clings, so too is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of dhyāna without any point of reliance.
Just as space has nothing for which it feels affection or attachment, so too is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of dhyāna free from all defiled attachments."
Just as space is not attached to any views, so too is it when a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, relinquishing all views.
Just as space is devoid of all pride, so too is it when a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, abandoning all arrogance.
Just as space is ultimately without cessation, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who cultivates dhyāna and skillfully enters the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), never regressing to the end.
Just as space cannot be destroyed, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who cultivates dhyāna and does not destroy the primordial limit (koṭi).
Just as space is without change or alteration, so too is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of dhyāna, which remains unchanging in suchness (tathatā).
Just as space is neither mind nor separate from mind, so too is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of dhyāna, which is free from mind, thought, and consciousness (citta-manovijñāna).
“Good son! A bodhisattva cultivates dhyāna with a mind of equanimity, not with a mind that is not equanimous.
What is meant by a mind of equanimity?

If the mind is neither high nor low, without seeking and without non-seeking, without action and without non-action, without discrimination and without non-discrimination, without practice and without non-practice, without grasping and without abandoning, without darkness and without light, without cognition and without thought, without non-cognition and without non-thought; if it is neither one nor different, neither dual nor non-dual, without movement and without non-movement, without going and without not-going, without cultivation and without non-cultivation, and if the mind does not take any objective realm as its object—this is called the equanimous mind.
Because the Bodhisattva’s mind is impartial, he does not grasp at form; having departed from and distanced himself from the two dharmas of eye and form, he cultivates dhyāna.

Because his mind is impartial, he does not grasp at sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects; having departed from and distanced himself from the two dharmas of mind and mental objects, he cultivates dhyāna.

“Good son! It is like empty space: when the calamity of fire arises, it cannot be burned; when the calamity of water arises, it is not swept away. In the same way, a bodhisattva is not burned by the fires of the various afflictions, nor is he swept away by the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. His own births are naturally free from distraction, yet he enables sentient beings with distracted minds to attain concentration. Having purified his own conduct, he does not abandon diligence; he manifests equality while demonstrating distinctions, yet he perceives neither the two marks of equality nor inequality. He is well able to universally contemplate the true nature of wisdom, and his mind is not covered by craving or views. Amidst all conditioned phenomena, his practice is without attachment, equal to empty space.”
"Good son! This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the dhyānapāramitā, which is equal to space. Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so that it is equal to space?
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they practice the perfection of wisdom so that it is equal to space.
What are these four?

Noble son, if a bodhisattva, because of the purity of the self, knows that sentient beings are also pure; because of the purity of knowledge, knows that cognition is also pure; because of the purity of meaning, knows that words and letters are also pure; and because of the purity of the dharma-realm, knows that all phenomena are also pure—this is for a bodhisattva to accomplish the four dharmas and practice the perfection of wisdom equal to space.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes eight dharmas, he can purify the prajñāpāramitā.
What are these eight?
"Good son! If a bodhisattva diligently strives to sever all unwholesome dharmas without clinging to the view of annihilationism;
and diligently strives to give rise to all wholesome dharmas without clinging to the view of eternalism;"
They know that all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions, yet they do not waver from the dharma of the forbearance of non-arising;
they skillfully analyze and explain all words and phrases, yet they remain eternally equanimous and beyond verbal expression;
they are adept at discerning and proclaiming that all conditioned things are impermanent and suffering, yet they remain unmoved within the quiescence of the selfless realm of reality.
They are able to skillfully discern all karmic actions performed, yet they know that all phenomena are without karma and without retribution;
they are skilled at discerning defiled phenomena and pure phenomena, yet they know that the nature of all phenomena is eternally pure;
they are skilled at weighing all phenomena of the three periods of time, yet they know that all phenomena have no past, future, or present.
These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the prajñāpāramitā. "Good son!
Just as space is neither movement nor non-movement, so too is the bodhisattva’s practice of prajñā that is free from all movements."
Just as space cannot be destroyed, so too it is that no māras can destroy a bodhisattva practicing prajñā.
Just as the nature of space is eternally quiescent, so too it is that a bodhisattva practicing prajñā perceives and realizes quiescence.
Just as the nature of space is eternally without self, so too is it when a bodhisattva practices *prajñā* and realizes the absence of self.
Just as the nature of space is not a sentient being, so too is it when a bodhisattva practices *prajñā* and is free from all views of sentient beings.
Just as the nature of space has no life-force (*jīva*), so too is it with the bodhisattva practicing *prajñāpāramitā*, who is free from all views of a life-force.
Just as the nature of space has no person (*pudgala*), so too is it with the bodhisattva practicing *prajñāpāramitā*, who is free from all views of a person.
"Just as space is neither a thing nor a non-thing and cannot be named, so too is it with the Bodhisattva practicing prajñāpāramitā, who is free from the views of things and non-things. "Good son!..."
Prajñāpāramitā is the meaning of the term "quiescence," because it is devoid of subtle discernment;
it is the meaning of the term "non-action," because its own-characteristics are pure;
it is the meaning of the term "unchanging," because it is devoid of the marks of conditioned activity.
This is the meaning of the phrase "reality," because it is non-arising;
this is the meaning of the phrase "non-deception," because it is without variation;
this is the meaning of the phrase "thorough penetration," because it enters into the single characteristic.
This is the meaning of the phrase "pervasive clarity," because it severs habitual tendencies;
this is the meaning of the phrase "fulfillment," because it is free from desire and seeking;
this is the meaning of the phrase "thorough penetration," because it enables correct vision.
This is the meaning of the foremost phrase, because there is nothing to be attained;
this is the meaning of the phrase of equality, because there is neither high nor low;
this is the meaning of the firm phrase, because it cannot be destroyed.
This is the meaning of the immovable phrase, because it has no basis;
this is the meaning of the vajra phrase, because it cannot be destroyed;
this is the meaning of the phrase of having crossed over, because what was to be done has been accomplished.
This is the meaning of the phrase "true purity," because its intrinsic nature is pure;
this is the meaning of the phrase "absence of darkness," because it does not rely upon light;
this is the meaning of the phrase "non-duality," because it is without accumulation.
This is the meaning of the phrase "exhaustion," because it is the ultimate characteristic of exhaustion;
this is the meaning of the phrase "non-exhaustion," because it has the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this is the meaning of the phrase "unconditioned," because it is free from arising and ceasing.
This is the meaning of the phrase "space," because it is without obstruction;
this is the meaning of the phrase "non-existence," because it is truly pure;
this is the meaning of the phrase "no location," because it leaves no trace.
This is the meaning of the phrase "without a lair," because there is nothing upon which to rely;
this is the meaning of the phrase "wisdom," because there is no discrimination;
this is the meaning of the phrase "unconquerable," because there is no peer.
This is the meaning of the phrase "without substance," because it does not assume form;
this is the meaning of the phrase "knowledge and vision," because one knows that suffering does not arise;
this is the meaning of the phrase "cessation," because one knows that the origin of suffering has no conjunction.
This is the meaning of the term "cessation," because it is ultimately without arising;
this is the meaning of the term "path," because it is the non-dual awakening;
this is the meaning of the term "awakening," because it is the awakening to equality.
This meaning of the Dharma-verse is ultimately unchanging.
"Good son! This prajñā is not obtained from another; it is because one personally realizes and perceives it through practicing according to its true nature."
Knowing that all words, phrases, and meanings are like echoes, he responds appropriately to all speech and sounds; his eloquence is uninterrupted, yet he remains unattached to words and language.

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to skillfully respond within all forms of discourse; knowing that all sounds and speech are like echoes because they are ultimately ungraspable, they give rise to no attachment and engage in no conceptual proliferation.
“Good son! This is how a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so that it is equal to space.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“Giving while free from attachment, extending universally to suit the dispositions of all beings, ultimately with an unimpeded mind and without giving rise to discrimination.
Because I am pure, the gift is pure; because the gift is pure, the aspiration is pure.”
May the purity of enlightenment be pure; may the purity of the Path bring purity to all.
Free from the notions of "self" and "mine," detached from craving and all views, having abandoned the marks of "other" and "self," may the mind of giving be like space.
Giving while detached from all conceptualizations, With no heart that hopes for recompense, Having abandoned the fetters of envy and jealousy, The mind of giving is like space.
Space is not form and has no dependence; It is without sensation, perception, or discrimination.
There is neither form nor consciousness; when giving, the mind is likewise so.
Like space, it benefits all beings, beginningless and endless from start to finish.
Understanding that the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, it brings benefit to all sentient beings.
Just as when an emanated person gives a gift, they do not hope for a reward for what is given;
so too does the wise one give—never hoping for its recompense.
With wisdom they sever the fetters and habitual tendencies, yet through skillful means they do not abandon the multitude.
Not perceiving fetters or a multitude, such giving is like space.
Knowing the body to be like a reflected image, knowing sound to be like an echo,
knowing the mind to be like a magical illusion, and the nature of phenomena to be like empty space.
Not forsaking supreme enlightenment, nor seeking the two vehicles,
they have always revered and carefully guarded the precepts before the Buddhas of the past.
Because they do not abandon their original vows, they are able, amidst all realms of existence, to...
Having successfully fulfilled their original vows, they restrain the mind and guard the pure precepts.
Like space, they are without expectation; they are free from feverish distress, high or low, turbidity, and change—so too is the one who possesses pure precepts.
Just as space receives all things, and the moon in water does not grasp at its reflection, so it is with the protector of the precepts: their pure morality is like empty space.
When faced with abuse, beating, anger, and the like, they do not give way to resentment by virtue of the power of patience.
Free from the notion of self and its views, having abandoned both these perceptions;
inwardly pure and supremely virtuous, outward conduct is likewise purified.
Being supremely pure, he is free from anger and is able to endure in accordance with the Dharma.

Free from all views, patient in emptiness, Abandoning discursive thought and detached from conceptualization, Without aspiration and free from longing, One relinquishes all conditioned activities and their grasping.
Like space, one is without craving; Neither frivolous nor harboring resentment.
Without frivolous play and seeking no reward, such is the one with untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
There is neither patience nor one who reviles; for that person, sound is like an echo.
It is neither existent nor impermanent; thus, there is no such conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Those who are deluded and I, who possess wisdom, manifest birth though there is no birth;
although we distinguish things in this way, we still cultivate the patience of non-arising.
It is like cutting a branch of a śāla tree: one does not distinguish it from the other branches.
Severing the body without discrimination—this patience is pure as space.
Diligently practicing without dependence, making offerings to the Buddha without the notion of a Buddha;
upholding the Dharma without attachment to words, delivering sentient beings without the notion of sentient beings.
Purifying the body, purifying the Dharma-body; Purifying the mouth, free from speech;
Purifying the mind, free from mental activity; Possessing all the pāramitās.
Possessing the factors conducive to enlightenment, The pure land is like empty space.
Having accomplished eloquence and dhāraṇī, they seek such Buddha-dharma as this.
Like space, they receive it without weariness; thus they can produce a forest of growth, reaching everywhere yet without form or color; their diligence is likewise like space.
Ever pure like space, without beginning and without end;
so too is human diligence, accomplished without beginning or end.
Like a wooden puppet moved by a mechanism, that which it performs is devoid of discrimination.
The practitioner is free from dualistic thought; their progress is like space.
Knowing how to rest within the inner mind, they gather the mind from external objects.
With one's own mind and the minds of others being equal, they rely upon the meditation of no-mind.
The nature of all phenomena is eternally empty; One knows this through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Not relying on the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*), Nor relying on the three realms (*tridhātu*), Not relying on the three realms, Nor relying on the elements, paths, or fruits.
As space is eternally without dependence, so too is the practitioner of dhyāna;
as space is devoid of craving, views, and pride, so too is the practitioner of dhyāna;
as space is without decline, destruction, or change, so too is the practitioner of dhyāna.
Equanimity, tranquility, and liberation—the wise do not take the elements as their object;
there is no fetter and no meditative absorption. Therefore, meditation is like space.
My purity is the purity of sentient beings; my wisdom is pure, and consciousness is likewise pure.
The meaning is pure and the letters are pure; the Dharma is pure and the realm is also pure.
Having severed unwholesome states along with their habitual tendencies, the Great Being accumulates all virtues.
Knowing that existence arises through conditions, he does not cling to non-arising nor to cessation.
Skillfully distinguishing words and letters, he teaches the dharmas of impermanence and suffering;
he manifests the receiving of karmic retribution and speaks of defilement and purity.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is eternally pure, he deliberates upon the three periods of time.
Emptiness has no activity, nor does non-activity; wisdom is likewise without activity.
Just as emptiness cannot be destroyed, it is devoid of self, person, or life-span;
it is neither a thing nor a non-thing, having uprooted and severed the two extreme views.
Knowing that words are provisional and untainted, The unchanging word of reality,
The fulfilling word of thorough penetration, The word of wisdom equal to the realization of meaning,
The word of equanimity, immovability, and firmness, The word of the pure vajra crossing over.
The phrase of the clarity of exhaustion and non-exhaustion; The phrase of the unconditioned and empty space;
The phrase of discerning the dwelling and the nest; The phrase of the wisdom-body that subdues;
The phrase of the cessation of the accumulation of suffering through the path; The phrase of the wisdom of the awakening to phenomena.
Just as an echo responds to sound, so too is inexhaustible eloquence;
preaching the Dharma without any dependence—this wisdom is pure like space.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Volume Fourteen.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Part Two.
The Buddha again addressed Gaganagañja, saying:
“Good son, what is meant by a bodhisattva whose practice of merit is equal to space?”
If a bodhisattva, hearing that the Buddha’s immeasurable dharmas are as vast as space, gives rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), they form this thought:
"Just as omniscience is immeasurable, so too the Buddha is immeasurable, and his sovereign awakening is immeasurable."

Within such immeasurability, one should give rise to immeasurable desire, diligence, and practice of heedfulness; for the sake of the Buddha-way, one should practice the immeasurable dharmas to be practiced by bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Just as the Buddhas possess bodies adorned with immeasurable merits, I too, in order to adorn my own body, should accomplish immeasurable roots of goodness.

Just as the Buddhas possess immeasurable merits that adorn their speech, adorn their minds, adorn their bodhimaṇḍas, and adorn their buddha-fields, so too shall I adorn my speech, mind, bodhimaṇḍa, and buddha-field;
I shall accomplish immeasurable roots of goodness, and I shall teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings;
for the sake of accomplishing these roots of goodness, I shall not give rise to weariness throughout immeasurable births and deaths.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable lands, immeasurable wisdom, and immeasurable supernormal powers.

Those sentient beings therein have immeasurable modes of conduct, immeasurable minds, and immeasurable differences in their faculties; within the cycle of birth and death, they undergo immeasurable masses of suffering and affliction, giving rise to various defilements.

In order to enter into the infinite dharmas of the Buddhas, and in order to abandon the mass of birth-and-death suffering and affliction associated with the various faculties and practices of infinite sentient beings, I have accomplished immeasurable roots of goodness.

With such a mind of right contemplation, the bodhisattva brings the merits they perform into correspondence with the various pāramitās, the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa), and the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma). They bring them into correspondence with the purification of sentient beings, the upholding of the true Dharma, the respectful offering and worship of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and the practices corresponding to the conduct of a bodhisattva.

The immeasurable merits thus performed are equal to space; because the nature of sentient beings is immeasurable, the wisdom of the Buddha is immeasurable, and the dharma-realm is immeasurable, that which is cultivated is likewise immeasurable.
Just as the nature of sentient beings is like space, the Buddha’s wisdom pervades the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without exception, so that all sentient beings receive its benefit.

The meritorious deeds performed by a bodhisattva are likewise: they reach every place to benefit sentient beings, because they are free from dependence and attachment, and by the power of their vows and skillful means (upāya).
“Good son! When a bodhisattva can practice in this way, their merit is equal to space. Good son!”
What is meant by "the bodhisattva’s practice of wisdom equal to space"?

If a bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), reflects upon it with skillful compliance and never becomes negligent regarding the various practices they undertake; having cultivated the perception of limited objects, they attain the perception of the immeasurable; having attained the perception of the immeasurable, they obtain such luminous wisdom (jñāna-āloka). Having obtained this luminous wisdom, they obtain the skillful means regarding the aggregates (skandha-upāya-jñāna), the skillful means regarding the elements (dhātu-upāya-jñāna), the skillful means regarding the sense bases (āyatana-upāya-jñāna), the skillful means regarding the truths (satya-upāya-jñāna), and the skillful means regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-upāya-jñāna).

He knows the defilements of sentient beings and he knows the nature of defilement; he knows the purity of sentient beings and he knows the nature of purity. That is to say, when a sentient being has a mind of attachment, he knows truly that there is a mind of attachment;
when there is no mind of attachment, he knows truly that there is no mind of attachment;
when there is a mind of anger, he knows truly that there is a mind of anger.
When there is no mind of ill will, he knows as it really is that there is no mind of ill will;
when there is a mind of delusion, he knows as it really is that there is a mind of delusion;
when there is no mind of delusion, he knows as it really is that there is no mind of delusion.
When there is a mind with afflictions, one knows as it truly is that there is a mind with afflictions;
when there is no mind with afflictions, one knows as it truly is that there is no mind with afflictions.
That bodhisattva does not perceive a defiled mind as inferior or an undefiled mind as superior. Why is this?

Because the bodhisattva has entered the wisdom of the dharma-gate of the purity of non-dual nature; as it is with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), so it is with the self-nature (*ātmatā*); as it is with the self-nature, so it is with the selfless nature (*anātmatā*); and as it is with the selfless nature, so it is with all phenomena, because their nature is pure.

If one enters into the purity of the nature of all phenomena, then one does not perceive any phenomena as being defiled or pure; nor does one perceive the characteristics or marks of the words for phenomena, because of non-acceptance and non-attachment; furthermore, one does not perceive any phenomena as being obstructed by hindrances or entanglements, nor as being unobstructed by hindrances or entanglements.
The Bodhisattva contemplates immeasurable realms; being free from the two dharmas of mind (*citta*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), this is called wisdom (*jñāna*) and not consciousness.

It is like space, which lacks mind, thought, or consciousness; the Bodhisattva is likewise, for he is free from mind, thought, and consciousness, knowing that the nature of all phenomena is equal to space. Because his practice of wisdom is unimpeded, it transcends all obstacles.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of wisdom that is equal to space. Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the mindfulness of the Buddha as permitted by the Tathāgata, which is never separated from suchness?

If a bodhisattva is in a forest hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, or in a wilderness, or in the open air, because they have attained the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are able to collect the mind so that it does not cling to various conditions. With an undistracted mind, they skillfully maintain the object of their recollection; through the aspects of practice, they accomplish the vision of the Tathāgata, whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics. Taking each individual mark and sign as the means to perfect their own body, their minds are directed toward the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), and they recollect the Tathāgata’s body emitting a net of radiant light.

The Bodhisattva, having attained the vision of liberation from desire, contemplates the body of the Tathāgata as filling one yojana, two yojanas, three, four, five, or ten yojanas, even up to a hundred yojanas.

If they pass beyond a hundred *yojanas*, through the attainment of the hope for liberation, they observe [the Buddha] seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), or see him turning the wheel of Dharma, or see him manifesting various dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) while preaching the Dharma to discipline sentient beings; or they see him performing buddha-works within a single buddha-world, or five buddha-worlds, or ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred buddha-worlds, up to performing buddha-works in hundreds of thousands of immeasurable worlds—this is the observation through the attainment of the hope for liberation.

Seeing for himself that he may act according to his will—whether listening to the Dharma, making offerings, or attending upon the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—he acts with sovereign freedom in all other modes of conduct. Having thus contemplated the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata, the bodhisattva recollects the Buddha’s meritorious qualities.

One may contemplate the precepts, or contemplation, or wisdom, or liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation; one may contemplate the powers and fearlessnesses, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, or the original practices of a bodhisattva, or the attainment of the stage of Buddhahood. Having universally recollected the merits accomplished by the Tathāgata, one then recollects the deeds of the Tathāgata: what are their characteristics?
How is karma created?
Is it created by the body,
or is it created by speech?
Is it created by the mind?
Is it created by deportment?
Is it visible?
Is it invisible? Is it expressible?
Or is it inexpressible?
In which lands were they created?
By how many types of bodies were they created?
Having thus performed various kinds of superior deeds and accomplished inconceivable roots of goodness, [he attained this state].
"Contemplating the Dharma of the Tathāgata: the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called Tathāgatas by virtue of their Dharma-body, not their form-body.

That Bodhisattva does not see form as the Tathāgata, does not see marks as the Tathāgata, does not see lineage as the Tathāgata, does not see the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases as the Tathāgata, and does not see deportment as..."
The Tathāgata does not perceive the past, future, or present worlds as the Tathāgata;
he does not perceive causes as the Tathāgata; he does not perceive conditions as the Tathāgata; he does not perceive reasons as the Tathāgata;
he does not perceive combinations as the Tathāgata; he does not perceive existence as the Tathāgata; he does not perceive non-existence as the Tathāgata.
One does not perceive the accomplishment of the Tathāgata; one does not perceive the disintegration of the Tathāgata;
one does not perceive the Tathāgata as being there; one does not perceive the Tathāgata as being here; one does not perceive the Tathāgata as being anywhere;
one does not perceive the Tathāgata; one does not rely upon the Tathāgata; one does not discriminate the Tathāgata; and one does not apprehend the Tathāgata.

For example, just as space has no names such as aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*), yet it is not without benefit to sentient beings; so too, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no names such as aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, yet they are likewise not without benefit to sentient beings.
“Good son! This is what the Tathāgata has authorized as the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Buddha that does not depart from suchness (tathatā). Good son!”
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being separated from the recollection of the Dharma as permitted by the Tathāgata?

It is when a bodhisattva recollects the Dharma, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the four noble truths, the profound twelve links of dependent origination, and the six perfections.
The treasury in which a bodhisattva should train, the three pure objects of the non-retrogressive wheel—these are the dharmas that a bodhisattva should keep in mind.
How should they be kept in mind?

He contemplates relinquishment; he contemplates the desire for detachment; he contemplates cessation; he contemplates the absence of coming and going; he contemplates the absence of a dwelling place; he contemplates the absence of intrinsic nature; he contemplates that which transcends the world; he contemplates thorough understanding; he contemplates exhaustion; he contemplates non-arising; he contemplates non-grasping; he contemplates the outflow-free; he contemplates the unconditioned; and he contemplates that nirvāṇa is without intrinsic nature.
To form such a thought is still to possess the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) among all phenomena.

Why is this? Because where there is a notion, there is mental agitation; because there is mental agitation, one dwells in perversion; and for one who dwells in perversion, there is no mindfulness of the Dharma.

"If one is free from the two notions of dharma and non-dharma, and having realized that all dharmas are unarisen, one severs the notion of dharmas and thereby attains the patience of the unarisen (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); this is because one attains non-attainment, as there is nothing to be possessed."
"Good son! This is what is called 'not being separated from suchness,' as permitted by the Tathāgata. Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva’s non-separation from the Tathāgata’s sanctioned mindfulness of the Saṃgha? "Saṃgha" refers to the four pairs and eight classes of noble beings.

Within the Saṃgha, there are those who are candidates for the fruit of arhatship and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship; those who are candidates for the fruit of anāgāmin and those who have attained the fruit of anāgāmin; those who are candidates for the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin and those who have attained the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin; and those who are candidates for the fruit of srotāpanna and those who have attained the fruit of srotāpanna. These constitute the śrāvaka-saṃgha.

"Furthermore, there is a Sangha consisting of those bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive, who have attained definitive patience (*niyata-kṣānti*), and who have entered the supreme, holy, and correct station (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Having already abandoned all signs, attachments, and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), they next attain the uninterrupted [realization] of the Tathāgata’s qualities."

That bodhisattva, mindful of such a multitude of great bodhisattvas, should offer them worship and praise, join his palms in service, circumambulate them to the right, and pay them homage; for they are a field of merit that is most auspicious, the foremost Sangha who have entered the ranks of the noble ones, and those who have already accomplished all that the Sangha ought to do.
This bodhisattva recollects the Saṃgha; he draws near to the bodhisattva-saṃgha and does not draw near to the śrāvaka-saṃgha.

Although that bodhisattva recollects the Saṃgha, he does not grasp at it as a numerical category, nor does he grasp at it as existing as a number. He knows that the Saṃgha is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); he recollects it as being without activity, without change, without arising, and without cessation. Recollecting it in this way, he does not give rise to the sphere of mental activity.
"Good son! This is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the Saṅgha as permitted by the Tathāgata, which is not separate from suchness. Good son!"
What is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of relinquishment as permitted by the Tathāgata?
It is the relinquishing of material wealth and the relinquishing of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is the relinquishing of body and life, and the relinquishing of all false paths.
Furthermore, there is relinquishment, which does not grasp at any phenomena. Why is this?
Where there is grasping, there is no relinquishment.
If one does not grasp, it is called ultimate relinquishment.
Within ultimate relinquishment, there is no seeking; one who does not seek does not hope for recompense. Because one does not hope for recompense, this is called true relinquishment.
If a bodhisattva practices such firm relinquishment, they make a vow in accordance with that relinquishment.

At the time of relinquishing and at the time of making the vow, they do not perceive a bodhi or the Buddha-dharma, but focus their mindfulness solely on relinquishment, reflecting: "How did the bodhisattvas of the past practice relinquishment when they were cultivating the path?"
"How should I now practice equanimity? Will I not fall short and be censured by the wise?
Thinking thus, he was able to relinquish everything.
Having relinquished it all, he analyzed that which was relinquished: "Who is the one who relinquishes?"
What objects are relinquished?
Who performs the recollection?
Having analyzed in this way, nothing at all is found.

Not perceiving the one who relinquishes, the object given, or that which is recollected—this is what constitutes a bodhisattva’s mindfulness of relinquishment as permitted by the Tathāgata, never departing from suchness. "Good son!..."
What is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the precepts as permitted by the Tathāgata, which is never abandoned?

It is when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts to the point of reaching the state of liberation, perfecting their deportment and conduct; they regard even the most minor precept with fear as if it were a vajra, constantly cultivating a pure livelihood, and skillfully guarding and upholding the precepts.

The Bodhisattva reflects that the precepts restrain body and speech; though these are of the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), he reverently observes them with vigilance. He cultivates the supreme right livelihood, never abandoning it for the sake of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*). Being pure and unshakable, he likewise never abandons great loving-kindness and great compassion. He gathers in and instructs sentient beings who have broken the precepts, and would rather sacrifice his own body and life than seek any other vehicle; this is called morality.

The Bodhisattva contemplates the superior precepts: the precept that is without flaw or defect, the precept that is not coarse or defiled, the precept that is not sought after [for gain], the precept that is unstained, the precept that is free from turbidity, and the precept praised by the wise; the Bodhisattva contemplates such precepts as these.

One does not rely on the observance of precepts nor disparage their violation; one does not praise one's own virtues nor criticize the faults of others; ultimately, one neither abandons the precepts, nor relies upon them, nor dwells within them.

Although he practices the conduct of form while having relinquished all reliance and attachment, this is the bodhisattva’s non-separation from the mindfulness of precepts as permitted by the Tathāgata. "Good son!..."
What is the bodhisattva’s non-separation from the recollection of the gods as permitted by the Tathāgata?
It is when a bodhisattva recollects the gods—namely, recollecting the gods of the desire realm, or the form realm, or the formless realm.

Because they recollect the karmic fruit of observing the precepts while in the heavens of the desire realm, they experience agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; they sport and enjoy themselves with the five celestial desires, freely satisfying themselves with celestial garments and food, experiencing exclusively love, joy, and pleasant satisfaction.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"All these prosperities must inevitably decline and perish; even these gods are subject to impermanence and transformation.
Because of negligence, they do not cultivate roots of goodness; the virtuous karma they previously possessed will now all be exhausted."
"Although these devas have been born in the heavens, they have not yet escaped the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva did not aspire to be born in any of the celestial abodes of the desire realm, with the sole exception of the Tuṣita Heaven palace.

In the Tuṣita palace, there is a Bodhisattva in his final birth who has reached the further shore in all bodhisattva practices; he has crossed to the further shore in all stages, all supernormal powers, all meditative concentrations, all dhāraṇīs, all eloquence, all bodhisattva activities, and all skillful means.
One should simply recollect such merits and give rise to a heart of joyful admiration for this deva realm; those who wish to be born in heaven should aspire to be born in such a celestial abode.
The Bodhisattva resolves, saying:
"When shall I attain such a celestial body?
The Bodhisattva further reflects:

"Regarding the devas of the form realm: these various devas are born in those celestial abodes as the fruit and retribution of the various dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Having transcended the afflictions of desire belonging to the desire realm, they dwell in one-pointed meditative concentration, taking joy as their sustenance, and experience exclusively the reception of the foremost reward of bliss."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Those devas of the form realm experience only slight flavors and yet take them as joy; they perceive permanence in the impermanent, pleasure in suffering, a self in what is non-self, and nirvana in what is not nirvana."
"These devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise subject to impermanence and change; they have not yet escaped their lot as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.

Thus, this bodhisattva does not wish to be born in the abodes of the devas of the form realm, with the sole exception of the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens—those from which one enters parinirvāṇa without returning to this world.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"These are the pure devas who have already been liberated from the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Because of this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of reverence and respect, yet does not desire or seek rebirth in those places.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:

"The devas of the formless realm receive the retribution of the formless meditative absorptions; having already transcended the desire realm and the form realm, their minds abide in the tranquility of meditative concentration."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"These devas of the formless realm are far removed from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Sangha. These devas do not know how to seek the way out of the formless realm; even if they dwell there for a long time, they will inevitably undergo transformation and extinction, and have not yet escaped their lot as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals."
"For this reason, I do not wish to be born even in those celestial realms.
I only form this thought:
'I shall become a God among Gods—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"

Although this bodhisattva contemplates the various devas, he does not rely on the celestial abodes of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; rather, he gives rise to great compassion for the sentient beings within the three realms. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva not departing from the recollection of the devas as permitted by the Tathāgata.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva practice the equality of all dharmas as being like nirvāṇa?

If a bodhisattva knows how to enter the equality of all dharmas as being like nirvāṇa, and perceives that the nature of all sentient beings is identical to nirvāṇa—having known this, they realize that for those who have entered nirvāṇa, there are no aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*).”

In this way, the bodhisattva perceives that the nature of sentient beings is identical to nirvāṇa, transcending the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; he sees them as like shadows and like dreams. Though there is no birth or death, they manifest birth and death; because ordinary beings are bound by fetters and afflictions, they create karmic actions of affliction, and having created such karmic actions, they undergo immeasurable retributions of suffering.

By the power of the prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the fetters and afflictions so as to sever them and prevent their arising; furthermore, he does not undergo the retribution of suffering due to the karma produced by those [fetters], and attains the state of equality that is nirvāṇa, which is termed the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Having transcended all paths of numerical calculation, because they do not forsake their original vows, they sport in great compassion; having reached the further shore of wisdom and skillful means, they have entered the supernatural powers of the Buddhas; they are already able to skillfully know and distinguish all conceptualizations. Having themselves attained deliverance, they deliver those not yet delivered; having themselves attained liberation, they liberate those not yet liberated; having themselves attained peace, they bring peace to those not yet at peace; having themselves attained nirvāṇa, they cause those who have not attained it to attain it. Regarding nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, they harbor no dualistic thoughts. This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the equality of all dharmas, which is like nirvāṇa.
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva who skillfully discerns the characteristics of practice?

It is when a bodhisattva exerts diligent effort in seeking the supreme wholesome dharmas, enters into and deliberates upon profound dharma-gates with the mind, and through pure, penetrating, and sharp distribution of wisdom-light, attains the gateway of great wisdom-light.”

By the power of this gate of great wisdom and clarity, one knows the inclinations and movements of the minds of all sentient beings; in brief, it is said that for each and every sentient being there are eighty-four thousand types of conduct, all of which can be fully known: namely, twenty-one thousand types of greedy conduct, twenty-one thousand types of hateful conduct, twenty-one thousand types of deluded conduct, and twenty-one thousand types of balanced conduct (equal parts). These constitute the eighty-four thousand types of conduct, and every single sentient being possesses these modes of behavior.
If explained in detail, there are immeasurable modes of practice.

Within each individual mode of practice, one knows there are eighty-four thousand faculties; within each individual faculty, one knows there are eighty-four thousand kinds of distinct inclinations. Thus, one fully knows the distinct characteristics of all practices, faculties, and inclinations, as well as the characteristics of what should be cultivated.
"What is knowing the characteristics of differentiation?

To know that these various formations (*saṃskāra*), faculties (*indriya*), and dispositions (*adhimokṣa*) are the characteristic of greed, the characteristic of hatred, the characteristic of delusion, the characteristic of equal proportions (*samabhāga*), the characteristic of decrease, the characteristic of increase, the characteristic of stability, and the characteristic of penetration—this is called knowing the characteristics of differentiation."
“What is the characteristic of that which should be cultivated?

It is knowing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), faculties (*indriya*), and dispositions (*adhimukti*) as having the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of non-self, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of cessation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of reality-as-it-is, the characteristic of nirvāṇa, the characteristic of the self-emptiness of characteristics, and the characteristic of the self-detachment of characteristics.”

If one can know these various activities, faculties, and inclinations—just as the Tathāgata, having accomplished unimpeded wisdom regarding all activities, knows the distinct characteristics of the activities, faculties, and inclinations of all sentient beings—and if the Bodhisattva likewise knows them through a wisdom that follows that of the Tathāgata, yet does not abandon the practices of a Bodhisattva, teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness, this is called "skillfully discerning the characteristics of activity."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva uphold the precious treasury of all Buddha-dharmas? Good son!”
The Tathāgatagarbha is inexhaustible and immeasurable; it reaches all places and brings joy to all sentient beings.
According to the various actions, faculties, and inclinations of sentient beings—of which there are immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas—it is inconceivable, incomparable, and unfathomable.
The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is likewise immeasurable, asanṅkhyeya, inconceivable, incomparable, and unfathomable.

Regarding the written words of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, even if all sentient beings were like Ānanda and others, they could not receive, uphold, read, or recite them for one kalpa or even up to a hundred kalpas, nor could they master them thoroughly apart from their meaning.

Why is this so? Because all the treasures of the Dharma of the Tathāgata have but a single meaning: namely, the meaning of detachment from desire, the meaning of cessation, and the meaning of nirvāṇa.

If a bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, receives it according to their capacity, upholds, recites, and masters it, and then skillfully accords with right contemplation by practicing exactly as received.
"When a bodhisattva enters the gateway of the Dharma-treasury, maintains firm contemplation, and does not rely on the practice of any signs, they then attain the gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi."

Having attained the gates of *dhāraṇī* and the gates of *samādhi*, they are able to uphold the words and meanings of the Dharma-treasury of a single Tathāgata—whether two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or even immeasurable, boundless, *asaṃkhyeya*, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, measureless, and beyond all measure—and with their minds undistracted regarding the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, they receive, uphold, read, recite, and master its words and meanings, explaining them extensively for others, relying on the meaning rather than the letter.
