Just as a great mass of dry charcoal does not burn empty space, one who understands afflictions is not burned by them.
As space is eternally abiding and subject to no decay, so too are all phenomena; they eternally abide within the Dharma-realm.
Just as space receives all forms, so too does the dharma-realm receive all phenomena.
As space is not form and its characteristics cannot be seen, the nature of the mind is likewise like space, without characteristics.
Space is a mere conventional designation and possesses no form or appearance; so too are mind, intellect, and consciousness, which are likewise spoken of as mere conventional designations.
Just as space is boundless and ultimately cannot be grasped, so it is with the wisdom of the Great Being, which is equal to space.
Just as a bird flies through the sky leaving no tracks, so it is with the practice of bodhi; its progress cannot be seen.
When the body has perished and passed away, it is equal to empty space; the present aggregates are likewise identical in nature to empty space.
The four great elements are likewise, identical to empty space; as after the three calamities, no diverse characteristics remain.
All sentient beings cannot fill the void; ordinary people are thus—the five desires can never be satisfied.
If one possesses noble wisdom and knows all phenomena, they are content and have no further seeking, being free from lustful attachment.
Just as space is vast and has no boundaries or shores, so too is the Buddha-dharma, having no limits.
One who knows the nature of all phenomena as being the Buddha-dharma does not rely on things, nor does he abandon things.
Knowing that things are non-things, he dwells in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); regarding things and non-things, he perceives no dual characteristics.
By means of sound one speaks of emptiness, yet the nature of emptiness is not sound; where there is no sound, that is called emptiness.
Although the Buddha spoke of emptiness, in the end he said nothing; the nature of emptiness is ineffable, and for this reason it is called empty.
Like illusions, transformations, dreams, mirages, echoes, and shadows— The teachings of all Buddhas are entirely like this.
To guide sentient beings, they speak such metaphors; Yet for the meaning of true purity, there is no further analogy.
All dharmas are without marks; yet they are spoken of as having marks according to convention. Both mark and marklessness are equally absent within the dharma-nature.
To take emptiness as a mark, and for emptiness itself to be without mark—to realize this nature of marks is what constitutes a bodhisattva.
Unobstructed and unimpeded, without playfulness and without movement, without beginning and without end— this is a bodhisattva.
Not departing from sentient beings, yet not included within the category of sentient beings, being like the very nature of sentient beings— this is a bodhisattva.
It is like a magician who kills many illusory people; in reality, there is no one who dies. Those who are delivered are likewise so.
Illusions and sentient beings, nirvana and the Buddha-dharma—know them to be of the same nature:
without nature and without marks.
This Great Being has attained the treasury of untainted emptiness, which suffices for all and is inexhaustible.
Having cultivated manifold virtues in the past, he has obtained this treasury; yet, because there is no hoarding or accumulation, he is able to act in such a manner.
One who can know that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions possesses an inexhaustible treasury, inconceivable.
The Great Sage, Savior of the World, has taught four things that are inexhaustible: emptiness, the mind of the Way, sentient beings, and the Buddha’s practice.
If wealth were a treasure, it could be accumulated; since it is not a treasure and possesses no inherent essence, it is therefore inexhaustible.
The ultimate nature of phenomena is emptiness; having reached exhaustion, there is no exhaustion, and this non-exhaustion is what is called "inexhaustibility."
"Those who know this gate are near to bodhi; by abiding in this gate, they shall swiftly accomplish bodhi.

By the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, such sublime teachings and material wealth rained down from the sky above, causing all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to obtain immeasurable, inconceivable happiness and to have their aspirations fulfilled.

Sentient beings afflicted by illness and suffering receive medicine and are healed; destitute and impoverished beings obtain immeasurable treasures; those in bondage and confinement attain awakening and liberation; those with impaired faculties all become fully endowed; those destined for execution have various emanated beings rain down from the sky to suffer in their stead; those separated from loved ones for a long time all rejoice in reunion; sentient beings tormented by grief all become free from sorrow; and sentient beings fallen into the three miserable realms, touched by the light, have all their sufferings removed and experience physical and mental bliss.

At that time, the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm each partook of food and drink, engaged in play, and fully enjoyed the five sensory pleasures together. Some practiced giving and performed various meritorious deeds; all sentient beings attained such joys as these and each exclaimed:
"It is because this Great Being, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, has appeared in the world, that he is able to bestow worldly happiness upon us."
"One who is able to bestow the nectar of immortality upon the world is indeed able to constantly and diligently provide happiness to all sentient beings without weariness.
Thus did the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha manifest such supernatural transformations, gladdening the dispositions of all sentient beings and demonstrating the spiritual power of a bodhisattva.

By means of material gifts and the gift of Dharma, he gathers in sentient beings, causing immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and causing immeasurable bodhisattvas to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, by causing immeasurable, asankhyeya, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas to exert diligent vigor, they cause them to achieve all the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, and to attain the gates of sporting in supernatural powers.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Arising Doubt had this thought:
"This is inconceivable and unprecedented!
Does the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha manifest such various supernormal powers only within the Sahā world?"
"Does he also manifest various kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) in other world-systems?

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Bodhisattva Saṃjātaśaṅka, immediately emitted light from his body; by the power of this radiance, he universally illumined the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Arising-Doubt and the other bodhisattvas all saw how, through the power of spiritual transformations, Ākāśagarbha was manifesting and transforming sentient beings in the infinite, boundless, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; this was exactly as it was in this Sahā world, without any difference, and was something that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas could possibly accomplish.
Upon seeing such a miraculous manifestation, the Bodhisattva Janmacitra’s net of doubt was immediately severed. He joined his palms, prostrated to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, and spoke these words:
“How marvelous, O Mahāsattva!”

How is it that you are able to place this inexhaustible treasury within the void of space, raining down in abundance upon immeasurable worlds without ever being depleted? Great Being, how long has it been since you placed this treasury in the sky?
Gaganagañja said: "Good son!
Since the time I first resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this treasury has always been present within space."
The Bodhisattva Jātasamśaya asked again: "Great Being!
How much time has passed since you first resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Ākāśagarbha replied, “World-Honored One, you should know that you may question him. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Saṃśayajaha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja first resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much time has elapsed?
We pray that you will explain this for us, so as to remove our doubts.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Saṃśayajaha, saying: "Good son!
This matter is remote, profound, and difficult to know."
"If it were to be spoken, it would cause all devas and humans to give rise to doubt and fail to believe the Buddha’s words; because of this lack of faith, they would incur immeasurable sin.
The Bodhisattva Birth-Doubt addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will explain it.
Those who have long cultivated roots of goodness will surely believe and accept it.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Seng-i (Arising-Doubt):
“Good son! Since you have so earnestly desired to hear this, how could I not speak?
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well.
I shall analyze and explain it for you, so that those who possess firm roots of goodness and have long cultivated the foundations of merit may give rise to joy.
"O son of good family!
Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and each grain of sand from all these Ganges Rivers represented a Buddha-field.

If all those Buddha-fields were ground into a mass of fine dust and placed in one location, and a long-lived person were to take a single grain of dust from this pile once every hundred kalpas until the entire mass was exhausted—the number of kalpas it would take for the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to have first resolved his mind toward enlightenment exceeds even that number; it is beyond the reach of calculation.
"Good son! You should know the length of time since Ākāśagarbha first resolved his mind upon enlightenment by means of this analogy. Good son!"

In the distant past, beyond as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the sands of the Ganges, and taking each grain of sand from all those Ganges Rivers to represent a Buddha-field, suppose one were to reduce all those Buddha-fields to atoms of dust.

After further passing hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas beyond that number, there appeared a Buddha named Pure All-Vows Majestic Virtuous Victorious King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That world is named Manifesting the Buddha-fields of Immeasurable Buddhas, and its eon is named Adorned with Myriad Jewels.
For what reason is that world named Manifesting the Buddha-fields of Immeasurable Buddhas?
"Good son! Because that buddha-field is truly pure, it can manifest the buddha-fields of the ten directions, just as a clear moon free from clouds appears in still water."

"Good son! For this reason, the immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as well as those Buddhas together with their lion-thrones, and all that sentient beings have created, appear within those lands. Therefore, that world is named 'Manifesting Immeasurable Lands.'"

"That world is equal in extent to ten billion trichiliocosms; it is vast, magnificent, pure, abundant, peaceful, and secure, with gods and humans flourishing in great numbers. Its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, free from hills, mounds, or any impurities and filth. It abounds in various precious gems, inlaid and interspersed to form a landscape that is both majestic and delightful."

It was adorned with suspended silken streamers, banners, and flowered canopies; sandalwood, aloeswood, and various exquisite incenses were burned; multicolored *karpāsa* cloth was spread over it, and the ground was strewn with wonderful flowers of many jewels.

In every place, there were trees of precious flowers, fruit trees, clothing trees, garland trees, music trees, jewel-vessel trees, incense trees, lamp trees, and medicinal trees, all of which served as universal adornments.
The eightfold path within that realm is level, straight, distinct, and clearly defined, adorned with pearl necklaces and jeweled nets, such that those who behold it never grow weary.

That world does not rely on the light of the sun and moon for illumination; rather, it is lit by various lamp-trees and mani-jewel trees. There is no distinction between day and night; the passage of time is known only by the opening and closing of precious flowers.

"In that world, there are no sentient beings who are blind, cross-eyed, hunchbacked, dwarfed, lame, or crippled; none with incomplete limbs, nor those with ugly countenances, soiled faces, or squinting eyes. There are no such unsightly sentient beings; all sentient beings are endowed with the thirty-two marks, which adorn their bodies."
In that world, even the names of the three miserable realms, the eight difficulties, and various evils do not exist; nor is the sound of heterodox teachers or those of divergent studies ever heard.
All sentient beings in that world are destined for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and there is not even the name of *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*.

That Buddha exclusively teaches the Bodhisattva Vehicle; in that world, there are no women nor those born from a womb. All sentient beings are born by spontaneous transformation sitting in the full lotus posture, and they exhaust their lifespans without even the names of old age or illness.
After his life comes to an end, he will be reborn in another pure buddha-field or return to his own original land. "Good son!
That land has accomplished such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merit that even if I were to speak of those merits for an eon or slightly less than an eon, I could never exhaust them."

“Good son! At that time, within the manifestation of immeasurable Buddha-fields, there was a universal monarch named Sarvadevābhiṣeka (Consecrated by All Devas), who ruled over a trichiliocosm. Having long planted the roots of virtue in the presence of various Buddhas, he possessed sharp faculties, fierce wisdom, and perfected majestic power.”
The consecrated holy king had thirty-six thousand sons, all of whom were born by transformation within lotus flowers, and all of whom had long planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas.

At that time, the Tathāgata King Victorious in the Majesty of All Purified Vows was respectfully surrounded by a great assembly of devas and humans; he traveled to the abode of the consecrated holy kings of the various heavens, accompanied by an immeasurable and incalculable host of bodhisattvas, beyond what could be calculated even by mathematicians or their disciples.
The lifespan of that Buddha lasts for a hundred thousand kalpas; the duration of those kalpas is equal to that of this Bhadrakalpa.
The sentient beings of that world perceive the passage of so many kalpas as being equivalent to a single kalpa.

"At that time, the Universal Monarch Sarvadevābhiṣeka invited the Tathāgata Viśuddhasarvapraṇidhānatejovikrāmin and the assembly of bodhisattvas for forty intermediate kalpas—the duration of which is as described for an intermediate kalpa—and made offerings of pleasing delicacies and food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, towers, pavilions, gardens, groves, bathing pools, and all such various necessities."

"At that time, the Universal Monarch Abhiṣikta, in order to make an offering to the Buddha, adorned a small chiliocosm as a sublime hall. Its ground was entirely embellished with lapis lazuli jewels; its surrounding walls were composed of various precious gems; its pillars were made of red sandalwood and Uotāra-pāra sandalwood; and its lintels and brackets were made of musaragalva jewels. Interspersed within this hall were such adornments, all combined to form a structure most delightful to behold."
After the World-Honored One had finished his midday meal, he arose from samādhi and preached the sublime Dharma for the great assembly within this hall.

He further adorned another hall to equal in size one four-continent world-system, desiring that the Tathāgata and the community of Bodhisattvas eat therein; the value of the precious jewels used daily for their food was like a mountain of piled-up treasure.

“Good son! At that time, the Universal Monarch Sarvaratnapratimaṇḍitābhiṣeka constantly maintained single-minded focus for forty intermediate kalpas; he never became negligent nor engaged in any other affairs, but always provided all manner of articles of pleasure as offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.”
Throughout that entire period, he performed meritorious deeds without ever making vows or seeking anything for himself.
After forty intermediate kalpas had passed, on the final day, he offered three priceless robes to the Tathāgata and presented one robe each to all the bodhisattvas in the assembly.
On that day, after the midday meal, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the great assembly.
At that time, the celestial consecrated holy kings (abhiṣikta-rāja), surrounded by their retinues, went to the Buddha’s dwelling in order to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the merits of that noble king were pure and wholesome, and that he was capable and fit for the task, remained together with the assembly of devas and the consecrated wheel-turning sage-kings for seven days and seven nights without any thought of food. Seated upon the lion throne, his body unmoving, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled "The Expedient Means of the Non-Retrogressive Wheel for Gathering Bodhisattvas in Pure Conduct."
The World-Honored One taught this Dharma in order that they might receive and uphold it entirely, never forgetting or losing it.

For seven days and seven nights, the consecrated noble king did not allow his mind to be distracted; having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, he was filled with joy and exultation, his heart overflowing with delight. Rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him seven times to the right. Having completed the seven circumambulations, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha with a profound and sincere heart, and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Then he spoke in verse:
"I have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, Invoking all living beings;
To those without refuge, I shall be their savior, Opening the great light in this dark world."
It is not for the practice of a single dharma, nor for making offerings to a single Buddha,
nor for the sake of a single sentient being; it is because of the vow to deliver all beings without exception from the sufferings of birth,
old age, sickness, and death, and from those oppressed by manifold afflictions.
Do not fear anything at all; I vow that I shall surely deliver you.
Those shrouded by desire, hatred, delusion, and pride, who have lost the Way and committed various evils—I shall rightly sever their wicked karma and lead them to the city of fearlessness.
Sentient beings fallen into the three miserable realms, Enduring manifold sufferings in those difficult places— Summon a firm resolve and do not fear; I have come to bestow upon you fearlessness.
Obscured by the delusion of ignorance, They do not recognize the gate of liberation.
I have lit the torch of the Dharma, Attaining clarity and reaching Nirvana.
For those drifting on the four currents, Sunk and unable to reach the shore,
I have fashioned a supreme Dharma-ship To ferry them across the streams of existence.
"Abiding in the famine of birth and death, their food—the sweet karma of their past—is exhausted;
I shall act as their guide and lead them to ultimate peace and happiness.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Śaṅkā-jāta, saying:
“Good son! At that time, when the consecrated holy king had spoken these verses, that buddha-world shook in six ways and was pervaded by radiant light.”
At that time, once the Holy King had given rise to the bodhicitta, he immediately attained a bodhisattva samādhi called "Non-retrogression of the Bodhicitta.
By the power of this samādhi, he was able to constantly see all Buddhas without obstruction; even within his dreams, no afflictions caused him any distress.

From that time forward, his mind was no longer accompanied by envy, nor by breaking the precepts, nor by anger, nor by indolence, nor by distraction; his mind was not associated with ignorance or the like.

That consecrated holy king served at the side of the World-Honored One for the remainder of his life, in order to hear the Dharma; furthermore, he constantly exhorted thirty-six thousand sons to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and likewise exhorted immeasurable and boundless other sentient beings to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son! As for that consecrated universal monarch of the gods at that time, could he have been anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought; it was none other than the present Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.”

At that time, those princes and the great assembly whom he instructed to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—I now see them here in this very assembly as these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of great power, diligence, and wisdom who are listening to the Dharma.
“Good son! Since the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he has practiced the bodhisattva path for such immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

From the moment he first resolved his mind, this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has never lost the bodhicitta and has never been born from a womb; he has constantly encountered all Buddhas, listened to the Dharma, and made offerings to the Saṅgha. Under the various Buddhas, he has upheld the True Dharma, taking its integration as his primary focus without ever losing mindfulness, and is able to skillfully discern and accomplish universal conduct.”

Having first resolved their minds upon enlightenment, they attain the profound and difficult-to-understand first stage (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; they are able to practice all forms of giving, achieve great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and become free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Without weariness, they exert diligent effort, study all treatises, and understand all worldly phenomena. They achieve a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) and attain firm power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).

"This Bodhisattva, dwelling in the first stage, throughout immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, incalculable, unfathomable, unspeakable, and beyond-description eons, is able to purify and fully perfect the practice of the dāna-pāramitā with utmost sincerity."

Constantly practicing great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, diligently cultivating the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), all the *pāramitās*, and all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), and accomplishing aspiration, diligence, heedfulness, and so forth—all these accord with the *dānapāramitā*.

"This Bodhisattva, dwelling in the first stage, constantly and diligently serves and makes offerings to all Buddhas, and diligently seeks skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands."

Abiding in the first stage, one attains entry into the light of wisdom of all stages without yet transcending the first stage; thereafter, one accomplishes immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom, obtains the sustaining power of the Tathāgata’s non-regressive supernormal powers, and becomes free from the obstructions of all stages.

From the first stage, they enter the second stage of the Bodhisattva and dwell therein for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, purifying the second stage and practicing the Śīla-pāramitā up to the tenth stage; the number of kalpas spent for the sake of each and every sentient being is likewise the same.

Within each and every stage, they accomplish the bodhisattva practices throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, manifesting buddha-activities for the sake of all sentient beings, yet never abandoning the conduct of a bodhisattva.

“Good son! There are few bodhisattvas who are able to practice such profound, inconceivable, supreme, and undistracted cultivation with single-minded diligence and progress, as has been accomplished by this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Arising-Doubt asked the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:
"How marvelous, O son of good family!
You are indeed able to make such a great vow, remaining for so long within the cycle of birth and death for the sake of this Mahāyāna without weariness?"
Ākāśagarbha replied: "Good son!

Does this great earth, which carries and supports the mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, trees, groves, all medicinal herbs, the hundred grains, crops, and all sentient beings, ever experience weariness?"
He replied: "No, Great Being!"
Gaganagañja said: "Noble son, the minds of all bodhisattvas are also like the great earth."
"In the same way, because of the perfection of pure devotion, practicing the bodhisattva path without weariness is also like this.
Ākāśagarbha spoke again: "Noble son!"
Just as this great earth rests upon the waters, and these waters sustain the earth without weariness, so too is it with the minds of the bodhisattvas:
by the power of their great compassion, they transform and guide sentient beings without weariness in the same way.
Ākāśagarbha spoke again:
"Good son! Just as this great water rests upon the wind, this wind sustains the water without ever becoming weary."
"The minds of all bodhisattvas are also like a great wind; because of the power of their great skillful means, they purify Buddha-worlds without ever becoming weary, and it is likewise so.
Ākāśagarbha spoke again: "Virtuous son!
It is like a great wind abiding in space without any support; this space sustains the wind without obstruction or weariness.
The minds of bodhisattvas are likewise like the wind and space: by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they gather all Buddha-dharmas without indolence, abandonment, or weariness, and it is just so.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva knows the characteristics of all phenomena; thus they accomplish the substance of non-arising, wherein there is no agent and no recipient, yet that which is produced exists through the synthesis of causes and conditions.

All dharmas that are performed likewise lack reality; because their original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is empty and their original limit is detached, they are not truly established. Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty, they are without arising and without cessation. Knowing that the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas are thus, one does not perceive any dharma that could give rise to weariness, nor any wearying agent.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are non-dual; he knows that the nature of birth and death is equal to the nature of nirvāṇa, that the nature of nirvāṇa is equal to the nature of all phenomena, and that the nature of all phenomena is equal to the nature of non-existence; therefore, he neither relies upon nor clings to them.

Knowing that all phenomena have no intrinsic nature at the limits of the past and the future, by the power of meditative concentration and the power of their vows, they are able to manifest all their activities without arising from that concentration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃśayajaha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Being will explain the practices and activities of the samādhis of all bodhisattvas."
"What is meant by samādhi?
What is meant by practicing the work of samādhi?
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied to the Bodhisattva Janmacitra:
“Good son! There are eighty-four thousand gateways of samādhi; these gateways of samādhi can comprehensively encompass all other samādhis.”
“What are these eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi?
Son of good family!
A bodhisattva possesses a samādhi called ‘Never Forgetting the Bodhicitta,’ which is able to accomplish the practice of non-distraction.”
There is a samādhi called "Subduing," which can purify and bring one to ultimate sincerity.
There is a samādhi called "Non-manifest Practice," which can ultimately accomplish and perfect that which is never regressed.
There is a samādhi called Non-Reliance, which can further the accomplishment of the ultimate.
There is a samādhi called Stainless, which can accomplish the pure mind.
There is a samādhi called Illumination, which can reveal and demonstrate wholesome dharmas.
There is a samādhi called True Purity, which can turn back all demonic activities.
There is a samādhi called Leaping Forth, which is never overcome by the various treatises of non-Buddhists.
There is a samādhi named "Renunciation," which can subdue all afflictions and fetters.
There is a samādhi named "Turning Back," which can cause all beings to enter the path of reality.
There is a samādhi called "Progressive Advancement," by which one can leave behind the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
There is a samādhi called "Delightful Roaming," by which one does not grow weary of birth and death.
There is a samādhi called "Proceeding," because it enables one to go from one stage to another stage.
There is a samādhi called "Delightful," because it enables one to accomplish the joy and satisfaction of the great assembly.
There is a samādhi called Unobstructed Light, which can bring about a mind of equality toward all sentient beings.
There is a samādhi called Knowing What Is to Be Done, because it can accord with all that is to be done without opposition.
There is a samādhi called Lion’s Mark, which can bring about fearlessness for the great assembly.
There is a samādhi called Courageous Mind, which can subdue the four māras.
There is a samādhi called Lotus Adornment, which can accomplish non-attachment to worldly dharmas.
There is a samādhi called Light Adornment, which can universally illumine all Buddha-worlds.
There is a samādhi called "Coolness," because it can sever and eliminate both hatred and attachment.
There is a samādhi called "Banner Mark," because it can accomplish the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas.
There is a samādhi named Torch King, which can accomplish the radiance of great wisdom.
There is a samādhi named Sunlight, which can accomplish the eradication of the darkness of ignorance.
There is a samādhi called "Accumulation of Merit," which can accomplish inexhaustible eloquence.
There is a samādhi called "Nārāyaṇa," which can accomplish a vajra-body.
There is a samādhi called "Firmness," which can accomplish the mind that is free from agitation.
There is a samādhi called "Sumeru Banner," which can accomplish the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
There is a samādhi called Firm Mastery, which can accomplish the fulfillment of original vows.
There is a samādhi called Vajra Being, which can accomplish the non-retrogressive superknowledges.
There is a samādhi called the Vajra Field, which can accomplish the ascent to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
There is a samādhi called Like a Vajra, which is well able to penetrate and discern all dharmas.
There is a samādhi called King of Conduct, which can observe the mental activities of all sentient beings.
There is a samādhi called King of Wisdom, which can accomplish supreme knowledge and discern those whose faculties are fulfilled and those whose are not.
There is a samādhi called "Conforming to Types," which can accomplish the preaching of the Dharma in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings.
There is a samādhi called "Cultivating All Bodies," which can accomplish the Dharma-body.
“There is a samādhi called ‘Unblinking,’ by which one can achieve unimpeded vision and behold all Tathāgatas.
There is a samādhi called ‘Non-contention,’ by which one can discern all causes and conditions.”
There is a samādhi called "Stainless Wheel," by which one can achieve the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma.
There is a samādhi called "Lightning Flash," by which one can awaken to the causes and conditions of all phenomena.
There is a samādhi called "Excellent Discernment," by which one can know that all realms are entirely one and the same realm.
There is a samādhi called "Adornment King," by which one can achieve the accomplishment of the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
There is a samādhi called King of Following Understanding, which can respond to all with a single voice.
There is a samādhi called Non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm, which knows that all samādhis are one and the same samādhi.
There is a samādhi called "Firmness," by which one can attain non-retrogression regarding the nature of all phenomena.
There is a samādhi called "Indestructible," by which one can know that all phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena.
“There is a samādhi called ‘Endless,’ which can know that the primordial limit is no limit.
There is a samādhi called ‘Unconditioned,’ which can accomplish suchness without any change.”
There is a samādhi called "Unshakeable," by which one can know that all dharmas are equal like space.
There is a samādhi called "Pure Abiding," by which one can achieve and perfect all the pāramitās.
There is a samādhi called "Skillful Gathering," which can accomplish the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
There is a samādhi called "Equal Practice," which can accomplish the four Brahma-vihāras.
There is a samādhi called Unobstructed Contemplation, which can bring to fulfillment all the factors conducive to enlightenment.
There is a samādhi called Ocean Seal, which can master and retain all that has been spoken by the Buddhas.
There is a samādhi called "Emptiness," which can sever all views.
There is a samādhi called "Signlessness," which can sever all discursive thoughts.
There is a samādhi called "Wishlessness," which can attain pure fulfillment of all vows.
There is a samādhi called "Definitive Comprehension," which can bring about the accomplishment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
There is a samādhi called "Non-Release," which can bring about the accomplishment of not losing the teachings one has heard.
There is a samādhi called "Unobscured," by which one can delight sentient beings with skillful speech.
There is a samādhi called "Attaining Abundance," by which one can achieve the attainment of the "Jeweled Hand."
There is a samādhi called Dharma-Cloud, which can rain down all dharma-gates.
There is a samādhi called Jewel-Adornment, which can achieve the uninterrupted, supreme lineage of the Triple Gem.
There is a samādhi called "Incomparable," which can accomplish the deeds performed by wisdom.
There is a samādhi called "Door of Space," which can bring about liberation from all obstacles.
There is a samādhi called the Seal of Wisdom (*jñānamudrā*), by which one is able to attain the universal knowledge of all phenomena.
There is a samādhi called Beholding All Buddhas of the Present, by which one is able to accomplish the merits of all Tathāgatas.
There is a samādhi called "Choice of Tranquility at Will," which can achieve the perfection of being free from the limit of beginning (anādikoti).
There is a samādhi called "Discernment of the Dharma-gate of a Single Characteristic," which can achieve the perfection of preaching the Dharma-gate of a single characteristic in future ages.
There is a samādhi called "Thoroughly Knowing the Equality of All Dharmas," by which one can achieve mastery in understanding all scriptures.
There is a samādhi called "Gathering All Meritorious Qualities," by which one can provide benefit and nourishment to all sentient beings.
“There is a samādhi called ‘Sporting with Supernormal Powers,’ which can bring about the accomplishment of inconceivable liberation.
There is a samādhi called ‘Self-Awakening,’ which can enter the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.”
There is a samādhi named Śūraṅgama, which can manifest even the Great Parinirvāṇa within the stages of a bodhisattva.
There is a samādhi named Sarvatraga, which can achieve birth wherever one appears.
There is a samādhi named "Crowned King" (*abhiṣeka-rāja*), which can bring to fulfillment all the practices of a bodhisattva without exception.
There is a samādhi named "Unconquerable" (*anabhibhūta*), which can bring to fulfillment the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Tathāgata.
There is a samādhi called "Inexhaustible," which can bring about the accomplishment of the four fearlessnesses.
There is a samādhi called "Peerless," which can bring about the accomplishment of the buddha-dharmas unique to a buddha.
There is a samādhi called King of Vows, which enables the accomplishment of all dharmas one has heard, so that the merit of benefiting oneself and others is never in vain.
There is a samādhi called Skillful Entry into the Stainless Seal, which enables the manifest realization and awakening to all Buddha-dharmas.
There is a samādhi called "Skillful Awareness," by which one can achieve the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) without remainder.
There is a samādhi called "Exhausting the Boundless," by which one can achieve all Buddha-works and receive and practice them without remainder.
“Good son! These are called the eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi.

Taking these as the foremost, when a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they immediately attain eighty-four thousand gates of all samādhis; each individual samādhi has immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis as its retinue.”
“Good son! These samādhis can know the eighty-four thousand types of practices of all sentient beings, and they can also manifest the eighty-four thousand clusters of dharmas.”

"Noble son! This is a brief explanation of the practices of all bodhisattvas and a small portion of the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; yet the practices of bodhisattvas are immeasurable and boundless, and the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is inconceivable."

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha was preaching this Dharma, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience in accordance with truth), and immeasurable samādhis manifested before them;
furthermore, eighty-four thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"Quickly explain these dharma-gates of samādhi; skillfully expound the supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata, for you have personally realized and practiced this dharma, having obtained it from no other.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Arising-Doubt joined his palms and addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying:
"How rare, O Mahāsattva!"

Thus one is able to accomplish such inconceivable merit; without hearing it from another, one is able to enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom. I too wish and desire that all sentient beings may attain this inconceivable Dharma, the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Bodhisattva Saṃśayaja: "Good son,
who gave you this name, 'Saṃśayaja' (Born of Doubt)?"
The Bodhisattva Birth-Doubt replied to Śāriputra:
"The bodhicitta has given me this name, 'Birth-Doubt. Why is this so? [Because...]"
If one does not resolve to attain bodhicitta, one will ultimately never give rise to doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma.

However, those who do resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* will give rise to doubts and uncertainties concerning all the Buddha-dharmas, because they desire to directly know and clearly comprehend all the Buddha-dharmas.

For example, it is like the eldest crown prince of an anointed Kṣatriya king who possesses the marks of royalty; he ought to become the sovereign of the nation and, following his father, succeed to the royal throne.
Therefore, that son constantly inquired about the methods of governing the state, asking:
"How should I oversee and manage the affairs of the kingdom?
O Great Virtuous Śāriputra!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: one who has ultimately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, following after the Tathāgata, likewise succeed to the supreme position of the Dharma-King; they should also constantly contemplate and inquire about the teachings associated with omniscience, thinking, "How should we uphold the Dharma of the Supreme Dharma-King?"
For this reason, one also constantly gives rise to doubt regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
Venerable Śāriputra, you should know that it is by virtue of this causal condition— the bodhicitta— that the designation "giving rise to doubt" is established.
The Bodhisattva Birth-Doubt addressed Śāriputra again,
saying, “Virtuous One!
Since the distant past, I do not recall ever encountering Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends without having inquired of them regarding the sublime Dharma.”
"For this reason, I truly say that doubt has arisen.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Volume 16;
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Volume 17.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eight, Part Four: The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja Addresses the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

The sphere of action of all Buddhas is inconceivable, and the dharmas that a bodhisattva should practice are likewise immeasurable. Therefore, this practice cannot be accomplished through the adornment of minor vows, nor through limited speech, nor by means of the path of the Hīnayāna.”
How wonderful!
World-Honored One!

We only pray that you will explain the great vow-adornments and the path-adornments of the bodhisattvas. Because bodhisattvas possess these great vow-adornments and path-adornments, they are able to mount the Great Vehicle and practice the true, supreme, supramundane path; thereby they shall attain the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of the transcendent world and accomplish all spontaneous great wisdom.
"Although you have not yet attained all-knowledge, you are able to perform the Buddha-work for the benefit of all.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, saying: "Good son!..."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain for you the great vows that adorn the bodhisattvas, their adornment of the vehicle, and their adornment of the path.
“Yes, World-Honored One! We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! A bodhisattva has twenty ornaments with which to adorn himself; having adorned himself, he is able to mount the Great Vehicle.
What are these twenty?

"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who ultimately resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, giving rise to the most supreme great compassion for all sentient beings and the mind that seeks to benefit them; having given rise to this mind to benefit sentient beings, they are then able to adorn their unsurpassed great vows."
"What is meant by the adornment of the great vow?
It is the adornment of the great vow for the sake of delivering those not yet delivered, because one boards the great vessel.
It is the adornment of the great vow for the sake of liberating those not yet liberated, because one releases them from false delusions and inversions."
He is adorned with the great vow to bring peace to those who are not yet at peace, because he establishes them in the fearless path.
He is adorned with the great vow to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain it, because he causes them to cast off the heavy burden of the five aggregates.
It is the great vow-adornment of constantly and diligently providing for and satisfying sentient beings, because of being diligent and untiring;
it is the great vow-adornment of not abandoning immeasurable births and deaths, because of being free from weariness.
It is the great vow-adornment for pleasing all Buddhas, because of making offerings and paying respect in their presence;
it is the great vow-adornment for upholding all Buddha-dharmas, because of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed.
It is the great vow-adornment of retaining all that has been heard without forgetting, because of attaining *dhāraṇī*;
it is the great vow-adornment of skillfully preaching the Dharma to delight all sentient beings, because of attaining eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
It is the great vow-adornment for accumulating immeasurable provisions of merit in order to achieve the primary and secondary marks;
it is the great vow-adornment for pleasing all spiritual friends in order to make one's practice firm and steadfast.
It is the great vow-adornment for restraining the distracted mind, so as to give rise to the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis;
it is the great vow-adornment for relinquishing body and life while dwelling in forest hermitages, so as to attain the six supernormal powers.
It is because they wish to achieve the great lion’s roar, free from fear and dread, through the adornment of their great vow, having realized before them the dharma of non-self;
and because they wish to reach all worlds through the adornment of their great vow, desiring to know that all dharmas are like illusions, like dreams, and like shadows.
It is the great vow-adornment of universally illuminating and adorning all worlds, by virtue of the power of the pure precepts being received, maintained, and accomplished.
It is the great vow-adornment for accomplishing the ten powers of a Tathāgata, by virtue of fulfilling all the pāramitās.
It is for the sake of attaining the great vow-adornment of the four fearlessnesses by practicing according to what has been taught;

and for the sake of fully attaining the great vow-adornment of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by not engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding the dharmas of the bodhisattva stages as they have been heard.
“Good son! These are the twenty great vows that serve as the adornments of all bodhisattvas. By the power of these adornments, they are able to mount the Great Vehicle.
Because the bodhisattva adorns himself with this power, he severs the causes and conditions for the three evil destinies; this is called adornment.”
Being fully endowed with goodness and protected by all Buddhas is called adornment.
Attaining rebirth wherever one desires is called adornment.
Abandoning all wombs and being able to undergo miraculous birth before the Buddhas is called adornment.
To be able to practice non-contentious actions of body, speech, and mind is called adornment.
To abide in heedfulness and conduct so as to be revered by the devas and the people of the world is called adornment.
To thoroughly master the three gates of liberation without realizing the limit of reality is called adornment.
To have all dharmas of non-self manifest before one while still not relinquishing the adornment of the great vow is called adornment.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be fully equipped with the adornment of the great vow.
"What is called the adornment of the bodhisattva vehicle? Good son!

"Vehicle" refers to the immeasurable; because it has no boundaries, it is universal like space, and because it extensively accommodates all sentient beings, it is not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle).
"Furthermore, the vehicle has the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) properly established as its wheels; the ten pure and true paths of wholesome action (*kuśalakarmapatha*) as its spokes;
the accumulation of pure merit as its hub; firmness, sincerity, and ultimate perseverance as its linchpins, axle-pins, nails, and bolts;
and the successful accomplishment of all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis as its shaft."
The four immeasurable minds serve as the skillful training; virtuous friends serve as the charioteer; knowing the proper and improper times serves as the impulse;
the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self serve as the whip; the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment serve as the reins;
the purification of the five faculties serves as the girth-straps; and the vast, universal, upright, and great...
Compassion serves as the ceremonial banner; the four right efforts serve as the net; the four foundations of mindfulness serve as the steady carriage;
the four bases of psychic power serve as the swift advance; the five superior powers serve as the vanguard for scouting the enemy lines;
the eightfold noble path serves as the direct course; and the unobstructed wisdom-light regarding all sentient beings serves as the ornamental frontispiece.
To dedicate the six perfections through non-abiding toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and to cross over to the other shore by means of the peerless Four Noble Truths—this is the Great Vehicle.

This vehicle is that which is received by all Buddhas, contemplated by *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and mounted by all bodhisattvas; it is that which should be venerated by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors; that which should be honored by all sentient beings; that which should be praised by all the wise; that which all the world should take as its refuge; that which no enemies or haters can disparage; that which no māras can destroy; that which no heterodox paths can fathom; and that with which no worldly wisdom can compete.
This vehicle is supreme and cannot be obstructed; it is protected by all worthies and sages, for this vehicle can reach all Buddha-realms according to one's vows.
This vehicle shines universally, for it can emit the light of a jeweled net.
This vehicle possesses great renown, for it can bring forth the Dharma gates.
This vehicle is powerful, for its resolve does not retreat.
This vehicle is firm and secure because it is free from laxity and indolence.
This vehicle is correctly established because it is unshakable.
This vehicle is fully equipped with all requisites because it can fulfill every aspiration.
"Good son! This is called the adornment of the great vows of the Mahāyāna. When a Bodhisattva mounts this vehicle, having mounted it, he is able to proceed from one stage to the next;

this is his adornment. He is able to abandon the faults and afflictions of the stages; this is his adornment. He is able to abandon all demonic activities; this is his adornment. He is able to transform and deliver sentient beings; this is his adornment. He is able to purify Buddha-fields; this is his adornment. He is able to manifest the spiritual transformations of a Bodhisattva; this is his adornment. He is able to cross over the great famine of birth and death; this is his adornment. He is able to enter the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas; this is his adornment."
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s adornment of the path? Good son!”

Having adorned themselves with the great vows and mounted the Great Vehicle, Bodhisattvas abandon all false paths; having abandoned all false paths, they proceed upon the true, correct path to reach omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

What is called the right path? It is said that because one does not abandon wholesome dharmas, one practices great aspiration; because one does not retreat from the bodhi-path, one diligently cultivates vigor; because one does not lose the roots of goodness, one practices non-negligence; being unshakable and pure in dedication, one does not sink in what is undertaken, but is surely able to reach the ultimate by aspiring to and climbing toward the higher Dharma. Seeking the provisions of merit without satiety, and seeking the provisions of wisdom without ever abandoning them—this is the right path of the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

That which is called the Bodhisattva path consists of: the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, the three bases of meritorious action, the three trainings, the six objects of veneration, the six recollections, the four means of attraction, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the skillful means regarding the aggregates, the skillful means regarding the elements, the skillful means regarding the sense-bases, the skillful means regarding the truths, and the skillful means regarding dependent origination. This is what is called the path."
When Bodhisattvas achieve mastery in these skillful means of the path, they are all able to accord with and enter the path of the six pāramitās.
This is because the Bodhisattva’s path of the six pāramitās is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
This path is praised by all Buddhas and issues from the mouths of all Tathāgatas.
A bodhisattva who has perfected skillful means and is able to know the true nature of all phenomena can abide in the noble path of the six supramundane pāramitās.
"What is meant by 'abiding'?
Son of good family!
If there is a bodhisattva who, having accomplished the skillful means of spontaneous wisdom, seeks enlightenment, regarding these five aggregates of clinging—"

Because they seek awakening in order to attain realization of reality as it is within the aggregates (*skandha*), these bodhisattvas practice generosity while knowing that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent;
they know that form is suffering, they know that form is selfless, they know that form is dull, and they know that form lacks wisdom.
They know that form is like an illusion, they know that form is like the moon reflected in water, and they know that form is like a dream.
One knows that form is like a shadow; one knows that form is like an echo; one knows that form is like a whirling firebrand.

One knows that form is without self, knows that form is without sentient beings, knows that form is without life, knows that form is without a person, knows that form is without a master, and knows that form is without a nourisher.
One knows that form is empty, knows that form is signless, and knows that form is wishless.
Knowing that form is without action, knowing that form is without birth, knowing that form is without arising, knowing that form is without emergence,
knowing that form is without shape, knowing that form is quiescent, knowing that form is detached, knowing that form has no end,
knowing that form is unconditioned, knowing that form is equal to space, and knowing that form is like the nature of nirvāṇa; yet...
He practices giving.
When a bodhisattva practices giving in this way, because giving is detached, he knows that form is also detached; because form is detached, he knows that giving is also detached.
Because both form and giving are detached, he knows that his vow is also detached; because the vow is detached, he knows that both form and giving are also detached.

Because form, giving, and vows are detached, one knows that bodhi is also detached; because bodhi is detached, one knows that form, giving, and vows are detached; and thus one knows that all phenomena share the same nature as bodhi.
“Good son! This is the supramundane dāna-pāramitā of the bodhisattva; feeling, perception, and mental formations are also like this.
One should practice giving by knowing that consciousness is impermanent, knowing that consciousness is suffering, knowing that consciousness is non-self, and knowing that consciousness is dull.”

Knowledge is without wisdom; knowledge is like an illusion, knowledge is like a mirage, knowledge is like the moon reflected in water, knowledge is like a dream, knowledge is like a shadow, knowledge is like an echo, knowledge is like a whirling firebrand;
knowledge is without self, knowledge is without sentient beings, knowledge is without...
Life is without a knower, knowledge has no master, knowledge has no nourisher;
knowledge is like space, knowledge is signless, knowledge is wishless, knowledge is without action;
knowledge is without birth, knowledge is without arising, knowledge is without emergence, knowledge is formless, and knowledge is quiescent.
With tranquility and the detachment of knowledge— knowledge that has no end, knowledge that has no attainment, knowledge equal to space,
and knowledge whose nature is like nirvāṇa— one practices giving.
"When a bodhisattva practices giving in this way, because giving is detached, they know that consciousness is also detached; because consciousness is detached, they know that giving is also detached.
Because both consciousness and giving are detached, they know that aspiration is also detached; because aspiration is detached, they know that both consciousness and giving are also detached.

Because consciousness, giving, and aspiration are detached, they know that awakening is also detached; because awakening is detached, they know that consciousness, giving, and aspiration are also detached, and they realize that all phenomena share the same nature as awakening."
"Good son! This is the supramundane dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, good son!"

The bodhisattva, knowing that form is impermanent, guards the precepts; even knowing that form is of the nature of nirvāṇa, he guards the precepts. It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations. Knowing that consciousness is impermanent, he guards the precepts; even knowing that consciousness is of the nature of nirvāṇa, he guards the precepts.

Because one is detached through the precepts, one knows that form is also detached; because one knows detachment through the precepts, one is detached even up to consciousness, and so on until one knows that all phenomena are identical in nature to bodhi.
"Good son! This is the supramundane perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva.
The perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) are also like this."
"Knowing that form is impermanent, one practices wisdom; even unto knowing that form has the nature of nirvāṇa, one practices wisdom.
Knowing that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one practices wisdom; even unto knowing that consciousness has the nature of nirvāṇa, one practices wisdom."
Because wisdom is equal, one knows that consciousness is equal; because consciousness is equal, one knows that wisdom is equal.
Because wisdom and consciousness are equal, one knows that aspiration is equal; because aspiration is equal, one knows that wisdom and consciousness are equal.

Because wisdom, consciousness, and aspiration are equal, one knows that bodhi is equal; because bodhi is equal, one knows that wisdom, consciousness, and aspiration are equal. Thus, one knows that all phenomena are identical in nature to bodhi.
"Good son! This is the supramundane prajñāpāramitā; this is the bodhisattva’s supramundane path of pāramitās, which is able to encompass all paths. You should know that all paths enter into it."
"Why is it called 'supramundane' (lokottara)? Good son! The five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are called the mundane.

When a bodhisattva skillfully discerns the five aggregates and contemplates them as impermanent, up to their being like the nature of nirvāṇa, he knows that within this path there is neither the mundane nor mundane phenomena. He knows that this path is untainted (anāsrava), supramundane, and free from all attachments; this is called 'supramundane'."
"Good son! This is called the path of the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, 'path' refers to seeking all dharmas as they truly are; through discernment and selection, one does not perceive any dharmas as having continuity, accumulation, duality, or distinction. For this reason, it is called the path."
Furthermore, this path is devoid of hatred and attachment; because it is free from hatred and attachment, it is called "equanimous.
Because it transcends the conceptual deliberations and observations of other vehicles, it is called "vast."
Because he has departed from flattery, he is called upright.
Because he has departed from a crooked mind, he is called free from guile.
Because he has severed all hindrances, he is called unimpeded.
Because one has departed from and abandoned thoughts of desire, ill-will, and harm, it is called "free from dust and defilement.
Because one does not crave forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, it is called "peaceful bliss.
Because one has departed from and abandoned all demonic activities, it is called "cool and refreshing."
Because it departs from and leaves behind the many thieves of affliction, it is called "fearlessness.
Because it can reach nirvana, it is called the "essential exit.
Because it accomplishes tranquil concentration, it is called "cooling water."
Because wisdom understands well, it is called "Ever-Luminous.
Because compassion is skillfully cultivated, it is called "Cool Refreshment.
Because great compassion is never abandoned, it is called "Advancing Without Weariness."
Because they constantly practice joy, they are called "delighted.
Because they have accomplished equanimity, they are called "faultless.
Because they accord with and gather the Dharma, they are called "greatly wealthy."

By virtue of accomplishing the power of the perfection of giving food, one attains the eloquence of the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*); because all Buddhas skillfully protect and uphold them, this is called the practice of the Dharma that transcends the four māras.
Because he does not abandon his original vow, it is called "advancement without obstruction.
Because he crosses over the flow of all afflictions, it is called "unsurpassed.
Because no one in any world can subdue him, it is called "without counterpart."

“Good son! This path accomplishes such qualities as these, as well as other immeasurable merits. Because all Great Beings ride upon this path, they are able to come and go to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings; this is what constitutes its adornment.”
To manifest entry into afflictions while remaining free from all afflictions is their adornment.

To contemplate birth and death without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and to reach the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness while being able to teach and transform sentient beings who practice in various views, signs, and vows, is their adornment.
To manifest entry into the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas while not abandoning saṃsāra is their adornment.

To manifest birth within the various realms of existence while remaining unmoved from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and to manifest the teaching of all verbal instructions while remaining unmoved from the ineffable, is their adornment.
To be able to manifest all Buddha-activities while not abandoning the bodhisattva practices—this is their adornment. "Good son!
This is the great vow-adornment of a bodhisattva, the Great Vehicle-adornment, and the Path-adornment."

Because Bodhisattvas adorn themselves with the adornment of great vows, they are able to mount the Great Vehicle and follow the supramundane noble path; although they have not yet attained *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they are able to perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ratnaśrī who asked the bodhisattva Gaganagañja:
"Son of good family,
have you already cultivated this supramundane noble path?"
Gaganagañja replied, “It has been cultivated. Ratnaśrī said:
"How is it cultivated? Akāśagarbha replied,
"It is cultivated in the same manner as one who has attained the pure path."
Ratnaśrī asked, "What is the path of purification? Ākāśagarbha replied:
“Good son! Because I am pure, the Path is pure. Ratnaśrī asked:
"What is meant by 'purity of self'? Akāśagarbha replied,
"It is like the purity of the world."
Ratnaśrī asked, "What is the purification of the world? Ākāśagarbha replied:
“Good son! The past limit of form is pure. Why is this so?
Because the original limit of form has no coming.”
The future limit of form is also pure.
Why is this so? Because the future limit of form has no going away. The present limit of form is also pure.
Why is this so? Because present form has no abiding.
Good son! This is the purity of the world.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure at their past limit.
The reason for this is that the fundamental limit of consciousness has no coming.
Thus, the future limit of consciousness is also pure.
The reason for this is that the future limit of consciousness has no going.
Consciousness is also pure in its present limit.
Why is this so? Because consciousness has no abiding in its present limit. Good son!
This is called the purity of the world.
Son of good family!
Because the world is pure within the world, the self is pure; because the self is pure, this is called the purity of the Path.
Ratnaśrī said: "Noble son! What can such a pure path accomplish?"
Ākāśagarbha replied:
"One can produce the light of great wisdom; by the power of this luminous wisdom, one is able to know all phenomena from the past limit to the future limit."
Ratnaśrī asked again:
"What is meant by the limit of past and future dharmas? Ākāśagarbha replied:
"All dharmas are without arising at the limit of the past and without cessation at the limit of the future; this is called knowing the limits of the past and the future.
Ratnaguṇa asked again:
"If one perceives the limits of the past and the future, what is it that is perceived?"
Gaganagañja replied, “I see them as being free from both.
Ratnaśrī asked again:
"What is meant by 'being free from both'?
Akāśagarbha replied, "It means being free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism."
Good son! If there are those who perceive the arising of dharmas and become attached to dharmas, they possess the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Why is this so? Because where there is arising, there is cessation; and because there is both arising and cessation, there arise the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

If one does not perceive any dharma arising from self-nature or other-nature, then one perceives dependent origination; if one perceives dependent origination, then one perceives dharmas; if one perceives dharmas, then one perceives the Tathāgata; if one perceives the Tathāgata, then one perceives suchness (*tathatā*); if one perceives suchness, then one does not stagnate in nihilism nor cling to eternalism. That which is neither eternal nor annihilated is without arising and without cessation.
Ratnaśrī asked again: "Noble son,
if there is neither arising nor ceasing, how can there be names and numbers?"
Ākāśagarbha replied: "It is merely a dharma named by means of conventional designations.
O son of good family!"

Just as because space exists, there are various designations for forms—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, purple, crystal color, and lapis lazuli color; coarse forms and subtle forms; long forms and short forms; square forms and circular forms—yet space is not defiled by such phenomena.
However, the intrinsic nature of all form is also empty; all phenomena are likewise thus, sharing the same nature as space, existing merely as names and categories through conventional designations.

Regarding what are called wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas, dharmas that should be practiced and dharmas that should not be practiced, tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas—the bodhisattva does not perform any non-meritorious actions; furthermore, regarding all meritorious actions performed, they perceive them as deceptive, unreal, and lacking solidity.

This bodhisattva knows that all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) are non-activities; having equanimously relinquished all signs (*nimitta*), by virtue of accomplishing the power of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they dedicate [their merit] toward enlightenment (*bodhi*) yet do not perceive any increase or decrease in enlightenment. They do not seek enlightenment within form (*rūpa*), nor do they seek enlightenment within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*). Because the bodhisattva is without seeking, they abide in the aggregate of pure ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and cultivate the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), thereby fulfilling all aspirations.

Knowing that the nature of birth and death is identical to the nature of nirvāṇa, although one enters ultimate nirvāṇa, one practices the bodhisattva path for the sake of severing the false and inverted views of sentient beings; yet, there is no dharma of practice to be practiced.
"Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva enters into nirvāṇa while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Whatever is performed is all birth-and-death; that which is without performance is called nirvāṇa.
The conduct of a bodhisattva is non-performance; therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva enters nirvāṇa while practicing the bodhisattva path.
"Good son! Whatever consists of attachment, nesting places, false conceptualization, frivolous discourse, and grasping at signs is called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Nirvāṇa is that which is free from attachment, nesting places, false conceptualization, frivolous discourse, and grasping at signs; this is called nirvāṇa."

When a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path by cultivating freedom from attachment to nests of dwelling-places, false conceptualizations, frivolous arguments, and the grasping of signs, this is called the bodhisattva entering nirvana while practicing the bodhisattva path.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Worthy one! You have eloquently explained the nature of dharmas, which accords with the bodhisattva practice and is true and not otherwise.
Thus, Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is the excellence of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
"Because of the World-Honored One’s illumination of wisdom, we have obtained this portion of eloquence.
World-Honored One!
It is like the sunlight illuminating Jambudvīpa; by the majestic power of the sun, those with eyes are able to see forms and colors and perform various activities."
By virtue of the Tathāgata’s great power of wisdom, his illumination of all sentient beings and all worlds is likewise so.
The true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is ineffable; the nature of all verbal expression is equal to empty space. Therefore, all phenomena cannot be numbered.

Whatever has numerical characteristics is limited; whatever is limited is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); whatever is conditioned can be known, abandoned, and cultivated; and whatever can be known, abandoned, and cultivated involves attainment, realization, and the enumeration of dharmas.
Through reflection, deliberation, and discernment, one does not perceive any dharma that can be known, abandoned, cultivated, realized, or attained;
therefore, there is no attainment. This is because all dharmas are unarisen.

One who can thus correctly view all phenomena does not give rise to attachment or defilement toward them; because there is no attachment or defilement, there is no clinging; because there is no clinging, there is no proximity; and because there is no proximity, there is neither grasping nor appropriation.
What is meant by "neither grasping nor seizing"?
It means that whether form is permanent or impermanent, there is neither grasping nor seizing;
whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent, there is neither grasping nor seizing.
Whether form is suffering or pleasure, whether it has a self or is selfless, whether it is pure or impure, there is no grasping and no appropriation;
whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are suffering or pleasure, whether they have a self or are selfless, there is no grasping and no appropriation.
Whether form is empty or not empty, there is no grasping and no taking up;
whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty or not empty, there is no grasping and no taking up.
Whether form is detached or not detached, there is no grasping and no taking up.
Whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are detached or not detached, there is no grasping and no appropriation.
Because the bodhisattva is without grasping and without appropriation, they attain the samādhi of non-grasping of all dharmas.

Having dwelled in this samādhi, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow upon this bodhisattva a prediction of enlightenment through their unsurpassed supernormal powers. Although this bodhisattva has entered nirvāṇa, they perceive that all sentient beings ultimately share the same nature as nirvāṇa; yet, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they do not abandon their great vow-adornments or their bodhisattva great compassion.
"How does a bodhisattva enter into nirvāṇa while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva? Good son,
whatever is performed is called saṃsāra."
That which is entirely without activity is called nirvana.

By means of right wisdom, the bodhisattva perceives that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are devoid of marks; because the bodhisattva sees with the clear eye of Dharma, they are able to expound the luminous wisdom of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī asked the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying: “Noble son!
"Why do you conceal your own wisdom and claim that all of this is solely the power of the Tathāgata?
Vimalākāśagarbha replied to Ratnaśrī, "Noble son!..."
"Does the Tathāgata not say that one should conceal good and reveal evil?
Good son, I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit."
"Good son! What do you think?
If the Dragon King Anavatapta were not present, would the Great Lake Anavatapta be able to produce the four rivers so that all sentient beings might enjoy their use?"
Ratnaśrī replied, "No. Ākāśagarbha said:

“Good son! If there were no Tathāgata, there would be no Dharma or Vinaya; the Bodhisattvas would have no means by which to realize the great ocean of wisdom, nor could they benefit all sentient beings.”

Because the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, there exists the Dharma and Vinaya; thus, all Bodhisattvas are able to realize the great ocean of wisdom and also bring all sentient beings across to liberation.
"Good son! Therefore, you should know that all the eloquence attained by bodhisattvas, which is able to benefit sentient beings, is entirely due to the spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
Ratnaśrī asked again:
"Noble son! Can the eloquence of the Tathāgatas be transferred into the mind of a bodhisattva?"
Gaganagañja replied, “No. Ratnaśrī said:
"How is it that one attains eloquence through the power of the Tathāgata? Ākāśagarbha replied, "Noble son!
It is like a skilled planter of fruit trees: when causes and conditions harmonize, the fruit is obtained; yet the tree is not the fruit itself, nor is the fruit separate from the tree. Good son!

Because the Bodhisattva practices in perfect accordance with the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, he gives rise to great wisdom and brilliant discernment; this is attained through the Buddha’s teaching and is without further transition.
Ratnaśrī said: "How rare, noble son!
The phenomena produced through causes and conditions are thus profoundly deep and difficult to fathom."
Ākāśagarbha said: "Son of good family!
All dharmas are ultimately unarisen."
Ratnaśrī said: "Good son! All phenomena are said to arise from conditions."
Gaganagañja said: "Good son, has it already arisen, or is it yet to arise?"
"Has that which has not yet arisen arisen? Ratnaśrī replied, "Noble son!"
"That which has already arisen does not arise; that which has not yet arisen also does not arise. Ākāśagarbha said:
"O son of good family!"
"Therefore, there is no arising. Ratnaśrī said:
"O son of good family!"
“Is there a cause within conditions? Ākāśagarbha replied, “No.”
Ratnaśrī asked, "Is there a condition within the cause? Ākāśagarbha replied:
"No," said Ratnaśrī. "What do you think?"
"Are these causes or conditions possessed of an intrinsic nature? Akāśagarbha replied, "No."
Ratnaśrī said: "Noble son, what do you think?"
"Are all phenomena produced without causes and conditions? Akāśagarbha replied, "No."

Good son! Therefore, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; they are without birth, without arising, and without emergence. Consequently, conditions do not produce causes, nor do causes produce conditions. Intrinsic nature does not produce intrinsic nature, nor does other-nature produce other-nature. Intrinsic nature does not produce other-nature, nor does other-nature produce intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are by nature unarisen.

Why is this? Because as suchness (tathatā) is neither arising nor ceasing, so too is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) neither arising nor ceasing. Just as suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit are, so too are all phenomena realized by the Tathāgata; they likewise are neither arising nor ceasing.
Ratnaśrī said: "Noble son, does it mean that even the Tathāgata does not appear in the world?"
Gaganagañja replied: "This should not be spoken of. Why is that? Because—"
Regarding all phenomena, the Tathāgata is ultimately ineffable; it cannot be said that he has appeared in the world, nor can it be said that he has not appeared.
If someone were to ask:
"Has the Tathāgata appeared in the world?"
"Or does he not appear in the world?
"The wise person, in order not to misrepresent the Tathāgata, should set aside such a question and remain without answering. Ratnaśrī asked:
"How should it be placed? Akāśagarbha replied,
"It should be placed in such a way that it abides as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
Ratnaśrī asked: "In what way does the nature of phenomena abide? Ākāśagarbha replied:
"Just as the nature of space abides—abiding in non-abiding—so too does the nature of phenomena abide;
as is the nature of phenomena, so too is the nature of sentient beings.
As is the nature of sentient beings, so too are all phenomena."

Just as all phenomena are, so too does the Tathāgata abide; he abides in non-abiding because there is no place of abiding. Since there is neither abiding nor non-abiding, one cannot say that he is born, nor can one say that he ceases.
Ratnaśrī said: "Noble son!
The matter of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is profoundly deep!"
"Profound! Akāśagarbha replied, "Noble son!
"If one can understand the phenomena of dependent origination as they truly are, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world. Ratnaguṇa said:
"O son of good family!"
"Who, then, would understand this teaching? Ākāśagarbha replied,
"One who perceives neither increase nor decrease within all phenomena."
