Ratnaśrī asked, "What is meant by 'increase'? Ākāśagarbha replied:
"Excess refers to what is called an 'excessive phrase,' meaning that one falsely gives rise to excess within what is non-existent.
The absence of excessive phrases is the phrase of equality; it is the phrase of non-equality, the phrase of no letters, the phrase of no phrases, and the phrase of no instruction."
Within the unmanifest (avijñapti), there are no phrases and no predominance, nor is there mind, thought, or consciousness; for this reason, it is not a phrase.
It is like the tracks of a bird in the sky: ultimately they do not exist, yet one speaks of "bird tracks" even though they are non-existent.

It is likewise with all phenomena (*dharmas*): they possess neither words nor phrases. Where there are no phrases, they are conventionally designated as "phrases," just as where there are no tracks, they are conventionally designated as "tracks."
The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is likewise no appearance; that he is conventionally designated as "appearing" is also thus.
Therefore, the wise should not grasp at or cling to this; because there is no grasping or clinging, he is conventionally designated as "appearing," yet he always abides in non-appearance.
Why is this so? Because non-arising is the true nature of all dharmas.
That which is non-arising is nothing whatsoever; therefore, it is called the "nature of the non-existence of all dharmas."

The nature of non-existence has no place of abiding; because it has no place of abiding, it is the limit of non-abiding. All dharmas and the limit of non-abiding are themselves the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi). The reality-limit is itself the limit of all dharmas; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are equal to the reality-limit.

What is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) is the limit where the three realms are severed; it is the indestructible limit, the limit that is neither interrupted nor eternal, the limit of suchness, and the limit equal to the three periods of time. By means of such limits as these, it is equal to the limits of all phenomena.

Why is this? Because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the limit of the self (*ātma-koṭi*) are non-dual and undifferentiated; the limit of reality and the limits of sentient beings, life-span, nourishment, and persons are non-dual and undifferentiated; the limit of reality and the limit of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi-koṭi*) are non-dual and undifferentiated. Within the view of a self, there is no limit of reality. One who can know this thus, according to reality, will not possess the twenty kinds of views of a self.

Why is this so? Because within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) there is neither one nor many; the limit of reality is equal to equality (*samatā*), without coming or going, without exhaustion or decrease. Since the limit of reality is ultimately empty, it is therefore said that all phenomena are the gate of inexhaustibility and the limit of inexhaustibility.
“Nirvāṇa is inexhaustible, because it is empty and because it lacks intrinsic nature.
Just as nirvāṇa is neither exhausted nor non-exhausted, so too are all phenomena. For this reason, it is said that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa.”
All phenomena are neither equal nor unequal, for they have no peer.
Just as space has no peer, so too it is with all phenomena.
If one perceives a counterpart and says that there is nirvāṇa, having already asserted that there is nirvāṇa, one then seeks nirvāṇa; this is to be in opposition to the noble ones.

Since it has already been stated that there is nirvāṇa, it follows that one must know this, abandon this, realize this, cultivate this, give rise to this, and extinguish this. One who does not practice in this manner cannot know things as they truly are and cannot see them as they truly are; thus, they do not recognize or understand, and they do not know or see.
Because they do not recognize or understand all phenomena, they become attached to words and letters, giving rise to false disputes and contention regarding all dharmas.
Those who give rise to such disputes and contention are objects of compassion within the Buddha-dharma.
"The reason for this is that the Tathāgata has declared:
'The dharma of a śramaṇa should not involve contention.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

This worthy gentleman’s eloquence is thus profoundly deep, clear, difficult to understand, and difficult to fathom. Regarding all phenomena, he has not received them from another; having personally realized them himself, he is able to speak in such a manner."
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha then said to Ānanda:
"Virtuous One!
I have personally realized this for myself; therefore, I speak thus according to what I have realized."
Why is this? My body is itself empty space; by means of empty space I realize all phenomena, which are sealed with the seal of empty space.
Venerable Ānanda!

All Bodhisattvas who cultivate the body and have a thorough understanding of its characteristics are able to perform all Buddha-works with this very body, manifesting various forms and images, yet without ever retreating from the true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, they do not depart from the body born of karmic bonds, nor do they transcend the nature of equality; they manifest transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) with complete mastery, universally appearing in all Buddha-lands, never concealing their responsive and transformative bodies. Practitioners such as these may all be called those who have attained "bodily realization" (*kāyāsākṣātkriyā*).
Ānanda asked, "Virtuous man! Have you perhaps attained some realization of the Dharma?"
Gaganagañja replied, “Venerable Ānanda!
I do not perceive any phenomenon that is separate from the body, nor a body that is separate from phenomena.”
Ānanda said: "Good son! If you have realized it through your own body, have you attained the fruit of arhatship?"
Gaganagañja said: "Virtuous One! There is neither attainment nor non-attainment."
"Because there is nothing to be attained, because one has no afflicted conduct regarding all phenomena, and because one is free from desire, hatred, and delusion—this is called an Arhat. Ānanda said:
"O son of good family!"
"When will you enter parinirvāṇa? Ākāśagarbha replied,
"Venerable One!"
An Arhat does not undergo parinirvāṇa; he knows that the ultimate nature of all phenomena is nirvāṇa, yet even this characteristic of nirvāṇa does not exist.
Ordinary, ignorant people engage in such conceptual proliferation and discrimination, saying, "This is saṃsāra" and "This is nirvāṇa";
the Arhat has no such conceptual proliferation.
The Venerable Ānanda said: "Good son!

As I understand the meaning of what you have said, a bodhisattva should not be called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), nor should they be called one in training (śaikṣa), nor should they be called one beyond training (aśaikṣa), because they have departed from these two characteristics."
Gaganagañja said: "Venerable Ānanda! Excellent, excellent!"
"Because he is neither an ordinary person, nor one in training, nor one beyond training, he is able to manifest himself everywhere, yet he does not grasp at or cling to any place.
At that time, the five hundred great śrāvakas each took the *uttarāsaṅga* robes they were wearing and offered them to Gaganagañja. Having presented their robes, they spoke these words with one voice:
"Those sentient beings who, with a profound mind, resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, have truly gained excellent benefit."
"Within such a treasury of the Dharma of great wisdom, one does not fall outside of it.
As soon as the offered robes vanished from sight, those śrāvakas asked Ākāśagarbha,
"Where have the robes gone?"
Gaganagañja replied, "Enter into my treasury.
He spoke again:
“The Tathāgata knows this; you may ask.
At that time, the śrāvakas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Where has the robe gone?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"To the east, passing beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya buddha-fields from here, there is a world named Kāṣāyadhvaja. In that realm there is a Buddha, titled Śailendra-rāja Tathāgata."
"Ākāśagarbha has already sent this robe to that world.
The śrāvakas then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason was this robe sent to that place?
The Buddha said,
"I wish to perform buddha-work in that world by means of this robe."

Regarding what has been spoken here by the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, such as the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi-Seals equal to the treasury of space, the sound of their meaning shall be expounded from within that robe by this samādhi.
The immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas in that world shall, upon hearing this Dharma, attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Monks, you should know that bodhisattvas employ such various skillful means to benefit sentient beings.

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable golden flowers rained down from the sky above, completely covering the Hall of Exquisite Jewel Adornments; from within those flowers, such sounds of the Dharma emerged.

Any sentient beings who have faith in this Dharma taught by Gaganagañja, and who properly contemplate and discern its meaning, shall all be sealed with the seal of non-retrogression and will certainly attain the unsurpassed site of enlightenment.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What auspicious omen is this, that these flowers rain down and such wondrous sounds emerge to comfort all sentient beings?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is a Brahmā named Radiant Adornment who, together with six million eight hundred thousand members of the Brahmā assembly from the Brahma Heaven, wishes to come here."

After the Tathāgata had spoken these words, the assembly of Brahmās suddenly arrived at the Hall of Wondrous Jewel Adornments, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
Having circumambulated him seven times, he stood to one side, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"It is rare, World-Honored One! The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is inconceivable. His aggregate of precepts is pure; he has skillfully cultivated all meditative concentrations; he is skilled in discerning great wisdom; he is skilled in sporting with great supernormal powers; he is skilled in fulfilling great and far-reaching vows; he is skilled in accomplishing great expedient means; he is skilled in adorning body, speech, and mind; and he is skilled in achieving the power of great mastery among all dharmas. Yet this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha’s body, speech, and mind perform no action at all, nor do they possess any conceptualization or recollection, yet he is able to manifest these inconceivable, adorned, and miraculous transformations."

Furthermore, they are able to manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and can also enter and emerge from hundreds of thousands of various samādhi gates, because from time immemorial they have always delighted in cultivating and accomplishing all wholesome dharmas.

"Bhagavān! Bodhisattvas should not remain ignorant of the causes of the roots of goodness they have cultivated in the past; furthermore, they should never grow weary of accumulating these roots of goodness. Why is this so?"
"It is because of the retribution from the roots of goodness planted in the past that he is able to manifest such inconceivable spiritual transformations.
The Buddha told Brahmā: "So it is, so it is!"

As you have said, because these bodhisattvas have already accomplished the provisions of roots of goodness and the skillful means of the wisdom of transcendence, they are able to manifest such inconceivable matters adorned with merit; yet they are without recollection, conceptualization, or discrimination, nor are they without non-discrimination.
The Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva gather the provisions of roots of goodness and the skillful means of the wisdom of transcendence?”
The Buddha addressed the Brahmā Prabhāvyūha, saying:
"There are three kinds of roots of goodness.
What are these three?"
What are called the roots of goodness—non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are termed "roots of goodness.
As for the provisions: what is called the relinquishing of all possessions and the cultivation of loving-kindness while contemplating all phenomena are termed "provisions."

Skillful means refers to departing from the stage of ordinary beings, having no aspiration for or delight in the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and entering the stages of the bodhisattvas; this is called skillful means.
"Wisdom" refers to the knowledge of abandoning unwholesome dharmas, the knowledge of accumulating wholesome dharmas, and the knowledge of dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi; this is called wisdom.
When a bodhisattva is able to abide in such correct practices, this is called the essential path to liberation.
"Furthermore, 'roots of goodness' refers to being able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
'Provisions' refers to seeking all wholesome dharmas."
Expedient means refers to never abandoning or forgetting roots of goodness, whether already performed or yet to be performed.
Wisdom refers to knowing that the mind is like an illusion or a magical transformation.
To clearly realize such dharmas as these before one is called the essential path of deliverance.
"Furthermore, 'roots of goodness' refers to pure devotion;
'provisions' refers to the arousal of energy;
and 'skillful means' refers to the profound mind."
"Wisdom" refers to being without grasping and without movement.
One who is able to practice such dharmas as these is said to have attained the essential way out.
"Furthermore, 'wholesome roots' refer to the desire for wholesome dharmas."
The provisions are what is called superior progress;
the skillful means are what is called abiding in heedfulness;
and wisdom is what is called relinquishing all attachments.
One who is able to practice such deeds as these is said to have attained the essential departure [from suffering].
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to right faith;
"provisions" refers to not abandoning one's original vow.
Skillful means refers to not abandoning mindfulness and concentration;
wisdom refers to insight.

One who is able to dwell correctly in such practices as these is said to have accomplished the essential path of emerging through the wisdom of skillful means and the provisions of the roots of goodness.
"Furthermore, 'roots of goodness' refers to being pleasing to all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
'Provisions' refers to providing what is required for their service, as well as honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and benefiting them."
Skillful means refers to conceiving of the spiritual friend as the World-Honored One.
Wisdom refers to knowing the proper and improper times to inquire about the Dharma.
One who can correctly abide in such practices as these is said to have attained the essential path to liberation.
"Furthermore, 'roots of goodness' refers to listening to the Dharma with proper compliance.
'Provisions' refers to receiving and upholding it without neglect or forgetting.
'Skillful means' refers to being able to contemplate according to what has been heard."
The wise person is one who acts in accordance with what they have heard.
One who is able to dwell correctly in such practices as these is said to have attained the essential means of deliverance.
Furthermore, "roots of goodness" refers to encountering a Buddha and being pleased by him.
The provisions (*sambhāra*) refer to the protection of all the *pāramitās*, the *saṃgrahavastus*, and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Skillful means (*upāya*) refers to the ability to proceed from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next.
"Wisdom" refers to the attainment of the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When a bodhisattva is able to dwell correctly in such practices as these, it is called the skillful means and wisdom of the essential departure that accomplishes the provisions of the roots of goodness.
At that time, the Brahmā Prabhālaṃkara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is able to summarize all the practices of bodhisattvas within the meaning of a four-line verse.”
“World-Honored One!
All Buddha-dharmas should be sought therein.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Brahmā, saying:
"A single phrase can also encompass all the Buddha-dharma. What is this one?
It is the phrase 'detachment from desire.'"
Why is this so? Because all Buddha-dharmas are identical to the state of freedom from desire; as it is with the Buddha-dharmas, so it is with all dharmas. Brahmā!
This is one phrase that comprehensively encompasses all Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore, Brahmā!
One single phrase of emptiness comprehensively encompasses all Buddha-dharmas, because all Buddha-dharmas are identical with emptiness; as it is with the Buddha-dharmas, so it is with all dharmas.
"Brahmā! These are the single phrases that comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas. They are:

the phrase of signlessness, the phrase of wishlessness, the phrase of effortlessness, the phrase of non-arising, the phrase of non-origination, the phrase of suchness, the phrase of dharma-nature, the phrase of the reality-limit, the phrase of detachment, the phrase of cessation, the phrase of exhaustion, and the phrase of nirvāṇa. These comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas because all Buddha-dharmas are identical to nirvāṇa; as it is with the Buddha-dharmas, so it is with all dharmas."
Brahmā! This is a single phrase that comprehensively encompasses all Buddha-dharmas. Why is this so?
Because such phrases as these are all non-phrases, all Buddha-dharmas are non-phrases, designated by name as "phrases.
Furthermore, Brahmā, desire is the phrase for the departure from desire.
Why is this? Because the nature of freedom from desire is itself desire, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Hatred is the phrase for freedom from hatred.
Why is this? Because the nature of being free from hatred is itself hatred;
delusion is the phrase for being free from delusion.
Why is this? Because the nature of delusion is itself delusion, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is a term for the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Why is this so? The nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is itself the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a synonym for clarity (*vidyā*).
Why is this? Because the nature of clarity is itself ignorance, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Even suffering and affliction are phrases for being free from suffering and affliction.
Why is this? Because the nature of being free from suffering and affliction is itself suffering and affliction; all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Form is a phrase for emptiness.
Why is this? Because the nature of space is itself form, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are phrases of non-action.
Why is this so? Because the nature of non-action is itself consciousness, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
The earth element is a phrase for empty space.
Why is this? Because space is itself the earth element, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
Water, fire, and wind elements are phrases for the dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is itself wind, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
The eye is a phrase for *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? Because the nature of nirvāṇa is itself the eye, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the phrase for nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the nature of nirvāṇa is itself the mind, and all Buddha-dharmas likewise share this same nature. Brahmā!
This constitutes a single phrase that comprehensively encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.
When Bodhisattvas enter each of these gates of wisdom, they perceive all Buddha-dharmas as entering into this single phrase.
“Brahmā! Just as the great ocean can swallow all flowing streams, so too does each and every phrase encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as empty space can entirely contain all forms and images, so too does each and every phrase encompass all Buddha-dharmas.”
All such Buddha-dharmas—whether subsumed or not subsumed, whether taught or not taught—neither increase nor decrease, because they are ultimately free from all characteristics.
“Brahmā! It is like a mathematician who repeatedly lays down counting sticks upon a calculating board; yet, within the board there are no sticks, and within the sticks there is no board.”
Why is this? Because they are ultimately non-associated and ultimately detached.

Thus, within each and every phrase, because they are merely designated by number, it is said that all Buddha-dharmas enter into a single phrase; yet the Buddha-dharmas cannot be named, numbered, or calculated, because they are ultimately non-associated and ultimately detached.
“Brahmā! The enumeration of the names of the Buddha-dharmas is itself the enumeration of the names of all dharmas. Why is this?

All dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma; these dharmas are neither dharma nor non-dharma, because their intrinsic nature is empty, because their intrinsic nature is detached, and because their intrinsic nature is ultimately without self-nature.

The absence of intrinsic nature is itself space; the nature of space is identical to the nature of all phenomena. This nature of phenomena possesses neither the characteristic of arising nor the characteristic of ceasing; it possesses neither the characteristic of having a location nor the characteristic of lacking a location. Therefore, all phenomena are said to be without characteristics and not without characteristics.
When this single Dharma-gate was thus expounded, twelve thousand Brahmās among that assembly of Brahmās all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
furthermore, five thousand Brahmās who had previously planted roots of virtue attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ratnapāṇi who addressed the bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"How marvelous, noble son!"
All phenomena and the dharmas of the Tathāgata are profoundly deep, difficult to fathom, and inconceivable.
Furthermore, son of good family,
what is meant by "the root that establishes all Buddha-dharmas"?
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied to Ratnapāṇi:
"Noble son! The bodhicitta is the foundation that stabilizes all Buddha-dharmas; because all dharmas abide within the bodhicitta, they are able to grow and flourish."
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"Noble son! By what dharma is the bodhicitta subsumed such that it is not forgotten and one can swiftly reach the stage of non-retrogression?"
Ākāśagarbha said: "Noble son!
The bodhicitta is encompassed by two dharmas, through which one attains non-forgetfulness and swiftly reaches the stage of non-retrogression."

What are these two? They are sincerity and ultimate resolve; these are what are called the two dharmas by which one is embraced, enabling one to avoid forgetfulness and swiftly reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Ratnapāṇi said: "Good son! By how many dharmas are these two subsumed?"
Gaganagañja said: "These two dharmas are subsumed within four dharmas. What are the four?"
That which is called "pure sincerity" is comprised of being free from falsehood and deceit, and being free from flattery and crookedness;
that which is "ultimate" is comprised of non-self and upward progress.
"These two dharmas are subsumed within four dharmas. Ratnapāṇi said:
"O son of good family!"
"By how many dharmas are these four dharmas subsumed?
Akāśagarbha replied, "Noble son!"
These four dharmas are subsumed within eight dharmas. What are these eight?
That which is not false or deceitful is subsumed under being free from hesitation and having a truly pure essence.
Being free from flattery and crookedness is subsumed under rectitude and right abiding;
being without self is subsumed under non-retrogression and progress;
and superior progress is subsumed under the equipment of merit and the equipment of wisdom.
"These four dharmas are subsumed within eight dharmas. Ratnapāṇi said:
"O son of good family!"
"By how many dharmas are these eight dharmas further subsumed?
Akāśagarbha replied, "Noble son!"
These eight dharmas are further subsumed by sixteen dharmas.
What are these sixteen?
That which is called "freedom from hesitation" is subsumed by great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*).
That which is essentially true and pure is subsumed by the discipline of body and the discipline of mind;
that which is upright is subsumed by patience and gentleness;
that which is correctly abiding is subsumed by the absence of pride and the absence of obstruction.
Not falling back is comprised of steadfastness and power;
advancing upward is comprised of acting according to what has been done and correct practice;
the equipment of merit is comprised of initial aspiration and never abandoning the ultimate goal.
"The accumulation of wisdom consists in seeking extensive learning and reflecting upon what has been heard;
it is comprised of these eight dharmas and sixteen dharmas.
Thus spoke Ratnapāṇi.
“Good son! By how many dharmas are these sixteen dharmas further subsumed?
Ākāśagarbha replied:
“Good son! These sixteen dharmas are subsumed within thirty-two dharmas.
What are these thirty-two?
That which is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is comprised of an unimpeded mind and a mind of equality toward all sentient beings;
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is comprised of tirelessness and the diligent provision of what is needed for all sentient beings;
and the cultivation of the body is comprised of non-agitation and non-infliction of harm.
A disciplined mind is comprised of meditative concentration and tranquility;
patience is comprised of receiving the true teaching and practicing in accordance with it;
gentleness is comprised of a sense of shame and dread of blame.
Being free from arrogance is subsumed by humility and reverent respect;
being free from obstruction is subsumed by being stainless and not being overbearing;
being firm is subsumed by not transgressing one's conduct and fulfilling one's original vows.
Power is subsumed by abiding in right intention and being undisturbed;
acting as one has resolved is subsumed by speaking accordingly and being able to practice;
right conduct is subsumed by right exertion and right progress.
Initiating the resolve is subsumed under "certain victory" and "non-retrogression";
not abandoning [the practice] is subsumed under "delighting in victory" and "supreme seeking";
and seeking extensive learning is subsumed under "approaching spiritual friends" and "pleasing spiritual friends."
Reflecting upon what has been heard is encompassed by wisdom and skillful observation.
Noble son, these sixteen dharmas are thus encompassed by thirty-two dharmas.
Ratnapāṇi said: "Good son! By how many dharmas are these thirty-two dharmas further subsumed?"
Ākāśagarbha replied:
"Good son! These thirty-two dharmas are subsumed within sixty-four dharmas."
What are these sixty-four dharmas?
That which is called the unobstructed mind is subsumed under protecting oneself and protecting others;
that which is equanimity toward all sentient beings is subsumed under non-differentiation and the single flavor.
Being free from weariness is subsumed by the contemplation of all things as dreams and the knowledge that birth and death are like illusions;
being diligently devoted to providing for all sentient beings is subsumed by the various supernormal powers and skillful means;
and not being provoked to anger is subsumed by a sense of shame and faith in the retribution of karma.
Non-harming is subsumed by fewness of desires and contentment;
meditative concentration is subsumed by the absence of provocation and the absence of distraction;
tranquility is subsumed by the relinquishing of the self and the detachment from what belongs to the self.
Those who receive the true teaching are comprised of seeking the Dharma and desiring the Dharma;
those who practice in accordance [with the teaching] are comprised of reverence and impartiality without weariness;
and those with a sense of shame are comprised of internal eradication and non-engagement externally.
A sense of shame is comprised of having faith and delight in the Buddha’s wisdom and not committing evil even in private;
humility is comprised of being free from arrogance and knowing how to humble oneself;
and reverence is comprised of physical uprightness and mental rectitude.
Being free from defilement is subsumed by possessing tranquil concentration and cultivating wisdom;
not being overbearing is subsumed by not being coarse or harsh and not engaging in divisive speech;
not transgressing one's practice is subsumed by not abandoning the bodhicitta and mindfulness of the site of enlightenment.
The fulfillment of original vows is comprised of the abandonment of demonic activities and being sustained by the spiritual power of the Buddha;
dwelling correctly in the mind is comprised of being neither frivolous nor distracted;
and being unshakeable is comprised of being like a rocky mountain and being immovable.
One who speaks as they have been taught is encompassed by the performance of wholesome deeds and freedom from feverish affliction;
one who is able to practice is encompassed by non-deceptiveness and not forsaking the refuge;
one who correctly sets forth is encompassed by being free from extreme views and by conforming to the contemplation of profound dependent origination.
Right progress is encompassed by skillful means and expedient methods;
certain victory is encompassed by lack of indolence and valor;
non-retrogression is encompassed by great aspiration and further advancement.
Delighting in excellence is subsumed by seeing the Tathāgata and hearing the Dharma;
seeking the supreme is subsumed by abandoning the faults of the stages and attaining the virtues of the stages;
and drawing near to spiritual friends is subsumed by freedom from malice and envy, as well as by faith and joy.
Pleasing the spiritual friend is subsumed under respectful compliance and not contradicting their instructions;
wisdom is subsumed under the contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of non-self;
and skillful observation is subsumed under the cultivation of signlessness and the non-reliance on nirvāṇa.
“Good son! These thirty-two dharmas are subsumed within sixty-four dharmas.
Precious Hand asked again:
“By how many dharmas are these sixty-four dharmas further subsumed?
Ākāśagarbha replied, “Good son!
These sixty-four dharmas are subsumed within one hundred and twenty-eight dharmas.
What are these one hundred and twenty-eight dharmas? They are as follows:
that which is called "protecting oneself" is subsumed under the severance of all evil and the accomplishment of all roots of goodness.
Protecting others is subsumed by patience and gentleness;
being without differentiation is subsumed by a mind like water and a mind like wind;
being of one flavor is subsumed by the contemplation of the dharma-realm and the contemplation of suchness.
That which is like a dream is subsumed by the contemplation of non-transmigration and the contemplation of lack of reality;
that which is like an illusion is subsumed by the manifestation according to dispositions and the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature;
and all supernormal powers are subsumed by the understanding of the definitive meaning and the understanding of wisdom.
Skillful means is subsumed by great compassion and the perfection of wisdom;
a sense of shame is subsumed by not concealing one's transgressions and by repentance;
belief in the retribution of karma is subsumed by heedfulness and the dread of the miserable realms.
Having few desires is subsumed under being pure in one's dwelling, having moderation, and being free from the defilement of staying overnight;
contentment is subsumed under being easy to satisfy and easy to support;
and being without provocation is subsumed under ultimate perfection and the ultimate limit.
That which is without dissipation is subsumed by the attainment of patience and the stage of non-retrogression;
that which abandons the self is subsumed by not reckoning the body or the life-span as "I";
that which is free from "mine" is subsumed by the absence of greed and the absence of delusion.
Those who seek the Dharma are characterized by wisdom and abandonment;
those who desire the Dharma are characterized by non-attachment to the five desires and the elimination of afflictions;
those who show reverence are characterized by conceiving of the Dharma as the World-Honored One and as a remedy for healing.
Being free from weariness is subsumed under physical lightness, alert diligence, and moderation in sleep;
the internal severing [of afflictions] is subsumed under the mindfulness of the body and the mindfulness of feelings;
and the non-engagement with external objects is subsumed under the mindfulness of the mind and the mindfulness of phenomena.
One who has faith and delight in the Buddha’s wisdom is encompassed by profound veneration and pure faith;
one who does not commit evil in private is encompassed by self-realization and the realization of the devas;
one who is not arrogant is encompassed by neither praising oneself nor disparaging others.
Knowing one's own inferiority is subsumed under not being falsely renowned and not manifesting one’s own virtues;
having an upright body is subsumed under not performing the three unwholesome physical actions and not violating the prohibitive precepts;
and having a straightforward mind is subsumed under constantly examining one’s own faults and not speaking of the shortcomings of others.
Those who possess tranquil concentration are encompassed by the pacification of the mind and the cessation of afflictions;
those who cultivate wisdom are encompassed by the discernment of all phenomena and the knowledge of non-self;
those who are not coarse or violent are encompassed by constant engagement in beneficial deeds and compliant patience.
One who refrains from divisive speech is embraced by having a sufficient retinue and by reconciling those who are estranged;
one who does not abandon the bodhicitta is embraced by sentient beings and by the wisdom of the Buddha;
one who recollects the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is embraced by the desire to destroy the hosts of Māra and by the attainment of perfect awakening.
Abandoning the works of Māra is subsumed by right contemplation and not forsaking the resolve for bodhi;
being sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power is subsumed by firm practice and excellent, pure dedication;
being free from frivolity is subsumed by firmly guarding the sense faculties and not abandoning the objective sphere.
Non-distraction is subsumed under the contemplation of suffering and the contemplation of emptiness;
being like a mountain of stone is subsumed under neither rising nor falling;
and being immovable is subsumed under the severing of craving and the removal of hatred.
The performance of wholesome deeds is subsumed under actions performed with wisdom and the abandonment of demonic activities;
freedom from feverish affliction is subsumed under pure ethical discipline and pure meditative concentration;
and freedom from falsehood is subsumed under truthful speech and the lack of expectation for karmic rewards.
Not abandoning the refuge is comprised by accomplishing the deeds of a noble person and by not acting with cowardice;
being free from extreme views is comprised by the contemplation of non-arising and the contemplation of non-destruction;
and conforming to the contemplation of profound dependent origination is comprised by the contemplation of causes and the contemplation of conditions.
Skillfulness is subsumed by being foremost in the absence of contention and the absence of arrogance;
skillful means is subsumed by the means of detachment and the means of non-arising;
and lack of indolence is subsumed by physical strength and mental strength.
The courageous are characterized by a mind of superior progress and the subduing of enemies;
those with great aspiration are characterized by not seeking gain and honor and by having no attachment to their own bodies or lives;
those who advance further are characterized by freedom from ignorance and by non-retrogression.
Seeing the Tathāgata is comprised of the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha and pure faith;
hearing the Dharma is comprised of delighting in going to the place of discourse and delighting in inquiring about it;
abandoning the faults and afflictions of the stages is comprised of non-distraction in practice and the abandonment of evil associates.
Attaining the merits of the various stages is subsumed by skillful dedication and not abandoning one's fundamental practice;
being free from malice and envy is subsumed by the ability to give everything and relinquishing according to one's intention;
having faith and joy is subsumed by stainless conduct and an unclouded mind.
Reverent compliance is subsumed under knowing what is appropriate for the world and practicing in accordance with it;
not contradicting instructions is subsumed under abandoning impurity and practicing pure and correct conduct;
the contemplation of impermanence is subsumed under the contemplation of movement and change and the contemplation of decay and disintegration.
The contemplation of non-self is subsumed under the non-apprehension of an agent and the non-apprehension of an experiencer;
the cultivation of signlessness is subsumed under the non-referencing of objects and the removal of what is expressed by conceptualization;
and the non-reliance on nirvana is subsumed under the elimination of ignorance and the severance of craving and attachment.
“Good son! These sixty-four dharmas are subsumed within one hundred and twenty-eight dharmas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, having heard from the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja this exposition of such dharma-gates, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at what he had never before experienced. He then addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"How marvelous, Great Being!
You are indeed able to achieve such swift eloquence and skillful analytical eloquence, being fully capable of explaining and resolving every question asked."

As I now understand the meaning, intent, and the words of what you have said, by such skillful means, even if one were to speak for an eon or slightly less than an eon, one could not exhaust them, nor would the exposition ever be interrupted.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying: "Good son! It is so, it is so!"

As you have said, if this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha were to expound the meaning of a single phrase, he could speak for an eon or even less than an eon without exhausting it, and his eloquence would never cease.
“The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha possesses such immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and inexhaustible eloquence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi covered the Hall of Exquisite Jewel Adornments with his hand; from within his hand, he produced immeasurable flowers and incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment, robes, ornaments for the body, as well as various banners, pennants, and exquisite parasols. He rained down such supreme and wondrous offerings to make offerings to the Tathāgata and Ākāśagarbha.
In the sky above, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; from among those sounds, sublime verses emerged to praise the Tathāgata:
"Upholding virtue and opening the gates of virtue, endowed with a hundred blessings; With superior intent, disciplined, and with unmoving mindfulness;
Śramaṇa, worthy sage, you have surpassed gods and humans; Son of the Buddha, possessor of the ten powers, you roar throughout the ten directions."
The Honored One of great renown, majestic power, and sovereignty, Subdues those who fear and dispels the darkness of ignorance;
He can deliver all devas and humans drifting in the current, Closing the gates to the evil realms and bringing them cool relief.
The Noble One’s skillful speech is subtle and wondrous; his voice is free from error or confusion and is serene.
Peerless throughout the three realms and devoid of the three defilements, what he proclaims in the ten directions bestows happiness upon all beings.
Firm in intention and delighting in tranquility, the Most Victorious One overcomes the powers of the ten directions;
having abandoned all guile, he has attained the nectar of immortality, free from worldly dust, and is venerated by the multitude.
The World-Honored One remains unmoved amidst the assembly, yet transforms immeasurable multitudes throughout the ten directions;
following the conduct of sentient beings, he is able to accord with them, and the sons of the Buddha likewise delight in cultivating this practice.
Just as the sun, free from obscuration, can shine everywhere and cause all flowers to bloom,
so too does the light of the Buddha’s wisdom shine upon the long-flowing stream, enabling all his children to attain awakening.
Like the wind that meets no resistance yet leaves the mountains unmoved, pure as the void and radiant as the sun.
The Buddha’s sons emit light and rain down nectar; therefore, I pay homage to the Buddha and his sons.

The waters of the great trichiliocosm oceans may yet be measured, the empty space of the ten directions may yet be traversed, and the minds of all sentient beings may yet be made one, but the merit of the World-Honored One can never be exhausted.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Seventeen. 5.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
In the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja," part five,
after these verses had been spoken,

Māra Pāpīyān arrayed his fourfold army and came to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he transformed himself into the form of an elder, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
These great beings are able to accomplish such inconceivable and manifold supernatural transformations, and are further able to manifest inconceivable matters of adornment."
"Bhagavān! In future ages, how many sentient beings will there be who, upon hearing of this inconceivable spiritual transformation, attain awakening and become free from doubt?"
The Buddha addressed Māra Pāpīyān, saying:
"In future ages, there will be few sentient beings—perhaps only one or two—who, upon hearing this sūtra of inconceivable spiritual transformations, will attain faith and understanding."

Pāpīyān! Suppose a single hair were divided into a hundred parts, and one part of that hair were used to take up a single drop of water from the great ocean. What do you think: is what was taken up more?
"Which is more numerous? Pāpīyān replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Those who take it up are very few, while those who remain [unaffected] are very many.
The Buddha again addressed Pāpīyān, saying:

"Just as the water taken from the ocean is very little, so too are those sentient beings who, upon hearing this sūtra of inconceivable spiritual transformations, are able to believe and understand it very few."

"Just as there is a vast amount of water remaining in the great ocean, so too is it with those who do not have faith or understanding in this Sūtra of Inconceivable Supernatural Transformations; they are many.
The Buddha again addressed Pāpīyas:

"If there were a person who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily took precious jewels filling a trichiliocosm and offered them in charity, the merit of a son or daughter of good family who hears this Sūtra of Inconceivable Supernatural Transformations and is able to believe and understand it would be far greater."
Why is this so? Pāpīyān!

If there are those who have faith and understanding in this sutra, you should know that such persons have personally heard this sutra from the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and have faith and understanding of it without doubt.
Why is this? Pāpīyān!
It is impossible for sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness to believe and understand this sutra, which is difficult for the world to believe.
“Pāpīyān! After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be many arrogant sentient beings.

Those beings, clinging to the literal words of what I have taught and not understanding skillful means, will each give rise to contention. They will abandon the contemplation of the Dharma and discard right practice for the sake of gain, fame, clothing, and food. Because they bind themselves, they will delight in discussing various worldly matters and secular literary expressions, rather than discussing the supreme ultimate truth. They will not take pleasure in practicing the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; instead, they will turn toward others to deride and criticize such true, profound, and wondrous sūtras. This constitutes slandering all Buddhas and accumulating an immeasurable mass of great suffering and affliction.”
The māras and devas will assist those people; for the sake of gain, honor, and fame, they will further increase their negligence and arrogance.

Because of this arrogance, when those people see bhikṣus who uphold the precepts and practice virtuous conduct, and who receive, maintain, read, and recite this sūtra, they will treat them with contempt, give rise to hatred and envy, and will slander and defame them without cause.

Those foolish people thus violate the prohibitions and precepts in this present life; among them, some who fear the inability to survive, or those who feel shame before others, falsely don the *kāṣāya* robe, while others abandon the precepts and return to lay life. When such persons die and their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo various bitter retributions.
The Buddha again addressed Pāpīyan:

“In future ages, there may be sentient beings seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle whose roots of goodness regarding various causes and conditions are slight and shallow; having newly resolved their minds on the Way, they cling merely to the literal words and are unable to comprehend the definitive meaning.”
When one receives, maintains, reads, recites, and explains such profound sūtras as these for others, one will be looked down upon, despised, and insulted by others.
Because of being so despised and insulted by others, one will then abandon such profound sūtras and instead read and recite sūtras associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because they are bound by various necessities such as gain, offerings, and fame, they instead slander and revile such true and profound sūtras;

furthermore, they despise those who receive, uphold, read, and recite these sūtras, refusing even to look upon them with their eyes. They constantly delight in base conduct and fall away from the Mahāyāna Dharma of the bodhisattvas—namely, they fall away from the sincere heart and the profound heart.
Because the māras and devas find such persons as these vulnerable, they diligently employ skillful means to corrupt their minds, even to the point of preventing them from hearing sūtras such as this.
If they were to hear it, they would give rise to great slander and lack faith.

Such persons would likewise accumulate immeasurable masses of evil karma and incur the grave offense of destroying the Dharma; they will be forever separated from the Triple Gem, unable to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or make offerings to the Sangha.
Why is this so? Pāpīyān!
It is because they have given rise to doubt and hesitation regarding the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, seeing his own transgression, was filled with sorrow, anxiety, and trepidation; he approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja asked Māra Pāpīyas:
"Why do you stand to one side, so sorrowful, emaciated, trembling, and gasping for breath, appearing like one who has lost his resolve?"
Māra Pāpīyas replied: “Good son!
Having heard from the Tathāgata such terrifying matters as these, I am therefore filled with sorrow and fear; to which realm shall I fall?”
"Who shall save me?
I have repeatedly committed countless obstacles against the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata; for this reason, I am filled with sorrow."
Gaganagañja said: “Pāpīyan!

Within the Buddha-dharma there is a method for the expiation of offenses. You should come to the presence of the World-Honored One and, with a sincere heart, repent for all the evils you have committed; do not commit them ever again.”
"If one can act in this way, one shall obtain wholesome benefit and not let it go to waste.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān immediately stepped forward and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the feet of the World-Honored One. Gazing up at the Tathāgata, he wept and shed tears as he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I now repent with a sincere heart for the countless obstacles I have repeatedly created within the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata since time immemorial.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will give rise to a heart of great compassion; out of loving-kindness and pity, I beseech you to accept my repentance.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Pāpīyān! That you are able to recognize for yourself the various evils you have committed is most excellent indeed!

One who can thus repent of their transgressions and offenses thereby expands the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata within the Buddha-dharma; the Buddhas will also accept the repentance of such a person. Therefore, from now on, do not commit them again.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "O noble sirs!
Each of you should speak on the methods for transcending the realm of Māra, out of compassion for the Māra Pāpīyān."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Golden Mountain King (Suvarṇaparvatarāja). Sitting among the multitude, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there is one who guards the internal realms, they have not yet transcended the realm of Māra."

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who perceives all realms as identical to the Buddha-realm, and knows that this Buddha-realm is itself no realm, this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who rely upon and take shelter in a nest or cave are within the realm of Māra.”

If there is a bodhisattva who does not rely on a nest-like dwelling and knows that all dharmas have no characteristic of attainment, then they can, for the sake of all sentient beings, preach the dharma of severing reliance on such nests; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who grasp at ‘mine’ and ‘I,’ this constitutes the realm of Māra.”
If there are bodhisattvas who do not grasp at "self" or "what belongs to self," they will have no contention.
Because they have no contention, they have no mental activity; how much less could there be a realm of Māra!
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend all realms of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Araṇavīrya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If there is contact and separation, then there is contention; where there is contention, Māra finds his opportunity.

If there is neither contact nor separation, one does not contend oneself and does not cause others to contend. Because one has attained non-self, for the practitioner who is free from affliction, it is possible to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnacintā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is conceptualization and discrimination, that is affliction; and wherever affliction exists, that is the realm of Māra.”
If there is a bodhisattva who knows that all dharmas are without marks, they will have no deluded thoughts regarding the afflictions.

Whether internal or external, they do not distinguish between them, for they have departed from all deluded conceptualization and discrimination; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Delight-in-Action addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a state of liking and disliking, then there will be hatred and attachment.”
If there is hatred or attachment, that is the realm of Māra.

If there is a bodhisattva who departs from hatred and attachment and practices with equanimity, they will have no dualistic conceptions regarding all phenomena; they will attain entry into the inconceivable realm, and this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vigataraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! The realm of Māra arises from the self. If a bodhisattva can know this self, they attain the patience of non-self (anātma-kṣānti) and thereby know the purity of the self. Because they know the purity of the self, they know the purity of all phenomena (sarvadharma). Because they know the purity of all phenomena, they know that the nature of all dharmas is pure like space; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one follows dharmas associated with afflictions and is driven by craving, then Māra will find an opportunity.”
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva who attains the highest mastery over all dharmas and awakens spontaneously, being thus granted a prediction by all Buddhas and never regressing from the dharma of Bodhi—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sound of Colliding Mountains said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If the mind has any deficiency or leakage, it is the realm of Māra.”

If a bodhisattva’s precepts are without flaw and their mind is without flaw, and they accomplish the practice of all dharmas of emptiness, this is what enables a bodhisattva to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, Māra will find his opportunity.”

If there is a bodhisattva who constantly beholds all Buddhas yet does not cling to their physical forms, and constantly hears all dharmas yet does not cling to words—because seeing the Dharma is to see the Buddha, and because being beyond verbal expression one can hear all dharmas—this is for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Diwang addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is reliance or agitation, this is the realm of Māra.”

If a bodhisattva practices diligence in accordance with wholesome signs, knowing that all phenomena ultimately lack the characteristic of accomplishment, they remain unshakable without relying on anything; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Virtuous Radiance addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who practice dualistic dharmas, then Māra will find an opportunity.”

If there is a bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they will not perceive any difference between the realm of Māra and the nature of phenomena.

Knowing that the nature of phenomena and the realm of Māra are equal because they possess the characteristic of non-duality, this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are bodhisattvas whose natures are weak and who fear the most profound Dharma, then Māra will find an opportunity to exploit them.”

If a courageous and valiant bodhisattva is well able to penetrate the three gates of liberation and is neither startled nor terrified by the profound Dharma—because they are able to directly realize and know the true nature of all phenomena—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Just as the water in the great ocean has a single salty taste, so too is it with the ocean of the Buddha-dharma; it likewise has a single flavor of Dharma, namely, the flavor of liberation and the flavor of detachment from desire."
"If a bodhisattva skillfully understands the single flavor of all phenomena, this is what constitutes a bodhisattva being able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
It is, for example, like space, which is ultimately stainless, ultimately luminous and pure, and ultimately not subject to being disturbed or obscured by any smoke, dust, clouds, or mist.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: their mind is like space, knowing that the nature of all phenomena is eternally pure and is never disturbed by adventitious afflictions. Having reached the further shore of Prajñāpāramitā and being free from all darkness, they attain the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena; this is what it means for a Bodhisattva to be able to transcend the realm of Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is speech, then there is obstruction.”
If there is any obstruction, that is the realm of Māra.
If a dharma cannot be expressed by any verbal discourse, then it is without obstruction.
What is meant by a dharma being inexpressible?
That which is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is such that within this ultimate truth there are neither words nor meanings.

If a bodhisattva can practice the ultimate truth, they will find that there is ultimately nothing to be practiced regarding any phenomena; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to transcend the realm of Māra, because there is nothing to be transcended.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyas, saying:
"Have you not heard the teaching on transcending the realm of Māra?
Pāpīyas replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We have indeed heard it.
The Buddha said:
“Pāpīyan! If there are those who practice such dharmas as these, all the māras will be powerless against them.
If any māras wish to instigate demonic obstacles for such practitioners, they will ultimately be unable to succeed, and instead will accumulate immeasurable heaps of transgressions.”
Therefore, Pāpīyan! You should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and you should firmly uphold and practice these dharmas that transcend the realm of Māra.
If you can practice in this way, then you will be able to transcend all the realms of Māra. Pāpīyān!

Just as the grime and grease of a hundred or a thousand years can be washed away in a single day until it is bright and clean, so too, all unwholesome karma accumulated over a hundred or a thousand kalpas can be entirely extinguished in a single day and a single moment through the power of the Buddha-dharma and by means of skillful, compliant reflection.
Pāpīyān! Just as a small fire cast into a heap of dry grass as vast as Mount Sumeru could quickly burn it all away,
so too, by means of even a small power of wisdom, can one eliminate the immeasurable mass of darkness.
Why is this? Pāpīyān!
It is because wisdom is brilliant and courageous, whereas ignorance is inferior and weak.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas had this thought:
"The World-Honored One of Great Compassion now takes pity on me and is able to teach me the Dharma of the Bodhicitta; I should now plant even a small root of goodness before the Tathāgata."

Thereupon, Pāpīyān immediately manifested eighty-four thousand exquisite jeweled parasols, as well as immeasurable flower garlands, necklaces, powdered incense, and ointments, and addressed his retinue, saying:

"The appearance of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the world is extremely rare; you all should come together to the place where the World-Honored One resides for the sake of making offerings."

At that time, among the retinue of the Māra-heavenly beings, there were eighty-four thousand followers along with Māra Pāpīyān; each of them together held exquisite jeweled parasols and immeasurable flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, and ointments. Having arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was and presented these offerings, they all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The other members of Māra’s retinue and those devas who had not yet resolved upon bodhicitta mocked and derided Pāpīyān, saying:
“How extraordinary, Pāpīyān! You are able to feign such an appearance of profound faith before the śramaṇa Gautama, acting as if you were his closest relative.”
The reason for this is that Pāpīyān may wish to learn the spells, illusions, and esoteric arts from the śramaṇa Gautama; therefore, he has now manifested before my very eyes to offer such praise.
At that time, the Māra-son Virūpamukha and the other Māra-sons, all lacking faith, each spoke these words:
"Even if the śramaṇa Gautama should employ various arts and stratagems to turn back the Māras, we shall together devise every means to ensure that such sūtras as these do not circulate."

Even if it were to be disseminated, it would be met with little protection or assistance; those who believe, accept, and practice it would likewise be very few. It would be held in contempt and mocked by many people, and it would constantly fall into remote regions rather than being proclaimed throughout the central lands.
May it be heard only by those sentient beings who lack majesty and are impoverished; let it never be heard by those of great majesty, wealth, and power, who would otherwise disbelieve and slander it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"Virtuous one! Did you hear these sons of Māra utter such evil words?"
Gaganagañja replied to the Buddha,
“Yes, I have heard it.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! For this reason, you should comfort, protect, and assist this sublime sūtra in order to subdue all māras and spirits.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have already protected and upheld sūtras such as these; we, too, shall comfort and uphold them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha spoke this dhāraṇī, which is as follows:
"The Four Kings always protect, as well as Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Brahmā, Lord of the World."
The various devas who revere the Buddha and protect bodhi— may such deities as these always provide protection and subdue all māras.
"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, you shall uphold the True Dharma, protect the Dharma-preachers, and provide full protection.
Having spoken this mantra, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha concluded.
At that moment, this Hall of Wondrous Jewel Adornments and the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Then, the sons of Māra saw in the space above five hundred Guhyapatis wielding vajra-clubs, blazing like fire and most terrifying.
At that time, the Guhyapatis proclaimed these words:
"If there are sons of Māra or any māra-demons who, upon hearing this mantra, do not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, we shall strike their heads and shatter them into seven pieces."

At that time, the sons of Māra and their retinues were struck with terror and trembling, the hair on their bodies standing on end; they immediately joined their palms in homage to the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“We now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will save us from this terror so that we may attain fearless bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed his attendant Ānanda, saying:

"Just as you have spoken here, sons of Māra, those of us who shall create obstacles for this sūtra in a future age must surely act in accordance with our original vow to create obstacles for such a sūtra as this."

It shall only be through the spiritual power of the Buddha and the upholding of the various bodhisattvas that it will circulate in the world; yet, there will not be many people who uphold, read, recite, analyze, or explain it.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"Do you see these sons of Māra who, for the sake of escaping their terror, have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, I have seen it.”
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"These words shall serve as the cause for the sons of Māra to abandon their demonic deeds, because they have not resolved upon bodhicitta with a profound mind."
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:

"In a future age, there shall appear in the world a Buddha named Vimalanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is at the place of that Buddha that this Māra Pāpīyān shall become irreversible and resolve his mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Ānanda! Because that Tathāgata Vimalalakṣaṇa knows that his profound resolve has been fulfilled, he shall bestow upon him the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, you shall likewise become a Māra-king who, with a profound heart of reverence and faith, honors the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Just as when Maitreya appears, there will be a Māra-king named Śāstṛ who, with a profound heart of reverence and faith, honors the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha.

These five hundred sons of Māra shall also be born among the māras there; for the sake of bodhi, they shall plant various roots of goodness under that Buddha, until the time when Pāpīyān attains buddhahood, at which point he shall grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This Māra Pāpīyān, although he has now resolved upon bodhicitta, remains wavering and uncertain, like a small piece of fine woolen cloth."
"Nevertheless, he shall gradually accomplish immeasurable merit and become a World-Honored One, just as my own body is now.

At that time, among the assembly were immeasurable and boundless devas, worldlings, Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors. Hearing that Māra Pāpīyas had been granted the prediction that he would attain Buddhahood, they leaped for joy at this unprecedented marvel. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke these words:
"How extraordinary! How rare!"
Those who behold the Buddha will surely attain the accomplishment of an immeasurable accumulation of the Dharma-treasures of merit.
Why is this so? Because there may be sentient beings lacking faith who, desiring to disturb and confound the Tathāgata, nevertheless come to behold the Buddha.
"Should there be those who encounter and are able to see the Buddha, I shall act as a cause for those sentient beings, even leading them to attain nirvana.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who else is able to discern and know the faculties of sentient beings in such a manner?
The Buddha addressed the devas and humans, saying:
"As you have said, there is no one who, having been able to see the Tathāgata, does not receive benefit."

"You all should know that there may be sentient beings whose roots of goodness are completely exhausted, such that for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* *nayuta* kalpas they lack the status of a human body. Yet, because such sentient beings see the Tathāgata, they immediately gain the cause of goodness and even attain *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the Tathāgata is able to act as an immeasurable, inconceivable, and unsurpassed field of merit."
The Buddha again addressed the devas and humans, saying:

"The nature of the mind is eternally pure, yet ordinary, ignorant sentient beings are unable to know and see it as it truly is. Because they cannot know and see it as it truly is, they say it is defiled;
because they are able to know and see it correctly, they say it is pure."
Yet within the ultimate reality, there is not a single dharma that can be purified or defiled.

You should know this: all afflictions have no direction and no location; they are neither internal nor external. Afflictions arise through improper reflection, whereas through proper reflection, there are no afflictions.
When there is increase or decrease, inequality arises, and thus afflictions are produced;
where there is no increase or decrease, there are no afflictions.
False and delusive conceptualization is itself affliction.
When there is no conceptual construction, there is no affliction. Therefore, I say:
knowing false views as they truly are is right view, yet false views themselves are not identical to right view.
"One who can know things as they truly are has no falsehood, no exaggeration or diminution, and no grasping; therefore, this is called Right View.
The Buddha again addressed the devas and humans, saying:
"It is like the great earth, which rests upon the water element; the great waters rest upon the wind element; the great winds rest upon space; and space has nothing upon which it rests."
In this way, the great earth has no basis upon which to abide, yet it is conventionally designated as having a basis for its abiding.

Therefore, you should understand it thus: suffering depends on karma, and karma depends on the fetters; yet suffering, karma, and the fetters have no basis at all, because the nature of the mind is eternally pure.

Thus one should know that all phenomena have no fundamental basis and do not abide anywhere at all; they are said to exist only by means of conventional designations, yet in reality they do not exist.
"Therefore, it is said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally pure, ultimately without birth and without arising.
The Buddha again addressed the devas and humans, saying:
"Therefore, you should know that this Dharma-gate is called the 'Dharma-gate of the Eternally Pure Nature.'"
The Bodhisattva who penetrates this gateway is not defiled by any afflictions, yet does not rely upon this gateway of purity.

Because they have relinquished all reliance and agitation, they attain the path of equanimity; they are able to transcend the realm of Māra and enter the realm of the Buddhas, and can also enter the realms of all sentient beings without wavering from the Dharma-realm.
Knowing that all phenomena are neither realms nor non-realms, they are able to swiftly give birth to the realm of omniscience.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the elder Śreṇya, who was among the assembly, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For my sake, you have preached such profound sūtras as these. Previously, because I wished to provoke and distress the World-Honored One, I prepared a great fire pit and set out poisoned rice; yet, since the Great Sage Tathāgata is one who cannot be harmed, I have conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Buddha.

From that time until now, the knots of doubt and regret have never been able to be eradicated; but now, having heard this most profound and subtle sūtra from the Buddha, my doubts and regrets are immediately dispelled, and with my mind free from hindrance, I attain the practice of peaceful bliss.
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, my heart of faith and reverence increases all the more.

Now that my household possesses abundant wealth and treasures, I shall offer them to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, as well as to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and the lowly beggars."
“World-Honored One!
Who would hear this profound sūtra that severs all bonds and yet give rise to craving and attachment toward any phenomena?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is exceedingly profound and difficult to fathom.
If there should be a bodhisattva in a future age who, having sacrificed their own body, life, gain, and reputation, is able to serve the Buddha’s bodhi, such a person would be extremely rare.”
At that time, there were sixty-eight billion bodhisattvas among the assembly who rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and simultaneously spoke these verses with one voice:
“After the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, we shall be able to endure it; we will sacrifice our bodies and lives to protect the True Dharma.”
Renouncing profit and fame, and being free from all attachments, one should vow to protect the True Dharma for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even when subjected to abuse, reprimands, and sarcastic insults, one should endure them for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
They will treat them with contempt and mockery, and spread their ill repute; yet one should protect this sutra through loving-kindness and patience.
They will side with Māra, slander the True Dharma, violate the precepts, and commit evil deeds.
Delighting in worldly entanglements and shrouded by gain, they take no pleasure in the True Dharma;
relying instead on mundane treatises, they are arrogant and heedless. Boasting loudly of their own interests, they despise those who practice correctly;
constantly abandoning solitude and quietude, they delight in dwelling amidst clamor and bustle.
They study worldly rhetoric and cling to the notion of "self";
they do not cultivate wisdom, abandon meditative sitting, and do not draw near to the Triple Gem.
Lacking wisdom, they form factions to seek profit; their every movement is accompanied by fetters.
Delighting in receiving offerings from others,
when others give with a compassionate heart, he cherishes them as if they were his own; he frequently visits them to discuss various worldly affairs—
matters of fields, houses, livelihoods, and trade— and diligently seeks profit and interest, yet still claims to be a śramaṇa.
Arrogant and attached to existence, relying on heterodox and perilous views, they will be greatly terrified upon hearing the teaching of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Claiming that the future is far off and seeking only for present retribution, they shall speak falsely, declaring what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma.
In such times of great calamity, wicked bhikṣus, Māra and his followers shall further provide their assistance.
While the scriptural texts remain the same, the explanations of their meaning will differ; each will preach according to their own treatises—such is the nature of the foolish.
Those profound and wondrous sūtras that can grant liberation—these they shall suppress and obstruct, as well as those that speak of superficial matters.
"I am superior and you are inferior; through superiority one attains the fruit"—thus shall they compete within the Buddha-dharma.
When there is such competition, the number of sentient beings is destroyed; they are tormented and oppressed by unrighteous kings.
In this final age, destruction is most fearsome; I uphold the True Dharma as taught for the salvation of the world.
I always maintain a heart of loving-kindness and do not abandon the Dharma and Vinaya; giving rise to great compassion, I act as a protector for the world.
Those who violate the precepts and commit evil, who do not abide in the True Dharma—I am constantly filled with sorrow and pity for them, wondering which path they will fall into.
Seeing those who intentionally commit evil and slander the upright, I shall never associate with them nor become their kin.
Constantly exerting my strength, I shall well guard against verbal transgressions; seeing those of no worth, I shall not speak of their faults.
I abide in the noble lineages, practicing the dhūtas and guarding the precepts; dwelling in concentration and cultivating wisdom, I am ever diligent in cultivation.
Leaving behind worldly clamor, I delight in seclusion and tranquility; unattached like a deer, I am well-tamed and content.
If they enter a village, they should restrain their senses and speak little; upon seeing those who preach the Dharma, they should discuss the True Dharma together.
With kind words and beneficial acts, they transform sentient beings, further preaching the Dharma for them so that they may sever unwholesome conduct.
For the sake of the True Dharma, I shall travel even to the furthest reaches to teach it for their benefit and for the welfare of all beings.
If I see ordinary, foolish people who are deficient, I shall simply guard myself and abide in the practice of patience through the Dharma.
Whether treated with contempt or with reverence, one should remain as steadfast as Mount Sumeru; unstained by worldly dharmas, one becomes a guide for the world.
If a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts comes to reproach me, I shall reflect upon my own conduct, considering it the ripening of past karma.
For the sake of such envious and wicked beings, one should first speak kind words with a benevolent mind and manifest respectful conduct.
They will then think: "I too am a śramaṇa; I have accomplished these virtues and possess no such evils."
Those who violate the precepts and the like are like people who have lost their resolve; hearing this sutra brings them distress, like a man whose nose has been cut off looking into a mirror.
They employ various means to avoid hearing it, and they further teach others, saying it is not the true Dharma;
they even instruct kings to corrupt the hearts of ministers and subjects, leading them to slander the true Dharma.
If it is said that this was not spoken by the Buddha,
we, at that time, shall— by the power of the Buddha— for the sake of upholding the True Dharma, not spare our own bodies or lives.
The World-Honored One knows me; my words are without duplicity. I shall firmly uphold and protect [the teaching], dwelling in this True Dharma.
Making speech that is truthful, acting according to what I have said, I shall please all Buddhas and thereby realize Bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha praised the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Beings!"
