"It is truly a great joy that you have been able to make such sincere vows and uphold the Tathāgata’s profound, subtle, and unsurpassed Great Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha said to Ākāśagarbha:
“O Worthy One!”

Suppose, for example, that the thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms in the eastern direction—and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—were all ground into fine dust, and that this entire amount of dust were gathered into a single heap.

Suppose there were a person who possessed immeasurable power through supernormal faculties and a long life; this person were to take up some atoms of dust and, having passed as many worlds to the east as there are atoms, drop a single atom, proceeding in this manner further and further to the east until all the gathered atoms were exhausted—yet even then, those worlds would still not be exhausted.

Just as it is with the worlds of the eastern direction, so it is with the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; having passed that many buddha-fields, one sets down a single mote of dust. Proceeding in this manner through all directions until this entire mass of motes is exhausted, yet the worlds themselves remain inexhaustible.
Gaganagañja! What do you think? Are these worlds not indeed many?
Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, very many,
World-Honored One!”
"It is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
The Buddha said, "Worthy One!"

All the places where the atoms of these worlds are attached and those where they are not, having exhausted all the worlds reached by these atoms, are again made into one great city, equal in length, breadth, height, and depth; within that city, it is filled with mustard seeds.
“Worthy sir! Can these mustard seeds be counted?
Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even by means of metaphors it cannot be fully understood, much less can it be known through calculation;
none but the Tathāgata is able to calculate it.”
The Buddha said to Gaganagañja, “So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said;
only a Tathāgata can know these mustard seeds, whether they be counted by the hundreds, the thousands, or the hundreds of thousands of millions.”
The Buddha said:

"Worthy one! Suppose there were a person who had perfected the immeasurable power and majesty of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), such that he could take these mustard seeds and scatter them throughout the ten directions with a single breath from his mouth, so that each mustard seed fell into a single Buddha-world and never more than one."
"Virtuous one! What do you think?
Is the world reached by all those mustard seeds indeed many?"
Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These worlds cannot be distinguished by the power of the mind.”
"If one were to engage in such conceptualization, it would cause the minds of people to become deluded and confused.
"Worthy One! I now tell you:

if there were sons or daughters of good family practicing the bodhisattva path who, day after day, took as many immeasurable treasures as fill those worlds and used them for giving, doing so without ceasing and attending to no other affairs; [the merit of this would not equal that of hearing this teaching]."

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe this profound sutra—not seeking gain or sustenance, but for the sake of bodhi—even if they explain it to but a single person so that, having heard it, that person is encouraged toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and even gives rise to a single wholesome thought, desiring that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.

The merit of this person exceeds that of the former donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, and even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy; how much more so for one who can cause another to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Why is this? Worthy one!
It is because they are able to speak thus of the accomplishment of immeasurable roots of goodness for the sake of all bodhisattvas, in order to protect and uphold the true Dharma.
"O worthy one!
I do not see any other dharma that surpasses this, whereby a bodhisattva may firmly practice right conduct, encompass all wholesome dharmas, and transform sentient beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare is the Tathāgata’s inconceivability; the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.”
Just as the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, so too the merit obtained by those who receive and uphold this sutra is inconceivable.

We pray only that the World-Honored One will protect and uphold this sutra, so that in future ages those good sons and good daughters who receive and uphold this True Dharma may obtain this sutra in their hands and hold it within their bosoms, never parting from it.

"If one is destined to transcend birth and death, they will naturally attain awakening to Bodhi without hearing it from another; having awakened to Bodhi, they shall extensively expound it for others.
The Buddha said, "Worthy One!"
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
For the sake of protecting this sutra, I shall now proclaim these verses to summon the Four Heavenly Kings who Guard the World, Śakra, Brahmā, and all other deities.
Because they are summoned by these verses, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā shall all protect those Dharma-preachers who uphold this sutra;

when they expound this profound sutra that is difficult for the world to believe, they shall ensure that no obstacles can arise—namely, whether it be kings or ministers banishing them from the country, contracting a grave illness, the outbreak of strife and contention, or the spread of pestilence within the land. When such events occur, by the power of these incantations, they shall be immediately extinguished and rendered ineffective.

23. Tatrabhadrika: "In accordance with the Buddha's intention, following the nature of the Dharma, and revering the Sangha,"
The World-Rulers have faith;
the Four World-Protecting Kings, for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas, shall receive and uphold this mantra and protect those who preach the Dharma.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We shall protect these sons of the Buddha who receive and uphold this sutra."
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

"Śvī (1) śvabhadri (2) śveti (3) indra-vaṅga (4) dhāri-vaṅga (5) dhāraṇī (6) phaddame (7) akhyoṅ-khyepa (8) amukhya (9) arani-dha-vaṅga (10) sauśrī-saheṇa (11) spiti-spitāre-santi (12) samai (13) vayamai (14) samaraimi (15) vasantārya (16) hū-hū (17) he-he (18) kulu-kule (19). At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, rose from his seat with a pure and joyful heart. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
"In the age of famine during the final dharma period, O Greatly Renowned Noble One, if you uphold and preach this sutra, I shall serve as your attendant."
Then, having spoken this verse, Śakra uttered this incantation:
"Arise from the bliss of dhyāna, you who come to protect and uphold the Dharma!
All the World-Honored Ones of the various worlds together receive and uphold it."
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, King of the Heaven of Great Brahmā, rose from his seat and praised those gods—the Śakras, Brahmas, and World-Protectors—saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
That you are able to don this great armor for the sake of protecting the True Dharma and for those who uphold and expound the Dharma is precisely what you ought to do; it is most appropriate.
For as long as the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya remain in the world, during that time there shall be those who can distinguish between right conduct and the practice of the Dharma;
during that time, the gods and people of the world shall be exceedingly flourishing and fill the palaces and dwellings.
"After this Dharma has ceased, the gods and people of the world will gradually diminish, and their palaces and dwellings will become desolate and abandoned.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!"
"You should receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and widely explain this profound sutra for others. Maitreya!

I now entrust such profound sutras as these to you, so that this Great Dharma may long abide in the world, to subdue all Māras, to benefit all sentient beings, to ensure that no non-Buddhists find an opportunity to prevail, to instruct all Bodhisattvas so that they may draw near to this sutra and not depart from it, to cause the great light of the Buddha-dharma to long abide in the world without declining or perishing, and to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha is never severed."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall always receive, uphold, and widely proclaim this profound sūtra.”
Why is this? One who upholds this Dharma upholds the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it is not merely the Dharma of a single Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
I also do so for the sake of protecting my own Dharma.
World-Honored One!
I constantly dwell together with the hosts of devas and humans, universally assembled in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, where I frequently expound such profound sūtras as these for them.

Furthermore, I shall cause those among humanity who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sūtra to obtain this scripture in their hands, holding it within their bosoms and never parting from the scroll.
World-Honored One!

If, furthermore, at the end of the age when the Dharma is about to perish, there should be those who receive and uphold this sutra and explain it to others, you should know that these are all established by the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya.

"Bhagavān! At that time, although there will be many demonic activities to disturb practitioners, those who preach the Dharma—being possessed by the demon of afflictions (kleśamāra)—will take no pleasure in this sutra, will not diligently practice it, and will engage in mutual disputes and accusations."

We shall all together diligently apply skillful means to cause the speaker of the Dharma to take delight in this sutra, so that he may constantly and diligently practice its cultivation, read and recite it until he masters it, and expound it widely for others.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Maitreya!”

You are indeed able to let out the lion’s roar for the sake of upholding the True Dharma; you have not only let out the lion’s roar before me now, but you have also let out the lion’s roar and upheld the True Dharma before immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the past.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda,
do you receive and uphold this sutra?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, I have already received and upheld it.”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

You should always extensively analyze and explain this for the fourfold assembly. If there are those who have previously planted roots of goodness and delight in the supreme Dharma, such people, having heard it, will be able to believe, understand, accept, uphold, read, recite, and widely proclaim it to others. Such persons shall obtain an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable mass of great merit.”
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "This sutra is titled 'Exhorting Bodhisattvas to Adorn Bodhi'; you should uphold it in this way."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇavyūha rose from his seat amidst the assembly, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma and those who preach it, has been able to skillfully and joyfully praise this sutra in such a manner.
World-Honored One!

If bodhisattvas who are newly trained, for the sake of awakening, plant various roots of goodness and diligently make offerings to the Tathāgata with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, and ointments, yet do not uphold this sutra—would such persons truly be performing the supreme offering to the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

This does not constitute the foremost offering to the Tathāgata, nor can one obtain immeasurable merit through this cause and condition; it is not equal to the vast merit of good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, and recite this sutra.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With my Buddha-eye, I behold the buddha-fields, pervading the ten directions,
vast and boundless."
If all those worlds were filled to the brim with precious jewels, and a bodhisattva were to constantly give them away in charity;
yet another were to receive and uphold the profound and wondrous sutras—the Dharma of non-attainment spoken by all Buddhas—and expound them for others:
the merit of this latter person [would far exceed the former].
Furthermore, in even greater measure than that,
with jeweled canopies, banners, and streamers, and most exquisite garments—
using such offerings to fill all realms universally, they make offerings to the Tathāgatas and dedicate the merit toward the Buddha-way.
If, in a future age at the time when the Dharma is about to perish,
one diligently practices to protect and assist the world-saving Dharma, upholds the True Dharma,
and acts without negligence— the mass of merit from this shall be even greater than that.
All the great oceans are filled to the brim with the finest fragrant oils;
forming great lamp wicks as vast as Mount Sumeru, they are lit as an offering to all the Buddhas.
When the torch of the Dharma is about to be extinguished, one knows that the beings of the world are shrouded by ignorance.
If one can kindle this great torch of the Dharma, the merit of such a person shall surpass even that [of the former].
As I have seen, though one were to offer various kinds of sublime and pleasing gifts to immeasurable Buddhas for billions of kalpas,
such offerings could not equal the upholding of this wondrous sutra.
Knowing there is a profound debt of gratitude, one protects and upholds the Triple Gem;
for the sake of repaying that kindness and desiring to benefit all sentient beings, one receives and maintains this sutra—
the merit of which surpasses that [of the former].

With my Buddha-eye, I behold all sentient beings; even if one were to teach them all until they had become Śakras or Brahmās, the merit thereby obtained would not equal that of one who copies and upholds this sutra—the merit of the latter is far greater.
If one were able to teach all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm so that they all attained the two vehicles,
yet another were able to give rise to the bodhicitta and uphold this sutra, the merit of the latter would be even more supreme.
If the merit of upholding this sutra were to take form, it would completely fill the worlds of the ten directions.
With the exception of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, supreme wisdom, there is no one else capable of knowing this merit.
Just as the wisdom of the Tathāgata has no limit, and as the dharma-realm of empty space likewise has no limit,
so too are the merits of one who can uphold this sutra-dharma of the Tathāgata boundless in the same way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to my understanding of the meaning and intent of what the Tathāgata has spoken, when the Dharma is about to perish during the final five hundred years, those beings who have set out in the Mahāyāna but do not accept this sūtra and its Dharma—let it be known that such individuals are possessed by Māra and have fallen outside of the Buddha-Dharma.”
“World-Honored One!
I am now capable of receiving and upholding this sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, desiring that the Buddha-dharma may long abide in the world.

At that time, in order to entrust this Dharma of the sutra, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions.

Those Tathāgatas, in order to entrust this Dharma of the sutra, all emitted light from the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows, which universally illuminated all worlds in the ten directions, reaching everywhere without exception.
Having spoken this sutra, the Tathāgata, by means of his great supernormal power, emitted a radiance.

At that time, immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-worlds shook in six ways; immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, and immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas who attained the roots of goodness of those in their final birth before Buddhahood;

moreover, beyond these immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, there were those who attained the vehicle of the śrāvakas and dwelt in the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra,

the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, the Venerable Ānanda, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the śrāvakas, devas, humans, and those of the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 18;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 19.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Section on the Jewel Banner, Part One: The Chapter on the Sufferings of Māra.

At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Great Jewel Enclosure between the realms of desire and form, surrounded by his retinue as he preached the Dharma. He addressed the great assembly, saying:
"In the past, when I first attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I resided in the Bamboo Grove of the Elder Kalandaka at Rājagṛha."
At that time, there were two wise men in the city:
the first was named Upatiṣya,
and the second was named Kolita.
He was fully accomplished in eighteen types of arts, and five hundred disciples constantly followed him.
At that time, the two men said to each other:
"If either of us first attains the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), we must certainly share it with the other."
"At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Aśvajit who rose from meditative concentration early in the morning and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in sequence.
On the road, Upatiṣya saw the bhikṣu Aśvajit from afar and thought to himself:
'I have lived in this city of Rājagṛha for a long time, yet I have never before seen a śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, or anyone else whose deportment is as composed and dignified as this man's.'"
"I shall go and ask whom he serves as his teacher and from whom he has received the Dharma.
Then Upatiṣya went toward that bhikṣu Aśvajit and spoke these words:
“Bhikṣu! Who is your teacher? From whom have you received the Dharma?”
Aśvajit replied: "Good son!

There is a Great Being, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who excels all those who have left the household life, the Unsurpassed Honored One, who has already crossed over birth and death and attained liberation, and who is able to deliver all immeasurable sentient beings; he is called a Buddha."

One who can awaken sentient beings, skillfully perform all practices, and dry up the river of suffering—one who fully accomplishes such qualities as these is my teacher; from him I receive the Dharma.
Upatiṣya said: "What kind of Dharma and meaning does your teacher constantly teach?
"O son of good family!..."
Listen attentively now;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Phenomena arise from conditions; thorough penetration is the cause. Because causes and conditions cease, that is itself tranquility.
The world is suffering; the cause of suffering is called its origination (*samudaya*). If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, the origination of the world ceases.
If there is neither suffering nor its origination, my Teacher declares that this is called Nirvana.
“Good son! My teacher teaches only such dharmas as these.
Having heard these words, Upatiṣya attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and was named a Srotāpanna; he then spoke this verse:
"I have heard the bhikṣu preach the Four Noble Truths; I have immediately transcended the three evil realms.
What I had never heard before, I now hear; what I had never attained before, I have now attained."
I have now transcended the three evil realms; Truly and clearly I know the path and what is not the path.
With a sincere heart, I now take refuge in the Buddha, Because he has been able to proclaim this Dharma.
Having spoken this verse, he again addressed the bhikṣu:
"In this way, World-Honored One, where does he now dwell? Aśvajit replied:
"The World-Honored One is currently in the great city of Rājagṛha, within the Bamboo Grove of the elder Kalandaka, together with a thousand bhikṣus including Kāśyapa and ten thousand bodhisattvas."
"You may go there. Upatiṣya said, "Bhikṣu!"
"I shall first go back and consult my fellow students and my own disciples.
Then Upatiṣya paid respectful homage to the bhikṣu Aśvajit, circumambulated him three times to the right, and returned to his dwelling place.
The brahmin Kolita saw Upatiṣya from afar and immediately asked him: "Upatiṣya!
Your faculties are now pure and serene, and your complexion is radiant; have you perhaps attained the flavor of the Deathless?"
“Good son! I have already attained it.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
I shall explain this for you: phenomena arise from conditions; the penetration of these causes is the path. Because causes and conditions cease, there is tranquility.
The world is suffering; the cause of suffering is called its origination. If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, the origination of the world ceases.
"If there were no suffering and no accumulation [of its causes], my Teacher would have called it Nirvana.
Kolita said, "Virtuous man!

Such words as these can exhaust all suffering; they are the holy life (brahmacarya), capable of severing all causes and conditions of false views, and they also declare that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are empty.
"O noble son! We pray that you will speak further.
Upatiṣya spoke again as he had before; having finished speaking, he immediately attained the fruit of srotāpanna.

Kullūta said: "These words are able to transcend the four floods and cross over birth and death; they penetrate the five aggregates and bring about the eternal extinction of afflictions. This is the flavor of the Deathless (amṛta) that I have now attained; it is not fitting for me to remain here."
"Good son! Where does such a teacher reside? Upatiṣya replied:
"I have heard that he resides in the great city of Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Upatiṣya and Kolita said to their disciples:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is now here; we have already received his teaching on the Dharma. Where do you intend to go now?"
At that time, the Māra King addressed the assembly of devas:
"In the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, there are two great men of supreme wisdom:
one is named Upatiṣya;..."
The second is named Kolita; he now wishes to become a disciple of that Gautama.
If these two men receive the Dharma from that śramaṇa Gautama, my realm will be empty. I shall now go to turn back their resolve for renunciation.
At that time, Māra immediately transformed his body into the likeness of Aśvajit and went to where Upatiṣya Kauṇḍinya was, saying these words:
"O son of good family!
What I previously said was merely to test your wisdom; since you have given no answer, Śākyamuni Tathāgata has not truly spoken such words.
The Tathāgata constantly says:

"There is no fruit of wholesome karma and no fruit of unwholesome karma; if one can intimately enjoy the pleasures of the five desires, that person shall immediately attain the flavor of the nectar of Dharma."
He further said:
"There is neither this world nor a future world; therefore, there is no karma.
If there is no karma, who performs it and who experiences its results?"
"If there is no seed, how can a fruit be obtained?
Śākyamuni Tathāgata spoke only these words.
At that time, Upatiṣya and Kolita said to one another:
"Such words as these are the utterances of Māra, not the words of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, they were not spoken by the bhikṣu Aśvajit.
Once Māra realized this, he immediately vanished.
At that time, the two men again addressed their disciples, the young brahmins:

"You have always observed with clarity that in this world, none are exempt from birth, old age, sickness, and death; yet we have now been able to eternally extinguish all suffering. What do you intend to seek today?"
At that time, Māra again transformed himself into the likeness of Aśvajit and spoke these words:
"Who is able to destroy birth, old age, sickness, and death?"
For example, it is as if someone were to say, "I can destroy that space"—there is no such possibility.
If one says they can destroy birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is likewise so.

Then Kolita said to Māra: "I wish to master the pure Dharma and remain far removed from all suffering. Since none among those who have gone forth possess liberation from such afflictions and suffering as these, I now wish to go to the Tathāgata."
The Māra King is like a wild fox howling; how can you claim it is a lion's roar?
Though the color may be similar, he is truly not a lion. O Māra!
Although you now bear the outward form of a bhikṣu, that which you have spoken is not the speech of a bhikṣu.
A true bhikṣu is one who has destroyed all afflictions; speech that destroys afflictions is pure speech. To speak of neither good nor evil is not the speech of a bhikṣu.
At that time, all the devas in the void each praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
Of all forms of renunciation, the Buddha-way is supreme; indeed, the Buddha-way is itself nirvāṇa. You must now not accept what Māra has said.
Excellent, excellent!
At that time, Māra, suffering great distress, immediately vanished.
Then the disciples said to their two teachers:
"Just as you, O Teachers, have now received the unsurpassed True Dharma from the śramaṇa Gautama, we too shall likewise go to receive it."
Then the two great masters, surrounded before and behind by five hundred disciples, proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove of the householder Kalandaka.
At that time, Māra again manifested a great chasm along their path, one hundred yojanas deep, intending to prevent the people from reaching the Buddha.
Having known this, the Tathāgata immediately employed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to cause those two men to see the ground as level, free from pits or precipices.
Māra again conjured a great mountain before them, thousands of li in height and breadth, but through the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, they were made unable to see it.
Then Māra again dispatched hundreds of thousands of lions to block their path;
upon seeing Upatiṣya and Kolita along with their five hundred disciples, the lions immediately conceived thoughts of goodness and remained silent, crouching low.

The people immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet in reverent salutation, then withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life; I wish to cultivate the pure brahmacarya of the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, sons of good family!"
"Let us freely cultivate and accumulate the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Having spoken these words, they fully undertook the bhikṣu precepts.
At that time, when the Māra King saw that these two had become renunciants, he immediately manifested the form of Īśvara and, approaching the Buddha, spoke this verse:
“If there are wise people in the world who have fully mastered the worldly arts and sciences,
and they all come to pay homage, respect, and make offerings to me, I shall likewise preach the path of purity to them.”
If you, Gautama, wish to cross over birth and death, you should now take refuge with a sincere heart.
The pure path I have now proclaimed is no different from what was taught by the Buddhas of the past.
At that time, I answered the Māra King with these verses:
“I truly know the Eightfold Noble Path, Which can forever bring about separation from and the destruction of all suffering.
You do not truly know this; Do not let a fox’s body roar the lion’s roar.”
At that time, Māra concealed his form as Īśvara and manifested the form of Brahmā, speaking in verse:

"Truly far removed from all afflictions, Able to transcend the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, Do not undergo various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings; You should remain silent and enjoy the bliss of dhyāna."
In this world, there is not even a single person capable of receiving and upholding the flavor of the nectar;
out of compassion for you, I now tell you: you should swiftly enter into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, I replied to Māra with these verses:
"I see many sentient beings in the world Who can cross the great, perilous river of birth and death;
Once those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities Have first attained deliverance, I shall then enter extinction."
At that time, Māra, King of the Demons, was overcome with great anguish and entered his abode of suffering to return to his dwelling.
His various attendants each spoke these words:
"For what reason does our King undergo such great suffering?"
Although he spoke these words, no one was able to understand them.
At that time, five hundred demon maidens, adorned with necklaces and various ornaments, performed music for Māra Pāpīyas, engaging in song, dance, and play to amuse him.
Pāpīyān then gestured with his hand to stop them; the court ladies thereupon remained silent. From two to seven times, Māra likewise stopped them up to seven times.
At that time, there was a woman named Vidyutprabhā who said to Pāpīyas:
"Great King, for what reason are you so distressed as if you had lost your celestial throne, as if a great fire were breaking out?"
"Is there no enemy who can destroy you? Pāpīyān replied, "I have a great enemy called the Son of the Śākyas;
he is a man of great evil who has mastered illusory arts. If I do not subdue him, my realm will become empty."
The court ladies said,
"By what means is that son of the Śākyas adorned?
What spiritual power does he possess?"
"Who are your allies that can empty the realm of the King?
The Mara-king replied, "Those people adorn themselves with precepts, generosity, and patience; they take impermanence, suffering, and emptiness as their armor."

If one destroys the various modes of existence and rebirth of sentient beings, I am unable to know their place of abode; being endowed with unsurpassed great supernormal powers and having great loving-kindness and great compassion as their companions, they are able to deliver all sentient beings within the three realms of existence, and for this reason, they are able to leave my realm empty.

"At that time, when the court ladies heard of the Buddha’s merits, they brought incense, flowers, and various musical instruments, coming to the Buddha’s dwelling to make offerings with all their hearts.
Within this great assembly, only the Buddha saw them; none of the other sentient beings beheld them at all."
At that time, the great assembly was filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is this offering of incense, flowers, and musical instruments not the work produced by the power of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others?"
The Buddha said: "No.
These are the offerings of five hundred maidens of Pāpīyān; the Māra King shall soon arrive here."
When the court ladies heard the Buddha’s words, their hearts were filled with joy, and they immediately attained the samādhi of not losing the bodhicitta.
At that time, the ladies knelt with palms joined and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has forever severed all afflictions, And is able to bestow upon sentient beings the pure Dharma-eye.”
Causing sentient beings to cross the river of birth and death, I therefore praise and prostrate with a sincere heart.
All humans and devas offer praise and worship; You possess infinite and boundless wisdom.
I pray that the Buddha will open for me the skillful means, Enabling me to attain liberation from this female body.
The World-Honored One cultivates the Great Emptiness Samādhi, Thoroughly penetrating the Supreme Truth;
As a great caravan leader fully endowed with the Dharma-treasure, May he destroy the power of Māra and discipline us.
At that time, having finished praising him with these verses, the court lady returned to Māra’s presence and spoke in verse:
“The King’s sovereignty is not eternal or self; He has likewise not escaped birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Multitudes of suffering and afflictions surround the King’s body; He constantly travels through the dark places of the evil paths.”
If you wish to cross the river of birth, old age, and death, You should give rise to faith and go to the Tathāgata.
I now desire to return to the Buddha’s presence To inquire and receive the nectar that cuts off all worldly flavors.
At that time, Pāpīyān conceived a great evil intent, wishing to bind the female attendants with fivefold fetters;
however, due to the Buddha’s supernatural power, he was unable to bind them, and the female attendants immediately returned to the Buddha’s presence.

Pāpīyān could not restrain himself even as he watched with his own eyes; furthermore, he created a vāyu-vilagna wind in the sky, wishing to scatter the women in all directions so that they would no longer see the Buddha, yet by the power of the Buddha, he was unable to destroy them.
At that time, Māra the King wept and lamented in distress, crying out with a loud voice to his wife and children:

"I have now lost my great supernormal powers! A poisonous tree has appeared in the world, preaching annihilation to all sentient beings; he has perfected great illusions and possesses skillful means."
When the various retinues of Māra heard these words, they all gathered together and went to the place where the Māra King was, saying:

"Great King, for what reason do you give rise to such great sorrow and suffering? There are no signs of your defeat, nor is there any conflagration, and within the realm of desire there are no enemies."
The Māra said: "My son!
Do you not see that there is now a man in this world sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, destroying the fourfold army just as a fierce fire consumes dry grass?"
All the wise people in the world have now already submitted to such as these; they are my enemies.
Do you not see that five hundred court ladies have abandoned me and gone to take refuge with them?
If you do not subdue that son of the Śākyas, this trichiliocosm will soon become empty.
Each of you must firmly arm yourselves and exert all your strength together to eliminate that son of the Śākyas.
The son of Māra said:
"Excellent, Great King! I shall adorn [the assembly] to the utmost extent of my supernatural powers."
"If I am able to remove it, how excellent! How wonderful!
But if I am unable, I shall once again take refuge [in you].
The Māra King spoke again:
“Evil man! Why do you now utter such words? “Great King!”

When the śramaṇa Gautama went forth alone and sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he was still difficult to overcome; how much more so now that he has an immeasurable and vast retinue—how could he be destroyed?
The Māra said: "Beloved son!
If you can kill that śramaṇa Gautama, it would be most excellent, most excellent!"
"If you are unable to do so, you must defend your own territory.

At that time, the fourfold army was immeasurable in number, filling Jambudvīpa to a height of eighty yojanas; they unleashed a great and fierce wind and poured down heavy rain, striking Mount Sumeru with their hands and shaking the four continents.

They let out a great, terrifying sound like that of a great nāga king, yakṣas, or various ghosts, shaking all rivers, ponds, and springs; all the nāgas, ghosts, humans, and devas were struck with such fear that their hearts trembled and their hair stood on end.
At that time, those hosts of Māras took a great boulder from Mount Sumeru, intending to cover over the Great City of Rājagṛha and the Kalandaka Grove.
"O virtuous sons!..."
At that time, I immediately entered the samādhi called "Shattering the Power of Māra.

As for the swords, spears, arrows, stones, fire, and poisons rained down by the sons of Māra, through my power they were all transformed into *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which fell upon Rājagṛha City; furthermore, various kinds of subtle, wondrous, and excellent fragrances were rained down.

These evil sounds were transformed into the voices of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the voice of supernatural powers, the voice of the *pāramitās*, the voice of non-retrogression, the voice of bodhisattvas, and the voice of shattering the four māras, as well as the sound of *nirvāṇa*; thus the malevolent winds were destroyed, leaving nothing behind.
All the grasses and trees within that land were entirely transformed into exquisite seven-jeweled substances.

At that time, my body reached as high as the First Dhyāna Heaven; endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, I emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm.

All the devas and humans therein, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the various classes such as those in the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—all of them beheld my body.

Immeasurable devas made grand offerings of flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and musical instruments; sentient beings of the three evil realms chanted "Namo Buddha" and immediately attained liberation, receiving bodies among humans and devas.
At that time, when the hosts of Māra saw the Buddha manifest such supernatural powers, they all conceived faith. Having conceived faith, they immediately spoke these verses:
"We now take refuge in the Tathāgata, Whose body, speech, and mind are pure and who possesses unsurpassed wisdom;
Who can show the Eightfold Noble Path within the realm of Māra, Bestowing great illumination upon sentient beings dwelling in darkness."

Possessing great power that none can surpass, viewing all beings with the thought of them as one's own children, his mind is as impartial as space; therefore, I prostrate before the Great Caravan Leader.
Unstained by afflictions while cultivating loving-kindness and compassion, Attaining auspiciousness and demonstrating cause and effect,
Able to bestow upon sentient beings true liberation— Therefore, I now prostrate in homage.
Greatly compassionate, most merciful, God among gods, Supreme and unsurpassed World-Honored One,
Who teaches that all phenomena are like the moon in water— I now pay homage to the Great Illusionist.
Sentient beings encounter the illness of heavy afflictions; therefore, they take refuge in the Great King of Physicians.
Sentient beings of the three evil realms are poor in the seven riches; now they shall take refuge in him who is free from all outflows.
I only pray that you will compassionately accept my confession for all evil thoughts I have harbored toward the Buddha;
for the Buddha is the compassionate father and mother of all sentient beings, and I now renounce all demonic activities.
I am able to summon all sentient beings and inspire them to give rise to the bodhicitta;
I pray that you will explain to me the unsurpassed path—endowed with what qualities does one attain enlightenment?
I now offer these exquisite incense and flowers, making this供养 (pūjā) to the Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings;
drawing near to virtuous friends and reflecting with right thought, may I listen and receive the teaching with a sincere heart and abide according to the Dharma.
“At that time, five hundred court ladies and the retinue of Māra made offerings to me with exquisite incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music.
These articles of offering reached as far as immeasurable worlds of Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, and simultaneously made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.”

All the hosts of Māras beheld the physical forms, colors, heights, and shapes—square or round—of all the Buddhas as being exactly equal and without distinction; only the lion thrones, the world-trees and groves, and the dwellings they inhabited differed from one another.
When the hosts of Māra saw this, each was filled with joy; they sat beside the Buddha and listened to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
Having heard and received the Dharma, they returned to the abode of Pāpīyān and addressed the Māra, saying:
"We went to that Gautama and exerted all our supernatural powers, yet we were unable to move even a single hair of his."
"Great King, you should know that I have now become the disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, Pāpīyas felt malice and anger arise in his heart, and he immediately thought:
"How shall I slay that son of the Śākyas and eliminate this enemy?"
At that time, Pāpīyān and his retinue felt sorrow and affliction in their hearts and entered the house of suffering.
Chapter Two: The Ancient Past, from the *Ratnaketu-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. "At that time, the hosts of Māra returned to my presence and addressed me, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
I desire the Mahāyāna and am mindful of the Mahāyāna; I wish to be endowed with supernormal powers, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
World-Honored One!
With how many dharmas must a bodhisattva-mahāsattva be fully endowed so that he does not associate with evil friends and swiftly achieves anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with four dharmas, he will not associate with evil friends and will swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these four?

First, if there is a bodhisattva who does not crave any phenomena and does not abandon any phenomena; who does not grasp at any phenomena and does not perceive any phenomena; and who is likewise devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," practicing generosity without seeking its karmic fruit, neither giving rise to attachment nor abandoning or grasping, and being without the perception of "I" or "mine"—and so it is likewise for up to the perfection of wisdom.

Second, if there is a bodhisattva who does not perceive sentient beings, life-span, or a person (pudgala), yet also does not abandon the realm of sentient beings; who neither craves nor grasps, and is likewise without the perception of "I" or "mine."

Third, if there is a bodhisattva who does not perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, yet does not abandon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; who neither abandons nor grasps them, and furthermore has no perception of a self or what belongs to a self;
fourth, if there is a bodhisattva who can deeply contemplate such dharmas as these, they will give rise to no discursive thought or investigation regarding the Buddha’s right gnosis.

Why is this? To sever all conditioned activities and sever all [limited] knowledge is called Buddha-knowledge. It is without vehicles; it is without sound, without thought, and without words. It is without measure;

it is without birth, without emergence, and without cessation. It is without conceptualization, without obstruction, and without hindrance. It is the tranquility beyond seeing; it is without self, without life-principle, and without name. It is without light and without darkness, without location and without realm. It is without faculties, without wings, and without deliberation. It is without food, without craving, without purity, and without defilement. It is without dust, without joints, without limit, and without number. It is without activity, without sensation, without karma, and without abode. It is without grasping, without action, and cannot be demonstrated. That which is without momentary arising and ceasing is precisely Buddha-knowledge.
It is just like space; as space is without cognition and cannot be described, it is free from defilement and free from perception.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with such qualities as these, they do not associate with evil friends and will swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! If there is anyone who can seek such wisdom, you should know that this person is able to contemplate two kinds of phenomena:
namely, the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas: saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
First, existence throughout a lifetime; second, existence after death.
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas:
first, permanence; second, annihilation.
Furthermore, there are two things:
sentient beings and the life-span.
Furthermore, there are two things:
First, this; second, that.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
first, internal; second, external.
"O sons of good family!
If there are those who seek such Buddha-wisdom and, apart from these two dharmas, contemplate other dharmas, you should know that such persons will not be able to attain it."

"Good son! It is like a person who seeks fire and takes water, seeks water and takes fire, seeks food and takes stone, seeks flowers and takes iron, seeks fragrance and takes a corpse, seeks clothing and takes wood, or seeks ointment-fragrance and takes empty space. If one seeking the wisdom of a Buddha likewise abandons these two and observes some other separate dharma, it is just the same."
At that time, within the great assembly at the Jewel Monastery, there was a bodhisattva named Dṛḍhamati. Having heard these words, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Can the meaning that is ineffable be realized?
If it cannot be realized, how can one be called 'Omniscient'? "Good son!
Ineffable wisdom is itself all-knowledge.
Good son, I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
“What do you think?
When I attain the all-knowledge of the Tathāgata, is there anything that is acquired?
The Bodhisattva Dharmanetrī then reflected:
"If we were to say that [the self] exists, this would be the view of eternalism;
if we were to say that it does not exist, this would be the view of nihilism.
We should avoid these two extremes and speak of the Middle Way."
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Such a principle is both existent and non-existent."
“World-Honored One!
If there is no arising or ceasing, neither number nor measure, neither light nor darkness, this is precisely the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vidyudmati.
“World-Honored One!
If there is neither going nor coming, that is the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sudarśana.
“World-Honored One!
That which is without attainment and without departure, without realization and without cultivation—this is the Buddha-wisdom.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
“World-Honored One!

If a dharma is not subsumed within the three periods of time, does not fall within the triple world, and is not the three fetters, the three knowledges, the three vehicles, the aggregates, bases, or elements—and is devoid of increase or decrease—this is precisely the Buddha’s wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Vajramati said:
“World-Honored One!

If one does not discriminate between ordinary dharmas and noble dharmas, nor between the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training, nor between the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas, this is itself buddha-wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Resolute Mind said:
“World-Honored One!
That which is non-turning according to the Dharma is itself the Buddha’s wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
“World-Honored One!

If one contemplates the characteristics of the arising and perishing of all phenomena, and having contemplated them, penetrates and realizes that there is neither gain nor loss, this is precisely the Buddha-wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Good Awakening Mind said:
“World-Honored One!
When sentient beings of the three realms observe the mind through the mind and yet do not perceive the mind, this is itself Buddha-wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Vibhakta-ripu-mitra said:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a person who neither delights in afflictions nor loathes afflictions; who is neither attached nor resentful; who neither abandons nor seeks; and who neither gives nor dwells upon thoughts—this is itself Buddha-wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha said:
“World-Honored One!
One who does not take pleasure in sin or merit attains the profound Dharma-patience; such a one neither perceives nor knows ‘self’ or ‘what belongs to self.’”
"If one does not perceive 'I' or 'mine,' that is the Buddha-wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha Kumāra said,
"World-Honored One!"
"If one can observe that all phenomena are like the moon reflected in water, and does not perceive any phenomenon as increasing or decreasing,
this is itself Buddha-wisdom. The Bodhisattva Youth Anantamati said,
"World-Honored One!..."
"If one does not perceive light or darkness regarding all phenomena, and does not perceive arising or ceasing within any mind, this is itself Buddha-wisdom.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
“If one can observe that the four kinds of Brahma-conduct and unwholesome conduct are equal and non-dual, this is itself Buddha-wisdom.
Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
“World-Honored One!
"If one contemplates that the two aspects of the six pāramitās across the three periods of time are without difference, this is itself the Buddha-wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said:
"World-Honored One!"

If, regarding all phenomena, the mind is free from greed and hatred; if one contemplates the profound realm of all phenomena, yet neither fully comprehends nor fails to comprehend it; if one does not perceive phenomena as increasing or decreasing, and does not perceive wisdom or ignorance—this is the Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ruci who addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son,
for what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, proclaim such profound meanings as these?"

Mañjuśrī said, “Good son! It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to distance themselves from wrong views and attain right view. Having attained right view, they do not give rise to defiled attachment and are free from stinginess; they do not associate with evil friends and sustain themselves through right livelihood; they do not cling to the three fetters yet feel compassion for sentient beings; they do not cling to the Three Jewels and do not deceive anyone; toward all sentient beings, they neither abandon nor cling; they do not cling to wealth and property, nor do they cling to the triple world. They are able to provide protection for those sentient beings who are terrified, and they are able to destroy the evil realms while revealing the true path. They do not cling to patience and remain free from all conceptualizations; they extinguish all defilements, remove all darkness, and do not seek karmic retribution.”

"Good son! For this reason, one seeks all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Having attained this knowledge, one does not give rise to discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*) regarding sounds, syllables, or phrases.

Whether it be the Buddha’s words or heterodox words, the Buddha’s conduct or other conducts, the Buddha’s teachings or other teachings, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), the adornment of merit, the adornment of wisdom, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), karma and its fruit, or worldly knowledge and the Buddha’s knowledge—one does not give rise to discrimination regarding such phenomena. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of these kinds of profound meanings."
The Bodhisattva Abhirati said: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
It is indeed as you have said: that which is of profound meaning is the wisdom of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because there is nothing to be awakened to.
If there is nothing to be awakened to, it cannot be described; that which cannot be described is precisely the Buddha’s wisdom.
If there is one who can know this ineffability, you should know that such a person has attained the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
He is well able to discern and proclaim the Buddha-wisdom. Why is this?
Non-attachment to all phenomena—neither arising nor ceasing—is itself Buddha-wisdom.

Good son! Non-attachment to all dharmas is neither the limit of emergence nor the limit of destruction. Ignorance and nirvāṇa truly have no limit of emergence. The limits of space-nirvāṇa, all dharmas, and all sentient beings are ineffable limits. These are the limit of space, the limit of non-obstruction, the limit of the absence of things, the limit of the absence of aggregates, and the limit of the emptiness of the three activities. Regarding the aggregate of dharmas, the aggregate of karma, the aggregate of fruits and non-fruits, and the aggregate of collections—all these are without substance; they are the limit of the absence of substance, the limit of space, and the ineffable limit of all dharmas.
"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva can fully possess such qualities as these, they shall immediately attain the Buddha-wisdom.

When this ineffable Buddha-wisdom was being spoken, the entire host of Māras attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); they cast off their coarse bodies and obtained subtle bodies—bodies of mind-intent and bodies manifested through the Dharma.
Furthermore, twenty-eight thousand sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding all phenomena;
ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas attained immeasurable *dhāraṇīs*.
All the māras made offerings of exquisite incense, flowers, and music, and praised the Tathāgata with these words:
"World-Honored One!
A virtuous friend is the very root of all wholesome dharmas. Because we have now encountered the Buddha as our virtuous friend, we have obtained great benefit."
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"You should contemplate all karmas with a sincere mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One then expounded upon past karma for the assembled multitude.
“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a kalpa named Vidyutdhara.
At that time, the lifespan of the sentient beings of the world was a full sixty-eight thousand years, and the world was named Gandhaprabhāsa.”
In that world there is a Buddha named Gandhaguṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, in a world possessed of the five corruptions, there was a wheel-turning king named Puṣpanetra who ruled over the four continents. Together with his retinue, ministers, and subjects, he went to the place where the Buddha was. With exquisite incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music, he made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. Paying homage with reverence, he prostrated and circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, then praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Buddha is praised by humans and devas; He has distanced himself from all evils and delights in tranquility.”
Fully endowed with the seven riches, you destroy poverty; how do you cause the multitude to attain profound wisdom?
By cultivating and gathering the three gates of liberation, you have already attained freedom from birth, old age, sickness, and death;
Able to deliver sentient beings from the three evil realms, how do you cause the multitude to transcend the deeds of Māra?
The Buddha said: "Great King!
By being complete in three dharmas, one attains profound wisdom."
What are these three?
First, to mindfully contemplate all sentient beings with a sincere heart;
second, to cultivate and accumulate great compassion to destroy the suffering of sentient beings.
Third, seeing that all phenomena are devoid of a sentient being, a life-span, or a person, one does not give rise to discrimination.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that can transcend the deeds of Māra:
first, not giving rise to an evil mind toward any sentient being; [the other two follow].
Second, when practicing giving, one does not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit;
third, one contemplates all phenomena as equal and non-dual, like empty space—neither arising nor ceasing, without activity or substance, devoid of characteristics and ineffable.
"When a Bodhisattva is fully endowed with such dharmas as these, they attain profound wisdom capable of transcending the works of Māra.
At that time, the Holy King had a queen named Sudarśanā, who, together with eighty-four thousand court ladies, made offerings to the Buddha.
Having made this offering, he immediately spoke these verses:
"In this great trichiliocosm, there is none superior; You always delight in tranquility and cultivate the thought of me as a son.
Through your virtuous conduct, you remain far removed from all defilements; How may you cause me to leave behind this female body?"
Having already attained freedom from all enmity, And having truly seen birth, old age, sickness, and death,
I only pray that you will expound the Path for me, So that I may be endowed with a male body.
Having transcended all states of existence, you have attained the unsurpassed state; you are able to bestow joy and increase wholesome dharmas.
Endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, how may you cause me to leave behind this female body?
Having crushed the four māras and cultivated the four brahma-vihāras, possessing truthful speech and skillful means,
endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics— how may you cause me to leave behind this female body?
The Buddha said: "Good woman!

There is a skillful means by which one may leave the female body and destroy female karma, even attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and never again receiving a female body—except for those who have made a vow through skillful means, namely, the *ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-mukha*."
If there are those who can cultivate this dhāraṇī, they shall be freed from the female body, purify their body, speech, and mind, and remain far removed from the three obstacles.

If there are those who hear the name of this dhāraṇī, they shall immediately leave the female body and receive a male body; they shall attain a complete body and subtle wisdom, purify their body, speech, and mind, delight in virtuous conduct, become endowed with extensive learning, remain far removed from evil karma and the retribution of suffering, and be able to extinguish the grave offenses of the five heinous acts and the uninterrupted hells.
Why is this? This Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī is that which has been expounded by the immeasurable Buddhas of the past, for the purpose of destroying evil karma and increasing wholesome dharmas;
it is also that which is currently being spoken together by the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, for the purpose of destroying evil karma and increasing wholesome dharmas.
In future ages, the Buddhas of the ten directions shall likewise proclaim it together, in order to destroy evil karma and increase wholesome dharmas.
I too, now in the present, proclaim this Dharma-door of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī; all the immeasurable Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions likewise praise this dhāraṇī together.

“Good woman! If, within the territory ruled by a Kṣatriya king, there exists the name of such a dhāraṇī as this, and it is praised, upheld, recited, read, and transcribed, that king shall be protected and praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing in the ten directions; furthermore, even the devas up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven will likewise protect and praise him.”

Wherever this king walks, stands, sits, or lies down, there too immeasurable devas, nāgas, and yakṣas will all together protect and keep him in mind, causing his kingdom to be harmonious and peaceful, free from strife, without pestilence, and with no outbreak of war. There shall be no calamitous winds or rains; it shall be neither too cold nor too hot. Grains and rice will ripen in abundance, and all malevolent spirits and wicked beasts will harbor hearts of joy and give rise to no evil thoughts.
In whatever land this sutra resides, any ill-omened stars, inauspicious signs, evil thoughts, or malignant diseases shall all be completely extinguished.

If a Kṣatriya king raises an army for conquest, by single-mindedly recollecting this sutra he can subdue his powerful enemies and achieve victory. If both kings maintain such mindfulness, then their two armies will become harmonious and will not harm one another.

If there be any kingdom, city, town, or village where humans or animals suffer from epidemics, one should transcribe this dhāraṇī and place it atop a banner; then all inauspiciousness and pestilence in that land will be entirely eradicated.

If there is a Dharma master who upholds the precepts and exerts diligence, who on the fifteenth day of the month bathes himself in purity and makes offerings of exquisite incense and flowers to the Triple Gem, and who ascends the lion throne to praise this dhāraṇī, such a person will be able to protect the land where he dwells; all evil omens will immediately vanish, and he will also be able to subdue and transform sentient beings, attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good woman! If there is anyone who can read and recite even a single verse of this sutra, such a person shall never again receive a female body, and they shall also attain non-retrogression in their bodhicitta."

At that time, after the Buddha Gandhaguṇa had spoken this dhāraṇī, he pressed the earth with his toe; immediately the great earth shook in six ways, and so it was likewise throughout the ten directions.
All the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas therein, through the power of the Tathāgata’s merit, felt joy in their hearts, and both saw and heard the preaching of the dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, saying:
"Śalacī śalacī mucī śale..."
Jara-jalane jara-varāte jahi-le parapuṣpa-sa.
