At that time, the World-Honored One immediately recited this dhāraṇī for the great assembly; upon hearing it, the five hundred court ladies immediately attained male bodies.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable women among the devas and humans who also received male bodies and attained the non-retrogressive mind of bodhi, forever severing all karmic determinations of womanhood.
“Good son! At that time, when the lady heard this upholding, the eighty-four thousand women she had brought along also transformed their female bodies and attained male bodies.”
Furthermore, there were immeasurable women among the devas and humans who also transformed their female bodies to obtain male bodies.
At that time, the Holy King entrusted the four continents to his thousand sons and, together with immeasurable people, left the household life to practice the Way.
"At that time, there were also immeasurable devas, each of whom thought to themselves:
'For what cause and by what conditions has the Wheel-Turning Sage King abandoned his kingdom to leave the household life?'"
They further said to one another:
"The Tathāgata of this realm is expounding the sublime Dharma; by the power of that Dharma, this woman has been transformed into a man.

There is one who has left the household life and can bestow the *kāṣāya* robe, who explains the joys of humans and devas to laypeople, destroys the sufferings of the three evil realms, extinguishes all existence, and crushes the works of Māra so that Māra suffers. Since Māra now suffers, he takes no pleasure in hearing the Dharma."
"The great illusionist is none other than the śramaṇa Gandhaprabhāsa.
Furthermore, others said:
"You should know that this śramaṇa is Māra himself."
"Why is this? Because she is able to transform her female body and obtain a male body.
At that time, there was a great minister named Śubhakārin who spoke these words:

"All my women have become men; you, my countless wives, concubines, and daughters, have likewise abandoned your original forms to receive male bodies. Having shaved off your hair and beards and donned the *kāṣāya*, you have all turned toward and submitted to that śramaṇa, while I alone remain here, staying behind and not going."
"We shall abandon this land and depart, so that we may never again see or hear of such an evil person.
When the people heard these words, they cried out: "Excellent!"
"If I now wish not to see or hear [them], and to distance myself from these wicked śramaṇas, I shall enter the deep mountains.
At that time, once those people had entered the mountains, they abandoned their homes to practice and cultivate the dharma of the brahmins, saying:
"There is no liberation; there are no fruits of good or evil."
In this world, there is currently a śramaṇa who has appeared, proclaiming the view of annihilationism.
He speaks of demonic activities that deceive sentient beings; he is a great master of illusion.

If anyone goes to see him, listens to what he says, and draws near to him, prostrating to him, making offerings, and honoring him, their minds will immediately become deranged and they will lose all understanding. They will shave off their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, abandon all their household possessions, undertake the discipline of begging for food, and dwell among burial mounds while practicing the rule of eating only once a day.

They conceive a sense of weary detachment toward birth and death, taking no pleasure in the enjoyment of the five desires, nor in perfumes, flowers, necklaces, or music; they take no delight in proclaiming worldly matters. Possessing such unwholesome qualities as these, they preach this nihilistic view and engage in demonic activities, acting as great enemies to all sentient beings by teaching immeasurable and boundless beings to give rise to nihilism, such that if they were not seen or heard, great benefit would be obtained.
At that time, the bhikṣu Puṣpanetra, hearing that immeasurable people had conceived great false views, immediately thought to himself:
"If I am unable to subdue such sentient beings with their false views, how shall I ever attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

Then the bhikṣu Puṣpanetra immediately went to invite the Buddha Gandhaguṇa, who, together with an immeasurable saṃgha of bhikṣus, traveled throughout the kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages, preaching the Dharma everywhere.

That is to say: distancing oneself from unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas; or preaching the Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, or the Śrāvakayāna; or the fruits of śramaṇaship; or the bhikṣu precepts, or the upāsaka precepts; or preaching the three refuges; or further expounding the method for transforming the female body; or preaching the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī gateway; or preaching the ten wholesome actions.

When this Dharma was being taught, it shattered the nets of doubt of immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to give rise to wholesome minds and resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and led immeasurable sentient beings to come into the presence of the Buddha.
Except for the minister Śubhakārin, who made this evil vow toward Padmākṣa:
"If you should attain the unsurpassed path in the future, I shall become an evil Māra in your buddha-field upon your attainment of Buddhahood, and go to the Bodhi tree to create great terror."
"If, after I have attained Buddhahood, you should destroy my Dharma,
and if I should give rise to faith in you, you must then grant me a prediction of enlightenment.
"O sons of good family!
At that time, the bhikṣu was none other than myself;
the lady Sudarśanā was Maitreya;
and the minister Sukṛta was Māra Pāpīyān.
Pāpīyān! At that time, you made this vow:
"To those who conceive faith in me, I shall grant the prediction of enlightenment."
"Therefore, I now fulfill your original vow and grant you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Pāpīyan! Because you previously paid homage and made offerings at Gandhamādana, by virtue of these roots of goodness, I now bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment."
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred court ladies attained male bodies, and immeasurable sentient beings were tamed through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

Chapter Three: Subduing Māra. From the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the "Jeweled Banner" Section. Chapter Three: Subduing Māra. At that time, ten billion Māras from throughout the world all gathered together and went to the abode of Pāpīyān.
Pāpīyān spoke to the various māra kings, saying:
"O sons of good family! Do you know?"
There appeared in the world a son of the Śākya clan who performed great magical feats; after six years of ascetic practice, he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree.
At that time, I led a host of thirty-six trillion beings to that place, yet despite my utmost effort, I was unable to move even the Vajrāsana.

At that time, Gautama achieved illusory powers at the Bodhi tree; by the power of these illusions, he caused this trichiliocosm to shake in six ways, making my followers fall headlong as if trees had been uprooted.

At that time, the son of the Śākyas accomplished the illusionary arts of signlessness; by the power of such illusions, all wise men of the ten directions submitted to him. When they sought out the sentient beings converted by Gautama to discover where their mental characteristics resided, no one could know their location.
If there is anyone who can take refuge with a sincere heart, not even a single hair on their body could be moved by all their might; such a person cannot be deceived nor need they fear intimidation.
Now, my assembly of five hundred court ladies and all my kinsmen have likewise turned toward him, and I am unable to restrain or turn them back.

"Your merit is now vast and great, and you possess much illusory power. If you can bring yourselves to heart and provide assistance, then I shall be able to destroy that son of the Śākyas and cut short his life; I shall also be able to crush those who take refuge in him, extinguish the Dharma of the śramaṇas, and increase the works of Māra."
"At that time, I shall receive unsurpassed bliss.
At that moment, there was a māra named Upasthāna who spoke these words:

"That son of the Śākyas has fully accomplished immeasurable merit; adorned with merit and adorned with wisdom, he does not dwell in any state of existence and is able to subdue all sentient beings. He can destroy various sufferings and afflictions, and his body and mind are pure. You cannot bring forth evil to harm him."
Pāpīyān said: "My various retinues have been deceived and deluded by that son of the Śākyas; if you do not employ skillful means, this world will soon become empty."
Again, another Māra said:
“The Tathāgata does not abide in any state of mind; his mind is pure and his body is pure. Having distanced himself from all evil afflictions, he has attained liberation within the triple world.”
"No conditioned phenomena can bind it; therefore, it is called the unsurpassed tranquility.
Who could harm such tranquility? Pāpīyān said:
"If there are sentient beings within the desire realm who, being greedily attached to the five desires, take refuge in the son of Śakra, such persons will be able to destroy the four māras.
If you do not subdue such wicked people, how can you possibly subdue the desire realm?"
Furthermore, another Māra said:
"That son of the Śākyas is like an illusion and like a mirage; he cannot be described, has no location, and is free from all obstructions. How can such a person be harmed?"
Pāpīyān said: "The son of the Śākyas receives offerings of food within this realm of desire and deceives sentient beings; how could I not punish him?"
Again, another Māra said:
"The supernatural power possessed by me now, as well as the supernatural power of my retinue, does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the supernatural power of the Son of the Śākyas."
"How could I possibly inflict harm upon him? Pāpīyas said:

"If that Gautama enters the city to beg for alms, I shall employ skillful means to ensure he does not obtain so much as a single grain for the entire day; I shall hurl large stones at him and revile him to provoke his anger. I hope that I alone can accomplish this, let alone you all with your many retinues!"
Again, another Māra said:
"Even if one were to perform such deeds as these against that son of the Śākyas, they would not cause him to give rise to thoughts of anger or joy.
If he neither feels anger nor joy, how can he be harmed?"

Pāpīyān said: "That son of the Śākyas possesses great wisdom; by the power of his wisdom, he does not feel anger where there is cause for anger, nor does he feel delight where there is cause for delight. He has cultivated and accumulated the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion, regarding all sentient beings with equanimity and without duality; therefore, he gives rise to neither anger nor delight toward me."
Again, another Māra said:
"If one were bound by the three realms, I could indeed harm them.
But that son of the Śākyas is not bound by the three realms; how could I possibly harm him?"
Pāpīyān spoke again:

"If you can follow my plan, it will not be difficult to harm him. All of you should assume the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and go to various kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages. Address the kings, ministers, and elders there, saying:

'We have already come under the sway of the śramaṇa Gautama; yet this śramaṇa Gautama is truly no śramaṇa—he is a mere empty word for a śramaṇa—and he is no brāhmaṇa, falsely claiming for himself that he is a brāhmaṇa.'"
In truth, they do not maintain the precepts, yet they manifest the appearance of maintaining them; in reality, they break the precepts and are no different from ordinary worldlings.
If you all believe this, excellent, excellent!
"If you do not believe this, after seven days there shall fall great stones, fierce fires, and sharp blades.
Having spoken these words, he then caused them to rain down from the sky.
"If such various expedients are employed, the followers of Gautama will soon be destroyed.
Then all the Māra kings said, "Excellent!"
At that time, the various Māras each adorned themselves; having completed their adornments, they proceeded toward the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha.
At that time, all the wicked retinues belonging to Pāpīyān, having likewise completed their adornments, proceeded toward the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, there was a seer in the Snowy Mountains named Prabhārasa, whose retinue of five hundred all possessed the five supernormal powers.
When Pāpīyas arrived, he prostrated with his head at the seer’s feet and spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has utterly destroyed all the various views of the non-Buddhists, and while standing amidst the great assembly, he proclaims this:..."
"Among all sentient beings, there are truly no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
"Venerable sir!
If you will go with me to the kingdom of Magadha, I shall then be able to defeat the śramaṇa Gautama."
The śramaṇa Gautama is utterly unable to engage you in debate or compete with you in supernatural powers.
Once the śramaṇa Gautama has been defeated and eliminated, all sentient beings will surely revere and make offerings to you.
At that time, after Pāpīyān had spoken these words, he returned and recounted the aforementioned matters in detail to the immeasurable host of Māras.
Then, one Māra spoke again, saying:

"When the śramaṇa Gautama enters the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms, I shall manifest the forms of lions, tigers, wolves, rākṣasas, and evil spirits along his path. Upon seeing them, he will give rise to a heart of fear; once fear has arisen, he will be unable to engage in debate or display his supernormal powers."
Again, another Māra said:
"I shall cause a rain of great stones to fall from the midst of the sky to destroy Gautama.
Yet another Māra said:
"I shall falsely pose as a disciple of Gautama; having become his disciple, I shall gain access to him, and once I have gained access, I shall take his life.
Another Māra said: "I shall manifest in the form of a householder, provide food, and invite him; if he accepts the invitation, I shall kill him."
Again, another Māra said:
"I shall manifest in the form of a courtesan and go to the various kings, saying that this Gautama has had sexual intercourse with me.
Yet another Māra said:
"I shall go to that ascetic Gautama and manifest the destruction of his body into seven pieces; you all should then say:
'This corpse was killed by Gautama.'"
Furthermore, another Māra said:
"I shall, from within that void of space, cry out in a loud voice: 'The śramaṇa Gautama is a most wicked man!'"
"If there be men or women who make offerings to them, at the end of their lives they shall be reborn in the Avīci Hell.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having known the mind of Māra, transformed this trichiliocosm entirely into vajra, so as to block the rain of stones, the rain of fire, and the rain of swords, ensuring that all sentient beings did not behold such demonic deeds with their eyes.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s four great disciples entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in succession.
Then Śāriputra entered through the eastern gate and encountered five hundred sons of Māra on the road, who were brandishing swords and staves. They said to Śāriputra:
“If you would dance and sing, it would be excellent, most excellent!”
"If you do not, I shall take your life. Śāriputra said, "Excellent!"
"Young man!
I shall now sing, and you all should dance.
The sons of Māra said:
“Excellent, Great Virtue! Then Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"I now seek not the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, for they have deceived and deluded me throughout immeasurable ages;
if one seeks such dharmas as these, that person shall never attain liberation."
When Śāriputra had spoken these verses, he further recited these dhāraṇī phrases:

“Vahara 1; Vahara 2; Varavahara 3; Marici-varahara 4; Sadāvaraha 5; Amogharahara 6; Svāhā 7. When Śāriputra had finished reciting this dhāraṇī, the minds of five hundred sons of Māra were tamed. Having been tamed, they prostrated, repented, and spoke these words:
“O Virtuous One!”
"I shall now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and abandon all the evil deeds of Māra.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered through the southern gate; midway along the road, he encountered five hundred sons of Māra holding swords and staves, who said to Maudgalyāyana:
"If you would dance and sing, how excellent! How excellent!"
"If you do not, I shall take your life.
Maudgalyāyana replied, "Excellent!"
"Young man!
I shall now sing, and you all should dance.
The sons of Māra said:
"Excellent, Great Virtue!
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
"I now seek not the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, for they have deceived and deluded me throughout immeasurable ages;
if one seeks such dharmas as these, that person shall never attain liberation."
When Maudgalyāyana had spoken this verse, he further recited these dhāraṇī phrases:

“Aṅgama 1, aṅgama 2, maraṇa 3, rāja 4, jahasa 5, mātaha 6, samātaha 7, samātaha 8, gaganaṅgama 9, svāhā 10. When Maudgalyāyana had finished speaking this dhāraṇī, the hearts of five hundred sons of Māra were tamed. Having been tamed, they prostrated and repented, saying:
“O Virtuous One!”
"I shall now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and abandon all the works of Māra.
At that time, Maitrāyaṇīputra entered through the western gate; midway along the road, he encountered five hundred sons of Māra holding swords and staves, who said to Pūrṇa:
"If you would dance and sing, excellent, excellent!"
"If you do not, I shall take your life. Pūrṇa said, "Excellent!"
"Young man!
I shall now sing, and you all should dance.
The sons of Māra said:
"Excellent, Great Virtue!
At that time, Pūrṇa spoke these verses:
"I now seek not the aggregates, sense-bases, or elements, for they have deceived and deluded me throughout immeasurable ages;
if one seeks such dharmas as these, that person shall never attain liberation."
When Pūrṇa had spoken these verses, he further recited this dhāraṇī phrase:

“Kha-khe-ḍe 1; Kha-khe-ḍe 2; Kha-khe-ḍe 3; Mocana 4; Mocana 5; Abadhani 6; Vibadhani 7; Svāhā 8. When Pūrṇa had finished reciting this dhāraṇī, the minds of five hundred sons of Māra were tamed. Having been tamed, they prostrated, repented, and immediately spoke these words:
“O Virtuous One!”
"I shall now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and abandon all the works of Māra.
At that time, Subhūti entered through the northern gate and encountered five hundred sons of Māra on the road, who were brandishing swords and staves and said to Subhūti:
"Virtuous One!..."
"If you dance and sing, it is well, it is well!
If you do not, I shall take your life. Subhūti said:
“Excellent, young man!
I shall now sing, and you all should dance.”
The sons of Māra said:
"Excellent, O Great Virtuous One!"
Then, Subhūti spoke these verses:
“I now do not seek the aggregates, sense bases, or elements, For they have deceived and deluded me throughout immeasurable ages.
If one seeks after such dharmas as these, That person shall never attain liberation.”
When Subhūti had spoken these verses, he further recited this dhāraṇī:

“Sama-ti (1) bi-ma-ti (2) ma-ri-śa-khe (3) si-le (4) si-le (5) si-le (6) va-si-le (7) va-si-le (8) a-gu-si-le (9) pu-tra-ku-tsi-si-le (10) svā-hā (11). When Subhūti had finished speaking this dhāraṇī, the minds of five hundred sons of Māra were tamed. Having been tamed, they prostrated, repented, and spoke thus:
“O Virtuous One!”
"I shall now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and abandon all the works of Māra.
At that time, through the power of the World-Honored One’s supernormal faculties, he caused all sentient beings in Rājagṛha to see the entire hundred-yojana area.

At each of the four gates of the city, there was a great disciple; from within the city emerged a great lotus flower, twenty-five *zhang* in length and breadth, with a stem of lapis lazuli and leaves of gold. Its filaments were made of diamond and it possessed immeasurable petals; its radiance shone afar, and all sentient beings saw it rise three *zhang* high.
From the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it was likewise seen to rise three *zhàng* high.
At that time, such verses were spoken from within the lotus, heard by all gods and worldlings wherever they were:
"A single Buddha has appeared in this world, Capable of utterly subduing all Māras."
He is able to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous Wheel of Dharma, To subdue all sentient beings here in this world.
The Honored One among two-legged beings is able to bring accomplishment;
Upatiṣya and Kolita, he can destroy the roots of the two kinds of afflictions. The Buddha desires to come here to discipline sentient beings.
Knowing the three periods of time as clearly as fruits in the palm of the hand, Fully endowed with the purity described by the threefold precepts,
Far removed from the three defilements and compassionate toward all— The Buddha desires to come here to discipline sentient beings.
Fully endowed with sovereign power and fearlessness, He tames the fourfold assembly and proclaims the four fruits;
Ever delighting in preaching the true meaning of the Dharma, The Noble Lion King has come for my sake.
Fully endowed with the five powers and the five faculties, He has accomplished merit and unimpeded wisdom.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Unsurpassed World-Honored One Cultivates compassion to pull them from the three evil realms;
He subdues the six sense organs to attain supreme faith, And remains far removed from the six sense bases while cultivating the six recollections.
Possessing the six supernormal powers and speaking words of truth, the World-Honored One desires to come to discipline sentient beings.
All sentient beings are bound by afflictions; dwelling in darkness, they do not know the path to liberation.
Constantly walking the way of Māra, they do not know reality; attached to perversity, they have lost their wisdom.
Not knowing this world or that, nor birth and death, they abandon dhyāna out of craving for the five desires;
therefore, they cannot attain liberation, nor can they cultivate the Path to repay past goodness.
Sentient beings do not understand birth, old age, and death; therefore, they do not cultivate the three gates of liberation.
They remain far removed from all generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom; therefore, they do not escape the three evil realms.
If sentient beings distance themselves from the pleasures of the five desires, Draw near to the Tathāgata and listen to the True Dharma,
And with a sincere heart uphold the meaning of even a single verse, Such people shall attain liberation just as the Buddhas of the past did.
Furthermore, the sound of these verses was heard throughout the sixteen abodes of the Form Realm:
"If one cultivates and accumulates the pure Dharma, Remains far removed from strife while practicing meditative concentration,
And with a sincere heart focuses single-mindedly on all liberations, There will be no distraction and the afflictions will be destroyed."
Having attained the thirteen dharmas of patience, They remain far removed from harmful contact and distracted minds;
Transcending all birth, aging, and death, They cultivate the four immeasurables and the various meditative concentrations.
Forever severing the views of eternalism and nihilism, Transcending the three evil realms and attaining right concentration;
Deeply contemplating impermanence, non-self, and suffering, One obtains the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma, as did the Buddhas of the past.
If one wishes to renounce pleasure like mucus or spittle, observing all things as empty and non-different,
purifying the dharma-realm and awakening, one will be unimpeded regarding phenomena, like space.
Able to destroy the four māras and extinguish afflictions, Cultivating and gathering the various skillful means of the right path,
Fearless before false views like a lion— One shall obtain this by drawing near to the Tathāgata.
When these verses and such sounds issued forth, immeasurable sentient beings proceeded toward the lotus grove.

At that time, Pāpīyān heard these verses with his own ears and saw the lotuses within the city of Rājagṛha, beneath which immeasurable sentient beings were all seated; this continued in succession up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where it was likewise so.
Afflicted by great suffering and distress, he addressed the māras, saying:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"

"The śramaṇa Gautama performs great illusory magic; you are unable to carry out the work of Māra, and before long you shall lose your dwelling place. You must rain down swords, stones, and fierce fire!"
At that time, there was a māra who said to Pāpīyān:
“The śramaṇa Gautama has fully accomplished immeasurable merit and is endowed with the two adornments, namely, merit and wisdom.”
"Because of his supernormal power, he has caused me to become frantic and unable to carry out the work of Māra; I now truly harbor fear toward him.
Another Māra said to Pāpīyas:
"You are now foolish and walk upon a deviant path. Even a mindless person who sees Gautama would give rise to faith and reverence, let alone one who possesses a mind."
"If you now wish to obtain great benefit, you should with a sincere heart take refuge in and revere him.
Another Māra then said to Pāpīyas: "Pāpīyas!..."
Why do you now constantly delight in evil conduct and perform evil deeds?
You should distance yourself from the works of Māra.
Do you not see that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is proceeding toward Rājagṛha, desiring to bestow upon sentient beings the flavor of the ambrosia of the Dharma?
"Come, let us go together to take refuge in Gautama.

At that time, an immeasurable host of Māras descended through the air and arrived at the city of Rājagṛha; some assumed the form of kings, others the form of universal monarchs (cakravartin) endowed with the seven treasures, while others manifested as the forms of Maheśvara, or as śramaṇas, brahmins, or nirgranthas, or as the forms of the four heavenly kings, the sun and moon, Śakra, or Brahmā.
Some sat, stood, or prostrated themselves while offering praises; some circumambulated the city of Rājagṛha; and some manifested themselves atop the city walls.

Some were blue in color, with white garments, white necklaces, white banners, and white canopies; some were yellow, with red garments, red necklaces, red banners, and red canopies; some were white, with garments of various colors, various necklaces, yellow banners, and yellow canopies; some were red, with blue garments, blue necklaces, blue banners, and blue canopies; some were the color of the seven treasures, with garments of the seven treasures, necklaces of the seven treasures, and banners and canopies of the seven treasures; some were the color of lapis lazuli, or the color of crystal, with garments of various colors, various necklaces, and various banners and canopies.
Some scattered various flowers before the Buddha, burning incense and prostrating; others sang hymns of praise, extolling him, and danced.
Upon seeing this, Pāpīyas raised his voice and wept, thinking to himself:
"I have now lost all my meritorious rewards; the entire host of Māras has surrendered to the śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, Pāpīyān said to the Brahmā:
"Although I have lost my merit and am without allies, I can still destroy the śramaṇa Gautama. I shall now display my final power; I can now pluck up this lotus."
At that time, Pāpīyān immediately rushed toward the lotus; yet, although he beheld it with his own eyes, he was unable to seize it.
It was as the people of the world say:
"I can catch lightning."
"Though lightning can be seen, it cannot be grasped; the lotus flower is likewise, for though Māra may see it, he cannot grasp it.
At that time, Pāpīyān felt deep distress in his heart, thinking:
"If even such a lotus flower is difficult to grasp, how can it be uprooted?"
He further thought to himself:
"I shall now produce immeasurable evil sounds, so that when the fourfold assembly hears them, they will be struck with fear; they shall then abandon Gautama and flee in all directions."
At that time, Pāpīyas immediately let out a great cry, yet none of the fourfold assembly heard it; only Māra himself heard it.
Having heard it, he was once again seized by a heart of great terror.
At that time, Pāpīyān was struck with terror and trembled violently; he struck the earth with both hands, yet his palms could not make contact, as if striking empty space.
He then sought to take up a staff to strike the fourfold assembly, but he could not even see it. His fear redoubled and his entire body shook like tree leaves tossed by a fierce wind.
He further thought to himself: "I have now forever lost all my merits and all my supernatural powers; it would be better for me to return quickly to my own abode."
"If I do not return, I shall surely die; there is no doubt of this. Thus, I wish to depart, yet I know not the path. He further thought:

"If I remain here, the śramaṇa Gautama will soon arrive with a great multitude of followers. Should he reach this place, I shall certainly be slaughtered. I now intend to sink my body into the earth, yet I fear that the sentient beings of this realm might see me."

At that time, Pāpīyas was unable to flee in any of the four directions—up, down, or across—and he saw his own body bound by five fetters; having seen this, he wept and was overcome with grief, sorrow, and distress.
At that time, there was a māra named Aryamārga who, appearing in the guise of a universal monarch (cakravartin), addressed Pāpīyān with these verses:
"For what reason do you utter such evil cries, Weeping, sorrowful, and tormented by suffering?"
The Tathāgata is now about to proceed to the Lotus [Assembly], capable of destroying the various sufferings of sentient beings.
If you wish to receive peace and happiness, you should with a sincere heart rely upon the Unsurpassed Honored One;
if you do not delight in the fivefold fetters, you should accept my words and take refuge in the World-Honored One.
At that time, having heard these verses, Pāpīyān immediately thought to himself:
"In order to achieve my own liberation, I shall feign taking refuge; it is not from a sincere heart."
He then turned toward the direction where the Tathāgata was staying, joined his palms, and spoke this verse:
“I now take refuge in the Honored One of the World, Who can destroy all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings.
I also repent for all my evils, And shall never again commit them before the Buddha’s retinue.”
When Māra Pāpīyas spoke these verses, he was immediately liberated from his fivefold bonds.
Having attained liberation, as he sought to return to his own realm, he was bound once again;
this occurred a second, a third, and so on, up to the seventh time.
At that time, Pāpīyān, being unable to depart, listened to the Dharma with a sincere heart: “1.
Jaruci, 2. Jarukamuci.”

Upādhyāyī, 5. Upādhyāyopādhyāya.
