“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall uphold and protect it.”

If there are members of the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen—who, whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, receive, uphold, recite, read, transcribe, and extensively expound this dhāraṇī, I shall be able to bestow eight things upon them.
What are the eight? First, heroic conduct;
second, delighting in hearing and receiving the Dharma.
Third, the mind is free from fear;
fourth, it is always luminous and without darkness;
fifth, it is fully endowed with virtuous vows.
Sixth, liberation; seventh, the possession of eloquence;
eighth, the increase of wholesome dharmas.
World-Honored One!
If the parents, brothers, wives, children, or kinsmen of an asura should harass such a person, we shall punish them.
If we do not protect the Buddha-dharma within this world, we would be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed the fourfold assembly, addressed the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya: “Kauṇḍinya!

This entire great assembly deeply desires to hear the Dharma. Beings from immeasurable worlds have all gathered here for the sake of the Dharma; they all wish to know the skillful means of practicing the Dharma, to achieve great wisdom, to remain far removed from greed and all afflictions, and to truly understand the skillful means of practicing the Dharma.”
Then Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"It is exactly as the holy teaching says,
World-Honored One!

Bodhisattvas from immeasurable worlds in the four directions all wish to come, bearing the empowerments granted by the four Buddhas, and they also wish to receive and uphold the Dharma-practice of the 'Eye of Space'."
Now is precisely the time; please deign to show compassion and proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Regarding what was said—“the practice of the Dharma” and “a bhikṣu who practices the Dharma.”
"What is meant by a 'dharma-practicing bhikṣu'?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and expound upon the dharma-practicing bhikṣu.
The Buddha said:
“Kauṇḍinya! Listen attentively and with a sincere mind; I shall explain this for you.

If there is a bhikṣu who recites and studies the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures—ranging from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas—this is called delighting in recitation, but it is not called practicing the Dharma.”

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who recites and chants the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras and delights in expounding and explaining them extensively for the fourfold assembly; this is called "delight in eloquence" (prātihārya), not "practice of the Dharma" (dharmācāra).

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who recites and chants the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, and is able to expound upon them extensively and contemplate their meaning; this is called "contemplation," but it is not called "practice in accordance with the Dharma."

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who receives, maintains, reads, and recites the twelve divisions of the scriptures, expounding upon and contemplating their meanings and principles; this is called "contemplating with joy," but it is not called "practice through the Dharma."

“Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who is able to contemplate the body and mind, whose mind does not greedily cling to any external signs, who is humble and modest in disposition and does not give rise to arrogance, who does not irrigate the field of karma with the water of craving, and who likewise does not sow the seeds of consciousness therein.

When the mind that engages in vitarka and vicāra has ceased and its objective sphere is entirely stilled, and one is forever free from afflictions with a tranquil mind—such a bhikṣu, I declare, is called a practitioner of the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
"In this way, bhikṣu, if one desires to attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the enlightenment of a Tathāgata, one shall be able to attain it. Kauṇḍinya!"
"Just as a skilled potter kneads clay and places it upon a wheel to fashion vessels according to his will, so too is the bhikṣu who practices the Dharma. Kauṇḍinya! "
If there is a bhikṣu who practices the Dharma, he should contemplate three things:
first, the body; second, sensation; [and third, the mind].
Third is the mind. Having contemplated these three things, one attains two kinds of knowledge: first, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna);
[and second, the knowledge of non-arising].
Second is the knowledge of non-arising.
"Kauṇḍinya! What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?

Knowing that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*); knowing that the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are exhausted is called the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the practice of non-action is called the knowledge of exhaustion; the knowledge of the fruit of non-action is called the knowledge of non-arising.

The knowledge that exhausts all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the knowledge that exhausts all afflictions (*kleśa*) is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, knowing the exhaustion of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is called the knowledge of exhaustion; knowing the exhaustion of all existence is the knowledge of non-arising.
Discerning the exhaustion of all things is called the knowledge of exhaustion; knowing the liberation from all bonds is called the knowledge of non-arising.

To know the realm of the extinction of the roots is called the knowledge of extinction (*kṣayajñāna*); to know the realm of the extinction of conditions is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

To not perceive the afflictions through vitarka and vicāra is called the knowledge of extinction; to not perceive the fruits of retribution through vitarka and vicāra is called the knowledge of non-arising.

Furthermore, the knowledge that exhausts the three stages is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Furthermore, the realization that "my births are exhausted and the holy life is purified" is called the knowledge of exhaustion; the realization that "there is no further state of existence" is called the knowledge of non-arising.
These two types of knowledge are called one single knowledge; they are also called "one-practice-knowledge" regarding the three paths.

If there is a bhikṣu who can sever the three paths, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma. Being able to perform this contemplation is the contemplation of the mind and its sensations.
“How does a bhikṣu observe the body?
If a bhikṣu contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, this is called observing the body, observing feelings, and observing the mind.”
"What is meant by 'contemplating the inhalation and exhalation of breath'?
Inhalation and exhalation are called *ānāpāna*: inhalation is called *āna* and exhalation is called *apāna*. One contemplates the inhalation and exhalation as being like a gate or a doorway."
If there is a bhikṣu who can contemplate in this way, this is called practicing the Dharma (dharmacārin).

If there is a bhikṣu who can observe and count [the breath], following its entry and exit—whether cold or warm, long or short—and whether it pervades the body; if he fixes his mind on the tip of the nose, can observe the new and the old, distinguishes various characteristics, and can observe arising and destruction; if he seeks śamatha and skillfully enters meditative concentration, and can also examine the coarseness or subtlety of the breath, even observing the internal body, perceiving the body as a body—this is called a bhikṣu cultivating the practice of the Dharma.
“Kauṇḍinya! When practicing the counting of breaths, one attains two things:
first, the abandonment of evil thoughts and reflections;”
Second, observing the characteristics of the breath.
Cultivating and accumulating this according to the occasion also achieves two things:
first, single-minded concentration of the mind; second, [the attainment of]... (as per the source context).
Second, one is separated from wholesome reflection and observation.
Observing cold and warmth also yields two matters:
first, the discernment of inhalation and exhalation; [second, the discernment of the body].
Second, observing the characteristics of mental factors.
When practicing the contemplation of the body, one also attains two things:
first, lightness of the body; [second, lightness of the mind].
Second, the mind becomes light.
Furthermore, observing arising and ceasing also yields two results:
first, one knows that all phenomena possess the characteristic of impermanence; [second, the mind becomes light].
Second, knowing that all phenomena are characterized by the absence of pleasure.
"Good son, a bhikṣu who practices the Dharma brings mindfulness to the inhalation and exhalation, binding the mind to a single point."
What is the reduction of numbers?
Two numbers become one, three numbers become two, and so on until ten numbers become nine; this is called the reduction of numbers.
What is the increase of numbers?
Counting one as two, and so on up to counting nine as ten—this is called the increase of number.
Why is this increase cultivated?
Because it destroys all discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).
When attaining the first dhyāna, one contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath as well as the characteristics of the mind.
"The five factors of the first dhyāna are:
first, applied thought (vitarka);..."
Second, contemplation;
third, joy born of seclusion;
fourth, experiencing bliss.
Fifth is concentration (*samādhi*).
When the five factors are complete, one is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.

If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with these five factors, he is called a practitioner of the Dharma (*dhammānusārī*); having distanced himself from five things and accomplished five things, he cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and achieves great merit.
“Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who is able to attain the second dhyāna, he is called one who practices according to the Dharma (dharmacārin).

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, fixing the mind on a single point and remaining detached from joy and pleasure, he attains the third dhyāna, which is neither joyful nor pleasurable.”
Why is this? Having unified the mind by binding the attention to the inhalation and exhalation of breath, one becomes detached from joy and bliss and attains the fourth dhyāna.
If a bhikṣu contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of breath, he then contemplates the five aggregates.
If one contemplates the five aggregates, this is called "practice of the Dharma" (dharmacaryā).
If a bhikṣu perceives the arising and ceasing of all dharmas, and even perceives the arising and ceasing of all afflictions, this is called "patience regarding the Dharma" (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).
If a bhikṣu sees that the eye is empty, up to seeing that the mental consciousness is empty, this is called the patience of emptiness (śūnyatākṣānti).
If a bhikṣu sees that the eye is signless, up to seeing that the mental consciousness is signless, this is called the patience of signlessness (animittakṣānti).
If a bhikṣu does not form aspirations regarding the eye, up to and including the mental consciousness, this is called the patience of wishlessness (apraṇihita-kṣānti).
If a bhikṣu contemplates suffering as distinct, pleasure as distinct, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as distinct, this is called the patience of the middle truth (madhyama-satya-kṣānti).
If one practices within the cycle of birth and death for the sake of sentient beings, this is called "patience that accords with the supreme truth.
What is meant by patience that accords with the faculties, accords with the powers, accords with applied and sustained thought, and even accords with nirvana?
When the mind does not cling to such dharmas, this is called "patience through faith" (śraddhā-kṣānti) and is termed "faith," but it is not termed the "faculty of faith" (śraddhendriya).
If one restrains body and mind so as not to commit evil, this is termed "diligence" (vīrya), but it is not termed the "faculty of diligence" (vīryendriya).
If one can single-mindedly attend to such dharmas as these, it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*), but it is not called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).

When the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are able to bind themselves to a single object, it is called concentration (*samādhi*), but it is not called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
If one is able not to contemplate such signs as these, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*), but it is not called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
If one contemplates such rootlessness, this is called the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).

“Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the stage of the summit (mūrdhan) and the stage of the highest mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma), and contemplates the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as impermanent, suffering, and empty, this is called the practice of the Dharma (dharmānusārin), and this is called the samādhi of emptiness.”
This samādhi takes as its object the absence of receiving life and the absence of mastery.
The signless samādhi takes as its objects exhaustion and disintegration, as well as cessation and revulsion.
The wishless samādhi has as its object the nectar but is not the practice of the nectar; there is the practice of the nectar but it does not have the nectar as its object.
The emptiness samādhi has as its object the nectar but is not the practice of the nectar; there is the practice of the nectar but it does not have the nectar as its object.
The signless samādhi has as its object the nectar but is not the practice of the nectar; there is the practice of the nectar but it does not have the nectar as its object.
Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who, taking wisdom as a condition, enters the wishless samādhi adorned with cessation, this is called "conditioning upon the nectar, but not practicing the nectar."
If there is a bhikṣu who attains liberation by taking wisdom as a condition for its cessation, this is called the practice of the deathless (amṛta), not the deathless itself as a condition.
It is the same for emptiness and signlessness.
"Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who can contemplate in this way, he is called one who practices according to the Dharma. Kauṇḍinya!"
If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates feeling and contemplates the mind, this is called "practice according to the Dharma" (dharmānusārin). Why is this?
Because he is able to destroy the twenty kinds of views of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).

Kauṇḍinya! There are five kinds of each of the view of annihilation and the view of self: from the annihilation of form up to the annihilation of consciousness, these are called the five views of annihilation;
from the selfhood of form up to the selfhood of consciousness, these are called the five views of self.
Kauṇḍinya! There are forty-four types of conceptualization regarding the five kinds of annihilationist views:

sixteen types of propounding perception, eight types of propounding non-perception, eight types of propounding neither-perception-nor-non-perception, six types of propounding various perceptions, and six types of propounding annihilation; these are called the forty-four types.
My views are distinguished into eighteen types:
four that assert a self, four that assert extremes, four that assert divergent matters, and six that assert the samādhi of wishlessness.
These are called the sixty-two views.

The twenty conditions of the view of self can give rise to four hundred and four kinds of afflictions. To become free from such afflictions, one contemplates the body and mind; this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma. In this way, a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the body and mind.
“Kauṇḍinya! What are the eight persons?
What is certainty?”

Kauṇḍinya! Those who hold the view of annihilationism say that [defilements] are severed in a single thought-moment, while those who hold the view of eternalism say they are severed through the eight patiences; both of these types of people attain certainty, and there is no hindrance to their later liberation from afflictions.

Kauṇḍinya! One who is able to attain the eight patiences is called an "eight-person" (aṣṭamaka); one who attains the sixteen moments of mind is called "one of fixed determination" (niyata), and this is called being in accordance with the Dharma. Kauṇḍinya!
"If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, he immediately attains the name of one of the eight persons and is also called 'one of fixed destiny.
Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes the counting of breaths, he immediately attains the faculty of faith, up to and including the faculty of wisdom."
If one attains the five faculties, one immediately attains the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
In this way, a bhikṣu is able to shatter the mind that is entangled in the net of all doubts; this is called the true cultivation and accumulation of noble conduct (*āryacaryā*).
If a bhikṣu accomplishes the knowledge of suffering, he severs ten kinds of afflictions; this is called cultivating the first untainted mental observation (*anāsrava-citta-vipaśyanā*).

At that time, he successively observes the wishless samādhi (*apranihita-samādhi*); while observing the wishless, he cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), which is called the wisdom of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi-jñāna*). He thereby attains the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*).

At that time, he contemplates the five aggregates of the form realm and the four aggregates of the formless realm; as with the suffering of the desire realm, so it is likewise for the form and formless realms.
Having observed in this way, one abandons the eighteen kinds of afflictions pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness.
Once these eighteen kinds have been abandoned, one reflects:
"From what karma do these various sufferings arise?"
"By whom was this created?
Having made this observation, he understands: "This suffering arises from the causal condition of craving; if I do not uproot such craving, suffering will inevitably arise."
"Therefore, one contemplates origination.
Having made this contemplation, one abandons the seven afflictions.
Having contemplated the origination of the desire realm, it is likewise for the form and formless realms."
Having observed thus, one attains subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). While performing this observation, one abandons the twelve afflictions.
"Kauṇḍinya! One who possesses the eight patiences is said to have 'seen the Dharma. Having abandoned the origin (*samudaya*) of the three realms, one again performs this observation:"
For what cause and condition is the cessation of the origin of suffering achieved?
It is for the sake of peace and bliss; indeed, peace and bliss are themselves the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

At that time, one first contemplates the Truth of Cessation within the desire realm and attains the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby severing the seven afflictions. The same applies to the form and formless realms.
Having performed this contemplation, one attains the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and extinguishes twelve afflictions.
One then performs this further contemplation:
"By what causes and conditions is this patience of conformity attained?"

By practicing the Eightfold Path, through the power of the Eightfold Right Path, one comes to know the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation within the desire realm, as well as the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation within the form and formless realms.
At that time, the subsequent patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) arises; having attained it, one is able to sever the eight kinds of afflictions.
At that time, he further contemplates the realms of form and formlessness, attaining the patience of conformity to the Path (*mārgānulomikakṣānti*) and severing fourteen afflictions.

Through this cultivation and accumulation, he becomes distanced from eighty-eight kinds of afflictions; this is called the definitive attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna*. This is called the sixteen moments of mind, this is called the certainty of attaining *bodhi*, and through these seven returns, all suffering is severed.
“Kauṇḍinya! Some persons attain certainty through faith; some attain certainty through the Dharma; and some, in a single lifetime, realize the fruit of srotāpanna, up to and including arhatship.”

Some enter the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom; some cultivate meditative concentration; some cultivate wisdom; some attain the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and enter definitive contemplation, observing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and arise and perish in succession, thereby distancing themselves from all the dharmas of ordinary worldlings.

There are those who contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure; as lacking self-mastery and devoid of tranquility; and as arising from conditions and ceasing from conditions.
Having performed this contemplation, one attains the tranquil Truth of Cessation; this is called a bhikṣu practicing in accordance with the Dharma. "Kauṇḍinya!

The Tathāgata fully knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, and he also knows the nature of the minds and the nature of the afflictions of all sentient beings. This is called the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, proclaiming the remedies in accordance with their various afflictions; for this reason, he is named Sarvajña-jñāna (the Wisdom of All-Knowledge)."

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s twelvefold scriptures, copying, reading, and reciting them; yet they will misinterpret their meaning and teach them erroneously. Because they conceal the treasury of the Dharma through such erroneous explanations, they shall be called Dharmaguptaka.”

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall uphold, recite, and transcribe the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras; yet they shall also read, recite, transcribe, and explain external treatises, accepting the existence of the three periods of time as well as the internal and external [phenomena]. They shall refute the heterodox paths and be skillful in expounding upon doctrines and meanings. They shall teach that all natures can receive the precepts, and they shall be able to answer all questions and challenges. For these reasons, they are called Sarvāstivāda.”

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall uphold, transcribe, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, proclaiming that there is no self nor any experiencer, and that they turn away from all afflictions as if they were a corpse; for this reason, they are called the Kāśyapīya school.”

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall receive, uphold, recite, and transcribe the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, without forming conceptions of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor conceptions of space or consciousness; for this reason, they are called the Mahīśāsaka school.”

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples will receive, uphold, recite, chant, and transcribe the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras; yet they will all say that there is a self and not speak of the characteristic of emptiness. Being like children, they shall therefore be called *bālaputraka* (foolish sons).”

“Kauṇḍinya! After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and widely study the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures across the five classes of texts; for this reason, they shall be called the Mahāsāṃghikas.”
"Good son! Although these five divisions are each distinct from one another, none of them obstruct the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas or Great Nirvana.
What is meant by 'following through faith'?"

If one has faith in the Triple Gem and is endowed with the faculty of faith, through the causal conditions of that faculty of faith, one enters into certainty, attains the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin, transcends the realms of form and formlessness, and attains the fruit of arhatship.

One who attains liberation through faith is called "liberated by faith" (śraddhādhimukta), also termed "one part" (ekadeśa), also termed "bodily witness" (kāyasākṣin), and termed "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta); this is called "one who follows by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
“Kauṇḍinya! What is meant by ‘practicing in accordance with the Dharma’?

If there is one who enters into certainty through the Dharma, is endowed with the faculty of wisdom, attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, or the fruit of *anāgāmin*; or if they transcend the realms of form and formlessness and attain the fruit of *arhat*—this is called ‘liberation through both vision and attainment. They are also called ‘one who has realized it with the body,’ or ‘one who attains liberation through wisdom. When the mind attains liberation and one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), for this reason they are called ‘liberated through both parts.’”

This is called the liberation of one beyond training; this is called the practice of the Dharma; this is called the accomplishment of the contemplation of the body, up to the accomplishment of the contemplation of phenomena within phenomena; this is called the accomplishment of vipassanā and samatha.
"What is called śamatha? Śamatha is termed 'cessation.
That which can extinguish the mind of greed, the mind of hatred, and the distracted mind is called śamatha."
What is called the characteristic of *śamatha*?
That which can extinguish the characteristics of greed, as well as the characteristics of hatred and delusion, is named the characteristic of *śamatha*.
What is called "entering into certainty by following *śamatha*"?
If one can practice śamatha accordingly, honoring and praising it, and adorning oneself with the skillful means of śamatha, this is called the characteristic of śamatha.
If there is a bhikṣu who reflects deeply within himself:
"My mind of greed can only be destroyed by contemplating impurity; the mind of hatred can be destroyed by loving-kindness; and the twelve links of dependent origination can destroy delusion."
This is called the characteristic of śamatha. What is called vipaśyanā?
If one cultivates noble wisdom and is able to observe the successive arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, this is called vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, if one contemplates all phenomena as being identical to the *dharmatā*, and truly understands their actual nature and true characteristics, this is called *vipaśyanā*.
What are the characteristics of *vipaśyanā*?

If one can achieve and maintain a mind of mindfulness, observing that all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions and cease due to conditions, and that all conditioned phenomena are without self-mastery, without an agent, and without a recipient, this is called the characteristic of vipaśyanā.
What is meant by "entering into certainty through vipaśyanā"?
It is to mindfully attend to vipaśyanā with a sincere heart, and with reverence and respect, to turn toward the path of adornment; this is called entering into certainty through vipaśyanā.
"What is meant by 'concentrating the mind through the method of emergence rather than the method of cessation'?

If a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the causes and conditions for the emergence of the mind, up to the causes and conditions for the emergence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), this is called concentrating the mind through the method of emergence rather than the method of cessation."
What is meant by "concentrating the mind on the dharma of cessation rather than on the dharma of emergence"?

If a bhikṣu is able to deeply contemplate the causes and conditions for the cessation of the mind, up to the causes and conditions for the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), this is called concentrating the mind on the dharma of cessation rather than on the dharma of emergence.
What is meant by "concentrating the mind on neither the dharma of emergence nor the dharma of cessation"?

If a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the nature of the mind, the nature of the eye, and so forth up to the nature of consciousness, this is called concentrating the mind on neither the dharma of emergence nor the dharma of cessation.
"What is concentration through an object (*ālambana-saṃgraha*) rather than through reflection (*manasikāra-saṃgraha*)?
If a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the out-breath without contemplating the in-breath, this is called concentration through an object rather than through reflection."
What is meant by "concentrating the mind through reflection rather than through an object"?
If a bhikṣu contemplates the inhalation of breath, this is called concentrating the mind through reflection rather than through an object.
What is meant by "not concentrated by means of an object" and "not concentrated by means of reflection"?

If a bhikṣu contemplates the nature of the mind, the nature of the eye, and so forth up to the nature of the mind-faculty (*manas*), this is called being neither concentrated by means of an object nor concentrated by means of reflection.
“Kauṇḍinya! If a bhikṣu is able to collect his mind, he will attain eighty gates of samādhi as well as cultivate the three gates of liberation.
If a bhikṣu contemplates his past body and cultivates adornment, observing the body and seeing the body, this is called cultivating the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha).”

If a bhikṣu, having contemplated his past body, sees only the mind and does not see the body, and while cultivating the contemplation of adornment, sees the body, this is called cultivating the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).

If a bhikṣu, having contemplated the past body, perceives neither the action nor the agent—wherein the agent has no body and the body has no agent—and cultivates the path of adornment by contemplating the body as the body, this is called cultivating the gate of liberation of emptiness.
The contemplation of feeling, mind, and phenomena is also like this. Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya!

One cultivates the adornment of the contemplation of the three gates of liberation: one contemplates all conditioned formations as neither arising nor ceasing; having arisen, they then cease, and in their cessation there is no destination; they do not arrive from the past, nor do they go to the future. This is called the adornment of the gate of wishless liberation.

"Furthermore, one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in future ages have not yet emerged; since these phenomena have not emerged, they do not undergo cessation. This is called the adornment of the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*)."

It is not an ultimate exhaustion; that which is ultimately exhausted is without arising or ceasing. If there is no arising or ceasing, that is ultimate exhaustion. If it is ultimate exhaustion, that is the causal condition of emptiness. To contemplate ultimate exhaustion in this way is called the adornment of the liberation door of emptiness.

If one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are ultimately exhausted, then there is neither arising nor ceasing; if there is neither arising nor ceasing, then there is neither existence nor emptiness.
Why is this? That which exists first and subsequently becomes non-existent is what is called "emptiness."
If there were no original non-existence, then there would be no subsequent non-existence.
If there were no subsequent non-existence, how could it be called emptiness?

If there were no activity, that would be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); yet that which is ultimately exhausted is neither conditioned nor unconditioned. Emptiness is neither activity nor non-activity; therefore, that which is ultimately exhausted is not subsumed under the conditioned, nor is it subsumed under the unconditioned. This is called the adornment of the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were ultimately exhausted, that would be *nirvāṇa*; it does not belong to the past, future, or present. Therefore, the cessation of past formations is not called *nirvāṇa*, nor is the cessation of future or present formations called *nirvāṇa*.
Those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna see this as nirvāṇa, and so on up to those who have attained the stage of Arhat, who also see this as nirvāṇa.
What is called the Truth of Suffering?

It is when one contemplates all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and does not perceive a first truth; contemplates all causes and does not perceive a second truth; contemplates all cessations and does not perceive a third truth; and contemplates all paths and does not perceive a fourth truth.
"What is called 'arising'? That which was originally non-existent and subsequently comes into being is called arising.
What is called 'ceasing'?"
That which exists and then returns to non-existence is called cessation (*nirodha*).
That there is no emergence from cessation is called exhaustion (*kṣaya*). For what reason?
The absence of arising and ceasing is called the Way (*mārga*). This Way has six aspects: cultivation and non-cultivation, practice and non-practice, knowledge and non-knowledge.

If there is a bhikṣu who can see such phenomena of arising and ceasing, this person will be able to become weary of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and will be able to perceive the characteristic of impermanence in all formations.
"What is the mark of impermanence that is not an impermanent dharma?

If there is the practice of the initial untainted faculties accompanied by signs; if there is the practice of the door of liberation of wishlessness accompanied by signs; or if there are the marks of emptiness, suffering, impurity, and non-self—these are called the mark of impermanence that is not an impermanent dharma."
What is meant by "impermanent phenomena that do not have the characteristic of impermanence"?

This refers to the characteristics of form throughout the three realms, up to and including the characteristics of mental phenomena (*dharmas*). These are called inverted characteristics and characteristics of relinquishment; they are not the characteristic of impermanence itself. This is what is meant by "impermanent phenomena that do not have the characteristic of impermanence."
What is the mark of impermanence that is also an impermanent dharma?

It refers to all sentient beings who have not yet attained certainty; they enter various samādhis by means of the worldly path and accord with the patience regarding the marks of dharmas. This is called the mark of impermanence that is also an impermanent dharma.
What is that which is neither the mark of impermanence nor an impermanent dharma?
It refers to the mark of quiescent permanence and the mark of pure liberation; this is called that which is neither the mark of impermanence nor an impermanent dharma.
"What is meant by attaining the foremost truth?
It is called attaining the foremost truth when one contemplates the six sense organs and the five aggregates as being like reflections in a mirror.
How does one contemplate the four truths with a single mind?"

If one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely causes of suffering, and because they are causes of suffering they can be seen, extinguished, and abandoned—this is called the mind taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object. Therefore, by single-mindedly attaining the Four Noble Truths, it is called "attaining liberation through a mind free from outflows" (*anāsrava-citta-vimukti*).

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the mind with the mind, this is called contemplating the mind with the mind through the gate of liberation of wishlessness. He has already contemplated twelve matters:
first, karma; second, formations; [and so forth].
Third, suffering; fourth, emptiness;
fifth, disintegration.
Sixth, lack of sovereignty;
seventh, the past; eighth, the present.
Ninth, the future; tenth, causes and conditions;
eleventh, non-action.
Twelfth is non-appropriation (*anupādāna*).
This is called seeing the mind within the mind, and it is named the gate of liberation through wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).

If a bhikṣu contemplates this mind and perceives that there is no master of the mind, no one who enters or exits, nothing capable of departing, and nothing to be departed from—this is called seeing the mind within the mind and attaining the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

If one contemplates that there is no mind entering meditative absorption, and thereby attains detachment from all afflictions—such that afflictions do not arise because of the absence of causes and conditions—this is called "detachment through seeing the mind within the mind," which is the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
If one contemplates in this manner, one will immediately become detached from the mind of outflows (āsrava) and attain untainted liberation (anāsrava-vimukti). "Kauṇḍinya!
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) lack any fixed certainty; if they are not fixed, how can one enter the stage of certainty (niyāma)?"
If it is claimed that one has already entered the stage of the rightly fixed (samyaktva-niyāma) by observing the three periods of time, this meaning is not tenable. Why?

Because the past has already ceased, the future has not yet emerged, and the present is impermanent; since the observations of the three periods differ, how could one enter the stage of the rightly fixed?
Therefore, all alternative views are of an indeterminate nature. "Kauṇḍinya!
It is like a hall that has four staircases."
If one were to say that it does not proceed from the first step of the ladder to the fourth step, such a thing is impossible;
yet, when one ascends the first step, one cannot be said to have already ascended the fourth, and likewise, these four steps are not called one.
Kauṇḍinya! If these four truths were but a single truth, they could be realized with a single mind. Kauṇḍinya!
The time of contemplation is different, and the time of attainment is also different.
Regarding the difference in the time of contemplation: cause and effect are both exhausted and destroyed.
Regarding the difference in the time of attainment: it consists of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates that conditioned formations are impermanent, suffering, non-self, impure, and unstable; that these are outflows, fetters, conditions, and the entirety of existence—this is called bondage.

Therefore, one does not seek after the aggregates or conditioned formations; one grows weary of all formations and joyfully seeks nirvana. With focused intent, one contemplates the merits of nirvana, deeply delighting in tranquility and being indifferent even to body and life as one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā. This is called a bhikṣu’s cultivation and accumulation of the practice of the Dharma.
“Kauṇḍinya! How is it that a bhikṣu’s mind can see the mind?

If a bhikṣu is able to contemplate the mind, seeing that the mind is impermanent and a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, this is called a bhikṣu whose mind can see the mind; such a bhikṣu cultivates the samādhi of emptiness.”
What is meant by emptiness?

It is the emptiness of the aggregates, bases, and elements; the emptiness of the truths; the emptiness of reality; the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination; and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
What is the emptiness of the aggregates?
That which is called form being empty of self and what belongs to self, up to consciousness being empty of self and what belongs to self—this is termed the emptiness of the aggregates (skandhas).
The same applies to the emptiness of both the sense bases (āyatanas) and the elements (dhātus).
What is the emptiness of the truths?
It means that regarding the truth of suffering there is neither acquisition nor relinquishment; this applies likewise up to the truth of the path.
What is the emptiness of reality?
Within all phenomena, there is no discursive thought (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*), nor "I" or "mine"; this is called true emptiness.
What is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination?

The twelve links of dependent origination are precisely the twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*); observing these twelve factors as being without "I" or "mine" is called the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination.
What is emptiness by nature?

If a bhikṣu contemplates that the eye is empty, devoid of self or what belongs to a self, and so on up to the mind, which is likewise empty—this is called the practice of the Dharma that is able to contemplate the mind and mental states.

In this way, a bhikṣu does not perceive a sentient being, a life-span, a person, or a "so-and-so"; he knows the nature of all phenomena and truly understands conventional truth. For the sake of dissemination, he speaks of the aggregates, bases, and elements, knowing that the nature of all phenomena is without arising or cessation.
In this way, a bhikṣu is able to cross over birth and death, is able to know the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and is able to sever the afflictions.
"Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates and accumulates the practice of the Dharma, he knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and cease from causes and conditions."
In this way, a bhikṣu attains the three gates of liberation and realizes the true characteristics of form (*rūpa*).

As for the true characteristics of form, they are: the characteristic of obstruction, the characteristic of feeling-feeling, the characteristic of perception-perceiving, the characteristic of formations-forming, and the characteristic of consciousness-knowing. This is called truly knowing the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*). Having contemplated in this manner, he attains the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

Seeing that all phenomena are without agent, recipient, life-span, or self-mastery, and seeing only impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth, this is called attaining the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
To contemplate all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing is called attaining the gate of liberation through signlessness. "Kauṇḍinya!

A bhikṣu who practices the Dharma is able to attain supernormal powers; he is free from evil thoughts and reflections, his mouth never speaks of the four kinds of evil transgressions, he engages in no quarrels, and he does not listen to malicious words."
At that time, he immediately becomes free from the five hindrances and increases the five roots of goodness; this practitioner of the Dharma attains the first dhyāna.

Having entered the first dhyāna and desiring to attain the supernormal power of the body, he fixes his mind on the tip of the nose and contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, clearly perceiving the movement of the breath through ninety-nine thousand pores.
One perceives that the body is entirely empty, and even the four great elements are likewise so.
Having observed in this way, one becomes detached from the marks of form and attains supernormal powers; even the four dhyānas are likewise so.
“How does a Dharma-practicing bhikṣu obtain the supernormal power of the eye?
Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who, observing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, truly perceives forms; having perceived these forms, he reflects as follows:”
“As I see all forms throughout the three periods of time, whenever I desire to see them, I see them immediately at will.
This applies likewise even up to the fourth dhyāna.
“How does a bhikṣu practicing according to the Dharma attain the supernormal power of the divine ear?”

Kauṇḍinya! If a bhikṣu attains the first dhyāna, having observed the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, he then successively observes sounds; this continues in the same manner up to the fourth dhyāna.
"How does a Dharma-practicing bhikṣu attain the knowledge of others' minds?

If a bhikṣu, while observing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, attains the first dhyāna and cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called the knowledge of others' minds; it is the same up to the fourth dhyāna."
"How does a Dharma-practicing bhikṣu attain the knowledge of past lives?

Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath and attains the first dhyāna, he thereby acquires the supernormal power of the divine eye. Having acquired the divine eye, he contemplates the time of the kalala at the very beginning of existence, up to the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, and the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates throughout immeasurable eons; this is likewise so even up to the fourth dhyāna."
"What is called 'dhyāna' (meditation)? Why is it named dhyāna?

Because it is swift, it is named dhyāna; because it is exceedingly swift, it is named dhyāna; because it is abiding, it is named dhyāna; because it is great abiding, it is named dhyāna; because it is stillness, it is named dhyāna; because it is great stillness, it is named dhyāna; and because it is the contemplation of cessation and detachment, it is named dhyāna."
The first dhyāna is also called "endowment" and also called "separation.
What is endowment? What is separation?
"Seclusion" refers to being secluded from the five hindrances.
"Endowment" refers to being endowed with the five factors, namely: applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, tranquility, and concentration.
What is meant by "awakening" (bodhi)?
When the mind awakens to the Great Awakening and contemplates the Great Contemplation, observing the nature of the mind—this is called awakening.
What is meant by "contemplation" (vipaśyanā)?
If one contemplates the mental activities as great activities, pervasive activities, and activities according to one's will, this is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
What is joy (*prīti*)?
It is knowing truly and with a great mind that the movement of the mind has reached the heart; this is called joy.
What is tranquility?
It refers to tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, and tranquility of feeling; experiencing pleasant contact—this is called tranquility.
What is concentration?
If the mind abides in the great abiding without distraction, is unerring regarding its object, and is free from inversion, this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
As for the second dhyāna, it likewise abandons five things, namely the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), and is endowed with three factors:
first, joy (*prīti*); second, tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); and third, concentration (*samādhi*).
Entering the third dhyāna, one is likewise free from five things and is endowed with five factors:
first, mindfulness; second, equanimity; [third, happiness; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind].
Third is wisdom; fourth is tranquility;
fifth is concentration.
Entering the fourth dhyāna, one likewise leaves behind five factors and is endowed with four branches:
first, mindfulness; second, equanimity; [third, happiness; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind].
Third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure;
fourth, concentration. Kauṇḍinya!
If there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the four dhyānas, he is called one who practices the Dharma (*dharmacārin*). "Kauṇḍinya!

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the body with revulsion, who distances himself from the marks of the body and all tactile sensations of joy, pleasure, and happiness associated with the body; who discriminates the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and distances himself from the aggregate of form; and who contemplates the sphere of infinite space—this is called a bhikṣu practicing the Dharma entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating and accumulating the practice of the Dharma."
“Kauṇḍinya! How does a bhikṣu attain the concentration of the sphere of consciousness?

If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, observes the mind, thought, and consciousness, and realizes for himself that this body is not subject [to them]; having known the three types of sensation, he attains detachment from these three kinds of sensation. Therefore, it is called attaining the concentration of the sphere of consciousness; this is termed ‘practice in accordance with the Dharma.’”
“Kauṇḍinya! How does a bhikṣu attain the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness?

If a bhikṣu contemplates the emptiness of the three periods of time and knows that the activity of all phenomena arises and ceases, and that the spheres of emptiness and consciousness also arise and cease—having made this contemplation, he next contemplates consciousness as follows:”
I now contemplate consciousness as being neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; that which is not consciousness is called tranquility.
How may I now utterly sever this consciousness?
Having made this contemplation, one attains a limited sphere of consciousness; this is called a bhikṣu attaining the concentration of the limited sphere of consciousness.
“Kauṇḍinya! How does a bhikṣu attain the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Kauṇḍinya!”
If there is a bhikṣu who possesses a non-conceptual mind and cultivates this compliant patience, thinking:
"This perception of mine is now suffering, it is an outflow, it is a sore, it is an abscess, and it is not tranquil."
"If I can sever such a state that is neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called tranquility.
If there is a bhikṣu who can sever such a state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he is said to have attained the door of liberation of non-perception.
Why is this? A bhikṣu who practices the Dharma reflects thus:

"Whether there is the perception of feeling, the perception of consciousness, the perception of contact, the perception of emptiness, the perception of consciousness, or the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—such perceptions as these are called coarse perceptions."
‘If I now cultivate the samādhi of non-perception, I shall be able to permanently sever such perceptions as these.
Therefore, seeing the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a state of tranquility, and having seen it thus, he enters the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"If, having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is without craving and without greed, and is thus able to destroy ignorance; having destroyed ignorance, this is called attaining the fruit of arhatship."
The first three types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are abandoned by the two paths;
the latter, the fourth concentration, can ultimately never be abandoned by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is detached from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), although they lack coarse afflictions, there are still ten factors present, namely:
1. Feeling, 2. perception, 3. formations, 4. contact, 5. volition, 6. desire, 7. resolve, 8. mindfulness, 9. concentration, and 10. wisdom.
What is feeling? It is so-called cognitive feeling. What is perception?
What is called "perception" (saṃjñā)?
What is "volitional formation" (saṃskāra)?
It is what is called "dharma-formation" (dharmasaṃskāra).
What is contact? It is so-called mental contact. What is volition?
This is what is called reflection on the Dharma. What is meant by "desire"?
It refers to the desire to enter and emerge from meditative concentration.
What is understanding?
It is the understanding of phenomena (dharma). What is mindfulness?
This is what is called mindfulness-samādhi.
What constitutes concentration?
It is when the mind abides in accordance with the Dharma.

What is wisdom? It refers to the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom; it is the contemplation directed toward the practice for the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], up to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship; it is the contemplation of arising and ceasing as well as the samādhi of emptiness; and it is the contemplation of the four great elements as being like four venomous snakes.
These ten dharmas are fully present in the fourth station of emptiness; because it is devoid of coarse afflictions, all ordinary worldlings claim this to be nirvana.

“Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates and accumulates the Noble Path, who becomes weary of and detached from the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, and who contemplates the path adorned by the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), he reflects thus:
‘All inhalations and exhalations are impermanent; if I can sever these inhalations and exhalations, that is true peace and happiness.’”

"Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising from causes and conditions are extinguished; feeling is extinguished, and so on up to wisdom being extinguished. Because initial and sustained mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*) are extinguished, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are extinguished; greed, hatred, and delusion are extinguished; all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are extinguished, and all non-mental factors are also extinguished. This is called the dharma not shared with ordinary persons; it is not a worldly dharma, but is the dharma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
“Kauṇḍinya! Neither a srotāpanna nor a sakṛdāgāmin can ever attain such a meditative absorption of cessation.

Even if one attains the fruit of srotāpanna through the sequential stages, one cannot attain it; nor can one attain it even if a srotāpanna, after casting off this body, attains the fruit of arhatship.”
"If there are those who are fully endowed with the eight liberations, such persons can attain it. Kauṇḍinya!
Even if the Tathāgata were to explain this Dharma-eye dhāraṇī method until the exhaustion of kalpas, he would never reach its end; this is called unimpeded knowledge of the Dharma."
Kauṇḍinya! This Dharmamukha dhāraṇī is inconceivable. Kauṇḍinya!
Suppose there were a person who could count every drop of seawater by using drops from a rabbit’s hair; they would still be unable to calculate the merits possessed by this Dharmamukha-dhāraṇī.
"If one were to exclude the Tathāgata’s intention to speak of their exhaustion, such a thing is impossible; even so it is with every single atom of the entire Sahā world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Vajraśikhara, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Is there any difference between the Dhāraṇī of Dharma-eyes that you have brought with you and what I have now spoken? "No,
World-Honored One."
“Noble son, do you speak thus? “World-Honored One, I do.”
"It is indeed as you have said.

'Good son! If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively explain this Dharma for others, you should know that such a person will always be protected by all humans, devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth; none of the four māras shall find an opportunity to harm them, and they shall cross the river of afflictions to enter the Eightfold Noble Path.'"
The youth Vajraśikhara said: “Excellent, excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"It is truly as the holy teaching says. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:

"If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās practice this Dharma, none shall be able to destroy it. This is called the Radiance of Giving, which is capable of purifying and bringing about tranquility; it has no place of activity, is free from turbidity and movement, and possesses no abode. It is neither small nor great, and is named the Practice Reaching the Destination, the Subtle Practice, and the Firm Practice. It can destroy the four Māras and their hosts, as well as all false views; it crosses the river of birth and death to enter the ocean of wisdom, is constantly praised by all the sages, and brings one near to the place entered by the Tathāgata."

Although they have not yet severed all afflictions, they may attain the supreme body, supreme enlightenment, supreme physical form, supreme strength, supreme eloquence, supreme mindfulness, supreme wisdom, and supreme station;
or they may attain the authority to rule as a king of the four continents—whether over three, two, or one;
or they may become Śakra, even up to becoming the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Whether he becomes a Brahmā King,

or further attains the vajra-seat beneath the Bodhi tree, his Brahma-voice is profound and far-reaching, his mind is equanimous, he attains great compassion and śamatha, and having destroyed all afflictions, he is named the Unsurpassed Honored One.
When this Dharma was being taught, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others attained the fruit of Arhatship while remaining in their seats.
At that time, all the people of the world and the various devas praised him, saying:

“The merit of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; immeasurable sentient beings have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, and have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Puṇyavatī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Wherever this sūtra circulates, we shall protect its fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as their kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, kings, and people.”
