Chapter Two: The Eye of the World; Section Ten: The Division on the Eye of Space (Part Two).

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the white tuft between his eyebrows a radiance that completely eclipsed the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the light of jewels, fire, and lamps throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, such that all rocky mountains and various thorny brambles were no longer visible.

When the sentient beings in immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, saw this light, they each focused their mindfulness and contemplated virtuous matters.
Therein, the various Buddhas, having seen this light, each addressed their own assemblies, saying:
"O sons of good family!
Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, replete with the five defilements.
A Buddha has appeared in that world, known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Innumerable bodhisattvas and innumerable śrāvakas from immeasurable worlds all gathered in that land and sat before that Buddha; that Buddha then proclaimed for them the dhāraṇī gate of the Dharma-practice and Dharma-eye.
Having taught the Dharma practice for the sake of the śrāvakas, he emitted a great radiance, intending to expound the dhāraṇī method of the "Pure Eye" (Vimalanetra) Dharma-gate.

For those of the middle vehicle, he enabled them to attain the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; for the bodhisattvas, he brought about the adornment and accomplishment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, endowed with the ten stages and the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata, turning the non-retrogressive wheel, destroying the three evil realms, and causing them to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to attain the unsurpassed fruit.
At that time, the assemblies in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, having heard these words, each addressed their Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to go to that Sahā world to the place where the Dharma is being preached, in order to hear and receive this Pure Eye Dharma-gate.”

At that time, an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas all came together to the Sahā world; having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, immeasurable Brahmā devas from this world went to where the Buddha was, paid him honor and respect, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Likewise, ten billion Māra devas, ten billion Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, ten billion Tuṣita devas, ten billion Yāma devas, ten billion Śakra devas, ten billion Cāturmahārājika devas, ten billion sun and moon devas, ten billion Īśvara devas, ten billion kings of the Yama realm, ten billion earth spirits, four hundred billion asuras, and four hundred billion nāga kings—all such multitudes as these went to where the Buddha was, paid him honor and respect, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Immeasurable śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having all attained supernatural powers, came to where the Buddha was, paid him respectful homage, and withdrew to sit on one side.
When the non-Buddhist diviners in the various worlds saw the radiance, they thought to themselves:

"This light is not the brilliance of the sun, moon, or stars; it must be an extraordinary light. Before long, seven suns will appear simultaneously, which shall scorch the four oceans, Mount Sumeru the king of mountains, and all grasses and trees. Thereafter, the fire calamity of the desire realm shall break out."
Others again said: "Before long, there will surely fall a rain of poison that shall harm all beings. Still others said:
"In no long time, there will surely be a rain of swords that will harm all people and things; as this evil age approaches, who can save us?
Others further said:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama has compassion for all beings; he alone is able to save us and bestow upon us our lives."
At that time, all the immeasurable sentient beings mindfully recited the Buddha with utmost sincerity;
having done so, they immediately beheld this Great Jewel Monastery, and by the power of the Buddha, they entered the monastery.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, King Prasenajit also beheld the jeweled monastery; by the Buddha’s power, he was able to enter within it.

King Udayana, King Duṣprasāha, King Śuddhodana, King Mahendra, King Śūdrasena, and King Bimbisāra—these kings likewise, through the Buddha’s power, were able to see the jeweled monastery. They all arrived within the monastery, made offerings and prostrations, and sat down in order, each thinking:
"In this assembly there is a Great Seer, a Buddha, a World-Honored One. To whom should we now inquire about the causes and conditions of this light?"
"Should one question the rishi,
or is it appropriate to question the Buddha? At that time, King Śuddhodana said:
"I now have a great brahmin teacher named Vidyujvāla, who is well-versed in the science of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), capable of interpreting and explaining them; he is the one most fit to be consulted.
Upon hearing this, Vidyujvāla immediately said:

"In all the treatises on marks that I have extensively studied, there is nothing like this. I truly cannot interpret this auspicious radiance; even all the five hundred masters of marks within Jambudvīpa are unable to explain it."
At that time, King Bimbisāra said to the kings: "Why are you so frantic?

Within this great assembly is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Śākyamuni. He is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, thoroughly knowing the characteristics of both the mundane and the supramundane; he has mastered the treatises on the auspicious signs of the twelve months. With great compassion, he pities all sentient beings; his speech is truthful and correct. Only the Buddha can explain the retribution for these lights."
At that time, all the kings and the great assembly, looking up to him with total devotion, addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray only that the Tathāgata will explain for us the script of the twelve months.”
The Buddha said, "Great King! In this great assembly,
one should not proclaim the worldly treatises on physiognomy."
King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are beings present in this assembly who do not believe in the merits of the Tathāgata, nor do they believe that he is the Omniscient One. We only pray that you will destroy such doubts and proclaim the truth.”
If these sentient beings, upon hearing this, give rise to joy and faith, and having given rise to faith, one may then preach the supramundane path for them;
such beings will also gladly receive it and be easily disciplined.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall explain it to you.
Great King!"

In the past, there was a seer on the Snowy Mountains named Bhagava. He cultivated a mind of loving-kindness by subsisting on fruits and roots, yet he was unable to eliminate the fetters of the various afflictions, nor could he subdue his heart of craving.
At that time, there was a tigress dwelling in that place who immediately engaged in sexual intercourse with him; the tigress then became pregnant.
When the months were fulfilled, she gave birth to twelve cubs at this man's location.
At that time, out of compassion, the seer took [the children] to bathe them and nourished them; the tigress mother, out of maternal love, suckled and raised them according to their needs.

Then the seer gave each of them a name: first, Keka; second, Bakapā; third, Vyāghra; fourth, Siṃha; fifth, Bhāradvāja; sixth, Pāruṣya; seventh, Padika; eighth, Brāhmaṇaka; ninth, Subhakṣa; tenth, Duḥśīla; eleventh, Siṃhabhāra; and twelfth, Suvikrānta.
"These twelve children were only seven years old at the start of the year, subsisting on grass roots, flowers, and fruits.
At that time, their parents both passed away simultaneously. The twelve children, their hearts filled with grief and distress, looked up to heaven and wailed:
'How is it that in a single day we have nothing to rely upon?'"
At that time, a tree deity, having heard these words, spoke thus: "Children, do not weep!

There is a place of refuge, namely Brahmā, who has compassion for sentient beings. You should bathe yourselves clean during the six periods of day and night, and with a sincere heart, prostrate toward the void and seek the mercy of Brahmā."
Brahmā shall hear your voices with his unimpeded divine ear; having heard them, he shall come to your dwelling out of compassion.

Once he has arrived, he shall destroy your darkness of delusion and bestow upon you the light of wisdom. Having attained this wisdom, all the devas shall make offerings to you, let alone the people of the world!
When the twelve sons heard these words, they acted according to the instructions for twelve years.
Thereafter, Brahmā heard their voices and immediately descended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, Śakra, seeing Brahmā approaching, immediately went forward to make offerings; having made the offerings, he addressed him again, saying:
"Great Being! Where do you intend to go?"
"Kauśika! Do you not see those twelve seers in the Snowy Mountains?
Kauśika, you should go there together with me."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, accompanied by immeasurable devas, descended together to the Snowy Mountains.
When the twelve seers saw Brahmā approaching, they leaped for joy and prostrated themselves in worship and offering.
Then the Brahma King addressed the twelve youths:
"For what reason have you diligently practiced austerities for twelve years to make offerings to me?"
"What do you seek?
Do you seek fame and reputation, physical strength, wealth and treasures, the noble path, wisdom, or the bodies of the devas?
Then the seer Garga addressed the Brahmā, saying:
“O Great Being!
We do not now seek such things as these; we wish to seek wisdom for the sake of sentient beings.
We are orphaned and young, having lost our protection at an early age; we follow our own whims, with no one to instruct or admonish us.”

I only pray that the Great Being will bestow wisdom upon me, enabling me to recognize and understand my own karmic actions of good and evil, as well as the karmic actions of good and evil of all sentient beings; furthermore, may I know the various characteristics of sentient beings—whether they be of the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes; male or female; great or small—and their experiences of suffering and pleasure resulting from such good and evil deeds.

As for those kings who greedily covet their kingdoms without satiety, raising armies to strike one another—whether in decline or in prosperity—I shall, having recognized these conditions, employ skillful means to instruct them in the cessation of such evil states, so that they may attain happiness.

**Chapter Three: Maitreya** From the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the "Section on the Eye of Space," Chapter Three: Maitreya. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, before the Buddha, spoke these verses from his heart, questioning the Tathāgata:
"There is no path, yet there is cyclic wandering; The Tathāgata likewise does not abide in any path. One does not see the path through a non-path, Nor does one see a non-path through a path."
The Buddha said: "Good son!

That which is not the path is that which neither arises nor ceases, does not abide, and is not wisdom; it is not the realm of wisdom, neither light nor darkness, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither good nor evil, and is not the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness. This is called true nature, this is called the dharma-nature, it is called all formations, it is called the limit of reality, and it is called the non-path—such is the Middle Way."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, turn the wheel of Dharma, yet they do not become greedily attached to such paths.

If there are sentient beings who perceive what is not the path as the path, or perceive the path as what is not the path, such beings are unable to penetrate the distinction between the path and the non-path, nor can they know the three paths.
The Tathāgata is fully able to analyze and explain them, as well as the path of their cessation. "Good son!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, turns the wheel of Dharma within the absence of a path, for the sake of destroying the three kinds of paths of sentient beings."
What are the three paths?
First, the path of afflictions;
second, the path of suffering.
Third is the path of karma.
The path of karma refers to the formations of existence (*bhava-saṃskāra*);
the path of afflictions refers to ignorance, craving, and grasping.
As for the path of suffering, it refers to consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, old age, death, and so forth.
By what causes and conditions do these three paths exist?

“With contact as condition, there is [feeling]. Good son! Because the eye sees forms, a mind of craving arises. This mind of craving is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). To perform karma for the sake of craving is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). The focused attention of the mind is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness together with form and formations is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The arising of greed through the six sense bases is called the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Seeking sensation because of the entrances is called contact (*sparśa*). The mind of greedy attachment is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Seeking such dharmas is called grasping (*upādāna*). The arising of such dharmas is called becoming (*bhava*). Their uninterrupted succession is called birth (*jāti*). Their successive cessation is called death (*maraṇa*). Being oppressed by the manifold sufferings caused by the conditions of birth and death is called affliction (*parideva*). Even up to the dharma of consciousness, the arising of greed through its conditions is likewise so.”
In this way, these twelve links of dependent origination are fully present within every single person and every single moment of thought.
There are three kinds of emergence:
first, emergence from causes; [and so forth].
Second is emergence from the beginning;
third is emergence through the path.
If there is a bhikṣu who practices the practice of the Dharma, he observes all the characteristics of the mind of attachment.
Monks, you should observe that if there is a mind of attachment, it is precisely ignorance; the essence of ignorance can give rise to two faults:
first, the production of formations;
second, the production of consciousness.
Consciousness also has two aspects:
first, the emergence of names;
second, the emergence of forms.
Name-and-form also has two aspects: first, non-abiding;
second, abiding in the six sense bases.
The six sense bases also have two aspects:
first, not being weary of desire;
second, being able to produce contact.
Contact also has two aspects:
first, that which gives rise to feeling;
second, that which seeks feeling.
Feeling also has two aspects:
first, experiencing pleasure and pain;
second, giving rise to craving and attachment.
Craving also has two aspects:
first, the firmness of bondage;
second, the seeking and grasping.
Grasping also has two aspects:
first, the mind of craving;
second, the seeking of existence.
Existence also has two aspects:
first, abiding in pleasure;
second, the causal conditions for birth.
Birth also has two aspects:
first, birth and old age;
second, the condition for suffering.
Old age also has two aspects:
first, it destroys the vigor of physical form;
second, it acts as the cause of death.
Death also has two aspects:
first, the destruction of the life-span;
second, separation from what is loved. These are called the causes of departure.
"What is meant by 'the first emergence'?
If there is a bhikṣu who cultivates the practice of the Dharma and contemplates these dharmas as both emerging and ceasing, this is called the first emergence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"What is meant by 'the path emerging'?
If a bhikṣu perceives that the path has two aspects:
first, the practice of cultivation; [second, the fruit of cultivation]."
Second is the practice of wisdom.
Kauṇḍinya! Do you know how to practice this practice of wisdom?
Kauṇḍinya said: “I do not yet know it,
World-Honored One.”

I only pray that the Tathāgata, for the sake of the bhikṣu who contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination so that he may attain great wisdom and destroy all afflictions, will provide a detailed explanation; having heard it, the bhikṣu shall fully receive and uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Ratnadhvaja: "Good son,
are you able to know the inhalation and exhalation of the breath?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
A bhikṣu practicing the Dharma first contemplates from ignorance up to old age and death.
How is it that he contemplates ignorance?

He first contemplates the intermediate state (antarābhava), wherein, due to the arising of craving and attachment toward the parents, the four great elements (mahābhūta) coalesce by the condition of that craving; the two drops of semen and blood merge into one drop, the size of a bean, which is called the kalala.
This *kalala* possesses three things:
first, life; second, consciousness; and third, warmth.
These are the karmic conditions and retributive fruits from past lives, wherein there is no agent nor recipient; the initial inhalation and exhalation of breath is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
At the stage of *kalala*, the inhalation and exhalation of breath proceed through two pathways:
namely, following the upward and downward movement of the mother’s breath, changing once every seven days.
This coming and going of the breath is called "vitality" (*āyus*), and it is termed the "pathway of wind" (*vāyu-mārga*).
That which is neither putrid nor rotten is called "warmth" (uṣman);
that which is the mental faculty therein is called "consciousness" (vijñāna). "Good son!

If there are those who wish to attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, they should contemplate these twelve links of dependent origination, and subsequently contemplate the causes and conditions of the three types of sensation:
the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
What is contemplation?

Following the mindful mind, one contemplates the exhalation and inhalation of the breath, and contemplates the internal body—its skin, muscles, tendons, bones, marrow, and brain—as being like clouds in the sky.

The winds within this body are likewise thus: there are winds that can move upward, winds that can move downward, winds that can fill [the body], winds that can cause emaciation, and those that can cause growth; therefore, the inhalation and exhalation of breath are called bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*).
Because these inhalations and exhalations arise from applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), they are called mental formations (*manas-saṃskāra*).
When combined with the production of sound, they are called vocal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*).
Due to these three types of causal conditions, consciousness arises.
Because of consciousness as a condition, there are the four aggregates and the aggregate of form; therefore, this is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
The six sense bases arise from the causal conditions of the five aggregates; therefore, they are called the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Because the faculties and their objects encounter one another, it is called "contact" (*sparśa*).
Due to the condition of contact, there arises mindfulness of forms up to mindfulness of mental phenomena; this is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).
Clinging attachment to forms, and so forth, up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because of the condition of craving, one seeks and pursues in the four directions; therefore, it is called grasping (*upādāna*).
Because of the condition of grasping, one undergoes a future body; therefore, it is called becoming (*bhava*).
Due to causes and conditions, there arise birth, old age, death, and all manner of sufferings.
These are called the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements—the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination.

"Therefore, conditioned by inhalation and exhalation, all suffering and afflictions are produced. For this reason, when ordinary persons are born, they are bound by afflictions, and it is the same at the time of death;
ultimately, they cannot attain mastery over body and mind, nor do they attain samādhi, nor do they exhaust the outflows."

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates inhalation and exhalation as being like the wind in space—devoid of self or what belongs to a self, devoid of an agent or an experiencer, arising from conditions and ceasing from conditions, signless, insubstantial, and free from vitarka and vicāra—he sees that the "wind" of sentient beings is likewise.

It moves together with the four great elements, entering and exiting through the nine apertures and even the ninety-nine thousand pores from the stage of the *kalala*. This wind enters and exits such a mass of flesh without action or experience; by these causes and conditions, there arises the accumulation of all sufferings, from ignorance up to old age and death.

“Good son! Just as space is devoid of substance and devoid of self, so too are the inhalations and exhalations, earth, water, fire, and wind, life-span, warmth, and consciousness, as well as ignorance up to birth, old age, sickness, and death. It is likewise.”

Sentient beings are subject to perversion; they falsely perceive a self within that which is not-self, and regarding such dharmas as are equal to space, they form conceptions of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Due to this perversion, all ordinary worldlings revolve through birth and death without end.

If a practitioner of the Dharma contemplates this breath as cool, his entire body becomes cool; if he contemplates this breath as warm, his entire body becomes warm; at that time, this body follows his will and follows the wind.
If, when contemplating cold, one does not attain meditative concentration and does not enter the stage of certainty, such a person will fall into the Cold Hell.
If, when contemplating warmth, one does not attain meditative concentration and does not enter the stage of certainty, such a person will fall into the Hot Hell.
If a disciple of the Buddha cultivates the practice of the Dharma and observes the inhalation and exhalation, such as its coolness or warmth, they will attain the Right Path.

When a bhikṣu practicing the Dharma observes, according to reality, everything from ignorance up to birth, old age, sickness, and death, with a mind free from inversion, this is called the Dhāraṇī of the Pure Eye.
“Good son! If you can receive this dhāraṇī, it is itself the true contemplation of the inhalation and exhalation.
Bodhisattva Ratnaketu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable; it is not something that can be reached by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Wherever this sutra may circulate, we shall certainly attend upon and protect it, ensuring that all evil matters are completely extinguished.”

4. Chapter on the Four Immeasurable Minds. From the *Gaganagañja-parivarta* of the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Four Immeasurable Minds. At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others practice the Dharma, Jambudvīpa is free from epidemics, famine, and calamities. World-Honored One,
if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the four immeasurable minds and is honored and respected by those of the four castes, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, the land in which they dwell will be endowed with eight superior qualities:

first, the people of that land will support their parents, increase in a sense of shame and remorse, revere śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, and those of virtuous merit, and uphold the prohibitive precepts."
"Great King!
If there are bodhisattvas in various lands who cultivate the four immeasurables, the people of those lands will be able to accomplish this first matter."
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever land he dwells, the people of that realm will cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness, remaining far removed from killing. Their minds will be harmonious and supple, free from turbidity and from thoughts of anger, being impartial and non-dual; this is called the second.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever land he dwells, the people of that realm will not covet wealth and treasures, will delight in practicing generosity, and will censure theft; this is called the third.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, in whatever land he dwells, the people of that realm will be naturally satisfied with their own spouses, remain far removed from unlawful conduct, and censure lustful thoughts; these are called the four.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever country he dwells, the people of that land will speak words of truth, words of reality, and words free from divisiveness, and they will constantly practice virtuous speech; this is called the fifth.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever land he dwells, the people of that realm will be free from the turbid and evil mind of envy; this is called the sixth.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever country he dwells, the people of that land will possess right view without error and be free from false views; this is called the seventh.
Furthermore, Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then in whatever country he dwells, the people of that land will all offer worship and respect to the Triple Gem and remain far removed from wrong views; this is called the eighth.
"Great King!
If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, then in whatever land they dwell, the people of that realm will be endowed with these eight kinds of merit."
“Great King! If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, in whatever land they dwell, that realm shall be free from the eight kinds of fearful things.
What are these eight?
First, there is no fear of internal or external armies;
second, there is no fear of various evil spirits;
third, there is no fear of malevolent stars and constellations.
Fourth, they have no fear of various malignant diseases;
fifth, they have no fear of various fierce beasts;
sixth, they have no fear of various wicked bandits.
Seventh, there will be no fear of drought or flood;
eighth, there will be no fear of crop failure. Great King!
If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, in whatever land they dwell, that realm shall be free from these eight fears.
“Great King! If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, in whatever land they dwell, that realm will be fully endowed with the eight qualities of a great man.”
What are these eight?
First, there are sentient beings who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, have deeply planted roots of goodness; such persons delight in being born in that land.
Second, there are also sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable past lives, have cultivated precepts and extensive learning; such persons delight in being born in that land.

Third, there are further sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable past lives, have made offerings to their parents, teachers, preceptors, elders, and those of virtuous character; such persons delight in being born in that land.

Fourth, there are also sentient beings who, having already accomplished the karma for rebirth as devas throughout immeasurable past lives and being destined to receive a celestial body, instead transform that celestial body to be born in that land.
Fifth, there are sentient beings who are able to destroy all karma leading to the three evil realms; such persons delight in being born in that land.
Sixth, there are sentient beings who possess the Śrāvaka vehicle; such persons delight in being born in that land.
Seventh, there are further sentient beings who delight in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; such persons come to be born in that land.
Eighth, there are further sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable past lives, have cultivated the six pāramitās; such persons delight in being born in that land.
"Great King!
If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, in whatever land they dwell, that realm will be fully endowed with these eight kinds of persons. Great King!"

If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the four immeasurables, in whatever land they dwell, that ground will be endowed with the supreme taste of the earth and water, the unsurpassed taste of the Dharma, and the taste of sentient beings; all sentient beings will feel mutual affection in their hearts, and after such beings relinquish this body, they will be reborn in the heavens, and even birds and beasts shall be likewise.
"Great King!
It is like a basket containing four kinds of incense:
the first is aloeswood;..."
Second, tagara; third, gośīrṣa-candana;
fourth, tamāla-leaf; these four types of incense together weigh four liang.

There were people of the four castes who placed four kinds of garments inside a basket; after several days had passed, each took their own garment away, yet the weight of the four fragrances did not diminish by even a single *zhu* or *liang*, and yet each of those garments was individually permeated with fragrance.
"Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four immeasurables, then according to the land in which he dwells, the people of that realm will each accomplish various kinds of merit, yet this will not cause any diminution to the bodhisattva."
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ cultivation of the four immeasurable minds is inconceivable.”
"Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through his own cultivation and accumulation, is able to bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Pure Light (Vimalaprabha) who addressed the Bodhisattva Invincible (Ajita), saying:
“Good son! You have now attained unsurpassed benefit. Why is this?
"You should constantly cultivate and accumulate the four immeasurable minds.
The Bodhisattva Anabhibhū said,
"O son of good family!..."
"How may I now obtain great benefit?
Within such a Dharma, there is no agent and no recipient; there is no perception, no view, and no cognition; there is neither 'this' nor 'that'."
Good son! It is like a person who says of themselves, "I can paint ornaments and decorations upon empty space.
Although they speak these words, in reality they cannot do so.

All phenomena are likewise thus: they neither emerge nor perish, neither arise nor cease; they have no location, no applied thought or sustained reflection, and are pure through the three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action.

Such is the dharma-realm: without transition or dispersion, without conjunction or obstruction, without turbidity or limit; it is like space, without combination, without desire, without intrinsic nature, without visibility, and without description.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is incalculable; it is neither small nor large, possesses no objective sphere, is non-dual and unattached, immeasurable and formless, soundless and tranquil, unchanging and infinite, just like empty space.

Peerless and unsurpassed, neither permanent nor annihilated, difficult to see and difficult to know, difficult to conceive, firm and without activity, free from anger, and encompassing all Buddha-realms—this is called the holy life (brahmacarya) and is termed the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni).

The Tathāgata’s cultivation and accumulation [of merit] is never weary or satisfied; he practices with diligent vigor—this is called the Buddha-dharma: great faith, great mindfulness, and great heedfulness, never forgetting with a sincere heart.
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates these four immeasurable minds, this is precisely the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound dharma-realm of a bodhisattva.

Such a bodhisattva is about to draw near to entering the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); practicing the six pāramitās, they protect all Buddha-dharmas and have already drawn near to the third patience that accords with the Dharma, truly beholding the body of the Buddha."

They are able to crush the hosts of Māras and destroy false paths; they cross the river of birth and death to enter the great ocean of wisdom, attain mastery over the realms of all Buddhas, and become fully endowed with the adornments of all Buddha-merits.

Possessing all forms of lineage and wealth that surpass those of all sentient beings, they shall successively sit upon the Tathāgata’s Dharma-seat, become fully endowed with all samādhis and dhāraṇīs, and never be disparaged by any of the noble ones.
They are praised by all pratyekabuddhas, are constantly protected and remembered by all buddhas, and are able to understand the various languages of sentient beings in all lands.
Among all phenomena, one does not perceive a recipient or a donor, nor a speaker or a listener of the Dharma; there is no agent or recipient, just like empty space.
Vimalaprabha said, "Noble son! For this reason,
I say that you have now accomplished immeasurable merit."
Why is this? Because it has been diligently cultivated and accumulated throughout immeasurable and boundless eons. Good son!

If a Buddha attains the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the Buddha-dharmas; renounces the world, practices asceticism, achieves perfect enlightenment, turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma, displays great supernormal powers, and enters great parinirvāṇa—all such matters arise entirely from the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds. Thus, these are the fruits of the four immeasurables.
"For this reason, sons and daughters of good family should cultivate and accumulate the four immeasurable minds.

When this Dharma was spoken, twenty thousand sentient beings attained the patience that accords with loving-kindness, immeasurable sentient beings were endowed with the four immeasurable minds, and the entire great assembly made offerings to the Buddha.

Chapter Five: The Chapter on Pure Eyes From the *Ākāśagarbha-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the Fifth Chapter: The Chapter on Pure Eyes. At that time, there was a bodhisattva youth named Ajitamatī who knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
What are the characteristics of the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness?
What is its essence?
What are its causes and conditions?
"What is the retribution?
How is it fulfilled?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are able to inquire about such a profound meaning.”
At that time, the Tathāgata entered a samādhi called "Taming Sentient Beings Without Fear.

Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance from his *uṣṇīṣa*. This light was fierce and magnificent, possessing various colors, and it illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds. Furthermore, a wondrous sound issued forth, speaking these verses:
"From within the mud grow water lilies, And likewise, various other flowers arise."
Sentient beings use these to make offerings to the Buddhas, as well as to all the various celestial deities.

All evil lands are likewise so; they give birth to sages and great Bodhisattvas who can discipline those difficult to discipline and those not yet disciplined, just like sentient beings making offerings with flowers.
The Sahā world is a land of evil; Śākyamuni dwells therein and proclaims the Dharma.
If you wish to obtain immeasurable benefit, you should go to that Sahā world.
When all sentient beings throughout immeasurable worlds heard these verses, each made offerings to the World-Honored One of their own land.
Having made these offerings, they all gathered together in the Sahā world by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, this great jeweled monastery was completely filled with immeasurable sentient beings. Each of these beings thought to themselves:
"I alone have come here to make offerings to the Tathāgata; I alone am in the presence of the Buddha to inquire about the True Dharma; the Tathāgata is speaking solely for me alone."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Anābhāsabuddhi:
"Good son! There are three kinds of loving-kindness (maitrī):"
First, the object of sentient beings;
second, the object of dharmas;
third, the objectless.

“Good son! Those who take sentient beings as their object of focus focus upon the five realms of existence. If there is a Bodhisattva practicing the Dharma who wishes to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, the great kindness and great compassion, and the ten stages of a Bodhisattva; who wishes to swiftly attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, subdue immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, cause them to cross the great river of birth and death, and destroy the hosts of immeasurable evil Māras to enter Great Nirvāṇa—[this is the practice of focusing on sentient beings].”
In this way, a bodhisattva should cultivate and accumulate the four immeasurable minds.
How should they be cultivated?

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and accumulates this loving-kindness for all sentient beings from the nadir up to the zenith, they regard all sentient beings as their father and mother, as their teacher and preceptor, and as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, one should reflect in this way:
"If there are sentient beings who recklessly commit various evil acts against me,
the Bodhisattva at that moment should form this thought:"
"If I were to harbor anger toward these evil sentient beings, I would be seen by the Buddhas of the ten directions, which would be deeply shameful.
I would surely be rebuked:
'How can this person, having set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, fail to subdue his own mind?'"

It is, for example, like a person who, being without feet, desires to travel to the land of Uttarakuru; or like one who, being without eyes, desires to read books; or like one who, being without hands, desires to perform manual labor. It is exactly the same for one who, being devoid of a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*), desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one cannot sever such a mind of anger, one will not even attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, let alone anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If I cannot subdue my own mind, I shall be rebuked by all the Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings.

If I cannot subdue my own mind, I shall incur great transgressions and undergo the sufferings of hell, failing to attain benefit in the present or the future; therefore, one should cultivate and accumulate a heart of loving-kindness.

Again, he reflects: "If anyone has done evil toward me, or is beginning to do so, or intends to do so; or if they have used harmful things against my relatives, or have benefited my enemies with matters of gain and sustenance—it shall be the same for them."

Having contemplated in this manner, the Bodhisattva first cultivates and accumulates a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings in one direction; he does the same for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s compassion that takes sentient beings as its object.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Morning Star, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, what kind of fruit does such a mind of loving-kindness have?
Is it in the present, or is it in the future? How much merit is fully accomplished?”
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva thus cultivates and accumulates a mind of loving-kindness, could they ever again fall into the three evil realms?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have already made offerings to and honored immeasurable Buddhas in the past; therefore, you are now able to pose such a question."

Having already planted the seeds of goodness, their roots of merit are firm; having cultivated and accumulated a mind of loving-kindness throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they do not share this with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but do so for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings. For these reasons, they are now able to pose such a question.
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.”

If there is a bodhisattva who can cultivate loving-kindness as I have previously taught, that person will obtain peace in sleep and peace upon waking, shall not see evil dreams, and will lack nothing among the necessities of life.

Guarded by the devas, they are a joy for gods and humans to behold; they do not hear evil sounds, nor do their bodies suffer from malignant diseases. They always delight in tranquility and practice with diligent vigor, taking pleasure in receiving the True Dharma. Having realized and seen non-self, they are constantly honored and supported by national rulers, śramaṇas, brahmins, men and women, the old and the young, and even by birds and beasts. They draw near to virtuous friends—namely, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas and bodhisattvas—and they delight in practicing generosity to deliver sentient beings.
All virtuous minds are not destroyed by the three poisons; their good names and excellent reputations spread in all four directions.

They can heal all the malignant diseases of sentient beings, enable sentient beings to distance themselves from all sufferings, and untie all the fetters of sentient beings. They can subdue the various evil afflictions of sentient beings, destroy all evil, heterodox, and divergent views, and bestow upon sentient beings the mind of faith and the mind of mindfulness.

With a mind of great wisdom, this mind abides in the Mahāyāna and cannot be shaken; it does not follow the words of others, and it can destroy the evils of body, speech, and mind in sentient beings. It can extinguish the three kinds of obstructive karma of sentient beings, with the sole exception of those who commit the five heinous crimes, those who slander the True Dharma and the worthy sages, and those who plunder the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters.

"Good son! If a bodhisattva can cultivate loving-kindness in this way, at the time of death, he will see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions with their own hands stroking his head. Because the Buddhas' hands touch him, his heart becomes joyful; because his heart is joyful, he immediately attains rebirth in those Buddha-lands and hears these excellent and wondrous words:
'Do not give rise to fear; do not give rise to fear.'"

"You are a person of pure goodness who cultivates loving-kindness; you shall certainly be reborn in a pure Buddha-world, where you will behold immeasurable Buddhas and World-Honored Ones. You will leave the three evil realms and surely enter Nirvana; you will also hear of the compassion based on dharmas and the compassion without object, and you will fully possess the four immeasurable minds, even attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, when the Devaputra Tārakā heard this Dharma, he attained mastery in entering and emerging from all meditative concentrations.
The youth Anuttarāśaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“By what power, O devaputra, do you thus enter and emerge so swiftly from meditative concentration?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

This devaputra has planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Tathāgatas; having cultivated the dharma-contemplating loving-kindness throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he was born in the realm of the Four Great Kings by the power of his original vow.

Ten thousand yojanas before the Sun Deity, there is a palace where he dwells, thirty-two thousand yojanas in length and breadth, composed of lapis lazuli, extending ten yojanas in front, behind, and to the left and right.

Surrounded by gods and goddesses, this person sits alone upon a jeweled couch within that space, three yojanas distant from their retinue, entering and emerging from meditative concentration for a day and a night.

In these four continents, there are eighty celestial abodes, sixty nāga abodes, four asura abodes, four garuḍa abodes, fifty-two kiṃnara abodes, forty-six mahoraga abodes, eight kumbhāṇḍa abodes, thirty preta abodes, and thirty piśāca abodes.
In such places, he is able to discipline such sentient beings by the power of his original vows.

In the past, he made this vow: "When five-fifths of the night have passed and one-fifth remains in this Jambudvīpa, I shall appear ten thousand yojanas before the sun; first, I shall destroy the darkness of Jambudvīpa and manifest the sign of light."

If there are virtuous sentient beings in Jambudvīpa who wish to cross over birth and death by practicing meditative concentration, I shall remove their sleepiness and bestow upon them the power of mindfulness for their sake.
If you wish to see me, I shall appear in your dreams as your preceptor, teacher, father, or mother.
If there are ordinary persons who cultivate the ways of external paths, I shall destroy their deviant minds and show them the right path.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to indolence regarding worldly or world-transcending matters, upon seeing me, they will cast off their indolence and diligently cultivate their tasks.
If there are sentient beings who have lost their way on the correct path, upon seeing me they shall regain their vision of the Way.

If there are sentient beings whose bodies are afflicted by serious illness, those who see me will find their suffering and pain stilled; their bodies will attain peaceful sleep and experience great happiness.

If there are elderly people whose bodies endure manifold sufferings and whose minds are prone to many lapses of memory, upon seeing me they shall regain their mindfulness; furthermore, when I appear, I am able to cause sentient beings to fix their minds on the recollection of what is wholesome.

If there are sentient beings whose lives are about to end, at their final moment of thought, I shall expound for them the Mahāyāna sūtras; having heard them, they shall behold the Buddha’s image face-to-face and, upon casting off this body, attain rebirth in a pure buddha-world.
If there are those who seek to become pratyekabuddhas, I shall expound for them the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
If there are those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, I shall likewise expound for them the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
If there are sentient beings who possess the three evil karmas, upon hearing my preaching of the Dharma, their evil karmas will be immediately extinguished.
World-Honored One!

I shall first travel through the land of Jambudvīpa, and after that, I shall next travel through Aparagoyānī; after Aparagoyānī, I shall next go to Uttarakuru; and after Uttarakuru, I shall next go to Pūrvavideha.
By the power of such original vows as these, they constantly practice the six pāramitās, until finally attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Devaputra Tārakā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall now proclaim this dhāraṇī.”

If these people do not achieve such matters as these, I would then be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions, and may I never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in future ages.
At that time, the youth Anuttaracitta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The people in all the buddha-fields of other directions constantly say this:”

Furthermore, the bodhisattvas of this world may manifest in the form of devas to discipline sentient beings; or they may manifest in the form of nāgas, or pretas, or asuras, or garuḍas, or kiṃnaras, or mahoragas, or yakṣas, or kumbhāṇḍas, or piśācas, or pūtanas, or humans, or animals, or the forms of birds and beasts, as they travel throughout Jambudvīpa to teach and transform such various classes of beings.

“Good son! Outside Jambudvīpa, in the southern ocean, there is a mountain of lapis lazuli called Tide.

“Good son! Outside Jambudvīpa, in the western ocean, there is a crystal mountain twenty yojanas high. This was also a dwelling place of a bodhisattva in the past, where a monkey cultivated the compassion of a śrāvaka.”

Furthermore, there is another cave named Vow, equal in length, breadth, height, and depth; it was also a place where the Bodhisattva dwelt in the past, and within it lived a hen who cultivated the compassion of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there is another cave named Dharma-Bed, whose length, breadth, height, and depth are likewise the same; it was also a place where a bodhisattva formerly resided, and within it dwells a dog that cultivates the compassion of a śrāvaka.

Within it there is a fire deity and a rākṣasī named Akṣidṛś (Eye-Witness), each surrounded by five hundred attendants; these two women constantly together make offerings to these three birds and beasts.

“Good son! Outside Jambudvīpa, in the northern ocean, there is a silver mountain named Bodhichandra, twenty yojanas in height. Within it is a cave called Vajra, equal in length, breadth, and height; this was also the dwelling place of a bodhisattva in the past, where a pig cultivated the compassion of a śrāvaka.”

Furthermore, there is another cave named Fragrant Merit, equal in length, breadth, height, and depth to the former; it was also a place where a bodhisattva dwelt in the past, and within it lived a mouse that practiced the compassion of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there is another cave named High Merit, equal in length, breadth, and height; it was also a place where a bodhisattva formerly dwelt, and within it lived an ox that cultivated the compassion of a śrāvaka.

On the mountain there was a wind deity named Vāyu-vikṣepa and a rākṣasī named Devaguptā, each surrounded by five hundred attendants; these two women constantly made offerings together to these three beasts.

“Good son! Outside Jambudvīpa, in the eastern ocean, there is a golden mountain named Guṇalakṣaṇa, twenty yojanas in height. Within it is a cave called Tārakā, equal in length, breadth, and height. This was also a place where a bodhisattva formerly dwelt; there lived a lion who cultivated the compassion of a śrāvaka.”

Furthermore, there was another cave named Pure Path (*viśuddhamārga*), equal in length, breadth, height, and depth; it was also a place where a bodhisattva had formerly dwelt, and within it lived a rabbit who practiced the compassion of a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there is another cave named Joy and Bliss, equal in length, breadth, height, and depth; it was also a dwelling place of the Bodhisattva in the past, where a nāga within it cultivates the compassion of a śrāvaka.

In the mountain there was a water spirit named Varuṇa and a rākṣasī named Hrīvyapatrāpinī, each surrounded by five hundred attendants; these two women constantly made offerings together to these three beasts.

"These twelve animals constantly travel within Jambudvīpa day and night; revered by devas and humans, they have accomplished meritorious virtues and have made profound and solemn vows in the presence of all Buddhas."
Day and night, one beast is always sent forth to travel and teach, while the remaining eleven beasts remain settled in the cultivation of loving-kindness; this cycle repeats itself.

On the first day of the seventh month, the rat begins its travels, teaching all sentient beings with rat-bodies by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna, causing them to abandon evil karma and encouraging them to practice virtuous deeds.
In this manner, proceeding sequentially until the thirteenth day, the mouse again began its journey, continuing in this way until the end of the twelfth month.
This continued for twelve years, always for the sake of taming and transforming all sentient beings.

“Good son! For this reason, this land possesses many merits; it can even transform and teach animals, expounding upon the path to unsurpassed bodhi. Therefore, the bodhisattvas of other directions should always pay respectful homage to this Buddha-world.”
At that time, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) in the assembly named Śuddhaguṇa who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
May I now behold these twelve animals?"

“Good son! If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who wish to behold these twelve animals; who wish to attain great wisdom, great mindfulness, great concentration, and great supernormal powers; who wish to receive all the scriptural collections and the four immeasurable minds; who wish to practice the right path and attain śamatha; who wish to attain tranquility and increase wholesome dharmas—such a person should fashion a mountain out of white clay, seven feet in length and breadth and twelve feet in height, anointing it with various fragrances and coating it with gold leaf. It should be twenty feet in circumference on all four sides. The *campaka* flowers to be scattered should be placed in a copper vessel, and various kinds of non-seasonal juices should be set at the four corners. Being pure and observant of the precepts, they should bathe three times a day and maintain reverent faith in the Triple Gem.”
Standing three *zhang* directly east of the mountain,
recite this mantra: "Candāroha svasti-sarpima."

"Dwelling for fifteen days, one shall see the image of the first moon upon the mountain."
At that time, one will know and see the twelve animals; having seen them, whatever one wishes for shall be obtained according to one's desire. Good son!
If one can practice such asceticism, one will immediately obtain the vision of these twelve animals with one’s own eyes.
At that time, the upāsaka Viśuddhaguṇa said to the bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna:
"Noble son! You are able to teach and discipline sentient beings."
How is one disciplined? Is it by means of the body,
the speech, or the mind?
“Good son! It is not by means of body or speech, but solely through mental karma.
“Good son! [he continued.]
If this is mental karma, is it past, future, or present?
“Good son! It is neither past nor future; it is solely the present. One restrains the present mind so that it does not commit evil.
“Good son! [he continued.]
"If you are still unable to bring about the liberation of the present mind,
how can you possibly subdue sentient beings?
The Morning Star replied:
"I shall now, by the power of upholding the Pure Eye Dhāraṇī of the Four Unhindered Knowledges, be able to subdue all sentient beings.
Viśuddhaguṇa said, "Even the Pure Eye Dhāraṇī of the Four Unhindered Knowledges cannot subdue sentient beings."
"Why is this? Because there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, how can you say that they are able to discipline sentient beings? "Good son!..."
I now ask you; answer according to your understanding.
Noble son! The inclusion within, the binding, liberation, the path of purity, and tranquility—though they are equal, they are also not equal.
Thus, from what causes and conditions do equality and inequality arise?
From what causes and conditions do they emerge?
And from what causes and conditions do they increase?
"Do you not know? Netde replied, "O noble son!"
"Such matters as these arise from and increase due to 'I' and 'mine.
The Bodhisattva Morning Star said: "Good son!
“What causes and conditions give rise to this ‘I’ and ‘mine’?
“Good son! This ‘I’ and ‘mine’ arise with wind as their cause and condition.”
The Bodhisattva Starlight said:
"Where does the wind abide?
[The Buddha replied: "Good son!
"The wind abides in space.
He asked again:
"In what does space abide?"
He replied, "Space abides in the ultimate destination.
He asked again:
"Once it has reached its destination, where does it abide?
He replied, "As for where that which has reached its destination abides, it cannot be described."
Why is this? Because it is far removed from all locations, not encompassed by any location, and because it is neither numerable, nor nameable, nor measurable.

It is neither vitarka nor vicāra; neither existent nor non-existent; neither activity nor birth; neither emergence nor cessation; neither increase nor growth; neither syllable nor thought; neither agent nor recipient; neither darkness nor light; neither increase nor decrease; neither vigor nor old age. This true nature is the gate of non-obstruction for all dharmas; therefore, wherever it reaches, there is no place of abiding.
The Bodhisattva Morning Star said:
"Good son! This is precisely the Pure Eye Dhāraṇī of the Four Unhindered Knowledges."

If there are bodhisattvas who cultivate and collect such dhāraṇīs, all their afflictions will be rotted away; they will enter into the compassion that takes phenomena as its object, and they will have no doubt regarding any phenomenon.

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions attained the Dharma-conditioned compassion (*dharmapratyaya-maitrī*), and immeasurable sentient beings attained the *Netra-viśuddhi-dhāraṇī* that is proximate to the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised these two people, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family!"
They will be able to question according to the Dharma and answer according to the Dharma, by the power of the causal conditions of this dhāraṇī.
O Four Heavenly Kings and others!
After my parinirvāṇa, you shall be able to protect the Dharma.

Chapter Six: The Holy Eye; Subchapter Ten: The Division of the Empty-Space Eye. Part Three of Six. Chapter Six: The Holy Eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Morning Star addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A śrāvaka practices the Śrāvaka vehicle, and a pratyekabuddha practices the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; how do these two types of persons cultivate compassion?”
"What dharma does reflection produce?
From what afflictions is one liberated?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who practice the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they do not contemplate the marks of pleasure possessed by sentient beings, nor do they form notions of enemies, relatives, parents, and so forth. Out of compassion for sentient beings, they cultivate and give rise to a mind of pity, and this extends even to the ten directions in the same way.”

If I am unable to cultivate and accumulate compassion toward evil sentient beings, I should contemplate these eight aspects of suffering—from the suffering of birth to the suffering of death—that such persons possess; since they are fully endowed with these eight sufferings, how could I not give rise to a heart of compassion for them?
"These people further have three kinds of great suffering and have likewise not yet attained liberation from the three evil realms; how could I not give rise to compassion for them?
What is meant by 'contemplating the suffering of birth'?"

Due to the causal conditions of karma and the union of the parents, when the initial consciousness first enters and forms the *kalala*, its body is as small as a mustard seed; at that time, there is as yet no inhalation or exhalation of breath, nor does it perceive pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

Having departed from the characteristics of prior form and not yet possessing subsequent form, they lack power and lack desire; they possess no vigor, no pride, no superior form, no superior nature, and no characteristic of superior mastery; they lack the characteristics of the five desires, and their sense faculties are incomplete.
Regarding such sentient beings, how could I not give rise to compassion?

For these sentient beings, the grasping at past objects of affection is called ignorance (*avidyā*); past karma is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the consciousness that first enters the womb is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); and within the *kalala* stage, the initial form and the four aggregates are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
At that time, although the twelve links of existence have not yet been fully formed, because they arise through causes and conditions, one may speak of the existence of the twelve causal links.
Since sentient beings are thus, what wise person would not give rise to compassion?
During the kalala stage, it remains for six or seven days; after six or seven days, it changes its name to arbuda, at which time its shape and color are like those of a small jujube fruit.
After seven weeks, it changes its name to peśī, at which time its shape and color are like the shell of a walnut.
After remaining for eight weeks, it is renamed *peśī*; its shape is like that of a *bimbara* fruit. At this time, five protuberances emerge from the body, namely the head, hands, and feet.

In the twelfth week, the appearance of the intestines first arises; in the twentieth week, the male and female sexual organs become distinct; in the twenty-first week, the bone joints first form; and by the thirty-sixth week, the body is fully endowed with flesh, blood, and the roots of the hair; in the thirty-eighth week, the limbs and members of the body are complete.
For four days and four nights, he dwells within the foul and putrid place of the womb.
Seeing that such is the condition of this person, how could I not feel compassion for him?
At that time, he recalls the events of his former birth; having recalled them, he is filled with sorrow and distress, and thinks to himself:

"Once I have emerged from the womb, I shall cultivate wholesome dharmas; may I never again be born in such a place, and through the cultivation of heedfulness, may I remain far removed from further rebirth.
As he first emerges from the mother's womb, at that moment his entire body suffers the pain of compression, and as the winds enter and touch his body, he likewise experiences suffering.
When the body first touches the ground, it is washed with water, yet it undergoes great suffering as if in hell; at that time, one again loses the memory of past lives.
Once born, one is pursued and never abandoned by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, as well as by wind-related illnesses and diseases such as the combination of white and yellow phlegm.
These four types of illness, numbering one hundred and one each, constantly pursue it; therefore, it is called "birth" as a great suffering.
Once birth has been received, old age further pursues it: the hair turns white, the face wrinkles, wisdom and a sense of shame are lost, and the hair on the head and body becomes thin and sparse.

Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are aged, the sense faculties (*indriya*) decline and mature; they become easily broken and easily destroyed, rotten, decayed, precarious, and fragile. They crave only two flavors, namely saltiness and sourness. These can destroy the faculty of the body’s bliss and cause universal affliction;

they are a great river of suffering that can shatter the vigorous physical form of sentient beings across the three periods of time. [Such beings] are as deluded as infants and as frantic as those possessed by demons.
"Sentient beings are possessed of such evil conditions; how could I not give rise to compassion for them?

At that time, they are further assailed and oppressed by death, losing their wisdom, their life-span, and all states of existence; they abandon the aggregates, their bodies perish, their lives end, and the four great elements disperse."
"The lifespan of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is the enemy; all sentient beings are subject to the law of death. How could I not give rise to compassion?
At that time, there are further unpleasant things that come to approach one, namely: cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wicked people, and vicious beasts."
"Sentient beings are thus; how could I not give rise to compassion?

Furthermore, there is the suffering of separation from what is beloved, namely: the prime of youth, wealth and treasures, health and vigor, life span, parents, wife and children, kinsmen and relatives, and the exquisite objects of the six sense-fields."
"Since sentient beings undergo such sufferings as these, how could I not give rise to compassion?
There are some sentient beings who, throughout the three periods of time, seek the six superior sense-objects but are unable to obtain them; by reason of this, they undergo all manner of suffering."
"If I do not give rise to compassion for these sentient beings of evil nature, how shall I ever attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
All sentient beings carry the burden of the five aggregates, and I am likewise the same."
If I do not cultivate the mind of great compassion, how can I cast off such a heavy burden?

All noble ones have already attained liberation from the heavy burden of the five aggregates; yet if one does not practice the three kinds of pure precepts, engages in unwholesome reflection, allows the mind to be negligent, and fails to walk the right path, such a person will not attain liberation and shall undergo a hundred kinds of suffering.
"Since sentient beings undergo these hundreds of sufferings, how could I not cultivate a mind of compassion?

If there are sentient beings who, for even a single day and night, can contemplate in this way, such persons will attain a mind like space; such persons will be able to cultivate and accumulate great compassion toward all sentient beings; such persons will be able to attain tranquility of body and mind."
Such a person is not far from the true and ultimate dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Through such skillful means, they are able to attain the compassion directed toward sentient beings characteristic of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"If there is a bodhisattva who, when first cultivating the path, reflects thus:"

"Even if I were to possess bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each as large as Mount Sumeru, and were to use these bodies for the sake of a single person by undergoing great and intense suffering throughout immeasurable eons, so that this one person might obtain happiness, I would never regret it, nor would I ever turn back from the bodhicitta."
"Furthermore, he forms this thought:
'Even if all sentient beings were each to take up mallets as large as Mount Sumeru and strike my body for immeasurable years.'"
"I shall endure it and not give rise to an evil thought, even for a single moment. He further reflects:
"The hundred kinds of suffering this person undergoes are the same as those undergone by all sentient beings, yet they do not know to mind *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
I am now training for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; why then would I not accept [this suffering]?
Swords, fire, stones, and so forth are likewise [unavoidable].
If I were to give rise to an evil mind toward any living being, all Buddhas and worthy sages would see me and reproach me, saying:
"This person desires to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; why then do they not practice patience in such a manner?
"The cultivation of a pure mind by a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is itself patience."

Patience is itself an ornament, the nature of the path of diligence, and the vessel for the four treasures; when a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates such patience, they can purify body and mind, achieve pure adornment and firm adornment, and attain great wisdom not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

He is the most preeminent among all sentient beings; none of the four māras can find an opportunity against him, nor can evil sway him. His afflictions are diminished, no enemies can do him harm, and the words he speaks are inexhaustible.

“His wisdom is profoundly deep, like the great ocean; his diligence is firm and stable, like Mount Sumeru; he treats all sentient beings with equality, like the single flavor of the sea; he is able to provide great benefit, like the great earth; he purifies all defilements, like clear water; and he is able to produce radiance, like the bright sun.”

He is unimpeded among the multitude like a fierce wind; he is unsullied by worldly dharmas like a lotus flower; he looks down upon sentient beings like a garuḍa; he is a joy for sentient beings to behold like a summer cloud; and he is a joy for sentient beings to receive like summer rain.

Seeing him, one has no further need for seeking, like a sick person meeting a physician; he destroys all poverty, like a wish-fulfilling jewel; he bestows various meditative concentrations, like Brahmā; he is unimpeded in birth and death, like space; he reveals the level and the uneven, like a bright lamp; and he is revered by humans and devas, like Śakra.

"If there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of anger, all enemies and thieves will find an opportunity to exploit them; they will lose all the treasures of their roots of goodness, and all Māras will seize their vulnerability. They will be defiled by various afflictions, enter into great darkness and lose all roots of goodness, and be rebuked by all the holy ones."

If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of anger for even a single thought-moment, they shall lose all wholesome dharmas; therefore, even if I were to receive from all sentient beings immeasurable billions of beatings, revilings, and insults, I should not give rise to a single thought of anger.
Why is this? Such sentient beings do not practice loving-kindness and compassion.
If those sentient beings have no thoughts of anger or violence, how could I cultivate and accumulate loving-kindness and compassion?
For this reason, when sentient beings are angry, I should give rise to joy.
Why? Because that is precisely the causal condition for my own compassion.

If there are good men or good women who can perform this contemplation, they will immediately attain the uncommon great compassion directed toward sentient beings—which is distinct from that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and they will also swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having contemplated the suffering of sentient beings in the three evil realms, cultivate and accumulate a mind of compassion.
Moreover, there are those who observe all the suffering of sentient beings within the triple world and thereby cultivate a mind of compassion.”
Furthermore, there are those who observe the five aggregates of sentient beings and cultivate a mind of compassion;
it is the same when entering the [eighteen] elements. "Good son!
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion. Why is that?
Indeed, compassion is the seed of all wholesome dharmas.
If there are sentient beings who obtain a body in the realm of form, this is likewise due to the causes and conditions of having cultivated and accumulated compassion.

Whether it be the formless body, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the various bodhisattvas who adorn and stabilize their practice by cultivating the six pāramitās, taming sentient beings, attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all these are due to the causes and conditions of the seeds of compassion.

When this Dharma of the causes and conditions of compassion was being taught, the Bodhisattva Mingxing attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), a patience not shared by Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas;
eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the patience in accordance with the Dharma;
and fifty-five thousand nayutas of sentient beings resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One hundred and eight thousand sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind;
twenty thousand sentient beings accomplished compassion;
and five thousand bhikṣus realized the fruit of arhatship.
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs exhausted all outflows;
one hundred trillion sentient beings shattered their great false views and attained the mind of right view.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Anābhibhūcitta:
“Good son! In the past there was a Buddha named Utterance of the Mind of Merit, who also preached such great loving-kindness and great compassion.
The youth Anuttarāśaya said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding that which is called ‘suchness’ (tathatā), what is meant by ‘suchness’?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! To be free from the marks of the body is called ‘suchness’ (tathatā).
The youth Anuttaracitta said:
"What is called the body is itself true nature; it is itself tranquility; it is itself the dharma-realm; it is itself the untainted; it is itself the inexhaustible."
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which is the body is the very body of all sentient beings; it is the limit of the past and the future, and it is quiescence."
The youth Anābhibhū said:
“World-Honored One!
If the suchness of all Buddhas is itself the body.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

Thus, the dharma-realm is without increase or decrease; it is equal throughout the three periods of time, neither arising nor emerging, nor ceasing. It is like empty space, and the body is likewise so.
When this Dharma was being taught, thirty thousand sentient beings attained the patience that accords with reality (*dharmānusāri-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Tiṣya, saying: "Good son!
What is the cultivation and accumulation of joy conditioned by sentient beings? Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who does not cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, who does not contemplate the marks of happiness possessed by sentient beings, and who does not even observe the various sufferings within the three realms and the three evil destinies, yet nevertheless observes the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates.

Having observed in this way, a mind of joy arises; one observes only the Dharma with delight, and having observed it, joy is born. When such a joyful mind aspires for the sake of sentient beings, this is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
“World-Honored One!
How does one cultivate equanimity? “Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who does not cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), or sympathetic joy (*muditā*), but cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) by abandoning thoughts of parents, and even when cultivating this equanimity toward śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas, remains far removed from all states of mind characterized by attachment or aversion, that person is practicing and accumulating emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Once these have been cultivated and accumulated, one will before long certainly enter nirvana.

If a person cultivates and accumulates such four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), that person shall be honored by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

In whatever land the fourfold assembly cultivates and accumulates these four immeasurable minds, that land will already be far removed from all signs of decline and calamity; the sentient beings therein will delight in abandoning unwholesome dharmas and will uphold wholesome dharmas.
“Good son! The four immeasurable minds are endowed with such immeasurable merit.

Chapter Seven: The Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. From the *Gaganagañja-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Seven: The Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Again, the youth Anuttara-mati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How do bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and sons and daughters of good family who practice the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas cultivate and accumulate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?”
The Buddha said: “Good son!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, good men, or good women who cultivate and accumulate the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, they contemplate the happiness of sentient beings and understand the happiness of sentient beings. They maintain the *maitrī* (loving-kindness) that takes phenomena as its object, never recollecting the *maitrī* that takes sentient beings as its object. Just as they experience pleasant things within their own minds, they likewise vow that all sentient beings may share in them.”
One contemplates the equality of phenomena, the equality of pleasure, the equality of the mind, and the equality of suchness.
Having contemplated in this way, one does not give rise to even a single thought of ill will toward another person.
If there should be causes and conditions that give rise to an evil mind, one should reflect thus:
"If I harbor an evil mind toward them, how shall I ever attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has accomplished immeasurable and purely virtuous merits should give rise to a single thought of anger or malice toward another person, they would still be unable to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how much more so for me, who have not yet perfected these various virtuous merits?

For these reasons, one cultivates the loving-kindness toward sentient beings (*sattvārambaṇa-maitrī*) and the loving-kindness based on phenomena (*dharmārambaṇa-maitrī*); the same applies to the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"Good son! If there are those who wish to study the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, they should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity in this manner."
When this Dharma was being taught, sixty trillion sentient beings attained abiding in the first bhūmi, or attained the second, third, fourth, or fifth bhūmi;
some sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti);
and some attained the path of the pratyekabuddhas and the path of the śrāvakas.
Immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
