Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Noble Unimpeded Wisdom, from the "Section on the Eye of Space" within the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. At that time, there was a youth in the assembly named Gaganasvara who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How does a bodhisattva adorn the path to unsurpassed enlightenment?

By practicing the skillful means of the eye of all-knowledge and the unconditioned Brahma-conduct; the skillful means of the eye of all dharmas and the unconditioned Brahma-conduct; the skillful means of the aggregates, bases, and elements; the skillful means of liberation; the skillful means of samādhi; the skillful means of dhāraṇī; the skillful means of attaining patience; and the skillful means of the stages?
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate the gateway of the eye of omniscience, attaining the shore beyond through wisdom equal to space, practicing the unconditioned Brahma-conduct, crossing over the four floods, and severing the bonds of the four Māras?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"

You are now able to enter the ocean of the four immeasurables and wish to deliver sentient beings from the river of birth and death; for this reason, you have now posed such a question, desiring further not to sever the great ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.

“Good son! In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, if there are bodhisattvas who practice the samādhi and wisdom identical to yours, they shall all serve as clear witnesses when I preach the Dharma.”
If there were no such bodhisattvas who have realized this, I would not speak of the objectless holy life (*anālambana-brahmacarya*). Why is that?
If I were to speak of it, many would give rise to doubt regarding this matter, and those who have not yet attained the objectless holy life would likewise fall into doubt.
"For this reason, it should not be proclaimed.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called the "Space Banner. Having entered it, a great radiance issued from his face, its manifold light illuminating the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and eclipsing the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared.
From within that radiance, a great voice proclaimed:

“In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni proclaims the pure conduct for the sake of all sentient beings to destroy all afflictions; he teaches the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the unconditioned pure conduct.”
Immeasurable sentient beings and various bodhisattvas sat in succession to listen to and receive the True Dharma, and he also expounded upon the pure practices for awakening.

Desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, he convened this great assembly to explain various practices, whereby immeasurable sentient beings attained [the state of] being born only once more, or being born thereafter.
When the sentient beings of the ten directions heard these words, they all gathered in the Sahā world.

Some bodhisattvas manifested bodies of pure gold and rained down golden sand; some manifested bodies of silver and rained down silver sand; some manifested bodies of lapis lazuli and rained down lapis lazuli sand; some manifested bodies of crystal and rained down crystal sand; some manifested bodies of aloeswood and rained down aloeswood sand; some manifested bodies of sandalwood and rained down sandalwood sand; and some manifested bodies of tamālapatra and rained down tamālapatra sand, making offerings to the Buddha.
Having completed the offerings, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet in respectful salutation and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Gaganasvara: "Good son!

Today, among the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions, there are some who have attained the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), the patience of non-arising (anutpattikadharmakṣānti), or those who are in their last birth or one birth before liberation; they all bear witness for me that such a bodhisattva has cultivated and accumulated the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, has clearly and thoroughly penetrated the nature of all phenomena, and is also able to remain far removed from the signs of the body and the signs of karma.

Their mind does not cling to the conditioned or the unconditioned, nor do they crave or become attached to anything from the eye up to the mind, or from forms up to mental phenomena; with a sincere heart, they cultivate and accumulate the objectless holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Free from discursive thought and examination, they do not give rise to arrogance; being without attachment, they know the nature of reality and contemplate all phenomena as entirely equal.
That is to say, regarding the three times, the three realms, and the three precepts, they also attain the increase of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity.

All sentient beings are far removed from the aggregates, sense bases, and elements of the triple world, and are free from all conditioned phenomena consisting of collections of letters, names, and phrases.

When one contemplates in this way, one immediately attains the perfection of great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; one cultivates and accumulates the Brahma-conduct and the six pāramitās, which are identical to emptiness, and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.

Possessing skillful means, they abide in the third stage of patience, surpassing the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and remain far removed from all causal conditions of eye and form, up to and including all causal conditions of mind and mental objects.
Observing the dharma-realm as it truly is, they accord with reality without error and attain the powers of great loving-kindness and great compassion.

Attaining great mastery over all phenomena, they do not give rise to weariness or regret regarding birth and death; possessing great power, they subdue sentient beings. They attain wisdom and skillful means within the three vehicles, can rain down the rain of Dharma, and achieve unimpeded knowledge, understanding the various linguistic conventions of sentient beings.
“Good son! This is called the Āryamukha-dhāraṇī; it possesses unimpeded wisdom and is cultivated through the practice of the holy life. Good son!”

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates this Brahma-conduct, such a bodhisattva will constantly behold the Buddhas, be able to fulfill the Buddha-dharmas, and purify Buddha-worlds. Their nature is pure, their assembly is pure, their conduct is pure, their wisdom is pure, and their intention is pure; their offerings are also pure. They are able to fulfill the ten stages and shall successively sit upon the Tathāgata’s Dharma-seat. This is called the pure practice of the Dharma; this is called the Tathāgata; this is called the World-Honored One; this is called that which transcends the four tides; this is called the path to Bodhi, by which one is able to attain Bodhi and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
"What is called 'all-knowledge' (sarvajñatā)?
It is the wisdom that can contemplate all things as equal: the equality of sentient beings, the equality of the three periods of time, and the equality of non-inversion.
To see all such phenomena as having the eye of emptiness, and to see the emptiness of phenomena—this is it."

The Eye of Emptiness that perceives non-action; the Eye of Emptiness that perceives the nature of phenomena; the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as empty; the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as internally empty;
the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as externally empty; the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as both internally and externally empty;
the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as great emptiness; and the Eye of Emptiness that perceives as the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
The eye of space sees as the emptiness of the conditioned; the eye of space sees as the emptiness of the unconditioned;
the eye of space sees as the emptiness of ultimate reality; the eye of space sees as the emptiness of that which has no beginning;
the eye of space sees as the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the eye of space sees as the emptiness of dispersion; the eye of space sees as intrinsic nature.
The gate of the empty void sees all phenomena as the empty void; the gate of the empty void sees as there is nothing to be perceived;
the gate of the empty void sees as there are no phenomena; the gate of the empty void sees as there is no intrinsic nature;
the gate of the empty void sees as there is the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the gate of the empty void sees as the reality-nature.
The eye of emptiness sees as the signless and the wishless; the eye of emptiness sees as all phenomena are boundless and placeless;
the eye of emptiness sees as great loving-kindness and great compassion;
the eye of emptiness sees as all-knowing vision; [it] sees all-knowledge.
Having seen this, he turned the wheel of the true Dharma; this is called the dharma-realm not shared with ordinary beings, this is called omniscience, and this is called the realm of the Buddha.

When he spoke these words on the Brahma-conduct without objective conditions, ninety-two thousand sentient beings accomplished this Dharma, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the patience in accordance with reality (*dharmānulomikī kṣānti*), sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges became free from defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, one thousand bhikṣus attained the fruit of arhatship, and immeasurable humans and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Nine: Protecting the Dharma From the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the "Section on Ākāśagarbha," Chapter Nine: Protecting the Dharma. At that time, all the devas of the desire and form realms made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has previously turned the wheel of the true Dharma in Jambudvīpa; now he again turns the great wheel of Dharma here within this Great Jewel Monastery for the sake of the practice of bodhi.
The entire assembly spoke again, saying:
"The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable. Why is this?"

When the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma within this great jeweled pavilion, all bodhisattvas from the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions gather here to hear such practices of the Dharma-eye of space.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, the youth Vajraśikhara, the youth Aparājitadhvaja, the youth Aparājita-mati, the youth Gaganasvara, and ninety-two thousand billion such youths addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I only pray that by the power of your vows, O Tathāgata, you will cause this Dharma-practice of Akṣayamati to abide long within this Sahā world and throughout the lands of the ten directions, so that it never perishes or disappears.
Why is this? Within these dharmas, three brahma-practices are taught.
If a bodhisattva practices these three practices, they will immediately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said, “Good son!

In the world to the south is the Tathāgata Vajraprabhāguṇa; in the world to the west is the Tathāgata Jñānaketu; in the world to the north is the Tathāgata Prabhāsa-guṇa; and in the world to the east is the Tathāgata Ratnacchatraprabhāsa-guṇa. These four Tathāgatas previously made vows, and by virtue of those vows, this sutra shall later be disseminated throughout the ten directions, causing all bodhisattvas to fully attain the practice of these three modes of conduct.”

I now entrust this True Dharma to the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Goddess Guṇakārandavatī, the Four Great Nāga Kings, the Deva Satyavādin, the four Asura Kings, the Deva Viśvadeva, Maheśvara, the Eight-Armed Deva, the Earth Goddess, and others.
Why is this? Good son!

There may be sentient beings whose nature is wicked and who possess great power; having committed many grave karmas, they do not accept this sutra. After such persons die, they take birth in the bodies of evil ghosts or evil dragons. These evil ghosts and dragons seek to destroy the Buddha-dharma by sending down calamitous rain, fierce winds, and flying dust, causing severe illnesses for those bhikṣus who cultivate the three karmas.

Reaching into his abdomen with his hand, he extracts the heart and liver, blowing foul vapors into food and drink; consequently, those who consume it contract a grave illness that even a skilled physician stands with folded hands, unable to cure.
When bhikṣus who practice in this manner have completely cast off their lives, this is called the extinction of the Dharma.

Furthermore, such evil spirits will cause all the Tathāgata’s disciples—kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, ministers, and elders—to give rise to malicious intentions; once these malicious intentions have arisen, they will slaughter one another.
At that time, the lands and cities within Jambudvīpa will be desolate and devoid of people; since there will be no inhabitants, who shall propagate such a sutra as this?

Therefore, I do not now entrust this sutra to bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or various rulers of nations; rather, I entrust it to the four kings and even down to the earth deities.

Thus, these celestial deities will protect and uphold with a sincere heart. If there are kings—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—or bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive, uphold, read, and recite such a sutra as this, these celestial deities shall protect them with a sincere heart and exhort donors to provide offerings, namely: clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine for illness, dwellings, and lamps and candles. By the power of these deities, any ill omens or afflictions of various evil diseases and emaciation among those donors shall be entirely extinguished. Through these causes and conditions, the Dharma shall increase and flourish without decline or disappearance.
At that time, all the devas and other celestial beings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whether in the present or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall certainly set aside our own affairs to protect this Dharma.”

If there are disciples of the Buddha—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—who are able to receive and uphold sūtras such as these and practice with diligent perseverance, even if they should accept and keep the eight impure things, or maintain a wife and children, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, fields and houses, slaves, or servants—for the sake of the Dharma, I shall likewise protect them and ward off all evil spirits so that they do not harass or approach them.

Wherever this sutra may be located, it shall cause the sun, moon, and five planets of that land not to deviate from their regular courses, and all enmities and military conflicts shall be entirely extinguished and subdued.
All sentient beings—whether male or female, great or small—all delight in receiving and reciting such sutras as these, maintaining pure precepts and practicing with diligent perseverance.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, all the devas delight in being among humans.

Such a person, upon casting off this body, will immediately attain rebirth in the heavens; the physical strength, vitality, and lifespan of the devas will increase, and all their inauspicious signs will be extinguished without remainder. As for those who lack faith, I am able to cause them to believe.”

If there are disciples of the Buddha—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—who are unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe such sūtras; who do not delight in tranquility and do not engage in skillful reflection; who seek offerings while failing to maintain pure precepts; who are indolent, lazy, and arrogant; whose minds lack shame and remorse; and who associate with laypeople.

In this way, a bhikṣu who, by means of worldly wealth and power, harms a disciple of the Buddha—whether by beating, killing, binding, or reviling them—and reports their faults and evils to kings and ministers.

When the disciples of the Buddha heard of these matters, they gave rise to great malevolent thoughts; having given rise to such evil thoughts, the various benevolent spirits abandoned them and departed for other lands, whereby the malevolent ghosts immediately gained the opportunity.

Once they had gained such power, the various kingdoms raised armies to attack one another; they brought down calamitous winds and rains so that the crops failed to ripen, and the people, suffering from famine, devoured one another.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have established prohibitive precepts for the sake of such beings of the five corruptions. We only pray that the Tathāgata will further establish prohibitive precepts so that the Dharma may abide for a long time.”

This refers to the precepts of body, speech, and mind: one must not accept or keep any evil things, harbor an evil mind of contention, associate with kings, ministers, or elders, or accept or keep any items belonging to worldly people—just as the pure precepts are prescribed in other Buddha-fields.
The Buddha said: "Good son, stop, stop!
The Buddha knows the proper time himself.
O son of good family!
As long as the causes and conditions have not yet arisen, the Tathāgata does not preemptively establish prohibitive precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra:
"Great King! According to the laws of your kingdom, what is designated as a grave offense?"
"What is called a minor offense? Bimbisāra said,
"World-Honored One!"
In the laws of my country, there are four grave offenses:
first, taking the life of another;
second, stealing property worth five coins or more.
Third, committing adultery with another’s wife;
fourth, deliberately speaking falsehood before a great assembly or a king for the sake of five coins.
One who commits any of these four offenses shall not survive.
The Buddha said:
"I now likewise establish these four grave offenses for my future disciples.
Furthermore, Great King!"
"At what age, Prince, are you not permitted to enter the palace?
"World-Honored One,
once I have passed twenty years, I am not permitted to enter."
The Buddha said, "I am likewise;
a śrāmaṇera who has reached twenty years of age, yet has not attained the Way, is not permitted to enter the assembly.
The King said:
“World-Honored One!

According to the laws of my country, those who commit crimes must die; there is no doubt of this. Alternatively, they may be beaten, reviled, imprisoned, fined, or banished beyond the borders. What is the meaning of this within the Dharma of the Tathāgata?”
"Great King! It is likewise within my Dharma:

for those who have committed offenses, I may have them perform arduous labor for one month or two months; or I may not speak with them, nor sit or eat together with them, nor dwell with them; or I may banish them, expel them from a single kingdom, or expel them from four kingdoms."

In places where the Buddha-dharma exists, once such evil bhikṣus have been disciplined, the virtuous bhikṣus will dwell in peace and receive the Dharma; thus, the Buddha-dharma is made to endure for a long time without perishing.
"Great King!

If in future ages there are my disciples who possess abundant wealth and many treasures, who have great power and influence, and whom the king holds dear—such that the entire assembly is unable to expel or discipline them—you all must discipline such persons."

If those of the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes are unable to cure it, these four classes will sever the lineage of my Three Jewels, extinguish the torch of the Dharma, destroy the ship of the Dharma, parch the flavor of the Dharma, and rob sentient beings of their eyes; when my Dharma is ruined, they will abandon me with their hearts.
"Great King!
Suppose one person were to rob everyone of their eyes; what do you think?
Would that offense be great?"
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
It is beyond measure and beyond calculation. “Great King!”

If there are kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras who possess great power and influence, yet upon seeing my Dharma perish, they abandon it and fail to protect it, the transgression they incur shall likewise be such as this.
"Great King!

If there is a sovereign who, having cultivated generosity, morality, and wisdom for immeasurable eons, sees my Dharma perish and yet abandons it rather than protecting it, all the immeasurable roots of goodness he has planted will be utterly lost."
In that country, there shall be three inauspicious events:
first, the price of grain will be high;
second, there will be war and conflict.

Third, there shall be pestilence. All benevolent deities will utterly abandon him; his subjects will not obey his commands; he will be constantly harassed and oppressed by neighboring states; violent fires will break out unexpectedly with many calamitous winds and rains; floods will swell and sweep away the people; and those within and without whom he trusts will all conspire together to rebel.
Before long, that king shall encounter a grave illness; after his life ends, he will be reborn in hell.

If, through the pursuit of past roots of goodness, he should again obtain a human body, for immeasurable lifetimes he will always be blind and sightless, living a life of poverty and wandering about to beg for his sustenance.
They constantly give rise to evil thoughts, and because of these evil thoughts, they shall again fall back into hell.
It is the same for kings, queens, crown princes, great ministers, city governors, village chiefs, generals, provincial governors, and high officials.
Upon hearing these words, King Bimbisāra wept with choked sobs; wiping away his tears, he said:
"World-Honored One!

Even though I have encountered the Tathāgata, I am still unable to rule the kingdom according to the Dharma. How much more so for the heedless kings of future ages, who will be unable to maintain the precepts and practice with diligence, nor to govern evil bhikṣus and protect the Buddha-dharma, nor to continue the lineage of the Triple Gem?"
"Such kings as these shall constantly travel through the three evil realms for a long night.
At that time, the kings, queens, crown princes, great ministers, city lords, village heads, generals, provincial governors, and officials all addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In this present world, we shall diligently protect the Buddha-dharma with a devoted mind; we shall also provide offerings to those who receive and uphold the Dharma—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and we shall discipline wicked bhikṣus so as to ensure the continuity of the nature of the Triple Gem."
The Buddha said,

“Good sons! If you are able to establish this matter, you will thereby make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time and shall also attain immeasurable, inconceivable, and virtuous merits.”

Chapter Ten: The Return of the Great Assembly. From the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the "Section on the Eye of Space," Chapter Ten: The Return of the Great Assembly. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the various devas:
"O sons of good family!

"You all should now not harbor any anxiety or concern. For the sake of protecting the Dharma for my future disciples, I shall now establish strict regulations; for the sake of ensuring that the nature of the Three Jewels is never severed; for the desire to increase all wholesome dharmas; for the purpose of increasing learning and filling the treasury of jewels; for the sake of being free from all suffering and afflictions; and for the purpose of accomplishing the path to unsurpassed Bodhi."

“Good son! What I have now spoken is for all śrāvakas to fully accomplish and attain the Śrāvaka Vehicle; for all pratyekabuddhas to fully obtain the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; and for all bodhisattvas to fully perfect the three kinds of brahma-conduct and attain unsurpassed wisdom.”

"Good son! This sutra can cause all evil sentient beings to leave their ways behind; it can destroy the evil and unwholesome dharmas of sentient beings; it can extinguish unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind; and it can shatter all retributions of evil."
"If any good man or good woman makes offerings to this sutra, they shall thereby be making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, all sentient beings in the Sahā world spoke with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"World-Honored One!
Previously I had never heard of this great collection of Dharma; now I have been able to hear it.
World-Honored One!"
I am able to receive, uphold, and protect this Dharma; for the sake of protecting the Dharma, I shall not spare my own body or life.
If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive this sutra, I shall provide offerings for them and grant them everything they require.

Furthermore, if there are those who are able to make offerings to such a person who upholds this sutra, we shall also diligently protect them, ensuring that their internal and external wealth and treasures suffer no loss or depletion; wherever this Dharma of the sutra is disseminated, we shall also protect that land, ensuring it is free from all evils.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
If you are able to protect the Dharma in this way, you shall be making offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Good son!

If sentient beings possess a mind that protects the Dharma, whether they are born among humans or devas, they will attain great sovereignty; even if they are born as animals, they will possess great power, be held in high esteem by others, and not undergo the sufferings of cold or hardship.
"Good son! Against this protector of the Dharma, evil cannot prevail; his mind is fearless and nothing can destroy it.
The various māras and afflictions find no opportunity against him; he possesses numerous retinues and is fully endowed with wisdom."

Whatever they preach is free from all obstruction; they delight in practicing the ten wholesome paths and cultivate right concentration. When their parents and various kings see them, they treat them with reverence. They are able to ascend the Dharma-seat and turn the wheel of the true Dharma; whatever they hear, they never forget.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Four;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, Part One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was still dwelling in the Great Jewel Enclosure between the realms of desire and form, seated upon the lion throne.

He emits great radiance like the sun and moon; he attains great sovereignty like Brahmā and Śakra; his merit is loftily manifest like Mount Sumeru; and the Dharma-realm is profoundly deep like the great ocean.

Within the great assembly, he expounds the True Dharma, which is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; its words and meanings are authentic, and it fully and purely proclaims the holy life (*brahmacarya*). For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he purifies the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it, may practice and cultivate it.

At that time, ninety-two thousand Buddha-worlds away to the east, there was a world named Supuṣpa. In that land there was a Buddha, titled the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Viśuddhavāsa, who was proclaiming the True Dharma for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

There was a bodhisattva named Ratnaśikhin, accompanied by eight thousand other bodhisattvas, who vanished from that world and intended to come to this land. Carrying exquisite jewel canopies to present to the Tathāgata, those canopies completely covered a thousand worlds; they also brought various fragrant flowers to make offerings to the Buddha.
Ghoṣadatta spoke these verses in praise of the Tathāgata:
“If any among gods or humans are able to behold the Buddha, They shall obtain a great benefit;
The suffering endured by the Tathāgata was immeasurable, Yet through diligent application of effort, he attained Bodhi.”
In the past, you cultivated enlightenment through diligence, surpassing all other bodhisattvas;
for the sake of bringing benefit to sentient beings, you have turned the unsurpassed wheel of the true Dharma.
A Tathāgata such as this is difficult to encounter; the True Dharma he teaches is likewise difficult to hear.
To obtain a human body is also difficult, and to possess all faculties intact is similarly so.
If sentient beings practice unwholesome deeds And are unable to perform the three types of wholesome karma,
If a person desires to obtain great benefit, They should go to behold the Honored One among the Śākyas;
If they wish to hear and receive the unsurpassed Dharma, And also see the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Endowed with the thirty-two wondrous marks, you should swiftly proceed to the Great Jewel Monastery.
If you do not plant various roots of goodness now, you will certainly not attain Great Nirvana later.
If you wish to be fully endowed with a human body, you should swiftly proceed to the Sahā world.
If you wish to destroy the three evil realms, And desire to enjoy the subtle and wondrous pleasures of humans and devas;
To attain the unsurpassed and incomparable bliss, You should proceed to the Sahā world.
The Great Physician now bestows the flavor of ambrosia, eradicating all the afflictions of sentient beings;
the Tathāgata, the Caravan Leader and Great Dharma King, today proclaims the unsurpassed realm.
When the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin spoke these verses, their sound pervaded the great trichiliocosm.
At that time, having heard these verses, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“From where was this verse-sound proclaimed?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!”
To the east, beyond ninety-two thousand Buddha-worlds, there is a world named Good Flower; in that land, there is a Buddha named Pure Abode.

There is a bodhisattva there named Ratnaśikhin who has come here together with eight thousand bodhisattvas; this is what he speaks, and his voice reaches throughout the great trichiliocosm, exhorting all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, together with eight thousand bodhisattvas and immeasurable humans and devas, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Pure Abode of the World of Exquisite Flowers sends his respectful greetings, inquiring:
Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Is your physical strength secure?
Do your retinue and the great assembly joyfully receive the Dharma?
“World-Honored One! I have come from that world to this world to hear the *Dharmamudrā of the Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas*.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion for all beings, will analyze and explain it for us, so that all bodhisattvas, having heard it, may cultivate and accumulate it; destroy all afflictions and habitual tendencies while practicing the bodhisattva path; understand the minds of all sentient beings; be able to practice all the aspects of a bodhisattva’s conduct; attain the practice of liberating wisdom; know all practices related to afflictions; be able to cultivate the dharma-practices taught by bodhisattvas; deeply observe all transgressions; and attain unimpeded vision of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now speak of even one-tenth of such pure conduct.
"O son of good family!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four practices. What are these four?
First, the practice of the pāramitās;
Second, the practice of assisting toward enlightenment;
third, the practice of spiritual powers;
fourth, the practice of disciplining sentient beings.
The practitioner of the pāramitās employs the skillful means of aspiration;
the practitioner of the aids to enlightenment employs the skillful means of cultivating the path;
the practitioner of the supernormal powers employs the skillful means of disciplining the mind.
The skillful means for disciplining the mind is the skillful means for making the bodhicitta firm. "Good son,
what is called the dānapāramitā?"

The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is itself pure conduct; it can destroy the mind of delusion and cultivate the mind of equanimity (*upekṣācitta*). Having cultivated the mind of equanimity, one is able to practice universal giving.
If there is a bodhisattva who is able to practice universal giving, they will immediately attain four kinds of non-conceptual minds.
What are the four?
First, not discriminating among sentient beings;
second, not discriminating among phenomena;
Third, non-discriminating mind;
fourth, non-discriminating aspiration—these are called the four.

"One does not discriminate among sentient beings as to whether they are worthy or unworthy of receiving [gifts], whether one gives much or little to them, whether one gives to those of high or low status, whether one gives with respect or with contempt, whether one gives in full or in part, whether they are observant of the precepts or violators of the precepts, whether they are fields of merit or not fields of merit, whether they will obtain great retribution or not, or whether they possess right view or wrong view."
"This conduct is a right assembly; this conduct is a wrong assembly. Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains such a mind, it is called a non-discriminating mind, a mind free from pride, a mind free from superiority or inferiority, and a mind free from obstruction.

This is the mind of equanimity, the truly authentic mind; it practices giving and precepts with equanimity and compassion with equanimity, being without discrimination like empty space. This is called not discriminating among sentient beings.
"Regarding 'non-discriminatory dharmas,' a bodhisattva ultimately does not make such discriminations as: 'I shall teach those who receive [the teaching], but not those who do not receive it';
or 'I shall provide what is necessary to those who accept the Dharma, but not to those who do not accept the Dharma';
or 'I shall never consider that ordinary persons are unworthy of gifts while noble and saintly persons are worthy of giving. This is called non-discriminatory dharmas."
"One whose mind is non-discriminatory observes that the minds of all sentient beings are equal; they do not give for the sake of recompense.
They are free from internal and external craving; they do not give for the sake of reputation, nor do they give seeking a karmic fruit."
To give away beloved objects without regret, practicing generosity for the sake of gathering in sentient beings—this is called the non-discriminating mind. Regarding "non-discriminating aspiration":

when giving, one does not do so for the sake of attaining the body of Śakra, the body of a Brahmā-king, the body of a Cakravartin king, the body of Māra, or the body of a householder or great minister; nor does one do so for the sake of great sovereignty or a large retinue.

To practice giving not for the sake of higher rebirth, nor for the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor even for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called the vow of non-discrimination.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the giving of gifts, by fully accomplishing these four matters, they will be able to remain far removed from the eight improper views:
first, the view of a self;”
Second, the view of a sentient being;
third, the view of a life span;
fourth, the view of a person; and—
Fifth, the view of eternalism;
sixth, the view of nihilism;
seventh, the view of existence;
Eighth, the absence of views—this is called the eighth.
Furthermore, one attains the distancing from four kinds of merit:
first, the merit of ordinary persons;
Second, the merit of the śrāvakas;
third, the merit of the pratyekabuddhas;
fourth, the merit of residual habits.
Having given such gifts, one does not contemplate four marks:
first, the mark of permanence; second, the mark of pleasure; [third, the mark of self; fourth, the mark of purity].
Third, the mark of self;
fourth, the mark of purity. These are the four dharmas that can be purified:
First, purification of the body;
second, purification of speech;
third, purification of the mind.
Fourth is the purification of vows.
It involves distancing oneself from three obstructions:
first, the obstruction of karmic retribution; [and so forth].
2. the hindrance of the śrāvaka;
3. the hindrance of remorse. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva practices such giving, they remain far removed from three fears:
first, the fear of arrogance;
second, the fear of overweening pride.
Third is the fear of demonic activities.
When a bodhisattva practices such giving, they possess four seals:
first, the seal of internal emptiness;...
Second, the seal of external emptiness;
third, the seal of the emptiness of sentient beings;
fourth, the seal of the emptiness of bodhi.
When practicing giving in this manner, one possesses four kinds of diligence:
first, the perfection of diligence for the sake of fulfilling the needs of sentient beings;
second, the perfection of diligence for the sake of protecting the Buddha-dharma.
Third, one possesses perfect diligence for the sake of being endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
fourth, one possesses perfect diligence for the sake of purifying the Buddha-fields.
At that time, they further attained the fulfillment of four recollections:
first, the recollection of the bodhicitta;
second, the recollection of the desire to see the Buddha.
Third, the mind constantly dwells upon loving-kindness;
fourth, mindfulness of being free from afflictions.
When giving in this manner, one purifies three things:
First, one's own body;
second, the bodies of others; third, bodhi.
When giving in this manner, one purifies four kinds of knowledge:
first, the knowledge of the realms;
second, the knowledge of the fulfillment of sentient beings.
Third, the wisdom of aspiration;
fourth, the wisdom that assists enlightenment.
"O son of good family!
If a bodhisattva can practice such dharmas as these, they will be able to purify the dāna-pāramitā.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva purify the practice of the śīla-pāramitā?"

"Good son! There is one kind of purity: namely, that a bodhisattva feels compassion for all sentient beings in the world, which surpasses the loving-kindness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; he is able to destroy the works of Māra and to discipline all sentient beings; he is fully endowed with an immeasurable accumulation of the jewels of merit, and is free from negligence."
“Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, not giving rise to malicious thoughts toward sentient beings;
second, disciplining sentient beings so that they turn toward Bodhi.”
“Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, purification of the body, because of being far removed from all evil deeds of the body;
second, purification of speech, because of being far removed from all evil deeds of speech;”
Third is purity of mind, because it is far removed from all greed, anger, and false views.
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
first, exhorting all sentient beings to uphold the prohibitive precepts;
Second, they exhort all sentient beings to fulfill pure precepts;
third, they are able to discipline those who violate the precepts;
fourth, upon seeing those who uphold the precepts, they make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise them.
"Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, not giving rise to arrogance after upholding the precepts;
second, not giving rise to contempt for those who violate the precepts."
Third, seeing those who uphold the precepts, their hearts are free from envy;
fourth, they never seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
fifth, they do not think of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, there are six kinds:
first, mindfulness of the Buddha, for the purpose of transcending precepts;
second, mindfulness of the Dharma, so that after transcending precepts, the mind does not give rise to regret."
Third is mindfulness of the Sangha, because it enables the complete fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s precepts;
fourth is mindfulness of the precepts, because it does not seek the karmic rewards of the various realms of existence;
fifth is mindfulness of giving, because it enables the total relinquishment of everything.
Sixth is mindfulness of the devas, for the sake of fulfilling all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, deep faith in all Buddha-dharmas;
Second, to practice with diligent vigor for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma;
third, to possess wisdom for the sake of knowing all the Buddha-dharmas;
fourth, to be able to expound all the Buddha-dharmas after having heard them.
Fifth, to make offerings to one's parents, teachers, and preceptors;
sixth, to fear evil karma in the present and future;
seventh, to possess a sense of shame and remorse.
"Furthermore, there are eight kinds:
first, not displaying extraordinary feats for the sake of gain or offerings to delude the masses;
second, not speaking of one's own affairs, being free from all such things."
Third, not praising offerings, because the mind is content;
fourth, practicing the noble lineages, because one delights in the wholesome Dharma;
fifth, following the dhūta practices, because one does not begrudge body or life.
Sixth, they delight in tranquility because they remain detached from discoursing on worldly affairs;
seventh, they deeply delight in the Dharma because they feel weary of the triple world;
eighth, they protect the Dharma with a sincere heart because they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
"Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
first, being free from the nine evil minds, because one has transcended the abodes where the nine classes of beings dwell;
second, pure mindfulness;"
Third, the cultivation of mindfulness;
fourth, the increase of wholesome dharmas;
fifth, the mind’s delight in tranquility.
Sixth, being free from the heat of afflictions;
seventh, adorning oneself with śamatha;
eighth, practicing diligence with vigor.
Ninth, not deceiving sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, purifying the three karmas of the body;
Second, purifying the four actions of speech;
third, purifying the three actions of mind;
fourth, remaining far removed from envy.
Fifth, to be free from a deceitful mind;
sixth, to mindfully contemplate the precepts with a sincere heart;
seventh, to practice diligence with assiduity for the sake of upholding the precepts.
Eighth, using gentle speech in order to harmonize sentient beings;
ninth, accepting rebirth as a servant for the sake of sentient beings;
tenth, not giving rise to contempt or arrogance toward any fields of merit.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), there are two kinds of pure conduct:
first, that which involves intention, signs, and adornment—wherein one would rather sacrifice their life than ever violate the precepts;”
Second, being without mind, without signs, and without adornment, one’s mind has no attachment to any phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, purifying the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
Second, not seeking any external sense objects.
This further consists of two kinds:
first, constantly aspiring for the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta); [second, not seeking external objects].
Second, not observing the characteristics of the precepts directed toward original enlightenment. "Good son!
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the pāramitā of kṣānti?"
Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is reviled, he does not retaliate, because his verbal karma is pure;
when he is struck, he does not retaliate, because his physical karma is pure.
When receiving anger, one does not retaliate because the mental karma is pure. Good son!
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva may suffer verbal abuse and humiliation, he does not repay it for the sake of protecting sentient beings.
One does not retaliate when undergoing various forms of torture and poison because one protects future generations;
when having one’s hands and feet severed, one remains free from anger with a mind of loving-kindness because one protects bodhi.

Upon seeing those who come seeking [help], one does not give rise to anger in the mind, because one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), because it increases the path to bodhi, and because it destroys the mind of stinginess and greed and shatters the works of Māra.
“Good son! Having cultivated the recollection of the Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices patience and endures all suffering for the sake of attaining the body of a Buddha.”
"Good son! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who cultivate patience for the sake of fully attaining the ten powers.
Moreover, there are bodhisattvas who cultivate patience for the sake of accomplishing the great lion’s roar."
Furthermore, there is the cultivation of patience for the sake of knowing the three periods of time without obstruction;
furthermore, there is the cultivation of patience for the sake of attaining the power of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
furthermore, there is the cultivation of patience for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of all-knowledge.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with two powers, is able to accomplish patience:
first, the power of wisdom;”
Second is the power of cultivation.
Because of the power of wisdom, one contemplates the body and mind; therefore, this is called patience.
Because of the power of cultivation, one does not cling to any phenomena; therefore, this is called patience.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva of pure patience is able to observe that among all phenomena there are no sentient beings; for this reason, he cultivates patience."
All dharmas are by nature liberated; therefore, the bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas as being without patience and without anger.
If the mind has no attachment toward any dharmas, this is called patience.
“Good son! A bodhisattva has two kinds of patience:
first, observing [all things] as being like the Dharma-body;”
Second, observing according to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can thus observe these two dharmas, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the *vīryapāramitā* (perfection of vigor)?

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cease nor regret their various practices, and their mind never feels satiated with regard to wholesome dharmas; furthermore, they delight in practicing the five *pāramitās*, constantly seeking to adorn all wholesome dharmas, protecting the true Dharma, and joyfully proclaiming it.”

To tame the minds of sentient beings without rest; to surpass the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; to protect the true Dharma of all Buddhas; to practice various ascetic disciplines without regret in heart; never to lose one's original roots of goodness; to extensively cultivate learning without weariness of mind; and to serve as a messenger for the masses without giving rise to sorrow or regret—this is called diligence.
Regarding such diligence, how is it called "pure"?

If one can contemplate the body as being like a reflection, remain silent with the mouth, and maintain ultimate purity of mind; if one contemplates all phenomena of cessation through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knows the exhaustion of all existence through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
When observing in this manner, one is then able to adorn three kinds of diligence:
first, the adornment of the essence;
second, the adornment of awakening.
Third is the adornment of discernment.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of unattached diligence:
first, non-attachment to the eye; [and so forth].
Second, non-attachment to form;
third, non-attachment to consciousness.
This applies likewise up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*); this is called the diligence of neither grasping nor rejecting.

Having fulfilled such diligent vigor, one does not grasp at giving nor abandon stinginess; one does not grasp at upholding the precepts nor abandon breaking them; one does not grasp at patience nor abandon anger; one does not grasp at vigor nor abandon indolence; one does not grasp at meditative concentration nor abandon a distracted mind; one does not grasp at wisdom nor abandon folly; one does not grasp at wholesome dharmas nor abandon unwholesome dharmas; one does not grasp at the Buddha-way nor abandon the two vehicles. These are called the two kinds of diligent vigor; these two forms of vigor can fully realize the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
namely, internal and external.
If a bodhisattva is able to cultivate such diligent effort, this is called the purification of the practice of vīryapāramitā.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure dhyānapāramitā?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes up the factors of dhyāna and contemplates those factors of dhyāna, and having contemplated them, enters meditative absorption.”
Having entered meditative concentration, one does not crave or cling to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is called dhyāna.
It is not clinging to the dhyāna of the eye, nor even to the dhyāna of the mind; this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the dhyāna of form up to the dhyāna of mental phenomena—this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the dhyānas of earth, water, fire, wind, or space—this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the dhyānas of the sun, moon, Śakra, Brahmā, or Maheśvara—this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to this or that dhyāna—this is called dhyāna.
Not contemplating the body or the mind as dhyāna—this is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the lower or higher dhyānas is what is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the dhyānas of the four graspings is what is called dhyāna.
Not being attached to the signs of sentient beings, life-span, the person (pudgala), the self, or the individual is what is called dhyāna.
Dhyāna that is not attached to views of permanence, annihilation, existence, or non-existence is called dhyāna.
Dhyāna that is not the ultimate exhaustion of outflows is called dhyāna.
Dhyāna that does not enter the stage of certainty is called dhyāna.
Not having attained the fruits of śramaṇaship through dhyāna, such dhyāna is not the ultimate practice of dhyāna; it is called the dhyāna of subduing through emptiness, but not true emptiness-dhyāna;
it is called the dhyāna of subduing through signlessness, but not true signlessness-dhyāna;
it is called the dhyāna of subduing through wishlessness, but not true wishlessness-dhyāna.
This Bodhisattva fully accomplishes the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of all-empty practices through great loving-kindness and great compassion.
What is meant by "possessing all emptiness"?

If one is able not to observe [as real] generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, the Four Noble Truths, the wisdom of enlightenment, the adornment of vows, *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, liberation, or a sense of shame and remorse—this is called the unimpeded knowledge of the Buddhas' expedient means, samādhi, and supernormal powers.

They have fully embraced the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; they are undefiled by the two vehicles, have severed all habitual tendencies, and are endowed with immeasurable great supernormal powers and wisdom, serving as a refuge for all sentient beings.

Adorning both mundane and supramundane dharmas, being able to skillfully subdue all sentient beings, crossing over the great ocean of birth and death with its four currents, being able to sever all bonds, and purifying the nature of all phenomena—this is called the tranquility of nature.

Not tending toward the tranquility of the Dharma, yet tending toward the nature of renunciation regarding the Dharma; clearly tending toward the nature of blindness regarding the Dharma, having hearing yet tending toward the nature of deafness regarding the Dharma; diligently subduing while tending toward stagnation regarding the Dharma; cooling, extinguishing, and tranquilizing, and subduing what is burning—this is called the emptiness of all conditioned activities (*sarvasaṃskāra-śūnyatā*).
“Good son! It is like this:

suppose all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were skilled in painting; among them, some might be adept at applying plaster, some at grinding pigments, some might understand how to paint the body but not the hands and feet, and others might understand the hands and feet but not the face and eyes.”
At that time, there was a king who gave a single piece of fine cotton cloth to these people and addressed them, saying:
"All those who are capable of painting, assemble here and paint my likeness upon this cloth."
At that time, all the people gathered together and worked on it collectively according to their respective abilities.
There was one painter, however, who for some reason was ultimately unable to come.
After the people had finished painting it, they brought it together and presented it to the king. "Good son!
Can it be said that all the people gathered together and made it?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
I have spoken this parable, yet its meaning has not been fully revealed. Good son!
Because one person has not arrived, it cannot be said that the assembly has gathered, nor can it be said that the image has already been accomplished.

It is the same for a practitioner of the Buddha-dharma: if there is even one practice that is not accomplished, they cannot be said to be fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s true Dharma. Therefore, one must fulfill all practices; this is called the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi.
When this Dharma was being taught, sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the perfection of emptiness regarding all conditioned phenomena. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the prajñāpāramitā?"
Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess twelve kinds of wisdom:
first, unimpeded knowledge of the past; [and so forth].
Second, unimpeded knowledge of the future;
third, unimpeded knowledge of the present;
fourth, unimpeded knowledge of the conditioned.
Fifth, unimpeded knowledge of the unconditioned;
sixth, unimpeded knowledge of all worldly activities;
seventh, unimpeded knowledge of the supramundane.
Eighth, knowing eloquence without obstruction;
ninth, knowing reality without obstruction;
tenth, knowing conventional truth without obstruction.
Eleventh, knowing the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) without obstruction;
twelfth, knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings without obstruction—this is called wisdom (prajñā).

It can refute that which is difficult to refute, contemplate that which is difficult to contemplate, and resolve that which is difficult to resolve; like a diamond, it cannot be destroyed. This is called supramundane wisdom, ultimate wisdom, and the wisdom of the true mind of liberation for all sentient beings.

"It is difficult to practice, difficult to enter, and difficult to see; it is profoundly deep and difficult to study. It is right view and the right aggregate, far removed from all views and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). One knows for oneself with clarity, perceiving the minds of all sentient beings; possessing the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*), one is free from attachment. It is vast and luminous, without contention and without confinement."

Skillfully knowing the proper seasons and transcending them, he protects the collection of the True Dharma; he attains ultimate awakening, true awakening, and actual awakening; remaining far removed from all defilements, he is not censured by anyone.

A single practice is non-practice; it is the practice of all sentient beings, a practice that leaves no trace. Although it is detached from all worldly practices, it does not remain apart from any worldly conduct.

Although he is detached from the world, he is not detached from the Buddha-fields; although he is detached from all the adornments of conditioned activities, he does not distance himself from the discipline of sentient beings.

Although he is detached from all activities, he is not detached from virtuous conduct; although he is detached from the causes and conditions of the mental activities of sentient beings, he is not detached from knowing the mental activities of sentient beings.
"Though one is detached from worldly activities, one does not depart from worldly dharmas; though one is detached from all bodies, one enters the minds of sentient beings—this is called wisdom.

Such wisdom is extremely difficult to obtain; it can never be attained unless one's roots of goodness are fully matured, nor can it be obtained by those who cannot constantly practice wholesome dharmas."

It is only beneath the Bodhi tree that one can attain it; truly knowing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), protected by all Buddhas, and crossing over to the other shore, one knows all dharmas and bestows the flavor of ambrosia—therefore, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
“Good son! Such wisdom ultimately and thoroughly understands all conditions, all marks, and the mental activities of all sentient beings; for this reason, it is called wisdom.”
Such wisdom has two kinds of tranquility:
first, the tranquility of knowing the characteristics of obstruction;
second, the tranquility of knowing the characteristics of non-obstruction.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, purity through non-conceptualization;
second, purity through being free from all views."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva with such wisdom constantly dwells among sentient beings of sharp and dull faculties, within the minds of sentient beings, and amidst all phenomena, observing that all afflictions are themselves wisdom.

Although the bodhisattva dwells within all realms, he dwells predominantly in the realm of the Buddha; he is able to skillfully observe the worlds of the ten directions, free from all hindrances. These are the root of all Buddha-dharmas, wherein all unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected. He does not study any dharmas nor does he depart from any dharmas; he neither destroys a single dharma nor establishes a single dharma.

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such wisdom, they are able to perform meritorious deeds, read, recite, and expound all Buddha-dharmas, fully attain all merits and virtues, and cultivate and perfect all wholesome dharmas; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure Prajñāpāramitā.

When this Dharma was being taught, twenty-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), five hundred bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind, and ten thousand devas and humans realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
At that time, all the devas and humans spoke with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are those who can believe in this sutra, it should be known that such persons are protected by all Buddhas; how much more so for those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to it!"
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the practice of enlightenment? Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the foundation of mindfulness of the body, there are two types of practice:
first, the practice of impurity;
second, the practice of purity.
Regarding the practitioner of impurity: they contemplate that the body is impure, filled with stench and filth, impermanent, non-abiding, and a deceiver of all ordinary worldlings.
Regarding the practitioner of purity: the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus:
"By means of this impure body, I shall now attain the pure Buddha-body, the pure Dharma-body, the body of pure merit, and the body that all sentient beings delight in beholding."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has contemplated the body as body, he is able to purify two practices:
first, impermanence; [second, suffering]."
Second is permanence.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the body is impermanent and that death is certain, having thus contemplated, they do not commit various evil deeds or live by wrong livelihood for the sake of the body, but instead cultivate the three firm dharmas: first, the firmness of the body; [the second is the firmness of speech;
the third is the firmness of mind].
Second is the firmness of life;
third is the firmness of wealth.
Having contemplated in this way, one is able to serve as an attendant for sentient beings, thereby attaining freedom from the crookedness of body, speech, and mind.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the body as impermanent in this way, they attain immeasurable merits such as these.
What is meant by "permanence"?

Having contemplated impermanence, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the permanent body; because of impermanence, they attain the body of merit; and because of impermanence, they do not sever the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, or the lineage of the Saṅgha.

Good son! Furthermore, that which is permanent is inexhaustible; that which is inexhaustible is unconditioned; that which is unconditioned is the sphere of activity of all-knowledge; and the sphere of activity of all-knowledge is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, that which is permanent is space; when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as being like space, this is called the "permanent practice" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

“Good son! Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the application of mindfulness to the body, observing that the bodies of all sentient beings will ultimately be the body of a Tathāgata Buddha. Just as the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s body is thus, so too are these two bodies and my own body likewise. This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the untainted body.”
Whatever wholesome dharmas the bodhisattva attains at that time, whether few or many, are all entirely without outflows (*anāsrava*).
By means of such dharmas, he makes vows and dedicates them toward all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); having attained the state without outflows, he never again gives rise to outflows.

What is called "outflow" (*āsrava*) refers to the three outflows: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Having clearly understood these three outflows, the Bodhisattva is born into the realm of desire for the sake of sentient beings, yet remains unstained by the outflow of desire; it is likewise so for the realms of form and formlessness.
The outflow of ignorance has already had its root pulled out.
Why is this? Because by pulling out ignorance, the outflow of views ceases to exist.

Having cultivated mindfulness of the body, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives neither a self nor what belongs to a self within this body and does not give rise to arrogance; because they are free from the notions of "self" and "mine," they do not seek or grasp at any material wealth.
Because one does not seek to grasp, there is no contention regarding things; because there is no contention, there is tranquility. That which is tranquil is precisely patience (*kṣānti*).
Abiding in patience, one is neither high nor low; being neither high nor low is to abide in accordance with the Dharma.
One who dwells in accordance with the Dharma neither practices wholesome dharmas nor unwholesome dharmas; having transcended both high and low, they immediately obtain virtuous friends.
Having obtained virtuous friends, they encounter spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*); because they encounter spiritual benefactors, they hear the True Dharma.
By hearing the true Dharma, one does not direct a defiled mind toward phenomena subject to outflows; this is called transcending the sphere of all outflows.

Having transcended the sphere of outflows, one constantly enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Once having entered concentration, not even a single phenomenon gives rise to applied or sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Because it is devoid of vitarka and vicāra, it does not create a single dharma nor transform a single dharma; this is called "in accordance with the Dharma" and is called "the equality of all dharmas.
If one attains such equality of all dharmas, this is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā).

“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can contemplate the foundation of mindfulness of the body in this way, it is called contemplating the body as the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Good son!”

At that time, the bodhisattva next contemplates the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). Toward those who possess feelings, he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and addresses all sentient beings as follows:
"Ultimate bliss consists in the severance of all feelings."
"If one can sever all sensations, that is eternal bliss.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion according to whatever sensation is experienced.
Whether experiencing a pleasant sensation oneself or in another, one remains far removed from the arising of craving and generates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
When experiencing suffering, one should distance oneself from aversion and give rise to compassion.
When experiencing neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, one should distance oneself from ignorance and give rise to equanimity.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva experiences a pleasant sensation, they do not give rise to craving; when experiencing a painful sensation, they do not give rise to aversion; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, they do not give rise to ignorance.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplates all sensations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; seeing those who experience pleasure, he knows it to be suffering;
seeing those who experience pain, he views them as like an abscess or a wound."
One perceives that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is not tranquil.
One contemplates pleasant feeling as impermanent, painful feeling as empty and non-existent, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as selfless.
When the bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he sees that these various sensations are themselves non-sensations; he sees that all sensations are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If they are conditioned, they are subject to arising and ceasing, to dispersion and leakage, and lack any abiding.
Having observed in this way, one perceives neither a self nor a recipient; this is called the bodhisattva’s great wisdom and skillful means.

By means of these skillful means, one sees that all sensations are impermanent, arising and ceasing; one contemplates that all phenomena are entirely empty and non-existent—there is no sensation and no recipient, no action and no agent. Arising from conditions and ceasing from conditions, they have no ownership and nothing to be grasped; regarding all causes and conditions, one gives rise to no discursive thought or deliberation.
Because there is no applied or sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), he speaks these words:
"All phenomena arising from causes and conditions are entirely empty.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates in this way, he accomplishes the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). He is able to bring both body and mind to complete tranquility and knows all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); this is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), and it is called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling within feeling.
“What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of the mind?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the bodhicitta, contemplates the nature of this mind: he does not perceive a mind within the internal sense bases, he does not perceive a mind within the external sense bases, he does not perceive a mind within both the internal and external sense bases; he does not perceive a mind within the aggregates, nor does he perceive a mind within the elements.”
Having failed to perceive it, he reflects thus:
"Are such mental objects distinct from the mind or not?
If the mind were distinct from its objects, then there would have to be two minds at one and the same time."
"If the mind were identical to its object, it would not be able to observe its own self, just as a fingertip cannot touch itself; the mind is likewise.

Having made this observation, one sees that the mind has no abiding place, is impermanent, and undergoes transformation; the locus of its objects ceases. One then knows that this mind is neither born from conditions nor unborn from conditions; it is neither permanent nor annihilated, neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent.
Observing the mind in this way does not hinder one from knowing, in accordance with the Dharma, that the mind is quiescent; this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the mindfulness of mind.
Furthermore, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the mind is not form and cannot be seen; it is not subject to vitarka and vicāra. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the application of mindfulness of the mind.
As it is with the mind, so it is with mental factors (caitasika);
as it is with mental factors, so it is with mental formations (citta-saṃskāra).
As is the activity of the mind, so too are the dharmas sought by the mind;
as are the dharmas sought, so too is bodhi;
as is bodhi, so too are all wholesome dharmas.

If a bodhisattva contemplates the mind, it is like a monkey, like drawing on water, like morning dew, like a queen bee, or like a mother fish; it is like a river, like a flame, like recollecting distant events, or like a solitary traveler without a body. It revolves constantly without ceasing, greedily attached to the various realms, arising and ceasing in succession.

To be able to gather such immeasurable states of mind, causing them to abide in a single place—unmoving, unswerving, without leakage, without error, without confusion, and without distraction—is called śamatha.

If a bodhisattva can perform such contemplation, this is called accomplishing the foundation of mindfulness of the mind by observing the mind; this is called knowing the sphere of the mind; this is called knowing the dharma-realm of the mind; this is called knowing the true characteristic of the mind; this is called knowing the true nature of the mind.

This is precisely extensive knowledge, which is true and pure knowledge; it is the thorough understanding that true knowledge and actual knowledge are like an illusion—this is called knowing phenomena.
It is called knowing the nature of the mind, knowing the exhaustion of the mind, and it is called non-apprehending knowledge and unimpeded knowledge.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has contemplated in this way, they thoroughly understand the mental nature of all sentient beings; having understood it, they preach the Dharma to them as is appropriate.
Just as they know their own mental nature, so too do they know the mental nature of all sentient beings.
Just as one knows the characteristics of one's own mind, so too does one know the characteristics of the minds of all sentient beings.
Just as one knows that one's own mind is empty, so too does one know that the minds of all sentient beings are empty.
Just as one contemplates the equality of one's own mind, so too does one contemplate the equality of the minds of all sentient beings.
Having performed this contemplation, one remains unmoved within the *dharmadhātu*; this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the mind.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva cultivate the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna)?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates in this way: phenomena arise and phenomena perish; there is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, and no person; there is no arising and no ceasing, no passing away and no emerging—this is called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
If one is able to seek the Dharma, this is called the emergence of the Dharma;
if one does not seek the Dharma, this is called the cessation of the Dharma.
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, that which emerges arises from conditions, and that which ceases arises from conditions.
When observing in this manner, one contemplates the three types of action: namely, unwholesome action, wholesome action, and imperturbable action.
Among these three types of action, I shall always practice virtuous and wholesome actions for the sake of the ten wholesome paths of conduct.
The ten wholesome dharmas consist of purifying the bodily karma; one who seeks the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Tathāgata cannot be harmed by others.
Purifying the verbal karma means that whatever one says will be joyfully heard and accepted by all.
Regarding the purification of mental karma: one maintains an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and constantly enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

One purifies the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and, because of purifying the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), bestows constant happiness upon sentient beings; because of purifying the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one undergoes suffering for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable lifetimes without regret;
and one purifies the ten powers (*daśabala*) in order to know the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings.
They purify the four fearlessnesses in order to know whether sentient beings have obstructions or no obstructions;
they purify the eighteen unique dharmas in order to know the three periods of time without obstruction;
and they purify all Buddha-dharmas so that they cannot be surpassed by any sentient being.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to contemplate in this way, they do not give rise to weariness or complacency regarding all wholesome dharmas and merits; they cultivate and draw near to virtuous conduct, while distancing themselves from unwholesome conduct and the habitual tendencies of afflictions, truly understanding immovable practice.

"Although they know this and are free from greed, their minds attain mastery; they are born according to their vows rather than through the birth of karmic bonds, being born in the realm of desire for the sake of sentient beings. Good son!"

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having attained skillful means, contemplates the foundations of mindfulness of dharmas, cultivates and accumulates the adornments that assist the factors of enlightenment, and remains far removed from all defilements that obstruct enlightenment.
Having attained these merits, one does not cling to the view of eternalism nor cling to the view of annihilationism; free from these two views, one practices the Middle Way.
Now, the Middle Way consists of two kinds of dharmas:
first, unwholesome thoughts; [the second is wholesome thoughts].
