Such a Middle Way cannot be seen by worldly wisdom; it cannot be proclaimed or displayed; it is without characteristics, formless, placeless, without grasping, and without relinquishing—pure and tranquil.

“Good son! As for the Middle Way, it cannot be seen by the eye, nor can it be touched, even by the sense of touch. It has no destination, belongs neither to the mundane nor the supramundane, and cannot be described as being either much or little; therefore, it is called the Middle Way.”
“Good son! ‘Self’ and ‘non-self’ are called the two extremes.

If one speaks of that which is neither eternal nor annihilated; neither life-principle nor person; neither perception nor non-perception; neither cognition nor non-cognition; neither real nor unreal; neither this nor that; neither existent nor non-existent; neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither activity nor non-activity; neither birth-and-death nor nirvana;”
Not acting in such a manner is called the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the mindfulness of phenomena as phenomena, yet does not discriminate within the dharma-realm."
As it is with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), so it is with the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).
These two realms are called the space-realm (*ākāśadhātu*); all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) entirely enter the dharma-realm.
Now, the dharma-realm is itself the realm of sentient beings, and the realm of sentient beings is itself non-discrimination (*avikalpa*); this is called the observation of all phenomena.
To view all realms as equal is itself the Dharma-realm; though one perceives them with clarity, the mind does not cling to them. Because there is no clinging, there is no conceptual discrimination.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not contemplate the foundations of mindfulness of phenomena by means of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, or the wisdom eye.
Why is this? Because these three eyes are without marks (*animitta*).

Therefore, when observing phenomena, one does so with the Dharma-eye; though one knows them with perfect clarity, the mind does not cling to them. Although there is no clinging, one does not lose the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); this is called Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*).

To be able to know such a profound dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) while also not losing mindfulness of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)—this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the application of mindfulness to dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna). "Good son!
For what reason do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate and accumulate these four foundations of mindfulness?
It is because they wish to distance themselves from the four perversions.

They cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body to abandon the perversion of purity; they cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of sensation to abandon the perversion of pleasure; they cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the mind to abandon the perversion of permanence; and they cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena to abandon the perversion of self.

Furthermore, by being apart from the four nutriments: one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body to be apart from edible food; one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of feelings to be apart from the nutriment of contact; one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the mind to be apart from the nutriment of consciousness; and one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena to be apart from the nutriment of volitional formations.

Furthermore, one distances oneself from the four stations of consciousness: by cultivating the application of mindfulness to the body, one distances oneself from dwelling in the station of form; by cultivating the application of mindfulness to feelings, one distances oneself from dwelling in the station of feeling; by cultivating the application of mindfulness to the mind, one distances oneself from dwelling in the station of perception; and by cultivating the application of mindfulness to phenomena, one distances oneself from dwelling in the station of formations.

Furthermore, being free from the five aggregates: one cultivates the application of mindfulness of the body to distance oneself from the aggregate of form; one cultivates the application of mindfulness of sensation to distance oneself from the aggregate of sensation; one cultivates the application of mindfulness of the mind to distance oneself from the aggregate of consciousness; and one cultivates the application of mindfulness of phenomena to distance oneself from the aggregates of perception and mental formations.
This is called the bodhisattva’s purification of the practice of the four applications of mindfulness. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of the four right efforts?"

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas always delight in cultivating and accumulating all wholesome dharmas; they practice with diligent vigor so that unarisen unwholesome dharmas do not arise; they practice with diligent vigor to eliminate unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen; they practice with diligent vigor so that unarisen wholesome dharmas may arise; and they practice with diligent vigor so that wholesome dharmas that have already arisen remain and are not lost.

“Good son! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have cultivated and accumulated virtuous conduct throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they are by nature good; thus, they do not need to employ expedient means to prevent evil from arising.”

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates the four right efforts and attains mastery over the mind through these four right efforts, then at that time the bodhisattva’s mind and mental factors proceed in unison with great compassion; therefore, they are called "right efforts."
"At that time, the bodhisattva sequentially cultivates and accumulates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):
first, desire; second, the mind;"
Third is diligence; fourth is wisdom.
To single-mindedly and with utmost sincerity focus one's thoughts upon bodhi is called aspiration.
Because one cultivates great compassion, the awakening mind becomes light and agile; this is called "mind.
Because one remains far removed from unwholesome dharmas, this is called "diligence.
Because one attains skillful means, it is called "wisdom."
“Once a Bodhisattva has cultivated the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), they attain four masteries:

first, mastery over lifespan. Because of this mastery, although they may be born with a short life, they naturally attain long life; for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, they preach the True Dharma to those with long lives, and while possessing a long life, they can manifest a short life. Wherever this Bodhisattva is born—whether among devas or humans—they attain mastery over life.”
Second, they attain mastery over the body; by virtue of this mastery, they manifest bodies and forms according to their will, displaying various modes of deportment for the sake of sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva wishes to make his body equal in size to that of sentient beings, he can manifest it as either vast and tall or minute and small.

Third, having attained mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), because of this mastery, he is able to know all mundane and supramundane dharmas and demonstrate all worldly affairs to sentient beings; yet his mind does not regress from supramundane practice. Clearly understanding the profound twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), he attains unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) and is able to preach various teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
Upon hearing this Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Fourth, he aspires to attain mastery;

by virtue of this mastery, he causes the four great oceans to merge into a single ocean, which neither comes nor goes and remains without movement or change, exactly as it was before and no different. He likewise causes all the Mount Sumerus of the trichiliocosm to merge into a single mountain, which neither comes nor goes and remains without movement or change, exactly as it was before and no different, without causing any obstruction to the Four Heavenly Kings or the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

If one wishes to cause the trichiliocosm to become entirely composed of gold, the seven treasures, sandalwood, flowers, incense, and necklaces, such that even space, water, and fire are all accomplished according to one's will, this is called the Bodhisattva attaining the four masteries.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva attains the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), he shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions face-to-face, converse with them, and dwell together with them in one place;
it is likewise for all Brahmās, Śakras, the Four Great Kings, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.”
"What is the adornment of the four bases of psychic power? Good son!

If one can make offerings to one’s parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and those of virtue; if, upon seeing sentient beings, one first greets them with a welcoming mind, speaks to them with gentle words, acts exactly as one speaks, and regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind—possessing a virtuous mind, a right mind, a respectful mind, and a sense of shame and remorse."

They remain far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion; they are without deceit, covetousness, envy, or stinginess. They attend to the affairs of others as if they were their own; they provide strength to those who lack it; they clear away earth and stones in muddy places; they construct bridges over rivers, streams, and ditches, either carrying them on their own backs or providing boats for rescue. They constantly give sentient beings whatever they require, never speaking of the misfortunes or afflictions of others, nor do they mock or criticize the transgressions of others.

One who is able to eliminate transgressions in accordance with the Dharma, who restrains all afflictions so that they do not arise, who is able to give away cherished objects to others, and who feels no regret in their heart after having given, and who makes vows and dedicates merit for the sake of all sentient beings.

With faith, they exhort all sentient beings toward goodness; they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, possessing few desires and knowing contentment; they harbor no longing for the gains and offerings of others, constantly mindful of renouncing the household life and likewise encouraging others to do so; and they remain mindful of spiritual friends, never intending to abandon them.

Maintaining impartiality and non-duality toward both enemies and kin, he provides various vehicles for those traveling on the road, gives beds and bedding to the weak and exhausted, and acts as a protector for those who are terrified; regarding all sentient beings as his own parents, he does not disparage those who have broken the precepts but bestows wealth and goods upon the poor.
To those who are ill or emaciated, he provides medicine; he bestows grace upon others without speaking of his own deeds.
He never severs the lineage of the Triple Gem and constantly contemplates the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Remaining far removed from all worldly affairs and every evil or unwholesome dharma, they are not defiled by worldly conditions and do not lose the mindfulness of their supreme resolve for bodhi.
This is called the adornment of the practice of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
*The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-Five.

Chapter Eleven: The Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa, Part Two.
"How does a bodhisattva purify the practice of the five faculties?"
The Bodhisattva’s faith that cannot be shaken or turned back is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To practice diligence without relying on the instruction of others is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Constantly recollecting *bodhi* is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Constantly cultivating great compassion is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*).
Gathering wholesome dharmas is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*).
Furthermore, having faith in all Buddha-dharmas is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhā-indriya*).
Seeking all Buddha-dharmas is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Mindfulness of all Buddha-dharmas is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Attaining the samādhi of the Buddhas is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
To sever all nets of doubt is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, for the mind to be directed toward Bodhi without any nets of doubt is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
To increase wholesome dharmas is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Seeking skillful means is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Viewing all sentient beings with an impartial mind is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
Contemplating the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
"Furthermore, the purity of mind free from turbidity is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Destroying the various turbid minds is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Mindfulness of pure phenomena is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)."
Contemplating the purity of the nature of the mind is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
Being able to cause sentient beings to abide in the pure Dharma is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, being far removed from all base and evil dharmas is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Seeking all wholesome dharmas is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Not losing what has been attained is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma once wholesome dharmas have been attained is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
Contemplating wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is the mind of giving.
The faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) is the delight in giving without ceasing.
The faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya) means that after having given, one does not seek karmic retribution.
The faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya) means that the mind of impartial giving is free from discrimination.
The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) means that one does not regard whether the recipient is a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) or not.
Furthermore, there is the faculty of faith, which is the mind that first enters into wholesome dharmas.
The faculty of diligence is able to destroy arrogance.
The faculty of mindfulness is to be free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self."
The faculty of concentration is to remain far removed from all sixty-two views.
The faculty of wisdom is to remain far removed from all evil afflictions.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the five faculties.
“What is the bodhisattva’s purification of the five powers?
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the five faculties (pañcendriya) and cannot be destroyed by any māras, it is therefore called ‘power.’”

That which no Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicle can reach; that which no sentient being can cause to retreat from the mind of the Mahāyāna; that which no afflictions can destroy; that which can cause the mind to be contented and have few desires; that which enables the body to attain great power, skillfully covering the sense faculties and attaining a vajra-body—this is called power.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the power of faith, he never commits any evil;
when he abides in the power of diligence, he performs all that is wholesome.”
When abiding in the power of mindfulness, one does not lose wholesome dharmas;
when abiding in the power of concentration, one is not destroyed by the pleasures of the five desires;
and when abiding in the power of wisdom, one remains far removed from all fetters and afflictions.
"Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one does not follow the words of others;
when abiding in the power of vigor, one seeks the good without ceasing;
when abiding in the power of mindfulness, one attains dhāraṇī."
When abiding in the power of concentration, one’s teaching of the Dharma is impartial;
when abiding in the power of wisdom, one is able to destroy the doubts of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one fully attains the power of understanding.
When abiding in the power of exertion, one possesses the power of diligence;
when abiding in the power of mindfulness, one possesses the power of liberation;
when abiding in the power of concentration, one is fully endowed with the power of aspiration.
When abiding in the power of wisdom, one is endowed with the power of all practices.
Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one perceives the faults of stinginess;
when abiding in the power of diligence, one distances oneself from stinginess and greed.
When abiding in the power of mindfulness, one directs the wholesome aspirations cultivated toward Bodhi;
when abiding in the power of concentration, the mind is equanimous;
and when abiding in the power of wisdom, the mind ultimately does not seek the retribution of giving, morality, or concentration.
"Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one is able to leave behind all defilements of broken precepts;
when abiding in the power of vigor, one possesses the precepts with a sincere mind;
when abiding in the power of mindfulness, one directs the precepts one upholds toward Bodhi."
When abiding in the power of concentration, one possesses the ground of purity;
when abiding in the power of wisdom, one remains far removed from artificial precepts.
Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one remains far removed from a mind of anger.
Abiding in the power of diligence, one cultivates patience;
abiding in the power of mindfulness, one directs the patience thus cultivated toward enlightenment;
and abiding in the power of meditative concentration, one protects all sentient beings.
When abiding in the power of wisdom, one does not conceptualize sentient beings, persons, or life-span.
Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one remains far removed from indolence;
when abiding in the power of diligence, one brings all cultivated practices to the ultimate shore.
When abiding in the power of mindfulness, one cultivates diligence directed toward bodhi;
when abiding in the power of concentration, body and mind are tranquil;
when abiding in the power of wisdom, one does not dwell in either good or evil.
"Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one remains far removed from all distracting affairs;
when abiding in the power of vigor, one diligently seeks the factors of dhyāna;
when abiding in the power of mindfulness, one directs the concentration thus cultivated toward bodhi."
When dwelling in the power of concentration, the mind is always concentrated;
when dwelling in the power of wisdom, one does not cling to any concentrations.
Furthermore, when dwelling in the power of faith, one remains far removed from ignorance.
When abiding in the power of exertion, one diligently seeks all that is wholesome;
when abiding in the power of mindfulness, one directs the wisdom thus cultivated toward enlightenment;
when abiding in the power of concentration, one cultivates virtuous reflection.
When abiding in the power of wisdom, one dwells in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, when abiding in the power of faith, one is endowed with the seven powers;
when abiding in the power of diligence, one attains the seven factors of enlightenment.
When abiding in the power of mindfulness, one attains the eight foundations of mindfulness;
when abiding in the power of concentration, one leaves behind the seven stations of consciousness;
when abiding in the power of wisdom, one leaves behind the eightfold wrong path.
"Furthermore, when the mind does not regress from bodhi, this is called the power of faith and the practice of pure faith;
when there is neither grasping nor rejecting, this is called the power of vigor and the practice of pure vigor;
when one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called the power of mindfulness and the practice of pure mindfulness."
To subdue the mind is called the power of concentration and the practice of purifying concentration;
to distance oneself from all views and know skillful means is called the power of wisdom and the practice of purifying wisdom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva purify the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment?
Never losing the dharmas that assist awakening is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.”
Śamatha that neither grasps nor rejects is called the awakening factor of discrimination.
Being free from all evil is called the awakening factor of energy.
Being free from all grief and affliction is called the awakening factor of joy.
The tranquility of body and mind is called the awakening factor of investigation (vīrya-sambojjhaṅga).
Attaining the taste of liberation is called the awakening factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga).
Having accomplished what was to be done is called the awakening factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga).
"Furthermore, not abandoning the bodhicitta is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.
Diligently protecting the Dharma with a sincere heart is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena.
Tirelessly taming all sentient beings is called the awakening factor of vigor."
Being fully endowed with wholesome dharmas is called the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Being free from all afflictions is called the factor of awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Being able to cause sentient beings to abide within samādhi is called the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Causing all sentient beings to fully know the dharma-realm is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, not recollecting the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
To discern the meanings of the words and phrases of all phenomena is called the factor of enlightenment of discrimination (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
To have no cessation of the three karmas when seeking wholesome dharmas is called the factor of enlightenment of diligence (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
To be free from the mind that discriminates between enemies and kin is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Being able to discipline oneself in accordance with the various worlds is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Not observing dualistic dharmas is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

“Good son! That which aids awakening consists in awakening to all dharmas and knowing all dharmas; it is the discernment of all dharmas and the deliberation upon all dharmas; it is knowing the mental natures and mental activities of all sentient beings. This is called the factors of awakening (bodhipakṣa), and it is also called the noble conduct (āryacaryā).”

Such noble conduct is not the practice of any ordinary person, nor of the hosts of Māras with their false views; it is not the practice of form, sound, fragrance, taste, or touch; it is not the practice of any marks, any sensations, or any mental consciousnesses—seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing—including all states of perception and non-perception. Therefore, it is called noble conduct.

Now, the noble practice is neither awakening, nor non-awakening, nor even great awakening; yet it is able to counteract all phenomena while remaining without contention or dispute with them—this is called the noble practice.
The practice of the noble ones is precisely the method for assisting in the realization of bodhi. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva purify the practice of the Eightfold Path?"
The Eightfold Path is what is called right view. What is right view?
Right view is seeing that all phenomena are entirely equal.
Such right view is not called the "view of emptiness.
Why is this? Because there exists right view that is not the view of emptiness.
These two views are also called "identical views.
Furthermore, the view of self, the view of sentient beings, and the view of emptiness are not called right view; these three views are likewise identical views.
Furthermore, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, and the view of emptiness are not called right view; these three views are likewise identical in their nature.
Moreover, the view of a self, the view of annihilation, and the view of emptiness are not called right view; these three views are likewise identical in their nature.
Furthermore, there are the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and the view of emptiness; these are not called right view. These three views are likewise identical [in their error].
Again, there are four views:

the view of the Buddha, the view of the Dharma, the view of the Sangha, and the view of emptiness; these are called right view, and these four views are not termed the "view of emptiness" [in the sense of nihilism].
"Good son! If there is anyone who clings to such a view, it is not called right view.
If one does not cling to it, only then is it called right view."
Why is this? For one who possesses right view perceives non-discrimination, equality, and non-duality.
What is meant by "the view of equality"?
If one thinks that the dharmas of ordinary beings are inferior and the dharmas of those in training are superior, this is called the view of inequality.

To hold that the dharmas of ordinary beings are with outflows (*sāsrava*) while the dharmas of those in training are without outflows (*anāsrava*); that the dharmas of ordinary beings are subject to nutriment (*āhāra*) while those of pratyekabuddhas are without nutriment; that the dharmas of ordinary beings are defiled while the dharmas of bodhisattvas are pure; or that the dharmas of ordinary beings are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while the Buddha is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—to see things in such a way is not the view of equality.
If one can observe that there is no distinction between the dharmas of ordinary beings and even the dharmas of the Buddhas, this is called equanimity.
If one can perceive that the dharmas of ordinary beings are empty, up to and including the emptiness of the dharmas of the Buddhas, this is called right view.
To observe that the dharmas of ordinary beings arise from causes and conditions, and that the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas likewise arise from conditions, is called right view.
To observe that the dharmas of ordinary beings are quiescent and the dharmas of bodhisattvas are quiescent is also called right view.
If one contemplates that the dharmas of ordinary beings are incomplete, and even the dharmas of the Buddhas are incomplete, this is called right view.
If one contemplates that there is no distinction between self and non-self, and possesses this vision of non-distinction, it is then called right view.
If one views things in this way, then one does not perceive superior, middling, or inferior dharmas; regarding all dharmas, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
This is called right view. Right view is defined as having nothing to see;
that which has nothing to see is itself right view.
If one views it in this way, such a person does not perceive even a single dharma, the characteristics of a single dharma, or the radiance of a single dharma.
Good son! To view it in this manner is called the right view of the Buddha-dharma.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus attained the fruit of arhatship. "Good son,
what is perfect awakening?"
The Perfectly Awakened One is free from all conceptualization; "awakening" refers to wisdom and skillful means.
To contemplate phenomena and know phenomena is called perfect awakening.
One observes all phenomena to discern which are defiled.
What is purity? Having observed in this way, one does not perceive equality or inequality at all; being free from all conceptualization, this is called right awakening.
What is right speech?

The words spoken from the mouth do not cause oneself distress nor distress others; they do not defile oneself nor defile others; they do not give rise to pride in oneself nor pride in others; they do not deceive oneself nor deceive others—this is called right speech.

Furthermore, as for right speech: whatever one says, one speaks of all phenomena as being entirely equal, and is well able to discern the characteristics of conditioned things; this is called right speech.

Furthermore, right speech is that which proclaims all phenomena to be empty, signless, and wishless, without arising, without ceasing, without emergence, and without disappearance; this is called right speech.
Furthermore, right speech is that which proclaims conditioned phenomena as suffering, impermanent, and non-self, and nirvana as tranquility; this is called right speech.

If there are sentient beings who say that what is called "sentient being" has no life-force or personhood at all, and that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and cease from causes and conditions—just like the fruit of a tree—this is called right speech.
Pure right speech is precisely the Buddha’s speech; this is called the practice of pure right speech.
What is right action? As for right action, although an action may be able to destroy all actions, it is nevertheless not called "action."
If karma can act as the cause of tranquility—being neither defiled nor pure, capable of destroying afflictions so they do not increase—this is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

Knowing that karma is thus, yet still performing wholesome karma, while also contemplating that all karmas are entirely empty and quiescent, lacking any solidity, being suffering and devoid of pleasure—this is called right action.
"What is right livelihood?
Right livelihood is that which does not harm oneself or others, does not increase any evil afflictions, and is not sustained by unwholesome actions; this is called right livelihood."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas purify their right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) regarding all sentient beings and, by means of this right livelihood, aspire toward enlightenment, this is called right livelihood; such right livelihood is able to benefit both oneself and others.
"Right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*) is the diligent application of skillful means to seek all wholesome dharmas, with a desire that does not cease and no weariness or regret; this is called diligence.

To investigate the nature of equality among all dharmas, neither observing whether dharmas are equal or unequal, neither acting nor non-acting, and to thoroughly understand the suchness and true nature of dharmas—this is called right diligence."
To proclaim the True Dharma so that all sentient beings may abandon wrong diligence, and to know the practices being cultivated by sentient beings—this is called right diligence.
What is right mindfulness?
If one brings to mind generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the four immeasurable minds, this is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

Furthermore, there is another form of right mindfulness: it gathers in all afflictions so they do not arise delusively; it keeps one far from all the deeds of evil Māras; it prevents falling into the evil realms and the arising of evil thoughts; and it constantly cultivates all correct and wholesome dharmas while remaining distant from all false and evil dharmas—this is called right mindfulness.
When a bodhisattva dwells within this right mindfulness and attains the true fruits of the śramaṇa’s right assembly, it is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
Practicing the noble conduct—knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path—it is called right concentration.
Furthermore, there is right concentration, which contemplates all phenomena as entirely equal.

If one contemplates that the self is pure, then all things are pure; if one contemplates that the self is empty, then all things are empty. Although one performs such contemplations, one does not enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*); this is called the right concentration of a bodhisattva.
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they attain all-knowledge (sarvajñā) in a single thought-moment; this is called right concentration.
When this Dharma was being spoken, sixteen thousand devas and humans gave rise to the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the purification of supernormal powers? Good son!”
The divine eye is of five kinds:

it can perceive all the worlds of the ten directions and see all the Buddhas of those ten directions; it also sees sentient beings being born and passing away. What it perceives throughout the ten directions is without obstruction, surpassing that of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and devas.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these five matters, they are able to clearly perceive all phenomena; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure divine eye.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of the divine ear, they hear five kinds of sounds:

the voices of humans, the voices of non-humans, the sounds from the hells, the sounds of the Dharma being preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and the vocal sounds of all sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the pure divine ear.
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the knowledge of others’ minds?
The knowledge of others’ minds also has five kinds:

fully knowing the minds of all humans and devas; knowing the minds of those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth; knowing past minds; knowing future minds; and knowing present minds. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the knowledge of others’ minds.”

Furthermore, there is the knowledge of others' minds, by which one knows whether these sentient beings belong to the group of those fixed in the right [path], the group of those fixed in the wrong [path], or the group of those who are not fixed. One knows that these sentient beings possess greed, hatred, and delusion; having understood this, one preaches the Dharma according to their needs. Upon hearing it, these sentient beings succeed in destroying their afflictions. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of purifying the knowledge of others' minds.

“What is the bodhisattva’s practice for purifying the knowledge of past lives? It is to fully understand that this body arises from the causes and conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion; to fully understand that this body arises from the causes and conditions of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; to fully understand whether this body is complete or incomplete; and to fully understand that this body arises from ignorance, craving, and the four inversions. Furthermore, to fully understand that through the cause and condition of generosity, this body comes to possess wealth and a retinue. Such forms of knowledge are called the bodhisattva’s practice for purifying the knowledge of past lives.”
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the purified supernormal powers?
There are five kinds of supernormal power practices:
first, manifesting forms;”
Second, they understand various languages and preach the Dharma accordingly;
third, they are skillfully able to comprehend the mind, intellect, and consciousness;
fourth, they are able to awaken to all phenomena and expound upon them—all these are called the bodhisattva’s pure superknowledges.

“Good son! These five supernormal powers are for the sake of the exhaustion of outflows; yet the bodhisattva cultivates them without exhausting the outflows, desiring instead to fully understand all outflows.”
Why is this? It is for the sake of disciplining sentient beings. Good son!

For example, suppose there is a city one yojana in length and breadth, with many gates; its roads are rugged, dark, and extremely terrifying, yet those who enter the city enjoy great peace and happiness.

Furthermore, there was another man who had an only son whom he loved and cherished deeply; hearing from afar that such happiness existed in that city, he immediately abandoned his son, intending to go and enter the city.
By these skillful means, the man successfully traversed the perilous path and reached the city gate; he had already set one foot inside, but before lifting the other, he thought of his son.
He then reflected: "I have but this one son.
When he came, why did I not go with him? Who will now nourish and protect him, keeping him free from all suffering?"
He immediately abandoned the city of Sukhāvatī and returned to where his son was. "Good son!

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: out of compassion, he cultivates the five supernormal powers; having cultivated them, he is on the verge of exhausting all outflows (āsrava), yet he does not realize [nirvāṇa]."
For what reason?
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he relinquishes the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows and even proceeds through the stages of ordinary persons. Good son!

The city is a metaphor for the Great Parinirvāṇa; the many gates are a metaphor for the eighty thousand doors of samādhi; the perilous and difficult path is a metaphor for the various karmas of Māra; reaching the city gate is a metaphor for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); one foot having entered is a metaphor for wisdom; and one foot not yet having entered is a metaphor for a bodhisattva who has not yet realized liberation.
The term "only son" is a metaphor for all sentient beings within the five realms of existence; "looking back and caring for the son" is a metaphor for the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Returning to the son's location" is a metaphor for taming sentient beings; that one is able to bring about liberation yet does not personally realize it is precisely skillful means (*upāya*).
“Good son! The great loving-kindness and great compassion of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva are inconceivable!
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, great loving-kindness and great compassion are inconceivable.
Indeed, as the holy teaching declares, not only are loving-kindness and compassion inconceivable, but the power of skillful means is also inconceivable.”

The Bodhisattva clearly knows for himself that he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet he does not realize it; for the sake of sentient beings, he wanders through birth and death, yet remains undefiled by birth and death.
“World-Honored One!
With what dharmas is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva endowed so that his mind does not feel weary or regretful while within saṃsāra? “Good son!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with twenty-one dharmas, they do not give rise to regret while within saṃsāra:
first, the wholesome dharmas they cultivate are conjoined with the practice of great loving-kindness;
second, the mind of loving-kindness they cultivate is conjoined with the practice of great compassion.
Third, the practice of great compassion shared with the harmonizing of sentient beings;
fourth, the practice of diligent effort shared with the subduing of sentient beings;
fifth, the practice of virtuous mind shared with the cultivation of diligence.
Sixth, the cultivation of a virtuous mind in conjunction with skillful means;
seventh, the cultivation of skillful means in conjunction with wisdom;
eighth, the cultivation of wisdom in conjunction with meditative concentration.
Ninth, the practice of the four dhyānas together with the supernormal powers;
tenth, the practice of the supernormal powers together with wisdom;
eleventh, the practice of cultivated wisdom together with aspiration.
Twelfth, the aspiration that is cultivated is practiced in conjunction with mindfulness;
thirteenth, the mindfulness that is cultivated is practiced in conjunction with the bodhicitta;
fourteenth, the bodhi that is cultivated is practiced in conjunction with the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
Fifteenth, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) practiced together with ethical discipline;
sixteenth, the observance of precepts practiced together with extensive learning (*bahuśruta*);
seventeenth, extensive learning practiced together with dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
Eighteenth, the practice of the dhāraṇī of dwelling together in accordance with the Dharma;
nineteenth, the practice of the dhāraṇī conjoined with unimpeded wisdom;
twentieth, the practice of unimpeded wisdom conjoined with the adornment of merit.
Twenty-first: practicing the adornment of merit together with the adornment of wisdom.
These are called the twenty-one dharmas of a bodhisattva, by which they do not give rise to weariness or regret while within saṃsāra.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva adorn his own person and also cause sentient beings to obtain great benefit?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with extensive learning, this is called 'adornment'; to expound it for others is called 'great benefit'."
Furthermore, attaining great dhāraṇī is called adornment; expounding it for others is called great benefit.
Furthermore, being free from negligence is called adornment; taming sentient beings is called great benefit.
Furthermore, the thirty-two marks are called adornment, while possessing great wisdom is called great benefit.
Furthermore, gentle speech is called adornment, while practicing what one preaches is called great benefit.
Furthermore, the ability to practice universal giving is called "adornment," while not seeking a karmic reward is called "great benefit.
Son of good family!
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva adorning their own person and also enabling sentient beings to obtain great benefit.

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a kalpa named Joyful Delight. In that time, there was a Buddha named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. That Buddha’s world was named Devavyūha.”
"Good son! For what reason is that kalpa named 'Joyful Delight'?
Because within that great kalpa, sixty thousand Buddhas appear in the world."
At the beginning of that kalpa, the Śuddhāvāsa devas proclaimed these words:
"In this kalpa, sixty thousand buddhas shall appear.
Upon hearing this, the hearts of all sentient beings were filled with joy; therefore, that kalpa is named Sukhāvatī (Joyful).

“Good son! That Buddha-world is adorned with subtle and wondrous refinements beyond measure; its joy and excellence are as exquisite as those of the heavens, with no difference between them. For this reason, that world is named ‘Heavenly Vision’ (Devadarśana).”
The ground of that land is entirely made of sandalwood; it is completely free of soil, sand, dust, or mist, and its fragrance pervades immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Throughout that land, various lotus flowers emerge everywhere, and each flower emits a great radiance that shines universally across the land.

The sentient beings in that land all attain supernormal powers and do not tread upon the ground; not even a single person is born from a womb, for all are born by transformation. No one hears the name of "woman," nor is there even the name of the three evil realms where suffering is experienced.
All sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their sustenance, and in that land, even the names of the Three Vehicles do not exist.
All are adorned with natural ornaments of pure gold, necklaces, celestial crowns, and precious decorations.
Although they do not shave their hair, dye their robes, or wear the *kāṣāya*, they may still be called persons who have left the household life. Why is this?
Because they have abandoned all things and are free from greed.
The Tathāgata of that land has a complexion like that of Brahmā and manifests in the form of Brahmā, expounding the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
When bodhisattvas from other worlds behold that Buddha, they receive great joy.

“Good son! Whenever that Buddha wishes to proclaim the Dharma to transform sentient beings, he ascends the great Dharma throne above the great assembly to the height of seven *tāla* trees and always teaches the Dharma in brief.”
Why is this? Because the faculties of all sentient beings are sharp and keen.
What the Tathāgata speaks is but a single phrase, yet sentient beings understand it as hundreds of thousands of phrases.
The Tathāgata has always spoken of the four dharmas of purity. What are these four?
First, the purity of the pāramitās;...
Second is the purity of assisting toward enlightenment;
third is the purity of supernormal powers;
fourth is the purity of disciplining sentient beings.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnakūṭa who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva adorn his own person and also cause sentient beings to obtain great benefit?"
That Buddha replied: "Good son!
If a bodhisattva possesses unimpeded wisdom, it is called adornment; being able to produce the light of wisdom is called great benefit."
At that time, while that Buddha was preaching this Dharma, six thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then those bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How does a bodhisattva adorn the Bodhi tree?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
If a bodhisattva is able to cultivate heedfulness, this is called adorning the Bodhi tree.
What is meant by "heedfulness"?
Heedfulness is dwelling in accordance with the Dharma; dwelling in accordance with the Dharma means dwelling as one has taught.

Furthermore, non-negligence is called: immeasurable adornment; immeasurable giving; immeasurable observance of precepts; immeasurable patience; immeasurable diligence; immeasurable meditative concentration; immeasurable wisdom; immeasurable Buddha-dharma; immeasurable self-discipline; immeasurable adornment of merit and wisdom; making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; possessing immeasurable learning because of being endowed with wisdom; and practicing immeasurable *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for the sake of increasing wisdom.
To accomplish such immeasurable dharmas as these is called adorning the Bodhi tree, and it also enables one to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Good son! All dharmas that assist toward enlightenment take heedfulness as their root; they possess the great adornment of all wisdom, do not lose any wholesome dharmas, remain far removed from all afflictions, and encompass all dharmas.

To be without obstruction regarding all phenomena, to subdue the sense faculties and protect all wholesome dharmas so that they do not decline or be lost, to know the timely and the untimely, and to be fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the crest-dharma of the Buddha’s teachings—this is called non-negligence.
“Good son! When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa was none other than you.”
"Good son! You should now know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with heedfulness is able to adorn the Bodhi tree. Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva purify their mastery?
Son of good family!

The conduct of sentient beings is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; mastery is likewise immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; and the conduct of the bodhisattva is also immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with single-minded and sincere resolve, tame sentient beings. "O noble son!

There are sentient beings who are tamed upon hearing teachings on generosity; some are tamed upon hearing teachings on ethical discipline; others are tamed upon hearing teachings on both generosity and ethical discipline. Furthermore, there are those tamed by gentle speech, those tamed by harsh speech, and those tamed by a combination of both types of speech. There are those tamed upon hearing teachings on physical action, those tamed upon hearing teachings on the sacrifice of the body, those tamed by superior ability, and those tamed by forceful means. There are those tamed upon hearing reprimands, those tamed at the time of giving, and those tamed at the very beginning.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain subduing upon seeing exquisite forms; the same applies to sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain subduing through constant proximity, others who attain subduing by remaining at a distance, and yet others who are subdued by seeing the Buddha.
“Some sentient beings are tamed by hearing the Dharma; some sentient beings attain taming by hearing the teaching on impermanence; and the same applies to suffering, emptiness, and non-self.”
There are sentient beings who are tamed upon hearing the sound of the teaching on generosity; the same applies to the sounds of morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
There are sentient beings who are tamed upon hearing the teaching that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; there are also sentient beings who are tamed upon hearing praise of humans and devas.
There are sentient beings who are tamed upon hearing the Śrāvaka-yāna; the same applies to the Pratyekabuddha-yāna and the Buddha-yāna.
Some are tamed by means of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), some by three, two, or one method of attraction, and others are tamed even without the methods of attraction.
Some are tamed through internal giving; the same applies to external giving and both internal and external giving.
Some are tamed upon hearing the proclamation of the sufferings within the hells; the same is true for hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
Some are tamed by hearing only of pleasure; some are tamed by hearing only of suffering; and some are tamed by hearing of both suffering and pleasure.
Some are tamed upon seeing the form of a bhikṣu, while others are tamed by the forms of a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā.
Or, they may achieve subjugation through various forms of singing, dancing, and music. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva is thus able to know the various ways of subduing sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva who can practice the six pāramitās, who is fully endowed with the dharmas that assist toward enlightenment, and who is fully endowed with supernormal powers to subdue sentient beings."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, he is able to subdue all sentient beings:
first, his mind is free from regret or weariness;”
Second, not coveting various pleasures;
third, knowing the proper and improper times;
fourth, thoroughly understanding all states of mind.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas. What are the four?
First, right speech;
Second, pleasant speech; third, pure speech;
fourth, speech in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings;
second, a heart of compassion;
Third, a mind intent on benefiting others;
fourth, self-discipline of the sense faculties.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, purifying one's own mind;
second, having compassion for the minds of others;
third, practicing with diligent vigor.
Fourth, they remain far removed from the enjoyment of pleasure. Good son!
Therefore, the practice of subduing by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

“Good son! In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a kalpa named ‘Affection. In that time, there was a Buddha named Vipulaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; the world was named ‘Tranquility.’”
That Buddha possesses an assembly of ninety-six trillion śrāvakas and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas; the lifespan of the people in that land is one hundred seventy-two thousand years.
“At that time, there was the son of a great king named Dhanaśrī, born of the Brahmin caste, whose countenance was handsome and whom all living beings delighted to behold.”
When he was sixteen years old, relying on his own physical beauty, he gave rise to arrogance and initially did not approach the Buddha with reverence or prostrate before him.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself:
"This prince is now about to fall away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; his roots of goodness are not yet mature."
"If one obtains a virtuous friend, then one may go to the Buddha to hear the Dharma and receive it for upholding.
At that time, the Tathāgata distributed voting sticks among the great assembly of eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas and said,
"Who is able to subdue this son of a brahmin?"
Who could, during these eighty-four thousand years, constantly travel back and forth to this prince’s house and undergo such manifold sufferings—
namely, being reviled and beaten— without giving rise to regret in their heart?
"Among the eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, not even a single person took a tally;
the second and third proclamations were likewise.
When the third proclamation had been made, a bodhisattva named Viśuddhavīrya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke:"
“World-Honored One!
I am now able to go to that prince’s house and willingly endure suffering.
When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook with a great trembling.
All humans and devas raised their voices in unison, crying out:
"Excellent, excellent! O Great Being!"
Then, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhavīrya immediately went to the gate of the prince’s residence and stood there.
When the prince saw him, he reviled and slandered him with harsh words, smeared his face with dirt, and struck his body with swords, staves, tiles, and stones.
At that time, the bodhisattva did not become angry, did not turn back, and his mind felt no weariness;
he endured such suffering for a thousand years until, after twenty thousand years had passed, he finally reached the threshold of the second gate.
When eighty-four thousand years had passed and seven days were yet to complete, he finally arrived at the gate of the seventh enclosure.
At that time, the prince saw this bodhisattva and spoke these words:
"O ascetic, what do you seek by coming here now?"
Thereupon, they conceived an inconceivable mind toward the Bodhisattva, thinking:
"How is it that this person, having undergone such manifold sufferings for so long a time, does not grow weary in heart?"
A second and a third time he spoke thus:
"Ascetic, what is it that you now seek to obtain?
At that time, the Bodhisattva, knowing that the prince's mind was already subdued, spoke these verses:
"Whatever wealth exists in the world—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, as well as the four types of offerings—I have no need for them; I have come here solely for the sake of the Dharma."
In this world there is a Buddha named Prabhāsa, who preaches the unsurpassed Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
having heard it, sentient beings are freed from afflictions and likewise partake of the flavor of immeasurable nectar.
The appearance of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in this world is rarer than that of the auspicious *utpala* flower;
yet now that the Unsurpassed Honored One has appeared in this world, you remain heedless, sinking into the ocean of desire.
All sentient beings always walk in darkness, yet the unsurpassed Tathāgata bestows the torch of wisdom;
though they harbor arrogance born of wealth and beauty, they do not go to seek the Honored One, the Tathāgata.
"All wealth, treasures, and the lives of sentient beings— The Buddha says these two are both impermanent.
If sentient beings hear this nectar-like teaching And yet do not go to the Buddha, they are called heedless."
In the past, when you practiced for enlightenment, you invited all sentient beings to partake of the flavor of the Dharma;
yet now you are still subject to the various afflictions—how can you possibly discipline those who are heedless?
I now entreat you to go together to the Buddha; destroy your pride and leave behind all afflictions.
Diligently cultivate vigor and renounce affairs of state, so that at the time of your end, your heart shall have no regrets.
At that time, having heard this, the prince abandoned arrogance and immediately gave rise to faith;
he praised and reverently honored pure diligence, and repented for the suffering he had previously inflicted.
"I have now renounced the affairs of my kingdom, as well as the most sublime pleasures of the five desires;
having shattered pride, I have come to the Buddha's presence to hear the nectar-like Dharma and to harmonize all sentient beings."
Surrounded by an assembly of eighty-four thousand, they carried exquisite incense and flowers to go and make offerings;
having arrived, they immediately presented them to the Buddha, and casting aside pride, they listened to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Prostrating with palms joined in joy, he addressed these words to the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"I now take refuge in You, whose pure diligence subdues me even as I endure suffering without regret.
Though I were to present many offerings, they could not repay Your kindness; I now, before the Buddha, repent with a sincere heart."
In the path of enlightenment that I practice, I tame sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion;
I shall no longer give rise to a negligent mind until I have attained the path of enlightenment.

“Good son! At that time, the prince immediately renounced the royal throne, left the household life to enter the Buddha-dharma, listened to the Dharma, and dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
"Good son! Do you think that the one named Pure Diligence at that time was anyone else?
Do not view it so; he was none other than myself."
As for the one of wealth and merit, he is none other than Maitreya.
Good son! Therefore, the bodhisattva’s practice of taming sentient beings is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
If there is a bodhisattva who is able to discipline sentient beings, this is the practice cultivated by a true bodhisattva. Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four kinds of activities:
First, the bodhisattva practice of purifying buddha-fields;
second, the bodhisattva practice of purifying the body;
third, the bodhisattva practice of purifying speech.
Fourth, the bodhisattva practice of seeking all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four practices:
first, knowing the mind;
Second, knowledge of the faculties;
third, knowledge of the afflictions;
fourth, the ability to treat them.

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin took from the top of his hair-knot a genuine jewel whose value was immeasurable and which had arisen from immeasurable karma, and offered it to the Tathāgata.
He made this vow:
"I now offer this crest-jewel to the Buddha; may this merit become the head for all sentient beings, and by means of these causes and conditions, may I attain unsurpassed wisdom."
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.
Then, from his mouth issued a great radiance of various and manifold colors, which was able to completely obscure all other lights.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣiprapratibhāna rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition does the Tathāgata smile?"
The Buddha said,
"Good son, do you see the jewel on the crown that Ratnaśikhin gave to me?"
“I have seen it, World-Honored One. “Noble son!”

Thus, this bodhisattva has already, in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; maintaining the precepts and exerting diligence, he has sought awakening, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and has likewise tamed immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

“Good son! Thus, in a future age, after ten asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, this bodhisattva shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, named Ratnasaṃbhava. His world shall be named Vimalaprabhā, and his kalpa shall be named Vimala.”

That Buddha-world is composed of the seven treasures, and its radiance shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Among all its inhabitants, there is neither hunger nor thirst; they are all exclusively pure bodhisattvas. From their very first hearing, they never hear the names of the two vehicles, but constantly hear only the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Ratnasaṃbhava (Jewel-Arisen).

All the bodhisattvas therein are fully endowed with supernormal powers; that land has no ruler other than the Dharma King. All sentient beings there are born by transformation, and even the names of the three evil realms, as well as the male and female sexual organs or the name of lustful desire, do not exist.
There are no sentient beings who do not possess their full faculties, nor is there any borderland; the lifespan of these sentient beings is forty thousand intermediate kalpas.

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of nothing else, except for the six perfections, the bodhisattvas' compassion, and all those of sharp faculties, who upon hearing a single phrase, awaken to and understand a thousand phrases.
"This Buddha constantly expounds the *dhāraṇī* vajra-words for all bodhisattvas.
What are called the *dhāraṇī* vajra-words?
The *dhāraṇī* vajra-words are, in fact, a single word."
This single phrase encompasses all phrases of phenomena and phrases of inexhaustible phenomena;
since these phrases of inexhaustible phenomena cannot be exhausted by any Buddha, they are called the practice of the phrases of inexhaustible phenomena.
The inexhaustible *dharmapada* encompasses all syllables (*akṣara*), and all syllables encompass all *dharmapadas*.

One cannot speak two syllables at once, nor can one syllable be joined with another; therefore, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "constructed phrase" (*kṛtapada*), and a "syllabic phrase" (*akṣarapada*).
If one does not differentiate between syllables and phrases, dharma-phrases and composed sentences, this is called the Vajra-phrase of dhāraṇī. "Good son!
This Vajra-phrase of dhāraṇī is that which that Buddha constantly teaches to all bodhisattvas."
"Good son! Whether in a full eon or slightly less than an eon, I could not fully exhaust all the merits of that Tathāgata through speech.
At that time, having heard this prophecy, Ratnaśikhin was filled with great joy and spoke these verses in praise:
"Knowing and seeing all things, having reached the further shore of all dharmas,
and being far removed from all afflictions— for these reasons, he is called the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Honored One."
I have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas; The Tathāgata understands them all as being like a single Buddha.
The Tathāgata has attained unimpeded wisdom, And thus knows the three periods of time without obstruction.
The Tathāgata now bestows upon me this prediction, causing my mind to be freed from the net of doubt;
I too shall attain the true path, just as the Honored Śākyamuni has done.
One might cause the entire great earth to disintegrate, Or cause the sun and moon in the void to fall;
But the words of the Tathāgata are without duality, Therefore, I shall certainly attain Bodhi.
With speech that is correct, truthful, and sublime, you grant me the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment;
if I truly attain enlightenment, I shall skillfully subdue immeasurable multitudes.
The Buddha has already described the pure and wondrous land that I have attained, as well as its great assembly;
having now heard this unsurpassed Dharma, my doubts are destroyed and I advance toward Bodhi.
I now cultivate bodhi with diligence, taming sentient beings without regret;
today the Buddha’s own mouth has bestowed upon me the power of faith, supreme wisdom, and the power of a buddha.
When these verses were spoken, twelve thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, each saying:
"May we all be born in that world."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this True Dharma, for the great benefit of all devas and people of the world.”
Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who believe in and accept this sutra, they shall certainly receive my prediction of enlightenment. Good son!

If one were to bestow upon sentient beings the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm for a full thousand years, it would not equal the merit of someone who receives, maintains, reads, and transcribes such a sutra as this.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?”
"How should it be upheld?
"Ānanda! This sutra is titled 'The Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Great Dhāraṇī: The Entrance for Bodhisattvas of Great Conduct.'"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda, along with all the devas and the people of the world, were filled with great joy;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly. *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle 26 [and] Fascicle 27.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Zhìyán and Bǎoyún of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. Part One of Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Tathāgata’s Practice Hall, Adorned with Jewels, in the city of Rājagṛha—a place accomplished through the cultivation of great merit, the fruit of the fundamental practices of all the Buddha’s dharmas, and a vast container for immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas.

All that he proclaims consists entirely of immeasurable and most profound meanings; all are sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, as he enters the subtle and wondrous gateway of unimpeded practice and wisdom.
Their minds are joyful, attaining mindfulness, diligence, and resolve; they possess discerning wisdom and are never disparaged by others.
If their merits were to be extolled and praised, they would remain inexhaustible throughout the entirety of the future world.

The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has awakened to the equality of all phenomena; he skillfully turns the wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes, attaining mastery over all dharmas. He knows the intentions of sentient beings and exhausts their very roots, skillfully severing all habitual tendencies for them, yet though he performs these buddha-activities, his mind remains free of deliberate action.

He was accompanied by six million great bhikṣus, all of whom were sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King; they had attained liberation well and severed the habitual tendencies of affliction, were thoroughly proficient in the profound *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, and had perfected their dignified deportment so that their conduct was upright and majestic. They were worthy of receiving offerings as fields of merit for the masses, and skillfully upheld the teachings and precepts spoken by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, numbering immeasurably, incalculable, inconceivable, and beyond description.

In a single thought-instant, these bodhisattvas were able to traverse immeasurable and boundless buddha-fields; they had already made offerings to the buddhas of the past and received the sublime Dharma without ever being satiated; they constantly and diligently transformed and taught immeasurable sentient beings, and were well-versed in skillful means and fully endowed with wisdom.

Their minds dwell securely in unimpeded liberation; they have skillfully eliminated discursive thoughts, grasping at signs, and frivolous proliferation. Approaching all-knowledge, they are all in their final birth before Buddhahood. Their names are:

Bodhisattva Electric Sky, Bodhisattva Victorious in Dispute, Bodhisattva Solar Treasury, Bodhisattva Valiant Hero, Bodhisattva Free from Evil Intent, Bodhisattva Wandering, Bodhisattva Eye-Contemplator, and Bodhisattva Free from Darkness. Such are the immeasurable bodhisattva mahāsattvas, whose virtues are all like this.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the sūtra of the unimpeded dharma-gates practiced by all bodhisattvas, namely: the profound Buddha-dharma that adorns the path of all bodhisattvas; the accomplishment of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and wisdom; the attainment of the sovereign seal-gate of dhāraṇī; the gate of great supernormal powers that distinguishes various eloquences; the turning of the irreversible wheel of the non-arising Dharma; the thorough penetration of all phenomena as being identical to a single mark; and the non-arising of discrimination regarding phenomena of a single mark.

He knows the faculties and natures of all sentient beings without obstruction; he is skillfully able to contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; he destroys all realms of Māra; he enters the gate of thorough penetration and wise reflection; he can eliminate all afflictions and views; and he possesses unobstructed wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

All Buddha-dharmas are equal and non-dual; one upholds the gateway to the wisdom of all Buddhas, expounds all dharmas according to their true marks, enters the gate of equality through recollection and the grasping of marks, accomplishes merit by entering deep causal conditions, and adorns the Buddha-body through the actions of body, speech, and mind.

He manifests the four truths through mindfulness, intention, diligence, and retention; he distinguishes sublime wisdom for the sake of transforming śrāvakas; he brings tranquility to body and mind for the sake of transforming pratyekabuddhas; he attains all-knowledge for the sake of transforming those of the Mahāyāna; and he enters into all dharmas to attain sovereign wisdom for the sake of praising the various merits of the Tathāgata. Through such gateways, he proclaims, reveals, instructs, and analyzes.

At that time, while the Buddha was preaching this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, a great golden light spontaneously appeared from the east, illuminating this trichiliocosm so that there was nowhere it did not pervade.

Except for the radiance of the Buddha, all the light of the sun, the moon, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, the various nāgas, ghosts, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas was completely eclipsed and no longer appeared.

The light thoroughly illuminated all walls, enclosures, trees, groves, small mountains, great mountains, Mount Mucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, and the spaces between the lands.

If all the hells within this world-system were to be bathed in that light, when its rays touched the bodies of the sentient beings therein, all their painful sensations would be eliminated and they would experience sublime bliss.

At that time, from within the great assembly before the Buddha, sixty billion pure and wondrous lotus flowers spontaneously emerged from the earth. A fragrant aroma spread abroad, and they were adorned with various ornaments; the diverse colors of the flowers gladdened the hearts of the multitude.

Each of those flowers has a hundred billion petals, covered above by nets of precious jewels; their substance is as soft and supple as celestial garments, and whoever touches them experiences sublime bliss.
The various fragrances emitted by each of these flowers pervaded the trichiliocosm;
within this world-system, all the fragrances belonging to gods or humans were completely extinguished and could no longer be perceived.
When the various classes of beings, including the nāgas, smelled this fragrance, they all attained sublime joy and gradually became free from afflictions.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, seeing this golden radiance and the lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Who has brought about this auspicious omen, this radiance, and these lotus flowers?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“There is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Akṣayamati who is here in the eastern direction, surrounded by a retinue of six billion bodhisattvas. Because he wishes to come here, he has first manifested this auspicious sign.”

Before long, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, by means of his supernatural power, caused this earth to tremble greatly; he emitted immeasurable light and rained down various kinds of flowers. Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of musical performances performed by billions of devas and humans, and surrounded on all sides by a multitude of sixty billion bodhisattvas, he arrived at the place where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he immediately stayed in the air before the Buddha at a height of seven *tāla* trees. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he uttered a subtle and wondrous sound; its resonance was heard throughout the great trichiliocosm. He then praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Pure and forever free from defilement, Valiant and strong, you have eliminated all desires.
Able to extinguish the multitude of afflictions, You have attained the pure and wondrous eye.”
The three stains, the wilderness, and the impurities— You have skillfully severed, vomited out, washed away, and extinguished them all without remainder;
I bow my head to the Greatly Compassionate Awakened One.
You have removed all fears and skillfully destroyed the net of ignorance.
The Holy Sovereign King of Ten Powers cannot be subdued by false doctrines.
Those of external paths and divergent views all harbor fear and dread;
like the lion king, he strides alone without any fear.
The Perfectly Awakened One’s pure radiance, Stainless and shining everywhere,
Amidst the worlds of devas and humans, Is able to dispel all darkness.
Having utterly eliminated the gloom of all obscurity, There is no longer the net of ignorance.
His light is ever bright and pure, like the sun emerging from clouds and mist.
For the sake of those sentient beings who suffer the pains of old age and death and have no one to protect them,
he undergoes immeasurable suffering in order to discipline them.
Only the Samyaksaṃbuddha can give rise to firm compassion;
like a great king of physicians, he diligently applies himself to curing the ailments of all beings.
The source of all dharmas is such that their nature is devoid of a self.
Just as an echo in a mountain valley arises from a multitude of conditions, so too sentient beings have no inherent nature;
there is neither an agent nor a recipient. Yet, for their sake, one gives rise to great compassion.
The ocean-deep abyss of all existence, where the darkness of ignorance is profound,
abounds with discursive thought and investigation, surging with waves of turbulence.
Without hearing the Dharma from another, he has spontaneously reached the further shore.
Like a lotus in the water, one moves through the world unstained;
as autumn leaves fall from the grasses and trees and rivers and ponds dry up in the intense heat,
through analogical reasoning one knows that worldly phenomena are subject to change and do not abide permanently.
Those whom the foolish associate with are reviled and abandoned by the noble and wise;
their understanding of the Dharma is not firm, yet they alone pull themselves out and cross over the stream of existence.
Their countenances are bright and clear, like the *utpala* flower.
Subtle and exceedingly pure, surpassing hundreds of thousands of suns and moons,
all that has been praised throughout the past and by all sentient beings in the present—
the Tathāgata is fully capable of receiving it all.
Because you have tamed that which was untamed, removing heat and attaining coolness, I today bow my head to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
You who transcend the world increase supreme merit; your virtues are without limit.
"Like a bull-king among men, I prostrate before the Buddha, the field of merit.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, having praised the Buddha with such truthful eulogies, descended from mid-air along with a multitude of sixty billion bodhisattvas. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; having paid homage, they circumambulated him three times to the right and sat cross-legged upon the flower pedestals.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
from where has this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati come?”
What is the name of that Buddha?
What is the name of that world?
And how far is it from here?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You may ask him yourself; Akṣayamati shall explain it for you.
Then, respectfully following the Buddha's instruction, Śāriputra questioned Akṣayamati.
"Indeed, son of good family!
From where have you come?
What is the name of that Buddha?"
"What is the name of that world?
How far is it from here? Ajita said:
“Indeed, Śāriputra, do you have the perception of ‘coming’? Śāriputra replied:
"Indeed, noble son! I have understood perception.
Thus spoke Akṣayamati.
"If one knows perception (saṃjñā), there should be no duality of characteristics; for what reason, then, do you ask from where it comes?
Indeed, Śāriputra, that which comes and goes constitutes the meaning of conjunction."

Just as the characteristic of conjunction is neither conjoined nor non-conjoined, so too that which is neither conjoined nor non-conjoined neither goes nor comes; this state of neither going nor coming is the sphere of the noble ones.

"O Śāriputra! That which has coming and going is the characteristic of karma. Just as the characteristic of karma is neither action nor non-action, so too that which is neither action nor non-action neither goes nor comes. That which neither goes nor comes is the sphere of the noble ones."

"O Śāriputra! That which comes and goes is the characteristic of a land. Just as with the characteristic of a land, there is neither a land nor a non-land; that which is neither a land nor a non-land is neither going nor coming. That which neither goes nor comes is the sphere of the noble ones."

"O Śāriputra! That which comes and goes is merely conceptualization based on conditions.
