It is to thoroughly understand that sentient beings are without self, without person, and have nothing to seek; to know that the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are identical to unconditioned liberation; and yet to be able to dedicate these toward all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is called the skillful means of the unconditioned.

"Furthermore, there is conditioned skillful means (*saṃskṛta-upāya*): if one cuts off the continuity of afflictions and birth-and-death so that they do not arise again, and ensures that all roots of goodness that assist awakening (*bodhi*) are not severed, even to the point of not engaging in even a fraction of affliction—this is called conditioned skillful means."
What is the skillful means of the unconditioned?

Although one contemplates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one knows that these three emptinesses are themselves the skillful means that assist the Path; therefore, one is able not to realize [nirvana prematurely]. This is called the skillful means of the unconditioned.

"Furthermore, there is the skillful means of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-upāya*): although one remains within the triple world, one is not defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the triple world; this is called the skillful means of the conditioned.
What is the skillful means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-upāya*)?"
Although one has emerged from the three realms, one does not realize an emergence; this is called the skillful means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As the Buddha has said, by knowing the skillful means of all dharmas, one is able to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is immeasurable and boundless, being fully endowed with right mindfulness, wisdom, and skillful means; therefore, it is called the "skillful means regarding all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-upāya*).
Śāriputra! These are called the eight skillful means that are the objects of focus for a bodhisattva’s wisdom. Śāriputra!
These eight skillful means can encompass the inexhaustible wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra! This wisdom is able to liberate, because it contemplates and thoroughly understands wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
This wisdom is like an arrow, for it is skilled in shooting at the Dharma;
this wisdom is the practice of wealth, for the noble Dharma is present before one;
this wisdom is true understanding, for it severs all views, afflictions, obstacles, and coverings.
This wisdom is concentration and aspiration, for it is able to fully satisfy all that was originally sought;
this wisdom is dissolution, for it can eliminate the burning fevers of the afflictions;
this wisdom is joy, for it does not sever the bliss of the Dharma.
This wisdom is right mindfulness, because it thoroughly understands the meaning of the objects of focus;
this wisdom is stable abiding, because it possesses the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
this wisdom attains the characteristics, because it can fully perfect the vehicle according to its practice.
This wisdom is characterized by liberation, for its nature is the illumination of knowledge;
this wisdom is able to cross over, for it transcends all floods;
this wisdom is able to advance, for it achieves the certainty of right concentration.
This wisdom is right view, for it is fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas;
this wisdom is joyous, for it can rescue those fallen into afflictions;
this wisdom is supreme, for it attains the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan).
This wisdom is subtle and sublime, because it is spontaneously awakened;
this wisdom does not function, because it does not approach the three periods of time;
this wisdom is all-encompassing, because it possesses all skillful means.
This wisdom is able to sever [delusion], for it transcends all conceptual thoughts;
this wisdom is non-negligent, for it abandons all darkness and ignorance;
this wisdom is the initial beginning, for it sets in motion all wholesome dharmas.
This wisdom is able to give rise [to all vehicles], for it is complete with all vehicles;
this wisdom is illuminating, for it removes the net of ignorance;
this wisdom bestows eyes, for all sentient beings obtain clarity according to their respective understandings.
This wisdom is without dependence, for it transcends the eye and visible forms;
this wisdom is the ultimate truth, for it emerges from reality;
this wisdom is without contention, for it is skillful in discernment.
This wisdom is lucid, for it is directed toward the gates of knowledge;
this wisdom is inexhaustible, for it is able to function universally;
this wisdom is non-opposing, for it perceives the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is liberation through wisdom, because all entanglements and fetters have been thoroughly severed;
this is wisdom unmixed, because it is free from all obstructive dharmas. "Śāriputra!

All mental activities of all sentient beings are fully illuminated and penetrated by such wisdom; likewise, the wisdom of contemplation regarding the mental activities of sentient beings, as well as the various gateways of afflictions, are all observed and understood by this wisdom.
Whatever wisdom there is of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, this bodhisattva is able to study it all thoroughly.
Śāriputra! This is called the inexhaustible wisdom of a bodhisattva; by means of this inexhaustible wisdom, they are endowed with inexhaustible knowledge.
When this Dharma was being taught, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas whose roots of goodness had matured attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume 28. Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume 29.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Zhìyán and Bǎoyún of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, Part Three.
At that time, Bodhisattva Akṣayamati spoke again to Śāriputra:
“The bodhisattva’s cultivation of loving-kindness is also inexhaustible. Why is this?

Because the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness is immeasurable and boundless; this cultivation of loving-kindness has no limits, being equal to the realm of sentient beings, as the bodhisattva cultivates loving-kindness with a resolve that universally covers all.”
Śāriputra! Just as space universally covers all without exception, so too is the loving-kindness of this bodhisattva; there is no sentient being who is not covered by it.

Śāriputra! Just as the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of loving-kindness; it is likewise immeasurable, boundless, and without end.

Because space is inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible; because sentient beings are inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s cultivation of loving-kindness is likewise inexhaustible. This is called the great being’s cultivated mind of loving-kindness, which cannot be exhausted.
Śāriputra said: “Good son, to what extent is the realm of sentient beings defined?”
Akṣayamati said: "The extent of the earth element, and the water, fire, and wind elements, is boundless; yet even so, they do not exceed the realm of sentient beings."
Śāriputra said: "Yes, noble son! Is it possible to provide a simile by way of comparison?"
Akṣayamati said: "It may be explained,
but one must not use a minor matter as a metaphor, Śāriputra!"

To the east, extending from here through as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, and likewise to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—throughout all these as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River—one forms a great ocean, its waters overflowing.

Suppose as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River were to gather together; they would take a single hair and divide it into a hundred parts, and with one such part of a hair, they would draw up a single drop of water. In this manner, as many as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River would together take one drop, and as many as there are grains of sand in two Ganges Rivers would together take two drops, continuing in this succession until all the water filling the great ocean is exhausted—yet the realm of sentient beings would still not be exhausted.
The compassionate mind of a Bodhisattva is able to universally encompass all such sentient beings.
Śāriputra, what do you think? Can these roots of goodness cultivated through loving-kindness and compassion ever be exhausted?
Śāriputra said: "Truly, it is inexhaustible.
Indeed, noble son!"
Even the nature of empty space may reach its end, but the compassionate mind of a bodhisattva can never be exhausted.
If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing this teaching, does not give rise to alarm or fear, one should know that this person has attained inexhaustible compassion.

“Śāriputra! This loving-kindness can protect one’s own person; this loving-kindness can also benefit others. This loving-kindness is free from contention; this loving-kindness can sever all anger, defilement, and bondage. This loving-kindness can distance one from all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). This loving-kindness is joyful; this loving-kindness does not perceive the transgressions of precepts in any sentient being. This loving-kindness is without feverish affliction, and body and mind experience bliss. This loving-kindness is far removed from all harm and injury; this loving-kindness can distance one from all fears. This loving-kindness can accord with the path of the noble ones; this loving-kindness can cause those who are angry to rejoice.”
"This loving-kindness can overcome all strife and contention; this loving-kindness can produce gain and praise;
this loving-kindness adorns the majesty and virtue of Śakra and Brahmā; this loving-kindness is always praised by the wise;
this loving-kindness always protects ordinary and foolish people; this loving-kindness can always accord with the Brahma-path; this loving-kindness is unmixed and far-reaching."
This loving-kindness transcends the desire realm; this loving-kindness can lead toward the dharma-gate of liberation;
this loving-kindness can encompass all vehicles; this loving-kindness can encompass non-material merit; this loving-kindness nurtures all merits;
this loving-kindness surpasses all merits of non-action; this loving-kindness is fully able to adorn the primary and secondary marks; this loving-kindness...
This compassion enables one to transcend inferior and dull faculties; this compassion can open the various wholesome, right paths to nirvana for devas and humans;
this compassion enables one to leave behind the three evil realms and the eight difficulties; and this compassion loves and delights in all wholesome dharmas.
"This loving-kindness is the sovereign accomplishment of all desires according to one's wishes; this loving-kindness is impartial toward all sentient beings;
this loving-kindness issues forth free from all signs of differentiation; this loving-kindness is correctly directed toward the gateway of ethical discipline;
this loving-kindness can protect those who have transgressed the prohibitions; this loving-kindness can accomplish the power of supreme patience."
Loving-kindness enables one to abandon all pride and negligence; this loving-kindness gives rise to non-contentious diligence and entry into the right path;
this loving-kindness is the root for entering noble meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); this loving-kindness skillfully discerns the mind and brings it free from all afflictions (*kleśa*);
this loving-kindness, arising through wisdom, produces the dhāraṇīs of speech and letters; this loving-kindness is the companion of meditative concentration.
This loving-kindness is free from the company of Māra; this loving-kindness always dwells together with joy; this loving-kindness is skillfully directed by the mind;
this loving-kindness firmly maintains the precepts of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*); this loving-kindness is able to leave behind all restlessness and the like;
this loving-kindness is able to extinguish various marks (*nimitta*); this loving-kindness is an excellent fragrance that anoints the body with shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*). This is...
Loving-kindness can eliminate the foul odor of afflictions. "Śāriputra!
One who cultivates loving-kindness is able to protect all sentient beings and can relinquish their own happiness to give it to other beings."
The compassion cultivated by śrāvakas is limited to their own persons, whereas the compassion of bodhisattvas extends to all immeasurable sentient beings.

"Śāriputra! Those who cultivate compassion are able to cross over the various torrents; the scope of their compassion encompasses sentient beings with whom they have a connection, or it takes phenomena as its object, or it is without any object."
Taking sentient beings as the object of focus is the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment.
Taking dharmas as the object of focus is the stage of having already practiced and cultivated.
Taking the non-object as the object of focus is the attainment of profound dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*).
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible cultivation of great loving-kindness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of great compassion is likewise inexhaustible.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Just as a person's life-faculty has exhalation and inhalation as its basis, so too the bodhisattva who trains in the Mahāyāna takes great compassion as the basis.
Just as a wheel-turning sage king has the wheel-treasure as his basis, so too the bodhisattva who cultivates omniscience takes great compassion as the basis.

Just as a great elder has an only son for whom he feels deep compassion and affection, so too is the great compassion of a bodhisattva; they love all sentient beings as if they were their own children.

Having thus practiced such great compassion, having thus performed such great compassion for my own benefit, such great compassion does not depend on external things; such great compassion is produced from one's own mind without guile or crookedness; such great compassion results in ultimate certainty through its practice; such great compassion, arising from its seed-nature, issues forth upon the direct path; such great compassion is born upright, with a mind free from perversity or distortion.

"Such great compassion is free from arrogance and emerges from the realm of sentient beings; such great compassion relinquishes one's own body and emerges as the body of a Tathāgata; such great compassion does not crave life and emerges as the non-commission of evil; such great compassion protects sentient beings and emerges as the pursuit of Bodhi; such great compassion guards the true Dharma and emerges as purity of mind; such great compassion beholds all who are in distress and emerges as the act of deliverance; such great compassion is firm in its original vow and emerges as an unshakable mind; such great compassion does not deceive oneself, humans, devas, sages, or saints, and emerges as freedom from falsehood."

"Such great compassion has its practice purified, arising from wholesome karma; such great compassion relinquishes one's own happiness to bestow happiness upon others; such great compassion does not inflict suffering upon others and arises free from burning affliction; such great compassion enables sentient beings to cast off their heavy burdens, arising from firm diligence; such great compassion possesses the power of patience and arises to protect the weak; such great compassion never tires of those who are defiled, arising from the care of the sick; such great compassion attains mastery over the Dharma, arising from the teaching of those with dull faculties; such great compassion conceals one's own virtues and arises to manifest the achievements of others; such great compassion issues forth from the departure from all sufferings; and such great compassion issues forth from the seeking of untainted bliss."

"Such is great compassion that it issues forth the relinquishing of beloved things; such is great compassion that it issues forth the performance of various wholesome deeds without affliction or distress;
such is great compassion that it issues forth the excellent upholding of prohibitions without abandoning those who have broken the precepts;
such is great compassion that it issues forth the teaching and transforming of sentient beings; such is great compassion that it issues forth the non-sparing of body and life; thus..."
Great compassion gives rise to the relinquishing of one's own limbs; great compassion gives rise to the roots of goodness in others;
great compassion gives rise to the roots of goodness for one's own benefit; great compassion gives rise to flavorless meditative absorptions;
great compassion gives rise to non-disgust for the desire realm; great compassion gives rise to contemplative wisdom; thus it is.
Great compassion gives rise to untainted roots of goodness; great compassion gives rise to the fulfillment of the aspirations of all sentient beings;
great compassion gives rise to both the conditioned and the unconditioned; great compassion gives rise to not realizing the unconditioned;
and great compassion gives rise to the knowledge that the nature of sentient beings is identical to the unconditioned, yet being able to teach and transform them. Thus it is.
Great Compassion emerges to protect those who violate the precepts; such great compassion emerges to praise the Buddha’s precepts;
and from the various forms of compassion within the Mahāyāna, Great Compassion emerges. For these reasons, it is called Great Compassion.

"It is said that one who possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) must certainly practice the various factors conducive to enlightenment—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—with perfect skill. To attain spontaneous, teacherless wisdom and to accomplish the tasks of other sentient beings, they apply themselves with diligent and exclusive focus as if cultivating their own affairs. For these reasons, it is called 'great compassion.'"
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of great compassion, which is inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of joy (*muditā*) is likewise inexhaustible.
What is meant by joy?

It is to constantly contemplate the Dharma with rapturous delight, giving rise to no indolence and being free from all afflictive heat; to leave behind the pleasures of the five desires and dwell in the bliss of the Dharma; for the mind to be harmonious and joyful, the body light and supple; to diligently exhort oneself with a mind that constantly gives rise to compassion, and to delight in seeking the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Dharma-body.

They delight in cultivating the primary and secondary marks to adorn themselves; they listen to the Dharma without weariness, contemplating and practicing the True Dharma; having practiced the True Dharma, their hearts give rise to joy; and having given rise to joy, they fully attain the compassion for the Dharma.

"Always not giving rise to obstructive thoughts toward sentient beings, one seeks the Dharma with superior aspiration and diligence; having diligently sought the Dharma, one attains deep understanding of the profound Buddha-dharma through a profound mind. Remaining far removed from the two vehicles, one resolves upon the unexcelled mind; removing all stinginess and parsimony, one gives rise to a mind of relinquishment. Seeing those who come to beg, one’s heart is filled with joy; while giving, one is joyful, and after giving, one has no regret. Thus, this giving is pure in three stages. Having attained such purity, the mind is then glad and content. One always practices giving toward those who uphold the precepts, and with a joyful heart, one embraces even those who violate the prohibitions."
By personally upholding the prohibitive precepts, the mind becomes pure.

One can cause sentient beings who fear the evil realms to attain fearlessness and remain far removed from evil places; with a single-minded dedication to the Tathāgata’s prohibitive precepts, one maintains them firmly and steadfastly so that they cannot be impaired, and when subjected to foul abuse, one endures it without retaliation.
"Regarding all sentient beings, his mind is free from arrogance; toward elders and superiors, he is humble and reverent; his speech is always harmonious and pleasant, free from frowning or scowling.

He begins with affectionate words and never resorts to flattery or crookedness; he does not deceive others with a wicked mind, nor does he employ himself for the sake of gain or profit for others; his mind is pure and free from coarse transgressions."

Regarding those things that are improper, one does not see their faults; one does not seek out the shortcomings of others nor expose their transgressions; with single-minded right mindfulness, one dwells in all dharmas of harmony and respect, and conceives the thought of Tathāgatas toward all bodhisattvas.
One should cherish those who preach the Dharma more than one's own body, and love and honor the Tathāgata as one would cherish one's own life.

One should regard all teachers and elders as one's parents; regard all sentient beings as one's own children; protect all modes of conduct as one protects one's head; cherish all perfections (pāramitās) as one loves one's hands and feet; regard all wholesome dharmas as precious jewels; regard those who offer instruction as sources of the five desires; regard the practice of contentment as freedom from illness; and regard the joyful seeking of the Dharma as the acquisition of excellent medicine.
One conceives the thought of a skilled physician toward those who point out one's faults; one restrains the sense faculties without indolence. For this reason, it is called joy (*prīti*).
This joy is because its awakening is tranquil and subtle; this joy is because its cessation is free from frivolity;
this joy is because its practice relies on non-proliferation (*aprapañca*); this joy is because its root is a mind that is undisturbed. This is joy.
This joy arises from taking up well-spoken words through extensive learning; this joy arises from the pliancy of a mind characterized by equanimity;
this joy arises from the courageous performance of wholesome deeds; this joy arises from the exclusive practice of virtue without regret; this joy arises from dwelling correctly without indolence;
this joy arises from being immovable because of having no dependence; and this joy arises from being uncommon and difficult to overcome.
This joy is because it does not forget the true meaning; this joy is because it is real and unchanging;
this joy is because it is truthful and acts according to what has been done; this joy is because its power of relinquishment is firm;
this joy is because its great power is invincible; this joy is because it can exercise the spiritual powers of all Buddhas to seek all Buddha-dharmas.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible cultivation of joy.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is likewise inexhaustible.
How is it that the bodhisattva’s cultivation of equanimity is inexhaustible?
When a bodhisattva practices equanimity, there are three kinds of equanimity.
What are the three? They are:
relinquishing all afflictions, relinquishing the protection of oneself and others, and relinquishing the timely and the untimely.
What is meant by "relinquishing all afflictions"?
When receiving respectful offerings, his mind is not elated; when encountering contempt or disparagement, his mind is not depressed.
When gaining profit and sustenance, his mind does not harbor greedy attachment; when meeting with decline or affliction, his mind feels no distress.
When encountering praise and acclaim, his mind has no sense of jubilation; when encountering those who revile him, his mind does not shrink back.
If one encounters those who revile them, their mind remains free from shame or dejection; if there are those who praise them, they dwell well within the *dharmadhātu*.
If they encounter suffering, they endure it with mental strength; if they encounter pleasure, they clearly perceive its impermanence.

Relinquishing what is cherished and severing ill-will, one attains a mind of equanimity toward both kin and non-kin; whether others uphold the precepts or violate them, one’s mind neither increases nor diminishes, perceiving no dualistic distinction between those who do good and those who do evil.

The mind has no attachment toward what is pleasant or unpleasant; hearing the good or the evil, the mind is able to endure it; the mind is not bound or attached to good or evil speech; and regarding the faults of sensory flavors, its measure is non-dual.

One attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; one attains equal radiance regarding those who are superior, middling, or inferior; and one regards body, life, and reputation—whether good or bad—as identical to the dharma-realm.

When the mind attains purity regarding both real and unreal phenomena, and when one attains the bodhisattva’s equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward worldly dharmas and so forth, this is called the bodhisattva’s relinquishing of afflictions.
How does a bodhisattva practice the relinquishing that protects both self and others?

If one's body and limbs are severed and cut, the mind remains free from anger and resentment, seeking no retribution; because one has attained the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one is able to relinquish both extremes, and thus neither body nor speech—within these two—gives rise to contention.

There is no defilement of desire regarding the eye and forms; it is likewise for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena. Thus, because no dispute arises between these two, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It is called equanimity (*upekṣā*) because it neither harms nor injures; it is called equanimity because it protects both oneself and others through relinquishment.

It is called equanimity because the mind acts with impartiality toward gain and loss; it is called equanimity because it does not give rise to dispute regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); it is called equanimity because it is well able to discern within one's own mind.
One observes the relinquishing of one's own body, and thus it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*); one does not harm the bodies of others, and thus it is called "equanimity.

While Bodhisattvas cultivate equanimity and constantly practice a mind of equanimity within all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not permit Bodhisattvas to practice a mind of equanimity toward sentient beings [in the sense of indifference].

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates diligence, striving to seek roots of goodness for the benefit of both self and others; this is called a bodhisattva’s relinquishing of protection for oneself and others.
What is meant by "relinquishing at the proper time and the improper time"?

They abandon and do not attempt to guide sentient beings who are not fit vessels; they abandon and do not accept decline, ruin, censure, or suffering; and they abandon those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and have reached a fixed determination.

When practicing generosity, they set aside the cultivation of ethical discipline; when cultivating ethical discipline, they set aside generosity; when cultivating patience, they set aside generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence; when cultivating diligence, they set aside generosity, ethical discipline, and patience; when practicing meditative concentration, they set aside generosity; and when cultivating wisdom, they set aside the five pāramitās. Whatever should not be done, they never do again.

When one thus abides in the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*) among all these dharmas, exerting oneself with vigor and fully accomplishing the cultivation, this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of inexhaustible relinquishment (*tyāga*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of bodhisattvas are likewise inexhaustible.
What are these various supernormal powers?

They are the supernormal power of the divine eye, the supernormal power of the divine ear, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, and the supernormal power of mastery over mental transformations.
"What is the supernormal power of the divine eye?

The Bodhisattva’s divine eye is the foremost among all the divine eyes possessed by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. It is subtle, exquisite, penetrating, and clear; it is accomplished through the merit directed toward omniscience, and is not shared with devas, nāgas, or the followers of the two vehicles."

If there are the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, with all their forms, appearances, and radiances—whether coarse or subtle, near or far—the Bodhisattva’s divine eye sees them all entirely; he illuminates, discerns, understands well, and perceives them clearly, and he also sees all the sentient beings born within them in their various realms of existence, with the exception of those in the formless heavens.
Furthermore, regarding the continuity of birth and death through residual karmic actions, he knows all the various faculties resulting from each specific karma without exception.

He sees, without omission, all the adorned and pure wondrous lands of the immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions; having seen them thus, he maintains pure precepts and vows to dedicate this merit toward adorning his own land.
Abiding in this observance of the precepts, they fully accomplish immeasurable great benefits according to their aspirations.

With the divine eye, the Bodhisattva also sees the great assembly of Bodhisattvas therein practicing the Path—their four modes of deportment and right mindfulness, their attainment of the Dharma of liberation and their abiding in *dhāraṇī*, as well as their eloquence, skillful means, and entry into the skillful means of wisdom.
Having seen this, he personally cultivates all such practices until they are fully perfected.
Because this Bodhisattva’s eye is pure and unobstructed in its seeing of forms; because this eye is unstained and unattached to forms;
because this eye is liberated through being far removed from all views and afflictions; this eye is pure.
Because its nature is lucid; because this eye does not rely on the separation from objects of perception; because this eye does not arise to sever afflictions;
because this eye is free of cataracts to sever the web of doubt; because this eye does not arise to sever obstacles;
because this eye attains clarity to illuminate and comprehend all phenomena; because this eye knows through mindfulness and does not function as ordinary consciousness; it is this...
This eye is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, for it can sever all fetters and latent tendencies;
this eye is the unsurpassed path to the noble foundation; this eye is unobstructed and equal, its radiance illuminating all sentient beings;
this eye is stainless, for it severs unwholesome dharmas; this eye is undefiled, for its nature is pure; this eye enters into the Buddha.
Because the eye is ultimately never abandoned; because this eye is neither bound nor severed from craving and aversion;
and because the functioning of this eye proceeds toward the ultimate meaning by means of practicing the pure path of mindfulness and knowledge.

Why is this? Because this Great Being dwells securely in great compassion and has a profound understanding of the characteristics of phenomena; he skillfully discerns their meanings without dispute, speaks in accordance with what he sees and hears while turning away from unwholesome dharmas, and proceeds toward the site of enlightenment with a mind free from obstruction.

Seeing those who are stingy, they cause them to relinquish wealth through giving; seeing those who violate the precepts, they cause them to cultivate and maintain pure morality; seeing those who harbor anger, they cultivate patience and refrain from contention; seeing those who are indolent, they gather them in and encourage them; seeing those with distracted minds, they demonstrate the various factors of dhyāna; to those lacking wisdom, they bestow the eye of insight; to those traveling on false paths, they show the true path; and for those practicing inferior ways, they expound the profound and subtle Buddha-dharma to lead them into omniscience, so that they do not regress from their supernormal powers and become fully endowed with bodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the divine eye, which is inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The divine ear superknowledge (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise inexhaustible.
What is the divine ear superknowledge of a bodhisattva?

It is the hearing of all sounds throughout the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—namely, the sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—as well as the noble sounds, namely the sounds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
Whatever sounds are encountered by the faculty of hearing—even those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, including flies, ants, mosquitoes, and gnats—all are heard without exception.

Whatever objects the minds of sentient beings take as their focus, and whatever actions they perform—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—they understand all the sounds that emerge from them.
If there are verbal actions that are wholesome, verbal actions that are unwholesome, or verbal actions that are indeterminate, he knows all such actions exactly as they are.

Furthermore, if there is a verbal action arising from desire that speaks of hatred or delusion; if there is a verbal action arising from hatred that speaks of desire or delusion; if there is a verbal action arising from delusion that speaks of desire or hatred; or if, based on desire one speaks of desire, based on hatred one speaks of hatred, and based on delusion one speaks of delusion—he is likewise able to know all such sounds.

There may be vocal karma where the mind is pure but the speech is coarse; there may be vocal karma where the speech is pure but the mind is coarse; there may be vocal karma where both speech and mind are pure; and there may be vocal karma where both speech and mind are coarse. All such cases are known as they truly are by one with unimpeded supernormal power of the ear.
This bodhisattva’s divine ear also discerns both noble sounds and non-noble sounds.
Upon hearing noble sounds, they do not give rise to attachment; upon hearing non-noble sounds, their mind does not give rise to obstruction.
Toward the voices of noble beings, they attain great loving-kindness; toward the voices of non-noble beings, they attain great compassion.
If they hear sounds of the past and future, they attain the true and correct knowledge that exhausts the ultimate limit.

This is the bodhisattva’s divine ear: it hears the sublime Dharma spoken by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; having heard it, they maintain it through mindfulness and the dhāraṇī of correct knowledge, neither forgetting nor losing it; they preach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, and they skillfully know the characteristics of the firmness and non-firmness of all phenomena.
It is impossible that such a bodhisattva, while listening to the Dharma taught by one Buddha, would fail to hear the Dharma taught by other Buddhas;

they are able to listen to and receive all that is expounded by all Buddhas. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva hears the sounds of dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, they thoroughly know both the appropriate and inappropriate times for them.
That is to say, if there is an assembly but it is not the time for preaching the Dharma, one remains silent after hearing [the request] and says nothing.
If it is the time for preaching but there is no assembly—meaning one is properly addressing a single person who is capable of receiving it—one therefore speaks, yet does not do so for everyone.

If a matter is true, one may refrain from speaking of it out of fear of harming others; if a matter is untrue, one may speak of it through skillful means with a pure mind for the sake of benefiting others.
If there are sounds they find pleasing, they are able to hear them; those that are not pleasing, they no longer hear.

When they expound the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings within a great assembly, the celestial ear of this bodhisattva hears and understands everything according to what their auditory consciousness can comprehend and receive.
When the Dharma is being taught, if there are sentient beings who are ready to attain understanding, they shall hear the Dharma; those who are not yet ready for understanding shall not hear it.

This is because the nature of this Bodhisattva’s auditory element (*śrotra-dhātu*) and the Dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) is pure, as he perceives that the self, persons, and sentient beings are all entirely pure.
This bodhisattva correctly discerns the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) according to the characteristics described by words and letters.

If there are sentient beings of various kinds within the five destinies, he preaches the Dharma to them according to the sounds and voices of their respective understandings. He dedicates this divine ear toward the ear-element attained by the Tathāgata, for he does not seek any other vehicle (*yāna*).
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the divine ear, which is inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The bodhisattva’s supernormal power of knowing the minds of others is likewise inexhaustible. What is the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of knowing the minds of others? It is that the bodhisattva fully knows the superior, middling, and inferior minds of all sentient beings.

He knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of giving; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of ethical discipline; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of patience; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of diligence; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of concentration; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculty of wisdom; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculties of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; he knows the mental characteristics of those sentient beings based on the faculties of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna vehicles; and he knows that these sentient beings have been born here because they possess superior roots of goodness through their powers, or because they possess superior roots of goodness through their practices.

He knows those sentient beings whose conduct is pure but whose minds are impure; he knows those sentient beings whose conduct is impure but whose minds are pure; he knows those sentient beings whose both mind and conduct are pure; and he knows those sentient beings whose both conduct and mind are impure.
To know the causes of the past minds, faculties, and conducts of sentient beings, and to know that these sentient beings awaken to the Dharma according to conditions—
this is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the minds of others.

Furthermore, he knows the minds of others in future lives; he knows that for these sentient beings there will be the cause of observing the precepts in future lives, and the cause of practicing generosity in the present life.
He knows that this sentient being has the cause for patience in future lives and the cause for upholding the precepts in the present life.
He knows that this sentient being has the cause for diligence in future lives and the cause for patience in the present life.
He knows that these sentient beings possess the cause for meditative concentration in future lives, while possessing the cause for diligence in the present life.
He knows that these sentient beings possess the cause for wisdom in future lives, while practicing the causes of worldly mind in the present life.

Knowing that these sentient beings will produce the causes for the Mahāyāna in future lives, yet possess the causes for inferior faculties in the present life—and knowing that such various causes and conditions exist for sentient beings in the future—the Bodhisattva understands these causes and conditions as they truly are. Thus, he never grows weary of sentient beings who have not yet been transformed; he understands their mental faculties and dispositions as they truly are, and teaches the Dharma according to their capacities.

If one delights in hearing little, one does not speak much; yet whatever one says is necessarily beneficial, and the effort is never in vain. This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the minds of others.

Furthermore, regarding the conduct of sentient beings in the present world, they know all mental states and mental factors exactly as they are: that is to say, they know a mind of desire as a mind of desire, and they know a mind free from desire as a mind free from desire.
He knows a mind of hatred as it truly is—a mind of hatred; he knows a mind free from hatred as it truly is—a mind free from hatred.
He knows a deluded mind as it truly is—a deluded mind; he knows a mind free from delusion as it truly is—a mind free from delusion.
He knows a distracted mind as a distracted mind, and he knows a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind.
He knows a slothful mind as a slothful mind, and he knows a diligent mind as a diligent mind.
One knows a low state of mind as it truly is a low state of mind; one knows a superior state of mind as it truly is a superior state of mind.
One knows a distracted state of mind as it truly is a distracted state of mind; one knows a concentrated state of mind as it truly is a concentrated state of mind.
He knows a mind not liberated as a mind not liberated, and he knows a mind liberated as a mind liberated.
He knows a mind not tranquil as a mind not tranquil, and he knows a mind tranquil as a mind tranquil.
He knows a limited mind as a limited mind, and he knows an immeasurable mind as an immeasurable mind, knowing them all as they truly are.

He knows every single affliction that binds and obscures the minds of each and every sentient being; having known this, he teaches the Dharma according to the path by which they may emerge from those afflictions.
Furthermore, wherever this bodhisattva dwells, he first observes sentient beings to discern the measure of their faculties, and accordingly expounds for them the Dharma that leads to liberation.
He knows the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all these sentient beings exactly as they are; when this bodhisattva’s mind knows the minds of others, there is no obstruction whatsoever.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas possess minds of sharp and keen intelligence that are skilled in discernment; because they know through mindfulness, intention, diligence, and wisdom; because they are well able to comprehend the characteristics of bodhi; because they have severed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); because they are pure and stainless; because they are clearly aware and free from contention; because they are devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*); because they are free from the deep currents [of saṃsāra]; because they illuminate all phenomena (*dharma*); and because they skillfully enter the minds of all sentient beings—they are able to understand in such a manner.

When this bodhisattva’s mental faculty is sharp and keen, and they correctly enter into and know such dharmas, this is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of knowledge of past lives is also inexhaustible.
What is the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of knowledge of past lives?

This bodhisattva recollects matters of past lives, whether his own or those of others, receiving and retaining them well; he dwells securely in the *dharmadhātu* without wavering, for one who does not waver is able to skillfully understand and perform wholesome deeds. This mindfulness is free from affliction because it dwells securely in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This mindfulness is fearless because it skillfully gathers wisdom. This mindfulness does not seek from others because it attains skillful knowledge in the present. This mindfulness is right recollection because it is ultimately never lost. This mindfulness assists merit because it skillfully understands the Mahāyāna. This mindfulness assists wisdom because it is fully perfected without depending on others. This mindfulness of roots of goodness and the perfections (*pāramitās*) is able to reach all Buddha-dharmas because they are fully perfected.

This is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*): whether recollecting one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, up to a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of births, immeasurable thousands of births, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, as well as the formation and destruction of the world-systems—immeasurable aeons of formation, immeasurable aeons of destruction, immeasurable aeons of both formation and destruction, and immeasurable kalpas of both formation and destruction.
He knows that all sentient beings are born therein, with such lineages, such names, such physical forms, such food and drink, such lifespans, and [experiences] of suffering and pleasure.
Dying here, they are reborn here; dying there, they are reborn there.

This bodhisattva contemplates such immeasurable births and deaths, reflecting upon his own past lives and those of other sentient beings throughout the limits of the past. This bodhisattva dedicates his own roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and regarding the roots of goodness of others, he vows that they shall all give rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
With a mind of right mindfulness, this bodhisattva skillfully contemplates impermanence, suffering, and non-self within the fundamental suffering of birth and death.

When contemplating impermanence, suffering, and non-self, they are entirely without greedy attachment to material desires, rank, emoluments, lifespan, or sovereign power over kin; nor do they crave the five sensual pleasures of Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, or universal monarchs, nor the joys of rebirth in various realms. Yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifest the taking of birth.

When this bodhisattva has contemplated impermanence, suffering, and non-self, they confess and repent for past defiled actions; regarding all evils in the present life, they will never commit them even at the cost of their own lives.

Desiring to cause past roots of goodness to increase and expand, they dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they share present roots of goodness with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because this bodhisattva has abandoned all evil vows and does not sever the lineage of the Three Jewels, they dedicate all their roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible knowledge of recollecting past lives. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The *ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna* (supernormal power of psychic transformation) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise inexhaustible.
What is the *ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna* of a bodhisattva?

It is that which is comprised of the factors of desire, exertion, mind, and wisdom; through the mastery of a mind made pliant and subdued by skillful cultivation and accumulation, one attains this supernormal power of psychic transformation in the present.

This bodhisattva performs various supernatural transformations; by means of these supernormal powers, he transforms sentient beings. This bodhisattva manifests each kind of supernatural power individually to teach and transform sentient beings—namely, whether through physical forms, through power and majesty, or through transformations.

This bodhisattva manifests various forms and appearances so that sentient beings, upon seeing them, may have their minds subdued. These include the form and appearance of a Buddha, the form and appearance of a pratyekabuddha, the form and appearance of a śrāvaka, the form and appearance of Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, or a cakravartin king, as well as other various and immeasurable forms and appearances, even manifesting the form and appearance of an animal. He manifests these for the sake of transforming sentient beings, and having manifested them, he teaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.

"If there are sentient beings who, claiming for themselves great power, give rise to arrogance, anger, and haughtiness, the Bodhisattva, wishing to subdue such beings, manifests great power—namely, manifesting one-quarter of Nārāyaṇa’s strength, or two-quarters, or three-quarters, or manifesting it in its entirety."

Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas in height and eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth; yet to lift it with three fingers and hurl it to immeasurable worlds in other directions—just as if tossing a single *āmalaka* fruit—does not diminish the power of a bodhisattva.
He can seize the trichiliocosm, from its base at the limits of the waters up to its zenith at the Peak of Existence, and lift it with his hand, holding it aloft for an entire kalpa.

When a bodhisattva has accomplished such a manifestation of great power, he is able to inwardly subdue sentient beings who are full of anger, pride, and arrogance; having subdued them, he then teaches the Dharma to them according to their needs.

"This Bodhisattva cultivates the supernormal power of psychic transformation (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), thereby attaining the power of wisdom for transformations; through this power of transformation, whatever he desires to do is entirely accomplished."

He can transform the great ocean into a cow’s footprint, yet the great ocean does not become small; he can also transform a cow’s footprint into the great ocean, yet the cow’s footprint does not become large.
When the kalpa is about to end and the calamity of fire arises, if he wishes to transform it into water, he can transform it as he desires;

when the calamity of water arises, he can transform it into fire; when the calamity of wind arises, he can transform it into fire; when the calamity of fire arises, he can transform it into wind; when the calamity of wind arises, he can transform it into water; and when the calamity of water arises, he can transform it into wind. Such transformations are all fully accomplished.

If superior, middling, or inferior phenomena are transformed at will, no one other than the Buddhas—neither Śakra, Brahmā, the celestial kings, nor Māra Pāpīyān and his retinue—is able to move, obstruct, or destroy the Bodhisattva’s supernormal power of mastery over the mind (rddhi-vidhi).
This bodhisattva performs various transformations, manifesting them to all sentient beings to bring them joy; thereafter, he preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations.

This bodhisattva’s supernormal powers are courageous, robust, and sovereign; he is able to transcend the realms of all Māras and afflictions, entering the Buddha-realm without distressing sentient beings. All his roots of goodness are fully accomplished, such that no host of Māras can sever them.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible supernormal power of mastery (ṛddhividhi). Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of a bodhisattva are likewise inexhaustible.
What are these four? First, generosity (*dāna*); [the others are: [kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality].
Second, pleasant speech;
third, beneficial conduct;
fourth, common purpose.
What is giving? There are two kinds of giving:
the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma.
What is kind speech?
It is speaking with gentleness to those who seek wealth as well as to those who listen to the Dharma.
What is beneficial conduct?
Regarding those who seek wealth and those who listen to the Dharma, one causes them all to have their requests fulfilled according to what they seek.
What is "common benefit"?
It is to establish those who seek wealth and the Dharma in the personal benefit of the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, as for giving, it is when one sees those who beg and gives rise to a pure mind.
As for kind speech, it is when one feels joy in one's heart toward those who beg.
As for beneficial conduct, it is when one enables those who beg to become fully endowed with whatever benefits they require."
"Common benefit" means constantly exhorting and instructing sentient beings through the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, giving" refers to the mind of relinquishment;
"loving speech" refers to practicing without limit or measure.
Regarding beneficial conduct, one ultimately has no regrets.
Regarding shared benefit, one dedicates [the merit] toward the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, regarding giving, one gives rise to loving-kindness and practices equanimity.
Loving speech means not abandoning a joyful mind.
Beneficial conduct means adorning great compassion to benefit sentient beings.
Shared purpose means relinquishing notions of high and low, and directing the aspiration toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
"Furthermore, regarding generosity: one seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and practices giving with purity.
Regarding kind speech: one guides those who are dear toward and establishes them in wholesome dharmas.
Regarding beneficial conduct: one speaks of one's own benefit in order to bring benefit to others."
"Benefiting others with common interests means causing all sentient beings to give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*).
Furthermore, 'generosity' means relinquishing both internal and external things;
'loving speech' means that the mind of merit and wisdom is free from stinginess."
"Beneficial action" means abandoning actions for one's own benefit to practice for the benefit of others.
"Shared benefit" means relinquishing a position of high status without the slightest regret in one's heart.
Furthermore, "Dharma-giving" means being able to expound all the teachings exactly as they have been heard.
Loving speech means preaching the Dharma not for the sake of gain or sustenance.
Beneficial conduct means instructing others in recitation without weariness of heart.
Shared benefit means that whatever sublime Dharma has been attained through the mind of omniscience, one uses that very Dharma to exhort and encourage sentient beings.
"Furthermore, as for the gift of Dharma: if there are sentient beings who listen to the Dharma one by one, he explains it to them in successive order without error.
As for kind speech: when preaching the Dharma for others, he does not decline on account of distance."

Regarding those who practice beneficial conduct: for those who seek the Dharma, they provide clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness so that they lack nothing; having first bestowed such comforts, they then expound the teaching to them according to their needs.
Regarding "common benefit," in all that one preaches and explains, one constantly exhorts sentient beings to dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, regarding the gift of Dharma, among all forms of giving, one recognizes it as the most supreme; thus, one expounds this supreme Dharma for others.
Loving speech is that which is always spoken for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Beneficial conduct is that which is spoken in accordance with the meaning rather than following the literal words.
Shared benefit is that which is always spoken for the sake of fulfilling the Buddha-dharma.
"Furthermore, giving is the fulfillment of the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
Kind speech is the fulfillment of the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla) and patience (kṣānti).
Beneficial conduct is the fulfillment of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā)."
"Common benefit" refers to being fully endowed with dhyāna and prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, "giving" is the initial aspiration for bodhi;
"loving speech" is the cultivation of bodhi.
Beneficial conduct is not retreating from bodhi.
Shared benefit is being one birth away from buddhahood.
Furthermore, giving is that which dwells securely in the root of the seeds of bodhi.
Loving speech nourishes and grows the sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves of bodhi.
Beneficial conduct gradually causes the flower of bodhi to bloom.
Shared purpose is already capable of bringing the fruit of bodhi to fruition.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible gathering of sentient beings through the four methods of attraction. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva are likewise inexhaustible.
What are these four? The first is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid).
Second is the unimpededness regarding phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid);
third is the unimpededness regarding expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid);
fourth is the unimpededness regarding eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
"What is the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*)? It is the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) among all phenomena;

it is the knowledge of inference, the knowledge of causes, the knowledge of conditions, the knowledge of conjunctions, the knowledge of not falling into extremes, and the knowledge of not abiding in the middle—these are the ten."

The wisdom of the two causal conditions is the wisdom that the dharmadhātu is not otherwise; it is the wisdom of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); it is the wisdom of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi-jñāna*);
it is the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of emptiness; it is the wisdom of the markless within marks; it is the wisdom of the wishless within wishes;

it is the wisdom of the unconditioned within the conditioned; it is the wisdom that contemplates the single characteristic; it is the wisdom that contemplates non-self; it is the wisdom that contemplates...
The wisdom that there are no sentient beings is the contemplation of the wisdom that there is no life-force; this is the contemplation of the wisdom of the ultimate truth of no-self;
this is the contemplation of the wisdom that is unimpeded regarding the past; this is the contemplation of the wisdom that is boundless regarding the future;

this is the contemplation of the all-encompassing wisdom regarding the present; this is the contemplation of the wisdom that views the aggregates as enemies and robbers; this is the contemplation of the elements...

It is the wisdom that regards [the world] as a venomous snake; it is the wisdom that contemplates the sense-bases (*āyatana*) as an empty village; it is the wisdom that contemplates internal phenomena as eternally quiescent;
it is the wisdom that contemplates external phenomena as having no place of movement; it is the wisdom that contemplates objects of perception as being like illusions and transformations;
it is the wisdom that contemplates mindfulness as correctly established; it is the wisdom that contemplates patience regarding the true Dharma; it is the wisdom that contemplates one's own self.
This is the wisdom that fully contemplates the various truths.
It is the wisdom that there is no conjunction with suffering; it is the wisdom that accumulation is not produced; it is the wisdom of the intrinsic nature of cessation;

it is the wisdom that the path is able to reach [the goal]; it is the wisdom that discriminates all phenomena; it is the wisdom that observes the faculties, minds, and activities of all sentient beings.
It is the wisdom that follows whatever enters [the senses]; it is the wisdom that no powers can subdue; it is the wisdom that understands all factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) as they truly are;
it is the wisdom that upholds meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); it is the wisdom that is the radiance of insight (*prajñā*); it is the wisdom that is the adornment of magical illusions (*māyā*);
it is the wisdom that is the delusion of a mirage (*marīci*); it is the wisdom of what is desired in a dream; it is the objective referent (*ālambana*) of an echo.
Wisdom is the knowledge that images in a mirror have no coming or going; it is the knowledge that various marks are markless; it is the knowledge of the yokes and the liberation from yokes;
it is the knowledge of grasping at birth and the liberation from birth; it is the knowledge of the Śrāvaka vehicle gained by hearing from others;

it is the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle through contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination; and it is the knowledge of the Mahāyāna, which is fully endowed with all roots of goodness.
Wisdom. Śāriputra, this is called the bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom regarding meaning.
"Furthermore, regarding the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): it is the contemplation of the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*). Why is this?

Because all these phenomena are without self (*ātman*), without sentient beings (*sattva*), without life-force (*jīva*), and without person (*pudgala*). That which is without self, without sentient beings, without life-force, and without person is precisely what is called 'meaning'."
Just as it is with the meaning of "life," so it is with all phenomena such as form; this is called the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, the unimpededness of meaning is the teaching of non-abiding, the inexhaustible teaching, and the teaching that attains all dharmas.
This meaning of non-obstruction is what all Buddhas authorize; it is the true meaning, without distinction or difference, wherein wisdom’s discernment encounters no hindrance.
This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible unimpeded knowledge of meaning.
"Śāriputra, what is the bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of phenomena?"

If one contemplates all phenomena—namely, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, mundane and supramundane phenomena, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, tainted and untainted phenomena, compounded and uncompounded phenomena, dark and bright phenomena, and the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvana—one realizes that this wisdom is equal in its dharma-nature, equal in its bodhi, and equal in its essence; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, regarding the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): one contemplates the mental activities of sentient beings—those with many desires, those with few desires, those who have first given rise to a desiring mind, those whose mental activities are characterized by desire, those whose desiring minds are currently focused on objects, and those whose desiring minds arise due to present conditions.

There are sentient beings who have internal conduct of desire but external conduct free from desire; there are those with external conduct of desire but internal conduct free from desire; there are those with both internal and external conduct of desire; and there are those with neither internal nor external conduct of desire.

There are those whose conduct is driven by desire for forms, but not for sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; there are those whose conduct is driven by desire for sounds, but not for forms, odors, tastes, or tangibles; there are those whose conduct is driven by desire for odors, but not for forms, sounds, tastes, or tangibles; there are those whose conduct is driven by desire for tastes, but not for forms, sounds, odors, or tangibles; and there are those whose conduct is driven by desire for tangibles, but not for forms, sounds, odors, or tastes.

Entering thus into the gate of observing the various modes of conduct of sentient beings, there are twenty-one thousand modes of conduct for those who act out of desire, twenty-one thousand modes of conduct for those who act out of hatred, twenty-one thousand modes of conduct for those who act out of delusion, and twenty-one thousand modes of conduct for those whose conduct is a mixture of these three.

Observing the eighty-four thousand modes of mental activity of these sentient beings, he knows them as they truly are and preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of dharmas, which is inexhaustible.
"Śāriputra, what is the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of expression?"

They fully observe and understand all sounds—namely those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—and are able to know all such speech, scripts, and voices.

Thus, for the various classes of sentient beings within the five destinies, he preaches the Dharma using their respective sounds, languages, and scripts, one by one; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Thus, when one contemplates and realizes the words and letters of the Dharma without obstruction, this Bodhisattva knows one word, two words, three words, and even many words; he knows masculine speech, feminine speech, and speech that is neither masculine nor feminine; he knows speech of the past, future, and present; and he knows the accumulation of words from a single syllable up to many syllables. This is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

This is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): when speaking, there is no error and no obstruction; his wondrous speech flows smoothly, what he says is precise, upright, and free from coarseness; all his phrasing is fully adorned, such that none among the great assembly who hear it fail to rejoice. With these various kinds of subtle and wonderful sounds—profound, far-reaching, vast, and universal—he adorns both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and with the arrow of wisdom, he skillfully shoots down false views.
This unimpeded eloquence is authorized by all Buddhas and is able to cause all sentient beings to attain joy.
Śāriputra, this is called the inexhaustible unimpeded knowledge of eloquence of a bodhisattva.
“Śāriputra! How is it that the bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is inexhaustible?
It is because what he speaks is unimpeded, what he speaks does not dwell [on objects], what he speaks is swift, and what he speaks is sharp and incisive.”

The answers given in response to questions are unimpeded answers, non-contradictory answers, appropriate answers, answers grounded in the power of patience, answers based on the two truths, answers based on generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, answers based on the chapters and phrases of all dharmas, answers based on the profound meaning of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path, and answers based on the contemplation of cessation.

What is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is this: regarding all speech and letters, one answers with direct discernment from the mouth; that is to say, one answers with the wisdom of the true reality (*tattva-jñāna*) concerning all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), and with fluent eloquence, one answers according to the mental activities of all sentient beings in accordance with the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
His speech is skillful and eloquent, not like that of a mute sheep;
all such words as those that are forceful, coarse, violent, impetuous, or frivolous are entirely absent.

What he proclaims is quiescence for the benefit of others; his majestic words are free from all entanglements, consistent and non-contradictory, subtle and supple, beyond reproach, and praised by the sages.

Just as the words taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are uttered in a Brahma-voice so pure and penetrating that all hear them, so too is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) authorized by all Buddhas.

To preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of other sentient beings, such that those who hear this Dharma attain supramundane bliss and extinguish all suffering—this is called the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence.
Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which are inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four reliances that are likewise inexhaustible. What are the four?
Rely on the meaning, not on the words; rely on wisdom, not on consciousness; rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, not on sūtras of interpretable meaning; rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
What is meant by relying on the meaning and not on the words?
Words refer to whatever is spoken when one enters into worldly phenomena; meaning refers to understanding the supramundane dharma as being devoid of the characteristics of letters.
"Speech" refers to speaking of generosity, self-restraint, and protection; "meaning" refers to knowing that generosity, ethical discipline, and patience enter into equality.
"Speech" refers to the discourse on birth and death; "meaning" refers to knowing that birth and death lack intrinsic nature.
"Speech" refers to describing the flavor of nirvāṇa; "meaning" refers to knowing that nirvāṇa is without intrinsic nature.

"Speech" refers to explaining the various vehicles according to where they are established; "meaning" refers to skillfully knowing that all vehicles enter the gateway of the wisdom of the single characteristic.
"Speech" refers to the teaching on various forms of relinquishment; "meaning" refers to the threefold purity.

"Speech" refers to the teaching on the merit and dignified conduct of upholding the pure precepts of body, speech, and mind; "meaning" refers to the realization that body, speech, and mind are all without action, yet are able to guard and maintain all pure precepts.
"Speech" refers to preaching patience that eliminates anger, arrogance, and pride; "meaning" refers to thoroughly comprehending all phenomena and attaining the patience of non-arising.
"Speech" refers to preaching the diligent cultivation of all roots of goodness; "meaning" refers to abiding in diligence without beginning or end.
"Words" refer to the explanation of the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis; "meaning" refers to knowing the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
"Words" refer to being able to hear, retain, and uphold all syllables, which is the root of wisdom; "meaning" refers to knowing that the meaning of this wisdom cannot be expressed in speech.
"Words" refers to the teaching of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; "meaning" refers to correctly understanding that the practice of these factors of enlightenment can realize the fruit.
"Words" refers to the teaching of the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path; "meaning" refers to the realization of the truth of cessation.

"Speech" refers to explaining that ignorance is the root and so forth, up to birth being the condition for old age and death; "meaning" refers to knowing the cessation of ignorance and so forth, up to the cessation of old age and death.
"Speech" refers to explaining the factors that assist concentration and wisdom; "meaning" refers to the clear knowledge of liberation.
"Words" refer to speaking of greed, anger, and delusion; "meaning" refers to understanding that these unwholesome roots are themselves liberation.
"Words" refer to speaking of obstructive dharmas; "meaning" refers to attaining unobstructed liberation.

"Speech" refers to proclaiming the immeasurable merits of the Triple Gem; "meaning" refers to the fact that the merits of the Triple Gem share the same unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) characteristic as the dharma-nature free from desire.

"Speech" refers to explaining the cultivation and accumulation of the meritorious adornments of enlightenment (*bodhi*), from the initial generation of the mind until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); "meaning" refers to awakening to all dharmas through the wisdom of a single thought-moment.
Śāriputra! To state the essentials:
that which can expound the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma is called "speech," while knowing that all written characters cannot be fully expressed is called "meaning."
"What is meant by relying on wisdom and not relying on consciousness?
Consciousness refers to the four stations of consciousness.
What are the four?"
The abodes of consciousness are form, feeling, perception, and formations;
the wise understand that the nature of these four types of consciousness has no place of abiding.
As for consciousness, it is the consciousness of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
As for "wisdom," it is that consciousness abides within the four great elements, yet their dharmic nature is without distinction.
As for "consciousness," eye-consciousness abides in forms; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness abide in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena.
As for "wisdom," its internal nature is quiescent and it does not engage externally; it thoroughly understands that all phenomena are devoid of conceptualization.
"Consciousness" refers to that which exclusively takes objects as its conditions, engaging in conceptualization and discrimination;
"wisdom" refers to a mind that has no objects of condition, does not grasp at appearances, and harbors no expectations regarding any phenomena.
Consciousness is that which functions within conditioned phenomena;
wisdom is that which knows unconditioned phenomena. Consciousness has no sphere of operation, for the nature of the unconditioned is devoid of consciousness and cognition.
Consciousness is characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
The wise have no characteristics of arising, abiding,
or ceasing. Śāriputra,
this is called relying on wisdom and not relying on consciousness.
"What is meant by relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not relying on sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*)?
Sūtras of provisional meaning differentiate the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), whereas sūtras of definitive meaning do not differentiate the fruit (*phala*)."
The *neyārtha* sūtras concern those who perform karmic actions and believe in their retribution; the *nītārtha* sūtras exhaust all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *neyārtha* sūtras censure the afflictions; the *nītārtha* sūtras praise the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
The *neyārtha* sūtras speak of the suffering and affliction of birth and death; the *nītārtha* sūtras teach that birth and death and nirvāṇa are of one mark and non-dual.
The *neyārtha* sūtras praise and describe various kinds of ornate language; the *nītārtha* sūtras teach profound sūtras that are difficult to uphold and difficult to understand.

Sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) mostly explain the characteristics of transgression and merit for the sake of sentient beings, causing those who hear the Dharma to experience joy and sorrow in their hearts;
sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), however, ensure that whatever they proclaim necessarily brings about the taming of the minds of those who listen.

A sutra of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is one that employs various expressions such as "self," "person," "sentient being," "life-span," "nourisher," "individual," "agent," or "experiencer," and while all phenomena are devoid of a giver or an experiencer, it speaks to others as if there were giving and experiencing.

A sutra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is one that teaches emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, and non-arising; it states that there is no self, person, sentient being, life-span, nourisher, individual, agent, or experiencer, and constantly proclaims the immeasurable gates of liberation.
This is called relying on sūtras of definitive meaning and not relying on sūtras of interpretable meaning.
What is meant by "relying on the Dharma and not relying on the person"?
A "person" refers to one who grasps at the views of a person, a doer, and an experiencer.
The Dharma is that which is understood as being devoid of a person who sees, an agent, or a recipient.

As for "persons," these include ordinary beings, virtuous persons, those who practice through faith, those who practice through the Dharma, the eight types of persons, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. Among these, there is one person who appears in the world who brings great benefit and causes many people to receive happiness; out of compassion for the world, he gives rise to the mind of great pity and provides abundant nourishment among gods and humans—this is what is called the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Names such as these are spoken by the Buddha based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
If there is anyone who grasps at such views, this is called "relying on the person."
The Tathāgata, in order to transform and gather those who hold views of persons, taught that one should rely on the Dharma and not rely on the person.
This nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unchanging and immutable, non-active and not produced by action, neither abiding nor non-abiding, and is entirely equal.
The equal is also equal, and that which is unequal is likewise equal.
Without cause and without condition, one attains right determination; regarding all phenomena, there is no distinction and no difference.
The non-obstruction between essence and characteristics is like empty space; this is called the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
If there is one who relies upon this dharma-nature, they shall never again depart from the dharma of the single characteristic.
Those who enter this gate contemplate all phenomena as being of one single dharma-nature; therefore, it is said that one relies on all phenomena and does not rely on the person. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s four reliances that are inexhaustible.
