*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Scroll 29. *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Scroll 30.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Zhìyán and Bǎoyún of Liángzhou during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, Part Four.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation and accumulation of the merits that assist the path, as well as their wisdom, are likewise inexhaustible.
How are the merits cultivated and accumulated so as to be inexhaustible?

If one practices giving and upholds the precepts, cultivating and initiating compassion through the mind; if one discloses and repents for all of one's own transgressions, and likewise discloses and repents on behalf of sentient beings; having performed such repentance, one should next practice sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

All sentient beings—those in training and those beyond training, as well as Pratyekabuddhas who have resolved their minds, and Bodhisattvas who have already practiced and abide firmly without regression, including those in their final birth before Buddhahood—one should, with a single mind, rejoice in accordance with the merit accumulated by such persons throughout the three periods of time.

"Furthermore, one should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward all roots of goodness belonging to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present; by such sympathetic joy, these Bodhisattvas shall all fully accomplish such merit and virtue."

Having completed the expression of sympathetic joy, one should next make requests to all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions: for those who have newly attained enlightenment, requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma; for those who manifest nirvana, requesting them to remain permanently in the world; and requesting all Bodhisattvas and holy beings to constantly dwell in the world to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus, these roots of goodness, which are identical in character to bodhi, are entirely dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi.
Such a bodhisattva encourages those who have not yet resolved their minds to do so, and for those who have already resolved their minds, he explains the various perfections (*pāramitās*).
To those who are impoverished, he provides relief and protection with material wealth; to the sick, he gives medicine and attends to them with timely medical care.
They encourage those who lack strength to practice patience;
they cause those who have committed transgressions not to conceal them;
and they encourage those who have already concealed them to reveal their faults.
One should resolve to offer worship and respect to all present Buddhas and those who have entered nirvana, honoring one's teachers with the same reverence as the World-Honored Buddha.

When seeking the Dharma, one should never grow weary even at the cost of one's life; regarding this Jewel of the Dharma, one should conceive the thought that it is priceless, and regarding the teacher of the Dharma, one should conceive the thought that they are a Buddha.
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, they travel beyond a hundred *yojanas*, their mental power being so courageous and sharp that they harbor no thought of fatigue.
Whatever they preach is never for the sake of gain or sustenance.

They recognize the kindness of their parents and repay it; in making offerings and serving them, their minds never feel regret. They are never weary or satisfied with the merit they perform, and they guard their body, speech, and mind so that they remain free from flattery and crookedness.
“The merit obtained from establishing a Buddha-stūpa is equal to the blessing of exhorting Brahmā.
One attains the primary marks because of practicing great giving by opening one’s doors;
one attains the secondary signs because of cultivating all roots of goodness.”
Adorning the body means being free from arrogance;
adorning speech means being free from verbal transgressions;
adorning the mind means not dwelling upon phenomena.
To adorn the Buddha-lands is to transform beings through supernormal powers;
to adorn the Dharma is to be free from all desires;
to adorn the great assembly is to refrain from double-tongued speech, harsh words, or causing dissension among others.
Because they teach the Dharma to those who receive it according to reality;
because they joyfully praise those who preach the Dharma, saying "Excellent!", so that the meritorious deeds performed are not in vain;
and because they are free from obscurations, going to listen to the Dharma.
Adorning the Bodhi tree means offering exquisite gardens and groves to the Buddha;
adorning the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) means accomplishing all roots of goodness;
giving birth to purity means not being defiled by afflictions (kleśa).
He is called "Jewel-Handed" because he is able to relinquish all that is most cherished;
he is called "Inexhaustible" because he bestows immeasurable treasuries of jewels;
and he is one whom all who see him rejoice in, because he is always harmonious and serene.
One who has realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) possesses the radiance of mind and wisdom that shines equally upon all sentient beings;
one who possesses the light of adornment does not disparage those who have not yet studied, but skillfully guides them;
one whose births are pure has fully accomplished the merit of upholding the precepts.
Those who are pure while dwelling in the womb do so because they do not perceive the faults of others;
those born among humans and devas do so because they have purified their practice of the ten wholesome paths;
and those whose wisdom shines peerlessly do so because they give rise to no discrimination regarding those whom they teach and transform.
One who possesses mastery over the Dharma does so because they have no stinginess regarding the cherished teachings;
one who is uniquely supreme in the world does so because they are ultimately pure;
one who has attained subtle and wondrous liberation does so because they do not seek after limited or partial practices.
One who practices all meritorious virtues does so because they do not abandon the mind of omniscience;
one who is fully endowed with the seven riches does so because faith is their foundation;
one who embraces the true Dharma does so because they do not begrudge body or life.
"He does not deceive the world because he is endowed with his original vows;
he is fully possessed of all Buddha-dharmas because he has already practiced the roots of all virtues. "Śāriputra!"
This is called a brief explanation of the bodhisattva’s merits; if explained in detail, they could not be exhausted even in the course of an eon or more than an eon.
"What is meant by the inexhaustibility of a bodhisattva’s wisdom?"
If one hears the teaching of wisdom through each individual cause, or attains wisdom through each individual condition,
what constitutes the cause?
It is the internal, predominant desire.
What is the condition?
It is to diligently seek the Dharma externally.

Such conditions rely upon the wisdom of the Buddha, not the wisdom of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; one draws near to the wise with a mind free from arrogance, always regarding such persons as the World-Honored One.

These wise ones, knowing that the minds of those who receive the Dharma have become supple, teach them the instructions of wisdom to provide a basis for reliance; according to their capacity as true vessels, they preach the undefiled Dharma.
For one who listens to the Dharma, to diligently cultivate and accumulate within this Dharma, and to possess the diligence that aids the Dharma, is what constitutes wisdom.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence that aids the Dharma?

If one is free from longing, cuts off worldly affairs, and minimizes speech; if the mind is always content with whatever is desired; if one reduces sleep during the first and last watches of the night;

if one is able to properly contemplate, deliberate upon, and discern all meanings heard; if one frequently seeks wholesome dharmas with a mind free from the turbidity of craving; and if one eliminates the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) so that there is no obstruction.

They are able to immediately eliminate any transgressions they commit. Their right practice is firm; they incline toward and revere it, honoring the practice of the Dharma with diligent application. They seek the Dharma without weariness, as if their hair were on fire. They are free from the notion of a self and act without slackness. They do not abandon their fundamental practice, but increase their superior resolve. They censure the conduct of crowds and delight in solitary practice. They direct themselves toward forest hermitages for contemplative practice, practicing contentment according to the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). They maintain the unshakable dhūta ascetic virtues and take joy in the practice of the Dharma.

The practice of not dwelling on worldly speech; the practice of seeking the supramundane Dharma; the practice of not losing right mindfulness; the practice of giving rise to the meaning of all dharmas; the practice of the truly correct path; the practice of knowing the total retention of conditions; the practice adorned with shame and remorse; the practice of wisdom that is firm and stable; the practice of purifying the eye of wisdom by removing the entanglements, knots, and fetters of the net of ignorance; the practice of skillful awakening; the practice of vast awakening; the practice of non-extinguishing awakening; the practice of analytical awakening; the practice of knowing the present; the practice of not relying on the merits of others; the practice of not being self-conceited regarding one’s own merits; the practice of praising the various merits of others; the practice of skillfully cultivating karmic actions; the practice of the immovability of cause and effect; and the practice of knowing pure karma.
"Śāriputra! This is called diligence that assists the Dharma. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four kinds of giving that are fully endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, they give paper, pens, and ink to Dharma-preachers so that they may transcribe the sutras.
Second, to bestow upon the Dharma Master a wondrous seat adorned with various ornaments;
third, to present to the Dharma Master all necessary articles for making offerings;
fourth, to praise the Dharma Master with a mind free from flattery or crookedness.
Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of giving by which a bodhisattva fulfills wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four ways in which a bodhisattva upholds the precepts and fulfills wisdom.
What are the four? First, upholding the precepts while constantly expounding the Dharma;
second, upholding the precepts while constantly and diligently seeking the Dharma.
Third, maintaining the precepts through the correct discernment of dharmas;
fourth, dedicating the maintenance of the precepts toward bodhi.
These are called the four kinds of maintaining the precepts by which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with wisdom.
“Furthermore, there are four kinds of patience through which a bodhisattva fulfills wisdom. What are the four?
First, when seeking the Dharma, one endures the malicious abuse of others.”
Second, when seeking the Dharma, one does not avoid hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, or rain;
third, when seeking the Dharma, one follows the conduct of the upādhyāya and ācārya;
fourth, when seeking the Dharma, one is able to endure emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Śāriputra! These are called the four kinds of patience through which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four kinds of diligence through which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with wisdom.
What are the four?
First, diligence in extensive learning;
second, diligence in dhāraṇī-retention;
Third, diligence in eloquent exposition;
fourth, diligence in right practice. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s four kinds of diligence that are endowed with wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of meditative concentration of the Bodhisattva that are endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, they always delight in dwelling alone;
second, they always delight in single-mindedness;
third, they seek meditative concentration and supernormal powers.
Fourth, seeking the wisdom of unimpeded analytical knowledge.
Śāriputra, these are called the four kinds of meditative concentrations through which a bodhisattva fulfills wisdom.
“Furthermore, there are four kinds of wisdom by which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, not abiding in the view of annihilation;”
Second, not falling into the view of permanence;
third, thoroughly understanding the twelve links of dependent origination;
fourth, practicing patience regarding the non-self nature of phenomena.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the four wisdoms to achieve the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four further dharmas of protection for the bodhisattva that achieve the perfection of wisdom.
What are the four?
First, to protect the Dharma teacher as one would one's own sovereign;
second, to protect all roots of goodness.
Third, protecting the world;
fourth, protecting the benefit of others. Śāriputra!
These are called the four dharmas of protection by which a bodhisattva is endowed with wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas of fulfillment by which a bodhisattva is endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, fulfillment in the teaching of the Dharma;
second, fulfillment in wisdom;
third, fulfillment in benefiting others.
Fourth, the fulfillment of all dharmas.
Śāriputra, these are called the four dharmas of fulfillment through which a bodhisattva is endowed with wisdom.
“Furthermore, a bodhisattva possesses four powers that are endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, the power of diligence, which seeks extensive learning in order to attain liberation.”
Second, the power of mindfulness, because the bodhicitta is never forgotten;
third, the power of meditative concentration, because it is free from discrimination;
fourth, the power of wisdom, because of the cultivation of extensive learning.
This is called the wisdom endowed with the four powers.
Furthermore, there is the wisdom endowed with the four skillful means. What are these four?
First, acting in accordance with worldly conventions;
second, acting in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings;
third, acting in accordance with all phenomena.
Fourth, acting in accordance with wisdom.
These are called the four skillful means that fully possess wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas by which a bodhisattva fully possesses wisdom."
What are the four?
First, the path of the various pāramitās;
second, the path that assists enlightenment.
Third, practicing the Eightfold Noble Path;
fourth, seeking the path of all-encompassing wisdom.
These are called the four paths that are fully endowed with wisdom.
“Furthermore, there are four practices of insatiability through which a bodhisattva fulfills wisdom. What are these four?
First, one delights in extensive learning without ever being satiated.”
Second, delighting in the preaching of the Dharma without weariness;
third, practicing wisdom without weariness;
fourth, practicing knowledge without weariness.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the four kinds of insatiability through the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, that which assists wisdom consists of following the mental activities of all sentient beings, following the practice of all dharmas, following the practice of giving, and following the practices of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; by following the practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one attains the fulfillment of wisdom.
Why is this? For all practices initiated by bodhisattvas have wisdom as their root; once wisdom is perfected, they in turn rely upon that wisdom.
This bodhisattva abides securely in wisdom based upon all-knowledge; the hosts of Māras cannot obstruct them, and for this reason, they are able to attain the full possession of all-knowledge.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible auxiliary wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The four foundations of mindfulness of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva are likewise inexhaustible.

This bodhisattva contemplates the body and cultivates bodily practice, seeing that all bodies of the past, future, and present are a combination of perversions; they exist through causes and conditions like external grasses, trees, walls, tiles, or stones—neither capable of being nourished nor possessing any inherent attachment.

This body is thus born from causes and conditions; it cannot be nourished and has no fixed attachment. Within these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, "self" and "what belongs to self" are empty, and permanence and impermanence are empty. This body is without self and possesses nothing that belongs to a self; this body is not solid and cannot be relied upon. One should seek instead the body of perfect awakening, bodhi.
"What is the body of the perfectly awakened one?
It is the Dharma-body, the vajra-body, the indestructible body, the firm body, and the body that has transcended the triple world."

Although my own body possesses immeasurable faults and afflictions, I vow to eliminate them and achieve the body of a Tathāgata; this is why the Bodhisattva is able to endure remaining for a long time amidst the four elements and the burning of all fetters, solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.

Just as the four external great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—manifest through various gateways, perform various functions, assume various forms, provide various vessels, and serve various purposes, all for the benefit of all sentient beings, so too is this body of mine now for the benefit of sentient beings.

Having seen such benefits as these, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the body’s manifold sufferings yet does not give rise to weary detachment; he contemplates the body’s impermanence yet does not loathe birth and death; he contemplates the body’s selflessness yet does not abandon the work of transforming others; he contemplates the body’s quiescence yet does not follow the path of mere renunciation.
When this bodhisattva contemplates the internal body, afflictions do not arise; when contemplating the external body, it is likewise so.

This bodhisattva abandons the defiled body and accomplishes pure bodily karma, adorning himself with the perfection of the excellent marks (*lakṣaṇa*). He brings great benefit among gods and humans; this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of contemplating and cultivating the body.
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate feelings, cultivate the practice of feeling, and engage in its conduct?
The bodhisattva reflects thus: 'All feelings are entirely suffering. He skillfully discriminates feelings and, through wisdom, evaluates them to know the cessation of feeling."
When experiencing pleasure, one does not crave desires;
when experiencing suffering, one contemplates the three evil realms and gives rise to great compassion without conceiving anger;
and when experiencing neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, one does not give rise to delusion.

This bodhisattva correctly attends to the bases of sensation; according to how they are experienced—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—they know their emergence and know their cultivation. They contemplate the adornment of the cessation of sensation for all sentient beings, yet these sentient beings do not know how to emerge from or cultivate themselves amidst those sensations.
When experiencing pleasure, one gives rise to craving and attachment; when experiencing pain, one gives rise to aversion; and when experiencing neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one gives rise to delusion.

I must now diligently cultivate wisdom to eliminate all sensations and give rise to all roots of goodness; I shall arouse great compassion to embrace wisdom, and for the sake of sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma to sever all sensations, for those who do not understand sensation suffer, while those who understand sensation experience happiness.
What is meant by the "experiencer"?
It refers to the absence of an experiencer—there being no self, person, sentient being, life-span, nourisher, or spirit.

Apart from the grasping of an experiencer, there is no grasper, no taker, no receiver of reception, no one who exists through reception, no one who experiences inversion, no one who experiences discrimination, no one who experiences various views, no one who experiences the characteristics of the eye, no one who experiences the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, no one who experiences the characteristic of form, and no one who experiences the characteristics of sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomena. Through the eye and its object, form, contact arises.

One experiences painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; through the ear, sound; the nose, odor; the tongue, flavor; the body, tangibles; and the mind, mental objects, contact arises, and one experiences painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—this is called feeling (*vedanā*).
"Furthermore, there is one feeling, which is fully cognized by the mind and intellect.
Furthermore, there are two feelings: internal feeling and external feeling.
Furthermore, there are three feelings: past, future, and present feelings."
Furthermore, there are four feelings that fully comprehend the four great elements.
Furthermore, there are five feelings that contemplate the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there are six feelings that discern the six sense bases.
Furthermore, there are seven feelings and seven stations of consciousness.
Furthermore, there are eight feelings, which are the eight wrong paths.
Furthermore, there are nine feelings, which are the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are ten feelings and ten unwholesome dharmas.
"Śāriputra, to state the essentials:
the immeasurable feelings, thoughts, and objects of focus of all sentient beings are all termed 'feelings'."

Within this, the Bodhisattva cultivates the practice of contemplating feelings and gives rise to great wisdom, knowing the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the wholesome and unwholesome feelings of all sentient beings. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s correct application of mindfulness, which is inexhaustible.
"What is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the application of mindfulness to the mind?

One contemplates the mind in this way: the bodhicitta is neither forgotten nor lost; right mindfulness is undisturbed. Once the mind has arisen, it ceases and possesses no abiding characteristic; it does not abide within, nor does it come from without."
That bodhicitta which I first generated has already passed away and undergone transformation; it does not reach any location, cannot be described, and has no place of abiding.

If the various roots of goodness and so forth accumulated by the mind are likewise of the past—exhausted, ceased, and transformed—they do not reach any location, cannot be described, and have no place of abiding.

If the roots of goodness of the mind are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these too are phenomena subject to extinction and transformation; they do not reach any location, cannot be described, and have no place of abiding.
The mind does not know the mind, the mind does not see the mind, and the mind does not give rise to the mind; by what mind, then, do I realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

This bodhicitta does not combine with the mind of roots of goodness; the mind of roots of goodness does not combine with the mind of dedication; and the mind of dedication does not combine with bodhicitta.
If a bodhisattva, when performing this contemplation, is neither startled nor terrified, this is called the diligent vigor of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, they reflect and observe the profound twelve links of dependent origination without losing sight of cause and effect; they know that the nature of the mind belongs to various causes and conditions, and is incapable of being nourished, unconditioned, and unbound.
All phenomena are likewise thus; one should practice according to the Dharma as it is adorned.
I shall now diligently cultivate and gather these adornments, never departing from the nature of the mind.
What is the nature of the mind?
What is its adornment?
As for the nature of the mind, it is like a magical illusion—without a master, without an agent, and without any established entity.
Adornment refers to dedicating all acts of giving toward the purification of Buddha-fields.
Nature of mind refers to the quiescence of mental characteristics, like those seen in a dream;
adornment refers to being fully endowed with the observance of precepts and the cultivation of the various supernormal powers.
The nature of the mind is like a reflection in a mirror, its characteristic being pure;
as for adornment, all the various forms of patience one cultivates are dedicated toward the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
The nature of the mind is ultimately quiescent, like a mirage in the heat;
adornment consists of generating profound diligence toward all virtues and dedicating them toward the fulfillment of unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas.
The nature of the mind is formless, non-obstructive, and devoid of purposeful activity;
adornment consists of dedicating all cultivated meditative concentrations, liberations, and attainments toward the fulfillment of the Buddha’s meditative concentration.
The nature of the mind cannot be seen and cannot be grasped;
adornment consists in being skillfully able to discern all difficult questions and dedicating them toward the fulfillment of a Buddha’s wisdom.
As for the nature of the mind, it does not arise without conditions;
as for adornment, one constantly contemplates roots of goodness.
As for the nature of the mind, it does not arise without causes.
Adornment refers to the arousal of the mind through the assistance of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
As for the nature of the mind, when one is detached from the six sense objects, the mind does not arise.
Adornment refers to entering the realm of the Buddha.

"In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates these mental activities and fixes his mindfulness upon the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having attained the supernormal powers, he is able to know the minds of all sentient beings; having known their minds, he teaches the Dharma to them according to the measure of those minds."
Furthermore, one contemplates the activities of the mind, binding mindfulness to great compassion, teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness;

and furthermore, one contemplates the activities of the mind, not giving rise to signs of exhaustion, cessation, or transformation, and not abandoning the afflictions that continue through birth and death.
Right mindfulness is the mind that knows there is no arising and achieves perfect certainty.

A practitioner who acts in this way does not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; by exerting the full power of this mind, they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the wisdom of a single thought-moment.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s station of mindfulness of the right mind, which is inexhaustible. Śāriputra!”
What is the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
Constantly perceiving all phenomena with the eye of wisdom, they never lose this vision until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

When this bodhisattva contemplates phenomena, they do not perceive even a single phenomenon or its subtlest characteristic; they see nothing apart from emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-ceasing, and the absence of substantiality. Furthermore, they do not perceive even a single phenomenon or its subtlest characteristic that does not enter into the twelve links of dependent origination.
“The Bodhisattva contemplates phenomena and sees that all non-dharmas are none other than dharmas.
What is meant by ‘dharma’?

It refers to the meaning of selflessness, the meaning of the absence of sentient beings, the meaning of the absence of a life-span, and the meaning of the absence of a person; these are called dharmas.”
What is the non-Dharma?

It refers to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a person, the view of annihilationism and eternalism, and the view of existence and non-existence; these are called the non-Dharma.
"Furthermore, all dharmas are dharmas; all dharmas are non-dharmas. Why is this?
To contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called 'all dharmas are dharmas.'"
The conceit of "I," arrogance, and the grasping at views of "I" and "mine"—these are called all dharmas that are non-dharmas.

When this bodhisattva contemplates dharmas, he does not see any dharma that is not a cause for bodhi or a cause for the supramundane path. This bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are entirely supramundane; he attains unimpeded great compassion and contemplates all dharmas—the afflictions, fetters, and bonds—as being like illusory transformations. He knows that these dharmas are neither possessed of afflictions nor devoid of afflictions.
Why is this? Because one realizes that the meaning of all phenomena is devoid of dual nature; these afflictions have no place of concealment and no place of accumulation.
If one understands afflictions, one understands bodhi; the nature of afflictions is precisely the nature of bodhi.

This bodhisattva dwells securely in right mindfulness; there is not a single dharma that can be subject to discrimination. Being free from all obstacles, they are well able to understand and correctly abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

To abide in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is to abide in the nature of sentient beings; to abide in the nature of sentient beings is to abide in the nature of space; and to abide in the nature of space is to abide in the nature of all phenomena.

When a bodhisattva contemplates phenomena, relying on the Buddha-dharma, they understand that all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma; at that time, their mind does not give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Although they have reached the end, they do not exhaustively enter the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), yet they contemplate sentient beings without abandoning conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the "application of mindfulness to phenomena" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): one dwells securely in right mindfulness regarding all phenomena—namely, all conventionally designated phenomena known by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and perfectly awakened ones—never forgetting them until the end of the future.

Furthermore, regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): it is said that by practicing immeasurable modes of conduct, one draws near to the Buddha-dharma, destroys all hosts of Māras, and attains self-arisen wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*). Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the true Dharma, which is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are also inexhaustible.
What are these four?
If unarisen evil and unwholesome states have not yet arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies mental focus, and strives correctly so that they do not arise.
If evil and unwholesome states have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies mental focus, and strives correctly so that they are abandoned.
For the sake of producing wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, and correctly strives with focused attention.

For the sake of maintaining, cultivating, increasing, and preventing the loss of wholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, and correctly strives with focused attention.
“In order that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, one generates desire, exerts effort, and applies diligence.
What is called ‘desire’ is wholesome reflection.
What is called ‘exerting effort’ is not abandoning wholesome reflection.”
"Collecting the mind and correctly eliminating" refers to observing wholesome reflection.
Why is this? Because when one reflects wholesomely, unwholesome and evil states are not allowed to enter the mind.
What are the evil and unwholesome dharmas?
Evil and unwholesome dharmas are not companions of the aggregate of morality, not companions of meditative concentration, and not companions of wisdom.
In what way are they not companions of the aggregate of morality?
If one violates the heavy precepts or otherwise destroys the remaining precepts, this is called the non-precept-group companion (*aśīlaskandha-sahāya*).
What is the non-concentration-group companion?
If one violates the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*) or other factors that disturb the mind, these are the non-concentration-group companions.
What is that which is not an associate of wisdom?
If one grasps at various views and other obstacles to vision, this is not an associate of wisdom; this is called an evil and unwholesome dharma.

When practicing right reflection, one does not allow such unwholesome states as these to enter the mind; this is called the first right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*): for the sake of abandoning unwholesome and non-virtuous states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, and correctly exerts the mind.
"As previously stated, evil and unwholesome dharmas do not aggregate within the mind; they have no location and no abode.

Because the mental activity of these unwholesome dharmas has been severed, because they have been fully understood, and because they arise from conditions: desire arises from purity, aversion arises from obstruction, and delusion arises with ignorance as its condition."

When one contemplates impurity with right reflection, the mind of desire is extinguished; by cultivating and accumulating a mind of loving-kindness, hatred is extinguished; and by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, delusion is extinguished. When such afflictions are eternally stilled and extinguished, this is the severing of all provisional designations (*prajñapti*), yet one does not perceive anything that can be severed. This is called the second right effort: generating desire, exertion, diligence, mental application, and right abandonment so that wholesome states not yet arisen may arise.
"These wholesome dharmas are said to be immeasurable. Why is this?

A bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates immeasurable wholesome dharmas; among these dharmas, desire is the root. Diligent application and cultivation lead to the gathering of the mind, which transcends wholesome dharmas; right elimination ensures that one is always present within wholesome dharmas everywhere. This is called the third right effort: to cause already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain stable and be further cultivated, so that they may increase and not be lost, thereby gathering the mind and abiding correctly."
"All these roots of goodness have already been dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because roots of goodness that are dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment can never be exhausted."

Why is this? Such roots of goodness do not rely upon the triple world; if they relied upon the triple world, they would be diminished and exhausted. Therefore, the various roots of goodness dedicated toward all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be exhausted. This is called the fourth right effort.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible cultivation of the four right efforts. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are likewise inexhaustible. What are the four?
They are: desire, vigor, mind, and reflection.
These four dharmas take loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as their foundation;
by constantly cultivating these four immeasurable minds, the mind becomes pliant and supple;
because the mind is pliant and supple, one attains entry into the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
Because they enter the various dhyānas, their bodies attain lightness and suppleness;
having accomplished such lightness of body and flexibility of mind, they enter the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);
having skillfully entered the bases of psychic power, they immediately give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Whether it be desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), or investigation (*mīmāṃsā*):

desire is the single-minded orientation toward those dharmas; effort is the accomplishment of those dharmas; mind is the observation of those dharmas; and investigation is the skillful means regarding those dharmas. Because these bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are thus fully perfected, one is able to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Zeal is adornment; diligence is accomplishment; the mind is right abiding; and reflection is the ability to discern well. Thus, the Bodhisattva attains the factors of mastery according to his understanding, and as he acts, his mind achieves sovereignty. He proceeds wherever he wishes, skillfully performing all deeds, ultimately fulfilling all fundamental practices, moving through them without obstruction, like the wind traveling through space.
"Śāriputra! These are called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) of a bodhisattva, which are inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The five faculties of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are likewise inexhaustible.
What are these five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
"What is the faculty of faith?
It is faith in four things.
What are the four?
While transmigrating through birth and death, they practice worldly right view and have faith in the retribution of karma, such that even at the cost of their lives they never commit evil;

they believe in the bodhisattva practices and do not follow various [erroneous] views, seeking exclusively for Bodhi and not other vehicles; they believe in and understand that all phenomena are identical with the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they accord with the ultimate truth and the definitive meaning, wherein the profound dependent origination is without self or sentient beings and free from all discrimination.
One believes in all Buddhas' ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities.
Having thus believed,
one eliminates the net of doubt and cultivates and accumulates the Buddha-dharmas.
This is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
Whatever phenomena are embraced by the faculty of faith are cultivated by the faculty of diligence; this is called the faculty of diligence.
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
Whatever phenomena are cultivated by the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), those phenomena are never forgotten or lost; this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?

If a phenomenon is subsumed under the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), such that it is not forgotten, not lost, and the mind is single-pointed and undistracted, this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?

If a phenomenon is subsumed under the faculty of concentration, and is that which is observed by wisdom, the very essence of wisdom, internally self-illuminating and not knowing through another, abiding in right practice—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
These five faculties arise in continuous succession; when they are fully endowed with all dharmas, one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

It is like the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of non-Buddhist seers, who cannot definitively know the distinctions within the womb until the signs of male or female appear, after which they know them.
Many bodhisattvas lack the faculties such as faith; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not bestow predictions upon them, but if they achieve these, they then grant them predictions. Śāriputra!
This is called the inexhaustibility of the five faculties of a bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the five powers of a bodhisattva are also inexhaustible."
What are the five?
They are the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
What is the power of faith?

This faith is consistently indestructible; even if a celestial Māra were to transform into the body of a Buddha and manifest entering and emerging from meditative concentrations and liberations, he could not shake the bodhisattva’s power of faith. This is called the power of faith.
What is the power of diligence?

A bodhisattva exerts diligence toward all wholesome dharmas and attains a firm strength; with the strength thus attained, they cultivate various meditative concentrations that cannot be destroyed by gods or humans, and they fully accomplish all their original vows. This is called the power of diligence.
What is the power of mindfulness?
It is that when a bodhisattva abides in all wholesome dharmas, they cannot be destroyed by afflictions. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva’s power of right mindfulness is able to subdue [all distractions], and such power of mindfulness cannot be destroyed by anything, it is called the power of mindfulness.
What is the power of concentration?
Staying far removed from clamor and always delighting in solitary wandering, this bodhisattva, although having something to say, is not hindered by speech or sound from the first dhyāna;
being well-established in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), he is not hindered from the second dhyāna;
and with the arising of joy in the mind, he is not hindered from the third dhyāna.
Although this bodhisattva delights in transforming sentient beings, he does not abandon the Buddha-dharma, nor is he obstructed by the fourth dhyāna.
When this bodhisattva practices the four dhyānas, no dharmas that hinder meditative concentration can prevail over him.

At that time, the bodhisattva does not abandon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor does he follow after it, yet he is able to be born freely wherever he wishes; this is called the power of concentration.
What is the power of wisdom (*prajñā*)?
This bodhisattva knows both mundane and supramundane dharmas, and there is not a single dharma that can destroy this wisdom.

In whatever place this bodhisattva is born, all arts and crafts are known naturally without being received from a teacher. Regarding the ascetic and difficult practices of the worldly non-Buddhists, this bodhisattva, for the sake of teaching and transforming them, likewise manifests the acceptance of these practices and acts in common with them.

This supramundane dharma, which is able to transcend the world, is due to the accomplishment of the power of wisdom; it cannot be overcome by gods or humans, and this is called the power of wisdom, Śāriputra.
This is called the bodhisattva’s five inexhaustible powers. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the seven factors of enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are also inexhaustible.
What are the seven?

They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
"What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?

If the awakening factor of mindfulness is able to contemplate phenomena, is able to discern phenomena and synthesize thought and wisdom, and is also able to observe the specific characteristics of all phenomena."
What is its specific characteristic?

Contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and maintaining mindfulness of such things so as to bring about clear realization—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
"What is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If one can analytically discern and clearly understand the eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings (*dharma-skandha*), such that regarding the teachings as they are understood: what is of definitive meaning is known as definitive meaning; what is of non-definitive meaning is known as non-definitive meaning; what is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is known as conventional truth; what is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is known as ultimate truth; what is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) is known as a provisional designation; and what is correctly understood without doubt is known as correctly understood without doubt—such analytical selection of these and other phenomena is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena."
"What is the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If, while recollecting the Dharma, discerning the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, removing [hindrances] through the Dharma, concentrating on the Dharma, and equanimously regarding the Dharma, one grasps with wisdom a vigorous and courageous energy, desiring not to regress but diligently practicing with exertion and perseverance, not abandoning the original intention and proceeding upon the right path—this is called the factor of enlightenment of energy."
"What is the factor of enlightenment of joy?

It is the Dharma-joy cultivated through practice; it is the gladness of mind toward immeasurable dharmas, free from indolence; it is the pure delight in the Dharma, a state of exultation that can eliminate both body and mind and abandon all afflictions. This is called the factor of enlightenment of joy."
"What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility?

If one removes [distractions] from body and mind as well as all afflictions, and by departing from hindrances enters the state of meditative concentration so that the mind abides correctly, this is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility."

"What is the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? It is the ability to fully awaken to and comprehend whatever meditative absorption one has entered; it is not the case that one awakens to these dharmas without having entered concentration.

Furthermore, it is the realization that all views, afflictions, fetters, and bonds are without beginning or end, that one's mind is equanimous, and that all dharmas lack any distinct characteristics. To be able to awaken to the equality of all such dharmas is called the awakening factor of concentration."
"What is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If, regarding phenomena, the mind neither sinks into sorrow nor rejoices, and is likewise not led away by worldly dharmas; if it dwells uprightly and immovably without being high or low; if it is free from all outflows (*āsrava*), free from joy and attachment, and free from all obstructions; and if it is straightforward and conforms to the true path of reality—this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
“Śāriputra, these are called the seven factors of enlightenment of a bodhisattva,
which are likewise inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra...”
The eightfold noble path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also inexhaustible.
What are these eight?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"What is right view? If one perceives that which transcends the world, and does not give rise to the views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, or a person; if one does not give rise to the views of annihilationism or eternalism, existence or non-existence; nor does one give rise to views concerning the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate, and so forth, up to not giving rise to the dualistic view of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—this is called right view."
"What is right intention? If an intention can give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, and various other afflictions, it is not called right.

This right intention does not contemplate nor give rise to such things; it contemplates only ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is right intention."
To be able to contemplate this dwelling in the aggregate of precepts and so forth—such contemplation is called right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
What is right speech (*samyag-vāc*)?

Whatever one utters does not cause one's own body to suffer affliction, nor does it harm others; achieving such virtuous, excellent, and well-spoken words that lead toward the right path is called right speech.
"What is right action?
If there is karma that is black with black retribution, white with white retribution, or black-and-white with black-and-white retribution, one never dares to perform it."

If there is karma that is neither black nor white and has a retribution that is neither black nor white, and if there is karma that can exhaust all karma, such karma must certainly be performed; this is the karma upon which a bodhisattva relies.
Diligently cultivating such right actions and so forth is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*). What is right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*)?

If one does not abandon the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), the dhūta practices, and the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); if one is unshakable and unwavering, free from guile and flattery; if one is not led astray by worldly gain and honor; if one is easy to support and easy to satisfy; if one constantly maintains one's own deportment and etiquette; if, seeing others obtain gain, one’s mind does not become feverish with envy; and if one always knows moderation and contentment regarding one’s own gain and honor—such right conduct praised by the Noble Ones is called right livelihood.
"What is right effort?

If an effort is directed toward what is wrong and not praised by the Noble Ones—namely, the afflictions of sensual desire, ill will, and delusion—one does not engage in such unrighteous exertion at all."

If a dharma can enter the noble path of the true truths, the tranquility of nirvana, and the correct way of objective focus, and if one cultivates, accumulates, and diligently practices this with right effort, this is called right exertion.
"What is right mindfulness?

It is when one’s mindfulness does not lose its object and does not waver from the Dharma; it is upright and not crooked; it perceives the faults of birth and death and advances toward Nirvana; it binds the mind so as not to forget or lose the right path—this is called right mindfulness."
"What is right concentration?
If concentration is undisturbed regarding all phenomena, when a bodhisattva abides in this way, they achieve right determination; this is called right concentration."
When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi for the sake of bringing liberation to all sentient beings and achieves right determination, it is called "right concentration.
This Eightfold Noble Path is the path of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; having awakened to it, the bodhisattva expounds, reveals, analyzes, manifests, and accomplishes the Buddha-way.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s eightfold noble path, which is likewise inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of concentration and wisdom is likewise inexhaustible. "What is concentration?

It is when the mind is tranquil, perfectly tranquil, and extinguished, not burning with passion; the mind is constantly undistracted as it guards the sense faculties; it is unmoving, unswerving, and free from abrupt violence; it is composed, silent, and firmly maintained without loss; it is well-tamed and supple, dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place; the body remains detached while the mind does not turn back toward worldly things, delighting in contemplation within empty and silent forest hermitages (āraṇya)."

He has no evil desires nor does he seek anything, yet he does not fail to seek much; his livelihood is pure, his conduct is upright, and his deportment is firm. Knowing the proper time and acting according to the occasion, he always knows moderation and contentment, being easy to support and easy to satisfy. By virtue of his power of forbearance, his mind is free from pride or dejection, and he is able to endure abusive speech.

To direct the mind single-mindedly toward wholesome dharmas and their contemplation, to delight in the objects of contemplation and the factors of dhyāna, to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, to enter into a mind of compassion, to abide in a mind of sympathetic joy, and to skillfully cultivate a mind of equanimity; to correctly enter the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and to be adept at contemplating the nine successive attainments—this is called concentration.

To state the essentials: the bodhisattva’s cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable and boundless aids to concentration through diligent practice is called the inexhaustibility of the bodhisattva’s concentration. What is wisdom?

This wisdom cultivates the path and enters into the selflessness of all phenomena—of persons, sentient beings, and life-span. Through such wisdom, one discriminates the aggregates as being like illusions and transformations; one realizes that the elements are equal and enter into the state of an empty village; one discriminates the truths with complete clarity; one contemplates and understands the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with reality; and one discriminates the causes, effects, and realizations regarding all views.

What is called "discrimination" (vikalpa) refers to being able to attain right view regarding all phenomena, seeing them as they truly are: the true view, the view of emptiness, the view of signlessness, and the view of wishlessness.
Furthermore, discrimination is so called because it is non-discriminatory.
That which is called "seeing" is itself without anything seen and without anything distinguished or known.
Such seeing is true seeing; one who sees the truth thereby attains skillful means.
When this bodhisattva thus perceives with wisdom and does not follow after the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), practicing all virtues with a mind that dwells nowhere—this is called wisdom. Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva’s inexhaustible cultivation of concentration and wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the dhāraṇī and eloquence of the bodhisattva mahāsattva are likewise inexhaustible.

"What is dhāraṇī? It is the accumulation of well-cultivated roots of goodness through right mindfulness; being able to correctly receive, uphold, and neither forget nor lose any of the eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma—this is called dhāraṇī."

Furthermore, dhāraṇī: if one is able to receive and maintain all the sublime teachings spoken by all Buddhas, as well as all the virtuous speech and sounds of all Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and ordinary sentient beings, this is called dhāraṇī.

Even if a kalpa-ending disaster arises and one’s life comes to an end in another birth, at that time the bodhisattva maintains right mindfulness through dhāraṇī, neither forgetting nor losing it; just as one observes an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand, so too does the bodhisattva perceive all phenomena. This is called dhāraṇī.

"What is eloquence? It is that what the bodhisattva speaks is without obstruction; what is spoken is without dwelling, what is spoken is without interruption, what is spoken is fluent, what is spoken is joyful, and what is spoken is swift. Such speech is entirely the fruit of retribution from the purity of past karma; it is protected by all Buddhas and sustained by all devas. What is spoken is without error, its merit is not in vain, and it advances toward nirvāṇa."

When a bodhisattva has accomplished such eloquence, regarding all forms and appearances as well as the various classes of sentient beings, their eloquence responds to the capacities of those present without prior deliberation or prior discrimination, skillfully praising and expounding upon the sūtras and verses.

Whether he enters among the great assembly, the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, the assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the assembly of Māras, or the assembly of Brahmās—in every such place, he is naturally able to know the measure of the faculties of those in the assembly and preach the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence. This bodhisattva, as originally delighted in proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma, continues without interruption for the rest of his life; this is called *pratibhāna* (eloquence).
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī and eloquence, which is likewise inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s compilation of four dharmas is likewise inexhaustible.
What are these four? They are:

the Bodhisattva’s knowledge that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, that all phenomena are selfless, and that all phenomena are the quiescence of nirvāṇa.
What is the meaning of impermanence?
That which is non-existent is the meaning of impermanence; that which cannot be destroyed is the meaning of impermanence.
This meaning of impermanence is itself the meaning of selflessness (*anātman*); if a phenomenon is without self, there is nothing capable of destroying it.
Because its nature is quiescent, this is called the meaning of impermanence.

What is the meaning of suffering? Because there is nothing to be sought, this is the meaning of suffering; because craving and defilement are exhausted, this is the meaning of suffering; because there is no aspiration, this is the meaning of suffering; because it is empty and non-existent, this is the meaning of suffering. This is called the meaning of suffering.
What is the meaning of non-self?

The ultimate absence of self is the meaning of non-self; as the meaning of non-self is the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-existence, and the meaning of being deceptive and unreal—this is called the meaning of non-self.
What is the meaning of quiescent nirvāṇa?
This meaning of quiescence is not the cessation of momentary thoughts; that which is not the cessation of momentary thoughts is itself quiescence.

When a bodhisattva attains this inexhaustible wisdom, they know that the characteristics of all phenomena are identical to quiescence, and that quiescence is itself nirvāṇa. This is called the meaning of quiescent nirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! These are called the four dharmas that a bodhisattva compiles and which are inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The single path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also inexhaustible.
What is this single path?
It is the true wisdom attained by the bodhisattva, which is not heard from another.
Furthermore, as for "a single path," it means that the bodhisattva is solitary and without companion, yet is already able to perform great adornment for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Through the power of one's own strength and diligence, one should undertake this practice, ultimately cultivating it oneself without relying on the actions of others. By means of the courageous power of one's own causes and conditions, one establishes such firm adornments, thinking: "Just as all sentient beings perform wholesome deeds, I shall likewise perform them all; and whatever practices the noble ones have performed since first generating the mind of enlightenment, I too shall perform them."

Generosity is not my companion; I am the companion of generosity. Morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are not my companions; I am their companion. The various pāramitās cannot command me; rather, I can command the various pāramitās. It is the same for all roots of goodness.
Although such dharmas as these are not my companions, I must nonetheless practice them.

Relying on no one else, with courageous self-reliance and alone without a companion, sitting upon the Vajra Seat at the site of enlightenment, I shall destroy the hosts of Māras; through the wisdom of a single thought-moment, I shall realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I shall awaken to and discern this in such a manner.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva’s single path that is inexhaustible. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The skillful means practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise inexhaustible.
What are these skillful means?
Seeing all phenomena is a skillful means; giving rise to all phenomena is a skillful means; acting as a messenger for bodhisattvas is a skillful means.
This is skillful means; ultimate discernment is skillful means; being without limit is skillful means;
constantly seeking the supramundane Dharma with one’s resolve is skillful means; being able to fulfill all the *pāramitās* at the very moment of practicing giving is skillful means;
and when upholding the precepts, being able to take birth with sovereign mastery in any place whatsoever is skillful means.
This is skillful means: when practicing patience, adorning one's own person and the path to enlightenment is skillful means;
when practicing diligence, the mind having no dwelling place is skillful means; when cultivating meditative concentration, being without regression or loss is skillful means;
when practicing wisdom, not realizing the unconditioned is skillful means; and when cultivating a mind of loving-kindness—this is skillful means.
Compassion for those who lack power and influence is the skillful means; not wearying of birth and death while cultivating the mind of compassion is the skillful means;

finding no pleasure in worldly pleasures while cultivating the mind of sympathetic joy is the skillful means; generating the resolve to cultivate and accumulate all roots of goodness while cultivating the mind of equanimity is the skillful means;
and being able to cultivate the divine eye in order to achieve the eyes of all Buddhas is the skillful means.
This is a skillful means: cultivating and gathering the divine ear for the sake of accomplishing the ears of all Buddhas; this is a skillful means:
cultivating the knowledge of others' minds for the sake of attaining the Buddha's wisdom to know the depth and shallowness of the faculties of all sentient beings;
this is a skillful means: cultivating the knowledge of past lives for the sake of attaining the Buddha's wisdom to know the three periods of time without obstruction.
Cultivating and gathering supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for the sake of attaining the supernormal powers of all Buddhas is skillful means.
Adapting to the minds of sentient beings is skillful means; having attained self-awakening and further awakening others is skillful means.
To have already attained self-liberation yet manifest as one not yet liberated, while diligently practicing the quest for liberation from the world—this is skillful means.

To be already free from afflictions yet manifest as having afflictions—this is skillful means. To have already laid down the heavy burden yet manifest as still bearing the heavy burden—this is skillful means.
To know the capacity of the faculties and to teach the Dharma according to that capacity is skillful means; to be adept at guiding and advancing sentient beings of dull faculties is skillful means;
to know the appropriate and inappropriate times is skillful means; to know those on the path who are falling into error and to establish them in the right path is skillful means;
to be able to make the measurable immeasurable and the immeasurable measurable is skillful means.
To cause that which has been damaged to return to its original state is an expedient means; to manifest superior grounds is an expedient means;

to teach and explain that there are the pleasures of the five desires within nirvāṇa is an expedient means; to manifest the presence of fetters for one who has already attained liberation is an expedient means;
to abide within birth and death without falling into birth and death is an expedient means; regarding all... [text ends]
To have no fixed attachment to one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) yet never to fall away from it is an expedient means;

to observe only sentient beings without observing whether they uphold or violate the precepts is an expedient means; to gather those with various views and conditions so that they do not give rise to contention is an expedient means;
to realize that all are merely sounds and provisional names without reality is an expedient means; to constantly traverse the three realms is an expedient means.
Attaining the marks of liberation through practice is skillful means; approaching ordinary beings as one approaches noble ones is skillful means;
not realizing nirvana while constantly dwelling in the cycle of birth and death is skillful means;
manifesting great radiance within the realm of Māra without affliction is skillful means; that "all is this" and "all is not this" is skillful means.
"Śāriputra! This is called the inexhaustible practice of skillful means by a bodhisattva."
“Śāriputra! These are called the eighty inexhaustibles of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
These eighty inexhaustibles are fully capable of containing and sustaining all Buddha-dharmas.”

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati preached this chapter on the Dharma-gate, sixty-seven hundred thousand sentient beings who had not yet resolved their minds for awakening immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five hundred and twenty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the great assembly made offerings of various flowers, incense, flower garlands, and flower canopies to the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, and this very sutra. Then, from the sky above, immeasurable celestial music spontaneously produced these sounds, saying:

"The unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) accumulated by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, over immeasurable kalpas—its meaning has now been expounded within this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra by the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati."

If there are those who hear this inexhaustible Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain it, you should know that such persons are fully endowed with this inexhaustible Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his shoulder-covering robe to Akṣayamati and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Great Being, you have eloquently explained this meaning; it is not only I who approves, but all the Buddhas of the ten directions do likewise."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati took the robe in both hands, placed it upon the crown of his head, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Devas and people of the world should regard this robe as being more venerable than a stūpa, for it is that which was used by the Tathāgata.

At that time, many kinds of precious robes, precious canopies, precious banners, precious trees, and precious garlands came spontaneously from the worlds of the ten directions, covering Akṣayamati as an offering.
At that time, the precious robes, banners, canopies, and tree-garlands spontaneously uttered these words:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"You have skillfully expounded this inexhaustible Dharma-gate; we grant what you have said.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
“From where did these precious robes and articles of offering come,
that they should utter such words?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"All those sentient beings whom this Bodhisattva Akṣayamati converted when he first resolved his mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi throughout the ten directions."

These Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, knowing gratitude and seeking to repay their debt of kindness, have sent this one here to extol and praise the true merits of Akṣayamati, and furthermore to make offerings to the sūtra he has preached.
At that time, the great assembly felt redoubled reverence, respect, and praise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, and spoke thus:

"We have now attained a most excellent benefit in being able to see the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, to pay him homage, make offerings, honor, and praise him, and furthermore to hear this Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible."
“If there are those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, they too shall obtain excellent benefit; how much more so for those who see him with their eyes and hear this sūtra!
At that time, having heard these words in the great assembly, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who study the Bodhisattva path, making offerings to all Buddhas throughout a kalpa, training in the precepts and dignified conduct, exhausting the limits of the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings through the power of forbearance, and diligently cultivating and accumulating [virtues] as if their hair were on fire, achieving concentration and wisdom with skillful means in all meditative absorptions—if such persons are separated from this sūtra, I say that they have not yet fulfilled the six pāramitās.”

“Śāriputra! If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this sutra, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it; read and recite it; explain its meaning; and practice according to what is taught—I say that such persons have already fulfilled all the pāramitās and will swiftly attain the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If there is a bodhisattva who receives and upholds this sutra and expounds it for others, they thereby fulfill the dānapāramitā.
Why is this? Among all forms of giving, the gift of the Dharma is supreme; it ensures that one never forgets the bodhicitta from the very beginning.
To uphold this sutra is itself to uphold the precepts; therefore, one is able to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā.
Why is this? Because all the precepts studied by bodhisattvas are subsumed within this sutra.
If one can endure and take delight in this sutra, one cannot be destroyed by any sentient being.
To be able to cultivate patience within this [teaching] is to fulfill the pāramitā of kṣānti.
To diligently practice and propagate this sūtra, and to assiduously cultivate and accumulate the actions of body, speech, and mind, is to fulfill the pāramitā of vīrya.

If, regarding this sutra, their mind is tranquil and free from distraction, and they single-mindedly concentrate their intent to discern the characteristics of dharmas, they thereby fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"If one attains direct knowledge regarding this sutra and gains the wisdom of right practice without hearing it from another, that constitutes the fulfillment of the prajñāpāramitā. Śāriputra!"
If there is a bodhisattva who diligently studies this sutra, it will not be difficult for them to fulfill all the *pāramitās*. Śāriputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who studies this sutra, upholds, reads, recites, practices according to the teaching, and transcribes its scrolls, you should know that all the Buddha-dharmas are already in their hands. Even if the nature of the four great elements could be changed into something else, the mind of such a bodhisattva can never again be turned back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! This sutra is the seal of the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas; therefore, a bodhisattva should seek this seal.
If there are good sons or good daughters who draw near to this seal, they are drawing near to all the Buddha-dharmas.”
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and their retinues rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We four kings are disciples of the Buddha who have already attained the traces of the Path.”

If there are good men or good women who receive and uphold this sutra, we shall be capable of providing protection, supplies, and service for them; we shall regard such persons as we would the Tathāgata.
"Why is this? Because from within this sutra, all vehicles emerge.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have frequently heard from the Buddha immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of sūtras, yet I have never before heard a sūtra such as this that analyzes the profound meaning.”
“World-Honored One!

Wherever in any land, district, city, town, or village there may be those who preach this sutra, I shall personally go with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to hear and receive it. Furthermore, I shall protect the Dharma-preacher and augment his vital strength, so that through courageous diligence, right mindfulness, and eloquence, this Dharma-preacher may attain fearlessness among the great assembly and be able to widely proclaim such a sutra as this.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!”
If you wish to protect these preachers of the Dharma so that they may attain courageous progress, right mindfulness, and eloquence, Kausika!
If you wish to protect these preachers of the Dharma, you are thereby protecting the True Dharma of all Buddhas; and those who protect the True Dharma are protecting all sentient beings.
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, King of the Gods, joined his palms, knelt on one knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Wherever this sūtra circulates, I shall personally, together with the other Brahma hosts and my retinue, renounce the bliss of dhyāna and go to that place to listen, receive, and inquire about it."
When I go there at that time, I shall manifest four omens to cause him to awaken to this knowledge. What are the four?
First, I shall cause him to see a subtle and wondrous radiance.
Second, they shall perceive extraordinary fragrances;
third, they shall cause the preacher of the Dharma to attain unimpeded eloquence and correct mindfulness, so that what is spoken is auspicious and the phrasing and sentences are not lost;
fourth, they shall cause the great assembly to give rise to a mind of wholesome aspiration, joyfully listening to the Dharma without ever becoming weary or satiated.
"By these four omens, you should know that Brahmā, King of the Gods, has come in person with his retinue to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the sixth Māra, Pāpīyān, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Such a sutra as this causes all my power to become utterly weak and inferior. Why is this?

If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing this sutra, receives, upholds, reads, recites, and extensively explains it for others, you should know that such a person has received a prediction of enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
Wherever such a bodhisattva goes, even reaching the realms of all Buddhas, one should know him to be like a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
All my current pride, jealousy, and arrogance have been utterly subdued by the power of the majesty of Akṣayamati.

I shall now protect such a sutra as well as those who preach it; wherever this sutra circulates and spreads, I will not even give rise to a single thought of creating obstacles, let alone go there in person to intentionally create the conditions for such hindrance!
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"From this day forward, for the sake of the long-term endurance of the True Dharma in the world, you should receive this sūtra, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it."
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes, rose, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now respectfully receive and uphold this sutra as taught by the Buddha; however, I regret that I am unable to widely proclaim and disseminate it as the various bodhisattvas do.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You need not worry; there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in this assembly who will themselves be able to protect and uphold it, so that this sūtra may be widely proclaimed and circulated."

At that time, there were sixty billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the assembly who were destined to protect the Dharma; they rose from their seats, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We must certainly proclaim this sutra so that it reaches the ten directions;
in the Sahā world, the Great Being Maitreya shall himself protect and uphold this scripture and its preachers therein.
World-Honored One!

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there should be bodhisattvas who hear this sutra and accept, uphold, read, and recite it, you should know that these are all established through the spiritual power of Maitreya.
At that time, the Buddha praised the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who protect the Dharma:
“Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!
"You all have not only upheld the True Dharma before me now, but you have also upheld the True Dharma of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I now expound this sutra by means of my own limited share of wisdom; its words, phrases, and meanings are surely incomplete. I now, before the Buddha and in the presence of the bodhisattvas who have achieved the inexhaustible Dharma, repent of these transgressions.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:

“Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), whatever they preach will be free from error. Such a bodhisattva, having attained the dharma-gate of discerning the meaning of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is then able to proclaim a sūtra such as this.”

"Good son! You have now reached the foremost state; having achieved mastery over the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) without obstruction, you are able to discern this Mahāyāna sūtra without having heard it from another."
"Good son! You have now accomplished such a stage of abiding, and your actions of body, speech, and mind are free from error. Why is this?
