The three karmas cultivated by Bodhisattvas are accomplished because they always take wisdom as their foundation. Good son!
There have already been immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who all together praise and approve what you have spoken.
“Anantamati! You have already, from the very beginning, performed ultimate repentance before me and before all the Buddhas, such that there is no longer any lapse.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This sutra is named ‘The Gateway of the Inexhaustible Meanings and Phrases Spoken by Akṣayamati,’ and it is also named ‘The Great Collection’ (Mahāsaṃnipāta); you should uphold it thus.”
Ānanda! You should believe and accept such a sutra as this. Why is that?
"Once you have received this, the power of your retention and mindfulness shall be a thousandfold greater than before; if you preach it to others, you will establish the work of a Buddha.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the Venerable Ānanda and Śāriputra, and the entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, and others—were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.

The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Thirty. According to this text, in the Song and Xiang editions of the canon, it consists of sixty fascicles in total comprising seventeen chapters; in the Dan edition of the canon, it consists of thirty fascicles comprising eleven chapters.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the scripture, the versions from the Song and the Xiang [catalogs] include the title "Chapter on the Necklace" (*Yíngluò pǐn*), which is absent from the Dan [Tang] canon.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Treasury of Space" (*Xūkōng zàng pǐn*), in the Song and Xiang versions it follows the "Ineffable Chapter" (*Bùkěshuō pǐn*), whereas in the Dan version it precedes the "Silent Chapter" (*Wúyán pǐn*).

Furthermore, following the "Ratnacūḍa-parivarta," the Song and Xiang editions contain four fascicles of the "Akṣayamati-parivarta," which are absent from the Danzang; instead, the latter contains three fascicles of the "Sūryaguhya-vibhāga."
Why is it that they differ in this way?
Now, examining the *Kaiyuan lu*, there are six versions of this scripture in total. The *lu* states:
According to the *Record of the Mahāsaṃnipāta* by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou, it states:
"There are twelve sections that together constitute a single sutra:

first, the 'Garuḍa-ornament Chapter' (*Ratnavyūha-parivarta*); second, the 'Dhāraṇī-vaśavartin Chapter'; third, the 'Ratnāvalī Chapter'; fourth, the 'Animiṣa Chapter'; fifth, the 'Sāgarabuddhi Chapter'; sixth, the 'Avacanā Chapter'; seventh, the 'Anabhilāpya Chapter'; eighth, the 'Gaganagañja Chapter'; ninth, the 'Ratnaketu Chapter'; tenth, the 'Gagananetra Chapter'; eleventh, the 'Ratnaśikhin Chapter'; and twelfth, the 'Akṣayamati Chapter.'"

According to the record, this is the first edition; examining the sequence of the fascicles now, it constitutes the first thirty fascicles among the sixty-fascicle version of the Song and Xiang editions.
Furthermore, it says: "Now, upon examining the manuscript of the sutra, it differs from Sengyou’s record:

first, the 'Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja'; second, the 'Chapter on the Jewel Woman'; third, the 'Chapter on Animiṣa'; fourth, the 'Chapter on Sāgaramati'; fifth, the 'Chapter on Gaganagañja'; sixth, the 'Chapter on Silence'; seventh, the 'Chapter on the Ineffable'; eighth, the 'Section on the Jewel Banner'; ninth, the 'Section on Gagananetra'; tenth, the 'Chapter on Ratnaśikhin'; and eleventh, the 'Section on Sūryaguhya'."
The commentary states: "This is the second version. Examining the sequence of the fascicles now, it corresponds to the thirty final fascicles of the present edition in the Danzang (Beijing Edition).
The compilation further notes:

'During the Sui dynasty, the monk Jiu combined the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, taking the *Pañcāśat-prajñāpāramitā-parīkṣā-sūtra* and titling it the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions," which he appended after the "Moon Store" (*Candragarbha*) chapter; thus it was made into fifty-eight fascicles including the "Inexhaustible Intent" (*Anutpādārtha*). This is incorrect, and as there is no authoritative basis for it, we do not follow that version.'"
The commentary states: "This is the fourth version.

Furthermore, it is said that when combined with the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there is also a version consisting of sixty fascicles; this is achieved because the thirty-first and thirty-second fascicles both contain the 'Ratnacūḍa-parivarta,' thereby completing the total of sixty fascicles."
The "Ratnacūḍa-parivarta" is contained within volumes twenty-six or twenty-seven, preceding the "Sūryagupta" chapter; its re-inclusion here remains unclear as to its intent.
Furthermore, since the Sanskrit manuscripts for the "Sūryagupta" and "Sūryagarbha" chapters do not differ, their repeated inclusion is a grave error.
The commentary states: "This is the fifth version; examining its sequence of chapters, it is the sixty-fascicle *Sūtra* currently held in the Song and Xiang editions of the canon."

However, it does not include the "Ratnacūḍaparivarta," which is its only minor difference; thus, it appears that from among the fifty-eight fascicles of the aforementioned fourth edition, the middle fascicles of the "Sūryagarbha-parivarta" were divided into twelve fascicles to complete the total of sixty.

As for the third and sixth versions, I shall not trouble to describe them here, as they are currently absent from the various canons; it is simply because the textual versions of the sūtra differ in this way that such discrepancies have arisen within the collections.

I have carefully examined the textual sequence of the *Kaiyuan lu*; as for this compilation of sixty fascicles of combined scriptures, it cannot be relied upon for practice because it contains six errors.

The *Lu* states: "There are also versions of the scripture that divide it into a 'Garuḍa-Necklace Chapter' (Yingluo-pin), but this is not correct; this is a single section and should not be divided into two."
The commentary states: "To divide this scripture [in this manner] is the first error.
Furthermore, it says:

"It is not the case that Sengyou’s catalogue lacks the *Rimik-bun* (Division on Sun-Mystery) and possesses the *Mujinyi-hon* (Chapter on Akṣayamati); for although the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, it was not translated by Kumārajīva, nor does it follow the sequential order [of the original], and thus it is inappropriate to include it therein."
According to the investigation, this scripture was included among the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and was also translated by Kumārajīva; these are two errors.
Furthermore, it is said:
"As for its *Gaganagañja-parivarta*, Sengyou places it after the *Avaktavya-parivarta*; the reason for this remains unclear."
The commentary states: "To claim that this sutra exists there [in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*] is the third error.
Furthermore, it says:
'The Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Dīrghāloka* and the *Sūryagarbha* are not different; to include them repeatedly is a most egregious mistake.'"
The commentary states: "This scripture is recorded twice; this is the fourth error. Furthermore, it says:

'The *Mingdu Wushi Jiaojijing* (Sutra on the Fifty Evaluations of the Perfection of Wisdom) has the title "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions. To compile it after the *Yuezang* (Moon Storehouse) is incorrect; since there is no authoritative basis for it, we do not follow that version.'"
According to the record, this scripture was based upon that [original], which constitutes the fifth loss.
Furthermore, while the *Mingdu jing* was translated by An Shigao, it is here stated to have been translated by Narendrayaśas.
The commentary states: This, too, misleads people; it is the sixth error.
Since there are these six errors, it is necessary in principle to rectify them.
How are they to be rectified?

In brief, it is correct that there are thirty fascicles, as in the *Kaiyuan lu* and the Danzang edition; in its full form, it comprises eighty fascicles, as in the sixth version within the *Kaiyuan lu*, which alone is complete.

Now, as for the two collections at Song and Xiang, they follow the *Kaiyuan lu* in their catalogs, yet they still retain the versions of the sūtras held by Sengjue; this is simply because they have had no intention of collating them.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Part Thirteen: The Division on Sun-Mystery (Sūryaguhya). Chapter One: Protecting the Dharma. Within the Division on Sun-Mystery, Chapter One: Protecting the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained in the Great Jewel Monastery situated between the realms of desire and form, together with an immeasurable number of great bodhisattvas. Having finished preaching for the great assembly the Gate of Ambrosia of the Exhalation and Inhalation of the Eye of Space, he sat in silence.
The entire great assembly was likewise; each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata today deeply understands that our minds desire the Dharma without weariness; he will surely pour down the nectar-like rain of the Dharma."

Having formed this thought, they joined their palms in reverent worship, longing to behold the Tathāgata, just as one suffering from a grave illness longs to see a skilled physician; as one in darkness longs to see the light; as one submerged in water longs to reach the other shore; and as one undergoing suffering longs to find refuge—the entire great assembly was likewise so disposed.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Great Brahmā Padmaprabha-guṇa, who had planted various roots of merit and cultivated all virtues under immeasurable and boundless buddhas; he was non-retrogressive in his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and had fully accomplished the compassion based on dharmas. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms in reverence, knelt on one knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The objects of focus for the minds of all sentient beings are without limit; they are swift, formless, and their nature is fundamentally pure.

Being unobstructed within all states of existence, and desiring to attain thorough penetration and knowledge of reality, one diligently cultivates and accumulates the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Through this cultivation and accumulation, one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
“World-Honored One!
If the nature of the triple world is fundamentally pure, for what reason do they cultivate and accumulate such knowledge of exhaustion?

We pray that the Tathāgata will expound and explain this for the sake of all bodhisattvas, so that those who have regressed may attain non-retrogression, so that the realms of immeasurable afflictions may be crushed and destroyed, and so that the boundless aggregates of suffering may be severed and broken.”

I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to take pity on us and speak what has never been heard before; once sentient beings have heard this which was unheard of, they shall cross the ocean of birth and death and break down the tree of craving.
For what reason?
All afflictions have craving as their root.

We pray that you will compassionately distinguish and expound upon the faults of craving; for the Tathāgata can purify the six sense faculties of sentient beings, we further entreat you to expound upon the collection of pure dharmas.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

If there are those who can practice the six pāramitās, they will be able to know for themselves the sphere in which their minds operate; such persons will never think of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Although they may practice immeasurable deeds without yet reaching their limit, they will not fear falling back into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

If bodhisattvas are unable to cultivate and accumulate the four immeasurables, such bodhisattvas will experience regression from the path to enlightenment; this is called not attaining the purity of the six sense faculties, and it is called having greed and stinginess regarding the Dharma.

This is called practicing the path of others while not practicing one's own path; it is called being unable to accomplish the seven riches and being unable to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death. Therefore, I say that such a practitioner follows the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"I have first expounded the practice of the Four Noble Truths, and shall subsequently continue to expound the practices of all Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the entire great assembly all had this thought:
"Is the Tathāgata about to speak of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and not the Mahāyāna?"
Is it not that the Tathāgata does not delight in such an assembly of bodhisattvas?
Does the Tathāgata not wish to sever the lineage of the Three Jewels?

For what reason do you not preach the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna so that devas and humans may gain faith, so that those who have not yet resolved for enlightenment may resolve their minds, so that those who have already resolved may increase in virtue, and so that all sentient beings may attain faith?

If the Tathāgata were to preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings would be inspired to give rise to the bodhicitta; by virtue of this, they would practice the uncommon dharmas and achieve the perfection of the dharma-dhāraṇī.
“Good son! The Śrāvaka Vehicle is itself the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is itself the Śrāvaka Vehicle; thus, there is no distinction between these two vehicles.”
At that time, the bodhisattvas dwelling in the ten stages within the assembly spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

We have already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); we are now able to practice the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Tathāgata; and we have fully understood both the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna. Yet, among this multitude, immeasurable sentient beings are unable to understand either the Small Vehicle or the Great Vehicle.”
“Sons of good family! You should cultivate the non-retrogressive meditative concentration.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas immediately entered its cultivation.

Having entered, some bodies emit radiance like a single torch, like the bodily light of Śakra or Brahmā, like the light of the sun and moon, like the light of three suns, like the light of four suns, like the light of eight suns, like the light of ten suns, or like the light of a hundred million suns.
In this way, it universally illumines the Sahā world.
This light is able to bring peace and tranquility to the bodies and minds of immeasurable sentient beings.

Those in the three evil realms are freed from all suffering and affliction; those with wrong views distance themselves from their evil perspectives; and they are forever liberated from the calamities of greed, hatred, delusion, fear, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
At that time, the sentient beings of this Buddha-world all together made offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, increasing their wholesome dharmas.

At that moment, this Buddha-world, as well as immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions—whether empty or non-empty, pure or impure—were entirely illuminated by light. All Bodhisattvas capable of practicing the noble conduct of the path to enlightenment gathered together within the Great Jewel Monastery in a single thought-moment; they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of śrāvakas:
"O bhikṣus, do you see such excellent supernormal powers?

Such supernormal powers can destroy all realms of evil Māras and all states of existence; they can protect the dharma-realm and traverse the realms of all Buddhas; they can distinguish the realms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, surpassing all other supernatural faculties."

“Good son! The reason all Bodhisattvas manifest great supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) is to increase the roots of goodness in sentient beings; to ensure that the nature of the Triple Gem is never severed; to cause those who have not yet gained faith to attain it; to cause those who already have faith to further increase it; to enable sentient beings to experience the five pleasures; to desire to nurture and grow the Mahāyāna Dharma; and to cause their bodies to attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity. For such causes and conditions as these, they manifest these supernatural powers to all sentient beings.”
“Good son! Following such spheres of practice of the bodhisattvas, the Buddha-dharma therein will increase.

If it abides for a long time in the present and future without perishing, there will be sentient beings who build stupas and temples and make offerings to the Sangha, seeking an inexhaustible body and a body free from suffering. All such offerings are made toward both the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Offerings to the birth-body consist of stupas and images; offerings to the dharma-body consist of copying, reading, and reciting the twelve divisions of the scriptures. This is superior to making offerings with the seven treasures, incense, flowers, music, banners, canopies, and necklaces.”
“Good son! At that time, my mind also accepted it.
By means of such giving, these sentient beings will fully attain the fruits and rewards of the three vehicles, and their minds will never regress.”
If sentient beings construct houses and walkways for me, I shall make use of them.

If they provide groves, flower gardens, lecture halls, and monasteries, as well as food, drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and dwellings for my disciples and myself, I shall likewise make use of them.
If Dharma masters ascend the high seat to preach the Dharma, I shall at that time listen with a sincere mind.

If they are given offerings of clothing, food, bedding, medicine for illness, dwellings, gardens, vehicles, fields, houses, servants, or slaves, I shall likewise accept them; this is called the offering of the Dharma.
“Such a person is able to purify the body and mind and adorn the body and mind; they are also able to adorn Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attain unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous bliss.”

To be able to give all things, to all people, at all times; and to be able to receive all fruits, from all people, at all times—this is called accomplishing the merit of generous giving. Such a person will never fall into the three evil realms and shall attain the state of non-falling.

Without turning back from the Three Vehicles regarding whatever they seek, such persons constantly attain the fulfillment of two kinds of things, namely wealth and the Dharma; whatever objects they seek are obtained according to their wishes, they are always kept in mind by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and they are able to destroy all realms of Māra.

If there are those with faith who offer whatever they possess to a Dharma teacher, and if one who has broken the precepts should receive such things—even as much as a single leaf, a single flower, or a single fruit—such a deluded person will, by reason of these causes and conditions, incur a great unwholesome retribution.
In the present life, one immediately incurs four great evil fruits:
first, an ill reputation spreads far and wide;
second, all those who are close—teachers and friends alike—distance themselves.

Third, they die from the suffering of a grave illness and misfortune; that is to say, at the time of death, they cannot consume food or drink, they behold foul sights, and because of these causes and conditions, they are unable to speak and lie fouled by excrement.

Fourth, their six requisites and other wealth do not reach the Sangha, but are instead consumed by fire or plundered by evil bandits; in future lives, they further undergo four kinds of evil retributions, namely: rebirth in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal, or, if they obtain a human body, they are born without hands or feet.
If one receives birth as a hungry ghost, for immeasurable years one will neither see nor even hear the name of water or drink;
if one receives the body of an animal, one will constantly eat earth and mud;

if one attains human status, one will dwell in a desolate land where the Three Jewels do not exist, in an age of the five corruptions, blind and sightless, constantly encountering grave illnesses and eating various kinds of filth.
After abandoning this body, they will fall back into hell.
Why is this? Because they accepted the goods obtained by the Dharma Master.
"This evil bhikṣu was able to destroy, extinguish, and sever the Three Jewels; for this reason, he has obtained such an evil retribution.
At that time, there was among the assembly a bhikṣu of great virtue named Gayākāśyapa, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Can such a person as this be called a "person"?
As I reflect upon it now, he is not a person. Why is this?
"This person upholds the prohibitive precepts solely because of a mind deeply attached to gain and profit; therefore, they are called a 'non-human' (amanuṣya).
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Kāśyapa! It would be better to take on the body of a being in the hells than ever to accept such things as these. Good son!

Having obtained the human body which is so difficult to obtain, having encountered the Buddha-dharma which is so difficult to encounter, and having received the prohibitive precepts which are so difficult to receive, yet failing to advance toward noble conduct and the holy life—this is called losing a matter of great benefit.
Such evil persons, because their minds are driven by greed for food, observe the prohibitive precepts not out of a mind for the Dharma.
Such deluded persons, by virtue of the power of their extensive learning and the power of kings and ministers, accept such things; they will immediately incur the karmic fruit of great evil.
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a person who has left the household life receives such things and attains such fruits, what is the offense for a householder who receives them?"
The Buddha said: "Great King!
You should not now ask such a question."
The King said, “World-Honored One!
Having cultivated the noble practice, I shall never accept such things as these; I ask about such matters only for the sake of future generations of wicked kings.”
The Buddha said, “Great King!

If I were to proclaim the karmic retributions that future evil kings will receive, there would be those who do not believe and would thus incur great sinful retribution. For this reason, I now set it aside and do not speak of it.”
The King said:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of those in future ages—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who possess faith and reverence, and who uphold the Buddha-dharma while protecting Dharma-preachers and their property, provide a detailed and thorough explanation.”
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent,
Great King!"
If, in future ages, various evil kings should plunder such things as these from Dharma masters, you should know that those kings will obtain twenty kinds of evils in their present life:
first, the devas will not protect them;
second, their ill repute will spread far and wide.
Third, one becomes estranged from friends;
fourth, enemies increase;
fifth, wealth and possessions are depleted.
Sixth, the mind is frequently distracted;
seventh, the body is not complete;
eighth, one cannot obtain sleep.
Ninth, they will constantly suffer from famine;
tenth, the food and drink they consume will turn into malignant poisons;
eleventh, the people will not love or respect them.
Twelfth, neighboring states frequently invade;
thirteenth, his own kinsmen do not obey his instructions;
fourteenth, secret matters are exposed by his ministers.
Fifteenth, all one's wealth and possessions are seized by water or fire;
sixteenth, one constantly suffers from serious illness;
seventeenth, medicinal decoctions and remedies do not take effect.
Eighteenth, medical treatment and medicine do not cure;
nineteenth, even water for rinsing the mouth cannot go down;
twentieth, one constantly dwells upon impurity—these are called the twenty.

Having abandoned this body, one will immediately be reborn in the Avīci Hell to suffer for one kalpa. Once that kalpa has passed, one will obtain the body of a hungry ghost in a vast wilderness; there, one will not even hear the names of water, drink, or food. With impaired faculties and an incomplete body, one will undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable years.

Having experienced these fruits, one will be born in the great ocean to take the body of a massive beast, many yojanas in size like a great mass of flesh, constantly being pecked and eaten by other beings while undergoing great suffering and affliction.
Even if they obtain a human body, they will be born in a world of the five corruptions where no Buddha resides, and their ears and eyes will be incomplete.
Great King! Future evil kings shall receive such great and evil retributions as these.
The king said,
“World-Honored One!
I would rather now take on the body of a hell-being than ever again receive such a wicked kingly body.”
The Buddha said,
"Great King! I now entrust this Dharma, these Dharma-preachers, and these material goods to you and all the other kings who possess faith."
"Why is this? For the Dharma Master is the treasury of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
The King said:
“World-Honored One!
If there are kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras who are able to protect and uphold such Dharma-treasures, what kind of merit and virtue will those people attain?”
The Buddha said,
“Great King! Such a person as this surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
"Great King!
It is as if there were someone who could sever the life-span of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, rob them of their eyes, and cut off their hands and feet.
Great King!"
"What would be the measure of the retribution for the sins incurred by such a person?
King Bimbisāra remained silent and did not answer.
The Buddha said:
“Great King! Why do you remain silent?
The king replied:
“World-Honored One!
The retribution for the evil karma obtained by this person is immeasurable and incalculable.
World-Honored One!”
"If the transgression of committing such evil karma against a single person is already difficult to calculate, how much more so when it concerns all people! "Great King!

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, if there are wicked kings—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who plunder such things belonging to a Dharma-master, let the retribution for the sins they incur be divided into one hundred parts; the sin incurred by the aforementioned [king] does not equal even one of those parts."
King Bimbisāra said: “World-Honored One!
It is rare for a king to rule his country according to the Dharma.”
"If one is not negligent, one can protect the Dharma; if one is negligent, one cannot protect it, World-Honored One!
What merit does one who can protect the Dharma obtain?"
“Great King! Suppose there were a person who could grant the aforementioned sentient beings their life-span, eyes, hands, and feet; would the merit this person obtains not be great?”
“World-Honored One!
If one were able to give life, eyes, hands, and feet to a single person, the merit thereof would already be vast; how much more so for that many people! “Great King!
"If the merit obtained by one who protects the Dharma were divided into a hundred parts, the previously acquired blessings would not equal even a single one of them.
The King said,
"World-Honored One!"
"If one were to take the property of a single Dharma teacher, would this constitute an offense?
And if one were to protect a single Dharma teacher, would one further obtain merit? "Great King!"

If one receives and takes the property of one Dharma teacher up to five Dharma teachers, protecting that one Dharma teacher and those five Dharma teachers, the resulting demerit and merit are exactly equal and no different.
"Great King! Whether it be a single temple, a single village, or a single grove where five Dharma-preachers reside,

if one strikes the *gandī* to assemble the Sangha from the four quarters, and once the visiting monks have gathered, provides them with dwellings, food and drink, bedding, and medicine in due order, without a heart of stinginess."

During the first and last watches of the night, they engage in recitation and discussion; they feel weary of birth and death and single-mindedly delight in Nirvana; they do not praise themselves nor disparage others; having few desires and being content, they always delight in praising [others]; with few desires and contentment, they apply themselves with diligent effort; their will delights in tranquility as they cultivate mindfulness and concentration, feeling compassion for all sentient beings.
"Great King!
This is called the Saṃgha dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.

Protecting the precepts, being diligent, and upholding the Buddha’s secret treasury; reciting, copying, and explaining the teachings—this is called the Saṃgha having compassion for sentient beings and benefiting sentient beings. They are able to uphold the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, and they are also able to reverently maintain the tranquil prohibitions and precepts, being fully endowed with shame, remorse, and the virtues of the noble ones."
"Great King!

This is called the Great Ocean of Merit of the Sangha; as the Teacher of Gods and Humans, they are able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, able to sever all the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, and able to bestow liberation upon all sentient beings. Even these five bhikṣus are called the Sangha, how much more so those who are immeasurable!"
“Great King! Even if an immeasurable number of monks have all broken the prohibitions and precepts, if there are but five who are pure and act according to the Dharma,
any donor who makes an offering will obtain immeasurable merit— beyond praise and beyond calculation.”

Why is this? Because there are those who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma; because they have compassion for all sentient beings; and because their minds are impartial and free from dualistic characteristics.
The King said:
“World-Honored One!
May a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts receive offerings of faith from the assembly?”

“Great King! Suppose there is a criminal within your kingdom who has not yet been banished. If you were to bestow gifts upon a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, would that person be able to enjoy the pleasure?”
"No, World-Honored One. "Great King!"
A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is likewise; although he receives offerings of faith from within the assembly, he cannot attain peace and happiness.
Why is this? Because he has violated the prohibitions and does not act in accordance with the Dharma.
"Great King!
Such a person is not protected or remembered by the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions; though they bear the name of a bhikṣu, they do not belong to the number of the Saṃgha."
Why is this? Because they have entered the realm of Māra.
Those who uphold the prohibitive precepts are disciples of the Buddha.
Those who violate the prohibitions and precepts are the disciples of Māra.
Furthermore, those who uphold the precepts follow the supramundane path;
those who break the prohibitions and precepts enter the mundane path.
I do not permit those who violate the precepts to receive the faithful offerings of others, even as small as a mustard seed. Why is this?
Because such persons have distanced themselves from the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The king said:
"World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of one who has broken the precepts?"
"Can this be known? "Great King! One who possesses wisdom can know it."

"Great King! If there is one who cannot revere the Triple Gem, who does not give rise to faith and lacks shame and remorse; who does not show respect toward their preceptors, teachers, elders, seniors, fellow disciples, or fellow students; who destroys the banner of the noble ones and does not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*); who increases stinginess and greed and delights in living as a householder; who cannot purify the four types of verbal karma; who constantly cultivates a mind for food while remaining distant from a mind for the Dharma; and who delights in speaking of worldly matters that are of no benefit—this is called the first sign of a bhikṣu’s breaking of the precepts, yet it is not yet termed the full violation of the prohibitions."

If one thus accepts and keeps male and female slaves, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, chickens, pigs, and even the eight kinds of impure items, this is called being fully possessed of the violation of the precepts.
Such a person is called the dregs among śramaṇas, the crooked among śramaṇas, the illusionist among śramaṇas, the thief among śramaṇas, the intoxicated among śramaṇas, and the caṇḍāla among śramaṇas.

In this way, such a bhikṣu should not dwell together with others nor live in harmony with them; he should not perform ninety-nine types of formal acts (karmavācanā) alongside them. This is called the loss of a bhikṣu’s vocation and falling into the realm of greed.
"Great King! It would be better to dwell together with a caṇḍāla than to dwell with such an evil bhikṣu. Why is this?
Such a bhikṣu burns away his roots of goodness and severs the heart of compassion for the three periods of time; he is an evil bhikṣu.
He is a latrine that increases the dharmas of birth and death, and he is the seed of all evils for humans and devas.
Why is this? Such a person deceives themselves, others, gods, and humans.

A bhikṣu such as this extinguishes the lamp of liberation and can topple the banner of the Dharma; he dries up the ocean of the Dharma and destroys those who preach it; he deceives donors and breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha.

If there are evil kings—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who protect such wicked bhikṣus, those kings will cause the three evil realms to increase and plant the seeds of evil for devas and humans.

“Great King! If wicked bhikṣus revile, abuse, or reproach those who abide in accordance with the Dharma, kings who possess faith and respect ought to banish them; if they do so banish them, the king will gain great merit.”

If the king lacks faith, a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma should not dwell together with that evil bhikṣu; rather, a wise bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma should first go to the king’s presence and speak these words:
“Great King!...”
"Are you now able to uphold the Dharma?
If the King replies,
"Venerable Sir!"...
"I am able to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the wise person should remain silent.
If that great king possesses a greedy mind, he will say to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!
There are many people in this temple; how could I drive them away for the sake of five bhikṣus?
Having heard this, the wise one should not go there again, but should instead depart and go to a place of tranquility.
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
If there were an evil king who followed the words of such an evil bhikṣu, how could this great earth bear that king?”

From this point forward, for immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he will ultimately be unable to regain a human body; even after immeasurable sentient beings have attained liberation, this king will still be unable to sever the karma of the three evil realms.

“Great King! If in future ages there are faithful kings—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who can protect Dharma-teachers by constructing stūpas and images, providing the monastic community with all their various necessities, and punishing wicked bhikṣus; who, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, can sacrifice their own bodies and lives, and would rather protect a single bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma than protect immeasurable wicked bhikṣus, such a king will, upon casting off his body, be born in a pure Buddha-land and constantly encounter the Triple Gem. Before long, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Great King! I do not now permit a single person to accept or possess the eight kinds of impure things; I permit only the community as a whole to receive, possess, and use them.
Great King!"

If there is anyone who can protect and uphold the Dharma, you should know that such a person is a great donor (*mahādānapati*) to the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions, for they protect and uphold the Great Dharma.
“Great King! The property of the Saṃgha is difficult to manage; I now permit only two kinds of persons to guard and protect it:
first, an Arhat bhikṣu who is endowed with the eight liberations;”
Second, there are those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Great King!
Apart from these two types of persons, there is no one else who may take charge of or protect the property of the Sangha.

2. Chapter on the Gathering of the Bodhisattvas from the Four Directions. In the second part of the "Chapter on the Gathering of the Bodhisattvas from the Four Directions" within the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta* of the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*: At that time, the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma for King Bimbisāra.
To the east there is a land named Immeasurable; therein dwells a Buddha named Five Virtues, who constantly preaches the sublime Dharma to transform and guide sentient beings.

There was a bodhisattva named Sūryagupta who, listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart, looked up into the void and saw immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas coming from the east and proceeding toward the west. He immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

“I see immeasurable bodhisattvas from the eastern direction proceeding toward the western direction. By what causes and conditions do they abandon a pure and wondrous land to proceed toward a defiled realm? “Good son!

To the west, beyond immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named Sahā, fully possessed of the five corruptions and filled with wicked sentient beings.

Within this, Śākyamuni Tathāgata proclaimed the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for the sake of increasing the Buddha’s true Dharma, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is not severed, for the sake of destroying the realm of Māra and erecting the banner of the Dharma, and for the sake of the long-term endurance of the Dharma so that it does not perish.
In that Buddha-world, there are immeasurable Buddhas and immeasurable Bodhisattvas who proclaim the Dharma of the Ratnaśikhara Dhāraṇī.

Once they have finished preaching this Dharma, Śākyamuni Tathāgata further teaches the three vehicles, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the four types of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). When immeasurable sentient beings hear this Dharma, their minds feel no weariness or fatigue because they delight in the ambrosia (*amṛta*). Furthermore, by the power of that Tathāgata’s original vows, immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from the four directions all gather in that land.

When the Buddha preached the Dharma, the assembly of bodhisattvas all entered meditative concentration; having entered concentration, their bodies emitted radiance, like a single torch extending to the brilliance of a hundred million suns.
“Good son! If you wish to protect the Dharma, you may arise from this samādhi and proceed to the Sahā world. Good son!”

All sentient beings in that Buddha-world have afflictions that are firm and deep-seated bonds that are heavy; their forms are ugly and foul, and they frequently give rise to arrogance. They use harsh speech and double-tongued talk, remaining far removed from truthful speech. In reality they are ignorant, yet they manifest the appearance of wisdom; they are full of stinginess and greed, yet they manifest the appearance of renunciation. They are full of flattery and crookedness, yet they manifest the appearance of integrity; their minds are mostly turbid and chaotic, yet they manifest the appearance of purity. They are full of jealousy, yet they manifest the appearance of gentleness; they delight in alienating others, yet they manifest the appearance of harmony; they frequently give rise to false views, yet they manifest the appearance of right view.
The people of that country followed the woman’s words; because they followed her words, they severed their roots of goodness and increased the three evil realms. "Good son!
Are you now able to act as my messenger and go to that country?"
I wish to bestow my desire so that that Tathāgata may skillfully expound the essentials of the Dharma.

What is called "desire" refers to the true dhāraṇī; this dhāraṇī is fully endowed with immeasurable merit and is able to sever desire for sense-pleasures, desire for form and the formless, pride, the conceit of self, all craving for grasping, and all five hindrances.

All views of a self, views of annihilation, views of attachment to precepts and rituals, views of grasping, views of permanence, views of a sentient being, views of a person, views of an agent, views of an experiencer, views of a human, views of a deity, views of form, views of sound, views of smell, views of taste, views of touch, views of the four great elements, views of emergence, views of birth, views of cessation, and views of abiding—these are called the patience that accords with reality as it is.

This dhāraṇī enables one to truly know form up to consciousness, the eye up to the mind, the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as all the gateways to liberation and the unsurpassed, wondrous bliss of the dharma-realm.

“Good son! The sentient beings in that realm are like those born deaf, born blind, and born mute, who are crazed and intoxicated by desire. Therefore, one bestows upon them the Dharma-door of the inconceivable treasury of all dharmas—the true dhāraṇī method according to reality—which is able to destroy all the factions of Māra and the realms of Māra.”

“Good son! This dhāraṇī can also subdue all hosts of Māras, terrify all evil and venomous nāgas, cause evil spirits to give rise to the thought of contentment, transform all the hosts of asuras, and tame all great garuḍas while terrifying the kiṃnaras.”
It causes all rākṣasas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras to give rise to reverence and faith, and enables them to destroy all craving for a woman's body.

It causes those who are learned to give rise to a heart of love and joy; it enables those who practice meditation to attain mental tranquility; it skillfully cures all manner of grave and evil illnesses; and it can eliminate all evil omens within a land, namely: wicked bandits, malevolent birds, predatory beasts, calamitous winds, disastrous rains, excessive cold, and extreme heat.
“Good son! If there is anyone who can recite this dhāraṇī, they shall be able to behold immeasurable Buddhas. Good son!”
"Go to that land with this dhāraṇī and proclaim it fully before those four assemblies.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sūryagupta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I am able to proclaim this mantra for them, yet I feel a sense of fear regarding that land. Why is this?

As the Tathāgata previously explained to me, the sentient beings in that land are for the most part corrupt and evil; they are like those born deaf, born blind, or born mute, who follow the whims of women.
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who comply with the wishes of women, you should know that such persons have forever severed their roots of goodness.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! You should now act not for the sake of your own present or future benefit, but for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; go and proclaim this teaching without giving rise to doubt or hesitation.”
“Good son! Are you not Vimalakīrti of that land? Why have you become afraid?
The Bodhisattva Sūryagupta remained silent and did not answer.
“Good son! Why do you remain silent? Sūryagupta replied:
“World-Honored One!
That Vimalakīrti is none other than myself.
World-Honored One!”
In that land, I manifest in the form of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) to proclaim the essential points of the Dharma for all sentient beings.

At times, I manifest in the form of a Brahmin, or a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra; or the form of Maheśvara, or Śakra, or Brahmā; or the form of a Nāga king, an Asura king, a Garuḍa king, a Kiṃnara king, a Pratyekabuddha, a Śrāvaka, an elder, a woman, a boy, a girl, an animal, a hungry ghost (*preta*), or a hell-being—for the purpose of taming sentient beings.
At that time, there were eighty thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly who entered and emerged from the same samādhi together.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas whose minds were restless, yet who focused their attention with single-minded intent, thinking:
"We wish to draw near to, behold face-to-face, and pay homage to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and the great assembly, and we also wish to hear and receive this subtle and wondrous Great Canon."
Thus, this great assembly is all of one mind, desiring to go to that realm; it is for their sake that I wish to expound upon this Great Matter. Why is this?
The minds of this great assembly are not yet settled; if they were to go to that realm, they might give rise to inverted views or draw near to evil associates.
At that time, that Buddha said to Sūryagupta,
“Good son! You should not now give rise to thoughts of fear.”

Why is this? I shall now bestow upon you all bodhisattvas the practice of the uncommon dharmas, the practice of non-conceptualization, the practice of subduing, the practice of liberation, the practice of discerning birth and death, the practice of not severing the Three Jewels, the practice of great kindness and great compassion, the practice of omniscience and liberation, the practice of destroying the four māras and evil heterodox arguments, the practice of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, and the practice of ultimate entry into nirvana. This is called the Lotus Dhāraṇī; it causes all bodhisattvas to take no pleasure in the three realms, to realize the gate of signless liberation, and to enter the gate of non-practice liberation.

“Good son! If there is one who has faith and can listen to this Lotus-Holding [Dhāraṇī] with a sincere heart, that person will diminish all greed and all afflictions. After seven lifetimes, they will always be reborn in the heavens and possess the knowledge of past lives. Although they dwell in the realm of desire, they will not be defiled by it; they will always delight in leaving the household life, and all humans and devas will joyfully offer them worship and support.”
“Good son! If there is anyone who can, with a sincere heart, practice this for seven days and listen to this dhāraṇī, they shall never fall into the three evil realms. Good son!”
If there are devas or humans who hear this upholder [of the teaching], they will distance themselves from the phenomena of desire and cultivate meditative concentration.
If there are those who can proclaim this dhāraṇī into the ears of kings, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras, those who hear it will immediately give rise to the mind of renunciation.

If there are women who can listen to this dhāraṇī with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, and recite it, they shall immediately transform their female bodies and obtain male bodies; they will never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will continue until they realize great parinirvāṇa, never again receiving a female body, except by their own vow.

“Good son! If there is anyone who uses this dhāraṇī-mantra to empower other medicinal herbs, and applies them to drums or conch shells—whether they are struck or blown—and if anyone hears them, no evil views, sorcery, or various malignant diseases shall be able to afflict them.”
"Good son! This dhāraṇī accomplishes such immeasurable merit.

Having arrived, he immediately rained down *campaka* flowers upon this Sahā world-system; he prostrated himself with his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then sat down to one side.
At that time, the Buddha was still preaching the practice of the Dharma for King Bimbisāra.
At that moment, to the south, past as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in a city one yojana in circumference, there was a world named Kāṣāyadhvaja.

The sentient beings therein are possessed of the five corruptions. In that land there is a Buddha named Śailendrarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who currently dwells there, proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
In that Buddha-world, there was a bodhisattva named Gandhahastirāja who looked up into the void and saw immeasurable bodhisattvas coming from the south and heading toward the north.
Having seen this, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas come from the south and proceed toward the north?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!

To the north, past worlds as numerous as the sands of one yojana of cities, there is a land named Sahā. Therein, Śākyamuni Tathāgata proclaims the sublime scripture of the Mahāsannipāta, distinguishing the three vehicles, so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may not be severed, so that the practice of the Dharma may not be interrupted, and so that the realm of Māra may be destroyed and the banner of the Dharma may be raised.”

All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions have all proclaimed and expounded the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī in those lands; having finished speaking, each has returned to their original dwelling place, while Śākyamuni expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
“Good sons! Do you wish to go to that world to hear and receive the Dharma?

I now also desire to go with that Buddha for the sake of what is called the *dhāraṇī* of severing karma that accords with the gate of emptiness, in order to sever attachment to form, conceit, arrogance, and the pride of ‘I am,’ and so forth, until the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.”

"Permanently sever all craving for desire, craving for form, and craving for the formless, and even eliminate all afflictions.
Son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Gandhahastirāja said:

I have already received and recited this dhāraṇī with a sincere heart and now wish to go there; however, I feel a sense of fear."
"Why is this? I have previously heard from the Buddha that the sentient beings in that world are corrupt and evil, possessing much greed, hatred, and delusion.
At that time, Śikhin Buddha addressed Gajapati, saying:

“Good son! You constantly manifest the form of a brāhmaṇa to teach and transform sentient beings; or the form of Maheśvara, or the form of Śakra, or the form of Nārāyaṇa; or the forms of ghosts, devas, nāgas, asuras, and universal monarchs (cakravartin); or the forms of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras; or the forms of ministers, elders, śrāvakas, men, women, and so forth, to teach and transform sentient beings.”
"How is it that you speak of giving rise to fear toward that world? 'Good son!'"

I shall bestow upon you the practice of the Great Dharma: the practice by which all wisdom knows all formations (*saṃskāra*); the practice that destroys the four Māras; the practice that can discipline all sentient beings; the practice that can gladden all sentient beings; the practice that does not sever the Three Jewels; the practice that can discipline all evil dragons; the practice that can destroy the evil karma of all sentient beings; the practice of great loving-kindness and great compassion; the practice that destroys the three evil realms; the practice of rescuing sentient beings; the practice that destroys evil views; the practice that can destroy the karma of women; the practice of the inexhaustibility of all dharmas; the practice that can destroy all stinginess and greed; the practice that can attain all samādhis and supernormal powers; the practice that can cause sentient beings to rejoice; and even the practice for attaining the path to Bodhi.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who hear of these practices, you should know that such persons will be able to destroy the causal conditions of evil karma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River and sever the three obstructions—excepting only those who commit the five heinous crimes, slander the Vaipulya sutras, or disparage the noble ones.”

“Good son! If there are those who, with a mind of faith, listen to and accept such practices as these, they will obtain the three vehicles according to their wishes. They shall not be separated from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and others of the ten directions; they will constantly purify the three karmas in accordance with the intentions of sentient beings. You should know that such persons are able to relinquish everything, even their heads and eyes, and no evil whatsoever can cause them harm.”

If this person practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they will attain the precepts of endurance, the precepts cherished by the noble ones, the precepts recollected by the noble ones, the precepts of great tranquility, and the precepts that subdue Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as the precepts that subdue Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

Such a person never praises themselves or disparages others; their mind constantly reproaches worldly gain and offerings. They sleep in peace and awaken in peace, their bodies free from the suffering of illness. They easily obtain food and drink, and they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold.
When such a person approaches death, they will behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas will praise them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
If you uphold the prohibitive precepts well and practice with diligence without indolence, you shall be born in my land.

I can cause you to abide in the stage of the ten dwellings; once you have seen the Buddha, your heart will give rise to joy. By these causes and conditions, upon casting off this body, you will attain rebirth in the Pure Land, ascending through the stages of the ten dwellings until you attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If this person practices the *vīryapāramitā*, they will achieve great power and remain free from physical or mental illness; they will vigorously practice the *dānapāramitā* and *śīlapāramitā*. Humans, devas, nāgas, ghosts, asuras, and others will all come to make offerings to and prostrate before this person, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When this person practices the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, they attain the patience that takes dharmas as its object (*dharma-ālambana-kṣānti*), perceiving neither awakening nor seeing any sentient beings.

Even if all sentient beings were to cut and flay them, they would never give rise to a single thought of malice; until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will always be venerated by humans and devas.

If this person practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, they will attain the samādhi and liberation of the dharma-conditioned dhyāna; the Buddhas of the ten directions will never cease to keep them in mind, and until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will always be venerated by humans and devas.

When such a person practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they are constantly protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Delighting in tranquility, they bring the realm of the mind under control and thoroughly penetrate the entire dharma-realm. Their minds are free from doubt or obstruction; neither humans nor devas can thwart or destroy their resolve, and until they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall always be venerated by humans and devas.
“Good son! Having undertaken these practices, you should not give rise to fear when going to the Sahā world. Good son!”

If those who have been expelled from the Pure Land are all present in that world—namely, those who commit the five heinous crimes, slander the Vaipulya sutras, revile the noble ones, or violate the four grave prohibitions—such people as these, who together defile and bring disgrace to the Sahā world, [the Buddha] manifests his body there due to the causal conditions of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s original vows.

"Good son! If all the wicked people in that world, upon hearing of this practice, cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for seven years, refrain from the four verbal transgressions, and practice the six recollections—good son!"

This person should further bathe themselves to purify, put on fresh and clean garments, and with a sincere heart pay homage toward the east while reciting this *Caryā-dhāraṇī* and other such mantras for as long as seven years; all evils whatsoever shall then be completely extinguished.
If there are women who can practice in this way, they will immediately transform their female bodies into male bodies, and eventually attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, to the west, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in forty Ganges Rivers, there was a Buddha-world named *Kendō* (Firm Banner), which was fully possessed of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

In that land there is a Buddha named Gao-gui-de-wang (King of Noble Virtue) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; he currently dwells there, proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.
Within that great assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Guptagunaprabha, who looked up into the void and saw various bodhisattvas coming from the west toward the east.
Having seen this, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do immeasurable bodhisattvas come from the western direction and proceed toward the eastern direction?"
The Buddha said,
“Good son! To the east of here,
past worlds as numerous as the sands of forty Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, which is fully possessed of the five corruptions.”

For these reasons, Śākyamuni Tathāgata proclaims the wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, entitled the Mahāsannipāta; he distinguishes the three vehicles in order that the nature of the Triple Gem may not be severed, to destroy the realm of Māra, and to raise high the banner of the Dharma.

All the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions gathered together in that land and collectively proclaimed the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī; having finished speaking, each returned to their own abode. Then Śākyamuni Tathāgata, for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, extensively expounded and proclaimed the pure brahmacarya of the four types of unimpeded knowledge.
“Good son! Would you now like to go to that world to see that Buddha?

I also wish to give to that Buddha what is called the *dhāraṇī* for severing karma, which accords with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), fully accomplishes immeasurable merit, and is able to sever desire and greed, greed for the realms of form and formlessness, pride, arrogance, and the conceit ‘I am,’ up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

The Buddha said, “Good son!

Are you not that Great Golden-Winged Bird who, for twenty-one days, terrified the sixty-four trillion great dragon kings of the great ocean in the space between the two worlds of the four continents in those lands, causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha and resolve to attain Bodhicitta?”
“World-Honored One!
It is truly as the holy teaching says. “Good son!”

"The land is suffering from a severe drought; are you not an elephant-dragon, a horse-dragon, or a garuḍa-dragon who, within seven days, will send down a great rain and cause all the evil dragons to be struck with terror?"
“World-Honored One!
It is indeed as you have said. “Good son!”
“Since you did not give rise to fear even among such evil nāgas, for what reason do you now feel terror?
“World-Honored One!
It is like a wise person who, hearing that there are many treasuries of jewels in another place, immediately goes there and seizes them with his hands.”
Having grasped it, my mind gradually gave rise to joy, and I never grew weary.
I am likewise; because I questioned the Tathāgata, I have been able to hear such true words;
because I have heard these words, I have gained great power, enabling me to uphold the Buddha’s seal and subdue that land.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

I shall bestow upon you a great and efficacious mantra capable of purifying all karma, purifying causes and conditions, purifying discipline, purifying desire, purifying growth, purifying equanimity, purifying malevolent winds, purifying conduct, purifying ignorance, purifying birth and death, purifying all afflictions, purifying all conditioned phenomena of the three realms, and purifying the distinction between self and other; this is what is called a mantra.

“Good son! Once this divine mantra has been heard in that land, the fetters of the superior, middling, and inferior grades will all become thin and weak. It is likewise for the realms of form and formlessness; all shall transcend the various karmas of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all evils of body, speech, and mind within the five states of existence shall be rendered pure.”

“Good son! If there is anyone who can hear and receive this mantra, and if they uphold, recite, and read it for up to seven days with a sincere mind without forgetting it, you should know that all their evil offenses will be completely extinguished—except for the five heinous crimes, slandering the Vaipulya sutras, disparaging holy beings, and violating the four grave prohibitions.”
Whatever this person seeks, even up to bodhi, shall be obtained according to their wish.
If they wish to practice the dāna-pāramitā, it shall likewise be accomplished; and so it is for all the others, up to the prajñā-pāramitā.
“Good son! Among all sentient beings in the Sahā world, there are none who receive the teaching of reprimand without cause. Why is this?

All those evil sentient beings who are expelled from the worlds of the ten directions shall all be reborn in that Sahā world; for this reason, they are able to commit the five heinous crimes, slander the Vaipulya sutras, revile the noble ones, and violate the four grave prohibitions.

Because of these karmic causes and conditions, such persons are mostly reborn in the evil realms to undergo immeasurable suffering; having already undergone such suffering, they are furthermore unable to attain the dharmas of the ten wholesome paths. Due to these causes and conditions, they return once more to be born in the Sahā world.
If such a person has originally cultivated and accumulated the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom, they will ultimately not be born in a corrupt and evil land.
Because of the causes and conditions of practicing such evil dharmas, they will be born in an evil land with impaired faculties;
lacking a complete human form and devoid of mindfulness, they will be deprived of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and ornaments.
The necessities for sustaining the body are difficult to obtain; one's lifespan is short and brief, and one cannot sleep in peace.
Wisdom, roots of goodness, and merit are incomplete; auspicious matters are rare and there is no heart of compassion.

One delights in practicing evil deeds, delights in cultivating wrong views, delights in reading heterodox books, delights in trusting evil friends, and delights in making evil vows; moreover, one suffers from many illnesses.

They have many sufferings, evils, and urgent affairs; they constantly delight in increasing the dharmas of the three evil realms; they revere and serve heterodox deities and are by nature corrupt and evil;
they are frivolous and jealous; they fully accomplish all unwholesome karmas; and they take pleasure in slandering the Triple Gem and delighting in practicing the three evil paths.

“Good son! When these evil sentient beings hear this mantra, they will give rise to a mind of repentance regarding the phenomena of birth and death. They will leave behind the three evil realms and cultivate the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom. They will also delight in practicing the six pāramitās and pure brahmacarya, increasing their lifespan and merit while eliminating the suffering of malignant diseases. Their wisdom will blaze forth, their close associates will suffer no harm, and all wholesome dharmas will not diminish. They will fully accomplish the ten wholesome paths of action, cause the Three Jewels to flourish, and delight in the practice of the Dharma, enabling all sentient beings to be endowed with such immeasurable wholesome dharmas.”

“Good son! In the Sahā world of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, if there are sentient beings who uphold the prohibitive precepts, respectfully believe in the Triple Gem, inquire about the sublime Dharma, recite, copy, or transcribe it, and thereby attain a heart of joy—by these causes and conditions, they shall immediately transcend the karma of the three evil realms.”

If there are grave evil offenses to be experienced in the future, they will instead be experienced as suffering in the present: such as encountering a slight headache, losing wealth and property, being separated from one's kin, having an ill reputation spread far and wide, or being beaten and reviled; through these, [the future retribution] shall be extinguished.

“Good son! This divine mantra is fully accomplished and endowed with immeasurable merit; it can destroy all evil karma, bring great benefit to sentient beings, wash away the immeasurable evil thoughts of sentient beings, produce great radiance, attain a mind of great mindfulness, and bring about great tranquility.”
This person will always be protected by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as by the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and human kings.
At the moment of death, this person shall behold the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions and hear what those Buddhas preach; the Buddhas will praise them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! Come and be born in my pure and wondrous land; I can cause you to swiftly abide in the ten stages.

At that moment, the person immediately gives rise to a heart of joy. Because of this joyful heart, they attain deep faith. By these causes and conditions, they are born in the pure and wondrous land; having been born, they immediately ascend to the correct position of the ten abidings and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! You should receive and uphold this divine mantra, reciting it until you have mastered it; then go first to the Sahā world to inquire after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s welfare, and only thereafter proclaim it.”

“Good son! By means of such immeasurable expedient means, I tame sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who encounter a grave illness, one should take a lion’s skin and consecrate it with mantras to give to the patient;

If there are many strange portents in that land—such as malignant winds, calamitous rains, or malevolent stars, suns, and moons—one should bathe oneself purely for seven days and consume milk gruel; by reciting this mantra throughout those seven days, all evils and strange anomalies will immediately vanish.
“Good son! If there is anyone who hears this dhāraṇī, all their afflictions will immediately diminish, and they shall enter the stage of right determination. Good son!”

Chapter 4: The Chapter on Discrimination The Great Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, within the *Divyaguhyaprabhāsa* Section, Chapter Four: The Chapter on Discrimination. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the four great bodhisattvas: "Good sons!
"If you abide in this world, cultivate and accumulate all wholesome dharmas according to your inclination.

At that time, the four bodhisattvas and their great assembly immediately each entered meditative concentration according to their own inclination. Having entered concentration, light issued from their bodies like a single lamp, even as much as the light of immeasurable suns and moons.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, thought to himself:
"If I were now to ask the Tathāgata about even a single point of meaning, the Tathāgata might, on account of this, analyze and explain at length these four dhāraṇīs."

When the Tathāgata speaks, his voice will surely be heard throughout the Sahā world; once sentient beings have heard it, the net of doubt in their minds will be destroyed, and they will attain great illumination regarding the Dharma they have turned toward. They will cross over to the other shore, reach the stage of right determination, and no longer fall into the evil realms, so that all shall practice exclusively the pure and wholesome Dharma.
Having had this thought, he immediately rose from his seat and stood silently with palms joined in reverence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"Do you not wish to inquire about the Great Meaning?"
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I truly wish to inquire and submit a request; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha said:
“Kauṇḍinya! You know the time; I shall now destroy the entire web of doubt. Kauṇḍinya said:
“As it is said in the Buddha’s sūtras, there are two kinds:
namely, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and the person (*puruṣa*) who wanders through birth and death.
What is called ‘craving’?”
"What is a person? For what reason does the Tathāgata say that there are these two types who wander in saṃsāra?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Kauṇḍinya!
You have asked this question most skillfully; it will bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings. This is a timely question, a question in accordance with the Dharma.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you. "Kauṇḍinya!
There are three kinds of craving:
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
Furthermore, there are another three kinds:
These are called craving for existence, craving for cessation, and craving for the Dharma. "Kauṇḍinya!
What is craving for desire?

What is called "desire" is termed "heedlessness. With heedlessness as its cause and condition, there arises "craving-contact. With contact as its cause and condition, the perception of pleasure arises. With the perception of pleasure as its cause and condition, one consumes the body and mind. Because the body and mind are consumed, one joyfully practices the ten unwholesome deeds. With the ten unwholesome deeds as their cause and condition, one is able to increase the suffering of the three evil realms.

If one receives a human body, one will suffer poverty and affliction; due to the causes and conditions of greed, one undergoes rebirth within the five realms, being born among sheep and enduring much suffering and distress. Although one undergoes such suffering, the mind lacks shame and remorse, and no repentance arises.

If, because of a small amount of merit, one regains a human body but the craving for existence increases, then due to that increase in craving, one’s body and speech become impure; one commits immeasurable grave evil karmas, even up to the five heinous crimes. By these causes and conditions, one undergoes great suffering and affliction once again in the hells.
"All suffering experienced arises from the mind of craving; therefore, for the sake of liberation from craving, the Tathāgata has proclaimed the True Dharma and censured the dharma of desire.

If there are sentient beings who, having heard such censure of desire, contemplate it as being like a mirage, like a great poisonous tree, a vessel of poison, or a walking latrine; like a sword, like a thief, like a *caṇḍāla*, or like a red-hot iron ball; like a shower of evil hail, like a violent gale, like a venomous snake, an enemy, or a *rākṣasa* in a desolate wilderness who kills and harms people; or like filth, or like a cemetery."

If there is anyone who can contemplate in this manner, all their craving and greed, their relish for objects, attachment, dwelling in craving, feverish passion, and aversion—all such phenomena will be immediately eliminated.

Having ceased [other thoughts], they mindfully contemplate the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, study the Dharma, receive the Dharma, grasp the Dharma, diligently seek the Dharma, and practice the Dharma as the treasury of wealth, the Dharma as purity, and the Dharma as conduct; taking refuge in the Dharma, such a person attains mindfulness of the Dharma at the moment of death.

"By means of mindfulness of the Dharma, one immediately hears the Buddhas of the ten directions proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings; having heard the Dharma, joy arises in the mind, and because of this joy, one is able to behold the form-bodies (rūpakāya) of the Buddhas."

This person, having cast off the body, will be born in a pure land where the three evil realms do not exist; they will always dwell and travel together with virtuous people, possessing perfect wisdom, practicing generosity and diligence, cultivating and accumulating compassion, taming sentient beings, severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions, and being fully endowed with immeasurable merit and adornments.
It is like a fragrant casket used to store clothing; the clothing becomes fragrant, yet the fragrance of the casket does not diminish. "Kauṇḍinya!

If sentient beings, by the power of their virtuous vows, are born in a pure land and engage in common activities together with other virtuous beings, it is also like this: they themselves increase in various virtues, yet the virtues of those others do not diminish."
“Kauṇḍinya! Therefore, if good sons and good daughters wish to benefit themselves, benefit others, and benefit both together, they should always diligently seek reliance upon virtuous friends.”
Kauṇḍinya! If a person can perform such an observation of the characteristics of the nature of desire, you should know that this person will before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
What is a virtuous friend? “Kauṇḍinya!”
Now, those who are virtuous friends are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats;
furthermore, the virtuous friend is none other than my own self. Why is this so?
I am always compassionate toward all sentient beings and am able to speak of all the faults and afflictions inherent in desires; therefore, the great assembly should accept my words.

The speech that issues from me is never dualistic; it is not false or deceptive, nor is it divisive. It is not meaningless speech, nor is it harsh or evil speech. What I say is truthful, a speech of loving-kindness, a speech of compassion, and a speech that brings peace to sentient beings.

I shall now speak of the faults and transgressions of all desires; you should receive and uphold them with a single mind. Having received and upheld them, you will escape the three evil realms and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, all sentient beings in the Sahā world raised their voices in unison and said:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that you will proclaim the faults and transgressions of desire; we shall now receive and uphold them with a sincere heart."
The Buddha said: "Sons of good family!
There are four kinds of desire:
First, desire for form;
second, desire for shape;
third, desire for celestial realms.
The fourth is the desire for sensual pleasures; these are called the four. What is the desire for form? It refers to the derivative matter produced by the four great elements.

Ordinary people do not perceive that there is no self or sentient beings, and thus they give rise to inverted perceptions, conceiving of male and female forms and superior or inferior appearances. They think, "This form is lovely" or "This form is loathsome. Because of these inverted views regarding the characteristics of male and female, greed and desire arise where they had not yet arisen, and having arisen, they increase. Consequently, such persons distance themselves from roots of goodness and virtuous friends, and are unable to properly guard their actions of body, speech, and mind. For this reason, it is called a collection of unwholesome dharmas.

Why is this? Because they are unable to observe [the truth] in order to seek liberation. For this reason, the three evil realms increase, and they undergo the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they experience great torment all because of craving. The causal conditions of craving cause desire to grow.

If there is one who possesses wisdom and observes the form of a woman, they see the marks of impurity: the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and blood vessels. Having seen this, their mind delights in cultivating and accumulating this perception. As it is with the body of a woman, so it is with the body of a man; as it is with what is near, so it is with what is far; as it is with this, so it is with that; as it is with another, so it is with oneself.

If this person can cultivate and accumulate this mind, they will swiftly attain liberation from craving and attachment; observing how the bones of this body are linked by tendons and joints, the mind follows the movement of the body.

At that time, one binds the mind to a spot on the forehead about the size of a jujube fruit. Once the mind has joyfully cultivated and accumulated such signs, the body attains tranquility; one no longer perceives unwholesome signs, unwholesome events, or unwholesome conditions. This is called *śamatha*, and it is termed the tranquility of the mind.
"What further is meant by 'the tranquility of the body'?
When this person enters meditative absorption and ceases the inhalation of breath, since there is no inhalation, how could there be exhalation?
This is what is called the tranquility of body and mind."
The tranquility of body and mind is the causal condition for *śamatha*.
