This person contemplates all the bones and joints of the body as being scattered like sand blown by the wind; having seen this, they immediately give rise to the perception that it is empty and devoid of substance. Contemplating empty space in this way is called the tranquility of body and mind; this is called attaining liberation by means of the concentration of *śamatha*.
“World-Honored One!
Is the characteristic of space a conditioned characteristic? “Kauṇḍinya!”
"These are the characteristics of the conditioned. "World-Honored One,
if space were a characteristic of the conditioned, would it be its own characteristic or the characteristic of another?"
“Kauṇḍinya! If one can observe the entire dharma-realm and the conditioned realm, this is called their specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). Why is that?
If one can contemplate the tranquility of form, one sees the body of the Buddha. Why is this?
If a person contemplates a skeleton such that it becomes like sand blown by the wind, that person is able to shatter attachment to and desire for form.

One who is able to deeply contemplate the true nature of form perceives all things as being like empty space; the forms of the ten directions are as empty as lapis lazuli, and within them one further beholds immeasurable Buddhas, and so it is throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, they see the Tathāgata with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and it is likewise so throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
If such a person attains repentance regarding the phenomena of birth and death, they will immediately reflect:
"I shall ask the Buddha: by whom was this space created?"
"How should it cease?
Having formed this thought, I have already asked and I have already known: "The nature of space has no agent; how could it possibly cease?"
That which is called "space" is without applied or sustained thought, without substance, and without number; it has no characteristics, neither arising nor ceasing. All dharmas are likewise thus.
When one contemplates in this manner, one attains the fruit of Anāgāmin.

This Anāgāmin has completely severed all minds of greed and desire, yet there remain five things that have not yet been eliminated: first, craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*); [the others being craving for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness].
Second, craving for the formless realm;
third, restlessness;
fourth, pride.
Fifth is ignorance.
If such a person were to see the body of the Tathāgata, they would think:
"I shall know its measure. At that time, this person observes little and sees little, or observes much and sees much.
Again, he formed this thought:
"From where do these Buddhas come?
Again, he formed this thought:

"Thus, these Buddhas come from nowhere and go nowhere; my mind within the triple world is the cause of this mind. According to my contemplation and observation, when desire is predominant, I see much; when desire is slight, I see little. The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are precisely my own mind."

Why is this? Because one perceives according to the mind; thus, the mind is my body and I am space. Through *vitarka* and *vicāra*, I perceive immeasurable Buddhas; through the awakened mind, I see the Buddhas and know the Buddhas. Yet the mind does not see the mind, and the mind does not know the mind. I contemplate that the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is without solidity; all phenomena arise from the causes and conditions of *vitarka* and *vicāra*. Therefore, all existing natures and characteristics are themselves space, and the nature of space is likewise empty.
If there are those who have first resolved their minds toward Bodhi, they should contemplate the causal conditions of immeasurable dharmas.

If such a person should give rise to the mind seeking the state of a Śrāvaka, at that moment they will immediately attain the Samādhi of Signlessness (animitta-samādhi), causing their ignorance to be forever extinguished and stilled, and they will further obtain the patience that accords with emptiness (śūnyatā-anulomikī-kṣānti).

If this person perceives that space is empty, at that moment they attain tranquility of body and mind; this is called the gate of liberation through emptiness, and for such a person, attaining arhatship is not difficult.
Furthermore, if one practices the liberation of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it serves to extinguish the causes and conditions of immeasurable dharmas.

When this Dharma was being taught, ninety-nine trillion sentient beings attained the patience of practicing concentration (*samādhi-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the patience of practicing emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*); sixty thousand sentient beings attained the liberation door of the samādhi of emptiness; twenty thousand sentient beings all attained the samādhi of directly perceiving all Buddhas; eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.

"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya! If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates his own body and forms the perception of impurity, yet is unable to subdue his own mind, that person should next carefully contemplate a corpse."
Whether it be blue-black, or festering, or reddish, or bloated, or dismembered, or bones white as conch shells—one should deeply contemplate where the mind finds its pleasure and dwells.
Having understood this, he then takes up [the practice] such that his own body is viewed in the same way as external forms:
whether they are blue, or even like a conch shell; as it is by day, so it is by night, and as it is by night, so it is by day;
as it is regarding what has gone and what has come, so it is regarding what is coming and what is going.

"At that time, if one perceives external objects—such as trees, people, livestock, and miscellaneous things—all as being composed of bone, and having made this contemplation, does not give rise to a mind of greed even unto the end of life, such a person is able to leave desire behind in the present life, though not yet in future lives."
If this person is able to attain the *śūnyatā-dhāraṇī*, they will then be able to contemplate bones as having the appearance of being dispersed like grains of sand or fine dust.

Whether regarding themselves or others, they will not perceive any form (*rūpa*) even as large as a single atom; immediately, they will attain the characteristic of space (*ākāśa-lakṣaṇa*), seeing all forms as if they were blue lapis lazuli.
Having seen this, they further contemplate the yellow color of space; they are able to contemplate yellow, red, white, variegated, and lapis lazuli colors.
If they see the earth and water as also being like lapis lazuli, this person can contemplate the entire great earth as being only four finger-widths thick.

If one wishes to cause movement, one simply treads upon it with the toes of the feet to move it as desired for as long or as short a time as intended; eventually, even the great earth, trees, mountains, and rivers will all be moved by it.

If one contemplates all waters as being of various colors—such as the color of the *pundarīka*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *padma* lotuses—one may walk, stand, sit, or lie down upon all such waters. One contemplates all mountains as being of various colors, their forms as fine and soft as *tūla* cotton, and therein one may walk, stand, sit, or lie down.

Furthermore, he observes his own body as light and drifting like the wind; having made this observation, he is able to travel through space in the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
This person then enters the fire-light samādhi, emitting various wondrous colors of radiant light from his body.
Furthermore, he entered the Yamakaprātihārya-samādhi, causing water to flow from his upper body and fire to issue from his lower body.
Having performed such great supernatural transformations, he again thought:
"How may I come to behold all the Buddhas?"
At that time, in whichever direction he looked, he saw the Buddha; the more he looked, the more he saw, and the less he looked, the less he saw.
Having seen him, he further reflected:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come from nowhere and go nowhere. My mind within the triple world is the cause of this body; following my contemplation (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), I wish to see much when there is much desire, and to see little when there is little desire."
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are precisely my own mind.
Why is this? Because they are perceived in accordance with the mind.

The mind is my body, and I am space. Through mental application and investigation, I perceive immeasurable Buddhas; yet it is by means of the awakened mind that I see and know the Buddhas. The mind does not see the mind, nor does the mind know the mind.
I contemplate that the nature of the dharma-realm is not solid; all phenomena arise from the causes and conditions of conceptualization and discernment.
Therefore, the nature of dharmas is itself empty space, and the nature of empty space is likewise empty.

Because of this mind, I see blue, yellow, red, white, and various colors within empty space; having performed these spiritual transformations, what is seen is like the wind and possesses no reality. This is called the "dhāraṇī of seeing things as they truly are, shared with ordinary worldlings."

This person further reflects: "If there is space, it is without grasping; it is devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and cannot be described. Just as my mind is detached from the characteristics of space, so too do I contemplate the characteristics of the mind without creating detachment. Detached from all activity, I do not give rise to the thought of awakening; even if such a thought arises, it is immediately extinguished because the mind takes extinction as its object. As this mind is thus extinguished, one purifies body, speech, and mind to cultivate and accumulate the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*). This person, throughout the long night, binds the mind within this concentration."
"Arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, one relinquishes that life-span and enters nirvana; this is called the 'dhāraṇī of reality not shared with ordinary persons.
What is called the 'dhāraṇī of reality shared with ordinary persons'?"
If there is one who can contemplate in this way:
"I observe at will that form is itself seeing, form is itself my mind, and my mind is itself form; just as I am detached from all marks of form, I contemplate the mark of empty space."
At that time, this person cultivates the characteristic of space; this is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality shared with ordinary worldlings.

If one can perform such contemplation—that form itself is space, and it is by means of such conditions of form that I attain the contemplation of space—and understand that the nature of space is called "unobstructed" and is the dwelling place of wind, and that such wind arises from the four great elements, and that my own characteristic of form likewise arises from the four great elements, and that space, wind, and form are thus without distinction;
and that the nature of all phenomena is inherently empty and quiescent, and that the contemplation of one's own and others' natures is likewise so.
Space is that which is neither born nor extinguished.

When one contemplates in this way and fixes the mind upon the Tathāgata, having formed this thought, one sees immeasurable Buddhas within space and immediately attains the fruit of Anāgāmin; this is called the "Dhāraṇī of Reality Not Shared with Worldlings."
Again, he thought: "That which is called 'space' is myself; it is my pure self, and it is my mind.
That which is the self is formless, like space which is boundless; I, too, am thus."
This is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality shared with ordinary worldlings.

If there is one who can contemplate that within all phenomena there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, and who speaks of the sphere of emptiness, it is precisely because form is without self and there is no self therein.
If one recollects the Tathāgata or contemplates the Tathāgata as being oneself,
and having seen the Buddha, attains the fruits of the śramaṇa up to the fruit of arhatship— this is called the dhāraṇī of reality that is not shared with ordinary persons.
If one contemplates purity and self, that very emptiness is the locus of emptiness and is my own mind.
If one can eternally sever all afflictions, that is the pure mind.
If one can cultivate and accumulate the Eightfold Noble Path, this is called the pure mind.
If one can practice in this way, one will be able to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat; this is called the "dhāraṇī of reality that is not shared with ordinary persons."
Furthermore, there is the contemplation of form; that which contemplates the characteristics of form is the characteristic of discrimination.
The characteristic of discrimination is the characteristic of aversion.

The characteristic of aversion is the characteristic of birth and death. Now, in order to sever the characteristic of birth and death, I contemplate the emptiness of the characteristics of the mind; this is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality shared with ordinary people.
Furthermore, I contemplate that the self is quiescent, yet I have not yet severed discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).

If I contemplate the self, the self is like space; that which is called "self" is suffering (*duḥkha*), and that from which suffering arises is called its origin (*samudaya*); such suffering and its origin are dharmas that can be severed, and this is called cessation (*nirodha*);
contemplating suffering, its origin, and its cessation is called the path (*mārga*).
To attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to arhatship is called the "dhāraṇī of reality that is not shared with ordinary beings.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"For what reason do I contemplate empty space?"

"Emptiness is precisely the self; if the self were to be far removed from the contemplation of emptiness, one would next contemplate the station of consciousness as being like the contemplation of emptiness.
The contemplation of consciousness is likewise: just as space is boundless, so too is the mind. This is called the dhāraṇī of reality shared with ordinary people."
If one can contemplate that consciousness itself is suffering, then knowing the source from which suffering arises is called the origin;
if that origin can be severed, it is called cessation;
and contemplating suffering, its origin, and its cessation is called the path.
To attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality that is not shared with ordinary persons.

"If one contemplates the sphere of consciousness as being the afflictions of vitarka and vicāra, which are like sores and tumors, and just as I have distanced myself from the sphere of emptiness and the sphere of consciousness to cultivate the sphere of non-perception, such a person, having cultivated non-perception, attains the attainment of non-perception; this is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality shared with ordinary persons."

If one contemplates the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), it is a state of affliction, like a festering sore; thus, having distanced myself from contemplating the characteristics of consciousness, I next contemplate the characteristic of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*). What is called "non-conception" is the characteristic of being without self and without what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmīya*).

Having performed this contemplation, one immediately attains the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat; this is called the "dhāraṇī of reality that is not shared with ordinary persons."
If there is one who can contemplate the sphere of non-perception (asaṃjñāyatana), that itself is a subtle perception;

as I have distanced myself from this sphere of non-perception and contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), this is called the "dhāraṇī of reality as it is, shared with ordinary worldlings."

If one contemplates that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is itself great suffering, and that this state can be severed and liberation attained therein—when performing such contemplation, one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat;

one permanently severs all craving for desire and craving for form, leaves behind the name of an ordinary person to receive the title of a noble one, and forever cuts off all causes for the three evil realms. This is called the *tathatā-dhāraṇī* (the dhāraṇī of reality as it is).

This was sent by those Buddhas, brought forth by the Bodhisattva Sūryagupta, and is capable of severing all fetters and afflictions. It can sever all evil views, including the view of self, the view of grasping, the view of precepts, the view of permanence, the view of annihilation, the view of a life-force, the view of an agent, the view of a person, the view of sensation, the view of form, the view of contact, the view of emergence, and the view of the four great elements. This dhāraṇī thoroughly understands the aggregates, sense bases, and elements; it can purify all views and cause the recipient to enjoy eternal peace and happiness. It crushes the various māras, subdues wicked nāgas, brings joy to the devas, destroys the asuras and tṛkacas, delights the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, and can sever evil desires.

It causes practitioners of dhyāna to delight in tranquility; it can heal all grave and evil illnesses, prevent all evil conflicts and disputes, increase the Dharma-realm, protect the Triple Gem, and enable the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, thereby destroying the mass of ignorance.

When the Tathāgata spoke this dhāraṇī, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of srotāpanna; immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhat; immeasurable sentient beings obtained this dhāraṇī; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Two The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra,
Scroll Thirty-Three Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Two The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra,
Scroll Thirty-Three Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty
In the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on Differentiation," within the "Division of the Secret of the Sun," Part Two:
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
What is called the Lotus Dhāraṇī?

As proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Sūryagupta, those who are wise and who receive, uphold, recite, read, and transcribe it will obtain great benefit. Those who take no pleasure in the three realms and have attained the gate of liberation of signlessness will all be able to sever all afflictions; they will constantly receive human and celestial bodies for seven lifetimes, and though they remain in the desire realm, they will not be defiled by desire, being always honored by gods and men.
The Buddha said, “Kauṇḍinya!
As for the Lotus Dhāraṇī you have asked about, it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this dhāraṇī is indeed the practice of the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).”

“Kauṇḍinya! Even if I were to proclaim this dhāraṇī for immeasurable kalpas, I could never exhaust it, nor would I cause those who hear it to give rise to a mind of confusion or distress. This dhāraṇī can only be spoken by a Buddha and can only be heard by a Buddha.”
"Why is this? This dhāraṇī is difficult to know and difficult to understand; the other three are likewise so.
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will preach the *dhāraṇī* of the practice of emptiness within emptiness. “Kauṇḍinya!
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall speak it for you.”

Kauṇḍinya! If there are sentient beings who, due to the causes and conditions of negligence, give rise to a mind of sensual desire through contact, such persons do not know the place of liberation; they wander through birth and death for immeasurable lifetimes, undergoing great suffering and affliction within the three evil realms.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see all sentient beings undergoing such immeasurable suffering and affliction, they give rise to a heart of compassion and diligently practice without ceasing, cultivating all paths; having performed these practices, they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained enlightenment, he preached liberation from suffering; upon hearing this, sentient beings immediately attained release from suffering.
This liberation from suffering refers to the first fruit of the path, up to and including the fruit of arhatship.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is the desire for touch?

To speak of the desire for touch means the coming together of two bodies. Because of the union of the bodies, touch arises; because of touch, pleasure arises; because of pleasure, suffering arises. Due to the conditions of suffering, the sufferings of birth and death arise from this.”
“Kauṇḍinya! Just as four venomous snakes can harm sentient beings through four causes and conditions—namely, seeing, hissing, biting, and touching—so too is desire.

There is the cause and condition of seeing, the cause and condition of hearing, the cause and condition of thinking, and the cause and condition of touching. Due to these four conditions, they cause all sentient beings to distance themselves from all roots of goodness and undergo great suffering within the cycle of birth and death.”
“Kauṇḍinya! What is called liberation through the desire for contact?
If there is a bhikṣu who can contemplate white bones and reflect thus:”

"Form is that which is produced by the four great elements; that which is produced by the four great elements is impermanent in nature and lacks solidity—it is a phenomenon subject to dispersal, consisting of skin, hair, flesh, and blood."
"How does a wise person give rise to pure and auspicious signs within this body?
Having performed this contemplation, he immediately perceives all pure forms throughout the ten directions as having the characteristic of being undesirable.
That bhikṣu further reflects:
"If I joyfully cultivate and accumulate these marks, I shall attain the severance of all afflictions, birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is called śamatha."
"If one contemplates the bones from the feet up to the skull, this is called vipassanā.

"Having thus attained both vipassanā and śamatha, one observes the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; seeing the breath as it goes out, one immediately forms this thought: 'From where does this wind come?'"
"Where has it gone?

When one contemplates in this way, one becomes detached from the characteristics of the body and gives rise to the characteristic of emptiness, no longer perceiving internal phenomena; this is called "internal emptiness.
Not perceiving what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*) nor external forms (*rūpa*), this is called "external emptiness."
Observing that internal and external forms are empty, he further reflects:

"I have now cultivated and accumulated the sign of inhalation and thereby achieved great benefit; it is capable of destroying all internal and external forms. That I destroy such signs of internal and external form is entirely due to the causes and conditions of the contemplation of inhalation."

By these causes and conditions, I am made not to see any internal or external forms; that I am without the marks of form is the power of emptiness. I now definitively know that all dharmas have no place of departure and no place of arrival.

Having made this contemplation, all discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and analytical reflections (*vicāra*) are forever severed. One then contemplates this consciousness (*vijñāna*), knowing it to be the causal condition for all such discursive thoughts and analytical reflections, and thinks: "I shall distance myself from the activities of mind, intellect, and consciousness."
Why is this? If there is anything that arises, one should know that it will certainly perish.
When practicing this contemplation, one may attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, up to the fruit of an arhat; some may obtain the patience that accords with the Dharma, while others may attain bodhi.

If one contemplates applied and sustained thought as having the characteristic of cessation, one immediately attains the concentration of cessation; this is called the "Space-like Dhāraṇī Unshared with Worldlings. By upholding it, one accomplishes immeasurable merit and forever severs immeasurable great sufferings and afflictions.

When this Dharma was being taught, ninety-two thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*; sixty thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of *arhat*; ninety-nine thousand sentient beings attained the *ākāśa-dhāraṇī*; eighty thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of *pratyekabuddha*; eight hundred billion sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive mind.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This ‘Wishless Dhāraṇī’ which the Buddha Uccakūṭa has brought forth and wishes to follow—may the Tathāgata please analyze and explain it.”
“Kauṇḍinya! I shall now speak; listen with a sincere and attentive mind. Kauṇḍinya!”

There are sentient beings bound by the fetters of sensory contact who do not know liberation; such persons should contemplate the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*) and form this thought:

"The desire for sense-pleasures, the desire for form, and the desire for the formless—the desire for contact and the desire for liberation—these various desires arise from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), which are themselves the causal conditions for all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*)."
In this way, all conditioned phenomena have no agent and no experiencer; they arise due to the wind.
My own actions of body and speech are likewise produced by the wind.
Because of this wind, the body attains growth;
because of this wind, the mouth attains growth.
As I contemplate the wind, it is precisely the inhalation and exhalation.

He contemplates minutely that all the pores of the body arise from the causes and conditions of wind; he further contemplates all impure things; and he further contemplates that at the time this body reaches the end of its life, this corpse no longer has the inhalation and exhalation of wind.
Again, he reflects: "The causal conditions for my bodily and vocal actions depend upon wind; if there were no wind, there would be no causal conditions for bodily and vocal actions.
Therefore, at that time, he attains the samādhi of emptiness, which is cultivated and increased; through this cultivation, he is able to sever sensual desire and even the desire for contact.
Having made this contemplation, they attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, or some may give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kalyāṇamati-vicāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a śrāvaka cultivates the mark of impurity and succeeds in accomplishing that mark, what kind of mark does he possess?”

“Good son! If, for the sake of destroying the fetter of sensual desire, one cultivates the sign of impurity and fixes the mind between the eyebrows to contemplate the bones of one’s own body, this is called the single sign;
if one contemplates both one’s own body and the bodies of others, this is called the double sign.”
Furthermore, observing that all things are entirely impure is called the three characteristics.
When such a person is able to contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and purity, this is called śamatha attaining the characteristic of the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata).

When this person contemplates the white bones in this manner, their insight is like a lamp; they contemplate the four modes of the body down to its subtlest particles. This is called the *mūrdhan* stage (the Summit).
Contemplating the Four Noble Truths is called the *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) of the *śrāvaka*.
To achieve and attain the concentration of śamatha is called the sign of the contemplation of white bones.
When contemplating this sign, one attains the Eightfold Noble Path.
By means of the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat.
"Good son! In the buddha-land of Prabhāsa, the śrāvakas contemplate such dharmas and immediately attain the fruit of the Way.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (dharmānulomikī-kṣānti), and immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience that accords with reality (yathābhūta-kṣānti).
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"If the Four Noble Truths could be realized in a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata should have expounded for all sentient beings a single practice, a single dharma, and a single matter."
If one person were to realize it, all sentient beings should likewise realize it simultaneously. Why is this?
Because their afflictions are identical, there should also be no distinction between the eighty thousand aggregates of dharmas.
Kauṇḍinya! For this reason, sentient beings should be tamed through various causes and conditions, not by means of a single condition. Kauṇḍinya!

All sentient beings do not truly possess a single vehicle, a single practice, a single craving, a single thought, a single desire, a single understanding, or a single faith; therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims various verses, names, and diverse Dharma gates.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with ten kinds of spiritual powers. “Kauṇḍinya!

All sentient beings possess various marks of perversion; therefore, in order to purify their perversions, the Tathāgata teaches the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, the mark of bloating, the mark of festering, the mark of bluish discoloration, the mark of decay, the mark of disintegration, and so forth.”
“World-Honored One!
What is called the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds?
And what is called the perception of the impurity of food?”
The Buddha said:
“Kauṇḍinya! You should not now ask such a question.”
Why is this? Because the attainment of the Way in that realm and the attainment of the Way in this realm have distinct characteristics, Kauṇḍinya!
"If I were to explain it in full detail, sentient beings who hear it might become confused or distressed.
"World-Honored One!
We only pray that, out of compassion, you will analyze and proclaim it for the sake of those bodhisattvas who are able to believe and understand."
World-Honored One!
If these sentient beings hear such an exposition of these two characteristics, they will be able to plant the seeds of goodness, increase their roots of merit, and shatter ignorance.
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings, due to the causes and conditions of ignorance and craving, delight in birth and death; therefore, birth and death have neither beginning nor end, World-Honored One.”
"World-Honored One, all sentient beings increase their greed due to the conditions of food.
Because all sentient beings have never before heard of these two characteristics, they wander through the five realms of birth and death and undergo great suffering."

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great kindness and great compassion; throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he has constantly kept sentient beings in mind. We only pray that, out of pity for us, the Tathāgata will explain the perception of non-delight and the perception of the impurity of food.

If the Buddha were to proclaim the perception of non-delight and the perception of the impurity of food, sentient beings who hear it would not give rise to craving for sensual desires, nor would they give rise to craving for food.
World-Honored One!
"If there are sentient beings who can harshly reproach the mind of desire and the mind of craving, you should know that such persons will swiftly reach the other shore.
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya!"
Listen attentively with a sincere mind; I shall now expound upon the perception of the lack of delight in all worldly things and the perception of the impurity of food. "Kauṇḍinya!
There are two kinds of worlds:
First, the world of sentient beings;
second, the receptacle world.
As for the world of sentient beings, it refers to the sentient beings of the five destinies.

Regarding the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*): within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there are twenty locations; the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) has sixteen; and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has four locations.
"What are the twenty locations of the desire realm?"
There are eight great hells, each surrounded by sixteen subsidiary hells:
first, the Reviving Hell;
second, the Black Rope Hell; [and so forth].
Third, the Hell of Crushing;
fourth, the Hell of Wailing;
fifth, the Hell of Great Wailing;
Sixth, the Heat Hell;
seventh, the Great Heat Hell; eighth, the Avīci Hell.
If there are sentient beings whose body, speech, and mind are evil, they will all be born in such great hells to undergo immense suffering and affliction.

Although these sentient beings see exquisite forms, they do not conceive thoughts of pleasure; for this reason, they further experience great suffering. It is the same with sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles. When a person of wisdom contemplates these matters, they conceive thoughts of non-attachment.

“Kauṇḍinya! If one contemplates the bodies of animals, they may be as minute as one-tenth the size of a mote of dust, or like a mote of dust itself, even down to the size of a jujube fruit; some are one yojana in size, while others are hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of yojanas.”
These sentient beings may have lifespans lasting from a single thought-moment up to seven thought-moments, or from one kalpa up to ten million kalpas.

These sentient beings lack practice in the Dharma, wisdom, a sense of shame, and a heart of compassion; they shall undergo suffering and distress and give rise to great terror. Each constantly harbors thoughts of mutual harm, remains far removed from all wholesome dharmas, and perpetually walks in darkness and upon deviant paths. For this reason, the wise cultivate the perception of non-delight.

“Kauṇḍinya! The wise person further contemplates the bodies of hungry ghosts: some are one foot tall, some are equal in size to humans, some are a hundred yojanas long, and some are like the Snowy Mountains.”

They constantly suffer from hunger and thirst, naked and without clothing; with disheveled hair wrapped around their bodies, they lack any sense of shame or modesty. Emaciated and reduced to mere skeletons, their bodies are devoid of flesh and blood; each gives rise to evil thoughts, their hearts are devoid of compassion, and all moist, cool vital energies have forever vanished.

Some eat iron broth, iron flour, and iron pellets; hot excrement, hot pus, hot blood, hot wind, hot grass, and hot fruit. Yet they cannot obtain these things constantly and they are never satisfied; for ten million kalpas they endure suffering and wander in darkness. Having observed this, the wise cultivate and accumulate the perception that the world is not to be relished.

“Kauṇḍinya! A person of wisdom next contemplates that within the human body there are all manner of sufferings: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death; the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; the suffering of hunger and thirst, the suffering of desire, the suffering of anger, and the suffering of jealousy and so forth; the suffering of double-tongued speech, harsh words, cold and heat, and so forth; and the sufferings of various evil beasts and evil kings. Within this human body, such sufferings are experienced.”
How is it that a wise person does not cultivate and collect the perception of the unattractiveness [of sensual pleasures]? "Kauṇḍinya!
How does a wise person contemplate the perception of the unattractiveness of the gods of the desire realm?"

The wise contemplate the six sense bases of the initial desire realm; therein, sentient beings are scorched by the craving of desire. Because the retributive fruits they receive are unequal, they suffer; because they are impermanent, they suffer; they suffer through grasping and the exhaustion [of conditions]; and they suffer through separation from what is loved.
How could a wise person not cultivate the perception of non-delight therein?

Next, one contemplates the sixteen abodes of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): the gods dwelling there practice mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), which are suffering because they are tainted (*sāsrava*). They suffer from a lack of tranquility, they suffer because of their desires, they suffer from the presence of superior concentrations, they suffer as a treasury of wholesome dharmas, and they suffer from not yet being liberated. Not knowing the further shore, they do not exhaust the causes and conditions for the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans.
Having contemplated this suffering, the wise person cultivates the perception of non-delight.

Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), some may cultivate and accumulate untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*). Yet these beings suffer because they cannot fully realize the Eightfold Noble Path; they suffer when striving for the means to realize the Eightfold Noble Path; they suffer because, upon attaining the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*), they lack mastery; they suffer because they do not attain the samādhi of a pratyekabuddha; they suffer because they do not attain the samādhi of a Tathāgata; and they suffer because they are unable to observe the realms of all sentient beings.
If sentient beings within the realm of form (rūpadhātu) undergo such suffering even upon entering nirvāṇa,
how could a wise person not cultivate the perception of the world as being unpleasurable within that realm?
"Next, one further contemplates the perception of the lack of delight in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The sentient beings therein suffer from practicing tainted meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*); they suffer from not attaining mastery while on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*); they suffer from not being able to hear the True Dharma; they suffer from being unable to ultimately sever sensation (*vedanā*); they suffer from the arising of wrong views at the time of death and regression; and they suffer from being unable to eternally sever the three evil realms."
"Upon the end of life, one falls into suffering; knowing this, at such a time one should cultivate and collect the perception of the world's lack of delight. Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya!
'The world' is precisely conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); there are three kinds of formations:"
There are bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations.
Bodily formations refer to inhalation and exhalation;
verbal formations refer to vitarka and vicāra.
The mental formations refer to perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*); these three types of formations share a single characteristic.
How can a wise person discern and know them?

The wise person contemplates the counting of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, deeply observing the coolness and warmth of the breath, even its entry into and exit from every pore. This person, contemplating the breath, truly knows that this breath was originally non-existent and now exists.

If that which was originally non-existent now exists, it possesses the characteristic of impermanence; it lacks a fixed nature, like lightning or a drawing on water. When observing in this way, one attains the characteristic of bodily conduct.

Observing from what causes and conditions such a characteristic arises, one immediately knows that this characteristic depends upon vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). The nature of vitarka and vicāra is originally non-existent and now exists; therefore, it is impermanent, a dharma that can be severed, and a dharma that can be liberated from.

These characteristics of vitarka and vicāra arise dependent upon the mind; yet the mind itself was originally non-existent and now exists. That which was originally non-existent and now exists possesses the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of being destructible, and the characteristic of having no refuge. It possesses the characteristic of being devoid of substantiality and the characteristic of being devoid of a self.
When one contemplates in this way, remorse arises toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), and one is able to cultivate the perception of the world as unattractive. "O bhikṣus!

If you can deeply contemplate these three types of formations, you will be able to forever sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), purify right view, and abandon the phenomena of birth and death. You will accomplish the level and straight path, be encompassed by the true assembly, and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of arhatship."
"Kauṇḍinya! The wise person cultivates the perception of non-delight amidst all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). Kauṇḍinya!"
How does a bhikṣu contemplate the robes he wears with the perception of non-delight?

If a bhikṣu cuts, sews, sees, touches, puts on, or takes off his robes, when he contemplates them at such times as being like blood-stained skin—putrid, foul-smelling, loathsome, an abode for worms, and a place devoid of anything pleasant—at that time, as he contemplates thus, the craving for robes is immediately extinguished.
“Kauṇḍinya! How does one cultivate and collect the perception of non-delight in food?
If a bhikṣu holds his alms-bowl, he regards it as being like a skull smeared with blood—putrid, foul-smelling, loathsome, and a dwelling place for insects.”
When obtaining food, one should contemplate this food as being like worms in a corpse.

When seeing parched flour, one should conceive of it as powdered bones; when obtaining rice gruel, one should conceive of it as excrement broth; when obtaining various cakes, one should conceive of them as human skin; the alms-bowl staff one holds should be conceived of as human bone; and when obtaining milk or curd, one should conceive of them as pus and blood-stained matter.
If one obtains vegetables, one should conceive of them as hair and body hair; if one obtains various kinds of drinks, one should conceive of them as raw blood.
Kauṇḍinya! If a bhikṣu practices such contemplation, this is called the perception of the unattractiveness of food.
“Kauṇḍinya! How does one conceive the perception of the dwelling as unpleasant?
When a bhikṣu enters a dwelling, he should give rise to this thought: ‘It is as if I were entering hell to undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.’”
In this way, the dwelling itself is a composite; the timber used is human bone, the earth is human flesh, and even all the beds, couches, and bedding are likewise so.
When one contemplates in this way, it is called the perception of the world as unlovely.

If one can observe such a perception, that person will immediately attain the patient acceptance of dharmas as they truly are (yathābhūta-dharma-kṣānti), following the patient acceptances of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

This person delights in cultivating the mark of emptiness; by virtue of cultivating the mark of emptiness, they perceive that all phenomena are entirely subject to arising and ceasing, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. They contemplate the aggregates, bases, elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, seeing that the nature of all phenomena is suffering, empty, and without self.
Having seen this, they immediately attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*.

"Kauṇḍinya! By cultivating and accumulating the perception of the world as unpleasurable, one is able to sever desire for the realm of form and the formless realm, as well as all pride, doubt, restlessness, and ignorance, until reaching the stage of *aśaikṣa*. This is called being fully endowed with the *dhāraṇī* that accords with the wishless (*apraṇihita*)."
"Kauṇḍinya! This dhāraṇī can destroy all evil Māras, and even cause the Three Jewels to increase.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable sentient beings attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; immeasurable billions of beings had their outflows (āsrava) forever exhausted; eight nayutas of beings followed the *apraṇihita-dhāraṇī*; immeasurable sentient beings resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; fifty-eight thousand sentient beings attained the non-retrogressive bodhicitta; and immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (*dharmānulomikī-kṣānti*).
At that time, immeasurable sentient beings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings were to hear this Dharma, how could they fail to resolve their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
"I shall now protect, uphold, listen to, and receive this Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"O great donors!
Since you now wish to protect the Great Dharma, by virtue of protecting the Dharma, you shall in future ages obtain immeasurable fruits of merit and retribution."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will expound the *Yùjìng* (Desire-Purifying) Dhāraṇī, which was sent by the Buddha Guṇakusumaguhya and brought here by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganaguhyaka.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well."
"I shall now explain for you the *Dhāraṇī of the Desire to Purify*, which was sent by the Buddha Guṇakusumaguhyaka to destroy the four inversions of the sentient beings in this land. Śāriputra!..."

The sentient beings of this land truly have no self; it is due to their inverted minds that they falsely give rise to the notion of a self. The wise, through deep contemplation, know that there is no self; having performed this contemplation, they then destroy their inversions.
“Śāriputra, how does the wise person contemplate non-self?
It means contemplating the body and truly knowing it to be without self.”
Why is this? Because it is a composite.
Furthermore, one observes that the eye also lacks a self.
Why is this? Because it is a combination of the four great elements.
If the eye blinks, that is the power of wind; such wind, moreover, comes and goes and turns about within space. Yet the nature of space is non-existent and cannot be described.
If that which is non-existent and ineffable is precisely non-self, then space truly has no self.
Within this space, wind likewise possesses no substance; it cannot be proclaimed, and therefore it is without self.
Just as with the observation of wind, so it is with earth; earth, too, is without substance and cannot be described, and for this reason it is without self. Water and fire are likewise.
Therefore, one should know that the four great elements of the eye are also without substance and cannot be described; for this reason, they are without self.
Furthermore, if it is said that there is a mark of self (*ātman*) due to the causal conditions of the eye and forms, this meaning is not correct. Why?
Because within the eye there is no self, and it is likewise with forms; moreover, within their conjunction there is also no self.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, eye-consciousness arises; yet within this consciousness, there is likewise no self.

From consciousness as a cause, form arises, which is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa). With name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise. With the six sense bases as a condition, contact (sparśa) arises. With contact as a condition, sensation (vedanā) arises. With sensation as a condition, craving (tṛṣṇā) arises. With craving as a condition, grasping (upādāna) arises. With grasping as a condition, becoming (bhava) arises. With becoming as a condition, birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth arise.
Such dharmas as these arise dependent upon eye-consciousness, yet this eye-consciousness likewise does not come from the ten directions.
The thought upon which it depends to arise is itself extinguished.

Visual consciousness does not abide within two moments of thought, nor does it say to thought, "You abide while I cease. Furthermore, this dharma of cessation has no location. Therefore, all dharmas arise through the conjunction of conditions and cease through the separation of conditions.

If something arises due to causes and conditions and ceases when those conditions are absent, one should know that there is truly no self; furthermore, these causes and conditions involve neither action nor reception, nor is there an agent, and for this reason, there is no self.

If there is no self, then that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is also non-existent. Therefore, the nature of the eye is without self or that which belongs to the self; being without conjunction or dispersion is itself arising and ceasing. All phenomena are likewise thus: the nature of all dharmas is without grasping or relinquishing, and it is not something created by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas.
Just as visual consciousness is empty, so too are all phenomena empty.
When one contemplates in this manner, one attains the gateway of the samādhi of emptiness, or attains the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat.
As it is with the observation of the eye, so it is likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

One observes that the body is without self; the hair is without self; the skin, hair, blood, flesh, sinews, bones, pus, marrow, intestines, saliva, vital warmth, and the various winds moving upward and downward—all these, as well as life-span and name, are entirely devoid of self. It is merely through the combination of various conditions that it is designated as "body."

Due to the causal condition of body-contact, body-consciousness arises; with consciousness as a causal condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as a causal condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as a causal condition, contact arises; with contact as a causal condition, sensation arises; with sensation as a causal condition, craving arises; with craving as a causal condition, clinging arises; with clinging as a causal condition, becoming arises; and with becoming as a causal condition, birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth arise.
Such dharmas as these give rise to body-consciousness, yet this body-consciousness likewise does not come from the ten directions.
The thought upon which it depends to arise is itself extinguished.
The body-consciousness does not abide for two moments; nor does it say to the thought, "You abide while I perish," for this phenomenon of cessation likewise has no location.

Therefore, all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions and cease through the dispersal of conditions; they arise when conditions exist and cease when conditions are absent. Thus, one should know that in reality there is no self, and these causes and conditions are without receiving or doing, having no agent; therefore, there is no self.
If there is no self, then that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is also non-existent; therefore, the nature of the body is devoid of both self and what belongs to the self.
The absence of conjunction and the absence of dispersion are themselves arising and ceasing, and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise so.

The nature of all dharmas is without grasping and without relinquishing; it is not something created by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or buddhas. Just as the body and consciousness are empty, so too is the emptiness of all dharmas.
When practicing this contemplation, one attains the gate of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, or attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*. "Śāriputra!

If there is a bhikṣu who can contemplate in this way that the eye and the body are without self, you should know that such a person attains the gates of *samādhi* and will be venerated by devas and worldly people."

When this Dharma was being taught, the past evil karma of immeasurable sentient beings was entirely extinguished; immeasurable sentient beings attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat; and ninety-four thousand sentient beings obtained such pure dhāraṇīs.

Immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; immeasurable sentient beings became non-retrogressive in their pursuit of enlightenment; immeasurable sentient beings attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (*dharmānusāri-kṣānti*); immeasurable sentient beings attained the destruction of desire for the realm of form and the realm of formlessness; immeasurable sentient beings attained the *dhāraṇī* of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and immeasurable sentient beings accomplished the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Immeasurable multitudes of beings attained *ānāpāna*; some attained *śamatha*, some attained *vipaśyanā*, some attained the stage of nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), some attained the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and some attained the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Upon hearing this, all women were transformed from their female bodies; all sentient beings of the desire realm experienced bliss as if they were in the third dhyāna stage.
At that time, all the devas, humans, and the eight classes of supernatural beings made offerings to the Buddha and dwelt in joy.
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this world, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who have accomplished such wondrously radiant colors; from the beginning of time, I have never before seen or heard of them.”
“World-Honored One!
This light of the bodhisattva can illuminate all Sahā worlds.
If this bodhisattva is close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, what will his light be like?”
“Great King! If there is a bodhisattva who has accomplished the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, his light can illuminate the worlds of the ten directions. Why is this?
Because they adorn all merits with wholesome dharmas; because they achieve and are fully endowed with the dharma of adornment;
because all roots of goodness increase extensively; because they draw near to the path of unsurpassed bodhi; because they are ultimately the path of unsurpassed bodhi;
because they receive the fruit of the Tathāgata’s true dharma; and because they analytically expound it boundlessly.
Because of the Dharma, because the body they have attained is free from obstruction, because they have obtained the pure and true Dharma,
because they have cultivated and accumulated the perfections (*pāramitā*), because their karma in future lives has already been exhausted,
because they have accomplished the immeasurable true Dharma of the Buddhas, and because they are able to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma, regarding all...
Because he has attained mastery over the Dharma, because he has thoroughly penetrated the faculties of all sentient beings,
and because he has forever severed all habitual tendencies of affliction, his radiance is thus able to shine universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"Great King!
By virtue of the great power of the Buddha's merit, you are also able to behold all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The King said:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to see the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas of the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"If my disciples—whether they be śrāvakas, householders, or those who have left the home life—each deeply contemplate all their wholesome dharmas, I likewise wish to enter the Tathāgata-samādhi."

If there are humans or devas who have attained suchness-patience (yathābhūta-kṣānti), or those who do not regress from the three vehicles, such sentient beings likewise enter into meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having gained a mind of faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem, likewise enter into dhyāna-concentration.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered a samādhi called "The Wisdom of the Practice of the Realm of All Buddhas, Vast as Space, Delightful to All-Knowing Ones, and Radiant as the Sun and Moon."
This samādhi cannot be known nor can it be measured by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any bodhisattvas; it is called the Buddha-realm samādhi.

Once the Tathāgata had entered this samādhi, the ten billion four-continent worlds, the ten billion Mount Sumerus, the ten billion suns and moons, and even the ten billion peaks of existence of the Sahā world—all such lands as these entirely entered the Buddha’s body.

In the Sahā world, those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, the heavens, and among humans who were undergoing suffering all attained the cessation of their pain and experienced universal joy, like a bhikṣu entering the third dhyāna.

All the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas arose from their meditative absorption and beheld the Buddha’s radiance; having seen this radiance, the light they themselves possessed immediately vanished and was no longer visible.
The happiness experienced by all śrāvakas is like that of a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna.

At that time, all immeasurable sentient beings each beheld the pores of the Tathāgata’s body; from every single pore issued forth immeasurable rays of light, equal in brilliance to the suns and moons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and also like the radiance possessed by the bodhisattvas of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Such light was able to shine universally throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
At that time, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions each addressed their respective assemblies:
"O sons of good family!
Do you see the great radiance of Śākyamuni Tathāgata?"

This radiance accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit; because this light arises from great kindness and great compassion for the sake of pitying all sentient beings, it now manifests to all sentient beings the signs of great supernormal transformations.
When all sentient beings saw this light, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Sentient beings from other worlds who possessed supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) all gathered here in this Sahā world; those who did not possess such powers paid homage and made offerings from afar.

At that time, all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas came to the Sahā world; all the Bodhisattvas made offerings of various flowers, incense, music, banners, and canopies of the seven precious gems, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them.
All sentient beings dwelling within the Buddha’s body saw him clearly;
having seen him, they further experienced immeasurable bliss.
At that time, all sentient beings in the Sahā world raised their voices together and spoke these words:

"By virtue of these wholesome causes and conditions, we vow that in the future we shall be born together in a single land, so that we may behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and cause the three evil paths of karma to be utterly extinguished."

If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha’s supernormal transformations, do not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should know that such persons constantly walk in darkness.

For the sake of sentient beings, various bodhisattvas undergo all manner of sufferings; they may manifest as Buddhas, or as pratyekabuddhas, or as śrāvakas, Brahmās, Śakras, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Nārāyaṇas, Maheśvaras, nāgas, pretas, asuras, or universal monarchs (cakravartins).

If there are those within the Buddha-realm who should be tamed by appearing as a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka; such transformations could not be accomplished by anyone other than those in the tenth stage.
"Therefore, the mind of unsurpassed bodhi accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit.
At that time, all sentient beings within the bodies of all Buddhas spoke in verse:
"Due to the causes and conditions of various evil minds, They wander through the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Because they do not associate with virtuous friends, they are therefore unable to reach the further shore.
If one can distance oneself from all evil thoughts, from all evil views and unwholesome conditions,
and is able to sever the cycle of birth and death within the three realms of existence, then one will be able to reach the further shore.
Sentient beings find it difficult to obtain a human body; having obtained it, it is difficult to encounter a virtuous friend.
A heart of profound faith is likewise difficult to attain; having attained it, it is difficult to hear the True Dharma.
If there are those who can give rise to the bodhicitta, these people can sever all afflictions and also teach and transform immeasurable multitudes,
manifesting great spiritual transformations just like the Buddha now.
If one can forever sever the two dharmas— namely, the two views of eternalism and nihilism—
and perceives that all conditioned phenomena are without self, such a person is said to possess right reflection;
if one can cultivate and accumulate the truths of suffering and its origin, such a person is able to sever all afflictions.
"If one can give rise to the bodhicitta, that person shall surpass all the worlds.
Having spoken this verse, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and there are sentient beings who give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka; some sentient beings attain immeasurable dhāraṇīs.

Moreover, there are sentient beings who attain the patience that accords with the Dharma, the patience of non-retrogression, and the patience of suchness; or some obtain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat.
At that time, Pāpīyas saw the entire Sahā world within the Buddha’s body.

Having seen this, he wept with tears streaming down his face; his heart was filled with grief and distress. Whether sitting, rising, walking, or standing—whether moving forward or backward, entering or exiting—he beat his head with his hands, experiencing intense suffering. All the members of Māra’s retinue did likewise.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas had a minister named Śūnyavṛkṣa (Empty Tree). Seeing Māra distressed, he spoke these verses:
"Why do you wander alone in such sorrow? Your mind is confused and disordered like a madman.
Wherever you go, your heart finds no joy; I pray only that the Heavenly King will explain the cause."
Then Māra Pāpīyas replied with a verse:
"I beheld the great supernormal power of Gautama; Therefore, affliction arose and I went mad.
My inner mind was agitated and found no peace; Grief and fever oppressed me and my retinue."
Beholding the Tathāgata’s boundless body, which encompasses the entirety of the Sahā world and renders my own realm entirely empty— therefore, I now give rise to sorrow and distress.
All the sages throughout the ten directions have gathered together in this world to perform a grand offering in worship of the Buddha; for this reason, I am filled with sorrow and distress.
Beholding the Tathāgata’s great supernormal power, and seeing his retinue taking refuge in the Buddha, I now wander alone without a companion; for this reason, sorrow and distress arise within me.
At that time, the great minister spoke again in verse:
"I now have many followers, Whose minds are wicked and who are fully armored;
Their power is such that they could destroy the body of the Tathāgata, And could likewise ruin his great supernormal powers."
Then Māra Pāpīyān spoke again in verse:
“My followers now stand in deep fear of the Buddha; how could they destroy his power of supernormal faculties?
If they wish to give rise to the thought of destruction, they will see their own bodies bound by the five fetters.”
At that time, the minister again spoke in verse:
"Just as when an enemy’s power is great, one should feign intimacy to bring about his downfall;
if you know that Gautama possesses great power, you should first feign a heart of close affection."
Then Māra Pāpīyas spoke again in verse:
"If I were to feign a heart of intimacy, Desiring to destroy the body of Gautama,
I would immediately manifest a corpse tied beneath my neck, And be censured by all people."
At that time, the minister spoke again in verse:
"All realms of desire are the domain of Māra; All humans and devas belong to the Tathāgata.
I pray the King will strictly command the evil Dragon King, For he is capable of destroying the body of Gautama."
Then Māra Pāpīyān spoke again in verse:
"If you truly know that the Dragon has power, I have already lost my mind and you have made your vow;
If you can truly destroy Gautama, I shall regain my realm and my original mind."
At that time, the minister immediately proclaimed to the various wicked dragon kings:
"You must destroy the body of Gautama for my sake.
Then those wicked dragons, wishing to fly through the air, were unable to move; they spoke to the minister:
"I have respectfully received your command and intended to go and destroy him; yet, as soon as this thought arose, I was unable to proceed.
At that time, the minister became terrified and thought to himself:
"If I were now to manifest the great power of Māra and cause the evil nāgas to give rise to anger, they would, through that anger, be able to destroy the body of Gautama."
At that time, the nāga palace was filled to overflowing with emanated corpses. When the nāgas saw this, they felt no joy in their own abode and thought to themselves:
"Who has manifested these corpses?"
Although he reflected thus, he did not know who it was.

At that time, all the great nāga kings throughout the four continents, along with their sons, daughters, elders, and retinues, emerged from their palaces and went to Mount Khadiraka. That mountain was level and vast, measuring forty thousand yojanas in both length and breadth; it was a place where former sages had dwelt, perfectly adorned with the seven treasures. Even Nanda and Upananda, the two nāga kings, abandoned their own abodes and came to this mountain.
All the dragon kings within the four great oceans, together with their immeasurable and boundless retinues—
namely, the Dragon King Elāpattra, the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita, the Dragon King Kūrma, the Dragon King Anavatapta,
the Dragon King Mucilinda, the Dragon King Guṇasāgara, the Dragon King Varuṇa, and the Dragon King Śata—
The Dragon King, the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Apalāla, the Dragon King Parvata,
the Dragon King Govinda, the Dragon King Elāpattra, the Dragon King Dīrghabāhu, the Dragon King Dīrghakeśa,
the Dragon King Śuci, the Dragon King Kakuda, the Dragon King Udaka, and the Dragon King Kṛṣṇakeśa.
King [of the Nāgas], the Golden Nāga King, the Śaṅkha Nāga King, the Smṛti Nāga King,
the Elephant Nāga King, the Sharp-Fang Nāga King, the Active Nāga King, the Doubt-Net Nāga King,
the Long-Face Nāga King, the Red-Eye Nāga King, and the Delight-to-Behold Nāga King— such as these were all those belonging to the land of Jambudvīpa.
Nāga King, eighty thousand nāga kings along with their retinues, and even all the nāga kings belonging to the forty-four thousand kingdoms, have all arrived at Mount Khararīṭika.
In Uttarakuru to the north, there are two dragon kings:
the first is named Ananta,
and the second is named Suvarṇakāya.
These two dragon kings, together with immeasurable hosts and forty-four thousand dragon kings from various lands, also arrived at this mountain.
In Pūrvavideha, there were two dragon kings:
one was named Candra; the other was named Soma.
The second was named Vasita.
These two nāga kings, together with immeasurable sentient beings and forty-four thousand nāga kings from various lands, arrived at this mountain.
In Aparagoyānī there are two dragon kings:
the first is named Ratnakeśa and the second is named Prabhākeśa;

forty-four thousand dragon kings from various lands have come to this mountain, as have the dragon kings of the four types of birth from the four continents, together with their retinues, all arriving at this mountain.
The bodies of these dragon kings were all like four-inch medicinal roots, yet because of their anger, their bodies became as large as Mount Sumeru.
When Māra Pāpīyas saw these dragon kings in such a state, he addressed his retinue:
"Listen closely, listen closely!"
"By my power, I shall cause these nāgas to emerge from their palaces; once they reach that great mountain, they will all lose their strength and be unable to destroy the śramaṇa Gautama."
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Thirty-Three. At that time, there was another minister named Śīlaskandha who addressed the Māra, saying: “Great King!
Thus, these dragon kings, desiring to destroy the body of Śākyamuni, assembled in one place and each thought to themselves:
"By what means shall I now destroy the body of Gautama?"
Pāpīyān replied: "I have such a thing.
If you wish to verify it, you should go and look."
At that time, the great minister, together with hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, desired to go to that mountain.
Then, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration and sat to one side, manifesting his eternal body.
When the minister saw that the Tathāgata’s permanent body was in the kingdom of Magadha, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has lost his supernormal powers; will he not perhaps feel fear toward me?"
"Do you wish to harbor great malice toward me?
I should go first to that Gautama’s place to engage him in discussion.
At that time, the minister, together with the great assembly, went to where the Buddha was and spoke these verses:
"Your own body has not yet crossed the ocean of birth and death; how then can you enable sentient beings to cross?
Gautama, do not deceive these sentient beings by claiming that they shall attain great nirvana."
At that time, the Tathāgata again answered in verse:
"I have already crossed the ocean of birth and death, And have also attained eternal liberation from all existence.
By reason of my compassion, I declare that sentient beings shall attain nirvāṇa."
In countless past eons, you have already resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
you have already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of World-Honored Ones.
"You shall certainly attain the Way of the Buddha; why do you say that I deceive sentient beings?
I now bestow upon you the power of great mindfulness, so that you may with a sincere heart contemplate your own original body."

At that time, having heard these verses, the great minister immediately examined his own past lives and clearly perceived that he had awakened the bodhicitta and made offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas.

Having seen this, his heart was immediately filled with great shame and remorse; he prostrated himself before the Tathāgata, confessed his transgressions, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

I now recall that throughout immeasurable lifetimes I have awakened the mind of bodhicitta; I have already made offerings to immeasurable billions of Buddhas, listened to and received the sublime Dharma from those Buddhas, and have already attained the practice of the six pāramitās.
“World-Honored One!
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who preached the Śrāvaka-yāna. Without reflecting upon it, I said:
‘These words are not the words of the Buddha; they are what Māra has spoken.’”

"Having already resolved upon Bodhicitta and practiced the path of a bodhisattva, it was for this cause and condition that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa did not bestow a prediction of my future enlightenment upon me. Because of this matter, I was born into the realm of Māra; since receiving this body, five hundred and seventy trillion years have already passed."
“World-Honored One!
I would rather undergo the sufferings of the hells with these past and future bodies than ever retreat from the mind of enlightenment.
The Buddha said:
“Great Minister!
Excellent, excellent!
If a person were to offer gold as vast as Mount Sumeru, along with the seven treasures, to the Buddhas throughout immeasurable eons, their merit would not equal that of generating the bodhicitta.”
"Why is this? One who gives rise to such a mind is indeed making an offering to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śīlatara attained the Dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti) while still upon his seat; he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and offered his upper robe to the Buddha. Even the great assembly of forty-four thousand followed suit in the same manner.
At that time, when Māra Pāpīyas saw that his ministers and their retinue had already taken refuge in the Buddha, he was filled with anguish; he firmly shut the gates and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately expounded for the great assembly three kinds of loving-kindness:
namely, that which has sentient beings as its object, that which has phenomena as its object, and that which is objectless, as taught in the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*.

At that time, all the devas and nāga kings assembled at Mount Kharādika, the dwelling place of the former sages; yet they were unable to move, nor could they walk, and though they wished to manifest their great bodies, they were likewise unable to do so. They then turned toward the kings Nanda and Upananda and spoke these words:
"Great Kings!..."
"The putrid and foul corpses created previously were all the work of Pāpīyān;
for this reason, he has caused us all to come here and receive these small bodies."
"If one can take refuge in Māra Pāpīyān, one may attain liberation.
At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra said:
"The Demon King has now lost his original mind and his supernormal powers; how could he possibly rescue you all?"

At that time, among the dragon kings, some took refuge in the Four Great Kings; some took refuge in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or the Yāma Heaven, or the Tuṣita Heaven, or the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, or the Brahmā Heavens, and so forth.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara spoke these words:
"Do you not see how Śākyamuni Tathāgata is being honored with a grand offering by all the worthy sages, devas, humans, and various other beings, who have taken refuge in him?"

At that time, some dragon kings took refuge with the seer Nata; others with the seer Ashvajit; others with the seer Vālmīki; others with the seer Prabhāsa; and others with the seer Bhārgava—thus taking refuge with these five kinds of seers.
These five sages had all attained the five supernormal powers and dwelt in the Snowy Mountains; they were all receiving and hearing the True Dharma from the great sage Prabhāsa-rasa.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-rasa also praised the Tathāgata with various and immeasurable eulogies.
At that time, the seer heard the voices of all the dragon kings.
Having heard them, he immediately said to the seer Prabhāsa-rasa,
"Have you not heard the sound of the dragons weeping?"
He replied, “I have heard it. “O Mahāsattva! [he continued.]
"I only pray that you will go there to rescue them from their suffering. Prabhārasa replied, "You may go; I cannot go."
"Why is this? Because now there is Mahādeva who wishes to hear and receive the teaching on unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*).
At that time, the four rishis prostrated before Prabhārasmi and went to Mount Kālañjara to rescue him.
When the nāgas saw this, they each raised their voices in lamentation, seeking mercy and rescue.
The rishi replied: "I cannot save you;
there is a bodhisattva in the Snowy Mountains named Prabhārasa who can deliver you, whereas we cannot. You should single-mindedly seek his mercy and pay him homage."
Then the dragon kings each with a single voice paid homage toward him.
At that time, having heard this sound, Prabhārasa, together with an immeasurable multitude of devas, went to Mount Kālañjara.
Having seen this, the Dragon King bowed his head in prostration and said,
"I only pray that the Great Being will save us from our suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Light-Taste (Prabhārasa), knowing that the hour had arrived, desired to speak of the constellations.
At that time, the Dragon King Mahāsamudra addressed the Bodhisattva Prabhārasmi, saying: "Great Being!
By whom was this teaching on the constellations spoken?"
Who created the great stars?
Who created the small stars?
Who created the sun and the moon?
On which day? Which star is foremost?
How is the full moon defined?
What is the season?
To which deity is this constellation assigned? What is its nature?
What is light and what is heavy?
What is good and what is evil?
What is food and what is almsgiving?
Who created this day? Who made this night?
How many paces does the shadow measure when it is called "revolving"?
"How does it turn south?
How does it turn north,
O Mahāsattva?"
"You are the foremost among all the sages; I pray that you will provide a full and detailed explanation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prabhārasmi addressed the dragon kings:
"Great Kings!..."

In the past, at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, there was a city named Caṇḍāyana. In that city there was a king named Anantaviśuddha, who ruled the country with the True Dharma; he did not crave sensual pleasures but always delighted in tranquility, and his wisdom and talent were keen and penetrating.
The king had a queen who, moved by lustful desire, went wandering with the king. While in a forest, she gazed at the king with a greedy mind and immediately became pregnant.
When her time was full, the queen gave birth to a son whose head, ears, neck, eyes, lips, and mouth all resembled those of a donkey, while the rest of his body resembled that of a human.
When his mother saw this, she was struck with fear and threw him into a latrine.
Before he had even reached the ground, the donkey-demon caught him in mid-air and went to the Snowy Mountains, where he looked after and nourished him as if he were his own son.
