At that time, there was a sweet medicinal herb within the Snowy Mountains; the donkey-demon gathered it and fed it to the child. Having eaten it, the child’s body underwent a transformation: he possessed great radiance, was endowed with the marks of merit, and was filled with wisdom and compassion.
For these reasons, the devas prostrated, made offerings, and offered praise on account of this son.

Among the various medicinal herbs, fruits, and melons in the Snowy Mountains, all other characteristics were transformed, yet his lips alone resembled those of a donkey; therefore, he was named the Rishi Donkey-Lipped. For sixty thousand years, he observed the prohibitive precepts while constantly standing on one foot.
All the Brahmā devas, Māra devas, and Śakras made grand offerings to him; with palms joined together, they addressed the Aśvakarṇa Rishi, saying:
"What wish do you seek?"
"I only pray that you will tell me; if it is within my power, I shall give it to you.
The seer replied, "I now wish to fully understand the stars and constellations, out of compassion for all people."
All the devas said: "If you would have compassion for all sentient beings and wish for us to know this, we pray that you will explain it. The rishi said:
“Brahmā! I truly do not understand the first watch of the night.
When these stars were thus described, the great nāga kings felt joy in their hearts toward the Bodhisattva Light-Taste (Prabhārasa).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Light Flavor (Prabhārasa) produced a subtle and wondrous sound for the sake of the dragon kings to praise the Triple Gem, and further spoke these words:
"I am truly unable now to deliver you from your suffering and affliction; only the Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, can save you."

For the sake of taming all sentient beings, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was able to renounce his most cherished possessions throughout immeasurable lifetimes, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion to rescue them from suffering and affliction.
At that time, all the dragon kings—male and female, great and small—with single-minded devotion called to mind the Buddha, praising him and taking refuge, saying:

"Homage to the World-Honored One, who is most preeminent among all sentient beings; who has attained mastery over the mind within all dharmas; who has already reached the further shore of the ocean of all dharmas; who is able to rescue all sentient beings from suffering and affliction, bestowing upon them peace and happiness that is impartial and non-dual."

Out of compassion for all beings, he is able to show the true path and bestow the eye of right wisdom; he is worshipped by all devas and nāgas, and is able to receive the subtle and exquisite offerings of all humans and devas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
“World-Honored One!
We are now suffering immeasurable afflictions; we only pray that you will compassionately deign to rescue us.
Once these dragon kings had brought the Buddha to mind, they immediately saw their own bodies restored, no different from how they were before.

The Bodhisattva Light-Taste said to the dragon kings: "The merit of the Tathāgata is inconceivable. For the sake of sentient beings, he has practiced and perfected the six pāramitās over immeasurable eons. He teaches the three types of compassion to subdue sentient beings; he teaches that all dharmas are without self and without agency; he teaches the aggregates, bases, elements, the four great elements, and afflictions; he teaches the nature of afflictions and the nature of sentient beings; he teaches that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature and without marks, without obstruction, without action, without defilement, and without purity; they are without light and without darkness, without grasping and without relinquishing, without activity and without abiding, and neither one nor two. The aggregates, bases, elements, and the four great elements are likewise thus—this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth."
Therefore, the Tathāgata is able to discipline sentient beings as the Unsurpassed Honored One; therefore, the Tathāgata is able to uproot your immeasurable sufferings and afflictions.
Chapter Six: The Rescue of the Nāgas from the *Sūryaguhya-parivarta*. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Prabhārasa: “Good son!
"Do you now wish to hear about the karma of the various nāgas?
The Bodhisattva Prabhārasa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Now is precisely the right time; I only pray that you will expound it.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! Listen attentively with a sincere mind; I shall speak for you.
At that time, all the devas and humans made offerings to the Buddha with fine incense, flowers, music, banners, and canopies.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with all the devas of the desire and form realms, an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, proceeded from the kingdom of Magadha toward Mount Sumeru.
At that time, Brahmā prepared a throne of the seven precious gems to await the Tathāgata and further constructed a streetway of the seven precious gems.
Then, the Brahmā King spoke these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will traverse this path and sit upon my throne."
At that time, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods further fashioned a bed and a path out of Jāmbūnada gold, and they also said:
"Tathāgata, we pray that you will travel this path and sit upon our seats."
At that time, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven again fashioned a bed and a path out of celestial gold, saying:
"May the Tathāgata please travel this path and sit upon our golden bed."
At that time, the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven again fashioned a bed and a path out of celestial silver, saying:
"Tathāgata, we pray that you will walk this path and sit upon our silver bed."
Then the Yāma devas further fashioned beds and paths out of lapis lazuli, saying:
"May the Tathāgata please travel this path and sit upon the lapis lazuli bed.
Then the Trāyastriṃśa devas further fashioned beds and paths out of pearls, and likewise said:
"The Tathāgata wishes to travel this path and sit upon the pearl throne.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings further fashioned beds and paths out of agate, also saying:
"The Tathāgata wishes to travel this path and sit upon the agate bed."
Then the four asuras further fashioned beds and paths out of sandalwood, also saying:
"Tathāgata, we pray that you will travel this path and sit upon these sandalwood seats."
At that time, out of compassion for them, the World-Honored One manifested transformed images of the Buddha that traveled throughout the six realms of existence and sat upon the six thrones.

With his true body, the Tathāgata occupied the dharma-seat prepared by the Brahma King; each of the transformed images was accompanied by immeasurable śrāvakas and bodhisattvas as their retinue, and the radiance of each transformed image was like the light of immeasurable suns and moons.
When these dragon kings saw the manifested images, they conceived a heart of reverence and each spoke thus:
"Is this Mount Sumeru, and even these thousands of suns and moons?"
Nanda and Upananda said, "This is the radiance of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who has gone with immeasurable Brahmās to Mount Sumeru; it is not that of the sun or the moon."
If you wish to attain liberation, you should with a sincere heart and single-minded devotion keep the Tathāgata in mind.
The World-Honored Tathāgata has already destroyed ignorance; therefore, there is now such radiance as this.
The Nāga King Anavatapta said:
"This radiance belongs to Māra; it is not the light of the Buddha. Why is this so?"
Since the entire realm of desire belongs to Māra Pāpīyān, it is he who is capable of committing such evils.
Now, out of compassion, Pāpīyān is able to rescue these dragon kings from their suffering.

Some said: "It is surely the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, Tuṣita Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Four Great Kings who, out of compassion, are able to rescue these nāga kings from their suffering."
The Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita said:
"This radiance is the light of the Bodhisattva Prabhārasmi; out of compassion, he rescues all the dragon kings from their suffering."
The Dragon King Ratnaśikhin said:
"This radiance is the light of a person of great virtue who has left the household life and shaved off his hair and beard; out of compassion, he rescues the dragon kings from their suffering."
The Dragon King Sāgara said:
"This radiance is the light of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"

Out of compassion, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, regards all sentient beings as his only son; he is able to rescue them from all suffering and affliction. Having fulfilled the six pāramitās through cultivation over immeasurable lifetimes, he does so solely for the sake of relieving the immeasurable suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings.
"Therefore, all the devas of the desire and form realms shall prepare great offerings and worship him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying: "Kauśika!"
"Just as I roam this Sahā world to transform sentient beings, so do you dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to deliver the devas. Kauśika said:
"World-Honored One!
"I do not yet possess boundless wisdom; how can I say that I am able to transform the various devas?
World-Honored One!

Upon this Mount Sumeru, there are immeasurable devas, immeasurable Brahmās, immeasurable spirits and ghosts, immeasurable gandharvas, immeasurable kiṃnaras, immeasurable garuḍas, immeasurable asuras, immeasurable mahoragas, immeasurable nāgas, immeasurable great seers, and immeasurable sages."
“I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of a heart of compassion, will transform and deliver such immeasurable sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and immeasurable rays of light issued from his mouth—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and variegated in color—which illuminated the dark and obscure places throughout the ten directions. This light surpassed the radiance of immeasurable billions of Brahmā deities and the suns and moons of immeasurable billions of Śakra deities, and was capable of destroying all the malevolent deeds of Māras.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying:
“Kauśika! Just as Mount Sumeru is the foremost among all the mountains in the Sahā world, so too am I the most supreme among all sentient beings.”
At that time, having heard these words, all the dragon kings addressed the Buddha individually, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray only that you will have compassion for us and rescue us from our suffering.”
The Buddha said: "O sons of good family!
You should first recollect the Buddha with a sincere mind, and I shall rescue you."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya, and his voice was heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions: "Kauṇḍinya!
All dharmas are entirely impermanent; all dharmas are impermanent in their arising and abiding."
Why is this? Because they arise from causes and conditions.
All phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves suffering.
“If a phenomenon arises, it is itself suffering, it is itself an ulcer, it is itself a link of existence, it is itself birth and old age, it is itself arising and ceasing. Kaccāyana!
The eye is impermanent.
If the eye arises, it is suffering, it is a festering ulcer, it is a constituent of existence, it is birth and old age, it is arising and ceasing; this applies even unto the mind.
“Kauṇḍinya! If the eye ceases, that is the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth; it is the cessation of all links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). This applies likewise to the mind.”

Sentient beings do not know the arising and ceasing of the eye; therefore, they transmigrate through the five realms of existence. To sever this arising and ceasing of the eye, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma, and he also teaches the truth of suffering and the practice of the path for the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is the Great Brahmā among Brahmās, the Great Deva among Devas, and the Great Elephant among Elephants;

he is the Great Śramaṇa among Śramaṇas, the Great Brāhmaṇa among Brāhmaṇas, the Great Benevolence among benevolent ones, and the Great Compassion among compassionate ones. He is the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Great Man, who has already reached the further shore of the great ocean of birth and death. He is the greatest field of merit and the peerless donor; his mind is impartial as he serves as the Great Dharma King. Upholding the great prohibitions and precepts with unsurpassed diligence, he has skillfully cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), thoroughly understood the right path, and acts as the Great Guide who masters all remaining karmic activities.

“Kauṇḍinya! One is called a Tathāgata because of thoroughly knowing the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the eye; one is called an ordinary person because of not understanding them.
In what way does not knowing constitute being an ordinary person?

“Kauṇḍinya! All sentient beings speak of having a self; for this reason, they do not perceive the marks of the arising and ceasing of the eye, and thus they revolve through the five realms of existence. Kauṇḍinya!”
There are certain non-Buddhists who say that the seer is called the self, and so on, up to the knower being the self.
They claim that the eye is the causal condition for the self, and the same applies to everything up to the mind.
“Kauṇḍinya! The various non-Buddhists say that the eye is like a window and the self is like the seer; if it were so, it would be called a perversion. Why is this?
What is called "seeing" is a conjunction; within this conjunction, the notion of a self arises, and for this reason it is a perversion.
If one were to say that the eye is analogous to the direction and seeing is analogous to the self, this meaning would not be correct.
Why is this? That which sees within the ear both sees and hears, and both cognizes and touches.
The eye is not like this; therefore, that which sees cannot be called the self. Although the ear is old, its seeing remains clear and distinct; if the eye were old, it could not be so.
The "self" is called permanent; if the self were subject to seeing and hearing, it would be impermanent. If it were impermanent, how could it be called a "self"? "Kauṇḍinya!

Because sentient beings possess these inverted causes and conditions, they do not see the Four Noble Truths. The Tathāgata, having fully realized the nature of these inversions, is termed 'Right Wisdom,' and the 'self' is precisely the Tathāgata."
If there is anyone who can know the Tathāgata as the self, that person will be able to destroy the marks of perversion.
If they destroy perversion, they will shatter the works of Māra; if they shatter the works of Māra, such a person will be able to rescue and deliver all the nāgas.
"Kauṇḍinya! For this reason, I am now able to save all the nāgas."
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty. Part 14:
The Division on the Sun Treasury (Sūryagarbha-vibhāga). Chapter One: Protecting and Upholding the True Dharma (Saddharmaparigraha-parivarta).
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, surrounded by an immeasurable and incalculable number of great bodhisattvas before and behind him, as well as an inconceivable, countless, and asaṃkhyeya multitude of great bodhisattvas and śrāvakas from the various buddha-worlds of the ten directions; they filled both the earth and the sky, having all come together for this assembly and surrounding him on every side.

Furthermore, there were the Śakra-devānām-indras, Brahmā-devas, the Four Great Kings, the great Nāga kings, Yakṣa kings, Gandharva kings, Asura kings, Garuḍa kings, Kiṃnara kings, and Mahoraga kings from immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions; such beings, infinite, countless, and beyond measure, all came together for this assembly.

Furthermore, there were devas of the desire realm and form realm, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, all of whom gazed upon the Tathāgata with single-minded devotion.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had taught the great assembly the nectar-like Dharma-door of the "Space-Eye Ānāpāna" and the four immeasurables, he sat in silence.

The entire assembly on the earth and in the void of the Sahā world likewise remained silent with palms joined toward the Buddha; they yearned only for the Tathāgata’s nectar-like rain of Dharma without ever being satiated—just like those with a grave illness longing to meet a skilled physician, like those in thick darkness longing to see light, like those drowning in a great river longing to reach the other shore, or like those beset by urgent peril longing to find protection.

In this manner, the great bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, Śakra and Brahmā kings, mahoraga kings, and even humans and non-humans who filled the earth and the void throughout the Sahā buddha-field remained silent with palms joined, gazing up at the Dharma King in the same way.

At that time, there was among the assembly a Great Brahmā King named Puṇyapadmaprabha. Having made offerings to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas in the past, he had planted roots of goodness under those Buddhas and attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. With his mind focused on the Dharma and having well-cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, he rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“By the power of the Great Sage’s supernormal faculties, He can swiftly pervade all lands;
Like the mind, unobstructed, His light illuminates the nations of the ten directions.”
He skillfully expounds śamatha, the knowledge of exhaustion, and expedient means,
as well as mindfulness of ānāpāna and the four immeasurables.
Within the three realms, the Buddha has already abandoned the limits of birth and death.
Pure wisdom is fully perfected; surpassing humans, devas, and asuras, he is already freed from the bonds of craving.
Having crossed over doubt, he has reached the further shore;
clearly understanding all bodhisattvas, he has realized the Buddha-dharma through direct manifestation.
Because the minds of sentient beings are distracted, they fall into the river of birth and death;
like the blind who see nothing, they are constantly submerged by suffering.
Having distanced themselves from virtuous friends, they do not hear the pure Dharma.
Within the cycle of birth and death, beings are bound by all manner of fetters.
The Buddha, having crossed the ocean of birth and death, preaches the Dharma out of compassion;
for the sake of sentient beings afflicted by defilements, he cuts through the net of birth and death.
Craving is the root of afflictions; all sentient beings are stained by attachment.
The Sage of Skillful Means discerns this thoroughly, leading them to the end of birth and death.
Due to the conditions of delusion and craving, they do not cultivate various meritorious virtues.
If one can sever these, the six sense-faculties will all be stilled.
The Greatly Compassionate King of Munis preached the Dharma out of his heart of pity;
having heard it, they eliminated delusion and craving, attaining the ambrosia of Nirvana.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great Brahma King Puṇyapadmaprabha, speaking in verse:
"In the past you cultivated the various perfections, and now you likewise practice them;
you take no delight in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor in the stage of the pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who repeatedly give rise to thoughts of anger, as well as thoughts of the two vehicles; these constitute obstacles.
Because of these various obstructions, they fall away and lose the Buddha-dharma.
Those who do not give rise to these hindrances attain the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharma.
There are beings of the four modes of birth who all come to this realm;
they are not merely those with bodies of desire, nor are they exclusively those mindful of impurity.
Among these, the person of great wisdom is able to practice the path to enlightenment;
having long cultivated samādhi, patience, dhāraṇī, and the like,
they are able to guard their sense faculties and sit cross-legged with right mindfulness.
Abiding in their own realm, the Buddha shall explain it for you.
For those beings who delight in the five aggregates, he preaches the dharma of impurity to sever their fetters,
so that the seven factors of enlightenment may be fulfilled.
I have no heart of envy; out of compassion, I speak this for you.
When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, they do not abandon the bodhicitta.
All Buddhas of the ten directions have already dwelt in this land.
Day and night, you shall constantly provide protection, causing the Buddha-dharma to abide for a long time.
You bodhisattvas, out of compassion for the sentient beings of this land,
should always give rise to joyful patience, so that my Dharma may endure for a long time.
I preach the Dharma for śrāvakas in order to sever the mind of craving;
I demonstrate the emptiness of the five aggregates, the various sense bases,
and the eighteen elements, as well as the thirteen types of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One who can sever craving, so difficult to sever, attains purity;
they proclaim the untainted practice and the four noble truths to śrāvakas.
Out of compassion for sentient beings and to ensure that the Dharma endures for a long time, [they teach].
I have preached this Dharma of the Four Truths to enable you to cross the ocean of birth and death.
I further address all bodhisattvas: "Do not give rise to doubt;
the Buddha shall extensively expound the bodhisattva practices for your sake."
At that time, all the sentient beings present in the assembly of the Buddha within this Sahā world thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata now intends to teach the Dharma for śrāvakas; he does not speak of the bodhisattva path."
The Bodhisattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions further thought:

“The Tathāgata, out of his compassionate pity, desires that we cultivate various meditative practices in this world so that the lineage of the Triple Gem shall not be severed; so that all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, and even humans and non-humans within this realm—those who have not yet attained faith may be led to faith, and those who already have faith may be made to progress; so that all sentient beings may fully receive peace and happiness, abandon all doubts and regrets, and fulfill the Eightfold Noble Path of Nirvāṇa; and so that this Buddha-field may possess great merit and be thoroughly cultivated with all wholesome dharmas.”
All sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions formed this thought:
"The Buddha-field of Sahā is a place of merit and auspiciousness; we now pay homage, revere, make offerings to, and prostrate before the bodhisattvas within that Buddha-field."
Each of them formed this thought:

"I should now sit cross-legged in this world, each entering various gates of dhāraṇīs of supreme patience and various samādhis, emitting great radiance for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
Having formed this thought, they immediately sat cross-legged in this very land and entered the profound samādhis of the *Vīradharaṇī*.

Among these bodhisattvas, some had practiced the bodhisattva path for as long as a hundred great kalpas; some had attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena) up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*); and all were fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and other such meritorious dharmas. By the power of the causes and conditions of the profound samādhis of the *Vīradharaṇī*, each emitted a great radiance.
Among them, some lights were as bright as lamps, torches, or forest fires; others were like the radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, the various devas, and the Great Brahmā King.

Furthermore, there was the light of one sun, and then two, three, four, five, and so on, doubling in succession until reaching the light of hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of suns; all these radiances shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm.

Among the sentient beings who encounter this light, their bodies and minds become peaceful and joyful, and they all experience great delight, like a person overcome by heat entering a cool, refreshing pool.

This light can eliminate the sufferings of the three evil realms for sentient beings, as well as various ailments such as hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, and afflictions such as greed, hatred, ignorance, and false views; it can even cause all sentient beings within the prison of the triple world who face terrors and calamities to reach the end of suffering.

At that time, by the power of this light, all sentient beings in this world-system, with deep sincerity, collectively paid homage, made offerings, revered, and praised the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they renounced all evils and diligently cultivated wholesome dharmas.

From these rays of light, they extend to universally illuminate the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, whether pure or defiled—and shine everywhere, regardless of whether a Buddha is present or not. It is just as if, in the midst of a thick night of profound darkness, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of suns were suddenly to shine simultaneously; so too do these lights and those from other lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shine everywhere with universal radiance.

At that time, from the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, arrived at this world-system in a single thought-moment. Each sat cross-legged on one side; some of these bodhisattvas had already practiced the bodhisattva path for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas, while others had even attained the perfection of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). They had all cultivated the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and other meritorious dharmas. By the power of their respective roots of goodness and merit, they entered profound samādhi and emitted great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. Within it, the splendors of all the māra kings, nāga kings, and even humans and devas were completely eclipsed and did not appear.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of śrāvakas and the fourfold congregation:

"You should now know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the power of their great roots of goodness, have entered into samādhi and emitted this radiance, which shines universally throughout the trichiliocosm."

Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions, having previously performed Buddha-works in this land and returned to their own realms, now collectively bestow their protective empowerment upon these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, causing them to enter meditative concentration and manifest supernormal powers, so that the Triple Gem may endure for a long time without interruption in both the present and future worlds.

By the power of these causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and radiant light, they cause devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who have not yet developed faith to do so, and cause those who already have faith to increase it; they inspire great diligence toward the True Dharma, practicing according to the Dharma with mastery and without obstruction, attaining non-retrogression, and even fully perfecting the study of the requisites for the true path to nirvāṇa.

"In whatever places these bodhisattvas may dwell, in those very locations they shall, in future ages, erect stūpas and temples and construct Dharma halls; therein they shall enshrine relics, the Dharma scriptures, and images, and perform offerings with various kinds of the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, crystal, pearls, conch shells, jade, and fine silks—as well as various garments, couches, bedding, banners, canopies, monastic robes, Dharma vestments, various necklaces, flowers, incense, powdered incense, ointment, and burning incense, and by performing music, prostrations, and offerings, they shall cause sentient beings who fear birth and death to seek the path to nirvāṇa and cultivate merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:

"If, in future ages, there are good men or good women who offer such gifts to the Triple Gem, I shall accept them all, causing those sentient beings to attain non-retrogression within the Three Vehicles according to their inclinations."

"Furthermore, if there is someone who, for the sake of making offerings, constructs a single dwelling or a monastery, or donates gardens and groves as places for walking meditation, and provides them with clothing, food and drink, bedding and mats, and various medicinal decoctions as offerings."

Or there may be those who establish lecture halls for recitation and debate, as well as walking paths and meditation chambers, wherein they bestow upon them slaves, fields and houses, elephants, horses, carriages, camels, donkeys, oxen, sheep, and various other items—clothing, bedding, and all necessary medicinal supplies and requisites for life—so that the bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma may have peace and stability of body and mind, practicing seated meditation, cultivating the Way, and lecturing on the meaning of the teachings; so that they may practice according to the Dharma, become fully adorned, and attain the supreme, sovereign path of Nirvāṇa; and so that the Buddha-Dharma may long abide in the world. To this end, they relinquish such various things, which I, at that time, together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, shall all accept.

If, in future ages, there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, for the sake of making offerings to the Triple Gem, are able to relinquish such various things as these to establish halls for lecturing and study, as well as rooms for walking meditation and dhyāna, and provide them with all that is required—I shall fully know and see this and give rise to sympathetic joy, and together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, we shall enjoy it in common.

Why is this? It is so that these beings may attain great rewards and be distanced from the three evil realms; so that, according to their aspirations, they may attain non-retrogression within the three vehicles and eventually enter parinirvāṇa within each of those three vehicles.
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family, by virtue of making offerings with such various things as these, they shall obtain two benefits in future lives."
What are these two? First, the benefit of the Dharma;
second, the benefit of material wealth.

In whatever place they are born, they will be endowed with abundant wealth and resources due to the causes and conditions of their past practice. Because of this, they will give rise to no stinginess toward these things and will be able to relinquish them all in charity. Desiring to make offerings to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, they will establish stūpas, monasteries, halls, and quiet chambers in accordance with where they dwell—whether in mountain forests, beneath trees, or in *āraṇya* hermitages free from clamor and noise, suitable places for sitting in meditation and fixing the mind.

Whatever they require, he is able to provide and bestow; because these bhikṣus practice in accordance with the Dharma after receiving those gifts, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas will protect them wherever they may be.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that the Buddhas of the ten directions have already, in this Sahā world, entered deep meditative concentration and manifested great supernormal powers; they have destroyed Māra and the various nāgas, and out of compassion for sentient beings, they have expounded the wondrous Dharma so that the Three Jewels may long abide in the world."
Having performed their Buddha-work in each of these lands, they returned to their own countries.

At that time, from as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—desiring to see me, prostrate before me, make offerings, hear the True Dharma, and receive and uphold it—and furthermore, desiring to hear me preach the *Ākāśanetra-sūtra* and the four kinds of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), gathered together in this land from various other directions. Out of compassion and pity for all sentient beings, they entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and manifested great majestic power to destroy the Māra kings and the various nāgas. This was so that the sentient beings of this land might provide offerings and provide whatever they required, thereby cultivating various merits and attaining liberation within the Three Vehicles.

In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family whose faith is pure, who, desiring to make offerings to those bhikṣus who practice according to the Dharma, may relinquish their homes, gardens, forests, fields, slaves, and even all manner of necessities for livelihood.

"At that time, if there should be a precept-breaking bhikṣu who accepts even a single flower or a single fruit offered by another, that evil bhikṣu, due to his ignorance, will receive a great evil retribution for accepting the various items donated with pure hearts by others; in this present life, he shall incur four kinds of evil retributions."
What are the four? First, one's ill repute will spread far and wide throughout the ten directions;
second, parents, teachers, elders, brothers, kinsmen, servants, and relatives will all be separated from one another.
Third, one contracts a grave illness and lies amidst excrement and filth, dying in agony as the signs of retribution manifest;
fourth, all one's possessions, including robes, alms bowls, and sitting mats, are dispersed among the five families—these are called the four kinds of evil retributions.
"In future ages, one shall further incur four kinds of great evil retributions. What are these four?
First, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the great hell."

Second, having endured long and arduous suffering within the hells, once the hellish retribution has ended, they are reborn among animals or hungry ghosts (*preta*), where they receive the karmic fruit of being without hands or feet; dwelling in waterless wildernesses, they undergo all manner of hardship for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Third, at the end of that life, they are born among venomous snakes, receiving the fruit of being blind; for immeasurable ages, they subsist solely upon earth.

Fourth, at the end of that life, they may be born among humans, yet fall into an age of five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) where they do not encounter the Buddhas; though they obtain a human body in that world, they are perpetually without eyes and without hands or feet, dwelling in the wilderness and eating only the filthy food discarded by others, never having sufficient sustenance, and unable to dwell together with other people.
When their lives there have ended, they fall back into hell, finding it difficult to escape from the three evil realms.

Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family, with pure hearts, gave away fields, houses, gardens, groves, clothing, medicinal decoctions, and various other things solely desiring to make offerings to monks who live according to the Dharma; yet those who had broken the precepts accepted what was given by others solely for the sake of their own bodies, and did not give it to monks who maintained the precepts in accordance with the Dharma. By reason of these causes and conditions, they incur such offenses.

"Furthermore, those who violate the precepts dwell for a long time in birth and death, fully experiencing all manner of suffering; even if they obtain a human body, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are inconceivable and extremely difficult to encounter."

Those who break the precepts sever the mother of the Dharma and do not seek diligence; because they do not apply themselves to seeing or hearing the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, for these reasons and conditions they do not encounter a Buddha in the world. Such evil bhikṣus will, in future lives, receive such great and evil retributions as these.
At that time, having heard these words, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa wept with tears falling like rain and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, I would rather dwell in hell and undergo all manner of suffering than ever again accept such a body of broken precepts.”

Why is this? Although they have obtained this human body and further left the household life, for the sake of food and clothing, they completely violate the prohibitive precepts and accept the pure offerings of others, thereby undergoing various kinds of such suffering and affliction.
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa! It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
It would be better to dwell in hell and undergo various sufferings than to receive a human body and give rise to such sinful karma of breaking the precepts.”

Why is this? Because once the retribution for hellish offenses has been completed and no new karma is created, one attains liberation from the bitter retribution once the old karma is exhausted. "Kāśyapa!..."

Among all forms of existence, a human body is difficult to obtain; having obtained a human body, it is even more difficult to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world; and although one may encounter the era of a Buddha, to leave the household life and receive the precepts is the most difficult of all.

Why is this? Because once they have received the precepts, by practicing according to the Dharma, they are able to reach the end of suffering, sever all outflows (*āsrava*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), and attain liberation.

If a son or daughter of good family with pure faith—whether a Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra—wishes to make offerings to a bhikṣu who maintains pure conduct and the precepts, they do so because he is endowed with merit and roots of goodness; thus, they may relinquish houses, gardens, quiet retreats, slaves, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and various other means of livelihood to establish them as the permanent property of the Saṅgha, so that the bhikṣu’s body and mind may remain peaceful and secure while he accumulates roots of goodness.

These foolish bhikṣus violate the pure precepts and abandon all roots of goodness; being far removed from tranquil mindfulness and devoted solely to what is not the Dharma, those sons of good family do not make offerings to them.
For these reasons, their clothing, bedding, and necessary requisites for life were all insufficient; they then said:
"I am a man of great wisdom and am worthy of receiving the various offerings bestowed by others."

Or, by resorting to the powerful influence of lay donors, they seize various items received by other monks who act in accordance with the Dharma, using them solely for their own bodies as private property, claiming, "This is my own; it is not the property of the Saṃgha."
"Because that foolish person has committed such an offense, they shall undergo these various evil retributions in future lives.
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

If good sons or good daughters, or kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others, wishing to make offerings to bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma, relinquish their fields, houses, gardens, groves, and various material necessities for livelihood, yet a precept-breaker seizes what has been received by others solely to provide for himself, by reason of this cause and condition, he shall obtain such great and evil retributions as these.

If laypeople were to seize such various requisites for life as have been given in alms by a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and practices the Dharma, and use them for themselves, how much sin would these people incur?
The Buddha said,
“Great King, there is no need to ask what kind of retribution for these offenses you will receive.”
The King addressed the Buddha again:

"If in future ages there are kṣatriyas and others who give various kinds of goods to bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma, and by reason of this, those bhikṣus come to possess many requisites for life—what measure of sin would those kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras incur who, because they do not believe in the Buddha-dharma and the law of cause and effect, and because they do not fear wrongdoing, should seize and use such things?"
The Buddha said, “Great King!

Because these people have seized the offerings of others, they shall receive immeasurable and great evil retributions; were I to describe them in detail, it would only further increase their transgressions.”

Why is this? Because these kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras give various kinds of requisites to those bhikṣus who practice the Dharma with a pure mind; thus, these bhikṣus possess many means of subsistence.
Such a foolish person is like that deluded donkey; because of their lack of faith, they seize various offerings received by others for their own use. For this reason, they shall incur great sin.

If such a person hears me explain the various karmic retributions resulting from the distinctions of evil deeds and yet slanders and disbelieves them, that foolish person incurs two kinds of offenses:
first, they rob others of what has been given as an offering;
second, they slander and disbelieve what I have taught.
Then King Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I pray that you will speak this; I pray that you will speak this. In future ages, among the four castes—the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—there may be those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, who deeply understand cause and effect, and who fear transgression. Upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken—which is good in the beginning, middle, and end, profound in its meaning and flavor, and which perfectly fulfills the pure Brahma-faring—they shall find fulfillment."

When such a person hears this, they will be able to believe it, practice according to the Dharma, and cultivate various merits; furthermore, for the sake of making offerings to those bhikṣus who practice the Dharma, they will relinquish all kinds of goods to provide for their needs.

If there are precept-breaking bhikṣus or foolish people who seize various kinds of requisites received by those dharmic bhikṣus, those faithful persons shall employ skillful means to protect the precept-observing bhikṣus, ensuring that they are never again subjected to such plunder, deception, or oppression.
After King Bimbisāra had spoken these words,
the Buddha said: "Great King!
Excellent, excellent! It is well said that these words were spoken.
"Great King!..."

In future ages, if there should be kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras who, desiring to make offerings to bhikṣus who practice the Dharma, relinquish fields and houses, gardens and groves, slaves and servants, elephants and horses, clothing, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, or whatever else is required for livelihood.

If there be any among the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras who, out of lack of faith, seize what has been given by others, that foolish person shall obtain twenty kinds of great evil retributions within their present body.
What are these twenty?
First, all the devas and benevolent deities will distance themselves;
second, a great evil reputation will spread throughout the ten directions.
Third, one's kinsmen and acquaintances will turn against and become estranged from them;
fourth, hateful and malicious people will gather together with them;
fifth, all their possessions and wealth will be completely lost.
Sixth, their minds are deranged and deluded, and they are constantly restless and agitated;
seventh, their sense faculties are incomplete;
eighth, they find no peace in sleep or rest.
Ninth, they are constantly hungry and thirsty;
tenth, whatever food they consume is like poison;
eleventh, all those they love are separated from them.
Twelfth, those with whom one works together will constantly engage in much strife and contention;
thirteenth, one's parents, brothers, wife, children, servants, and slaves will not trust one's words;
fourteenth, all secret and concealed matters will be exposed by one's acquaintances and close friends.
Fifteenth, all one's wealth and possessions will be dispersed among the five families;
sixteenth, one will constantly encounter serious illnesses with no one to attend to them;
seventeenth, the necessities for livelihood will never be as one desires.
Eighteenth, their physical forms are withered and emaciated;
nineteenth, they endure toil and suffering for a long time, finding it difficult to escape;
twentieth, they constantly dwell amidst filth and impurity until the end of their lives.
"Great King! This foolish person shall receive twenty such kinds of evil retributions within his present life, and after his death, he will fall into the Avīci Hell to suffer for one kalpa."

Hungry, they eat iron balls; thirsty, they drink molten copper; they use hot iron sheets as clothing; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, everything they encounter is a mass of fire, with blazing flames from the six directions mutually penetrating one another.

Those sinful beings undergo all such various sufferings in the Avīci Hell. When their lives there end, they are reborn among the Maghacarḍa hungry ghosts. Dwelling in desolate wildernesses where there is no water, they are born without eyes and lack both hands and feet. Hot winds blow from the four directions and strike their bodies; their forms are tormented as if being cut by swords. As they writhe upon the ground, they endure great anguish; their fat, marrow, and grease flow like they are in a hot cauldron. Their spirits are bewildered and confused as they emit terrible cries. Having undergone hundreds of thousands of such sufferings for immeasurable years, they finally die and are reborn in the great ocean with a body of flesh-mass, its form vast and reaching a full hundred *yojanas* in length.

However, in the place where those offenders dwell, for a distance of one *yojana* surrounding their bodies, there is boiling water filled to the brim, resembling molten copper; they undergo such various kinds of suffering for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, no different from those in the hells.

When his life there comes to an end, he will suddenly be born by transformation in the midst of a wilderness marsh in Jambudvīpa, his form like a mass of flesh resembling a great mountain. Hot winds from the four directions will come to burn his body, and flying birds and running beasts will vie with one another to devour him. After passing through immeasurable years, he will then die and fall back into hell.

Furthermore, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of years, they undergo all manner of sufferings; thereafter, at the end of their lives, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts. Even with bodies as mere lumps of flesh, they pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, wandering back and forth in saṃsāra and fully experiencing all forms of suffering.

Their sins gradually diminish, and they manage to emerge as human beings; yet they are born into a world of five turbidities where no Buddha resides, blind from birth with impaired faculties, their physical forms so hideous that people take no pleasure in seeing them.
The Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying: "Great King!
Such a sinner shall, in a future world, obtain such great and evil retributions as these."

Why is this? Because these Dharma-holding bhikṣus practice according to the Dharma, those with faith provide them with various kinds of material requisites in abundance; yet those wicked bhikṣus and foolish people seize these for their own use, and therefore they obtain such evil retributions as these.
At that time, having heard these words, King Bimbisāra wept with tears falling like rain and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I would rather undergo the body of one in the hells than ever again accept such a human body."
"Why is this? Because these people have committed such sins, they receive such various fruits of great suffering as retribution.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:

“Great Kings! You kings, as well as the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, village heads, and others—both those present now and those in future ages until the Dharma remains—I entrust to you all the bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma during that time; you should protect them well.”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who possess faith and, for the sake of making offerings to bhikṣus who practice the Dharma, relinquish various kinds of life-sustaining necessities and miscellaneous items, you should protect them well, ensuring that non-Dharma bhikṣus and other evil persons do not deceive, seize, or oppress them.
"If there are wicked people who deceive and plunder the faithful offerings received by bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma, you all should punish them according to the law.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

the Buddha said.

From my present existence through the future until the exhaustion of the Dharma, during that interval, if there are sons or daughters of good family with faith who all renounce such necessities of life as fields, houses, gardens, groves, elephants, horses, slaves, servants, clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, and bestow them upon bhikṣus who practice the Dharma.

At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:

The king addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha said, “Great King! Those kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas,

vaiśyas, śūdras, and village headmen— both those of the present and those of future ages until the end of the Dharma— who, by means of the True Dharma, govern those bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma and those who are foolish, shall obtain even greater merit than they.”

Furthermore, if there are faithful sons or daughters of good family who, in the present, in future ages, or even until the time when the Dharma is about to perish, provide various necessities to those bhikṣus who practice the Dharma; and if there are unrighteous and evil persons who would encroach upon, seize, or treat them with contempt, and if someone else should skillfully teach and transform them so as not to allow such encroachment, saying:
"If you do not now follow this instruction, I shall punish you for your offense."

"If those wicked people follow this instruction and cease their deceitful intent, no longer encroaching upon or seizing the faithful offerings received by Dharma-upholding bhikṣus, then the kṣatriyas and others, even down to the village headmen, will acquire very great, indeed immense, merit!"
The King spoke again to the Buddha:

If there should be even a single bhikṣu who abides in accordance with the Dharma regarding all his possessions, and if there should be wicked people who treat him with contempt, oppress him, or seize his property, we—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or even village headmen—shall not act according to the law [toward them], and we shall incur great sin.”

If any person who acts contrary to the Dharma and is evil should seize or plunder the requisites for life belonging to this bhikṣu, we—whether they be kṣatriyas or even village headmen—shall protect him in accordance with the Dharma so that such a person does not seize, deceive, or oppress him; furthermore, by punishing him according to the Dharma, one shall obtain great merit.
The Buddha said,

Why is this? Within my Dharma, there are bhikṣus who, even if they act in accordance with the Dharma, I do not permit them to receive permanent monastic property—such as fields, houses, gardens, groves, elephants, horses, carriages, or male and female slaves—if they are from one person up to four persons; only when there are five persons or more may such property be received.

Whether in a monastery or in a forest hermitage, if a Dharma-holding bhikṣu resides therein, the community shall assemble by the ringing of the bell for matters such as the harmonious uposatha and formal acts (karmavācanā), and they shall collectively share and utilize the dwellings, couches, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.

Even when hundreds of thousands of monks are gathered in a single monastery or in a forest hermitage, ringing the bell to assemble for the harmonious *poṣadha*, they share and utilize dwellings, bedding, robes, and medicinal decoctions with a unified mind; yet they do not harbor greed or attachment, nor do they fixate their thoughts upon them—unlike the ṛkṣa bird, which greedily clings to various meats, eating until they are exhausted before finally ceasing, never stopping midway.

The Dharma-holding bhikṣu is not like this: throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he diminishes his sleep, diligently reciting the sūtras, practicing dhyāna, and cultivating the Path. Turning his back on birth and death, he proceeds toward the road to Nirvāṇa. Such a bhikṣu does not praise the shortcomings of others nor speak of his own virtues; he is humble, modest, and does not act with pride or arrogance. He is content with food and clothing, practices the dhūta ascetic virtues, and is diligent and non-negligent in his conduct. Binding his mindfulness in contemplation, his mind does not wander; toward all sentient beings, he gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, cherishing and protecting them.
"Great King!
Thus, within the Saṃgha, those who plunder incur a great retribution for their sins, while those who protect and benefit it attain great merit.
Furthermore, Great King!"

Wherever they may be—whether in a monastery or a forest hermitage—if five bhikṣus dwell therein, maintaining the precepts without violation, fully pure, and even feeling great dread regarding minor offenses.

As for the practice of emptiness taught in the Buddha’s sūtras: if one recites it oneself or teaches others to recite it; if one does not slander others nor speak of their faults; if one does not boast of one's own virtues but remains humble and self-effacing; if one gives rise to no pride, arrogance, or envy; and if one possesses compassion and pity for all sentient beings, seeking the path to liberation and emerging from the ocean of birth and death.

When such a community of monks is gathered at a monastery or a forest hermitage, they assemble by the ringing of a bell to harmoniously utilize the property of the Saṃgha, including even medicinal decoctions.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who makes offerings according to the Dharma, they will obtain great merit; yet if one robs, seizes, or insults them, one will receive the retribution of a great sin. "Great King!

These five bhikṣus were diligent in upholding the precepts and fully possessed of shame and remorse; they felt great dread toward even minor transgressions, practiced the dhūta austerities, and dwelt in the four noble lineages."

The merit possessed by such a Sangha is like the great ocean; it is the supreme field of merit among all worldly beings, including devas, humans, and asuras, capable of causing all sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and affliction and attain nirvana.
How much more so for ten, twenty, thirty, or even hundreds of thousands!

If there are faithful Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras who, for the sake of making offerings, strike a bell to assemble the Saṃgha, and at the time of this assembly there are among them some unrighteous bhikṣus—whether many or few—who gather together with righteous bhikṣus; yet within that assembly there are even as few as five bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts and are fully possessed of shame and remorse, who always feel fear regarding even minor transgressions and never violate them.

Thus, this Sangha has cultivated great diligence, renouncing all worldly affairs and aspiring solely to the supramundane path of Nirvana; their merits are immeasurable and boundless, and as a great field of merit, they deserve the offerings of the world’s devas and humans.
Therefore, Great King! You should provide them with proper protection and establish them according to the Dharma; you must supply all their necessities so that they lack for nothing.

If there are those who act contrary to the Dharma, seeking to deceive, oppress, or insult them with a contemptuous mind, you must guard and sustain them well, ensuring that such people do not harass or disturb them.
King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.”
The Buddha said, "Great King!
Ask whatever you wish."
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha said to the Great King:

When the king at that time convenes a great assembly, and during the gathering for song, dance, music, and joy, would this criminal be permitted to take his place in the assembly to eat, sing, dance, enjoy himself, and make music together with them?
The king said to the Buddha:
"Such a person should not be permitted to remain in the assembly; they should not even be allowed to see me, let alone join me in the joys of the gathering."
The Buddha said: "Great King! So it is, so it is."
If there is a bhikṣu who breaks the precepts and commits offenses, who is not truly a śramaṇa yet claims to be one, and who does not truly practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet says,
"I practice the holy life"— such a person is like one who is blind, wandering, falling, and sinking within saṃsāra.

"Great King! Such a person has completely violated the prohibitive precepts within the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. For this reason, they are abandoned by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas; they are not disciples of the Buddha but are the retinue of Māra. "Such a person as this is outside the Buddha-dharma and is abandoned by all.

“World-Honored One!
What kind of conduct, categories, and physical characteristics does such a person who has broken the precepts possess, so that they may be recognized?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! This mark of broken precepts is difficult to discern when it has not yet appeared.
What is the initial sign of broken precepts?

That which is called not delighting in making offerings to the Triple Gem, the preceptors (upādhyāya), and the instructors (ācārya); furthermore, not placing faith in or honoring the four noble lineages (catvāri āryavaṃśāḥ) and failing to practice them; and also not practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣadharmāḥ)—this is termed the first sign of breaking the precepts.

Their minds crave gain and offerings, lacking both shame and remorse; they form intimate friendships with worldly people, praising their own virtues to become self-conceited, while looking down upon, slandering, and reviling others. Their hearts take no pleasure in speaking words of the True Dharma, but only delight in talking of useless matters.

They exclusively engage in demonic deeds to harass and disturb the Sangha; when another speaks but a single word or ten phrases, they retaliate with tenfold harshness. They indulge their own minds in dissipation and never yield, being just like a vicious dog.

Furthermore, they are like a flock of flying crows whose clamorous voices cry out only for victory; though they have left the household life and dwell among the assembly, they are sycophantic, deceitful, and hypocritical, solely practicing piercing malice.
Furthermore, they are like merchants carrying various goods who, while traveling on a road, encounter wicked bandits; these persons of broken precepts are the thieves among śramaṇas.

Again, they resemble monkeys that, having smeared their bodies with excrement, rush headlong into people; amidst the assembly, they are like *kuraṇṭaka* flowers—lacking both color and fragrance. Their minds are not harmonious and they constantly utter words of contention; they are always greedy for gain, offerings, fame, and the like, and delight in taking evil bhikṣus and laypeople as companions with whom to converse.

"As long as these bhikṣus have not yet stolen the community's fields, houses, gardens, groves, slaves, elephants, horses, camels, mules, oxen, donkeys, or such like items—which are difficult to identify—this is called the first sign of broken precepts."

If one steals such items as these, it is called the characteristic of violating the precepts and so forth; once this characteristic has arisen, one loses the status of a bhikṣu. This is a pārājika offense, and one is no longer a śramaṇa; one may not dwell together with the Saṃgha of the Dharma and should be expelled.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"This bhikṣu who upholds the precepts would rather dwell together with a caṇḍāla than dwell together with one who has broken the precepts."
"Just as fire arises from within a tree that has withered and decayed, so that once the root is burned, the branches and leaves are also utterly consumed;

so too it is with a bhikṣu who violates the precepts. By the fire of his broken precepts, he burns away all his merits, such that the fruits and rewards of his roots of goodness are completely exhausted without remainder. For example, it is like a latrine that can never be made clean; such a person slanders the worthy sages and saints, severs the lineage of the Triple Gem, dries up the ocean of Dharma, destroys the city of the True Dharma, deceives and deludes donors, and troubles and disturbs the pure assembly.

When the Saṃgha of bhikṣus is in harmony according to the Dharma, if one opposes and does not comply with the assembly, that bhikṣu who has broken the precepts will, due to the cause and condition of stealing the property of the Saṃgha, result in the rulers—whether Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—and even men, women, or all other donors, though they relinquish their necessities, obtaining nothing at all; they lose the path of humans and devas and fall into the evil realms.
"Therefore, Great King!
You should know that those who break the precepts lack shame and remorse; with a mind of robbery and theft, they take the property of the Sangha and claim it as their own."

Such monks who act contrary to the Dharma, wherever they may dwell—whether in the forest or within a monastery—should not be allowed to live with them; rather, one should give rise to compassion for them and employ skillful means to instruct and guide them so that they are expelled from the community.
He spoke thus: "Elders! You should not remain here."
If, after these three admonitions, that person who has broken the precepts departs, it is well;
if they do not leave the assembly, the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma must not scold or revile them.
They should inform the king, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and those who possess power, saying:
“There is a bhikṣu here who acts contrary to the Dharma and constantly disturbs us, not allowing us to practice the Path with a settled mind.
We pray that you will investigate this matter and ensure he does not cause further harassment.”
"Then that king—whether a Kṣatriya or even a village headman—should punish them and drive them out.

If those Kṣatriya kings and others accept the food, drink, wealth, or property of such precept-breaking bhikṣus and do not expel them, the bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma should likewise not become angry. They should not covet their dwellings or the necessities of life, but should depart in silence to seek another place free from difficulties, whether it be among mountains and forests, in caves, or in an araṇya, and dwell there in whatever secluded spot they find."
Having heard these words, King Bimbisāra wept and wailed aloud, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and even village headmen, for the sake of clothing, food, and material wealth, protect those precept-breaking bhikṣus and provide them with influence, causing these bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma to abandon their dwellings.”

For this reason, in future lives they will fall into the great hells and undergo immeasurable suffering; they will cycle back and forth through the three evil realms, finding it difficult to escape. Although in future ages there will appear in the world immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—Buddhas endowed with great compassion who enter the cycle of birth and death to deliver suffering sentient beings—they will not be able to cause those kings, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and village chiefs to abandon the retribution of the evil destinies and obtain bodies among gods and humans.

Why is this? Because they do not accept the words of bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma, and because they fail to provide them with offerings and support, they undergo such great retributive fruits as these.
The Buddha said: “Great King!
In future ages, within various lands, there will be kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and vaiśyas who possess faith.”
Śūdras, for the sake of providing and making offerings to bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma,
may construct monasteries or secluded dwellings, or erect halls and chambers in forest hermitages (āraṇya) and offer them to such bhikṣus;
or they may donate fields, houses, gardens, groves, slaves, and various other necessary articles for the livelihood of their sustenance.

Even down to medicinal decoctions—by virtue of such causes and conditions of making offerings, those donors will, in future lives, be born into families of great clans such as the Kṣatriyas or Brāhmaṇas;
or they will be born among the gods of the six heavens of desire up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra);
or they will be born in the pure Buddha-worlds of other directions, where they shall encounter the Buddhas and hear the Dharma before long.
One shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, if there is anyone within my Dharma who, for the sake of seeking merit and the path to *nirvāṇa*, should provide offerings and support to bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma.

The king said to the Buddha:

Such a person is not a disciple of the Buddha, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya; among the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time, they are a person of great transgression. In this way, if kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others do not expel those evil bhikṣus, then even if they further cultivate merit and perform various kinds of giving, they will ultimately be unable to extinguish this transgression; they must inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Therefore, Great King!
If there are those who wish to achieve their own benefit and the benefit of others, they should not protect those who have broken the precepts. Why is this?"

If kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others protect bhikṣus who practice the Dharma, preventing those evil bhikṣus from dwelling together with them or sharing in their use of robes, food, and drink, then these kṣatriyas and others—though they may not personally give alms or cultivate other merits—are nonetheless the great *dānapatis* of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and are able to uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
When this person’s life comes to an end, they will be reborn in a pure buddha-field in another direction and shall before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Therefore, Great King!"

"You, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and others, should protect, honor, and provide for those bhikṣus who practice the Dharma; even until the time when the Dharma is about to perish, you should protect, honor, and provide for all such bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma. By these causes and conditions, you will be able to cause the Three Jewels to endure long and not perish."

"If you do not protect the bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma, my teaching will perish; but if the Dharma remains in the world, it can cause the realms of gods and humans to flourish and the evil destinies to diminish.
The King said, "World-Honored One!"
"Who are those capable of serving as administrators to protect the property of the Sangha and provide offerings and support for bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
There are two kinds of persons capable of managing monastic affairs and guarding the property of the Sangha. What are these two?
First, those who are Arhats endowed with the eight liberations; [the second is...]
Second, there are those in training who have attained the three fruits beginning with stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
These two types of persons are capable of managing monastic affairs and making offerings to the Saṃgha.
As for other bhikṣus, if their precepts are incomplete or their minds are not impartial, one should not allow such individuals to manage monastic affairs.
