"Good son! This Great Prophecy Dhāraṇī possesses great merit, great power, and great benefit.

It can exhaust all evil karma, compassionately protect all sentient beings, and completely wash away all defilements of sin. It renders the body and mind radiant and pure, bestowing the power of mindfulness and the power of cessation."

If there are sentient beings who listen and receive this with a single mind and practice according to what is taught, all Tathāgatas, all Bodhisattvas, all Pratyekabuddhas, and all Arhats will provide their protection; even the heavenly kings and human kings will constantly guard and keep them in mind, honoring, loving, prostrating to, making offerings to, and providing for them.

When that person approaches the end of life, they shall behold all the Buddhas of the ten directions whom they have previously recited and contemplated. Those Buddhas will all place their hands upon his head and speak these words:
"Come, son of good family! I shall now lead you to be born in a pure Buddha-field; once born in my land, you shall swiftly abide in the ten stages."

That person, upon seeing the Buddha, attained great joy; because of that great joy, at the end of life, they were reborn in a pure buddha-field. Having been born there, they attained the stage of the ten bhūmis and, before long, achieved anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! This wisdom relies upon the great dhāraṇī; it possesses such power that it can purify evil karma, accomplish a pure mind, and realize the path to nirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Buddha Jñānaguṇakūṭarāja addressed the Bodhisattva Arciṣmatigarbha, saying: “Good son,
take this dhāraṇī and go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, and speak these words on my behalf:”
"Jñānaguṇaśikhararāja Buddha sends his greetings to the World-Honored One.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jvālākara replied: "So be it;
I shall receive your instructions."
At that time, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within that assembly spoke with one voice, saying:

"We now desire to behold that Śākyamuni Buddha of the Sahā world, to pay him homage and make offerings, and to see the great assembly, so as to hear and receive the *dhāraṇī* gate of the Sun-Treasury that Destroys the Realm of Dragons and Exhausts All Evil Karmas."

"Since the distant past, we have never before gone to that Sahā world; now, having arisen from meditative concentration, we wish to go to that land. We pray only that the World-Honored One will grant us permission to go."
At that time, the Tathāgata Jñānaguṇakūṭarāja addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
You may go as you wish; however, you should travel to that land with your minds well-restrained. Each of you should transform your bodies so that they are fully adorned like those of Nārāyaṇa."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jvālāgarbha, together with the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all manifested the adornment of the body of Nārāyaṇa; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and immediately departed from there, reaching the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha in the kingdom of Magadha within the four continents of the Sahā world-system in the time it takes for a single thought to arise.
Having arrived, he scattered powdered Jambūnada gold over the Buddha.
Having made this offering, he prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Jñānaguṇaśikhararāja inquired after the World-Honored One:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy, and is your physical strength at peace?
Do you turn the wheel of the true Dharma without hindrance?"
Having spoken these words, he withdrew and stood to one side.

At that time, eighty Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields to the north of this Sahā world, beyond that number, there was a Buddha-field named Universal Superior Fragrance (Samantottaragandha), filled with the five turbidities.
In that land there is a Buddha named Guṇakusumagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.
Among the assembly of that Buddha is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gaganagañja, who is present in the gathering listening to the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja looked up into the sky and saw immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas coming from the north and proceeding toward the south; he further saw a great radiance in the southern quarter.
Having seen this, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Just as I arose from meditative concentration and was listening to the Dharma in this assembly, I saw immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas coming from the north and proceeding toward the south; furthermore, I saw a great radiance in the southern direction."
"By what causes and conditions does such a thing occur?
At that time, the Buddha Guṇakusumagarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, saying:
"O son of good family!"

To the south of here, passing through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-world named Sahā, which, like my own field, is filled with the five corruptions.

In that world-system there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells in the world, preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings. This is so that the Mother of the Dharma may long abide in the world, so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may not be severed, and so that the great banner of the Dharma may be raised to destroy the net of Māra.
The Buddhas of the ten directions all assembled in that land to proclaim the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī; having finished speaking, they each returned to their own lands.

Śākyamuni Buddha convened a great assembly for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas, and by means of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, he expounded the three gates of liberation.

In that buddha-field, the earth and the void were filled with a great assembly. The Tathāgata sat upon a lion throne, emitting great radiance and preaching the profound and wondrous Dharma: the pure brahmacarya and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); the "Dragon Realm-Destroying Flame Chapter" from the *Sūryagarbha-dharmaparyāya*; and the dhāraṇī gateways that eliminate the unwholesome and evil karma of all sentient beings. All beings delighted in hearing it without ever being satiated, constantly thinking thus: [May we also attain such a realm].

If there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas in all the lands of the ten directions who have practiced the bodhisattva path for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, and who desire to attain the stage of being "born only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and who wish to personally possess unobstructed wisdom without following the teachings of others—those Bodhisattvas should all assemble in this Sahā world. By means of their own roots of goodness, they should enter various samādhis so that this world’s great earth may receive immense benefit, so that all sentient beings do not lose their power of mindfulness, and so that through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence, they may attain great wisdom, just as it is in the pure Buddha-lands of other directions which are endowed with all merits.
"Now, in this Sahā world, there are also great assemblies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the ten directions who have all gathered here.

Those bodhisattvas, according to their respective capacities within the Sahā world, each enter into samādhi and emit light from their bodies and sides; some are like great lamps, while others are like the light of hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, or even immeasurable and boundless suns and moons."
All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have gathered together in that Sahā world-system; for this reason, there is a great radiance.

Those assemblies of bodhisattvas from the buddha-fields of the ten directions who have not yet arrived rise from their samādhi and proceed toward the south, going to the Sahā world-system desiring to see Śākyamuni Buddha and the great assembly, and desiring to hear the *dhāraṇī* gate that destroys all evil karma.
They sat cross-legged, each entering profound meditative concentrations of vigorous play. "Good son,
you may now go to that Sahā world."

"Good son! The sentient beings therein have short lifespans and many ailments; they possess little wisdom, few roots of goodness, and meager merit. They feel no dread toward the three evil realms; they lack the necessities of life and are full of greed and desire. They engage in impure conduct, lacking both shame and remorse, and delight in practicing the ten unwholesome deeds. When such sentient beings cast off this body, they fall into the evil realms."

Furthermore, there are those born among the evil yakṣas, the kaṭapūtanas, and even the ākapūtanas; having been born there, they extract the vital essence of the earth and the various flavors of grains, flowers, fruits, plants, trees, and all such things, causing the physical strength of those who consume them to diminish.

Those various evil spirits increase their power and constantly watch for opportunities, dwelling within the womb during gestation and emerging at birth; they follow the being through its growth until they even snatch away its life.

For this reason, those sentient beings suffer from many illnesses and short lifespans, lacking the power of mindfulness and wisdom; they do not fear the suffering of the three evil realms in the future, and even delight in practicing the ten unwholesome karmas, thereby falling into the evil paths.

“Good son! In the past, when I was practicing as a bodhisattva, I made such a vow: to be firm and courageous, to practice with diligence without rest, to make offerings to all Buddhas, and to practice according to their teachings. I questioned those Buddhas about which dhāraṇī mantras could protect the womb and the mother’s body, enabling them both to attain peace and security?”

May all evil nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pīlitas, piśācas, putanas, kaṭapūtanas, umarās, and avasmaras—whether they cause malarial fevers lasting from one day up to four days, or administer poisons and evil spells, or employ malevolent medicines that afflict the body and mind with suffering—be unable to find any opportunity to harm?

Whether in the mother’s womb, or upon emerging from the womb, during nursing and growth, when various foods and drinks absorb his vital essence, how could the turbidity and confusion of body and mind find any opportunity?

May those sentient beings dwell in safety within the womb, and until they are nurtured by breast milk, may their bodies and minds remain untainted; may they be free from illness, enjoy long life, and increase in wisdom; and may they eventually be able to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, delighting in practicing generosity and upholding the precepts, while fearing the suffering of the three evil realms in the future.
What kind of dhāraṇī can attain such [a state]?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it for me; having heard it, I shall teach and transform sentient beings in future ages.
"At that time, that Buddha immediately taught me the *Śamathavipaśyanā-siddhi-maṇḍala*, the Great Prophecy Dhāraṇī.

Having heard this mantra, I have upheld and disseminated it for immeasurable billions of kalpas, and have constantly used this mantra to transform and guide sentient beings, enabling them to practice the six pāramitās with firm diligence."
Furthermore, by means of this mantra, one shall protect all women and protect the womb.

Whether it be devas, umarā, apasmārā, humans, non-humans, or others, they shall be unable to cause the four great elements of those women or their wombs to become unbalanced, nor cause their bodies or minds to become turbid and disturbed. They shall not be able to seize the vital essence of humans through evil spells or evil medicines, nor even asuras or other worldly beings who destroy the womb; such beings shall find no opportunity. The womb shall be secure, and the birth shall be without difficulty. The faculties shall be complete, the body pure, and the countenance upright. One shall be endowed with wisdom and never lose the power of mindfulness. Great powerful devas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, along with their immeasurable retinues, shall constantly follow and provide protection.

It enables them to attain the wisdom of recollecting past lives, to give rise to a heart of compassion through fear of the evil realms, to delight in practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and to find joy in spiritual friends so as to easily attain noble wisdom.
They will be able to exhaust suffering and attain perfect wisdom.

Delighting in empty and tranquil places, they will extinguish all afflictions; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and various spirits will provide them with offerings and support. Disgusted with birth and death, they will resolve to seek nirvāṇa, eventually giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In every place of rebirth, they shall never forget the bodhicitta and will swiftly achieve the samādhis of a bodhisattva.
If one gives rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, one will presently attain the patience that accords with truth (anulomikī-kṣānti) and will become a pratyekabuddha in a future life.
If one resolves upon the mind of a śrāvaka and attains the patience that accords with the Four Noble Truths, one will not fall into the three evil realms but will be reborn among gods and humans.
“Good son! In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I used immeasurable skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to dwell in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Good son! This dhāraṇī possesses such great power and brings such great benefit. Good son!"
If any sentient beings encounter severe leprosy, one should take this dhāraṇī and enchant lion’s milk with it, then have the patient drink it; all diseases will be completely cured.

If one cannot obtain lion’s milk, one may take food from the side of a sacrificial offering for the dead and, having empowered it with this dhāraṇī-mantra, administer it to the patient; thus all illnesses will likewise be completely cured.
If no such food is available, one should take dust from discarded medicine, empower it with this dhāraṇī mantra, and give it to the patient to consume; thus, all illnesses shall also be cured.

“Good son! In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I diligently sought skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings in this way, even leading them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If I see trees that have no flowers or fruit, I shall immediately use this mantra to consecrate rainwater and sprinkle it upon the roots of those trees; thus, their flowers and fruit will flourish and grow lush, even causing grapes and all varieties of grains and grasses to thrive and prosper.

If it does not rain, take various impure liquids from ditches and channels, place them within a tortoise shell, and consecrate them with mantras. Wrap this tortoise shell in leaves of the *campaka* tree and place it in a dragon pond; immediately a great rain will fall.

If excessive rain from the heavens damages the sprouts and fruit, one should take the jewel from the head of the Aṭakāra snake, enchant it with mantras, and place it within a dragon spring; the rain will then immediately cease.

If there are untimely black winds, extreme cold or extreme heat, if the sun, moon, and stars lose their regular courses, or if the years, seasons, and four quarters undergo strange transformations and calamities, one should compassionately cultivate the pure Brahma-faring for seven days and seven nights, bathing the body and subsisting on milk gruel or merely vegetables, with single-minded concentration and no other thoughts.

If one recites and upholds this dhāraṇī for seven days and seven nights, and further uses this dhāraṇī to consecrate pure chrysanthemums, wrapping them with *mātuluṅga* fruit and placing them within a celestial temple, then untimely winds, rains, cold, heat, and various calamities will immediately cease, and the sun, moon, and stars will once again follow their regular courses.
“Good son! When I was practicing for enlightenment in the past, I desired to bring peace and security to all sentient beings wherever they may be.
Whenever I saw sentient beings who were deluded by false imaginings and inverted views, at those times I would preach this dhāraṇī mantra for them.”

Upon hearing this mantra, those sentient beings completely abandon all false views and delusions; they cultivate the ten wholesome actions, give rise to virtuous vows, and their lustful desires become thin and few.

“Good son! In the past, by means of skillful power, I taught and transformed sentient beings, causing them to abide in the six pāramitās; I myself also fully practiced the six pāramitās, until I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

“Good son! This dhāraṇī can bestow such great power upon sentient beings and grant them great benefit; it can eliminate all suffering and affliction of disease, protect pregnant women and their fetuses, destroy all fetters of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and provide knowledge of the four great elements, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) while demonstrating the path of skillful means. It can awaken one to the peace, security, and bliss of nirvāṇa, cause the faith of sentient beings to become pure, enable entry into the various gateways of the differentiated dharmas, subdue all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and destroy the realm of Māra.”

“Good son! The power of this dhāraṇī can cause all the devas to rejoice; it causes yakṣas and malevolent spirits to feel contentment in their hearts; it causes the asuras to experience extreme terror; it causes the garuḍas, kinnaras, and others to likewise rejoice; and it prevents the mahoragas from even looking back.”
It subdues and overcomes heterodox arguments, enabling Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras to attain faith and joy, and it enables women to diminish their lustful desires.

It increases the power of mindfulness for those who are learned; it causes those who cultivate meditative concentration to delight in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages). It can repel all thieves, strife, famine, epidemics, droughts, floods, cold, heat, coarseness, and harsh, unpleasant contacts; such matters as these are all completely extinguished. The "Mother of Dharma" increases, the Buddha-dharma spreads, and the Three Jewels remain uninterrupted. It removes the fear of birth and death, shatters the mass of ignorance, and casts off the burden of suffering, enabling one to attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | mana kha tsyeh (with the 'tsyeh' pronounced with a retroflex 'c' and a reversed 'e') |"

"Saheha 42. At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī, sixty trillion people within that great assembly attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); furthermore, sixty *bimbara* of people attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*).
“Good son! You may take this dhāraṇī of mine and go to the Sahā world, speaking these words on my behalf:
‘To the north of here, beyond eighty Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields, there is a Buddha-world named Universal Superior Fragrance, which likewise possesses the five turbidities.’”
In that world-system there is a Buddha named Guṇakusumagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.
He inquires after the Śākyamuni Buddha, asking:
"Are you free from illness? Are you free from affliction? Is your physical strength at ease?"
Do the assembly of disciples delight in hearing the Dharma and practice according to what they have heard?
Are they able to subdue the four māras and all evil nāgas?
Is the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma free from obstacles?

"Good son! At the place of that Śākyamuni Buddha, he preached the Dharma-gate of the *Sūryagarbha* (Sun Treasury), which can destroy the realms of Māra kings and Nāga kings and eradicate evil karma. He preached this *Śamapaita-siṭi-mahāvyākaraṇa-dhāraṇī*, desiring to cause this dhāraṇī to possess great power and great benefit, so as to enable sentient beings to dwell in peace and happiness, extinguish all afflictions, and even cast off the burden of suffering."
At that time, the assembly of disciples of the Buddha Guṇakusumagarbha all praised him together, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
How rare, World-Honored One!”
"How rare, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata’s wisdom is unobstructed and unhindered regarding all phenomena. From the distant past until now, we have never before heard such a profound and great dhāraṇī, which can bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings. Having heard this dhāraṇī, we shall all rouse our courage to read, recite, and uphold it."
"Why is this? Because this dhāraṇī possesses such immeasurable and boundless great merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who fear birth and death and rejoice in nirvana, who single-mindedly invoke the name of, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Buddha Virtue Flower Treasury (Guṇakusuma-garbha), and who recite this dhāraṇī while giving rise to a mind of rare wonder—those sentient beings will increase their roots of goodness and obtain great benefit.”
At that time, the Buddha Guṇakusuma-alaṃkāra addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, saying: "Good son, it is so, it is so!"
"It is as you have said, son of good family!

In the past, when I was cultivating bodhi, I diligently sought skillful means and made this vow: 'When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if there are any sentient beings in the buddha-fields of the ten directions who delight in practicing giving, up to and including wisdom [the six perfections],'"

If one can with a sincere heart invoke my name, prostrate, and make offerings, there shall be no gods, humans, asuras, or others who can inflict harm upon that sentient being, nor shall there be anyone able to obstruct their practice of the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, it can increase immeasurable roots of goodness, with the sole exception of those who have committed extremely evil deeds in the past.
If this vow is not fulfilled, I swear that I shall not attain supreme perfect enlightenment.

"Good son! If there are women who desire to conceive a child, or those who do not wish for many children, or those who are pregnant and fear the perils of childbirth—all such persons should, with a sincere heart, invoke my name, pay homage, and make offerings."

If humans or non-humans were able to find an opportunity to harm me, or if evil spells or poisonous drugs could cause my body and mind to suffer oppression—even for a single thought-moment—should anyone be able to inflict such evil upon me, I vow not to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! In the past, when I was seeking Bodhi, I made such a vow to protect and benefit all sentient beings. Therefore, sentient beings should single-mindedly invoke my name, prostrate to me, and make offerings; all their evils will be completely extinguished, of this there is no doubt—except for those who are currently experiencing the retribution of extremely heavy karmic offenses from the past.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! It is inconceivable!

I now wish to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha; however, those sentient beings there are corrupt and evil, envious, lacking a heart of compassion, ignorant of repaying kindness, their speech always coarse and vulgar, and they frequently practice false views. Might they not cause me distress? As I am now going there, will it perhaps be of no benefit?”
The Buddha said, “Good son! Such a thing does not exist.
Who could inflict harm upon one who has accomplished the four immeasurable minds? Even if there were hundreds of thousands of māras and their retinues, they would be unable to create any obstacle.”
"Good son! Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, you have constantly practiced the four immeasurable minds;
do not be afraid, good son!"
I possess a dhāraṇī born from the four immeasurables and the Brahma-conduct, which can extinguish all evils, even including bad dreams; you should receive and uphold this dhāraṇī.

At that time, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas spoke these words with one voice:

“We now thirst with longing to see the Great Virtuous World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage, make offerings, revere, and praise him; we also wish to observe that great assembly and hear the *Sūryagarbha-dharmaparyāya*, the Chapter on the Blazing Destruction of the Dragon Realm, for the sake of eliminating all evil karma of sentient beings. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us permission to go there.”
The Buddha said, “Good sons! You may go as you wish;

you should travel to that land with a single-minded focus. Each of you should transform yourselves into universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven treasures and a full thousand sons, adorning your bodies according to the dharma of a universal monarch.”

Immediately, eighty million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, together with the bodhisattva Gaganagañja, respectfully surrounded the Buddha Guṇakusumagarbha; after circumambulating him three times, they ascended into the void.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas each manifested themselves as the bodies of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), endowed with the seven treasures and a full thousand sons, and equipped with elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—all arrayed in various ornaments according to the dharma of a universal monarch. Departing from there, they reached the Sahā world in a single thought-instant. They scattered powdered Jambūnada gold over the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of śrāvakas in the Sahā world; thus, this powdered gold completely filled the entire Sahā world.

Furthermore, he scattered powdered nāga-candana sandalwood; he also scattered pearls; he also scattered pearl necklaces and golden ornaments; he also scattered necklaces; he also scattered various kinds of necklaces and various garments; and he also scattered various banners, pennants, and precious parasols.
All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were there for the purpose of making offerings to Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having made these offerings, that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas respectfully surrounded and circumambulated the Sahā world three times to the right.
Having completed the circumambulation, they came to this Jambudvīpa, to the land of Magadha, to where the Buddha Śākyamuni was.
Having arrived, they paid respectful homage, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, King Bimbisāra beheld for the first time immeasurable asaṃkhyeya numbers of Brahmā devas, Śakra devas, Nārāyaṇa devas, and universal monarchs (cakravartin) of the four continents.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sūryagatigarbha scattered *campaka* flower garlands over Śākyamuni Buddha and praised him,
saying: "Most supreme among all who possess feet, Bestowing great radiance upon those with evil views,
Able to expound the supramundane practice of equality, Granting the Dharma-seal to those who walk the right path."
He has crushed the venomous dragon and the four Māras; the Buddha is supreme in liberating the world from afflictions.
He raises the firm banner of the Dharma and bestows liberation; with the great torch of the Dharma, he extinguishes all darkness.
By drawing near to virtuous friends, he cultivates and accumulates meditative concentration; out of compassion for sentient beings, he proclaims the field of merit.
The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is extremely difficult to encounter; so too are a human body and faith difficult to find.
Though one has obtained a human body, a virtuous friend is rare; those who obtain such a friend destroy their afflictions.
Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and afflictions; may they swiftly be able to extinguish the web of these afflictions.
Sentient beings are submerged in the river of afflictions; the Buddha, like a great ship, can rescue them.
We, the emissaries of the Buddhas, proclaim our desire, and we rejoice in the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sūryagatigarbha addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the east, beyond buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Anantaguṇa. There, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Campakapuṣpavarṇa currently dwells, teaching the Dharma.”
That Buddha-Tathāgata has sent me to deliver this message and to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you without many troubles?"
Are your disciples and retinue physically strong and at ease?
Are they always secure and peaceful?
Do they delight in hearing the Dharma?
"Have you heard what the Buddha has taught? Do you practice according to the instructions?
Do you delight in the *āraṇya*?
Thus did the World-Honored One, having here destroyed the hosts of Māras and alone transcended all sages, turn the unimpeded, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma.

However, because these sentient beings of the five turbidities have not yet exhausted their obstacles and do not believe in or accept the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma, for their sake, that Buddha, whose color is like the *campaka* flower, preached this *dhāraṇī* called the "Dhāraṇī of Accordance with the Four Truths" (*catur-āryasatya-anuloma-kṣānti-dhāraṇī*), which belongs to the chapter on the "Blazing Realm of the Dragon's Destruction of the Sun-Treasury Dharma Practice" and exhausts the evil karma of all sentient beings. This *dhāraṇī* possesses great power and great benefit; it can exhaust all desire and greed for the realms of form and formlessness, as well as all pride, overweening pride, and the conceit of self.

As explained above, this *dhāraṇī* of the compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) regarding the Four Noble Truths can destroy all the power of the Māras; it can cause the hearts of the devas to rejoice; it can cause the asuras and garuḍas to feel great terror; it can cause the kiṃnaras to feel joy; it can cause the mahoragas to feel fear; it can defeat the heretics; and it can grant contentment to the kṣatriyas.

It can lead Brahmins to enter the Buddha-dharma; it can cause Vaiśyas to give rise to great faith; it can cause Śūdras to give rise to a heart of joy; it can cause women to be free from all lustful desires; it can cause wise people to give rise to a heart of joy; and it can cause those who practice seated meditation to delight in the āraṇya.
It can avert all manner of evil events, as well as various conflicts, famines, epidemics, and untimely deaths;
it can eliminate external enemies, unseasonable cold and heat, malignant winds and rains, wild beasts, torrential floods, and all harsh, bitter, parched, and astringent unpleasant tactile sensations;
it can establish the banner of the Dharma and bring forth the light of the Buddha-dharma, causing the Mother of the Dharma to abide for long and the lineage of the Buddhas to remain undying.

It can comfort sentient beings wandering in the stream of birth and death; it can give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); it can awaken the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); it can tear asunder the entire mass of the darkness of ignorance; it can lay down the burden of all suffering; and it can dry up the ocean of all suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sūryagatigarbha spoke the following dhāraṇī of the compliant patience regarding the Four Noble Truths:
“Namasthā | Vaye vayabale pare ||”

For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the Tathāgata has performed no other activity than expounding the meaning of this dhāraṇī; among all devas and humans, there is none who can understand it, and even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages cannot know it, with the sole exception of the Buddhas.

This dhāraṇī is thus profound and thus possesses great power; it can bestow great benefit, swiftly fulfill unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and furthermore fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion to transform and guide sentient beings.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana!
You should receive, uphold, recite, and chant this dhāraṇī, and explain it extensively for others within the great assembly.

Those who hear this dhāraṇī shall obtain great benefit; those beings with much anger who would otherwise have to undergo evil retribution in future lives will have all such [karmic seeds] extinguished and shall not experience the fruit of their retribution. They will be able to recognize the many faults and evils of birth and death, cultivate great roots of goodness, and attain great merit and virtue. By drawing near to, supporting, and making offerings to great spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they will swiftly attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Maudgalyāyana!
This dhāraṇī can kindle the lamp of the Dharma and perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem.
*Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle 37.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of the Sui Dynasty. Part Four:
The Section on the Sun-Treasury; Chapter Four: The Chapter on Samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the four emissary bodhisattvas and their retinues of bodhisattvas:
"Sons of good family!

If you wish to dwell in this Sahā world, each of you may, according to your own inclination, enter the samādhi-dhāraṇī of the roots of goodness and merit cultivated through your respective practices, as well as the samāpatti and samādhi."

Then the four bodhisattvas and their retinues each entered meditative absorption according to their own inclination. Having entered dhyāna-concentration, light issued from their bodies; some bodhisattvas’ light was like that of a great torch, while others’ light was even like that of hundreds of thousands of millions of suns and moons.
At that time, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, thought to himself:
"I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about a certain matter; because of this, the Tathāgata may perhaps analyze and explain in detail the words and meanings of the four dhāraṇīs of the Tathāgata."

If the Tathāgata were to speak, and the multitudes of the ten directions within this Sahā world were to hear it, they would destroy the mind of doubt’s net and attain great illumination regarding all dharmas, swiftly attaining the four fruits: those who have not yet attained the fruit of Srotāpanna will swiftly attain Srotāpanna; those who have not yet attained Sakṛdāgāmin will attain Sakṛdāgāmin; those who have not yet attained Anāgāmin will attain Anāgāmin; and those who have not yet attained Arhatship will attain Arhatship.
"Having transcended the three evil realms, they shall obtain bodies among gods and humans, and all shall attain purely wholesome dharmas.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and stood there in silence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"Do you not wish to inquire about the meaning from me?
Kauṇḍinya replied to the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I truly wish to ask; may the Buddha grant me permission to speak according to my intention."
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it extensively so as to gladden your heart.
When all the devas and humans heard these words, they were filled with joy.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, there are two kinds [of beings], namely craving and the *pudgala* (person), who wander through birth and death.”
What is meant by "craving"?
What is meant by a "person" (pudgala)?
For what reason did the Tathāgata say that these two types of beings wander in saṃsāra?
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
“Excellent, excellent! It is well that you have asked this question.”

Kauṇḍinya! You have asked this question out of compassion for all sentient beings; you have asked this question because you wish to bring happiness to all sentient beings. Such a question is one that asks at the proper time.
"Kauṇḍinya! Listen with a focused and attentive mind; I shall now speak. Kauṇḍinya replied:
"So it is, so it is. As the Buddha has spoken, I shall receive and uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"There are three kinds of craving: namely, craving for sensual desire, craving for form, and craving for the formless;
furthermore, there are another three kinds: namely, craving for existence, craving for non-existence, and craving for the Dharma."
“Kauṇḍinya! What is the craving for desire?
‘Desire’ refers to heedlessness; with heedlessness as a condition, there arises greedy contact; with contact as a condition, there arises the perception of pleasure.”

Sentient beings delight in and become attached to such phenomena as these; their desire-mind is stirred up and consumed like being burned by fire. Due to the conditions of desire, they take pleasure in committing the ten unwholesome actions and abandon the ten wholesome ones.
By these causes and conditions, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and are born among the impoverished yakṣas.

Due to the causes and conditions of desire, they undergo bodies composed of the five aggregates within the cycle of birth and death, experiencing all manner of sufferings; yet, even while undergoing such suffering, they do not give rise to fear.
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, they take no pleasure in cultivating goodness; thus, within the cycle of saṃsāra, it is difficult for them to obtain a human body.

Even if they do obtain a human body, due to the causes and conditions of desire, their bodies and speech are impure, and they commit immeasurable grave evil karmas, even up to the five ānantarya crimes.
Because of these causes and conditions, they further undergo great and heavy suffering within the cycle of birth and death and the three evil realms.

All experiences of suffering stem from the mind of desire; the accumulation of the causes and conditions of desire is like a dung-eating pig that is bound and fettered, heading toward the three evil realms to undergo all manner of afflictions and distress.
Therefore, for the sake of severing craving and desire, the Tathāgata proclaims the True Dharma and censures the nature of desire.

If there are sentient beings who, having heard such censure of desire, are able to contemplate all desires as they truly are—impure like the fruit of a poisonous tree, like a great mass of fire, like a jar filled with poison, like a bottle full of excrement, like a sharp blade or a thief, like a Caṇḍāla wearing a *kaṭhina* robe, like a red-hot iron ball, like a great rain of hail, like a malevolent *vairambha* wind, like a venomous serpent, like a treacherous wild marsh, like the island of Rākṣasas, like Vadhaka-dūtas, like various heaps of refuse, or like a *śītavana* cemetery—such persons, thus knowing the faults and afflictions of desire, will give rise to great fear toward the objects of desire, and their bodies will tremble violently.

Loving the Dharma, delighting in the Dharma, and training in the Dharma, they shave their hair and beard and don the dharma-robes; seeking the True Dharma and seeking mastery over the Dharma, they give rise to a pure mind within the True Dharma and practice the rescue and salvation of beings through the path of the Dharma.
One who possesses such joy will attain right mindfulness at the time of death.

Because they recollect the Dharma, because they delight in the flavor of the Dharma, and because they recollect the fruit of the Dharma, they see the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the essentials of the Dharma and transforming sentient beings amidst great assemblies. Having heard the Dharma, they attain a heart of joy; because their hearts are joyful, they repeatedly behold the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas.

After this person dies, they will leave behind the three evil realms and be reborn in a Buddha-field, constantly dwelling and associating with virtuous people. They will be able to practice generosity, patience, and diligence, delighting in meditative concentration; they will cultivate the five supernormal powers and take pleasure in the path to Nirvana. With great compassion, they will teach and transform sentient beings, attaining the body of merit adorned with the necklaces of all Buddhas, wherein all past afflictions and habitual tendencies are completely extinguished.

Those sentient beings attain such adornment of body and mind; it is like a fragrant casket containing various garments, all of which become fragrant, yet the weight of those perfumes and flowers is not increased, nor is their color diminished.

"In this way, Kauṇḍinya! If there are sentient beings who, through the causal conditions of delighting in the Dharma, are able to see the Buddhas at the time of their death; and by virtue of seeing the Buddhas, they attain a heart of joy; and because their hearts are joyful, they are reborn in a Buddha-field where they share in the activities of virtuous beings—likewise, they increase their own roots of goodness for themselves, obtain various necklaces and ornaments to adorn their body and mind, and before long attain the awakening of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet their goodness does not diminish."

"Therefore, Kauṇḍinya! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who perceive their own benefit, perceive the benefit of others, and perceive the benefit of both, they should always draw near to virtuous friends and study the teachings of virtuous friends; they should constantly hear from virtuous friends the various faults and afflictions of the dharma of desire, as rebuked by them."
Having heard this, they shall proceed until they attain the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Kauṇḍinya! Those who are called 'virtuous friends' are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats."
Furthermore, the virtuous friend is none other than myself.

Why is this? Having now appeared in the world out of compassion for sentient beings, I desire to sever all their suffering and afflictions and am able to explain all the faults and perils of sensual desires; therefore, the great assembly should accept my words.
I do not speak falsely, but always speak words of truth; I do not speak meaningless words nor harsh words, but speak with a heart of compassion.

I shall now proclaim the faults and evils of all sensual desires; you should receive and uphold them with a single mind. Having received and upheld them, you will swiftly attain liberation from the three evil realms, and even go on to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the entire assembly gathered from throughout the great trichiliocosm of the Sahā world raised their voices in unison, saying:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim the faults of desire; having heard it, we shall receive and uphold it with a sincere heart, just as the Buddha has taught."
The Buddha said:
“Kauṇḍinya! Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
There are four causes and conditions by which sentient beings give rise to desire. What are these four? They are:
craving for form—craving for things such as long or short, red or white; and so forth.
Craving for touch;
craving for pleasure—namely, pleasure in song and dance;
and craving for various ornaments, necklaces, garments, and the like.
What is craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*)?
"Form" refers to the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which arise and perish without ceasing, being without self (*anātman*) and without sentient beings (*niḥsattva*).

These four great elements are without self and without sentient beings; yet all ordinary people, through the inversion of ignorance (*avidyā-viparyāsa*), give rise to discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) regarding form, [discriminating]: "This is male," "This is female," "This is beautiful," "This is ugly," "This is pleasant," or "This is unpleasant. The fire of desire enters their hearts as if they were possessed by a demon; when a man sees a woman's body, he grasps at its characteristics and becomes attached to its long or short, black or white features.
For these reasons, they cause unarisen desire to arise and already arisen desire to increase.

As such a person thus contemplates desire, it becomes ever more abundant and they never abandon it; all their roots of goodness diminish, they no longer take delight in spiritual friends, they cannot properly guard the actions of body, speech, and mind, they become united with all manner of transgressions, and they fail to see the faults and perils inherent in all desires.
Because they do not see [the truth], at the end of their lives they immediately enter the three evil realms—whether in hell, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost.
Within those evil realms, they undergo various great sufferings for immeasurable lifetimes; all this is due to craving, for the causes and conditions of craving cause desire to increase.

"Any wise person who contemplates the form of a woman should bring to mind the perception of impurity; they do not dwell on the hair, fur, skin, flesh, sinews, or blood of the woman's body, but contemplate only the white bones with single-minded focus and without distraction. As it is with the body of a woman, so it is with the body of a man;
as it is when seeing a body nearby, so it is with one at a distance;
as it is with another's body, so it is with one's own."
One contemplates only the white bones and does not contemplate the hair, fur, skin, flesh, sinews, or blood.

Having contemplated thus, one repeatedly reflects upon it; if the mind constantly maintains this mindfulness without forgetting, this is called the "Dharma-gate of the Initial Severance of Desire," which is the practice of the mind following the path.

That person further contemplates the samāpatti within those bones, abiding at a point between the eyebrows the size of a jujube fruit; having contemplated thus, they repeatedly reflect until the mind remains steady without loss.

At that time, that person’s mind attains tranquility; the breath neither issues forth nor enters within; one perceives no evil signs and perceives no evil events; one finds no pleasure in them, does not dwell upon them, and does not even take a single dharma as an object of focus. This is what is called *śamatha*, and it is called the tranquility of the mind.
This is called the second dharma-gate for severing desire within the path conducive to the afflictions.
What is physical tranquility?
Because this person maintains such mindfulness, they are able to bring the inhalation and exhalation within the body to a state of concentration, where there is neither entering nor exiting.

That wise person, Parāśabuddha, finds joy in the tranquility of body and mind; because he contemplates in this way, his mind swiftly accords with śamatha. This is called the third dharma-gate of the path for severing afflictions by taking tranquility as its object of focus.

This person further contemplates the area at the crown of the skull, about the size of a small jujube fruit; having contemplated this repeatedly, they see that its interior is empty. Contemplating emptiness in this way again and again, they see that skull bone as being like a grain of sand, and thus, for the second and third time, they see it as fragments of bone.

By means of this method, one visualizes all skull bones as being like fine dust; seeing those bone fragments blown about by the wind, one likewise visualizes all the skeletal remains of the body as entirely reduced to dust and blown away by the wind.

In this way, from not seeing the bones of the body up until seeing empty space, within that state, the body and mind are *prasarabuddhi*. This is called the fourth dharma-gate of the path for severing afflictions through the tranquilizing of objective conditions (*ālambana*) in accordance with *śamatha*.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the characteristic of space a conditioned characteristic?”
The Buddha said, "So it is,
son of good family!"
"The characteristic of space is a conditioned characteristic.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If the characteristic of space were conditioned, would it be its own characteristic or another’s characteristic?
The Buddha said, “Kauṇḍinya!”
If one can observe all dharma-realms and the realm of conditioned phenomena, this is called their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why is this?
If one can observe the quiescence of form (*rūpa*), it should be known that such a person is able to see the Tathāgata.

Why is this? If a person contemplates bones and sees them as fragments blown about by the wind, having seen this, they are able to deeply observe the true nature of form (*rūpa*). At that time, this person sees all forms as entirely empty and quiescent, even to the point of not perceiving any characteristics (*nimitta*), seeing only empty space and contemplating only empty space, repeatedly practicing upon that empty space.
He saw that all forms in the ten directions were entirely empty, like pure lapis lazuli.
Within them, he further beheld immeasurable Buddhas; this was likewise the case throughout the ten directions.

Having beheld the Buddha’s body, they further saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; indeed, they saw the form-bodies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, complete and perfect, their radiant light perfectly circular like a nyagrodha tree.
If that person had previously practiced the path to nirvana and possessed roots of goodness, they would immediately think:
"I shall ask the Buddha: 'By whom was this space created?'"
"How long will it be before they are extinguished?
Having had this thought, he immediately questioned the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata then proclaimed for him:
"Furthermore, that which is called 'space' exists only as a name; there is no creator of it, so what could possibly be extinguished?

To speak of space means it is devoid of applied and sustained thought, without substance and without number, without characteristics, and without arising or ceasing. The marks of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are likewise unobtainable; both the one who conceives and the object conceived are entirely non-existent."
Having realized this, he was completely liberated from all bonds of perception and immediately attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin, being able to sever all hearts of craving and desire.
"There remains only the fetter of craving for the form realm, the fetter of craving for the formless realm, as well as restlessness, conceit, and various forms of ignorance.
At that time, having seen the Buddha’s body, that person thinks:
'I shall now know the dimensions—the length, height, breadth, and width—of the Tathāgata’s body.'"
Having formed this thought, he saw Tathāgatas everywhere throughout the empty space of the ten directions in the place where he was.

At that time, if that person wished to see a small number, he would immediately see a small number; if he wished to see many according to his vision, he would see many; and it was likewise for immeasurable and boundless numbers.
"Furthermore, that person again thinks:
'From where do these Buddhas come?
Then he further thinks:"
"Thus, the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
At that time, having seen that the Buddhas have no coming or going, the person further reflects:

"The body and mind that experience the three realms are merely provisional and false. For this reason, according to my contemplation and observation, if I wish to see much, I see much; if I wish to see little, I see little. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are none other than my own mind."

Why is this? Because the Buddha is created by one's own mind and seen by one's own mind; the mind is my body, and the body is empty space. It is because of my *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) that I see immeasurable and boundless Buddhas. I see the Buddhas and know the Buddhas through the awakened mind; it is not that a mind knows another mind, nor that a mind sees another mind. Those who perceive the characteristics of the mind cannot sever them.

I contemplate that the nature of the dharma-realm is without solidity or reality, for it arises in accordance with thought; therefore, all existing natures and characteristics, as well as the mind’s conceptualization and observation, are themselves empty space, and the nature of empty space is likewise non-existent.
"If one can perceive that emptiness in this way, they have already awakened the bodhicitta in the past.
Through the causal conditions of that person’s cultivation of samādhi, all Buddhas will immediately appear before them."
If such a person gives rise to the mind seeking the state of a śrāvaka, they will immediately attain all signless samādhis.

Having cultivated these, they further attain a mind of unattached, pure wisdom that is far removed from ignorance, and they also obtain the patience that accords with emptiness; before long, they shall attain the true realization of the four fruits.

If that person perceives emptiness as being emptiness itself, at that moment they attain tranquility of body and mind; having attained such tranquility, this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.

Once one has entered this gate, it is not difficult to attain the fruit of arhatship; this is called the fifth true dharma-gate for practicing emptiness and quiescence, severing all objects of attachment, and eliminating afflictions.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, among the great assembly, nine hundred and ninety billion devas and humans attained the *śamatha* conforming patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand people attained the emptiness conforming patience; likewise, sixty thousand devas and humans attained the liberation dharma-gate of the emptiness samādhi; twenty thousand sentient beings all attained the Buddhas’ Presence Samādhi (*pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi*); immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*; and eight million four hundred thousand bhikṣus attained the path free from outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"If there is a person who observes their own skull, yet the mind does not remain steady or find delight therein, this person is not yet tamed;
being untamed, they are likewise unable to attain liberation."

At that time, that person should go once more to the śītavana (cemetery) to observe the dead; they may see corpses that are livid and bloated, smeared with blood, or see them with pus flowing and soaking everywhere, the skin and flesh rotting away while tendons and veins remain intertwined, as birds and beasts come and go, vying with one another to devour them.
Alternatively, one may see white bones, their color like that of a conch shell, with skulls and jaws displaced and hands and feet scattered.
Having seen this sign, one should carefully examine the mind to discern where it finds pleasure and dwells.

Having known this, one should immediately contemplate it with constant mindfulness and never abandon it: all external forms are subject to such decay; considering one's own body, it too must be thus—from the initial stages of livid discoloration, foul odors, and putridity, until finally reaching the state of bleached bones, fragmented and dissolving away.

Keep the mind constantly focused and do not allow it to be distracted by other conditions. Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, diligently cultivate the practice of contemplation so that it becomes smooth and flowing. Let it continue uninterruptedly day and night without allowing it to wander or disperse. Whether eyes are closed or open, always keep the visualization clear and distinct. Starting from small objects and proceeding to larger ones, penetrate both the internal and external until it reaches such a state that even mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, forests, humans, animals, and all such things are all perceived as skeletal forms; treat them in this same manner.

In all four modes of conduct, one constantly contemplates the skeleton and other such phenomena of one's own body, never abandoning them; thus the mind abides immovable like a mountain, always concentrated and undisturbed within a single object, fully perfecting the mindfulness of impurity and so forth.

"At that time, having performed this contemplation within this body, until the end of his life he does not give rise to defiled thoughts; he is able to be free from lust in the present, though not yet in future lives."
"If this person attains the *Ākāśānugata-dhāraṇī*, they will then be able to contemplate the bones as having the appearance of being dispersed.
Having thought thus, he causes winds to arise simultaneously from all four directions to blow upon this skeletal body, grinding and scattering it entirely until it becomes like fine dust.

In this way, once one's own body has been reduced to dust through the causal conditions of wind, all forms and the entire great earth likewise scatter like fine particles through the power of the causal conditions of wind.
Having done this, the body and all things follow the wind; the dust flies up and disperses until nothing remains to be seen, just like empty space, free from all verbal expression.

Having observed in this way, one attains the characteristic of space and perceives all objects as being like blue lapis lazuli; by practicing this repeatedly, one prevents such thoughts from wandering or dispersing.
Having observed in this way, one further observes the void as yellow, fixing the mind upon it through recollection and visualization, thereby also achieving a state of non-dispersed attention.
Having observed in this way, one further observes the color red and contemplates the color red.
Having contemplated the red color, one further forms the mental image of white and contemplates the white color.
Having contemplated the white color, one further contemplates the purple color.
Once the purple color is established, one contemplates the crystal color.
In the midst of space, he formed this thought:
"May these myriad phenomena—the forms, the earth, and all such things—all appear as blue and crystal-colored, so that they do not disperse."

Having performed this contemplation, one next forms the perception of water; one sees all colors, such as blue and crystal, as being entirely water, with no other perceptions remaining, except that one sees the great earth for only about the thickness of four fingers, while everything else is water.
Having seen that the ground was four finger-widths deep and remained without increase or decrease, he further thought:
"I shall now move this great earth with my toe, causing it to shake and turn according to my will for as long or as briefly as I desire."

If he wishes to cause even a small portion to move, it moves accordingly as he intends; furthermore, he can cause all mountains, the great earth, the great oceans, and the rivers to move in unison, producing a great sound whose resonance reaches far and is heard in other directions.

Furthermore, he observes that the various waters possess diverse colors; there are blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), red lotuses (padma), and white water lilies (puṇḍarīka)—all such various flowers appear to him according to his thoughts.
Furthermore, one contemplates empty space as entirely becoming earth, and upon that ground, one walks, stands, sits, lies down, looks up, looks down, bends, and stretches.

One further contemplates all earth, stones, and mountains as being of various colors, their forms fine and soft like *tūla* cotton; upon those mountains, one turns back and forth, comes and goes, paces, and sits in meditation.

Having performed such various external observations at that time, he completely relinquishes them and again withdraws his mindfulness. He further observes his own body, forming the perception of it being light and subtle, cultivating this practice even more until it is perfected, like cotton-wool drifting and scattering with the wind.

Having performed this contemplation, they walk, stand, sit, and lie down in mid-air; these persons further enter the fire-light samādhi, and their bodies manifest various wondrous colors and radiances—blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal.

Furthermore, he enters the *jvālāmukha* (Flaming Mouth) samādhi, whereby water and fire issue forth alternately from his upper and lower body; even within the earth, he manifests appearing and disappearing as if a bird in the sky, free from all obstructions. Regarding the sun and moon, whose majestic power possesses great radiance, he is able to touch them with his hand without giving rise to fear or alarm.
Furthermore, having ascended from his body as far as the Brahma Heaven and manifested such supernatural transformations, he again formed this thought according to his inclination:
"Within my body, there may be blue, yellow, red, or white; or perhaps purple and crystal are seen."
Again, he formed this thought:
"How may I come to see all the Buddhas, beholding them in every direction?

At that time, if that person wishes to see them on a small scale, they appear according to his recollection; if he wishes to see them on a large scale, they likewise appear according to his recollection, even filling and pervading the entirety of space.
Again, he reflects:
"These various Buddhas come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are created solely by my own mind. Within the three realms, these causes and conditions of the body are created solely by the mind."
Following my contemplation and reflection, I wish to see much when there is much desire, and to see little when there is little desire.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are precisely my own mind. Why is this?

Because one sees according to the mind, the mind is itself my body, which is identical to empty space. Through contemplation and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*), I see immeasurable Buddhas; by means of this awakened mind, I see the Buddhas and know the Buddhas. Yet the mind does not see the mind, and the mind does not know the mind. I observe that the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is without solidity; all phenomena arise from the causes and conditions of contemplation and observation.

Therefore, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is identical to space, and the nature of space is likewise empty. Because of this mind, I perceive various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—as well as all mixed colors and space. Having manifested various supernatural transformations, that which is seen is like the wind, lacking any reality; it is merely the deluded mind that relies upon form.
"This is what is called the dhāraṇī of the four truths in common with ordinary persons.
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya!"
What is called the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Truths that is not shared with ordinary worldlings?
If there is someone who can form this thought:
"This space cannot be grasped; it is devoid of applied and sustained thought and cannot be described. The mind is likewise like space—ungraspable and indescribable."

These two kinds of things are entirely false, causing sorrow, distress, and agitation; they are like a burning fire, deceptive and contentious. I now renounce all such thoughts, distractions, perceptions, and reflections regarding emptiness, form, and so forth.

"Having thus abandoned all false conceptualizations and discursive thoughts regarding space, form, and so forth, the mind no longer arises; because it is free from all recollections, the mind attains stillness, and having attained stillness, it does not arise again."

Why is this? Because when the objects of the mind cease, the mind itself ceases; physical and mental joy are all relinquished. Through this relinquishment, the body attains tranquility; by abandoning applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the mouth leaves off speech, and the mind rests on a single object as one cultivates the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

At that time, for one day and one night, this person enters such a samādhi of quiescent extinction; with mastery over his will, he remains within this samādhi for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, enduring it without distraction.
Arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one relinquishes all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) along with one's lifespan and enters *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the first gate of liberation: the *dhāraṇī* of compliance with the Four Truths, which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and uncommon to ordinary beings.
The Buddha again addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"What is called the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Truths shared by ordinary persons?
If there is anyone who can form such a thought as this:"

"Following my investigation and contemplation, I contemplate such form as 'this is me,' and my mind is identical to form while form is identical to my mind; or, if I am detached from all marks of form, I contemplate the mark of empty space."
At that time, this person cultivates the mark of space and immediately enters the samādhi of the immeasurable sphere of space.
This is called the meaning of the dhāraṇī that accords with the Four Truths for ordinary persons.
"If there is someone who can think thus:
'Form is itself emptiness; because this form is empty by reason of its conditions, I am able to see space.'"
What is the characteristic of the sphere that is space?
The nature of space is called non-obstruction; it is the dwelling place of wind.

Such wind is a characteristic of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); my form (*rūpa*) is likewise comprised of the four great elements. These two phenomena are without distinction, and the mind is also like this, just like space.
Again, he formed this thought:
"What is the substance of these four great elements?
The nature of all dharmas is inherently empty and quiescent; the natures of self and other are likewise all empty and quiescent."
"Indeed, empty space is that which possesses nothing; it is neither born nor extinguished, having no location and no abode.
When he contemplates in this way, he fixes his mindfulness upon the Buddhas.
Having fixed his mindfulness, he sees immeasurable Buddhas within empty space. With single-minded recollection, he attains the fruit of Anāgāmin.
This is called the second liberation gate, the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Noble Truths that is not shared with ordinary beings.
Furthermore, the practitioner forms this thought:
"What kind of object has the characteristic of space?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called the mark of self?
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"That which is called space is precisely the self; that which is pure self is precisely my own mind."
"The self is formless, like space which is boundless; the self is also thus.
This is called the *dhāraṇī* of reality shared with ordinary persons.
If there is one who can contemplate that all phenomena are empty and devoid of self or what belongs to a self—
whereas that which is called the "sphere of emptiness" means that there is no self in form and no self in sensation—

if they contemplate the Tathāgata as being the self, and having seen the Buddha, they attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, or Anāgāmin, and eventually, with the exhaustion of all out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas, attain the fruit of Arhatship.
This is called the third liberation door, the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Truths that is not shared by ordinary persons.
Furthermore, if a practitioner contemplates the self as pure and untainted, this is the station of emptiness, and emptiness is my own mind.
If one can forever sever all afflictions, this is the pure mind; if one can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, this is called the pure mind.
By training in this manner, one can attain the fruit of srotāpanna and even realize the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the fourth liberation gate of the *dhāraṇī* for acceding to the Four Truths, which is not shared with ordinary beings.

Furthermore, if a practitioner wishes to contemplate the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), they are immediately conceptualizing marks; conceptualizing marks is itself the mark of aversion (*dveṣa-lakṣaṇa*); and the mark of aversion is the mark of birth and death (*saṃsāra-lakṣaṇa*).
"I now contemplate the emptiness of the characteristics of the mind in order to sever the characteristics of birth and death.
This is called the *dhāraṇī* of the Four Truths in accordance with the common worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

If a practitioner contemplates the self as being quiescent, yet has not yet severed discursive thought (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra), they should contemplate the self and what belongs to the self (ātman and ātmīya) as they would contemplate empty space; for that which is "self" and "what belongs to the self" is precisely suffering.

That from which suffering arises is called the origin; that such suffering and its origin are subject to cessation is called extinction; the contemplation of suffering, its origin, and its cessation is called the path. By this, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and even attains the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the fifth liberation gate, the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Truths that is not shared with ordinary beings.
Furthermore, the practitioner forms this thought:
"For what reason?"
I have now observed this characteristic of space; for that which is space is indeed myself.
If I were to move beyond the contemplation of space, I would next observe the sphere of consciousness.
"Just as the contemplation of space is, so too is the contemplation of consciousness; just as the sphere of space is immeasurable and boundless, so too is consciousness immeasurable and boundless.
This is called the dhāraṇī of the four truths in accordance with the stream [of practice], shared with ordinary worldlings.

If a practitioner contemplates consciousness, it is called perception and is also called vitarka and vicāra. Consciousness itself is suffering; knowing the source from which suffering arises is called origination; that suffering and its origination can be severed is called cessation; and contemplating suffering, origination, and cessation is called the path. By this, one attains the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.
This is called the sixth liberation gate, the *dhāraṇī* of compliance with the Four Truths that is not shared with ordinary persons.

Furthermore, if the practitioner contemplates the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) as being identical to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), like a thorn piercing the body, like a wound, or like a disease—just as I previously distanced myself from the sphere of infinite space, and having distanced myself from the sphere of infinite space, I also distanced myself from the sphere of consciousness—and having distanced myself from the sphere of consciousness, I cultivated the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

At that time, having attained the state of non-conception, this person no longer takes any dharma as an object and immediately dwells in the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This is called the meditative attainment shared with ordinary worldlings.

If one contemplates the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) as being a state of festering wounds and affliction—like a disease, like an abscess—one distances oneself from it and contemplates the characteristics of consciousness.
Next, one contemplates the non-conceptual (*asaṃjñin*); that which is called "non-conceptual" is precisely the absence of self (*anātman*), the absence of the notions of "self" and "mine" (*ātmiya*).
One contemplates the purity of Great Parinirvāṇa.
While performing this contemplation, one immediately attains the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and even the fruit of Arhatship.
This is called the seventh liberation door, the dhāraṇī of compliance with the Four Truths that is not shared with ordinary beings.

Furthermore, if a practitioner is able to contemplate the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*), this is itself a subtle perception; just as I am detached from this sphere of non-perception, so too is the contemplation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This is called the "dhāraṇī of reality shared with ordinary persons.
If one contemplates the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as being great suffering, this state can be severed and liberation attained.
When one contemplates in this manner, that person immediately attains the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin, up to and including the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the eighth liberation gate, the *dhāraṇī* for acceding to the Four Truths, which is not shared with ordinary worldlings. "Kauṇḍinya!

This *dhāraṇī* possesses such inconceivable and manifold benefits; it can further sever all craving for sense-desires, all craving for form, and all craving for the formless. It causes one to leave the stage of an ordinary worldling and attain the Dharma of a noble one, forever cutting off all causes for the three evil realms, so that in future lives one shall no longer undergo rebirth as a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost. This is called the *dhāraṇī* for acceding to the Four Truths."
"You should now know that this is the message sent by the Tathāgata Campakapuṣpavarṇa and brought by the Bodhisattva Sūryagatigarbha.
Because I am currently here preaching the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, that Buddha has sent this message to me."

This dhāraṇī can sever all fetters and afflictions; it can also forever exhaust all resentment, all forms of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and all jealousy. It can repel all worldly domestic affairs and all frivolous merriment. It can sever all views of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), all views of doubt, and the *brahmadatta-sparśa*. It can sever all views of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), views of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), views of a life-principle (*jīvita-dṛṣṭi*), views of *pudgala*, views of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), views of agency (*kartṛ-dṛṣṭi*), views of knowledge (*jñātṛ-dṛṣṭi*), and all views regarding form (*rūpa-dṛṣṭi*), up to and including views regarding contact (*sparśa-dṛṣṭi*), views regarding birth (*jāti-dṛṣṭi*), and views regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta-dṛṣṭi*). It can sever all such views as these.
It is able to know all five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements;
it can cause those who receive it to attain the bliss of nirvana; it can destroy the various māras and subdue evil nāgas;
it can cause all devas and yakṣas to give rise to joy; and it can terrify asuras, garuḍas, and kinnaras.
Naras and mahoragas, you are able to destroy all evil and heterodox outsiders;
you are able to gladden all kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras; you are able to cause women of great greed to contemplate few desires;
you are able to cause those of much learning to give rise to joy; you are able to...
The practitioner of seated meditation delights in the *āraṇya*, for it can cure all grave and evil illnesses;
it can ward off all strife, famine, pestilence, misfortune, and untimely deaths;
and it can eliminate external enemies, as well as adverse winds, rains, floods, and rivers, and unseasonable cold and heat, along with various bitter, pungent, coarse, and harsh unpleasant tastes.

They can illuminate the Mother of Dharma and establish the banner of the Dharma; they succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall never be severed; they can comfort sentient beings terrified by the cycle of birth and death, bringing them joy; they can give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion and realize the knowledge of non-arising; they can rend ignorance and shatter the mass of all darkness; and they can cast off the burden of suffering and enter into nirvana.

When the Buddha taught this dhāraṇī of patience that accords with the Four Noble Truths, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes of devas and humans became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
ninety-six billion nayutas of sentient beings abandoned all afflictions and attained liberation of mind;
and eight billion hundred-thousand nayutas of sentient beings attained this dhāraṇī that accords with the Four Noble Truths.
Immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya sentient beings resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and likewise attained the path of non-retrogression;
forty-two thousand sentient beings attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, all praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

O Unsurpassed World-Honored One! Your speech and voice are subtle and wondrous, inconceivable; they are most supreme, immeasurable, and beyond description. For those lacking the eye of wisdom, you bring forth the light of knowledge; for sentient beings burdened by suffering, you are able to remove it; in the ocean of saṃsāra, you act as a great ship and raft.
"Who that hears such an exposition of skillful and unimpeded wisdom would not joyfully resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is called the *Sūryacakṣuḥ-padma-dhāraṇī*?

It is as proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sūryagatigarbha: if a wise person receives, maintains, recites, reads, and transcribes it, they will obtain great benefit; they will not conceive thoughts of pleasure regarding the prison of the triple world, they will attain the liberation door of the signless samādhi, they will attain the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*, and they will attain the twofold extinction of fetters.
