If there are those who hear this, they will be able to attenuate their afflictions; for seven lifetimes they will constantly receive the bodies of humans and devas, and within those human and celestial realms they will attain the Noble Path, remaining unstained by desire and always revered by gods and men alike.
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
“Listen attentively, receive this with care!
Apply yourself with diligence and do not give rise to weariness or indolence.”
Regarding this *Dhāraṇī of the Sun-Eye Lotus* that you have asked about, it is not within the sphere of mental activity of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Why is this?
This dhāraṇī arises from the power of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) that are utterly pure.

Kauṇḍinya! Even if I were to recite this Sūryacakṣu-padma-dhāraṇī for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, I could never reach its end; furthermore, it would cause confusion and distress to arise in the minds of all gods and humans who hear it.
This dhāraṇī can only be spoken by a Buddha and can only be heard by a Buddha. Why is this?

This dhāraṇī possesses immeasurable meanings that are difficult to know and difficult to awaken to, such as the Sūryacakṣuḥ-padma-dhāraṇī; likewise, the Aparasamudra-mūla-dhāraṇī, the Jñānāśraya-dhāraṇī, and the Duḥsvapna-sattva-dhāraṇī of the other three directions are also thus.
Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, we pray that you will proclaim this *śūnyānukūla-dhāraṇī* sent by the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin from the Tathāgata Śailendrarāja in the southern quarter.”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Listen attentively with a sincere mind, and I shall explain it for you."

Kauṇḍinya! If there are sentient beings who, due to the conditions of sensual desire, become intoxicated and deluded, they do not know the place of awakening that is liberation; they wander through birth and death for immeasurable kalpas within the three evil realms, undergoing various intolerable sufferings.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a heart of great compassion, seeing all sentient beings undergoing such immeasurable suffering and affliction, gives rise to great vigor and practices the various paths; having practiced these paths, he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he expounds the path for escaping suffering.

"If there are sentient beings who can listen with a sincere heart and practice in accordance with what has been taught, they shall immediately be liberated from suffering and attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*.
The Buddha addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"What is the desire for contact?"
If there are sentient beings who engage in the act of sexual union, because of that union, contact arises; from contact, pleasure arises; from pleasure, suffering arises.
Due to these conditions of suffering, the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death arise from this.

Kauṇḍinya! Just as four venomous snakes can harm sentient beings through four causes and conditions—namely, the poison of their gaze, the poison of their breath, the poison of their bite, and the poison of their touch.

In this same way, all sentient beings who dwell on desire are likewise so: through the causal condition of seeing, the causal condition of hearing, the causal condition of thinking, and the causal condition of contact—by means of these four conditions—they cause all sentient beings to distance themselves from all roots of goodness and undergo great suffering within the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha said to Kauṇḍinya:
"What is called liberation through the desire for contact?
If that practitioner forms such a thought:"
"By what skillful means can one become free from desire for touch? He further thought:
"If I can contemplate the skeleton to distance myself from greed and desire, this shall be called the most excellent skillful means."

He reflects thus: "Form is that which is composed of the four great elements; that which is composed of the four great elements is impermanent, its nature lacking solidity, subject to destruction and dissolution. Skin, flesh, hair, nails, pus, blood, sinews, and bones—no wise person would ever give rise to perceptions of purity or beauty within this body."

Having performed this contemplation, whether by day or by night, one sees all the ten directions as pure as a conch shell; having seen this, one immediately attains the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in.
The practitioner further reflects in this way:
"This cycle of birth and death is produced by the afflictions; if I joyfully cultivate this perception, I shall be able to sever all afflictions, as well as birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"When a practitioner has thus correctly contemplated all the bones with right awakening, maintaining single-minded right mindfulness without loss or wavering, this is called *śamatha*.
When one proceeds in this sequence to correctly contemplate from the skull down to the foot bones, maintaining single-minded right mindfulness without loss or wavering, this is called *vipaśyanā*."
Again, he thought: "By what skillful means can I break through birth and death?
Reflecting thus, he observed the wind entering and exiting through the union of the mouth and nose; by this skillful means of the wind, he broke the drum of birth and death.

In this way, the practitioner observes their own body bones as if they were pulverized fragments blown about by the wind; within their own body, the perception of bones is completely exhausted, and no bodily form is seen.

When observing in this manner, one distances oneself from the characteristics of the body and gives rise to the characteristic of emptiness; not perceiving internal phenomena, this is called the first gate of emptiness.
Furthermore, the practitioner further contemplates within his own body:
"All external forms are destroyed by the power of the wind."
Having performed this contemplation, one neither thinks of nor perceives any internal or external forms; this is called the second gate of emptiness.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects thus:

"I now do not perceive any characteristics of internal or external forms; all of this is due to the power of emptiness. I now definitively know that all dharmas have no characteristic of going and no characteristic of coming."
When one contemplates in this way, all discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) are forever severed; this is called the third gate of emptiness.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects thus: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a great fault.

He further observes that this consciousness is the causal condition for all discursive thoughts, and thinks: "I shall swiftly depart from the activities of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*)."

Why is this? If there is any phenomenon that arises, one should know that it will certainly cease; the essence of all existing phenomena is not real, and the nature of all existing phenomena is quiescent extinction.
"This is called the fourth gate of emptiness.

When one performs this contemplation, one may attain the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat; some may obtain the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti), while others may obtain the realization of bodhi."

"Furthermore, if a practitioner contemplates that initial and sustained mental application (vitarka-vicāra) are of the nature of cessation, they immediately attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). This is called the 'Dhāraṇī of Emptiness Accordant with the Unshared [Path] of Ordinary Beings.'"

"This dharani accomplishes immeasurable and all-encompassing merit; it possesses great power and can bring vast benefit, forever severing immeasurable and great sufferings and afflictions. It is well able to eliminate all craving for sense-desires and all craving for form, even up to all craving for the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It can cast off the burden of all afflictions and suffering; this is what was sent by that Tathāgata Śailendrarāja, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gandhahastin."
"Because I have preached this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, that Buddha has sent forth this dhāraṇī.

When this Dharma was spoken, ninety-two million hundred thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of srotāpanna; six million sentient beings were no longer subject to afflictions and attained the liberation of mind through the wisdom of the untainted path;
and ninety nayuta hundred thousand sentient beings, among those at the stage of initial practice, attained this *śūnyatānugata-dhāraṇī*.
Eight million sentient beings attained the meditative concentration of the realized wisdom of pratyekabuddhas;
sixty-six *bimbara* of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable sentient beings likewise established themselves on the path of non-retrogression.
The entire assembly all praised him,
saying, "Excellent!
and the heavens rained down various flowers as well as scattered fragrant powders.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray only that the Tathāgata will explain for me that 'Wishless Accordant Dhāraṇī' sent by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jvalanaguhya from the Buddha Jñānaguṇaśikhararāja."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kauṇḍinya!"
Listen with a sincere and attentive mind, and I shall explain it for you.

There are sentient beings dwelling in the world who delight in sensual desires; day and night they crave flavors, unaware of the path to liberation. Because they do not know the way out, they undergo great suffering and affliction within the cycle of transmigration.
This person should contemplate the liberation door of wishlessness and form this thought:

"The desire for sense-pleasures, the desire for form, and the desire for the formless; the desire for contact and the desire for liberation—all such desires arise from vitarka and vicāra, and exist due to the conjunction of the conditions of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)."
Furthermore, the practitioner further reflects in this way:
"These conditioned phenomena have no creator and no experiencer; they exist because they are produced by the wind."
The activities of my body, speech, and mind are likewise thus: they arise because of the wind; by reason of this wind, the body attains growth, and by reason of this wind, speech attains growth.
He further thought: "If body, speech, and mind are created by wind, I shall shatter my body into particles as fine as dust.
Having thought thus, he carefully observed himself:

"The inhalations and exhalations within this body of mine are identical to that wind; by observing closely, one sees that all the pores of the body exist through the causal conditions of wind, and thus there is birth and death."
Furthermore, he contemplates that all impure things—flesh, blood, hair, and nails—are formed by means of wind;
he further contemplates that at the time of this body's end of life, this corpse no longer has the inhalation and exhalation of wind.
Again, he reflects:
"The activities of my body and speech have wind as their causal condition; if there were no wind, there would be no activity of body or speech.

For this reason, at that time, he attains the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, which he cultivates and increases. Because of this cultivation, the leaves of the root of all existence become thin and its flowers wither, until he gradually becomes able to sever sensual desire and achieve liberation from desire.
Having made this contemplation, they attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, or some may give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, when the practitioner's mind is distracted, they should contemplate in this way:
'Due to the causal conditions of desire, one recollects various forms, even up to the devas; it is because of this that the mind is scattered.'"
At that time, the practitioner further reflects thus:
"If, within all my various places of birth, desire has not been severed, this mind will arise again.
It is like cutting down a tree without removing the root; by merely clearing away the branches and twigs, the tree grows back because its root has not been eliminated."
Craving is also like this: as long as craving has not been severed, it can give rise to all forms of suffering.

Furthermore, the practitioner does not dwell on grasping, but practices with single-minded concentration until he visualizes his own body as a skeleton, white as snow and like a conch shell, with all the bones connected by tendons.

Having seen the skeleton, at that time, if one sees internal and external forms with the eye, or again sees them all as empty, there is only the skeleton connected to form, white like a conch shell, neither increasing nor decreasing.
At that time, when the practitioner has reflected in this way and does not lose his mental focus, this is called *śamatha*.
Furthermore, if the practitioner trains in this manner:
"This is my skull bone, the teeth bone, the neck bone, and so on, up to these are my toe bones."
"One who reflects in this manner will not attain dhyāna while sitting. Why is this?
Because the mind cannot attain dhyāna due to the presence of these two types of reflection: śamatha and vipaśyanā."
At that time, the practitioner should collect the mind and fix it upon the object so that it remains unmoving; thus, with joy and happiness, they will swiftly attain cultivation.
If one is practicing vipassanā alone and the mind is correctly established, one should swiftly recollect that skeleton and focus one's contemplation exclusively upon it.
If this practice is clear, one should further observe how the skeletal form becomes dust, being ground down, destroyed, and dispersed according to causes and conditions.
One who performs this contemplation is said to possess the awakening of *anulomikī kṣānti* (conformity-patience) within *vipaśyanā*.

If one contemplates that all bones are free from impurities and white in color, and that when ground into powder they become dust and merge with the mind—this kind of reflection is called the awakening of the compliant patience of birth (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

If that practitioner contemplates all forms as free from defilement, pure white, and reduced to bone-dust, and perceives them as being devoid of a self-aggregate and as the coming and going of consciousness—
such contemplation is called the awakening of the *kṣānti* (patience) of thorough conformity to non-self.
If all forms that come before the eye as objects of consciousness—excluding those that are stainless, pure white, or skeletal dust—one should form this thought:
"They cannot be described, they cannot be grasped, and they do not abide."
One who contemplates in this way is said to possess the awakening of compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) associated with *śamatha*.

Because such a practitioner has attained these causes and conditions for the awakening of compliant patience, all craving regarding the present and future within the three periods of time is entirely eliminated, as are the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Having been liberated from the bonds of the three defilements within the triple world, one immediately enters the three gates of liberation.
Having reflected thus, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*; likewise, one who maintains such single-minded mindfulness attains the fruit of *arhat*.

"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates all forms and the skeleton as being like a conch shell; having seen the skeleton, free from impurities and connected only by sinews, the mind of that practitioner becomes settled and immovable."
If the mind is unmoving, one constantly binds it to a single object throughout walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
One who maintains such mindfulness is said to be practicing the cultivation of *śamatha* with pliancy.

At that time, the practitioner further observes emptiness both internally and externally; by recollecting internal and external emptiness, they enter samādhi. They observe all forms as having entirely blue characteristics and recollect these skeletal remains (*asthisaṃkalā*) as also being blue. Having seen the skeletal remains as blue, the practitioner then reflects as follows:
"Who created this color and this skeleton-blue?
Who fashioned it and who established it?
This continues even unto the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal.
Having formed this contemplation and conceptualization, he further reflects thus:
"This perception of blue is seen through the causal conditions of the mind; it is a false perception, not a real perception."

Having reflected thus, one knows that dharmas arise from conditions and practices them with diligent effort, constantly performing prostrations and making offerings to sentient beings throughout all worlds.
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:

“This is the meaning of the *Anapraṇihita-anuvartinī-dhāraṇī*, which eliminates thoughts of dissatisfaction and removes all inverted perceptions regarding food; it was sent here by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jvālāguṇagarbha at the command of the Tathāgata Jñānaguṇaśikhara-rāja.”
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Samyaksmṛtijñāna who addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
when śrāvakas cultivate the sign of impurity and śamatha, once they have attained the signs, what are those signs?"
The Buddha said:

“Good son! If one wishes to destroy the fetter of sensual desire, one should cultivate mindfulness of impurity by fixing the mind between the eyebrows and observing one’s own body as three hundred fragments of bone; thus shall the signs arise and the mindfulness of impurity be established.”
At that time, the body of the practitioner becomes both hot and agitated; this is called the first sign (*nimitta*).

Having attained this sign, one constantly contemplates such signs until one perceives the sensation of roughness and other qualities in one's own body, and likewise in the bodies of others; this is called the second sign.
Furthermore, when that practitioner cultivates an undistracted mind and contemplates all things as entirely impure, this is called the third mark.
When such a person is able to contemplate the cessation and purification of suffering and its origin, it is called *śamatha*.

When such signs emerge within the practitioner’s body, they attain the stage of *ūṣmagata* (the stage of warmth); it is like warm milk being poured over the body and mind, and this is called the sign of the immovable mind.

"At that time, if the practitioner finds such signs pleasing within the mind, they should relinquish the state of mindfulness; for these signs are pure, and the defilement of greed is naturally eliminated because ignorance pollutes the mind and wisdom cuts it away."

When the practitioner thus contemplates white bones, recollecting the causal conditions for these skeletal marks up to their ultimate cessation, they engage in such observation and perceive warmth emerging from within the entire body. When such a sign is fully perfected through *śamatha*, it is called the "wholesome root of the sign of warmth."

At that time, the practitioner takes past merit and roots of goodness as an object of focus; now performing this cultivation of mental conduct, they attain purity, and through insight like a lamp, they know it within their own mind.

"Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the four aspects of the body, from the small bones down to the subtlest atoms, penetrating them with complete clarity, as if looking at the flame of a lamp within one's own forehead; thus they see all forms, as well as their own mind and its mental factors, knowing them all through discernment."

For example, when the light of the sun shines through a window, motes of dust swirl about without ceasing for even a moment; all conditioned phenomena are like the nature of these dust motes. One should form this thought:
"Until I perceive the selflessness of all existing things in the world and realize the wisdom of the reality of cessation."
At that time, the practitioner attains the wholesome root of the "Summit," which is called the Dharma of the Summit.
Furthermore, having attained the Dharma of the Summit, the practitioner again contemplates his own body.
Sometimes they see fire emerge, sometimes they see fire burn, and sometimes they see a great light filling the ten directions.

Born from the roots of goodness of the stages from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, such is the subtle nature of the four great elements of this aggregate of form; the body of that practitioner likewise attains the same bodily color as what is seen, and being fully satisfied with the bliss of dhyāna, it is no different from that of the devas.
At that time, the practitioner again produces rays of light from within the heart, seeing sun-discs filling every place throughout the ten directions.

Having seen this sign, he does not give rise to discursive thoughts; at that moment, he enters the *śūnyatā-samādhi*. He further sees various colors emerge from the crown of his head like a parasol; this is called the merit and root of goodness of the "Crown Sign" (*uṣṇīṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

"Furthermore, when the practitioner does not grasp at the signs of the conditions—the patient acceptance (kṣānti) that accords with the Four Noble Truths—at that time, they attain the realization of the Four Noble Truths therein.
Son of good family!

This is called the śrāvaka’s cultivation of impure right mindfulness and the impure right mindfulness based on causes and conditions. Once these causes and conditions are perfected, one attains śamatha; this is called the sign of the 'Bones-and-Bones Lamp-Light' contemplation."

Furthermore, within that state, such signs arise; he sees these signs, and having seen them, he attains a mind of joy. By reason of this joy, he attains the Eightfold Noble Path. By means of the Eightfold Noble Path, he is able to sever all afflictions and the fetters of craving, thereby attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*.

“Good son! In your own land, the Buddha-field of Jvalanottama, those śrāvakas and individuals who delight in arhatship contemplate such dharmas as the causes and conditions of impurity and thereby attain the fruit of the Path.”

When this Dharma of the liberation through the impure was taught, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings realized the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma regarding the Four Truths, and even immeasurable and boundless sentient beings attained the fruit of reality as it is.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya, saying: "Good son!

If all sentient beings were to unite their minds as one, such that the Four Noble Truths could be realized in a single thought-moment, then the Tathāgata would have preached for all sentient beings only a single practice, a single dharma, and a single matter; there would likewise not be eighty thousand aggregates of dharmas, differentiated according to the variations of causes and conditions."
If one person attains realization, all sentient beings should likewise attain it;

if one person severs [afflictions], all sentient beings should likewise sever them. There should not be separate Śrāvakas or the three vehicles, nor should there be separate Bodhisattva stages of the ten bhūmis.
Why is this? Because their afflictions are identical, the place where they are realized at the time of severance is the same. Kauṇḍinya!
Therefore, sentient beings should be tamed through various causes and conditions, not by means of a single condition or a single matter. "Kauṇḍinya!

If all sentient beings have not yet exhausted their discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), then during such a time, all existing phenomena are like great sores and great thorns; there are various modes of arising, and within these various arisings, phenomena increase with various characteristics, various colors, and various minds."
At that time, the practitioner reflects thus:

"If one wishes for the mind to find joy and grasp its signs within itself, one contemplates how this skeleton arises through the combination of mental factors. By taking that mindfulness as the causal condition, one performs this initial sequential contemplation; in this way, it will not be difficult to certainly attain the realization of the fruit of the path to Nirvana, and because one sees that this body attains the causal conditions for happiness and does not regress."
"Furthermore, the practitioner forms this thought:
'By what causes and conditions does the harmony of the mind arise?
For those causes and conditions, one joyfully explains the skillful means.'"
"One who can know this is said to possess the second superior mind.
Directly perceiving the joy of the Dharma, they abide in a state of certainty and attain non-retrogression.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects in this way:"

"This mind of mine now arises through the conjunction of various causes and conditions; it discriminates and observes, grasping and rejecting objects everywhere. Because such a body and mind possess pleasant sensations, one may dwell in conceptual construction; yet, I seek the quiescence within that body and mind."
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
"If I arise due to the conjunction of causes and conditions, then because of the skeletal frame as a condition, my body and mind experience peace and happiness, after which they again cease."
"If that practitioner gives rise to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, the causes and conditions for their arising, abiding, and ceasing are likewise all quiescent.

Forming this thought is called the third superior state of mind: the direct realization of the joy of the Dharma. One will certainly not regress and shall attain the path to Nirvana; by these causes and conditions, the attainment of the four fruits will occur before long and without difficulty.
"Furthermore, the practitioner reflects thus:

'If this body of mine were to penetrate all dharmadhātus through skillful means, its essential nature would be pure; yet even that essential nature does not abide in the skillful means of quiescent extinction.'"
Again, he thought thus:

"I abide through the skillful means of the cessation of all mental characteristics; furthermore, I abide with a mind that is tranquil through the extinction of all mental characteristics, including vitarka, vicāra, and saṃjñā."
This is called the fourth superior mind. One experiences the joy of the Dharma in the present life;
thus, one will certainly attain the path to Nirvana, and though the body has not yet realized it, its realization will not be difficult.
“Kauṇḍinya! When these four kinds of most excellent and harmonious mental states are present, one immediately attains clear vision of eighty-four hundred thousand gateways of samādhi practice.”
Seeing these practices, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and even attains the fruit of *arhat*.

At that time, one further attains two kinds of liberation; possessing great power and great supernormal faculties (*mahābhijñā*), one becomes an object of veneration and offerings for all devas and humans.

"Kauṇḍinya! All sentient beings do not truly possess a single vehicle, a single practice, a single craving, a single thought, a single desire, a single understanding, or a single faith; therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims various verses, names, and various Dharma gates."
For this reason, the Tathāgata is endowed with ten kinds of spiritual powers. Kauṇḍinya!

All sentient beings possess various kinds of inverted perceptions; therefore, in order to purify the inverted perceptions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata teaches the perception of impermanence, or the perception of suffering in what is pleasant, or the perception of non-self, or the perception of delighting in death, or the perception of bloating, or the perception of delighting in putrefaction, or the perception of delighting in pus, or the perception of bluish discoloration, or the perception of delighting in being devoured by various insects, or the perception of delighting in foul odors, or the perception of delighting in the dispersal of skeletal remains, and so forth.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in?"
"What, then, is meant by the perception of the impurity of all food in the world?
Kātyāyana! You should not ask such a question now."

Why is this? Within my realm, there are distinct skillful means for attaining the path to nirvana and the dharmas of the four fruits; whereas in that realm, the faculties and natures of the sentient beings differ, their faith and practices vary, and they attain the path to nirvana through different powers of skillful means.
Since the realms of the world are distinct, their characteristics differ accordingly. Kauṇḍinya!

If I were to explain such a Dharma in full detail, only those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) would be able to believe and accept it; all other sentient beings, upon hearing it, would immediately become confused and overwhelmed.
Then Kauṇḍinya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that out of compassion you will analyze and proclaim it for the sake of those bodhisattvas who are able to believe and understand.”

"Bhagavān! If these sentient beings hear the proclamation of the perception that all worlds are not to be relished and the perception of impurity in food—having heard these two kinds of signs—they will be able to produce various sublime and excellent roots of goodness; they will be able to shatter the various obstacles of ignorance; they will [sever] the union of the sense-bases through craving of all sentient beings; and they will [loosen] the fetters of deluded views like a *kathora* flower. Thus, they will no longer take birth in various places within saṃsāra, nor perform various karmic formations throughout the course of transmigration."

Furthermore, within the various cycles of transmigration throughout the past limit, they cannot be seen or known; for this reason, they take pleasure in birth and death, and thus birth and death have neither beginning nor end.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings, while wandering in saṃsāra, have not heard of such a perception of food as being unpleasurable; due to the conditions of food, their craving increases.
Furthermore, because they have not heard this Dharma-gate, they undergo the suffering and exhaustion of wandering through birth and death across five realms.
Thus, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has constantly kept sentient beings in mind throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will preach this *paripūrṇa-apraṇihitānukūla-dhāraṇī*.
*Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Fascicle Thirty-eight;
*Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Fascicle Thirty-nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Five: The Accumulation of Evil Karma, from the Division on the Sun-Treasury.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:

“Good son! That Tathāgata Jñānaguṇaśikhararāja, out of compassion for the sentient beings of the five turbidities in this world, as well as for the devas and humans, has commanded the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Arciṣmatguṇagarbha to bring this [letter] here, desiring to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.”
Then Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One! So it is, so it is!”

I only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively expound and analyze the perception of the lack of delight in all worldly things and the perception of the impurity of food; if the Buddha proclaims these perceptions of the lack of delight and the impurity of food, sentient beings who hear them will be able to abandon sensual desire and no longer cling to various flavors.

"Bhagavān! If there are sentient beings who are able to give rise to fear toward all desires and food and drink, and who, regarding these two matters, develop a mind of weary detachment and sternly reproach themselves, they should practice purification. It should be known that such persons will cross the river of saṃsāra and swiftly reach the other shore, being able to attain liberation from the bonds of all existence."
The Buddha said, “Kauṇḍinya!

As you have said—regarding the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in, the impurity of food, and so forth—these were sent by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jvālāguṇagarbha from the presence of the Tathāgata Jñānaguṇaśikhara-rāja to the assembly of devas and humans and the rest; receive them with a sincere mind.”
Kauṇḍinya replied, “Yes, World-Honored One!
I shall now listen attentively.”
The Buddha said to Kauṇḍinya:
"What is called the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in? Kauṇḍinya!"
Regarding what is called the "world," there are generally two kinds:
first, the world of sentient beings;
second, the world of the vessel (the physical environment).
"What is called the world of sentient beings?
It refers to the sentient beings of the five destinies:
devas, humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings; these are called the world of sentient beings of the five destinies."

Regarding the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*): within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there are twenty locations; in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), sixteen; and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), four.
These forty types are called the receptacle world, the dwelling places of sentient beings.
Regarding the twenty locations within the desire realm:

first, as for the eight great hells, each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary hells on its four sides as its retinue, surrounding it on all sides; therein, one should contemplate and give rise to the perception of dissatisfaction.
"What are the eight great hells?
First is the Hell of Alternating Death and Revival;
second is the Black Rope Hell."
Third, the Saṃghāta Hell; fourth, the Raurava Hell; fifth, the Mahāraurava Hell;
Sixth is the Reviving Hell;
seventh is the Great Reviving Hell; eighth is the Avīci Hell.

If there are sentient beings in the past, future, or present who, having committed various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, are born in that great hell and undergo all manner of hundreds of thousands of sufferings for immeasurable eons.

Even if one should behold exquisite forms within that hell, because the mind is so oppressed, no perception of pleasure arises; and because the perception of pleasure does not arise due to those causes and conditions, great suffering is produced once again.
In this manner, they pass from one hell to another in succession; the suffering within them is the most extreme of all, unbearable and beyond description.
It is likewise when sounds are heard by the ear, odors are smelled by the nose, flavors are tasted by the tongue, tactile objects are felt by the body, or mental phenomena are perceived by the mind.

All their minds were devoid of love, joy, or delight; everything was unpleasant, and not a single thing was agreeable. Their bodies were constantly ablaze as they ate glowing iron balls and drank molten copper; every place they touched was entirely fire, and they experienced unbearable, extreme suffering.

Because those sentient beings have not yet exhausted their evil karma, they do not die in this manner; as long as they have not yet experienced all the retributions for that karma, they continue to be born there. Furthermore, because they subsequently create evil karma through the actions of body, speech, and mind while among humans, they likewise undergo retribution there.
Kauṇḍinya! The sentient beings of the world mostly delight in pleasure and do not delight in hardship and toil; who among them would wish to enter that hell?
This is called the first dwelling place of hell-beings for those of evil karma; having observed this matter, a person of wisdom gives rise to the perception of aversion.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is called the second dwelling place for animals, observing which one gives rise to the perception of dissatisfaction? Kauṇḍinya!”

Among animals, there are differences in body size; while some sentient beings have bodies that are vast, there are also those with inconceivably subtle bodies, as small as a single hundredth part of a hair split in ten.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose bodies are like motes of dust floating in a window, and there are sentient beings whose bodies are ten thousand *yojanas* in size.

There are sentient beings whose lifespan lasts for the duration of a single *muhūrta*, and there are sentient beings whose lifespan lasts for seven *muhūrtas*. There are sentient beings whose lifespan is one *kalpa*, and even up to a hundred *kalpas*, ten million, a hundred million, or a billion *kalpas*.

Due to their evil karma, they are born there; they take no delight in wholesome dharmas and do not plant roots of goodness. They possess neither the practice of the Dharma nor wisdom; they lack shame and remorse, and have no heart of compassion. Constantly undergoing suffering and affliction, they give rise to great terror; each harbors a mind of mutual harm toward others. They remain far removed from all wholesome dharmas, constantly practicing unwholesome deeds within the darkness of ignorance. Amidst these perilous and evil paths, they create the karma for the hells, giving rise to hearts of anger and resentment, having no joy in merit or virtue.

When this retribution ripens, one undergoes it within the evil realms; born with a base body and a base mind in such a place, one constantly endures various forms of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, beating, and being ridden; burdened by heavy loads until exhausted, with the neck pierced and the spine broken, mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects vying with one another to bite and eat them—such suffering and affliction are immeasurable and boundless.
What wise person would take pleasure in such a place?

Having observed these matters, a person of wisdom does not conceive a thought of delight within the animal realm; this is called the second dwelling place of sentient beings of evil karma, the animal realm.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is called the third place of abode for hungry ghosts? Observe that place and conceive the perception of it as unpleasant. Kauṇḍinya!”

Among the hungry ghosts (preta), there are differences in their bodies: some hungry ghosts have bodies one foot tall; some have body proportions like those of humans; some have bodies as large as a thousand yojanas; and others have bodies as vast as the Snowy Mountains (Himavat).

Those hungry ghosts are naked and without clothing; their hair hangs down, entangling them, and they are black, emaciated, and withered. They have nothing but skin wrapping their bones, for their flesh and blood are entirely gone. Their bodies are coarse and rough like dry trees; they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst, and though they long for food and drink, they can never obtain it. Fire burns within their mouths, with flames issuing forth from outside.
Their minds are constantly filled with anger and resentment, devoid of compassion; they are feverish and agitated, seeking coolness but finding none.

Furthermore, they are tormented by hunger and thirst, compelled to drink molten copper and eat glowing iron balls, as well as various hot, foul-smelling, putrid pus and blood, hot excrement, hot urine, hot parched grain, and hot gruel. They encounter hot winds or even hot rains, and regarding all grasses, trees, rivers, seas, ponds, and streams—leaves, flowers, fruits, and whatever food there may be—it is extremely difficult for them to find, and they can never obtain it.

Even if one were to obtain it and live for a thousand years or even a hundred thousand years, such a lifespan would be constantly plagued by suffering and affliction, spent in darkness and ignorance whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
What wise person would take pleasure in that?

Having contemplated this matter, a person of wisdom does not give rise to thoughts of delight regarding the realm of hungry ghosts; this is called the third abode of sentient beings who have committed evil karma, the dwelling place of hungry ghosts.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is called the fourth human dwelling place? How does one observe that place so as not to give rise to the perception of pleasure? Kauṇḍinya!”

The wise person next contemplates among human beings that all possess various kinds of suffering, namely: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging;
the suffering of hunger and thirst, the suffering of greed, anger, and envy;
and the suffering of false speech, frivolous talk, and divisive speech, as well as the suffering of harsh words, abuse, and slander.

The suffering of cold and heat; the suffering of evil winds, evil rains, epidemics, and locusts; the suffering of injury by venomous and malevolent birds and beasts; the suffering of an evil age, wicked kings, and imprisonment; and the suffering of poverty, low birth, and a short life.

Having already contemplated this suffering, one gives rise to further heavy suffering; conditioned by suffering, suffering arises, and one again creates the causes of suffering. Thus, in future bodies, one undergoes the retribution of suffering once more. In this way, it turns and turns on without limit or bound, undergoing all manner of hardships and pains that never come to an end.
What wise person would take delight therein?
This is called the fourth dwelling place for sentient beings among humans; having observed this matter, a person of wisdom does not conceive a sense of pleasure within the human realm.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is meant by ‘the fifth abode of the gods born in the desire realm,’ and how does one observe that place and conceive the perception of non-delight in being born there? Kauṇḍinya!”

A person of wisdom observes that within the six heavens of the first desire realm, sentient beings are constantly delighted by sensual matters and entangled by sensual craving. The retributions they receive differ and are not equal, giving rise to feelings of suffering; or rather, their retributions vary in quality—some superior and some inferior, some higher and some lower. When those with lower retribution see those with higher retribution, they feel shame, embarrassment, and humiliation, which constantly gives rise to feelings of suffering. Furthermore, those who came here having cultivated merit in the past now find their retribution coming to an end and their merit about to be exhausted; when they reflect in this way, they then give rise to feelings of suffering.

Furthermore, because of various activities and endeavors involving diligent toil and hardship, one experiences painful sensations; or because beloved people and cherished objects are divided and scattered, one experiences painful sensations; and when all the fruits and rewards of merit are exhausted, seeing a pleasant place and feeling affection and joy toward it, yet being unable to be reborn there, one experiences great painful sensations.

Furthermore, one knows that through such karmic actions, one will swiftly fall into the evil realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and hells; because of this, one undergoes manifold and immense suffering.
Given these various and immeasurable sufferings, what wise person would take delight in those places?

This is called the fifth place where the six heavens of the desire realm receive their retribution; having observed this matter, a person of wisdom does not give rise to thoughts of pleasure regarding those heavens of desire.
"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya! Why is it said that one does not conceive the notion of pleasure among the gods of the form realm?

A person of wisdom observes all the gods dwelling in the sixteen abodes of the form realm: having cultivated worldly dhyāna, they are born there; yet because their cause is conditioned and constitutes outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and because suffering is not yet exhausted, they do not attain the bliss of a tranquil mind nor the various other superior pleasures. Therefore, this is a sensation of suffering."
Furthermore, because they have not yet reached the further shore of bliss, they do not know the path out of this flow of suffering.
For this reason, they have not attained liberation from the three evil destinies; therefore, they experience painful sensations.
How could a wise person take delight in that place?

This is called the sixth realm of the gods of form subject to outflows (*sāsrava-rūpa-deva*). Having contemplated this matter, a person of wisdom does not conceive a notion of pleasure toward those gods of form.

"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya! The wise one observes those sentient beings in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): because they have practiced such untainted meditation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), they attain residence in those heavens; yet, because they have not fully perfected the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), they experience suffering."
Because one applies diligent effort for the sake of fulfilling the Eightfold Noble Path, there is the experience of suffering.
Furthermore, because the mind has not yet attained the stage of samādhi belonging to all those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the experience of suffering arises.
Because those Pratyekabuddhas have not yet attained mastery over the various dhāraṇīs, they experience painful sensations.
Because they have not yet attained mastery over the realm of the samādhis of the Tathāgatas, they experience painful sensations.

The realm of all sentient beings is entirely suffering; thus, when these sentient beings within the form realm desire to enter parinirvāṇa simultaneously, they must fully undergo the various kinds of suffering as described above.
How could a wise person take delight in such a place?
This is called the seventh heaven of untainted form; having contemplated this matter, a person of wisdom does not conceive a notion of pleasure within the heavens of form.
"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya! How is it that one contemplates the formless heavens (*ārūpya-deva*) and does not give rise to the perception of pleasure?

A person of wisdom contemplates the four types of celestial abodes in the formless realm; because they have been able to cultivate tainted samādhi (*sāsrava-samādhi*), they are born there. Yet, because they have not attained liberation from all taints (*āsrava*), suffering arises."
Because they have not yet attained mastery over all the stages of training and the stage of no-more-training, suffering arises;
because they are unable to hear the true Dharma of the Buddhas, suffering arises.
Because all cravings have not been completely severed, one lacks mastery within the cycle of existence; therefore, suffering arises.
When life ends there, one fails to attain a superior rebirth and is instead born into wrong views—such is the great suffering.
The suffering of birth consists in the fact that all three types of evil afflictions and karmic paths have not yet been permanently severed;
the suffering of birth consists in the fact that one has not yet attained liberation from all three evil realms.
What wise person would take delight therein?

This is called the eighth [heaven] among the four formless heavens. When a person of wisdom has contemplated this matter, they do not give rise to thoughts of pleasure regarding the formless heavens; thus, they escape from the prison of all existence (*bhava*) and detach themselves from birth within all realms of existence.

When these eight kinds [of factors] are observed in conjunction, a person of wisdom is then able to attain them; though they do not give rise to [discursive] thoughts, they constantly cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path with a sincere mind.
"Kauṇḍinya! This is called the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in. Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya!"
That which is called "the world" is precisely what is termed "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Why does the wise person not give rise to the notion of pleasure regarding the world of conditioned formations?
There are three kinds of conditioned formations.
What are these three?
First, bodily action; second, verbal action;
[and third, mental action].
Third, mental activity (*manosaṃskāra*).
What is bodily activity (*kāyasaṃskāra*)?
Bodily activity refers to the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; this is called bodily activity.
What are verbal formations?
Verbal formations refer to vitarka (initial application) and vicāra (sustained application) as well as speech; these are called verbal formations.
What are mental formations?
The mental formations (*manas-karman*) are called perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*); these are termed mental formations, and these are the three types of formations.

Since the characteristics of these three types of formations are such that all sentient beings possess a single kind of mental perception, how can a wise person discern and know the arising of perceptions of displeasure within body, speech, and mind?

The wise practitioner observes the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, counting up to ninety-nine; while counting, they deeply contemplate the coolness, warmth, and their harmonious integration as the breath moves through all parts of the body.

All the breaths entering and exiting his entire body—whether through the mouth and nose, or even through the passages of all his pores—the person contemplates these breaths and knows them with clarity:
fundamentally, these breaths have neither arising nor ceasing.

If something was originally non-existent and now exists for the first time, it possesses the characteristic of impermanence and lacks the characteristic of certainty, like a bubble upon water or a flash of lightning in the sky.

When observing in this way, one perceives the characteristic of bodily formations within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). One then contemplates from what causes and conditions such characteristics arise.
One then knows that these signs are caused by vitarka and vicāra.
The nature of vitarka and vicāra is originally non-existent and now exists; therefore, they are impermanent, they are dharmas that can be abandoned, and they are dharmas that lead to liberation.

Yet this vitarka and vicāra arise from the deluded mind; and the nature of this mind, which was originally non-existent but now exists, possesses the characteristics of being impermanent, destructible, lacking refuge, lacking substantiality, lacking a self, and lacking reality.
When one contemplates in this way, remorse arises toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and one is able to cultivate the perception of the world as unsatisfactory.

Furthermore, if a wise person can deeply contemplate the three periods of time in this manner, they will be able to permanently sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the twelve bases (*āyatana*). They will purify right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and eliminate the dharmas that constitute the continuity of transmigration, thereby accomplishing the level and straight path subsumed within the aggregate of rightness (*samyak-saṃbhāra*).
When practicing through such skillful means as these, one will certainly attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship.

Kauṇḍinya! This is called the wise person’s attainment of the perception of non-delight within all conditioned phenomena; for this reason, it is termed the skillful means of taking non-delight as the object of focus.
"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya! How does the wise person contemplate the clothing they wear and form the perception of non-delight? Kauṇḍinya!"

If a wise person contemplates clothing—from its being made, sewn, cut, or dyed, until it is finished and placed by their side—whether seeing it, touching it, wearing it, or taking it off, they should reflect upon it thus: "This is like human skin. Upon seeing a garment of fresh color, they should conceive of it as smeared with blood, a dwelling place for all manner of foul-smelling insects, and filled with impurities such as mosquitoes, gadflies, lice, and nits.
Having seen this, the wise person does not give rise to a mind of delight. In this way, Kauṇḍinya,
this is called the wise person’s perception of dissatisfaction regarding clothing.
“Kauṇḍinya! What is meant by a person of wisdom perceiving the thought of non-delight within food? Kauṇḍinya!”

If there is a practitioner who, when holding his alms-bowl, forms this perception: "This vessel is like a flayed skin, defiled by pus and blood; it is an impure skull, rotten and foul-smelling, loathsome, with swarms of flies and maggots filling its interior, such that nothing within it is worthy of desire."
When seeing food, one should contemplate that food as being filled with the impurities of corpses and worms;
if one obtains parched grain flour, one should contemplate it as being like the dust of bone fragments;
if one obtains rice cakes, one should contemplate those rice cakes as being human skin.
If one obtains broth or a gruel, or rice porridge or soup, one should contemplate them thus: "This is like pus and blood, or like excrement and urine, or like human fat, or like human brain.
If one obtains various mixed vegetables, one should again observe them thus: "This is like horse hair, or like human hair.
If one obtains radish pickles, one should further reflect: "This is like human teeth."
If one obtains meat, one should form this thought: "This is like human flesh.

If one obtains white rock-honey or yellow rock-honey, or grape juice, or pomegranate syrup, or milk, curd, clarified butter, cream, fresh or processed ghee, and so forth, one should form this thought: "This is like human blood, or like human pus, mucus, saliva, marrow, spittle, and the like"—such foul secretions, stinking places, difficult to behold.
The wise person, therefore, does not give rise to the perception of pleasure regarding food. Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya,
how does the wise person give rise to the perception of non-pleasure regarding dwellings?
When a wise person thus enters various halls, corridors, rooms, or even towers, having entered, they should contemplate with a sense of dread:
"I have now entered this place which has four gates outside; it is like a great hell that will burn my body."
If one sees the rafters, purlins, pillars, and ridgepoles of a house, one should observe that these wooden members support one another, just as all the fragmented bones of a human body do.
He sees the plastered walls as if they were flesh covering a skeleton; he sees the painted decorations as if they were blood smeared all over.

Furthermore, he contemplates the various beds, mattresses, and mats as being like human skin; he contemplates his places for sitting, reclining, sleeping, and resting as being either like skeletons or like corpses.
In this way, regarding various kinds of drinks, decoctions, pills, powders, infusions, and ointments, one should give rise to such perceptions to cultivate a sense of weary detachment. "Kauṇḍinya!
This is called the wise person’s perception of dissatisfaction toward all food."
What benefit is gained by having such mindfulness?
One is able to attain three kinds of compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). What are these three patiences?

These are the conforming patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anulomikī kṣānti*), the conforming patience of signlessness (*animitta-anulomikī kṣānti*), and the conforming patience of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-anulomikī kṛṣānti*).

Having thus attained these three patiences, such a person delights in cultivating the perception of emptiness; by virtue of cultivating the perception of emptiness, they abide within this emptiness and see that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely empty. Having entered into this emptiness, they further attain benefit and are able to know the skillful means of arising and ceasing for beneficial conduct. Thus, regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity, they perceive the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) and the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), up to the four truths (*catuḥ-satya*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), seeing that the nature of all phenomena is suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Having reflected thus, he attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, and attained the mark of liberation.
"Furthermore, Kauṇḍinya!"

This samādhi is the liberation of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); such is its benefit for all the world that it does not give rise to the notion of pleasure. It is well able to sever all craving for sense-desires, all craving for form, and all craving for the formless; all doubt and conceit; all frivolity; and all ignorance. Furthermore, it can establish one in the stage of one beyond training.
“Kauṇḍinya! This is called the two kinds of perception that all the world finds unpleasurable.

Such various names constitute the subtle meaning of the *aparigraha-anulomā dhāraṇī* (the wishless conforming dhāraṇī) in its full perfection. This dhāraṇī possesses great power; it can eliminate desire, form, and formlessness, as well as pride and arrogance. It can realize the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). It can tear asunder the entire web of darkness and cast off the heavy burden of all suffering and affliction.”

Because I have spoken this Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, that Tathāgata Jñānaguṇakūṭarāja has commanded the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jvālāguṇagarbha to send forth from his hand this *apraṇihitānulomikī-dhāraṇī* so that it may come here.

“Kauṇḍinya! This dhāraṇī can crush all evil māras and the like; it can overcome all venomous nāgas; the devas will revere and believe in it with redoubled joy; the yakṣas will submit to it with great exultation; and the asuras will feel fear within their hearts.”

Furthermore, he can terrify the Garuḍa kings, inspire love and joy in the Kiṃnaras, and naturally subdue the Mahoragas; he can shatter all heterodox views of outside paths, cause Kṣatriya kings to give rise to hearts of joy, and increase the faith of all Brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, it causes the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to give rise to universal joy; it is able to cause the greedy minds of lustful women to cease;
it causes those of great learning to advance further in their upholding [of the Dharma]; and it causes practitioners of seated meditation to delight in the āraṇya.

It can eliminate all manner of afflictions and repel all strife, enemies, famine, untimely calamities, external bandits, and violent death; it can dispel evil winds, hail, rain, floods, frost, cold, heat, bitter and pungent tastes, and harsh tactile sensations—all such portents it can utterly eliminate. It gloriously praises the Mahāyāna, perpetuates the lineage of the Triple Gem, illuminates the Mother of Buddhas, and erects the banner of the Dharma. It brings comfort to sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra who are struck with fear; this is called the "Subtle and Wondrous Wishless Accordant Dhāraṇī."

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; ninety-eight *bimbara* of people attained the fruit of Arhatship; eight *nayuta* of sentient beings attained that *dhāraṇī* of compliance with wishlessness; immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained non-retrogression; and five million eight hundred thousand sentient beings attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the entire immeasurable great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans—spoke with one voice in unison, praising him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
O Great Sage, World-Honored One!
It is inconceivable!
Most great, most wondrous, and inconceivable!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, having attained unimpeded wisdom, clearly perceives that among us there might be those who dare not give rise to a heart of joy regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, knows all sentient beings; he thoroughly knows their faculties, knows their afflictions, knows their skillful means, and knows how they reach the other shore. He is able to cause sentient beings to be fully satisfied with the flavor of the Dharma, able to cause sentient beings to see the Eightfold Noble Path, able to remove from sentient beings the burden of suffering, and able to provide sentient beings with the burden of happiness for them to bear. Now, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all others join their palms and, each with such a unified mind, proclaim:

"Wherever and in whatever place the Buddha-Bhagavān has taught this *dhāraṇī* of the four kinds of wishless compliance (*apraṇihitānulomikī-kṣānti*), and wherever kings, ministers, elders, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and other assemblies have been able to transcribe and place this sūtra, or where there are those who can read, recite, or expound it—in such places as these, we shall provide protection, bestow empowering majesty, and provide all necessary offerings for whatever they require. We shall ensure that those who preach the Dharma are never lacking in worship or provisions, suffer no decline or loss, and that no unfavorable circumstances or enemies can find an opportunity against them; we shall cause all their means of livelihood to be constantly complete."
Free from physical illness and affliction, they shall attain a heart of joy; I shall thus protect those who delight in the Dharma.
Such persons shall never again be reborn in the evil realms; by these causes and conditions, they shall become vessels of the Dharma, and all their offerings shall be fully and perfectly fulfilled.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent! O great donors!"
You who now wish to protect the Great Dharma—by virtue of protecting the Dharma, the Triple Gem shall remain unbroken, and in future ages you shall obtain immeasurable fruits of merit and reward.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha Guṇakusumagarbha has dispatched the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja with this *śamapaita-siddhina* dhāraṇī, intended to induce sleep in those sentient beings of evil karma who lack faith.
“I and all the devas and humans of the world desire to hear and know this; we only pray that the Tathāgata will explain it extensively.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
Reflect upon this well.
I shall explain for you in detail the pure *dhāraṇī* of desire sent by the Buddha Guṇakusumagarbha.

That Tathāgata has sent this desire because the sentient beings of this land possess meager roots of goodness and are burdened with many afflictions. Due to these afflictions, they give rise to the four inverted views and take pleasure in attachment to the notion of a self (*ātman*). Because they are attached to the notion of a self, they become deluded and confused, wandering through birth and death and losing the Eightfold Noble Path; for this reason, that Buddha has sent this desire here.
“Śāriputra! All sentient beings truly have no self; it is because the sentient beings of this land possess perverted minds that they falsely give rise to the notion of a self. Śāriputra!”
A person of wisdom observes deeply within themselves and knows that there is no self.
When performing this contemplation, they destroy the four inversions. Śāriputra!
How does the wise person contemplate non-self?
It is said that they contemplate the body and truly know it to be without self. Why is this so?
Because of their being a composite.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the eye also lacks a self. Why is this?

When visual consciousness first arises, one observes and contemplates with focused attention in this way, perhaps seeing various ornaments, garments, mats for reclining, or bedding, while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Having sat down, one collects the mind; all six sense faculties do not function in mutual separation, for it is thus visible because the mind does not abandon them.
Furthermore, this eye faculty arises from the combination of the four great elements: tendons connect it, it is filled with water, and nothing else can move it.
When the eye moves, it is solely through the power of wind;

because of the wind, it is able to move. Yet that nature of wind depends upon space (*ākāśa*); entering and exiting the sense organ, it revolves to the left and right. Because the organ is pure, one is able to see clearly. However, that nature of space is non-existent and has no basis of support; it cannot be grasped and cannot be described.
If that which is non-existent cannot be described, it is precisely because it is without self; therefore, space truly has no self.
Within this space, wind likewise possesses no substance; because it lacks substance, it cannot be proclaimed, and for this reason, it is without self.

These winds, through their causal conditions, also enter the sense organs, circling to the left and right, pure and clearly illuminating; yet those winds, though they blow like an illusion, cannot be grasped nor can they be described, for apart from the notion of "mine," they cannot be found when sought.

In this way, one should contemplate with a focused and attentive mind that the earth element within the eye is as solid as a *nyagrodha* seed; having contemplated it thus, one extracts it, grinds it into powder, and blows the dust away until it is scattered. By seeking in this manner, one never perceives a "self" at all; thus, one definitively knows that there is no self.
Within this earth element, one analyzes and finds no self; the characteristics of each respective stage exist merely as names, being ungraspable, without self, and without a master.
One should observe the water element and the fire element in this same sequence, contemplating them just as one has contemplated the wind element.
Having reflected thus, one definitively knows there is no self; therefore, one no longer doubts that the "self" exists within the four great elements of the eye.
Thus, it should be understood that all four great elements of the eye are devoid of any substance and cannot be described; for this reason, they are without self.
"Furthermore, if it is said that there is a self because of the causal conditions of eye-consciousness, this meaning is not so.

Why? Because there is no self within the eye, and form is likewise so; yet there is also no self within their conjunction. Eye-consciousness arises from the causal conditions of this conjunction, and thus there is also no self within this consciousness."
Within the wind and within space, there is likewise no self; thus, when sought through investigation, it cannot be found.
This consciousness is merely the cyclic flow of the twelve links of dependent origination; apart from the twelve links of dependent origination, consciousness cannot be seen.

However, conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise; this is called "name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise. With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises. With contact as condition, feeling arises. With feeling as condition, craving arises. With craving as condition, clinging arises. With clinging as condition, existence arises. With existence as condition, birth arises. With birth as condition, there are aging, sickness, and death.

“Such dharmas as these arise dependent upon eye-consciousness; yet this eye-consciousness does not come from the eastern direction, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or the zenith and nadir—it is likewise for all. The thought upon which it depends to arise gives birth to the eye-consciousness, yet that thought also ceases, and the eye-consciousness does not abide.”
In the second moment of thought, one does not think:
"You abide while I cease.
Yet this dharma of cessation likewise does not go to the ten directions, nor does it dwell fixedly in a single location; therefore, all dharmas arise by way of causes and conditions.

"If one is separated from causes and conditions, birth cannot occur; it is through causes and conditions that there is birth, and through causes and conditions that there is cessation. Such causes and conditions are termed 'the law of continuity.

Therefore, you should know that although in reality there is no self, there are these causes and conditions. Furthermore, there is no agent, no experiencer, no originator, and no one by whom things are originated; therefore, there is no self."
If there is no self, then since the self is empty, that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is also empty.
Why is this so? Because such is its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the nature of the eye is without self or what belongs to a self; it is without accumulation, neither conjoined nor dispersed, because it is subject to arising and ceasing.

All phenomena are likewise so: the nature of all phenomena is without grasping and without relinquishing; it is not made by Arhats, nor is it made by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Bodhisattvas, nor by Tathāgatas.
Just as visual consciousness is empty, so too is all phenomena empty; because they are empty of self and non-self, they are not perceived.
When one thus contemplates the three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—one is able to completely sever all stinginess, greed, and all afflictions.
Having reflected thus, some attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and others the fruit of Arhat; as it was with the eye, so it was likewise with the ear, nose, and tongue.

"Furthermore, the practitioner knows that the body is without self; next, they contemplate the hair, dividing each individual strand into a hundred parts, burning them until they become ash, which is then blown away and extinguished by the wind.
In this way, since the essential nature of even a single hair is empty, the doubts in the practitioner’s mind are naturally clarified. Why is this?

Within a single hair, no "self" is to be found; likewise, within the skin, flesh, blood, saliva, mucus, intestines, brain, bones, marrow, sinews, veins, nails, claws, breath, cold and heat, and the various winds moving upward and downward—within the life-force and even in names—all are devoid of a self. It is merely through the mutual conjunction of causes and conditions that it is called a "body."

Having reflected thus and contemplated with a focused mind, one knows that bodily contact is the cause for the arising of body-consciousness; consciousness has name-and-form as its condition; name-and-form has the six sense bases as its condition; the six sense bases have contact as their condition; contact has feeling as its condition; feeling has craving as its condition; craving has grasping as its condition; grasping has becoming as its condition; becoming has birth as its condition; and birth has old age and death as its condition.

Because all phenomena rely upon the mind-consciousness, bodily consciousness arises; yet this bodily consciousness does not come from the eastern direction, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or the zenith and nadir—it is likewise so for all others.

Regarding the thought that serves as the cause for the arising of body-consciousness: when that thought ceases, the body-consciousness does not abide; nor does it say to the second moment of thought, "You remain while I cease."
Furthermore, this phenomenon of cessation has no location; one sees neither a place where it gathers nor a place where it disperses.

Therefore, all phenomena arise because conditions conjoin and cease because conditions separate; they arise when conditions exist and cease when conditions are absent. They are perceived through the continuity of causes and conditions, yet if this continuity is severed, they cannot be seen. Thus, one should know that in reality there is no self.

Furthermore, these causes and conditions have no agent, no one who abides in them, no one who originates them, and no one who causes them to originate; because such causes and conditions cannot be apprehended, there is therefore no self.
If there is no self, then that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is also non-existent. Therefore, the nature of the body is without self or that which belongs to the self;

it neither aggregates nor disperses, for it is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing. All dharmas are likewise so; within that dharma-nature, nothing can be apprehended, and there is neither grasping nor relinquishing. It is not made by śrāvakas, nor is it made by pratyekabuddhas, nor is it made by bodhisattvas, nor is it made by Tathāgatas.

Just as body-consciousness is empty, so too are all phenomena empty; their essential nature is without self and without what belongs to a self. Because they are empty, a self cannot be perceived; all phenomena are entirely devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self, and because they are devoid of these, they are empty.

When one contemplates in this manner, one is immediately able to attain the three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—and through the practice of emptiness, realize the conditions of dependent origination, thereby severing all afflictions of stinginess and greed; some may even attain the fruit of a Srotāpanna up to the fourth fruit of an Arhat.

In this way, the wise person investigates each [constituent] one by one and finds no self; because it cannot be found, they know for themselves that there is no self. Contemplating the absence of self with clarity, their mind is freed from the net of doubt; at that time, they know the body with perfect certainty to be without self.

“Śāriputra! If there are practitioners who can contemplate in this way, you should know that such persons attain these three gates of emptiness—the signless, the wishless, and liberation—and will be venerated by Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, who will protect their bodies and cause them to constantly experience bliss just like Śakra.”

Thus, Brahmā, as well as all other kings among the devas, all nāga kings, all yakṣa kings, all garuḍa kings, all kiṃnara kings, and all mahoraga kings—these various kings shall likewise pay homage, provide offerings and provisions so that nothing is lacking, constantly provide protection, and personally attend to their needs, so that sentient beings with evil intentions may find no opportunity against them.
If one is among all kings of men, the protection obtained through prostrations and offerings shall likewise be so.

"Śāriputra! This is called the *Śamapaidasiṭi* (Skt. *śamapradīpa*) Dhāraṇī. The Tathāgata Guṇakusumagarbha sent the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja here; because I am preaching the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra of the Sun Treasury* in this realm, he has come with the desire to uphold it."
This dharani possesses great power and can bring immense benefit;
it is compassionate and merciful toward all sentient beings, able to rescue them from all perils, calamities, and sufferings;
it can abandon all afflictions and fetters, know all aggregates, bases, and elements, discern the distinctions among all phenomena, and reveal...
All skillful means can bestow the bliss of the path to nirvana upon all, can enter the gates of all dharmas,
can crush all demons who are difficult to subdue, can shatter all heterodox arguments and external paths,
can grant joy to all devas, and can cause all yakṣas to attain contentment.
It can terrify all asuras, cause all garuḍas to give rise to joy in their hearts,
cause all kinnaras to rejoice without weariness, cause all mahoragas to be unable to look back, and cause all kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas to be filled with delight.
The faith of the Brahmins increased and expanded; the Vaiśyas, their kin, and the Śūdras all rejoiced and leaped for joy.
It caused women of excessive desire to diminish their greed and enabled pregnant women to attain peace and security.
It causes those who maintain mindfulness to delight in extensive learning, and those who cultivate meditative concentration to delight in the *āraṇya*.

It can avert strife and famine within nations, and eliminate the calamities of death as well as various thieves and bandits. It wards off untimely winds and rains, cold and heat, bitter hardship, coarse and harsh textures, and foul odors—such unpleasant tactile sensations. It illuminates the Mother of Dharmas and raises the banner of the Dharma; amidst the cycle of saṃsāra, it continues the lineage of the Triple Gem and liberates sentient beings from all fetters and fears.

It can give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and realize the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); it can destroy darkness and bring forth great radiance; it can lay down the heavy burden of the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings.

This *Śamapradā-siddhi-dhāraṇī*, the Great Prophecy Dhāraṇī, enables all sentient beings within the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*) to cross the stream of evil karmic paths and enter the Buddha-realm. It grants mastery and unimpededness regarding all phenomena, up to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) further shore of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). It can turn the wheel of Dharma and rain down the rain of all teachings, skillfully teaching and transforming all sentient beings so that they all may abide upon the path to nirvāṇa.
When this Dharani-method for the exhaustion of evil karma was preached, the past evil karma of immeasurable sentient beings was entirely eradicated;
immeasurable asankhyeyas of devas and humans distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;
and immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Srotapanna.
One hundred thousand *bimbara* of sentient beings attained the fruit of the outflow-free *arhat*;
seventy *nayuta* of sentient beings obtained the *śamapaita-siddhi-dhāraṇī*, and having obtained this *dhāraṇī*, they shall never again regress from the Three Vehicles;
and immeasurable, incalculable, *asaṃkhyeya* devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Immeasurable sentient beings also attained a state of mind within bodhi that does not regress from the path;
eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
