All sentient beings within the lands of the present Sahā world, having heard the meaning of these four kinds of dhāraṇīs—the Four Noble Truths, which accord with emptiness, accord with wishlessness, and accord with śamatha-vipaśyanā—shall all attain the destruction of all craving for desires, craving for forms of long or short stature, craving for touch, craving for pleasure, and craving for both material and immaterial forms.
Furthermore, when sentient beings attain the knowledge and vision of reality as it is and realize that desire is an obstacle, and having heard the Dharma,
there are among them those who attain the roots of goodness of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), those who attain mindfulness of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana-smṛti*),
or those who attain the roots of goodness of the universally non-distracted mind, or those who attain universal roots of goodness, or those who attain...
Regarding those with roots of goodness in *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing),
some attain *śamatha*, some attain *vipaśyanā*, some attain the first *dhyāna*,
some attain the intermediate *dhyāna*, some even attain up to the fourth *dhyāna*, and some attain the four [immeasurables].
Regarding those in the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), some have attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) that accords with the Four Truths;

some have attained the stage of the person of nature (*prakṛti-pudgala*); some have attained the stage of the eight dharmas (*aṣṭadharma-bhūmi*); some have attained the harmonized roots of goodness of the Hīnayāna;
some have attained the non-harmonized roots of goodness of the Hīnayāna; and others have attained the goodness known by omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
As for the roots of goodness, some among them attained the roots of goodness of samādhi, kṣānti, and dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, among that assembly there were women who gave rise to a mind of weary detachment, observing that the female body possesses all manner of faults and is utterly base and evil.
"Why have I received this body and become attached to sensual desires?
Thus he rebuked himself.

Because they had heard the Dharma, all the women practiced mindfulness and took no pleasure in their own bodies; among them, ninety-one *bimbara* of women transformed their female characteristics and attained male bodies.

Ninety-nine hundred billion women among the devas, eighty-four thousand women among the nāgas, eight million six hundred thousand women among the yakṣas, eighty-four thousand women among the asuras, seventy thousand women among the garuḍas, twelve *bimbara* of women among the kiṃnaras, one thousand women among the mahoragas, ninety *bimbara* of women among the pretas, and forty-two *bimbara* of women among the piśācas—all such women as these completely lost their female organs and became men.

If there are pregnant women among them, their wombs will be secure and free from any injury; even for animals, it shall be likewise. Those who give birth shall be endowed with the five faculties, being intelligent, wise, and handsome, whether male or female.

Some may give birth prematurely within the womb, while others may have various ailments that are all able to be eliminated; they are made entirely secure and peaceful, just as a practitioner who cultivates the third dhyāna attains the bliss of meditative concentration, with body and mind equally joyful and content.

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans—all the great assembly together raised this cry:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Buddha Bhagavān, such a sublime Dharma is inconceivable. We have never before heard or received it;

now, through the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata, all our evil karmas and obstacles are completely eliminated. We cross over all states of existence within saṃsāra, drink the nectar of immortality to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa, and teach and protect all sentient beings. Having abandoned the five turbidities, we obtain supreme wisdom and enter the realm of the Buddha, illuminating the Three Jewels so that they shall never be severed.
"The Tathāgata now descends with the rains of all Dharmas; we shall offer worship with single-minded devotion according to our own strength.

Thus it was, until the various devas, including the Kaṭapūtanas, performed all kinds of celestial music and rained down fine powdered gold and silver from the heavens like falling rain, as well as flowers, incense, robes, silken fabrics, various necklaces, and various celestial garlands, scattering them over the Tathāgata for the sake of making offerings. All devas and humans gathered there like clouds, with the sole exception of those who were sitting in meditation and absorbed in samādhi.

In this way, each of these sentient beings, having made offerings of whatever flowers, incense, clothing, necklaces, gold, silver, and jeweled garlands they possessed in their respective places of birth to the Buddha, dwelt there with joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Thirty-nine;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Volume Forty.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Six: On Protection and Sustenance, from the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*. Chapter Six: On Protection and Sustenance.

At that time, all the great kings of the devas together with their retinues; all the nāga kings; all the yakṣa kings, asura kings, garuḍa kings, kiṃnara kings, mahoraga kings, preta kings, piśāca kings, pūtana kings, and even the khaṭvāṅga-pūtanas—all these various kings, each with their own retinues, prostrated before the Buddha. With one mind and palms joined, they spoke these words: “World-Honored One!
From this day forward, wherever there may be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas or upāsikās, or any man or woman who possesses faith,
should they be able to practice such contemplation on impurity and the samādhi of cessation as previously taught by the Buddha,
they shall, through these roots of goodness and their causal conditions, attain the gathering of the mind.
As for those who dwell [in this practice], we and all our celestial retinues,
as well as those with pure faith— whether men or women— shall always provide relief like a guide, causing them, their bodies and minds,
and their retinues to make offerings of food, clothing, bedding, seats, mattresses, and medicinal decoctions.
He provides all manner of necessities for life, thus fulfilling their needs and bringing them peace and security,
so that they no longer worry about the fifteen kinds of turbid and evil matters.
Furthermore, should such things occur, we shall always provide mutual protection therein.
What are the fifteen types of turbid minds? They are:

being pelted with stones, beaten with clubs, hacked with knives, pierced by spears, poisoned, thrown from cliffs, or encountering wicked people; or being met with lack of faith, or the agitation of the four elements—we shall provide protection against these.
If someone, with a malicious mind, sends that person their favorite food, drink, or medicinal decoctions, I shall provide protection for them;
if they wish to inflict such evils as greed, hatred, envy, jealousy, double-tongued speech, or harsh words, I shall provide protection for them;

or if there is a wicked person who, with a turbid and evil mind, constantly acts as a donor by providing robes, alms bowls, bedding, furniture, and medicinal decoctions for illnesses; [in all these cases, I shall provide protection].
Whether it be for those who exhort and convert others, or for those who personally provide offerings for their kin and friends—I shall provide protection against all such evil matters;
or again, whether it be from enemies or malevolent spirits—against such evils as these, I shall provide protection;
or protection against poisons, or against malevolent devas, or within one's own country or in foreign lands—whenever such bandits arise, I shall provide protection.
These are the fifteen kinds of turbid and evil matters.

Whether it be a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, or other men and women of faith—whether in the present or in the future, even until the end of the kalpa during the age of the final dharma (mofa)—[these shall prevail].
What is meant by the period of the Dharma-ending age?
It refers to a time when those who recite and chant do not practice according to the path of the *prātimokṣa*.

If they do not practice seated meditation, they will be unable to attain *samādhi*, nor even the fourth fruit [of the śramaṇa], nor even the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*); this is what is called the period of the Dharma-ending age.

If, as described above, one remains awake throughout the first and last watches of the night, reciting this sutra or practicing seated meditation, and abides in such a manner, then for all those kinsmen—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as for all faithful men and women, their entire retinues, and even their dwellings; whether in villages, towns, cities, or kingdoms; whether in forest hermitages (āraṇya), or in the homes of village chiefs—in whatever place these fifteen turbidities exist, I shall provide complete relief and protection, ensuring that all such evils are entirely eliminated.

"In whatever village there may be a person of merit who dwells permanently—whether many people dwell there or only one, or even if they practice merit for but a single day and night, or reside in such a place for but a single day and night; whether it be a city, a town, or a household—I shall rescue and provide protection and assistance to them all, so that no such person shall encounter evil matters. This applies without exception to all households of donors, whether they be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, or whether they be men, women, boys, or girls; I shall rescue them all and constantly provide guardianship so that they do not enter into evil."

If there are those who thus cultivate merit with vigor of body and mind, and if someone makes offerings, pays homage, shows respect, and provides various necessities—whether by building houses or great monasteries, or forests or gardens, or by making robes, or providing food, drink, bedding, and seating, or even by providing medicinal decoctions, acupuncture, moxibustion, and various medical treatments for the sick—we shall protect all such donors throughout all fifteen turbidities.
"If there are women who are pregnant and carrying a fetus, when they make offerings to such people of merit, we shall protect and sustain them, never abandoning them for even a moment.

Should any evil persons or malevolent spirits wish to inflict harm upon them, we shall turn back those malicious intentions and cause them all to rejoice. Thus, wherever children and grandchildren cultivate merit and mindfulness of roots of goodness, they will be loved and respected by others; or other sentient beings may encourage, assist, and praise them; or family members may speak their names; or one may employ incantations and knots to protect sentient beings; or teach them merit, or teach them to abandon evil. Toward such sentient beings as these, during the fifteen turbidities, we shall constantly provide close protection so that no malevolent ghosts or spirits may find an opportunity to harm them."

“If there are those who cultivate merit in this way, whether they be humans or non-humans, and can believe their words and act according to their instructions—all such as these we shall likewise protect.”

If there are wicked people who, toward those practitioners who cultivate merit, become angry, revile them, seek to inflict harm upon them, or create obstacles—toward such evil beings as these, we shall not provide protection.
"What are the names of those who cannot be protected by the fifteen turbidities?
As for the fifteen turbidities:
the first is the affliction of evil."
The second is the loss of sovereignty;
the third is the dispersal of various means of subsistence;
the fourth is the severing of various limbs within the body—whether eyes, ears, mouth, nose, hands, or feet—or else the decapitation of the head.
Fifth, the loss of beloved wives, children, and all kinsmen;
sixth, the loss of official rank;
seventh, the loss of one's home.
The eighth is being invaded by various enemies;
the ninth is having a mind constantly filled with sorrow;
the tenth is being angry toward kṣatriyas and constantly practicing evil in one's heart.
Eleventh, the sentient beings of the towns, districts, kingdoms, and cities will be turbid and evil;
twelfth, various stolen goods will be lost through acts of theft;
thirteenth, one's own wives and women will constantly engage in mutual strife and contention.
Fourteenth, the land will be ravaged by thieves and bandits from foreign nations;
fifteenth, there will be short lifespans and premature deaths.
If evil sentient beings possess these fifteen kinds of conditions, we shall not protect them.
The puggalas replied:

"Furthermore, if there is someone who, though practicing meritorious deeds, does not accept wholesome words and constantly gives rise to evil anger; if such a person wishes to perform meritorious acts for another but instead commits various evil deeds, thereby creating obstacles amidst their manifold merits."

If such evil beings come to take refuge in me, hoping to obtain various powers through incantations—even though such incantations possess all manner of ritual applications—we shall not provide them with protection, nor grant them power, nor offer them any rescue.
If those sentient beings desire to seek and hope to obtain such and such things, we likewise shall not give them.

If there are sentient beings who, toward those who constantly cultivate and constantly recollect merit, give rise to anger and commit various evil acts of obstruction, we shall deal with them as previously described.
Furthermore, whether in the present life or in the future, they may rely upon this Dharma to practice with mindfulness;

yet when the Dharma is about to perish, there will always be gods, nāgas, spirits, and even kaṭapūtanas who harbor evil intentions and wrathful anger, lacking compassion, taking no delight in their future sublime bodies, and having no fear for the retributions of the three miserable realms.
If there are such persons who create merit and virtue, who delight in the *āraṇya* and plant various roots of goodness—
whether dwelling among burial mounds, or beneath trees, or in monastic dwellings, or in the abodes where they walk and stay within the *śītavana* (cemetery)—
all such persons of merit and virtue are as described above, including devas, nāgas, and even *kāṭapūtanas*.
Those with evil views and evil minds— whether they dwell in the vicinity of such persons of merit,
or cause turbidity in their body or mind, or steal their vital energy; or whether they are practitioners who receive offerings from donors—
I, along with the various devas, nāgas, and even the kāṭapūtanas, being devoid of compassion and ignorant of gratitude, [will act] in the future...
One who is born does not fear the evil realms; yet defilements turbid the body and mind and rob them of their vital essence.
This can only be avoided through past extremely heavy evil karma; otherwise, within such evil karma, protection cannot be obtained.

“If I, along with the devas, nāgas, and even the kaṭapūtanas, should fail to provide protection where it ought to be given, I would then be deceiving all the Buddhas of the three periods of time in this present life; I would not encounter arhats or pratyekabuddhas amidst the cycle of saṃsāra, and my body would forever fail to become a vessel for merit and would not attain nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”

That you are able to give rise to this mind in such a way is no different from the practice of all Buddhas of the three periods of time in their past lives; it continues the lineage of the Triple Gem, erects the banner of the Dharma, and illuminates the Mother of Dharmas. By acting thus, you shall be making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time.
"O son of good family!

Whether male or female, whoever is able to exert such diligent and energetic resolve and takes delight in guarding the True Dharma—for such a person who practices the Dharma, one shall always protect, always mindfully attend to, and always provide for their needs."

Thus, these sentient beings, within the cycle of transmigration, shall always obtain noble status and harmonious kinship; they shall constantly experience peace and happiness without undergoing hardship, until they swiftly accomplish the path of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good sons! You seek happiness and do not seek suffering; therefore, you should always be diligent and energetic in cultivating all roots of goodness.
The devas and others replied:
“Excellent, excellent!
From this day forth, I shall cultivate myself in this way and resolve my mind in this way.

At that time, within this Sahā world, there were various hungry ghosts with malicious minds who constantly lived by looking upward to devour the vital essence, blood, and flesh of all sentient beings.
Thus, immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of such spirits and others addressed the Buddha in unison, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have been summoned by the retribution for our evil karma; we constantly devour human flesh, blood, and vital essence to sustain our lives.”
Today I have resolved to enter the abode of the Buddha’s Dharma and become a disciple of the Buddha; henceforth, I shall commit no further evil nor give rise to evil thoughts.

If I, as a disciple of the Buddha, do not constantly cultivate and practice the method of the contemplation of impurity exactly as the Buddha has now taught—practicing it in this single way without deviation—and if my mind does not dwell upon the person (pudgala) as prescribed, may my eyes remain perpetually blind in darkness, may all my four limbs be unable to move, and may I be deprived of the five sense faculties within my body.

We, like the *pudgala*, shall also protect these people of merit along with their donors who have constructed monasteries, chambers, groves, gardens, and bathing pools, as well as provided all necessities such as robes, bowls, food and drink, bedding, couches, and medicinal decoctions; we shall likewise protect such donors.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
"You should cultivate a good resolve and always remain thus; do not allow yourself to become heedless.
At that time, the Earth Deity Dṛḍhā rose from her seat and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!

If a disciple of the Buddha constantly restrains the five sense faculties and practices with focused mindfulness and a sincere heart according to the method of the contemplation of impurity as taught by the Buddha today, then we, the earth deities, shall for the sake of such a practitioner constantly bring forth the essence of the earth to nourish that person, causing their lifespan to increase within their body. Through the causal condition of this overflowing vital energy of the earth, the practitioner’s body will attain physical form, strength, mindfulness, joy, diligence, and great wisdom.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!

You, a great donor, are able to give rise to such a mind; you are truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by the Dharma. By providing such food that benefits their bodies, through these causes and conditions of merit, you shall swiftly achieve fulfillment in the Mahāyāna.”
At that time, a venerable deva among the assembly rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are such bhikṣus who practice the Dharma and are disciples of the Buddha, those donors may provide them with various kinds of gold, silver, precious jewels, various necessities for life, and various grains and rice in full abundance."

If the disciples, following the method of the contemplation of impurity as taught by the Buddha, up to the gate of emptiness of the samādhi of cessation, thus bind their mindfulness—whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing from the first watch of the night until the middle and latter watches—contemplating the Dharma in this way with a mind free from external conditions.

Those donors built monasteries for him—some constructing a single hall, others a grove of trees, and still others providing clothing, food, bedding, seats, and couches—as well as constantly supplying various necessities for life, such as medicine for illness and other requisites.
Having thus attained freedom from lack, his body became secure and free from sorrow; his mind was constantly joyful, and he obtained an excellent field of merit, becoming a vessel for the Dharma.
Having given such gifts, one will obtain great rewards in future lives; with a deep mind that delights in the Dharma, one will not be born in the evil realms nor create unwholesome dharmas.

When I protect them in this way, those people will immediately cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and their various kinds of excellent and wondrous roots of goodness will increase without diminishing.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent! Great Dānapati!"
"This is the power of your diligence; within the Mahāyāna, you shall swiftly increase the strength of your merit.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi among the assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata has preached this Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, the great donors along with their retinues will each resolve to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma for the benefit of sentient beings."
"By reason of that cause and condition, within this Sahā Buddha-field, the Mother of the Dharma shines forth, and its radiance increases.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, desiring to benefit those of the future, addressed the Vajrapāṇi within the assembly, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!"
What is the nature of space?
Is it visible? If it is not visible, how can this thing be described?
He asked again: "What is meant by the 'conjunction of all dharmas'?
Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya:
“Because the shore of the *bhūtakoṭi* cannot be seen, this dharma of harmony is also not to be seen.
Maitreya asked again: “Good son!...”
"What is that which is called the 'true dharma of non-conjunction with empty space'?
The Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya:
"In that, there is no difference."
Maitreya asked again:
"Good son, what is called the dharma of space?"
"What is called the 'non-concordant dharma'? Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya:
"The entry into the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), which is immovable and unarisen, is therefore not different."
Maitreya asked again:
"Good son, what are called conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, and tainted and untainted phenomena?"
The Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya, saying:

"As it is fundamentally real, suchness and the nature of suchness are without difference; because the outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas are in harmony with space, they are therefore not different."
Maitreya asked again:
"Good son, what are those dharmas called 'true suchness' that are both with outflows and without outflows?"
The Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya, saying:
"Because space is joined, it is the true Suchness; it is neither a defiled dharma nor a non-defiled dharma.
Maitreya asked again:
“Good son! What is called the dharma of the union with space?
The Vajrapāṇi replied to Maitreya:
"All dharmas are free from obstruction; because they are in harmony, they are empty, neither accumulating nor dispersing.
Why is this? Because their essential nature is never lost."
Furthermore, because neither the object nor the emptiness can be apprehended within that emptiness, it is called the "dharma of emptiness.
Son of good family!

Because of this skillful means among all dharmas, you should know that the essential nature of all things is suchness (*tathatā*). This essential nature is empty because it is originally empty; likewise, the ten thousand dharmas are empty because they are a composite. Being free from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), this emptiness is not conceptualization; yet even non-conceptualization is empty.
Why is this? Because all such composite phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty and inexpressible; for such is the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.

This Dharma is not created by śramaṇas, nor by arhats, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas, nor by Tathāgatas. Such is the reality of *tathatā*: all outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) dharmas are entirely empty because they are composite phenomena, because they are not separate [from that nature], and because they are not distinct phenomena.
“Maitreya Bodhisattva!
You should know it thus.

At that time, when the Vajrapāṇi had spoken this Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings who had previously studied emptiness in the past had all their evil karmas completely eliminated; they became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Ninety-two nayutas of sentient beings gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within this Dharma;
immeasurable sentient beings also attained the stage of non-retrogression and reached the ultimate realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter Seven: The Buddha Manifests Supernatural Powers The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Division on the Sun-Treasury, Chapter Seven: The Buddha Manifests Supernatural Powers At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard the Buddha preach this method of the contemplation of impurity, and with the entire great assembly each desiring to protect and uphold it, leaped for joy. He immediately rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The merit of such a Dharma-gate is supreme and inconceivable. Within this land, the Sahā world Buddha-field, there are immeasurable great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have achieved radiant and wondrous forms; such as these, I have never before seen nor heard of from the very beginning.
“World-Honored One!
This light of the Bodhisattva is able to illuminate the entire trichiliocosm, even filling all the way up to the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Now, my eyes see no other forms; I see only this Sahā world-system, from within its Buddha-fields down to the great and small Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*), all filled with radiance.”
"Bhagavān! If such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, what will their radiance be like?"
What are the characteristics of the light emitted when the Tathāgata enters into samādhi?
Can I see the Tathāgata’s light?
By means of that light, can I also see the various wonderful, marvelous, and extraordinary things in other Buddha-fields?
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
Great King!"
If there are bodhisattvas who have accomplished the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, their light can illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.
Why is this? Because they are able to practice the power of the adornment of great merit within the realm of the Tathāgata.
Because in the bodhisattva practices of past lives, they have accomplished and perfected the adornment of the Dharma through the power of great merit;
because their roots of goodness cultivated through all bodhisattva practices have greatly increased;
and because, possessing immeasurable merit, they were born into the family of the Buddhas and drew near to the path of unsurpassed enlightenment.

Because it is the ultimately unsurpassed, wondrous path of bodhi; because it is the swift and supreme wisdom within the Buddha’s realm, which is free from all obstacles and possesses the power of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, vigorous wisdom;
because it is the entry into the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom and the True Dharma;
and because it is the basis for discerning the boundless realms of the Buddha-dharma throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past.
This ground is the most supreme turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma; it is the body attainable by all those who possess mastery, because such merit is free from obstruction;
because one has attained the pure and true Dharma;
and because one has reached the further shore through what is to be cultivated.
Because all karma in future lives has already been exhausted;
because they have attained penetration into the roots of goodness of all sentient beings and have forever severed all habitual tendencies of affliction;
and because they are free from obstructions and abide within the Buddha-realm—for these reasons, their radiance is able to shine universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"Great King!
In this way, by the power of the light of the Buddha’s merits, you are also able to behold all the infinite, innumerable, and incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions."
The King said,
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to see such Buddhas of the ten directions— immeasurable, innumerable, and asaṃkhyeya— as well as their bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and assemblies of śrāvakas.”
At that time, King Bimbisāra and his retinue, along with immeasurable billions of sentient beings, spoke to the Buddha with one voice:
“So it is, World-Honored One!”

We also pray that the Tathāgata will manifest for us the realm of all Buddhas and the unobstructed matters of the meritorious adornments practiced in the past; having seen these, we shall give rise to a heart of joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya:

“You great assembly—both householders and renunciants, as well as my śrāvaka disciples—all of you should each bind your mindfulness and contemplate with deep thought; by the power of your own roots of goodness, enter into meditative concentration. I, too, now wish to enter the Tathāgata-samādhi.”

At that time, among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and all humans and non-humans within this buddha-field, some perceived the Four Truths, some attained the patient acceptance of accordance (anulomikī-kṣānti), and some attained non-retrogression in the Three Vehicles; all such beings sat cross-legged and entered meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings who, having attained a heart of faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem, likewise entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered the *sarvatathāgataviṣayacandrasūryasamādhi* (the Samādhi of the Sun and Moon of the Realm of All Tathāgatas). His practice of wisdom was vast and expansive, fully pervading all of space, and he caused all sentient beings possessed of wisdom to give rise to joy.

This samādhi is immeasurable and invisible; it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor even by the bodhisattvas who are one step away from buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Only the Buddha-Tathāgata can attain it; this is called the Tathāgata-realm Samādhi.

Once the Tathāgata had thus entered this samādhi, the three thousand great thousandfold worlds of this Sahā world—including ten billion four-continent systems, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and even ten billion heavens up to the Peak of Existence—all appeared as reflections within the body of the Buddha.

In this way, once all the Buddha-fields of the Sahā world had entered the body of the Buddha, all sentient beings therein—whether in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, or among gods or humans—whatever suffering they experienced, whether physical or mental, was entirely extinguished. They all attained complete mastery and gave rise to joy, just as a bhikṣu entering the third dhyāna attains perfect bliss.

At that time, all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were previously seated in the assembly and had entered into samādhi arose from their concentration. Having arisen from concentration, they beheld the Buddha’s radiance; having beheld the radiance, the light they themselves possessed immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
In this way, the śrāvakas and disciples of the Buddha, as well as all the hosts of devas and humans who had entered meditative concentration, each arose from it.
Those great assemblies experienced joy in body and mind, just like a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna.
At that time, all the infinite multitudes of living beings experienced great joy, leaping for joy in ways immeasurable, inconceivable, and never before heard or seen.

Furthermore, their six sense-faculties were entirely purified as they appeared within the body of the Buddha—whether sitting, walking, standing, or reclining—and they further beheld immeasurable rays of light issuing from every single pore of the Tathāgata.

It is like the light of the sun and moon in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it is like all the great maṇi jewels, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and it is like the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the tenth stage, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, simultaneously emitting a vast, blazing radiance.

In this way, these radiances are able to shine universally throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; thus, the radiances emitted from each and every pore of the Tathāgata fill every place within the lands of the ten directions, being the most supreme of all.

At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, dwelling with sovereign ease within their respective lands, each praised my name in a single voice before their great assemblies, reciting this verse:
"Behold him, replete with perfected merit, Who compassionately regards all sentient beings;
With wisdom and great power, he is able to uproot [afflictions]— Śākyamuni Tathāgata is supreme among the victors."
Out of compassion, he emits this light, which fills all Buddha-fields;
furthermore, out of pity for these sentient beings, he causes them all to appear within his own body.
Each and every Buddha-field is filled with light; all sentient beings who behold it rejoice, their resolve becoming pure and entirely firm, as they attain the supreme, unsurpassed, true Bodhi.
If among you there are those who have attained supernormal powers,
all should go with utmost haste to pay respect by touching his feet and prostrating before the most supreme Honored One, the Lion of the Śākyas.
If there are those who have not yet attained supernormal powers, they should bow their heads in prostrate worship from afar toward him;
by swiftly giving rise to the thought of true wisdom regarding Bodhi, they shall behold the body of the Muni, the Perfectly Awakened One.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions each spoke such verses within their respective lands for the sake of compassionately teaching and transforming all sentient beings.

Furthermore, because the adornments of the vows cultivated by the Tathāgatas in the past were fully perfected, in each of those Buddha-fields, every Tathāgata was likewise surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—as well as great disciples, Śrāvaka bhikṣus, and immeasurable billions of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other immeasurable multitudes. All these great assemblies, surrounding those Buddhas, each mounted their supernatural powers and came together to this Sahā world.
Having arrived at this land, they approached the Tathāgata, bowed their heads to his feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.

Having completed the circumambulation, each of them brought forth all manner of various precious objects, various precious robes, various *kāṣāya* garments, various necklaces, various banners and canopies, various assorted flowers, various incenses, various ointments, various kinds of music, various hymns of praise, and various songs and dances to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Having made these offerings, he and his retinue each returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, all sentient beings within the Buddha’s body in this Sahā world were able to see them.
Having seen this, they rejoice and further experience immeasurable and boundless bliss.
Moreover, all sentient beings behold all the Buddhas of the ten directions, seated upon diamond thrones within their respective lands, expounding the Dharma.

Furthermore, he saw that in each of the various buddha-fields, at their respective seats, the Buddhas were teaching all sentient beings about the merits of Śākyamuni Tathāgata of this world: his great renown, his power of great wisdom, his adornment of merit and virtue, and how he teaches and transforms sentient beings through great diligence and the power of great compassion.

In those various lands, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of sentient beings, equal to the sands of the Ganges, resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and received predictions of enlightenment within their own respective lands; likewise, immeasurable sentient beings received predictions of enlightenment through the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas*.
That great assembly also saw all sentient beings of this land enter the body of the Buddha and likewise receive such predictions of enlightenment.
Among those sentient beings, some were experiencing pleasure and others were experiencing suffering; they all appeared dwelling within the body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

If sentient beings in a Buddha-field afflicted by the five turbidities were able to see the Tathāgata, as well as the immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas throughout the ten directions preaching the Dharma, each Tathāgata surrounded by immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who paid him respectful homage; having seen this, they would give rise to great love and reverence, and their hearts would be filled with joy.
Within the bodies of all those sentient beings, every painful sensation is entirely eliminated, and they attain peace, stability, and happiness.

If the five-turbid worlds were not empty, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the tenth stage and others would see the Buddha in whatever land they might be, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Having seen this, they gave rise to faith; having attained faith, they listened to and received the sublime Dharma.
Those bodhisattvas each manifested the body of a Buddha in that place, filling all lands with a single voice, each speaking these verses with different mouths but in unison:
“The Buddhas of the ten directions share a single vehicle; Having perfected their roots of goodness, they have come here.”
Apart from the Buddha and the assembly of other bodhisattvas, there is no one else of such great virtue.
Each and every one of you sentient beings, quickly resolve upon the unsurpassed path of Bodhi;
if you do not exert yourselves with courageous diligence, you will wander in the ocean of suffering with no time of escape.
All of you should come together; quickly follow me as we go to make offerings to the Lion of the Śākyas among men, and pay homage by circumambulating that World-Honored One to the right.

At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having manifested the bodies of Buddhas and spoken these verses, each arrived here together with immeasurable and boundless numbers of sentient beings—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—who had all attained supernatural powers; having seen Śākyamuni Buddha, they circumambulated him three times to the right.

Having circumambulated him, they each brought with them various precious objects, various precious garments, various sounds, and various songs and dances, using these to make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Having completed the offerings, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There were also some sentient beings who made vows for the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddha*; in this way, they all attained the path of non-retrogression.

Those sentient beings also each attained various kinds of patience (*kṣānti*), various kinds of dhāraṇīs, and various kinds of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); having attained these, they each returned to their own original lands.

There may be bodhisattvas who manifest as the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, or again manifest as the bodies of arhats; or they manifest as the bodies of Brahmā kings, or manifest as the bodies of Śakra devānām indra; or they manifest as the bodies of the four heavenly kings, or manifest as the bodies of Nārāyaṇa; or they manifest as Maheśvara, or manifest as the bodies of Īśvara; or they manifest as the bodies of the celestial constellations, or manifest as the bodies of asuras; or they manifest as universal monarchs (cakravartin), and likewise in various forms such as the bodies of nāgas and spirits, throughout whichever buddha-fields they may be located.
If there are sentient beings who delight in seeing the body of an arhat, and having seen an arhat, receive the Dharma with joy,
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of teaching and transforming those sentient beings, manifest in the form of an arhat therein and preach various Dharmas to them.

When those sentient beings see the great radiance and Śākyamuni Buddha, and having seen the Buddha, they give rise to love and reverence in their hearts and experience great joy; their six sense faculties become complete, all their vows are fulfilled, their evil karma is entirely exhausted, and they all delight in taking birth [in the pure land].

Furthermore, those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest within the Buddha-fields such bodies of Arhats to teach the Dharma and transform beings. Because they possess a great mass of merit and have fully accomplished the power of roots of goodness, they are able to pervade all fields with a single voice, employing various modes of speech to recite these verses:
"Sentient beings have long dwelt within the cycle of transmigration; Out of ignorance, they do not know the essential path to liberation.
Due to their various kinds of sinful karma, They obtain this body of birth-and-death, fraught with suffering and affliction."
Therefore, you should swiftly abandon evil thoughts, The afflictions of wrong views and inversions.
Cross the stream of existence early to reach the other shore; How is it that you do not realize this?
The Guide, so difficult to behold, has now been seen; The human body, so difficult to obtain, has now been attained;
The virtuous friend, so difficult to meet, has now been encountered; The True Dharma, so difficult to hear, has now been heard.
Therefore, you all should with a sincere heart Swiftly resolve to attain the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Having emerged from the prison of all birth and death, one realizes the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous body of merit.
If one can forever leave behind the two kinds of perversions— namely, the two views of annihilationism and eternalism—
and know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without self, this is called entering the gate of right contemplation.
Craving leads to grasping, which enters into existence and results in birth; The water of wisdom washes them all away until they are pure.
Together we shall go to the Sahā world, To reverently make offerings to the Lion of the Śākyas.

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having thus manifested themselves in the form of arhats and spoken these verses, set out together with immeasurable sentient beings—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—who had attained supernormal powers, and arrived at this realm.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and his retinue; having respectfully circumambulated the Buddha three times, he brought forth the various precious objects, various precious robes, various *kāṣāya* garments, various necklaces, various parasols, various banners and streamers, various precious flowers, various precious incenses, and various musical performances, verses of praise, songs, and dances, using them to make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

Having completed their offerings, they each returned to their own lands; once arrived at their respective lands, they sat upon their thrones and, for the sake of their own assemblies, extolled and praised Śākyamuni Tathāgata, saying:
"Śākyamuni Tathāgata compassionately teaches and transforms all sentient beings, and is able to bestow every benefit upon them."

Each of these bodhisattvas spoke thus within their respective assemblies; upon hearing this, all in those assemblies praised Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and having offered their praise, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable sentient beings resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, there are those who resolve their minds toward the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and others who resolve their minds within the Śrāvaka Vehicle; each attains the path of non-retrogression within their respective vehicles.

There were those who had attained various dhāraṇīs, various patiences, and various roots of goodness, and they also saw all the sentient beings of this Sahā Buddha-field entering into the body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

When these sentient beings witnessed this inconceivable transformation of divine power, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Among them, some who had conceived the aspiration for the vehicles of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas each attained non-retrogression in their respective vehicles;
others assumed the subtle bodies of Cakravartin wheel-turning kings and received predictions of their future enlightenment.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Forty;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Forty-one.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Constellations, Part One, within the Section on the Sun-Treasury.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, the Lord of the Desire Realm, saw all sentient beings throughout the entire Sahā world-system, as well as the inhabitants of all celestial palaces and their families and retinues, within the body of the Buddha.

When Māra Pāpīyas saw this, he wept with tears streaming down his face; his heart was filled with great anguish, and sweat broke out over his entire body as he wailed until his voice failed, crying out in bitter lamentation.

Sometimes they rise, sometimes stand, sometimes sit, or walk; they enter and exit houses, running frantically here and there; they yawn and stretch, trembling with fear and alarm; they sigh in indignation, heaving long and short gasps for breath; they close their eyes, gape with open mouths, protrude their tongues, and lick their bodies; they expose their backs and chests, extend their arms and contract their legs; they shake their heads and necks, seeking hands to rub and stroke them. They engage in all manner of such actions while undergoing great suffering and affliction; even all the retinues of Māra experience such inner grief and anxiety in the same way.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān had a general named Śīlāśraya. Seeing the King’s body and mind thus tormented and oppressed, he spoke a verse to ask him:
"Why do you dwell alone in such sorrow and distress? Why do you cry out and run about as if mad?
Entering and leaving your home, your heart is not at peace."
"Please tell us, O King, what the causes and conditions for this are.
When Māra Pāpīyān heard these words, he became even more distressed and wept with tears falling like rain, replying in verse:
"Now sweat flows all over my body, And my heart is split asunder as if cut by a blade."
Tears like blood flow from my weeping eyes, for I behold Gautama manifesting his supernatural transformations.
His form is vast and boundless; all buddha-fields dwell entirely within his belly.
I have lost my subjects, ministers, and kinsmen; my realm and palace are now utterly empty.
Furthermore, if great assemblies from the ten directions were to come,
filling this Sahā world, each offering boundless great offerings, prostrating, circumambulating, or coming and going,
they would cause me to lose my sovereign power and majesty, and my companions and retinue would turn to them.
“The Tathāgata possesses such great supernormal power; why then should my heart not be sorrowful?
Then the Great General of Māra’s Army, Reliance on Precepts, spoke again in verse to Pāpīyān:
“The various hosts of troops commanded by me are strong, valiant, and truly difficult to withstand.”
“With a wheel of swords brandished and struck, it shall shatter your body into fragments in an instant.
Then Māra Pāpīyān replied in verse:
“We, along with our armies and retinues, have long since taken refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One.”
"If you wish to give rise to an evil mind within yourself, you will immediately see a cangue and shackles around your neck.
Then the Great Mara General, Kai-yi-zhi, spoke again in verse:
"I shall now employ many skillful means to entice and deceive that wicked enemy."
"Feigning intimacy and acting as a friend, I shall wait for an opportunity and then destroy him.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas replied in verse:
"If I were to give rise to a poisonous and evil mind, and thus employ such expedients to destroy the Buddha..."
He immediately saw a corpse hanging from his neck, so foul and loathsome as to be difficult to behold.
Then the great leader of Māra’s army, Śīlāśraya, spoke again in verse:
"All that belongs to the realm of desire is subject to Māra; only those gods and humans who have faith and take refuge in the Buddha [are not]."
"The various evil venomous dragons are also under his command; I pray you, issue the order to swiftly harm the body of Gautama.
Then Māra Pāpīyas replied with a verse:
"If you truly know that the dragon possesses such power, I am already bewildered and confused; you yourself must issue the command."
"If I can truly defeat Gautama, I shall regain my realm and restore my original mind.
At that time, the great commander of Māra’s army, Śīlāśraya, thought to himself:
"There are three poisons in the world that are difficult to crush:"
First, the celestial Māras;
second, the malevolent nāgas;
and third, the sages who have attained meditative concentration and the five supernormal powers.
"The palace of Māra has now been destroyed; only the realm of the nāgas remains firm, its radiance shining upon the ocean, its sovereign power and surrounding retinue being inconceivable."
Since the Dragon is already under the influence of Māra, he shall command all the remaining troops; you must now act as king and issue orders to go quickly and destroy that Gautama.
Māra Pāpīyān said, “Excellent!”
"Excellent!
O General of Wisdom, you may depart at once; go to that dragon palace and deliver these urgent instructions: engage in battle with Gautama as soon as possible."

Then the great commander of the Māra army, Śīlāśraya, having finished his leave-taking with the king, raised his hand and addressed the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of troops, proclaiming these words:

"You should all quickly adjust your robes and armor; I now wish to go to that palace of the Dragon King to cause the evil dragons to raise up poisonous winds, to harm the life of Gautama and cause him to be shattered."
When he had spoken thus, the entire host of troops was unable to move.
Since the army and their leader could not advance, tears flowed from their eyes and their body hairs stood on end. Joining their palms toward Māra Pāpīyān, they said: "We can no longer proceed.

The śramaṇa Gautama is treacherous and full of illusions; he knows our homes and has bound us. Within our bodies, all fires are ablaze, seething and burning with such torment as if we were being boiled in a cauldron. Now that we are thus powerless and lack self-mastery, how can we seek to borrow strength from another?"
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān became even more distressed, sorrowful, and unhappy; he commanded the Dragon who was his preceptor for the precepts to announce the foregoing matters to all the dragons:
"You must destroy the body of Gautama for my sake."
At that time, the various evil nāgas, wishing to fly through the air, were unable to go. They said to the Precept-Dependent:
"We respectfully received your command and intended to go and destroy [the place], but as soon as this thought arose, we were unable to proceed."
At that time, Śīlāśraya was struck with terror and thought to himself:

"If I were now to manifest the great power of Māra, I could cause the evil nāgas to give rise to wrathful indignation; through that wrathful indignation, they would be able to destroy the body of Gautama."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas and his followers transformed the interior of the nāga palace into a place filled with mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, stinging insects, venomous creatures, corpses, and human excrement; it was a foul-smelling place, strewn with filth and overflowing within.
When the nāgas saw this, they felt no joy in their own palaces and thought to themselves:
"Who has conjured these foul things? Though they pondered it, they did not know who had done so.

At that time, all the great dragon kings throughout the four continents, together with their male and female offspring and their retinues of both large and small, became filled with wrath and indignation; they immediately departed from their palaces and went to Mount Khadiraka at the foot of Mount Sumeru.

That mountain was level and smooth; at its summit was the place where a Great Sage had previously resided. The circumference and dimensions of that mountain were exactly forty thousand yojanas, and all its adornments were composed purely of the seven precious jewels. Even Nanda and Upananda, the dragon kings, together with their immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues, abandoned their own palaces and went to the Great Sage on Mount Kharāṭika to request his protection and deliverance.
Those nāgas exerted themselves like Mount Sumeru; yet upon reaching that place, their bodies all became as small as copper ladles.

Although they knew this to be so, they were unable to speak, each saying to themselves, "We wish to go, yet we cannot move. They then became greatly distressed and sat there in a state of angry resentment.
At that time, there was also the Naga King Sagara, accompanied by immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of followers; likewise the Naga King Elapatra,
the Naga King Supratiṣṭhita, the Naga King Takṣaka, the Naga King Anavatapta, and the Naga King Mucilinda...
The Nanda Dragon King, likewise the Sāgara Dragon King, likewise the Varuṇa Dragon King, likewise the Mahābhoga Dragon King,
likewise the Cakravāka Dragon King, likewise the Apalāla Dragon King, likewise the Śailabhadra Dragon King, and likewise the Gośīrṣa Dragon King.
Thus it was with the Nāga King Ālambūṣa; thus it was with the Nāga King Elāpattra;
thus it was with the Nāga King Ucchakalpa; thus it was with the Nāga King Varuṇa; thus it was with the Nāga King Salmali;
thus it was with the Nāga King Karkoṭaka; thus it was with the Nāga King Khiraki.
Thus there is the Dragon King Jalavāhana, thus the Dragon King Anjanasucitti, thus the Dragon King Kanakapiṇḍana, thus the Dragon King Śakrośravas,
and so on up to the Dragon King Nimīlita, up to the Dragon King Śvetahastapārśva, and up to the Dragon King Devila.
...down to the nāga king Deva-pāñcāla, down to the nāga king Devaka, down to the nāga king Elāpattramukha,
down to the nāga king Divyacakṣus-rakta, down to the nāga king Abhirūpa, down to the nāga king Prabhācara,
and down to the eighty-six thousand [nāgas] of this Jambudvīpa land.
At that time, all those great nāga kings— each one of them with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues—
came together to this place where the holy man was, entreating him for rescue and relief.

In this manner, throughout the eighty-four thousand oceanic islands, in each and every island there were immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of nāgas, who each abandoned their palaces and residences and came to the great holy site of Kharatī for the sake of rescue and relief.

Likewise, in the continent of Uttarakuru, the dragon kings Nidhāna and Mahāviśva, each surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of dragons, came to this dwelling place of the holy one, seeking rescue and deliverance.

Likewise, from the continent of Pūrvavideha, the Naga King Sumālīkṣa and the Naga King Vāsukī, these two Naga Kings, surrounded by immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of attendants, have all come here seeking deliverance.

Likewise, from the continent of Aparagoyānī, the Naga King Hradodana and the Naga King Kumbhapa, these two Naga Kings, surrounded and followed by immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of naga attendants, came to this place where the Great Holy One dwells in order to seek rescue and relief.

At that time, furthermore, among all the eighty-four thousand islands within these four continents, there were all manner of nāgas—nāgas born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation—including their nāga wives, nāga men, nāga women, and nāga sons. For the sake of seeking salvation, they all came to the dwelling place of this Great Sage, the Muni; having arrived, they all became small in stature, like copper ladles.
Those nāgas, filled with anger and resentment, each thought to themselves:
"Our original bodies were like Mount Sumeru; how is it that we have now become so minute?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān saw all the nāgas coming into this abode of the Muni and all assuming such small bodies.
Having seen this, Pāpīyān felt distress in his heart; he was filled with anger, resentment, fear, and unease, and spoke to his armies and retinue: "Look at all these nāgas!

By my power, I have transformed their palaces into swarms of mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous flies, as well as various foul-smelling excrement and filth. They have all abandoned their own homes to come to the place of the Sage on the great mountain, yet they have entirely lost their power and no longer possess any autonomy; they are unable to harm the śramaṇa Gautama."
Then the great commander of Māra’s army, Śīlādhiṣṭhāna, addressed Pāpīyān, saying:
“Great King, do not grieve; please listen to my words.

These nāgas who have received such bodies were not transformed by the śramaṇa Gautama; rather, the nāgas themselves gathered in one place and, in jest, assumed these forms in the hope of finding a means to harm that son of the Śākyas.”
Māra Pāpīyas said: "That is well.
You should go quickly and inquire of that nāga: what words should be spoken and what means should be employed so that this śramaṇa Gautama may be broken and dispersed?"
"If it is reduced to fragments, my realm shall be superior, and the dragon palace will remain intact.

Then, the Great General of Māra’s Army, Kai-yi-zhi (Kai-ī-shih), surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions before and behind him, set out for that mountain from his own residence, traveling through the air.

At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed all past vows, penetrating and revealing them exhaustively and without remainder; he manifested the realization attained by all sages currently existing in the present world, the deeds performed by all Munis in their respective abodes, the completion of the conversion of all sentient beings, and the display of the vigorous spheres of activity of all Buddhas born into their families.
The life-spans attained by all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are of one kind, without any difference.
All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, and non-humans behold all the buddha-fields; their minds are filled with joy as various adornments are universally illuminated by light.
Among all the other Buddha-fields in the ten directions, this field’s radiance is the most supreme and magnificent; it has attained such excellence through the causes and conditions of merit.
All those possessing the five supernatural powers from the other Buddha-fields come to this field to make offerings to and pay homage to Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, all sentient beings of this Sahā world and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions entered within the Buddha’s body; such was the power of the samādhi of the Buddhas’ domain of supernormal penetrations.

When those sentient beings behold the light of the Buddha’s body, it extends beyond all the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, filling them entirely; its radiance is so extraordinary that it eclipses all other lights.
At their respective seats, they spoke thus:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is inconceivable; we have never before heard of or seen such a one.

Having spoken these words, those bodhisattvas each made offerings to the Tathāgata with various flowers, incense, precious robes, *kāṣāyas*, necklaces, and all kinds of music. Having completed their offerings, they circumambulated him to the right hundreds of thousands of times, prostrated themselves, and then all withdrew to sit down.

At that time, this great assembly—including all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and even all humans and non-humans—also prepared various kinds of offerings. Having performed prostrations and circumambulated him to the right as before, they all withdrew to sit down and listened to the Dharma in this manner.
At that time, the great leader of the māra armies, Śīlāśraya, was wandering upon the land of Jambudvīpa together with his retinue.
At that moment, the Tathāgata sat amidst the assembly, manifesting his eternal body, serene and unmoving.
Upon seeing this, the Great General of the Māra army thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama manifested a massive body, yet now he has returned to his original form and sits upright in the kingdom of Magadha no differently than before. He might see my great host of Māra troops; fearing them, he may lose his strength and no longer possess his supernormal powers."
Then that Great General of Māra’s army, Śīla-adhiṣṭhāna, thought to himself:

“The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great skill and wisdom; he might perhaps conceive an evil intent toward me. I shall now go first to where Gautama is, to observe his magical arts and skillful means, and test him through discussion to examine his deceptions.”
Then the great Māra general, Śīlāśraya, surrounded by his retinue, approached the Buddha’s dwelling and stood before the Tathāgata,
speaking these verses: “Having not yet been able to deliver yourself, nor having escaped from the ocean of birth and death,
why do you deceive other classes of sentient beings by saying, ‘I shall establish you in nirvāṇa’?”
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to the great Māra general, Śīlāśraya, speaking in verse:
"I have long since transcended the ocean of saṃsāra, And shall no longer be born within the various realms of existence.
Out of compassion and pity for all living beings, I therefore proclaim the path of definitive deliverance."
In the past, throughout countless eons, you already gave rise to the most supreme bodhicitta;
having encountered the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, you practiced generosity and upheld the precepts.
Thus, having already reverently made offerings to billions of past Buddhas,
you shall attain this pure vehicle; I now decisively grant you this prediction that in the future you will become a Buddha just like me— how then can you say such things to deceive sentient beings?
"I now bestow upon you the eye of wisdom, so that you may reflect upon the origins and details of your past lives.
At that time, Mārajit, who relied upon the precepts, immediately attained the knowledge of past existences;
having practiced the ascetic disciplines and the rigors of *dhūta* while cultivating meditation, he became fully clear regarding the fruits of karma and his own merit.

At that time, having heard this verse, the Great Mara General Śīlāśraya recalled his past roots of merit and fortune; he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the Tathāgata, tears falling from his eyes, and kneeling with palms joined, spoke these words:
“Tathāgata, World-Honored One!

I am filled with great remorse and profound shame; I am like a great fool, as if lost, as if intoxicated, or as if possessed by a demon. I recall that in the past, throughout one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I exerted the power of great diligence to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I practiced the six pāramitās, cultivated the noble path, and performed various meritorious deeds. I encountered Buddhas appearing in the world, making all manner of offerings, hearing and receiving the sublime Dharma, and giving rise to great vows.

Even during the Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, there was a bhikṣu who taught the Dharma of the śrāvakas and a follower of the Mahāyāna who taught the Dharma of the bodhisattvas; at that time, my mind was deluded and my speech was wicked as I slandered those teachers, claiming their words were the speech of Māra or his retinue, and I spoke of the faults of the Hīnayāna to those followers of the Mahāyāna.
Because of such causes and conditions of harsh speech, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa did not bestow upon me the prediction of my attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi therein.
Due to the karmic conditions of those sins of harsh speech, I was born here in this realm of the Lord of Death; it has already been fifty-seven billion thousand years since I received this body.
“World-Honored One!

I would rather undergo the sufferings of hell for another six hundred thousand years than, for even a single thought-moment, lose the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much less would I ever retreat from the mindfulness of the four *brahma-vihāras*?”
"Having thus repented for the first and second times, and likewise for the third time, as well as for their remaining kinsmen, they further resolved:

'Throughout the past cycle of transmigration, and likewise in the future within the ocean of birth and death or in the hells, we shall never for a moment retreat from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"
The Buddha said: "General, excellent, excellent!"

"Good son! If there were someone who lit a great lamp as large as Mount Sumeru and offered it, along with the seven precious treasures, to all Buddhas throughout immeasurable ages, this mass of merit would not equal that of someone who, with a sincere heart of compassion, gives rise to the bodhicitta."
Why is this? For one who gives rise to such a mind, even the merit of making offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past is surpassed by this; it is the most supreme.
You, son of good family!
"Now exhaust these sins and harbor no other thoughts; within the five aggregates of birth and death, amidst all states of existence, you shall attain the body of a Guide.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Precept-Dependent (Śīlāśraya) attained the Dharma-patience of Accordance (Anulomikī-kṣānti) right where he sat. Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and immediately removed the priceless precious robes, pearls, and necklaces from his person to offer them as an offering to the Tathāgata.
Having finished the gift, he spoke a verse, asking:
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate all dharmas?
How does one realize that everything is entirely empty, observe the world as being like a bubble of water, and exhaust the bonds of ignorance within all realms of existence?"

All false views are by nature unreal; having attained the supreme mind of patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one constantly proceeds upon the path to enlightenment and is able to bring sentient beings to liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered the one who relied on the precepts by speaking these verses:
"The four kinds of minds, immovable as mountains, Only those of wisdom can possess;
They endure all manner of sufferings for immeasurable billions of kalpas, Out of compassion for all sentient beings."
The Buddha taught that one should firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts, not violating even a single point;
thus, one can fully and perfectly practice all the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

At that time, the eighty-four thousand māra armies and the retinue of the Bodhisattva Śīlāśraya, having heard that Śīlāśraya had received his prediction, were filled with great joy. They immediately repented before the Buddha with all their hearts, and they all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this bodhicitta is called the "samādhi-conforming bodhicitta."
Having attained this state of mind, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; each one removed their garments to offer as alms, and having given them, they sat down.

At that time, Pāpīyān, seeing that his military commanders and their retinues had taken refuge in the Buddha, felt a surge of anger and resentment, becoming distressed and uneasy. He was struck with even greater terror and spoke these words:
"I have now escaped from the belly of the śramaṇa, yet I have lost my followers; I do not know how many others will escape from here."
"How many people are there who have become disciples of the Buddha?
Quickly close the city gates; do not allow a single person to go outside, so that they may dwell in peace within the realm of Māra."

At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded three kinds of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) for that assembly of Māra and his retinue: namely, the objective support of sentient beings, the objective support of phenomena, and the absence of objective support, as explained in the "Chapter on the Eye of Space."

At that time, all the devas and nāga kings assembled together and dwelt within the abode of the Sage Muni on Mount Kharadī. Each of those nāgas saw their own forms become as small as copper spoons; they wished to move but were unable to do so. Their wanderings were cut short and they fell into despair, longing for their former bodies. Distressed by their tiny forms, they writhed there, lacking any autonomy. Their hair stood on end with fear, and they all went together to the presence of the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda, prostrated themselves, and spoke these words:
"Great Kings!..."
"In my dragon kingdom, all the mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, venomous insects, filth, and various impurities that exist now are all the doing of Gautama."
Therefore, we have all abandoned our palaces and homes to come here seeking salvation, yet we are still unable to escape this small body and its terrors.
"If you can take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, you may obtain liberation.
At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda spoke these words:

"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses many skillful means and various illusory arts; he was able to place all the buddha-fields of Sahā within his own body. He has likewise conjured all manner of evils upon our dragon abode, causing us to be terrified and come here to seek salvation."

"Now this śramaṇa has lost his own power; he possesses no further skillful means, divine powers, or esoteric arts. His body is now just as it was before, sitting upon his old seat; how could he possibly save me?"
"Since these small-bodied beings have already created this hell and placed me within it such that none can depart, how could they possibly rescue us and free us from fear?

All dragons are subject to Pāpīyān; in the Desire Realm, there is only the power of Māra as sovereign. You should now pay homage and seek deliverance from this calamity, so that each may return to his home and dwell in peace."
At that time, the Dragon King Elāpattra spoke again, saying:
"You dragons, do not give rise to distress. Why is this?

The śramaṇa Gautama has already subdued the retinue of Māra; his ministers and the people have become his disciples. Only the King of Māras remains, having lost both his original resolve and his supernatural powers; how then could he possibly rescue you?

When the dragon kings heard what Elāpattra had thus said, some prostrated before the Four Great Kings, some prostrated before Śakra Devendra, some prostrated before Suyāma, some prostrated before Saṃtuṣita, some prostrated before Nirmāṇarati, some prostrated before Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and some prostrated before Mahābrahmā.
At that time, Sāgara the Nāga King spoke again to all the nāga kings, saying:
"Do you not see those various celestial kings, humans, non-humans, and the diverse classes of sages and worthies, who pay homage and make offerings to the śramaṇa Gautama and take refuge in him?"
At that time, the nāgas returned once more to take refuge with other sages and seers.
At that time, there were six sages on the summit of that mountain:
the first was named Suśīma; the second, Nātha; the third, Arciṣmat; the fourth, Vīryaka; the fifth, Bhargava; and the sixth, Jyotirasa (translated into Chinese as Guǎngwèi, "Light-Taste").

Among all those nāgas, some took refuge at the side of Suśīma and prostrated; some took refuge in Naḍa; some prostrated to Aśokadatta; some prostrated to Vīraka; some took refuge in Bhagīratha; and some took refuge in Śuci-rasa.

All those nāgas, having taken refuge in these six sages, entreated them for rescue and deliverance; these six sages, who had attained the five supernormal powers, each resided on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains.
Those five holy men were all in the presence of the great sage Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suciloma, listening to the True Dharma.
At that time, Bodhisattva Suciloma also praised the divine virtues of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni with various and immeasurable words.
At that time, the five sages all heard the sound of all the dragon kings weeping and begging for deliverance.
Having heard it, they immediately arose and addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suśīlaprabha, saying:
"Virtuous One, have you perhaps heard the sound of those dragons crying out, wailing, and seeking rescue?"
He replied, “I have heard it. “O Mahāsattva! [he said.]
"O Holy One, at this moment all the nāgas are in a state of great anguish; if we, upon hearing of this, still wish to go and rescue them, how much more so should you, O Virtuous One?
We pray only that you will, out of compassion, go to that place and deliver all the nāgas, granting them liberation."
Then the great sage Śucivara said: "You may go;
I have not yet reached the point of going. Why is that? Because—"

Within this assembly, hundreds of thousands of Mahādevas, nāga kings, and yakṣas now sit before me; they inquire about the four Brahma-vihāras that are free from obstacles, and with joyful hearts, they listen to what I say.

Then the five holy men, having prostrated before the Great Being Viśvāmitra and circumambulated him three times, flew up into the air by means of their supernormal powers and arrived at the dwelling place of the Sage Muni on the summit of Mount Kailāsa.
At that time, all the dragon kings there, seeing the five noble ones, felt great joy in their hearts; they paid homage with reverence and spoke these words:

"O great seers, you who possess merit and virtue, adorned with all wisdom and skillful means, you have already reached the further shore amidst suffering and affliction. We pray that you will rescue us from this evil prison and grant us liberation."
Those five noble ones replied thus:
"We cannot rescue you. Why is that? Because..."

Nowadays, there is a great bodhisattva on the Snowy Mountains named Suśīla, who possesses the greatest wisdom and profound skillful means among all holy beings. That bodhisattva can grant you liberation; you should seek his compassion with a single-minded heart and entreat him.

Upon hearing this, the nāgas, though possessing diverse bodies, joined their palms together in unison and, from afar, paid respectful homage toward the sage Śucivira, all proclaiming these words: "O Virtuous Sage!
"May you rescue me! May you have compassion for me!

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suḍṛśa, hearing the Dragon King cry out for rescue, immediately set forth from the Snowy Mountains with Mahādeva, Kiṃnaras, and hundreds of thousands of millions of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas surrounding him before and behind. By means of his supernormal powers, he ascended into the air and traveled to the summit of Mount Kālaparvata.
At that time, the various dragon kings, seeing the holy man, each paid homage with palms joined in reverence. With one mind and in unison, they spoke these words:

"Great Sage, Holy One, we pray that you will rescue and deliver us! Grant us liberation from within this prison, so that we, ourselves and our retinues, may return home in safety, free from all suffering and affliction."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śuddharaśmi, who was skilled in expedient means and understood the causal conditions of the world, wished to explain the laws of the constellations for the sake of the nāgas:
"As for the laws of the constellations, each has its specific degrees and its harmonious seasonal timing; when they coincide, it is easy, but when they do not, it is difficult."
"The time has not yet converged, so liberation cannot be attained. Listen attentively to the sequence, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
This present month is named Śravaṇa; the lunar mansion is named Punarvasu. Punarvasu belongs to this fifth month, and this month, in turn, is governed by the Sun Deity."
"You dragon kings, the timing has not yet harmonized with these constellations.
At that time, Sāgara Dragon King addressed the Bodhisattva Sucitti-rasa, saying: "Great Being!"
By whom were these constellations originally taught?
Who created the great stars, who created the small stars, and who created the sun and moon?
On which day does which star appear first?
Furthermore, who established the thirty days of the month, the twelve months, and the year within the empty sky?
What constitutes time?
To what is it bound, what is its lineage, and who is its name?
What is good and what is evil? What is food and what is almsgiving?
What constitutes day and what constitutes night? How do the sun, moon, and stars move? What is called the first day of the lunar month, and what is the full moon?
If they are categorized by time-periods or by their course through the heavens, how many are there in each case?
Furthermore, how do they pause, and for how long do they travel? Which are light and which are heavy?
What is conjunction and what is non-conjunction?
What constitutes great power and what constitutes little power?
What is meant by the successive progression of the day?
How many shadows does it cast when moving upward, and how many when moving downward?
How many paces of shadow are designated as the first turning of the cycle?
Why is it that the moon moves north and south?
What is the sequence, O Great Being?

You are the foremost and most honored among all holy ones; we pray that you will compassionately explain it fully for us, so that having heard it, we may be liberated from suffering and practice accordingly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Suḍṛśa addressed the nāgas, saying: "Great King!
In a past age, at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there was a great city named Campā, where the people lived in harmony and great prosperity."
