"In the dark fortnight of the second month: on the first day it coincides with Kṛttikā; on the second day, Rohiṇī; on the third day, Mṛgaśiras; on the fourth day, Ārdrā; on the fifth day, Punarvasu; on the sixth day, Puṣya; on the seventh day, Aśleṣā; on the eighth day, Maghā; on the ninth day, Pūrvaphalgunī; on the tenth day, Uttaraphalgunī; on the eleventh day, Hastā; on the twelfth day, Citrā; on the thirteenth day, Svātī; on the fourteenth day, Viśākhā; and on the fifteenth day, Anurādhā—thus the dark fortnight is complete."

"In the white fortnight: on the first day it is in conjunction with Wei; on the second day with Mao; on the third day with Bi; on the fourth day with Zi; on the fifth day with Shen; on the sixth day with Jing; on the seventh day with Gui; on the eighth day with Liu; on the ninth day with Xing; on the tenth day with Zhang; on the eleventh day with Yi; on the twelfth day with Zhen; on the thirteenth day with Jiao; on the fourteenth day with Kang; and on the fifteenth day with Di—this is the full moon of the white fortnight."

"In the second month, when the moon is full in conjunction with the lunar mansion *Viśākhā*, day lasts for fifteen periods and night lasts for fifteen periods; the sun moves toward the north, and at midday the shadow is six footprints long. The lunar mansion *Jyeṣṭhā* moves through the night and *Mṛgaśiras* is before the sun. The teacher of the Asuras, named Venus (*Śukra*), presides over this time. This is the season of the second month, and the deity of the bull (*Vṛṣabha*) presides over this month."

"In the dark fortnight of the third month: on the first day, it is in conjunction with the lunar mansion Fang (Hāstā); on the second day, with Xin (Citrā); on the third day, with Wei (Svātī); on the fourth day, with Ji (Viśākhā); on the fifth day, with Dou (Anurādhā); on the sixth day, with Niu (Jyeṣṭhā); on the seventh day, with Nü (Mūlā); on the eighth day, with Xu (Pūrva-āṣāḍhā); on the ninth day, with Wei (Uttara-āṣāḍhā); on the tenth day, with Shi (Abhijit); on the eleventh day, with Bi (Śravaṇā); on the twelfth day, with Kui (Dhaniṣṭhā); on the thirteenth day, with Lou (Śatabhiṣaj); on the fourteenth day, with Wei (Pūrvabhadrapadā); and on the fifteenth day, with Mao (Uttarabhadrapadā). This is the completion of the dark fortnight."

"In the bright fortnight, on the first day it is in conjunction with the asterism Bi; on the second day, with Zi; on the third day, with Shen; on the fourth day, with Jing; on the fifth day, with Gui; on the sixth day, with Liu; on the seventh day, with Xing; on the eighth day, with Zhang; on the ninth day, with Yi; on the tenth day, with Zhen; on the eleventh day, with Jiao; on the twelfth day, with Kang; on the thirteenth day, with Di; on the fourteenth day, with Fang; and on the fifteenth day, with Xin—this is the full moon of the bright fortnight."

"In the third month, when the moon is full in conjunction with the lunar mansion Heart (Hṛdayā), the day lasts sixteen periods and the night fourteen periods; the sun moves toward the north, and at midday the shadow is four footprints long. The mansion Base (Vaiśravaṇa) moves through the night and the Beak (Mṛgaśiras) stands before the sun. The solar day is named Buddhakaṣṭha; during this time, soft activities are performed. This is the third month, presided over by the deity of the Twin Birds (Yamī)."

"In the dark fortnight of the fourth month: on the first day, it is in conjunction with the constellation Wei (Tail); on the second day, with Ji (Winnowing Basket); on the third day, with Dou (Dipper); on the fourth day, with Niu (Ox); on the fifth day, with Nu (Woman); on the sixth day, with Xu (Emptiness); on the seventh day, with Wei (Danger); on the eighth day, with Shi (Room); on the ninth day, with Pi (Opening); on the tenth day, with Kui (Crane); on the eleventh day, with Lou (Maiden); on the twelfth day, with Wei (Stomach); on the thirteenth day, with Mao (Horn); on the fourteenth day, with Bi (Net); and on the fifteenth day, it is in conjunction with Zi (Beak)—thus the dark fortnight is full."

"In the bright fortnight: on the first day it is in conjunction with the constellation Zhen (參); on the second day, with Jing (井); on the third day, with Gui (鬼); on the fourth day, with Liu (柳); on the fifth day, with Qi-xing (七星); on the sixth day, with Zhang (張); on the seventh day, with Yi (翼); on the eighth day, with Zhen (軫); on the ninth day, with Jue (角); on the tenth day, with Kang (亢); on the eleventh day, with Di (氐); on the twelfth day, with Fang (房); on the thirteenth day, with Xin (心); on the fourteenth day, with Wei (尾); and on the fifteenth day, it is in conjunction with Ji (箕)—this is the full moon of the bright fortnight."

"In the fourth month, when the moon is full in conjunction with the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā, the day lasts for seventeen time-units (muhūrta) and the night for thirteen; the sun travels toward the north, and at midday the shadow of the sun is two footprints long. The lunar mansion Rohiṇī moves through the night, and the sun follows the asterism Puṣya. This is the time of the fourth month, when the deity Karkaṭaka presides over that month."

"In the dark fortnight of the fifth month: on the first day, the moon is in conjunction with the *Dou* mansion; on the second day, with *Niu* and *Nü*; on the third day, with *Xu*; on the fourth day, with *Wei*; on the fifth day, with *Shi*; on the sixth day, with *Pi*; on the seventh day, with *Kui*; on the eighth day, with *Lou*; on the ninth day, with *Wei*; on the tenth day, with *Mao*; on the eleventh day, with *Bi*; on the twelfth day, with *Zi*; on the thirteenth day, with *Shen*; on the fourteenth day, with *Jing*; and on the fifteenth day, with *Gui*. This is the completion of the dark fortnight."

"In the waxing moon, on the first day it is in conjunction with the constellation Willow (Jyeṣṭhā); on the second day, with the Seven Stars (Uttarā-phalgunī); on the third day, with the Tension (Pūrvā-phalgunī); on the fourth day, with the Wings (Hasta); on the fifth day, with the Pivot (Citrā); on the sixth day, with the Horns (Viśākhā); on the seventh day, with the Neck (Anurādhā); on the eighth day, with the Base (Jyotiṣka); on the ninth day, with the Chamber (Mūla); on the tenth day, with the Heart (Pūrva-āṣāḍhā); on the eleventh day, with the Tail (Uttara-āṣāḍhā); on the twelfth day, with the Winnowing Basket (Abhijit); on the thirteenth day, with the Dipper (Śravaṇā); on the fourteenth day, with the Ox (Dhaniṣṭhā); and on the fifteenth day, it is in conjunction with the Woman (Śatabhiṣaj). This is the fullness of the waxing moon."

"In the fifth month, when the moon is full in conjunction with the lunar mansion Nǚ (Virgo), the day lasts eighteen *muhūrta* and the night lasts twelve *muhūrta*. The sun reaches its northernmost limit; at midday, the shadow is half a footstep long. The lunar mansion Jī (Bootes) moves through the night while the Heart (Cancer) mansion stands before the sun; at this time, the radiance of the sun’s flames is most intensely blazing."
During this fifth month, the deity Lion presides over it. "In the dark fortnight of the sixth month: on the first day, it is in conjunction with *Xū*; on the second day, with *Wēi*;

on the third day, with *Shì*; on the fourth day, with *Pì*; on the fifth day, with *Kuī*; on the sixth day, with *Lóu*; on the seventh day, with *Wèi*; on the eighth day, with *Miǎo*; on the ninth day, with *Bì*; on the tenth day, with *Zǐ*; on the eleventh day, with *Shān*; on the twelfth day, with *Jǐng*; on the thirteenth day, with *Guǐ*; on the fourteenth day, with *Liù*; and on the fifteenth day, it is in conjunction with *Qīxīng*. Thus, the dark fortnight is complete."

"In the bright fortnight, on the first day it is in conjunction with the constellation Zhang (Jyeṣṭhā); on the second day, with Yi (Śravaṇā); on the third day, with Zhen (Dhaniṣṭhā); on the fourth day, with Jiao (Aśvinī); on the fifth day, with Kang (Bharaṇī); on the sixth day, with Di (Kṛttikā); on the seventh day, with Fang (Rohiṇī); on the eighth day, with Xin (Mṛgaśiras); on the ninth day, with Wei (Ārdrā); on the tenth day, with Ji (Punarvasu); on the eleventh day, with Dou (Puṣya); on the twelfth day, with Niu and Nü (Maghā and Pūrvaphalgunī); on the thirteenth day, with Xu (Uttaraphalgunī); on the fourteenth day, with Wei (Hasta); and on the fifteenth day, with Shi (Citrā). This is the full moon of the bright fortnight."

"In the sixth month, when the moon is full in conjunction with the lunar mansion Śravaṇā, the day lasts for seventeen muhūrtas and the night for thirteen muhūrtas. The sun moves strongly toward the south; at midday, the shadow of the sun is two footprints long. The lunar mansion Rohiṇī moves through the night, while Revatī stands before the sun. The moon-child named Jñāna presides over this period."
During these six months, the goddess of the heavens presides over each month.

In the dark fortnight of the seventh month: on the first day it conjoins with Bi; on the second day, with Kui; on the third day, with Lou; on the fourth day, with Wei; on the fifth day, with Mao; on the sixth day, with Bi; on the seventh day, with Zi; on the eighth day, with Shen; on the ninth day, with Jing; on the tenth day, with Gui; on the eleventh day, with Liu; on the twelfth day, with Qi-xing; on the thirteenth day, with Zhang; on the fourteenth day, with Yi; and on the fifteenth day, it conjoins with Zhen—thus the dark fortnight is complete.

"In the bright fortnight, on the first day it is in conjunction with the constellation Ārdrā; on the second day, with Rohiṇī; on the third day, with Mṛgaśiras; on the fourth day, with Ārdrā; on the fifth day, with Punarvasu; on the sixth day, with Puṣya; on the seventh day, with Āśleṣā; on the eighth day, with Maghā; on the ninth day, with Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī; on the tenth day, with Hastā; on the eleventh day, with Citrā; on the twelfth day, with Svātī; on the thirteenth day, with Viśākhā; on the fourteenth day, with Anurādhā; and on the fifteenth day, it is in conjunction with Jyeṣṭhā—this is the full moon of the bright fortnight."

"In the seventh month, when the lunar mansion Revatī is full, the day lasts sixteen periods and the night lasts fourteen periods; the sun moves closer to the south, and at midday the shadow is four footprints long. The lunar mansion Rohiṇī moves through the night while the lunar mansion Viśākhā stands before the sun; at this time, the teacher of the asuras named Venus exercises his influence."
"In this seventh month, the deity presiding over the scales shall take charge of that month.
At that time, Kharaśva addressed the host of devas, saying:
"Each of these months has its own presiding deity; you should provide relief and protection for the four kinds of sentient beings."
What are these four?
They are to rescue those on earth—humans, nāgas, yakṣas, and even scorpions and the like; all such beings as these are entirely to be saved.

For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, I have arranged the constellations according to their respective divisions, and have fully explained them down to the *muhūrta* periods and so forth; in whatever region or direction one may be, the activities undertaken therein shall accordingly increase and flourish.
Kharoṣṭhī joined his palms before the great assembly and said:
"In this manner, the sun, moon, years, seasons, and the major and minor constellations are established.
What are called the six seasons?"

The first and second months are called the season of warmth; the third and fourth months are called the season for sowing and planting; the fifth and sixth months are the time for seeking rain; the seventh and eighth months are the time when things are about to ripen; the ninth and tenth months are the time of cold and frost; and the eleventh and twelfth months are the time of heavy snow—thus these twelve months are divided into six seasons.
"Furthermore, there are eight great celestial bodies (nakṣatras), namely: Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, Venus, Mercury, the Sun, the Moon, and Rāhu."
Furthermore, there are twenty-eight minor lunar mansions, namely those from Mūla to Bharaṇī.
Having established them in this sequence and explained their dharmas, you all must both see and hear them.
"What do all you members of the great assembly think?
Is the matter of the Dharma I have established correct?
Do you take pleasure in the various karmic activities performed by the twenty-eight lunar mansions and the eight great stars?"
"Whether this is right or wrong, each of you should declare it.
At that time, all the devas, humans, ṛṣis, asuras, nāgas, kinnaras, and others joined their palms and spoke thus:
"As for this Great Ṛṣi, he is the most honored among devas and humans; even among the nāgas and asuras, none can surpass him. His wisdom and compassion are the foremost."

Because they have not forgotten their compassion for all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas, they have obtained meritorious retributions; having fulfilled their vows, their merit is like the ocean, and they are able to know all matters of the past, present, and future.
Among gods and humans, there is no one with such wisdom or such application of the Dharma as this:

regarding the application of the Dharma concerning days and nights, *kṣaṇas* and *kalās*, the great and small lunar mansions, and the phases of the moon—half-months, full moons, and the completion of years—no other sentient being is able to perform such a Dharma as this; may they all rejoice and bring us peace and happiness.
"Excellent, Great Virtuous One!
You bring peace and security to sentient beings.
At that time, the seer Kharoṣṭha spoke again, saying:
"These twelve months constitute the beginning and end of one year. Thus, the methods regarding the large and small stars, as well as the *kṣaṇa* and *nimeṣa*, have all been fully explained.
Furthermore, the Four Great Heavenly Kings are established; one King is placed at each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru, and each of these directions governs its respective sentient beings."
The Heavenly King of the North is named Vaiśravaṇa; within his realm there are many yakṣas.
The Heavenly King of the South is named Virūḍhaka; within his realm there are many kumbhāṇḍas.
The Heavenly King of the West is named Virūpākṣa; within his realm there are many nāgas.

The Heavenly King of the East is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; within his realm there are many gandharvas who provide protection in all four directions and intermediate quarters, and he likewise stations spirits and deities to guard all continents, islands, cities, and towns.

At that time, after the ṛṣi Kharoṣṭha had finished preaching the Dharma, the great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all exclaimed, "Excellent! and rejoiced immeasurably.
At that time, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others made offerings to Kharoṣṭha day and night.

Subsequently, after the passage of immeasurable aeons, another seer named Gargya appeared in the world; he further explained in detail the arrangement of the lunar mansions, as well as the essential rules regarding the small and large months and the seasons.
At that time, the nāgas at the hermitage of the sages on Mount Khararīṣṭha honored and revered the seer Arciṣmān with all their nāga power, making offerings to him.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 42; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 43.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: Dispatching Messengers, from the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the Bodhisattva Light-Taste, saying:
"Virtuous One!..."

He is thus able to recollect various kinds of wholesome karma and immeasurable past events from such eons of his former lives, never forgetting them; furthermore, he fully understands and explains, without omission, the methods for illuminating and establishing the constellations and stars in space, being the most honored and supreme within the three realms, with wisdom foremost and unsurpassed by any other.

Therefore, that nāga and we ourselves have, through such skillful means, attained liberation from this hell and are freed from suffering and affliction. Out of compassion for sentient beings and loving-kindness toward all, our meritorious conduct and precepts, as well as our *brahmadatta*, adorn the mind and bring all things to fulfillment.
At that time, Prabhāsa spoke to the nāgas, saying:
"I am not now the ascetic seer Khaṇḍa-kaśyapa, nor am I able to place the constellations in the midst of the sky; what I speak of now is known through the power of supernormal knowledge."
"You, Sāgara and all you dragon kings, do not speak thus, saying that I truly cannot.
However, the account of the past causes and conditions concerning this seer Khaṇḍa has not yet been fully told."
"At that time, Śakra and the various Brahmās each turned toward the seer Kharassṭha, joining their palms together and speaking thus:
'We wish to hear; we pray only that you will speak further.'"
We, the Brahmās, are the most honored among the gods, just as the Great Sages are the most honored among holy men.

Among my gods, there are those who practice the holy life; whatever various divine spells or incantations they may employ, I fully understand them all and am likewise able to analyze and explain them extensively for others.
Then the Ṛṣi Śita said, "If you can do so, you may likewise teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to know this.
At that time, Śakra Devendra, the Lord of Devas with blue eyes, was present in the assembly; the Ṛṣi Śita spoke to Śakra, saying:
"O Lord of Devas!
May all wholesome dharmas be fully established and maintained in the world so that they may always illuminate it; protect those who practice wholesome dharmas and do not abandon them."

If there are sentient beings who are diligent, delight in the good, uphold the precepts, possess much learning, cultivate meditation, and study wisdom—such as these multitudes—the Lord of Devas should provide them with all necessities: clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; bestowing these various gifts without end.

Having already expounded the dharmas of the void and the constellations, I shall now speak of how, within each of the various regions of this world, there are nāga kings who reside and maintain watch. Such as the nāga kings Sāgara, Varuṇa, Takṣaka, Ratnapāla-mahācaryā, Gośara, Vasuva, Hurukukṣa, and Vāsikukṣa—these eight nāga kings protect the great ocean and are able to ensure that the great ocean neither increases nor decreases.
Anuṭaci, Vicakṣus, Varuṇa, and Utpalaka—these four nāga kings protect the lake from which all rivers issue; therefore, the various rivers flow forth without ever being exhausted.
Nanda and Upananda—these two dragon kings protect the mountains; therefore, the mountain forests are lush and verdant.
Vasuki, Sālirah, Karkoṭaka, and Gomati also act as guardians.
Viliśa, Jambuka, and Rakta-akṣa Śarabhadri protect the small rivers.
Siddhamanu, Arasuma, and Harucandra provide protection for the sages and all medicinal herbs; Dṛḍha, Kiṃśuka, and Nandika provide protection within the earth.
Jyotiṣprabha, Vidyutprabha, and Vīryaśikhin—these provide protection against fire.
Cundī, Māṇibhadra, and Kuberaka—these provide protection against wind.
Urapo, Rājāya, and Tilasara—these provide protection among trees.
Uluhañca and Phaggurāsī—these provide protection among flowers.
Gandharva, Cāṇḍāla, and Pūrṇakalā—these provide protection within the fruits.
Aśvalamba, Viṣkambha, Dāruṇī, and Drumarāja; among them, Viśvakarman, Somasūrya, Āśvaki, and Hayaśya—these four types provide supreme protection for all crafts.
The four types of yakṣas—Kira, Hūhū, Saṃghanāsa, and Araṇa, along with Bhayūka—are able to act as protectors in all matters such as merit and giving.
Vajranetra, Siṃhanetra, Sudarśananetra, and Triśūla—these four protect all nāgas; each of them acts as a protector in this manner.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Prabhārasa was the most supreme and most excellent among all sages, saints, devas, humans, and nāgas; out of compassion for all suffering beings, he therefore rescued these nāgas from their calamity and caused them to attain liberation.
The Bodhisattva Light-Taste reflected thus:
"How may I cause those nāgas to turn their minds toward and take refuge in the Triple Gem?
He then used skillful means and eloquent speech to instruct all the nāga kings in succession, saying:
"Those who place their faith in me, I truly cannot deliver and save them.

Now there is a Great Sage, a possessor of all-knowledge, who alone can bestow upon you peace and fearlessness. Regarding the merits of the rishi Kharassatha that I have praised, it was not through my own meager virtues that this matter was accomplished; such is the Dharma he teaches."
That noble one, in the past, during immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, had already cultivated various kinds of merit and was able to relinquish all things difficult to give up.

That is to say, elephants and horses, various precious chariots, wives and children, kingdoms and cities, gold and silver, palanquins and carriages, slaves and servants, clothing, couches, and bedding—whatever sentient beings require, he gives to them according to their wishes.

Furthermore, whether it be their hands, feet, ears, nose, tongue, body, head, eyes, sinews, bones, skin, flesh, or integument, they seek to give them away without any stinginess, so as to swiftly fulfill the six *pāramitās*. Possessing great compassion, they are able to bring suffering beings to liberation; for the sake of securing peace and stability for all sentient beings, they remain even within the midst of hell, never for a moment abandoning their resolve to rescue beings. They do not do this for their own attainment of the Buddha-way, but desire to cause all sentient beings in the evil realms to escape the various sufferings of old age, illness, and death.
"This Great Seer, throughout boundless kalpas in the distant past, has undergone these various kinds of vows and practices.
Throughout life after life, this Seer has maintained firm diligence, valor, and compassion, guiding and receiving sentient beings to establish them on the path to Nirvana."

Furthermore, that rishi Kharasvatha had, throughout immeasurable kalpas, fully perfected all manner of merit and virtue; he was even born into the house of King Śuddhodana and conceived within the womb of Queen Māyā. Once born, he raised his hand and proclaimed:
"I am the most honored and most supreme in the three realms."

He emitted various kinds of light that were able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; by reason of these lights, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, humans, and non-humans were moved, and they all came together to make offerings.

Furthermore, at the time of birth, he took seven steps in each of the four directions; wherever his feet trod, lotus flowers emerged to support his feet. By the causal conditions of this walking with such footsteps, all mountains, rivers, lands, and the great oceans were stirred and trembled. Such was the manifestation of the merit of his birth.

Furthermore, O son of the Śākyas, you are able to bring about the liberation of all of us sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death; you lead us to the city of Nirvāṇa, which is tranquil, secure, and free from all fears.

When these words were spoken, all the devas, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, each scattered various kinds of precious jewels, mixed flowers, ointments, and powdered incense from the midst of the sky, raining down as it were, as an offering and with various praises.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Light-Taste (Prabhārasa) spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"In immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, They practiced various forms of giving (*dāna*),
Maintained pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), Exerted diligence in seated meditation, and studied wisdom (*prajñā*)."
For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, he fully endured all manner of bitter sufferings.
Abandoning the sixty thousand queens and concubines within the palace as if casting off a pair of sandals,
he dwelt alone for six years practicing asceticism, consuming but a single sesame seed, a single grain of rice, or a single grain of barley each day.
Exerting diligence day and night without sleep, his body was reduced to nothing but skin and bone.
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree in deep contemplation, eight hundred thousand hosts of celestial Māras came;
from the four quarters, above and below, the earth and the sky were entirely filled for eighty *yojanas*.
Thus, the Māra armies and their retinues, all were able to be destroyed and brought to submission;
having accomplished unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi, they attained the fruit of the ultimate truth.
Seeing and hearing various things, they have no fear; their minds are as tranquil as nirvana.
Among all sentient beings, they always maintain an impartial mind of compassion, without partiality or favoritism.
Fully endowed with true wisdom, he instructs all devas and humans;
not a single sentient being gives rise to evil, for his compassion thus penetrates to the very marrow of his bones.
Furthermore, toward all classes of sentient beings, even down to ants and crawling insects,
they do not give rise to thoughts of affliction, disturbance, or malice; throughout the cycle of transmigration of all beings,
they are able to cause them all to attain liberation.
He pulls sentient beings out [of suffering] so that they may attain peace; whether they are as small as a mustard seed or large, the Great Sage goes to rescue them all.
He can dispel their evils and sorrows; therefore, the Great Sage comes out of compassion.
Through a mind of loving-kindness, I deliver you from this prison.

I shall extensively expound the boundless, profound, and essential secrets; may those who lack self-mastery all have their hearts' desires fulfilled, and may everyone return home to dwell in peace and security.
Those who obtain the salvation of that holy one do not fear the various kings of the garuḍas;
each returns to their own dwelling to roam at will, enjoying themselves as they did before, with no difference in their hearts.
The Great Sage, in the past, cultivated myriad practices, Never permitting the affliction or disturbance of a single sentient being.
Whatever calamities and evils you all possess, They are the deeds of the Mara King, not those of the Buddha.
Do not harbor further thoughts of slandering or reviling the Buddha; Accept my instruction and resolve for Bodhi.
"Do not give rise to doubt or malice, nor allow yourselves to be deluded and submerged; each and every point is exactly as I have previously explained.

At that time, all the great Dragon Kings, along with their entire retinues—male and female, great and small—who were in the presence of the Sage Muni, having heard this teaching, each focused their minds and together joined their palms, saying:
"Namo, Namo to the Great Sage!"
The most excellent among all beings in all worlds!

Possessing all dharmas and having reached the shore of mastery, you are able to grant liberation to all sentient beings, able to grant peace and happiness to all sentient beings, able to grant joy to all sentient beings, and able to cause all to reach the further shore of wisdom.

With impartial compassion toward all sentient beings, he causes them to cultivate and fully perfect wholesome dharmas; he brings to fruition all sentient beings who perform virtuous deeds, establishes them in the good paths and the eye of the true Dharma, and serves as a supreme field of merit among devas and nāgas.
"Most supreme and most honored among the three realms, you who are able to receive all the offerings of the world.
We dragons have together undergone great hardship, remaining within this prison unable to escape; thus, with utmost sincerity, we prostrate and take refuge in you."
Having spoken these words, all the nāgas and others regained their original forms; yet, despite returning to their former bodies, they were still unable to escape from that mountain.
At that time, all the dragon kings again addressed the Bodhisattva Light-Taste, saying:
"We pray that you will rescue us.
As the Great Virtuous One has said, those holy ones do not give rise to affliction or disturbance toward sentient beings, but always bestow peace and happiness."
These words are true; we now accept them with faith and without doubt.
If you have compassion for sentient beings and would rescue us with mercy, we pray only that you come quickly to deliver us from that demonic prison.
At that time, Prabhārasa addressed the nāgas, saying:

"That Great Sage is fully endowed with wisdom; the Muni Tathāgata’s mind is ever compassionate toward all sentient beings. He cultivates all that is wholesome and abandons all that is unwholesome, his great compassion universally covering all. Amidst the cycle of saṃsāra, he is diligent and courageous in guiding sentient beings, leading them to find peace and security upon the path to Bodhi."

Manifestly perceiving the accomplishment of the Buddha-eye through cause and effect, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, due to causes and conditions of non-anger throughout the distant past, fully perfected the four Brahma-vihāras of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

"Furthermore, regarding the arising of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path through causes and conditions: having arisen from causes and conditions, all matters concerning the various evil destinies as well as practices such as loving-kindness have already been fully explained."

"Furthermore, that Buddha, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, dwells in immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; because he has practiced the immeasurable and boundless pure conduct of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for as many eons as there are atoms, he has fully perfected the six *pāramitās*. Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas have emerged from the ocean of saṃsāra, he has reached the further shore of the wisdom of Great Nirvāṇa. Because he has destroyed the four Māras and succeeded to the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it remains unbroken, he is able to wash all sentient beings with the water of the Dharma, purifying all the stains of their afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, the Tathāgata, forever free from objective clinging, teaches the four Brahma-vihāras."

"Furthermore, it is said that the nature of reality (tathatā) transcends characteristics and is free from characteristics, and is detached from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). It is the inexhaustible skillful means (*upāya*) by which all phenomena are equal.

This means that through the contemplation of the true reality (*satya*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*), all phenomena such as the distinctions of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are extinguished. By these skillful means, one becomes detached from greed, hatred, and delusion; the essential nature of all afflictions (*kleśa*) is entirely empty."

There is no realm of sentient beings, free from all攀缘 (pāraṇa, objects of attachment); there is no joy, free from joy; no activity, free from activity; no things, free from things; and no perceptions, free from perceptions. It is without obstacles and without location; it is without dust, without defilement, without darkness, and without light; it cannot be grasped or held.
Without self and without other, neither coming nor going, without difference and free from conditioned activity—this extends to all aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The essence of the eye of wisdom is neither dark nor bright; it does not function and is not produced; it is the reality of the *dharmadhātu*.

It is neither extinguished nor destroyed; it is suchness (*tathatā*) and non-arising. The reality of the *dharmadhātu* is entirely empty; one thoroughly penetrates all past phenomena within this equality. This is the true object of focus, from which the Tathāgata is born.

If there is a bodhisattva who reaches the other shore within this Dharma, fully perfecting the six pāramitās—just as space is devoid of form and devoid of tangibility—and thus attains unobstructed wisdom of mind that universally severs everything, such that all views and habitual tendencies are entirely eradicated; having thus become free from all afflictions, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the fourfold Brahma-conduct that is free from conceptual observation.

When Prabhāsa had thus spoken this Dharma, the Dragon King Sāgara, the Dragon King Vikaṅgasusīma, the Dragon King Sumāhulu-kasa-ratnapāla, and other such dragon kings within that assembly—who had already cultivated merit and made great vows during their past bodhisattva practices—recalled their past lives and immediately attained the *dhāraṇī* of Radiant Illumination.
Furthermore, eighty nayutas of other dragon hosts, who had also in the past cultivated various vows and practices, all gave rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained samādhi.

At that time, Prabhārasa immediately transformed himself into the body of a sage with the form of a bodhisattva; together with the various seers, he traveled through the air by means of supernatural power to the place where the Tathāgata was.

Chapter Ten: The Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Division on the Sun Treasury, Chapter Ten: The Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha At that time, all the hosts of nāgas, having received with faith the words of the Bodhisattva Light-Taste (*Prabhārasa*), all with sincere hearts took refuge in the Buddha, took refuge in the Dharma, and took refuge in the Saṃgha.

When he was making this return, Māra Pāpīyān saw him with his own eyes and heard him with his own ears; having seen and heard this, he was greatly struck with wonder, alarm, and unease. With anger and sorrow, sweat flowed over his entire body; raising his hand to touch his head, he spoke this verse: "Haha!
Look at that great laughter— The deceitful and illusory deceiver of Śākya śramaṇas!
He has enticed and deluded all the nāgas to return to him, Bewildering and opposing all sentient beings."
Within the path of delusion, things are falsely established; in truth, what is expressed as "I" is not my true dharma.
When such true dharmas are attained, they should never be lost from beginning to end within that state.

At that time, after Pāpīyān had spoken these verses, there was among that assembly a māra-daughter named Vigatatamas. This māra-daughter, having planted many roots of virtue in the past, spoke as follows: "The śramaṇa Gautama possesses renown and merit;

if any sentient being hears the Buddha’s name and takes refuge with a single mind, no māras whatsoever can inflict harm upon that sentient being. How much more so for one who has seen the Buddha and personally heard the Dharma—whose various skillful means and profound, vast wisdom and understanding are so deep!"
"Your Majesty, the King, now wishes to give rise to an evil mind toward the Tathāgata and those who study the Buddha-way, but in the end he will not succeed.
At that time, Māra said:

"The śramaṇa Gautama has mastered the wisdom of True Suchness (tathatā), which is vast and great; he has deeply entered and become firm within the dharma of emptiness. Having himself crossed over the great ocean of birth and death, he also teaches sentient beings so that they too may escape it."
The demoness replied:

"As Your Majesty has said, if one awakens to the reality-limit within the dharmas of emptiness, even if there were a thousand million billion armies of all Māras, they would ultimately be unable to cause harm for even a moment."
"The Tathāgata has now opened the path to nirvāṇa; I wish to go there to take refuge in the Buddha.
She then spoke a verse for her father:
"Free from marks and unattached, the most excellent among men; Abiding eternally in suchness, the most honored among devas."
Having reached the city of wisdom on the other shore, I now wish to go and take refuge in them.
By training in the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I shall deliver all suffering sentient beings;
having attained mastery over all phenomena, may I in the future become like a Buddha.
At that time, after Vimardakāra had spoken these verses, all five hundred sisters of the māras who were his retinue within the palace of the father-king conceived the aspiration for bodhi.

At that time, when the Māra-king saw that the five hundred maidens in his palace had all taken refuge in the Buddha and resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), he became even more intensely enraged, terrified, and sorrowful. He then thought to himself:

"I shall now employ the power and majesty of a great Māra-king; within my own palace, at the seat where the Māra-king sits, I will exert the utmost supernatural transformations. At that place where the Sage-Muni resides, and at the gathering place of all the nāgas, I shall create great fire-stones and cause them to rain down like hail from the void all at once, shattering those nāgas and the seer Prabhāsa so that they are dispersed far and wide."
"If that one departs, my palace as the Māra King will then be at peace.
Having formed this thought, he immediately released great fire-hail from the sky, raining down upon him like rain.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Tathāgata transformed those fire-stones entirely into celestial flowers, which fell in profusion and scattered across the summit of Mount Khadiraka, completely filling the dwelling places of the sages; all the dragon kings were filled with joy.
At that time, when Māra saw the hailstones falling upon the dwelling place of the Holy One, he pointed to his five hundred women and said:

"Look well, my daughters! Now, as for all those dragon retinues and great assemblies who have taken refuge with the śramaṇa Gautama, I have already crushed them all into dust; how much more so could I not destroy my own palace!"
“If there be anyone in my palace who seeks to take refuge in Gautama, I must ensure that they become exactly like him and no different.
At that time, five hundred demonesses spoke these verses to Pāpīyān:
“If there are sentient beings who take refuge in the Buddha, Those people shall not fear billions of Māras.”
How much more so for those who wish to cross the stream of birth and death, reaching the shore of unconditioned nirvana!
If there are those who can take even a single flower or incense and scatter it before the Triple Gem— the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—
giving rise to a firm and courageous resolve, no demons whatsoever shall be able to destroy them.
How much more so for those who resolutely seek to become Buddhas!
Or again, those who come with a sincere heart to the presence of the Buddha and hear and receive even a single phrase of the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
they immediately resolve upon the non-regressive path to Bodhi and will certainly become the Honored One among all the multitudes.
Having attained the Buddha’s indestructible vajra-body, he is able to crush all the hosts of the four Māras.
Father King, merely observe how these nāgas and others each scatter clouds of various fragrant flowers;
only the World-Honored Buddha can fully comprehend this—it is not within the realm of the Māra King.
The sole Teacher abides in the world, Proclaiming the sublime and inconceivable;
All that he does is auspicious, Able to eliminate the karmic offenses of sentient beings.
All the immeasurable evils of our past have likewise been extinguished without remainder;
having taken refuge in the Buddha with utmost sincerity and single-minded devotion, we shall certainly attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, having heard these verses, Māra’s anger and fear redoubled, his mind consumed by distress; he sat alone within his palace, haggard and sorrowful.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhārasa, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma—whereby all sentient beings had completely abandoned objective clinging and attained the four Brahma-vihāras—descended from the air before the Buddha.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, the Bodhisattva Prabhārasmi, together with his great assembly, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew to stand with palms joined, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has taught this *dhāraṇī* for relying upon the mind and recollecting the four dhyāna stages; by the power of this *dhāraṇī* incantation, I recall that in the past there were two sons of Brahmins who, due to matters of desire, deserved to be put to death according to the law.

When his execution had not yet arrived, the king commanded the officials to place him in prison. For every half-month, he was given but a single meal; his body was bound with five fetters, his two hands and two feet were all secured in shackles, and his throat was constricted by a collar. Unable to endure the hunger and thirst, and further terrified that the time of his death was drawing near, he took refuge single-mindedly in the Buddha within the prison.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Mandāravagandha, who focused his mind on the Buddha’s side and cried out from afar for deliverance.

Then, out of compassion for sentient beings and for us, that Buddha manifested within his own seat the great supernormal power of the Buddha-realm and taught the *dhāraṇī* of the mental recitation based upon the four dhyāna stages, speaking these words:
"By the power of the Buddha, I cause those two brahmins in the hell to hear this *dhāraṇī* of the mental recitation based upon the four dhyāna stages."

Having heard this, they rejoice and maintain it with sincere mindfulness. By these causes and conditions, all their evil karma and all obstacles—whether the evil karma and obstacles of this present life, or the various obstacles of evil karma from many past lives; whether obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), obstacles to the Dharma (*dharmāvaraṇa*), obstacles regarding sentient beings (*sattvāvaraṇa*), obstacles to giving (*tyāgāvaraṇa*), obstacles to wisdom (*prajñāvaraṇa*), obstacles to livelihood (*ājīvāvaraṇa*), or obstacles of untimely death before the end of one’s natural lifespan; or the power of karmic forces that bind them to rebirth in realms where they do not wish to be born; or the obstacles of the heart that prevent them from going to pure Buddha-fields when they sincerely desire to be born there—all such things shall be eliminated.

Due to the cause and condition of hearing this *dhāraṇī* on the mental recollection based upon the four dhyāna stages, all such obstacles of evil karma—the fivefold shackles of the throat, hands, and feet—will spontaneously fall to the ground at once; they shall then obtain the power of the *dhāraṇī* within that very prison.

By means of his supernormal powers, he emerged from the prison and traveled through the air to the abode of the Buddha Maṇḍārava-gandha. There he paid homage and made offerings for the duration of his life, and immediately attained rebirth in the buddha-field of Mount Radiance (Giriprabhāsa).
“That Buddha-World-Honored One is named Cloud-Colored (Meghavarṇa).

Having requested ordination from Cloud-Colored Buddha, throughout immeasurable kalpas in birth after birth, he never failed to be born in a Buddha-field where a Buddha was present, always encountering the era of a Buddha just as in this current field. Within the Sahā world—the great trichiliocosm Buddha-land—filling both the earth and the void up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, humans and non-humans alike were all completely present.”

“At that time, all sentient beings in that buddha-field—whether on the earth, in the air, or up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—were likewise so: all those beings were fully possessed of evil karma and various obstacles. For the sake of these beings, that Tathāgata preached this *dhāraṇī* of mental recollection based upon the four dhyāna stages; thereby, all evils of body, speech, and mind were completely eliminated. If one hears and hears this *dhāraṇī*, by its power, all sinful karmas of the three periods of time will be extinguished without remainder.”
Furthermore, those sentient beings shall obtain various kinds of the *dhāraṇī* of the Human-Endurance Samādhi (*manuṣya-kṣānti-samādhi*).

Even when their lifespan is about to end and they have died here, if they desire to be born in a pure Buddha-field in another direction according to their wish, they shall be born there immediately upon that thought. They shall attain the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), always practice with diligent vigor the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), never again fall into the three evil realms, constantly be able to practice the six *pāramitās*, constantly practice the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), constantly behold the Buddhas, constantly hear the Dharma, constantly make offerings to the Saṅgha, constantly attain the four dhyānas and the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and constantly be fully endowed with the mindfulness of the four sublime abodes (*catvāri brahmavihārāḥ*).
"In life after life, may we always be born in harmony with that Dharma, never to be parted from it until the attainment of Nirvana.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! For the sake of bringing great benefit to sentient beings, you have spoken thus regarding the causes and conditions of your past lives and the initial resolve for enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Light Flavor (Prabhārasa), saying:
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or men, or...
Alternatively, there may be women who possess faith and, within the Three Vehicles or other paths, aspire to swiftly realize the path to *nirvāṇa* and exhaust all suffering;
who wish to attain the ability to retain all that they hear in their minds; who desire that all their actions of body, speech, and mind be pure;
who wish to protect the Buddha-dharma; and who seek various kinds of benefits. Planting [these roots...]
All kinds of clothing and food will be abundant; one will possess sovereignty, excellence, physical beauty, and great strength.

One’s retinue will be powerful and flourishing, and the land will be wealthy and peaceful. One’s rank will rise to high positions, and many will revere and honor them. Possessing intelligence and wisdom, they shall be most honored and supreme.

In all four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—they will never lack for anything, and they will delight in various forms of giving, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration.
In meditation, they attain all samādhis up to those of the Peak of Existence within the formless realm,
and they likewise delight in the four Brahma-abodes.

"If there are those who delight in dhāraṇīs and hope to obtain such various matters, yet their evil karma is firm, heavy, and thick— obstructed by karmic hindrances and afflictive hindrances— even their desire to be born in a pure Buddha-field will not be hindered."
For this reason, various virtuous vows will not be fulfilled according to one's heart's desire.

If one wishes to cause such various evil karmas to be swiftly extinguished, these sentient beings should bathe themselves clean, put on fresh and pure garments, observe the long fast with a vegetarian diet, and refrain from eating pungent or foul-smelling foods. In a quiet place, they should adorn a *bodhimaṇḍa*, and with right mindfulness, sit cross-legged—whether walking or seated—recalling the physical marks of the Buddha’s body so as not to allow the mind to become distracted, and must not entertain other conditions or think of other matters.

Whether for one day and night, or seven days and nights, without performing other activities, one should mindfully recollect the Buddha with a sincere heart. To the extent that one sees the Buddha—whether with slight mindfulness one sees him slightly, or with great mindfulness one sees him greatly—even one who possesses immeasurable mindfulness sees the Buddha’s form-body as infinite and boundless. Regarding that Buddha’s physical body and its thirty-two marks, one should both recollect and contemplate each individual mark until they are all clearly understood. Following whichever mark is seen, one perceives a blue light; one should focus the mind intently upon that radiant mark, ensuring the mind does not become distracted.
When forming this thought, recite this mantra:

"Tadyathā | Viśilinba | Viśilinba | Utpādāpaya viśilinba | Sna-pa-pha | Rosna-pa-thu | Ra-a-nu-na-ta-tha | Thi-a-nu-na-ta-tha | Thi-pu-hu-ta-koṭi-viśilinba | Viśilinba | Svāhā. In this manner, with a single mental image present before the mind, one should maintain focused mindfulness without giving rise to distracted thoughts. Then, recite this dhāraṇī mantra until one visualizes blue light radiating from the physical marks of the Buddha’s body; once that light has issued forth, it enters through the crown of the practitioner’s head.

At that time, settle your mind and do not be startled or terrified. Within your own body, you will see this light; like that blue color, contemplate this blue light as it travels through each and every limb throughout your body, until fire blazes within your entire body. Having seen the fire blazing, it continues until the body is reduced to ashes, which are then blown away and extinguished by winds coming from the four directions.

When contemplating in this way, one sees that one's own body possesses not a single characteristic, but exists only as emptiness; even throughout the ten directions, all is entirely empty, and not a single form is seen.
Thus, by reciting and upholding this mantra through the causal power of mindfulness of the Buddha’s blue color, one accomplishes this practice. "Good son!

If there is another person who, with a focused mind free from distraction, trains in the four dhyāna stages and relies upon the mind-recollection dhāraṇī, all that sentient being's karmic obstructions, afflictive obstructions, and obstructions to the Dharma—all their sinful karma—will be completely exhausted, with the sole exception of the five heinous crimes, the destruction of the True Dharma, and the slandering of noble beings."

"If there should be another person who delights in this way and is able to practice the aforementioned mindfulness of the Buddha-samādhi for one day and one night, they will be able to orally recite and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas, as well as the superior points of wisdom regarding the eighteen types of treatises of all non-Buddhist paths; thus, all such various phrases, meanings, and literary compositions shall be remembered and upheld without any forgetfulness."

Furthermore, in a single day and night, he attained the four dhyānas, the four kinds of supernatural powers, the four immeasurable practices, the four kinds of eloquence, as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); all such dharmas were fully accomplished and realized by him.
One who practices in this manner can, in as little time as a single snap of the fingers, reach a single buddha-field and even immeasurable fields.

Furthermore, with a single foot they can shake such immeasurable lands, and they can also cause even more than these lands to tremble. They can fill all these fields while sitting cross-legged with a single body.
In this way, they can cause the worlds to be filled with water; they can count and know all the atoms of the ten directions; and they can fill all realms with the seven treasures.
Furthermore, in a single thought-moment, those people can fully know the karmic retributions of birth and death—past, present, and future—as well as all the mental activities of every sentient being.

Furthermore, that practitioner is able, with a single body, to manifest various transformations into the bodies of all Buddhas, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devānām-pati, Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Cakravartin kings, extending even to water and fire pervading all of space.

Furthermore, for a person who contemplates in this way, within a single thought-moment, all the lands and spaces of the ten directions can be filled with various flowers and an abundance of the seven treasures; all manner of fragrant parasols, canopies, banners, and pennants, as well as various garments and various necklaces, can completely fill the entirety of empty space.

"If there is another person who, with a sincere heart, practices these four dhyāna stages and relies upon the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, thoroughly discerning and penetrating each of their distinctions, then that sentient being’s immeasurable evil karma will be completely exhausted.

Such a person will swiftly attain fulfillment within other vehicles regarding immeasurable merit, diligence, various *samādhis*, various *dhāraṇīs*, various *kṣāntis*, and the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). They will certainly and rapidly emerge from the ocean of saṃsāra; however, those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), slandered the Dharma, or reviled the noble ones shall not obtain this teaching."

That person must pass through seven periods of seven days; by relying upon this stage of the fourth dhyāna and internally cultivating the mind of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, one who constantly practices and does not abandon this teaching within this Dharma will have all their sins exhausted.

If one does not focus the mind, two parts of the transgression will be exhausted; if one applies the mind in the ordinary way, one part of the transgression will be exhausted. One must practice in this manner with a mind of diligence, pure faith, and reverent devotion; for those who can do so, that evil will be completely exhausted.

"Furthermore, if there is a person who, relying on these four dhyāna stages, practices the Buddha-remembrance samādhi—whether expounding it among the devas or among humans—and if those devas and humans listen to and receive this samādhi with faith, they will inwardly reflect upon it and give rise to joy."
If such a person is imprisoned with their body bound by fivefold shackles, or undergoes suffering and hardship in other places, they shall all be liberated and released.

Whether they have lost their livelihood or seek wealth; whether they are beaten or burned, or stand on the brink of a river; whether they are afflicted by poison or various enemies come to invade them; whether it be all manner of ghosts or all manner of illusions; whether it be the various terrors of kings, or quarrels and disputes within one’s own home, or others coming unprovoked in anger; whether it be the fear of death or the fear of falling into the evil realms—through these [practices], all such fears and karmic obstacles will be exhausted, and they will be reborn among gods and humans.

"Furthermore, if there should be a person who, upon hearing this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* based on the four dhyāna stages, single-mindedly believes in and accepts it—know that this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* possesses great power and great benefit. If even with slight application of the mind one obtains such results, how much more so when one applies oneself with a sincere heart free from doubt!"

When this dharma of samādhi was being taught, among the assembly there were eighty-six *bimbara* nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans who had come from the ten directions; those who had previously been perfumed and cultivated by this samādhi all attained that which was described above.

Furthermore, eighty-four nayutas of sentient beings attained the patience of the knowledge of suffering; immeasurable sentient beings attained this samādhi, or [attained fruits] ranging from the stage of stream-enterer to arhatship.

When immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta, those five hundred demonesses who had abandoned darkness, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, while in the palace of the Māra King, all attained this Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
they all cast off their original forms and obtained male bodies, because in the past they had practiced and studied this very Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.

At that time, these five hundred daughters of the Māra kings, having attained this samādhi and acquired male bodies, felt great joy in their hearts and desired to go to the Buddha’s dwelling. They all transformed themselves into the bodies of Great Brahmās, each Brahmā King surrounded by immeasurable thousands of billions of attendants;
or they manifested as the bodies of immeasurable Śakra-devānām-indras, likewise surrounded by thousands of billions of attendants.

Each having manifested such adornments with immeasurable varieties of music and ornaments, they descended from the palace of Māra toward the place where the Tathāgata was, and presented offerings; scattering various flower garlands, powdered incense, and unguents upon the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and circumambulated him three times to the right.
[He] withdrew to stand to one side. Chapter Eleven:

Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. From the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the "Sūryagarbha" Section: Chapter Eleven, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhārasa, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!"
"You should now know that all those dragons have completely exhausted the karmic offenses for rebirth in the evil realms.
He further addressed Prabhārasa:
"This is because they contemplate emptiness with their minds."
Then Prabhāsa said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with pure conduct; the Tathāgata shall act as an adornment for all the nāgas.”
"Furthermore, Prabhārasmi!
At that time, I was indeed among the nāgas, because I wished to explain extensively the distinctions in the karmic retributions of inconceivable deeds."

At that time, all the gods of the desire realm, down to the yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others, rained down various flowers from the midst of the sky, scattering various perfumes, garments, banners, pennants, necklaces of the seven precious gems, and various kinds of music.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas simultaneously raised their voices in song and praise, producing sublime sounds, while humans and non-humans alike paid them reverent homage.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and looked toward the north, surveying the four directions:
"What mountain here joins with Mount Sumeru, situated near the heavens of the Desire Realm and the Form Realm?"

At that time, the Tathāgata, surrounded on all four sides by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and all the eight classes of beings, proceeded toward Mount Sumeru with them escorting him from before and behind.
At that time, the Tathāgata wished to ascend the mountain by treading upon its base with his feet, proceeding step by step.

Knowing that the Buddha intended to climb to the summit of Mount Sumeru, Mahābrahmā and the other deities immediately created for the Tathāgata a staircase and bridge made of the seven precious gems, adorned with various celestial garments, flowers, incense, and powders.
Having done so, he came before the Buddha and said:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon my bridge.

For the sake of the Buddha, the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) likewise fashioned a precious bridge out of Jambūnada gold, scattering powdered nāga-candana upon it, and spoke these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon my bridge.
For the sake of the Buddha, the deva Sunirmita also fashioned a precious bridge out of celestial gold and scattered various powders of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood upon it, saying these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon my bridge."

The Tuṣita Heaven, likewise for the sake of the Buddha, fashioned a precious bridge out of celestial silver. They scattered upon the bridge the finest black sandalwood powder—subtle fragrances that emerge at the appropriate time—and spoke these words:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon our bridge."
The Suyāma devas likewise, for the sake of the Tathāgata, fashioned a jeweled bridge out of celestial lapis lazuli and scattered various kinds of fine powdered incense of tāmarasa leaves, saying:
"We pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon our bridge."

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, also for the sake of the Buddha, manifested a jeweled bridge out of red pearls; he scattered all kinds of celestial sandalwood and powdered jewels upon the bridge, and further covered it with celestial silks and exquisite nets of the seven precious gems.
Having covered it, they spoke these words:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon our bridge.

In this manner, the four Great Kings who guard the quarters likewise used rare celestial stone-treasure jewels to create jeweled bridges for the sake of the Tathāgata, and they also held various kinds of fine and exquisite celestial garments to cover the bridges.
Having covered it, he spoke these words:
“I pray only that the Tathāgata will ascend Mount Sumeru by means of my bridge.

At that time, the four great Asura kings, together with their retinues, for the sake of the Tathāgata, fashioned a precious bridge out of the *masāra* jewels they produced, and scattered fine powders of celestial gold and silver upon the bridge.
Having scattered [the flowers], he spoke these words:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will walk upon my bridge.

At that time, out of compassion for all those Brahmās, Śakras, the Four Great Kings, and the various celestial kings of the asuras, the World-Honored One simultaneously manifested eight Tathāgatas. These Buddhas were indistinguishable from one another in their thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and they were surrounded and escorted by the eight classes of beings, the fourfold assembly, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas.

When all those devas, asuras, and others had thus made such extensive preparations for the adornments, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, ascended the precious bridge to the summit of Mount Sumeru, or arose from one place and departed for another.

The bodies of those eight Tathāgatas were brilliantly radiant; from each and every Buddha-body, light was emitted, illuminating all at once like the radiance of hundreds of thousands of billions of suns and moons.

When these eight Buddhas had thus emitted light from their bodies, all the hosts of nāgas who were gathered and dwelling there at the site of the sages on Mount Kharaṭa saw them and all spoke in wonder:
"What place is this? Are these the eight Great World-Protectors who have now come to take up residence upon Mount Sumeru?"
At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda spoke these words:
"This is Brahmā, surrounded by all those of the desire and form realms, the most preeminent among all devas who has reached the shore of wisdom; out of compassion for us, he has come here."
"Now, all you dragons who wish to escape this prison of suffering may pay him homage.
At that time, the Dragon King Anavatapta spoke these words:

"This is not Brahmā, but rather the Māra King, who possesses sovereign power within the realm of desire. Out of compassion for us, he has come surrounded by his wife, children, and retinue; desiring to liberate all sentient beings within the realm of desire from fear, he has come here to rescue us from our dragon calamity."
Then the Dragon King Dṛḍhavīryavarṇa spoke these words:
"This is not the Māra King.

Rather, it is a deity from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*) and other heavens of the desire realm who has come here, wishing to bring liberation to all the dragons."
At that time, all the dragon kings within the assembly raised their voices in unison and spoke these words:
"May the devas grant us liberation;
grant us liberation and bestow upon us peace and happiness, so that we may quickly emerge from this prison."
Then the Naga King Sagara spoke again, saying:

"That is not the Tuṣita Heaven, nor the Transformation of Self-Enjoyment, and so forth; this is the radiance emitted by Śakra Devānām Indra, the Lord of Devas, which illuminates the realm of desire and the four continents."
Observe that all sentient beings of the four quarters delight in wholesome dharmas.
You all should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; do not harbor further anger. Seek liberation from those celestial realms and quickly depart from this suffering.
Then the Dragon King Susthitu spoke these words: "This is not Śakra;
rather, it is all the devas of the form realm who have abandoned their meditative bliss and descended from there, wishing to rain down the Dharma-rain to bring happiness to sentient beings."
"You nāgas, all of you, with single-minded devotion, prostrate yourselves and beg for deliverance.
Then the Nāga King Vikaṅka-susīra spoke again:

"This is not the arrival through supernatural power of the gods of the Form Realm; rather, it is Vaiśravaṇa and the others of the Four Great Kings, each leading their own retinue, who have come to protect the four directions and to eliminate the sinful among all sentient beings."
At that time, the Dragon King Ratnapāla spoke again, saying: "These are not the Four Heavenly Kings.

I see one whose hair and beard have been shaved off, who wears the dyed robes and the saffron-colored *kāṣāya*, whose marks and signs are upright and serene, and who possesses sovereign great virtue. He is gazed upon by all devas and humans, who respectfully make offerings to him while surrounding him with palms joined, like the sun, moon, and stars encircling them."

These eight great sages are all resplendent; their bodies are firmly illuminated with purple-gold light, and endowed with the thirty-two marks, they compassionately regard all beings and receive offerings within the triple world.
At that time, the Nāga King Viṣkambhasusīma spoke further: "I have personally seen the True Guide;

he is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings and dry up the ocean of suffering. He can grant the bliss of liberation within this very hell and now dwells nearby upon the summit of Mount Sumeru."
Thus, by the supernatural power of the World-Honored One, this summit of Mount Sumeru suddenly became even more vast and wide, measuring eighty-four hundred thousand yojanas.

At that time, all the devas of the desire and form realms, each desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata, constructed for the Buddha stairways and bridges of the seven precious gems, with pavilions and steps arranged in successive tiers, reaching all the way up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Each was adorned with various inconceivable nets of celestial lapis lazuli, like exquisite jeweled canopies rarely equaled, which all sentient beings could never tire of beholding; they were further embellished with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of rare treasures, as well as various celestial garments, various necklaces, various parasols, silken banners and streamers, conchs, drums, bells, and gongs, along with flowers, incense, and musical performances—such offerings filled the entirety of space.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying: "Lord of Devas!

Thus, in this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, all the Buddhas, along with the great Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great Arhats, the great sages and holy ones, as well as the powerful Māras who delight in merit and fortune, and the various classes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans—all have finished their dwelling and enjoyment within this trichiliocosm."

Thus it is, Śakra! This Mount Sumeru is where the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One; the bodhisattvas who have come from the buddha-fields of the ten directions; all the great arhats and holy ones; Māra, the King of Delights; the devas of great virtue; and even the nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, and non-humans—all of them reside upon this Mount Sumeru. You devas shall gain great power in future worlds.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha, the Tathāgata, would have compassion for me, [please grant this] as a feat of supernatural power to be utilized, as well as for all the Bodhisattvas, Great Arhats, Great Brahmās, Māras, and Śakras of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven within this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds; and even for all the kings of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas in this Sahā world."

Furthermore, there were sentient beings of great power and merit, sages among the gods, and sages among humans; all of them came to make offerings to the Buddha, to behold the Buddha, to prostrate before the Buddha, and to listen to the Dharma.
"If this Mount Sumeru were to be enjoyed by such a multitude as these, I would, in the future, increase my supreme bliss and attain great peace and security.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted Śakra’s invitation to dwell therein; he sat upright in right mindfulness, with a serene and joyful smile upon his face.
Having smiled, various rays of light issued from his mouth—
blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of purple crystal— illuminating this trichiliocosm Buddha-field.

The palaces of ten billion Māra kings, ten billion Śakra kings, ten billion Brahmā kings, ten billion kings of all the celestial realms, ten billion asura kings, and ten billion dwelling places of the holy sages (muni)—all these were illuminated by such light. As previously described, all those powerful Māra kings of great merit, up to the holy sages, were suddenly awakened; each followed the light and, by means of their supernormal powers, arrived here at the summit of Mount Sumeru in the space of a single thought-moment.
At that time, having manifested divine light, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, saying:
“Lord of Devas!
Within this single Buddha-field of a trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Sumeru Kings of Mountains.”
At that time, among all the Sumerus, this Sumeru is the most honored and most excellent.
Why is this? Because I and all the devas have gathered here in a great assembly to enjoy [the offerings] and deliver the nāgas.
When these words were spoken, immeasurable hundreds of billions of Śakras and all the Brahmā kings were filled with great joy.
Through such supernatural power of the Tathāgata, the four dragon kings were then able to emerge from that dwelling place of the holy man.

Having emerged, each returned to their own quarter; thus, the Naga King Sagara returned to the great seashore in the south, resumed his original form as large as Mount Sumeru, and even raised his head to the palace of Śakra, where he beheld the Buddha himself.

In this way, the Nāga King Ratnapāla of the west, the Nāga King Vicaragasusīra of the north, and the Nāga King Sumāhuluṣa of the east each returned to the great ocean and within their former palaces, all assuming their original forms once more; they even came as before to the summit of Mount Sumeru to behold the Buddha in person.
The remaining immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nāyutas* were still there, unable to escape.
At that time, all the *nāgas* addressed the Great Holy One in this way:
"We pray for our deliverance; we pray for our deliverance! Grant us swift liberation from within this hell."

At that time, the two dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, from their dwelling place on Mount Kāla where sages reside, each used their own bodies to rely upon Mount Sumeru and miraculously created a great bridge reaching to the palace of Śakra. They spoke these words:

"We pray only that the Tathāgata will tread upon this bridge, descend from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the dwelling of the sages on Mount Kāla, and sit there to preach the Dharma for the refuge of all dragons."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"This dragon’s body is rough and its skin emits a poisonous vapor; it might injure the Tathāgata’s feet, making them uncomfortable.

Having had this thought, he immediately covered the dragon’s body with celestial garments. Furthermore, he took celestial gośīrṣa sandalwood, uragasāra sandalwood, and tamāla fragrance—these three kinds of incense—as well as various celestial flowers and powdered essences, scattering them over the bridge and covering the dragon’s body.
At that time, by the power of the Buddha, the abode of the muni Kharadī became even more vast and extensive, measuring eighty-four billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of yojanas.

Once that place had been expanded, the Great Brahmā King fashioned a lion throne made of celestial gold and silver from Mount Sumeru, adorned with various banners, flowers, canopies, and parasols, and established it there.
At that time, having heard these words, all the dragon kings and their retinues addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray only that you will take pity on us and rescue us from our suffering."
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"You all should first recollect the Buddha with a sincere mind; I shall rescue them.
At that time, the World-Honored One was atop Mount Sumeru and addressed the Elder Kauṇḍinya, saying:

“Kauṇḍinya! Such is the power of the Buddha’s domain, his display of supernormal powers, and his empowerment as he preaches this Dharma; and among all the infinite sentient beings within these entire three-thousandfold great thousandfold Sahā world-systems of Buddha-fields, those sentient beings who hear my preaching of the Dharma and are able to receive and uphold it.”
"Kauṇḍinya! All dharmas are entirely impermanent; all dharmas are impermanent in their arising and abiding. Why is this?
Because of the conditions of arising:
just as visual consciousness arises, having arisen it abides, having abided it is recollected, and from recollection it arises again—this is itself suffering.

These conditions of arising are the arising of suffering; they are the abscess and the ulcer; they are all twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); they are the conditions for birth, old age, sickness, and death.
In this way, they arise and perish from moment to moment; as it is with the eye due to its causes and conditions, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
"Kauṇḍinya! Although they abide for a brief time, they cease and then gradually arise again; this is like a window."

This is the condition for dwelling in this life; this is the causal condition for suffering. There are these hundred kinds of aging, sickness, and death, which thus arise through a succession of gradual causal conditions.
One sees with the eye the commission of karma; as one sees, so one recollects; as one recollects, so one acts. The causal conditions for birth and death thus created are inexhaustible.

“Kauṇḍinya! Just as when the eye is extinguished, because its light has vanished it no longer perceives various forms—just as one cannot see through a window when the sun has set—if the causes and conditions are extinguished, all afflictions are extinguished;
the twelve links of existence are entirely extinguished, and birth and death are extinguished like the condition of the setting sun. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.”

“Kauṇḍinya! Just as when the mind is stilled, its objects of perception are also extinguished, and these windows and their causal conditions are as if never having arisen from the beginning, so too are all phenomena.”

This is called the cessation of suffering and the extinction of all afflictions; it is the complete stillness of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and likewise the ultimate exhaustion of birth and death and the end of all states of being.

“Kauṇḍinya! Sentient beings do not know the arising and ceasing of the eye; they pursue and follow what is defiled by the ear, nose, tongue, and body, and for this reason they wander through the five realms of existence.”

My noble Dharma can bring one away from birth and death to the further shore; therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma in order to sever all arising and ceasing of the eye, and he also teaches the Dharma of the practice for abandoning suffering, so that within all sufferings, their very bottom may be reached.

Therefore, having attained this Dharma, the Tathāgata is the Great Brahmā among all gods and Brahmās, the Great Deva among all devas, the Great Man among men, the Great Śramaṇa among all śramaṇas, and the Great Brāhmaṇa among all brāhmaṇas. He is the most supreme among the great compassionate ones, the unsurpassed Honored One, the Great Being (Mahāpuruṣa), who has already crossed to the other shore of the flowing stream of birth and death, and is the most excellent among all in the world regarding *dāna*, *dharma*, and *saṃyama*.
What is *dāna*? It is giving and relinquishing;
one is able to give away even the head, eyes, hands, feet, and all necessary limbs as required, let alone other things!
This is called *dāna*. What is *dharma*?

It is the pure upholding of the precepts such that, even if someone comes and demands one's head and one gives the head, the mind feels no anger or resentment and compassion is never lost; this is called *dharma*.
What is *saṃyama*?

It is not abandoning the six sense faculties while remaining single-mindedly in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and not forgetting all merits, words, recitations, and mindfulness through cultivation. Having cultivated these two modes of reflection and contemplation, these two types are called *saṃyama*, the dharma of the impartial mind toward all sentient beings.

If I were to abandon the Dharma, the giving of the Dharma (*dhammadāna*), as well as the Saṃgha, Yama, the four Brahma-vihāras, and the Noble Eightfold Path—because such dharmas as these are permeated by a mind of loving-kindness, and because all these dharmas have been cultivated with a mind of loving-kindness throughout immeasurable eons.

Just as I have realized all dharmas, I shall extensively proclaim and expound them among sentient beings; acting as their guide, I shall compassionately pity sentient beings and clarify their understanding, expounding this matter without any omission or deficiency.

You all should now, with a single mind, believe in, accept, uphold, and train in the various dhyānas. Whether dwelling in various aranyas, or beneath forest trees, or among burial mounds, or within various mountain crags and precipices, you should practice seated meditation there. For the sake of exhausting birth and death, exert great diligence so that body and mind do not grow weary; do not harbor a lowly mind, for through such lack of accomplishment, you will feel regret and distress at the time of death.
“This is all the Dharma I have taught.
