Having spoken thus, within this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold Buddha-fields, there were ten billion sets of four continents; in each set of four continents, there were immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Those sentient beings were fully endowed with various roots of goodness and merit; some attained dhāraṇīs, some attained patience (kṣānti), some attained the Dharma-eye, and some attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to that of an arhat.
There may be sentient beings within the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts whose remaining retributions for evil karma are all completely extinguished.
Likewise, yakṣas who were impoverished due to various causes and conditions shall have them all exhausted and attain great wealth.

There may be sentient beings among humans whose retributions for the evil karma of poverty are exhausted, and their various malignant diseases are all cured; those beings imprisoned in dungeons shall all receive liberation.
At that time, Sāgara, the Dragon King, spoke these verses in praise before the Buddha:
“With a face like pure gold, free from stain, and like the full moon, Possessing pure conduct, you are the most supreme field of merit;
Honored among the devas, humans, and nāgas of the three realms, You are able to remove the turbidity, defilement, and afflictions of sentient beings.”
Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence, you have perfected a mind of true equanimity;
having liberated all nāgas and bestowed peace and happiness, you recall the power of your past vows.
Having long cultivated the various practices of compassion, your resolve is more steadfast than that of all other sentient beings.
Thus he underwent all manner of bitter suffering, never forgetting the various afflictions caused by those nāgas;
through various transmigrations, he attained transcendence and crossed over to the far shore beyond the ocean of birth and death.
Having liberated himself, he rescued all sentient beings, purifying the nāgas with the water of wisdom.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 43; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 44.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: Saving the Dragon through the Three Refuges, from the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*.

At that time, various kinds of fragrant flowers, various precious robes, various musical instruments, and various songs and dances rained down spontaneously from the sky, filling the void; all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and asuras paid them their utmost respect.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded on all sides by the great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who followed him in front and behind, descended from the summit of Mount Sumeru across the bridge of dragon bodies to the abode of the sages on Mount Khadiraka, where he sat upon the precious lion throne spread out by the Brahmā gods.

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as the asuras, kiṃnaras, and others in the void, each presented offerings; scattering various powdered incenses, various flower-incenses, and various precious robes upon the Buddha, they circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated, and sat down.
At that time, the Naga King Sagara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions have we all been born among the nagas?”
The Buddha said: "Dragon King!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
I shall now explain to you, O King, in detail and at length.
There are ten kinds of karma by which one is reborn among the nāgas. What are these ten?

There are sentient beings who practice the six pāramitās, desiring to attain the awakening of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and also wishing to be free from evil obstacles; or again, those who wish to extensively cultivate the perfection of giving by practicing timely relinquishment, and by reason of these vows and conditions, are reborn among the nāgas.
"Furthermore, Dragon King!
There may be sentient beings who practice giving within the Mahāyāna; by reason of the causal conditions of the karmic fruit and retribution of that merit, they vow to be born among the dragons."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

There are some sentient beings who practice giving for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; although their meritorious rewards are many, they cannot attain purity. Because they fear the causes and conditions within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, they vow to be born among the dragons."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

There are sentient beings who, when they desire to practice for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, give rise to a haughty mind and the power of great pride due to certain causes and conditions, and therefore vow to be born among the dragons."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

There are sentient beings who, having resolved upon bodhicitta and practicing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, frequently give rise to anger and resentment toward other sentient beings. Because they direct their wrath and indignation toward the causes and conditions for rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, they persistently cultivate such anger; thus, after death, they vow to be born among the dragons."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

There are sentient beings who seek the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), desiring to become fields of merit and seeking to be among the noble ones; yet they abandon the fruits of their giving, their meritorious virtues, and their offerings. Through such causes and conditions and by the power of their own vows, they are reborn among the dragons."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!
There are sentient beings who, due to jealousy and pride, are born among the dragons as a result of those karmic causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Dragon King!"
There are sentient beings who frequently give rise to arrogance and are full of idle talk; by virtue of their own karma, they come to be born among the dragons. "Furthermore, Dragon King!

There are sentient beings who do not have faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; nor do they provide for their preceptors, ācāryas, or other virtuous ones; nor do they make offerings to their parents. Due to various causes and conditions such as anger, resentment, poisonous intent, attachment and aversion, arrogance, and delusion, and because they have acted erroneously toward fields of merit, they come to be born among the dragons through these karmic conditions."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!

There are sentient beings who, due to their various forms of delusion, arrogance, and the great power of their evil karma, possess little merit; because their minds are filled with fear, they vow to be born among the dragons."
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
There are sentient beings who engage in false speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh words, and who lack compassion; by reason of these three types of karma, they are born among the dragons."
The Buddha said,
“Nāga King! It is because of these ten kinds of karmic causes and conditions that one is born among the nāgas.”
"Furthermore, O Dragon King!
There are three further karmic causes and conditions by which one is born among the dragons.
What are these three?

There are sentient beings who, having firmly established evil karma through body, speech, and mind, are born within the hells due to the ripening of that karma and remain there for immeasurable eons, undergoing extreme suffering from which it is difficult to attain liberation. Even when they have escaped the great karma, because their minor karma is not yet exhausted, they are born among the nāgas, or among animals, or among hungry ghosts; by reason of these three types of evil karmic causes and conditions, they come to be born among the nāgas.
Then Sāgara the Nāga again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is so, World-Honored One!

Among these nāgas, there are some who receive the retribution of pleasure just like the devas; others receive pleasure like humans; some are like pretas or like animals; and yet other nāgas undergo great suffering and hardship as if they were in hell.”
When he had spoken these words, the prince of the great nāga Sāgara, named Utpalaka, addressed the Buddha from before him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions of evil karma and transgression have I been born among the nāgas? Though my body is large and upright, and whatever colors, textures, garments, or places for sitting and reclining I enjoy at all times, my body experiences them as if they were being burned by fire; I am constantly without clothing and walk about naked."
"Is the experience of supreme pleasure like that of my father, the King, and is the karmic fruition like that of a Wheel-Turning King?
The Buddha said to Huamian:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well.
I shall now relate for you a past event.
Thirty-one eons ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Śikhin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, there was a king in that world named Pradyota.

During the three months of the rainy season, King Pradyota made offerings to that Buddha, as well as to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, and *arhats*, along with the assembly of great *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas*. He provided them with various kinds of clothing, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions, and listened to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Having heard the Dharma, he immediately resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

After making offerings for three months in this manner, King Puṣya constructed monasteries for Śikhin Buddha and the rest of the Saṅgha, providing them with an abundance of various robes, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, beds, couches, and bedding.

The eldest son of that King Puṣya was named Bimbisāra. Having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, Bimbisāra conceived a profound fear of cyclic existence; he prostrated before his father the king and petitioned him, requesting permission to approach the Buddha and seek ordination as a renunciant.
The king replied to his son, "Go as you wish; you may leave the household life as you please.
Once he had left the household life, he spoke again to his father, saying:
"I wish to stay at my father the King's temple.
Puṣya-rāja said, "I shall also grant your wish; you may reside within that temple."

"At that time, the monks and disciples of Śikhin Buddha were sitting, reclining, using the bedding, and consuming food and drink within that monastery. Pippalāyana, the son of a wealthy man, gave rise to a heart of envy and jealousy; he became enraged at those resident disciples of the Buddha and constantly scolded and reviled them."
At that time, having been reviled with anger, the assembly of monks all departed from the monastery. Seeing the monks leave, Satyaka felt great joy and thought to himself:
"It is well that they have gone; I am now in great peace."
"After the assembly of monks had departed, at that time Satyaka used the robes and food within the monastery as he pleased; if anyone else came, he would not allow them to stay.

Having committed such various evil karmas, after his life ended, Satyaka was reborn in the great hell, where for immeasurable thousands of millions of nayutas of years he suffered being burned by fires.
Upon escaping from the hell, he was reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta), where for another immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of years he endured suffering and hardship."
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they fall back again into hell;
having escaped from hell, they are born among the hungry ghosts—thus they pass through thirty-one kalpas.
You nāgas, listen attentively and receive this well: thus did Śatadruha endure all such hardships throughout his cycle of transmigration.
The Buddha said,
"Padmavaktra! Could that Śatadruṣṭi have been anyone else?"
It is none other than your own body.

Due to the causes and conditions of evil karma in the distant past, you were born in the great hells, as hungry ghosts, and as animals, transmigrating through them to undergo suffering. For thirty-one great kalpas, you have experienced every kind of misery without a moment’s respite; because of the remaining residue of that karma, you have now been born among the nāgas to undergo this evil retribution.
When the dragon Huamian heard these words, he wept aloud and threw his entire body to the ground, prostrating with his four limbs spread out. He bowed to the Buddha and spoke thus:

"I now repent before the Buddha with a sincere heart. Driven by great delusion, great arrogance, and ignorance, I failed to understand the distinctions between skillful means and the difference between good and evil, thereby committing this sinful karma. With my head bowed and palms joined, I confess it with a sincere heart and dare not conceal it."
"O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!

I now enter with utmost sincerity into my very marrow, taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. From this moment when I first resolve my mind until the end of my life, during that time, I shall act as an upāsaka."
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”

"You currently possess karmic retributions for the evil realms of hell and hungry ghosts; by thus taking refuge in me with a sincere heart, you shall exhaust those karmas. After dying here, you will encounter Maitreya Buddha and obtain a human body, whereupon you will leave the household life within the Dharma of Maitreya Buddha and realize the fruit of Arhatship."
The Buddha said, “Puṣpamukha!
Do not harbor further doubts.

Formerly, that King Prasenajit of Vaiśālī made various offerings of the necessities of life to the Tathāgata Śikhin and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas for three months. Because of this, he has now obtained this retribution: he has received the body of the great nāga king Sāgara, which is like celestial music; for thirty-one kalpas he shall not be born in the three evil realms, but will always be born among devas and humans, receiving such rewards as these.”
“They too have come among these dragons for the sake of the causal conditions for practicing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wishing to be born here.
When these words were spoken, all the dragons were greatly distressed and repented of their past faults; they all made offerings with a sincere heart before the Buddha.
At that time, there was among the assembly a blind nāga named Phalakiṃkara, who raised his voice and wept aloud, saying these words:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One!
"May you rescue me! May you rescue me! All Buddhas are compassionate and take pity on all beings.

Now, within my body, I endure great suffering and affliction; day and night, I am constantly being bitten and eaten by various insects, small snakes, and frogs. Dwelling in hot water, I have not a moment’s peace."
The Buddha said, “Reverend Liśa!

In a past life, you were once a bhikṣu within this Buddha-dharma. You violated the prohibitions and precepts, harboring deceit within while manifesting various signs of virtuous demeanor and deportment without. You greedily sought a vast circle of followers and had many disciples; your fame spread far and wide, such that there was no one who did not know of it.”
Those disciples spoke thus: "Our preceptor has attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Because of this cause and condition, they received much offerings; having received these offerings, they consumed them for themselves alone, and when seeing those who maintained the precepts, they instead treated them with malice and spoke ill of them.
That person, filled with remorse, thought thus:
"In every birth throughout my lives, may I always eat the flesh of your body.

Due to such evil karma, he was reborn among the dragons; because of the aspirations of sentient beings, he ate your body in his previous life, and through the causal conditions of that evil karma, he has received this retribution of blindness and dwells within hot water.
"Furthermore, throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, within the hell of molten red copper, you were constantly devoured by various insects.
At that time, having heard these words, the assembly of nāgas wept in sorrow and lamentation, saying:
"We now all repent with a sincere heart; may we be swiftly liberated from this suffering."
At that time, the Tathāgata extended his golden hand, stroked the face of that nāga, and spoke these words:
"Listen attentively! In the past, I was once a king named Sunetra. At that time, there was a blind brāhmaṇa who came to me and begged for one of my eyes; I then joyfully gave both eyes to him."
"If these words of mine are truly not false, may pure eyes arise for you, Liśa, and may all your sins be entirely eradicated.
Then he spoke the mantra: "Tadyathā..."
Cakṣu-kāva-saraṇa-kāva-karma-kāva.
Ānanda-jñāna-vīra-śakrabharaṇḍa-yama.
Nīvaraṇaduryodhābhidhānataruḥ.
Bhīṇḍu-sthita-kṣipra-sthita-phala-sthita-aśi.
Tāttale tāttale

*vaseṭa saṃkete saṃkete ulūrava mahā-ulūrava tebu-ālata-nāvara-te svāhā.* At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this *Dhāraṇī of the Truly Pure Eye*, that Liśa dragon attained the pure eye; the remaining fifty-three thousand dragons also attained the pure eye; and furthermore, eighty-four *nayutas* of yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and others, their defilements and stains extinguished, all attained the pure eye.
At that time, the Devaputra Sudatta joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke in verse:
"Behold the World-Leader of Ten Powers, Who is able to purify the eyes of all nagas.
If they do not encounter a Buddha in this life, All who have lost their sight will remain forever blind."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Kauṇḍinya:
"You should uphold this Net-Eye Dhāraṇī mantra.

If there are sentient beings who, due to past evil karma, whether in the present or in future lives, suffer from the four great diseases, or curses from wicked people, or through poisonous drugs—and by reason of these conditions, they lose their sight."

Sentient beings such as these should recite this Vimalanetra Dhāraṇī, repenting of the evil karma they have committed in the past; they should give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, mindfully recollect the Buddha with utmost sincerity while setting aside all other affairs, and for seven weeks, during the six periods of day and night, wipe their eyes with their hands. By these causes and conditions, they shall obtain pure eyes.
"If there are sentient beings who, in past lives, committed various evil deeds—

whether by destroying the Dharma, slandering noble ones, creating obstacles for those who preach the Dharma, or by copying scriptures and erasing the characters, or by damaging the eyes of others or obscuring their vision— it is due to the conditions of these karmic actions that they now receive the retribution of blindness."

If, due to such causes and conditions of grave evil karma, one does not recover within seven weeks, one should transcribe this dhāraṇī and, with a sincere heart, recite and uphold it to repent for that karma.

Furthermore, take these five medicinal substances—sea foam, licorice (*yaṣṭimadhu*), *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *bhallātaka*—and grind them into a powder mixed with honey. Place this within an old tortoise shell and boil it over a fire with aged ghee. Recite this *dhāraṇī* one thousand and eight times and consecrate the medicine with this mantra; then apply it to the eyes. For seven weeks, set aside all other affairs, recollect the Buddha, fashion an image, and make a vow with a sincere heart. At that time, the evil karma of those sentient beings will be completely exhausted, and they shall obtain pure eyes.

If one possesses wealth, they should further construct monasteries and provide the necessities of life as offerings according to their means; by doing so, all such evil karma will be exhausted, and throughout immeasurable future births, they shall never lose their sight.
At that time, the entire assembly of nāgas spoke these words:

“Homage, homage to the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, who is able to bestow benefit upon sentient beings of the three periods of time; having lost their eyes, they regain their sight, and all their evil karma becomes pure and stainless.”
At that time, there was a dragon named Blue who cried out in a loud voice and spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One can eliminate all stains of sin, Just as a great river washes away everything;
He fully knows the various conducts of sentient beings, Therefore he is praised as the Most Honored One among the multitude.”
The place where I dwell is in the midst of a marsh; in the great wilderness, the dried-up springs have no water.
A hot wind blows upon my body more fiercely than fire, and the stench of my physical dwelling is unbearable.
For eight thousand million years I have lived there, never for a single day having experienced joy or pleasure.
"They are constantly devoured by sentient beings, and the same is true for their entire retinue, both great and small.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, answering:
"If there are sentient beings who commit various transgressions, yet further cultivate and perform meritorious deeds,"
Establishing monasteries and offering bells and chimes, providing various kinds of food and drink as offerings to the Sangha—
by virtue of these diverse causes and conditions of merit, one receives their fruits according to one's karma in whatever place of birth one takes.
Committing evil brings bitter suffering like that of hell, while giving food brings happiness like that of heaven;
or one may even be reborn among the nāgas, all due to the causal conditions of those virtuous deeds.
From within the dragon’s head, there naturally emerges the rare and wondrous King of Jewels that grants all wishes;
whatever one desires is fulfilled according to one's will, and all manner of karmic fruits are fully provided.
Though dwelling in parched springs or arid marshes, they can produce the most sublime and pure flowing water;
though the clear sky spreads dense clouds, level ground like the palm of a hand wells up with springs and pools.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, wherever they may be, they can cause all manner of waters to arise in response to their thoughts.
If there are any sentient beings who, though having obtained a human body,
commit all manner of evil deeds and fail to make offerings to the Triple Gem,
after death they will gather amidst all manner of suffering and undergo the torments of hell and the realm of hungry ghosts.
Even if one should obtain the body of a dragon king, with all one's retinue and wife and children,
one will suffer the torments of poverty, hunger, and thirst; lacking the wish-fulfilling jewel upon the crown of the head,
one dwells in desolate marshes teeming with venomous insects, where everything is parched, perpetually dry, and devoid of water.
All this is due to their past lives, when they were once bhikṣus within the Buddha-dharma;
or when they saw forest-dwellers practicing austerities, they harbored jealousy and stinginess, begrudging food and drink.
When visiting bhikṣus came to stay with them, they felt anger and resentment, their hearts full of displeasure.
When a donor offers food and drink with impartiality, One who obstructs it therein will revile them.
Even if there were pure, fine flowing water, Excrement, urine, and filth would fill its midst;
In all places where one dwells, walks, or sits, Everything would be foul, stinking, and impure.
There may be those who maintain pure precepts; having seen such [a place], they all distance themselves from it.

If there are virtuous people elsewhere who hear of this and have no desire to come here, it is due to the causes and conditions of their own evil karma that, after death, they fall into hell for immeasurable eons.
In the Ash River and the Boiling Excrement, they endure the burning of molten copper for immeasurable billions of years, suffering bitter torment.
Thus, among the hungry ghosts, they suffer from hunger and thirst; throughout their lives, they have never even heard the names of water or broth.
With this remaining retribution, they are reborn in the realm of dragons, where they fully experience hardship and suffering for many years.
Though they have attained the bodies of dragons, they are perpetually hungry; wherever they are born, it is empty and devoid of water.
Sometimes in parched marshes or on scorched, desolate mountains, they are cut off from water, eternally dry, and without food or drink.
After death, they repeatedly enter the hells, where great fires and scorching torments pervade their entire bodies.
In that sutra it is said that for immeasurable years, one will thus circulate among the hungry ghosts;
were it not for the practice of dhyāna to provide rescue, or the prostration and making offerings to the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
Uphold the precepts, cultivate wisdom, and study extensively; Exert diligence and abandon thoughts of stinginess and pride.
The poisonous mind of envy and jealousy is the most evil; Such karmic causes and conditions must be severed.
Recall that at the time of death you will suffer this calamity; Do not doubt this certainty, but repent early.
At that time, when the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, twenty-six billion hungry nāgas among that assembly of nāgas, recollecting their past lives, all shed tears and spoke thus:
"We pray only that you will have compassion for us and deliver us."
O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

We recall that in past lives, although we had left the household life within the Buddha-dharma, we committed various kinds of such evil karma. Because of this evil karma, we passed through immeasurable lifetimes in the three evil realms; furthermore, due to the remaining retribution, we were born among the nāgas and undergo extreme suffering, just as this Blue Nāga and I do.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the nāgas:
"You may take water and wash the Tathāgata’s feet, so that your calamities and transgressions may gradually be extinguished."

Then all the nāgas cupped water in their hands, but the water turned entirely into fire and transformed into great stones; as soon as it filled their hands, a fierce, blazing flame arose, and upon discarding it, it was produced again—this occurred up to seven times.
When all the hosts of nāgas had seen this, they were struck with terror and distress, weeping and shedding tears like rain.
The Buddha addressed the nāgas:
"You have committed sinful karma and thus received this evil retribution; those who cultivate wholesome karma receive excellent fruits. I shall now instruct you to utter a truthful oath."

If the Buddha, the Guide, out of compassion for all, regards all sentient beings with impartiality and without distinction, may these words not be in vain, and may the flames of our fires be extinguished at once.
Having made this vow, the flames were all extinguished.
Then the famished nāgas and others, up to eight times, cupped water in their hands and washed the Tathāgata’s feet, repenting with a sincere heart:
"From this day forward, we shall no longer commit evil."
Having thus repented, they each addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata,
in your great compassion, we pray that you will deliver us.
The Buddha said:

“O nāgas! Since there remains a residue of this evil karma of yours that has not yet been exhausted, you shall obtain a human body during the era of Maitreya Buddha. There, you will encounter the Buddha, leave the household life, practice with diligence, uphold the precepts, and attain the fruit of arhatship.”
At that time, the nāgas attained the recollection of their past lives; reflecting upon their own past karma, they wept until their faces were drenched with tears, each speaking thus:

"I remember in the past, within the Buddha’s Dharma, whether due to the circumstances of being relatives of laypeople, or due to the circumstances of coming and going to hear the Dharma, I possessed a mind of faith and offered various flowers, fruits, food, and drink, which I shared with the bhikṣus so that they might eat in due order."
Some said: "I have previously consumed the flowers, fruits, food, and drink belonging to the Sangha from the four directions. Others said:
"I went to the monastery to give alms to the community of monks;
or else I paid my respects, and so I ate and drank.
Or again, he might say:
"I was once a layperson during the time of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin," or again, some say:
"I was once a layperson during the time of the Tathāgata Śikhin."
Or again, some say: "I was once a layperson within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin. Or again, some say:
"I was once a layperson during the Dharma of Krakucchanda Buddha," or again, some say:
"I was once a layperson during the Dharma of Kanakamuni Buddha."
Or again, some say: "In the Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa Buddha, I was once a layperson. Or again, others say:
"Within the Dharma of me, Śākyamuni Buddha, I have formerly been a layperson;
whether on account of visiting with old acquaintances,
or again on account of coming and going to hear the Dharma, I have traveled back and forth between the temples and my home."
Because those with faith make offerings to the Saṅgha, they give away flowers, fruits, and various kinds of food and drink.
When the bhikṣus receive these, they transfer them as gifts to me, and I then eat them.

Due to those karmic causes and conditions, they undergo suffering within the hells for immeasurable kalpas, being burned or boiled amidst great, fierce fires, drinking molten copper, or swallowing iron balls.
Emerging from hell, they fall among the animals; casting off their animal bodies, they are born among the hungry ghosts. In this manner, they undergo all manner of bitter sufferings.

As their evil karma is not yet exhausted, they are born among these nāgas and constantly endure affliction: hot water rots their bodies and hot winds blow upon them; there is hot sand, hot earth, hot excrement, and hot ashes. When food enters their mouths, it turns into molten copper or becomes iron balls.

At all times, whatever food they eat, when it enters their mouths their mouths are scorched; when it enters their throats their throats are seared; when it reaches their bellies their bellies burn; it passes straight through and falls to the ground, leaving perforations throughout their entire bodies. They undergo such unbearable suffering that it cannot be endured; we only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and deliver us.
The Buddha told the nāgas:

"This evil karma is no different from stealing the property of a Buddha; the crime of a bhikṣu’s act of rebellion is like half [of that], yet because the retribution for this sin has not yet been fully experienced, it is difficult to escape."

"You all should now fully receive the three refuges and cultivate goodness with a single mind; by virtue of this cause, you shall encounter the final Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa, named Ruci, and in the world of that Buddha, your sins shall be extinguished."
When the nāgas heard these words, they all with sincere hearts and for the remainder of their lives each received the Three Refuges.

At that time, among that assembly there was a blind nāga girl whose mouth was swollen and festering, filled with various kinds of worms and resembling excrement and urine; it was even more foul and loathsome than the impurities within a woman’s private parts, being rancid, stinking, and unsightly. Various creatures devoured her, pus and blood flowed forth, and all her limbs were constantly being bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, and various evil, venomous flies; the stench of her body was such that it was difficult even to look upon or hear of.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, saw that the nāga woman was blind and suffering, and asked her thus:
"Sister, for what reason have you obtained this wretched body? What karma did you perform in past lives?"
The nāga woman replied, “World-Honored One!
This body of mine is now oppressed by manifold sufferings without a moment’s respite; even if I wished to speak further, I would be unable to do so.”

I recall that for thirty-six billion hundred-thousand years in the past, I was born among evil dragons and underwent such suffering, which continued day and night without ceasing even for a single kṣaṇa. This was because during ninety-one kalpas in the past, while under the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, I had been a bhikṣuṇī whose thoughts on sensual desires exceeded those of a drunken man; thus, although I had left the household life, I was unable to act in accordance with the Dharma.

Within the monastery, he prepared beds and bedding, repeatedly committing acts contrary to celibacy; with a mind of lustful desire, he gave rise to feelings of great pleasure, or greedily sought after the property of others and accepted many offerings from the faithful.
"Because of this, for ninety-one kalpas, she was never able to receive the body of a deva or a human, but constantly underwent the torments of burning and boiling within the three evil realms.
The Buddha asked again:
"If this is so, where was this woman born when this intermediate kalpa came to an end?"
The nāga woman replied, "By the causal conditions of my past karma, I was born in another world; when that kalpa ended there, driven by the winds of evil karma, I have returned to be born here."
When the nāga woman had finished speaking these words, she said:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!
I pray that you will rescue me; I pray that you will rescue me!"
At that time, the World-Honored One cupped water in his hand and addressed the nāga girl, saying:

"This water is called *Candālī-lepa-miśra*. I now speak these words to you with absolute sincerity: in the past, for the sake of saving a pigeon, I sacrificed my own life without ever giving rise to a thought of doubt, stinginess, or regret. If these words are true, may your malignant ailment be entirely cured."
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, took water in his mouth and sprinkled it upon the body of that blind nāga woman; all her ailments and foul odors were completely cured.
Having recovered, she spoke these words:
"I now seek from the Buddha to receive the Three Refuges."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately conferred the Three Refuges upon the nāga girl.

Then, within that assembly, there was another nāga who was foul-smelling and loathsome; his mouth was filled with all manner of insects, and pus and blood flowed from within his throat. Those who saw or heard of him all fled and abandoned him.
At that time, the Buddha, having seen this, immediately asked: "Good son,
what evil karma did you commit in the past to receive such retribution?"
That dragon opened its mouth, and from within its mouth issued forth various kinds of worms; pus and blood flowed out in abundance like a blazing fire.
Although it opened its mouth, it was ultimately unable to speak, and immediately closed it again.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for that nāga:
"Because of the causes and conditions of your past theft, And your frivolous mockery of a sage, you have received this retribution;
Listen with sincerity to these true words of mine, And you shall immediately attain coolness and extinguish all suffering."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words of truth, he poured a small amount of water into the dragon’s mouth, and the fire, along with the worms and pus, were all completely extinguished.
The dragon’s mouth became cool and refreshing, and he spoke these words:
“Great Sage, Tathāgata!”
I recall that in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was once a layman plowing a field.
A bhikṣu came to me and begged for fifty coins; I replied at that time, "Wait until the grain is ripe, and I shall give you food."
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"If fifty coins cannot be obtained, I pray you will grant me ten.
At that time, I became angry with that bhikṣu and said to him:
"Even ten coins shall not be given to you.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt deep resentment in his heart.
On another occasion, he went to the monastery and entered beneath a grove of trees, where he immediately stole ten āmra fruits belonging to the currently resident Sangha and ate them privately.

Due to the causal conditions of those karmic actions, he suffers in hell; when his evil karma is not yet exhausted, he is reborn in a wild marsh as the body of a starving nāga, constantly being devoured by various kinds of insects, with pus and blood overflowing as he endures the torment of hunger and thirst.

Furthermore, due to the karmic conditions of his malice and anger, that bhikṣu, upon death, immediately took birth as the body of a small venomous dragon; he was born beneath my armpit and sucked my blood, and the heat of his breath touching my body was unbearable, which is why my body is now filled with hot pus and blood.
The nāga addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
I pray only that you will take pity on me and deliver me, so that I may be freed from those enemy venomous nāgas."
At that time, the World-Honored One took water in his hand and, uttering words of truth, spoke thus:
"In the past, during an age of famine, I made a vow to become a being with a vast and immeasurably long body. By means of my supernormal powers, I proclaimed these words from mid-air:
'In that marshy wilderness there is a large-bodied insect named Aśatru (Non-Anger). You all should go and take its flesh for food and drink, and you shall not suffer from hunger.'"
"At that time, when the humans and non-humans there heard this sound, they all went together in competition to seize and eat it.
When these words of true and faithful truth were spoken, the small dragon from beneath the armpit of that great dragon emerged.
Then these two nāgas both addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How long will it be before we leave this nāga body and are liberated from our calamities and transgressions?"
The Buddha said to the dragon:
"This karma is extremely grave, second only to the five deeds of immediate retribution. Why is this?"

If one privately consumes or takes out for external use any property belonging to the permanently resident Sangha of the four quarters, or property belonging to the present Sangha, or items given with deep faith by a donor—whether flowers, fruits, trees, gardens, food and drink, means of livelihood, bedding, mats, or medicinal decoctions for illness—all such necessities as may be required, this offense is heavier than the retribution received in the Avīci Hell.

"Therefore, you should receive the Three Refuges; once you have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, you may remain within these cold waters. Thus he recited this three times and they received it three times; their bodies immediately became peaceful and secure, and they were able to enter the water.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of the nāgas:
"Better to cut one's own body with a sharp blade— The limbs, joints, skin, flesh, and all parts of the body—
Than for a layperson to consume The offerings given out of faith."
It would be better to swallow a great red-hot iron ball, causing flames to burst forth from one's mouth,
than to privately use for oneself any food or drink belonging to the community of monks.
It would be better to take up a great fire as large as Mount Sumeru with one's own hands and eat it oneself,
than for any layperson living at home to ever eat food that has been offered to the Sangha.
It would be better to butcher and mince one's own body with a sharp blade and eat one's own skin and flesh,
than for laypeople living at home to accept or take the various foods belonging to the Saṃgha.
It would be better to throw one's own body into a room filled with a great fire of fierce flames;
those who are householders and laypeople should not sit or lie upon the beds and mats of the Sangha.
It would be better to grasp a red-hot iron spike with one's clenched fist until it is scorched and seared;
those who are householders and laypeople alike must not privately appropriate the property of the Saṃgha.
It would be better to use a sharp, superior blade to cut one's own flesh into pieces than to give rise to even a single thought of anger toward a person who has left the household life in purity.
It would be better to pluck out both eyes with one's own hands and cast them away upon the ground than to look upon one who practices the wholesome Dharma with a mind of malice or anger.
It would be better to wrap one's body in glowing iron sheets and move about, stand, walk, sit, or lie down east and west,
than to wear the pure offerings given to the Saṃgha with a mind of anger, resentment, or envy.
It would be better to drink ash-water or brackish salt water, hot and boiling so as to scorch the mouth like fire,
than to harbor a greedy and poisonous evil mind while consuming the pure medicines offered in alms to the Saṃgha.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the assembly of fourteen thousand nāgas all received the Three Refuges; they attained liberation from all the sufferings and afflictions resulting from their past and present karmic retributions, and with deep faith in the Triple Gem, their minds never regressed.
Furthermore, there were eight billion assemblies of nāgas who likewise gave rise to a mind of refuge and reverence toward the Triple Gem.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya: "Observe these evil sentient beings who deceive their own minds;

some, due to the causes and conditions of fearing poverty, or out of fear of the miserable realms, practice wholesome dharmas. Or, as bhikṣus, they receive various requisites for life, all of which are gifts bestowed by faithful donors. Yet these beings either eat them themselves, or give them to others, or share them with the multitude; they steal and hide them away to use them privately. Because of such karma, they fall into the three evil paths and undergo arduous suffering for a long time."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are poor, lowly, and lack autonomy; for this reason, they leave the household life in the hope of attaining wealth, liberation, and peace.

Having left the household life, they are indolent and lazy, failing to recite the scriptures; they abandon diligent application to meditation and wisdom while delighting instead in managing monastic affairs.

Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who, day and night, apply themselves with diligence, delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; they recite the sūtras, practice dhyāna, and train in wisdom without relinquishing them for even a moment. By these causes and conditions, they receive various offerings from the fourfold assembly.

At that time, having obtained offerings and sustenance, the administrator either consumes them for his own private use or steals them to give to relatives and worldly acquaintances. Due to such causes and conditions, he remains long in the evil realms; even after emerging from them, he enters them again. Thus, being ignorant and deluded, he does not perceive the gravity of the retribution that will come in the future.
I now exhort my śrāvaka disciples: mindful of the Dharma and maintaining it, you must not claim for yourselves, "I am a śramaṇa who practices the true Dharma," on account of relying upon the Saṃgha.

Regarding the offerings given by others—whether cakes, fruits, vegetables, or flowers—whatever items are intended for the consumption of the Sangha must not be given indiscriminately to laypeople, nor should one say, "This is my own property," and eat it apart from the assembly.

Furthermore, one must not accumulate the property of the Sangha to engage in trade or various forms of commerce under the pretext that it is "profitable," thereby inviting public reproach and suspicion; nor should one buy low and sell high to compete with the world for profit.

Moreover, one must not cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms on account of food and drink or for the sake of the Sangha; rather, one should exhort and lead them toward wholesome dharmas, causing the community of bhikṣus to have true faith in the Triple Gem, and gathering in all sentient beings, even their parents, to bring them peace and security within the three gates of liberation.
The Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 44;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 45.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: The Protection of Stūpas, from the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*.
At that time, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This *Sūtra of the Treasury of Days* provides long-lasting illumination, explaining that the karmic retributions for the evil deeds of all nāgas are inconceivable, and further elucidating the authentic methods of practice for bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kauṇḍinya!"

In these four continents, there are great caityas and dwelling places of sages; if there are sentient beings who apply themselves with diligent skillful means, practicing seated meditation and right wisdom, you should know that such places will not be empty. In this way, these lands of merit shall become the sites where the Dharma-treasure of the *Sūryagarbha* is disseminated.
What is called a great caitya site?

Within this Jambudvīpa, in the city of Rājagṛha, the great caitya that is the dwelling place of the Sages is where countless Tathāgatas of the past, countless Bodhisattvas, countless Pratyekabuddhas, and countless Śrāvakas once practiced the Path and attained parinirvāṇa; they all exist there now, and it shall be so in the future as well.
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy beings of the past all entrusted this to the Naga Varuṇa, commanding him to protect, maintain, and establish it.
I now likewise desire that the light of this sacred site endure for a long time, and thus I entrust it once more to the Naga Varuṇa.

If there are sentient beings who are able to protect my Dharma, diligently applying skillful means through seated meditation and right wisdom, all *pudgalas* should constantly guard, provide for, and make offerings to them.
At that time, the Nāga King Varuṇa spoke these words: “So it is, so it is.
It shall be according to the instruction of the Blessed One.”

In the distant past, when Kāśyapa, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, was in the world, he also entrusted this place to me for protection, support, and offerings; he appointed me as the donor (dānapati) for those who diligently apply skillful means, practice meditative concentration with right wisdom, and cultivate wholesome dharmas. At that time, I provided support and protection for them until the extinction of the Dharma.

Next, there were further Buddhas named Kanakamuni up to Kāśyapa, who likewise entrusted this place to me for its protection and veneration; at that time, I provided for it and protected it, and so it shall continue until the Dharma comes to an end.

Within that Buddha-dharma, there may be disciples who do not accept slaves, servants, or fields, but instead practice diligent asceticism with a pure mind; all such as these I shall protect and sustain. Today, the Tathāgata further entrusts this place to me to maintain and protect.

At that time, the World-Honored One further entrusted the place known as Cloud-Exhausted (Meghakṣaya), a dwelling of sages located on Mount Kharasvati beneath Mount Sumeru in Aparagoyānī, to the Dragon King Ratnapāla.
Then the nāga Ratnapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! It is so, it is so.”

As the World-Honored One has instructed, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa of the past likewise entrusted these clouds of dwelling places of the noble ones to me; at that time, I guarded these places, as well as those disciples of the Buddha who practice according to the Dharma, until the extinction of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One further entrusted the holy dwelling place known as Sūryodaya, located on Mount Kāraṇḍava beneath Mount Sumeru in Pūrvavideha, to the Dragon King Somahuluṣka.
Then that Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so; it is just as the World-Honored One has taught.”

At that time, the World-Honored One further entrusted the sanctuary on Mount Kūṭaśaila—known as Gandhamādana-muni, located on the northern flank beneath Mount Sumeru—to the Naga King Vighuṣṭaśvasita, and likewise entrusted it to all bhikṣus who practice the pure Dharma.
Then that Nāga King spoke these words:
"So it is, so it is, according to the instruction of the World-Honored One.

In the past, the Tathāgata Krakucchanda likewise entrusted this Perfumed Peak, the dwelling place of the noble ones, to me, as well as the practice of the Dharma and the bhikṣus who maintain and make offerings to it."
Even so it was with the Tathāgata Kāśyapa. Today, the Tathāgata has likewise entrusted this site of the Fragrant Peak Caitya to me, and I shall protect it.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
You, Great Dragon King!"

In this way, you are able to protect my Dharma and uphold the Mother of the Dharma; you are my companion, a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and a donor who acts in accordance with the Dharma. All sentient beings rely upon my Dharma, and thus the land shall endure for a long time, bringing benefit and illumination.

At that time, the World-Honored One further entrusted the site of the sage Nāṭamuni in the continent of Aparagoyānī to the nāga king Gopālaka, and so forth; the manner in which his disciples who practice the Dharma were to guard, honor, and make offerings was likewise as described above.

Furthermore, he entrusted the dwelling place of the holy man Nīkarada-padmamuni in the continent of Pūrvavideha to the Nāga King Vasimudrakṣa, and likewise commanded his disciples who practice the Dharma to protect and make offerings there in the same manner.

"Furthermore, he entrusted the abode of the Perfected Sage Jvalanaprabha on Mount Gandhamādana in the northern continent of Uttarakuru to the Earth-Walking Dragon King, and likewise [entrusted it] to his disciples who practice according to the Dharma, charging them with guarding and making offerings in the same manner."

Furthermore, he entrusted the palace of the Naga King Sagara within the great ocean—the dwelling place of the holy sage Maṇigarbha-jvālāmuni—to the Naga King Sagara, and likewise [instructed him] to provide offerings there in the same manner.

"Furthermore, he entrusted the Flower Treasury Palace (Kusumita-alaṃkāra-maṇḍala), the dwelling place of Śakra atop Mount Sumeru where the Sage Muni resides, to the Dragon King Elāpattra; the manner in which it was guarded and venerated was likewise the same."
"Furthermore, this abode of the Great Virtuous Sage Muni, Nandopananda, within this Jambudvīpa, is likewise entrusted to the Nāga King Jambuka for his protection and veneration."

"Furthermore, this Vairaṇyā, the dwelling place of the sage Śrī-Susthita-Muni within Jambudvīpa, is entrusted to the Naga King Vasuki; he shall likewise protect and make offerings to it in this same manner."

"Furthermore, he entrusted this abode of the Sage Kāṇakamuni—Kapilavastu, the 'Good Fragrance' in Jambudvīpa—to the Nāga King Anavatapta, charging him with guarding and making offerings there in the same manner."

"Furthermore, the dwelling place of the holy sage Vimalaprabhāsa in the mountain range of Vipula in the kingdom of Magadha within Jambudvīpa was entrusted to the Dragon King Śailaśrī; the manner in which he was to guard and make offerings there was likewise as described above."
Furthermore, he entrusted the dwelling place of the holy sage named Maitrāyaṇīputra, known as Mathurā in Jambudvīpa, to the Naga King Yamavaktra.
"Furthermore, he entrusted the dwelling place of the holy man Śākyamuni, known as the Kingdom of Kośala within Jambudvīpa, to the Naga King Kṛmīla."
Furthermore, he entrusted the Suvarṇakṣaya-sāccha-muñjindhara incense, located in Jambudvīpa at the dwelling place of the Muni Sage, to the Dragon King Muñjindhara.
Furthermore, he entrusted the place in Jambudvīpa known as the kingdom of Gandhāra—the dwelling of the holy man Mahāśrīyanāmamuni—to the Naga King Elapattra.
Furthermore, he entrusted the palace named Gomaṇikhāmaṇi, the dwelling place of the holy sage Muni within the kingdom of Kaśmīra in Jambudvīpa, to the Naga King Ullola.
"Furthermore, he entrusted the dwelling place of the sage named *Archanmunī*, known as *Aṃbūli-ma* in the land of Jambudvīpa and called *Koṭigarbha-jvālā*, to the Naga King Lohitākṣa."
"Furthermore, he entrusted the land of China within Jambudvīpa—the dwelling place of the sage Nārāyaṇaparivāsa Muni—to the Dragon King Sāgara."

"Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Khotan, on the banks of a river by the Ox-Head Mountain near the river's edge, at the site of the stūpa of the Great Sage Gopāla, I entrust it to the Naga King Kṛtīhapradatta to protect and make offerings."

"These great caityas are all dwelling places of past great sages, bodhisattvas, great pratyekabuddhas, great arhats, śramaṇas who have attained the fruits [of the path], and ṛṣis possessing the five supernatural powers."
Therefore, all Buddhas of the past have successively entrusted this teaching, desiring that sentient beings who wander in fear may increase their roots of goodness and attain Bodhi.

In this way, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past from immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya lands throughout the ten directions all abide at that great caitya and constantly provide protection, so that the evil karma of all sentient beings may be exhausted.

In future ages, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable lands, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas shall likewise dwell at these twenty great caityas and constantly provide protection, so that the merit and virtue of all worlds may increase and the evil karma of all sentient beings may be exhausted.

"Furthermore, all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all Pratyekabuddhas, all Arhats—those śramaṇas who have attained the fruit—and all sages of the five supernatural powers shall constantly provide protection and support within these twenty great caityas, the dwelling places of the noble ones, so that the merit of all sentient beings may increase and the evil karma of all sentient beings may be exhausted."
In this way, all the noble ones of the past entrusted these twenty caityas to me.

Now I likewise entrust them, just as the previous Buddhas did, desiring that all sentient beings wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra may attain peace and happiness, and so that they may be firmly protected and preserved without being destroyed.
At that time, after all the nāgas had received the Buddha’s entrustment regarding the twenty stūpas and sacred sites, they spoke these words:
“Great Sage, World-Honored One!

We nāgas are prone to many obstructions; we are so addicted to sleep that we are no different from the ignorant. A single night of our sleep is equivalent to twenty-one years among human beings; thus, while we remain asleep and unaware, there may be evil humans or non-humans, or even water or fire, that destroy the stūpas.”

Whether we were sleeping, eating, drinking, or indulging in worldly pleasures and desires, due to such causes and conditions, these evil deeds could not be averted; therefore, within all the Buddhadharma of the past, present, and future, we have committed various unwholesome acts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the twenty-eight yakṣa generals, saying:
"I now entrust this dwelling place of the sages to you. You must regard these twenty caityas—this meritorious abode—with great reverence and protect them with a focused and diligent mind."
Then the twenty-eight yakṣa generals said:

"We respectfully obey the Buddha’s teaching; how would we dare not uphold the twenty caityas entrusted by the Tathāgata? However, as for the single location of Mount Gandhamādana, it is difficult for us to accept and take possession."
Then the Naga King Śrīghoṣadatta addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has now entrusted to me the great caitya of Gomasagandhamuni on Mount Vṛṣabhaśṛṅga in the kingdom of Khotan. However, the cities, towns, and villages of that land are all desolate; all its inhabitants have come from other regions, other kingdoms, or from other worlds. These include Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, great Pratyekabuddhas, great Arhats, śramaṇas who have attained the fruits [of the path], and those with the five supernormal powers, who have come to that place for the sake of making offerings through the power of their dhyāna. In Gomasagandha there were originally no sentient beings; all who have come are from other countries.”
World-Honored One!
These twenty-eight yakṣa generals are unwilling to provide protection and support; this now causes me wonder. Why is this so?
"Because they do not protect us, we nāgas have acquired an evil reputation.
The Buddha said,
"Nāga King, do not speak thus."
Why is this? Now there are twenty thousand people of great merit who have realized the Four Noble Truths; they have departed from the kingdom of Śākala and are dwelling there.
Because those twenty thousand meritorious beings possess great power, they constantly come day and night to this stūpa site on Mount Gomasāra to offer all manner of worship.
Nāga King, you should know that at such times there is never hunger or want.

Furthermore, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, that country of Khotan was named Karāśama; its territory was vast, peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with various flowers and fruits for the enjoyment of sentient beings. In that country, there were many hundreds of thousands of noble ones possessing the five supernatural powers who served as fields of merit for the world; they dwelt therein, fixing their mindfulness in seated meditation, and delighted in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because that land was peaceful, secure, and prosperous, the sentient beings there were largely given over to negligence and greedily attached to the five desires; they slandered and reviled the noble ones, bringing ill repute upon them, and even smeared those noble ones with ashes, dust, and soil.
When the practitioners had suffered this humiliation, they each departed from that country and scattered toward other regions.

When the beings of that land saw the sages leave, their hearts were filled with great joy; because of this cause and condition, the water deities and fire deities within that realm all became enraged. Consequently, all the waters—rivers, ponds, springs, and wells—completely dried up. At that time, because the beings lacked both water and fire, they all died of hunger and thirst, and the land naturally fell into desolation.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:

"I shall now go shortly to the abode of the Muni Gomasara, where I will sit cross-legged for seven days to experience the bliss of liberation. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this kingdom of Khotan shall once again be established; it will abound with cities, districts, counties, and villages, its population will flourish, and all shall delight in the Mahāyāna, living in peace and happiness. There will be no lack of various foods, drinks, fruits, or flowers."
Then the great yakṣa general Saṃgīti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! It is so, it is so.”
The Buddha said,
"Great Yakṣa General!
Do you remember events from the distant past?"
Saṅgharakṣita said:

"I recall that in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this was the dwelling place of sages on Vṛṣabhagiri Mountain. There, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa also sat cross-legged for seven days to experience the bliss of liberation; after those seven days had passed, he arose from meditative concentration."
At that time, I went to the dwelling place of the Muni Gomasara, where I paid homage and made offerings.

That Buddha Kāśyapa also entrusted me with those bhikṣus who practiced the Dharma with equanimity, who were diligent in skillful means, who sat in meditation with right wisdom, and who cultivated wholesome dharmas.
Then the Nāga King Śrīgṛhapati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I vow to constantly protect this great stūpa of Gomasara incense and never abandon it, even unto the time when the Dharma of the Buddha’s disciples—the bhikṣus who practice the Dharma with diligent cultivation of goodness and who do not accept offerings—is exhausted. Whether by water or fire, or by nāgas, yakṣas, or kumbhāṇḍas, or at the time of Maitreya Buddha when those who harbor anger and commit evil arise—I shall provide protection during such times; however, I shall not be the one to protect them.”
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent,
O Dragon King!"

If you can thus give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity, protecting my Dharma and upholding the Mother of the Dharma so that the Dharma may long endure, you shall be my true companions and excellent patrons.

At that time, sixty billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present in the assembly, together with all the bodhisattvas from other buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, all gathered in the Sahā world to listen to the *Sūryagarbha-mahāvyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
Having heard this, they all addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!

From this day forth, we shall constantly come to this dwelling place of the Muni within these four continents to pay homage and make offerings. We shall hold various flowers, various banners and canopies, and various gold and silver, scattering them as offerings; furthermore, we shall uphold this *dhāraṇī* for the exhaustion of evil karma through the prophecy of the Sun-Treasury, and proclaim it extensively for the sake of all sentient beings, just as the Buddha has taught.”

Now, for the sake of benefiting myself and others and bringing my evil karma to an end, I practice the path of Bodhi to fulfill the six perfections. Within this assembly, there are many billions of Māras, as well as immeasurable asaṃkhyeya numbers of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, all gathered here in this congregation surrounding the World-Honored One.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will entrust all these dwelling places of the twenty sages and munis to you, so that future māras, devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kiṃnaras, asuras, and others may not give rise to heterodox thoughts, leaving these twenty great caityas without protection and allowing those evil persons and non-humans to attempt their destruction.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
Do not be afraid. Why is this?
The Buddhas of the past likewise entrusted this place to all the dragon kings and yakṣas.
I am likewise; I entrust these twenty great *caityas* to the various *nāgas* and *yakṣas*. Why is this?

Because future sentient beings will mostly dwell within the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), I desire that their evil karma be exhausted, their pride diminished, and that they take delight in *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, so that there may be no lack of the necessities of life—food, drink, and medicinal decoctions—and so that winds and rains may fall in season, flowers and fruits may flourish, the five grains may ripen, and there may be constant peace and happiness, I entrust them to the various *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and others for these reasons.

"In all future ages, all Buddhas shall likewise, at these twenty great caityas, dwell among the forest trees, practice walking meditation, sit in dhyāna, and perform asceticism; they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turn the wheel of Dharma, and even enter parinirvāṇa to establish stūpas and shrines. Furthermore, the Buddha’s disciples—the bhikṣus who practice the Dharma and the noble ones of the four fruits—shall also reside there."
All devas and humans there perform prostrations and make offerings, generating vast merit and giving rise to the path to nirvana.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise entrusted twenty great caityas and his disciples to the dragon kings, yakṣas, and others, charging them with their protection.

“Good son! I shall now, for your sake, proclaim the Great Prophecy Dhāraṇī Mantra, which causes all sentient beings with evil minds to attain joy, enables them to give rise to the power of various samādhis, and eliminates all evil, heterodox, and afflictive mental states.”
This dhāraṇī is empowered and rejoiced in by all Buddhas of the past and future.
This mantra can cause sentient beings with evil minds to attain gentleness; it teaches the cultivation of all merits and virtues;
it causes those who practice evil to feel joy; and it brings all merits and virtues to fulfillment. In various ways...
Because their great vows have reached the further shore; because they dwell in peace and security within great wisdom;
because they have attained the *dhāraṇī* of great hearing and retention; because they have reached the ultimate consummation of great skillful means and knowledge;
because all enemies give rise to joy; because they can eliminate all calamities and afflictions; because they emerge from great perils; and because they are free from fear.
Therefore, it is because they accomplish great tasks, because they perceive the Great Truths, because they attain Great Patience,

because they enter deeply into the ocean of Great Wisdom, because they attain the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) which can eliminate all false views,
and even because they are able to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
And he spoke this divine mantra: "Tadyathā amā amā babba."
Amabari babha sayajeba baribaba.
Mitrā-mitrā-śaraya-mitrā-paripava-mitrā-saṃjñāya-niguluta-saṃjñāya.
Mokṣa kṣāṇe jaye śrīkukāpā upayirāja vināśaye.
Samāśarāyate rānabhaga raṇma babhaga raṇma śirid vikaravaṇa samajñā apobhaga.
Narayana-bhagavata-sarvadharmatathatagatavisuddha-bhaga.
“Svāhā. At that time, having spoken this mantra, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:

“This dhāraṇī is also named ‘Worthy Face’ (Bhadramukha). It is protected by the empowerment of all Buddhas; it can give rise to dhyāna and samādhi, it can exhaust all evils, and it can even lead to the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

If, in the present or future ages, at any great *caitya*, there should be other beings—whether they be Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or even rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, or non-humans—who, by means of water, fire, or various evil deeds, seek to destroy the *caitya*, you all should call to mind the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Having called the Buddhas to mind, you should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward those sentient beings and recite and maintain this great *dhāraṇī*, so that the evil-minded intentions of all such sentient beings shall be entirely extinguished.
If any Māras, humans, or non-humans have no joy in the presence of the Tathāgata, may they all give rise to joy, reverence, and offer worship.

Then, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, Māra Pāpīyas was immediately made to dwell in peace within his own palace; he naturally heard this dhāraṇī, and having heard this mantra, he immediately conceived a heart of joy toward the Buddha and attained great faith.
Having attained faith, he wept with tears falling like rain and, gathering his kinsmen together, spoke these words:
"All of you, listen attentively, listen attentively!
I have now, in the presence of this Great Muni, attained a mind of great forbearance, immovable as a mountain."

That Honored Muni is fully endowed with compassion; he emits great radiance that illuminates all nāgas, all devas, and all asuras. I too was among them, having committed various evils against the Muni; I now wish to repent and receive the three refuges.

If you have ever committed evil deeds against the Buddha, you may now repent and receive the Three Refuges. I shall now go with you together to see the Buddha, where we shall pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart. By severing the demons of affliction, you shall enter the pure path, leave behind all fear, and reach the city of Nirvana.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, surrounded before and behind by a retinue of eight billion beings, went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings, is supreme in the world; Having attained quiescence himself, he also teaches it to others.”
Patient and diligent, you have compassion for all sentient beings;
we were foolish and gave rise to evil intentions, unaware of our past karmic actions—only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can fully understand them.
Encompassing the lands within my own body, may you cause my mind to distance itself from all manner of delusions.
The Great Compassion of the Buddhas of the three periods of time accepts my prostrations and repentance for all calamities;
the same applies to the two jewels of Dharma and Sangha—to whom I take refuge with utmost sincerity, without distinction.

May that which I have offered today, Out of reverence and respect for the World’s Teacher, Cause all evils to be forever exhausted and never arise again; For as long as life endures, I take refuge in the Tathāgata and the Dharma.
When Māra Pāpīyas had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is equal toward me and all sentient beings, without distinction; his mind is always joyful, compassionate, and patient."
The Buddha said, “It is so.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was filled with great joy and gave rise to a pure mind. Once again before the Buddha, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined in reverence, withdrew to stand to one side, gazing up at the World-Honored One without weariness.

At that time, among the assembly, there was a son of Māra named Karaji who, together with his retinue, rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
What is meant by "eye"?
Is the eye the causal condition for form, or is form the causal condition for the eye?
This applies likewise, even unto the mind and mental phenomena as causal conditions.
The Buddha said:

"Good son! It is not that the eye is the causal condition for form, nor that form is the causal condition for the eye; and so on, up to: it is not that the mind is the causal condition for phenomena, nor that phenomena are the causal condition for the mind."
"Good son! The eye is empty of the nature of the eye; eye-consciousness is empty of the nature of consciousness. Good son!"

With the eye as a condition, visual consciousness arises; because of that condition, visible forms can be seen. This continues up to: with the mind as a condition, mental consciousness arises; because of that condition, mental phenomena can be known, yet no visual consciousness is to be apprehended.
Why is this? It does not come from another place, nor does it go to another place.
The eye is not permanent; throughout the three periods of time, it is entirely empty.
Such an eye neither sees fully nor sees deficiently; it does not see through conjunction, nor does it see through separation; it neither touches nor does it rely [upon anything].

For example, when the sun rises and its light illuminates everything, the brilliant radiance enters through any windows and shines upon the walls; yet that light on the wall does not form the thought, "I am dark" or "I am bright."
This light does not exist solely on a single wall or on many walls; rather, this light arises due to causes and conditions.

This wall and the light are neither joined nor separate. One perceives the light because of the wall, yet this wall and the light do not have the thought, "The sun can produce me," nor does the sun think, "I am producing this light."

Why is this? Once the sun has set, its light also ceases to exist; its place of departure and its place of arrival are entirely empty, with not a single thing visible. It is by reason of the sun as a condition that one is able to perceive these luminous colors, and it is by reason of the brilliant illumination of the light that they become visible. The production of consciousness regarding them is likewise so.

These six internal sense bases give rise to the six external sense bases, and likewise the six external sense bases give rise to the six internal sense bases; yet the six external sense bases are not the causal conditions, nor are the six internal sense bases the causal conditions.

Why is this? Because these and that are devoid of intrinsic nature, neither aggregated nor conjoined, neither combined nor dependent, extending even to the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
That consciousness which arises from their conjunction is likewise not aggregated, not conjoined, and not dependent.
Why is this? Because they do not depend upon one another, as their objective spheres are distinct.

"These phenomena and consciousness—the wisdom that knows and sees the causal conditions of all formations (saṃskāra)—arise because of the causal conditions of formations; and when this consciousness arises, it consists of three kinds of formations."
What are the three types of formations?
They are bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations.
What are bodily formations?
Bodily activity refers to the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; this is called bodily activity.

As these breaths move in and out, coming and going, each inhalation and exhalation is unaware of the other. If new consciousness arises, old consciousness does not remain, because such is their essential nature: they are neither an accumulation nor distinct entities, and within suchness, they do not depend upon one another.
The wind moves through space with equality; yet the wind is not space, and space is not the wind.
Why is this? Because they do not touch one another and neither constitutes the domain of the other.
Both of these are empty and likewise ineffable. Why is this?

Because they are devoid of characteristics, because there is neither increase nor decrease, because they do not rely upon this shore or the other shore, and because they abide as suchness within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this is called the activity of the body.

Therefore, bodily formations are not the support for consciousness, nor its companion, nor its conjunction, nor its accumulation; they are never supported by it because their characteristics are distinct. Likewise, consciousness is not supported by the body because it is free from conjunction. This is called "bodily formations."
"What are verbal formations?
Verbal formations are of two kinds, namely vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). What is vitarka?"
What is contemplation?

When two types of mental states arise regarding the inhalation and exhalation, reflecting upon and recollecting them is called *vitarka* (applied thought). Furthermore, as the mind gradually becomes subtle until it finally gives rise to a pure mind through such progressive elimination, this is also called *vitarka*.

This awakening arises because it depends upon the entering and exiting [of breath]; having arisen, it immediately ceases. Furthermore, the faculties and their objects do not perceive "this" or "that," because the characteristics of the objective sphere are mutually separated and its nature and marks are non-existent; thus, one cannot even describe it as long or short—this is called awakening.
What is contemplation?
If there is a person who contemplates the sensation of coldness touching the body and practices accordingly, or further contemplates that all breaths are characterized by heat and are like wind.

To contemplate that wind through its causal conditions and know it as contact is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). Each remains distinct from its respective object, and their mutual characteristics are separated; even to the point where one cannot describe them as long or short—this is called "applied thought and sustained thought" (vitarka-vicāra).
"What is mental activity? Mental activity is called 'perception.
What is meant by 'perception'?"

He knows all phenomena, even to the point of knowing the inhalation and exhalation of breath at the proper time and the inhalation and exhalation of breath at improper times; he knows that this exhalation is not that inhalation, and that that inhalation is not that exhalation, knowing all such distinctions.

Reflecting in this way, one discerns the characteristics conducive to practice and those not conducive to practice; this is called the basis of that wind, and these two kinds cannot be described as being obtainable.
What is volition (*cetanā*)? What is the characteristic of the mind (*citta-lakṣaṇa*)?

Up to the discernment of the distinctions between formations (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), once these have been performed, one enters the path to *nirvāṇa*, transcends the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), and is said to be "born beyond birth-and-death" (*cyuti-bhava*). Within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the mind is able to eliminate these [distinctions]; this is what is called volition.

Such winds neither go nor come; they abide thus within that consciousness of thought. From the eye as eye, up to the mind as mind, each does not touch the other. When the three types of sensation are exhausted, one is called a noble person (*ārya*).
"In this way, son of good family!

It is not that the eye is the causal condition for form, nor that form is the causal condition for the eye; and so on, up to: it is not that the mind is the causal condition for phenomena, nor that phenomena are the causal condition for the mind."
Why is this? These two objects are neither distant nor near; they are neither aggregated, nor conceptualized, nor conjoined. Why is this?
"Because it is ineffable; because it does not rely upon this shore, the other shore, or that which is between them; and because it relies upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

When the Buddha had spoken these words, at that time the son of Māra, Karaji, together with his twenty thousand followers—who had previously practiced merit within the teachings of the Buddhas of the past—all attained the Patience of Accordance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who have also planted various roots of virtue in the past; some have attained the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; some have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin; some will serve as seeds of merit within the Lesser Vehicle in the future, even serving as seeds for the state of a pratyekabuddha in the future; and others have resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, among that assembly there were sixty *bimbara* of nāgas who, from the distant past until now, had never encountered a Buddha; having now heard this Dharma, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
