At that time, the great earth of this entire trichiliocosm Buddha-field shook in six ways, trembling and quaking violently. All the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions each attained various Bodhisattva samādhis. Having attained these samādhis, they each scattered various jewels, various garments, various incenses, and various flowers upon the Buddha as an offering to the Tathāgata, saying these words:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
It is inconceivable.

Since time immemorial, we have never before seen or heard such a great assembly expound this *samādhi-bala-dhāraṇī*. This is the second turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma for the benefit of beings by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. We shall now single-mindedly uphold this *Sūtra of the Great Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury* (*Divyāvadāna*) and explain it in detail for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the assembly of Māras, devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, and piśācas who were gathered there all spoke thus:
"It is inconceivable!"
“Śākyamuni Tathāgata is able to bring such benefit to sentient beings!

Each was filled with great joy and, from the sky, scattered various kinds of music, various jewels, various garments, various necklaces, flower garlands, burning incense, and powdered incense as offerings to the Tathāgata.
At that time, Sāgara, the Dragon King, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that the Tathāgata will temporarily enter the ocean and come to my abode to accept my humble offering out of compassion for me."
"If the Buddha, the Tathāgata, should come to my palace, all of my retinue shall be able to hear this Great Dharani of the Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury.
Then the Naga King Sagara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If all the men and women within that great ocean were to hear this Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury and listen with single-minded devotion, how much merit would they obtain?
The Buddha said, “Nāga King!

If a son of good family were to offer as alms to the Tathāgata the seven treasures filling the four continents, and there were another sentient being who, having fully heard this Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury, listened with single-minded devotion, the former merit would not equal even a hundredth part of the latter; it would not equal a hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor could it even be reached by calculation.”
"Great King!
If there are those who hear this profound sutra, their merit will be immeasurable.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara spoke again, saying:

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not enter the great ocean, I shall transcribe this *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* on the Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury and place it within my palace; by this cause and condition, the merit and virtue of as many nāgas as there are in that sea shall increase."
The Buddha said, “Nāgarāja!

In whatever place this *Mahāvyākaraṇa-sūtra of the Sun-Treasury* is transcribed and installed according to the Dharma, and is venerated and offered to with respect, one shall obtain ten kinds of benefits.”

What are these ten? If there is anyone who can transcribe this sutra according to the Dharma and make offerings to it with single-minded devotion, all auspiciousness will prevail within their household;
they shall attain great mastery among the assembly, and the five grains will be abundant, while all kinds of livelihoods, money, wealth, and treasures will be fully provided.
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

If within a house or amidst a multitude, one extracts this *Mahāvyākaraṇa-sūtra of the Sun-Treasury* and makes offerings to it, then sixty billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will come to that place in great numbers to pay homage and make offerings to this sūtra."

By these causes and conditions, all manner of evil matters—strife, quarrels, epidemics, and various malignant diseases—as well as the high price and scarcity of grain, national famines, bandits from other regions, and untimely winds and rains, shall all be extinguished.
Those sixty billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We shall provide various forms of protection and support for them, ensuring they have all their wishes fulfilled.”
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

If within a household or amidst a great assembly, this *Sūtra of the Great Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury* is transcribed and installed according to the Dharma, then Śakra Devendra, the various Brahmā deities, the Four Heavenly Kings, the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals along with their retinues, and even the Great Virtuous Deity (*Mahādeva*) together with his sons and daughters, the Sārasvata deity, the Sthira-bhūmi deity, the Susthitasukha deity, and all their followers will come to that land. Day and night, they will constantly provide protection with a sincere heart and bestow peace and happiness upon it."
At that time, Śakra Devendra and the gods up to those of the Sudṛśa and Sudarśana heavens, having heard these words, spoke thus: "So it is, Tathāgata!"
“I and my retinue shall always go with a sincere heart to protect that land.
“Furthermore, O Dragon King!

If there are those in households or even in nations who copy this sutra—whether they be humans of merit or devas—who in past lives have made offerings to many Buddhas, practiced giving, and observed the precepts—such persons will go there to take birth.”
"Furthermore, Dragon King!

If there are households, or even entire nations, that transcribe this sutra, the sentient beings therein will be diligent and courageous, taking no pleasure in the five desires, and constantly practicing the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Dragon King!
If there are householders, or even entire nations, that transcribe this sutra, those beings who are fields of merit will always delight in dwelling in peace.
Furthermore, Dragon King!"
If there is a land where this sutra is transcribed, various kinds of wholesome dharmas will constantly rain down upon that country.
Furthermore, Dragon King,
if there is a land where this sutra is transcribed, the sentient beings therein will constantly practice and never abandon the ten wholesome courses of action.
"Furthermore, Dragon King!
In whatever land this sutra is transcribed, the sentient beings therein will constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, Dragon King!"
If there are those who transcribe this sūtra in their homes, or even throughout entire kingdoms, the sentient beings therein—whether humans or devas—shall never enter the evil realms.
Great King!

In whatever kingdom this *Sūtra of the Great Prophecy of the Sun-Treasury* is transcribed according to the Dharma, established for worship, and recited repeatedly, one shall fully obtain these ten kinds of benefits.
Why is this? If there are those who read, recite, and practice according to the teachings of this *Sūryagarbha-sūtra*, the mass of their merit could not be fully described even in a hundred kalpas.
“O Dragon King!
This *Mahāsaṃnipāta-mahāvyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the *Sūryagarbha*, is thus profound, capable of fulfilling great vows and bringing great benefit.

Having spoken this sūtra, the bodhisattvas who had come from all the buddha-fields of the ten directions gathered at this great assembly in the Sahā world-system of the trichiliocosm, together with this host of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and even including the Māras, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, humans, and non-humans—all attained realization according to their respective capacities, their hearts were satisfied, and they all rejoiced greatly, each making offerings and remaining there in unison.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 45; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 46.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
15. The Section on Candragarbha, Chapter One: The Moon-Banner Divine Incantation.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Kāraṇḍava, the abode of the sages and seers, together with a great assembly of six million bhikṣus—both those still in training and those beyond training—who had all attained liberation from the firm fetters of the afflictions and were now diligently applying skillful means to sever their residual habitual tendencies. He was also accompanied by an immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and innumerable multitude of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, all of whom had attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*) and were transforming the hosts of nāgas.

When the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* had been preached, immediately a great cloud of flowers appeared in the west—namely, *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, and *vārṣika* flowers—and such clouds of flowers all manifested and arrived.

Within those flower clouds appeared a half-moon, ten yojanas in width; within that half-moon, there further appeared a lecture hall consisting of multi-storied pavilions of pure gold, exquisitely adorned and subtle.
The radiance of that hall surpassed the light of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of suns and moons; its light illuminated Mount Kālaṃjara in its entirety.

Furthermore, various extraordinary clouds of flowers appeared—namely, *utpala* flowers, up to and including *pāriyātaka* flowers. The brilliance of these flowers shone upon the dwelling place of the Sage Seer, the lecture hall with its seven-jeweled five-pillared multi-storied pavilion, which was so exceedingly marvelous and subtle that it eclipsed the light of the sun and moon, rendering them invisible.
Within that hall, there further appeared a half-moon; within the half-moon was a blue lotus with a thousand petals, and upon its calyx sat the World-Honored One, seated upright, preaching the Dharma.
That light shone universally upon the entire assembly, and upon the head of each individual appeared a subtle celestial wreath in the shape of a crescent moon;
furthermore, there rained down various jewels, various flowers, and various fragrances.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, seeing such miraculous transformations and feeling a sense of wonder, and knowing that the great assembly harbored doubts in their hearts, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“Only the Buddha has completely eliminated all afflictions; He awakens those who are blind and in darkness.
For the sake of all living beings, he closes the gates to the evil realms, Causing all sentient beings to abide in the wholesome paths.”
Only the Buddha subdues billions of māras, causing all non-Buddhists to lose their radiance;
he tames sentient beings so they may abide in dāna and śīla, drying up the ocean of their afflictions.
They cause beings to bathe in the water of eight virtues, And deliver sentient beings with the jewels of the factors of enlightenment;
Countless billions of beings enter nirvana, As they are able to turn the jewel of the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
All the various hosts of nāgas, driven by anger, commit all manner of evils;
oppressed by craving, they possess no compassion.
Only the Buddha can benefit them and cause them to take refuge in faith.
The dragons from the four continents all assemble, With single-minded devotion they take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
Having exhausted all karmic obstructions and afflictions, They all protect the True Dharma and dwell in peace.
Furthermore, here there appear clouds of exquisite flowers, within which the light of the half-moon shines;
all these manifest as garlands of half-moons—what Buddha-activity do they now intend to perform?
These various flowers were accumulated like a great mountain; rain fell of incense, flowers, and many jewels.
When the great assembly beheld this auspicious omen, doubt arose in their hearts: "What kind of Dharma-rain will now fall?"
This place is subtle and most supreme; this great assembly all relies upon it.
Having cultivated offerings to the Buddhas of the past, these lions among men have come in this manner.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“In the western direction there is a world named Candravijaya; the Buddha there is named Sūryacandraprabha.

There is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha-kumārabhūta, who, leading a retinue of eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, wishes to come here to see me, pay homage, and make offerings. He wishes to assemble with the great multitude to express his sympathetic joy, and furthermore, he wishes to entrust the Eye of the True Dharma to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others.”

At that moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha, together with his retinue of eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, came from that world to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood before the Buddha. With palms joined, they all spoke these verses in a single voice:
"Throughout countless auspicious kalpas, You have practiced for the sake of sentient beings;
Auspiciously you behold sentient beings, Who are oppressed by the suffering of birth and death."
Auspiciousness lies in giving through almsgiving; the Great Sage brings benefit by practicing generosity, thereby transcending both humans and devas.
Auspiciousness lies in guarding pure precepts; sentient beings cannot shake them.
May auspiciousness cause those who are angry to abide in a mind of loving-kindness;
may auspiciousness inspire diligence in those who are indolent;
and may auspiciousness lead those away from evil realms and establish them in the happy destinies.
Auspicious is the well-cultivated patience that forgives angry and evil minds;
auspicious is this rare occurrence, and therefore I take refuge in it entirely.
Auspicious is the cultivation of the various dhyānas, which brings about rare wonders among the devas.
Auspiciousness completely dries up the ocean of all sentient beings' suffering;
auspiciousness cultivates wisdom, turning back the wheel of the evil realms;
auspiciousness leads to supreme enlightenment, reaching the most difficult-to-attain place.
Auspicious one who subdues the hosts of Māra, Who establishes the banner of the True Dharma;
That which is turned by the Auspicious One Is the most excellent Wheel of the Dharma.
The Auspicious One, out of compassion for those in other views, Has subdued all the non-Buddhists.
Auspiciously descending the rain of Dharma, It satisfies the thirsty world.
Auspiciously acting as the witness, For devas, humans, and gandharvas;
Auspiciously filling the world, I am the supreme teacher.
Auspiciously establishing the four fruits, Worthy of receiving the world's offerings;
Auspiciously causing billions of beings To dwell securely in nirvāṇa.
While the Auspicious One remains for long, The Eye of Dharma is established.
May auspiciousness long abide in the world, for there is none equal to it in the world.
May there be the auspicious fruit of awakening, the great benefit obtained by all beings.
For the sake of sentient beings, may auspiciousness proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma.
With the water of the Dharma, Śrī bathes all sentient beings;
Śrī is well able to deliver these gods and humans.
Śrī is able to manifest the stainless, truly wondrous Dharma.
Auspiciously removing all the afflictions of sentient beings;
Auspicious are the Saṅgha, the foremost in the world;
Auspicious is their birth in the world, Which brings benefit to humans and devas.
May auspiciousness cause the fourfold assembly to be bright, pure, and radiant with excellent light;
may auspiciousness cause the fourfold assembly to fully protect the discipline of the precepts.
May auspiciousness lead them to practice generosity, maintain ethical conduct, and apply diligence.
Auspicious is the cultivation of patience and dhyāna, as well as sublime prajñā.
Auspicious is the Great Brahmā King, the lord of the Sahā world.
Auspicious is the Great Māra King, the sovereign of all desires.
Auspicious Kauśika, with his retinue of attendants;
auspicious hosts of devas, along with their palaces and so forth;
auspicious Vaiśravaṇa, and the hosts of yakṣas.
Auspicious Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with his retinue of gandharvas;
auspicious Virūḍhaka, together with the kumbhāṇḍas;
auspicious Virūpākṣa, along with the hosts of nāga armies.
Auspicious Sūrya and Candra, the planets and the lunar mansions;
auspicious Maheśvara, his son, and the Lord of the Elements;
auspicious Vāyu and Agni, as well as the Earth Goddess and the others.
Auspicious hosts of nāgas, as well as asuras;
auspicious rākṣasas, along with kiṃnaras; auspicious garuḍas, mahoragas, and the rest.
Auspicious one who rains down sweet rain, great divine king who brings the rain;
auspicious protector of the land, sovereign among all men.
Auspicious brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra.
To the most excellent and honored Teacher, who is the object of auspicious offerings,
may those who hear [this] with auspicious intent hear the truly faultless Dharma.
To all those in the past and the future who make offerings to the Triple Gem, may there be auspiciousness.
Auspicious to all beings, may they extinguish all afflictions;
auspicious to all sentient beings, may they dwell together in the True Dharma.
Auspicious are generosity and ethical discipline, and the perfection of diligence.
Auspicious is the perfection of dhyāna, the perfection of kṣānti;
auspicious are all things for those who have reached the shore of wisdom.
Auspiciously, may all diseases be entirely healed and cured.
May all auspiciousness come to rest; may all beings in this turbid and evil world attain auspiciousness and be completely liberated;
may all beings through auspiciousness attain all that is free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
May all that grows from seeds upon the auspicious earth—
may all auspicious crops, medicinal herbs, forest trees, and fruits,
all of them auspicious, ripen in full accordance with the seasons.
The essence of the auspicious supreme place fills all locations;
the vital energy of the auspicious person abides everywhere;
the vital energy of the auspicious Dharma fills all beings.
May all auspiciousness come to rest, and may all evils and misfortunes cease;
may auspiciousness cause sentient beings to attain supreme enlightenment,
and may they reach the further shore with mastery over all phenomena.
The auspicious rain of the True Dharma universally moistens all sentient beings;
may all these auspicious sentient beings be completely delivered from the three realms of existence.
May all be rendered auspicious, and may they all realize Great Nirvana.
“O Great Virtuous Bhagavān!

I now wish to proclaim auspicious verses and a mantra of great power. This mantra was proclaimed by the sages of the past; it establishes and protects, is well able to increase matters of auspiciousness, can eliminate all stains of sin and evil views, and leads one into the roots of goodness to increase great compassion.”

By means of these mantra-syllables, one is able to provide benefit and support to all sentient beings; even those among the deer, birds, and beasts who hear them shall have their minds brought to peace and stability. They shall be freed from all obstacles of the turbid and evil world, and such hindrances as those of sentient beings and those of the Dharma shall all come to rest. All roots of goodness, according to whatever they encounter, shall enter their hearts; their mindfulness and wisdom shall become firm and stable; their reputation, appearance, and form shall be pleasing to others; and they shall be courageous and fearless regarding the ten paths of wholesome action, remaining steadfastly established in the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

They are firmly established in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they are firmly established in great loving-kindness, great compassion, the power of great skillful means, all-knowledge, and even ultimate, unsurpassed nirvana—except for those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, slandered the true Dharma, reviled the noble ones, or held the two views of eternalism and nihilism. It is only these various sinful persons who are excluded.

This is an auspicious phrase, constantly established and protected by the former sages. Such a mantra phrase can also cause the various devas to believe and accept it, leading them to enter the path of the ten wholesome karmas; it can also lead them to enter the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the power of great skillful means, and even up to all-knowledge and unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it can cause all the retinues of those māras to attain faith and take refuge.

He causes all devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras to enter the ten paths of wholesome action, from the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā; he establishes them in great loving-kindness and great compassion, the power of great skillful means, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, omniscience, the knowledge of all modes, and unsurpassed nirvāṇa—except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes, slandered the true Dharma, or reviled the worthy and holy ones.
Having spoken these words, he uttered this mantra: "Tadyathā | candālī..."
Candara-viti candara-mati candara-bha-śiḥ.
Candrabhāte candrabhale candrabhāve.
Candālakṣite candrāja candrākṣi.
Candālati candālaṃmi candaulu.
Candara-varo candara-mudari candara-bhadiye.
Candarasame candarakakṣe candarindare.
Candāla-acara candāli-vi candāla-pali-vi.
Candālavatsi candrāsiti candrapāṭe.
Candāla-ne-candāra-kiḷi-candāra-pakṣa.
Candālaseni candāralūmi candāragopī.
Candrasaṃbhe candrasvare candrapratiṣṭhe.
Candāla-accha candāra-suti candāra-gaṇi.
Candālaśvi candālasiphaśi candālamaṇi.
Candrabhadrī Mṛgībhadrī Kāruṇyabhadrī.
Satyavati, Tāḍitavati, Kṣayavati, Śāntavati.
*Trilapatī-candraloke svāhā.* "World-Honored One!..."

This divine mantra was established and protected by the Buddhas of the past, the Munis, and the sages. This divine mantra is named Candradhvaja-candra; it enables all sentient beings to attain auspiciousness, take refuge in the Triple Gem, eliminate all evil and grave offenses, and even attain unsurpassed Nirvana.

When the Bodhisattva Candragarbha spoke this mantra, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; all sentient beings dwelling in the desire realm and the form realm were struck with great terror, trembling, and became restless with fear.

At that time, the various devas rained down diverse kinds of jewels, diverse kinds of flowers, diverse kinds of incense, diverse kinds of powdered incense, diverse kinds of garments, diverse kinds of bedding, and diverse kinds of necklaces.
When such various things as these rain down, these objects strike against one another and produce the sounds of various sublime Dharmas:
namely, the sound of the Triple Gem, the sound of the three codes of discipline, the sound of the three liberations,

the sound of the three types of supernormal knowledge, the sound of the three trainings, the sound of being free from the desires of the three realms, and the sound of the three kinds of enlightenment.
The sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of non-self, the sound of emptiness, the sound of wishlessness,

the sound of detachment from joy, the sound of non-arising, the sound of the nature of reality (*tathatā*), the sound of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the sound of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*),
the sound of suchness, the sound of neither going nor coming, and the sound of being nowhere established and never regressing.
The sound of exerting diligence that is without a dwelling place or basis; the sounds of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*);
the sounds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
the sounds of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); the sounds of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*); and the sounds of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The sound of upholding the True Dharma; the sound of the law of causes and conditions; the sound of protecting the True Dharma.

Like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, or the moon reflected in water, they gather in those among sentient beings who are ready to be delivered. Having grown weary of and detached from cyclic existence, they depart for secluded forest hermitages (*āraṇya*). They themselves practice what they preach without contradiction, remaining steadfastly established in accordance with the Dharma. [They utter] the sounds of seeking all roots of goodness; the sound of the ten stages (*bhūmi*); the sound of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the sound of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); the sound of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); the sound of turning the wheel of Dharma; the sound of causing those wandering in birth and death to abide in the Eightfold Noble Path rather than following the flow of transmigration; and the sound of subduing the four Māras to lead them into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Having heard these sounds, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—including those in the hells—each of them, by the power of causes and conditions from having been close friends in previous lives, receive into their ears all the aforementioned sounds according to their respective planted roots of goodness: whether it be through generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), or the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); whether it be the resolve and vows made toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; or the great aspirational vows made toward the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). To each of those beings, the sounds accord with what they have previously practiced, just as described before.

According to the roots of goodness they have previously cultivated and the karmic conditions they have created, they are all able to recollect these matters of their past lives; cherishing, respecting, and placing faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they quickly come to take refuge, and among those sentient beings, whatever karmic obstructions they naturally possessed are entirely eliminated.
Having passed away from those realms, they were born simultaneously in the heavens and among humans, where they all went together to the Buddha’s presence to sit and listen to the Dharma.

Likewise, animals and hungry ghosts also all gathered there; through the power of causes and conditions involving their former karma and virtuous spiritual friends, and by virtue of having planted roots of goodness—whether through generosity (*dāna*) or ethical discipline (*śīla*), even up to the point where their karmic obstructions were completely extinguished.

Among them, some come in their very bodies to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma; others, having passed away there, are reborn among gods or humans and then come to the Buddha’s presence to listen to and receive the True Dharma.
Thus, all humans and devas came to where the Buddha was, with the sole exception of the Māra king and his retinue, as well as the four asura kings and their retinues.
At that time, the ground of the trichiliocosm was as level as the palm of a hand.

At that time, Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, the Black Mountains, and all such mountains, as well as the great oceans and forests, were entirely invisible, with the sole exception of Mount Khadiraka.

That mountain was as vast and expansive as the fourteen worlds, with no empty space between humans and non-humans; above it, too, it was like the fourteen worlds—immeasurable, incalculable, and without limit—as the great assembly filled the void to behold the Buddha, to pay homage, and to make offerings.
To mature sentient beings, he saw a great assembly gathering, having come together for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

Within this trichiliocosm, all existing palaces, dwellings, groves, trees, medicinal herbs, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and various miscellaneous precious objects—all such things as these were entirely transformed into crescent moons and appeared there.

Within each half-month, they emit this colored light, like the combined radiance of a thousand suns and moons, which universally illumines the trichiliocosm Buddha-field; such are the vast and magnificent adornments of these colored forms.
At that time, all the boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions appeared before them.

In those Buddha-fields, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devānām-indra, and other kings of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and all the kings of spirits, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, were able to see this Buddha and the great assembly gathered there, and they further beheld such wondrously colored radiance.
Having seen this, they all resolved to come.

Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, they arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling in a single thought-moment, where they paid homage, made offerings, and listened to the Dharma with a sincere heart.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candragarbha scattered divine powdered jewels, celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial garlands, and celestial garments over the Buddha. Having scattered them three times, he circumambulated him to the right three times, stood before the Buddha with palms joined, and addressed him, saying:
"O Bhagavat of Great Virtue!

"I have committed transgressions and was unable to join this great assembly. All the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the ten directions have gathered here, and it is only due to certain circumstances that I arrived here later."
“O Bhagavat, Great Virtuous One!

While in my own land, the world-system of Candravijaya, I entered the Apramāṇābha samādhi together with my retinue for seven days. Upon arising from that samādhi, I immediately asked the Tathāgata Sūryacandraprabha:
‘O Bhagavat, Great Virtuous One!’”
"Where have your followers and retinue gone now?
The Buddha Candrasūryaprabha replied to me, saying:
"O son of good family!
To the east, passing beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds from here, there is a world named Sahā.

In that land there is a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who dwells in the world teaching the Dharma and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; he is currently present there amidst a great assembly.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas residing in the buddha-lands of the ten directions gathered together in that world in order to see Śākyamuni Buddha, pay him homage and make offerings, and listen to the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.
"Therefore, my retinue has also gone there.
You too may now go to that Buddha’s abode to pay homage, make offerings, and recite the Moon Banner Moon-Dhāraṇī.
For this reason, I have come here last."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Candragarbha spoke these verses:
"The Buddha alone is the father of all sentient beings; He rescues them from the fires of affliction.
I now repent before the Most Victorious Buddha, For it was due to my own circumstances that I arrived late."
Only the Buddha is the Great Illuminator for humans and devas, Universally shining upon all lands in the ten directions;
I now repent before the Dharma-King of Buddhas, For it was due to my own circumstances that I arrived late.
Only the Buddha can show the path to nirvāṇa, turning back those who are heading toward evil realms;
I offer my thanks to the Muni, the Great Caravan Leader, for coming later on account of me.
The Buddha alone is the great physician of the world; To those who have lost their sight, he grants the Dharma-eye.
I offer my apologies to the most supreme Great King of Physicians, For it was due to my circumstances that I arrived later.
Only the Buddha can show the various rafts and floats, enabling sentient beings to cross the river of the four afflictions;
I offer my thanks to the Most Victorious among Men, for it was due to my own karmic conditions that I came later.
Only the Buddha’s cloud of compassion sends down the rain of Dharma, Washing away the defilements of affliction within the minds of sentient beings.
I offer thanks to the Great Sage, the Honored One of Supreme Dharma, For having come later due to my own karmic conditions.
Only the Buddha alone, amidst the four currents, Can ferry sentient beings across the ocean of the three realms of existence;
I offer my apologies to the World-Honored One, the speaker of truth, Because I have come late due to my own circumstances.
Only the Buddha opens the treasuries of all true dharmas, Saving sentient beings with the seven riches of the noble ones;
I thank the Great and Victorious Master of Dharma-Gifts, Because I have come later due to my own causes and conditions.
Only the Buddha can grant eyes to sentient beings, Uprooting the blindness and darkness of ignorance.
I was originally seated in a single samādhi, With my mind dwelling peacefully in āpana-dhyāna;
Yet I did not see the Buddha manifest his supernatural transformations, Because I arrived later due to my own karmic conditions.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”

"You possess great diligence, being able to enter deep meditative concentration for seven days; such a wondrous concentration is the dwelling place of a manly hero, the dwelling place of a Tathāgata, and the unsurpassed dwelling place."

“Good son! You and your retinue shall dwell for seven days in the Āpānaka-dhyāna. By virtue of this principle, you shall now fully accomplish [the path] for immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, asuras, kiṃnaras, humans, and non-humans, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; their karmic obstructions, sentient-being obstructions, dharma obstructions, dhyāna obstructions, affliction obstructions, and awakening-factor obstructions shall all be extinguished without remainder.”
Among those sentient beings, there are some who attain the samādhi of the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta and do not regress from the unsurpassed path.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who attain the great illumination-patience (mahā-vidyā-kṣānti) regarding all Buddha-dharmas; by virtue of these roots of goodness, such beings will before long achieve perfect awakening in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"In this way, son of good family!
Because you have entered meditative concentration for seven days, you are able at once to extinguish the great suffering of sentient beings and cause them to achieve a great mass of merit."

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who, relying solely on recitation and chanting, seek to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such persons will mostly take pleasure in and become attached to worldly matters. Because of their attachment to the worldly, they cannot even subdue their own minds and afflictions; how then could they possibly subdue the afflictions of others?”

Good sons and good daughters who delight in reading and reciting while seeking bodhi will become envious, seeking fame, profit, wealth, and nobility; with arrogant hearts, they consider themselves right and disparage others. Because of this self-exaltation, they cannot even attain the roots of goodness of the desire realm, let alone attain all the roots of goodness of the form and formless realms!
Furthermore, they cannot even attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, much less the path of a pratyekabuddha or unsurpassed enlightenment! Why is this?

Because the ultimate truth of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; therefore, it cannot be attained through worldly means, but rather through the most supreme roots of goodness and the great mass of merit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son! Just as a spark from a firefly cannot dry up the profound great ocean, even so, even so!”
"Good son! One cannot exhaust the great ocean of one's own afflictions by means of worldly methods; how then could one exhaust the afflictions of other sentient beings? Good son!"
For example, the wind blown by the mouth of a single person cannot damage the great earth of the world.
In the same way, son of good family,
one cannot achieve great loving-kindness and great compassion through worldly means.
"Good son! For example, a lotus fiber cannot move Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, by means of weighing it.
In the same way, good son!"
If one cannot fulfill the wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of worldly [attainments], how could one enable others to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Thus it is, son of good family!
The wisdom that can achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not of the mundane world.
What is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
It is the cultivation and performance of all meritorious deeds.
If one cultivates merit, one should also repeatedly cultivate and refine both body and mind;
if one cultivates the body, one is then able to cultivate the mind;
and if one is able to cultivate the mind, one is then able to cultivate wisdom.

If one can cultivate the body and mind through the cultivation of wisdom, such a person will be able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās, employ the four means of attraction to gather all sentient beings, and bring them to maturity in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"One attains equal and perfect enlightenment not by means of worldly convention.
Within the realm of worldly convention, there are sentient beings who cling to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism; these are not the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings within the realm of worldly convention who hold the view of self and the view of extremes; these, too, are not the ultimate truth."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, within the mundane world, seek happiness in the present life as well as in future lives; yet this is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

I do not see any other single dharma that can exhaust karmic obstructions and even afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), enabling immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, in a single day and night, to all attain reverent faith in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and to mature and dwell securely in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
"If there is a practitioner of dhyāna who, although unable to fully maintain the precepts and whose dhyāna methods are incomplete such that they have not yet attained samādhi,
nevertheless— whether sitting or walking during the first and last watches of the night— abides in accordance with dhyāna-concentration,
then they will be able to sever immeasurable karmic obstructions and cause many hundreds of millions..."
If even those nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all attain faith and take refuge,

thereby maturing various roots of goodness and accumulations of merit for enlightenment, how much more so for one who fully maintains the precepts, attains the true Dharma-samādhi, various dhāraṇīs, and patience,
and achieves the four Brahma-vihāras and the tranquility of meditative concentration— what would be the merit obtained in seven days?
It is inconceivable and beyond all analogy; how much more so its ability to exhaustively eliminate the obscurations of sentient beings,
such as the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations, leaving none remaining, and even bringing immeasurable sentient beings to maturity toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
while also accumulating immeasurable masses of merit and fulfilling the six *pāramitās*.
...the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Why is this?

For one who practices dhyāna, whether walking or sitting, removes all obstructive dharmas so that the mind becomes pure; by relinquishing all conceptualizations of objective referents within every activity, this is the perfection of giving.
To constantly and without rest relinquish thoughts of objective referents is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
To give rise to no afflictions or wounds amidst all sensory objects is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Not abandoning detachment is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Not allowing the mind to be lax regarding any activity is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Joyfully enduring the non-arising nature of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, if one does not give rise to agitation or turbidity regarding sense objects, this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
If one is free from wounds or blemishes regarding sense objects, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
If one is not defiled by sense objects, this is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
If one is unshakable regarding sense objects, this is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
If there is no conceptualization or recollection regarding objects of perception, this is the perfection of dhyāna.
If one practices with exclusive purity regarding objects of perception, this is the perfection of prajñā.
"Furthermore, relinquishing all aggregates is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Not forming conceptual attachments to the aggregates is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Seeking the notion of non-self within the aggregates is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."
To conceive of the aggregates as enemies is the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
To prevent the aggregates from burning intensely is the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).
The ultimate relinquishing of all aggregates is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, the relinquishing of all elements (*dhātu*) is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
To remain undisturbed and unpolluted amidst all realms is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To relinquish the causes and conditions of all realms is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
To repeatedly renounce all realms is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Not giving rise to [discriminative] activity regarding the various realms is the perfection of dhyāna.
Regarding the various realms as being like illusions is the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, this is the perfection of dāna.
To have a mind free from hatred or attachment toward all sentient beings is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To give rise to thoughts of compassion toward all sentient beings is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
To give rise to the thought of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To embrace all sentient beings with the thought of joy is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
To not conceive notions of "this" or "that," or of "self" and "other" regarding all sentient beings, is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva bestows the gift of Dharma upon all sentient beings without giving rise to dualistic thoughts, this is the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
To speak with gentle and loving words to all sentient beings is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To refrain from giving rise to any evil toward all sentient beings is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Not withdrawing from kind speech toward all sentient beings is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Bringing benefit and compassion to all sentient beings is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
To practice the Dharma together with all sentient beings is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, to establish sentient beings in various states of goodness is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Not relying upon any phenomena is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Entering into all phenomena by means of a single path is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
To have no thought of agitation or turbidity regarding all phenomena and all difficulties is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
To not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
To be able to enter all phenomena through a single word and explain them for the sake of sentient beings—this is the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Good son!
It is by means of this essential teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, not through worldly means."
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), employ this very dharma for themselves and for others; by diligently practicing until the six pāramitās are fulfilled, they shall swiftly attain perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."

In this way, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas currently existing in other worlds throughout the ten directions, through their skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), shall all, by means of these very dharmas of the path, swiftly attain perfect enlightenment in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

In the future, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions will all diligently cultivate such profound skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), practicing the six pāramitās, and thereby attain perfect enlightenment in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is not of the mundane world.

“Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently seek and practice in order that the Dharma-eye may long endure and the lineage of the Three Jewels may not be severed; for the sake of all sentient beings, they hold aloft the great bright torch to provide illumination, causing them to bring rest to the suffering of the path of afflictions and the path of cyclic existence, and bestowing upon them the eye of wisdom.”
They cause all beings to cross over the flow of the three realms of existence and establish them on the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.

Regarding the noble Dharma, they remain silent; during the first and last watches of the night, they abandon gain and dwell in accordance with it; they are well able to give rise to samādhi and right reception, and they abide in association with the three gates of liberation.

“Good son! Because you have now entered meditative absorption in the *apānaka* dhyāna for seven days, and because you have brought immeasurable sentient beings to maturity, I therefore exhort you and all good sons and daughters: whether in the present age, the future, or the final age, within my Dharma, you should always dwell in association with equanimity during both the first and last watches of the night, illuminating with the eye of the True Dharma so as to uphold and prosper the Triple Gem and ensure it is never severed. For the sake of maturing sentient beings, you should diligently cultivate this ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and dwell in diligent cultivation to fulfill the six *pāramitās*.
The Buddha addressed all the hosts of devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and yakṣas:

"You should nurture and provide for this person, giving them clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, providing everything they require. You should also protect them, removing calamities and misfortunes, and cause all凶衰 (inauspicious decline), 殃惡 (calamitous evils), and diseases to be completely extinguished."
Why is this? Those who are in accord with dhyāna are my true children; they are born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma.
If there are donors, devas, nāgas, or yakṣas who, in the present life and in future lives...
It is associated with equanimity; because it fulfills the six pāramitās by means of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);

because it eliminates the path of afflictions and the path of suffering for all sentient beings; and because it causes the Dharma-eye to abide long so as to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels without interruption—you donors, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas—should all protect and sustain it.
Furthermore, one should provide them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness as they require, giving them all completely;

one should also exhort and praise them, saying: "Because these donors—devas, nāgas, and yakṣas—uphold my True Dharma, they desire to cause my Eye of the Dharma to abide long and to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem."
Because they are never-severed, such as these are my true children, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by the Dharma.

Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or other faithful laymen—whether good sons or good daughters—who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through the ultimate truth, and those who provide for and protect them, I entrust them to you, with Maitreya at their head and all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa. You should receive and transform them by means of the four bases of sympathy, and confer upon them the prohibitive precepts.

Furthermore, they shall be established in the four immeasurable minds, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, great skillful means, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; thereafter, they shall be granted the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, acting as the leader, together with the various bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"So be it, so be it, Great Virtuous Blessed One!
I shall protect and sustain those sentient beings, even bestowing upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Whether in the present age, the future age, or as long as the Dharma remains, those donors who act as great luminaries shall also receive the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others who, in forest hermitages, practice in silence seeking the ultimate truth, shall have faith and joy in receiving, upholding, making offerings to, and providing for them with robes, bedding, and even medicinal decoctions—whatever they may require.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When the sun rises in this world, Countless billions of flowers all bloom;
Just as when a single Buddha appears in the world, The flowers of merit longed for by sentient beings manifest."
If you wish to swiftly attain the ten supreme powers, And cross over the firm delusions of affliction,
And further desire to swiftly attain the most excellent concentration, Dwell in solitary silence within an araṇya.
If you wish to receive the faith and respect of humans and devas, and to eliminate the thirst of mental afflictions;
if you wish to sever the heavy burden of mental suffering, settle your mind in the noble path of śamatha.
If you wish to dispel all evils and hardships, And adorn yourself with all manner of merit,
And desire to cross over the ocean of suffering by yourself, You should settle your mind in the wondrous Bodhi.
If you wish to obtain those seven treasures of Dharma, And wish to attain the patience of skillful means,
And wish to preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, You should always delight in dwelling in an araṇya;
With the six sense faculties constantly united with samādhi, You should dwell in peaceful stillness within an araṇya.
With few desires, practicing *dhūta* austerities, and being well-contented—such a person can enter the path of the noble ones (*ārya*).
If one can swiftly renounce the pleasures of the five desires, one will extinguish the afflictions by attaining the five powers (*pañcabala*).
If one delivers sentient beings within the five realms of existence, while personally abandoning faults and evils to abide in *samādhi*;
If one wishes to attain the four immeasurables, And the four unhindered analytical knowledges,
And wishes to reach the further shore of the four dhyānas, That person should cultivate the ultimate truth.
If you wish to swiftly understand the three realms of existence, if you wish to know that all phenomena are suffering and impermanent,
and to realize that the nature and characteristics of all conditioned formations are empty, you should joyfully dwell in an araṇya.
If you wish to swiftly know the two kinds of dharmas— vipaśyanā and śamatha—
and if you wish to swiftly know the faults of the conditioned, you must dwell in the bodhicitta.
Dwelling alone in quietude and free from negligence, one can swiftly abandon conventional truth;
by seeking the ultimate truth with diligence, one can quickly leave all evil realms behind.
If you wish to dry up the ocean of pus and blood, And wish to dry up the ocean of afflictions;
If you wish to swiftly exhaust the ocean of the three realms of existence, Always remain in accord with the mind of the noble lineages;
If you wish to bring the ocean of sentient beings to maturity, And wish to fulfill the ocean of all great vows;
If you wish to know the limits of birth and death, Seek a secluded and tranquil place as if your head were on fire.

If you wish to know your past lives and dwellings, And from where you have come through long ages and subtle transitions, Employ various skillful means to delight in tranquility; Gather your mind therein and attain samādhi.
If you wish to sport in the ocean of meditative concentration; if you wish to awaken to the ocean of supernormal powers;
if you wish to cross over the ocean of craving and thirst; if you wish to attain supremacy among the gods;
if you wish to drink from the ocean of the True Dharma; or if you wish to behold the adorned lands—
If you wish to behold the ocean of all Buddhas, If you wish to inquire into the ocean of profound meanings,
If you wish to attain such supreme merit, And if you wish to swiftly attain supreme Bodhi,
You should leave behind all afflictions and dwell in an araṇya; By this means, attaining the Way will not be difficult.
If a person were to constantly make offerings for many years at the abodes of ten billion Buddhas,
yet another were able to dwell in an araṇya for seven days and attain meditative concentration by restraining the senses, the latter’s merit would far exceed that of the former.
If a person recites ten billion dharmas and understands their wondrous meaning as taught by the Buddha;
yet if another dwells in an araṇya for seven days, the mass of merit from that samādhi far exceeds the former.
If a person spends many years attending to the affairs of the Saṅgha, yet performs no other kind of meritorious action;
and if another person dwells for seven days in an araṇya, the latter’s accumulation of merit is greater than that of the former.
If one preaches the Dharma for the multitude, explaining its profound meaning, and remains free from other activities for many years,
yet another were to dwell with a mind fixed in tranquility for just seven days, the mass of their merit would be beyond counting.
If a person constructs many Buddha-stūpas and bestows monasteries, fields, and property upon the Saṃgha;
yet if one can dwell in an araṇya for seven days, their merit will be far greater than that.
The realm of the Buddhas is tranquil and unconditioned; therein one can attain pure enlightenment.
If anyone slanders those who dwell in meditative concentration, they are said to be slandering all the Tathāgatas.
If a person destroys hundreds of thousands of stupas, or burns hundreds of thousands of monasteries;
yet if another slanders one who dwells in meditation, the latter’s sin is far greater than that.
If there are those who make offerings to one dwelling in dhyāna— be it food, drink, clothing, or medicinal decoctions—
that person shall extinguish immeasurable sins and shall not fall into the three evil realms.
Therefore, I now announce to you all: those who wish to attain the Buddha-way must always abide in dhyāna.
If one cannot dwell in an araṇya, one should instead make offerings to such persons;
if one can abide in dhyāna without negligence, then one will swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās.
If you seek the path to great enlightenment, you shall reach it swiftly through these skillful means;
if you seek enlightenment and abide in tranquility, you should relinquish all conditioned activities,
abandon afflictions, and forsake all worldly pleasures, whereby you will quickly reach the other shore of generosity.
If one relinquishes the spheres of objects, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and abandons the faults of greed, hatred, and delusion;
if one casts off all afflictions and cultivates wholesome deeds, by this one can reach the further shore of giving.
One should regard sentient beings with compassion, Ceasing all conceptual discriminations and not asserting oneself as superior;
By always being able to feel pity for all sentient beings, One fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Diligently abandon sinful karma and cultivate the various dhyānas; you should also abandon the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Cherishing all skillful means, constantly seek dhyāna, and by removing hindrances, reach the shore of diligence.
Unshaken by sense objects and without attachment to them, they cultivate compassion and joy as causes for relinquishment;
with a single path of purity, they remain immovable, thereby fulfilling the perfection of patience.
Not dwelling on thoughts within the realm of objects, Free from agitation, one finds joy;
When all phenomena are free from restlessness and non-conceptual, Untainted and without sorrow—this is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The aggregates and elements are like illusions, without arising or activity; yet one continues in practice without interruption.
By skillfully cultivating and thoroughly understanding such dharmas, one thereby fulfills the perfection of wisdom.

Therefore, I now address the entire assembly: if there are those who wish to eliminate all sinful karma and seek the samādhi and dhāraṇī of patience, they should know that they must abide thus in tranquility.
If one wishes to transcend the Śrāvaka vehicle, And wishes to transcend the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
Furthermore, wishing to swiftly attain the supreme stage of Buddhahood, One should quickly dwell in an araṇya.
If the mind is gathered and settled in an araṇya, this itself is an offering to all Buddhas;
therein one can abandon all transgressions and thus fulfill the six perfections.
When you attain Buddhahood as the supreme among the three realms of existence, you shall be able to turn the pure wheel of the True Dharma,
dry up all the evil destinies of sentient beings, and deliver them across the ocean of the three realms of existence.

One should abandon all conditions associated with evil views, Constantly give rise to the most supreme bodhicitta, And should swiftly proceed to a forest hermitage (araṇya); Therein one shall accomplish such virtues as these.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was preaching this sutra, among the great assembly gathered there, ninety-two thousand people who had well cultivated and accumulated merit in the past heard this profound *paramārtha-dhyāna* (meditation on the ultimate truth) and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Seventy billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
Eighty-one thousand people received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their future attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

All sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who had not yet resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, shall all now resolve their minds and attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 46; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 47.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Arrival of Māra Pāpīyān at the Buddha’s Abode; Section Fourteen: The Moon-Treasury.

At that time, within the palace of King Māra, all the various groves of trees, fruits, flowers, and leaves, as well as garments, crowns, necklaces, and all objects of adornment, were transformed into half-moons and appeared there. They emitted a great radiance that illuminated the palace of King Māra, making both its interior and exterior transparently bright. Lutes, harps, *konghous*, and all other musical instruments, as well as non-musical jeweled ornaments and all other objects, spontaneously produced these verses:
"The peerless Great Teacher of the world, Most sovereign among all dharmas, ... [The remainder of the verse follows]"
Now dwelling on Mount Kāliṅga, he reveals for the sake of the multitude the ocean of the Buddha-dharma;
he expounds the single path of the pure Dharma, and those who hear it shall surely attain supreme enlightenment.
Pāpīyān, you are fierce and cruel, yet you are not my equal; you shall cause your realm of Māra to become entirely empty and void.
Because you once performed a single perverse act of merit, you now receive such a reward of sovereign power.
You should now, according to the Dharma, fall away; why do you not go quickly to see the Teacher?

All the sentient beings who have come here, having performed hundreds of billions of crores of mistaken virtues, this great assembly gathered as a treasury of merit, has come to hear and receive the supreme, illness-free Dharma.
Each one directed their heart toward the Buddha with reverence and esteem; seeing the Honored Teacher, they practiced offerings.
Through that pure faith, they extinguished their afflictions and would no longer be reborn in the realm of desire.
Devotedly believe in and pay homage to the Honored Teacher; He extinguishes the bonds of suffering and affliction within the three realms.
For billions of lifetimes one shall receive supreme and wondrous retribution, And swiftly become a close friend to the three realms.
Furthermore, he acts as the Dharma King within the three realms, preaching the true Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
all phenomena are like bubbles on water, and the marks of the conditioned appear like illusions.

The retribution of merit is impermanent and entirely empty; you should swiftly abandon the view of self and quickly resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta, for by this you will surely receive supreme and wondrous blessings.
At that time, when Māra Pāpīyān and his retinue saw and heard this, they were struck with terror and fell from their seats; covering their ears with both hands, they spoke these words:

"Behold, this śramaṇa performs such illusions and deceptions! He will surely seize our demonic powers and cause all our forms to become half-moons, while further emitting these various kinds of sounds."

The śramaṇa Gautama has manifested great supernormal power and has completely taken possession of the desire realm as his own; you should quickly beat the drums and assemble the great multitude to come to this place.
Having spoken these words, he immediately had the drum beaten within his palace.
As that drum was struck, a voice issued forth from it in the form of these verses:
"All phenomena are empty and quiescent, like the harmony of the winds; They are far removed from any basis and all manifold forms."
Useless in their actions, they deceive sentient beings; their manifested forms are deceptive, like illusions.
Letters are formed through the conjunction of causes and conditions; like writing in space, the letters do not abide.
The aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus) are empty and quiescent, devoid of all colors; the meaning of impermanence appears, yet it is not inherently real.
The sensory object of sound enters the gateway of the ear-faculty; the meaning of impermanence manifests without pausing for a moment.
Its consciousness is like an illusion; if one discriminates it, it reveals selflessness and a lack of autonomy.
The eye-faculty is empty and quiescent because of its rapid movement; it accords with the meaning of the intrinsic nature of suffering.

The nose-faculty and its objects of fragrance, the tongue and its objects of taste, the body-faculty and all tactile sensations, as well as mental phenomena, are all accompanied by impermanence; yet deluded sentient beings remain unaware of this.
Thus these six objects give rise to all suffering and cause one to lose the path to Nirvāṇa.
Because of this, ordinary beings transmigrate through the five realms; unable to leave their bonds, they find no liberation.
By removing craving for all sensory objects, one can swiftly reach the supreme and wondrous state.
This mind has the characteristic of natural purity; by contemplating this, one realizes the path to enlightenment.
If one attains mastery over the spheres of experience, one will then be able to compassionately pity all sentient beings.
Therein one shall attain generosity, morality, and patience, adorning oneself with the merit of wisdom;
attaining the most unsurpassed knowledge of enlightenment, one is able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings.

When this verse was spoken, all sentient beings within the palace of Māra were struck with terror and agitation; men and women, boys and girls, called out to one another and went to the abode of the Māra King, standing before him.
The Māra King addressed the assembly with these verses:
"You all behold this palace of Māra, Thus immeasurably and utterly loathsome;
With ceaseless sounds producing great suffering, It will surely seize away our demonic power."
The śramaṇa Gautama has uttered this sound, desiring to extinguish the activities within the realm of Māra’s power;
you should go quickly to Gautama’s presence and all together offer praise and take refuge.
At that time, a son of Māra named Aṅgulīmāla addressed his father in verse, saying:
"I shall now prepare my chariot and don my armor, Leading forth brave and sturdy warriors.
With bows, swords, spears, lances, and razor-edged wheels, And with faces like blades, drums, and various beasts."
The māra armies, yakṣas, nāgas, and asuras, together with all their retinues filling the void,
shall swiftly go to the presence of the evil-minded Gautama and crush him until he is like dust.
At that time, Māra the King spoke in verse, replying:
"From the past until now, I have repeatedly created immeasurable obstacles for that man;
you too must have seen the Bodhi tree, where Gautama has triumphed over me and my host."
Thus we have repeatedly troubled and disturbed him; yet Gautama is always victorious over us.
We see no god, nāga, or asura capable of moving even a single hair-tip of that man.
At that time, there was another minister of Māra named Śaṃlu-cana, who spoke these verses:
"We should quickly abandon the desire realm; We must simply protect our own palaces.
Gautama has never come here before; Now that he has arrived, we must resist him and not let him pass."
At that time, Māra was deeply distressed and remained silent, offering no reply.
Then, another minister named Utpannabhaya spoke these verses:
"Only through skillful means can an enemy be subdued; one should feign intimacy with deceit and guile."
"We shall lead the multitude to visit him, and with guileful pretense, we shall praise that śramaṇa.
Furthermore, a great minister named Pi-chant-t'o-hsing spoke in verse:
"In the past, this palace was filled with crowds; now it has diminished as the śramaṇa has encroached upon and seized [our wealth]."
"Those who have already gone for refuge are very numerous; we too should go to take refuge.
At that time, upon hearing what was said, the Māra immediately grew angry with his minister, and having become angry, he remained silent.
Furthermore, there was a minister named Old Wisdom (Jñānavṛddha) who spoke these verses:
"Gautama’s power has suffused all the palaces, Causing these various and extraordinary sounds to emerge.
If we do not go to him swiftly, The śramaṇa will surely arrive here with speed."
No one here can provide protection or use force to stop that seer Gautama;
therefore, let us all together quickly go and take refuge in that Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, the great assembly dwelling within those various palaces—the men and women, the elders and the young, along with their retinues—all formed a single faction and spoke these words:
"O Great King!
"Now you may take your retinues and go quickly to that place; we shall now protect these cities, towns, and palaces.
At that time, the Māra King spoke thus: "So be it, so be it."

I, together with the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, along with his armies and all his retinue, great and small, went to that place; and together with the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Suyāma Heaven, as well as Śakra Devendra and his armies, we all went to that place.

Furthermore, together with King Vaiśravaṇa and his host of troops, King Virūḍhaka and his host of kumbhāṇḍas, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his hosts of gandharvas and kiṃnaras, and King Virūpākṣa and his host of nāgas, they proceeded to that place.
When these words were spoken, there was another minister of the Māra-king named Sañcalana, who addressed him, saying: "Great King!

All the celestial palaces are now utterly empty and silent. The gods of the desire realm, along with all their celestial maidens and retinues, are staying at the place of the great śramaṇa Gautama to listen to the Dharma. Likewise, the kinnaras, nāgas, pretas, yakṣas, garuḍas, and kumbhāṇḍas are all at that place making various offerings to the śramaṇa Gautama and receiving his teaching."

At that time, the Māra-king, having observed for himself, saw that all the palaces throughout the desire realm were entirely empty and silent; that all the devas, humans, and non-humans within the desire realm had gathered at the place of Gautama and were sitting there listening to the Dharma, with the sole exception of the asuras who had not yet arrived there.
And he spoke these words:

"I shall now go together with the asuras to that place, so that the entire assembly there will be utterly deluded and unable to attain right faith; do not let Gautama teach that great multitude that all dharmas are like illusions—neither going nor coming, neither uniting nor dispersing, neither arising nor ceasing—and cause my realm of desire to become entirely empty and quiescent."
He further spoke these words:

"I shall now go together with all the asuras and their armies to that place in haste, to obstruct the sentient beings so they do not quickly cross the sea of suffering to reach the other shore; for by the power of the śramaṇa, they are swiftly turning their backs on the law of death, causing the strength and dominion of my realm to diminish. I shall now go quickly to block and protect those humans and non-humans."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, by means of his demonic supernormal powers and spheres of influence, thought of the four Asura kings, their armies, and all their retinues, commanding them to swiftly assemble upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Thereafter, they would descend together to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama resides, feigning eloquent speech and humble praise, and manifesting the pretext of seeking an audience for the sake of taking refuge. By such skillful means, he intended to cause the entire great assembly to give rise to fear and sever their right faith, and furthermore, to prevent them from conceiving any respect for Gautama, thereby causing that śramaṇa Gautama to become weary of the world and quickly enter parinirvāṇa.

In this way, the Māra king repeatedly harbored expectations regarding the host of asuras; yet, because the asuras were sustained by the Buddha’s supernatural power, they remained utterly bewildered and unaware of the Māra’s intentions.
At that moment, Māra conceived an evil intent toward the Buddha and all the asuras, and spoke these words:
"Observe how this single individual, Gautama, has already attained liberation within my realm and cannot be turned back; I have attained complete mastery over the entire desire realm."

"These common, lowly beings—the animals and asuras—do not accept my teaching; I shall cause them great distress so that they will quickly abandon the palaces they govern. Thereafter, I shall use my supernormal powers to lead my retinue to go and see Gautama."

Furthermore, surrounded by his great ministers, brave generals, and the various troops of his retinue—both men and women—he prepared the most excellent music of the five tones for play, song, and dance. With all manner of garments and ornaments, and a harmonious blend of various jewels, incense, flowers, banners, streamers, precious parasols, and sounds, he quickly made ready to go and see Gautama.

Now I too shall take my queen, my court ladies, and my sons and daughters, surrounded by a great assembly, and with the first and most excellent of Māra’s realms—the playful manifestation of supernormal powers through the harmony of the five musical tones—I shall go to see Gautama.

Why is this? With the sole exception of Gautama, he intends to cause all the rest of the great assembly—the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, humans, asuras, and the multitudes of the world—to fall into delusion; he will ensnare them with a firm net of desire so that they cannot quickly cross the great ocean of birth and death. For this reason, he has come to him.
"The rest of you shall remain here to guard this palace.

Then Māra Pāpīyas immediately took with him nine million six hundred thousand *bimbara* followers—men and women, boys and girls, as well as ministers and attendants—and through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of his own realm, he produced the most excellent five-toned music, song, dance, and playful performances, providing everything that causes people to feel great delight and gives rise to attachment.
Then Māra Pāpīyān went to those various palaces and announced:
"All of you, come forth and proceed to that place.
He then joined his palms and spoke these verses:
"Only the Buddha has utterly eliminated all afflictions; Only the Buddha can transform all worlds;
Only the Buddha can kindle the lamp of the True Dharma. Within the three realms, I take refuge in the Supreme One."

At that time, having thus manifested the power of such demonic supernormal realms, Māra emerged from his palace and scattered flowers with his hands. The scattered flowers formed flower-canopies throughout the four continents, remaining suspended in the air; in every place, they rained down various jewels and various flowers, descending like clouds.
At that time, the World-Honored One was still preaching the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of dwelling in an araṇya.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"All of you, guard and restrain your sense faculties; bind your minds in single-minded mindfulness so that they do not wander or scatter."

This Māra Pāpīyān has brought many followers who sing, dance, and sport; they play music with the five tones as various performers join together, and he comes surrounded by his retinue of women, both great and small.
At that time, Māra, together with his retinue, immediately arrived at Mount Kharatī, the dwelling place of the sages and seers.
Having reached the Buddha’s location, he manifested a canopy of the seven precious gems in the sky above the Buddha, measuring seven yojanas in length and breadth, to cover the Buddha’s head.

Furthermore, he adorned the top of the Buddha with priceless pearl necklaces, and again made offerings to the World-Honored One with various kinds of jewels, flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, celestial garlands, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, gold threads, pearls, necklaces, and music performed by the five musical instruments.
Circumambulating him three times to the right, he spoke these verses:
“I now take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One; From this moment forth, I shall never again give rise to an evil mind.
May Gautama, with a mind settled in concentration, forgive me; I shall protect the True Dharma of the Buddha.”
In this world, there is none like the World-Honored One, who out of compassion benefits all sentient beings;
having attained liberation himself, he enables others to attain it as well—therefore, I take refuge in the Most Victorious Honored One.

Only the Buddha has compassion for all beings; having already transcended the mountain of birth-and-death and afflictions, he constantly and joyfully seeks to deliver all sentient beings—now we quickly take refuge in you, O World-Honored One.
Able to comprehend the conditioned and the unconditioned, Free from both like a lotus unstained by water,
The body upon which the accumulation of merit and the holy life depend— Therefore, I now take refuge in the Buddha.
In the world there is no dharma of tranquility or freedom from illness, nor anything pure that eternally overcomes the afflictions;
only the True Dharma and Nirvana exist—therefore, I take refuge in this peerless Dharma.
In this world, there is none equal to the Saṅgha: the eight noble men who are harmonious and liberated, able to sever all bonds of affliction; therefore, I take refuge in the virtuous Saṅgha.
Dwelling in seclusion and silence, always eating but one meal, their minds are constantly in accord with the ultimate truth;
out of compassion they take pity on all sentient beings—to them, as well, I go for refuge.
May they cause the lineage of the Triple Gem to blaze forth and protect and nourish all the Buddha’s śrāvakas;
I exhort all sentient beings to make offerings of famous garments and exquisite food.
At that time, the great assembly gathered there—whether gods, humans, gandharvas, or others—spoke with one voice in praise:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
speaking in verse: “I have already instructed you, my assembly of śrāvakas, All those who seek liberation through appropriate practice,
To always delight in the four noble lineages as their reliance, So that they may fulfill the path to bodhi.”
As a tree with abundant fruit quickly brings about its own ruin, and as bamboo and reeds likewise perish when they bear fruit,
and as a mule loses its life by conceiving a foal, so too it is for the ignorant who seek profit.
Just as a shower of fierce hail in the height of summer destroys all the crops,
so too will those who greedily seek gain and offerings surely and swiftly lose their supreme enlightenment.
Just as when the flowers of various trees have blossomed, they may yet be consumed by fire;
