so too shall those who greedily seek gain and offerings fall away from the path to enlightenment.

If there is a bhikṣu who receives offerings, yet delights in seeking gain and remains stubbornly attached to them, there is no evil in this world greater than this; it prevents him from attaining the path of liberation.
One who thus greedily seeks gain and honor, having already attained the path, will lose it once again.
At that time, having heard these verses, Māra the King thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama knows my hypocrisy and my feigned taking of refuge."
Ashamed and silent, he withdrew to sit on one side and remained there listening to the Dharma.

The women of Māra—whose faculties, features, countenances, and complexions had previously been radiant—now all became withered and emaciated, turning an ugly hue; they were hunchbacked, lame, crippled, and hideously deformed.

None of the men were able to sing, dance, or engage in playful dalliance; the five musical tones and all instrumental music were completely silenced so that no sound could emerge. They withdrew to sit on one side, remaining there to listen to the Dharma.

Chapter Three: All the Asuras Approach the Buddha’s Abode. *The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Moon Treasury Section. Chapter Three: All the Asuras Approach the Buddha’s Abode. At that time, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha, for the sake of gathering and transforming all sentient beings, was reciting the moon-bannered moon-mantra phrases, everything existing within the realms governed by the four great asura kings—namely all grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, various jewels, necklaces, articles of adornment, clothing, and bedding—all transformed into the shape of half-moons and appeared before them.

As those various objects struck one another, they produced five kinds of sounds; all the drums, conchs, *caṇḍa*-drums, *mṛdaṅga*-drums, lutes, and zithers played together in perfect harmony, and from within those sounds, these verses were also proclaimed:
“Only the Buddha guides with peace and security, Together with the assembly dwelling on Mount Khadiraka;
From the stench of afflictions, he uproots sentient beings, And for their sake, he preaches the Dharma to bring about eternal severance.”
Ordinary beings all fall into the sea of birth and death, Where the swift river of afflictions stirs up waves;
In the three realms of existence there is no one so compassionate As the Muni, the Honored One, with his heart of loving-kindness.
A great multitude has gathered at one place— gods, humans, kumbhāṇḍas, nāgas, and yakṣas—
all relying upon Mount Kharādi, seeking liberation from all suffering and fear.
Let us all go there together with haste, desiring to hear the True Dharma;
before long, the Māra King may come here and create obstacles for us.
Listen with single-minded devotion to the supreme and wondrous Dharma; from that pure mind, you shall gain great merit.
Through this merit, may you have long life and eliminate all enemies, and may you always enjoy majestic power and bliss within the world.
If one seeks liberation through this merit, one will sever all afflictions to attain arhatship;
by severing all conditions, one becomes a pratyekabuddha, and may likewise achieve buddhahood, endowed with all bliss.
Thus you shall attain this without doubt; therefore, quickly cast off all bonds of conditions.
All should give rise to a pure mind and swiftly go to the Buddha’s presence to practice offerings.
Since the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there has never been such a great assembly;
though Maitreya shall arise after a vast eon, we shall not attain a lifespan lasting that long.

At that time, within those four cities, palaces, and abodes of the asuras, such things occurred: through the majestic empowerment and adornment of the Bodhisattva’s power, upon hearing the meaning of these words, they all conceived faith. Each gathering together from their respective cities, palaces, and abodes in one place, they said to one another:
"What matter is there that we should now attend to here?"
Why is this? That which we have never seen before, we now see; that which we have never heard before, we now hear; and that which no one else knew, [we now know].
Then Māra Pāpīyān descended from his own palace and went to scatter flowers as an offering to the Buddha; the flowers he scattered fell as a floral rain over the four continents.

When it rains, throughout all the cities, towns, and palaces of the four asura realms, everything is transformed into the most extreme stench and filth; moreover, foul smoke, dust, ashes, and soil swirl everywhere until they fill every place, while mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and various venomous flies likewise swarm in great numbers, causing such grief, distress, and agitation that no joy can be found.

At that time, all the cities, towns, palaces, and mansions of the asuras became pitch black. All the asura men and women, boys and girls, were filled with the utmost sorrow and agitation; they found no joy dwelling there and gathered together in the streets and alleys, going before their king and standing in his presence.

Seeing these various calamities and afflictions, the Asura King experienced extreme distress and anguish. The Asura King Vemacitra, together with his retinue and all the asuras—men, women, boys, and girls—of his realm; and the Asura King Pāraṭa, along with the Asura King Vairocana, together with their retinues and all the asuras—men, women, boys, and girls—of their respective realms, proceeded toward the cities, villages, and palaces governed by the Asura King Rāhu.

Having seen those various evils and harassments—the mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and venomous flies—they all three asura kings went together to where Rāhu, the asura king, was, and stood before him.
The Asura King Vemacitra questioned the Asura King Rāhu, speaking in verse:
"All the palaces of the asuras Are no different from the hells;
When hot winds arise in violent gusts and reach here, Everything appears as if consumed by fire."
All the fruits upon the trees have fallen to the ground;
all the lotuses and bathing pools, as well as the grasses, sprouts, and various flowers, have completely withered.
Smoke, dust, and ashes fall upon us, and the palaces within the cities of the asuras—
There are mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and malevolent flies, as well as immeasurable varieties of evil venomous insects.
Now hearing such various evil sounds, sentient beings are greatly distressed and find no joy;
the asuras undergo this suffering, all of them oppressed and tormented by hunger and thirst.
Oppressed by suffering, with no place of refuge, all are struck with terror and their hearts wither away.
By whose power can the fears of birth and death be overcome so as to benefit us, O devas and nāgas?
By what skillful means may these various kinds of fearful matters be brought to rest?
"Is it not because an evil dragon has come here that we Asuras have been subdued?
Then, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, answered in verse:
"O you hosts of Asuras, listen attentively! In days of old, we were possessed of every happiness."
All that is required for the five desires shall accord with one's wishes; though possessing great power and courageous supernatural faculties,
the bows, swords, arrows, spears, lassos, barbed darts, blades, wheels,
and all such weapons now shall utterly fall away, leaving the cities and streets entirely desolate.
Men and women who were formerly fierce and vigorous, whose complexions were handsome and who possessed great power—
though they were once equal to the gods themselves— all shall surely come to an end in this present time.
When life is exhausted, the white dharmas are exhausted; Shame, modesty, and the mind of liberation are exhausted, as are the knowledges of the wise;
Skillful conduct and the noble wisdom of the virtuous are exhausted, As are the crops, the various flowers and medicinal herbs, The flavors of fruits, and all the precepts are exhausted.
All desired music shall come to an end; all precious garments, food, and drink shall come to an end;
all joyful affairs, humans, and devas shall come to an end; yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras shall come to an end;
brahmins and kṣatriyas shall come to an end, along with all vaiśyas and śūdras.
Alas, together with all such evil beings—those who are unholy, deceitful, and prone to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
those who engage in lying, divisive speech, frivolous talk, and harsh words; those possessed of greed, anger, arrogance, delusion, and false views;
those characterized by stinginess, meanness, and the increase of hunger and thirst; and those who suffer the pain of separation from loved ones, encounter with enemies, and the pursuit of hunting.
Seeing others obtain gain, they give rise to envy and jealousy; they inflict cutting, slicing, hacking, and destruction.
Poisonous harms increase with knives, spears, and sword-wheels; tears stream down their faces as they suffer in grief and sorrow.
Mosquitoes, gadflies, foul winds, smoke, and dust—these all come together to cause irritation;
the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts are a great ocean of suffering.
This is no time for engaging in unwholesome conduct, for moment by moment one falls away from right view.
For those of pure karma, evil deeds increase; thus all such evils flourish and prevail.
This is the time when the asuras are brought to their end; only the peerless vehicle can restrain them.
At that time, the Asura King Pāratas addressed the Asura King Rāhu, speaking in verse to inquire:
“O King, for the sake of all sentient beings, You always exert yourself with diligence to cultivate all dharmas;
Possessing great merit, virtue, and supernormal powers, As well as wisdom, you adorn your body.”
What power is this, and by whom was it wrought, that seeks to destroy us, the asuras?
Who can provide protection for us?
We shall pay homage to him and take refuge in him.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, spoke in verse, answering:
"This is not the power of Śakra or Brahmā, Nor of Īśvara or Nārāyaṇa, Nor of yakṣas or nāgas; It can only be the sovereign will of the Māra King."
In the past, he likewise distressed the various nāgas; the Great Sage Gautama has now severed it for us.
We pay homage to that sage Gautama, for he is able to bestow peace and happiness upon us.
At that time, the asura king Vajravairocana addressed him in verse, saying:
"Are you a deva, a human, a nāga, or a yakṣa, The one who can bestow all peace and happiness?
By what power of supernatural faculties and diligence Do you employ such skillful means to create these illusions?"
In what phenomena does one attain mastery? Who is able to receive such instructions?
To achieve liberation from the power of Māra, by what power is this made possible?
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, replied in verse:
"In the past, I saw a handsome Great Śramaṇa, Sitting upright in the shade of the Bodhi tree.
When the hosts of Māra’s generals approached him, He swiftly subdued them through the power of his compassion."
There he attained supreme enlightenment, transcending all the hosts of devas;
endowed with great compassion, he entered nirvāṇa, and thus was able to dry up the ocean of all suffering.
This most excellent banner among all sages, endowed with the ten powers as the medicine for sentient beings—
to him the Śakras, Brahmās, Īśvaras, Asuras, and ṛṣis, the Kāmeśvaras, Māras, and Nārāyaṇas,
all pay homage and take refuge; this person can show the liberation of all.
Within all the three realms, you surpass all the hosts of devas.
Tamed, serene, and having subdued the senses, adorned with the seven riches of the noble ones, you delight in tranquility;
abiding in nirvana and having reached the further shore, you are able to completely dry up the ocean of afflictions.
Therefore, we, the entire assembly, all take refuge in the one who can extinguish all suffering;
holding various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers, each with palms joined, we offer our supplication.

At that time, the four asura kings Rāhula, Vemacitrin, Bali, and Vairocana, along with their male and female attendants, and boys and girls—all the hosts of asuras—gathered like clouds. Some made offerings of burning incense, prostrated before the Buddha, and offered supplications;

some brought various kinds of exquisite flowers of diverse colors; some brought various maṇi jewels; some brought various banners, pennants, precious canopies, golden threads, pearls, necklaces, and garments, offering them to the Buddha and seeking his grace;

and some played various musical instruments such as the *kinnara*, the lute, the *vīṇā*, the flute, and the drum, performing music in the five tones to make offerings, prostrate, and supplicate the Buddha.

The Asura King Rāhula, by the power of his own supernatural realm, manifested his great body in play; with both hands he grasped Śakra’s Vaiḍūrya-maṇi jewel garland, prostrated with his head at the feet, and paid homage to the World-Honored One from afar.
He spoke a verse in praise, saying:
“The Buddha acts for the joy of sentient beings; Having long practiced various ascetic austerities, Out of compassion for all the multitudes, May he likewise have compassion for us.”
Patience is like the great earth; with compassion for all sentient beings, you bring rest to all turbid evils and cover us with your mercy.
Having delivered all from fear, the Buddha has attained unsurpassed wisdom.
With an impartial mind toward all beings, may he take pity on the asuras.
With the eightfold noble vessel, the Buddha delivers suffering beings;
having filled them with the flavor of nirvana, he regards the asuras with compassion.
"The Buddha, toward all sentient beings, Is not ashamed of lowly birth;
To all he is like an only child. Therefore, we take refuge in the Buddha.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin, with both hands, held up the mani-jewel wreaths worn by all the devas upon their accession to their thrones. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and praised him in verse:
"Surpassing the hosts of devas and nāgas, asuras and kumbhāṇḍas,
having utterly eliminated all afflictions and the evils committed by the mind,
they have subdued the path of karmic suffering and reached the further shore."
Distant from both the perception of existence and the perception of non-existence among sentient beings,
yet out of compassionate concern for them, he does not enter nirvana.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he is able to endure every suffering.
Behold all sentient beings as a mother thinks of her only child;
may you have compassion for them and sprinkle the waters of mercy upon their state of suffering.
May you bring rest to those touched by affliction and those drowning in the waters of the defilements.
O you who have roused firm valor, may you vow to rescue sentient beings from suffering.
As they now face the arrival of intense suffering and are destroyed by the power of Māra,
as the Asuras are touched by pain, may you sprinkle upon them the waters of great compassion.
If sentient beings give rise to thoughts of anger or malice toward the Buddha,
they cannot move even a fraction of the Buddha’s body or mind. Whatever joy they possess,
whatever objects of their senses, and whatever experiences of body and mind—
The Buddha’s constant and impartial compassion is no different toward this [place].
Only the Buddha can bestow all happiness upon devas and humans;
we, however, are tormented by Māra, our hearts solitary and without refuge.
There is no other sentient being capable of extinguishing the works of Māra;
only the Buddha can swiftly dispel them, destroying them utterly without remainder.
This is witnessed and known by the devas and nāgas, as well as the yakṣas and asuras.
As the Buddha is supreme among all sentient beings, able to rescue them from every suffering;
as Māra desires to swiftly extinguish me and the various palaces of the asuras—
may you quickly radiate the light of the precepts and bestow upon me the bliss of fulfillment.
At that time, the Asura King Pāratas held in both hands a Brahma-light-bannered *maṇi* jewel combined with celestial garlands; bowing his head in prostration, he spoke these verses of praise:
"Bound by the prison of saṃsāra, Deprived of all happiness, In this most evil and vast great ocean, They are submerged with no place of refuge."
Only the Buddha practiced with such diligence; throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he crossed over to the other shore by himself and completely exhausted the ocean of afflictions.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he performed ascetic practices for six years.
And having attained supreme wisdom, you have extinguished those afflictions.
We are tormented by Māra; we lack the power to endure these various sufferings.
We pray that you will remove what Māra has inflicted upon us and bathe our palaces for us.
"These multitudes of monks are tormented by various sufferings;
may you save them from these miseries—let us go to see the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Asura King Vajravairocana took in both hands the Brahmā-like radiant *maṇi* jewel garland, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and praised him in verse:
"Now I pay homage to the Honored Muni, who possesses mastery over all dharmas;
he has transcended the kings Śakra and Brahmā, subdued Māra and his hosts,
and surpassed the light of the sun and moon, as well as the Four Heavenly Kings."
Compassion is like the sun and moon, universally illuminating all sentient beings.
When five suns rise at once, the waters of the great ocean are entirely exhausted;
yet the merit of making offerings to the Buddha can never be exhausted.
Transcending the three realms, they enter the city of fearlessness;
with great compassion covering all sentient beings, all sufferings are utterly extinguished.
With a mind equal toward all beings, they regard them as a mother looks upon her only child.
We are obscured by the veil of sorrow; we pray that the wind of your compassion may blow it away.
We have no other refuge who can rescue us from this suffering.
Since your merit is as full as yours, O Buddha, do not abandon the palace of the Asuras.

At that time, with the ear of a Buddha and the eye of a Buddha, the World-Honored One perceived the cities and palaces of the asuras. He saw that they were all overwhelmed by the power of Māra; every kind of calamity pervaded them without exception, and they all suffered from burning affliction.
[He thought: "May they joyfully seek my shelter and protection, taking me as their refuge and resort."
"I shall protect all the asuras; now is precisely the right time.

At that moment, the World-Honored One, through the majestic power of his great compassion, manifested universal bliss and immediately entered the *samādhi* of the Light-Rays of Compassionate Wind. By the power of this *samādhi*, all the painful afflictions inflicted by the supernatural might of Māra within the palaces of the four asuras were made to cease in a single thought-moment and were restored to their former state. Furthermore, they became like the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, wherein appeared the foremost wondrous pleasures and delightful things.
When those asuras saw this, they leaped for joy, their hearts filled with gladness; their mouths and eyes were all pleased and radiant with smiles, and they all spoke these words: "Namo Buddhāya."
"Homage to the Buddha!
Having spoken these words, he immediately took the exquisite and wondrous jewel garlands of the devas and cast them from afar toward the direction of the Buddha as an offering.
The jewel garland cast by the Asura King Rāhu reached the place where the Buddha was and remained suspended in the air above the Buddha’s head.
The jeweled garland hurled by the asura king Vemacitrin also reached the Buddha and remained suspended in mid-air upon his right shoulder.
The jeweled garland hurled by the asura king Pāraṇata also reached the Buddha and remained suspended in mid-air upon his left shoulder.
The precious garland cast by the asura king Vairocana also reached the Buddha’s presence, where it remained before the Buddha, emitting light that shone forth.

All the other asuras likewise took various kinds of precious incense, flowers, banners, pennants, jeweled parasols, as well as golden threads, precious gems, celestial garlands, pearls, necklaces, various garments, ointments, and powdered incense; they all cast these toward the World-Honored One from afar to offer them, thereby making their offerings.
At that time, upon this Mount Khadiraka, the dwelling place of the sages and seers, a rain of various flowers down to powdered incense fell like a torrential downpour.

At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Seeking the Severance of Doubt. Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and asked in verse:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One of immeasurable wisdom, You have already rained down such rain as this;
Having manifested various supernatural powers, transformations, and auspicious omens, The Bodhisattva Candragarbha has arrived here."
Now there falls again a rain of various jewels; who could have come here?
Are these the great virtuous Bodhisattvas, or are they messengers from the Buddhas of other realms?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prārthitavicchittisaṃśaya, saying: "Good son!

This is Māra Pāpīyān, who, within the four cities and palaces of the asuras, has conjured darkness, dust, smoke, mist, mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous flies, and various poisonous snakes, bees, and scorpions. He has caused all the trees, forests, grasses, woods, flowers, fruits, springs, and ponds there to wither and dry up, leaving all the asuras in bitter distress, on the verge of death."

They took refuge in me with single-minded devotion, joined their palms in salutation, and, with various flowers up to powdered incense, made offerings by casting them from afar toward me from the city where those asuras dwell.
The jeweled garland cast by Rāhu, the Asura King, is the one now upon my head;
the jeweled garland cast by Vemacitrin, the Asura King, is the one upon my right shoulder.
The jeweled garland cast by the Asura King Pāratā, which is upon my left shoulder, is this one;
the jeweled garland cast by the Asura King Vajravairocana, which is now before me, is that one.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha in reverent prostration, and spoke these words:
"These asuras have received the grace and merit of the Buddha; I, too, shall now cause the asuras to once again obtain full benefit, prosperity, and peace."
The Buddha told Pāpīyas:
"You need not speak such words now; I have already caused them to be fully satisfied and at peace.
All the cities, palaces, and dwellings of the asuras, along with their increasingly sublime and exquisite articles of enjoyment, have been restored to their former state."

Why is this? Those four great asura kings are my close friends; likewise, all other asuras have conceived faith, reverence, and respect for me, and their minds are filled with wonder. They shall soon arrive here for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.
Māra Pāpīyān again gave rise to an evil thought and reflected:
"I am the most supreme and sovereign within the entire realm of desire; I am able to inflict both suffering and pleasure upon all sentient beings."

This śramaṇa is but a human being; how could he be so crafty and deceptive, a heretic of heterodox and malevolent ways with such loquacity, as to dare to compete with me and seek to measure himself against me?
Neither Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, nor the Wheel-Turning Sage King, nor any sentient beings whatsoever, are able to rival, compare with, or oppose me.

Now this Gautama performs illusions to delude all sentient beings; filling the four continents, the earth, and all of space, they have all come because they wish to see Gautama. Even these lowly, beast-like classes of asuras are now included within his influence.

"I shall now employ the supernatural powers, majestic authority, and playful manifestations of Māra’s realm; furthermore, I shall create further illusions and delusions to vex that śramaṇa Gautama and to subdue all those gathered in this assembly."
Then Māra Pāpīyān surveyed his retinue and spoke in verse:
"Each of you demons should form this thought:
'I shall subdue the enemy, and harass this assembly, as well as imprison the asuras.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"You should behold my power: In the past, beneath the Bodhi tree, The devas served as witnesses As I cultivated the true and correct Dharma."
"Exert whatever power you possess; manifest it as you wish! If you can afflict me, I shall take refuge in you.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān further intensified his first and most grievous resentment. Employing all the magical powers, spheres of influence, and supernatural displays at his disposal, he called upon the scorching winds from the four directions, causing a hot wind to strike and distress the entire assembly that had gathered, thereby seeking to subdue them.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Subduing the Power of Māra; by the power of this samādhi, there arose from the four directions a supreme, wondrously fragrant, cool breeze, which touched his body so that he experienced total bliss.
When Māra Pāpīyān learned of this matter, he again manifested a great mass of fire before the Buddha;
the World-Honored One immediately manifested a vast, cool pond at that spot, from which water gushed upward.
When the Māra King saw this, he again rained down large stones from the sky;
the Buddha immediately transformed those falling stones so that they all became various celestial flowers, which rained down upon that place.
The Māra Pāpīyān, together with his retinue, again grasped Mount Khadiraka with both hands, wishing to swiftly shake the trichiliocosm;
yet the Buddha further transformed this terrestrial realm into adamant, so that they could not move it even by a single speck of dust, much less more.

The Māra King, again by the power of his wrath, directed a breath from his mouth toward the direction where the asuras dwell, forming a cloud of black vapor that cast a gloomy darkness over their cities and palaces, causing all the asuras to become once more bewildered and unable to come or go.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately transformed the clouds of breath he had blown into various kinds of exquisite celestial flower clouds.
Then, upon those four cities, palaces, and dwellings of the asuras, there fell a rain of various celestial flowers;
from within that rain of flowers, hundreds of thousands of subtle and wondrous Dharma gates were proclaimed, namely, the voice of the Buddha.
The sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Saṃgha, the sounds of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the sound of the three types of wholesome conduct, the sound of the three refuges, the sound of the three restraints, the sound of the three forms of non-protection,
the sound of the three reliances, the sound of the three kinds of awakening, the sound of the three vehicles, and the sound of the three cultivations.
The sound of the three kinds of roots of goodness; the sound of transcending the three realms; the sound of the three types of sensation;
the sound of the three liberations; the sound of the three manifestations; the sound of the four foundations of mindfulness; the sound of the four right efforts; the sound of the four bases of power;
the sound of the four indestructible faiths; the sound of the four dhyānas; the sound of the four Brahma-abodes; and the sound of the four means of integration.

The sound of the [four] analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the sound of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the sound of the four noble truths (*āryasatya*), the sound of the five faculties (*indriya*),
the sound of the five powers (*bala*), the sound of the five-limbed samādhi, the sound of the five entrances to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the sound revealing the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
the sound of the sixfold respectful harmony (*ṣaḍabhiprasannā*), the sound of the six recollections (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*), and the sound of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The sound of the seven noble treasures, the sound of the seven stations of consciousness, the sound of the seven factors of enlightenment, the sound of the eightfold noble path,
the sound of the nine successive meditative attainments, the sound of the ten noble abodes, the sound of the ten powers of a Buddha,
the sound of great loving-kindness and great compassion, the sound of dependent origination, the sound of the indestructibility of the mind, and the relinquishing of all things.
The sound of the elimination of evil views; the sound of not forgetting the bodhicitta; the sound of non-retrogression; the sound of patience; the sound of samādhi; the sound of dhāraṇī;
the sound of receiving the prophecy of ascending to the throne; the sound of the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
the sound of ascetic practices; the sound of the ten stages (daśabhūmi); the sound of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma); and the sound of reaching awakening (bodhi).
The sound of turning the wheel of Dharma; the indestructible Buddha-sound; the sound of relinquishment; the sound of wearying detachment; the sound of liberation and meditative concentration;
the sound of cessation; the sound of maturing sentient beings; the sound of embracing the true Dharma; the sound of eloquence; the sound of impermanence;
the sound of suffering; the sound of non-self; the sound of emptiness; and the sound of non-action.
The sound of tranquility, the sound of non-arising, the sound of suchness, the sound of the limit of reality, and the sound of entering the dharma-realm.

There were sounds of "no sentient beings, no life, no nourishment, no recipient"; sounds of suchness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor interrupted, neither departing nor arriving, neither abiding nor moving; sounds of great supernatural transformations; sounds of the protection of the Three Jewels; sounds even of Great Parinirvāṇa; sounds of the heavy burden of the five aggregates—the sufferings of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; sounds of the repeated wandering through birth and death and the pain of separation from loved ones; sounds of the prison of the conditioned cycle of existence being like an illusion, a plantain tree, the moon in water, or an echo; sounds of faith, diligence, patience, and wisdom, and the protection of the ten paths of wholesome action; and sounds of escaping that prison of the cycle of existence. From the falling rain of flowers, these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of sounds emerged.

Those sounds were able to cause immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* asuras to gain profound reverence and faith in the Triple Gem, to respect and take refuge in them with a sense of wonder, and to longingly desire to see Śākyamuni, to hear the Dharma, and to make offerings to the Saṅgha. They became utterly terrified of the cycle of birth and death, of wandering through saṃsāra, and of being separated from those they love; thus, they yearned for *nirvāṇa*.
All those asuras together raised their voices and said:
"Homage to Śākyamuni Tathāgata! Homage to Śākyamuni Tathāgata!"

We now go to see the Tathāgata Śākyamuni in order to pay homage and make offerings, to listen to the Dharma, and to serve the Saṃgha; for the sake of beholding the Great Assembly; for the sake of seeking the vehicle of unsurpassed Bodhi; for the sake of felling the banner of Māra; for the sake of establishing the banner of the Dharma; for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed; for the sake of hearing the Dharma-gate of the supreme noble truths; for the sake of bringing rest to the path of afflictions and the path of suffering; for the sake of severing the bonds of Māra; for the sake of drying up the river of craving; for the sake of filling the ocean of Dharma; for the sake of entering the ocean of wisdom; for the sake of maturing the ocean of sentient beings; and for the sake of making offerings to the ocean of all Buddhas.
Therefore, we and our retinues shall go to where the Buddha is, so that the evil Māra may no longer gain mastery over us; from this day forward, we shall never again encounter such suffering.
At that time, the Asura King Mucilinda spoke again, saying:

"I now come together with my wives, concubines, palace attendants, sons, daughters, and all my retinue of Asura women—eighty-four thousand in all—all wearing blue garments and adorned in blue. We carry blue parasols, blue canopies, blue banners, blue pennants, blue chariots, and blue flowers; we possess blue-colored mani-jewels, lutes, harps, and lyres, as well as blue jewels and blue drums."

I shall now take these five musical tones to perform music, song, dance, and playful merriment as the foremost adornment; together with my retinue, I shall go to see the Buddha, to pay respectful homage, to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma, and to make offerings to the Sangha; for this reason, I am proceeding to the Buddha’s abode.
At that time, the Asura King Sujiṭhila spoke again, saying:

"I too shall now go to the place where the Buddha is, together with my wives, concubines, palace attendants, sons, daughters, and retinue, as well as nine million nine hundred thousand Asura women, all of whom are adorned in yellow robes, for the sake of making offerings to the Saṃgha."
At that time, the Asura King Śambhala again spoke these words:

"I now also go with my wives, concubines, palace attendants, male and female kinsmen, and hundreds of thousands of billions of Asura women—all of us wearing deep blue garments and adorned with necklaces and ornaments—to serve and honor the assembly of monks as we proceed to the Buddha’s dwelling."
At that time, the asura king Vajravairocana again spoke these words:

"I too shall now go to the place where the Buddha is, accompanied by my wives, concubines, palace attendants, male and female kinsmen, and ninety-nine *bimbara* of asura women, all of whom are dressed in vermilion garments and adorned with necklaces and ornaments."
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra spoke again, saying:

"I shall now go to the place where the Buddha is, together with my wives, concubines, palace attendants, male and female kinsmen, and ninety-nine thousand *koṭis* of wicked Asura women, all of whom are dressed in garments the color of crystal and adorned with necklaces and ornaments."
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, spoke again as follows: “I now also come with my queens,
court ladies, sons, daughters, and retinue, as well as the lords of the lands and tributary kings,
along with elders, ministers, generals, attendants, cities, towns, and villages.”
All the multitudes, including as many asura women as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
were all adorned with amaranth-colored garments and necklaces; they further carried amaranth-colored robes,
banners, pennants, precious parasols, gold thread, pearls, necklaces, mani-jewels, incense, and flowers.
The unguents and the vehicles they rode were all the color of agate;
likewise, the drums, horns, lutes, harps, *konghou*, flutes, pipes, and musical instruments—all such things—were the color of agate.
Together they performed music, singing, dancing, and laughing, while the most excellent adornments hovered in the void.
"Desiring to see the Buddha to pay him homage and make offerings, and for the sake of hearing the Dharma and supporting the Sangha, we are going to where the Buddha dwells.

As previously described, they all fully prepared those various forms and appearances—supremely subtle, marvelous, and unprecedented—which had never been heard of before; thus, from their dwelling place among the asuras, they emerged and remained suspended in mid-air.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with his retinue, performed music with the five tones, singing, dancing, and laughing as they proceeded to lead the way before the Asura King Rāhu.
At that time, the asura king Pāratas, together with his retinue, all fully arrayed in armor, arrived and led the way on the right side of the asura king Rāhu.
At that time, the asura king Vajravairocana, together with his retinue, likewise equipped with great adornments, arrived at the left side of the asura king Rāhula and led the way.
At that time, the Asura King Śambhara, together with his retinue, also fully prepared themselves and followed behind the Asura King Rāhu as they proceeded.
At that time, the Asura King Mucilinda, together with his retinue, also prepared a grand procession and arrived, leading from above the Asura King Rāhu.
At that time, the asura king Sujiṭhara, together with his retinue, adorned in such a manner, also arrived and followed behind the asura king Rāhu as he moved below.

At that time, Rāhu the Asura King, together with his retinue, adorned themselves with such magnificent physical forms; the five kinds of musical instruments played all at once, and amidst the harmonious sounds of singing, dancing, and laughter, they proceeded to where the Buddha was.

Again, with both hands holding various precious flowers, celestial garlands, and fragrant unguents, they scattered them from afar toward the direction of the Buddha as an offering; upon reaching Mount Khadiraka, these transformed into a great cloud that remained suspended in the air.
Upon that Mount Khadiraka, the dwelling place of the sages and seers, there rained down various jewels, various flowers, various celestial garlands, and various ointments.
At that time, there were beings in the assembly who thought to themselves:
"What matter do they wish to address? By what power has this omen been manifested first?
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Yaśas, saying:
“O bhikṣus, you should dwell with right mindfulness, binding the mind within;
do not allow it to become distracted. The World-Honored One further addressed the venerable Yaśas:

“O bhikṣus, you should dwell with diligent application of mindfulness, binding the mind within; do not allow it to become distracted. If you can diligently apply mindfulness without distraction, you will be able to rest from the path of afflictions and eliminate the path of suffering; you will be able to abide in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and fulfill the six pāramitās, before long attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

These are the asuras and all their retinues and courtesans who now wish to come; they have prepared an array of musical performances with the five types of sounds to adorn themselves, in order to pay homage to me, make offerings, and listen to the Dharma.
"Therefore, you all must not be distracted; remain with your mindfulness focused.
At that time, all the asuras and their retinues immediately arrived at Mount Khadiraka.
Having arrived, he immediately circumambulated the mountain three times to the right; having finished, he led his retinue to the place where the World-Honored One was.

At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood before him. He took a *maṇi* jewel from the radiant and brilliant crest of a Brahmā and placed it before the Buddha;
furthermore, he offered various kinds of precious flowers, powdered incense, banners, streamers, jeweled canopies, as well as golden threads, pearls, and necklaces.
Furthermore, they made offerings with various songs, dances, and music, and joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke these verses in praise:
“O Best among those who have tamed the mind, You are able to bestow all happiness;
As a lamp of Dharma, you constantly give the gift of Dharma, Increasing the wisdom of the Dharma.”
The World-Honored One has lit the torch of Dharma; gods and humans all know it.
Having fully realized the dharma that transcends longing, he dwells securely in the path of nirvana.
Only the Buddha provides shelter for all beings, like a canopy covering everything.
Having subdued the māras of the aggregates, the māra of death, and the māra of afflictions,
and having conquered the hosts of Māra along with their evil-minded followers,
I bow my head to the World-Honored One, the courageous and valiant one who has compassion for all beings.
This Māra possesses an extremely evil mind; he constantly performs all manner of wicked deeds.
This is his sport and laughter: he desires to bring suffering upon sentient beings.
These palaces of the asuras are entirely shrouded by clouds of misery.
The Buddha immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion and touched all of us asuras.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha completed various ascetic practices;
for many kalpas he cultivated generosity and precepts, and practiced patience and wisdom.
The World-Honored One no longer performs any other evil deeds;
by such actions as these, the Buddha has brought me sufficient joy.
The Buddha alone is a man of diligence; in the three realms, there is no equal to him.
Free from the bonds of all afflictions, liberated from the three realms of existence,
the Buddha continues to turn the wheel of compassion for sentient beings;
I pay homage to the Buddha, the Immovable Mountain, who dwells in perfect peace with a heart of loving-kindness.

At that time, the asura king Vemacitra and his retinue prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the feet of the World-Honored One in worship. They circumambulated him three times to the right and stood before the Buddha, immediately placing a thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* of Jāmbūnada gold before him.

Furthermore, he placed the *sūryakānta* (sun-loved) *maṇi* jewel above the Buddha, and made offerings with various kinds of jewels, various fragrant flowers, and even various songs, dances, and musical performances. With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these verses of praise:
“Śakra, Brahmā, Maheśvara, Cakravartins, Nārāyaṇa, The World-Protectors, and Pāpīyas— None possess such power as this.”
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, humans and asuras alike—none possess such great power of compassion as the World-Honored One.
Only the Buddha is supreme among all beings; like the earth, he is neither angry nor pleased.
One who can endure all evils and even perform evil deeds themselves,
yet regards all sentient beings equally as a mother loves her child,
with a mind impartial toward all— for this reason, I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
May you protect this single Dharma, so that Māra does not return;
do not allow him to prevail and inflict such evil affliction and harm.
May all evil wrath and the most extreme malice [be stilled].
Please speak the mantra of truthful words to subdue all demonic hosts.
Just as a person who is free from illness has no need to seek out physicians,
so too the asuras have no reason to think of the Buddha.
I am now filled with great joy, having come to the presence of the Buddha;
I pray that you will preach the pure Dharma, leading us to the path of Bodhi.
Reveal to us the various noble sages, whose tranquil concentration is like space.
Staying far removed from all evils, And free from the notions of "I" and "mine," One swiftly realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), Is able to eliminate all afflictions (*kleśa*),
Swiftly severs all bonds, And attains knowledge of the supreme path.

At that time, the asura king Pāṭala and his retinue prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and holding various multicolored trees made of diverse jewels—shaped like *pāṭala* trees of the seven precious substances—they placed them behind the Buddha.

Various jeweled leaves, flowers, and fruits; golden-threaded pearl necklaces; celestial jewel garlands; celestial necklaces and robes; finger-rings, bracelets, and bangles; precious parasols, banners, and streamers; and jeweled ornaments for the hands, feet, and arms—all these precious adornments hung down from the air above the Buddha’s head. Furthermore, they made offerings to the Buddha with various songs, dances, and musical performances.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and spoke these verses of praise:
“Sentient beings are constantly tormented by the fires of affliction;
Though they seek happiness, they never find it, For they do not encounter one who can bestow it upon them.”
All who dwell in the evil realms, for them the Buddha alone is the medicine for sentient beings;
abiding securely in the path of liberation, he is able to rescue all from suffering.
The Buddha alone is the sovereign of merchants; within the three realms of existence, there is none other.
With the waters of compassion, vigor, and wisdom, you are filled with all virtues like the ocean.
For those who are blind and have lost their way, you establish them upon the correct path;
you guide all sentient beings so that they may abide in the supreme path of nirvana.
Ordinary beings suffer from hunger without satiety; only the Buddha can satisfy them.
Constantly submerged in the afflictions, only the Buddha can rescue them.
Suffering from the disease of being drowned, they lose their mindfulness when oppressed by pain.
For those suffering in such bitter pain, the Guide acts as their intimate savior.
Even sentient beings with evil minds, nāgas, ghosts, and various rākṣasas,
upon seeing the Buddha, attain right mindfulness and abide in a heart of great compassion.
Only the Buddha within the three realms Is able to act as our protector;
We have already become solitary and alone, All submerged by manifold sufferings.
With one mind, we all abide In the joy of the Dharma.
I pray you will explain the supreme meaning, so that I may attain bodhi.
Having attained the Buddha-eye and the supreme wisdom of all Buddhas, may I swiftly subdue all demonic adversaries; I pray you will let fall the rain of the True Dharma.

At that time, the asura king Vajravairocana, together with his retinue, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right. He then piled Jāmbūnada gold to the left and right of the Buddha;

furthermore, he made offerings with various jewels, various flowers, various powdered incenses, precious canopies, banners, and streamers, as well as golden threads, pearls, necklaces, songs, dances, and music. With palms joined in homage, he praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Field of merit, water of merit, Seed of merit, sprout of merit, The field of merit is vast and boundless, The water of merit is pure and cool.”
The tree of merit, with its branches of merit, Its twigs of merit and leaves of merit,
Its flowers of merit and fruits of meritorious flavor, And the most supreme juice of meritorious flavor;
With its color of merit and shade of merit, It brings to fulfillment the children of merit.
The Buddha’s merit is firm and solid; the courage of his merit can subdue others.
His meritorious form is that of a valiant hero; his merit is an immovable mountain.
His merit is like flowers covering the earth; his merit is the medicine upon which his body relies.
At the supreme summit of merit, The waters of merit and wisdom are released;
The ocean of merit is profoundly deep, And sentient beings rely upon this merit.
Sublime merit is the source of all treasures, And the flavor of merit is like the great sea.
The vessel of merit is filled with nectar; May our meritorious vows be fully perfected.
May we, as merchants of merit, ever proceed toward The precious land of the outflows-free.
As all our merits are now exhausted, We therefore take refuge in the Buddha.
“O Vessel of Merit, Virtue, and Jewels, we pray that you will compassionately bestow [your favor] upon us.

At that time, there was another asura-ṛṣi named Sarvabodhimaṇḍala, who possessed great merit, great majesty, great wisdom, and great asceticism; he was adorned with the bodhicitta, had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), was free from all defilements, dwelt securely in the accomplishment of benefiting all sentient beings, and constantly transformed all asuras and others so they were capable of receiving his offerings. As the unsurpassed guide of all those asuras, he was surrounded before and behind by ninety-five thousand asura-ṛṣis who were likewise endowed with the five supernormal powers. They came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and placed a vessel of pure gold filled with water of eight virtues before the Buddha, along with offering a precious staff.

Furthermore, together with ninety-five thousand followers, each holding various kinds of precious parasols, they offered them to the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses in praise:
"Patience is like the great earth; The water of patience is ever full.
Abiding securely in pure patience, The mind is tranquil and nothing is lost."

With the exhaustion of the thirst of afflictions, Abiding securely in the wealth of faith, the Buddha dwells in a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, Placing all beings upon the path to enlightenment.
His preaching of the Dharma is like water; If one hears such a teaching as this,
Delighting in the bodhicitta, one can accomplish the ultimate truth.
With the great compassion of the vow to subdue,
may you accept these inferior practices and the various precious offerings presented by me, an asura.
All offerings existing within the three realms, he renounces without seeking defilement;
only the Buddha is free from afflictions and is worthy of receiving the world’s worship.
With Great Bodhi, the Buddha adorns the sentient beings of the three existences.
I pray that you will explain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for the sake of attaining bodhi.
Under Krakucchanda, I once heard the ultimate truth;
it was likewise under Kanakamuni and Kāśyapa Buddha.
By the power of my own vow, I manifest as an asura;
for the sake of transforming asuras, I practice the path to enlightenment.
Having heard the Dharma and attained the treasury of virtues, I am further able to turn it over and show it to others.
Having subdued the hosts of evil Māras, he causes the fellowship of the True Dharma to blaze forth.
In this defiled and evil world, it is rare to find a person of merit who manifests such deeds of the Buddha’s realm; this is the wondrous supernatural power of the Buddha.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 47; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 48.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Past Deeds, Section Fourteen: The Moon-Treasury. Chapter Four: The Past Deeds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these words:

"World-Honored One, you are of the noble Śākya lineage, a great clan of the Kṣatriyas, the son of King Śuddhodana of the city of Kapilavastu. These four Asuras are of the animal realm and are exceedingly lowly; for what reason does the World-Honored One say that they are my kinsmen?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:

“In the past, during the thirty-first kalpa, there appeared a Buddha named Viśvabhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Damya-sārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. That Buddha constantly preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.”

At that time, there was a great brahmin named Puṣyayaśas, who had already planted various roots of goodness under countless Buddhas in the past; he was non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, possessed profound faith and took refuge in the Triple Gem, and having received and upheld the five precepts, he was free from all negligence.
At that time, the Vṛṣa Yakṣa had eight younger brothers:
the first was named Vṛṣavajra; the second was named Vṛṣanābhi.
The third was named Puṣyaśrī; the fourth was named Puṣyavarman;
the fifth was named Puṣyaketu.
Sixth, Puṣya; seventh, Puṣpavilī; eighth, Puṣyanadī.
Then the brahmin Puṣya advised his younger brothers, saying: "O virtuous ones!
You should now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; uphold the five precepts, abandon all negligence, and resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, none of those younger brothers were willing to take refuge in the Triple Gem, nor were they even willing to resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
After Vṛṣagañja had exhorted his younger brothers repeatedly over many years, he questioned them again: "You all!..."
"Why is it that you all refuse to take refuge in the Triple Gem, and even refuse to resolve to attain Bodhicitta?
What is your ultimate intention, and what do you seek?
At that time, those eight younger brothers spoke as follows:

"Brother, if you can cultivate two modes of deportment for a thousand years—practicing only walking and standing, neither sitting nor reclining—and for seven days and nights limit yourself to a single meal, completing this difficult practice for a full thousand years, then I shall take refuge in the Triple Gem, receive and uphold the five precepts, abandon all negligence, and give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi."
“Maitreya! At that time, having heard these words, Puṣya Śāriputra was filled with single-minded joy and immediately made a vow before his eight younger brothers:

‘If you are able to take refuge in the Triple Gem, and even if you are able to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi so as not to fall back, I shall now for a thousand years neither sit nor lie down, and for seven days and seven nights limit myself to a single meal.’”
Having made this vow, if for a thousand years—whether by day or by night, even for the duration of a single kṣaṇa—I should think of sitting or lying down;

or if, during seven days and nights, I should eat more than one morsel of food, may I forever transgress against the Buddhas of the three periods, transgress the six pāramitās, and transgress the ten paths of wholesome action, and may I fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of immeasurable devas in the air praised him, saying:
"Great Being! Excellent!"
Excellent!

You, who possess firmness, courage, great power, and resolve, shall in a future age, amidst a world of blind and ignorant beings, attain Buddhahood as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with your fame resounding throughout the world.
At that time, Viśvabhū Buddha, on account of Puṣya’s head-to-foot dhūta merit, praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

"Great Brahmin! Because you now practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) through these ascetic observances, in a future age—during the thirty-first Great Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan is one hundred years—you shall attain Buddhahood there, known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, your fame resounding throughout the world."
"At that time, you shall bestow upon these eight younger brothers the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Maitreya! That Brahmin Puṣya, for a full thousand years, neither sat nor lay down; for seven days and nights he limited himself to a single morsel of food. Having completed those thousand years, he established his eight younger brothers in the Three Refuges and caused them to uphold the Five Precepts, as well as to resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed bodhi."

"Good son! After Puṣya Yaśas had brought his eight younger brothers and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of others—including brahmins, elders, householders, men, women, boys, and girls—to spiritual maturity, they all went forth from home to study the Path within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū."

"At that time, having explained the sūtras, śāstras, and various non-Buddhist texts, and having memorized them without forgetting so as to explain them to others, he then went to a secluded grove and dwelt there for fifty thousand years in accordance with the dhyāna-pāramitā of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."

During that time, he brought to maturity immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, animals, pretas, piśācas, humans, and non-humans, causing them to turn toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and never to regress.
“Maitreya! As for that brahmin Vasiṣṭha, would you think he was someone else?
Do not view him as another; it was I myself.”

At that time, desiring to bring those eight younger brothers to maturity, for a thousand years I neither sat nor lay down, but only walked and stood; for seven days and nights I limited my food to a single morsel.

For the sake of bringing those brothers to maturity, I remained in a secluded grove dwelling in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) for fifty thousand years, maturing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, animals, pretas, piśācas, humans, and non-humans, directing them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* so that they would never fall back.
"At that time, Puṣya-vajra was the present Asura King Rāhu; Puṣya-nābhi was the present Asura King Vemacitrin;
and Puṣya-śarī was the present Asura King Pāra-datta."
Puṣyavarman is now the asura king Vajravairocana; Puṣyaketu is now the Māra Pāpīyas; and the Puṣya tree is now you, Maitreya.
By these causes and conditions, you have attained unimpeded wisdom and abide securely in the Mahāyāna as one who will attain buddhahood in this very life.
Puṣya Vīra was none other than the present-day Vimalakīrti;
Puṣya Nandi was none other than the present-day Devadatta. You should view it thus:

in the past, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and desiring to bring about the downfall of Māra Pāpīyas, I performed such immeasurable acts of hardship, distress, and terrifying conduct that would cause one's hair to stand on end.
Therefore, because this Māra Pāpīyas is adorned with both merit and wisdom, he possesses such supernatural powers and majesty, great capability, and supreme sovereignty within the desire realm.

"This Māra Pāpīyān and his remaining retinue have now conceived a mind of slaughter toward me; they have conceived a mind to topple the banner of the True Dharma; they have conceived a mind to destroy the Jewel of the Sangha; they have conceived a mind to sever the Eightfold Noble Path; they have conceived a mind to extinguish the lamp of the True Dharma; they have conceived a mind to obscure all wholesome dharmas of sentient beings, a mind to create obstacles, a mind to incite terror, a mind devoid of compassion, a mind of opposition, and a mind to cause sentient beings to retreat from and abandon the path of goodness so that they fall into the evil destinies."

Conceiving a sense of alarm and fear toward the host of nāgas, and a mind intent on destruction toward the palaces of the asuras, he came here because he desired to obstruct this great assembly for the preaching of the Dharma; furthermore, giving rise to the intention to disrupt the gathering of the assembly, he sat down while casting about his gaze with such malevolent thoughts.

"If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of obstructing others, for the sake of harassing others, for the sake of subjugating others, for the sake of insulting others, for the sake of seeking praise, for the sake of seeking renown, for the sake of the playful delights of the five desires, or for the sake of seeking wealth and status, practice giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—not for the sake of liberation, not for the sake of faith and reverence, not for the sake of detachment and tranquility, but solely for the sake of the pleasures of the five desires for their own bodies—and thus practice giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom: being bound by such fetters as these and mired in delusion, when the karmic fruit ripens within the desire realm, they will suffer such afflictions as those of Māra Pāpīyān."

"This Māra Pāpīyān, because he obstructed others in the past, because he tormented others, because he subdued others, because he treated others with contempt, because he sought praise, because he sought renown, and because he relied on the play and pleasure of the five desires while seeking wealth and status, practiced giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū."

By these causes and conditions, now that the pure dharmas have completely perished in the present, you have become a Māra-king in this world of the five turbidities; toward the Triple Gem, you do not give rise to faith or respect, nor do you possess a heart of veneration or admiration.
In this way, Pāpīyān constantly commits various evils against sentient beings because he does not benefit them, causes them suffering and affliction, and leads them to fall;
Devadatta is likewise the same.

"This Rāhu Asura King, Vemacitra Asura King, Pāraṭa Asura King, Bāli Vairocana Asura King, Mucilinda Asura King, and other asuras likewise, during the Dharma of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, were arrogant, self-exalting, and did not diligently practice."

Furthermore, harboring doubts and various afflictions—namely greed, anger, delusion, and false views; ignorance, flattery, and a mind fixated on annihilationism or eternalism—they practice giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Due to these causes and conditions, they are now born in the lower realms of the suffering animal and asura paths; bound by various fetters, possessed of doubt and delusion, they are unable to even give rise to mundane right view, let alone give rise to unsurpassed roots of goodness!

"Only Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Vimalakīrti, the Asura Rishi Bodhimaṇḍala, and others, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, did not practice the six pāramitās for the sake of obstructing others, nor even for the sake of seeking wealth and status; rather, they did so solely because they delighted in transcending desire and transforming sentient beings."

By these causes and conditions, this Great Being Maitreya Bodhisattva, Vimalakīrti, the asura-sage Bodhimaṇḍala, and others, have attained unimpeded wisdom; adorned with the merits of all bodhisattvas, they skillfully prepare the medicinal elixir of wisdom for all sentient beings.

"Therefore, I now tell you all: if there are those who seek unexcelled wisdom, such persons should have profound and pure faith, seeking bodhi through the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and not through worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
For example, just as the five great rivers are able to fill the great ocean, whereas small streams cannot, so too,
by relying on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one can swiftly fill the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), whereas conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) cannot.
Furthermore, just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, abides long and remains unmoving by relying upon the great earth, and not by relying upon the water;
so too, all roots of goodness attain firmness by relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and not by relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, just as all grasses and trees grow by depending upon the great earth, and not upon the blades of grass themselves,

so too do the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion, grow by depending upon the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and not upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Furthermore, just as a fierce wind, relying upon empty space, is able to blow away and disperse smoke, clouds, dust, and mist, yet does not rely upon the earth;

so too, sons and daughters of good family who seek bodhi, by relying on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), are able to blow away the clouds of false views, the smoke and mist of afflictions, and the dust of the ten unwholesome paths, but not by means of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Furthermore, it is by relying on the great radiance of the sun that one can perceive elevations and depressions, as well as various forms and diverse activities, rather than by relying on the small light of an oil lamp.
Thus, by relying on the bodhicitta of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one performs all virtuous deeds without confusion, not by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Therefore, one should abandon all matters of attachment, grasping, and acquisition, dwell in secluded forests, and practice the ultimate truth without negligence, not by means of conventional truth.
"In this way, you shall be able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās and attain perfect enlightenment in unexcelled, complete, and perfect awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Born in the same life as Maitreya, He questioned the Honored Teacher:"
"How can those of the animal realm claim kinship with humans?
The World-Honored One, seeing this from long ago, spoke to Maitreya:
"In the past, the asuras and others were all my brothers."
In the thirty-first eon, during the time of Viśvabhū Buddha,
I was a brahmin named Yaśas; wise and intelligent,
I was constantly endowed with the six perfections and never regressed from bodhi.
At that time, I had eight younger brothers who were Brahmins with wrong views;
I exhorted them to have faith in the Triple Gem and to resolve upon the Bodhicitta,
but they were all unwilling to practice, due to their ignorance and false views.
After many years had passed, the one of dull faculties spoke these words:
"Brother, you have been able for a thousand years to remain constantly free from sitting or lying down;
furthermore, for seven days and nights, you have limited yourself to a single morsel of food."
"When thus a thousand years are fulfilled, I shall abide in Bodhi.
At that time, with a single-minded joy, I vow to remain in two postures;
once the thousand years are complete, I shall finally bring them to maturity."
Furthermore, having transformed many sentient beings so that they left the household life and departed from worldly俗俗 (vulgar) existence,
I then remained in accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha) for fifty thousand years.
In this way, I have always dwelt in that ultimate truth.
They transform immeasurable multitudes, Firmly abiding in the unsurpassed path.
Rāhu and Vemacitra, Bali and Prahlāda, Pāpīyas and Vemacitrin, Maitreya and Deva.
These eight individuals were formerly my brothers;
for their sake, I practiced austerities to bring them to maturity in enlightenment.
For the sake of the unsurpassed path, I underwent all manner of hardships and difficulties.
Pāpīyān Devadatta always sought to harm me.
Although Māra performed various wholesome deeds in the past, he never possessed faith or reverence;
he constantly desired to afflict sentient beings.
Driven only by the desire for wealth and status, seeking fame rather than respect,
during the time of Viśvabhū’s Dharma, they practiced the six perfections.
When the pure dharmas had been utterly extinguished and the unwholesome dharmas were flourishing,
He became Māra Pāpīyas, exercising sovereignty over the realm of desire.
Furthermore, regarding the Triple Gem, he was unwilling to give rise to faith or reverence.
This Pāpīyas Devadatta constantly sought to afflict sentient beings.
Thus, this asura king, a man of excessive pride and negligence,
possessed by doubt and the defilement of desire, and characterized by various acts of envy,
now dwells among the class of animals, having become an asura king.
Regarding these most supreme dharmas, those lacking wisdom cannot comprehend them;
yet Maitreya, Vimalakīrti, Mārgalamkāra, and the ṛṣi Asura attained faith in the Vimala [Samādhi] and practiced the unsurpassed path.
He is united with the six perfections and constantly transforms all sentient beings;
therefore, he is now preeminent and has matured unimpeded wisdom.
Thus, I now show this to you: you should abandon all doubts and hesitations.
Diligently cultivate the ultimate truth, and the realization of bodhi will not be difficult.
Just as the ocean is ever filled with all manner of precious treasures,
so too by practicing the true reality, one can bring wisdom to fulfillment.
Furthermore, just as all crops grow depending upon the great earth,
so too, when conjoined with the True Reality, can supreme enlightenment be produced.
Moreover, just as the wind, relying on space, blows away all dust and gloom, [so does wisdom rely on the Dharma-body].
Thus, by practicing the True Truths, one can extinguish all afflictions.
Just as by relying on the light of the sun, one clearly perceives all forms and images;
so too, by abiding in the Ultimate Meaning (paramārtha), one can behold the teachings of all Buddhas.
Therefore, if you wish to attain Buddhahood swiftly in this world,
you should abandon all attachments to views and dwell securely in the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Retire to a secluded grove, sit upright, and cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).
Courageous and resolute, he is without peer, seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Diligent and self-subduing, he guards his own mind;
casting aside all false views, he remains far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
"Angry-minded nāgas and yakṣas, Along with all the spirits and ghosts, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions— I shall transform them through the True Dharma. Chapter Five:

The Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya) The Great Vaipulya Saṃnipāta Sūtra, Moon Store Section, Part Fourteen At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that the Tathāgata will, at this opportune time, grant me permission to explain it for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha, saying:
“Good son! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, grants you leave to ask whatever you wish; I shall answer according to your inclination to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, we shall receive your instruction, Blessed One!

How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in an araṇya cultivate the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) so as to become like the moon, and by means of the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), mature sentient beings and fulfill the six pāramitās?”
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! You have asked well about this meaning.

In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past, you planted various roots of goodness and cultivated meritorious deeds and perfect practices; you have already previously inquired about this profound meaning."
You now ask about this matter solely for the sake of those sons and daughters of good family who have not yet practiced but seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

"Good son! If there are faithful sons or daughters of good family who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should form this contemplation: 'All sentient beings within the three realms are being scorched by the fierce fires of the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—and are likewise ablaze with birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, unable to attain liberation.'"
While making this contemplation, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward those sentient beings and further reflects:
"All sentient beings do not fail to loathe suffering and seek happiness; yet they are thus driven by suffering like a five-jointed wheel."
Again, he thought: "By what causes and conditions do these sentient beings experience an increase in manifold sufferings without any rest?
While reflecting thus, he knew that all sentient beings are gripped by the causes and conditions of craving and grasping; therefore, they undergo this suffering, which increases without ceasing.

Therefore, I shall renounce the causes and conditions comprised of craving and grasping, and go forth into the secluded forest alone and without companion, dwelling in contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In this way, having first eliminated my own suffering, I will then be able to eliminate the suffering of sentient beings.

In this way, when a bodhisattva, with a mind of truth, desires to cause sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness, one should know that this mind arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abandons all causes and conditions of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), goes forth toward the quiet forest to dwell alone without companion like the horn of a rhinoceros, and dwells with joy in the four noble lineages (*catur-ārya-vamśa*). He does not think of earth, nor does he think of "my earth," nor does he think of "earth and I"; it is the same for the elements of water, fire, and wind.
One does not conceive of form, nor conceive of "my form," nor conceive of "form as me. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One does not conceive of the eye, nor conceive of "my eye," nor conceive of "the eye as me"; likewise, one does not conceive of eye-consciousness, nor conceive of "my eye-consciousness," nor conceive of "eye-consciousness as me."
In this way, one does not attend to eye-contact, nor does one attend to "my eye-contact," nor does one attend to "eye-contact is mine.

Likewise, regarding the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact, one does not attend to the pleasure, nor to "my pleasure," nor to "pleasure is mine"; and so it is for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as well. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

One does not attend to the mind, nor to "my mind," nor to "the mind is mine"; and so on, up to the feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mind-contact: one does not attend to pleasure, nor to "my pleasure," nor to "pleasure is mine"; and so it is likewise for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

One does not contemplate the four great elements; one does not contemplate "the four great elements are mine," nor "the four great elements are my self. This extends even to not contemplating the three types of sensation, the six perceptions, the three formations, or the six consciousnesses. It is likewise for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
He does not attend to the sphere of infinite space, nor the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor the sphere of nothingness, nor the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He does not attend to what is seen, nor what is heard, nor what is sensed, nor what is cognized; he does not attend to change, nor to applied and sustained thought, nor to the mind; he does not attend to this world, nor to that world.

One does not contemplate the past, nor the future, nor the present; one does not contemplate annihilation, nor permanence; one does not contemplate samādhi, nor dhyāna; one does not contemplate relinquishment, nor exhaustion, nor utility; one does not contemplate arising, nor ceasing; one does not contemplate self, nor number; one does not contemplate black, nor white; one does not contemplate superior, nor inferior; one does not contemplate walking, nor standing, nor sitting, nor lying down; one does not contemplate darkness, nor light.
Do not dwell on formations, do not dwell on the three realms, and do not dwell on moments;
it is likewise so. "Ha ha ha ha ha | Dārami | Dharaniye | Dhavakṣe | Dhavagacchaye | Dhavamokṣaye | Svāhā. "O son of good family!"
"This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in a secluded forest and cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

When the Buddha spoke thus on the ultimate truth of the araṇya, eighty billion hundred thousand *bimbara* devas and humans who had previously cultivated the ultimate truth all attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there were gods and humans as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Moreover, there were sentient beings exceeding the measure of space who attained the samādhi of not forgetting the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand bhikṣus who attained the untainted liberation of mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again, saying:
"O sons of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, as previously described, abandons the causes and conditions comprised by craving and grasping, and even practices the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as I have taught—how does such a bodhisattva mahāsattva become like the moon, mature sentient beings through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*)?

“Good son! Just as a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes that all sentient beings are ablaze with the fierce fires of the three poisons, and that birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are likewise ablaze, such that they do not attain liberation.

When practicing this contemplation, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion toward all those sentient beings; this is how the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains likeness to the moon, illuminating and dispelling the dark ignorance of sentient beings, just like the rising moon.

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of eliminating the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, relinquishes the causes and conditions comprised of craving and grasping—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva attaining likeness to the moon, illuminating and removing the darkness of ignorance for sentient beings, maturing them through association with unimpeded mastery over meaning, and fulfilling the six pāramitās; thus, they are like the second-day moon."

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva goes out toward a secluded forest, dwelling alone and without companion like the horn of a rhinoceros, finding joy in the four noble lineages—this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attaining likeness to the moon. He illuminates and dispels the darkness of ignorance of sentient beings, and through being in accord with unimpeded Dharma, he brings sentient beings to maturity; for the sake of fulfilling the six pāramitās, he is like the third-day moon.”
