"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva attaining likeness to the moon: illuminating and dispelling the darkness of ignorance for sentient beings, maturing them through mastery of unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and for the sake of fulfilling the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), being like the moon on its fourth day."

"Just as a bodhisattva-mahāsattva completely renounces the realms of the three worlds and all worldly pleasures to cultivate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), so too does this bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain the likeness of the moon; illuminating and removing all the thirst and craving of sentient beings, and being endowed with the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech to bring sentient beings to maturity, he acts like the fifth-day moon in order to fulfill the six pāramitās."

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes the pleasures of humans in the present and does not even aspire to the pleasures of the five desires while cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha), this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains likeness to the moon. He illuminates and dispels all the darkness of anger in sentient beings; he brings sentient beings to maturity and is able to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on its sixth day toward all sentient beings."

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains śamatha-concentration regarding all objects, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of being like the moon; they are able to mature sentient beings and fulfill the śīla-pāramitā. Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the seventh-day moon for all sentient beings."

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva corresponds to the cessation of the spheres of the three realms, neither discriminating between anger nor discriminating between loving-kindness—this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva matures sentient beings and is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on the eighth day."

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva is in accord with the cessation of all three realms, neither conceptualizing nor even non-conceptualizing them—this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva matures sentient beings and is able to fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*. Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon in its ninth day."

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the ultimate truth for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s maturing of sentient beings and his fulfillment of the dhyāna-pāramitā; therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on its tenth day toward all sentient beings.”

"Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of sentient beings, does not conceptualize and thoroughly non-conceptualizes regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the three types of sensation within the triple world, but dwells in accordance with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) while practicing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva matures sentient beings and is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on the eleventh day toward all sentient beings."
"In this way, noble son!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in a secluded forest while cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha), becomes like the moon; through the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), they bring sentient beings to maturity and are able to fulfill the six perfections (pāramitā)."
"Furthermore, good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), bring sentient beings to maturity and become like the moon?

“Good son! When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he relinquishes all conceptualization regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the three realms, and abides in non-conceptualization while cultivating the ultimate truth.”

At that time, the devas who roam the various earths, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas—afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, and mutually terrified—they oppressed their own bodies and minds, constantly harboring anger and malice. They felt no compassion for sentient beings and paid no heed to the terrors of future lives.

Those gods, nāgas, and even the kaṭapūtanas, having gone to where the Bodhisattva was and seen him, laughed loudly; they sought to seize the Bodhisattva’s vital energy, further attempted to exhale foul breath upon him, and desired to strike and harm him in order to distract his mind.

Although those spirits and ghosts may give rise to such evil intentions, they cannot travel even one yojana to reach the place where that bodhisattva resides; how then could they blow upon him with their breath to steal his vital energy, or strike and harm him to distract his mind?
Those spirits and ghosts felt extreme wonder in their hearts; they further manifested the most horrific forms and colors, wishing to cause the Bodhisattva’s heart to split with fear.
Yet, whether he was walking or standing, the Bodhisattva could not even move a single hair, let alone allow them to inflict any other affliction or disturbance!
Those gods, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas cannot, by any means whatsoever, cause even the slightest disturbance to that bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

They then conceived a sense of reverence, faith, respect, and veneration toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and their minds were filled with wonder. Because they gave rise to such reverence and faith toward the Bodhisattva, the suffering of their bodies and minds was exhausted, and they attained a state of overflowing bliss.

They again frequently went to the Bodhisattva’s abode, prostrated at his feet in reverence, and returned to their own places to wander and dwell; furthermore, they showed mutual respect toward one another among the sentient beings, constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind free from fear, a mind free from flattery, a mind free from malice, a mind free from enmity, a mind free from contention, a mind of equanimity, and a mind that has ceased killing, up to and including a mind that has ceased all wrong views.
They repeatedly showed the utmost reverence toward the Bodhisattva, prostrating their heads at his feet, making vows, and repenting for all their sinful karma, saying:

"From this day forth until the distant future, throughout as long as we wander in the cycle of birth and death, we shall always respectfully make offerings to you, serving as your attendants, friends, spiritual teachers, brothers, kinsmen, and patrons, until the Bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, O Benevolent One, you shall bestow upon us the prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles.
By virtue of your power, we shall attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death and enter the City of Fearlessness.

"This is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while cultivating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), brings sentient beings to maturity and is able to fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on the twelfth day to all sentient beings."

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha), all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas who are cruel, malicious, and wrathful toward sentient beings—lacking compassion and disregarding the fear of future lives, and who manifest such evil forms and improper conduct—cannot disturb even a single hair of that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the secluded forest who cultivates the ultimate truth; how much less could they cause any other form of disturbance!"
Those devas and nāgas then conceived respectful faith toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and even ceased from the ten unwholesome paths.

Repeatedly approaching the Bodhisattva, they made vows and repented of all their sinful karma, saying: "O Noble One, grant us the prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles; we shall then attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death and enter the city of fearlessness."

"This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, when practicing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), maturing sentient beings and being able to fulfill the six *pāramitās*; for this reason, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is like the moon on its thirteenth day toward all sentient beings."

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest cultivating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), those gods, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas approach that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and repent of their karmic obstructions, sentient-being obstructions, dharma obstructions, and afflictive obstructions. Furthermore, because these sentient beings attain maturity, they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās; therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the moon on the fourteenth day for all sentient beings."

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha), those devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas become fierce, cruel, and full of anger."

Lacking compassion for sentient beings, they neither deeply revered nor had faith [in others], nor did they regard the terrors of future lives; yet, toward those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who cultivate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they developed profound faith, respect, reverence, and a sense of wonder. They completely abandoned all evil deeds and their homes, and day and night went to the presence of those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who cultivate the ultimate truth, practicing as described above.

Ceasing the taking of life, one dwells with a mind of compassion, a mind of benefit, and a mind of pity toward all sentient beings; ceasing theft, sexual misconduct, and false speech—this is the practice by which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) in the ultimate sense.
Just as he refrains from divisive speech, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Just as he refrains from harsh speech, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Just as he refrains from frivolous speech, this is how the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*.
Just as he refrains from greed and hatred, this is how the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the *dhyānapāramitā*.
Just as one who has rested from wrong views and attained right view repeatedly makes this aspiration:
"May we attain unsurpassed wisdom," so too is this the way a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

"Just as those devas, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas have attained deep reverence and faith toward that bodhisattva mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth (paramārtha), they likewise do not feel any diligent fear toward kṣatriyas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras; nor do they fear men or women, boys or girls; nor do they fear elephants, horses, lions, tigers, leopards, dholes, wolves, deer, or birds and beasts; nor do they fear kingdoms, cities, villages, or dwellings; nor do they fear earth, water, fire, or wind; nor do they fear medicinal herbs, forests, trees, flowers, fruits, or other such things."

This is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while cultivating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), brings sentient beings to maturity and is even able to fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Therefore, toward all sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is like the moon on the fifteenth day—perfectly complete in every respect.
In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest and cultivates the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), they are able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās.

Just as the moon on the fifteenth day is subtle and lovely, surrounded by the host of stars, so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth subtle and lovely, surrounded by those of faithful mind—devas, nāgas, and even kṛtya-pūtanas—who follow their virtuous conduct.

Just as the moon on the fifteenth day illuminates and dispels all the darkness of ignorance, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) illuminate and dispel the ten unwholesome obscurations of devas, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas.

Just as the nature of the moon is cool and refreshing, enabling all sentient beings afflicted by heat and distress to attain peace of body and mind, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth cause those gods, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas who are tormented by anger to abide in a mind of loving-kindness and attain physical well-being.

Just as the moon causes those who have lost their way to see the path, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) cause all those who have lost their way—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas—to give rise to compassion for both gods and humans, and ultimately enable them to see the paths of the three vehicles (triyāna).

For example, when the moon on the fifteenth day is fully complete, it illuminates the *candrakānta* (moon-love) maṇi jewel; because that jewel is illuminated by the moonlight, it can produce abundant water that fills small streams, great rivers, and even the great ocean. In the same way, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) possesses such power of majestic deportment that even the *kāṭapūtana* spirits attain deep reverence and faith. They are not afraid of kṣatriyas, nor of boys or girls, nor of cities, nor even of trees, flowers, and fruits.

By this causal connection, humans, non-humans, and even *kāṭapūtanas*, deer, birds, and beasts—each shall have their needs fully satisfied. Because their needs are thus fulfilled, they will not harm one another, and their bodies and minds will abide in peace and happiness.

They are capable of practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, and even attain the full enjoyment of happiness as karmic retribution among devas and humans; by these causes and conditions, they attain non-retrogression within the three vehicles, whereby many such devas and humans receive abundant benefit.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest cultivating the ultimate truth (paramārtha), they are able to bring peace and security to all devas and humans; by means of such practices, they are swiftly able to fulfill the six pāramitās.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in a secluded forest to cultivate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), so that regarding all roots of goodness, samādhis, and dhāraṇīs, they may attain maturity through firm endurance.

"Just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is well-established, so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth is well-established in all roots of goodness, beginning with the perfection of giving."
Like the lion, king of beasts, he subdues all afflictions through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Like Nārāyaṇa, he overcomes all evil views within the three realms through the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Just as the flowers of the Pārijātaka tree begin to bloom, so too do the various flowers of the roots of goodness through the *vīryapāramitā* come to full bloom.
Like the blazing radiance of the solar orb, the *dhyānapāramitā* is able to dispel all the darkness of ignorance.
Like the moon on the fifteenth day, when it is perfectly full, his vows are fulfilled through the adornment of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Like a wish-fulfilling jewel that can eliminate poverty, his various roots of goodness are inexhaustible through the power of skillful means (*upāya*).
May the Dharma of inexhaustible wisdom and wealth be fulfilled, just as a great cloud is able to bring down a heavy rain.
In this way, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest practicing the ultimate truth, they are then able to pour down the rain of the jewels of all dharmas.

Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva who cultivates the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is well able to abide in the bodhisattva practice, such that no demonic activities can ever shake them; they attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and further obtain the complete adornment of various jewels and flowers of merit, reaching the luminous wisdom of all dharmas.

Just as the maṇi jewel atop a banner can accomplish all purposes; just as King Vaiśravaṇa’s auspicious vase can reach the torch of omniscience; and just as when one holds the moon-loved maṇi jewel in the palm of one's hand, all that is to be known becomes perfectly fulfilled like the great ocean.

"Furthermore, it is like wearing the raiment of shame and remorse during the winter; like a valiant and strong person skillfully employing various firm and sturdy weapons; and like one who skillfully transforms hidden treasures to nurture and sustain all sentient beings."
Just as at Lake Anavatapta, the kinnaras and others receive their retributions with perfect equality;
they are like lotus flowers, which cannot be defiled by the mud of the various afflictions.
Like a cluster of precious flowers, it is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of various Dharma gates;
like a precious garland, it is gazed upon by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
It is like a spring or pond filled with pure water, which washes away the defilements of the afflictions of sentient beings.
It is like the great river Sītā, which sweeps away all the defilements of the afflictions and evil views of sentient beings.
Like a boat upon a great river, he is able to ferry sentient beings across the river of all afflictions.
Like Kiśarī the lion, he subdues all heterodox and deviant paths.
Like Śakra’s vajra, it subdues all the asuras of the afflictions;
like a parasol, it shields sentient beings from the rain of their various afflictions.
Just as the Great Brahma King causes all sentient beings to cross over the flow of existence, showing the path to nirvāṇa within the wilderness of birth and death,
so too is it called the maturation of such immeasurable merit when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a secluded forest cultivating the ultimate truth.

"In this way, son of good family! What is the meaning of the term 'ultimate truth' (*paramārthasatya*)? The ultimate truth is the meaning of the five faculties; it is the meaning of the roots of samādhi;

it is the meaning of great loving-kindness and great compassion; it is the meaning of deep faith in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*); it is the meaning of gathering in all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); it is the meaning of protecting and upholding the true Dharma; it is the meaning of diligently seeking all Buddha-dharmas; it is the meaning of remaining far removed from all calamities; it is the meaning of abiding in the merits of a Buddha; it is the meaning of transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is the meaning of being able to purify the three karmas; it is the meaning of adorning the mind with various samādhis; it is the meaning of purifying the three evil destinies so that all sentient beings may abandon false paths; it is the meaning of the patience of faith and understanding; it is the meaning of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) for maturing sentient beings; and it is the meaning of relinquishing hatred and attachment."

The meaning of decisive judgment regarding all phenomena; the meaning of discerning all phenomena; the meaning of diligently seeking omniscience; the meaning of attaining all factors conducive to enlightenment; the meaning of awakening to the twelve links of dependent origination; the meaning of discerning the foremost qualities; the meaning of the three ways in which there is nothing to guard against; the meaning of the four fearlessnesses; the meaning of the ten powers; the meaning of great loving-kindness and great compassion for maturing sentient beings; the meaning of skillfully and diligently seeking the ultimate truth of the Tathāgata’s ten powers; the meaning of the ten stages; the meaning of ascending the stage of succession; the meaning of subduing Māra; the meaning of attaining the knowledge of all modes; the meaning of turning the wheel of Dharma; the meaning of raining down the rain of Dharma; the meaning of delivering all sentient beings; and the meaning of establishing the Eightfold Noble Path.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) possesses such immeasurable great meanings as these.

"Good son! The ultimate truth washes away the defilements of all fetters and extinguishes all evils; it can ferry sentient beings across the mire of afflictions, dry up the river of craving, and cause them to transcend the vast wilderness of all saṃsāric wandering. It shatters the net of false views, illuminates and eliminates ignorance, subdues all enemies, and cuts off grief and sorrow. It brings harmony and joy to the faculties, leading one into the right path; it awakens one to all dharmas, increases roots of goodness, causes one to abandon the state of ordinary fools, and leads one to enter the stage of the noble ones and reach the path of Bodhi."

“Good son! Thus, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is fully perfected in all its merits; it brings to maturity the unsurpassed and most excellent wisdom, and is able to cause sentient beings to reach the other shore of all saṃsāra.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘samādhi,’ of what body is this samādhi?”
What is this object of clinging?
What is this perception?
What is this sign?
What is its nature?
What is its body in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
What is its object of apprehension (ālambana)?
What is its perception?
What is its characteristic? What is its nature?
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You have long practiced samādhi and your roots of goodness are perfected; it is for the sake of all sentient beings that you now ask the Tathāgata about such matters as these."
"Good son! Listen now with close attention and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The samādhis of the various Śrāvaka vehicles are called ‘unwholesome samādhis. They consist of the bodies of the three realms, involve inverted objects of focus, possess notions of impurity, have the characteristic of weary detachment, and lack the nature of joyful delight.”

"The earth-element samādhi is that which, inseparable from the body, takes as its object of focus the perception of heaviness and the characteristic of solidity, yet has the nature of being broken and destroyed.

The water-element samādhi is that which, inseparable from the body, takes as its object of focus fullness, the perception of moisture, and the characteristic of fluidity and softness, yet has the nature of drying up."
“The fire-element samādhi is that which, inseparable from the body, takes maturation as its object, has the perception of heat, the characteristic of burning, and the nature of total extinction.

The wind-element samādhi is that which, inseparable from the body, takes blowing and lifting as its object, has the perception of non-obstruction, the characteristic of rapidity, and the nature of lightness.”

“The Samādhi of Discerning the Aggregates (skandha-vibhāga-samādhi) consists of the thirst for the body, taking dependent origination as its object, the perception of relinquishment, the characteristic of suffering, and selflessness.

“The Samādhi of Emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) consists of penetrating the Dharma-body, taking all phenomena as its object, the perception of non-substantiality, the characteristic of opening vision, and ultimate emptiness.”

"The signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi) involves abandoning the body of the three fetters, taking nirvāṇa as its object, the perception of emptiness, the cessation of signs, and the thorough exhaustion of the nature of activity.

Likewise, the wishless samādhi of mind and mental factors involves the five groups of consciousness, taking causes and conditions as its objects, constantly practicing the perception [of impermanence], the characteristic of rapidity, and the nature of non-reliance; these are the samādhis of the Śrāvaka vehicle."
"Cultivating this samādhi of dependent origination is called the samādhi of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
One dwells securely in the Mahāyāna,
O son of good family!"

The samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) consists of recollecting the body, taking sentient beings as its object, possessing the perception of non-obstruction, the characteristic of non-aversion, and a nature free from turbidity.

The samādhi of compassion (*karuṇā*) consists of recollecting the body, taking sentient beings as its object, possessing the perception of non-harming, the characteristic of rescuing and uprooting [suffering], and a nature of sympathetic pity.

"The *muditā-samādhi* (samādhi of sympathetic joy) involves recollecting the body, taking sentient beings as its object, and having a nature of constant celebration characterized by attachment to perceptions of pleasure and fondness for signs.

The *upekṣā-samādhi* (samādhi of equanimity) involves recollecting the body, taking sentient beings as its object, and having a nature of effortless equanimity characterized by the absence of both aversion and perceptions of joy."

“Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection: it is the Dharma-nature body; its objects of focus are physical forms; its perceptions are of the sense-sphere of form; its characteristics are those of affection and reverence;

and its nature is one of joy. “Regarding the Samādhi of Mindfulness of Ānāpāna: it takes the body as the body; mindfulness serves as the object of focus; its perceptions do not abide; its characteristics are those of cold and heat; and its nature is that of arising and ceasing.”
“Good son! Thus, the first noble truth—the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the four dhyānas, cessation, emptiness, and samādhi—depends upon mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
What is meant by mindfulness of breathing?
*Āna* means inhalation; *apāna* means exhalation; *smṛti* (mindfulness) refers to a mental factor.
"Good son! One should practice that inhalation and exhalation. Having practiced them, the body becomes tranquil and the mind also attains tranquility."
How should one practice? First, counting;
second, following along.
Third, abiding; fourth, observing characteristics; fifth, returning.
Sixth is "excellent purity.
There are two types of cultivation:
first, relying on that [state] to eliminate applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Second, taking up the signs of inhalation and exhalation.
"Accordance" also has two aspects of practice:
first, relying on exhalation to eliminate vitarka and vicāra; [second, relying on inhalation to eliminate vitarka and vicāra].
Second, taking up the sign of inhalation.
"Abiding" also has two aspects of function:
first, it manifests the gradual diminution and exhaustion of the inhalation and exhalation; [the second is]...
Second, abiding in samādhi. "Contemplating the signs" also has two aspects of practice:
first, manifesting the gradual diminution and exhaustion of inhalation and exhalation; [the second is]...
Second, one observes that the mind and all mental phenomena are variously distinct and abide in different locations.
Furthermore, there are two aspects to the process of turning back and returning:
first, the cessation of the three types of sensation; [the second is...]
Second, by ceasing three types of activity, one attains the pure *śūnyatā-samādhi*.
What is this *śūnyatā-samādhi*?
It is seeing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without life-force (*jīva*), observing that all phenomena are without a master (*svāmin*), and thereby abiding in the seven kinds of emptiness.
What are these seven?

They are the emptiness of the aggregates, the emptiness of the elements, the emptiness of the sense bases, the emptiness of the truths, the emptiness of dependent origination, the emptiness of phenomena, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature; these are called the samādhi of emptiness.

Abiding in this emptiness-samādhi, the growth of causes and conditions ceases; when the growth of causes and conditions ceases, activity comes to rest; because activity comes to rest, the path comes to rest.

"Good son! This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fourth dhyāna, the samādhi of attaining the ultimate truth through the unobtainable and the ineffable. It is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this state of meditative concentration, they ultimately do not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they are able to fulfill the six pāramitās and, in seven days and nights, bring to maturity immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas and so forth—let alone over many days and nights. In whatever kingdoms or cities they may dwell, there are those who abide in such dhyāna of the ultimate truth!"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have twelve kinds of meritorious benefits in that land. What are the twelve? First, in that world, kings do not cause anger or affliction;

brahmins do not cause anger or affliction; śramaṇas do not cause anger or affliction; vaiśyas do not cause anger or affliction; śūdras do not cause anger or affliction; nor do men, women, boys, girls, or even the classes of animals, birds, and beasts cause anger or affliction.”
Second, in that land, enemies from other regions shall not come to invade the country, nor shall weapons be raised;
third, in that land there shall be no bandits, no deceit, and no hypocrisy;

fourth, in that land evil persons shall not enter, and there shall be no epidemics—except for those illnesses arising from the imbalance of the four elements—and none shall die an untimely death except when their own karma is exhausted.
Fifth, in that land there shall be no unseasonable winds, rains, cold, or heat;

sixth, among all sentient beings in that land there shall be none who are malicious, impetuous, or coarse, nor any who are obscured by ignorance through inverted views and attachments, nor any gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, lions, white elephants, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous snakes, vipers, or scorpions;

seventh, in that land there shall likewise be no mosquitoes, gadflies, evil flies, lice, fleas, field mice, wild foxes, owls, hares, owls, or hawks and falcons, nor any other insects that cause harm or devour crops.

Eighth, in that land, flowers, fruits, and delicious flavors are all sweet and crisp; there are no bitter, pungent, astringent, or tasteless things, nor is there famine, for fruits and medicinal herbs abound.

Ninth, in that land, the great earth is level and even, without wildernesses, elevations, depressions, or treacherous difficulties; the ground is free of salt marshes and lacks pits or ravines. The flower and fruit trees and forests are always verdant, spreading wide and luxuriantly; therefore, sentient beings do not lack food or clothing, and they constantly obtain abundance, benefit, and peace.

Tenth, in that land, people will have no enmity, strife, slander, or litigation; they will all give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of harmony, a mind of joy, a mind of generosity, a mind of ethical discipline, a mind of patience, a mind of diligence, a mind of meditative concentration, a mind of wisdom, a mind seeking the Dharma, a mind free from transgression, a mind diligently seeking the Three Vehicles, a mind seeking liberation, and a mind of contentment—except for those instances of enmity arising from past unwholesome karma.

Eleventh, in that land, Buddhas shall dwell in the world; if there are no Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas shall dwell there; if there are no Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas shall dwell there; and if there are no Śrāvakas, there shall be seers possessing the five supernormal powers; thus, in that land, there will always be such persons worthy of receiving offerings.

Twelfth, in that land there shall be no ill repute or unpleasant sounds, namely: the sound of punishment; the sound of strife and litigation; the sound of imprisonment and bondage; the sound of killing; the sound of donning armor; the sound of hunting; the sound of theft; the sound of abuse; the sound of making deadlines; the sound of scarcity; the sound of famine; the sound of lacking clothing; the sound of oppression; the sound of illness; the sound of sexual misconduct; the sound of lying; the sound of divisive speech; the sound of harsh speech; the sound of frivolous speech; the sound of greed; the sound of anger; and the sound of taking refuge in evil deities.
"In that land, such evil and false sounds as these shall never exist; rather, it shall always be filled with such excellent sounds as these:

namely, the sound of the Three Jewels, the sound of the three types of restraint, the sound of the four divine abodes, the sound of the four means of attraction, the sound of the six perfections, the sound of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the sound of ascending the throne, the sound of not being subject to further existence, the sound of subduing Māra, the sound of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the sound of raining down the Dharma. In that land, it shall be constantly filled with all such sounds."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the dhyāna of the ultimate truth, all sentient beings in the lands where they dwell shall attain progress toward unsurpassed bodhi, and their fame shall resound throughout the world within the three realms.

“If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās, and who wish to bring immeasurable, incalculable tens of billions of sentient beings to maturity so that they may swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should go to a secluded forest and dwell in accordance with the four noble lineages; in this way, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will, by means of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), attain the wisdom of the eighth stage.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Candragarbha asks the Honored Teacher of Gods and Humans: ‘I pray you will explain for me the supreme words:
How does a bodhisattva dwell in an araṇya?’”
How does one cultivate the ultimate truth?
How does one become like the moon therein?
One can bring countless billions of sentient beings to maturity and swiftly fulfill the six perfections.
Severing afflictions and all conditioned formations,
seeing that the three realms are ablaze with the fires of suffering and affliction— aging, sickness, grief, lamentation, and death—
one gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings and swiftly abandons craving and grasping, which are the causes and conditions of bondage.
Delighting in the noble lineages, they dwell in forest hermitages, Constantly in accord with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Practitioners of dhyāna abandon the six sense faculties, And likewise abandon craving, grasping, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
With craving for the objects of the three realms utterly eliminated, They remain far removed from the three times and the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
When one does not dwell on the diminution or exhaustion of dhyāna, that person attains liberation from the dusts of black and white,
as well as from all discriminations of light and darkness, and constantly cultivates the ultimate truth.
Having relinquished the aggregates and elements, you abide in awakening;
like the moon among all worlds, you cause beings in the lands to cease their fear, just as the full moon illuminates the world.
Thus sentient beings attain peace and happiness; Like the moon’s nature of coolness and radiant light, Evil sounds cease throughout all lands; Such merit is also like the moon.
If a person cultivates the ultimate truth, subtle and wondrous sounds will fill the world;
famine, disease, and strife will all be stilled, causing all sentient beings to turn toward Bodhi.
Through faith and compliant patience, one accomplishes the ultimate truth; awakening to the patience of non-arising is likewise so.
By this also, one accomplishes unimpeded wisdom; by this also, one can swiftly fulfill the six perfections.
By this Dharma, one brings sentient beings to maturity; by this Dharma, one swiftly attains Buddhahood.
Śrāvakas should likewise abandon unwholesome states and perversions;
the earth element cannot be separated from its nature of solidity, heaviness, and susceptibility to breaking,
nor can the water element be separated from its nature of moisture, wetness, and drying.
The fire element burns and cooks; its nature is the total extinction of the perception of heat.
All aggregates (skandhas) are of the nature of craving; through causes and conditions, they find rest.
Emptiness exists in seven ways; it causes the phenomena and things to manifest.
By means of signlessness, one eliminates craving; by resting from all fetters and relinquishing all causes and conditions for their accumulation,
one practices dependent origination through the power of wishlessness— this alone is the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
All sentient beings of the Mahāyāna, practicing the various Brahma-abodes,
the mindfulness of *ānāpāna*, and samādhi, reveal these within body and mind;
when the mind can abide in the non-substantial, it brings rest to the three kinds of grasping.
Inexpressible and beyond verbal description, this is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha);
it is not the domain of the two vehicles, for they abide here in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
If, by means of this samādhi, one brings countless beings to maturity, [one attains this state].
One whose fame fills the world will swiftly attain Buddhahood. Therefore,
if you wish to fulfill the perfections such as generosity,
and if you desire to achieve the path of the Buddha, always delight in the *araṇya*.
"If one always delights in the araṇya, cultivates the practices of the noble ones,
and swiftly abandons all conditions and hindrances, one shall attain the Bodhi of a Buddha. At that time,

when the World-Honored One spoke this primary truth, five hundred and seventy bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within that assembly— those who had previously cultivated this Dharma in the past— all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Furthermore, there were sixty hundred thousand *bimbara* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had previously cultivated this Dharma; they have all attained spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) through the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, there were sixty hundred thousand nayutas of *bimbara* sentient beings who, having previously cultivated the four Brahma-abodes and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) in the past, all attained the Moon-Treasury Samādhi (*Candragarbha-samādhi*), whereby they naturally matured and attained the wisdom of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, eighty-four thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of all outflows and their minds were liberated.
As many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River who had not yet resolved to attain unexcelled bodhicitta, all attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll Forty-eight;
Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll Forty-nine.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Tianqi period of the Gao Qi dynasty.
Chapter Six: Causing Māra to Attain Faith and Joy; Section Fourteen: The Moon-Treasury.
At that time, there was a Śakra-devānām-indra named Jyotir-dhvaja who was seated in the assembly together with a great multitude. He addressed Śakra Kauśika, saying: "Kauśika!..."
Does this Māra Pāpīyān intend to diligently create disturbances so that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who dwell in secluded forests and correspond to the ultimate truth (paramārtha) may attain samādhi?
"Is it because he wishes to cause them to fall away from that samādhi?
At that time, Kauśika replied to the Devendra Agniśikha: "It is Māra Pāpīyān;

throughout all places within the four continents, he diligently creates affliction and confusion in order to cause sentient beings to lose their wholesome companions and to create obstacles for them."
Furthermore, they diligently create disturbances in order to cause the loss and obstruction of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
They also diligently create disturbances in order to cause the loss of the lineage of gods and humans, the loss of the three types of *bodhi*, and the increase of the three evil realms;
the various retinues of Māra do likewise, diligently creating disturbances because they desire to increase the great ocean of suffering for all sentient beings.
After Kauśika had spoken these words, the entire great assembly that had gathered there gazed upon the Māra King with hearts of loving-kindness.
There were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, out of compassion, exhorted and admonished the Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Fire-Light, together with ten thousand Śakra-devas, all joined their palms toward Māra Pāpīyān and spoke these words: "Great King!
“Rejoice, Ānanda! Rejoice!
You should give rise to faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, together with sixty billion hundred thousand Brahma hosts and the Four Great Kings, gazed upon Māra Pāpīyas with eyes of loving-kindness and spoke these words as well:
“Rejoice, Ānanda! Rejoice!

You, Māra Pāpīyān, if you do not gain faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, you will suffer great loss throughout the long night of the future; you will find no benefit and will fall into the various evil realms.”

Then Māra Pāpīyas, regarding all those who had gathered as the great assembly—each with eyes of loving-kindness—as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protecting kings who were offering exhortations, rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and spoke these verses:

“The wise man resolutely abandons the royal throne; Because of afflictions, jealousy, and pride, he causes one to lose and ruin the supreme path of goodness, And fall into various evil and unwholesome realms.”
Due to the intoxication of wealth and status, I created many obstacles for the Good Teacher;
I hindered the various wholesome deeds of sentient beings and, failing to see the Buddha at first, gave rise to a mind of anger.
The World-Honored One is ever-constant in patience, Compassionate and merciful toward all sentient beings;
With a mind equal toward all, his pride has been eliminated, Drying up the ocean of afflictions of sentient beings.
Only the Buddha has burned away the fuel of afflictions And can show the path of liberation to humans and devas;
He causes billions of sentient beings to cross the ocean of existence, While I, blind and without wisdom, have entered into the darkness.
I now entreat the great assembly: may you, out of compassion, assist us;
having apologized to the Tathāgata and abiding in firm faith, we shall never again give rise to a mind of affliction and disturbance.
I now single-mindedly protect the Buddha-dharma, Vigorously illuminating the Eye of the True Dharma;
Having abandoned all greed, envy, and pride, I repent for all karmic offenses without exception.

I now resolve upon the great bodhicitta, and likewise exhort all sentient beings to cultivate diligence for themselves and fulfill the six perfections, establishing those beings upon the Eightfold Path.
For the sake of each and every sentient being, I have extensively expounded immeasurable Dharma-gates;
according to their capacities, I cause them to enter the city of the Dharma, thus diligently exhorting the entire multitude.
Never before have I seen such an assembly, all of whom possess pure faith in the Triple Gem;
because I was loathed and despised due to my evil mind, I now renounce it along with all my transgressions.
From now on, may I dwell forever in pure faith; May I never again be subjected to contempt or disdain;
May my mind always be in accord with noble virtue, And never again commit various evil deeds.
At that time, having spoken these verses, Māra approached the Buddha.
Upon arrival, he prostrated and spoke in verse:
“I have created obstacles for the World-Honored One; I pray that you will accept me with the highest patience and grant me forgiveness.”
"May the Savior of the Orphaned and Solitary accept my confession; the Greatly Wise One, compassionate and benevolent, harbors no anger.
At that time, the entire great assembly who had gathered spoke with one voice, addressing the Buddha: "Bhagavān!"

I only pray that you will grant forgiveness to Māra Pāpīyān; for Māra now possesses deep faith and sincerely repents. He shall uphold the Buddha-dharma and keep the Eye of Dharma ablaze, causing the World-Honored One’s teaching to abide long in the world, and further ensuring that gods and humans obtain benefit and peace throughout the long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Patience is supreme in the world; Patience is the path of peace and happiness.
Patience brings freedom from loneliness; It is what the noble and holy ones delight in."
Patience can reveal sentient beings; patience can act as a kinsman and friend;
patience increases one’s good reputation; patience is loved by the world;
through patience one attains wealth and sovereignty; and patience can endow one with physical beauty.
Patience can obtain power; patience illuminates the world;
through patience one attains all desired pleasures; patience can accomplish skillful arts;
the power of patience subdues enemies and eliminates sorrow and affliction.
Patience brings forth a beautiful countenance; patience enables one to possess a retinue;
patience summons all superior rewards; patience leads to the good realms.
Through patience, one gains the favor of others' gazes; through patience, one attains exquisite excellence.
Patience can extinguish all sufferings; through patience one attains a long life.
Through patience one becomes a Great Brahmā King; through patience one attains mastery over desires.
Through patience one becomes Śakra, Lord of Devas; through patience one becomes a Wheel-Turning King endowed with supernormal powers.
Through patience one becomes a lord among men; the power of patience is difficult to overcome.
Through patience one gains mastery over nāgas and yakṣas, and sovereignty among the asuras.
Patience can extinguish all enmity and does no harm to sentient beings.
Patience can cause one to abandon stealing; patience can cause one to renounce sexual desire;
patience can stop false speech, double-tongued talk, frivolous chatter, and harsh words.
Patience can eliminate greed and anger, as well as the mind of wrong views.
The power of patience accomplishes generosity and ethical discipline, as well as diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; it is able to fulfill these six perfections.
Patience can eliminate all delusions, and through patience one attains the bliss of an Arhat.
One may also attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, And abide in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Patience can fulfill the ten stages (*bhūmi*), And swiftly lead to the path of Bodhi;
Through patience toward all sentient beings, One attains supreme and unsurpassed victory.
Patience can subdue all Māras and conquer all non-Buddhists;
patience can, within this world, turn the most supreme wheel.
Patience causes many sentient beings to dry up the three evil realms.
Patience cuts off the afflictive obscurations and can purify the Dharma-eye;
patience bestows predictions upon sentient beings according to their pursuit of the three vehicles;
patience can subdue the fierce and evil, such as yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Patience bestows upon all kinds of people the prediction of the most supreme path;
having endured, one subdues all enemies and can likewise extinguish all evils.
Patience can pacify everything, even untimely violent winds and rains.
Patience can bring about a great assembly, such as this multitude who have come here.
I forgive you, Pāpīyan, for all your harshness toward me;
simply repent within your own mind—this is my foremost forgiveness.
"Now, before this great assembly, I bear witness and exhort you:
do not destroy the true Dharma of all Buddhas, which I have practiced.
At that time, the entire great assembly that had gathered—the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—spoke with one voice in praise, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhagavān!
The Tathāgata always regards all sentient beings with compassion and pity, benefiting and bringing them peace and happiness through various wholesome dharmas.”

The Māra Pāpīyān constantly harbors feelings of hatred, enmity, and malice toward the World-Honored One; he acts as an evil friend to all sentient beings, perpetually creating obstacles to wholesome dharmas and causing them to abide in unwholesome states.
At that time, there was a Brahmā named Tejodhipati, who addressed the Great Brahmā King Acala with these verses:
“As space is boundless and without equal, And as it is the support upon which all sentient beings dwell,
So too is the Buddha’s wisdom inconceivable, Having reached the further shore of all phenomena.”
The World-Honored One has praised the practice of giving, out of compassion for all sentient beings;
by means of giving, one becomes a person of merit and is swiftly able to fulfill all the pāramitās.
Some may extensively explain morality, patience, diligence, As well as meditation and prajñā;
yet within each of these, The World-Honored One is fully able to manifest all six perfections.
The Tathāgata teaches that only through the dharma of meditative concentration can one proceed toward the path to enlightenment;
therefore, one should always delight in dwelling in meditation, for it enables the swift realization of great bodhi.

At that time, there were also all the Brahma Kings, the various Śakra Kings, the various other Heavenly Kings, the various Dragon Kings, the various Yakṣa Kings, the various Asura Kings, the various Garuḍa Kings, the various Kiṃnara Kings, the various Gandharva Kings, the various Mahoraga Kings, the various Rākṣasa Kings, the various Kumbhāṇḍa Kings, the various Preta Kings, the various Piśāca Kings, and others, who rose from their seats, turned toward Māra Pāpīyān, joined their palms in salutation, and spoke these words:

"Great King, pay homage with reverence, pay homage with reverence to the World-Honored Muni! For by means of this World-Honored One, one is liberated from all faults and reaches the further shore of all merits."
"Out of compassion and pity for all sentient beings, he bestows all happiness, realizes all dharmas, abandons all cyclic existence, and dwells on the other shore.
He further said:
"Great King!..."

If there are sentient beings who, for even a single thought-moment, have deep faith in the Tathāgata, looking up to him with reverence and respect, and exclaiming that he is unprecedented; because of this reverent faith, they shall become wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents with the seven treasures complete, or even become Śakra, King of Devas, or Māra Pāpīyān, Lord of Desire, or Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World—how much more so for those who can constantly possess faith in the Triple Gem!
Therefore, Great King!

You should abandon the demonic views and all defiled, turbid minds, and be endowed with pure faith. Through the cycle of birth and death, you shall attain sovereignty over wealth and honor and receive various karmic fruits; subsequently, having attained perfect enlightenment, you will be able to bestow all peace and happiness upon sentient beings, becoming the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
At that time, Māra again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with his ministers, and with single-minded devotion and reverence, he sincerely apologized to the World-Honored One, the Muni.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed him in verse:
“Evil intent and treacherous wit you have aroused; I have always been patient and forbearing, as witnessed by gods and men.”
"Practicing the path to enlightenment with a sincere heart, you shall become a Buddha of boundless wisdom.

At that time, the Māra King gave rise to pure faith and immediately took up a priceless maṇi-jewel garland, a priceless necklace for the throat, armlets, anklets, and finger-rings, and offered them to the World-Honored One. Joining his palms in prostration, he spoke these words:
"In the past, I frequently created obstacles for the Buddha, desiring to destroy the Eye of the True Dharma, sever the seeds of the Triple Gem, and extinguish the torch of the Dharma."
Why is this? Because their minds were deluded and far removed from wholesome dharmas.

Now, having attained profound reverence and faith in the Triple Gem, they have repented all karmic obstructions committed in the past; they have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and have received the prediction of their future enlightenment.
“May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, graciously accept from us this mani-jewel garland, necklace, and finger-seal.
At that time, out of loving-kindness and pity for Māra Pāpīyas, the World-Honored One immediately accepted them.
At that time, the Māra King gave rise to great joy and spoke these words:

"If any of the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—or even others, who dwell in quiet seclusion in the forest in accordance with the ultimate truth (paramārtha), whether in the present or the future; if there be Māras, sons of Māra, wives of Māra, daughters of Māra, or the various attendants of Māra, male and female; as well as all sentient beings who dwell under the influence of Māra; or if there be devas, sons of devas, wives of devas, daughters of devas, or the various attendants of devas, male and female; or if there be nāgas, sons of nāgas, wives of nāgas, daughters of nāgas, or the various attendants of nāgas, male and female; even down to the kaṭapūtanas, their sons, wives, or daughters."
If various attendants—men or women—disturb, afflict, or harm them by seizing their vital essence (*ojas*), causing their breath to falter and their minds to become distracted;
or if they rob them of clothing, food, drink, or medicinal decoctions; or if they incite others to rob them or deprive them of their flavors;
or if they sniff at them with the nose or release foul odors throughout their dwelling; or if...
Furthermore, if I do not diligently provide offerings and support— such as clothing, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions— to those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and other sentient beings dwelling in secluded forests who cultivate the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
I shall cause them to be afflicted by Māra, the sons of Māra, and even by the Kā... [omitted].
The male and female *ḍāka* and *ḍākinī* attendants suffer from diseases of the head, eyes, ears, and abdomen;
thus afflicted by such ailments, they lose their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and can no longer fly through the air to distant places,
becoming utterly lost and shrouded in darkness in every direction.
After Māra Pāpīyān had spoken these words,
he immediately uttered this incantation: "Amocā kṣa hrāmocā amomocā."
Mokṣa-vijāpate mokṣa-sudūte abhakṣi.
Abadhi riṣi naṭi na-maga-sabha-kṣetra-rajā-gama-nati riṣi.
Vajravati akhaṇḍe kṣame kṣāntimite āviśa rakṣa viśa.
Mudrā-khavi-biri-ti-vine-mati-utka.
Nemide jina nemide bhayava nemide akasamale.
Nirmāṇa-nirmita-nārāyaṇa-khaḍga-nirmita-maheśvara-nirmita.
Aśvaghnanivṛtti-stūpa-saṃkhyeya-vatsara.
Nirvañci-pramārdha-nirvañci.
Prakara-pratāna-nirvṛti-cittaḥ.
Tobabarada-nemuda-pramāttā.
*Nyavendhi ra svāhā*.
At that time, all those in the great assembly who had come there—those with evil conduct and evil minds, and those who lacked compassion for sentient beings—were all struck with terror.
Māra Pāpīyān spoke again, saying:
"If there be anyone who violates this command of mine, they shall suffer from the various ailments and afflictions mentioned above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

I shall now protect and sustain the sons of the Buddha and the śrāvakas, subduing all evil conduct so that they do not suffer any decline or affliction in the present or future worlds; I shall enable the World-Honored One’s Dharma-eye to abide for a long time and ensure that the lineage of the Triple Gem is not severed in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One again praised Māra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! So it is, Pāpīyan!"
"Throughout the long night, you have accumulated great merit; henceforth, there shall be no more evils or any form of decline or affliction.
At that time, the entire great assembly who had gathered—including devas, humans, gandharvas, and others—all praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

The Māra Pāpīyān has attained profound and pure faith in the Triple Gem; thus, the Buddha-dharma shall blaze brightly through the long night, and gods and humans shall enter the city of fearlessness. The evil paths shall be closed off, while the gates to the happy realms and liberation shall remain ever open. All strife, pestilence, famine, and unseasonable winds and rains throughout the four continents shall come to rest.
"Furthermore, may the four continents always enjoy peace, abundance, joy, and delight, and may they be filled with vast multitudes.
At that time, the Māra-king prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the great assembly, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The mind of Māra has attained certain joy; He prostrates in repentance before the Tathāgata and his retinue.
With a heart of true delight, he utters these words: 'Before the Compassionate One, I renounce all evils.'"
Just as space is without limit, so too is the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom;
having awakened to all boundless phenomena, he is the foremost in teaching the Dharma within the world.
Some say that giving (*dāna*) is supreme and peerless, for through giving one can attain wondrous Bodhi;
others again speak of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Through such various skillful means, they demonstrate the peerless Great Bodhi.
Devas, humans, and asuras should know: The World-Honored One has subdued the sovereign Māra.
In this sutra, the Buddha taught that patience is supreme; It can bring about all peace and happiness.
Patience can bring rest to all afflictions, And can point the way to the city of supreme, wondrous liberation.
With humble hearts and palms joined, all turn toward the Buddha;
having repented for all evil deeds committed, we shall now resolve upon the most supreme vow for bodhi: "We shall surely become guides."
Once the Tathāgata has bestowed this prediction upon him, Māra shall swiftly attain equal and perfect enlightenment;
and as for the hundreds of thousands of other sentient beings, they too shall be granted the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi.
Having fulfilled the perfection of patience, you shall swiftly become an unequaled Great Teacher;
as the refuge for all wholesome dharmas, you have spoken this mantra to protect all śrāvakas.
If Māra, or any of his attendant spirits and ghosts, yakṣas, asuras, or pūtanas,
should cause harm or affliction to a son of the Buddha, they shall be struck by malignant diseases that take hold of their bodies.
The entire great assembly leaped for joy, and with delight they all spoke these words:
"Because of this karma, the Dharma shall flourish and thus abide long in the world."
The Māra King abides in a mind of pure patience; the springs of the Triple Gem cannot be exhausted.
He shall quell all the turbidities of the world—famine, violent winds, and drought.

Therefore, humans and devas obtain all forms of happiness; through the practice of patience they have cultivated from the beginning, and by delighting in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and skillful means, they reach the great further shore of diligence, dhyāna, and wisdom.

At that time, as the World-Honored One clearly expounded these merits of patience, nine million eight hundred thousand devas and humans who had previously cultivated patience all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
ten *bimbara* hundred-thousand people attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
and a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* devas and humans attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
More beings than can be numbered attained mundane right view;

ten *bimbara* hundred-thousands of devas, humans, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas who had never before resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all resolved their minds upon it and attained non-retrogression;
and one million beings received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Seven: The Assembly of All Ghosts and Spirits. The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Moon Store Section, Part Fourteen. Chapter Seven: The Assembly of All Ghosts and Spirits. At that time, the four world-protecting Great Heavenly Kings rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and spoke these words: "Bhagavān!..."

In all the various lands, cities, towns, villages, gardens, monasteries, mountains, marshes, and other such places within this Jambudvīpa, there dwell various malevolent devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas. These beings are wrathful, evil, and fierce; they lack shame and remorse, possess no compassion for sentient beings, and constantly take the lives of others and cause them distress and turmoil.

Those devas, nāgas, and even the kaṭapūtanas frequently cause untimely droughts, violent winds, hailstorms, torrential rains, darkness, dust clouds, severe cold, and toxic heat within Jambudvīpa. By means of these calamities, they destroy all crops, the five grains, flowers, fruits, grapes, sugarcane, cotton, and other such things; consequently, sentient beings are afflicted by many kinds of famine, epidemics, and the suffering of separation from loved ones, being oppressed by manifold afflictions. Each fears the others, engaging in strife and combat, their minds constantly filled with dread.

These Kṣatriya kings take no pleasure in the fivefold sensual enjoyments belonging to their own retinues; they cause distress to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, as well as men, women, boys, and girls within their own kingdoms. Furthermore, they cause distress to elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, dogs, and all other birds and beasts, afflicting them all.

They oppress and afflict sentient beings through various causes and conditions; day and night they kill, burn, boil, and cut them, causing all five grains, wealth, silks, desired requisites, physical and mental pleasures, as well as all virtuous deeds, to utterly diminish.

For these reasons, the number of beings in the happy realms, such as those of gods and humans, will diminish; furthermore, because virtuous deeds in Jambudvīpa will perish, it will no longer be a place of delight, and none of us will be able to protect or shield it.

Now, at this place where the World-Honored One is gathered in great assembly, all the great beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the multitude of śrāvakas have assembled like clouds; all the celestial kings and their retinues, all the nāga kings and asura kings, and even all the piśāca kings, together with their retinues, have all come to this gathering.
“World-Honored One!
In all the lands, cities, towns, villages, mountain valleys, monasteries, and groves of this Jambudvīpa, those people—”

I only pray that the World-Honored One will distribute and entrust [this teaching] to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, and others, so that each may protect and uphold it.

If those devas, nāgas, and even piśācas should cause any form of conflict, affliction, untimely wind or rain, pestilence, famine, cold, or heat within Jambudvīpa, each shall protect and shield against them according to their respective capacities.

If all conflicts, provocations, epidemics, famines, untimely winds and rains, cold and heat, and other such occurrences throughout Jambudvīpa are entirely brought to rest; and if all the flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, cotton, silks, five grains, sugarcane, grapes, as well as curds, honey, and so forth in Jambudvīpa are made to ripen, and all crops are prevented from withering or being destroyed.
Throughout all regions of Jambudvīpa, among humans, deer, birds, and beasts, there shall be no lack of anything according to their desires.

Because they lack nothing, those sentient beings will cultivate various virtuous deeds, practice the conduct of the True Dharma, and dwell diligently in the cultivation of authentic practice, causing their various virtues to increase and never decline.
By these causes and conditions, this Jambudvīpa shall be peaceful, prosperous, and densely populated, being most delightful.

The True Dharma of the World-Honored One shall endure for a long time; the aspirations of all devas and humans shall be fulfilled; all sentient beings shall attain the path leading toward wholesome realms and Nirvana, departing from the three evil destinies; and the lineage of the Triple Gem shall never be severed.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"In all the lands within this Jambudvīpa,
there are evil devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas."
Pretas, piśācas, and kaṭapūtanas— malicious, ungrateful,
and devoid of compassion for sentient beings—
they lack shame and remorse, and they provoke and harass the kṣatriyas.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas and śūdras, lions, elephants,
tigers, and leopards, untimely evil winds and rains,
pestilence and famine— these can cause suffering for sentient beings.
They harm sentient beings and destroy the world;
they ravage all crops and extinguish the lamp of the True Dharma.
We, the Four Great Kings, cannot restrain such evil.
May the Buddha distribute [this teaching] throughout the lands, cities, and towns,
entrusting it to the nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas,
so that they may each provide protection against untimely evil winds and rains.
May all fears and afflictions be stilled; may there be no disease or famine.
May flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and crops abound with every kind of delicious flavor.
May sentient beings never lack anything, including all the various requisites for offerings.
May all wholesome dharmas increase, may they bring about desirable things,
may the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time, and may sentient beings proceed toward the good paths;
may the seeds of the Triple Gem never be severed— may the Buddha always look upon us with compassion.
The great earth is endowed with manifold excellences, free from all bitter and acrid flavors;
flowers and fruits are fully abundant, and it is filled with various tastes.
Springs, ponds, pools, rivers, and the like are always filled with pure water.
Regarding all crops and the like, they cannot steal away their vital essence.
As for the food and drink they consume, their minds are gentle and free from coarseness;
they always maintain thoughts of loving-kindness toward one another, flowing with purity and stainlessness.
Having renounced home and worldly affairs, dwell in an araṇya;
diligently cultivate the practices of bodhi so as to inspire faith in many sentient beings,
increase the assembly of Dharma friends, and cause the hosts of Māra to diminish.
"The four continents are abundant and joyful, and people fill every place.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, and the others, saying: "O Heavenly Kings!

When you saw or heard that at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, when Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and the others appeared in the world, how did they distribute and entrust all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth within this Jambudvīpa? Was it not done in the same manner as I have now, having first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, distributed and entrusted all these devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth within Jambudvīpa for their placement?
Having been asked thus, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of the Sahā World, and others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Bhagavān of Great Virtue!

We have seen and heard that at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, when Krakucchanda Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment beneath his Bodhi tree, he distributed and entrusted this Jambudvīpa to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others; this is no different from how the present World-Honored One, having first attained perfect enlightenment beneath his Bodhi tree, has likewise distributed and entrusted this Jambudvīpa to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others.

When that Buddha Krakucchanda appeared in the world, the lifespan of sentient beings was forty thousand years. At that time, the vital essence of the great earth, the vital essence of sentient beings, and the vital essence of the Dharma all attained preeminence; their flavor, their majesty, their virtue, their compassion, their excellence, and their wisdom all attained preeminence, and all such matters likewise reached a state of excellence.

At that time, all sentient beings who consume the fruits, flavors, various flowers, medicinal herbs, and so forth derived from the earth will attain a supple mind, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of equanimity, a mind of generosity, a mind of ethical discipline, a mind of patience, a mind of diligence, a mind of meditative concentration, a mind of wisdom, and a mind free from killing, up to and including a mind free from wrong views.

Having few desires and being content, they possess little defilement and affliction; possessing great merit and long life, they dwell in seclusion apart from desire. They love and delight in the True Dharma, loathe the cycle of transmigration, and cause the seeds of the Triple Gem to flourish.
By these causes and conditions, they shall be freed from the evil realms and proceed toward the good realms.
At that time, all beings, from the various devas down to the kāṭapūtanas and all birds and beasts, shall fully attain such matters as these.

Thereafter, sentient beings will be characterized by the decline of lifespan; because of the decline of lifespan, merit and virtue will decline; because of the decline of merit and virtue, the vital essence of the earth will decline; because of the decline of the vital essence of the earth, the vital energy of sentient beings will decline; because of the decline of the vital energy of sentient beings, the wholesome mental factors of shame and remorse will decline among sentient beings; and because of the decline of these wholesome mental factors of shame and remorse, the vital essence of the nectar of the True Dharma will decline.

Those sentient beings are said to have their lifespan diminished, and so forth, up to the point that the vital essence of the nectar of the True Dharma has been diminished; consequently, they extensively engage in killing and so forth, up to wrong views, and even among birds and beasts it is likewise so.
Thus, these sentient beings, having abandoned the path of virtue and the path to nirvana and instead heading toward the evil realms, are reborn within those evil realms after their lives end.

If such beings are born among the yakṣas, up to the kaṭapūtanas, they are full of malice and lack compassion; they do not regard the terrifying consequences of future lives and extensively commit acts ranging from killing to holding wrong views.
Those sentient beings in Jambudvīpa have not yet entered the stage of being entrusted with and protected by [the Dharma].

"In this same way, when Konākamuni Buddha and Kāśyapa Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, they distributed and entrusted this Jambudvīpa to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth; it is no different from how the present World-Honored One, having first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Tree of the Path, has likewise distributed and entrusted this Jambudvīpa to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth."

"In this way, as pure dharmas gradually diminish and dark dharmas increase, from that time forth, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of evil nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas have been born and multiplied. They are constantly wrathful and fierce, devoid of shame and remorse; they harbor no compassion for sentient beings, disregard the terrifying consequences of future lives, and take the lives of others to devour their flesh and blood."

They do not enter among the ranks of the ordained and have no fixed dwelling place; these evil nāgas and others do not protect humans or even animals, but constantly seek to seize the vital energy of humans and sever their life-faculties. They destroy kingdoms, cities, villages, monasteries, and other such places, causing kings to fall into anger and distress, and even bringing affliction to animals and the like.

Furthermore, there are untimely winds, rains, severe cold, and scorching heat that destroy all flowers, fruits, and crops; because such evil nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas, do not accept my teachings, I have no mastery over them. Consequently, in this present age of the five turbidities, the most extreme evils prevail and the white dharmas (pure qualities) decline.

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, all sentient beings develop reverence, faith, respect, and affection for their compassionate guide. The words spoken by the Buddha accord with their capacities and bring them benefit; he is a perfect mass of merit and wisdom who has realized great compassion."

In accordance with the six pāramitās, they bring their ultimate aspirations to fulfillment; they attain the six supernormal powers and achieve mastery over all dharmas; they provide protection and support for all sentient beings, and are able to bestow upon them all wholesome paths as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa.

Now, at this place, there has never before occurred, nor has it ever been heard of since time immemorial, such a great assembly as this, wherein all the celestial kings and their retinues have gathered; all the nāga kings, and even the sun kings, yakṣa kings, rākṣasa kings, asura kings, gandharva kings, kiṃnara kings, garuḍa kings, mahoraga kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, preta kings, and piśāca kings—all together with their retinues—have come to assemble here.
Regarding those who have not yet arrived, we now pray that the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, will gather them all completely.

Should there be various evil spirits and ghosts who are without allegiance, who do not accept the instructions of others, who are wrathful, cruel, and coarse, lacking any compassion, who disregard the terrifying consequences of future lives, and who harm the lives of others, drinking their blood and eating their flesh—[may they all be gathered].

As for those who have not yet arrived, we pray that the World-Honored One will again look upon them with compassion; by means of his supernormal powers, may he command those spirits and their retinues to come here, so that they may be distributed among other regions and no longer repeatedly harass sentient beings. By this expedient means, may the remaining essence of the great earth throughout the four continents not quickly perish, and may its vital energy remain stable and no longer diminish.
Because the vital essence of the earth is not diminished, the vital essence of sentient beings remains undiminished;
because the vital essence of sentient beings is not diminished, the vital essence of the nectar of the True Dharma remains undiminished;
because the vital essence of the nectar of the True Dharma is not diminished, the wholesome mental states of sentient beings increase equally.
By these causes and conditions, the lineage of the Triple Gem shall not be severed.
In this way and that way, the Eye of the Dharma will abide for a long time; the three evil realms will be closed, and the gates to the happy destinies and nirvana will be opened.
In this way, in this way, wholesome dharmas increase and unwholesome dharmas diminish.
In this way, in this way, devas and humans increase, and immeasurable devas and humans all obtain the abundant bliss of nirvāṇa.
When the Four Heavenly Kings and the others had spoken these words, the World-Honored One observed them and remained silent.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, Kauśika, the various Śakras, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings all joined their palms together and addressed the great assembly:

“We all address the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all śrāvakas, and all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and all others: we pray that you all entreat the Tathāgata, the Honored One of the Dharma, so that the World-Honored One may cause the hosts of devas to gather here, and likewise cause all the hosts of nāgas, up to and including all the kaṭapūtanas, to assemble as well.”

They shall distribute and entrust all the lands, cities, towns, villages, monasteries, gardens, groves, mountains, valleys, wildernesses, rivers, wells, springs, and ponds throughout Jambudvīpa—wherever beings dwell, stay, or reside—to all the various benevolent devas and nāgas, even down to the kaṭapūtanas, assigning them to take up residence therein. Each shall protect their respective domain with impartiality, neither neglecting nor abandoning it, and not causing distress. They shall each instruct those beings to practice the Dharma together, constantly cultivating wholesome thoughts and subduing evil intentions.
