Furthermore, they shall cause each to guard their own portion, neither being negligent nor causing harm to others.

"If each of you were to provide protection and support according to your respective shares with impartiality, your fame would spread far and wide, you would attain great valor, and you would obtain great merit and reward.

At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all the śrāvakas, and the entire assembly of those who had gathered—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and all others—rejoiced and leaped for joy. They rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and simultaneously spoke these words with one voice:

“We exhort the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: out of compassion for us and for the benefit of all sentient beings, may he arouse his great compassionate heart and cause all the devas, down to the kaṭapūtanas, to assemble here.”

Regarding those who dwell within this Jambudvīpa—in cities, villages, and even those who rely upon springs and ponds—he shall distribute and entrust them, commanding the devas, nāgas, and even the kaṭapūtanas to take possession of and settle them.

If those gods, down to the kaṭapūtanas and others, each abandon their own portion yet continue to cause affliction and harm, or do not restrain themselves from afflicting others, they should be punished and subdued.
"I pray that the Buddha will exert his vigor to perform great buddha-works, so that all may be distributed and established.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"In this Dharma of the Buddha, There is no principle of causing affliction to others."
Having crossed to the other shore of suffering, with a mind equanimous toward all realms,
seeing that all phenomena are non-dual, and having abandoned both aversion and attachment—
the Guide’s single path is like space; this is the realm of the Buddha.
"If there is a conditioned mind that contemplates past and future events, it can, through both the Dharma and non-Dharma, summon spirits and deities to appear.

At that time, there was another Great Brahmā named Right Discernment (*Samyak-vibhakti*), who dwelt in the tenth stage as a holy and unsurpassed saint; adorned with the merits of all bodhisattvas, he sat in the assembly.
The goddess Cunda addressed the various kings of the devas, all the nāga kings, all the asura kings, and even all the khaṭvāṅga-pūtana kings, saying:
"In this manner, you have now heard this meaning from the Tathāgata: just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, does not afflict sentient beings."
Now you all should simultaneously raise your voices in unison to make this aspiration and request:

"May all those non-humans—whether comprised among devas, nāgas, or spirits—who constantly consume vital energy and cause harm to others by eating flesh and drinking blood, be subdued by the power and majesty of the Four World-Protecting Kings.

Furthermore, may all those belonging to the four modes of birth—those born miraculously, from moisture, from the womb, or from eggs—including all classes of nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas—be likewise [subdued]."
They are all subdued by the power of the Four Great Heavenly Kings; may the Four Great Kings cause all those who have not yet come to gather here.
At that time, all the heavenly kings, down to the king of the Kāṭapūtanas, made this vow, saying:

"With the exception of those below the Heaven of the Thirty-three, may all those in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, as well as the hosts of nāgas, down to the Kāṭapūtanas and all others without exception who rely upon the four modes of birth, take refuge entirely in the Four Great Heavenly Kings."

Subdued by the power of those four kings, if there are any gods, or even as far as the kaṭapūtanas, who act in violation toward the Four Heavenly Kings—should they fail to obey the commands of each individual king’s power—their ears and noses shall be severed with a blazing iron wheel.
If they still persist in their defiance even after having their ears and noses cut off, he shall cause iron wheels to sever their hands and feet.
If they still persist in their defiance even after having their hands and feet severed, he shall further decapitate them.
"If there be anyone who violates even the commands and exhortations of the Four Heavenly Kings, I shall surely cause such a thing to happen.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa took a blazing, fiercely radiant iron wheel and hurled it toward the north from afar, and spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | kuṃkuṇi-lā-kuṃ-kha-pa-kuṃ | ka-ka-ga-ga | ni-ka-kha-ja-ra-cī | svāhā. At that time, King Virūpākṣa also took a blazing, fiercely radiant iron wheel and hurled it toward the west from afar.
He further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | Śirike | Śīlake | Gaganake | Śirike | Kṣīrake-ti | Śāri | Svāhā. At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka also took a fiercely blazing, radiant iron wheel and hurled it from afar toward the southern direction.
He then spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | Jarābhirīśa | Jarābhirīśa | Sītapa | Jarābhirīśa | Darasi | Jarājarā | Bhirīśa | Svāhā. At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also took a fiercely blazing, radiant iron wheel and hurled it from afar toward the eastern direction.
He then spoke the mantra:

"Tadyathā | Anaye anaya anaye | Anabuve akāśabuve | Makhidute | Svāhā. At that time, the devas of the four quarters, down to the kāṭapūtanas, as well as the deities of the various large and small forests and medicinal herbs, saw from afar the iron wheel blazing with fierce flames; they were all greatly terrified, filled with grief and distress, fearing for their very lives.
Having surveyed the ten directions, they each thought to themselves:
"Who is there capable of saving us? To whom may we go for refuge, who might grant us our lives?

They then beheld the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, who truly benefits all sentient beings, dwelling upon Mount Kālaṃjara as the abode of the sages and seers, surrounded and seated amidst a great assembly.
"Only he can save our lives. They immediately went to where the Buddha was, arriving before him as swiftly as a flash of lightning and standing there.
In this manner, all the devas of the ten directions, down to the *kāṭapūtanas* and others, all went to where the Buddha was and, having arrived, stood there.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"At that time, I, the Honored One among two-legged beings, Questioned Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings:
'Have you seen or heard of those Past Guides?'"
Distributing [the teachings] throughout the four continents in order to cause the devas and others to protect them—would it not be as I do now, distributing [them] beneath the tree of enlightenment?
The Heavenly King answered me, saying: "In this same way, the Buddhas of the past,"
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he shared [his merit] with the yakṣas and others;
later, when the time passed, various mixed evils were produced:
kumbhāṇḍas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
Fierce and devoid of compassion, they constantly devour the flesh and blood of others;
they afflict the various kingdoms as well as the people of the four castes,
bringing untimely winds and rains, as well as cold and heat.
Famine, disease, and strife shall destroy the very essence of the great earth;
lacking compassion for all, they will afflict and harm many sentient beings.
There will be none able to protect them, nor will they submit to us.
Therefore, the vital essence of the earth and the vital essence of sentient beings have vanished;
the wondrous vital essence of the True Dharma, so difficult to obtain, is daily diminished.
Because the conditions of the times have passed, gods and humans alike are decaying.
As all evil worlds increase, friends of the Dharma will be difficult to find;
the Dharma will not long remain in the world, and the lamp of the True Dharma will be extinguished.
The seeds of the Triple Gem will be severed, and the world shall fall into blinding darkness.
Now the Buddha, the Great Hero, appearing in Jambudvīpa at the time when the white dharmas were fading away,
is the medicine for sentient beings through his great compassion;
his central teaching possesses the six supernormal powers, and he has thoroughly realized the further shore of all phenomena.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this great assembly has been convened.
All the devas, nāga kings, world-protectors, and others have gathered here;
yet there are various ghosts who are cruel and devoid of compassion, constantly devouring the flesh and blood of others.
Nāgas, ghosts, and pūtanas—may they not come here;
having no one to receive their commands, they shall not be subject to another’s authority.
May all who accept the Buddha’s word cause them to assemble here.
May they share [their power] with those beings, each entrusting them so that no further harm or affliction may occur; may they not seize the vital essence of others,
but rather abide in the three kinds of vital essence, causing people to practice the Dharma.
Wholesome qualities increase, and unwholesome qualities are extinguished;
thereby the evil realms are stilled, and gods and humans attain growth.
The gates of liberation open, and the lineage of the Triple Gem flourishes.
May the stream of merit flow to all sentient beings, so that they may swiftly attain liberation.
At that time, I remained silent and did not comply with them—
the Brahma kings, the Śakras, and the four world-protecting kings.
They addressed the entire assembly, all those gathered in the congregation,
entreating the Teacher of Gods and Humans: "Please summon the various spirits here,
and distribute them among these cities, towns, and villages."
Day and night they shall constantly protect and uphold [the teachings], each remaining steadfast in their own domain.
The great assembly of Bodhisattvas and others rose from their seats, joined their palms, and entreated the Great Teacher: "Please summon all the spirits to come here."
Dividing all things into their constituent parts, protect Jambudvīpa;
do not afflict sentient beings, but rouse your courage as the supreme among men.
I shall not disturb others, remaining far removed from the affairs of coming and going.
Realizing that phenomena are non-dual, he is free from all notions of sentient beings.
The Great Brahmā King, in his correct discourse, addressed the various heavenly kings, saying:
"The Teacher does not afflict others; such a thing does not exist within the Buddha's Dharma."
They all together made this vow: "May the spirits not cause harm;
may we each take refuge separately in those Four Heavenly Kings.
The kings spoke these words: "We now rely upon your words."
I issue this solemn command to them, that they shall all be granted their share.
If they do not comply with these instructions, they shall swiftly be consumed by the wheel.
At that time, the Four Great Kings shall cause the wheel to turn toward the four directions.
In a mere instant, they all arrived at the place where the Buddha was;
prostrating at the feet of the World-Honored One, they stood there with palms joined.
(Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 49)
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Fifty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Part Fourteen of the Candragarbha-parivarta: Chapter Eight, "How All Malevolent Ghosts and Spirits Attain Reverent Faith. Chapter Eight: How All Malevolent Ghosts and Spirits Attain Reverent Faith.

The Eighth, Part One. At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who Guard the World saw immeasurable asaṃkhyeya numbers of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas, all possessing various colors, various forms, various desires, various conducts, and various dispositions.

They lack compassion for the nature of sentient beings; they are hateful, evil, and coarse. Disregarding the terrors of future lives, they do not enter into the domains of others nor provide them with protection. They repeatedly afflict those from the kṣatriya class down to animals, robbing them of their vital essence and devouring their flesh and blood.
When all these spirits and deities had assembled together, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; each then questioned the great general under his command.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa asked the yakṣa general Saṃjñeya:

"Do all the yakṣas within these four continents—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether dwelling in cities, villages, houses, stūpas, temples, gardens, forests, mountain valleys, rivers, wells, springs, ponds, among graves, beneath trees, in wildernesses, fields, secluded groves, empty dwellings, the great ocean, or on jewel islands; whether they travel on land, by water, or through the air—all of them without exception now gathered at the place where the World-Honored One resides?"
The Great General Vaiśravaṇa said: "Great King!

All the yakṣas within these four continents, even those on the jewel-islands of the great ocean—whether they travel by land, by water, or through the air—all have gathered here without exception at the presence of the World-Honored One."
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked the Gandharva General Rucirakāma:
"Regarding all the gandharvas within these four continents, the rest is as previously described."
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka asked the Great General Dantī Kumbhāṇḍa:
"Regarding all the kumbhāṇḍas within these four continents, the rest is as previously described."
The Deva King Virūpākṣa asked the Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita:

"Have all the nāgas, mahoragas, garuḍas, and pretas within these four continents—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether dwelling in cities, villages, or houses, or even in the great ocean and jewel islands; whether moving on land, in water, or through the air—all of them without exception now gathered at the place where the World-Honored One resides?"
The Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita said: "Great King!
All the nāgas within these four continents, down to the hungry ghosts, have now gathered here before the World-Honored One without exception."

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of the Sahā World, and Brahmā Saṃjñeya joined their palms toward the Buddha, paid homage with single-minded devotion, and spoke these words:
“O Bhagavān of Great Virtue!

All the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, mahoragas, garuḍas, and various hungry ghosts within these four continents—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether moving on land, in water, or through the air—all without exception have now gathered together in the presence of the World-Honored One.

We, having received the exhortations and requests of these great wise ones, beseech the Tathāgata: May the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us and all sentient beings, cause evil beings to attain respectful faith; so that the Eye of the True Dharma may abide for a long time; so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may be sustained without interruption; so that the vital essence of the earth, the vital essence of sentient beings, and the vital essence of the True Dharma may long endure and increase; and furthermore, so that the paths of the good realms, the path to Nirvāṇa, and the Eightfold Noble Path shall never perish but always flourish.
“World-Honored One!

All cities, towns, villages, and residences within this Jambudvīpa, even down to the jewel islands—without exception—you should distribute and entrust these to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even the kāṭapūtanas according to what is appropriate for each, so that they may protect and uphold them.”

Now, all these great assemblies of the kings of devas, the kings of nāgas, and even the kings of piśācas, each leading their retinues, have all gathered here; I entrust them all to you, so that you may instruct, remind, and sustain them, causing them to practice this Dharma together.

Command all those devas, down to the kaṭapūtanas, each to protect and nurture their respective domains; do not abandon yourselves to negligence, nor cause harm to others; and should you see anyone harming others, ensure they are restrained and protected, so that no one is abandoned to such acts.

He causes each of them to exert great courage and strength to provide proper protection and nurture; if they exert great courage and strength, they should give rise to joy, for they will then find delight, their fame will spread, and they will obtain great rewards of merit.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted their exhortation; out of compassion and pity for those multitudes, he surveyed the entire assembly of those who had come and raised his right arm, saying:
"O you virtuous ones, entire assembly!
Each of you listen attentively; I shall now explain.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; escaping the eight difficulties is as rare as the seasonal sandalwood tree;
hearing the True Dharma is as rare as rain falling upon Jambūnada gold; and encountering the Sangha of precept-keepers and concentration-attainers to offer them support is as rare as [reaching]...
To attain pure faith in the Triple Gem within the great ocean of the jewel-island is as difficult as seeking a wish-fulfilling gem;
to encounter the Triple Gem is as difficult as finding the goddess Puṇyavatī with her auspicious vase;
to uphold the precepts is as difficult as reaching the island of Gośīrṣa-candana; and to give rise to compassion for sentient beings is as difficult as encountering [such a rare opportunity].
When a valiant enemy wielding a vajra makes it difficult to escape, one must protect one's life;
yet, contentment is as rare as the *aśvamedha* sacrifice. Here, *aśva* means "horse," *medha* means "sacrificial pillar," and *yajña* means "offering."
Only a king of Jambudvīpa is capable of performing this sacrifice. "O noble leaders!

There are ten kinds of equality; if sentient beings possess this equality, they will constantly receive superior retribution during the cycle of transmigration and will swiftly be able to enter the great city of fearlessness."
What are the ten? First, the equality of sentient beings;
second, the equality of dharmas.
Third, the equality of purity;
fourth, the equality of giving;
fifth, the equality of ethical discipline;
Sixth, the equality of patience;
seventh, the equality of diligence;
eighth, the equality of meditative concentration;
Ninth, the equality of wisdom;
tenth, the purity and equality of all phenomena. "O virtuous ones!
In that regard, what is the equality of sentient beings?
"Sentient beings" refers to all sentient beings within the three realms.
If there are sentient beings who cherish their own bodies, desiring to remain alive, seeking happiness, and wishing to be free from suffering, they should train themselves in this way:
If there is a person who, as a living being, performs actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—by doing them themselves or by instructing others, they will visibly experience the retribution thereof.
Therefore, O worthy ones, if you seek happiness and wish to leave suffering behind, you should act in this way:

through body, speech, and mind, perform all kinds of wholesome deeds and refrain from unwholesome deeds; whether in this life or in future lives, benefit yourselves and others, cultivate goodness for yourself and for others, and do not commit unwholesome acts.
"Virtuous ones, this is called the equality of sentient beings.
Virtuous ones, what therein is the equality of phenomena?"

Regarding the Dharma: if there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to leave suffering behind, who rejoice in life and fear death, and who desire never to be parted from those they love nor encounter those they detest—such people are submerged in the ocean of the human mind.
Why is this? Because if there are sentient beings who cling to a self, they will transmigrate through birth and death, failing to see the pure path of liberation.

Therefore, one should contemplate and observe the equality of all phenomena: there is no phenomenon apart from sentient beings, and no sentient beings apart from phenomena. Just as the essential nature of sentient beings is the essential nature of the self, so the essential nature of the self is the essential nature of all phenomena; and just as the essential nature of all phenomena is the essential nature of the Buddha-dharma.

When observing all phenomena as equal in this way, sentient beings cannot be found within the aggregates (*skandha*), nor can they be found apart from the aggregates; they cannot be found as a combination, nor can they be found apart from the combination; they are neither phenomena (*dharma*) nor non-phenomena.
When such a person thus abides in the signless, this is called the equality of dharmas.
"O virtuous ones! Among those, what is the purity of equality?"
It means to have attained a human body endowed with ten complete virtues. What are these ten?
First, being born away from low and base families;
Second, not being dull-witted;
third, not being mute;
fourth, having no deficiency in the sense faculties.
Fifth, one obtains a male body;
sixth, one’s countenance is upright and handsome;
seventh, one acquires excellent kinsmen and associates.
Eighth, one will not be poor;
ninth, one will not be deceived by others and one’s speech will be meaningful;
tenth, many people will look up to one with reverence.
"Why is it said that obtaining a human body is called 'pure equality'?

Because by obtaining a human body, one attains the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), leaves the three evil destinies behind, and is able to seek the three vehicles and the three kinds of enlightenment, attaining them as they correspond."

What is pure equality? If a person can attain bodhi, their mind has no dependence upon any phenomena; their mind has no dependence upon any internal or external objects. Such a person does not rely upon any phenomena.

In suchness, there is nothing to be grasped; seeing all phenomena, one does not grasp at the internal mind nor grasp at the external mind, attaining profound tranquility and concentration regarding these two spheres.

When this person thus perceives the purity of the Dharma through right view, they do not perceive, either internally or externally, any sentient being, life-principle, soul, living being, person, individual, nourisher, sustainer, agent, instigator of action, originator, instigator of origination, experiencer, instigator of experience, knower, or seer.

In this way, such a person perceives the pure equality of non-self among all sentient beings; being without a sentient being, without a life-principle, and without a self, they are free from desire and pure, and do not give rise to extreme views. Thus they enter into the pure equality of sentient beings; thus they enter into the seal of the wisdom of emptiness, non-action, signlessness, and wishlessness regarding all phenomena; thus they enter into the pure equality of sentient beings.
This person matures sentient beings through those dharmas without destroying the self, nor does he destroy phenomena or wealth.
If one knows that the essential nature of all sentient beings is equal, then one knows the essential nature of all dharmas.
If the essential nature of all phenomena is itself the essential nature of the Buddha-dharma, this is called the equality of all phenomena with the Buddha-dharma; this is called pure equality.
"O worthy ones! Among those, what is the purity and equality of giving?
O worthy ones!"
Through the purity and equality of the four kinds of giving,
by means of such generosity, sentient beings constantly receive superior retributions during their journey through saṃsāra and are swiftly able to enter the great city of fearlessness.
What are the four?
First, giving rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings;
second, a mind of equanimity.
Third, the mind of great loving-kindness;
fourth, the mind of great compassion.

These constitute the four kinds of pure and equal giving, through which sentient beings constantly receive superior retribution during their wandering in saṃsāra and are swiftly able to enter the great city of fearlessness.
"O virtuous ones! What is that pure equanimity which arises toward all sentient beings?

If there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to be free from suffering, who desire not to be separated from those they love and not to encounter those they hate, and who wish to obtain long life, gain, fame, wealth, and the five sensory pleasures, they should train themselves in this way: [as follows...]"
Just as I cherish and value my own body and life with no sense of satiety, protecting them through every possible means in a manner that is unsurpassed and beyond measure;

so too do I cherish and value the body and life of every single sentient being, down to the smallest insect or ant, with no sense of satiety, protecting them through every possible means in a manner that is unsurpassed and beyond measure.
Why should I cause affliction or harm to other sentient beings or other living beings, deprive them of the necessities of life, sever their life-faculties, or destroy their life-faculties?

If I were to cause harm or deprive another sentient being, another living soul, of their life, then for each individual life taken, I shall, for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, undergo the suffering of being deprived of life myself in every successive birth.

From this day forward, toward all sentient beings, I shall conceive of them as my parents and as my sons and daughters; even toward insects and ants, I shall conceive of them as my parents and as my sons and daughters. I shall no longer harm or injure the lives of others, nor shall I seize the means by which others sustain their lives, nor shall I deprive them of life. Furthermore, I shall not instruct others to rob them of their vital energy or to sever their life-faculties. Thus, as I transmigrate through birth and death for hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas, and in every lifetime when I receive a body and life, there shall be none who can harm me, seize my means of livelihood, or deprive me of life.
Why is this? Because among all sentient beings, there is none who has not been my father, mother, brother, son, daughter, or the like.

Just as I have not failed to be their father, mother, brother, son, daughter, or the like toward all sentient beings, for this reason, I have been intimate with all sentient beings, and all sentient beings have been intimate with me. If I were to give rise to affliction toward those who have been intimate, it would be improper.

"Regarding what is called 'affliction': if I were to afflict a kṣatriya, I would cause that kṣatriya to lack contentment regarding his own realm, territory, and subjects; and likewise for brahmins, down to animals, I would afflict their minds so that they know no satisfaction."
For these reasons, they engage in mutual combat, contentious debate, slander, litigation, flattery, deception, and lying; they dismember one another and even sever the life-faculty.
Therefore, I now cease from harming and taking the life-force of all sentient beings.

By virtue of this cause and condition of pure and impartial giving, while wandering through the cycle of existence, no one shall be able to harm me, nor engage in combat, dispute, revilement, litigation, flattery, deception, lying, dismemberment, or the taking of my life; these are what constitute "harming."
"In that regard, what is the taking of life?
He should train himself thus:
'All sentient beings are my kin; I am the kin of all sentient beings.'"
If I were to take the life of a living being, that would be improper.

If I were to cause untimely winds and rains, droughts, calamitous hailstorms, rains of dust, darkness, or the drying up of all waters; if I were to diminish the flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and various flavors—by these causes and conditions, sentient beings would suffer from hunger and thirst, the four elements would become disturbed, giving rise to various diseases, and because of those diseases, they would meet their end.
Therefore, I have desisted from taking the lives of all sentient beings; because of this desistance, the vital essence of the earth no longer vanishes.

By these causes and conditions, I cause all sentient beings to be free from hunger and thirst, their four elements remain stable, no diseases arise, and they do not meet their end through those causes.
"By means of this pure and impartial generosity, even while transmigrating through the cycle of existence, may I never again suffer from hunger, thirst, or illness"—this is called taking life.
"In that regard, what are the requisites for sustaining life?
As for those things by which one sustains body and life, one should train as follows:
'All sentient beings are my kin, and I am the kin of all sentient beings.'"
If I were to deprive them of their means of sustaining life, that would be improper.

If I were to take away from sentient beings the essence of flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and the five grains—the very means by which they sustain their lives—then I would cause those sentient beings to consume inferior flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and the essences of the various grains. This would cause their bodies and minds to become emaciated, weak, and forgetful; it would make them prone to anger and malice, fickle and coarse, with an ugly complexion and many ailments.

Therefore, following the instructions of the celestial seers of the past, from each of the sixty-four portions of the vital essence of flowers, fruits, and various delicacies, I shall take one portion of that essence to sustain my own life, while leaving the remaining sixty-three portions to sustain all sentient beings and allow them to experience peace and happiness.

By virtue of this cause and condition of contentment, even throughout the course of saṃsāra, I shall no longer consume food that lacks essential flavor, lacks vital energy, or is harmful; I shall possess great power, a retentive memory, a gentle heart, a fine complexion, and freedom from disease—these are called the requisites for sustaining life.
"In this regard, what is the severance of life?

If one looks upon sentient beings with an evil mind, breathing upon their bodies and distracting their minds, one seizes their vital essence joint by joint. Because of seizing their vital essence, one causes their body and mind to be afflicted by suffering.
One should train thus: 'I am kin to all sentient beings; even this [evil] is not appropriate for me.'"

If I were to look upon my relative with an evil mind, breathe upon their body, distract their mind, or seize the vital energy from their limbs and joints, it would cause suffering to arise in the body and mind of my relative.

By these causes and conditions, even during the time of transmigration, no non-human being will look upon me with an evil mind, nor will they breathe upon my body or distract my mind; they shall not seize my vital essence—this is called "separation from death."
"In that regard, what constitutes the destruction of life?

It is when sentient beings, for the sake of their own food, cut off limbs and joints and completely rob them of their vital energy; or push them to fall from high mountains, trees, or deep waters and great rivers; or administer poison; or employ *vetāla* (reanimated corpses)."

If one performs sorcery of loathing or other harmful acts, such as cutting off food and drink, or severing the head to terminate the life-faculty—due to these causes and conditions, if you love yourselves and desire long life, seek happiness and avoid suffering, seek renown, wealth, and honor, and seek liberation, you should train yourselves thus:
"I am kin to all sentient beings; all sentient beings are kin to me."
If, for the sake of my own food, I were to seize their vital energy, sever their limbs, or even decapitate them, that would be improper.
By virtue of this cause and condition, throughout the course of saṃsāra, no one will be able to decapitate me or destroy my life; this is what is called "destroying life," and it is pure and equal.
"O virtuous ones!

If you further wish to have compassion for all sentient beings, you should, for their sake, accumulate merit and wisdom, sever all false and illusory views, and attain firm and courageous resolve to seek all that is wholesome, practicing according to the teachings."

For the sake of the conditions of life, one should not give rise to evil thoughts toward other sentient beings, nor harbor a harmful mind toward any sentient being; one should share the precepts one upholds with all sentient beings and feel profound joy upon seeing sentient beings find happiness.
Regarding one's own happiness, one is naturally able to be content with its conditions; there is nothing among all objects of affection that one cannot relinquish.

One has no sense of stinginess regarding any phenomena, is constantly fearful of the triple world, possesses the strength and capacity to endure all matters requiring patience, and, believing in the characteristic of impermanence, is able to practice according to the teaching.
One is able to observe one's own faults and, upon seeing the faults of others, gives rise to compassion.
One never tires of wholesome dharmas, constantly confesses and repents, attains boundless dedication, and is able to seek the profound Dharma.
Regarding all sentient beings, they cultivate the mind of a field of merit and seek the wisdom of wearying detachment.

They are able to feel dread toward the afflictions that cause wandering within the prison of the triple world; they diligently alleviate all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings; they are able to seek all Buddha-dharmas; they are able to give rise to the mind that brings rest to all evil realms; and they are well-established in all dharmas.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the worldly purity and equality.
O virtuous ones!"
"I shall now proclaim the ultimate truth of pure equality.
Having spoken these words, he immediately uttered this mantra:

"Tadyathā | jyāme jyāme | prākṣyāme | utpala-kṣyāme | jayāme kṣayāye kṣaye | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being taught, eight million six hundred thousand kiṃnaras, gandharvas, and others were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | gokhale | nyapokhale | upanyapokhale | svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | dhāraṇidhāraṇi | upadhāraṇi | dhāraṇidhāraṇi | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being taught, ninety-four million yakṣas were distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | Ajaṇe | Cakṣajaṇe | Gajakṣajaṇe | Maurājaṇe | Caca svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was spoken, seventy million nāgas attained the samādhi of being free from dust and defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | haha haha haha haha | kiyūba | haha ha | śiyo śiyo śiyo | haha ha | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being spoken, three million nayutas of asuras attained the samādhi of the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | Anuna | Anapuna | Apānanuna | Apārīṇya | Apānanuna | Svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was spoken, eighty-four thousand *bimbara* of *kumbhāṇḍas* attained the Samādhi of Joyful Delight.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | dhagadhaja | avadhagadhaja | avagadhajaja | gandhagandhaja | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being taught, seven million nayutas of hungry ghosts, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas attained the Vidyutpatisamādhi;
and countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas who had never before resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, all now resolved their minds upon it.
"O worthy ones! This is called the purity and equality of the ultimate gift. O worthy ones!"
In this regard, what is the equality of the purity of ethical discipline?

Whether it be the wholesome paths of the mundane world or the supramundane, or the bliss of nirvāṇa, ethical discipline is their root; it enables one to abide on the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and it enables one to abide in the wisdom of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This purity and equality of precepts consists of the so-called ten paths of wholesome action:
abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
"O virtuous ones! By refraining from taking life, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, attaining fearlessness toward all sentient beings;
second, attaining a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
third, severing evil habitual tendencies.
Fourth, one has few illnesses or afflictions and is capable of making decisive judgments;
fifth, one attains a long life span;
sixth, one is protected and sustained by non-human beings.
Seventh, they shall be peaceful and secure in both waking and sleeping, free from all evil dreams;
eighth, they shall have no enemies or adversaries;
ninth, they shall have no fear of the evil realms.
Tenth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one will be reborn in a happy destination.
O virtuous ones!
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained by refraining from taking life.
If one can dedicate the roots of goodness from this abstention from killing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that person will before long realize unsurpassed wisdom.
When that person attains enlightenment, in that land, long-lived beings who are free from all weapons and harm will come to be born in that country.
"By refraining from stealing, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, to possess great karmic fruition as the basis for decisive action;
second, to not share one's wealth and possessions with others.
Third, he does not share [his wealth] with the five types of families;
fourth, he is loved and respected by the multitude such that they never tire of him;
fifth, as he travels through various regions, he encounters no obstacles or hindrances.
Sixth, they are fearless in coming and going;
seventh, they give with joy;
eighth, they naturally and swiftly obtain wealth and treasures without seeking them.
Ninth, one’s acquired wealth shall not be dissipated;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one shall be reborn in a happy destination.
O virtuous ones!
This is called obtaining ten kinds of merit by ceasing from stealing.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from ceasing stealing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom.

When that person attains enlightenment, in that land there will be an abundance of various flowers, fruits, groves, garments, necklaces, and ornaments of adornment; it will be filled with every kind of rare and precious treasure.
"By abstaining from sexual misconduct, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, one attains the restraint of the sense faculties and achieves decisiveness in one's undertakings."
Second, one abides in the purity of detachment from desire;
third, one does not afflict others;
fourth, one is cherished and delighted by all people.
Fifth, being pleasing for all people to behold;
sixth, being able to arouse diligent effort;
seventh, seeing the faults of birth and death.
Eighth, they always delight in practicing generosity;
ninth, they always delight in seeking the Dharma;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they attain rebirth in a favorable realm.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the ten kinds of merit obtained by abstaining from sexual misconduct.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from abstaining from sexual misconduct toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, such a person will before long attain supreme wisdom."
When that person attains enlightenment, there will be no foul odors in that land, nor will there be female organs or the practice of sexual desire; all beings shall be born through transformation.
"By refraining from false speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, all people will guarantee that whatever one says shall be believed."
Second, in all places, even among the devas, his speech attains the middle way;
third, his mouth emits a fragrance like that of the utpala flower;
fourth, he alone acts as the witness among humans and devas.
Fifth, he is loved and respected by all people and is free from all doubts;
sixth, he always speaks words of truth;
seventh, his mind and intentions are pure.
Eighth, they are always free from deceit, and their speech is invariably appropriate to the occasion;
ninth, they are constantly full of joy;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they attain rebirth in a happy realm.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the ten kinds of merit obtained by resting from false speech.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting from false speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom."
When that person attains enlightenment, there shall be no foul odors in that land; it will be constantly filled with the fragrances of various exquisite jewels.
"By refraining from divisive speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, the equality of the indestructibility of the body;
second, the equality of the indestructibility of one's retinue;
Third, the unbreakable equality of spiritual friends;
fourth, the unbreakable equality of faith;
fifth, the unbreakable equality of the Dharma.
Sixth, the equality of unimpaired dignified conduct;
seventh, the equality of unimpaired śamatha;
eighth, the equality of unimpaired samādhi.
Ninth, patience that does not destroy equanimity;
tenth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one attains rebirth in a good realm.
O virtuous ones!
This is called resting from divisive speech and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting from divisive speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom.
"When that person attains enlightenment, all their retinues in that land shall be indestructible by any Māras, adversaries, or hostile factions.
By ceasing harsh speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, attaining gentle speech;
second, swift and sharp speech;
Third, speech that accords with reason;
fourth, speech that is beautiful and refined;
fifth, speech that invariably hits the mark.
Sixth, straightforward speech;
seventh, fearless speech;
eighth, speech that does not dare to be arrogant or contemptuous;
Ninth, their speech regarding the Dharma is pure and eloquent;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, they attain rebirth in a favorable realm.
O virtuous ones!
This is called the ten kinds of merit obtained by ceasing harsh speech.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from ceasing harsh speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this person will before long attain supreme wisdom.
When that person attains enlightenment, the sound of the Dharma will pervade their land, free from all harsh speech.
By refraining from frivolous speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
What are the ten? First, being loved and respected by devas and humans;
second, being rejoiced in by the wise.
Third, they always delight in reality;
fourth, they are not resented by wise people and dwell with them without separation;
fifth, they are able to comprehend what they hear when it is spoken.
Sixth, they will always be respected and loved;
seventh, they will always delight in dwelling in araṇya hermitages;
eighth, they will delight in the silent composure of the noble ones.
Ninth, to distance oneself from evil persons and draw near to the noble and holy;
tenth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, to attain rebirth in a favorable realm.
O virtuous ones!
This is called resting from frivolous speech and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting from frivolous speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom.

When that person attains enlightenment, sentient beings who are upright and handsome will be born in that land; they will possess strong memory and non-forgetfulness, and will delight in dwelling apart from desire.
“Resting from sensual desire yields ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, one’s physical faculties will be unimpaired;”
Second, purity of verbal action;
third, non-distraction of the mind;
fourth, attainment of superior karmic fruition.
Fifth, one attains great wealth and nobility;
sixth, all people delight in beholding one;
seventh, the karmic retribution of one's retinue cannot be destroyed.
Eighth, one will always associate with wise people;
ninth, one will never be separated from the sound of the Dharma;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one will be reborn in a favorable realm.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the ten kinds of merit obtained by resting from sensual desire.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting from sensual desire toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain supreme wisdom."
When that person attains enlightenment, they will be free from the enmity of Māra and all non-Buddhist paths in that land.
By ceasing anger, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
What are the ten? First, being free from all anger;
second, delighting in not accumulating wealth.
Third, being delighted in by the multitude of noble ones;
fourth, constantly meeting with sages and saints;
fifth, attaining matters of benefit.
Sixth, his countenance is upright and handsome;
seventh, he gives rise to joy upon seeing sentient beings happy;
eighth, he attains samādhi.
Ninth, one attains a luster and pliancy of body, speech, and mind;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in a happy realm.
O virtuous ones!
This is called obtaining ten kinds of merit by resting from anger.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting from anger toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom.
When that person attains enlightenment, all sentient beings in that land will attain samādhi; those who are born in that land will have minds that are utterly pure.
"By resting from wrong views, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, a mind-nature that is gentle and virtuous, with companions who are noble and good;
second, having faith in the retribution of karma such that one does not give rise to any evil—even at the cost of one's life.
Third, they respectfully believe in the Triple Gem and, even for the sake of their livelihood, do not believe in celestial deities;
fourth, they attain right view and do not marvel at strange occurrences, nor do they select auspicious days or favorable times;
fifth, they are constantly reborn among humans or devas, remaining far removed from all evil realms.
Sixth, they always delight in merit and virtue, being praised by wise people;
seventh, they discard worldly etiquette and constantly seek the noble path;
eighth, they abandon the views of annihilationism and eternalism and enter into the dharma of dependent origination.
Ninth, one will always encounter those who have correctly entered the path and correctly resolved their minds;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one will be reborn in a happy realm.
O virtuous ones!
This is called resting from wrong views and attaining ten kinds of merit.

If one can dedicate these roots of goodness from resting in wrong views toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that person will swiftly fulfill the six *pāramitās* and attain perfect enlightenment in a pure and sublime Buddha-land.

Having attained bodhi, sentient beings adorned with all roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom will come to be born in that buddha-field; they will not believe in celestial deities and will be free from the fear of the evil realms, and when their lives there end, they will return to birth in the good realms.
"O virtuous ones!

When one practices the pure equality of giving, and when one observes the precept of abstaining from taking life and cultivates the practice of equality, one possesses the great, pure, and equal fruit of retribution, attaining long life and freedom from all fears."

"When he practices the pure and impartial giving of alms, he refrains from stealing within the precepts and cultivates impartial conduct; he possesses the great, pure, and impartial fruit of retribution, which is not shared with others, and he cultivates all virtues without hindrance."

"When he practices the pure and impartial giving of alms, he refrains from sexual misconduct regarding the precepts and cultivates impartial conduct, thereby possessing the great, pure, and impartial fruit of retribution; he cultivates roots of goodness without hindrance, and free from thoughts of sexual misconduct, he regards the wives of others as his own."

"When he practices the pure and impartial giving of alms, he refrains from false speech within the precepts and cultivates impartial conduct; he possesses the great, pure, and impartial fruit of retribution, is not subject to slander, and his resolve is firm as he practices according to his word. Among gods and humans, he alone acts as a witness, and his mouth emits a fragrance like that of the *utpala* flower."

"When he practices giving with pure equanimity, he refrains from divisive speech regarding ethical discipline and cultivates the practice of equanimity; possessing the great, pure fruit of equanimity, he obtains an indestructible retinue, a retinue of noble men, and a retinue of those who possess respectful faith."
"When he practices the pure and impartial giving of alms, he rests from harsh speech within the precepts and cultivates impartial conduct; thus he attains a sublime voice and hears no evil sounds."

"When he practices the pure and impartial giving of alms, he refrains from frivolous speech within the precepts and cultivates impartial conduct; possessing the great, pure, and impartial fruit of retribution, his speech is moderate, he cuts through all doubts, and sentient beings delight in seeing him."

"When he practices giving with pure equanimity, he rests from transgressions regarding the precepts and cultivates the practice of equanimity; he possesses the great, pure fruit of equanimity, and having received that fruit, he is again able to relinquish it, attaining the fruit of liberation and possessing great power."

"When he practices giving with pure equanimity, he rests from transgressions regarding the precepts and cultivates the practice of equanimity toward anger; he possesses the great fruit of pure equanimity: his countenance is upright and handsome, he is loved and respected by all, he is unimpeded in his affairs, and his faculties are complete."

"When that person practices giving with pure equanimity, they rest from [transgressions of] precepts, abandon wrong views, and cultivate the practice of equanimity; they possess the great, pure fruit of equanimity, are born in a land of right view and a family of right view, and constantly encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Saṅgha."
Cultivating the practices of awakening, one never abandons pure equanimity.
"O virtuous ones! This is the purity and equanimity of ethical discipline."

Those who adorn themselves with this purity and equanimity of precepts will, before long, attain the merit of Buddhahood; they will be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks and possess pure vocal qualities, subduing all demonic adversaries and attaining purity and equanimity.

Before long, this person will attain all Buddha-dharmas—pure meditation, mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct, as well as great knowledge, great kindness, and great compassion—and even be able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas in pure equality; this is called the stage of pure equality in worldly ethical conduct.
"O noble ones! What therein is the state of purity and equality of supramundane ethical conduct?

It is when one who practices with faith and resolve in the perfection of ethical conduct does not maintain that precept by relying on the aggregate of form; does not maintain it by relying on the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not rely on the eye, nor on forms, nor on eye-consciousness, nor on eye-contact, nor on the feelings, craving, grasping, becoming, and birth produced through the condition of eye-contact; and so on, up to not maintaining it by relying on the mind, nor on phenomena, nor on mind-consciousness, nor on mind-contact, nor on the feelings, craving, grasping, becoming, and birth produced through the condition of mind-contact."

One does not maintain the precepts by relying on the earth element; one does not maintain the precepts by relying on the water, fire, or wind elements; one does not maintain the precepts by relying on the sphere of infinite space, and so on, up to not maintaining the precepts by relying on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One maintains the precepts without relying on the realm of desire or the realm of form; one maintains the precepts without relying on this life or future lives; one maintains the precepts without relying on the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); one maintains the precepts without relying on hearing, without relying on dhyāna, and without relying on wisdom (*jñāna*). One maintains the precepts without relying on the power of listening, the power of samādhi, the power of dhāraṇī, the power of patience (*kṣānti*), the power of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) states, the power of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states, the power of the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), the power of the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), the power of the wholesome or the unwholesome, and the power of light or darkness.
"O virtuous ones!

This is called the supramundane purity and equality of the precepts; this is called the holy path of the Brahma-faring cultivation of the precepts, which can lead one into the great city of unsurpassed fearlessness. It is the purity and equality of the precepts upon which all sages rely; because it protects the ultimate purity of the precepts, one is able to enter pure wisdom."
"What is the meaning of 'precept' (śīla)?

It is, for example, like the winds of scorching affliction between the Great Iron Ring Mountains and the Vajra Mountains; because these mountains act as a barrier, they prevent those winds from reaching the four continents."

Thus, one trains in the noble, pure, and equal precepts; because the wind of the heat of craving is stilled through the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, it is for this reason that they are called "precepts" (śīla).
For example, just as the foul and stinking winds between the great Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are prevented from reaching the four continents by the barrier of those mountains,
so too is the pure and impartial precept that protects the noble ones.
Because of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), one prevents the arising of the foul stench of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*); for this reason, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).
It is like the darkness between the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*Mahācakravāḍa*): because of the obstruction of the mountains, [the light] cannot reach the four continents (*caturdvīpa*).

Thus, by guarding the holy, pure, and impartial precepts, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment through the characteristics of ignorance, conditioned phenomena, and outflows, so that they do not arise; for this reason, it is called "precept" (śīla).

The meaning of detachment is the meaning of precepts; the meaning of liberation is the meaning of precepts; the meaning of cessation is the meaning of precepts; the meaning of inexhaustibility is the meaning of precepts; the meaning of extinction is the meaning of precepts—these various meanings of the terms are called the meaning of precepts.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the purity of conditioned and unconditioned precepts.
If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world who abide in this equality of the purity of conditioned and unconditioned precepts, such persons are called fields of merit for the world."

If there are those who, with reverence, faith, respect, protection, and nurturing, provide them with all necessities—clothing, bedding, seats, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and so forth—such persons, by virtue of these roots of goodness, will constantly receive superior rewards throughout their cycle of rebirth and will swiftly be able to enter the great city of fearlessness.
"O noble ones! Among those, what is the purity and equality of patience? There are two kinds of patience: [the patience of enduring harm and the patience of reflecting on the Dharma]."
The first is the patience of relinquishment;
the second is the patience of subduing anger. "O virtuous ones!
In this regard, what is the patience of equanimity?
If there are sentient beings who seek all happiness and bring all suffering to rest, this is called the purity and equality of the patience of equanimity.

Furthermore, if there is a person who seeks happiness and wishes to leave suffering behind, that person contemplates the poisonous heat of afflictions within all the paths of suffering in the three realms—excluding only the noble ones—and for the sake of their own benefit, gives rise to great fear.

With such fear, one contemplates that the three realms are all ablaze, being consumed by the great fires of the various afflictions; every single sentient being is afflicted by manifold sufferings, rushing and wandering through the cycle of existence, unable to liberate themselves.
"Just as he was oppressed by suffering and had not yet attained liberation, so too am I oppressed by suffering.
By what means can I liberate myself from this suffering?
He then formed this thought:
"Without any other motive, I shall abandon [worldly things] through patience and liberation from all suffering, so as to provide all forms of happiness.

Having formed this thought, he immediately exerts himself; through patience and contentment, he is able to relinquish various requisites for sustaining the body—namely, food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, elephants, horses, and vehicles—and provides them all according to whatever is required.

This person, through patience and giving, desires to extinguish all sufferings; this person repeatedly cultivates patience and contentment, and while abiding therein, is able to practice relinquishment toward what is correct. One who follows the path of correctness should go to such a person, attend upon them, make offerings, and comply with their instructions. By means of making such offerings, one hears in this way and that way about the various faults and afflictions of saṃsāra and the benefits of nirvāṇa.

Such a person may resolve their mind upon the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or resolve their mind upon the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or resolve their mind upon the Mahāyāna; for the sake of their own happiness, they further increase their patience and contentment while protecting and nurturing sentient beings. This is called the pure equality of the renunciation of patience.

Even to the extent of relinquishing external wealth and one's own happiness, enduring all manner of suffering so that others may obtain happiness—this is called the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment (*tyāga-kṣānti*).

"If one sees beggars of various appearances, various demeanors, various voices, various outbursts of anger, various insults, various forms of contempt, and various harsh and unpleasant words coming to solicit [something], such a person, in this way and that way, has not yet tamed or softened their mind; their anger is not yet purified, and they do not yet abide in pure patience."
He thinks to himself: "Who could surpass me?
For what reason?"

Those evil yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and others who feed on flesh and blood have not heard of the suffering of birth and death nor the merit of nirvāṇa; they do not contemplate the terrors of future lives and are tormented by manifold sufferings, having not yet attained liberation from all forms of suffering.
Why is this? Because they have been separated from virtuous friends and have not heard the true Dharma, they remain submerged in the suffering of birth and death.

Having repeatedly heard of the afflictions of birth and death and the merits of Nirvana, and having contemplated the terrors of future lives to diligently cease all sufferings, I have drawn near to virtuous friends and obtained hearing of the true Dharma.
I now wish to cross over the drowning in birth and death; for what reason, then, should I give rise to anger?
Therefore, I should reflect as follows: abusive sounds and all adverse circumstances are entirely like the wind; I should abandon them and must not give rise to anger.
"In this way, regarding all sentient beings, one desires to relinquish various perceptions; all distinctions of written words and speech are entirely like the wind.
Toward all sentient beings, one abandons various perceptions and cultivates the purity of patience and equanimity."
This person repeatedly abandons various perceptions regarding sentient beings, as well as all conceptualizations involving words and letters, and cultivates the purity of patience and equanimity.
In this way, and in this way, this person’s mind abides in the purity of patience and equanimity, attaining joy and attaining purification.

In this way, in this manner, such a person cultivates the four kinds of analytical knowledge—analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of eloquence.

This person repeatedly cultivates the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas up to the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence; such a person is then able to relinquish their own body—skin, flesh, sinews, bones, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, head, and even their beloved life.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the pure equality of the patience of discernment and non-discernment; this is called the Bodhisattva’s pure equality of the patience of relinquishment.
"O virtuous ones!
In that regard, what is the purity of equanimity through the patience of subduing anger? "O noble ones!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can relinquish conceptualization regarding all speech, sounds, and letters;
Furthermore, they abandon conceptual discrimination regarding all physical forms, appearances, movements, deportment, coming and going, mental karma, and playful laughter;
they also abandon all that is comprised by craving and grasping, seeking no karmic retribution and remaining detached from suffering and pleasure, free from conceptual discrimination.
Even regarding their own bodies and lives, they abandon both conceptual and non-conceptual discrimination, attaining the purity and equanimity of the foremost dharma-patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*).

Just as space is neither angry nor delighted, and makes no distinctions between light and darkness, so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), remaining free from conceptualization and discrimination regarding all conditioned activities, laughter, speech, letters, forms, colors, painful sensations, and pleasant sensations; he is neither angry nor delighted.
The Bodhisattva, free from conceptual discrimination regarding those sentient beings, abides in the purity and equality of the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*).
Just as space is unmoving yet not improperly moving everywhere, unshaking yet not improperly shaking everywhere;

so too, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, amidst all karma, conditioned phenomena, and formative activities, remains unmoving in body and mind, not improperly moving everywhere, and likewise unshaking, not improperly shaking everywhere.
"Just as space is pure and free from defilement,
so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), attains perfect purity regarding all conditioned bodies and minds."
"Just as space nurtures all sentient beings,
so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (paramārtha-kṣānti) nurture all sentient beings."
"Just as space cannot be burned by the fires at the end of an eon, nor destroyed by the waters or winds of an eon;

so too, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-kṣānti), until they reach unsurpassed enlightenment, their mind cannot be corrupted by greed, hatred, or delusion."

"Just as the pure sky on the fifteenth night holds the perfectly full moon, which radiates cool light everywhere to bring refreshing peace to the bodies and minds of sentient beings afflicted by heat;

so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, abiding in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), extinguish the heat of all afflictions in sentient beings through the majestic deportment of body and speech."
"Just as the pure sky on the fifteenth night holds the perfectly full moon, surrounded by the multitude of stars, which shines with radiant light over the four continents;

so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, abiding in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), wherever he dwells, always remain surrounded by devas, nāgas, and even khaṭvāṅga-pūtanas, illuminating them with brilliant splendor."

"Just as when the pure sky is clear on the fifteenth night of the month, the perfectly full moon illuminates a sea island, and from that *candrakānta* (moon-love) jewel within it, a great flow of water issues forth capable of filling the vast ocean; so too,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the purity and equanimity of the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*),
all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, [and other beings...]"
The *pūtana* and *kaṭapūtana* demons are coarse, violent, and malicious, devoid of compassion;

they show no regard for the terrors of future lives. Yet this bodhisattva, through the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), emits a supreme radiance that illuminates all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Even unto the *kāṭapūtanas* and others— by this means, he causes those gods, nāgas, yakṣas,
and even the *kāṭapūtanas* to all attain a pure and virtuous mind; they give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion, thoughts of benefiting,
and thoughts of bringing rest to the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, causing them to abide in all forms of happiness.
With a mind that contemplates the fear of future lives, a mind detached from all evil,
and a mind of great diligence toward all wholesome dharmas, they attain an exceedingly pure mind; thus,
they even give rise to a mind of great heroic vigor toward all wholesome dharmas.
They gradually and successively distance themselves from all unwholesome states, fully attain all roots of goodness, and are able to fulfill the ocean of Great Nirvana.
"O virtuous ones!

You all should observe this bodhisattva: although he has not yet reached the ultimate, because he dwells in the purity and equality of the foremost dharma-acceptance (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), he has already surpassed the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and through that foremost dharma-acceptance, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
In the past, when I was practicing as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, I constantly dwelt in the forest eating various sweet fruits.
At that time, there was a king named Kali who dismembered my body into eight pieces.

At that time, because I had skillfully cultivated the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), white milk flowed from the places where I was cut. Through these causes and conditions of such patient asceticism, I brought to maturity immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, garuḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth.
At that time, immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of humans and non-humans all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In the past, when I was born as a human in a non-difficult place, performing such ascetic practices was not difficult for me.
"O virtuous ones! Listen attentively.
In the past, when I was born in a place of hardship and took the body of a rabbit dwelling in the forest, I leaped into a great mass of fire of my own accord in order to provide food for a rishi."
Because I was able to skillfully cultivate the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), I caused that mass of fire to transform into a lotus pond filled with pure water.
At that time, I lay upon a flower pedestal; by virtue of these causes and conditions of ascetic practice, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

At that time, the immeasurable Śakras, Brahmās, and Cāturmahārājakāyika kings, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas, along with various ṛṣis, humans, and non-humans, made offerings to me with all kinds of ritual implements and made this vow, saying:
"When you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you shall grant us the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"In the past, when I was in the body of a rabbit, I was able to skillfully cultivate the supreme patience of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), which is pure and equanimous—a patience not shared by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

When I was a rabbit in former times, the Brahmā and Śakra kings, the four world-protecting kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even humans and non-humans, all used various kinds of fragrant flowers, unguents, powdered incense, various precious jewels, jeweled banners, flags, and canopies, as well as manifold exquisite music, to honor, praise, and make offerings to me with a sense of unprecedented wonder—something that Arhats do not possess today."
"O virtuous ones!
Thus does a bodhisattva skillfully cultivate the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (paramārtha-kṣānti). O virtuous ones!"
This is the purity and equanimity of the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*); what is the meaning of this phrase?
"Ultimate truth" means that because one has reached the further shore of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is called the ultimate truth.

"Patience" (kṣānti) refers to seeing that the aggregates (skandha) within the three realms are ultimately empty, and seeing that all elements (dhātu) and sense-bases (āyatana) are ultimately empty; therefore, it is called patience.

"Purity" (viśuddhi) means that by means of noble wisdom, one eliminates and purifies the paths of affliction, the paths of karma, and the paths of suffering within the three realms; therefore, it is called purity.

"Equanimity" means that by means of noble wisdom, one knows all conditioned phenomena of the three realms and the suchness of the nature of all dharmas as they truly are—the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). One knows as it truly is that which is not the limit of reality and that which is not non-limit of reality; because one has severed the path of all afflictions, it is called "equanimity."
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the bodhisattva’s purity and equality of ultimate patience.
O virtuous ones!"
In this regard, what is the purity and equality of diligence?
Because diligence serves as the cause for the purity and equality of generosity, it is called the purity and equality of diligence.
Furthermore, because diligence can serve as the cause for the purity and equality of *prajñā*, it is called the "purity and equality of diligence.
Because diligence can abandon all views, and because diligence can serve as the cause for the purity and equality of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Through diligence, one is able to surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; through diligence, one is able to act as the cause for the four right efforts and the four bases of power.

Through diligence, one is able to abandon all afflictions; through diligence, one is able to act as the cause for the four means of attraction, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, the four Brahma-abodes, the four formless attainments, the five faculties and five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive meditative concentrations, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the twelve links of existence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Because diligence can serve as the cause for great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the purity and equality of *prajñā*, it is called the purity and equality of diligence.
Because diligence can serve as the cause for the purity and equality of maturing sentient beings, it is called the purity and equality of diligence.

Taking diligence as the means to accumulate the various roots of goodness of immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, and even to accumulate immeasurable wisdom of skillful means and immeasurable supreme vows; practicing immeasurable merit and wisdom, and acting as the cause for birth and grasping for immeasurable and diverse sentient beings—this is called the purity and equality of diligence.
"By means of diligence, he dwells in the Tuṣita heaven palace and observes the proper time for his birth as the one who fills the place;
even by means of diligence, he relinquishes that palace and clearly knows his entry into the mother’s womb;
and even by means of diligence, he emerges safely from his mother’s right side in the Lumbinī grove. And so forth.
He took seven steps, causing the great earth, its mountains, and its oceans to tremble;
he even, through diligence, accepted the bathing with water poured by the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda;
he even, through diligence, manifested all arts and crafts in the play of a youth; and he even, through diligence, remained within the palace for five...
Unstained by desire, and so forth, he exerted himself until at midnight he leaped over the city walls and went to a secluded grove;
and so forth, he exerted himself until he approached the sages Udraka Rāmaputra and Arāḍa Kālāma to practice offerings;
and so forth, he exerted himself for six years in ascetic practices; and so forth, he exerted himself toward Anuttara-...
Attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and realizing perfect enlightenment,
and even turning the wheel of Dharma through diligence with immeasurable humans and devas as witnesses— this is called the purity and equality of diligence.

"By means of my diligence, I have now convened this great assembly on Mount Khadiraka, the dwelling place of the sages and seers; all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, have been made to gather here."

There were as many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, mahoragas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas as there are atoms in a buddha-field who all came together in a great assembly for the sake of hearing the Dharma; this is called the purity and equality of diligence.
"O virtuous ones!

If one were to divide the waters of the four great oceans into individual drops, and if one were to cultivate diligence with such purity and equanimity as there are those drops, one would enable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others to fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*; this is called the purity and equanimity of diligence."

*The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Scroll 50; *The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Moon-Treasury Sūtra*, Scroll 5, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Tianqi era of the Northern Qi dynasty. Chapter Eight (Part One): "All Evil Ghosts and Spirits Attain Reverent Faith. At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who protect the world saw an immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas, who possessed various colors, various forms, various desires, various conducts, and various natures.

Those sentient beings are by nature devoid of compassion; they constantly give rise to thoughts of anger, malice, and harm toward all beings. They do not contemplate the terrifying consequences of future lives, remaining without any sense of obligation or protection. Such individuals perpetually afflict and harass everyone from kṣatriyas down to animals, seizing their vital energy and devouring their flesh and blood.
When the Four Heavenly Kings saw that all the ghosts and spirits had assembled together, they leaped for joy and each questioned the great generals under their command.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa asked the yakṣa general Saṃjñeya:

"In these four continents, there are all manner of yakṣas and rākṣasas—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—who dwell in cities, villages, houses, stūpas, temples, gardens, groves, mountain valleys, rivers, wells, springs, ponds, marshes, burial mounds, beneath trees, in wildernesses, fields, secluded forests, empty dwellings, and upon the many wondrous jewel islands within the great ocean."
"Have all those spirits— whether they move on land, move through water, or move through the air— come together here at the place where the World-Honored One is,
without exception? Vajrapāṇi the Great General replied, "Great King!"

As Your Majesty has said, all the yakṣas within these four continents, even those on the jewel-islands of the great ocean—whether they travel by land, by water, or through the air—all have now assembled before the World-Honored One without exception.
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked the Gandharva General Saṃtuṣita, saying:
"Regarding all the hosts of Gandharvas within this four-continent world, the rest is as previously described."
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka asked the great general of the kumbhāṇḍas, Dhanañjaya, saying:
"Regarding all the hosts of kumbhāṇḍas within this four-continent world, the rest is as previously described."
The Deva King Virūpākṣa asked the Naga King Supratiṣṭhita:
