"Have all the hosts of nāgas, mahoragas, garuḍas, and pretas within these four continents—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether dwelling in cities, villages, or houses, or even on the various wondrous jewel-islands within the ocean; whether moving upon the earth, in the water, or through the air—all of them without exception now gathered at the place where the World-Honored One resides?"
The Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita said:
"Great King! It is as you have said."
"All the nāgas, up to and including the pretas, throughout these four continents—without exception—all have now gathered together here in the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā, and Brahmā Sahāmpati joined their palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!"

All the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, mahoragas, garuḍas, and various pretas within these four continents—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; all those who move on land, in water, or through the air, without exception—all have now gathered together in the presence of the World-Honored One.

We, this great assembly, all join in this exhortation: We pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us out of his compassion for all sentient beings; that he may cause evil beings to attain respectful faith; that he may cause the Eye of the True Dharma to abide for a long time; that he may ensure the lineage of the Triple Gem continues without interruption;

that the vital essence of the earth, the vital essence of sentient beings, and the nectar-like vital essence of the supreme flavor of the True Dharma may abide long and increase in benefit; and furthermore, that the paths of the virtuous realms and the path to Nirvāṇa may never perish or be destroyed, but rather increase in benefit.
“Venerable World-Honored One!

All the cities, towns, villages, and dwellings of this Jambudvīpa, even down to the jewel-islands—without exception—all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even the kāṭapūtanas and so forth, have now all gathered here.”
The kings of the devas, the kings of the nāgas, and even the kings of the piśācas have all brought their retinues and gathered here.

We pray that the World-Honored One entrust this king with the practice of the Dharma, so that he may be mindful and provide protection. May the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and even the kaṭapūtanas each have their respective domains, nurturing and upholding them according to their own portions; may they never abandon them, nor cause them distress. Should they see others causing distress, may they prevent and protect against it, never forsaking them so that they may attain peace and security.
If each of them, within their own respective domains, exerts diligence and provides impartial protection, they will attain joy, renown, and receive abundant rewards of merit.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted their exhortation; out of compassion and pity for them all, he surveyed the great assembly. Having surveyed the assembly, he raised his right arm and spoke these words:
"You virtuous ones, you entire great assembly, each of you listen attentively; I shall now explain."

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as difficult as the blooming of the udumbara flower; escaping the eight difficulties is as difficult as waiting for the seasonal fragrance tree to bloom; hearing the True Dharma is as difficult as rain falling upon Jambūnada gold; encountering the Sangha of precepts and concentration and receiving their offerings is as difficult as entering the great ocean to reach the Isle of Wondrous Jewels; having faith and reverence for the Triple Gem is as difficult as seeking the wish-fulfilling jewel; making offerings to the Triple Gem is as difficult as seeking the goddess Puṇyavatī and her auspicious vase; and upholding the precepts is as difficult as reaching the land of ox-head sandalwood, which is hard to attain.
It is difficult to give rise to compassion for sentient beings, like encountering a brave and powerful enemy who wields a vajra-pestle, from whom it is hard to escape;

it is difficult to be prudent and content, like performing the *aśvamedha*—in Sanskrit, *aśvamedha*, here translated as the "Horse-Treasure Pillar Sacrifice"—for such a sacrifice can only be performed by a sovereign of Jambudvīpa.
"O virtuous ones! There are ten kinds of equality.

If sentient beings possess these ten equalities, they will constantly receive superior retributions within the cycle of birth and death, and will swiftly be able to enter the great city of fearlessness."
What are the ten? First, the equality of sentient beings;
second, the equality of dharmas.
Third, the equality of purity;
fourth, the equality of giving;
fifth, the equality of ethical discipline;
Sixth, the equality of patience;
seventh, the equality of diligence;
eighth, the equality of meditative concentration;
Ninth, the equality of wisdom;
tenth, the purity and equality of all phenomena. "O virtuous ones!
In this regard, what is the equality of sentient beings?
If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of seeking life and experiencing pleasure while avoiding suffering, should hold this view:

"If a recipient performs an action—whether by body, speech, or mind, whether wholesome or unwholesome—whether acting themselves or instructing others, that recipient shall experience the retribution in the present life as well as the retribution in future lives."

Therefore, if you wish to be free from suffering and seek the happiness of both this life and the next, you should cultivate the virtues of body, speech, and mind, and refrain from committing any evil.
If you seek to benefit yourself and others in both lives, to bring joy to yourself and others, and to bring well-being to yourself and others, do not commit any evil deeds.
This is the equality of sentient beings.
"O worthy ones! Among those, what is the equality of phenomena?

If there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to avoid suffering, who rejoice in life and fear death, who desire not to be separated from those they love and do not wish to encounter those they hate—such people are submerged in the ocean of the human mind.
Why is this? Because if there are sentient beings who cling to a self, they will transmigrate through birth and death, failing to see the pure path of liberation.

Therefore, one should contemplate and observe the equality of all phenomena: sentient beings are not separate from phenomena, and phenomena are not separate from sentient beings. If the essential nature of sentient beings is the essential nature of the self, and if the essential nature of the self is the essential nature of all phenomena, then the essential nature of all phenomena is the essential nature of the Buddha-dharma.

If one contemplates all phenomena as equal in this way, that person attains non-existence; they do not perceive sentient beings, nor is there any coming, going, joining, or dispersing of sentient beings. Furthermore, they do not perceive any sentient beings as obtainable, being neither dharma nor non-dharma. Such a person thus abides in the signless; this is the equality of dharmas.
"O virtuous ones! What therein is pure equality?
It is the attainment of a human body endowed with the full ten virtues."
What are the ten? First, being born away from lowly families;
second, not being dull-witted.
Third, not being mute;
fourth, having no deficiency in the sense faculties;
fifth, obtaining a male body.
Sixth, one will have a handsome and upright countenance and obtain excellent companions;
seventh, one will not be poor;
eighth, one will not be deceived by others.
Ninth, his speech possesses the middle way;
tenth, many people delight in seeing him.
Why is it said that he has attained the purity and equality of a human body?

Just as having obtained a human body, one obtains the three types of restraint, leaves the three evil destinies, and is able to seek the three vehicles; by this means, one attains the three kinds of bodhi, and not by any other dharma.
"How does purity and equanimity lead to bodhi?

This person causes the mind not to rely on any dharmas, causes the mind not to rely on internal or external objects, and does not rely on the vision of suchness (*tathatā*). All dharmas lack the characteristic of combination; they do not grasp at an internal mind nor grasp at an external mind, attaining profound tranquility and concentration regarding these two spheres."

When one thus purifies and contemplates the principle of right view, one does not perceive a self, nor an internal sentient being, nor an external life-principle, a vital span, a born being, a person, a numerical category, a nurtured entity, an agent, an instigator of action, an originator, an instigator of origination, an experiencer, an instigator of experience, a knower, or a seer; these sixteen names all arise from false conceptualization.

"Such a person, regarding all sentient beings, attains the vision of the purity and equality of non-self; for this reason, they are free from desire and purity, and do not give rise to extreme views."
In this way, one enters into the purity and equality of sentient beings, as well as the seal of wisdom that is empty of all phenomena, non-active, signless, and wishless.
Having thus entered into the purity and equality of sentient beings, one further matures sentient beings through those very dharmas, neither destroying oneself nor destroying one's resources.
If one knows that the essential nature of sentient beings is equal, then one knows that the essential nature of all phenomena is equal.
If the essential nature of all phenomena is equal, this is the equality of the essential nature of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, all phenomena are called the Buddha-dharma, and this is pure equality.
“O worthy ones! What therein is the purity and equality of giving?
It refers to the four kinds of pure-minded giving.”
By means of giving, sentient beings constantly receive superior retributions during their cycle of existence and are able to swiftly enter the great city of fearlessness.
What are these four?
First, to give rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings;
second, a mind of equanimity;
third, a mind of great loving-kindness.
Fourth is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Regarding the purity and equanimity of the compassionate mind: if there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to leave suffering behind—desiring that they not be separated from those they love and not encounter those they hate—and who desire long life, benefit, widespread fame, wealth, and the five sensory pleasures all to their heart's content, one should train in this way:
"Just as I cherish and delight in my own body and life, protecting them with every possible means as something unsurpassed and beyond measure, so too should I act for others."

In this same way, for all sentient beings—even down to a single insect or ant—each likewise delights in and cherishes their own life and body, and there is no price or measure for the supreme protection they provide through every possible means.

If I were to afflict or harm sentient beings, or further deprive them of the means of livelihood or sever their life-force, then throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes in the cycle of birth and death, I would in turn be afflicted and harmed, deprived of the means of livelihood, have my life-force severed, and undergo immeasurable suffering.

From this day forth, regarding all sentient beings, I shall conceive of them as my parents and my children; even down to insects and ants, I shall regard them as my parents and my children. For this reason, I shall no longer afflict or harm sentient beings, nor shall I seize their means of livelihood or sever their life-faculties, nor shall I instruct others to rob people of their vital energy or sever their life-faculties.

In this way, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas of saṃsāric wandering, I shall be unable to be harmed or afflicted, nor shall my means of sustaining life be taken away, nor shall my life-force be severed.

Why is this? Among all sentient beings, there is not a single one who has not been my parent, brother, son, or daughter; likewise, among all sentient beings, there is not a single one who is not my parent, brother, son, or daughter.

For this reason, I have at one time been no other than a relative to all sentient beings, and all sentient beings have likewise at one time been no other than relatives to me; therefore, it is not possible that anyone could cause harm to their parents, or even to their sons and daughters.
"O virtuous ones! Among those, what is non-affliction?
If all sentient beings seek happiness and wish to be free from suffering, they should train themselves in this way:

If I were to provoke the mind of a kṣatriya, causing that kṣatriya to find no joy or pleasure in what he originally desired regarding his own domain, kingdom, and subjects; or if I were to provoke the minds of anyone from brahmins down to animals, causing them to find no joy or pleasure in what they originally desired.

For these reasons, they wage war against one another, engaging in strife, contention, and litigation; they practice flattery and utter falsehoods, and they dismember and sever one another's life-faculties.

Because of these causes and conditions, from this day forward, I shall desist from harming and severing the life-faculties of all sentient beings. By virtue of these causes and conditions of pure and impartial acts of giving, throughout my long journey through the cycle of birth and death, no one shall be able to provoke me, engage in strife or contention with me, or sever my life-faculties.
For this reason, it is called "not causing provocation.
"O virtuous ones! Among those things, what is 'not taking life'?"
If there are sentient beings who seek long life and refrain from harming others, they should train themselves in this way:

"All sentient beings are none other than my own kin. If I were to send down torrential rain or unseasonable rain; or if I were to rain down dust and ash, causing great darkness and gloom; or if I were to cause a prolonged drought that dries up streams and springs, thereby diminishing the flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, the five grains, and all flavors—by these causes and conditions, it would bring famine and suffering to those whom I know as my kin, agitating their four elements so that they develop various illnesses and even reach the end of their lives."
If one were to inflict such harm, this principle would not hold.

For this reason, I distance myself from taking the lives of sentient beings, so as not to cause a depletion of the essential nutrients of the earth; thereby, I ensure that those I know intimately suffer no distress of famine, that the four elements do not become disturbed to give rise to various diseases, and that they do not meet with untimely death.

By means of this pure and impartial giving, one will not undergo the sufferings of famine, illness, or death throughout the long cycle of birth and death; for this reason, it is called "not harming life."
"O worthy ones! Among those things, what is not an instrument for depriving others of their livelihood?
Those sentient beings who seek their own lives and sustenance should train themselves in this way: [They should think: 'I shall not take the life of any living being.'"

All sentient beings are none other than my own kin. If I were to deprive them of their flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, five grains, and the vital essence that serves as their means of sustenance, those sentient beings—because they would no longer consume those excellent essences, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and the flavors of the five grains—would become emaciated and lose their strength; they would lose mindfulness, become malicious in nature, flighty and coarse, turn pale and haggard, and fall prey to various ailments.
If one were to add this suffering, such a principle would not hold true.

Therefore, I ought to accept the instructions of those former sages and devas: from among all those flavors, I should take only one sixty-fourth part of the vital essence to sustain my own life, while leaving sixty-three parts of the vital essence of the earth's flavors to sustain other sentient beings and allow them to enjoy peace and happiness.
By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of my practice of contentment, throughout the long cycle of birth and death, I shall never again consume food that lacks fine flavor or vital energy.
Because of this food, one possesses majestic power and strength, is able to maintain firm mindfulness, has a supple nature and mind, an upright countenance, and is free from all suffering of illness.
This is called "not depriving others of the means of livelihood."
“O virtuous ones! Among those things, what is the non-separation from life?
One who seeks life should train as follows:”

All sentient beings are none other than my own kin; it would be contrary to this principle that one should look upon them with an evil eye or blow upon them with the breath so as to cause them to lose their minds, or seize the vital energy from their limbs and joints, thereby causing my kin to experience suffering in body and mind. Such a thing is not right.

By these causes and conditions, I shall undergo the long-term cycle of birth and death without encountering non-human beings who might breathe upon me, gaze at me with malevolent eyes, distract my mind, or steal my vital essence; for this reason, it is called "life not being separated."
"O virtuous ones! Among those things, what is the indestructible life?
If sentient beings cherish their own lives and seek happiness while avoiding suffering—whether for the sake of fame, wealth, status, or even liberation—they should train themselves in this way: "

All sentient beings are none other than my own kin. If, for the sake of food and drink, I were to rob my kin of their vital energy, or dismember them limb by limb; or push them from mountain peaks, trees, high pavilions, or deep rivers so that they fall; or administer poison to them; or dispatch zombies and malevolent spirits to harm them; or employ sorcery and curses, or deprive them of food and drink; or use swords and blades to sever their bodies and heads—using such means to cut off their life-force—if I were to inflict such suffering upon them, this would not be right.

For this reason, throughout the long flow of birth and death, I have not had my vital energy stolen by sentient beings, nor have I been subjected to dismemberment or the severing of the life-faculty; for this meaning, it is called "indestructible life," which is the pure equality of giving.

"Furthermore, regarding the purity and equanimity of giving: out of compassion for all sentient beings, one accumulates merit and wisdom for their sake; with firm diligence that eliminates all illusory views, one seeks all that is wholesome and is able to act according to what has been taught, never giving rise to an evil mind for the sake of sustaining one's livelihood."
One does not give rise to harmful intentions toward sentient beings; the precepts one upholds are shared with all beings; seeing the joy of sentient beings, one feels profound delight.
Regarding the conditions for one's own happiness, one is naturally able to be content; whatever things one holds dear, one is able to relinquish them all.

Regarding all supreme dharmas, he is free from the mind of stinginess; he is constantly fearful of the three realms and possesses mastery through the power of patience. He has faith in the characteristic of impermanence and practices according to the teachings.

When he observes his own failure in capacity, he examines himself; seeing others fail in their capacity, he gives rise to compassion. In cultivating goodness, he is never weary; regarding transgressions, he diligently repents. He performs boundless dedications of merit and joyfully seeks the true principle. He always regards sentient beings as fields of merit and diligently works for them so that they may cease from the evil paths.
The mind abides nowhere with respect to all phenomena; this is the purity and equality of giving according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
I shall now explain the purity and equality of giving according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | jyāme jyāme | prakhāye | upaprakhāye | jame | yajyāme | khāyakhāye | svāhā. When this Dharma-door was spoken, eight million six hundred thousand kinnaras, gandharvas, and others were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:
“Tadyathā | gokare | gokare | yavagokare | upayavagokare | svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

“Tadyathā | dhare | dhāre | dhāradhare | upadhāre | dhāre | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being taught, nine million four hundred thousand yakṣas became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | Ajaṇe | Cakṣa ajaṇe | Gakṣa cakṣa ajaṇe | Mauro ajaṇe | Caca | Svāhā. When this dharma-gate was spoken, seventy million nāgas attained the supreme samādhi of the dharma that is free from dust and defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | ha ha ha ha ha ha | heḍava | ha ha ha | ja ja ja | ha ha ha | svāhā. When this dharma-gate was spoken, three hundred thousand nayutas of asuras attained the samādhi of the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | Anuna | Anuna | Apānanuna | Apāyari | Apānanuna | Svāhā. When this dharma-gate was spoken, eighty-four thousand *bimbara* *kumbhāṇḍas* attained the Samādhi of Joyful Bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke this mantra:

"Tadyathā | dhagadhaja | avadhagadhaja | avadha | gadhajaja | gandhagandhaja | svāhā. When this Dharma-gate was being taught, seven hundred thousand nayutas of *preta*s, *piśāca*s, *pūtana*s, and *kaṭapūtana*s attained the Vidyutpati-samādhi. Furthermore, countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even kaṭapūtanas who had never before resolved their minds toward supreme, true bodhicitta all now gave rise to that resolve.
This is the purity and equality of giving according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "O virtuous ones!
Among those, what is the purity and equality of ethical discipline (*śīla*)?"
Whether it be all mundane or supramundane wholesome paths, as well as the bliss of nirvana, ethical discipline is their root.
By this cause and condition, one attains the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, as well as the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The so-called ten paths of wholesome action consist of abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
"O virtuous ones! By the cause and condition of abstaining from taking life, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, attaining great fearlessness toward all sentient beings;
second, attaining a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
third, attaining the severance of habitual tendencies.
Fourth, they shall be free from all illness and affliction;
fifth, they shall attain a long life span;
sixth, they shall be protected by non-human beings.
Seventh, one will be peaceful and secure in both waking and sleeping, free from all evil dreams;
eighth, one will have no enemies;
ninth, one will not fear the evil realms.
Tenth, one attains birth in the good realms.
By dedicating these roots of goodness from having distanced oneself from killing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person will before long realize unsurpassed wisdom.
"Once he has attained enlightenment, long-lived beings from that buddha-field who have abandoned all killing will come to be born in his land.
O virtuous ones! By being far removed from the causes and conditions of stealing, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, possessing great wealth and reward;
second, not sharing with others.
Third, not sharing [one's wealth] with the five families;
fourth, being loved and respected by the multitude, never being weary of or abandoning them;
fifth, traveling afar throughout the ten directions without any doubt or apprehension.
Sixth, fearlessness in one's sphere of activity;
seventh, constant delight in giving;
eighth, the spontaneous and swift attainment of wealth and treasures without seeking them.
Ninth, to give away wealth as soon as it is obtained;
tenth, to be born in the good realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from abstaining from stealing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once bodhi is attained, that Buddha-land will be fully endowed with various kinds of flowering and fruit-bearing groves, garments, necklaces, and ornaments, and will be filled with all manner of rare and precious objects.
"O virtuous ones! By the cause and condition of abstaining from sexual misconduct, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, attaining the restraint of the sense faculties;
second, abiding in the purity of detachment from desire;
third, not causing affliction to others.
Fourth, one is praised by the multitude;
fifth, one is beheld with joy by the multitude;
sixth, one is able to arouse diligent effort.
Seventh, seeing the faults of birth and death;
eighth, always delighting in relinquishment and giving;
ninth, always delighting in seeking the Dharma.
Tenth, one attains rebirth in the happy realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from abstaining from sexual misconduct toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once bodhi is attained, that buddha-field will be free from foul odors and devoid of women; there, no sexual desire is practiced, and all beings are born through transformation.
"O virtuous ones! By the cause and condition of abstaining from false speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, his words are trusted by all people;
second, he speaks with propriety in all places, even among the devas;
third, his mouth emits a fragrance like that of the utpala flower.
Fourth, he alone serves as the witness among the assemblies of humans and devas;
fifth, he is loved and respected by all people and is free from all doubts;
sixth, he always utters truthful speech.
Seventh, purity of mind and intention;
eighth, being constantly free from flattery and speech that does not miss the opportune moment;
ninth, being constantly full of joy.
Tenth, they attain birth in the happy realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from being far removed from false speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once they have attained bodhi, their buddha-field will be free from any foul odors, and various sublime fragrances will pervade it everywhere.
"O virtuous ones! By the cause and condition of abstaining from divisive speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, one attains an indestructible body;
second, one attains an indestructible retinue;
third, one attains indestructible friends.
Fourth, attaining indestructible faith;
fifth, attaining indestructible Dharma;
sixth, attaining indestructible discipline.
Seventh, attaining unshakable *śamatha*;
eighth, attaining unshakable *samādhi*;
ninth, attaining unshakable patience (*kṣānti*);
Tenth, one attains birth in the good realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from being far removed from divisive speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once bodhi has been attained, the sentient beings and retinues in that Buddha-field will not be destroyed by various Māras or others.
"O virtuous ones! By the cause and condition of being far removed from harsh speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, their speech and tone are gentle and supple;
second, their diction is fluent;
third, their speech and tone are moist and lustrous.
Fourth, attaining harmonious speech;
fifth, ensuring that one's words always hit the mark;
sixth, attaining straightforward speech.
Seventh, they attain speech that is fearless;
eighth, they attain speech that is without flattery;
ninth, they attain speech that is in accordance with the Dharma.
Tenth, they attain birth in the happy realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from having distanced themselves from harsh speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once they have attained bodhi, the sounds of the Dharma will fill their buddha-field, and all vulgar and evil speech will be eliminated.
"O worthy ones! By the cause and condition of abstaining from frivolous speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, they are loved and respected by devas and humans;
second, they are followed with joy and praised by devas and humans;
third, they always delight in truthful speech.
Fourth, one should always dwell together with wise people and never leave them;
fifth, one should fully comprehend whatever is heard;
sixth, one should be loved, respected, and honored by those who possess wisdom.
Seventh, one constantly finds joy in dwelling in forest hermitages;
eighth, one delights in the silent composure of the noble and holy ones;
ninth, one distances oneself from evil people and draws near to the noble and holy ones.
Tenth, they attain rebirth in the good realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from having distanced themselves from frivolous speech toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once they have attained bodhi, those who possess upright countenances, strong memories, and a delight in seclusion will come to be born in that buddha-field.
"O virtuous ones! By means of that cause and condition of being free from desire, one attains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, the faculty of the body is unimpaired;
second, the karma of speech is pure;
third, the mind is undistracted.
Fourth, one attains superior karmic retribution;
fifth, one attains great wealth and nobility;
sixth, one is beheld with pleasure by all people.
Seventh, one obtains an indestructible retinue and indestructible wealth;
eighth, one constantly associates with wise persons;
ninth, one is never separated from the sound of the Dharma.
Tenth, one attains birth in the good realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness from being far removed from sensual desire toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once bodhi has been attained, that buddha-field will be free from those Māras, enemies, and all non-Buddhist paths.
"O virtuous ones! By means of that distance from the causes and conditions of ill-will, one attains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, one attains freedom from anger;
second, one takes no pleasure in amassing wealth;
third, one accords with the noble ones.
Fourth, one constantly associates with the worthy and the noble;
fifth, one attains beneficial matters;
sixth, one’s countenance is upright and dignified.
Seventh, seeing sentient beings experience joy, one gives rise to sympathetic gladness;
eighth, one constantly attains samādhi;
ninth, the three karmas are harmonious and supple.
Tenth, one attains rebirth in the happy realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness that distance one from ill-will toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, once bodhi has been attained, all sentient beings in that Buddha-land will attain samādhi and their minds will be utterly pure.
"O virtuous ones! By means of that cause and condition for being far removed from wrong views, one attains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, their mental nature is gentle and virtuous, and they associate with those who are noble and good;
second, they believe in the retribution of karma to such an extent that they will not commit any evil, even at the cost of their own lives;
third, they take refuge in and honor the Triple Gem, and do not believe in celestial deities.
Fourth, they attain right view and do not select auspicious or inauspicious times based on the year, month, day, or lunar mansion;
fifth, they are constantly reborn among humans and devas, remaining free from all evil realms;
sixth, they attain a virtuous and excellent mind that is praised by wise people.
Seventh, to abandon worldly pursuits and constantly seek the noble path;
eighth, to distance oneself from the views of nihilism and eternalism and to have faith in the principle of dependent origination;
ninth, to always encounter those who possess right faith, right practice, and the right aspiration for enlightenment.
Tenth, they shall be born in the good realms.

By dedicating these roots of goodness—which consist in remaining far removed from wrong views—toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such persons will swiftly fulfill the six *pāramitās* and attain perfect enlightenment in a pure and sublime Buddha-field.

Having attained enlightenment, sentient beings adorned with all roots of goodness—merit and wisdom—will come to be born in that buddha-field; they will have no faith in celestial deities and will be free from the fear of the evil realms, and upon the end of their lives there, they will return to birth in the good realms.
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and equal giving toward them, one practices the equal abstention from taking life through the precepts.
By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition and is free from all fears."
"O worthy ones! When practicing the pure and equal conduct of giving, one practices the equal conduct of abstaining from theft within the precepts.
By these causes and conditions, one possesses great rewards not shared with others, and there shall be no obstacles in cultivating all virtues."
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and impartial conduct of giving, one practices the impartial conduct of abstaining from sexual misconduct through the observance of precepts.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great rewards and cultivates roots of goodness without hindrance, remaining free from thoughts of sexual misconduct and regarding the wives of oneself and others with equanimity."
"O worthy ones! When practicing the pure and impartial giving of those [virtuous deeds], one practices the impartiality of the precepts by remaining far removed from false speech.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great rewards. Even if one is slandered and not believed, one’s resolve in practicing as taught remains unshakable. Among the hosts of devas and humans, one alone acts as a witness, and the mouth emits a fragrance like that of the *utpala* flower."
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and impartial giving of those [gifts], one practices the impartiality of abstaining from divisive speech through the precepts.
By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition and attains an indestructible retinue, a retinue of noble men, and a retinue of respectful faith."
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and equal giving of those [offerings], one practices the equal distancing from harsh speech through the precepts.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition; being free from coarse and wild speech, one attains a subtle and wondrous voice, fully endowed with purity and free from base and evil sounds."
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and equal conduct of giving, one practices the equal conduct of abstaining from frivolous speech within the precepts.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition; whatever words one speaks are appropriate, one cuts through the doubts of the great assembly, and all people delight in seeing one."
“O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure and impartial giving of those [gifts], one practices the impartiality of observing the precepts free from greed.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition; having correctly received that retribution, one is further able to practice relinquishment and giving, thereby possessing superior rewards and great majestic power.”
"O worthy ones! When practicing the pure and impartial giving of those [wholesome deeds], one practices the impartiality of observing the precepts while remaining free from ill-will.
By these causes and conditions, one possesses great karmic fruition: being handsome and magnificent, loved and respected by all, and having all faculties unimpeded and without deficiency."
"O virtuous ones! When practicing the pure equality of giving, one practices the equality of precepts that distance oneself from wrong views.

By these causes and conditions, one possesses great retribution: being born in a land of right view and a family of right view; constantly encountering all Buddhas, as well as Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Sangha; and cultivating the Bodhisattva practices while never abandoning pure equality."

"O noble ones! This is the purity and equality of the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Those who adorn themselves with this practice of ethical discipline will, before long, be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*), achieve the merit of Buddhahood, and possess pure vocal resonance. They shall subdue the hosts of Māra and enemies, and through the purity of meditative concentration, mindfulness, and wisdom, attain great knowledge, great loving-kindness, and great compassion. Ultimately, they shall be able to accomplish the purity and equality of all Buddha-dharmas; this is the arising of the purity and equality of the practice of ethical discipline in the world."
"O worthy ones! What therein is the purity and equanimity of the supramundane arousal of ethical conduct?

It is when one who practices with faith and resolve in the purity of ethical conduct and samādhi does not maintain the prohibitions by relying on the phenomenon of form, nor does one maintain the prohibitions by relying on the phenomena of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

One does not uphold the precepts by relying on the phenomenon of the eye; one does not uphold the precepts by relying on the phenomena of forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or the feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and so forth arising with eye-contact as their condition.

This extends even to not relying on the phenomenon of the mind; one does not uphold the precepts by relying on the phenomena of mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, or the feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and so forth arising with mind-contact as their condition.

One maintains the precepts without relying on the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; one maintains the precepts without relying on the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One maintains the precepts without relying on the phenomena of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
One maintains the precepts without relying on phenomena of the present or the future.
One maintains the precepts without relying on the phenomena of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed Great Vehicle’s omniscience.
One does not maintain the precepts by relying on matters of hearing, meditation, or wisdom;
nor does one maintain the precepts by relying on the power of hearing, the power of samādhi, the power of dhāraṇī, or the power of patience.

One does not uphold the precepts by relying on the power of the tainted or the untainted, the conditioned or the unconditioned, the power of the wholesome or the unwholesome, or the power of light or darkness.
This is the supramundane arousal of pure and equal conduct, the Brahma-path and Noble Way that enters the city of fearlessness.
The ethical conduct upon which those noble and holy ones rely is pure and equal; it is the ultimate truth that enters into pure wisdom.
"O virtuous ones! As for what is called 'ethical conduct' (śīla), what is its meaning?"

For example, just as the winds of burning affliction between the Vajra and Cakravāḍa mountains are prevented from reaching the four continents because they are blocked by those mountains, so too the power of the pure and equanimous cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness through noble precepts can block the wind of the heat of craving, preventing it from arising. For this reason, it is called "precept" (śīla).

For example, just as the foul and stinking winds between the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are prevented from reaching the four continents by the obstruction of those mountains, so too does the pure and impartial noble precept cultivate the four fearlessnesses and powers, able to obstruct that evil, stinking vapor and prevent it from arising. For this reason, it is called "precept" (śīla).

For example, the space between the Cakravāḍa mountains is filled with profound darkness; because these mountains act as a barrier, they prevent that darkness from obscuring these four continents. In the same way, the power of cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment through pure and impartial noble precepts can obstruct the characteristics of ignorance, conditioned existence, and outflows, preventing them from arising. For this reason, it is called "precept" (śīla).

"O worthy ones! The meaning of detachment is the meaning of morality; the meaning of liberation is the meaning of morality; the meaning of cessation is the meaning of morality; the meaning of exhaustion is the meaning of morality; the meaning of extinction is the meaning of morality—these various meanings of these terms are called the meaning of morality."
"O worthy ones! This is the purity of conduct that is equal in both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who cultivate this equality of conduct regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned, such persons should receive the offerings of the world."

If people of the world revere, trust, respect, protect, and support those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas by providing them with clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal decoctions for the sake of illness, as well as the necessities for sustaining life, then those people, while wandering through birth and death, will constantly receive superior rewards and will swiftly be able to enter the great city of fearlessness.
"O virtuous ones! Among those, what is the purity and equality of patience?
There are two kinds of patience: "
First is the patience of relinquishment;
second is the patience of quelling anger.

Regarding the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment: if one desires to attain all happiness and relinquish all suffering, this is called the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment.

If there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to leave suffering behind, they perceive that all paths of suffering within the three realms and the heat of the fires of affliction oppress them, with the sole exception of the noble ones.
This person has already given rise to great fear.

When they perceive this, they see that all sentient beings in the three realms are tormented and scorched by the blazing fires of afflictions; each and every being undergoes various sufferings and harms, driven along in the cycle of transmigration, unable to save themselves.
"Thus, I, together with all sentient beings, am afflicted by suffering; by what skillful means can I save myself?
He then thought: "Not by any other means, but only by practicing patience should one liberate oneself from all suffering and be endowed with all happiness."
He is then able to joyfully cultivate impartial patience (*samatākṣānti*).

He can relinquish various requisites for sustaining the body—namely food and drink, vehicles, clothing, bedding, dwellings, and couches—and bestows them all according to their needs, using patience and generosity to extinguish all sufferings.

"When this person repeatedly cultivates patience and abides therein, they are able to practice relinquishment and giving; one should go to the place of such a person who has correctly resolved their mind and is correctly practicing, and there cultivate offerings."
Because they have made offerings many times, they hear from those people about the faults and sufferings of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa.

Such a person, whether seeking realization through the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, acts for the sake of that joy; they repeatedly delight in patience and nurture sentient beings. This is the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment.

Even if one relinquishes external material wealth, being able to endure suffering oneself so that others may obtain happiness, this is also called the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment.

If various forms and colors, various modes of conduct, various sounds, and various expressions of anger, abuse, bullying, and harsh, untrue, or unpleasant words are directed at a mendicant who comes seeking [alms], and if this person’s mind is not yet supple and their hatred is not yet purified, they will not be able to abide in patience.
This person thinks:
"Who can surpass me? For this reason, when insulted, they are unable to practice patience.
Again, he thought:

"Why is it that those flesh-eating yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and others, have not yet heard of the great suffering of birth and death or the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa?"

Failing to contemplate the terrifying matters of future lives and being afflicted by manifold sufferings such that they cannot yet attain liberation, one should know that these individuals are separated from virtuous friends and have not heard the Dharma; therefore, they are submerged in the suffering of birth and death.

I have already drawn near to spiritual friends and have repeatedly heard of the suffering and affliction of birth and death, as well as the peace and bliss of nirvana. Contemplating the terrors of future lives, I constantly and diligently practice to sever all suffering; I shall surely attain deliverance from that sinking and drowning in birth and death.
Why do anger arise and why do I not practice patience?

Therefore, I should make this distinction: abusive sounds and all adverse circumstances are entirely like the wind; I should abandon them and not give rise to anger, and in this way, I should relinquish the notion of "sentient beings."

"When one reflects in this way, the sounds of abuse and all adverse circumstances pass away like the wind; free from the notion of a sentient being, one practices patience that is pure and equanimous."

If this person repeatedly abandons various notions regarding those sentient beings, and remains free from discriminative thoughts toward abusive sounds and all adverse circumstances, practicing patience that is pure and equanimous, then this person abides in a patient mind and attains purity through joy; thus they are able to cultivate unimpeded wisdom, namely the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
In this way, one is able to relinquish all internal wealth—namely, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, and head, as well as the cherished life itself.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus cultivates the purity and equanimity of patience that is neither discriminative nor non-discriminative, it is called the purity and equanimity of the patience of relinquishment.
"O virtuous ones! What therein is the pure equality of patience that extinguishes anger?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva can abandon conceptualization regarding all speech, sounds, and letters; abandon conceptualization regarding all forms, bodies, perceptions, gestures, deportment, coming and going, and playful laughter; further abandon craving and grasping, not seeking karmic retribution, remaining free from the conceptualization of pleasure and pain, and even maintaining no conceptualization regarding one's own body or life—thereby attaining the pure equality of the patience of the ultimate truth."

For example, just as space does not become angry when encountering darkness nor rejoice upon obtaining light, and does not give rise to such discriminative thoughts, so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the purity and equality of the foremost patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether they be speech, form and color, or the sensations of suffering and pleasure, he remains free from discrimination; he does not discriminate, he is neither angry nor joyful, and regarding all sentient beings, he is free from conceptualization. Thus he attains the purity and equality of the foremost patience.

"Just as space does not move yet pervasively moves, does not tremble yet pervasively trembles, so too the bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all karma, conditioned states, and formative activities, neither moves nor trembles in body or mind, yet pervasively moves and pervasively trembles."

"Just as space is pure and free from defilement, so too the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abiding in the purity and equanimity of the foremost dharma-patience attains perfect purity of body and mind regarding all conditioned phenomena."
"Just as space nurtures all sentient beings, so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (paramārtha-kṣānti) nurture all sentient beings."

"Just as space cannot be burned by the fire at the end of a kalpa, nor destroyed by the waters or the winds at the end of a kalpa, so too the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, abiding in the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (paramārtha-kṣānti), until reaching unsurpassed bodhi, does not have his mind burned or destroyed by the blazing fires of the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion."

"Just as the pure sky holds the full moon on the fifteenth night, which radiates cool light so that the bodies and minds of sentient beings tormented by heat find refreshing peace, so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in the purity and equanimity of the foremost patience (paramārtha-kṣānti) calms all distress and agitation within his own majestic deportment, and likewise calms the heat of all afflictions in sentient beings."

"Just as the pure sky on the fifteenth night holds the perfectly full moon, surrounded by the multitude of stars, illuminating the four continents; so too, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the purity and equanimity of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), wherever he may abide, he is surrounded by devas, nāgas, and even kaṭapūtanas, radiating brilliant light."

"Just as when the pure sky is clear, on the fifteenth day of the month, the perfectly full moon illuminates the moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*) on a sea island, causing great water to flow forth from that jewel which fills the great ocean; even so, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). By means of this purity and equality of ultimate patience, he emits supreme light that shines upon all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and even kaṭapūtanas, causing them all to attain purity of virtuous mind. He gives rise to a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings, a heart of profound benefit, a heart that brings rest to suffering and affliction, a heart that causes them to abide in all happiness, a heart that contemplates the terrors of future lives, a heart detached from all evil, and a heart of diligent application toward all that is wholesome."

Because those spirits and deities have attained such superior and wholesome states of mind, they gradually and successively distance themselves from all that is unwholesome; as they become fully suffused with all wholesome waters, they are thus able to flow and fill the great ocean of nirvana.
“O virtuous ones!

You should observe these roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas: although they have not yet reached the ultimate state, because they abide in the purity and equality of the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), they have already surpassed all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are able to bring sentient beings to maturity through wholesome dharmas.”
In the past, when I was practicing as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, I constantly dwelt in the forest eating various sweet fruits.
At that time, there was a king named Kali who dismembered my body into eight pieces.

At that time, because I had skillfully cultivated the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), white milk flowed from the place where [my flesh] was cut. By means of these causes and conditions of patient endurance and ascetic practice, I brought to maturity immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, garuḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas.
At that time, immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, and even humans and non-humans, all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"O worthy ones! When I was formerly born as a human being in a place that was not difficult, performing such ascetic practices was not considered difficult.

However, when I was previously born in a difficult place and took the body of a rabbit, for the sake of providing meat for a rishi, I leaped into a great mass of fire. Because I had skillfully cultivated the foremost patience of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*)—which is pure and equanimous—the great mass of fire was transformed into a lotus pond."
At that time, the body of that rabbit lay upon the flower pedestal; by virtue of the causes and conditions of his ascetic practice, this great trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Then Śakra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even the kaṭapūtanas, as well as various ṛṣis, humans, non-humans, and others, made diverse offerings and said to me:
"If you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, at that time we too shall certainly receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"O virtuous ones! Because I was formerly able to skillfully cultivate the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*) while in the body of a rabbit, I have already attained the unique offerings that are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

Therefore, at that time, the Brahmā and Śakra kings, the Four World-Protecting Kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even humans and non-humans, all used various kinds of superior incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, music, many jewels, banners, and flags to offer praise, veneration, and rare offerings—things which Arhats do not possess today.
"O noble ones! A bodhisattva thus skillfully practices and abides in the purity and equality of the ultimate patience (*paramārtha-kṣānti*).
The meaning of these four phrases shall now be explained:
The "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha) is so called because it enables one to reach the other shore; thus, by this definition, it is named the Ultimate Meaning.

"Patience" (kṣānti) is so called because one perceives that the aggregates (skandha) of the three realms are ultimately empty, and perceives that the elements (dhātu) and sense-bases (āyatana) are ultimately empty; thus, by this definition, it is named patience.

"Purity" (viśuddhi) refers to the removal and purification of the path of afflictions, the path of karma, and the path of suffering within the three realms by means of noble wisdom; thus, by this definition, it is named purity.

"Equanimity" means that by means of noble wisdom, one attains knowledge of things as they truly are regarding the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within all phenomena operating in the three realms; because there is no path of afflictions, no path of karma, and no path of suffering, it is for this reason called "equanimity."
This is the first-level purity and equality of patience for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"O virtuous ones! Among those, what is the purity and equality of vigor?"

By means of this diligence, one can act as the cause for the pure equality of giving, up to acting as the cause for the pure equality of the *prajñāpāramitā*; through this, one is able to relinquish all views.
By means of this diligence, one can act as the cause for the pure equanimity of the four foundations of mindfulness, thereby surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
By means of this diligence, one can act as the cause for the four right efforts and the four bases of power, whereby one is able to abandon all afflictions.

By means of this diligence, one is able to act as the causal condition for the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), the four Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the severance of the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), and the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*), eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the pure equality of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By means of this diligence, one can act as the cause for the pure equality that brings sentient beings to maturity.
By means of this diligence, one accumulates all roots of goodness in order to attain the immeasurable, supreme dharmas of the Buddhas.

By means of this diligence, one is able to cultivate immeasurable wisdom of skillful means; immeasurable wisdom of vows becomes increasingly superior, as one cultivates a vast accumulation of great merit.
By means of this diligence, he takes birth according to his vows to teach and benefit others.
Because of his diligence, while dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven palace, he observes the proper timing to leave that palace, and with perfect awareness and clarity, he enters the mother’s womb.
By virtue of his diligence, he emerged safely from his mother’s right side in the Lumbinī grove.
By virtue of his diligence, having taken seven steps, he caused the great earth, along with its mountains and seas, to tremble.
By virtue of his diligence, he accepted the bathing ritual performed by the Naga kings Nanda and Upananda, brothers;
by virtue of his diligence, as a youth, he manifested all manner of artistic skills and extraordinary talents in his play.
By virtue of his diligence, he remained within the palace untainted by the five desires.
By virtue of his diligence, at midnight he scaled the city walls and proceeded toward the secluded forest.
By virtue of his diligence, he went to the abodes of the seers Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma to practice offerings.
By means of diligence, he practiced those difficult and painful austerities for six years;
by means of diligence, he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"By means of diligence, he turns the great wheel of Dharma, enabling immeasurable humans and devas to realize the noble path.
This is called the purity and equality of diligence. O virtuous ones!"

By means of this diligence, I have now convened this great assembly on Mount Kharatī at the dwelling place of the sages and seers. All the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, have been made to gather here; likewise, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, mahoragas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and others, equal in number to the atoms within a buddha-field, have all come to this great assembly for the sake of hearing the Dharma. This is called the purity and equality of diligence.
"O virtuous ones!

If one were to divide the waters of the four great oceans into individual drops, and if, according to that number of drops, one were to cultivate diligence with complete purity and equanimity, such as would enable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others to fulfill the *vīryapāramitā*, this is called the purity and equanimity of diligence."
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra: The Candragarbha-parivarta, Scroll 5.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 51.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
The Fourteenth Division: The Moon Treasury, Chapter Eight, Part Two: "The Chapter on All Evil Ghosts and Spirits Attaining Reverent Faith.
"O virtuous ones! Among those [qualities], what is the purity and equanimity of dhyāna?

There is dhyāna shared by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas; there is dhyāna shared by pratyekabuddhas and Tathāgatas but not shared with śrāvakas; there is Tathāgata-dhyāna that is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and there is Tathāgata-dhyāna shared with śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings.
"O virtuous ones! Regarding that, what dhyāna is shared by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas?

If there are sentient beings who seek happiness and wish to leave suffering behind, observing the fears of future lives, and while practicing pure and impartial generosity, there should be those who correctly enter and correctly resolve their minds; one should go to such persons, cultivate a humble mind, and provide them with compliant offerings, so as to hear the true Dharma from them."

Having heard [the teaching], they understand its meaning and practice in accordance with the Dharma; their minds delight in detachment, and as the flow of continuity proceeds, these persons, having become detached from all desires and unwholesome states, enter the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
They enter the second dhyāna, which is without directed thought or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.
They enter the third dhyāna, which is free from joy, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and supreme clear comprehension.

Abandoning both suffering and pleasure, and having previously stilled sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

Transcending all perceptions, one extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance and does not attend to perceptions of diversity, thereby entering the sphere of infinite space. Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness. Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

"O worthy ones! One who dwells in the first dhyāna extinguishes the thorn of sound; one who dwells in the second dhyāna extinguishes the thorns of applied and sustained thought; one who dwells in the third dhyāna extinguishes the thorn of joy; and one who dwells in the fourth dhyāna extinguishes the thorns of inhalation and exhalation."

One who dwells in the sphere of infinite space eliminates the thorn of form; one who dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness eliminates the thorn of space; one who dwells in the sphere of nothingness eliminates the thorn of consciousness; one who dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception eliminates the thorn of nothingness; and one who dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling eliminates the thorn of perception and feeling. This is called the eight liberations of a practitioner of dhyāna, in which the activities of body, speech, and mind have attained repose.

The Arhat who has attained the samādhi of cessation and reached the further shore, by relying on this state, attains the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, and the four unhindered analytical knowledges; by relying on this state, he attains śamatha and vipaśyanā.

This is not the pure equality of a bodhisattva’s practice; it does not attain the four means of attraction, the four Brahma-abodes, the three ways in which there is nothing to guard, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, or the knowledge of all modes of knowledge. This is called the equality of the perfection of meditation that is common to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas.

"O virtuous ones! Suppose there is a person who first practices the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, then regresses and enters the practice of the Śrāvaka vehicle. This person enters the first dhyāna, up to and including the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Relying on these absorptions, they attain the three gates of liberation and the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), yet they do not attain the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the three ways in which there is nothing to guard (*trārakṣya*), nor even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is called the equality of dhyāna shared by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas."

"O noble ones! If there is a person who, having previously practiced the Mahāyāna, subsequently regresses and enters the Śrāvaka-yāna, and this person enters the first dhyāna up to the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and attains the three gates of liberation, the four means of attraction (saṃgraha-vastu), and the four sublime abodes (brahma-vihāra), yet does not attain the three forms of self-protection (trīṇi arakṣāṇi), nor even the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—this is called the 'equality of dhyāna' shared by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas."
“O noble ones! Regarding those meditative concentrations shared and unshared by Pratyekabuddhas and Tathāgatas with Śrāvakas:

if there are sentient beings who, having long cultivated the Śrāvaka vehicle, subsequently enter the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, such persons have not previously attained the first dhyāna; yet once it is attained, they contemplate and seek the law of causes and conditions (pratītyasamutpāda). Continuing thus up to the fourth dhyāna, they contemplate and seek the law of causes and conditions, entering the samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness. By means of those samādhis, they contemplate the relinquishing [of grasping] and realize the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti). Through those three gates of liberation, they enter the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). In all states, they contemplate and seek the Pratyekabuddha Dharma, seeking the extinction without remainder of the three types of formations within the ultimate truth of causes and conditions, which is the cessation of perception and feeling. This is called the equality of dhyāna of the Pratyekabuddhas shared and unshared with Śrāvakas.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who has not yet studied the Śrāvaka vehicle but has well studied the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and this person enters the first dhyāna to contemplate and seek the law of causes and conditions, relying on the first dhyāna they transcend the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments, entering the cessation of the three activities—the ultimate cessation without remainder. This is called the equality of dhyāna shared by Pratyekabuddhas and Tathāgatas, but not shared with Śrāvakas.

"O virtuous ones! Suppose there is a person who, having not yet studied the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, first studies the Mahāyāna but then regresses and enters the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
This person enters the first dhyāna and, within that meditative state, contemplates and seeks the Dharma of causes and conditions."
In this way, up to the fourth dhyāna, one contemplates and seeks the law of causes and conditions;
likewise, throughout all stages of the four formless absorptions, one contemplates and seeks the law of causes and conditions.

Thus, through the cessation of these three modes of activity—the ultimate cessation without remainder—one attains the unspeakable samādhi by means of the three gates of liberation; in that state, there is no arising.
It is without extinction; it is neither realized nor cultivated, neither existent nor non-existent;
it is neither this shore nor the other shore, neither darkness nor light; it is neither measurable, nor conceptualized, nor non-conceptualized.
This is called the *khagaviṣāṇa-kalpa*. *Khaga* means "rhinoceros" and *viṣāṇa* means "horn"—the Pratyekabuddha of the world.
The solitary field of merit is called the supreme, ultimate truth of the purity and equality of dhyāna, shared and unshared by pratyekabuddhas and tathāgatas, as well as śrāvakas.

In that state, the entire ocean of existence within birth and death is severed; the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned formations are all brought to an end. Being able to personally awaken to and know the ineffable meaning is called the supreme, ultimate truth of the purity and equality of dhyāna.
"O virtuous ones! Among those, what is the Tathāgata’s first-principle dhyāna that is pure, equal, and not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"

If the Tathāgata enters the first dhyāna, he does not enter it by relying on the aggregates (*skandha*), nor by relying on the sense bases (*āyatana*), nor by relying on the elements (*dhātu*). He does not enter it by relying on the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element; he does not enter it by relying on the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he does not enter it by relying on the element of cessation. He does not enter it by relying on the present or future worlds; he does not enter it by relying on arising or ceasing; he does not enter it by relying on existence or non-existence. Without any basis and not relying on a basis—just as the Tathāgata enters the first dhyāna, so it is with the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and likewise with the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

When the Tathāgata enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he does not rely on the aggregates (*skandha*) or the sense bases (*āyatana*), nor even upon any support (*āśraya*). This entry of the Tathāgata into the meditative absorption of cessation is called the Tathāgata’s ultimate (*paramārtha*) dhyāna-purity and equanimity, which is not shared with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"O worthy ones! Among those, what is the Tathāgata’s pure and equal dhyāna, which is shared with śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings?

When the Tathāgata enters the first worldly dhyāna up to the fourth worldly dhyāna, the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas are also able to enter the first worldly dhyāna up to the fourth. Furthermore, when the kalpa of all sentient beings is nearing its end, they too have been able to enter the first worldly dhyāna up to the fourth."

Thereafter, due to the causes and conditions of their evil minds, they fall away from the practice of dhyāna; being hateful, cruel, and coarse, they do not contemplate the terrors of future lives, and lacking compassion for sentient beings, they consume their flesh and blood and head toward the three evil destinies.
"Furthermore, when the Tathāgata enters the first worldly dhyāna up to the fourth worldly dhyāna, all those sentient beings—whether devas, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, or hell-beings—think thus:
'In what place do the Tathāgata’s mind and mental factors operate? In what abode does he dwell? "

"By the power of the Buddha’s加持 (adhiṣṭhāna), all those sentient beings, down to the insects and ants, likewise know in accordance with reality the Buddha’s mind and mental factors as they abide in the first dhyāna, up to knowing them as they abide in the fourth dhyāna."
This, moreover, is the Tathāgata’s samādhi, which is equal and shared with all sentient beings.
This samādhi is impartial; it is not the domain of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is called the purity and equality of dhyāna.
"O worthy ones! Among those, what is the purity and equality of the vessel of wisdom? Wisdom is of two kinds: [the wisdom of phenomena and the wisdom of their meaning]."
First is mundane wisdom; second is supramundane wisdom.
O virtuous ones!
What is mundane knowledge?

It consists of secular scriptures, that which is spoken and compiled through oral discourse, the path of speech expressed through sounds, and that which is revealed by written characters as heard in various treatises.

Whether it be writing characters and phrases, calculation, arithmetic, or sealing; whether it be various methods of ascetic practice or the study of crafts—regarding all such diverse activities as these, whatever one seeks shall be accomplished.

All other three mundane applications of mindfulness—whether contact, feeling, perception, volition, or attention—all such things as these are not vessels for nirvāṇa; this is called the equality of the vessels of worldly knowledge.
"O worthy ones! Among those, what is the equality of the world as a vessel for wisdom?
O worthy ones!"

Regarding the equality of the world as a vessel for wisdom: it is the equality of the vessels for generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the wisdom derived from hearing.
"What is the equality of the worldly vessel of wisdom for giving?
O virtuous ones!

If there is a person who, for as long as they live, refrains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and all forms of intoxication such as drinking alcohol; and who dwells with a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, and a desire to rescue toward all sentient beings—such a person is a vessel for Nirvāṇa."
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the world's wisdom-vessel of giving. O virtuous ones!"
In that regard, what is the equality of the worldly vessel of ethical discipline and wisdom? O noble ones!

It is when one possesses a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, observes the terrors of future lives, and constantly abides in a mind of loving-kindness, a gentle mind, a mind intent on benefiting others, a mind free from enmity, a mind free from jealousy, a mind free from harshness, a mind free from double-tongued speech, a mind free from arrogance and negligence, and remains established in a mind of loving-kindness.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the world’s precepts, wisdom, and vessels. O virtuous ones!"
In this regard, what is the equality of the world’s receptacles of patience and wisdom?
O noble ones! It is when one hears the various kinds of harsh speech and purely coarse, savage words uttered by sentient beings.

Having heard it, they do not grasp it; they do not give rise to sudden violence, nor do they produce turbidity or manifest signs of anger; they are likewise able to endure all sentient beings and do not follow after the words or sounds that issue forth.
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the world’s receptacles for patience and wisdom. O virtuous ones!"

If one sees sentient beings commit evil deeds, transgressions, or sinful acts against what belongs to oneself—whether by destroying one’s form, sound, smell, taste, or touch, or by harming one’s body or life—one should always cultivate patience toward such beings and train as follows:
"These sentient beings have, since beginningless saṃsāra, habituated themselves to greed, hatred, and delusion; having been separated from spiritual friends, they have never practiced or studied.
I, however, am close to spiritual friends, I am able to practice and study, and I seek all forms of happiness."
If one does not give rise to anger or aversion toward any sentient being, that person attains all forms of happiness.

Therefore, having seen all those sentient beings, one does not grasp at them; one does not become violent, does not become turbid, and does not manifest signs of anger. This is called the equanimity of the vessel of worldly patience and wisdom.
“Virtuous ones! Among those, what is the equality of the world’s vessel for the wisdom of diligence?
Virtuous ones!”
If one diligently practices giving to sentient beings without interruption, and cultivates ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom without interruption—
O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the world’s vessel of diligence and wisdom.
"Virtuous ones, what among those is the equality of the world’s vessels for meditative concentration and wisdom?
Virtuous ones!"
If one enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna of the mundane realm, or enters the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the vessel of mundane meditative concentration and wisdom. "O virtuous ones!
Among those, what is the equality of the vessel of mundane wisdom consisting of hearing?
"O virtuous ones!

If one is capable of reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding such Mahāyāna teachings that correspond to this emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and if one explains them to others with pure speech, free from flattery and deceit, so that all afflictions, evil karma, and obscurations are exhausted, and one knows both the phenomena (*dharma*) and their meaning (*artha*)—such a person, knowing the phenomena and their meaning within those teachings, shall diligently strive day and night to seek unsurpassed wisdom."
"O virtuous ones!
This is called the equality of the vessel of wisdom consisting of the worldly wisdom of hearing. O virtuous ones!"
In that regard, what is the equality of the vessel for supramundane wisdom? Noble sirs!

If a son of good family does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not grasp at the eye or forms; does not grasp at eye-consciousness; does not grasp at eye-contact; and does not grasp at whatever suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arises conditioned by eye-contact—and likewise, up to and including, does not grasp at the mind or mental phenomena; does not grasp at mind-consciousness; does not grasp at mind-contact; and does not grasp at whatever suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arises conditioned by mind-contact.

In this way, one does not grasp the earth element, nor the water, fire, or wind elements; one does not grasp the space element, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
