At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the hosts of nāgas and asuras, saying:
"You should not fight; you ought to cultivate forbearance."
O Benevolent One!
If you can distance yourself from anger and achieve patience, you will swiftly attain ten states. What are these ten?
First, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who rules over the four continents as a sovereign king;
second, one becomes the celestial king Virūpākṣa;
third, one becomes the celestial king Virūḍhaka.
Fourth is the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
fifth is the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa;
sixth is the Heavenly King Śakra.
Seventh, the King of the Suyāma Heaven;
eighth, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven;
ninth, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
Tenth is the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations. O virtuous ones!
If one is fully endowed with patience, such a person will swiftly attain these ten proximate fruits of patience.

"Furthermore, sirs! If one is able to deeply cultivate patience so that it further increases and becomes fully perfected, you should know that such a person will further attain five states. What are these five?
First, the assembly of Brahmā;
second, the Great Brahmā King;
third, the fruits of the śrāvaka path.
Fourth, the pratyekabuddhas;
fifth, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. O virtuous ones!
If one can deeply endure and further increase this perfection, such a person will swiftly attain these five states.

Furthermore, if one fully practices patience, one will naturally and soon obtain all the supreme and wonderful five desires of the world; all necessities for livelihood will be completely provided, and if that person further reaches the point of cultivating the merit of patience, they will attain noble peace and happiness.

If there are those who are non-noble and of base character, who are fierce and arrogant by nature and constantly prone to anger, manifesting great wrath in the presence of many people, one should know that when such persons die and their lives end, they will fall into hell.
If, by some chance, they should escape from that hell and be born into the inferior realm of animals, they will take the form of lowly dragons or asuras.

If they are born among humans, they will be extremely base and lowly, with impaired faculties—either having elongated organs, being organless, possessing double organs, or having oversized organs; their appearance will be hideous, they will be lame or hunchbacked, and their bodies will be foul-smelling and filthy. They will be born into families such as those of *caṇḍālas* or performers who practice deceitful seduction, or into other such low-born households. Or they may be born in borderlands where clothing and food are scarce, born into lowly families, or in places devoid of fields of merit where they delight in performing various unwholesome deeds.
By these causes and conditions, such a person will successively fall again into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. "O virtuous ones!
I have now briefly explained the retribution for such intolerant anger."
O virtuous ones!
Because of anger, one increases immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas within the cycle of birth and death.
By reason of these causes and conditions, such a person will further fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
"O virtuous ones!

For this reason, I now address you all—the nāgas, asuras, and others—saying that for a long night you have each lived in mutual opposition. You all must now, before me and this great assembly who has gathered, each give rise to a mind of thorough patience toward one another, and you must extinguish the long-accumulated anger within your hearts."
If you cannot endure [this], it will inevitably cause you to obtain results that you do not desire; therefore, each of you should practice mutual forbearance.

If you can refrain from anger, strife, derision, litigation, and jealousy, and remain steadfast in self-restraint, then you shall certainly attain supreme and wondrous things, free from all faults and evils.
At that time, the entire assembly that had gathered all exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to receive the Buddha’s instructions in this way, and that you each exercise mutual forbearance toward one another in this manner, means that you shall obtain constant superior retribution within these four continents and be free from all evil matters."

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha again addressed the Dragon King Sāgara, the Asura King Rāhula, the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Asura King Vemacitrin, the Dragon King Varuṇa, the Asura King Muchilinda, the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita, and the Asura King Vajravairocana, instructing them with these verses:
"You have received the prediction of enlightenment, The most supreme, not of any other vehicle;
Why, then, do you feel no shame or remorse Toward the Teacher?"
One who clutches at a raft while drowning, followed by a great multitude into a swift current—
such is one who abandons the Most Excellent One, who is then loathed and despised by all.
Whether it be an ordinary dragon or an asura, through anger they are loathed and despised.
You who are sublime beings, you should all abandon anger and wrath.
Loving-kindness leads one to the good realms and allows one to fully enjoy all sensual pleasures;
loving-kindness enables one to leave behind all hardships and act as a virtuous friend.
Loving-kindness enables one to attain great wisdom, And to rely upon a master of great brilliance;
Loving-kindness enables one to leave all evils behind, And causes others to view one with joy.
Through loving-kindness one attains great wealth, And is always able to bestow everything upon all.
Loving-kindness enables one to delight in the precepts and meditative concentration, and further attains the most supreme wisdom;
loving-kindness enables one to acquire skillful arts and learn all matters well;
through loving-kindness, in the most supreme place, one sits upright and transforms sentient beings.
Through loving-kindness one attains a supreme and wondrous body, complete with the marks and a handsome countenance;
through loving-kindness one possesses a sublime voice, which all people delight to hear;
through loving-kindness one gains virtuous kinsmen and companions, practicing the holy life free from jealousy.
Delighting in the Dharma and possessing a sense of shame and remorse, the wise person always rejoices with them.
Through loving-kindness one may attain official rank and sit upon a supreme throne;
one can pacify the evils of sentient beings and establish them on the path to enlightenment.
Loving-kindness can attain the ten stages, as well as patience and dhāraṇī;
loving-kindness can accomplish compassion and abandon all attachments.
Loving-kindness can attain the bases of spiritual power and encounter the enlightened Teacher.
Loving-kindness can attain a pure land, Pure and free from afflictions.
Loving-kindness can subdue all demons, Reaching the shore of Great Bodhi.
Among gods and humans, loving-kindness Can turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
Loving-kindness can transform sentient beings, placing them in the stations of the Three Vehicles;
loving-kindness can skillfully expound the Dharma, subduing all non-Buddhists.
Through the Eightfold Noble Path, loving-kindness delivers and liberates devas, humans, and others.
You shall all be able to enter the state of immortality.
Now I bestow upon you this *dhāraṇī* of the compassionate heart;
at the abodes of billions of Buddhas, I have heard it with single-minded devotion.
"By establishing your own retinue in a state of loving-kindness and patience,
and by giving rise to thoughts of compassion toward one another, you shall attain peace and happiness throughout the long night.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha spoke this mantra:
Tadyathā medini mahāmedini.
Ṛmī-tara-nu-vadate-mī-tara-rasī-mī-tara-kṣe.

You should teach it to your own retinues and those of others, so that they may pacify their anger and malevolent intentions."
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha had spoken this Dharani of Loving-kindness,
the Tathāgata exclaimed, “Excellent, excellent!
All those present in the great assembly— devas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, non-humans, and others— all likewise exclaimed:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the various devas each came to abide in a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of patience, a mind free from enmity, and a mind free from dispute, and they apologized to one another in turn.

The devas apologized to the nāgas, and the nāgas apologized to the devas; with hearts of loving-kindness, patience, freedom from enmity, freedom from contention, and freedom from dispute, they mutually confessed their transgressions.
The devas approached the asuras, and the asuras approached the devas, even going so far as to apologize.
The nāgas approached the asuras, and the asuras approached the nāgas, even going so far as to apologize.
The devas [applied themselves] toward the yakṣas, and the yakṣas toward the devas; even the expressions of apology were all as described above.

In this manner and in this way, the devas [applied themselves] toward the rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and kaṭapūtanas, abiding in a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of patience, a mind free from enmity, a mind free from strife, and a mind free from dispute.
Even the *kāṭapūtanas* directed their thoughts toward those devas, abiding in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*), and even their expressions of apology were as described above.
The nāgas directed their thoughts toward the yakṣas, and so on down to the *kāṭapūtanas*, abiding in a mind of loving-kindness, and even their expressions of apology were likewise.
From the yakṣas down to the kaṭapūtanas, their approach toward the nāgas—and even their offering of apologies—is likewise in every respect.
Even from the kaṭapūtanas toward the kaṭapūtanas, they abide in a mind of loving-kindness, and even their offering of apologies is likewise in every respect.

By virtue of the power of the Great Compassionate Heart Dhāraṇī, all devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth, will dwell in mutual states of loving-kindness, patience, freedom from enmity, freedom from litigation, freedom from strife, freedom from anger, and freedom from jealousy.

By reason of the power of this Great Compassion Dhāraṇī, all human beings will dwell in mutual kindness, patience, compassion, freedom from enmity, freedom from litigation, and freedom from strife. Furthermore, all animals—whether birds or beasts, even down to the most lowly and minute insects—will dwell in mutual kindness, patience, compassion, freedom from enmity, freedom from strife, and freedom from hostility.

At that time, the great assembly—including the devas down to all the khaṭvāṅga-pūtanas, humans, and non-humans—joined their palms toward the Buddha and paid him reverent homage. Simultaneously, with one voice, they spoke these words:

“Having all received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, we have mutually apologized for our transgressions and have each dwelt in a mind of loving-kindness, patience, compassion, freedom from enmity, and freedom from contention. We all now likewise offer our apologies to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Whatever transgressions we have committed in the past against the World-Honored One through body, speech, or mind;
those committed against the Dharma and the Sangha through body, speech, or mind;
and even those committed against a single disciple of the World-Honored One through body, speech, or mind—[all such offenses].

Even those who have shaved their heads for the Buddha, donned a fragment of the *kāṣāya*, yet engage in contrary conduct and are unworthy vessels of the Dharma—whatever transgressions they have committed through body, speech, or mind—all such sins shall be sincerely repented before the Buddha as they cultivate the precepts and dignified deportment.
We pray that the Buddha will grant us forgiveness and accept our repentance, so that we may come to abide in the majestic deportment of the precepts.

Furthermore, from this day forward, even until the time when we shave our heads and don a fragment of the *kāṣāya* robe and act as transgressors, we shall regard all those who are disciples of the Buddha’s voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*) as our teachers; we shall protect, nurture, and provide them with everything they require, ensuring they never lack for anything.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent! You noble men have accomplished patience.

As for whatever transgressions you have committed against me, the Buddha, through body, speech, or mind; whatever transgressions you have committed against the Dharma or the Saṅgha; whatever transgressions you have committed against even one of my śrāvaka disciples through body, speech, or mind; or whatever transgressions you have committed against those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned a fragment of the kāṣāya through body, speech, or mind—you must each deeply contemplate such karmic offenses and sincerely repent them. Then they shall all be extinguished, and you will not suffer their evil retribution.”

In this way, you all should protect, uphold, and nurture my Dharma; even those who have left the household life for my sake, having shaved their hair and donned a fragment of the kāṣāya robe, though they do not maintain the prohibitive precepts—you all should likewise protect, uphold, and nurture them.
If you are able to protect, uphold, and nurture these individuals, it is truly worthy of praise.

"If any of my śrāvaka disciples are fully endowed with the precepts, and are likewise complete in their extensive learning, renunciation, wisdom, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, you all should protect, uphold, and nurture them."
Those who, by virtue of their own past roots of goodness and merit, have successfully obtained offerings are already fortunate.

However, if there are sentient beings in future ages who lack wisdom and merit, yet shave their heads and don a fragment of the kāṣāya robe—whether they do not receive the prohibitive precepts or violate them, and thus fail to accord with various wholesome dharmas—I shall act as a virtuous guide for such individuals, out of compassion and for their benefit, so that those who protect and nurture them may obtain immeasurable merit.
Why is this? In future ages there will be wicked sentient beings who perform only meager virtuous deeds toward the Triple Gem.

Whether practicing generosity, observing the precepts, or cultivating various meditative concentrations, they will become kings by virtue of such slight roots of goodness; yet they will be foolish and ignorant, devoid of shame and remorse, with rampant arrogance, lacking compassion, and failing to contemplate the terrifying consequences of the afterlife.

They will harass all my śrāvaka disciples, beating, binding, reviling, or even forcing them into service to provide for their needs; they will seize their food, drink, robes, bowls, medicinal requisites, monasteries, gardens, and fields; they will cast them into prison, exile them, or punish them—even those who have merely shaved their heads and donned a fragment of the *kāṣāya* shall be treated in this same way.

Furthermore, there will be ministers and judicial officials who are foolish and ignorant, devoid of shame and modesty, lacking compassion, and heedless of the terrifying consequences in future lives. They will harass and disturb my śrāvakas, even to the point of imprisoning them, banishing them, or subjecting them to punishment; they will treat in the same manner even those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned fragments of the kāṣāya robe for my sake.
"I now entrust all these renunciants to you; do not allow them to perish from hunger, thirst, or loneliness.
At that time, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya rose from his seat and spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, World-Honored One!"
If those kṣatriyas, or brahmins, vaiśyas, or śūdras—such persons as these—should harass and disturb the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples, how much demerit would they incur?

Setting aside the matter of observing the precepts, suppose one has shaved off their hair and beard for the sake of the Buddha and donned a fragment of the kāṣāya robe; yet, having not received the prohibitive precepts, or having received them and then violated them, how much sin does one incur by causing distress to such a person?
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! Kauṇḍinya!"
"Do not inquire about this matter.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Bhagavat of Great Virtue!..."
I only pray that you will speak of it,
O Great Virtuous Sugata!
I only pray that you will speak of it!

If there is one who has shaved off their hair and beard for the sake of the Buddha and donned the saffron robes, yet has not received the prohibitive precepts or, having received them, has violated them—if a Kṣatriya king were to cause him distress, harass him, revile him, beat him, or bind him, how much demerit would he incur?
The Buddha said, “Great Brahmā!
I shall now briefly explain it for you.”
If there were someone who drew blood from the bodies of ten trillion Buddhas,
what do you think? Would the person’s transgression not be great?
The Great Brahma King said:

"If a person incurs the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) by shedding the blood of even a single Buddha, they will already fall into the Avīci Great Hell in numbers so vast and immeasurable as to be beyond calculation; how much more so for one who sheds the blood of ten trillion Buddhas!"
"In the end, no one at all would be able to fully describe the retribution for that person's karmic offenses, except for the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "Great Brahmā!"

If there are those who harass, revile, beat, or bind one who has shaved their head for my sake and wears a fragment of the kāṣāya—whether they have not received the precepts or have received them but violate them—the offense incurred is greater than that [of the former].

Why is this? Because such a person has left the household life for my sake, having shaved their head and donned a fragment of the *kāṣāya*; even if they have not received the precepts or have violated them, this person is still able to show the path to *nirvāṇa* to all devas and humans. This person has already attained respectful faith within the Triple Gem, surpassing all ninety-five heterodox paths.
Such a person will surely be able to enter nirvana quickly, surpassing all lay householders, with the sole exception of those householders who have attained the stage of patience (kṣānti).
Therefore, gods and humans ought to make offerings to them; how much more so for those who are fully able to uphold the prohibitive precepts and bring their three karmas into accord!

"O worthy ones! Should any Kṣatriya kings, ministers, or judicial officials see one who has gone forth in my Dharma committing great sinful karma—such as great killing, great theft, great unchastity, great lying, or other unwholesome acts—they should merely expel such a person from the kingdom, city, or village in accordance with the law. They must not permit them to remain in the monastery, nor may they participate in the communal affairs of the Saṅgha. No offerings or requisites should be shared with them; yet they must not be beaten, for it is improper to do so."
Furthermore, one should not insult them with verbal karma, nor should any physical punishment be inflicted upon their bodies.

If one intentionally violates the Dharma by penalizing them, that person will fall away from liberation and be reborn among the lower classes; they will be severed from all the wholesome paths of humans and devas and will certainly head toward the Avīci Hell—how much more so for one who beats those who have gone forth as Buddhist practitioners and maintain the precepts!

At that time, there were also all the devas, all the nāgas, and even all the kaṭapūtanas and the entire great assembly who had gathered; having attained superior faith, reverence, respect, and a sense of wonder toward the Three Jewels, they further spoke these words:

“From this day forward, we shall all protect, uphold, and nurture the True Dharma of the World-Honored One, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—even those who have violated the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, we shall likewise embrace and protect them. Even those who have shaved off their hair and beards for the sake of the Buddha, donned fragments of the kāṣāya robe, yet have not received the prohibitive precepts and possess no stores of merit—we shall regard them as our teachers, protecting, nurturing, and providing them with all necessities, so that they may be fully provided for.”

If any kings see those who have gone forth from home for the sake of the Buddha and uphold the prohibitive precepts, or even those who have shaved off their hair and beards and donned a fragment of the saṃghāṭī robe but do not receive the precepts, or having received them, violate them and possess no accumulation of merit—should such persons be punished for their offenses against the body by being whipped according to the circumstances of their deeds, we shall no longer protect, support, or nourish them.

When a king thus abandons his kingdom, because of that abandonment, various forms of deceit, strife, pestilence, famine, and warfare will arise together within that land; untimely winds and rains, droughts, and scorching heat will damage the crops.

Furthermore, if we were to abandon that land, we should diligently employ skillful means to cause all the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples residing in that land to go to other lands, thereby leaving that land empty and devoid of fields of merit.

If there are disciples of the Blessed One’s śrāvaka community, even those who merely wear a fragment of the saffron robe, and if officials should whip them and the Kṣatriya king does not protect them, we too shall depart from that land.
They further spoke these words:
"We shall now all join together, each according to our capacity, to diligently perform various offerings to the World-Honored One.

At that time, by the power of the causes and conditions arising from the simultaneous resolution of the devas, nāgas, and even all the kaṭapūtanas, all the mountains within these four continents immediately transformed into mountains of the seven treasures, solely for the purpose of making offerings to the World-Honored One.

All the trees, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits likewise transformed into the seven treasures; from these flowers and fruits further emerged various sublime and wondrous articles of offering, and the five musical tones were played as an act of worship.

All medicinal herbs and sprouts growing upon the earth within the four continents likewise all transformed into the seven treasures as an offering; furthermore, the entire earth-element of these four continents transformed into ground of blue lapis lazuli as an offering.

Those devas and nāgas, up to and including the kaṭapūtanas—everything existing within the four continents, from the highest reaches down to the entire realm of desire—each made offerings according to their respective capacities.
There was a rain of various jewels, various flowers, various garments, various necklaces, and various celestial, exquisite flower-parasols, banners, and streamers as offerings.
Some made offerings by holding various celestial, exquisite banners and pennants, jeweled parasols, gold threads, pearls, necklaces, mani-jewels, and precious vessels.
Some made offerings to the World-Honored One with music using various kinds of lutes, harps, *konghou*, flutes, transverse flutes, *qigu* drums, *lugu* drums, and *leigu* drums.

Some made offerings through the sounds of various songs and music; some made offerings by raining down various musical instruments; and others made offerings by adorning the land with various kinds of ornaments.

All those who dwell within the four continents—humans, non-humans, and even all insects, both large and small—all see and hear [this]. All their painful sensations cease, and they give rise to pleasant sensations; according to their various physical contacts and perceptions, they obtain sufficiency in happiness and attain a rare, unprecedented state of mind, gaining deep reverence and faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity for all sentient beings, acted to bring them to maturity.
"All those sounds and languages are empowered by the noble ones."

All such speech as that of humans and non-humans, as well as the sounds produced from within the jewels, and the sounds produced by branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, lutes, harps, *konghou*, flutes, transverse flutes, *qigu* drums, *chigu* drums, and thunder-drums—all these are empowered by the holy power.

All of them attained a marvelous and unprecedented voice, empowered by the establishment [of truth], namely: form is empty of form, sensation is empty of sensation, perception is empty of perception, formations are empty of formations, and consciousness is empty of consciousness.

In this way, the eye-base is empty of the eye-base; the ear, nose, tongue, and body bases are empty of the ear, nose, tongue, and body bases; and the mind-base is empty of the mind-base. Likewise, the form-base is empty of the form-base;
the sound, odor, taste, and tangible-object bases are empty of the sound, odor, taste, and tangible-object bases; and the mental-object-base is empty of the mental-object-base.
In this way, the eye-element is empty of the eye-element, up to the consciousness-element being empty of the consciousness-element.

Thus one knows that the body is pure through detachment from desire; one knows that all phenomena are pure through detachment from desire; one knows that the realm of all phenomena has the characteristic of detachment from desire; and one knows that all phenomena are suchness.
One who knows thus is unmoved by emptiness; such a person is capable of rescuing all sentient beings from their conceptualizations and brings them to liberation within all conditioned phenomena.

Regarding the perception of sentient beings, the perceptions of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; from the perception of the eye-base up to the perception of the consciousness-element—such a person is thus capable of establishing all sentient beings within the unconditioned realm of the three vehicles.
“How does a practitioner demonstrate and discern those various dharmas?

It is by practicing internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.”

Furthermore, there is the emptiness of phenomena in their own nature (*dharmadharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-phenomena in their own nature (*adharmādharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), the emptiness of phenomena in their own nature as self-phenomena (*svadharmasvadharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), and the emptiness of phenomena in their own nature as other-phenomena (*paradharmaparadharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*).

If one can thus cultivate and discern this emptiness of all phenomena, such a person is capable of establishing all sentient beings, even unto the ultimate, in the unconditioned realm of the three vehicles.
“By what dharma-gate do those practitioners come to know inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
It is by means of the gate of liberation that is emptiness itself that they are able to cultivate the discernment of internal, external, and other such phenomena.”
What are called internal and external phenomena?
Internal phenomena refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The practitioner knows the eye as it truly is: the eye is empty; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of these dharmas.
Even up to the knowledge that the mind is empty of mind—neither an accumulation, nor indestructible, nor graspable.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is thus.
This is called internal emptiness.
"In this way, the practitioner should know external phenomena as they truly are—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
The practitioner knows form as it truly is: empty of form, and so on, up to mental objects as empty of mental objects; they are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they are ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called "external emptiness."
"A practitioner should know this as it truly is: what is called 'internal and external emptiness'?
Internal and external phenomena refer to the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases."
The practitioner knows, as it truly is, that the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) are empty; they are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they cannot be grasped.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is called internal-and-external emptiness.
In this way, a practitioner should know things as they truly are: what is called "emptiness of emptiness"?
Emptiness refers to the emptiness of all phenomena.
Because it is empty, it is emptiness; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
"In this way, a practitioner should know it as it truly is: what is called the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*)?
The eastern direction is empty of the eastern direction, and so on up to the four intermediate directions; they are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they are ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is thus.
This is called the Great Emptiness.
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'emptiness of the ultimate meaning' (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?
The ultimate meaning is what is known as nirvāṇa; thus, nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa itself, for it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"A practitioner should know this as it truly is: what is called 'the emptiness of the conditioned' (saṃskṛta-śūnyatā)?

Conditioned phenomena refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are empty; they are not accumulated, they cannot be destroyed, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned.
"A practitioner should know this as it truly is: what is called 'emptiness of the unconditioned' (asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā)?

That which is without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without change is called the unconditioned. Because the unconditioned is unconditioned, it is empty; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is thus.
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
"A practitioner such as this should understand according to reality: what is called 'ultimate emptiness' (atyanta-śūnyatā)?
'Ultimate' refers to the fact that all phenomena are ultimately unobtainable; they are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called ultimate emptiness.
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'emptiness of that which has no beginning' (anavarāgra-śūnyatā)?
It is such that coming and going cannot be apprehended; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of that which has no beginning.
"A practitioner should know this as it truly is: what is called 'emptiness of dispersion' (anavakāra-śūnyatā)?
It is without anything to be grasped or abandoned; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of dispersion.
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'emptiness of intrinsic nature' (prakṛti-śūnyatā)?

The intrinsic nature of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is not made by śrāvakas, not made by pratyekabuddhas, and not made by Tathāgatas. This emptiness of dharma-nature is not an accumulation; it is indestructible and cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know things as they truly are: what is called 'emptiness of self-characteristic'?

That which is afflicted and disintegrating is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*); that which is capable of feeling is the characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*); that which grasps characteristics is the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*); that which performs conditioned activity is the characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*); and that which cognizes is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*). In this way, all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, are empty of their own self-characteristics; they are not accumulations, they cannot be destroyed, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is thus.
This is called the emptiness of self-characteristics.
“A practitioner who acts in this way should know things as they truly are: what is called the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

‘All phenomena’ refers to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; from the eye up to the mind; from forms up to phenomena; and the consciousnesses produced by the conditions of the eye and forms, up to the consciousness produced by the conditions of the mind and phenomena—all these conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are called ‘all phenomena. Those phenomena are empty; they are not an accumulation, they are indestructible, and they are ungraspable.”
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of all phenomena.
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'the emptiness of the unobtainable' (anupalambha-śūnyatā)?
All phenomena are unobtainable; they are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
"A practitioner such as this should know things as they truly are: what is called the 'emptiness of non-existence' (abhāva-śūnyatā)?
It refers to all non-entities that are unobtainable, which are not accumulations, indestructible, and ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence.
"A practitioner should know this as it truly is: what is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*)?
Within a combination there is no entity; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
Non-entities are empty of non-entities; entities are empty of entities. They are not accumulations, they are indestructible, and they are ungraspable."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'the emptiness of phenomena (dharma) and their characteristics'?
'Phenomena' refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*). The five aggregates are empty; they are not a collection, they cannot be destroyed, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena. This is called the emptiness of phenomena in their own characteristics (*dharmadharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*).
"A practitioner who acts in this way should know it as it truly is: what is called 'the non-existence of phenomena' and the 'emptiness of the characteristics of non-existent phenomena'?

'Non-existent phenomena' refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). These unconditioned phenomena are empty; they are not an accumulation, they are indestructible, and they are ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is thus.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence and the characteristic of non-existence.
"A practitioner such as this should know things as they truly are: what is called 'the emptiness of self-dharmas in themselves'?
All dharmas are empty of their own nature; this emptiness is not produced by wisdom, nor is it produced by views; it is not an accumulation, it is indestructible, and it is ungraspable."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of dharmas being empty of their own characteristics.
"A practitioner should understand this as it truly is: what is called 'the emptiness of other phenomena and the characteristics of other phenomena'?

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma abides, its characteristics abide, its position abides, and its realm abides, just like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Its nature and characteristics are eternally present, without change or deviation. These phenomena are empty; they are not an accumulation, they are indestructible, and they cannot be grasped."
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is such.
This is called the emptiness of other phenomena and the characteristics of other phenomena.

A practitioner such as this should know things as they truly are; having known them, they are able to cause sentient beings to abandon the notion of "sentient beings," to abandon all notions of formations, perceptions, feelings, forms, and consciousness, to abandon notions of the eye up to the mind, and to abandon notions of form up to phenomena. Thereafter, they establish all sentient beings within the unconditioned realm of the three vehicles.
"If there is a practitioner who realizes these phenomena as they truly are through direct perception, they are said to be 'well-cultivated.
For those sentient beings who have previously practiced these teachings, this foremost sound of the most profound Dharma enters their faculty of hearing."
There may be sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, yet even such sounds of the Dharma enter their ears.

Or there may be those who behold the Buddha and gaze upon him with single-minded devotion; for them, all inexhaustible roots of goodness will manifest before them, until they attain the stage of non-retrogression, becoming great vessels of the Dharma by perfecting the ten powers and fearlessnesses.
"There may be sentient beings for whom the sound of impermanence enters their faculty of hearing; or the sound of suffering, the sound of emptiness, the sound of non-self,
the sound of the threefold restraint, the sound of the four foundations of mindfulness, the sound of the four right efforts, the sound of the four bases of power,
the sound of the five faculties, the sound of the five powers, and the sound of the seven factors of enlightenment."
The sound of the eightfold path, the sound of the *tattvārtha-śāstra*, the sound of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the sound of the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*),
the sound of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the sound of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), the sound of dhyāna, the sound of liberation (*vimokṣa*),

the sound of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the sound of the six *pāramitās*, the sound of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), the sound of samādhi, dhāraṇī, and patience (*kṣānti*), and the sound of the śrāvakas.
The sound of the vehicle of the Hearers, the sound of the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, the sound of the Great Vehicle, the sound of the stage of non-retrogression,

the sound of the exhaustion of karmic obstructions, the sound of the exhaustion of afflictive obstructions, the sound of the exhaustion of sentient-being obstructions, the sound of the exhaustion of dharma obstructions,
the sound of the adornment of the merits of conditioned lands, the sound of the purity of the unconditioned mind, and the sound of great compassion.
The voice of great compassion; the voice of the three forms of non-protection; the voice of the four fearlessnesses; the voice of the ten powers;
the voice of the eighteen unique qualities; the voice of those in their final birth before Buddhahood; the voice of the ten stages; the voice of the final body; the voice of subduing Māra;
the voice of unsurpassed wisdom; the voice of turning the wheel of Dharma; appearing according to those who are to be saved.
The sound of divine transformations, the sound of relinquishing all life-faculties, and the sound manifesting the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa to all sentient beings—

such sounds, each distinct from the others, enter the faculty of the ear. To these sentient beings, including those in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates enter their ears.
“Those sentient beings attained a most rare joy and leaped for joy; they gained supreme faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem.
As for those sentient beings’ affliction-obstructions, karmic obstructions, sentient-being obstructions, and dharma-obstructions, two-thirds of them were already exhausted.”

When those sentient beings hear this sound, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings who previously possessed evil minds all attain a supple mind, a mind of compassion, and a mind of wholesome karma; they come to perceive the terrifying things of future lives and plant the complete roots of goodness for gods and humans. By means of those various sounds, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings are led to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Among all those who uphold the pure precepts, some have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), up to and including those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness in the vehicle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhayāna*).
Furthermore, there were immeasurable, incalculable numbers of sentient beings who gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, there were immeasurable, incalculable numbers of sentient beings who attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"The Fire-Taste Asura pointed out Rāhula."
"This is my most supreme teacher, adorned with merit and wisdom.
The Buddha told them: "Cease all envy, anger, and malice;
entrust yourselves to this Eye of the Dharma, and receive it for the sake of its protection and preservation."
Those asuras were filled with joy and respectfully replied to the Honored Teacher:
"We shall protect the Eye of the Dharma until the Dharma remains for a long time.
We proclaim this most excellent, unhidden divine mantra of the Dharma."
Causing all those nāgas to lose the power of their pride.
At that time, the various nāgas each became enraged;
wishing to rely on the power of their pride, they sought to battle together with the asuras.
The Buddha addressed the various dragon kings and the lords of the asuras:
"Throughout the long night, each of you has been constantly fierce and unruly;
if you do not eliminate your anger and wrath, you shall not be vessels for any happiness."
Constantly touched by suffering, this inferior, foul,
and impure body lacks the integrity of its limbs and members, and is perpetually destitute of the necessities of life.
Upon hearing that these various sufferings all have anger as their root, [one should abandon it].
Harsh punishments and various shackles, Prisons, hunger, thirst, and the like— The sufferings of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals Are all endured because of anger.
One should practice patience toward all; For one who is patient, these [sufferings] cease to exist.
The husband has attained supremacy, possessing wealth, honor, and all desires.
You two groups of followers—the nāgas and the asuras—each practice patience; through patience, there is no evil.
The great assembly was filled with joy, and all offered praise;
having now heard these words, they have all attained patience (*kṣānti*).
The devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, and various spirits likewise rejoiced.
All have attained patience, gazing upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
Humans and animals alike, having attained patience, are all harmonious and submissive;
even birds, beasts, and small insects treat one another with compassion and pity.
The great assembly all joined their palms, gazing up at the words of the Guide:
"We have mutually sheltered one another, and all have come to abide in a mind of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, we, the great assembly, [rely] upon the Buddha, the Honored Guide."
Whatever sinful karma I have committed, Whether through transgressions of body,
speech, or mind, Toward the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or even a single individual—
O steadfast hero among men, I pray only that you will grant me your forgiveness.
Regarding all the evil deeds I have committed against the Dharma of the World-Honored One, I now come before you to confess them all; may the Buddha compassionately accept them.
At that time, the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings addressed the great assembly, saying:
When you have finished repenting for your evil karma, there will ultimately be no bitter retribution.
Even if one has shaved their hair but not received the precepts, and wears but a fragment of the kāṣāya robe,
yet conceives the thought of being a guide, they are superior among men.
The evil king obstructs the eye of the Dharma; Out of greed and delusion, he strikes the bhikṣus.
Just as shedding the blood of a guide, He shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
The great assembly spoke these words:
If there are wicked kings who harass the assembly of śrāvakas,
we shall abandon all matters in that country;
if there are śramaṇas in that land, we shall cause them to go elsewhere.
We shall destroy those lands, causing famine, war, and pestilence to arise.
To whatever kingdom a śramaṇa goes, we too shall go there,
ensuring that all obtain supreme happiness and are fully provided with clothing, food, and drink.
Toward that blazing Eye of Dharma, the Supreme among Men, they made offerings;
throughout the four continents without exception, everything was transformed into the seven treasures,
and there fell rains of various fragrant flowers, precious gems, and garments.
With songs, dances, music, and the like, they made offerings to the Teacher.
Whatever sentient beings saw or heard thereby attained sufficient joy;
through the Sage’s empowerment, all those sounds were transformed into the voice of the Buddha.
It is taught that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, impermanent, empty, and without self;
all dharmas of the three times are entirely empty and non-existent.
Both accumulation and dispersion are empty, and the same is true for the eye and consciousness.
Even unto the realm of mind and mental phenomena, The aggregates, the body, and all such dharmas are empty.
Knowing all dharmas in this way, One is then able to save sentient beings.
If one knows the three realms are empty, One can untie the bonds of sentient beings.
All the twelve links of existence are entirely empty of intrinsic nature.
Those who have practiced this Dharma in such a manner in the past will all attain patience upon hearing any sounds whatsoever.
With the power of wisdom and fearlessness, they abide upon the path to enlightenment.
Sentient beings of meager merit hear the sounds of conditioned phenomena;
immeasurable multitudes, through diligent effort, enter the practice of enlightenment.
Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
through the power of diligence, the blessings that adorn the Buddha-fields are purified.
You shall all become Buddhas and reach the further shore of all dharmas.
Having subdued Māra and his hosts, he brings down the rain of the True Dharma.
To the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, he can bestow the eye of the True Dharma.
You, all members of this assembly, quickly enter the city of peace and security.
Countless multitudes, hearing his voice, attained the path to Great Bodhi;
some attained the paths of the Two Vehicles, some obtained the bliss of gods and humans,
and some reached the fruit of Arhatship and samādhi.
"Such evil sentient beings, having attained a gentle mind and fearing all evil karma, abide in a heart of kindness and compassion. —
*Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Scroll 54.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll 55, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty. Chapter 17:
The Distribution in Jambudvīpa; Part 12 of the Candragarbha Section: Chapter 17, "The Distribution in Jambudvīpa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the entire great assembly who had gathered had conceived deep faith,
respect, and veneration toward the Triple Gem— attaining what they had never experienced before and no longer placing their trust in other deities—
addressed the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the King of the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Suyāma Heaven King, the Śakra Heaven King, the Four Great Heavenly Kings and their retinues;
the Sāgara Dragon King, the Anavatapta Dragon King, Rāhula Asura King, Vemacitra Asura King, and Śambhara Asura King.
...the Asura King Vajravairocana, the Kinnara King Mahādruma, the Gandharva General Rati, the Kumbhāṇḍa General Dantī,
the Yakṣa General Indra, the Preta King Śītaparṇa, the Piśāca King Lambauṣṭha, and Anagha...
The Pūtana King, the Khaṭvāṅga-śabda Pūtana King, and others spoke these words:
"O virtuous ones!..."

All of you have thus exhorted me to distribute and establish [this teaching] throughout all the lands, cities, palaces, royal capitals, villages, mountain crags, monasteries, gardens, ponds, wildernesses, and various groves of trees in this Jambudvīpa, entrusting it to you for protection and preservation so that no evil may arise.
Furthermore, may the vital essence of the great earth, the vital essence of sentient beings, and the vital essence of the True Dharma increase and flourish.

May the Buddha’s eye of the True Dharma long abide in the world, perpetuating the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed. May the evil realms be diminished and the paths of goodness increased, bringing peace, abundance, and joy to all within this Jambudvīpa.

For this reason, I now divide these four continents and entrust them to all you great celestial kings, all dragon kings, and even all the kṣata-putana kings. Each of you should resolve to renounce your own retinues and distribute yourselves to establish, protect, and nurture [these lands], together with all your celestial retinues, and even including the kṣata-putana kings and their entire retinues, so that they likewise establish, protect, and nurture every land and forest throughout this Jambudvīpa.

Therefore, you great celestial kings and your retinues, down to the king of the kaṭapūtanas and his retinues, should all with sincere hearts rejoice and offer praise throughout Jambudvīpa; do not be angry, do not harbor resentment, and do not give rise to wrath.

At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the devas of the form realm, the humans and devas of the desire realm, all the hosts of nāgas, all the gandharvas, and even all the kaṭapūtanas and others among the great assembly who had gathered there, joined their palms and each spoke these words:
“We all sincerely rejoice and respectfully accept the Buddha’s teaching, just as the World-Honored One has distributed and established it throughout this Jambudvīpa.”
"We have resolved to receive the Buddha’s instructions, to protect and nurture them, and to cause the Buddha’s True Dharma-eye to blaze forth.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"O noble beings! You should all thus speak with a sincere heart, expressing your desire for sympathetic joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those devas who subsist on the food of Dharma, the food of joy, and the food of dhyāna, saying:

“Within the great ocean waters of these four continents, across all the lands of the eighty thousand islands and territories, you gods who subsist on the food of Dharma, the food of joy, and the food of dhyāna, should protect and nurture my Dharma. You should protect and nurture those bhikṣus who abide in the Dharma, who accord with the Dharma and follow the Dharma, who have resolved to practice with their three karmas in harmony, and who have shaved off their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes.”
Then, those devas who subsist on the food of Dharma, the food of joy, and the food of dhyāna each spoke these words:
"We shall protect and uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas throughout the lands of the eighty thousand islands and continents within the great ocean."
If there are disciples of the Buddha who do not even keep women, livestock, fields, houses, or assets, we shall all protect, uphold, and provide for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised that deva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
The entire great assembly likewise praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candragarbha, saying:
“O pure gentleman who has attained full understanding!”

If I were to remain in the world, my assembly of śrāvakas would be fully endowed with ethical discipline, renunciation, learning, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; my True Dharma would flourish in the world, and even all devas and humans would be able to manifest the impartial True Dharma.
In the five hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus shall remain firm in liberation within my Dharma;
in the next five hundred years, my True Dharma of dhyāna-concentration and samādhi shall remain firm;
in the subsequent five hundred years, the practice of recitation and extensive learning shall remain firm.
In the next five hundred years, within my Dharma, many stūpas and monasteries will be constructed and shall remain firm and stable;
in the subsequent five hundred years, within my Dharma, there will be strife and litigation, and the pure Dharma will become obscured, diminished, and lose its stability.

“O Pure One! From this time forward, within my Dharma, there shall be those who, though they shave their hair and beards and wear the kāṣāya robes, violate the prohibitions and act contrary to the Dharma—these are merely pseudo-monks by name.”

If a donor makes offerings, provides support, and nurtures such a bhikṣu who is merely a name in name alone for having broken the precepts, I say that this person still attains an immeasurable, incalculable mass of great merit.
Why is this? Because they are still able to benefit many sentient beings; how much more so is this true for me, who am now present in the world?

"For example, if there were no genuine gold, silver would be priceless; if there were no silver, brass would be priceless; if there were no brass, counterfeit gems would be priceless; and if there were no counterfeit gems, red and white copper, iron, tin, lead, and pewter would be priceless treasures."

Thus, among all the worlds, the Buddha-jewel is unsurpassed; if there were no Buddha-jewel, the Pratyekabuddha would be unsurpassed; if there were no Pratyekabuddhas, the Arhat would be unsurpassed; if there were no Arhats, the other noble assemblies would be unsurpassed; if there were no noble assemblies, the ordinary persons who have attained meditative concentration would be unsurpassed; if there were no such practitioners of concentration, those who purely maintain the precepts would be unsurpassed; if there were no such pure-keepers of the precepts, even a bhikṣu of defiled precepts would be unsurpassed; and if there were no such defiled-precepted bhikṣus, a bhikṣu by name alone—who has shaved his hair and beard and wears the kāṣāya—would be the unsurpassed jewel, more honored than the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths, the foremost and supreme, worthy of receiving the world’s offerings as a field of merit for all beings.
Why is this? Because they are able to show sentient beings what is to be feared.
If there are those who protect, nurture, and establish such a person, that person will before long abide in the stage of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devas of the six heavens of the desire realm, saying:

"You all should diligently protect and uphold, each according to the portion assigned to you during the time of past Buddhas. Furthermore, from time to time within these four continents, you should diligently contemplate the meaning of the Buddha’s True Dharma, so that my Dharma may endure for a long time and the lineage of the Triple Gem may be maintained without interruption."
Then those devas each spoke these words: "So be it;
we accept your instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
The entire great assembly likewise praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"You and your retinues should, according to the respective portions assigned during the time of past Buddhas, once again provide protection, establish, and nurture my True Dharma."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings each spoke these words:
"We shall do as you command.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the gandharvas and others, saying:
“O virtuous ones!

"You and all the celestial seers who dwell within such groves as the Udumbara forest, the Āmra forest, the Jambu forest, the Harītakī forest, the Āmalaka forest, and the grapevine forest, together with the sons of gods from the palaces of the Four Great Kings, should contemplate the meaning of the Buddha’s True Dharma so that my Buddha-dharma may endure for a long time."
Then the gandharvas and others all said: "So it is,
O Great Virtuous Bhagavān!"
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King Sāgara, the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, the Dragon King Suprabha, the Dragon King Varuṇa, the Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Takṣaka, the Dragon King Ānanda, the Dragon King Aruṇa, and the Dragon King Ketumatī, saying:
"Each of you shall dwell in your respective original palaces within the great ocean and protect, uphold, and nurture my True Dharma."
Then the dragon kings and the others each said,
"We shall do as we are instructed.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon Kings Anavatapta, Supratiṣṭhita, Śuddhapārśva, Mālinī, Utpala, Gandharva, Meghasara, Aśani-pati, Mahāmāndāra, and Manojña, saying:
“Each of you shall dwell in your respective palaces and protect, uphold, and nurture my True Dharma.”
Then the dragon kings and the others each said,
"We shall do as we are instructed.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the generals Kumbhāṇḍa Dandika, Upadandika, Karaka, Mahāpārśva, Mahodara, Khujjuttarā, Vaḍiśā, Aṅgulimāla, Virūḍhaka, and Ekākṣa, saying:
"Each of you shall dwell in your respective palaces and protect, uphold, and nurture my True Dharma."
Then the great generals of the kumbhāṇḍas and the others each spoke these words: "So be it;
we shall receive your instructions.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great yakṣa generals Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Vajrapāṇi, Baladhvaja, Īśāna, Candana, Candrākṣa, Bhadrajit, and Hemavata, saying:
“Each of you shall dwell in your respective palaces to protect, uphold, and nurture my True Dharma.”
Then the yakṣa generals each spoke these words: "So be it;
we accept your instruction, O Blessed One, Great Virtuous One!"

We shall protect, sustain, and establish the World-Honored One’s True Dharma, and provide for the needs of the monks who abide in the Dharma; we shall likewise provide all necessary requisites even for those who have shaved their heads but do not maintain the precepts.

In order that the Buddha-dharma may endure for a long time; so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may be inherited without interruption; so that the three kinds of vital essence may increase; so as to bring rest to all strife, litigation, enmity, pestilence, famine, and scarcity; and to eliminate untimely droughts and the transgressions of the planets and constellations; and furthermore, so that the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples who are in accord with the three karmas and do not accumulate [defilements] shall be diligently nurtured.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
"You have acted thus for the sake of the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings within the three realms.
Then the entire great assembly also praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the piśācas who dwell in the wilderness, all the vetālas who dwell in empty houses, all the pūtanas who dwell in wild fields, and all the kaṭapūtanas who dwell among burial mounds and beside latrines, saying:
"Each of you shall protect, maintain, and nurture my True Dharma within your respective abodes."
Then Pīṭhila and the others each said,
"We shall do as you command.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again, saying:
"O virtuous ones!

All the devas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāga kings, asuras, and kumbhāṇḍas—just as the World-Honored One formerly assigned specific territories, cities, towns, villages, and dwellings to each, may you provide protection, establish yourselves therein, and sustain them according to those respective locations; I shall rejoice in this, and the entire great assembly shall likewise rejoice.

Furthermore, if there are gods, nāgas, yakṣas, or even kaṭapūtanas who, regarding the territories and cities previously assigned by the World-Honored One, fail to properly protect, establish, and sustain them, I shall transfer them to other gods and nāgas, commanding them to establish, protect, and sustain them, each providing excellent protection according to their respective territories.

“I now entrust the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to you: to the Gandharva Sunetra and his thousand followers; to the Yakṣa-ṛṣi Anila and his five hundred followers; to the Asura Suvarcas and his immeasurable followers; to the Nāga King Takṣaka and his hundred followers; and to the Great Black Goddess and her five hundred followers. May you protect and nurture the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, so that my Dharma may endure for a long time, so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may be maintained without interruption, and so as to ward off all evil sentient beings.”
At that time, the Gandharva Sunetra, the Yakṣa-ṛṣi Anila, the Asura Suvarcas, the Nāga King Takṣaka, the Great Black Goddess, and others, each with their retinues, all spoke these words:
“O Bhagavat, Great Virtuous One!

We shall protect, nurture, and establish [the Dharma] throughout the entire territory of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; we shall ward off that which is unbeneficial and nurture that which is beneficial, even to the point of warding off all unwholesome and evil beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! The great assembly that had gathered there likewise praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Kapilavastu to the fire-protecting Kinnara seer with his thousand followers, the *kuci-rava* Gandharva with his ten thousand followers, the yakṣa general Vātāpati with his thousand followers, the asura Śamanacī with his twenty thousand followers, the nāga king Varuṇamucī with his ten thousand followers, the kumbhāṇḍa general Mahābhasa with his five hundred followers, and the two great goddesses Cāndrī and Cāndralikā, each with their ten thousand followers:
“You all shall together protect the kingdom of Kapilavastu and even ward off all evil beings.”
They all spoke these words:
"We, along with our retinues, shall protect, sustain, and nourish the entire territory of the kingdom of Kapilavastu, even to the point of warding off all evil beings."
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the Kingdom of Magadha to the thousand-fold retinue of the Devaputra Sthitajvālā, the thousand-fold retinue of the Gandharva Utpala, the thousand-fold retinue of the Asura Rutasvara, the ten-thousand-fold retinues of the Naga Kings Subāhu and Sumati, the five-hundred-fold retinue of the Asura Mayūravarṇa, the three-thousand-fold retinue of the Great Yakṣa Kunāla, the hundred-thousand-fold retinue of the Yakṣa Senāpati, the hundred-thousand-fold retinues of the two Kumbhāṇḍa Generals Daśagaja and Mahāgaja, and the ten-thousand-fold retinues of the two Devīs Caṇḍī and Manoharā.
“You all should together protect the kingdom of Magadha, even to the point of obstructing all evil sentient beings.
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the Kingdom of Kosala to the divine son Maitreya-ke-na with his retinue of one thousand, the Gandharva General Ratiśvara with his retinue of ten thousand, the Kiṃnara Umā with his retinue of one thousand, the Nāga King Guṇavat with his retinue of one thousand, the Asura Puṣyapati with his retinue of five hundred, the Yakṣa General Varuṇa and the Yakṣa General King Varuṇa each with their retinues of fifty thousand, the Kumbhāṇḍa Nataka with his retinue of five hundred, and the celestial maiden Maṇivīrī with her retinue of one thousand, saying:
"You all shall together protect the Kingdom of Kosala."
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Aṅga to the Devaputra Candrasvara with his ten thousand followers; the Gandharva General Rucira and the Gandharva General Jambhala, each with ten thousand followers; the Kinnara Amaramalla with five hundred followers; the Asura Siṃhagarbha with five hundred followers; the Yakṣa Candana and the Yakṣa Baladhvaja, each with five thousand followers; the Kumbhāṇḍa Nūraccha with two thousand five hundred followers; and the goddess Mahākālī with two thousand five hundred followers.
“You all should together protect the land of Aṅga.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Pañcāla to the divine son Raṇasiṃha with his retinue of five hundred, the Gandharva Ruciraghoṣa with his retinue of seven hundred, the Kinnara Māyāvin with his retinue of one thousand, the Yakṣa general Pañcika with his retinue of five thousand, the Asura Anavatapta with his retinue of one thousand, the Kumbhāṇḍa Dharmaruci with his retinue of five hundred, and the goddesses Śyāmāvatī and Mālatī each with their retinues of two thousand five hundred:
"All of you together shall protect the kingdom of Pañcāla."
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the Kingdom of Soma to the divine son Ratnaśikhin and his retinue of five thousand; the Gandharva Mātṛmandita and his retinue of one thousand; the Kiṃnara Jayasūtra and his retinue of one thousand; the Yakṣa general Upapāñcika and his retinue of two thousand; the Nāga King Kāla and his retinue of one thousand; the Asura Jñānakāma and his retinue of one thousand; the Kumbhāṇḍa Gaurava and his retinue of six hundred; and to the goddesses Śakunī and Vatsalā, each with their retinue of five hundred.
“May you all together protect the land of Soma.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Aśmaka to the divine son Rohitāśva and his retinue of twelve hundred; the Gandharva Śrotas and his retinue of one thousand; the yakṣa general Maṇivara and his retinue of five thousand; the Asura Ajūra and his retinue of six hundred; the Naga King Sūryaprabha and his immeasurable retinue; the Kumbhāṇḍa Maṇivara and his retinue of five hundred; and to the goddess Anāhārā and the goddess Aśvajit, each with a retinue of two thousand five hundred, saying:
"You all shall together protect the kingdom of Aśmaka."
The Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Mathurā to the Devaputra Sunetra with his ten thousand followers; the Gandharva Śāntaprabha with his one thousand followers; the Kinnara Vītika with his two hundred followers; the Yakṣa Jayakāma and the Mahāyakṣa Puruṣavāhana, each with their fifteen hundred followers; the Nāga King Vimala with his one thousand followers; the Asura Ghaṇṭaka with his one thousand followers; the Kumbhāṇḍa Kṛṣṇavarṇa with his one thousand followers; and the Devī Manoharā with her two thousand followers.
“You all should together protect the country of Mathurā.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the country of Cetiya to the divine son Bhadra with his retinue of five hundred, the gandharva Aṭaka with his retinue of five hundred, the kinnara Vimala with his retinue of one thousand, the yakṣas Vigata-grantha and Asaṃga each with their retinues of five hundred, the nāga Subhadra with his retinue of one thousand, the asura Viśāla-veṇu with his retinue of five hundred, the kumbhāṇḍa Go-rāja with his retinue of three hundred, and the goddess Vijayotpalā with her retinue of one thousand, saying:
"All of you together protect the country of Cetiya."
When the Buddha and the great assembly had all praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! at that time,

the World-Honored One entrusted the country of Vatsa to the ten thousand attendants of the Devaputra Candraprabha, the thousand attendants of the Gandharva Padmagandha, the five thousand attendants of the Kinnara Madanaphala, the five thousand attendants of the Yakṣa Mahāphala, the thousand attendants of the Nāga Aruṇa, the hundred attendants of the Asura Duṣṭavṛkṣa, the five hundred attendants of the Kumbhāṇḍa Parṇākṣa, and the thousand attendants of the Apsaras Anaghapuṣpā.
“May you all together protect the land of Vatsa.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the country of Śākya to the five thousand retinues of the celestial seer Maheśvara; the one thousand retinues of the Gandharva Asura; the one thousand retinues of the Vimala Kinnara; the two thousand five hundred retinues each of the Indra Yakṣa and the Sumana Yakṣa; the one thousand retinues of the Bhadra Nāga; the five hundred retinues of the Mucilinda Asura King; the two thousand five hundred retinues each of the Upatandhi Kumbhāṇḍa and the Kṛkīśa Kumbhāṇḍa;
and the ten thousand retinues each of the goddess Haritī and the goddess Surakṣitā: "May you all together protect the land of Śākya."
...until the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Ujjayinī to the five hundred attendants of the devaputra Candrābha, the thousand attendants of the gandharva Mūka, the five hundred attendants of the gandharva Maṇikarṇa, the thousand attendants of the yakṣa Pañcaka, the five hundred attendants of the nāga-king Parvatabhuja, the three hundred attendants of the asura Dāruhasta, the five hundred attendants of the kumbhāṇḍa Suprabha, and the thousand attendants of the goddess Romadantī.
“You all should together protect the kingdom of Ujjayinī.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Śūroṭa to the Dharma-flower Devaputra and his hundred thousand retinues; to the Gandharva General Suyāma and his ten thousand retinues; to the Kinnara Sage Parvata-bhaya and his one hundred retinues; to the Naga King Nanda and his ten thousand retinues; to the Asura Khara-akṣa and his five hundred retinues; to the Great Yakṣa Sudīpa and his one thousand retinues; to the Great-Kukṣi Kumbhāṇḍa General and his one thousand retinues;
and to the Goddess Kṣema and her one thousand retinues, saying: "All of you together protect the kingdom of Śūroṭa."
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Mahāraṭṭha to the divine son Peacock Hair with his retinue of five hundred; to the Gandharva Joyful Desire and the Gandharva Tiger-Approach, each with their retinue of five hundred; to the Kinnara Milk Flavor with his retinue of one hundred; to the Dragon King Lord of Water with his retinue of one thousand; to the Asura Jewel-Lover with his retinue of five hundred; to the Great Yakṣa Goat-Foot and the Great Yakṣa Manara, each with their retinue of one thousand; to the General of the Kumbhāṇḍas Padmaka with his retinue of five hundred; and to the Great Goddess Bhāruṇī with her retinue of five thousand.
“You all must together protect the country of Mahārāṣṭra.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Śūrpāraka to the Thousand-Golden Son of Heaven with his thousand retinues, the Gandharva Suvakṣa with his thousand retinues, the white-colored Kinnara with his five hundred retinues, the Yakṣa Lokaprabha with his thousand retinues, the Mahādhana Kumbhāṇḍa with his five hundred retinues, and the two goddesses, Atiraudrā and Maṇiphala, each with their five hundred retinues, saying:
"All of you together shall protect the kingdom of Śūrpāraka."
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Maṇicandana to the five hundred attendants of the Devaputra Puṣpasvara, the two hundred attendants of the Gandharva Nārāyaṇa, the three hundred attendants of the Kinnara Maheśvara-puṣpa, the five hundred attendants of the Yakṣa Piṇḍākṣa, the one hundred attendants of the Asura Vārāṇasīputra, the one hundred attendants of the Kumbhāṇḍa Raktākṣa, and the one hundred attendants of the Devī Haimavatī.
"You all must together protect the kingdom of Maṇicandana.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra to the divine son Śāradvatīputra and his retinue of one thousand; to the gandharva Manuṣyapuṣpa and his retinue of five hundred; to the kinnara Maṇicūḍa and his retinue of three hundred; to the yakṣa Śaṅkhaputra and his retinue of five hundred; to the asura Śāradvatī and her retinue of five hundred; to the nāga Śrīgupta and his retinue of eight hundred; to the kumbhāṇḍa Pūrṇika and his retinue of one hundred; and to the goddess Vairocanī and her retinue of five hundred, saying:
"All of you together shall protect the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra."
...until the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

Subsequently, when [the Buddha] was about to descend upon the kingdom of Aṅga, at that time the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Gandhāra to the devaputra Agnibhūti with his three thousand retinues; the gandharva Priyagīta with his thousand retinues; the kinnara Mahājayanta with his five hundred retinues; the yakṣa Siṃhakeśa with his five hundred retinues; the nāga king Elāpattra with his thousand retinues; the nāga king Bhadralabdha with his thousand retinues; the asura Vīryapati with his five hundred retinues; the kumbhāṇḍa Markaṭasvara with his hundred retinues; and the celestial maidens Maṇicandrā and Bimbicandrā, each with their thousand retinues.
"You all should together protect the kingdom of Gandhāra.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the country of Avanti to the divine son Siṃhaprema and his retinue of five thousand, the gandharva Māramanda and his retinue of two thousand, the kinnara Jayanetra and his retinue of one hundred, the yakṣa Soma and the earth-walking yakṣas each with their own retinue of one thousand, the asura Bhṛṅgīraja and his retinue of three thousand, the nāga Vāsukīta and his retinue of one thousand, the kumbhāṇḍa Senāraja and his retinue of one hundred, and the goddesses Utpalā and Nandīghoṣā each with their own retinue of two thousand, saying:
"All of you together shall protect the country of Avanti."
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly all praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted the kingdom of Varanavati to the celestial son Kesi with his retinue of one thousand; to the gandharva Citraka with his retinue of five hundred; to the kinnara Vatsaruci with his retinue of two hundred; to the naga kings Gaja and Upagaja each with their retinues of two thousand; to the asura Vemacitra with his retinue of one hundred; to the kumbhanda Candravarcas with his retinue of three hundred; and to the goddesses Svāhā and Maṇicūḍā each with their retinues of one thousand.
