At that time, there was a great yakṣa named Mukhamaṇḍitikā.
Having conceived deep faith in the Buddha and revered the Buddha’s true Dharma,
he used a vajra-pestle to kill that Aṅga; by killing the Arhat, the unattached Sūrata.
Furthermore, there was an evil bhikṣu named Kīṭa;
with both hands he also grasped a staff and likewise killed that Tripitaka master.
All the bhikṣus rose up together and each began to kill the others.
Of the hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, few remain alive. At that moment,
for a brief instant, the great earth trembled everywhere,
and from the midst of the void, a great and terrible sound issued forth.
Great evils arise from the four quarters; hundreds and thousands of fires blaze up, their towering flames most fearsome, appearing and dwelling in the sky.
Comets and malevolent stars fall and stream down from all four directions.
Trillions of devas all spoke these words:
"The Dharma gathered by Śākyamuni shall today vanish.
The sons of gods from the form realm and all the devas of the desire realm [lament likewise]."
Once the True Dharma has vanished, they wail and cry out with great lamentation.
Seeing the Buddha, the yakṣas fall to the ground and roll about;
from this day forth, there shall be no more Buddha-dharma in the world.
The discipline of the Prātimokṣa precepts is entirely empty and non-existent;
darkness pervades the world, leaving no refuge and no place of resort.
Before long, all people will be no different from deer.
The banner of the Dharma shall be broken and snapped; the sound of the Dharma drum shall also cease.
The gate of the ambrosia shall be closed; the Dharma Master shall also pass away.
The torch of the Dharma shall be extinguished; the Wheel of the Dharma shall no longer turn.
The bridge of the True Dharma is destroyed; the feet of the Dharma no longer walk.
The water of the Dharma ceases to flow; the river of the Dharma is forever parched.
The mountain of the Dharma is about to collapse; the ocean of the Dharma shall surely dry up.
When he dwelt in the forest hermitage, all the sons of the gods were seized with great terror;
they wailed piteously and threw themselves down.
There were also the retinues of Māra and the evil factions of wrong views.
All rejoiced in song and dance, leaping for joy and tossing their garments;
as for those who have entered the nectar taught by Śākyamuni,
it is fitting that they should pass away, so that my Dharma may flourish.
When King Durdarśa learned that the True Dharma had vanished,
from the beginning of the night until its end, he left the city and went to that place;
seeing the corpses of the bhikṣus, he fell to the ground and immediately fainted.
After a long while he regained consciousness, yet once more he wept in sorrow:
"Seeing an Arhat slain, the Tripiṭaka master lost,
and immeasurable bhikṣus dead, I too shall not live much longer."
Having gathered the remains of the Arhats, they separately took the corpses of those from the Tripiṭaka and the deceased bhikṣus, and performed their cremations in various ways.
As for the remaining bhikṣus, they were summoned and assembled in one place.
With various delicacies and many flavors, he made offerings in manifold ways.
He further renounced ten million treasures, each worth hundreds of thousands;
with these myriad precious objects, he intended to construct five hundred monasteries.
To each and every one of the bhikṣus, we shall each offer hundreds of thousands of things;
while you, O Teachers, dwell here, we shall provide for your sustenance.
Please preach the True Dharma to us, and we shall listen with a sincere heart.
All remained silent; there was no one to preach the Dharma.
The King urged them three times, and having addressed the bhikṣus, they likewise all remained silent, with none among them speaking a word.
The king said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you not know the Dharma?
Having spoken, his saffron robe turned white; the dyed color no longer appeared.
They all fell from their beds, rolling about upon the ground.
They all cried out the words of the Buddha: "The Dharma, the Jewel of the Buddha, is vanishing;
our beards, hair, and nails have grown long, and we have forgotten all the teachings."
At that time, a great sound in the void shook the earth;
everything trembled throughout, like wheels upon the water.
The city walls crumbled and fell, and all the houses collapsed and were torn asunder.
The roots, branches, and leaves of the forests, the flowers, leaves, fruits, and medicinal herbs— all are exhausted.
With the sole exception of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, throughout all places in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
the seven flavors and three vital essences have diminished until nothing remains.
All excellent treatises on liberation have vanished; at that time, everything is exhausted.
The fruits, flowers, and flavors that arise are rare and lack luster.
All wells, springs, and ponds have completely dried up.
The land is entirely salty and barren, split open to form hills and ravines.
All the mountains are scorched, and the devas and nāgas do not send down rain;
the crops all wither and die, as do the sugarcane, cotton, and medicinal herbs.
All that is born shall perish; no further grass shall grow.
The rain turns to dust, shrouding all in darkness; the sun and moon no longer manifest their brilliance.
All four quarters suffer from drought, and various ill omens appear repeatedly.
The ten unwholesome courses of action, greed, hatred, and delusion increase twofold;
toward their own parents, sentient beings regard them as if they were deer.
The lifespan of sentient beings, their physical form, strength, majesty, and happiness all diminish.
They abandon the joys of humans and devas, and all fall into the evil realms.
Such unwholesome karma— wicked kings and wicked bhikṣus—
destroys my True Dharma and diminishes the paths of gods and humans.
The various devas, virtuous kings, and lords who feel compassion for sentient beings have all abandoned this turbid and evil land and departed for other regions.
That which previous Buddhas did not do, I now perform for the sake of sentient beings.
Renouncing body and life to increase the three vital energies,
out of compassion for sentient beings, he relinquished one-third of his lifespan so that the ocean of my Dharma might be filled, providing a bath for all devas and humans.
The Tathāgatas of the past, having passed into parinirvāṇa according to their lifespans,
saw their True Dharma vanish after seven days.
Now, after my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall endure for five hundred years.
Dwelling within the world, when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted,
the diligent Bodhisattvas fulfill the six perfections;
those who practice can swiftly enter the stainless city of peace and security.
The Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world for a full thousand years;
those who shave their heads and don the kashaya— whether they uphold the precepts or violate them—
shall always be provided with nothing lacking, being venerated by devas and humans alike.
To make such offerings to them is to make offerings to me.
If there are those who have entered my Dharma, who take refuge and shave their heads,
and who wear the saffron robes— I declare them to be my sons.
Even if they should break the prohibitive precepts, they all abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
If anyone strikes them, it is as if they strike my own body;
if anyone reviles them, it is as if they revile me.
This person’s mind desires to extinguish the great bright lamp of the True Dharma; therefore,
whether they be worthy vessels or not, he shall relinquish one-third of his lifespan so that the multitude may attain peace and happiness, and all devas and humans may receive benefit.
In the past, when I practiced austerities for the sake of all sentient beings,
I relinquished my own personal happiness so that the Dharma might long remain ablaze;
in the past, I sacrificed my body and life for the sake of those who were ill.
For the sake of impoverished sentient beings, I shall cause the Dharma to blaze brightly for a long time.
In the past, for the sake of Bodhi, I renounced wealth, wife, and children,
as well as precious elephants, horses, and chariots, so that the Dharma might blaze brightly for a long time.
In the past, I made offerings to all Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas,
as well as to my parents and all my teachers and elders, so that the Dharma might long remain ablaze.
For the sake of hearing about bodhi, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have practiced.
Enduring all manner of sufferings, may I cause the Dharma to blaze long.
Having cultivated the discipline of the precepts, constantly practicing with diligence through the long night,
with the Buddhas of the ten directions as my witnesses, may I cause the Dharma to blaze long.
In the past, I was always patient, enduring all evil beings;
for the sake of the multitude, I removed their afflictions, so that the Dharma might long remain ablaze.
In the past, I was diligent and energetic, steadfast and ever-subduing others.
To deliver all sentient beings, I cause the Dharma to blaze long and brightly.
I have cultivated meditative concentration and liberation, as well as formless samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; I cause the Dharma to blaze long and brightly.
In the past, for the sake of Prajñāpāramitā, I dwelt in a secluded forest,
expounding immeasurable discourses so that the Dharma might long remain ablaze.
In the past, out of constant compassion, I gave away the flesh and blood of my own body.
And even when giving up my limbs and joints, it was to increase the eye of the True Dharma.
Out of compassion for evil sentient beings, I have brought them to maturity through loving-kindness;
establishing them in the three vehicles, I have increased the gift of the True Dharma.
In the past, through wisdom and skillful means, I delivered all those with evil views and established them in right insight, causing the rain of Dharma to flow without ceasing.
In the past, by means of the four methods of attraction, I rescued and delivered all sentient beings.
Extinguishing the fire of evil afflictions, you cause the fourfold assembly to dwell for a long time.
In the past, I removed the nets of various evil and heterodox views from the outsiders and established them on the true path, so that the fourfold assembly may receive offerings.
For their sake, I shall relinquish my life; out of compassion, I shall deliver sentient beings so that the world is not left in darkness and has a place of refuge.
Thus, at a later time, I desire that the Dharma shall not perish.
Therefore, entrust the Dharma-eye to benefit all sentient beings.
After my parinirvāṇa, may bodhisattvas turn toward other regions so that the teachings of all the worthy and holy ones shall not perish or be destroyed.
Therefore, I now speak this mantra, so that the Dharma may long remain ablaze.
It is the adamantine secret, without flaw, the basis for the flavor of liberation.
May all the Buddhas of the ten directions grant me their approval.
"Those who have come here, the great assembly also grants their consent.
At that time, for the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time, the World-Honored One spoke this Great Dhāraṇī mantra:

*Tadyathā | Apamuki | Pamuki | Ciṭṭhamuki | Kharāmuki | Carāmahe | Ahe | Ahe | Daravati | Mahādharite | Siddhaparāhe | Jāgari | Maśpari | Darāmukhi | Nāgameśvari | Śvarāmanepabha | Svāhā.* At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these dharani-words of the essence of the flavor of the adamantine, firm, and profound liberation, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the heavens rained down flowers, and all musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
The great assembly that had gathered filled the earth; they all wept with tears of sorrow and offered praise, saying:

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni is truly extraordinary! Possessing the unprecedented Dharma and endowed with great compassion, for the sake of maturing those sentient beings and for the sake of establishing and manifesting the future Dharma, he has relinquished one-third of his lifespan."
When these words were spoken, the minds of those beings in the assembly who were bound by bodies of affliction attained reverent faith;
all beings throughout the measure of empty space who had not yet resolved upon supreme bodhicitta now all resolved their minds upon it;
ninety-two nayutas of beings attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); and eight nayutas of beings...
They attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and the Holy Lamp Samādhi; one hundred thousand yakṣas perceived the Four Noble Truths;
two thousand bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Measuring the Vinaya in Common Practice;
sixty-four hundred thousand asuras attained the Nārāyaṇa Samādhi of Supreme Conduct; and eight hundred thousand nayutas of beings...
The deva attained the Samādhi of Pure Conduct; three hundred thousand nayutas of kumbhāṇḍas attained the Samādhi of the Supreme Banner’s Exalted Lamp;
two hundred thousand nayutas of nāgas attained the Samādhi of Unconquerable and Resolute Power;
and twenty thousand bhikṣus, having exhausted all outflows, attained liberation of mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānolkadāraka addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “O Knower of Purity!
Contemplate this Tathāgata Śākyamuni, whose great renown fills the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
How does he fill them?

It means that since Śākyamuni Buddha first resolved his mind to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he has impartially established all sentient beings; with the mind of a field of merit, he has diligently practiced various forms of giving and performed the most supreme deeds upon all bodhisattva paths. For the sake of maturing all sentient beings, he made the most supreme vows, relinquishing a pure land to come to this world of the five turbidities and manifold sufferings, where he attained perfect awakening in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

By the power of the causes and conditions of great compassion, for the sake of those beings who are bound by the karma of immediate retribution, by slandering the True Dharma, by reviling the noble ones, and by all manner of unwholesome and evil deeds—beings who are cast out from all the pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions and are fettered by various afflictions—he seeks Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world and cultivates the most supreme practices on the path of all Bodhisattvas. It is for the sake of bringing such beings to maturity that this person has now attained perfect enlightenment in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within this world of five corruptions.

These sentient beings who commit immediate transgressions (ānantarya-karma) reviled and slandered the Tathāgata in various ways, treating him with contempt and disparagement, and assiduously inflicting suffering upon him.

Driven by the causes and conditions of envy, they sought to kill him through various means; furthermore, they employed various weapons such as swords, arrows, spears, lances, axes, and battle-axes, as well as hurling down massive mountains of rock, using poisons, water, and fire, and even releasing mad elephants, lions, tigers, leopards, vicious oxen, and savage dogs to diligently harm the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata still regards those sentient beings with great compassion and pity, protecting them as parents look upon their only child; he employs skillful means to rescue them from the ocean of suffering. For this reason, the name of the present Buddha, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, is now universally renowned throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
Now, for the sake of all these sentient beings, I entrust all dharmas to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits, so that the eye of the Dharma may long endure and blaze brightly.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he relinquished a third portion of his lifespan; likewise, so that the Eye of the Dharma might abide long and blaze brightly, and for the sake of protecting and not harming all those who are vessels or non-vessels among the śrāvakas, as well as all those who have shaved their heads and donned the *kāṣāya*, and in order to increase the three vital essences (*ojas*), Śākyamuni Tathāgata has attained supreme renown throughout all Buddha-fields in these ten directions, among all Tathāgatas, all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all gods and men of great wisdom, such that his fame fills the ten directions.

Therefore, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have come together, each according to their own capacity, have prepared the foremost and most excellent offerings to honor, revere, and pay homage to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered there rose from their seats, their mouths and eyes smiling.

Those bodhisattvas, throughout this Sahā world, rained down various precious articles of offering to worship the World-Honored One: some rained down fragments of gold; some rained down fragments of silver; some rained down fragments of lapis lazuli; some rained down fragments of crystal; some rained down red pearls; some rained down fragments of agate; some rained down fragments of musaragalva; some rained down fragments of sandalwood highly prized by dragons and serpents; some rained down ox-head sandalwood; some rained down tamālapatra incense; some rained down black, solid aloeswood incense; some rained down various kinds of exquisite and wonderful jewel-flowers; and some rained down canopies of the seven treasures, banners of the seven treasures, pennants of the seven treasures, as well as golden threads, pearls, necklaces, and bracelets.

Some held *kalpa* wish-fulfilling jewel trees; some held jewel-cloth trees; some held jewel-flower trees; some held jewel-vessel trees; and some held jewel-incense trees, making offerings to the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who transformed all the trees, forests, flowers, leaves, fruits, and all vegetation in the Sahā world into the seven treasures as an offering to the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who transformed all the mountains, stones, bricks, and tiles throughout the Sahā world into the seven treasures to make offerings to the Buddha.
Moreover, there were bodhisattvas who transformed every portion of the great earth within the Sahā world into exquisite celestial precious incense to make offerings to the Buddha.
All sentient beings who dwell upon the earth experienced physical and mental bliss for seven days and seven nights, as if they were gods.

Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva who transformed all the great water realms within the Sahā world-system into a water realm of the first-microbe celestial nectar—exquisite in flavor, fragrant, pure, and perfectly endowed with all qualities—and for seven days and seven nights, the sentient beings experienced physical and mental bliss as if they were gods.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who transform all winds into subtle, pure, fragrant breezes to make offerings to the Buddha. Because these fragrant breezes touch every single sentient being in the three evil realms without exception, for seven days and seven nights their bodies and minds experience happiness as if they were among the devas.

At that time, from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the gods of the Four Great Kings below, including all the celestial maidens without exception, praised the World-Honored One with various subtle and exquisite voices, and further made offerings to the Buddha with diverse songs, dances, and music.

All yakṣas, all rākṣasas, all kumbhāṇḍas, all gandharvas, all asuras, all kiṃnaras, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—all of them, according to their respective capacities, offered various praises and even various kinds of offerings to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the foremost Maitreya and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, saying:
"O sons of good family!

In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I made such offerings to the Tathāgatas of former Buddhas; by means of these roots of goodness, they have become the cause for my attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall now divide this fruit of retribution into three parts: one part I shall set aside for my own enjoyment;
the second part, after my parinirvāṇa, I shall give to those śrāvakas who are firmly established in dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, so that they may have no lack;

the third part, I shall give to those śrāvakas associated with the breaking of precepts yet engaged in the recitation of the sūtras—those who, during the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma periods, shave their heads and don the kāṣāya—so that they too may have no lack.

“Maitreya! I now entrust into your hands all the assemblies of śrāvakas associated with the three karmas—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—so that they may not pass away in poverty or solitude. Furthermore, I entrust into your hands those who, during the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, have broken the prohibitions yet wear the saṃghāṭī; do not let them pass away lacking the necessities of life, nor let them be afflicted by Caṇḍāla kings or suffer in body and mind.”

I now entrust those donors into your hands; as for all those who possess vessels or lack vessels and have gone forth under me as my disciples to offer worship, you too shall protect, sustain, and nurture them.
“Maitreya! Those who read, recite, receive, and uphold this Dharma-gate in the present and future ages shall obtain ten kinds of pure merits.”
What are these ten?
Because the body is pure, one abstains from killing, abstains from stealing, and abstains from sexual misconduct;
because the speech is pure, one does not engage in false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, or frivolous speech.
Because the mind is pure, one is free from greed, free from hatred, and free from wrong views; these constitute the ten [purities].
From this point onward, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of births, one will constantly attain these ten kinds of pure merit.
"If there are those who listen to this Dharma-gate with a sincere mind, such persons will abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain eight kinds of pure merit.
What are these eight? "
First, long life; second, physical excellence;
third, wealth and nobility.
Fourth, renown; fifth, constant protection by the devas;
sixth, never lacking in whatever is required.
Seventh, they exhaust all karmic obstructions;

eighth, at the time when their lives are about to end, the Buddhas of the ten directions and their great assemblies emit a great radiance that illuminates their eyes, enabling those people to see and be reborn in favorable realms.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall constantly obtain these eight kinds of merit.
To speak further in brief, such a person shall also obtain thirteen kinds of pure merit.
What are the thirteen?
First, though transmigrating through birth and death, one shall never again give rise to inverted or evil views;
second, one shall not be born in the five turbidities or in a Buddha-less land.
Third, they shall always behold the Buddha;
fourth, they shall always hear the True Dharma;
fifth, they shall always be able to make offerings to the Sangha.
Sixth, encountering virtuous spiritual friends;
seventh, constantly corresponding with the six pāramitās;
eighth, not falling into the Lesser Vehicle.
Ninth, they constantly mature sentient beings through great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the power of great skillful means;
tenth, they constantly give rise to supreme vows;
eleventh, until they reach bodhi, they never depart from the aforementioned dharmas.
Twelfth, they are able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās;
thirteenth, they attain perfect enlightenment in unexcelled, complete, and perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

If there are those who uphold, transcribe, read, recite, explain to others, and practice according to the instructions this *Candragarbha-dharmaparyāya*, the merit they shall obtain will be as previously described.

When these words were spoken, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Candragarbha, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and the entire great assembly that had gathered—including devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and all other sentient beings—having heard what the Buddha taught, were filled with joy and reverently accepted and practiced it.
Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 56; Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Volume 57.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
16. The Section on the Treasury of Mount Sumeru, Chapter One: The Disciples. Chapter Fifteen of the Section on the Treasury of Mount Sumeru: The First Chapter on the Disciples.
Homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on Mount Kharadīśvara, at the abode of the sage Muni, together with a great assembly of Śrāvakas exceeding all count— all of whom were the great disciples of the Buddha—

and an immeasurable and boundless assembly of great Bodhisattvas, who had all come from the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions to assemble there, following the sequence of the *Brahmaparivarta-vyākaraṇa* section.

At that time, in the midst of the assembly, Guṇakārandavatī stood before the Buddha not far from him; for the sake of hearing the Dharma, she rose from her seat, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Bhagavān of Great Virtue!
There are bodhisattvas who, by means of the ship of the merit of giving, cross over the ocean of birth and death. Why is this?
Because this Buddha-world is extremely defiled by the five turbidities, and there are many sentient beings whose merit and wisdom have all diminished.
For these reasons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Furthermore, these sentient beings propound the doctrine of non-causality; lacking material resources, they strive with great hardship yet are unable to obtain them.
If these bodhisattvas do not practice giving, they will be unable to transform those sinful sentient beings.
Therefore, the bodhisattvas form this thought:
"I shall now don the armor of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and arouse great diligence; launching the vessel of giving, I shall cross the ocean of birth and death."

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing the meritorious deeds of giving, cause others to enter the unsurpassed great ocean of all buddhas, until they attain the station of the Dharma King through the supreme consecration.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cling to the view of eternalism; they lack abundant resources and, though they exhaust their bodies in pursuit, they cannot obtain them.
If a bodhisattva does not practice the precepts and generosity, he will not bring those sentient beings to maturity.”
Therefore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva arouses great compassion for sentient beings who cling to the notion of permanence, and further reflects:
"I shall transform those sentient beings who cling to permanence; armed with the armor of such observance of the precepts, I desire to cross the great ocean of birth and death."
"Thus, they eventually attain the rank of a Dharma King who has received consecration.

By means of the merit of observing the precepts, the practice of the ten paths of wholesome action, and so forth, these bodhisattvas bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to enter the great ocean of the unsurpassed Buddhas, and ultimately establishing them in the rank of a Dharma King who has received consecration."
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who practice the ten paths of wholesome action yet do not do so purely. Because their merit and wisdom are diminished—such as those sentient beings who harbor views of a self regarding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and even greed and hatred—they lack wealth and resources; though they strive and toil in pursuit of them, they cannot obtain them. For such sentient beings, were it not for the pure precepts of renunciation, there would be no means to bring them to maturity.”

Therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, toward those sentient beings who engage in unwholesome physical actions—such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, greed, and anger—arouses great compassion. Through the skillful means of impermanence, he causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma, maturing them through the precepts of renunciation.
This is precisely my armor of patience and diligence.
These are the precepts of renunciation, serving as the vessel for crossing the ocean of birth and death.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the merit of upholding the precepts and the skillful means of impermanence, teaches, transforms, and brings to maturity those beings who observe the precepts of the monastic discipline.

By virtue of this karma, that bodhisattva leads others as far as entry into the great ocean of the unsurpassed Buddhas, and even establishes them in the position of the consecrated Dharma King; thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to enter the great ocean of the unsurpassed Buddhas by his own power.
At that time, Puṇyavatī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Great Virtuous Bhagavān!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva first cultivate and study the fundamental practice of the dhyānapāramitā? Having studied it, how does he come to know the constituent factors of the dhyānas, so as to be able to emerge from the desire realm, abandon the five hindrances, and accomplish the five faculties? How does he sport with the supernormal powers of the four bases of psychic power, travel to all buddha-fields as swiftly as lightning, and make offerings to and listen to the Dharma at the abodes of all Buddhas? This is for the sake of exhausting the three paths of sentient beings—what are these three?”
That is to say, the path of karma, the path of afflictions, and the path of suffering—these fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
How does one fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā?
By being complete in the six pāramitās.
"Once you have fulfilled the six pāramitās, you will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"
O Pure Wisdom! O Pure Wisdom!
You have exerted yourself in this Dharma and fulfilled its practice; for the sake of sentient beings, you are able to inquire about this meaning from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"O Viśuddhamati! You should listen with a focused mind and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Guṇakārandavatī said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I shall listen and receive it; I only pray that you will speak of it.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Puṇyavatī, saying:
“Vimalajñāna! It is as you have asked.

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva first train in the fundamental practice of the dhyānapāramitā? Having trained, they understand the factors of dhyāna and are able to transcend the desire realm; they eliminate the five hindrances and accomplish the five limbs [of dhyāna]. They sport with the supernormal powers of the four bases of psychic power and are able to travel to all buddha-fields as swiftly as lightning. At the abodes of all Buddhas, they make offerings and listen to the Dharma in order to exhaust the three paths of sentient beings.”
What are the three?
They are the path of karma, the path of afflictions, and the path of suffering.
These are able to give rise to the meritorious deeds performed on the path of cultivation, thereby fulfilling the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Because the dhyāna-pāramitā is fulfilled, one becomes fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“O Viśuddhamati! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva first practices meditative concentration, he binds his mind to the signs of all inhalations and exhalations as objects of mindfulness.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva exhales and inhales with an undistracted mind.”
Following the in-breath as it touches the mind, that in-breath touching the mind is called *vitarka* (applied thought).
Following the out-breath as it touches the mind, that out-breath touching the mind is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).

Progressing further, with a mind of joy and bliss that is single-minded and undisturbed, he is about to emerge from the desire realm and become detached from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Having severed the hindrance of sensual desire and ill-will, and having subdued all unwholesome states, he attains the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought.
At that time, such signs arise: all parts of the body tremble and vibrate throughout the entire frame.

If the Bodhisattva applies superior vigor and maintains focused mindfulness, he is then able to extinguish applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and with joy and bliss and a unified mind, he attains the second dhyāna.
To eliminate the fault of joy, he applies himself with unremitting diligence; once joy has been extinguished, he attains the bliss of the third dhyāna.

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body experiences a sublime ease, as if his entire frame were being drenched with warm milk, attaining a rarefied bliss comparable to the perception of a celestial body.
Having attained such supreme bliss, he gained superior faith in the Triple Gem.
He further thought:
"For the benefit of all sentient beings, I have donned the great armor and diligently cultivated meditative concentration; I should now renounce my bodily pleasure."

"Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cease inhalation and exhalation, abandon the mind that clings to continuous objects of perception, fix their attention on the tip of the nose, and dwell with the mind observing the inhalation and exhalation."
Furthermore, he contemplates that mind as disintegrating moment by moment, knowing its arising and knowing its ceasing.

He further knows that mind, in its momentary association and disintegration, is without arising—like the moon in water, like a reflection of light, like a mirage, and like lightning; that mind, mentation, and consciousness, along with all aggregates, elements, and sense bases, are like bubbles.
"Therefore, having relinquished bodily pleasure and contemplating the arising and ceasing of those phenomena, he enters the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, such signs arise; although the Bodhisattva has closed his eyes, he sees with clarity as if illuminated by the light of the Great Sun."
That bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Because of this objective support of the mark of light, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of all sentient beings continue to grow and blaze forth; I should now, with my mind, bring the cessation of activity to rest upon the objective support of light."

Furthermore, by means of this method of cessation, he relinquishes feeling, perception, volition, contact, and the arising and ceasing of mental formations; he enters the city of supreme purity and sublime tranquility, and abides in the restraint of bodily, verbal, and mental actions.

That bodhisattva emerges from concentration and takes up the signs of inhalation and exhalation; observing the signs of contact and mindfulness, he re-enters the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

Emerging from the concentration of emptiness, he again observes the signs of the arising, ceasing, and objective conditions of inhalation and exhalation, and thereby enters the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
Arising from the wishless samādhi, one perceives the cessation of inhalation and exhalation and abides in the signless concentration.
In this way, one is able to cultivate and fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness and the three gates of liberation.
"By observing the arising and ceasing of inhalation and exhalation, that bodhisattva, through observing arising and ceasing, fulfills the cultivation of the four right efforts.
By observing the characteristics of the emergence and submergence of inhalation and exhalation, that bodhisattva is then able to fully cultivate and perfect the four bases of psychic power."
By observing the inhalation and exhalation, he is able to dissolve his body like fine dust in a window.

At that time, he attains the full cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Through the skillful means of the emergence and submergence of inhalation and exhalation, he contemplates the three types of formations; in this way, he is able to fully cultivate the five powers (*pañcabala*).

By means of the skillful means of removing the perception of inhalation and exhalation, he contemplates their removal and cessation; thus he cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment.
By means of the mindfulness of the wind of inhalation and exhalation, he disperses and destroys the entire earth element and all form, leaving nothing behind.

It is without marks, without language, without characteristics, and without provisional names; the three activities are tranquil, utterly tranquil, and extinguished, as one attains the objectless samādhi.
This is called the fundamental practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) consisting in the play of *samādhi*.
It is the fundamental practice of meditation shared by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If one were to abide in this state, through inferior diligence, one might realize the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or a non-returner (anāgāmin), or even abide in the fruit of an arhat; yet for a bodhisattva who possesses firm diligence and a heart of great compassion, mindful of all sentient beings, the accumulation of immeasurable merit and wisdom becomes a source of weariness.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling through skillful means in this samādhi of the fundamental activity of playing with such dhyāna, does not retreat from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does not fall into the fixed group of śrāvakas, and does not cast off the great armor of the fundamental activity of dhyāna-concentration.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the dhyāna-pāramitā; having fulfilled the dhyāna-pāramitā, he is then able to fulfill all six pāramitās.

“Pure Wisdom! Furthermore, in whatever land there may be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who wish to enter the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Mahāyāna; or good sons and good daughters who, in this Samādhi of the Play of the Fundamental Karma of Dhyāna, maintain mindfulness and contemplation—in whatever place they dwell, all the celestial kings of that land shall constantly provide excellent protection. All dragon kings, all yakṣa kings, all asura kings, all kiṃnara kings, all mahoraga kings, all preta kings, all piśāca kings, and all rākṣasa kings shall likewise well protect that land.”
“If there are those who dwell as fields of merit associated with such dhyāna within a land, that kṣatriya king of that land shall obtain ten kinds of desirable qualities.”
What are the ten? First, to dwell in peace and extinguish all afflictions;
second, to possess long life;
Third, obtaining a most excellent and sublime physical form;
fourth, having skin that is fresh and soft;
fifth, having limbs and joints that are lovely to behold.
Sixth, one obtains virtuous associates;
seventh, one is able to cultivate wholesome deeds;
eighth, one maintains mindfulness of compassion and skillful means.
Ninth, one is always endowed with a reputation that accords with being a vessel of merit;
tenth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens. These are the ten.
"Furthermore, that land shall also achieve ten kinds of extraordinary benefits. What are these ten?
First, it shall not be plundered or harmed by internal thieves or external enemies."
Second, there are no evil bandits, venomous beasts, mosquitoes, gadflies, or locusts;
third, there is no drought or flooding, nor untimely winds, rains, cold, or heat;
fourth, the land is level and even, free from mounds, ruins, gullies, ravines, or treacherous wastes.

Fifth, all seeds, the five grains, medicinal herbs, grasses, trees, and forests in that land will be lush and flourishing; its flowers and fruits will be free from bitter, pungent, or astringent tastes.
Sixth, there will be no harsh sounds, nor strife, rebellion, famine, illness, or untimely death.

Seventh, the beings of that land will have long lives, be handsome, and enjoy abundant prosperity; they will be free from defiled minds, sporting in happiness, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma to be reborn in the heavens.
Eighth, the various vessels of merit within that land dwell in reliance [upon it], delighting in and conforming to dhyāna and samādhi;

ninth, the food and drink required by the sentient beings of that land are entirely without lack, providing excellent and lovely sustenance for the four great elements, harmonizing with their faculties and increasing them without contradiction;
tenth, the people of that land are courageous, strong, and possessive of keen memories; endowed with a heart of compassion, they are reborn in the heavens after death.
"Pure Wisdom! These ten kinds of dharmas are well able to adorn that land. Pure Wisdom!"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, due to karmic obstructions, abandons the Mahāyāna and dwells on the level of the śrāvaka, thereby contravening the transformation of sentient beings. This is the śrāvaka’s samādhi of sporting in the dhyāna-pāramitā; by means of this, the śrāvaka fully understands and masters the factors of dhyāna, emerges from the cave-dwelling of the triple world and the bonds of existence, severs the five factors and accomplishes the five factors, transcends the triple world and dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), sports with supernatural powers, and reaches the further shore of the eight liberations and meditative concentrations. Having practiced for one kalpa, he becomes a son of all Buddhas, born from the mouth of the Buddha and transformedly born from the Dharma.

Although he was thus, he was still unable to travel to the lands of the Buddhas to make offerings to the Buddhas and listen to the Dharma from them; nor was he able to dry up the three paths of sentient beings.
"If one can thus sport within this samādhi, then in whatever land they dwell, they shall obtain the great merit and benefits described above.
Chapter Two: The Fundamental Karma of Bodhisattva Dhyāna Fifteenth Section: The Sumerugarbha-vibhāga of the Mahāsannipāta-sūtra At that time, the Buddha addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: "O Pure Wisdom!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the distinction of the fundamental practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā that is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having fulfilled the dhyāna-pāramitā, is then able to fulfill the remaining five pāramitās.

“Pure Wisdom! This bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the arising and ceasing within all inhalations and exhalations as well as within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Having performed this contemplation, he dries up and exhausts craving and thirst, and does not fall into the fixed assembly of the śrāvakas.”

Sporting with the supernormal powers of the four bases of psychic power, they are able to travel to all buddha-fields as swiftly as lightning; at the abodes of all Buddhas, they make offerings and listen to the Dharma, completely drying up the three paths of all sentient beings—namely, the path of afflictions, the path of karma, and the path of suffering.

Although he has emerged from the desire realm, he does not abandon it; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he manifests birth in the various realms of existence, yet he is not defiled by the womb. He cuts through the net of afflictions of sentient beings, yet regarding these sentient beings, he perceives nothing to be attained.

“O Viśuddhamati! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates each inhalation and exhalation individually; he understands them as they truly are, as being new and not old. In this way, he understands the aggregate of form and feeling within these inhalations and exhalations as they truly are; he also understands the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations as they truly are. Likewise, he understands the aggregate of consciousness within these inhalations and exhalations as it truly is. He knows the difference between exhalation and inhalation; he knows the difference in exhalation and knows the difference in inhalation. Within the difference of inhalation, he knows the feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention; regarding the difference in exhalation, his knowledge of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention is likewise. When there is the feeling of inhalation, there is no feeling of exhalation; when there is the feeling of exhalation, there is no feeling of inhalation.”

"In this way, the wheel of the three realms of existence revolves; because of the conditions of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention, it continues in an uninterrupted succession. One is carried away by the ocean of birth and death and cannot cross over; having undergone birth, old age, and death again and again, one is born once more. One is unable to realize these phenomena as they truly are, unable to emerge from that cycle of birth and death as it truly is, and unable to correctly observe the inhalation and exhalation of the breath as they truly are."

"Furthermore, these inhalations and exhalations pass in and out, coming and going, through the nine orifices; likewise, they all circulate through the inhalation and exhalation of ninety-nine nayutas of hundreds of thousands of pore-openings. Yet, within those ninety-nine nayutas of hundreds of thousands of pores, there is neither increase nor decrease. One cannot perceive them as being of the past, the future, or the present; nor can one perceive them as being at the beginning, the middle, or the end. One knows not their abiding, nor their departure."
Again, he reflects:
"I shall now abide in accordance with the characteristics of arising and ceasing through the skillful means of the arising and ceasing of the exhalations and inhalations from all my pores."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, following the arising and ceasing of the exhalations and inhalations through the nine orifices, likewise observes the arising and ceasing of the breath within each of the ninety-nine nayutas of hundreds of thousands of pore-openings; he dwells observing the arising and ceasing of the exhalations and inhalations in accordance with that observation.
If a bodhisattva wishes to contemplate the subtle marks of the pores, merely seeing the breath moving in and out at the tip of a hair, they are able to see the small.
If they wish to see the large, they are then able to see it as being the size of a mustard seed.
If one wishes to see [the Buddha] as large as an *āmala* fruit, one will immediately be able to see him.
If one wishes to see him as large as a *bimba* fruit, one will likewise immediately be able to see him.

If one wishes to see a distance of one yojana, a thousand yojanas, or even up to a four-continent world-system, one may observe each and every pore; according to the extent one desires to see, one is able to see that much.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Sentient beings are deluded by their eyes; bound within the cycle of birth and death, they continue in succession without interruption, drifting in the stream of saṃsāra and undergoing all manner of suffering."
That bodhisattva further reflects:
"I have now abandoned all perceptions of form and have attained the wordless samādhi, which is not the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

In that earth element nothing is apprehended; likewise, in the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element, nothing is apprehended. One does not engage with the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; there is no prior limit nor a subsequent limit, no this world nor another world, no retribution for wholesome karma nor retribution for unwholesome karma, no arising nor cessation, and neither the presence of afflictions nor their departure—there is nothing to be apprehended.
"In this way, the bodhisattva dwells in the dwelling of quiescence.

If he wishes to abide in or exert himself within this samādhi of the ineffable emptiness of all phenomena for immeasurable kalpas, then by the power of the samādhi sustained by his own wisdom, the bodhisattva is able to dwell in this samādhi of the ineffable emptiness of all phenomena for immeasurable kalpas, and is also able to fulfill the six pāramitās for the sake of the causes and conditions for the maturation of sentient beings."

“Pure Wisdom! Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha has reached the further shore of mastery in this ‘Speechless Emptiness of All Dharmas’ Samādhi. Whenever this Bodhisattva wishes to enter this samādhi, he does so through the power of his merit and wisdom for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.”

First, he made this vow: "Until I have emerged from this samādhi, during this interval, I shall cause all the necessities of life required by all sentient beings within the realms of this land and the four continents of this Buddha-world—whether according to their appearance, their quantity, or their preferences; namely, food and drink, clothing, bedding, necklaces and ornaments, gardens, groves, houses, and dwellings; as well as forms, colors, shapes, limbs, body parts, and desirable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures—to appear whenever they wish to see such things."
At that time, the Bodhisattva entered this samādhi.

Having entered this samādhi, according to the appropriate seasons, all sentient beings within the four continents of this Buddha-world obtained, as previously described, whatever requisites they required, becoming fully satisfied.
Or again, one might think:

"In accordance with the duration of my dwelling in meditative concentration, and in accordance with the extent of the number of sentient beings, I wish to eliminate the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings—namely, diseases caused by wind, bile, and phlegm, or those produced by humans and non-humans—and likewise wish to extinguish the diseases of the afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as to extinguish the ten unwholesome karmas so that they may abide in the path of the ten wholesome karmas."
He then immediately entered this samādhi.

For as long as that bodhisattva-mahāsattva remained in meditative concentration, and for as many sentient beings as he acted upon, all the aforementioned physical and mental illnesses and sufferings were entirely eliminated.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:

"For as long as I have remained in meditative concentration, may I extinguish the various sufferings of the hells; the sufferings of animals devouring one another; the sufferings of hunger and thirst in the realm of Yama, as well as the sufferings of cold and heat, the suffering of meeting those one hates, the suffering of being separated from those one loves, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—according to the extent of my vow."

May all sentient beings be freed from all suffering, affliction, and unwholesome dharmas, and may they accomplish all wholesome dharmas. May all sentient beings direct their minds toward one another with loving-kindness, giving rise to a mind of benefit, an immovable mind, a mind free of enmity, a mind free of contention, a mind free of strife and litigation, and a mind of compassion; even to a mind well-established in dhyāna-samāpatti, an undeluded mind, and a mind that extinguishes the ignorance and delusion of sentient beings.

Furthermore, they extinguish the common views of eternalism and nihilism, as well as all clusters of views; they show reverence and make offerings to the Triple Gem, engendering a sense of rare wonder, and cause all sentient beings to leave the four inversions and abide in the four non-inversions.
"His mind is well-settled upon the Four Noble Truths and the ultimate truth.

Thus, empowered by the power of a bodhisattva’s merit, wisdom, and skillful means, when that bodhisattva wishes to enter samādhi for the sake of transforming sentient beings, from the moment he intends to enter until he has not yet emerged from that samādhi, he causes all sentient beings within this land, the four continents of Jambudvīpa, and indeed this entire buddha-field, to obtain the matters of peace and happiness according to their respective capacities, as described above; only then does he enter the wordless samādhi of the emptiness of all phenomena.

"When that bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters this samādhi, for as long as he remains in it—extending even to the full extent of sentient beings within the buddha-field according to his vow—that bodhisattva, by the power of his merit, wisdom, and samādhi, causes all those various means of subsistence and articles of pleasure mentioned above to be obtained by all sentient beings, until he emerges from that concentration."

When that bodhisattva enters this samādhi, there is no physical suffering nor mental suffering, nor hunger or thirst; fire cannot burn them, water cannot sweep them away, and even the kalpa-ending fires cannot harm them, nor can the kalpa-ending floods rot them, nor can they be scattered or destroyed by the calamity of wind.
Furthermore, they shall not have their life-faculties exhausted by calamities such as epidemics, famine, or warfare; they may enter parinirvāṇa at will and with mastery;
and neither humans nor non-humans, nor poisonous winds or violent fevers, shall be able to afflict them.

Furthermore, while that bodhisattva remains in meditative concentration and has not yet arisen from it, according to his intention, he desires to cause immeasurable buddha-fields to enter into a single minute atom;
moreover, he is able to see all the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, and assemblies of śrāvakas throughout the lands of the ten directions within a single fingernail, without exception;
and he causes all sentient beings to enter into a single pore, yet those sentient beings perceive their own environments exactly as they were before.

Furthermore, all the winds existing throughout the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions, the Bodhisattva causes to enter into a single hair-tip; traversing the void according to the realm of those winds, whether wide or narrow, coming or going, there is no obstruction, yet within that hair-tip there is neither increase nor decrease, remaining as it was without change.

Moreover, all the water elements existing within every Buddha-world of the ten directions, the Bodhisattva is able to cause to enter into a single bean husk; following the breadth or narrowness of the water, its flowing and its coming and going are likewise without obstruction, yet within that bean husk there is no increase or decrease.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas no longer dwell in a womb—except by the power of their own vows—and they are not born in the evil realms, do not take female form, and are never born into inferior states. Their faculties are complete and never deficient; their actions of body, speech, and mind are free from fault; and they are never born in worlds where no Buddha resides—except by the power of their own vows for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

This bodhisattva is never separated from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and serving the Saṃgha; nor is he ever separated from merit, wisdom, fearlessness, and skillful means for teaching and transforming sentient beings, until they enter unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
"In this way, O Pure Wisdom!

That bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned such a great and firm armor, first cultivates the fundamental practice of the dhyāna-pāramitā; he is able to transcend the desire realm and comprehend the factors of dhyāna, severing the five hindrances and accomplishing the five limbs, even to the point of sporting with the four bases of psychic power."

They are skillfully able to travel to all Buddha-fields with the swiftness of lightning, making offerings to all Buddhas and hearing the True Dharma; they dry up all three paths of sentient beings—namely, the path of afflictions, the path of karma, and the path of suffering.
Thus it is, O Pure Wisdom!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has fulfilled the dhyāna-pāramitā, they are then able to fulfill the six pāramitās; having fulfilled the six pāramitās, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was expounding this fundamental practice of the Dhyānapāramitā, fifty thousand sentient beings within that assembly—who had practiced this dharma in the past—thereby attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
ninety-nine thousand bodhisattvas attained fulfillment in the Dhyānapāramitā.
Immeasurable and boundless sentient beings gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta never before arisen; having given rise to this mind, they dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.

Chapter Three: The Extinction of Untimely Wind and Rain The Great Collection Sūtra, Section Fifteen: The Storehouse of Mount Sumeru At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed Śrīdevī, saying: "O Pure Wisdom!

You should now observe that these four continents are magnificent and exquisite, worthy of being honored, remembered, and protected by all bodhisattvas; you should pay them respect throughout the long night.

Now, because Śākyamuni Buddha has gathered all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he reveals the non-retrogressive wheel of all practices on the path to enlightenment, the ultimate stage of the Buddha’s empowerment through skillful means, and even your own practice of the *dāna-pāramitā*, fulfilling the supreme, non-retrogressive conduct.

If you cultivate offerings of various foods and drinks toward such a supreme field of merit, through this diligent effort you will swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās; having fulfilled the six pāramitās, you will then be able to dwell ultimately in omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).
Then, Puṇyavatī spoke these words: “So it is, so it is.
Just as you have said, noble sir, I pray that you will listen as I relate my original causes and conditions.”
I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, I and Śākyamuni Buddha cultivated the bodhisattva practices together and made this vow:

"When you attain the Unsurpassed Way, may I reach the place of merit within those four continents; having reached that place of merit, I shall provide all sentient beings with whatever clothing and food they require."

“Virtuous one, listen well. In the past, beyond immeasurable kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Indraketudhvajarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; at that time, the human lifespan was one thousand years.”

At that time, there was a lay follower named Vimalaguṇaprabha, who was wise, disciplined, learned, and fearless; he preached the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, and being one whom the multitude revered and submitted to, he had many followers.
He had an eldest son named Vimalaśrī, who addressed his father in verse: "Father,
for what reason now do you exert yourself with such diligence, refusing to rest, and abandoning both your worldly affairs and your own life?"
"To protect sentient beings, I increase my diligence with valor; why then does this body not enter parinirvāṇa?
At that time, Prabhāsa-vimala-guṇa replied to his son in verse:
"I behold the suffering of the world and sentient beings who are utterly deluded by birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Oppressed by these [afflictions], the fire of defilement blazes fiercely as they sink and flow into the evil realms; therefore, with great courage and vigor, I seek to extinguish that fire.
Furthermore, with diminished wisdom, they do not see the future; they fall into the river of birth and death, into the most grievous and evil states.
Facing the miserable realms, they lose their way on the true path; it is for the sake of delivering them that I practice.
Yet they constantly distance themselves from the peace and bliss of humans and devas,
and always turn their backs on spiritual friends.
I pray that you will show sentient beings the essential path for transcending the world.
Within the prison of afflictions, sentient beings are constantly bound; they lack eyesight and have no savior.
Clinging to evil views, they devour flesh and blood. It is for their sake that [this is done].
Therefore, I practice with such compassionate reflection: for the sake of each and every person,
may they dwell in the Avīci Hell and fully undergo all manner of most intense sufferings and afflictions.
As it is for one person, so it is for many.
I do not delight in seeking the wisdom of the śrāvakas, nor do I wish to seek the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas;
I seek only the unsurpassed, most supreme wisdom.
Even until an immeasurable number of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
have not yet been liberated from suffering— desiring to deliver all those sentient beings—
I shall never take up the perfect awakening of Bodhi.
It should likewise be so: toward all sentient beings, one should always give rise to compassion, always be courageous, and practice wholesome dharmas.
Dedicate this toward the unsurpassed noble path.
Amidst the fires of affliction, you shall rescue and liberate sentient beings; you ought to be courageous and fierce—what need is there for such extreme suffering and distress?
"You should practice giving with a gentle and disciplined mind; you shall attain the Way of the Buddha, of this there is no doubt.
When I have attained unsurpassed Bodhi, you shall provide food and drink to sentient beings."
"At that time, I bestowed upon you the prediction of supreme enlightenment; you should now abide firmly in your steadfast vow.
Then, Puṇyavatī addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!..."
At that time, in the presence of the Buddha King of the Indra-Banner Sign, I made this vow:

"For as long as I remain in the world, whether for a short or long duration, I shall practice all manner of diligent and difficult austerities; I shall cultivate generosity and self-mastery, restraint against negligence, and all meditative concentrations; I shall assist in various affairs, practice extensive learning and the perfection of relinquishment, and be able to give up whatever is difficult to give."

"In this way, my father shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future world where the lifespan is one hundred years, a world defiled by afflictions, strife, turbidity, and delusion; and I shall appear in that land as the Lord of Merit."
Regarding the sentient beings within the realm of Śākyamuni Buddha and their retinues, they shall obtain the gift of unsurpassed clothing, food, drink, and the requisites for sustaining the body.
Immediately before Śākyamuni Buddha, they shall receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If the sentient beings in that land are violent, cruel, and coarse, lacking a heart of compassion, and further engage in treacherous conduct and evil intentions, thereby accomplishing such various evils; if wind and rain do not come at their proper times, whether through drought or flooding, or if cold and heat are unbalanced, causing various calamities; if all the flowers, fruits, five grains, medicinal herbs, and exquisite flavors possessed by sentient beings are utterly destroyed and deprived of their vital essence; and if the assets of sentient beings all decline and waste away, resulting in darkness and obscurity.
May I, at that time, through the empowerment of my merit toward those sentient beings and by the power of my wisdom, cause all [obstacles] to be halted and inspire in them faith.

Furthermore, may I ensure that sentient beings do not lack the necessities of life, refrain from committing evil, and increase in wholesome dharmas. May those sentient beings who are to be delivered and transformed by the Buddhas succeed in upholding the nature of the Triple Gem so that it remains uninterrupted, and may their spiritual power flourish and increase.
Furthermore, may I attain mastery over the environment and its rewards (*niṣyanda-bhoga*), so that I may teach and transform sentient beings, enabling them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the vows I have now made before the Buddha, which I wish to fulfill in future ages, I pray only that you grant your approval and bestow upon me the words "Excellent! (*sādhu*).
At that time, the Buddha King of the Indra-Banner Mark immediately confirmed this and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"Your wish shall surely be fulfilled.
Furthermore, son of good family!

I shall bestow upon you the *dhāraṇī-heart* called 'The Dwelling of the World’s Water. By means of this *dhāraṇī-heart*, you will be able to bring many sentient beings to accomplishment; you will cause immeasurable sentient beings to have their livelihoods and karmic rewards abundant and free from lack, and you will also enable them to cross over the turbulent flood of afflictions."
Then he spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā jvalambā..."
Mahā-jaḷamba, anu-ha-jaḷamba, sa-ra-jaḷamba, ugra-jaḷamba.

"Vārāśi svāhā.
"If one recites these dhāraṇī phrases for the sake of others or for oneself, calling their names, all fears and all calamities shall be completely extinguished."
"Good son! This is the Heart Dhāraṇī of the Water-Abode of the World. If you employ this Heart Dhāraṇī, you will be able to bring many sentient beings to accomplishment."
"O son of good family!

In the past, at the place of that Buddha Indraketudhvajarāja, I received and upheld this *dhāraṇī* called 'The Mind-Mansion of Water for the World. At that Buddha’s place, I made various kinds of offerings, observed the precepts, studied extensively, practiced generosity, and applied myself with diligence."
From that time onward, he further advanced his vows and practices in the presence of ten thousand buddhas.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he has now attained a station of great merit within this Bhadrakalpa; yet even now, he is still not yet capable of accomplishing this great enterprise.

Why is this? Since time immemorial, immeasurable evil nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, and others have been born into the world; toward all sentient beings they are poisonous, cruel, and violent, lacking faith and compassion, and devoid of a heart of mercy as they practice unwholesome dharmas. They cause untimely winds and rains, droughts and floods, calamitous hail, and irregularities of cold and heat—various forms of rebellion. They provoke strife and contention between their own armies and those of others, and amidst hatred and enmity, fierce winds suddenly arise, heedless of the future life.
"These sentient beings do not give rise to faith or joy regarding the *Cittadhāraṇī of the World-Water-Abode*, which was empowered by those past Buddhas.

Because those wicked beings lack faith and joy, they destroy, ruin, and seize the vital essence of all seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, delicious flavors, the five grains, medicinal herbs, and all means of subsistence."

They emitted poisonous vapors upon the essences of the earth, causing those essences to become tainted with poison, coarse, and foul; they became mixed with diseases, greasy, putrid, and flavorless, making this great earth such as it was. For this reason, sentient beings found no delight in it.

If sentient beings who subsist on the essence of the earth consume these seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, various flavors, the five grains, and medicinal herbs as means of sustaining their bodies, they will give rise to evil thoughts that are harsh, fierce, and poisonous.

Lacking a heart of compassion for all sentient beings and disregarding the future life, they are oppressed by various illnesses, their physical appearance is coarse and ugly, they are afflicted by the sufferings of manifold afflictions, and they are possessed of evil views while dwelling in false refuges.

They do not give rise to faith, joy, respect, reverence, or a sense of the marvelous toward the Triple Gem; even down to birds and beasts, they likewise cling to various evil views, losing their way and becoming deluded. They are sycophantic, crooked, and insincere, possessing nothing but empty words.
Those sentient beings, within the Three Jewels, violate the wholesome Dharma through body, speech, mind, and intention; they are unable to restrain themselves as monks who have broken the precepts.

They act with reckless abandon toward those monks of great virtue and eloquence who uphold the precepts, constantly keeping them at a distance and failing to approach them. They revile, slander, mock, and harass them, proclaiming their faults. Having abandoned shame and remorse and departed from the ten paths of wholesome action, their hearts take no delight in any virtuous conduct, giving rise instead to a spirit of alienation.

"At that time, sentient beings will be devoid of merit and wisdom, their lifespans will be short, and they will head toward the evil realms; therefore, I am currently unable to provide these sentient beings with all their necessities, nor can I bring them to spiritual maturity."
At this time, you are a great man who has attained mastery and skillful wisdom within the True Dharma.

Furthermore, you have already crossed over all samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences; you are well able to observe the further shore of wisdom, and you have completely crossed over the further shores of the adornments of compassion and the supernormal knowledges.

Furthermore, among those bodhisattvas, you are the most excellent banner; you have already been able to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment. Now, for my sake, you ought to give rise to a heart of compassion within these four continents and observe with your own wisdom: how may we cause all the evil dragons, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, and kaṭapūtanas—all such malevolent spirits—to be completely subdued; so that winds and rains follow their proper seasons, floods and droughts are harmonized, autumn harvests are bountiful, and cold and warmth are balanced?

By these causes and conditions, the potency, flavor, and fragrance of the various earth-essences are increased; when consumed, they cause no harm but augment the power of mindfulness. One’s physical appearance becomes full and lustrous, exceedingly pleasing to behold, and all things that accord with one's wishes emerge in the world. Relying upon this great earth, all sentient beings may consume it without fault, and their power of mindfulness shall increase as previously described.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: "O Pure Wisdom!

I am now able to cause all the four great elements within this buddha-field to be universally and entirely transformed into celestial food and drink, such that all sentient beings could not exhaust them even by eating for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have meager merit and are thus unable to eat it; they are not suitable vessels for such sublime retribution. "O Pure Wisdom!

Furthermore, I am able to transform this Sahā Buddha-field into celestial palaces and celestial bedding, and to create all manner of ornaments such as garments, fragrant flowers, and fruit trees, as well as various sounds and manifold exquisite music—all adorned with the seven precious gems.

These sentient beings are devoid of merit and are not suitable vessels, unable to partake of it; except for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and those who dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and have attained mastery, they alone are able to partake of it.
“O Viśuddhamati! Furthermore, since I am able to establish all sentient beings without exception in the fourth dhyāna, how could I not be able to subdue nāgas, pūtanas, and the like?”
Furthermore, it would be improper for me to manifest supernatural transformations without having first received the Buddha’s permission.
For example, it is impossible for a minister in charge of the military treasury of a Wheel-Turning Sage King to mobilize the fourfold army without following the king’s command.

Thus, all these bodhisattvas are the children of the Buddha; they are born from the mind of the Buddha, born from the mouth of the Buddha, and born through transformation from the Dharma. Therefore, among all these bodhisattvas, there is none who manifests supernatural transformations without having first requested the Tathāgata to do so.

“Pure Wisdom! Furthermore, there is a dhāraṇī-wheel named ‘The Assembly of All Mantra-Phrases of the Water-Wind Maṇi Palace,’ which establishes the nature of the Triple Gem of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.”
"O Pure Wisdom!
You may now question the Tathāgata regarding the Great Dharani-wheel Collection of All Mantra-arts and Verses of the Water-Wind-Maṇi Palace; if the Buddha speaks of it, I shall likewise rejoice."
“If you are able to receive and uphold this dhāraṇī, all your aspirations shall be completely fulfilled.

At that time, the goddess Mahāpuṇyavatī, together with the goddess Mahāprajñāvatī, the goddess Mahādṛḍhā, the goddess Mahāprabhāsa-karī, the goddess Priyaṅkarā, the goddess Kṣemaṅkarā, the goddess Tamāladṛḍhā, the goddess Tārādhīśvarā, the goddess Śyāmāvatī, and the goddess Sphaṭikā—these and other leading goddesses, accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of devas and hundreds of thousands of followers surrounding them in front and behind, rose from their seats and joined their palms toward the Buddha.
Then the goddess Puṇyavatī spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Capable of extinguishing the most evil and turbid afflictions, Free from defilement, with stainless and pure conduct— We thirstily yearn for this dhāraṇī;
We pray that you will expound the wheel of total retention.”
The Muni has taught tranquility free from defilement; the Three Jewels are the blazing, most supreme words.
May they cause the asuras and others to attain a pure mind, increasing the essence of the earth and eliminating all poison and evil.

May you be able to dispel cold, heat, and violent winds and rains; I pray you will explain how to protect against those who steal vital energy, and how to cause them to consume grains, medicines, fruits, and flavors instead, so that they may possess strong memory, eliminate afflictions, and cultivate virtuous conduct.
Having eradicated the harm of all evil views and taking refuge with faith in the most supreme and unsurpassed Dharma,
how should one teach and transform those sentient beings who rob others of their vital essence and are possessed of many afflictions?
These gods, toward the Sage, aspire to the most supreme, profound, and wondrous;
they reveal the path leading toward Bodhi, causing all sentient beings to enter the Mahāyāna.
The great assembly has gathered and their aspirations are fulfilled; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions praise the Buddha’s virtues:
"How shall you subdue all the evil dragons so that the rains fall in due season and the crops flourish?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: "Pure Wisdom!

This great dhāraṇī is proclaimed by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, only at rare intervals. Now, before this great assembly, the Tathāgata makes this solemn vow: 'This water-wind-maṇi-palace dhāraṇī-wheel is empowered by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; I shall now reveal it.'"

All the bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions and hear this shall be able to dwell in the five-turbidity worlds of the Buddha-less lands throughout the ten directions; they shall be able to manifest this Water-Wind-Maṇi-Palace Dhāraṇī-wheel, and by the power of this dhāraṇī, all untimely winds, heat, cold, warmth, drought, and floods within those lands shall be entirely extinguished.

By means of this dhāraṇī, may those venomous and evil beings who lack compassion and disregard the future life—namely, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, non-humans, and even birds and beasts—attain a mind of faith and joy, becoming gentle, mild, and virtuous; may they possess skillful power of mindfulness, delight in seeking the true Dharma, protect and uphold the true Dharma, and continue the lineage of the Triple Gem.
"By the power of this dhāraṇī, all sentient beings in that buddha-field shall increase in lifespan,
increase in physical appearance, increase in the five grains, increase in the necessities of life, increase in peace and happiness,
increase in freedom from affliction, increase in reputation, and increase in the observance of the precepts."
Increasing in erudition; increasing in generosity; increasing in compassion; increasing in wisdom;
increasing in skillful means; increasing in samādhi; increasing in dhāraṇī; increasing in the contemplation of the stages;
increasing in the aspiration for world-transcendence; increasing in the transformation of sentient beings; increasing in entry into the Mahāyāna; and increasing in excellence.
May there be an increase in the progressive entry into each successive stage; an increase in the contemplation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
an increase in shame and remorse; an increase in the gathering of merits for the adornment of Buddha-fields; an increase in the practice of the six pāramitās;
an increase in being constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas of the ten directions; and an increase in meeting with all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva’s spiritual friends increase his playful mastery of the supernormal powers; they increase the destruction of all afflictions so that they do not increase;
they increase his supernormal faculties for crossing to the other shore; and they ensure that no wholesome dharmas, up to and including unsurpassed nirvana, ever decline.
