The great assembly that had gathered trembled with unease; their hearts were struck with terror, and they cried out in unison: “Namo, namo buddhāya!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Puṇyavatī, saying:

“O Viśuddhamati! By the power of this Water-Wind Maṇi-Palace Dhāraṇī-wheel, you shall be able to eliminate all strife and contention, as well as all poisonous harms from yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, and evil nāgas, even including humans, non-humans, and various birds and beasts. Furthermore, all calamities such as untimely winds, heat, cold, frost, hail, drought, and excessive rain shall be entirely extinguished.”

“O Viśuddhamati! This dhāraṇī can cause the five grains to all ripen excellently; it causes all sentient beings to increase their lifespan and augment their karmic rewards, even extending to the growth of all wholesome dharmas, ensuring they are not lost or destroyed until they have entered unsurpassed nirvāṇa.”

"If anyone hears this dhāraṇī, receives and maintains it, reads and recites it, and practices according to its instructions, that person will certainly proceed toward nirvāṇa and dwell beyond the three realms.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I also wish to proclaim the Great Dharani of Whetting the Blade; by the power of this dharani, may all that is required for the karmic retribution of all beings, as well as the essence of the earth, never diminish, and may no one be able to destroy or seize the vital energy of the earth.

Furthermore, there is no one capable of emitting poisonous vapors, nor can anyone spoil its fine flavor, nor cause it to turn bitter and foul, nor cause it to vanish, nor prevent the five grains, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and grasses from growing upon this great earth, nor can anyone rob it of its vital essence.

"Furthermore, it shall not have any poisonous vapors, nor shall it wither or dry up; it shall not be harsh or foul, nor shall it be unripe or harmed by cold and heat; there shall be no impediment to its consumption, and once eaten, it shall be free of poison."

If food contains poison, it can cause the eater to suffer from abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea; it afflicts both body and mind, causing the limbs to contract, and leads to feverish illness, insanity, mental confusion, and loss of mindfulness. It causes mutual plundering and strife, as well as killing, stealing, and even wrong views.

All these sentient beings are constantly associated with the aforementioned evil dharmas—namely, whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, pretas, piśācas, or pūtanas, kāṭapūtanas, humans, or non-humans—and yet they are unable to afflict or harm other sentient beings.

"By these dhāraṇī phrases, may this lord of the land be protected."
Svāhā. "O Pure Wisdom! This is the Great Dharani for Sharpening the Blade.
By the power of this Great Dharani for Sharpening the Blade, you shall be able to perform the aforementioned great deeds for all sentient beings and act as a great medicine."
"For this reason, you are now able to cause all sentient beings to receive your transformation.
Thereupon, the entire great assembly that had gathered praised the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
At that time, the World-Honored One also praised Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
You are now able to serve as a great and wondrous medicine for all sentient beings. Why is this?

Your very body is a subtle and sublime great medicine; among all sentient beings within these four continents, you are the medicine for beings, capable of extinguishing the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings and bestowing upon them all the requisites of happiness, thereby perfecting great compassion.

Because you are able to manifest the power of this profound *Kṣuramāṇa-mahā-dhāraṇī*, you cause the essence of the earth, vital energy, seeds, sprouts, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, all flavors, the five grains, and medicinal herbs among these sentient beings not to decline; they grow free from poison and are fully perfected as food for sentient beings. You cause the impurities and strife of those sentient beings to be entirely extinguished, so that they may be capable of practicing wholesome deeds.

In these four continents, untimely winds, heat, cold, humidity, drought, and floods are all entirely eliminated; likewise, the anomalies of the sun, moon, and stars, day and night, the waxing and waning of the moon, the seasons, and the years are also extinguished. For the sake of subduing these, this Great Razor Dhāraṇī is taught.

By the power of this dhāraṇī, may my lineage of the Triple Gem and the Eye of Dharma endure for a long time in the world. May those who are ruined by ignorance, darkness, meager merit, and arrogance—namely, wicked kṣatriyas and ministers who do not cultivate roots of goodness—not cause the destruction or ruin of this Dharma, which I have accumulated through diligent ascetic practices over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas. May bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās be free from affliction and disturbance; because they are free from affliction, the devas shall not be provoked to anger; and because the devas are not provoked to anger, all sentient beings shall obtain the aforementioned articles of happiness.
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 57;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Scroll 58.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Dhāraṇī Section; Chapter Fifteen: The Sumerugarbha Section.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: “O Viśuddhamati!

"In the past, you and I, the two of us, together made a vow before the Buddha Indraketudhvajarāja. Now our vows have been fulfilled; I have now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and you likewise abide in the station of merit."
Gunaśrī said: "So it is, so it is, O Great Virtuous Bhagavat!"
"So it is, so it is, Great Virtuous Sugata!

My aspirations together with those of the World-Honored One have been fulfilled; my virtuous desires together with those of the World-Honored One have been fulfilled. Formerly, I and the World-Honored One made a common vow together in the presence of King Indradhvaja-lakṣaṇa Buddha; now that vow is entirely fulfilled and our hearts are satisfied. Therefore, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, and I now abide in a place of merit."
Although I have now attained this state of merit, I am still unable to fulfill my original vow to bring sentient beings to maturity. Why is this?
Because in this place there are many elephant-nāgas, horse-nāgas, snake-nāgas, fish-nāgas, and frog-nāgas.
Among the sentient beings of this realm, he has committed evil deeds; although he has preached the profound *Prabhāsa-dhāraṇī*, he has still not been able to subdue these various evil nāgas.

That dragon constantly brings about untimely cold and heat, malignant clouds, torrential rain, and irregular droughts or floods, thereby harming sentient beings as well as the sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs of the five grains.
“O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!

Now, within this world-system of four continents, all the nāgas, mahānāgas, and their retinues—male nāgas, female nāgas, nāga boys, and nāga girls—whosoever are born into the nāga realm, have all gathered here.”

Furthermore, all the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from all the Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions gathered there; likewise, all the devas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth, all assembled there.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, the śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha, humans, non-humans, and others have also all gathered at this great assembly; for the sake of hearing the Dharma, they stand before the Buddha. All sentient beings subsist by means of the four kinds of nutriment.
“O Great Virtuous Blessed One! Now is the very time.

We pray only that you will remove these calamities and expedients of the evil, venomous nāgas—those who have no faith in the Tathāgata, whose minds are constantly associated with unwholesome dharmas, who harass and disturb sentient beings, who destroy the means of subsistence for sentient beings, who are poisonous, wicked, and coarse, who lack compassion for all beings, and who do not see the future life—and do not allow them to create obstacles and difficulties for the beings whom I transform.”
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
you should give rise to great compassion for those sentient beings and extinguish all their evils.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nāgarāja Sumerugarbha, saying:
“Good son! In the past, at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, you made a great, courageous, and far-reaching vow to transform all nāgas.
You, Sumerugarbha!”

There are four kinds of birth among dragons and great dragons who are venomous and malevolent: all those dragons of the past, future, and present who possess the poison of breath, the poison of sight, the poison of touch, the poison of biting, as well as the poison of greed, the poison of hatred, and the poison of delusion.

Regarding these evil nāgas, how should we now lawfully eliminate all their evil karma so that the various means of subsistence belonging to all sentient beings shall not be diminished, so that they may have faith, joy, and reverence for the Triple Gem, and with deep conviction in future lives, abstain from evil karma?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sumerugarbha Nāga-ṛṣi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I shall enter the palace of that venomous dragon and sit cross-legged, entering the Dragon-Frequency-Stretching Samādhi (*nāga-vijṛmbhita-samādhi*). By the power of this samādhi, I will cause the greed, anger, and arrogance of that evil dragon to be completely extinguished. I will soften and subdue him so that his mind becomes tranquil and he develops deep faith in future lives. I will inspire compassion and pity for all sentient beings and give rise to a heart of rescue and relief, causing that venomous dragon to conceive a heart of reverence and faith, so that he no longer harasses or disturbs any sentient beings, but instead establishes them upon the ground of rescuing and relieving all beings.”

Furthermore, whenever there is wind, rain, drought, or flooding in the world, or when clouds and great clouds cause harm through cold or heat, those sentient beings should invoke my name, join their palms together, and speak these words:
"O Greatly Compassionate One!"
Think of me, think of me!

O Bodhisattva Sumerugarbha, who is able to transform and subdue dragons, and who employs various skillful means, wisdom, and valor to practice the path to unsurpassed bodhi—may you only deign to save me and eliminate my suffering.
Having spoken these words, he then uttered this mantra:

*tadyathā | sadambabhuja | viliḍhabhuja | śukulibiḍhabhuja | meruśavaga | cchavabhuja-yaṃ-yaṃ-anibhabhuja | somarābaddhabhuja | jñapubhuja | svāhā ||* "By this dhāraṇī-mantra phrase, may [the name of the person] be protected! Svāhā! "O Bhagavat of Great Virtue!"

If there are sentient beings who are tormented and disturbed by various venomous dragons, they should invoke my name and recite this dhāraṇī; this will be able to extinguish these dragons' greedy, hateful, arrogant, jealous, and poisonous evil minds.

With my pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, I hear this; having heard it, if the four classes of nāgas—the great nāgas, the nāga fathers, the nāga mothers, the nāga sons, the nāga daughters, and their retinues—cannot be made to give rise to reverence and faith, they will continue to produce such untimely winds and rains, cold and heat, drought and flooding, calamitous clouds, and other evils.

If I do not extinguish [these afflictions], and if I do not provide all sentient beings with the causes and conditions for peace and happiness to fulfill their vows, then I would be deceiving all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; furthermore, may I never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"So it is, Blessed One! In the past, in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and before the great assembly of his retinue, I made such firm and great vows."
From that time forward, he has always dwelt securely in the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Furthermore, from that time onward, in the presence of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddhas currently residing with their retinues, he has likewise made such firm and great vows.

I constantly abide in the power of great diligence, teaching and transforming sentient beings with tireless exertion; just as I am now before the World-Honored One, my firm diligence is no different from this, for the purpose of subduing and converting all evil dragons.
“World-Honored One!

I recall that from incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past until now, I do not remember ever for even a single moment relinquishing firm, courageous, and vigorous diligence. My mind has always dwelt securely in firm diligence to teach and transform sentient beings, and even unto this day, I continue to teach and transform all sentient beings.”

These dragon kings diligently practice the Mahāyāna Dharma; that is to say, this King Supratiṣṭhita is the lord of all elephant dragons, this King Nanda and this King Upananda are the lords of all serpent dragons, this King Anavatapta is the lord of all horse dragons, this King Varuṇa is the lord of all fish dragons, and this King Mānasa-vatsī is the lord of all frog dragons.
These great nāga kings are capable of inflicting various forms of decay and affliction upon sentient beings; as for the other nāgas, their own power is insufficient to cause such superior calamities.

These five great nāga kings abide in the Mahāyāna and possess great majestic power; each of these great nāga kings, together with their respective retinues, pledges before the Buddha not to incite the aforementioned calamities, so that the lamp of the Buddha-dharma and the lineage of the Triple Gem may long endure in the world and not quickly perish.
At that time, the entire great assembly who had gathered there praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sumerugarbha Nāgarāja with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
At that time, the Dragon King Susthitu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"O Bhagavān of Great Virtue!

All the nāgas and mahānāgas who belong to me—namely those born from wombs, from eggs, from moisture, or by transformation—who follow the assembly of disciples, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas of the Buddha, shall dwell in their respective lands with hearts of loving-kindness toward one another, free from thoughts of enmity or harm, and abiding in a state of peace and equanimity.

Furthermore, those who attain the status of kings in that land shall gain pure faith in the Buddha-dharma and protect it. They shall not, out of pride in their noble rank or sovereign power, give rise to arrogance and destroy the Buddha-dharma. Nor shall they harass bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. Toward all who have gone forth in reliance upon the Buddha—whether they be worthy vessels or not—who have shaved off their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes, such persons shall be protected by their faithful support.
If there are other sentient beings within that land who give rise to animosity or hostility toward the Buddha-dharma, the king should restrain them in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the fields, houses, and fiefs previously bestowed by former kings upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas out of reverent faith, he should permit them to continue using them and shall not confiscate them.

If there are wise ministers and high officials who harmonize their minds to govern state affairs together, who acquire stable wealth and constantly extend the hand of charity, then this Kṣatriya king will well protect his kingdom. All the strife, contention, and defilements within the entire realm, as previously described, shall cease; we, the various kings, will each command our own retinues not to give rise to calamities or disturbances.
"Why have I now issued such a decree?
This dyed robe of the *kāṣāya* has always been sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas of the past.

Furthermore, this *kāṣāya* is the seed of all Bodhisattvas; it is the direct path leading toward *nirvāṇa*; it is a sharp sword capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is the seed of *nirvāṇa*; it is the lamp for those who have lost their way, and it is also the medicine for those afflicted by disease."

It is like a great, violent wind that blows away the clouds of ignorance; it is the staff for those who would travel the evil paths of desire; it is the emetic that can vomit up the poison of afflictions; it is the vajra that destroys the enemies of the asuras; and it is the treasury of all wholesome dharmas.

"Just as pure water can wash away the defilement of sin, contemplate all unwholesome dharmas as being like a bright mirror; it can gather a distracted mind like a net, and it can contain meditative concentration like a precious casket."
Just as the great earth can give birth to all the pāramitās, one should carry them upon the crown of one's head like a bright jewel in a topknot.
Being able to endure insults is like having a dwelling; it is a pure vessel that contains the practices of the ten stages.
He acts as a citadel to obstruct all non-Buddhists; he is a skilled physician who cures the disease of afflictions.

To those in training, he is like Mount Sumeru; he dispels the heat of afflictions like the bright moon; he removes the darkness of false views like the pure sun; and he serves as a treasury of wisdom like the great ocean.

Regarding the factors of enlightenment, it is like a flower garland; regarding the knowledge of all modes, it is like an auspicious vase; and as for the protection of all Buddhas, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Furthermore, this kāṣāya is blessed by all Buddhas because it rains down the rain of Dharma upon all sentient beings.

"Therefore, Blessed One! If a wicked Kṣatriya king destroys the Buddha-dharma and harasses bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or even those who have gone forth under the Buddha—whether they are worthy vessels or not—and if he punishes their bodies, seizes their property, or even takes their lives; [may his merit be lost]."

Therefore, within that country, there may be those who revere and have faith in devas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, and others of great majestic power; should they give rise to a mind of malice toward any of those kṣatriya kings, they will cause strife, famine, pestilence, and the concurrent outbreak of weapons to arise in that land. Furthermore, untimely winds and rains, droughts and floods, and extremes of cold and heat will damage the five grains, their seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and medicinal properties.
"This is not the fault of the nāgas; these nāgas are truly innocent, yet they have been unjustly subjected to an evil reputation. O Bhagavān, Mahābhadra!
It is like a brāhmaṇa who, having himself eaten garlic and then consorted with a precious woman, does not say that he himself is foul-smelling, but falsely accuses the precious woman, saying:"
"O World-Honored One! This wicked Kṣatriya king is just like that:

he abandons the dharma of a Kṣatriya and practices the conduct of a Śūdra. Because of this cause and condition, the gods who protect the kingdom and possess majestic power, down to the preta spirits, give rise to anger and resentment and destroy the kingdom. Yet the king, his ministers, and the people do not examine their own faults, but falsely ascribe ill repute to the nāgas and mahānāgas."
The Buddha said to the Dragon King:
"I have already issued instructions to all kings: if they follow these teachings, they will attain the happiness of humans and devas, and even obtain the bliss of nirvana."
If an evil Kṣatriya king does not act in accordance with these teachings, he shall even fall into the Avīci Hell.
He further addressed the Dragon King:

“Each of you must admonish your own retinue, establishing strict instructions so that they do not commit transgressions, ensuring that in both the present and future worlds they do not destroy my Dharma or the lineage of the Triple Gem.”
At that time, the Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
so it is, Bhagavān!”
"So it is, so it is, Sugata! World-Honored One!"

In whichever lands there may be those who uphold the precepts and possess great learning, wherever my retinue resides within those countries—whether they be male nāgas, female nāgas, nāga fathers, nāga mothers, nāga sons, nāga daughters, or other nāga followers—in all places throughout those lands, such as cities, towns, and villages, they shall produce untimely winds, rains, frost, hail, cold, and heat, thereby destroying the five grains, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and all means of livelihood.

"Bhagavān! If there are any nāgas who contravene my instructions at the dwelling place of that field of merit, I shall make a vow to cause those evil nāgas to have their bodies withered and emaciated and to lose their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). With burning heat touching their bodies, their primary and secondary supports (*upadhi*) will be destroyed; they will no longer possess eloquence and will be incapable of performing any service."
He then spoke the mantra:

"Tadyathā | nāgānubhai | nāganime | nāgadara | sugara | sugara | jarasugara | abhimakīsa | paha | saramuṣiṇa | karatebūśe | nabasadambai | tejayapavale | vimuśakale | svāhā | By these dhāraṇī phrases, may [Name] be protected, and may all fears and all calamities be completely extinguished. Svāhā. At that time, the entire great assembly praised the Dragon King Suvikrānta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Great Dragon King!
You are able to protect all sentient beings.
At that time, the entire assembly of dragons was struck with alarm and fear.
At that time, the Dragon King Nanda and the Dragon King Upananda rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"O Bhagavān, Great Virtuous One!

Whether in the present or future age, if there should be a wicked Kṣatriya king who is stingy with his wealth and resources, neither using them himself nor giving them to others; who is miserly and attached to his own possessions and does not extend a hand in charity; who has no faith in śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and does not provide for the poor, travelers, or beggars; and who likewise does not bestow upon those in his own palace or among his retinue the pleasures and comforts that accord with the Dharma.

Those various devas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, and others who protect the land and possess great majesty and power—all of them will give rise to a mind of anger toward wicked kṣatriya kings, causing strife, famine, pestilence, and weapons to break out in competition within those lands, even to the point that the five grains and medicinal flavors will all be ruined.
"It is not the fault of those nāgas or great nāgas; those dragon kings are truly without fault, yet they have undeservedly acquired an evil reputation.
It is like when a wind blows over a putrid corpse, and the people of the world say:
'This is a foul wind.'"
"However, the nature of that wind is actually not foul-smelling.

In the same way, World-Honored One, it is likewise with an evil Kṣatriya king: because of his stinginess and greed, all those who protect the kingdom give rise to a mind of anger; because of that anger, they bring ruin and disorder to the country, and he is falsely given an evil reputation among the nāgas."
Although I have issued this command for the sake of those nāgas, if any of those nāgas— whether past or future— should violate my command,
then in whatever lands inhabited by the śrāvaka disciples of these Buddhas who are observant of the precepts and possessed of great learning,
or wherever my own retinue exists— whether born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, or by transformation— [may they be subject to my power].
If male nāgas, female nāgas, nāga fathers, nāga mothers, nāga sons, nāga daughters, and their nāga retinues,
within those cities, villages, mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys, should cause unseasonable winds and rains,
droughts and floods, calamitous hail, or extreme cold and heat, thereby harming sentient beings— (5)
Regarding those who cause harm to the grains, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, flavors, and the various necessities of life belonging to the Buddhas,
Śrāvakas, disciples, and persons of merit— those nāgas who disobey my command shall take an oath so that their bodies become cramped and they are unable to move about,
losing their supernatural powers and being consumed by burning heat.
When his body is touched, all his physical supports and enjoyments will be utterly destroyed; he will no longer possess eloquence or the ability to act.
He then spoke this mantra:

“Tadyathā | Paranāśume | Kujūpātulakīvaruṇakuve | Akārakī | Kṣaṇivimāharākī | Kunābi | Araki | Adāśre | Nayana-dambi | Karakuśe | Śyāṅku-parājite-gandha-haravasi | Svāhā | ‘By these dhāraṇī-words, may [so-and-so] be protected! Svāhā! At that time, the entire great assembly praised Nanda and Upananda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
At that time, the Nāga King Anavatapta also made a vow before the Buddha to provide protection, commanding his retinue as previously described.
He then spoke this mantra:

“Tadyathā | Namaḥ piliśe | Nabhanama piliśe-anucana-paṅga-ja-ni-kī | Khaga-pe-kha-pratolū-aṃ | Ḍe-tu-mai-ha-ya-sre | Nārāyaṇa-gumi-bi | Na-si-su-re | A-sa-kara-me | A-cu-se-ni | Yi-she-mu-ni-sa-vi | Svāhā. “This dhāraṇī shall protect [Name], causing him to be free from fear and calamity. Svāhā. At that time, the Dragon King Varuṇa also, before the Buddha, instructed his retinue and made his own vow, as was previously described.
He then spoke this mantra:

“Tadyathā | himavemi | varakīṇa gune | tamapini | dutele | varakhadale migasaṃkume | piyamukhiṃ | kṣe | turumudimeye | donakus | camakhike | caraharaṅgi | naṭadaṭi gaṇḍakadule | svāhā. “This dhāraṇī-phrase protects [Name] | svāhā. At that time, the Nāga King Maṇasvāti rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: “Bhadanta Bhagavan!”

"O Bhagavān! Among those nāgas and mahānāgas who rely upon me—whether born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, or by transformation—if there should be wicked kṣatriya kings in the present or future who abandon the dharma of kṣatriya kings and practice evil deeds, such kings will follow the preliminary path to the Avīci Hell. One should know that all this is the fault of the wicked kṣatriya kings; the nāga kings are innocent, yet they are falsely subjected to ill repute. Due to these causes and conditions, the nāga kings become enraged and commit various evil karmas."
Nevertheless, we respectfully accept the teaching of the Tathāgata.
"World-Honored One!

It is as if, among a great multitude of people, there were a woman of exquisite jewels who had bathed until she was pure, anointed her body with fragrances, and donned the most sublime garments of a wheel-turning sage king."

Upon his head he wore a supreme wreath of the seven precious gems, and he adorned himself with armlets, bracelets, and rings of pure gold; mounted upon a great elephant and surrounded by his retinue, he was escorted to the presence of the Kṣatriya king.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Our bodies, which belong to the category of nāgas and animals, are ruined and defiled by greed, hatred, and pride.
The Tathāgata, however, is now the King of the Dharma-Wheel."

Bathe us with the water of the foremost self-subjugation; clothe us in the raiment of shame and remorse; adorn our heads with the garlands of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and embellish our mind, intellect, and consciousness with the various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and stages of patience, so that we may ascend the vehicle of the Mahāyāna.

I now wish to go to a pure buddha-field, free from the five corruptions, to the place where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a multitude of pure great bodhisattvas, is preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Therefore, we respectfully accept the Buddha’s teaching.

From this day forth, together with our own retinues, we shall abide in firm and steadfast great vows and aspirations. In every place—whether in cities, towns, villages, mountain ranges, or border fortresses—whenever there are those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or those of the Bodhisattva vehicle; whether they be monastics or laypeople, whether they observe the precepts or break them, whether they are learned or of little learning, and whether they are diligent or indolent.

Whether in a state of concentration or distraction, whether with mindfulness or loss of mindfulness, they simply give rise to a sense of wonder toward the Tathāgata through love, faith, and reverence; it is likewise so toward the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the noble precepts. They incline their minds toward the three types of enlightenment as they wish, giving rise to a sense of wonder through love, faith, and reverence, remaining firm and securely established wherever they abide.

Whether they be my own retinue, or dragon fathers and dragon mothers, male dragons and female dragons, or dragon sons and dragon daughters along with their followers—wherever they may be, in cities, towns, villages, mountains, rivers, or remote wildernesses—if untimely wind and rain, drought or flooding, calamitous hail, or sudden cold and heat arise, causing injury to the five grains, seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, and all medicinal herbs and means of livelihood.

Wherever there are shrines of the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples—the fields of merit—should any nāgas violate my commands and instructions, I now make this vow: I shall cause their bodies to contract entirely, causing them to lose their supernormal powers so they cannot travel; their bodies shall be scorched by heat and their sense faculties blocked, such that their external environment will be ruined and they will be unable to perform any functions.
He then spoke the mantra:

"Tadyathā | Buddhasya jaye | Varṣe | Amamini bodhisāriḷi | Apamatte | Pratyenili apanirame | Kṣipa śūṣṇa sudubhiparibhi | Śvavi śāntaparibhi | Varṇakṣīye | Svāhā. "May this dhāraṇī protect [Name]! Svāhā! At that time, the entire great assembly who had gathered rejoiced and leaped for joy; with palms joined, they praised the Naga King Manasvati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Great Being! That which you ought to do is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
At that time, the entire assembly of nāgas was struck with alarm and trepidation; they were bewildered and lost their composure.
At that time, there was a gandharva seer named Bhaiṣajyasena who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:

"May the great assembly of Buddhas attend with single-minded mindfulness. Whether in the present or the future, if there are wicked kṣatriya kings—foolish, lacking wisdom, and ruined by arrogance—who disregard the next world, are deceitful and devoid of compassion, and who harass and disturb bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, even those who have taken refuge in the Tathāgata, shaved their hair, and donned the saffron robes, I shall, through the power of samādhi, make this vow before those wicked kṣatriya kings to cause those evil kings to receive the retribution in this very life."

It shall cause the king’s person, his retinue, and their means of livelihood and enjoyments to be plundered by hostile nations; it shall cause internal rebels and insurgents to stir up turmoil, rivers and ponds to dry up or overflow with floods, and the people to be afflicted by epidemics and portended by the appearance of malevolent stars. Bandits shall rise up in competition, while the king becomes addicted to and attached to sensual pleasures. Family members and kinsmen shall be scattered and live in insecurity; the four great elements shall undergo transformations and spirits shall cause disturbances. All those possessing power and majesty, from the devas and nāgas down to the hungry ghosts, shall all become ill at ease.

There are kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras—whether men or women—who are all likewise ill at ease; even lions, tigers, wolves, predatory beasts, and venomous insects are all likewise ill at ease.
I now make this vow because I wish to destroy the evil kingdom of that wicked king.

Why is this? Because these wicked kings have caused turmoil for those who have gone forth from home under the Tathāgata to shave their hair—those whom all Buddhas sustain and through whom the seeds of the Triple Gem are made to flourish.
He then spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā vane..."
Yebanabale mahāvanide dulo.
Maca cī kusoma parāti yuta sampraca.
Vaimatī-tāṣa-ulo-paṇaya-paripāri-bu-ma-duru-kara.
Mimi he lian shaji luomi dili peimo bodu (Mimihelianshijiluomidilipomobodu)
Maśurukha śinayana kien-kie pi-p'o-che pi-li-ch'ie.
Namo Cchamkha-viśākha-pārāśarī-pāramin.
Dhātrī-bhūmi-pārśva-je yu-lu-ma-dhāri-vanaga-śe-bhūma-je.
Āvāce paṇaye bīre śiśvakārami sūtradhara.
"Gandharva-sme svāhā.
"By this dhāraṇī phrase, may [the name of the person] be protected, so that they shall have no fear or calamity, svāhā.
May those wicked kṣatriya kings and those who do not see the future world and who harass bhikṣus incur such evil retribution.
At that time, all the gathered hosts of nāgas and gandharvas each spoke these words:
"We pray that you release us.

If a kṣatriya king violates the Dharma, commits evil deeds, and disturbs the Saṅgha of the Dharma, we shall fulfill our vow and allow ourselves once more to sport, sing, and dance within our own palaces, enjoying pleasures with complete freedom."
At that time, the entire great assembly that had gathered raised their voices in unison and praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha joined his palms, prostrated before the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I possess the supernormal power of sporting in all samādhis, and I now wish to proclaim the Great Dhāraṇī Door of the Banner-Staff.

If anyone hears this Great Dhāraṇī Door of the Banner-Staff even once, all diseases of the ear shall be completely cured; furthermore, all diseases of the afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion shall be eliminated, or at the very least, rendered light and thin.”

By reciting this mantra over sea-calf skin one hundred thousand times while remaining in meditative concentration, it shall be used to coat the king’s drum. Any who hear its sound will find all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion completely attenuated; they will attain pure faith, reverence, love, and a sense of rare wonder toward the Buddha-dharma, and will also gain courageous compliance with the practice of the Dharma. They will have deep faith that their provisions for future lives will be abundant, and all people will love them and take delight in seeing them.
He then spoke the mantra:

"Tadyathā | bhaṃgabha | madi alupa | madikitarabhu | kṣepana-kaṇṭi | kuṇama-kṣile-matsa-nule | kāharanadi-naṣṭa-vami | bandha-haraśumi | bhāgarakiri-milu-hita-haravi-ṅgala-su | bhagana-jili-ni-andhaja-śerika-ra-buśe | kṣeluhu | samādhi-tupari | svāhā. "This dharani-verse shall protect [Name], causing him to be free from fear. Svāhā. At that time, the Tathāgata praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
"Excellent, O noble being!
and the entire great assembly also joined in praise, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:

"Buddha and the great assembly, I pray that you will rejoice in this; I now wish to proclaim a great dhāraṇī called 'The Wish-Fulfilling Eye of the Jewel Banner Arising from the Speech and Sounds of All Tathāgatas. It possesses great majesty, great power, and great might; it fulfills the treasury of learning and fulfills the treasury of wisdom, and is that which has been accomplished by all Buddhas and śrāvakas."
If there is anyone who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, dwells in pure precepts for as long as life lasts,
dwelling in the precepts of an upāsaka, or dwelling in the śrāmaṇera precepts, or dwelling in the full precepts— whether they be a fit vessel or not—
if they are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this Great Dhāraṇī of the Banner, Parasol, Maṇi, and Vow-Eye for seven days and seven nights...
At night, with wisdom-observation and skillful means, he constantly contemplates the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Reciting this *Dhvaja-vitāna-praṇidhāna-cakṣus-mahā-dhāraṇī* repeatedly, if he can complete one hundred thousand recitations over seven days and seven nights, he will immediately attain the power of hearing and retaining (*śruta-dhara*), receiving [the teachings] as soon as they are heard; he will obtain immeasurable eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and be able to [influence] the Kṣatriyas...
Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all sentient beings will give rise to respectful faith; furthermore,
they will be made abundant in wealth and resources, proceed toward the heavenly realms, and constantly attain proximity to the presence of all Buddhas.
He then spoke this mantra before the Buddha, saying:

“Tadyathā | Tiriṇa | Sañjaya-ke | Vidiriṇa-pinvi-karaṇḍe | Pūvasuve | Cāmara-cinne | Aparakhe | Akṣaye-lu | Atyayadumati-mili-śiri-bavi-śavari-aṅgīra-jāte-siṇḍe | Jajjara-nume | Anama-śuddhi-mili-kha-khili-khe-kurava-je-miga-pakṣa-pau | Śavaśavari | Abhidi-su-pu | Śavarakhase | Sumati-mune | Svāhā. “This dhāraṇī protects [the name of] so-and-so. Svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"O virtuous man!
You have skillfully maintained my Dharma. You are able to manifest this Great Dhāraṇī of the Banner, Parasol, and Vow-Eye, and you are able to show the eye of great learning to all sentient beings."
At that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas praised the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! O virtuous man!”

In the present and in future lives, for all sentient beings who aspire toward the Mahāyāna, you will be able to increase and sustain the accumulation of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), because you are now able to manifest this great *dhāraṇī* of the fulfillment of extensive learning through the Eye of the Vow of the Banner and Parasol.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

I now likewise desire to cause all the trees, flowers, fruits, five grains, medicinal flavors, sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves, as well as the necessities for the sustenance of the sentient beings dwelling upon the earth within these four continents, to be abundant and sufficient; for the sake of their protection, I shall proclaim a great dhāraṇī named Kūṣmāṇḍī Śrī-jinā.

Within these four continents, such a great assembly performed by the Tathāgata is rare, unprecedented, unseen, and unheard of. I shall now proclaim this *Śrīputra-jinu-mahādhāraṇī*, which possesses great majestic power; it increases all seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, medicinal flavors, and moisture, making them all sweet, succulent, and abundant. It enables all sentient beings to cultivate faith, precepts, extensive learning, generosity, wisdom, compassion, and skillful means, thereby nourishing all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
He then spoke this mantra before the Buddha:

"Tadyathā | amanye-ke-vi-kṣa-pi-śe-ku | ru-cara-ru-mi | paṭṭa-kṣa-ru-mi | śrīya-kṣa-ku-su-mi-na | ba-gu-man | ti-ha-ra-ja-bha-mi-ca-ṭa-ba-bha-ma-ce | pi-su-laṅ-gi-a-bhra-su-le | ha-sa-ga-ja-ca | ru-ma-bhu-ja-ca | kṣaṃ-vi-ra-bha-su-mi | a-nu-ma-ya-sa-ri-pra-śa-du-ye | svāhā | This dhāraṇī phrase protects [Name] | svāhā. At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Write this dhāraṇī upon a high banner and recite it with a loud voice.
Furthermore, chant this dhāraṇī-spell over the juice of the madana fruit one thousand times and scatter it over trees, field crops, and the five grains.

If one consecrates various conch shells and drums with this mantra and blows or strikes them, then wherever the sound reaches, all flowers, fruits, the five grains, medicinal herbs, and flavors that grow from the earth shall not be destroyed by any calamity, nor shall they be withered, nor can they be burned away, nor can their vital essence be stolen.
Furthermore, one cannot impair their power, nor can anyone plunder it.

Whether they be devas, nāgas, or even highly majestic preta spirits; whether they be Māras, sons of Māra, or the retinues of Māra—none can cause them harm, much less other sentient beings or those categorized as such, except for the fixed obstructions of past karma!
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
You have now skillfully mounted the vehicle of meritorious giving within the four continents.
Son of good family!
You are furthermore able to assist immeasurable sentient beings in accomplishing the path to unexcelled bodhi.
At that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas praised the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! What you have done should always be thus.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

“I shall now bestow upon you a great dhāraṇī named ‘Vessel-Flower Merit. By means of the phrases of this dhāraṇī, you shall don the armor of great compassion for all sentient beings and preach the Dharma with its voice.”

By the power of your samādhi and supernormal faculties, these sentient beings shall hear the True Dharma; they shall eliminate all evil intentions, false views, evil associates, and wicked companions. They will constantly recollect the roots of goodness of compassion, give rise to a heart of pity toward all sentient beings, deeply perceive the future world, and distance themselves from the ten unwholesome paths of action while abiding in the mind of the ten wholesome paths. They will be able to purify the minds of all sentient beings, raining down the rain of Dharma according to their inclinations, causing all enemies to rejoice and give rise to a heart of faith and delight.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā lambu svāhā."
Kaśyapavami, thrice recite Yibajie, Tuopohelengqiejie.
Muli chasu hecha sabhari suha vāji.
Aparogale siddhābhyavacarīhana piṇḍasiri.
Abhiśānta avyāpāda-cara-aparādhya-roṣiṇi.
Brahācūḍilaka haradūte samādhi-kani.
Vrajaṇite mahāpudgala-akṣaye āraṇi-le.
*Brahāśame nīlagu-sume svāhā*.
"This dharani-phrase protects the sovereign of the land, svāhā. Thus it is, Maitreya!
This is the Great Dharani of the Merit of the Flower Boat. Clad in the armor of this dharani, the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

If any sentient beings hear the sound of this dharani even once as it passes through their ears—even down to the most minute mosquitoes, gnats, and insects—all turbid and evil thoughts will be completely extinguished, and they will attain a mind that dwells securely within wholesome dharmas; how much more so for humans who hear this dharani!

If there is anyone who desires rain, they should go to the source of a spring where dragons dwell and recite this dhāraṇī one thousand and eight times each day, continuing in this manner for seven days.

Furthermore, they scattered various kinds of fine flowers, famous incenses, and food and drink of a hundred flavors into the dragon pond, with the sole exception of alcohol, meat, the five pungent roots, and other impure foods.

From the seventh day of the month until the fourteenth, on the morning of the fifteenth, one should take powdered black pepper mixed with castor oil and recite the mantra over it one thousand and eight times. Then, applying this mixture to a piece of white cotton cloth, one should cast it into a dragon spring. This will cause the dragon to feel great joy toward that person and pour down heavy rain.

At that time, the great nāgas, nāga-sages, and all those assembled in the assembly, having heard this Great Dharani of the Merit of Ship-Flowers, were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. They felt profound gratitude and gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and a conviction in future lives. Within the Triple Gem, they developed pure faith and reverence, giving birth to a heart of veneration and a sense of wonder. They repented for their own minds that had produced evil karma leading to rebirth in the animal realm, and entered into the mind of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.

Each of those nāgas, according to their respective power and ability, desired to make offerings to the Buddha. Among the nāgas and mahānāgas, some rained down gold powder, silver powder, gośīrṣa-candana, solid black aloeswood, nāga-karkaṭika-candana, and tamāla-leaf incense; others rained down utpala flowers, padma flowers, various other flowers, various garments, various canopies, various banners and pennants, golden cords, and pearl necklaces.
All the nāgas and mahānāgas joined their palms toward the Buddha and, at one time with a single voice, spoke these words:
“O Bhagavān of Great Virtue!
We all abide in a mind of superior faith and joy toward the Triple Gem.”
We now, before the World-Honored One, utter this oath of truth: wherever there may be cities, towns, or villages, we shall manifest this Ship-Flower Merit Dhāraṇī among the people.

In this way, all these other dhāraṇīs—namely, the Water-Abode Mind Dhāraṇī, the Whetstone Dhāraṇī, the Banner and Canopy Vow Dhāraṇī, the Able-to-Solicit Śrī and Jīvanu Dhāraṇī, the Boat-Flower Merit Dhāraṇī, as well as the dhāraṇīs spoken by the Four Heavenly Kings, together with the Four Dragon-Mind Dhāraṇīs—and such great dhāraṇīs as these, are displayed, expounded, maintained, and recited individually in every place.
We nāgas, wherever there are cities, towns, borderlands, mountains, or rivers, shall, according to the seasons, raise clouds and send down rain so that the cold and warmth remain perfectly balanced.

In various places, we shall eliminate the strife and conflict between our own armies and those of others, as well as disputes, epidemics, famine, and death; we shall cause every region to be peaceful, prosperous, and abundant, so that the people may dwell in happiness and find great delight.

I further cause those seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, trees, the five grains, and medicinal herbs to increase in flavor without any diminution; I cause the secondary environment of sentient beings to be abundant, producing rich, fatty, sweet, and exquisite flavors along with wondrous fragrances.

We are also able to cause all the kings of Jambudvīpa to give rise to minds of loving-kindness, minds of benefit, minds free from enmity, and minds free from contention; likewise, we can cause Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, even up to yakṣas, to give rise to loving-kindness, and even up to upāsakas and upāsikās, to give rise to a mind of harmony.
"Wherever this dhāraṇī reaches, we shall be able to perform the matters described above.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the nāgas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
At that time, the entire great assembly that had gathered also praised the nāgas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Sumerugarbha also offered praise:
"Excellent! Having thus praised her as excellent, he addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: "O Pure Wisdom!
Although you now have such immeasurable great bodhisattvas as your virtuous friends, you are still unable to turn the wheel of subduing and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Then, Puṇyavatī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sumerugarbha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by virtue of the power of their vows and through the conditions of mastery, takes birth in this defiled buddha-field of the five corruptions and encounters such a spiritual friend as a companion—as I have today encountered such a corresponding and virtuous friend—then that person’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is already within the palm of their hand, and they shall fulfill the six pāramitās.”

"If there are bodhisattvas who are courageous and diligent, and who are embraced by virtuous friends, then all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) will be within the palm of their hand. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
"O Pure Wisdom!

Just as you have said, if there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses mastery over the power of vows and, for the sake of the conditions to mature sentient beings, is born into the world of the five turbidities; who is courageous, diligent, firm, and non-retrogressive; who acts in accordance with the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu); and who is embraced by such great spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)—then the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) is already within the palm of his hand."

One should know that such a person has fulfilled the six pāramitās and is free from the three evil realms; one should know that this person is far removed from the womb; one should know that this person dwells on the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*); one should know that such a person is remembered and protected by all Buddhas; one should know that this person dwells on the stage of freedom from desire (*vairāgya*).
At that time, in the assembly, there was Śakra, Lord of the Devas, named Vimalatejas. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he addressed him thus:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason do these nāgas and mahānāgas destroy the worldly resources and wealth of sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
"There are two causes and conditions by which these nāgas and others are able to destroy the worldly resources and wealth of sentient beings."
What are these two? First, the causal condition of the power of greed;
second, the causal condition of the power of anger.

For these reasons, untimely clouds, rain, frost, hail, cold, and heat arise, destroying all the seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, five grains, and medicinal flavors of sentient beings; they cause them all to be scorched, withered, and fallen, diminishing the means of subsistence for sentient beings and causing them to perform various kinds of grave evil karma through body, speech, and mind.

Because sentient beings possess these heavy karmic obstructions, they burn away all past roots of goodness without exception, remaining far removed from spiritual friends and constantly dwelling within the three evil realms.

There may be sentient beings who, for the sake of food and clothing in the present life, commit even the five grave offenses of immediate retribution; because of these evil karmas, they shall not obtain a human body for immeasurable kalpas. Even if, after a long time, they should obtain a human body, their faculties may be impaired or deficient, or they may lose right mindfulness; they will be born into the families of Caṇḍālas, low-caste lineages, or households of artisans, being impoverished, base, lacking sufficient food and clothing, and destitute of the means of livelihood.

Furthermore, due to their evil karma, they are separated from virtuous friends; because their physical, verbal, and mental actions are obstructed by evil karma, they fall again into the three evil realms, even taking the Avīci Hell as their primary path, such good sons, because they lack sufficient food and drink.
"These sentient beings have long dwelt in birth and death, sinking and drifting without interruption, fully experiencing the various extreme sufferings of the three miserable realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All sufferings that arise, Are entirely due to food and drink."
"If one is free from food and drink, all sufferings will not arise.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Gods of Immaculate Splendor, spoke these verses:
"How marvelous is the snare of craving! It reaches even unto the Peak of Existence."
Such vast snares all arise from food and drink.
For ordinary beings, these two causes bind the body with the ropes of craving;
they cannot escape, just as a deer caught in a snare.
Sometimes running, sometimes walking slowly; having risen, they fall back down again.
Because of the poison of craving, they sometimes weep and sometimes laugh.
Pressed by the painful wheel of the mechanical device, they are like sesame seeds being crushed for oil.
All humans and devas are likewise oppressed by craving.
Though one may witness hundreds of thousands of arts and various skills,
craving’s playfulness with humans and devas is more clever and subtle than those.
The fault of the poison of craving can harm all people;
even if one were to train in martial prowess against an enemy, one could not match its power.
Like one possessed by a yakṣa, it causes various kinds of madness and delirious speech.
Seized by craving, the yakṣa, one’s madness exceeds even this.
There is a person of auspiciousness in the world who can leave behind the fear of affection;
if one can dry up craving, one will cross to the other shore of the world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara also spoke in verse:
“Greed, hatred, and delusion delude people; They become frantic and lose right mindfulness.
Far removed from all that is wholesome, They commit grave and evil karma.”
Disrespecting one's venerable parents, one is scattered and destroyed from the path of goodness;
lacking reverence and faith in the Triple Gem, one further commits various heinous karmas.
Devoid of a heart of compassion, such violent evil is truly terrifying.
By the power of that mind of hatred, they enter the Avīci Hell.
Because sentient beings harbor anger, they devour one another;
repeatedly within the evil realms, they are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Far removed from virtuous friends, tripped up by an evil mind,
they constantly dwell within the ocean of existence and wander upon paths of darkness.
For the sake of such sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests a body of great compassion.
Having renounced one's own happiness for the sake of enabling others to attain liberation,
one cultivates the practices of enlightenment and performs three kinds of deeds:
raising the banner of the supreme Dharma and extinguishing the evils of sentient beings.
For the sake of even a single sentient being, They extensively gather various ascetic practices,
Diligently cultivating the methods of the Path, And relinquishing wealth as well as body and life.
For the sake of each and every sentient being, They undergo suffering for immeasurable eons.
To rescue and deliver sentient beings, She endures the afflictions of the world.
The courageous Guṇakārandavatī dwells in the teaching and transformation of beings;
For the sake of sentient beings who are driven by desire, She inspires them to give rise to the bodhicitta.
At that time, Puṇyavatī took a vessel holding one *droṇa* of various seeds and offered them to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"I now give all these seeds to you, O virtuous man, desiring to increase all seeds; may my heart's desires be fulfilled."

Furthermore, may I be able to provide all beings throughout the four continents with the necessities of life; and for those beings who are wicked, tyrannical, and have severed their roots of goodness, may I uproot their suffering and distress, enabling them to dwell securely in the seed of Bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara took the vessel of seeds in his hand, displayed it throughout the ten directions, and spoke these words:

"May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as all the nāgas currently present, please attend to me! May all the seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, the five grains, and various medicinal flavors found within all the four continents of the world-systems; may the vital essence of the earth, the vital essence of sentient beings, and the vital essence of wholesome dharmas increase and not diminish."

Furthermore, may the lineage of the Three Jewels within these four continents continue without interruption; may the goddess Puṇyavatī have all her aspirations fully satisfied; and may she always enable all sentient beings to have abundant wealth and resources. May she also be able to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from all evils and resolve to attain bodhicitta, and further enabling all beings to leave the three evil realms and be reborn among the devas.
He then spoke the mantra:

"Tadyathā | Muniśiva | Muninakha | Munipara | Munibali | Sarvabhūtasaṃceti-kṣatraparāna | Nīlabhaya-bhasava-sarvaviśaye | Bhavasilili | Svāhā | This dhāraṇī-phrase protects [Name] | Svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Goddess Guṇavatī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
He addressed Puṇyavatī, saying: “O Pure Wisdom!

All the Buddhas and the great assembly have already bestowed their protection, causing the five grains, seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves throughout these four continents to ripen in full. Furthermore, they have empowered you to transform sentient beings; you should now proceed to teach and transform them.”
At that time, Śakra Kauśika addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-gate be named?”
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Kauśika:

"This sutra is titled 'The Sutra on the Essential Vows of the Tathāgata Together with Guṇakārandavatī'; it is also titled 'The Vow of the Bodhisattva Sumerugarbha,' also titled 'The Casket of Dhāraṇīs,' also titled 'Increasing the Essence of the Earth,' and also titled 'The Skillful Means of Samādhi for Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings.'"

When this Dharma was being taught, the Great Deity Guṇamahādeva, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sumerugarbha, all the nāgas and mahānāgas who had come together with their retinues, and the entire assembly of ṛṣis, devas, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha spoke, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Fifty-Eight;
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Fifty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter 13: The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions.
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha at the site of the Dharma-Purity, there spontaneously appeared lion thrones draped with ornamental curtains.
At that time, the Buddha sat manifesting the thirty-two marks, the radiance of which extended throughout the ten directions.
All the bodhisattvas came to visit and inquire of the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions, O Bodhisattva, [do you attain this]?"

There are those who are deluded and those who are clever; there are those who possess wisdom and those who are able to fly; there are those who are able to sit and practice *samādhi* and *dhyāna*, and those who are able to see through with clairvoyance; there are those who cannot fly, and those who cannot sit and practice *dhyāna* or enter *samādhi* to attain a concentrated mind for long; and there are differences in the thickness or thinness of their wisdom.
If they are identical in their bodhisattva practices, by what causes and conditions do differences in depth and breadth arise?
If they are identical in possessing mind, intellect, and consciousness, and identical in their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and faculties,
by what causes and conditions do their practices become different?
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!

The Buddhas of the past, present, and future throughout the ten directions all declare that when one can calculate the mind, consciousness, and the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they are all said to be of the same Dharma.”
The Buddha said:
"If a person can calculate that the six sense-faculties constitute all things, they shall attain the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Buddha then addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“There are degrees of thinness and thickness among the bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What constitutes these degrees of thinness and thickness?”
The Buddha said:
"A 'thick' bodhisattva is one whose practice of the path follows the path deeply.
A 'thin' bodhisattva is one who cannot fully follow the practice of the path; that is, their practice is partial and they follow the path only slightly—this is what constitutes a thin bodhisattva."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"What is the practice of the bodhisattva who constantly follows the path without losing it?
The Buddha said:
It means that a bodhisattva constantly guards the mind, intellect, and consciousness so they do not waver, returning them to the seed-planting of the path to extinction;
it means that a bodhisattva can guard the eye so that forms do not adhere, returning them to the seed-planting of the path to extinction;
it means that a bodhisattva can guard the ear so that sounds do not adhere, returning them to the seed-planting of the path to extinction.
This means that the bodhisattva is able to guard the nose so that fragrances do not adhere, returning to the seed of the path that leads to extinction;
this means that the bodhisattva is able to guard the mouth so that flavors do not adhere, returning to the seed of the path that leads to extinction;
this means that the bodhisattva guards the body so that tactile smoothness does not adhere, returning to the seed of the path that leads to extinction.

"When a bodhisattva is thus able to guard the six sense-faculties, remaining unmoved by the pleasant and the unpleasant, and constantly maintaining the state of cessation, this is called 'thickly following the Way' with depth.
The bodhisattva again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing 'thinly'?"
The Buddha said:

"This refers to a bodhisattva who has lost their practice; at times they attain the practice and at times they do not. At times the bodhisattva is able to guard the mind, intellect, and consciousness so as to follow the Path, but at times the eye cannot be guarded, whereby they lose the practice and no longer follow the Path."

At times one can guard the eyes but cannot guard the ears; at times one can guard the ears but cannot guard the nose; at times one guards the nose but cannot guard the mouth; at times one can guard the mouth but cannot guard the body; at times one can guard the body but cannot practice seated meditation; at times one can practice seated meditation but cannot engage in analytical investigation; at times one can engage in analytical investigation but cannot practice walking meditation; at times one can practice walking meditation but cannot perform discernment; and at times one can perform discernment but cannot know the subtle, soft, and minute movements of the mind.
"For this reason, as the Bodhisattva follows the Way, there are instances of faulty practice and instances of successful practice;
for this reason, the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Way varies in degree, being sometimes slight and sometimes profound.
The Bodhisattva asked the Buddha:
"What kind of practice should one perform in this way?
The Buddha said, "A bodhisattva must personally engage in discernment; he must know for himself whether he has fallen into discernment or has not fallen into discernment."
"One who falls into calculating deliberation is a fool; that a Bodhisattva does not engage in calculating deliberation is wisdom.
He asked: "What is meant by 'calculating deliberation as wisdom' and 'calculating deliberation as folly'?"
The Buddha said:
"Once one has calculated delusion, one is then able to calculate wisdom.
The Buddha said:

"Human beings are deluded by one hundred and eight types of craving; yet, if one wishes to exercise discernment and attain wisdom, there are fifty modes of calculation. By understanding the subtle and minute transgressions within these fifty modes of calculation, one attains cleverness."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"What are the fifty reckonings?
The Buddha said:
"The fifty reckonings refer to that which arises from the fundamental mind. Those who wish to know them should first reckon the one hundred and eight delusions;

second, reckon the one hundred and eight doubts; third, reckon the one hundred and eight inversions; fourth, reckon the one hundred and eight desires; fifth, reckon the one hundred and eight falls; sixth, reckon the one hundred and eight cravings; seventh, reckon the one hundred and eight root-seeds; eighth, reckon the one hundred and eight consciousnesses; ninth, reckon the one hundred and eight attachments to causes and conditions; and tenth, reckon the one hundred and eight types. These constitute the ten reckonings."
The Buddha said: “A bodhisattva further has ten reckonings: first, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight gates of arising;

second, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight practices of cessation; third, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight severances of birth and death; fourth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight extinctions and non-extinctions; fifth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight transgressions entering emptiness and not being seen; sixth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight non-abandonments and exhaustions; seventh, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight non-abandonments of purity entering purity; eighth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight refinements returning to the precepts; ninth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight advancements entering the Path; tenth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight precepts of patience. These are the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva.”

“Furthermore, there are ten reckonings for a bodhisattva: first, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight paths of humiliation; second, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight vows of union with the Path; third, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight original faiths that enter the Path; fourth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight ways of emerging from delusion and entering wisdom; fifth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight cessations of joy; sixth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight instances of not yet attaining the Buddha’s compassion; seventh, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight instances of not yet attaining the Buddha’s sorrow; eighth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight instances of not yet attaining the Buddha’s affliction; ninth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight instances of not yet attaining the Buddha’s sūtras, nor attaining the Buddha’s essential *nirvāṇa*; tenth, one should reckon the hundred-and-eight essentials for emerging from transgressions but not yet attaining entry into the essential *nirvāṇa*. These are the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva.”
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are ten reckonings for a bodhisattva:

First, one should calculate the hundred and eight methods for seeking entry into wisdom and emerging from transgressions; second, one should calculate the hundred and eight methods for seeking entry into emptiness and crossing over to emerge from emptiness; third, one should calculate that when the hundred and eight transgressive dharmas arise as empty, one should know that at the time of their cessation they return to emptiness; fourth, one should calculate the hundred and eight dharmas of maintaining emptiness to understand the dharma of exhaustion; fifth, one should calculate the hundred and eight dharmas of exhaustion so that they do not arise again; sixth, one should calculate the hundred and eight *nirvāṇa*s of long life and non-extinction; seventh, one should calculate the hundred and eight recollections of corresponding signs; eighth, one should calculate the hundred and eight recollections of relinquishing signs; ninth, one should calculate the hundred and eight recollections of mixed signs, knowing the nature of mixed signs; tenth, one should calculate the hundred and eight recollections of the signs of receiving [the fruit], which are long-lived and non-extinguished. These are the ten calculations of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are ten reckonings for a bodhisattva:
first, one should reckon the beginnings and ends, the successes and failures, of the births and deaths of all things throughout the eighteen directions; second..."

First, one should examine and calculate the hundred and eight directions to realize success and failure; second, one should examine and calculate the hundred and eight directions to realize that all people possess ignorance;

third, one should examine and calculate the hundred and eight directions to realize that all people possess ignorance; fourth, one should examine and calculate the hundred and eight directions to realize that ignorance is drawn forth from the ten directions;
fifth, one should examine and calculate the hundred and eight directions to realize the parinirvāṇa of the Arhats, wherein nothing remains.
The sixth realization is to calculate the one hundred and eight [factors] that lead the Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions into parinirvāṇa and to take this as a witness;
the seventh is to calculate the one hundred and eight [factors] that lead the former teachers of the ten directions into parinirvāṇa and to take them as witnesses;
the eighth is to calculate that the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions shall likewise enter parinirvāṇa.
In the future, when I have become the Buddha Śākyamuni and am the master of heaven and earth, possessing sovereign power over transformations, I must ultimately enter *nirvāṇa*.

If they should drag me forward to act as a witness, this is the ninth; one should calculate that the Buddhas of the future in the one hundred and eight directions shall likewise enter *nirvāṇa*, and if they should drag them forward to act as witnesses, this is the tenth; one should calculate that the one hundred and eight [realms] will reach their end.
"By exerting power to repel greed and seeking the Buddha-nature as I have, one shall likewise enter parinirvāṇa; this constitutes the fiftieth reckoning of a bodhisattva.
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads and received the instruction.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"How should one calculate the one hundred and eight delusions that arise from the root of the mind?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:

"If there is a bodhisattva whose mind has thoughts, yet does not know that within the arising and ceasing of the mind there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and does not realize this, it is ignorance."

"When consciousness turns toward the mind (*manas*), and the mind has thoughts, one does not know that within the arising and ceasing of the mind there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); not knowing this is delusion."

“When consciousness enters into transformation, consciousness has that which is cognized; yet it does not know itself as consciousness arising or consciousness ceasing. Within this there are the five aggregates and within this there are habitual tendencies; not knowing [this] constitutes delusion.”

“Engaging with the eye, when the eye sees a beautiful form, not knowing attachment and not knowing cessation—within which there are the five aggregates and within which there are latent tendencies—is ignorance.
When the eye sees a neutral form, not knowing attachment and not knowing cessation—within which there are the five aggregates and within which there are latent tendencies—is ignorance.
When the eye sees an ugly form, not knowing attachment and not knowing cessation—within which there are the five aggregates and within which there are latent tendencies—is ignorance.”

“When it enters the ear and the ear hears a pleasant sound, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.
When the ear hears a neutral sound, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.
When the ear hears an unpleasant sound, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.”

When the mind turns toward the nose, regarding the pleasant fragrances perceived by the nose, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency, yet this ignorance is delusion.

Regarding the neutral fragrances perceived by the nose, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency, yet this ignorance is delusion.

Regarding the foul odors perceived by the nose, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency, yet this ignorance is delusion.

When [consciousness] turns toward the mouth, regarding the fine flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.

Regarding the moderate flavors and moderate speech obtained by the mouth, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.

Regarding the foul flavors and unpleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one is unaware of attachment and unaware of cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is accumulation—this lack of knowledge is delusion.

“Entering into the body, when the body encounters something pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, one does not know the attachment nor the cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation [of karma]—not knowing this is delusion.

When the body encounters something neutral, subtle, and soft, one does not know the attachment nor the cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation—not knowing this is delusion.

When the body encounters something unpleasant, harsh, painful, and disagreeable, one does not know the attachment nor the cessation; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation—not knowing this is delusion.”
"A Bodhisattva practicing the Way must certainly count the breaths and perform such calculations.
The Bodhisattvas then bowed their heads and accepted the practice.
The various Bodhisattvas said:
"Although the Buddha has spoken of delusion for my sake, I have not yet understood it.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"If I were to know the hundred and eight attachments of delusion and know their cessation, would that be considered delusion or wisdom?"
The Buddha replied to the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Though you know attachment and know cessation, you still continue to be deluded and have not yet attained liberation.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha again:
“I have not yet heard the Buddha speak of delusion during the practice of counting the breaths; now that I have heard the Buddha’s teaching, I understand it.
For what reason is this called delusion?
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:

"It is like a newly initiated bodhisattva who has not yet attained the power of flight; though they hear of the Buddhas of the ten directions and desire to go to them with earnest aspiration, they are unable to fly. In this way, would they be able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions?"
The bodhisattvas replied,
“Is it thus that there is merely a vow and commitment, yet one does not see the Buddhas of the ten directions?
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

"Although you have now heard me speak of the extinction of the hundred-and-eight delusions and attachments, you are like newly initiated bodhisattvas who merely wish to reach the buddha-fields of the ten directions but are unable to fly there."
The Buddha again asked the bodhisattvas:
"Newly initiated bodhisattvas!
For what reason do you vow to reach the buddha-fields of the ten directions yet are unable to fly there?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“Because we have not yet eliminated the offenses that cannot destroy delusion, we are unable to fly to the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
The Buddha said:
"By analogy, it is called 'delusion' when bodhisattvas are only able to speak of arising and speaking of cessation, yet speak without practicing.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"From what shall we attain wisdom?"
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"That which is clung to is delusion and must be extinguished; non-clinging is the essential state of non-delusion, yet it is not yet wisdom.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"Why is it that they are still not wise?
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"It is because there are yet one hundred and eight doubts that they have not resolved."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What are the one hundred and eight doubts?
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva does not know for himself that within the arising and ceasing of the mind there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and does not understand this, it constitutes doubt;

if he does not know for himself that within the arising and ceasing of the mental faculty (*manas*) there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies, and does not understand this, it constitutes doubt;

if he does not know for himself that within the arising and ceasing of consciousness (*vijñāna*) there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies, and does not understand this, it constitutes doubt."

“Entering into the eye, when the eye sees a beautiful form, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.
When the eye sees a neutral form, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.
When the eye sees an ugly form, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.”

“When it enters the ear, regarding pleasant sounds heard by the ear, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); not knowing this constitutes doubt.
