Regarding neutral sounds heard by the ear, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.

Regarding unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.”

"Turning toward the nose, when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.
When the nose perceives a neutral fragrance, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.
When the nose perceives a foul odor, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt."

“Turning toward the sense of taste: when the mouth encounters pleasant flavors and elegant speech, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies;

not knowing this constitutes doubt. When the mouth encounters neutral flavors and neutral speech, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies;

not knowing this constitutes doubt. When the mouth encounters unpleasant flavors and harsh speech, one does not know that within their arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; not knowing this constitutes doubt.”

“Entering into the body, when the body obtains what is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein lies habit-energy (*anuśaya*); this lack of knowledge constitutes doubt.

When the body obtains what is moderate, subtle, and soft, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energy; this lack of knowledge constitutes doubt.

When the body obtains what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, one does not know that within its arising and ceasing there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energy; this lack of knowledge constitutes doubt.”
The Buddha said,
"If a bodhisattva does not depart from these [dharmas], they should not yet be considered a bodhisattva.
The bodhisattvas then asked the Buddha:
"For what reason should one not be a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:
"Because they do not practice *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and do not examine the hundred-and-eight inversions."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What are the one hundred and eight inversions?
The Buddha said:

"It means that when the mind of a bodhisattva gives rise to many thoughts, there are the five aggregates within the offenses of birth-and-death, and therein lies habitual tendency (*vāsanā*). Yet they say of themselves, 'I am without offense. In this way, throughout countless kalpas of birth-and-death, they remain in perversion."

“Shifting one’s mental attention, one reflects that within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies therein; yet one says to oneself, ‘I am without fault. Thus, throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, one remains in perversion.”

"When the mind transforms into consciousness, within the many consciousnesses of birth-and-death and the midst of offenses, there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). Yet one says of oneself, 'I am without offense. Thus, for countless kalpas of birth-and-death, one remains in perversion."

“Entering into the eye, when the eye frequently views beautiful forms, there are the five aggregates within the cycle of birth and death and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for incalculable eons in perversion.

When the eye frequently views neutral forms, there are the five aggregates within the cycle of birth and death and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for incalculable eons in perversion.

When the eye frequently views ugly forms, there are the five aggregates within the cycle of birth and death and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for incalculable eons in perversion.”

"Entering through the ear, when one hears many pleasant sounds, there are the five aggregates within the karmic offenses of birth and death, and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, 'I am without offense,' and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion.

When one hears many neutral sounds through the ear, there are the five aggregates within the karmic offenses of birth and death, and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, 'I am without offense,' and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion.

When one hears many unpleasant sounds through the ear, there are the five aggregates within the karmic offenses of birth and death, and therein lies habitual tendency; yet one says of oneself, 'I am without offense,' and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion."

"When the [consciousness] turns toward the nose: if one frequently perceives pleasant fragrances with the nose, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and one says of oneself, 'I am without fault,' then such wandering through birth and death for incalculable eons is called perversion.

If one frequently perceives neutral fragrances with the nose, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies, and one says of oneself, 'I am without fault,' then such wandering through birth and death for incalculable eons is called perversion.

If one frequently perceives foul odors with the nose, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies, and one says of oneself, 'I am without fault,' then such wandering through birth and death for incalculable eons is called perversion."

“When it turns toward the mouth, if one frequently encounters delicious flavors and pleasant speech, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and one says to oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ thus wandering through birth and death for incalculable kalpas—this is perversion.

When one frequently encounters moderate flavors and moderate speech, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies, and one says to oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ thus wandering through birth and death for incalculable kalpas—this is perversion.

When one frequently encounters unpleasant flavors and unpleasant speech, yet within the cycle of birth and death there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies, and one says to oneself, ‘I am without fault,’ thus wandering through birth and death for incalculable kalpas—this is perversion.”

“Entering into the body, there are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the karmic offenses of birth and death when the body frequently experiences what is pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable; yet one says, ‘I am without offense,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion.

There are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the karmic offenses of birth and death when the body frequently experiences what is moderate, fine, and soft; yet one says, ‘I am without offense,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion.

There are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the karmic offenses of birth and death when the body frequently experiences what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable; yet one says, ‘I am without offense,’ and thus undergoes birth and death for countless eons—this is perversion.”
The Buddha said, "These are the one hundred and eight inversions; thus, these bodhisattvas do not understand.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
"Although I am subject to the cycle of birth and death and its inversions, I wish to rely on the Dharma of the sutras to deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"In delivering sentient beings, what kind of path do you wish them to attain?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We wish to cause all people to attain the path of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“You are many in number.
For what reason do you not each attain Buddhahood yourselves, rather than merely following one another in a crowd?
The Bodhisattvas replied:
"Although I follow you, I shall not depart from my walking meditation.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"Could all of you possibly attain Buddhahood together in a single day?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We cannot all become buddhas together.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Why is this? the bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:

"Among us there are those whose marks are not yet complete; among us there are those whose merits are not yet fulfilled; among us there are those whose offenses of birth and death are not yet exhausted."
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"Among you there are those whose marks are not yet complete, those whose merit is not yet fulfilled, and those whose transgressions are not yet exhausted."
If it is as you say, that those who have not yet perfected the marks cannot attain Buddhahood themselves, how can they cause others to attain Buddhahood?
If your merits are not yet complete and you cannot attain Buddhahood yourself, how can you cause others to attain Buddhahood?
The Buddha said, "If you all have not yet exhausted the karmic intentions of birth and death, you cannot attain Buddhahood yourselves; how then could you enable others to attain Buddhahood?
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in shame.
The bodhisattvas again asked the Buddha,
"By what causes and conditions do we thus fail to attain Buddhahood?
The Buddha replied to the bodhisattvas:

"You all sit here because you do not practice *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), nor do you maintain mindfulness (*śīlamanasikāra*) to examine and calculate the one hundred and eight desires; it is because you do not abandon these desires.
The Bodhisattvas asked:
"How does one practice *ānāpāna*, maintain mindfulness, and examine and calculate so as to abandon the one hundred and eight desires?"
The Buddha replied to the bodhisattvas, saying:

"If your minds give rise to thoughts, and those thoughts further give rise to more thoughts of desire—within that desire there are the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and within them there is habitual tendency (anuśaya); this is what constitutes desire."

“Turning toward the mind (*manas*), the mind further conceives of desire; within this desire for desire there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*);

this is the desire for desire. Turning toward consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness becomes the desire for desire; within this desire for desire there are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency; this is the desire for desire.”
“Turning toward the eye: when the eye perceives a pleasant form, there are the five aggregates therein and there is accumulation;
this is sensual desire. When the eye perceives a neutral form, there are the five aggregates therein and there is accumulation; this is sensual desire.
When the eye perceives an unpleasant form, there are the five aggregates therein and there is accumulation; this is sensual desire.”
“Turning toward the ear: pleasant sounds heard by the ear constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire.
Neutral sounds heard by the ear constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire.
Unpleasant sounds heard by the ear constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire.”
“Turning toward the nose: the pleasant fragors smelled by the nose constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency—this is sensual desire.
The neutral fragors smelled by the nose constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency—this is sensual desire.
The foul odors smelled by the nose constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency—this is sensual desire.”

"Turning toward the mouth: the pleasant tastes and pleasant speech encountered by the mouth constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire.
The moderate tastes and moderate speech encountered by the mouth constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire.
The unpleasant tastes and unpleasant speech encountered by the mouth constitute sensual desire; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency, which is sensual desire."

"Entering into the body: regarding the pleasant, subtle, and soft sensations obtained by the body that are desirable, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency; this constitutes sensual desire.
Regarding the moderate, subtle, and soft sensations obtained by the body that are desirable, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency; this constitutes sensual desire.

Regarding the unpleasant, coarse, hard, and painful sensations obtained by the body that are undesirable, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency; this constitutes sensual desire."
The Buddha said: “O Bodhisattvas!
You merely sit there without understanding desire and craving.”
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We have no desire for desire.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Do you wish to seek Buddhahood and deliver the people of the ten directions?
The bodhisattvas replied, "Indeed!"
"We wish to seek Buddhahood and deliver the people of the ten directions.
The Buddha replied to the bodhisattvas, saying:
"To act thus is to have desire; why then do you say you are without desire?"
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Do you, in your minds, think of the people in the ten directions who undergo toil and suffering?
The bodhisattvas replied:
"Indeed! We consider ourselves diligent and hardworking people.
The Buddha said:
"If you conceive of those who undergo various hardships as being driven by desire, for what reason do you say they are without desire?
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"When you went to the abodes of the Buddhas of the ten directions to inquire about this sutra, have you forgotten it now?"
The bodhisattvas replied,
“Regarding the sūtras we have asked about, we all recognize them and have not forgotten them.
The Buddha then questioned the bodhisattvas:
"Do you recognize the sutras spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions? Would you not transmit them and preach them for others?
The bodhisattvas replied, "Indeed!"
"I spend my days expounding the sutras for others.
The Buddha said,
"When you expound the sutras for others, do you wish for people to understand them?"
The bodhisattvas said: "Indeed!
We wish to cause people to understand."
The Buddha said:
"If you preach the sutras for others with the desire to cause them to understand, this is itself the desire for desire; why then do you say you are free from desire?"
The Buddha again asked the bodhisattvas:
"When you preach the sūtras for others, do you ever teach them to practice giving?
The bodhisattvas replied:
"Indeed! We teach people to practice giving. The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"If you teach people to give, what do you offer to the Buddha?"
The bodhisattvas replied,
“We first wish for someone to carry fine-colored flowers.
The Buddha said:
"If you do not desire form, for what reason did you have someone hold five-colored, beautiful flowers pleasing to the eye and offer them to the Buddha?
If this is so, you do desire form; why then do you say, 'We do not desire form'?"
The Buddha again asked the bodhisattvas:
"Would you rather hear the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the sutras?
The bodhisattvas replied:
“It would be acceptable for the Buddhas of the ten directions to preach the sutras for me; we would all rejoice.
The Buddha said:
“If you rejoice upon hearing the sutras because of desire, for what reason do you say you are without desire?”
The Buddha again asked the bodhisattvas:
"Would you like to teach others how to burn incense for the sake of becoming a buddha?
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
"I personally go every day to gather various flowers and famous incenses, which I carry to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Just as you go to gather various flowers and incenses with the desire to obtain what is pleasing to the nose, so too do you carry them to offer to the Buddha."
The Buddha said, "If you wish to obtain fragrant flowers to please the nose, such is desire; why then do you say there is no desire?
The Buddha further questioned the bodhisattvas, saying:
"When you expound the sutras for others, do you wish them to be merely pleasant to the ear?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"When we expound the sutras for others, we wish to distinguish them so they are pleasant to the ear, and we wish to cause people's minds to understand."
The Buddha said:
"If that which is to one's liking constitutes desire, for what reason do you say you have no desire?
The Buddha then questioned the bodhisattvas again, saying:
"Would you rather possess a body endowed with the thirty-two marks?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"We strive to perfect these marks only because we desire a beautiful body."
The Buddha said:
"If you can take this body as desire, for what reason do you say you have no desire?
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads and each felt ashamed.
The Buddha said,
"Such bodhisattvas have not yet attained anything to rely upon.
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads in prostration and said:
“I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me and explain this to me. The Buddha then spoke to him:

“When practicing the bodhisattva path—whether through the practice of counting the breaths in dhyāna or by relying on one’s own concentrated mind—one should calculate the one hundred and eight transgressions. Those that are extinguished correspond to true dhyāna; those that are not extinguished do not correspond to dhyāna.”
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:

"Dhyāna is for the abandonment of evil; the extinction of the one hundred and eight transgressions constitutes the abandonment of evil, whereas their non-extinction does not constitute the abandonment of evil."

Whether arising from meditative awakening, or while walking, sitting, or rising, if one obtains the conditions to preach the sutras for others, and regarding all things seen, is able to examine and calculate them through the "one hundred and eight falls," such that one does not become attached and does not fall into transgression—this is the bodhisattva’s practice of examination and calculation.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“From what do the reckoning of the one hundred and eight transgressions arise?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:

"Regarding the calculation of the one hundred and eight falls: when the mind (*citta*) gives rise to mental formations (*manas*), there are therein the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); this is a fall.
When the mental formations give rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is a fall."
“Entering into the eye: when there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies within the beautiful forms seen by the eye, this is falling;
when there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies within the neutral forms seen by the eye, this is falling;
when there are the five aggregates and the latent tendencies within the ugly forms seen by the eye, this is falling.”
“Entering through the ear, if there are the five aggregates and the underlying tendencies within the pleasant sounds heard by the ear, this is called falling;
if there are the five aggregates and the underlying tendencies within the neutral sounds heard by the ear, this is called falling;
if there are the five aggregates and the underlying tendencies within the unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, this is called falling.”
"Entering into the nose: when there are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the pleasant odors smelled by the nose, this is called falling;
when there are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the neutral odors smelled by the nose, this is called falling;
when there are the five aggregates and latent tendencies within the foul odors smelled by the nose, this is called falling."
“Turning toward the entrance of the mouth, when the mouth encounters pleasant tastes and elegant speech, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this is called falling.
When the mouth encounters moderate tastes and moderate speech, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this is called falling.
When the mouth encounters unpleasant tastes and foul speech, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this is called falling.”
“Entering into the body: when the body obtains what is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called falling.
When the body obtains what is middling, subtle, soft, and agreeable, therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called falling.
When the body obtains what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called falling.”
"These are the one hundred and eight ways of falling.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

"They calculate the one hundred and eight ways of falling, yet they do not realize they are committing offenses. Suffering will surely follow them later, yet they feel no shame; they claim for themselves that they can sever the path of the one hundred and eight ways of falling."
The Buddha said:

"This person is like a lustful and jealous woman who, having become pregnant through her own excessive lust, does not know how much the fetus grows day by day within her womb. While the lustful and jealous woman continues her excessive lust, until the child is fully formed after ten months and is about to be born—whether the child is moving or not, whether it has been born or not—the mother suffers from abdominal pain and feels shame and regret."

When the pain of childbirth descends, the wailing of the envious woman is heard as far as the seventh heaven. Once the child has been born and the mother’s pain has subsided, she immediately thinks of sexual indulgence; she no longer feels shame and no longer remembers her pain, resuming her lewd behavior as before. Such suffering is beyond words, yet the envious woman is unable to perceive her own agony.
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva practices the Way, they do not calculate the one hundred and eight transgressions. It is like a licentious and envious woman who does not know the extent of her own sins, nor does she weary of her suffering; she does not calculate for herself to feel shame for her offenses, nor does she understand the suffering of the five realms of birth and death. She does not realize she is falling into the three evil paths, yet she feels no shame for her conduct, saying, ‘I am on the path.’”
"In this way, life after life, one receives calamity for oneself.
Returning to self-reflection, one finds no benefit in this; disciples who study the Way must learn with earnestness.
All these bodhisattvas rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and received the teaching into practice.
The Buddha said,
"Even for a bodhisattva who practices in this way, it is not yet appropriate to provide an explanation.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"For what reason is it said that they have not yet understood?
The Buddha replied,
"It is because the bodhisattvas are unable to calculate the one hundred and eight types of craving."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"How does one calculate the one hundred and eight types of craving?
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, they are unable to unify their mind and bring it to cessation; this is because they remain seated while clinging to the hundred and eight [afflictions].

First, when the bodhisattva’s mind has thoughts that cannot be extinguished, it is because within craving there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein lies habitual tendency (*vāsanā*); this is what constitutes craving."

When the mind turns into mental attention (*manasikāra*) and cannot be extinguished, because within craving there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein lies habituation (*vāsanā*), this is called craving.
When the mind turns into consciousness (*vijñāna*) and cannot be extinguished, because within craving there are the five aggregates and therein lies habituation, this is called craving.
"Entering into the eye, when one cannot extinguish the perception of beautiful forms, there are therein the five aggregates and therein the latent tendencies; this is craving.
When one cannot extinguish the perception of neutral forms, there are therein the five aggregates and therein the latent tendencies; this is craving.
When one cannot extinguish the perception of ugly forms, there are therein the five aggregates and therein the latent tendencies; this is craving."
“When it enters the ear, if one cannot extinguish attachment to pleasant sounds heard by the ear, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.
If one cannot extinguish attachment to neutral sounds heard by the ear, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.
If one cannot extinguish attachment to unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.”

When the sense of smell is engaged, if one cannot extinguish attachment to pleasant fragors perceived by the nose, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.
If one cannot extinguish attachment to neutral fragors perceived by the nose, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.
If one cannot extinguish attachment to foul odors perceived by the nose, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this is called craving.

“Turning toward the mouth, when the mouth encounters delicious flavors or pleasant speech and cannot extinguish [craving], there are the five aggregates within that craving and there is accumulation therein; this is called craving.

When the mouth encounters neutral flavors or neutral speech and cannot extinguish [craving], there are the five aggregates within that craving and there is accumulation therein; this is called craving.

When the mouth encounters unpleasant flavors or unpleasant speech and cannot extinguish [craving], there are the five aggregates within that craving and there is accumulation therein; this is called craving.”

“Entering into the body, when the body encounters what is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, and one cannot extinguish it, there are therein the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation; this is called craving.
When the body encounters what is moderately subtle, soft, and [agreeable], and one cannot extinguish it, there are therein the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation; this is called craving.

When the body encounters what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, and one cannot extinguish it, there are therein the five aggregates and therein is the accumulation; this is called craving.”
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva practices the Way, they do not calculate or eliminate the one hundred and eight cravings, nor do they realize that these one hundred and eight cravings lead to falling into transgression.
It is like a newborn infant who, from childhood until adulthood, cannot know for itself by how much it has grown each day.”
It is like this: when a bodhisattva practices the Path, they may not be able to discern the extent of their transgressions.

If a bodhisattva practicing the Path becomes aware of the offense of falling into the hundred-and-eight cravings, they should immediately feel shame, immediately sever them, immediately distance themselves from them, and immediately extinguish them. When such cravings are severed, one is a true bodhisattva.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in reverence and accepted his teaching.
The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva practicing the Way must examine and calculate the one hundred and eight types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). If one practices the Way without examining and calculating the one hundred and eight latent tendencies, this should not be considered the practice of a bodhisattva. Only by removing these latent tendencies does one accord with the practice of a bodhisattva."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What is meant by ‘one who should remove the roots’?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:

“A bodhisattva dwelling alone in a secluded place should sit and practice dhyāna, counting the breaths, following them, and attaining stillness through śamatha and vipaśyanā until purity is reached. Through this purity, one eliminates the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); that which is not pure constitutes the failure to eliminate these tendencies. Thus, upon arising from dhyāna and being among people, one should practice discernment and sever these underlying tendencies.”
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"How should one calculate that which eliminates the underlying tendencies?
The Buddha said:
"If one practices the Path without attaining single-minded concentration, it is called 'not extinguishing the root.
The Buddha said:

"One who does not attain single-minded concentration has thoughts within the mind; therein lie the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and therein lies habitual tendency (*anuśaya*), whereby the root arises."
“Turning toward the mind (*manas*), there are the five aggregates within it and there are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within it; thus a root of existence arises.
Turning toward consciousness (*vijñāna*), there are the five aggregates within it and there are latent tendencies within it; thus a root of existence arises.”
"Entering into the eye: when the eye sees a pleasant form, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency;
thus a sprout arises. When the eye sees a neutral form, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency; thus a sprout arises.
When the eye sees an unpleasant form, therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency; thus a sprout arises."
“Entering through the ear: when a pleasant sound is heard by the ear, there are the five aggregates therein and there is latent tendency; thus a root of existence arises.
When a neutral sound is heard by the ear, there are the five aggregates therein and there is latent tendency; thus a root of existence arises.
When an unpleasant sound is heard by the ear, there are the five aggregates therein and there is latent tendency; thus a root of existence arises.”
“Turning toward the nose: when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency (anuśaya), whereby a seed is produced;
when the nose perceives a neutral fragrance, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, whereby a seed is produced;
when the nose perceives a foul odor, therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, whereby a seed is produced.”

“Turning toward the entrance of the mouth: when the mouth encounters pleasant tastes and elegant speech, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); thus a root of growth arises.
When the mouth encounters moderate tastes and moderate speech, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies;
thus a root of growth arises. When the mouth encounters unpleasant tastes and harsh speech, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; thus a root of growth arises.”
“Entering into the body, when the body obtains what is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; thus a root of existence arises.
When the body obtains what is intermediate, subtle, and soft, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; thus a root of existence arises.

When the body obtains what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, there are therein the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; thus a root of existence arises. In this way, the roots are not severed.”
The Buddha said:
"If there is a bodhisattva who practices the Path yet says, 'I have no such roots,' this constitutes arrogance.
By planting these roots for oneself, one is unable to liberate oneself; thus, one lacks wisdom and cannot know the extent of the fault of those roots."
For example, when hair grows on a person's body, that person cannot calculate it for themselves one by one, nor can they know for themselves how much hair there is.
Likewise, when bodhisattvas practice the Way, they cannot eliminate their own offenses, yet they instead say, "I seek the Buddha-way and desire to deliver all beings throughout the ten directions."
If one is thus unable to save even oneself, how can one save the ten directions?
A bodhisattva who practices the Way and is able to remove the stumps can then save the ten directions;
if they do not remove the stumps, they cannot save the ten directions.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas joyfully accepted and practiced his teaching.
The Buddha said:
"Even so, these bodhisattvas have not yet attained full understanding."
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads once more and said:
"We do not yet understand this; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattvas have one hundred and eight consciousnesses of transgression; if these are not extinguished, they should not be considered bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha, “What are these one hundred and eight consciousnesses of transgression?”
The Buddha said:

"It refers to that which the bodhisattva’s mind conceives as a transgression; therein are the five aggregates (skandhas), and therein are the habitual tendencies (vāsanās) which constitute consciousness (vijñāna). This is what is meant by 'transgressive consciousness.'"

"Entering into the mind (*manas*), that which the mind thinks and repeatedly contemplates becomes an offense; therein are the five aggregates (*skandha*) and therein are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which constitute consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is the consciousness of offense. Entering into consciousness, that which consciousness thinks and does not forget becomes an offense; therein are the five aggregates and therein are the latent tendencies, which constitute consciousness. This is the consciousness of offense."

“Entering into the eye, the sight of beautiful forms by the eye is a fault; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habituation that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of fault.
The sight of neutral forms by the eye is a fault; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habituation that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of fault.
The sight of ugly forms by the eye is a fault; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habituation that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of fault.”

“Entering through the ear, the pleasant sounds heard by the ear constitute a transgression; therein are the five aggregates (skandhas), and therein is the habitual tendency (vāsanā) which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression.

The neutral sounds heard by the ear constitute a transgression; therein are the five aggregates, and therein is the habitual tendency which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression.

The unpleasant sounds heard by the ear constitute a transgression; therein are the five aggregates, and therein is the habitual tendency which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression.”

"Entering through the nose: when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, this constitutes a transgression; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habitual tendency which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression.

When the nose perceives a neutral fragrance, this constitutes a transgression; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habitual tendency which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression.

When the nose perceives a foul odor, this constitutes a transgression; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the habitual tendency which constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of transgression."

“Turning toward the sense of taste, the mouth’s acquisition of delicious flavors and pleasant speech constitutes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein is the habitual tendency that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of a fault.

The mouth’s acquisition of middling flavors and middling speech constitutes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein is the habitual tendency that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of a fault.

The mouth’s acquisition of unpleasant flavors and unpleasant speech constitutes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein is the habitual tendency that constitutes consciousness—this is the consciousness of a fault.”

"Entering into the body, that which is obtained by the body as pleasant, subtle, soft, and suitable for the body becomes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein the habitual tendencies become consciousness—this is consciousness of a fault.

That which is obtained by the body as moderate, subtle, and soft becomes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein the habitual tendencies become consciousness—this is consciousness of a fault.

That which is obtained by the body as unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and unsuitable for the body becomes a fault; therein are the five aggregates, and therein the habitual tendencies become consciousness—this is consciousness of a fault."
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Do you all have such offenses?
The bodhisattvas replied:
"I have only the five aggregates; I have no transgression.
The Buddha again asked the bodhisattvas:
"What in this world causes a person to have transgressions and fail to attain the Way?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“All people in the world fail to attain the Way because they are mired in greed.
The Buddha said:
"All people in the world crave birth and death; is this because they have the habituation of the five aggregates?
The bodhisattvas replied, "It is a fault."
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"If you all maintain the view that the body is the Buddha, you shall continue to undergo birth and death.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
"We must undergo birth and death again; we shall not attain Buddhahood through this present body.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"How many more births and deaths must you all undergo before you shall attain Buddhahood?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We have not yet reached a definitive end to birth and death.
The Buddha again questioned the bodhisattvas:
"Why is there no essential core?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"I do not know for myself the extent of my own transgressions or merits."
"For this reason, I do not know the essential point.
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"In this way, what difference is there between you and the people of the world?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha, “We can fly to the buddha-fields of the ten directions; we can understand what the Buddha has spoken.
The Buddha said:
"If you can fly to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and understand what the Buddhas of the ten directions say, why do you not attain Buddhahood immediately?
For what reason do you continue to undergo the cycle of birth and death?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:

"Because we still have our original offenses that are not yet exhausted, and because the merit and blessings of our original vows are not yet fulfilled, for these reasons we should not attain Buddhahood at this time."
The Buddha said:

"If you say that all people in the world have offenses solely because they dwell upon the habits of birth and death within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), then you yourselves must likewise undergo the habits of birth and death and possess offenses."
"For what reason do you all say to me that there is no offense?
All the bodhisattvas felt ashamed, prostrated themselves, and accepted the teaching with practice.
The Buddha said:
“Although I have spoken thus, the bodhisattvas have not yet understood.
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads and said,
“We pray that the Buddha will further explain this for us.”
The Buddha said:
"Bodhisattvas have one hundred and eight causes and conditions for attachment to suffering.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
“What are the one hundred and eight causes and conditions for attachment to suffering?
The Buddha said:

“When the mind of a bodhisattva has thoughts, these serve as causes and conditions for attachment to suffering; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency (*vāsanā*), whereby one must sit amidst the suffering of birth and death caused by those conditions.”

"Entering into the mind, the mind's thoughts serve as the causal conditions for attachment to sensation; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency. One shall sit amidst the suffering of birth and death caused by these conditions."

"When consciousness turns and enters, and consciousness has an object of cognition, this becomes the causal condition for attachment to feeling (*vedanā*). Within this there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and within this there are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); one shall sit amidst the suffering of birth and death caused by these conditions."

“Entering through the eye, attachment to pleasant forms seen by the eye serves as the causal condition for suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency (*anuśaya*); one shall sit amidst the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.

Attachment to neutral forms seen by the eye serves as the causal condition for suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; one shall sit amidst the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.

Attachment to unpleasant forms seen by the eye serves as the causal condition for suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; one shall sit amidst the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.”

"Entering through the ear, hearing pleasant sounds becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency (anuśaya), which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions.

Hearing neutral sounds with the ear becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency, which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions.

Hearing unpleasant sounds with the ear becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency, which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions."

“Turning toward the nose: when the nose perceives pleasant fragrances, this becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies (anuśaya), which will result in the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.

When the nose perceives neutral fragrances, this becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies, which will result in the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.

When the nose perceives foul odors, this becomes a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies, which will result in the suffering of birth and death due to these causal conditions.”

“Turning toward the mouth, the mouth’s acquisition of delicious flavors and pleasant speech serves as a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency (*vāsanā*), which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions.

The mouth’s acquisition of moderate flavors and moderate speech serves as a causal condition for attachment and suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions.

The mouth’s acquisition of unpleasant flavors and unpleasant speech serves as a causal condition for suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, which one must sit through as the suffering of birth and death due to causal conditions.”

“Entering into the body, one becomes attached to the pain caused by the body obtaining what is pleasant, fine, soft, and suitable; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency (anuśaya), which will result in the pain of birth and death due to causal conditions.

One becomes attached to the pain caused by the body obtaining what is moderate, fine, and soft; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, which will result in the pain of birth and death due to causal conditions.

One becomes attached to the pain caused by the body obtaining what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and unsuitable; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency, which will result in the pain of birth and death due to causal conditions.”
The Buddha said:
"The bodhisattvas have not yet grown weary of the suffering of birth and death caused by causes and conditions. The bodhisattvas said:
"I have become a bodhisattva precisely because I am weary of the suffering of birth and death.
The Buddha said,
"You all are weary of the suffering of birth and death."
"For what reason do they not plant the seeds of the Way?
For what reason do they plant the seeds of the suffering, transgressions, and karmic retributions of birth and death?
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
"I plant the seeds of the Way every day.
The Buddha said,
"If you plant the seeds of the Way, for what reason do you still have the one hundred and eight pains of birth, death, and their causal conditions?"
The bodhisattvas immediately felt shame, bowed their heads, and accepted the practice.
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads and asked the Buddha, saying:
"Although the Buddha has preached this sutra for us, we do not understand it."
The Buddha said, "I see that you all plant the seeds of one hundred and eight pains; I know that you do not understand.
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads again and said:
“I pray that the Buddha will explain this to me. The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva’s mind has a thought and desires to attain it but cannot, he consequently experiences pain while sitting. Within this there are the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and within this there are latent tendencies (anuśaya); this is what constitutes the planting of pain.”

"Entering into the mind, when the mind has a thought, it further conceives of what is agreeable and what is disagreeable as the planting of suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the underlying tendency—this is the planting of suffering."

"Entering into consciousness, when there is an object of consciousness that one cannot take as 'I,' therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this is the planting of suffering.
Entering into the eye, when the eye perceives a pleasant form, it is suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency;
this is the planting of suffering. When the eye perceives a neutral form, it is suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this is the planting of suffering."
Unpleasant forms seen by the eye are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
Turning to the ear, pleasant sounds heard by the ear are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
Neutral sounds heard by the ear are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the latent tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
Hearing unpleasant sounds with the ear is suffering; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
Turning to the nose, hearing pleasant fragrances with the nose is suffering; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
Hearing neutral fragrances with the nose is suffering; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency—this is the planting of suffering.
The smelling of foul odors by the nose is suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are the latent tendencies—this is the planting of suffering.

When it turns to enter the mouth, the obtaining of delicious flavors and pleasant speech by the mouth is suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are the latent tendencies—this is the planting of suffering.
The obtaining of moderate flavors and moderate speech by the mouth is suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein are the latent tendencies—this is the planting of suffering.
Unpleasant tastes and harsh speech obtained by the mouth are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency (*anuśaya*); this is the planting of suffering.
When it enters the body, the subtle and soft sensations obtained by the body are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency; this is the planting of suffering.
The moderate subtle and soft sensations obtained by the body are suffering; therein are the five aggregates and therein is the tendency; this is the planting of suffering.

"When the body encounters what is evil, coarse, hard, painful, and unbearable, it experiences suffering; within this there are the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency (*vāsanā*). This is called the 'seeding of suffering.

The Buddha said, "A bodhisattva must sever these one hundred and eight types of suffering to be truly practicing the bodhisattva path; one who does not sever suffering is not practicing the bodhisattva path. These constitute the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva."
The Buddha said:
"Even though the bodhisattvas understand it thus, they should further investigate and calculate.
The bodhisattvas then asked the Buddha:
"What further should one calculate and examine?
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should calculate and examine the hundred-and-eight gateways of arising."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What are the one hundred and eight gates of birth?
The Buddha said:

“The bodhisattva’s mind penetrates sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; therein lie the five aggregates and therein lies habituation—this is what is meant by ‘penetrating birth.
The Buddha said:
“If one attends to the mind so that it does not enter sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then there will be no five aggregates and no habituation.”
The Buddha said:
"To block the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) so that the mind does not waver is to sever the suffering of birth and death.

'Blocking' means to penetrate earth, water, fire, wind, space, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and birth-and-death; within these there are the five aggregates and within them there are habitual tendencies—this is what constitutes the penetration of birth."
When the mind is focused, it remains unmoving.
It does not receive earth, water, fire, wind, space, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Within these there are the five aggregates and within them there are habitual tendencies; this is what constitutes the continuity of birth.

When the mind is restrained, it remains unmoving; it does not accept earth, water, fire, wind, or space, nor does it accept feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, or the habitual tendencies of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
One who fails to restrain themselves falls into transgression; one who restrains the mind so that it remains unmoving enters the Path. This is called "restraining birth."

"When consciousness turns and enters, that consciousness also permeates earth, water, fire, wind, space, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; thus there arise the habitual tendencies of the five aggregates, and one thereby permeates birth and death."
Those who do not apply the crossbar fall into the suffering of birth and death; those who apply the crossbar fall into the Path and do not undergo birth and death.

When it turns toward the eye, within the beautiful forms perceived by the eye there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energy; this is called piercing through birth and death. To apply the crossbar so as to remain unmoved is to fall into the Path;

failing to apply it is to fall into transgression. Within the neutral forms perceived by the eye there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energy; this is called piercing through birth and death. To apply the crossbar so as to remain unmoved is to fall into the Path; failing to apply it is to fall into transgression.

Within the foul forms pierced by the eye, there are the five aggregates and therein are latent tendencies; this constitutes being pierced by birth and death. Those who close the gate so as not to move fall upon the Path; those who do not close it fall into transgression.

“Entering through the ear, within the pleasant sounds that pierce the ear there are the five aggregates and therein is latent tendency (*anuśaya*); this constitutes piercing the cycle of birth and death. To block it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; failing to block it is to fall into transgression.

Within the neutral sounds that pierce the ear there are the five aggregates and therein is latent tendency; this constitutes piercing the cycle of birth and death. To block it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; failing to block it is to fall into transgression.

Within the unpleasant sounds that pierce the ear there are the five aggregates and therein is latent tendency; this constitutes piercing the cycle of birth and death. To block it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; failing to block it is to fall into transgression.”

“Turning toward the nose: within the pleasant fragrances encountered by the nose there are the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency (*vāsanā*); this constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death. To block it so that it does not move is to fall upon the Path; to fail to block it is to fall into transgression.

Within the neutral fragrances encountered by the nose there are the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency; this constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death. To block it so that it does not move is to fall upon the Path; to fail to block it is to fall into transgression.

Within the foul odors encountered by the nose there are the five aggregates and therein lies habitual tendency; this constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death. To block it so that it does not move is to fall upon the Path; to fail to block it is to fall into transgression.”

"Turning toward the entrance of the mouth, within the fine flavors and eloquent speech pierced by the mouth there are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency (*anuśaya*); this constitutes being pierced through birth and death. To close it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; not to close it is to fall into transgression.

Within the middling flavors and middling speech pierced by the mouth there are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this constitutes being pierced through birth and death. To close it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; not to close it is to fall into transgression.

Within the foul flavors and foul speech pierced by the mouth there are the five aggregates and therein is habitual tendency; this constitutes being pierced through birth and death. To close it so as to remain unmoved is to fall upon the Path; not to close it is to fall into transgression."

“Entering the body, there are pleasant, subtle, and soft sensations that are agreeable to the body; within these there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energies (vāsanā). This constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death; one who applies the bolt so as to remain unmoved falls upon the Path, while one who does not apply the bolt falls into transgression.

Within the body there are neutral, subtle, and soft sensations; within these there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energies. This constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death; one who applies the bolt so as to remain unmoved falls upon the Path, while one who does not apply the bolt falls into transgression.

Within the body there are unpleasant, coarse, hard, and painful sensations that are disagreeable to the body; within these there are the five aggregates and therein lies habit-energies. This constitutes the penetration of birth-and-death; one who applies the bolt so as to remain unmoved falls upon the Path, while one who does not apply the bolt falls into transgression.”
The Buddha said:
"The essential practice of a bodhisattva must pass through the gate without wavering; to waver is to be unenlightened.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
"We shall practice dhyāna so as to remain unmoving.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"After practicing dhyāna, do you move again?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“The meditative absorption is disturbed again.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Why does it move again?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"It moves spontaneously."
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"For what reason does it move spontaneously?
The bodhisattvas replied:
“I do not understand; I do not know from what causes and conditions this movement arises.
The Buddha said, “Even these bodhisattvas have not yet understood.”
The bodhisattvas said:
“We pray that the Buddha will further explain this for us.
The Buddha said:

"As for why the dhyāna of a bodhisattva spontaneously moves and awakens, it is because the bodhisattva possesses one hundred and eight gates of arising; since these are neither moving nor non-moving, they do not cease.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas bowed their heads and received his teaching with practice.
The Buddha said:
"Bodhisattvas, even with this, you have not yet attained understanding. The bodhisattvas said:
"Why is it that they have not yet attained liberation?
The Buddha said,
"It is simply because these bodhisattvas still possess fundamental attachments and do not cease to dwell upon the one hundred and eight activities."
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads and said,
"We pray that the Buddha will again explain this for us.
The Buddha said:
“The mind of a bodhisattva originally has many thoughts; because it does not abide in restraint, the mind’s original offenses consist of one hundred and eight modes of activity.

When it turns into the mental faculty (*manas*), that mental faculty originally has many thoughts; because it does not abide in restraint, the mental faculty’s original offenses consist of one hundred and eight modes of activity.”

“Entering into consciousness: because the fundamental nature of consciousness involves many thoughts and lacks restraint, the fundamental fault of consciousness consists of one hundred and eight modes of activity.

Entering into the eye: because the fundamental nature of the eye involves seeing many beautiful forms and lacks restraint, the fundamental fault of the eye consists of one hundred and eight modes of activity;
because the fundamental nature of the eye involves seeing many neutral forms and lacks restraint, the fundamental fault of the eye consists of one hundred and eight modes of activity.”
The eye originally sees many unwholesome forms; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight modes of the eye’s original transgression.
Turning to the ear: the ear originally hears many pleasant sounds; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight modes of the ear’s original transgression;
the ear originally hears many neutral sounds; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight modes of the ear’s original transgression.
The ear originally hears many unpleasant sounds; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the ear’s original faults.
Turning inward to the nose: the nose originally smells many pleasant fragrances; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the nose’s original faults;
the nose originally smells many neutral fragrances; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the nose’s original faults.
The nose originally perceives many foul odors; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the original offenses of the nose.

Turning into the mouth: the mouth originally obtains many delicious flavors and pleasant speech; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the original offenses of the mouth.
The mouth originally obtains many middling flavors and middling speech; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of the original offenses of the mouth.

The mouth inherently experiences many unpleasant tastes and harsh words; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of action that constitute the inherent faults of the mouth.

When these turn toward the body, the body inherently experiences many pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable sensations; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of action that constitute the inherent faults of the body.

The body inherently experiences many sensations of moderate fineness and softness; because it does not maintain restraint, there are one hundred and eight courses of action that constitute the inherent faults of the body.

"The body is fundamentally characterized by many acquired evils—coarse, hard, painful, and unbearable—which do not cease because one does not maintain restraint; thus, the body is fundamentally possessed of the hundred-and-eightfold actions of transgression.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas joyfully accepted and practiced his teaching.

The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Fifty-nine. These final two scrolls of this scripture are not found in the Danzang (Dunhuang) collection; therefore, there is currently no version with which to cross-check them.
However, both the Song and Xiang editions contain three distinct textual segments within this scroll, where the prose is broken and the meaning is severed, making the passages difficult to interpret.
On the first and ninth scrolls, line 17 states:
"Among the five aggregates... followed immediately by: "...the many flavors and words obtained therein.
On the second and tenth scrolls, line 21 states:
Regarding the phrase "those whose characteristics are not yet complete," immediately following "not of themselves," it says: "they habitually say of themselves, 'I am without fault,' and so forth.
Thirdly, at the end of the second line of the twelfth fascicle, it says:
"This is inverted speech," followed by: "How can one attain Buddhahood, and how can one cause others to attain Buddhahood? These are the points where the three sections of the text are divided.

Now, according to the *Prasannapadā* (or *Mingdu jing*), these two versions have both erroneously transposed the twenty-seven lines totaling three hundred and seventy-nine characters—beginning from "the section on inverted speech" (*diandao kou*) down to "those whose characteristics are not yet complete" (*xiang wei ju zhe zi bu deng*)—to the position below "within the five aggregates" (*wu yin zhong you*). Conversely, they have moved the twenty-seven lines totaling three hundred and seventy-six characters—beginning from "the section on habitual self-assertion 'I am without fault'" (*xi zishuo wo wu zui*) down to "this is inverted speech" (*shi wei diandao kou*)—to the position below "those whose characteristics are not yet complete. Consequently, the textual continuity of these three sections has been severed, resulting in a total disjunction of meaning.

Now, based on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, I shall rectify this by advancing and retreating through the text; furthermore, for the sake of those who consult the old editions or the Song-dynasty canon, I have briefly recorded the authentic text below:

Within it [the text], regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it says: "If one immediately claims 'I am without fault,' and so forth, this is called a perversion. Regarding speech, it says: "Whatever much one obtains of middling flavors or middling words," and so forth, until: "One whose marks are not yet complete should not claim for themselves that they can attain Buddhahood, let alone enable others to attain Buddhahood," and so on.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Scroll Sixty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Part Two of the Chapter on the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions.
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva practices seated meditation by counting the breaths, they fail to attain a concentrated mind, or if concentration is attained, it does not endure. This is because they merely sit without severing their fundamental offenses, which causes their dhyāna to remain unstable."
The Bodhisattva said himself,
"By what causes and conditions do my fundamental offenses remain unsevered?
The Buddha said:
"Because the Bodhisattva sits without calculating or reckoning the severance of birth and death, his fundamental offenses are not severed.
The Buddha said:
"One who wishes to sever fundamental offenses should sever the intention toward future birth and death; one should extinguish the intention toward birth and death rooted in fundamental offenses."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
“What is it that should sever the intention for future birth-and-death, and what is it that should extinguish the fundamental sinful intention for birth-and-death?
The Buddha said:
"The movement of the mind constitutes the primary offense that serves as the causal condition for the offenses of future birth and death.
One must sever these future births and deaths to truly correspond with the state of a Bodhisattva."
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in prostration and said,
"We pray that the Buddha will further explain for us the offenses of birth and death in the future.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"When the mind moves and encounters the convergence of causes and conditions, there arises within it the fullness of the one hundred and eight births and deaths.
A bodhisattva must certainly sever this fullness of the one hundred and eight births and deaths.

When the intention of the bodhisattva moves and encounters causes and conditions, if he cannot distance himself from that intention, there arises within it the fullness of the one hundred and eight births and deaths; the bodhisattva must certainly sever this fullness of the one hundred and eight births and deaths."

“The Bodhisattva is moved by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and furthermore, within that consciousness there is the accumulation of the one hundred and eight births and deaths; the Bodhisattva must certainly sever this accumulation of the one hundred and eight births and deaths.”

“Entering into the eye: when the eye of a bodhisattva perceives pleasant forms, this is the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these pleasant forms, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the bodhisattva must decisively sever.

When the eye perceives neutral forms, this is the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these neutral forms, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the bodhisattva must decisively sever.

When the eye perceives unpleasant forms, this is the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these unpleasant forms, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the bodhisattva must decisively sever.”

"Entering through the ear: when a bodhisattva hears pleasant sounds, these pleasant sounds serve as the basis for desire and discrimination, within which there is the intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths; the bodhisattva must certainly sever this intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths.

When neutral sounds are heard by the ear, these neutral sounds serve as the basis for desire and discrimination, within which there is the intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths; the bodhisattva must certainly sever this intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths.

When unpleasant sounds are heard by the ear, these unpleasant sounds serve as the basis for desire and discrimination, within which there is the intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths; the bodhisattva must certainly sever this intense cycle of one hundred and eight births and deaths."

“Turning toward the nose: when a bodhisattva perceives pleasant fragrances through the nose, this is the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these pleasant fragrances, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. The bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. When he perceives neutral fragrances through the nose, this is the basis;

within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these neutral fragrances, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. The bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. When he perceives foul odors through the nose, this is the basis;

within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these foul odors, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. The bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death.”

“Turning toward the mouth: when a Bodhisattva obtains delicious flavors and pleasant speech through the mouth, these serve as the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these delicious flavors and pleasant speech, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death.

The Bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. When he obtains moderate flavors and neutral speech through the mouth, these serve as the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these moderate flavors and neutral speech, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death.

The Bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. When he obtains foul flavors and unpleasant speech through the mouth, these serve as the basis; within the movement of desire and discrimination regarding these foul flavors and unpleasant speech, there are one hundred and eight instances of birth and death. The Bodhisattva must certainly sever these one hundred and eight instances of birth and death.”

“Entering into the body: when the body obtains that which is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable to the body, this is its basis; within the movement, desire, and discrimination of that subtle softness, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the Bodhisattva must sever.

When the body obtains that which is neutral, subtle, and soft, this is its basis; within the movement, desire, and discrimination of that neutral subtle softness, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the Bodhisattva must sever.

When the body obtains that which is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable to the body, this is its basis; within the movement, desire, and discrimination of that unpleasant, coarse, hard, and painful state, there are one hundred and eight flourishing cycles of birth and death, which the Bodhisattva must sever.”
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva must certainly sever this to be worthy of the name 'bodhisattva'; one who does not sever it is not a bodhisattva. Even so, you have not yet understood."
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We have already understood dependent origination.
The bodhisattvas said:
"I have heard what the Buddha has taught, and I shall not fall into any transgression whatsoever.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Do you see anyone among the bodhisattvas who has shaved his head and beard to become a śramaṇa?"
The bodhisattvas said,
“Yet we see them acting as śramaṇas.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"When a śramaṇa shaves his head and plucks out his beard, is the hair and beard on the śramaṇa’s head completely removed?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"It is completely removed."
The Buddha said:
"When one's hair has been completely shaved off, would a śramaṇa wish for his head-hair and beard to grow back?
The bodhisattvas replied:
"The śramaṇa does not wish for them to grow.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"For what reason do the hair of his head and beard grow back?"
The bodhisattvas said, “They arise spontaneously; even a śramaṇa does not cause them to arise.
The Buddha said:
“Shramana, as your head hair and beard grow, can you know for yourself by how much they increase each day?
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“Shramana, as our head hair and beard grow, we cannot know for ourselves by how much they increase each day.”
The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva cannot perceive for himself the subtle increase of the one hundred and eight offenses of wrongdoing. It is like a śramaṇa who has hair growing on his head but does not know by how much it grows each day;
likewise, when a bodhisattva sits amidst offenses yet cannot recognize them for himself, how can he say, ‘I have no offenses’?”
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Is there such a thing as this?
The bodhisattvas immediately bowed their heads in shame and accepted his teaching for practice.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
"We pray that the Buddha will further explain this for us.
The Buddha said:
"A Bodhisattva must not rely on themselves, saying, 'I have no offenses' or 'my offenses are extinguished.
The Buddha said:
'One must examine and calculate whether or not the one hundred and eight fundamental offenses are extinguished.'"
The Bodhisattva asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes the extinction or non-extinction of the one hundred and eight fundamental offenses?
The Buddha said:

“The arising and transformation of the Bodhisattva’s mind is immediately extinguished; within that extinction, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] that will arise again and be experienced in future lives, and they are not extinguished.

It transforms and enters the manas; the arising and transformation of the manas is also extinguished; within that extinction, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] that will arise again and be experienced in future lives, and they are not extinguished.”

“Entering into consciousness, consciousness arises and then turns toward extinction; within that extinction there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and they do not cease.

Entering into the eye, when a beautiful form seen by the eye arises and then turns toward extinction, within that extinction there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and they do not cease;

when a neutral form seen by the eye arises and then turns toward extinction, within that extinction there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and they do not cease.”

When an unwholesome form seen by the eye arises, it passes away as soon as it has arisen; yet within that passing away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and do not cease.

When a pleasant sound heard by the ear arises, it passes away as soon as it has arisen; yet within that passing away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and do not cease.

When a neutral sound heard by the ear arises, it passes away as soon as it has arisen; yet within that passing away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and do not cease.

When an unpleasant sound heard by the ear arises and passes away, as it passes away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that will arise and be experienced again in future lives and are not extinguished.

When a pleasant fragrance smelled by the nose arises and passes away, as it passes away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that will arise and be experienced again in future lives and are not extinguished;

when a neutral fragrance smelled by the nose arises and passes away, as it passes away there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] that will arise and be experienced again in future lives and are not extinguished.

When a foul odor perceived by the nose arises, it passes away; as it passes away, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and do not cease.
