When it turns toward the mouth, a delicious flavor or pleasant speech obtained by the mouth arises, it passes away; as it passes away, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and do not cease.

When a middling flavor or middling speech obtained by the mouth arises, it passes away; as it passes away, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] that shall arise again and be experienced in future lives, and do not cease.

When an unpleasant taste or an unpleasant speech encountered by the mouth arises and passes away, within that passing there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and are not extinguished.

When a pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable sensation encountered by the body arises and passes away, within that passing there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and are not extinguished;

when a neutral, subtle, soft sensation encountered by the body arises and passes away, within that passing there are one hundred and eight [afflictions] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives and are not extinguished.

When unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations arise within the body, they pass away as soon as they have arisen; yet within that cessation, there are one hundred and eight [tendencies] which will arise again and be experienced in future lives, and do not cease.
The Bodhisattva said:
"For what reason do my offenses arise and then cease?
For what reason do I not perceive them at all?"
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Has your mind undergone transformation?
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha:
“My mind arises; even if my mind did not arise, it still could not converse with the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
“When the mind arises, does it recognize that the mind has arisen?”
The bodhisattvas said, “We only perceive the time of the conditions; we do not perceive the moment of its initial arising.
The Buddha said:
“As you have said, if one cannot even know when the mind first arises, how could one possibly be without fault?
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas felt ashamed, bowed their heads, and accepted his teaching for practice.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha, “Your explanation for us was too brief; we pray that the Buddha will explain it to us once more.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Since you were born, have you ever been able to perceive how many fires there are within your body that produce warmth?
Have you perceived how many winds there are within your body that produce cold?
How many waters are contained within your entire body?"
The bodhisattvas said,
“We cannot return to fully discern and know how many there are.
The Buddha said:
"If you do not know how much there is, how could you know whether cold and heat are water and fire?
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
"We know that cold and heat involve water and fire."
The Buddha said,
"If you still know cold and heat, water and fire, for what reason do you not know their measure?
The bodhisattvas replied:
“I can only perceive cold and heat, but I cannot know their quantity.

The Buddha said, “A bodhisattva does not himself perceive the arising of the mind, nor the number of the one hundred and eight offenses of wrong reception; it is like being unable to perceive the amount of fire that has arisen since its inception, even while perceiving cold and heat.”
The Bodhisattva does not know for himself how much time has passed since his successive births.
Thus, the Bodhisattva can only perceive the branches but cannot perceive the root; in this way, the Bodhisattva’s transgressions have entered into the void and remain unresolved.
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in prostration and asked the Buddha,
"We pray that you will further explain for us how transgressions enter into emptiness.
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva has one hundred and eight offenses that enter into emptiness and cannot be seen.
What are these one hundred and eight offenses?
If a bodhisattva’s mind has a thought, it arises within emptiness and again ceases within emptiness; therein are the one hundred and eight offenses, invisible as the mind arises and ceases.”
For example, when a person speaks, there is sound that cannot be seen; yet it must exist as sound in space, merely being invisible.
When [the voice] turns inward into the mind, the mind arises in space and again perishes in space; within this process, the one hundred and eight offenses exist but are invisible.
“Entering into consciousness, consciousness arises in empty space and again ceases in empty space; within it, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
Entering into the eye, when the eye perceives beautiful forms, they arise in empty space and again cease in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
When the eye perceives neutral forms, they arise in empty space and again cease in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.”
When the eye perceives an unwholesome form, it arises in space and again ceases in space; within this, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
When it turns to the ear, and the ear hears a pleasant sound, it arises in space and again ceases in space; within this, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
When the ear hears a neutral sound, it arises in space and again ceases in space; within this, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
When evil sounds are heard by the ear, they arise in space and again perish in space; within them are one hundred and eight offenses that cannot be seen.
When they turn to enter the nose, when pleasant fragrances are smelled by the nose, they arise in space and again perish in space; within them are one hundred and eight offenses that cannot be seen.
When neutral fragrances are smelled by the nose, they arise in space and again perish in space; within them are one hundred and eight offenses that cannot be seen.
The foul odors perceived by the nose arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible. They then turn toward the mouth:
the exquisite flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
The moderate flavors and moderate speech obtained by the mouth arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
Regarding the foul tastes and harsh words encountered by the mouth: they arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.

When they turn into the body, regarding the fine, soft, and pleasant sensations experienced by the body: they arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.
Regarding the moderate fine and soft sensations experienced by the body: they arise in empty space and again perish in empty space; within them, the one hundred and eight offenses are invisible.

"When the body encounters what is evil, coarse, hard, painful, and unbearable, it arises in empty space and again ceases in empty space; within this, there are one hundred and eight offenses that cannot be seen.
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"If you do not see these offenses arising in empty space, nor see them ceasing in empty space, then such bodhisattvas have not yet attained understanding."
The bodhisattvas said,
"In this way, I have realized and understood it.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"If they awaken through such causes and conditions, for what reason do the bodhisattvas not constantly practice seated meditation?
For what reason, moreover, do they fly to the abodes of the Buddhas of the ten directions?"
The Bodhisattva said:
“Because of my original vow, I cannot but practice.
The Buddha said:
"If you have an original vow to reach the abodes of the Buddhas of the ten directions, for what reason would you practice seated meditation to abandon your transgressions?
Even if you were to abandon your transgressions through seated meditation, your original vow would surely be extinguished."
The bodhisattvas said, “In our practice of dhyāna, we merely extinguish future offenses; we have not yet extinguished the offenses of our original vows.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
“Will the past offenses of birth and death committed by you all since incalculable kalpas be extinguished?
The bodhisattvas replied,
“We shall extinguish our original offenses from incalculable kalpas in the past.”
The Buddha said:
"If you are even able to extinguish the fundamental sins of incalculable kalpas, for what reason alone do you not extinguish the sin of your original vows?
The bodhisattvas replied:
“The Buddha asked me about this, yet I could not fully understand it.
The Buddha said,
“If you all have not yet understood in this way, for what reason do you say that you understand?”
All the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in shame and accepted the practice.
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha, saying:
"Although the Buddha has explained it for us, we have not yet understood."
"I pray that the Buddha will further explain for me: what kind of practice should one undertake?
The Buddha said, "Since the countless kalpas ago when the Bodhisattvas began practicing the Way, they have taken the fundamental nature of birth and death as their primary intention."

It is like a fruit seed planted in the earth that grows into a great tree; once it has become a great tree, hundreds of billions upon billions of branches grow upon it, each branch produces billions upon billions of leaves, and from every branch grow billions upon billions of fruits, each single fruit being capable of producing another tree in turn.

When a bodhisattva practices dhyāna, they abandon their fundamental offenses, just as if one were to take the leaves of a tree and extinguish them one by one, take the fruits and extinguish them one by one, so that they no longer sprout;
or take the branches and extinguish them one by one—until the leaves, fruits, and branches are all completely exhausted, leaving only the root.

The "roots" serve as a metaphor: they are like the fundamental offenses arising from the single-mindedness of one's original vows. Just as the roots of a tree give rise to branches and leaves which must then be extinguished, those that are not extinguished should be nurtured; yet even those that have truly arisen and been extinguished shall not arise again.

When a bodhisattva guards the mind, it is like guarding the root of a tree so that branches, leaves, and fruit do not grow; for their growth would increase future offenses, whereas their cessation prevents future offenses from increasing and serves to extinguish past offenses.
"In this way, for a bodhisattva whose fundamental offenses have not yet been exhausted, one should constantly contemplate the hundred and eight [offenses] until they are abandoned and exhausted.
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads and said,
"We pray that the Buddha will explain for us what we do not understand."
The Buddha said:

"When one does not abandon the exhaustion of whatever thoughts arise, and those thoughts, having arisen, return to exhaustion, then the hundred and eight [defilements] are exhausted; this is called 'not abandoning exhaustion.
When they further enter the mind (*manas*), and the thoughts arising in the mind return to exhaustion, then the hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called 'not abandoning exhaustion.'"

“Entering into consciousness, when the thought that arises in consciousness returns to exhaustion, the one hundred and eight [defilements] are exhausted; this is called ‘exhaustion without abandonment.
Entering into the eye, when the thought regarding the beautiful forms seen by the eye returns to exhaustion, the one hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called ‘exhaustion without abandonment.
When the thought regarding the neutral forms seen by the eye returns to exhaustion, the one hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called ‘exhaustion without abandonment.’”
When the mindfulness of unwholesome forms seen by the eye returns to its cessation, the one hundred and eight [afflictions] are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment.

When it turns to the ear, the mindfulness of pleasant sounds heard by the ear returns to its cessation, and the one hundred and eight are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment.
When the mindfulness of neutral sounds heard by the ear returns to its cessation, the one hundred and eight are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment."
When the mindfulness regarding unpleasant sounds heard by the ear returns to its cessation, the hundred and eight [afflictions] are exhausted; this is called "not abandoning exhaustion.

When it turns to enter the nose, the mindfulness regarding pleasant fragrances smelled by the nose returns to its cessation, and the hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called "not abandoning exhaustion.
When the mindfulness regarding neutral fragrances smelled by the nose returns to its cessation, the hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called "not abandoning exhaustion."
When the mindfulness regarding foul odors perceived by the nose returns to cessation, the one hundred and eight [tendencies] are exhausted; this is called "exhaustion without abandoning.

When it turns toward the mouth, the mindfulness regarding delicious flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth returns to cessation, and the one hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called "exhaustion without abandoning.
The mindfulness regarding moderate flavors and moderate speech obtained by the mouth returns to cessation, and the one hundred and eight are exhausted; this is called "exhaustion without abandoning."

When the thoughts regarding foul tastes and foul speech obtained by the mouth are brought back to cessation, the hundred and eight [afflictions] are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment.

When they turn toward the body, the thoughts regarding pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable sensations obtained by the body are brought back to cessation, and the hundred and eight are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment.

When the thoughts regarding middling, fine, and soft sensations obtained by the body are brought back to cessation, the hundred and eight are thereby exhausted; this is called "exhaustion through non-abandonment."

When the unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations experienced by the body are brought back to their cessation, the one hundred and eight [afflictions] are thereby exhausted; this is called "not abandoning exhaustion.
In this way, when the bodhisattva does not abandon exhaustion, they enter the purity of the one hundred and eight.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas rejoiced, bowed their heads in prostration, and undertook to practice it.
The bodhisattvas again bowed their heads and asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes the one hundred and eight purities?"
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva gives rise to a thought of birth, they immediately return to cessation; this is entry into purity, for it is the cessation of the one hundred and eight [afflictions] without abandoning purity."

“Turning toward and entering the mind (*manas*), as soon as the mind arises it returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight [defilements] without abandoning purity.

Turning toward and entering consciousness (*vijñāna*), as soon as consciousness arises it returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight [defilements] without abandoning purity.”

"Entering into the eye, when a beautiful form perceived by the eye arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight [defilements] that do not abandon purity.

When a neutral form perceived by the eye arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight [defilements] that do not abandon purity.

When an ugly form perceived by the eye arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight [defilements] that do not abandon purity."
"When a pleasant sound enters the ear and arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.
When a neutral sound enters the ear and arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.

When an unpleasant sound enters the ear and arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity."

"Turning toward the nose: when a pleasant fragrance perceived by the nose arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.

When a neutral fragrance obtained by the nose arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.
When a foul odor perceived by the nose arises, it immediately returns to cessation; this is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity."

“Turning toward the entrance of the mouth, when a delicious taste or pleasant speech is encountered by the mouth, it arises; as soon as it arises, it returns to cessation, which is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.

When a neutral taste or neutral speech is encountered by the mouth, it arises; as soon as it arises, it returns to cessation, which is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.

When a foul taste or unpleasant speech is encountered by the mouth, it arises; as soon as it arises, it returns to cessation, which is entry into purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.”

“Turning toward the body: when pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable sensations arise in the body, they immediately return to cessation for the sake of entering purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity;

when neutral, subtle, soft sensations arise in the body, they immediately return to cessation for the sake of entering purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity;

when unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations arise in the body, they immediately return to cessation for the sake of entering purity, for the sake of extinguishing the one hundred and eight non-abandonments of impurity.”
"When a bodhisattva practices in this way without abandoning purity, they are able to diligently restore the one hundred and eight precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas joyfully accepted and practiced it.
The bodhisattvas again prostrated themselves and asked the Buddha:
"What is the 'hundred-and-eightfold reversion through refinement' that corresponds to the precepts?
The Buddha said:

"When the Bodhisattvas give rise to the mind that practices the Way, they immediately and precisely extinguish the one hundred and eight [defilements]; this constitutes returning to correspond with the precepts.

When they further enter into the mental faculty (*manas*), as soon as the mind arises, they immediately and precisely extinguish the one hundred and eight [defilements]; this constitutes returning to correspond with the precepts."
“Entering into consciousness, as soon as consciousness arises, the essence returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight [afflictions]; this is the returning that accords with the precepts.
Entering into the eye, when a beautiful form seen by the eye arises, the essence returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight; this is the returning that accords with the precepts.
When a neutral form seen by the eye arises, the essence returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight; this is the returning that accords with the precepts.”
When an unwholesome form is seen by the eye, the essence immediately returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight [afflictions]; this is the return that accords with the precepts.

When it turns to enter the ear, when a pleasant sound is heard by the ear, the essence immediately returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight; this is the return that accords with the precepts.
When a neutral sound is heard by the ear, the essence immediately returns and extinguishes the one hundred and eight; this is the return that accords with the precepts.

When an unpleasant sound is heard by the ear, one immediately concentrates on returning and extinguishing the hundred and eight [afflictions]; this constitutes returning in accordance with the precepts.

When it turns to the nose and a pleasant fragrance is smelled, one immediately concentrates on returning and extinguishing the hundred and eight; this constitutes returning in accordance with the precepts.
When a neutral fragrance is smelled by the nose, one immediately concentrates on returning and extinguishing the hundred and eight; this constitutes returning in accordance with the precepts.
When a foul odor is perceived by the nose, one immediately refines and extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions]; this is the precept of returning.
When it turns to the mouth, and delicious flavors or pleasant speech are perceived by the mouth, one immediately refines and extinguishes the hundred and eight; this is the precept of returning.
When middling flavors or middling speech are perceived by the mouth, one immediately refines and extinguishes the hundred and eight; this is the precept of returning.

When unpleasant tastes or harsh words encountered by the mouth arise, one immediately refines the essence to extinguish the hundred-and-eight [afflictions]; this is returning to correspond with the precepts.

When pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable sensations encountered by the body arise, one immediately refines the essence to extinguish the hundred-and-eight; this is returning to correspond with the precepts.
When neutral, subtle, and soft sensations encountered by the body arise, one immediately refines the essence to extinguish the hundred-and-eight; this is returning to correspond with the precepts.

When unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations arise within the body, one immediately refines and extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions]; this is what it means to "return" in accordance with the precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the bodhisattvas joyfully accepted and practiced it.
The Buddha said:
"All bodhisattvas, by returning their vigor to correspond with the precepts, advance in practice and enter the Way.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
“What is meant by ‘refining and returning the precepts so as to advance and enter the Path’?
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva has a thought arise in the mind, he exerts all his strength from that mind; by exhausting what was thought, he extinguishes the one hundred and eight [afflictions]. This is called advancing and entering the Path.”

“Turning toward the mind, when the mind has something to think, one exerts effort from the mind; by exhausting what is thought, the one hundred and eight [afflictions] are extinguished—this is advancing into the Path.

Turning toward consciousness, when consciousness has something to cognize, one exerts effort from consciousness; by exhausting what is cognized, the one hundred and eight [afflictions] are extinguished—this is advancing into the Path.”

“Turning toward the eye: when the eye perceives a beautiful form, one exerts effort regarding that beautiful form; by exhausting the beautiful form, one extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions].

This is called proceeding toward the entrance into the Way. When the eye perceives a neutral form, one exerts effort regarding that neutral form; by exhausting the neutral form, one extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions].

This is called proceeding toward the entrance into the Way. When the eye perceives an ugly form, one exerts effort regarding that ugly form; by exhausting the ugly form, one extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions]. This is called proceeding toward the entrance into the Way.”

"Turning toward the ear: when the ear hears pleasant sounds, one exerts effort regarding those pleasant sounds; by exhausting pleasant sounds, one extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions]. This is called progressing into the Way.
When the ear hears neutral sounds, one exerts effort regarding those neutral sounds; by exhausting neutral sounds, one extinguishes the hundred and eight. This is called progressing into the Way.

When the ear hears unpleasant sounds, one exerts effort regarding those unpleasant sounds; by exhausting unpleasant sounds, one extinguishes the hundred and eight. This is called progressing into the Way."

“Turning toward the nose: when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, by exerting effort regarding that pleasant fragrance, one exhausts the pleasant fragrance and extinguishes the hundred and eight [afflictions]; this is called progressing into the Path.
When the nose perceives a neutral fragrance, by exerting effort regarding that neutral fragrance, one exhausts the neutral fragrance and extinguishes the hundred and eight;

this is called progressing into the Path. When the nose perceives a foul odor, by exerting effort regarding that foul odor, one exhausts the foul odor and extinguishes the hundred and eight; this is called progressing into the Path.”

“When it turns toward the mouth, regarding the fine flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one exerts effort from those fine flavors and pleasant speech; through the exhaustion of those fine flavors and pleasant speech, the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished—this is called advancing into the Path.

Regarding the middling flavors and middling speech obtained by the mouth, one exerts effort from those middling flavors and middling speech; through the exhaustion of those middling flavors and middling speech, the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished—this is called advancing into the Path.

Regarding the foul flavors and unpleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one exerts effort from those foul flavors and unpleasant speech; through the exhaustion of those foul flavors and unpleasant speech, the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished—this is called advancing into the Path.”

“Turning toward the body: when the body encounters what is pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, one exerts all effort from that pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable state until the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished;

this is called advancing into the Way. When the body encounters what is moderately subtle and soft, one exerts all effort from that moderate subtlety and softness until the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished;

this is called advancing into the Way. When the body encounters what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, one exerts all effort from that unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable state until the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] are extinguished; this is called advancing into the Way.”
The Buddha said:
"By proceeding forward and entering the Way, one is able to endure and maintain the practice of the precepts.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"What is the precept of patient endurance and upholding?
The Buddha said:
'If a bodhisattva has already been able, or will be able, to patiently uphold the precepts without departing from them, this accords with the practice of a bodhisattva.'"
When the Bodhisattva’s mind moves, he should endure the hundred and eight [afflictions] and not allow them to turn; this is the precept of the endurance of the mind and the practice of endurance.

When they turn into the mental faculty (*manas*) and there is something thought by the mind, he should follow the endurance of the mind and not allow it to turn; then the hundred and eight [afflictions] will not proceed. This is the precept of the practice of endurance.

"When consciousness turns and enters, and there is that which is cognized by consciousness, one should practice patience regarding consciousness so as not to allow it to turn; thus the hundred and eight [afflictions] will not proceed. This is called the precept of practicing patience toward the patience of consciousness."

"When the eye turns toward it and sees a beautiful form, one should exercise patience regarding that beautiful form so as not to allow [the mind] to turn; thus the 'one hundred and eight' do not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring beautiful forms, the practice of patience which is the precept.

When the eye sees a neutral form, one should exercise patience regarding that neutral form so as not to allow [the mind] to turn; thus the 'one hundred and eight' do not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring neutral forms, the practice of patience which is the precept.

When the eye sees an ugly form, one should exercise patience regarding that ugly form so as not to allow [the mind] to turn; thus the 'one hundred and eight' do not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring ugly forms, the practice of patience which is the precept."

“When sounds enter the ear, regarding pleasant sounds heard by the ear, one should exercise patience toward them so as not to allow them to cause a shift; thus the hundred-and-eight [delusions] cannot proceed—this is the practice of the precept of patience toward pleasant sounds.

Regarding neutral sounds heard by the ear, one should exercise patience toward them so as not to allow them to cause a shift; thus the hundred-and-eight [delusions] cannot proceed—this is the practice of the precept of patience toward neutral sounds.

Regarding unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, one should exercise patience toward them so as not to allow them to cause a shift; thus the hundred-and-eight [delusions] cannot proceed—this is the practice of the precept of patience toward unpleasant sounds.”

"When the sense of smell turns toward it, regarding the pleasant fragrances perceived by the nose, one should exercise patience toward these pleasant fragrances so as not to allow them to turn [the mind]; thus the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] shall not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring pleasant fragrances, the practice of the precept of patience.

Regarding the moderate fragrances perceived by the nose, one should exercise patience toward these moderate fragrances so as not to allow them to turn [the mind]; thus the hundred-and-eight shall not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring moderate fragrances, the practice of the precept of patience.

Regarding the foul odors perceived by the nose, one should exercise patience toward these foul odors so as not to allow them to turn [the mind]; thus the hundred-and-eight shall not proceed—this is called the patience of enduring foul odors, the practice of the precept of patience."

"When [the sense] turns toward the mouth, regarding the fine flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one should exercise forbearance so that they do not cause [the mind] to turn; thus the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] cannot proceed—this is called the practice of the precept of forbearing fine flavors and pleasant speech.

Regarding the middling flavors and middling speech obtained by the mouth, one should exercise forbearance toward those middling flavors and middling speech so that they do not cause [the mind] to turn; thus the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] cannot proceed—this is called the practice of the precept of forbearing middling flavors and middling speech.

Regarding the foul flavors and unpleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one should exercise forbearance so that they do not cause [the mind] to turn; thus the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] cannot proceed—this is called the practice of the precept of forbearing foul flavors and unpleasant speech."

"When the body encounters what is pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable, one should endure it from that state of being pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable, not allowing it to turn [into attachment]; thus the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] do not proceed—this is the precept of practicing patience toward what is pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable to the body.

When the body encounters what is moderately fine and soft, one should endure it from that state of being moderately fine and soft, not allowing it to turn; thus the hundred-and-eight do not proceed—this is the precept of practicing patience toward what is moderately fine and soft.

When the body encounters what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, one should endure it from that state of being unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, not allowing it to turn; thus the hundred-and-eight do not proceed—this is the precept of practicing patience toward what is unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable to the body."
The Buddha said:
"These are the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattvas further have ten forms of calculation.
The bodhisattvas bowed their heads and asked the Buddha,
“What are these ten forms of calculation?”
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should be able to endure insults; by being able to endure insults, one enters the Way.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
“What is meant by ‘enduring humiliation to enter the Way’?
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva has a thought arise in the mind, they must humiliate that mind so that it cannot persist; thus, they humble the one hundred and eight offenses so that they do not prevail. This is called entering the Way by humiliating the mind.”

“Turning toward the mind: when the mind has thoughts, one should subdue the mind so that it does not give rise to them; thus one subdues the hundred and eight offenses so that they do not prevail. This is called subduing the mind to enter the Way.”

"When consciousness enters into transformation and consciousness has objects of thought, one should subdue the consciousness so that it does not give rise to thoughts; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight offenses and does not allow them to prevail—this is called subduing consciousness to enter the Way."

“Turning toward the eye: when the eye perceives a beautiful form, one should subdue that beautiful form so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing beautiful forms to enter the Path.

When the eye perceives a neutral form, one should subdue that neutral form so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing neutral forms to enter the Path.

When the eye perceives an ugly form, one should subdue that ugly form so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing ugly forms to enter the Path.”

"When the ear turns toward sounds, regarding pleasant sounds heard by the ear, one should subdue those pleasant sounds so that they do not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [defilements] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing pleasant sounds to enter the Way.

Regarding neutral sounds heard by the ear, one should subdue those neutral sounds so that they do not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [defilements] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing neutral sounds to enter the Way.

Regarding unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, one should subdue those unpleasant sounds so that they do not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [defilements] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing unpleasant sounds to enter the Way."

"Turning toward the nose: when the nose perceives a pleasant fragrance, one should subdue that pleasant fragrance so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred and eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing pleasant fragrance to enter the Path.

When the nose perceives a neutral fragrance, one should subdue that neutral fragrance so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred and eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing neutral fragrance to enter the Path.

When the nose perceives a foul odor, one should subdue that foul odor so that it does not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred and eight [afflictions] and does not succumb to them—this is called subduing foul odors to enter the Path."

"When the [sense] enters the mouth, regarding the fine flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one should subdue those fine flavors and pleasant speech so that they do not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not allow them to prevail—this is called subduing fine flavors and pleasant speech as entry into the Path.

Regarding the moderate flavors and moderate speech obtained by the mouth, one should subdue those moderate flavors and moderate speech so that they do not give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not allow them to prevail—this is called subduing moderate flavors and moderate speech as entry into the Path.

Regarding the foul flavors and unpleasant speech obtained by the mouth, one should not allow them to give rise to thought; thus one subdues the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] and does not allow them to prevail—this is called subduing foul flavors and unpleasant speech as entry into the Path."

“Turning toward the body: regarding those bodily sensations that are pleasant, subtle, soft, and agreeable, one should subdue them so that they do not give rise to thought; thus subduing the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] without being overcome is called entering the Path by subduing pleasant, subtle, and soft sensations.

Regarding those bodily sensations that are moderately subtle and soft, one should subdue them so that they do not give rise to thought; thus subduing the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] without being overcome is called entering the Path by subduing moderately subtle and soft sensations.

Regarding those bodily sensations that are unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable, one should subdue them so that they do not give rise to thought; thus subduing the hundred-and-eight [afflictions] without being overcome is called entering the Path by subduing unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations.”

The Buddha said: “When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they act in accordance with the bodhisattva’s practice of patience and precepts. By means of patience, the bodhisattva attains one hundred and eight vows for unifying with the Way; they attain one hundred and eight fundamental faiths for entering the Way; they attain one hundred and eight ways of emerging from delusion and entering wisdom; they attain one hundred and eight joys for returning to cessation; they attain one hundred and eight compassionate minds of the Buddhas; and they attain one hundred and eight sorrows regarding not yet having attained the Buddha-way.”
"What are the one hundred and eight compassionate minds of a Buddha?
What are the one hundred and eight sorrows of not yet having attained the Buddha-way?
It is said that when a Bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s compassionate mind, he reflects upon the people in the hells throughout the ten directions, who are difficult to deliver."
This means that the Bodhisattva, having attained the Buddha’s mind of compassion, reflects on how birds, beasts, and all crawling and flying insects find it difficult to attain liberation.
It means that the Bodhisattva, having attained the Buddha’s mind of compassion, reflects on how the hungry ghosts within the realm of *preta* find it difficult to attain liberation.

This means that when a bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s mind of compassion, he reflects upon the inhabitants of the twenty-eight heavens and other celestial beings who, due to their long lives, pride, and pleasures, do not recognize suffering or its origin and thus find it difficult to attain liberation.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s mind of compassion, he reflects upon the world’s emperors, kings, and the wealthy and noble, who likewise find it difficult to attain liberation.
This means that when a bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s compassionate mind, he reflects that the deluded people of the world do not understand how difficult it is to attain liberation;
that is, when a bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s compassionate mind, he reflects that many people in the world are deluded and find it difficult to attain liberation.

This means that when a bodhisattva attains the Buddha’s mind of compassion, they reflect upon all beings in the five realms across the ten directions, seeing that it is difficult for those who share the same dharma to attain liberation.
Thus, because the bodhisattva has attained the Buddha’s mind of compassion, they likewise attain the Buddha’s sorrow.

This means that when a bodhisattva contemplates the suffering of the five realms of existence throughout the ten directions and the sorrow of the difficulty in attaining liberation, the bodhisattva already feels compassion and sorrow; yet, even as these hundred and eight forms of craving increase further, the bodhisattva must not, because of this increase in the hundred and eight cravings, cease to feel compassion and sorrow.
The Buddha said:

"I attained Buddhahood solely because of my compassion and sorrow for the suffering of the five realms throughout the ten directions; this constitutes the one hundred and eight compassions of a bodhisattva who has not yet attained Buddhahood, and this constitutes the one hundred and eight sorrows of a bodhisattva who has not yet attained Buddhahood."
The Buddha said: "Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the Buddha’s freedom from the one hundred and eight afflictions.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"What are the one hundred and eight afflictions of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:

"It refers to when a bodhisattva, before having attained Buddhahood, sees those in the hells throughout the ten directions being tortured and suffering agonizing pain; wishing to go and deliver them, yet being unable to deliver them, he gives rise to affliction."

This means that when a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they see birds and beasts, crawling and wriggling insects, as well as human beings, inflicting torture upon one another, suffering agonizing pain, and killing each other; seeing this, the bodhisattva wishes to deliver them but is unable to do so, and thus gives rise to vexation.

This means that when a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they see the *preta* hungry ghosts who have nothing to eat; wishing to deliver them but being unable to do so, they give rise to distress.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they see the people of the world committing evils—such as greed, lust, anger, hatred, slaughtering for sacrificial offerings, coveting profit, robbery, and acting with unrestrained pleasure and will—and they see such people undergoing birth and death within the five realms of existence, their suffering never ceasing.

Although there is no difference even when one is among the higher heavens, as long as there is the suffering of birth and death within the five destinies, one will not immediately attain Buddhahood; instead, affliction arises and the hundred-and-eight modes of craving increase. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva who has not yet attained Buddhahood experiencing the hundred-and-eight afflictions.
"This means that Bodhisattvas have not yet attained the essential wisdom of the hundred-and-eight [teachings] of the Buddha’s sutras, nor have they attained the essential Nirvana of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattvas then asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes the hundred-and-eight attainments of the wisdom of the Buddha’s sutras?"
The Buddha said:
"It means that when a bodhisattva can protect their own six sense-faculties so that the one hundred and eight [afflictions] do not arise, they have attained wisdom regarding the Buddha's sutras.
[The interlocutor asked: "What constitutes not yet having attained the essential of the Buddha’s nirvana?"
The Buddha said:
"It means that the bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, nor has he attained the essential state of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"All Bodhisattvas should calculate the essential points for the emergence from the one hundred and eight offenses; by doing so, they shall attain the essential point of entry into Nirvana.
The Bodhisattva again asked the Buddha:
"What are the essential points for the emergence from offense that lead to the attainment of the essential point of entry into Nirvana?"

The Buddha said: "It means that whatever the bodhisattva contemplates as a transgression must be extinguished; this extinction constitutes the essential gateway to entering nirvāṇa. When all six sense-faculties and the one hundred and eight [afflictions] are extinguished, this likewise constitutes the essential gateway to entering nirvāṇa. This is called the bodhisattva’s emergence from the one hundred and eight transgressions and entry into the essential gateway of nirvāṇa; this is the bodhisattva’s tenth reckoning."
The Buddha said:
"Bodhisattvas further have ten reckonings:

first, when Bodhisattvas gather together, they should only reckon upon the one hundred and eight [delusions] to bring them to an end; they should seek entry into wisdom and the emergence from transgressions, which accords with the Dharma of a Bodhisattva."

Second, one should calculate the bodhisattva’s hundred and eight inquiries into entering the dharma of emptiness, thereby emerging from the dharma of sinful emptiness; this is called the bodhisattva’s hundred and eight calculations for emerging from sin and entering the emptiness of the Path.

Third, when the bodhisattva calculates the hundred and eight sinful dharmas at the moment they first arise in emptiness, he should know that calculating their cessation is their return to emptiness; this is the bodhisattva’s calculation of the hundred and eight arisings and cessations, whereby he unites with emptiness to understand arising and cessation—this is the bodhisattva’s thorough calculation.
Fourth, the bodhisattva should calculate the hundred and eight dharmas of maintaining emptiness and the exhaustion of all dharmas.
The bodhisattvas again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by upholding the dharma of emptiness and understanding the dharma of exhaustion?
The Buddha said:

"Once the Bodhisattva has realized that all things throughout the ten directions, from their beginning to their end, are entirely empty, he knows emptiness and knows that all existing things shall likewise be extinguished.
When the Bodhisattva realizes this extinction as the truth, he no longer craves the one hundred and eight [afflictions]."

No longer practicing attachment to desire, the bodhisattva is able to liberate himself; one should know that this is the exhaustion [of all things]. This is the bodhisattva’s reckoning of upholding the dharma of emptiness and the dharma of the exhaustion of [defilements]; this is the bodhisattva’s reckoning of the one hundred and eight dharmas of liberation through exhaustion.

"5. Fifth, the Bodhisattva should calculate that the hundred-and-eight [defilements] are exhausted and will not arise again; having known that they will not arise again, this is the Bodhisattva’s calculation of the dharma of the exhaustion of phenomena and the knowledge that they will not arise again. 6.

Sixth, the Bodhisattva should calculate the hundred-and-eight exhaustions, whereby he shall attain Nirvāṇa—long life without further extinction, deathlessness—and by attaining this calculation, the Bodhisattva knows suffering for himself; this is the Bodhisattva’s dharma of knowing the bliss of Nirvāṇa through the calculation of dharmas. 7.

Seventh, the Bodhisattva should calculate the mindfulness of the hundred-and-eight exhaustions and Nirvāṇa; this is the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the characteristics of the calculation of Nirvāṇa."

Eighth, the Bodhisattva should calculate the one hundred and eight thoughts of the sign of relinquishment through cessation, such that they no longer arise; this is the Bodhisattva’s calculation of the one hundred and eight thoughts of the sign of relinquishment so that they no longer arise.

Ninth, the Bodhisattva should calculate that if the thoughts are not fully exhausted, thoughts of various signs will arise; by knowing these thoughts of various signs, he should calculate the non-existence of Nirvana, for what reason would there again be thoughts of various signs that must be extinguished?

This is the Bodhisattva’s calculation of knowing the thoughts of various signs. Tenth, the Bodhisattva should calculate that he knows for himself their extinction and non-existence, long receiving the sign of Nirvana; Nirvana is eternally present and does not undergo further extinction. This is the Bodhisattva’s calculation of receiving the sign of Nirvana.
"These are the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said,
"Bodhisattvas further have ten other reckonings."
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha,
"What are the ten reckonings of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:

"First, the Bodhisattva knows for himself the one hundred and eight offenses, and he shall also speak of these one hundred and eight offenses to people of the ten directions; he shall also speak to others of the suffering and pain of birth and death within the five realms of existence throughout the ten directions; and he shall constantly speak to people of the ten directions regarding the rise and fall of all things, their origins and ends, and that birth and death are ultimately non-existent—this is the first calculation of the Bodhisattva.

Second, the Bodhisattva shall calculate the rise and fall of the ten directions and employ evidence to demonstrate them to others; this is the Bodhisattva’s calculation of evidence to explain the Dharma to people."

Third, a bodhisattva should calculate that all people in the ten directions are attached because they sit within greed; since attachment arises from greed, it is entirely due to delusion (*moha*). A bodhisattva should constantly explain away attachment for others and resolve the delusion of others. Furthermore, a bodhisattva should take greed and delusion as a standard for self-reflection, thinking: "When I did not yet know the Bodhisattva path, my greed and delusion were also intense. This is the calculation attained by a bodhisattva;
he should always maintain a mind of loving-kindness to resolve the greed and delusion of others—this is the bodhisattva’s calculation.
Fourth, a bodhisattva should constantly calculate the hundred and eight [afflictions] that drag those deluded people of the ten directions toward [suffering], taking them as witnesses.
The bodhisattvas again asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes drawing foolish people from the ten directions to bear witness?
The Buddha said:

"The thoughts of people in the ten directions are all rooted in the one hundred and eight delusions; therefore, when a Bodhisattva eliminates these one hundred and eight [delusions], he is no longer deluded.

If a Bodhisattva loses his practice regarding these one hundred and eight practices, he becomes deluded. He must always lead those deluded people of the ten directions as witnesses so that they do not lose their practice; this is the Bodhisattva’s method of calculation."
"Fifth, a bodhisattva must further calculate the one hundred and eight [factors] that draw upon the Arhats of the ten directions as witnesses.
The bodhisattvas asked:
"How does one further calculate the one hundred and eight [factors] that draw upon the Arhats as witnesses?"
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva loses their practice only because they sit idly attached to it; therefore, one should be drawn toward the nirvāṇa of an arhat, which is non-existence.
Why should I be concerned about losing my practice?"
"What is the contemplation of sitting amidst this suffering?
To constantly bring about the realization of the Arhat’s Nirvana—this is the bodhisattva’s method of calculation.

Sixth, if one further loses their practice, they should calculate the hundred-and-eight [delusions] by bringing about the realization of the Pratyekabuddha’s Nirvana of non-existence; this is the bodhisattva’s method of calculation."

Seventh, if a bodhisattva loses their practice, they should again calculate that the one hundred and eight [dharmas] are non-existent; they should draw upon the parinirvāṇa and non-existence of the Buddhas of the past throughout the ten directions, reflecting: "The Buddhas of the past throughout the ten directions were all my teachers, and they have all attained parinirvāṇa and departed. Why should I lose my practice and remain in the world?"
When a bodhisattva has already drawn forth realization, they then return to the practice; this is the bodhisattva’s method of reckoning through the drawing forth of realization.

Eighth, when a bodhisattva again loses their practice, they should once more draw forth the present Buddhas of the ten directions—even those who are about to enter *nirvāṇa*—and should constantly draw forth their own realization; having realized it for themselves, they should immediately return to practice; this is the bodhisattva’s method of reckoning through the drawing forth of realization and returning to practice regarding the one hundred and eight [delusions].
Ninth, the bodhisattva should reckon upon the one hundred and eight ways in which they may again lose their practice.

The Buddha said: “I am now Śākyamuni Buddha; all that I govern—the heavens, the earth, emperors, kings, and the people—belongs to me. Possessing sovereign power to fly about with great majestic spiritual might, yet I shall enter parinirvāṇa and return to non-existence. You must always lead me as your witness; you must always resolve your mind firmly to seek Buddhahood, holding me as your witness so that your intent does not waver. To waver is to lose one’s practice, whereby one falls into the midst of the hundred-and-eightfold activities of craving. This is the bodhisattva’s reckoning.”

"Tenth, a bodhisattva should always exert all effort to repel greed so that it does not result in seeking; for one who seeks is not fit to be a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should earnestly seek, discern, and reflect upon what I have calculated. This constitutes the fifty calculations of a bodhisattva."
The Buddha said, "When bodhisattvas practice *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), they constantly suffer from losing their practice; there is none who does not lose it.
At that time, the bodhisattvas asked the Buddha:
"Why is this? We who act as bodhisattvas constantly suffer from the failure of our practice.
The Buddha said:

“Because Bodhisattvas do not weary of the habitual tendencies of the suffering of birth and death; because they do not personally awaken to the habitual tendencies of birth and death; because they do not clearly know that birth and death are exhausted and non-existent; and because they do not clearly know the path of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said:
"Bodhisattvas must not become arrogant or superior toward the people of the ten directions on account of practicing the bodhisattva path for themselves.
The Buddha said:

“Since they have not yet attained Buddhahood, their suffering of birth and death has not yet been joined with its cessation, nor has it been joined with the Path; they constantly experience physical pain, as well as the sufferings of cold and heat, and the afflictions of hunger and thirst which they cannot sever. Thus, such a bodhisattva may not yet rely upon his own goodness.”
The Buddha said:

"Before I attained Buddhahood, I thought to myself that no one could equal me in wisdom; I thought to myself that no one could equal me in knowing dhyāna; I thought to myself that no one could equal me in knowing the subtle extinction of the mind."
The Buddha said:
"I have already established myself as the Śākyamuni Buddha; let us now compare what I know now that I have become a Buddha with what I knew when I was still a bodhisattva.
For example, the wisdom of a single bodhisattva is like this; yet now that I have become a Buddha, there is that which I know."
"For example, among all the myriad things and bodhisattvas within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions," the Buddha said,
"the wisdom of all the bodhisattvas of the ten directions is not yet equal to the wisdom of a single minute speck of dust belonging to a single Buddha of one direction."
The Bodhisattva immediately prostrated himself and asked the Buddha, "We are deluded;
why is it that we cannot equal even a single speck of dust of the Buddha's wisdom?
The Buddha said:

"Because you do not weary of the habitual suffering of birth and death, because you have not yet early on attained Buddhahood, because you do not understand the subtle and minute mind, and because you do not know how to extinguish the source and sever the root."
"You all must exert yourselves with diligent practice; you shall also come to know the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The bodhisattvas asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions do we have such an abundance of birth and death?"
The Buddha said:

"You all do not practice with clarity the subtle meaning within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the twelve gates, and the three stages of the *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) Sūtra; nor do you know how to discern and calculate the subtle meanings within the one hundred and eight aspects of birth and death. Therefore, birth and death are many for you, and it is difficult to attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha said:
"When your mind has not yet arisen, there are five hundred and forty sets of one hundred and eight modes of craving within it.
When the mind turns into mental attention (*manas*), there are likewise five hundred and forty sets of one hundred and eight modes of craving within it."
When the mind transforms into consciousness, there are five hundred and forty sets of one hundred and eight modes of craving.
When it enters the eye, regarding the beautiful forms seen by the eye, there are five hundred and forty sets of one hundred and eight modes of craving;
regarding the neutral forms seen by the eye, there are five hundred and forty sets of one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Regarding the unwholesome forms seen by the eye, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Turning to the ear, regarding the pleasant sounds heard by the ear, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving;
regarding the neutral sounds heard by the ear, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Regarding the unpleasant sounds heard by the ear, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving.
When it turns to the nose, regarding the pleasant fragrances smelled by the nose, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving;
regarding the neutral fragrances smelled by the nose, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Regarding the foul odors smelled by the nose, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Turning into the mouth, regarding the fine flavors and pleasant speech obtained by the mouth, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving;
regarding the middling flavors and middling speech obtained by the mouth, there are therein five hundred and forty times one hundred and eight modes of craving.
Regarding the foul tastes and foul speech obtained by the mouth, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving.
When they turn toward the body, regarding the excellent, fine, soft, and agreeable things obtained by the body, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving;
regarding the middling, fine, and soft things obtained by the body, there are therein five hundred and forty-one hundred and eight modes of craving.

Regarding the unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable sensations experienced by the body, there are within them five hundred and forty and one hundred and eight modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
The Buddha said:

"Within a single moment of mind, there are five hundred and forty and one hundred and eight modes of craving. Among these five hundred and forty and one hundred and eight modes of craving, each single mode of craving leads to the experience of one birth and death; each single mode of craving leads to the experience of one body. In this way, if the five hundred and forty [modes] are not exhausted, one will undergo five hundred and forty births, deaths, and bodies."

The same applies to the mind and the consciousness; the same applies to pleasant forms, neutral forms, and unpleasant forms; the same applies to pleasant sounds, neutral sounds, and unpleasant sounds; the same applies to pleasant odors, neutral odors, and foul odors; the same applies to delicious tastes and pleasant speech, neutral tastes and neutral speech, and unpleasant tastes and unpleasant speech; the same applies to pleasant, fine, soft, and agreeable tactile sensations, neutral fine and soft sensations, and unpleasant, coarse, hard, painful, and disagreeable tactile sensations.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas,
"Do you know this? The bodhisattvas replied:
"Upon hearing what the Buddha has said, we all understand.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Do you believe that such a thing exists or not?"
The bodhisattvas said:
“We believe this to be so;
the assembly has no doubt, yet we do not understand.”
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Since you have set out and come to my presence, do you know how many times your thoughts have turned?
Since you heard me begin preaching this sutra, do you know how many times your thoughts have turned?"
The bodhisattvas replied to the Buddha,
“We do not know how many times.
The Buddha asked the bodhisattvas:
"Why do you not know how many times [the wheel] has turned?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"When we heard the Buddha preaching the sutra, we were so filled with joy that we did not realize how many times it had turned."
The Buddha said:

"Since you first came here until now, you have not realized that your minds continue to fall into the cycle of birth and death; it is like the dust in the kingdom of Mahākośala, the amount of which is unknown."
"Bodhisattvas merely sit and fail in their practice, not knowing for themselves the extent of their birth and death; therefore, they do not attain Buddhahood immediately.
Each of the bodhisattvas bowed their heads in reverence and joyfully accepted and practiced [the teaching].
The various bodhisattvas each prostrated themselves and said:

"Before we heard the Buddha’s exposition on the fifty reckonings, we considered ourselves to have maintained our practice without fail; now that we have heard the Buddha’s explanation of the fifty reckonings, we realize for ourselves that our practice was flawed."
The Buddha said:
"You have both lost your practice and not lost your practice.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
"Why is it that one both loses right conduct and does not lose right conduct?
The Buddha said:

"If you go before the Buddhas of the ten directions and, out of self-conceit and self-praise, say, 'I understand that there are no such fifty reckonings of offenses,' you thereby fall into offense and lose right conduct; this is what is meant by both losing right conduct."
The Buddha said:

"One who does not lose their practice is a bodhisattva who, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, always feels self-reproach—feeling reproach for their physical body and feeling reproach for birth-and-death. When they give rise to transgressions and are unable to calculate or recognize them, they constantly maintain the fifty reckonings and return to self-reproach. This is the bodhisattva’s non-loss of practice; those who do not reproach themselves constantly lose their practice."
When the Buddha had spoken thus,
each of the bodhisattvas felt shame within themselves, each repented within themselves, and each thought to themselves:
"All things are subject to cessation, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self."

Upon hearing this sutra, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha, touching their heads to his feet, and having received and practiced its teachings, they departed.
*Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Fascicle 60.
